## Questions

### Why are deep office floor plates hard to convert to housing?

Habitable rooms need daylight and ventilation. Deep plates leave too much space far from windows, so designers must sacrifice area or cut light wells, both of which reduce viability.

### What is usually the largest technical cost in an office conversion?

New plumbing and drainage to every unit, together with ventilation, typically drives cost and complexity, along with fire and acoustic separation between dwellings.

papers.title: Most of the Buildings of 2050 Already Exist
papers.question: Why does existing building stock matter more than new development for the future of commercial property?
papers.answer: New construction adds only a small share to the total stock each year, so most of the buildings that will be in use in 2050 already exist. Their performance, adaptability and renewal will shape cities, emissions and returns far more than new buildings, which makes capital planning for existing stock the central task.
papers.summary: The future of commercial property will be lived mostly in buildings standing today. The decisive capital is the capital spent on keeping, adapting and renewing them.
papers.limitations: A thesis that interprets external economic, policy and market developments through the physical reality of buildings. It is a view to test against individual assets, not a forecast or a finding from the Moyne Ross dataset.

sections.heading: Why the arithmetic is so stable

technicalPages.why: What upgrades to existing buildings achieve

papers.contentMarkdown:
Each year, new construction adds a small percentage to the total stock of buildings in a mature economy. Demolition removes a smaller share. The arithmetic is simple and its consequence is large: most of the buildings that will be in use a quarter of a century from now are already standing. In Britain the point is often made with an estimate that around four in five buildings of 2050 already exist; independent estimates put it somewhat lower, and the share will be smaller again in faster-growing Australia and the United States. Even there, it is a large majority.

Real estate attention gravitates to the new. Launches, towers, the prime grade. But the economic and physical life of cities happens mostly in the stock we already have.  Research note

Checked 3 November 2026. The UK Green Building Council states that 80 per cent of the buildings that will be occupied in 2050 already exist; no underlying primary dataset for the figure was found, and an independent estimate based on English housing data puts it nearer 72 per cent. It is best read as a British estimate in a range of roughly 72 to 80 per cent. The share is lower in faster-growing Australia and the United States, though still a large majority, because annual additions are a small fraction of stock in all three. Deepened 4 November 2026 with a worked illustration of the stock arithmetic. Deepened 11 November 2026 against the Technical Library: the layered 1975 office read against its service lives.

## The renewal economy

If most future buildings already exist, most future building work is renewal: replacing roofs and plant, upgrading facades, electrifying heating, meeting new safety rules, adapting for new uses. This is a vast, continuous economy of decisions made one building at a time, usually without the attention a new development gets.

It is also where the forces in Part I of this publication land. Electrification, industrial demand, AI and physical climate risk all arrive at buildings that were designed for other conditions. Their response is a capital programme.

## Why the arithmetic is so stable

Annual new construction in a mature economy adds a small share of total floor space, typically a low single-digit percentage, and annual demolition removes less. Compound those two rates over twenty-five years and the stock of 2050 is dominated by buildings already standing, even in fast-growing cities. The share is highest in older urban centres and lowest in new industrial precincts, but nowhere is it small.

The consequence for capital is direct. The money that will shape cities over the next quarter century is mainly the capital spent on roofs, plant, facades, controls and compliance in buildings that already have addresses.

## The arithmetic, worked

The share of the 2050 stock that already stands depends on only two rates: how fast new floor space is added and how fast old floor space is removed. The illustration below uses round numbers to show how robust the conclusion is. How much of the stock in 25 years exists today: illustrative arithmeticNew floor space added each yearFloor space removed each yearShare of the stock in 25 years that exists today1%0.5%About 78%1.5%0.5%About 69%2%0.5%About 61%1%1%About 78%, in a stock that has not grown

Moyne Ross illustration: today’s stock surviving at the removal rate, divided by total stock after 25 years of additions and removals.

Even at rates of new construction that most mature markets rarely sustain, well over half of the floor space in use in 2050 is already built. The UK Green Building Council has long put the figure for Britain at around 80 per cent. Whatever the precise number, the capital consequence is the same: the decisive work of the next quarter-century is renewal of what exists.

## What “existing” hides

An existing building is rarely one building. It is an original shell plus decades of alterations, renewals and repairs, each on its own clock. A 1975 office may carry a 2004 chiller, a 2012 lift modernisation, a 1998 facade reseal and an original switchboard. Read against the library’s service lives, each layer is at a different point: the chiller, at twenty-two years, inside the twenty-to-thirty-year life of a water-cooled machine; the lift controller nearing the fifteen to twenty years after which parts support ends; the reseal, at twenty-eight, past the life of even a good silicone joint; and the switchboard past the thirty to forty years a main board lasts ([chillers](/technical/central-cooling-plant#service-life), [lifts](/technical/passenger-and-goods-lifts#service-life), [sealants](/technical/sealants-and-joints#service-life), [switchboards](/technical/main-electrical-supply#service-life)). Reading the stock means reading these layers, not just the date on the facade.

That is why the generation studies that follow in this part treat age as a prior to test rather than a verdict. The era predicts the materials and systems the building started with. Evidence shows what has been done since.

## Carbon points the same way

The carbon argument now reinforces the economic one. A large share of a building’s lifetime emissions is embodied in its structure and materials. Demolishing and rebuilding spends that carbon again. Keeping the frame and renewing what surrounds it is often the lower-carbon path, and planning systems and investors increasingly ask developers to justify demolition.

The future of commercial property is mostly a [retrofit](/technical/energy-efficiency-upgrades) story, and that retrofit will be either planned or discovered.

## Planned or discovered

Renewal can happen in two ways. It can be planned: the owner knows what the building will need over the next decade, sequences the works sensibly and prices them into decisions. Or it can be discovered: a chiller fails, a facade panel slips, a tenant’s fit-out triggers an upgrade, a buyer’s due diligence finds what the seller never looked for.

Discovered renewal is more expensive, more disruptive and worse for value. It is also the default for much of the existing stock, because few owners hold a clear, current view of what their buildings need.

## Reading the stock we have

The rest of this part of the publication reads the existing stock generation by generation: the [1970s office](/insights/the-1970s-office), the [services-heavy buildings of the 1980s and 1990s](/insights/the-services-generation), the [tilt-up shed](/insights/the-roof-nobody-designed-for-solar), [heritage buildings](/insights/the-economics-of-heritage), [shared buildings](/insights/why-shared-buildings-defer) and [what age conceals](/insights/what-age-conceals). Each generation has its own capital signature, a pattern of elements that tend to come due together.

A generation’s signature is a prior to test against evidence, not knowledge of a particular building, but it explains why the same questions keep surfacing across very different assets, and why a structured ten-year view is the right instrument for the stock we already have.  In the register

The renewal economy appears in every register as lifecycle replacement of structure, envelope and services, sequenced across the 2–5 yr and 6–10 yr horizons.   Key signal

Because most of the buildings of 2050 already exist, planned renewal of existing stock is the decisive capital task, and discovered renewal is its expensive alternative.

## Sources

## Questions

### Is it better to retrofit or demolish and rebuild?

It depends on the building, its location and its potential use. Retrofit often has lower embodied carbon and can be faster, but some buildings cannot adapt without works approaching the cost of new. The decision should rest on a physical reading of what the existing building can support.

### What does a generation’s “capital signature” mean?

Buildings of similar age and type tend to share materials, systems and design assumptions, so their major capital needs often arrive in similar patterns. It is a starting expectation to test against the actual building, not a substitute for evidence.

papers.title: The 1970s Office
papers.question: What capital issues are typical of office buildings built in the 1960s and 1970s?
papers.answer: Offices from the late 1960s and 1970s commonly combine original or once-replaced central plant, early facade systems near the end of their life, concrete and hazardous-material issues, low floor-to-floor heights and compliance gaps that major works will trigger. Because these needs tend to arrive together, the decision often moves from maintenance to whether to refurbish deeply, convert or redevelop.
papers.summary: Office buildings from the late 1960s and 1970s are reaching the point where facade, services and compliance tend to come due together. Few generations hit the wall so completely at once.
papers.limitations: A research note drawing on public sources and Moyne Ross practice. It describes patterns that commonly matter to capital planning; any particular building needs its own evidence before a conclusion is drawn.

papers.contentMarkdown:
The office boom of the late 1960s and 1970s gave Australian, British and American cities a large generation of mid-rise and high-rise buildings. Concrete frames, precast or early curtain-wall facades, central air conditioning, and the first generation of tall-building fire and lift systems. Many of them are now fifty years old or more.

They were built quickly, often well, and to the standards and materials of their time. That is exactly what makes their present capital position so recognisable.  Research note

Asbestos bans: Britain banned the import, supply and use of all asbestos in 1999; Australia prohibited asbestos and asbestos-containing products nationally from 31 December 2003; the United States moved more gradually, with the EPA finalising a ban on ongoing uses of chrysotile asbestos in March 2024; that rule was challenged in the Fifth Circuit, argued in June 2026, and has not been stayed. The description of 1960s and 1970s office construction is general practice knowledge and should be tested against each building. Deepened 4 November 2026 with a service-life reading of a 1975 office and asbestos ban dates. Deepened 11 November 2026 against the Technical Library: service lives now come from its tables, with the refrigerant, controller, breaker and sealant clocks added, and the chloride test that tells corrosion causes apart.

## A generation coming due together

Most buildings have staggered cycles. Roofs, plant and [lifts](/technical/passenger-and-goods-lifts#service-life) fall due at different times and can be managed one by one. The 1970s office is different because so many of its systems have reached the end of their second cycle or the end of their original design life at around the same time.

Central [plant](/technical/central-cooling-plant#service-life) may have been replaced once, in the 1990s or 2000s, and is due again; a chiller of that vintage may also run on R22, a refrigerant now out of production in developed countries, and refrigerant rules often end a machine’s useful life before wear does ([The Services Generation](/insights/the-services-generation)). Lifts may have had one modernisation, but [lift controllers](/technical/passenger-and-goods-lifts#service-life) lose parts support after fifteen to twenty years, so even a lift modernised in the 2000s is coming due again. Facades, including sealants, gaskets, fixings and glazing, are often original or patched: a face-sealed [precast joint](/technical/sealants-and-joints#service-life) lasts ten to twenty years, so an original one is long gone, and in the United States caulk of this era can contain PCBs. Electrical switchboards and distribution may be original, and their breakers lose manufacturer support after twenty to twenty-five years. Fire services have often been added to over decades rather than renewed as a system.

## Fifty years of clocks

A building completed in 1975 is now past fifty. Set against typical service lives, it shows why so much falls due at once, and why the plant in such a building is rarely original. A 1975 office against typical service livesElementTypical life (years)Cycles since 1975What that usually means[Water-cooled centrifugal chillers](/technical/central-cooling-plant#service-life)20 to 30About twoSecond set at or near end of life; refrigerant may end it sooner[Cast iron and steel shell boilers](/technical/central-heating-plant#service-life)25 to 35One or twoSecond boilers due, and the electrification decision with them[Indoor air handling units](/technical/air-handling-units#service-life)25 to 30About twoOriginal units replaced once, or overdue; a sound casing can be refurbished in place[Main switchboard](/technical/main-electrical-supply#service-life)30 to 40; breakers supported 20 to 25One to twoOriginal boards near or past life, and their breakers long out of support[Lift controllers and drives](/technical/passenger-and-goods-lifts#service-life)15 to 20Two or threeModernised at least twice by now, or overdueGeared lift machines25 to 35One or twoReplacement due or recently done[Fire detection panel](/technical/fire-detection-and-alarm-systems#service-life)15 to 20Two or threeSeveral renewals; compliance with current codes is the question[Plant controllers](/technical/building-management-and-control-system#service-life)15 to 20Two or threeOften a patchwork of generations[Face-sealed precast joints](/technical/sealants-and-joints#service-life)10 to 20SeveralThe original sealant is gone; what replaced it, and when, is the question

Typical lives: the Technical Library’s service-life tables, linked from each row, which run close to published facility condition assessments such as the Menlo Park Fire Protection District’s Appendix 4. Actual buildings vary with maintenance and duty.

The table also explains the hazardous materials question. [Asbestos](/technical/hazardous-materials) use continued into the 1980s in many buildings, and bans came late: Britain prohibited all asbestos in 1999, Australia on 31 December 2003. A 1970s office will almost always need a hazardous materials survey before significant works, whatever its renewal history.

## What the fabric hides

This generation sits squarely in the era of asbestos-containing materials. Britain banned asbestos in 1999 and Australia in 2003, but buildings of the 1960s and 1970s commonly used it in insulation, fireproofing, ceilings, floor tiles, risers and plant. It may be managed safely in place, but any significant refurbishment has to deal with it first, which adds cost and time.

[Concrete](/technical/structural-frame#concretes) frames and facade panels can suffer reinforcement corrosion from carbonation or chlorides, visible as cracking and spalling, often called concrete cancer. Concrete of the 1950s to 1970s sometimes carried calcium chloride as an accelerator, which makes the corrosion aggressive and localised, with little warning on the surface; [chloride testing](/technical/structural-frame#investigation) at the depth of the steel, against a threshold generally taken as 0.2 to 0.4 per cent by mass of cement, tells the two causes apart, and the cause decides the repair. Precast panel fixings may be hard to inspect. Early curtain-wall systems were not designed for today’s thermal or air-tightness expectations. [What Age Conceals](/insights/what-age-conceals) covers these concealed conditions in more detail.

## The compliance trigger

Ordinary maintenance rarely forces a building to meet current codes. Major works often do. A significant refurbishment can bring requirements for fire upgrades, accessibility and energy performance into scope, and the extent depends on the jurisdiction and the work. For a 1970s office, the gap between existing and current standards can be wide, which means the cost of a deep refurbishment includes a compliance component that may be hard to see from the outside. In Australia, for instance, the National Construction Code requires sprinklers throughout a new building with any part more than 25 metres in effective height ([the value, kept by market](/technical/automatic-sprinkler-systems#thresholds)), so where major works bring fire safety toward current provisions, a taller tower of this generation can face a full sprinkler installation.

## A typical register for this generation

The shape is recognisable across the three markets. In mechanical services, central plant, often on its second cycle, with air-handling units, cooling towers and controls close to the end of useful life. In electrical, an original or lightly upgraded main switchboard with limited spare capacity and parts availability, and emergency lighting and distribution added over time. In vertical transport, lifts with one modernisation behind them and another due. In fire, detection and suppression assembled in layers rather than designed as a system, with [passive fire separation](/technical/passive-fire-protection#compartments) often compromised by decades of fit-out.

In the envelope, precast or brick facades with sealant, fixing and concrete questions; single-glazed or early double-glazed windows; flat roofs on their second or third membrane. In structure, usually sound, with investigation items for concrete condition in car parks, balconies and exposed elements. And across the building, a hazardous materials survey as a gating item before any of the above can be programmed.

Read together, the near-term horizon is heavy and the uncertainty is wide until investigation narrows it. That is the signature.

## Where this generation differs by market

Australian 1970s offices often sit in central business districts and inner suburbs where land value has run ahead of building value, which is why redevelopment analysis appears so often; many also predate the fire and accessibility provisions that major works now trigger under the National Construction Code and state regimes. British examples are more likely to carry cladding and system-build questions and, for larger let buildings, to face the energy-rating pressure described in [the British note](/insights/britain-when-the-energy-rating-becomes-a-letting-rule). American examples vary by city, with local performance standards and seismic considerations adding to the programme in some markets.

## Refurbish, convert or redevelop

Because so much falls due together, owners of this stock face a real decision rather than a maintenance plan. Deep refurbishment can extend life by decades and suit occupiers who want character and location. Conversion, discussed in [Conversion Is an Engineering Question First](/insights/conversion-is-an-engineering-question), suits some buildings and not others. Redevelopment becomes rational when the capital required approaches what the building can earn, as in the Melbourne office described in [When the Building is Not the Asset](/insights/when-the-building-is-not-the-asset).

The register for a building of this generation is where that decision starts. Its shape, heavy near-term items across mechanical, electrical, [facade](/technical/cladding-and-wall-systems), lifts and fire, with investigation allowances for hazardous materials and concrete, is often the clearest signal of which path the building is on.  In the register

A typical 1970s office register shows mechanical plant, lifts, switchboards, fire services and facade items clustered in the 1 yr and 2–5 yr horizons, with investigation allowances for asbestos and concrete condition.   Key signal

The 1970s office is defined by coincidence: plant, lifts, facade, fire and compliance needs falling due together, which turns maintenance into a strategic decision.

## Questions

### Is asbestos in a 1970s office building dangerous?

Asbestos-containing material that is in good condition and undisturbed can often be managed in place under a management plan. It becomes a significant cost and safety issue when works disturb it, so it must be identified and dealt with before refurbishment.

### Why do refurbishments of older offices cost more than expected?

Major works can trigger upgrades to fire, accessibility and energy performance, and they often uncover hazardous materials and concealed defects. These costs are hard to see without investigation.

papers.title: The Services Generation
papers.question: What capital issues are typical of office buildings from the 1980s and 1990s?
papers.answer: Buildings of the 1980s and 1990s rely heavily on mechanical, electrical and control systems that are now on their second or third cycle, including chillers, air-handling and variable air volume systems, building management controls, lifts and switchboards. Their facades, often curtain wall or glazed systems, also depend on sealants and gaskets with finite lives, so capital concentrates in services renewal and envelope maintenance.
papers.summary: Offices of the 1980s and 1990s were built around their services. Thirty and forty years on, those services, and the controls that run them, carry most of the capital.
papers.limitations: A research note drawing on public sources and Moyne Ross practice. It describes patterns that commonly matter to capital planning; any particular building needs its own evidence before a conclusion is drawn.

papers.contentMarkdown:
If the 1970s office was built around its structure and facade, the office of the 1980s and 1990s was built around its services. Larger floor plates, more glass, more equipment, more cooling. Variable air volume systems, centralised chilled water, raised floors for cabling, the first building management systems, faster lifts with electronic controls.

Thirty to forty years on, the structure of most of these buildings is sound. The capital sits in the services and in the systems that keep the envelope sealed.  Research note

Checked 3 November 2026. Refrigerant phase-outs follow the Montreal Protocol and its Kigali Amendment: hydrochlorofluorocarbons such as R22 were phased out of production in developed countries, with US production and import of R22 ending in 2020. Hydrofluorocarbons are now being phased down in developed countries to 40 per cent below baseline from 2024, 70 per cent from 2029 and 85 per cent from 2036, through the AIM Act in the United States, Australia’s own phase-down and Britain’s F-gas regime. Service-life ranges for plant are indicative practice ranges, not standards. Deepened 4 November 2026 with refrigerant phase-out dates for Australia (Australian Government), the United States and Britain. Deepened 11 November 2026 against the Technical Library: plant, controls, sealant, lift and breaker lives from its tables, and the US leak-repair trigger for R22 plant.

## Second and third cycles

Mechanical plant has shorter lives than structure. Chillers, cooling towers, [boilers](/technical/central-heating-plant) and air-handling units installed when these buildings opened have often been replaced once and may be approaching a second replacement. The clocks are well known: water-cooled centrifugal chillers last twenty to thirty years and air-cooled machines fifteen to twenty; galvanised [cooling towers](/technical/heat-rejection-plant#service-life) fifteen to twenty; cast iron and steel boilers twenty-five to thirty-five and condensing boilers fifteen to twenty; indoor [air-handling unit](/technical/air-handling-units#service-life) casings twenty-five to thirty, though their motors, actuators and humidifiers turn over faster. Pumps, fans and terminal units follow their own cycles. The question for an owner is rarely whether the plant works today. It is when the next major replacement falls and whether it should be like for like.

Refrigerants add a regulatory layer. Older refrigerants were phased out under international agreements, and newer ones face their own phase-down schedules. Plant that runs on a [refrigerant](/technical/central-cooling-plant#refrigerant) that is becoming scarce becomes more expensive to maintain and may be replaced earlier than its physical condition alone would suggest.

## The refrigerant clock

Plant from this generation often runs on refrigerants that are being phased out, and the phase-out dates now drive replacement as much as wear does. Refrigerant phase-out dates by marketMarketR22 (HCFC)HFCs such as R134a and R410AAustraliaBulk imports limited to servicing from 2020; banned entirely from 1 January 2030; reclaimed R22 still allowedImports phased down from 2018, reaching 85% below baseline by 2036United StatesProduction and import ended on 1 January 2020AIM Act phase-down of 85% by 2036United Kingdom and EUVirgin HCFC banned for servicing from 2010, recycled from 2015F-gas regulation phase-down, with bans on high-warming refrigerants in new equipment

Australian Government R22 and HFC guidance; US and UK dates as enacted. Check current regulations before planning a replacement.

For an owner the effect is practical. A chiller on R22 can still run, but every leak repair draws on a shrinking and dearer supply, and a major failure may make replacement the only economic choice. A chiller on R410A has longer, but its refrigerant is on the same path. Leakage is regulated too: in the United States, a comfort cooling system holding 50 lb (about 23 kg) or more of an ozone-depleting refrigerant such as R22 must be repaired once it leaks more than 10 per cent of its charge a year ([the value, kept by market](/technical/central-cooling-plant#thresholds)), so a leaking R22 machine there is a compliance item as well as a supply problem. Recording the refrigerant against each item of plant, as the [plant room](/technical/plant-rooms) reading in this paper suggests, turns a regulatory schedule into a capital one.

## Controls are the weak link

The first and second generations of building management systems were proprietary, and many controllers installed in the 1990s and 2000s are no longer supported. The parts age at different speeds: head-end hardware lasts five to eight years and its software five to ten before a major upgrade, plant controllers fifteen to twenty, and it is vendor support rather than wear that ends them ([controls lives](/technical/building-management-and-control-system#service-life)). Spare parts are scarce, integration with newer plant is difficult, and the system often cannot support the analytics described in [What AI Takes Out of the Building](/insights/what-ai-takes-out-of-the-building).

In this generation, the controls often date the building more than the chillers do.

## The envelope relies on sealants

Curtain walls and glazed facades from this era depend on [sealants](/technical/sealants-and-joints), gaskets and structural glazing compounds that age with sun and movement. A facade can look fine from the street while seals fail, letting water and air in and allowing condensation behind the glass. Silicone on well-designed joints lasts fifteen to twenty-five years, polyurethane eight to fifteen, and most surviving polysulphide is past its life, so a facade of this era on its original joints is usually due; joints on the sunny and weather faces can need replacing in half the time of sheltered ones ([sealant lives](/technical/sealants-and-joints#service-life)). Facade maintenance programmes, reseal works and, eventually, glazing upgrades are recurring items.

Some buildings of this period, and later, used cladding materials that are now the subject of remediation programmes in Australia and Britain and of tighter code requirements in the United States. Identifying cladding type is part of reading any building from the 1990s onward.

## Reading the plant room

The quickest way to read a building of this generation is to walk its plant rooms with a list. For each major item: year installed, refrigerant, hours run, maintenance record, parts availability, and whether the [controls](/technical/building-management-and-control-system#support) that run it are supported. Chillers and cooling towers first, then boilers or heat pumps, air-handling units, pumps and the main switchboard. Then the building management system: who made it, what version, whether the vendor still supports it and whether it can be integrated.

The register that results is usually services-heavy in the two-to-five-year horizon, with the envelope reseal and lift modernisation close behind. The structure rarely appears except where car park concrete or balcony elements are exposed.

## The electrification question

Many of these buildings heat with gas boilers and cool with electric chillers. Electrifying heating means replacing boilers with heat pumps that produce lower-temperature water and draw more electrical load, which pushes the question back to the switchboard and supply. For larger let buildings in England and Wales, the expected EPC B standard from 2031 makes this a sequenced programme rather than a choice, and in American cities with performance standards the same works are a compliance path. In Australia the driver is more often NABERS performance, tenant expectation and gas pricing than regulation.

The practical reading is that the plant replacement already due in this generation is also the moment to decide the building’s energy future. Replacing like for like can lock in a second gas cycle. Replacing with electrified plant brings the switchboard and distribution forward. Either way, the decision deserves to be made explicitly.

## Lifts and electrical

Lift controllers, drives and door equipment from this period are commonly due for modernisation. [Lift controllers](/technical/passenger-and-goods-lifts#service-life) last fifteen to twenty years before parts support ends, so the controllers of the 1990s are on their second modernisation. Electrical switchboards installed with the building are now old enough that spare capacity, safety features and parts availability matter, with breakers typically out of manufacturer support after twenty to twenty-five years, especially if the owner wants to electrify heating or add charging. As [Energy Becomes a Building Function](/insights/energy-becomes-a-building-function) argues, the main switchboard often gates later decisions.

A services-led plan suits this generation: map the plant, its age, its refrigerant, its controls and its dependencies, then sequence replacements so that each one prepares the building for the next.  In the register

Registers for 1980s and 1990s offices typically carry chillers and central plant, building management controls, lifts, switchboards and facade resealing across the 2–5 yr and 6–10 yr horizons, with refrigerant and controls obsolescence noted in the cost basis.   Key signal

In offices of the 1980s and 1990s, capital concentrates in services renewal, controls obsolescence and facade sealing rather than in the structure.

## Questions

### How long does commercial chiller plant usually last?

Service life varies with type, maintenance and operating conditions, and many chillers are replaced at somewhere around twenty to thirty years. Refrigerant availability and efficiency can justify earlier replacement.

### Why do curtain wall facades need resealing?

Sealants and gaskets degrade with UV exposure, temperature cycling and movement. When they fail, water and air can enter even though the facade looks intact, so periodic inspection and resealing are normal maintenance.

papers.title: The Roof Nobody Designed for Solar
papers.question: Can existing industrial and warehouse roofs carry rooftop solar?
papers.answer: Many portal-frame and tilt-up industrial buildings have lightweight roofs designed for minimal additional load. Adding solar can affect structural capacity, wind uplift, roof sheeting life, waterproofing and fire safety, so rooftop solar on existing sheds should start with an assessment of the roof structure and sheeting rather than the panel layout.
papers.summary: The modern industrial shed was built to be cheap and quick, with a roof designed for little more than weather. Now that roof is being asked to carry a power station.
papers.limitations: A research note drawing on public sources and Moyne Ross practice. It describes patterns that commonly matter to capital planning; any particular building needs its own evidence before a conclusion is drawn.

papers.contentMarkdown:
The industrial shed of the last forty years is one of the most efficient buildings ever designed. Tilt-up concrete or clad steel walls, a steel portal frame, light purlins and a metal roof spanning large distances for very little material. It was built to keep weather off goods at the lowest possible cost.

That efficiency is now being tested. In [When the Shed Becomes a Power Station](/insights/when-the-shed-becomes-a-power-station) we argued that energy capacity is becoming a primary determinant of industrial value. Much of that capacity is meant to sit on the roof.  Research note

Checked 3 November 2026. The National Construction Code 2025 introduces mandatory on-site solar photovoltaics for new Class 3 and Class 5 to 9 buildings under Section J. Adoption runs state by state, with several states on NCC 2022 until at least May 2027; see [where each state stands](/insights/australia-supply-constraint-and-the-staircase-code#where-each-state-stands). NCC 2022 required new commercial buildings to keep 20 per cent of the roof clear for solar and to provide switchboard space for solar and batteries, and Part B required new Class 7b warehouses to allow for the future structural load of panels; an earlier version of this note said NCC 2022 made no structural provision, which was wrong for warehouses. Existing buildings are not retrospectively covered. Deepened 4 November 2026 with roof service lives set against typical solar warranties. Deepened 11 November 2026 against the Technical Library: the roof-life table now uses its lives by covering and exposure, with the zones that fail first, the life of asbestos cement sheet and the roof safety values by market.

## Designed for weather, not equipment

Lightweight industrial roofs were typically designed for the loads they needed to carry: their own weight, maintenance foot traffic, wind and, in some places, snow. Additional dead load was often minimal. Solar arrays add weight, change how wind acts on the roof, and concentrate loads at mounting points. On many roofs this is fine. On some it is not, and the difference can only be known by checking the [structure](/technical/roof-structure#loads) and connections.

In Australia, the 2022 National Construction Code required new commercial buildings to keep at least 20 per cent of the roof clear for future [solar](/technical/solar-photovoltaic-systems#roof) and to provide switchboard space for solar and batteries. For warehouses it went further: Part B required long-span warehouse roofs to allow for the future structural load of panels. The 2025 edition goes further again by requiring on-site solar on new commercial buildings. None of it reaches back to existing buildings, and most sheds built before 2022 were never designed for the load.

## The sheeting clock

Metal roof sheeting has a finite life that depends on coating, environment and maintenance. Coastal and industrial atmospheres shorten it sharply: zinc-aluminium coated steel that lasts forty years and more inland may last fifteen to twenty-five within about a kilometre of surf, and a [roof wears by zone](/technical/roof-coverings#service-life), with the bottom metre above the gutter, the slope facing the weather and the bays below plant going first. A solar array installed on sheeting with ten years of life left will have to come off when the roof is replaced, at real cost. The sensible sequence is often roof first, panels second, which can move a roof replacement earlier than condition alone would justify.

Putting a twenty-five-year array on a roof with ten years left is a capital decision, whether or not anyone made it consciously.

## Two clocks on one roof

The sequencing problem is a mismatch between two lives. Solar modules commonly carry performance warranties of around 25 years; many roofs under them have far less left. Roof life against solar lifeRoofTypical life (years)Risk under a 25-year arraySingle-ply membrane (TPO, PVC)15 to 25Likely to need renewal during the array’s lifeEPDM membrane20 to 30Can outlast the array if new; renewal likely if halfway throughModified bitumen, exposed15 to 20Will almost certainly need renewal under the arrayCoated steel sheet, benign inland40 and moreMatched or better, if the sheet and its fixings are soundCoated steel sheet within about a kilometre of surf15 to 25Mismatched; renewal likely under the arrayExisting coated steel near the coast, 15 years oldUp to about 10 remainingRemoval and reinstatement of the array likely

Roof lives: the Technical Library’s service-life tables for [roof coverings](/technical/roof-coverings#service-life) and [membranes](/technical/waterproofing-membranes#service-life). Some published nominal lives run shorter: the Menlo Park Fire Protection District’s facility condition assessment gives 10 to 15 years for torch-on and about 25 for prefinished metal. Solar life reflects typical manufacturer performance warranties.

The same coated steel can outlast an array inland and fail under it near the coast, so exposure moves the answer more than material does. The arithmetic favours doing the roof first where its remaining life is shorter than the array’s. Removing and reinstating an array to renew the roof beneath it adds cost, downtime and risk to a job that would have been simpler done in the right order.

## Skylights, safety and fire

Older sheds often have translucent roof sheets and [skylights](/technical/skylights-dormers-and-glazed-atria#fragile) that become brittle with age and present a fall hazard. Solar installation means more people on the roof, which brings fall protection, safe access and walkways into scope. Some older industrial roofs in Britain and Australia still carry [asbestos cement sheeting](/technical/roof-coverings#ac), which must not be walked on or drilled without specialist management, and which weathers toward loose fibre after forty to sixty years, so on a shed of the 1970s or early 1980s the sheet itself may be at its end. The edge protection, anchors and fall arrest each market requires differ, and the library keeps them apart ([the values, by market](/technical/roof-safety-systems#thresholds)).

Fire is the other consideration. Arrays add electrical equipment across the roof surface. [Insulated panel](/technical/cladding-and-wall-systems#panels) roofs and walls with combustible cores, used in some buildings, change the fire risk. Insurers and fire authorities increasingly take an interest in how arrays are designed, isolated and accessed.

## What the engineer checks

A structural assessment for rooftop solar on an existing shed typically covers five things. The additional dead load of panels and mounting against the design capacity of purlins, rafters and portal frames, including any corrosion loss. Wind effects, since arrays change uplift and can concentrate load at mounting points and roof edges. Connections, which are often the weakest link in light steel roofs. The condition and remaining life of the sheeting the mounts attach to. And the roof’s ability to take the foot traffic and access equipment that installation and maintenance bring.

The outcome is usually one of three: the roof can take the array as designed; it can with local strengthening or a lighter layout; or it should be re-sheeted first and the array designed with the new roof. Knowing which before procurement avoids the common failure of buying an array for a roof that cannot carry it.

## Three markets, one roof

The physics is the same in Dandenong, Doncaster and Dallas. The drivers differ. Australian owners of existing sheds face tenant demand, NABERS and the example set by the new-build mandate. British owners face minimum energy standards for letting and grid connection constraints. American owners face local performance standards in some cities and incentive regimes that change with federal and state policy. In all three, the roof is the physical gate, and the register should read it as one system: structure, sheeting, drainage, skylights, access, hazardous materials and the array itself.

## Roof first

Read the roof as one system: structure and connections, sheeting and its remaining life, penetrations and drainage, skylights and access, and any hazardous materials. That reading says whether the roof can host solar now, after strengthening, or only after replacement.

It also turns an energy decision into a sequenced capital plan, which is the right place for it. The roof is no longer just weatherproofing. It is part of the building’s energy system.  In the register

Roof readiness appears as roof structure, sheeting, skylights and fall protection, and roof drainage rows, with solar-related works often recorded as conditional allowances sequenced after sheeting renewal.   Key signal

On existing sheds, rooftop solar is a roof structure and sheeting-life decision before it is an energy decision, and the sensible sequence is usually roof first, panels second.

## Questions

### How do I know whether a warehouse roof can take solar panels?

A structural engineer should check the roof structure and connections for the additional load and changed wind effects, and the sheeting should be assessed for remaining life. Skylights, access and any hazardous materials also need review.

### Should the roof be replaced before installing solar?

If the sheeting is near the end of its life, replacing it first usually avoids removing and reinstalling the array later. The decision depends on remaining sheeting life compared with the expected life of the array.

papers.title: Why Shared Buildings Defer
papers.question: Why do strata, condominium and multi-owned buildings tend to defer major capital works?
papers.answer: In buildings with many owners, major works need collective agreement and funding through levies or reserves, while individual owners have different hold periods and appetites for cost. That structure rewards deferral, which is why many jurisdictions now require long-term maintenance plans, capital works funds or reserve studies.
papers.summary: When a building has many owners, every capital decision becomes a collective one. Collective decisions are slow, and slow decisions let buildings wear out.
papers.limitations: A research note drawing on public sources and Moyne Ross practice. It describes patterns that commonly matter to capital planning; any particular building needs its own evidence before a conclusion is drawn.

Roof lives behind a sinking fund
Waterproofing: the defect that hides longest

papers.contentMarkdown:
A building owned by one party can make a capital decision in a meeting. A building owned by forty, or four hundred, has to make it through a governance process. In Australia that is an owners corporation or body corporate. In Britain, a freeholder or management company recovering costs through service charges. In the United States, a condominium or homeowners association. The forms differ. The dynamics are similar.

This paper is about why shared buildings defer, and why it matters beyond residential towers. Commercial strata offices, industrial unit estates and mixed-use buildings share the same structure.  Research note

Checked 3 November 2026. Florida’s post-Surfside regime, created by Senate Bill 4-D in 2022 and refined in 2023 and by HB 913 in 2025, requires milestone structural inspections at 30 years and every ten years after, and structural integrity reserve studies, for condominium and cooperative buildings of three or more habitable storeys. Reserves for those components cannot be waived, though HB 913 allows a pause of up to two budget years after a milestone inspection so that repairs can be funded. Buyers are entitled to the reports. Australian and British requirements for maintenance plans, capital works funds and service charge reserves differ by state and scheme type and should be checked for the building concerned. Deepened 4 November 2026 with a summary of capital planning rules for shared buildings in Australia, Florida and England. Deepened 11 November 2026 against the Technical Library: the predictable cycles a fund must carry, the English fire door check cycle and the records a buyer should ask for.

## The arithmetic of collective decisions

A major capital item, a roof, a facade, [lifts](/technical/passenger-and-goods-lifts#service-life), a waterproofing programme, benefits the building over decades. It is paid for now, by whoever owns a lot today. An owner planning to sell in two years carries the cost and gets little of the benefit. An owner planning to hold for twenty years sees it differently. Every vote balances these interests.

Add competing priorities, limited information and the discomfort of a large special levy, and the easiest decision is usually to patch and wait. Each individual deferral is rational. Together they let the building decline.

## Funds that are too small

Reserve and sinking funds are meant to solve this by collecting money steadily for future works. Many are set too low, because higher contributions are unpopular and because the forecast of future works is weak or out of date. When the major item arrives, the fund cannot cover it. The items are predictable, which is what makes an underfunded reserve avoidable: [lift controllers](/technical/passenger-and-goods-lifts#service-life) lose parts support after fifteen to twenty years, exposed [membranes](/technical/waterproofing-membranes#service-life) on podiums and balconies last fifteen to twenty-five, and facade [sealants](/technical/sealants-and-joints#service-life) eight to twenty-five depending on type, and a forecast should name each of them.

Regulators have responded. Australian states require various forms of long-term maintenance or capital works planning for owners corporations, with obligations that differ by state and scheme size. In Britain, service charge regimes and professional guidance govern reserve funds in leasehold buildings. In the United States, the 2021 collapse at Surfside in Florida led that state to introduce mandatory milestone structural inspections and structural integrity reserve studies for condominium buildings of three or more habitable storeys.

## What the law now asks

Several jurisdictions have responded to deferral in shared buildings by prescribing how far ahead owners must plan and save. The requirements differ widely. Capital planning rules for shared buildingsJurisdictionWhat is requiredNoteNew South WalesA 10-year capital works fund planPlans must use a prescribed standard form from 1 April 2026QueenslandA sinking fund budget covering at least the next nine yearsA reserve, not a full forecast documentVictoriaA maintenance plan for larger owners corporationsRequirements depend on the scheme’s sizeFloridaMilestone structural inspections and structural integrity reserve studies for condominiums of three or more habitable storeysIntroduced after Surfside in 2022; reserve funding temporarily eased in 2025England and WalesNo mandatory reserve; leasehold reform under the Leasehold and Freehold Reform Act 2024Building safety duties under the Building Safety Act 2022 for higher-risk buildingsEnglandFire door checks in blocks with a storey over 11 metres: communal fire doors at least every three months, flat entrance doors every twelveFire Safety (England) Regulations 2022; a running cost the fund carries ([values by market](/technical/common-circulation-areas#thresholds))

State and national legislation as summarised at review. Rules change; check the current instrument for a particular building.

None of these rules guarantees adequate funding. A ten-year plan can be optimistic, and a reserve can be set to the minimum the law allows. What they do is make the gap visible, which is the first condition for closing it.

## Florida’s lesson, in capital terms

The Surfside collapse in June 2021 made the cost of collective deferral visible. The legislative response is instructive for owners anywhere. Buildings of three or more habitable storeys must now have a milestone structural inspection by a licensed engineer or architect at a prescribed age and every ten years after, and a structural integrity reserve study every ten years that visually inspects the [roof](/technical/roof-coverings#service-life), structure, fireproofing and other critical components and states their remaining useful life and the reserves needed. Owners can no longer vote to waive those reserves, although 2025 amendments allow funding to pause for up to two budget years after a milestone inspection while repairs are paid for. Prospective buyers are entitled to the inspection reports and the reserve study.

Strip away the Florida specifics and three principles remain: inspect the structure on a schedule tied to age; forecast the capital for critical components on a fixed cycle; and make both visible to buyers. Those principles translate directly to commercial strata in Australia and leasehold blocks in Britain, whatever the local law requires.

## Reading a shared building as a buyer

For a buyer of a lot or a unit, the [common property](/technical/common-internal-areas#collective) is part of the purchase. The useful reading has four parts. The fund balance against the forecast of works. The age of the forecast and who prepared it. The minutes, which show what has been raised, deferred and disputed. And the building itself, read as any other: roof, facade, lifts, fire services, car park structure, hydraulics. A low levy with a thin fund and an old forecast is a signal, not a saving. The records worth asking for are set out in the library: the [common property records](/technical/common-internal-areas#what-to-ask-for), the defects history and the fire door and essential services records.

## Commercial strata carries the same risk

Strata offices, medical suites, industrial units and small retail lots are common in Australian markets in particular. Their owners are often owner-occupiers or private investors with limited technical support. The building’s common property, roof, facade, lifts, fire services, carparks, depends on the same collective process, and the same deferral logic applies.

For a buyer of a lot in a shared building, the condition and funding of the common property are part of the asset. A low levy can be a warning rather than a bargain.

## A plan everyone can read

The most effective remedy is a clear, credible capital plan that every owner can understand: what the building needs, why, roughly what it will cost, and when. It turns abstract warnings into specific decisions, lets the fund be set sensibly, and makes it harder for deferral to pass unnoticed.

That is the same instrument we argue for in single-owner buildings. In shared buildings it does one more thing: it gives a group of people with different interests a common, evidence-based picture to decide from.  In the register

Shared buildings carry the same register as any other, with an added reading: which items fall on common property, and whether the fund forecast matches the 2–5 yr and 6–10 yr horizons.   Key signal

Shared ownership rewards deferral because costs fall now and benefits arrive later, so a credible, readable capital plan is the strongest protection for the building.

## Questions

### What is the difference between a sinking fund and a reserve study?

A sinking or capital works fund is money set aside for future works. A reserve study is the analysis that estimates what those works will be and how much needs to be collected. Terms differ between Australia, Britain and the United States, but the relationship is the same.

### Should a low strata levy worry a buyer?

It can. A low levy may mean the fund is underfunded against future works, which can lead to large special levies later. The capital plan and fund balance should be read together.

papers.title: What Age Conceals
papers.question: What concealed conditions should be considered when assessing an older commercial building?
papers.answer: Older buildings commonly conceal hazardous materials such as asbestos, deteriorating reinforced concrete, era-specific materials like reinforced autoclaved aerated concrete in Britain, combustible cladding from more recent decades, corroded fixings, and services hidden in walls and floors. These cannot be confirmed from appearance, so a good capital plan carries them as visible uncertainty with investigation allowances rather than ignoring or assuming them.
papers.summary: Each building generation hides its own problems behind finishes: hazardous materials, failing concrete, unsuitable cladding, corroding fixings. Concealed conditions are where uncertainty, and capital, concentrate.
papers.limitations: A research note drawing on public sources and Moyne Ross practice. It describes patterns that commonly matter to capital planning; any particular building needs its own evidence before a conclusion is drawn.

Concrete and its reinforcement
RAAC planks: how they fail and how to tell
Cladding: combustibility and fixings
Wall tie corrosion and the cracking it causes

papers.contentMarkdown:
A building shows its owner a surface: ceilings, paint, cladding, finished floors. Behind that surface sit the materials and systems that decide most of its capital future. Some are fine, some were acceptable when installed and are now known to be problems, and others have simply aged out of sight.

Every generation of construction has its own concealed conditions. Knowing them does not tell you what any particular building contains. It tells you what to ask.  Research note

Dates and materials in this paper were checked on 3 November 2026: asbestos bans in Britain (24 November 1999), Australia (31 December 2003) and the United States (EPA chrysotile rule of March 2024, under challenge but not stayed); RAAC use in Britain from the 1950s to the mid-1990s per Department for Education guidance. Cladding remediation programmes run in Australia and Britain, where the government has committed to remediating buildings over 18 metres by the end of 2029; the United States relies on code requirements rather than a public remediation programme. Whether any particular building contains these materials can only be established by inspection and testing. Deepened 4 November 2026 with the RAAC case and IStructE’s view of the 30-year lifespan claim, and a table of concealed conditions with known dates. Deepened 11 November 2026 against the Technical Library: PCBs in mid-century sealants, calcium chloride concrete and the chloride threshold, the dates of high-alumina cement, and the English external wall line, each linked to the library page that holds it.

## Hazardous materials

Asbestos is the most widespread. It was used extensively in insulation, fireproofing, sheeting, flooring, ceilings, gaskets and plant until bans took effect, in 1999 in Britain and 2003 in Australia, while the United States has moved toward a ban more gradually. In the commercial stock of all three markets it remains common in buildings of the mid twentieth century. Lead-based paints and some older electrical and insulation materials raise related questions, and so do [the sealants](/technical/sealants-and-joints#pcb): caulk installed between 1950 and 1979 can contain as much as 40 per cent PCBs, which migrate into the concrete or masonry beside the joint, so the waste stream from a facade reseal can be hazardous before anyone has looked at the substrate.

These materials are often safe if undisturbed and managed. They become capital items when works disturb them, which is why refurbishment budgets for older buildings so often expand after investigation.

## Concrete and its reinforcement

Reinforced concrete protects its steel through cover and alkalinity. Over decades, carbonation and chlorides, from coastal air or de-icing salts, can lead to [reinforcement](/technical/structural-frame#concretes) corrosion, cracking and spalling. Balconies, car parks, facade panels and exposed frames are typical locations. Early stages are hidden; by the time spalling is visible, repair is already due.

Britain has its own era-specific example in reinforced autoclaved aerated concrete, a lightweight material used mainly in roofs and some floors from the 1950s to the 1990s, which drew national attention in 2023 when problems in schools and public buildings forced closures. High-alumina cement, used in precast beams in schools, offices and industrial roofs in Britain from the 1950s to the early 1970s, is another. So is concrete mixed with calcium chloride as an accelerator, common in the 1950s to the 1970s, where the chloride sits in the concrete itself and corrosion is aggressive and localised ([what each concrete of its era carries](/technical/structural-frame#what-it-is)). Each requires identification by a qualified engineer rather than assumption.

## RAAC: a lesson in evidence

Reinforced autoclaved aerated concrete, a lightweight material used in roof planks, floors and walls in Britain from the 1950s to the mid-1990s, became front-page news in August 2023 when the Department for Education closed schools containing it. It is a concealed condition in the purest sense: it looks like ordinary concrete from below, and its failures can come with little warning.

It is also a lesson in how evidence travels. The material is widely said to have a lifespan of 30 years. The Institution of Structural Engineers describes that claim as misleading, traced to a 1995 exchange of correspondence, with no specific data behind it. The real risks are moisture, poor bearing details and inadequate reinforcement, and they depend on the building, not the calendar. A register that recorded [RAAC](/technical/roof-structure#concrete) as expiring at 30 years would be confidently wrong; one that records it as present, unassessed, with an investigation priced, is right. Concealed conditions with known datesConditionWhere and whenWhat to recordAsbestosCommon until bans: Britain 1999, Australia 31 December 2003; the US has never had a complete banPresence, survey status and management planRAACBritain, roughly 1950s to mid-1990s; mainly public buildingsPresence, structural assessment and remediation statusCombustible claddingMany markets, roughly 1990s to 2010sFacade materials, fire assessment and remediation programmeConcrete deteriorationAny reinforced concrete, faster with chlorides or low cover; calcium chloride accelerators in the 1950s to 1970sCover, carbonation and chloride testing where warranted, against a chloride threshold generally taken as 0.2 to 0.4 per cent by mass of cementPCBs in sealantsCaulk installed between 1950 and 1979, documented in the United StatesSampling of joints and adjoining substrate before any reseal or removal

IStructE; national asbestos bans as enacted; the Technical Library for the concrete and sealant rows (chloride threshold from the Institute of Corrosion, PCB dates from the US Environmental Protection Agency). Britain’s remediation programme for unsafe cladding on buildings over 18 metres targets completion by the end of 2029.

## Cladding and facades

From the 1990s into the 2010s, some buildings used aluminium composite panels with combustible cores, expanded polystyrene systems and other materials now subject to remediation programmes in Australia and Britain and to tighter code requirements in the United States. Their presence can affect insurance, financing and sale long before any remediation is required. The line each market now draws is precise: in England, for example, external walls of residential buildings with a storey more than 11 metres above ground are expected to reach Class A2-s1, d0 or better, so a building just under or over that height carries a different question ([the values, kept by market](/technical/cladding-and-wall-systems#thresholds)).

The cost of a concealed condition is rarely the repair alone. It is the uncertainty it puts into every other decision until it is resolved.

Older facades have their own concealed issues: corroded wall ties and fixings behind masonry, failing anchors on stone and precast panels, and water tracking behind [cladding](/technical/cladding-and-wall-systems#combustible). These are often found during other works or after a visible failure.

## A concealed-conditions checklist by era
- Pre-1940: embedded steel in masonry and stone facades, corroded cavity [wall ties](/technical/masonry-brickwork#ties), lime mortar and render incompatibility with later cement repairs, timber decay behind renders, lead paint, early electrical.
- 1940s to 1970s: asbestos-containing insulation, fireproofing, sheeting, flooring and gaskets; reinforced concrete carbonation and chloride attack in car parks, balconies and panels; in Britain, reinforced autoclaved aerated concrete in roofs and some floors; high-alumina cement in some structures; original switchboards and distribution.
- 1980s to 1990s: late asbestos use in some products until the bans; curtain wall [sealant and gasket failure](/technical/sealants-and-joints#ageing); early combustible insulated panels; proprietary [building management controls](/technical/building-management-and-control-system#support) now unsupported; [refrigerants](/technical/central-cooling-plant#refrigerant) now phased out.
- 1990s to 2010s: aluminium composite and expanded polystyrene cladding systems now subject to remediation programmes in Australia and Britain; [waterproofing membrane](/technical/waterproofing-membranes#wet) failures in podiums and planters; lithium-ion and electrification retrofits that outgrow original electrical design.

Each line is a prompt for investigation, not a finding. The point of the checklist is to make sure the right questions are asked for the right era.

## How investigation is priced

Investigation allowances are usually small beside the works they may reveal: a [hazardous materials](/technical/hazardous-materials) survey (in Britain, the HSE expects a refurbishment and demolition survey before such works), a concrete condition assessment with cover and carbonation testing, a facade inspection from access equipment, a cladding identification and fire engineering review. Their value is that they convert a wide range into a narrow one. A register that carries them in the near term, with conditional works beside them, tells an owner exactly what the next decision costs to make well.

## Carrying uncertainty honestly

A capital plan cannot confirm what it cannot see. What it can do is make the uncertainty visible. Where a concealed condition is plausible given the building’s era, type and evidence, the register should say so, carry an investigation allowance, show a range for the possible outcome and state what would resolve it. [Pricing What You Don’t Know](/insights/pricing-what-you-do-not-know) describes how.

This is also where evidence grading matters most. A suspected condition inferred from age is different from one observed in a photograph, which is different again from one documented in a survey. [Documented, Observed, Inferred](/insights/documented-observed-inferred) explains why that distinction should be carried on every line.  In the register

Concealed conditions appear as investigation items and provisional allowances with low or medium confidence, each with the action needed to confirm or close it.   Key signal

Concealed conditions concentrate uncertainty in older buildings, so the honest response is a visible investigation allowance and range rather than silence or assumption.

## Sources

Named sources consulted for this paper. Consequential claims link to their source in the text. Reviewed 3 November 2026; next review by 3 November 2027.

- [Asbestos Safety and Eradication Agency](https://www.asbestossafety.gov.au/), Australian Government. Accessed 3 November 2026.
- [Asbestos](https://www.epa.gov/asbestos), United States Environmental Protection Agency. Accessed 3 November 2026.
- [Reinforced autoclaved aerated concrete: estates guidance](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/reinforced-autoclaved-aerated-concrete-estates-guidance), Department for Education. Accessed 3 November 2026.
- [Fifth Circuit probes standing in challenge to EPA asbestos rule](https://www.law360.com/articles/2483907/5th-circ-probes-standing-in-challenge-to-epa-asbestos-rule), Law360, June 2026. Accessed 3 November 2026.
- [IStructE statement and FAQs: reinforced autoclaved aerated concrete (RAAC)](https://www.istructe.org/resources/news/istructe-statement-reinforced-autoclaved-aerated-c/), Institution of Structural Engineers. Accessed 3 November 2026.

## Questions

### What is RAAC and why does it matter?

Reinforced autoclaved aerated concrete is a lightweight concrete used mainly in roofs and some floors in Britain from the 1950s to the 1990s. It can deteriorate and has limited tolerance to defects, so buildings where it may be present should be assessed by a qualified engineer.

### Can a desktop assessment confirm whether asbestos is present?

No. It can indicate that asbestos-containing materials are plausible given a building’s era and type. Confirmation requires inspection and sampling by appropriately qualified people.

papers.title: Patient Capital and the Long Building
papers.question: How does the length of ownership affect how commercial buildings are maintained and renewed?
papers.answer: Buildings renew on long cycles, while many owners hold for far shorter periods, which rewards deferring work onto the next owner. Patient capital that holds for longer, or any owner who plans as if it will, can align spending with the building’s own cycles and capture the value that short holding leaves behind.
papers.summary: Buildings live for generations and renew on cycles of fifteen to forty years. Most ownership is far shorter. The mismatch explains much of how buildings are treated.
papers.limitations: A thesis that interprets external economic, policy and market developments through the physical reality of buildings. It is a view to test against individual assets, not a forecast or a finding from the Moyne Ross dataset.

technicalPages.why: An element’s life, read zone by zone

papers.contentMarkdown:
A well-built commercial building can stand for a century. Its structure is designed for that. Its roof, facade, lifts and plant renew on shorter cycles, typically somewhere between fifteen and forty years. Its fit-out turns over faster still.

Ownership often runs on a different clock. Funds have terms. Investors have hold periods. Managers have reporting cycles measured in quarters. A building may pass through several owners within a single cycle of its major systems.  Research note

Service-life ranges for building elements are indicative and depend on design, exposure and maintenance; ISO 15686 sets out the principles of service life planning used internationally. The relay argument is a thesis about incentives rather than a measured finding. Deepened 4 November 2026 with a table setting typical holding periods against building cycles.

## The relay problem

When ownership is shorter than the building’s cycles, each owner holds a section of a relay. What matters is what each passes on. An owner who renews the [roof](/technical/roof-coverings#service-life) late in the hold gets little of its benefit. An owner who defers it can show stronger income and pass the problem to the next holder, at least until a buyer’s due diligence notices.

Markets are meant to price this, and to some extent they do. But pricing relies on information, and information about building condition is uneven and often prepared in a hurry at the point of sale. Much deferral is priced roughly or not at all.

## What patience buys

Long-horizon owners, pension funds, sovereign capital, family offices, owner-occupiers, can align spending with the building’s own rhythm. They can replace a system near the right point in its life rather than at the last possible moment. They can sequence works so that each prepares the building for the next. They capture the full benefit of what they spend.

This connects to the macro argument earlier in the publication. If returns no longer come mainly from falling yields, as [Forty Years of Cheap Money](/insights/forty-years-of-cheap-money) argues, they have to come from the building. Owners who understand their building’s cycles are better placed to earn them.

## Cycles, not dates

Every building runs on several clocks at once. Fit-out may turn over every ten to fifteen years. Mechanical plant, lifts and switchboards commonly run twenty to thirty. Roofs and facade systems may run twenty-five to forty or more, depending on material and exposure. The structure runs for the life of the building. Service life planning, as set out in ISO 15686, treats these as overlapping cycles to be managed rather than dates to be waited for.

Patient capital is capital that plans across these cycles. It asks, at each point in the hold, which clocks are about to strike and whether acting slightly early, slightly late or together with another item gives the best result over the building’s life rather than over the next reporting period.

## Holding periods against building clocks

The relay problem is easiest to see when typical holding periods are laid beside the building’s own clocks. How long owners hold, and how long the building runsElement or ownerTypical span (years)What it meansTenant fit-out10 to 15Turns over within most holdsMechanical plant15 to 30One renewal falls in most holds, often near the endRoof coverings15 to 40May or may not fall in a given holdFacades and curtain walls30 to 60Rarely planned by the owner who faces themStructure50 and moreOutlasts almost every ownerClosed-ended fundCommonly 7 to 10Sees one or two of the building’s cycles at mostOwner-occupier, pension fund, family officeOften 20 or moreCan plan whole cycles and time renewals to the building

Element spans from published service-life data and Moyne Ross practice; holding periods are typical, not universal.

The practical lesson is in the middle rows. A facade programme with a forty-year cycle is almost always decided by someone who did not commission the last one and will not own the building when the next is due. Without a record that carries the reasoning across owners, each one inherits the decision cold.

## Planning beyond the hold

Even a short-term owner can borrow some of the benefits of patience. The method is to plan over the building’s horizon rather than the investment horizon. A ten-year view of capital, built item by item, shows what will fall due during the hold and immediately after it. That second part is what the next buyer will price, as [What the Next Buyer Will Read](/insights/what-the-next-buyer-will-read) explains.

A ten-year horizon is a practical compromise. It is long enough to cover a typical hold and the decade a buyer will think about, short enough to keep estimates meaningful.

## The register as the baton

If ownership is a relay, the most useful thing to pass on is a clear record: what was done, what is due, what is uncertain. A building with a living capital record transfers its knowledge with its title. Without one, each owner starts from nothing and the building’s history is lost between sales.

That record is the subject of [The Living Record](/insights/the-living-record). It is also the most practical form patient capital can take for an owner who will not hold forever.  In the register

Hold period is not a register field, but it changes how the 2–5 yr and 6–10 yr horizons are read: one owner’s later years are the next owner’s first.   Key signal

When ownership is shorter than a building’s renewal cycles, deferral is rewarded unless capital is planned over the building’s horizon rather than the hold.
