## Questions

### Why does a ten-year capital horizon suit most owners?

It covers a typical hold period and the years a buyer will consider, while remaining short enough for estimates of condition, timing and cost to stay meaningful.

### Do short-term owners always defer maintenance?

No, but the incentive exists because costs fall within the hold and benefits often fall after it. Clear capital information and buyers who price it reduce that incentive.

papers.title: Timing Is Not Risk
papers.question: Should high-risk building items always be funded in the first year of a capital plan?
papers.answer: No. Risk describes what happens if something fails; timing describes when intervention is actually needed. A high-consequence item may need monitoring or investigation now and works later, so near-term capital should be reserved for items whose intervention window genuinely falls within the next twelve months.
papers.summary: A serious consequence does not mean a building must spend now. Separating how much an item matters from when it needs action is the most useful discipline in capital planning.
papers.limitations: Explains how Moyne Ross reads buildings and builds a Capital Strategy. It describes the method and its reasoning; it is not a statement about any particular asset.

sections.heading: Why a published life is not a date

technicalPages.why: Life is a property of each zone, not a date
How serious a finding is, graded on one scale

papers.contentMarkdown:
Capital plans often confuse two different questions. How much does this item matter? And when does something need to be done about it? The first is about consequence. The second is about the item’s condition, remaining life and the window in which intervention makes sense.

When the two are merged, every serious item drifts into year one. The near-term budget swells, credibility falls, and owners learn to discount the plan. Keeping them separate is one of the main disciplines of the Moyne Ross Capital Register.  Research note

The timing discipline described here is the Moyne Ross Capital Register method. Professional guidance in building surveying and technical due diligence, including RICS standards, distinguishes urgent works from planned works and leaves the timing of intervention to professional judgement; it does not prescribe the one-year, two-to-five-year and six-to-ten-year horizons Moyne Ross uses. Deepened 4 November 2026 with the ISO 15686 factor method for service life. Deepened 11 November 2026 against the Technical Library: the library’s lives and the roof read zone by zone.

## Three horizons, one question

A Moyne Ross register expresses timing in three horizons: within one year, years two to five, and years six to ten. The near-term horizon is protected. An item belongs there only when the whole intervention window falls inside the next twelve months.

The test is simple to state: why must this happen within twelve months? If the honest answer is “because it is important”, the item probably belongs later, with monitoring or investigation now. If the answer is “because it is failing, unsafe, non-compliant with a current obligation or about to cause consequential damage”, it belongs now.

Every dollar in the first year should be able to answer one question: why must this happen within twelve months?

## Consequence is carried separately

Consequence still matters. In the register it is carried by impact, on its own scale, and by the item’s description of what failure would mean. A fire system with modest remaining life may be impact four and still a two-to-five-year replacement, with inspection and testing confirmed now. A lift with serious safety implications may need immediate attention. The impact rating tells the reader why the item matters. The timing tells them when to act.

This is consistent with the way professional guidance treats the question. The RICS approach to building surveys and technical due diligence distinguishes urgent works within a short period from planned works over longer horizons, and leaves the timing of intervention to professional judgement on the evidence. Risk is not treated as the same thing as expenditure timing.

## Why a published life is not a date

Service life planning has an international standard, and it makes the same separation this paper argues for. ISO 15686 estimates a component’s life by starting from a reference life and adjusting it for the conditions it actually faces. The Technical Library applies the same idea element by element: every page sets out typical lives with what moves them, and for a roof it goes further, treating life as a property of each zone rather than of the whole, because the bottom metre above the gutter and the slope facing the weather reach the end first ([roof lives by zone](/technical/roof-coverings#service-life)). The factors ISO 15686 uses to adjust a reference service lifeFactorWhat it coversExample that shortens or lengthens lifeAQuality of the componentA premium coating against a basic oneBDesign levelSheltered detailing against an exposed oneCQuality of installationSealant joints prepared properly or notDIndoor environmentA dry office against a humid plant roomEOutdoor environmentAn inland site against a coastal oneFConditions of usePlant running continuously against part-timeGMaintenance levelA planned regime against reactive repair

ISO 15686-1, service life planning: the factor method. Factors are judgements, not constants.

The factor method is a reminder that timing is an estimate about a particular component in particular conditions, which is why the register records the evidence behind each timing rather than a table value alone. Consequence is a different question, and it stays on its own scale.

## Two worked rows

Consider two rows from an office register. The first is a fire detection system: twenty-two years old, functioning, with parts becoming harder to source. Impact is high, because the system protects life. But it passes its tests and its intervention window opens in three to four years when parts support lapses. Timing: two to five years, with annual testing confirmed in the first year. The second is a section of [roof](/technical/roof-coverings#service-life) membrane: fifteen years old, with active leaks over a tenancy and staining spreading. Impact is moderate. Timing: within one year, because the window for intervention is now, before consequential damage.

A risk-weighted plan would put the fire system first and the roof second. A timing-disciplined plan puts the roof in the first year and the fire system in the middle years, with testing now. Both items are still visible and both are taken seriously. The first-year budget is smaller and every dollar in it can say why it is there.

## Checks are not works

Many near-term actions are investigations rather than works, surveys or tests that resolve uncertainty: a roof survey, a facade inspection, a hazardous materials survey, a structural assessment. These can and should sit in the first year, with their own small cost, while the works they may lead to sit later as conditional allowances. Treating the check as the works overstates year one. Ignoring the check understates risk.

[Pricing What You Don’t Know](/insights/pricing-what-you-do-not-know) develops how conditional allowances are carried without inflating the base programme.

## Why it matters for decisions

A plan that separates timing from risk is more useful to an owner. It shows the true near-term commitment, which is usually smaller and more defensible than a risk-weighted plan would suggest. It shows which items need watching rather than spending. And it lets the owner bring items forward for strategic reasons, a tenant’s requirement, a refurbishment, a sale, rather than because the plan defaulted them there.

It also produces a better rating. The [MR Index](/methodology/mr-index) reads consequence and timing separately too, and attention needed soon weighs more than attention needed later in the decade. A building does not look worse simply because it has important systems; it looks worse when important systems need attention soon.  In the register

Every row carries impact and timing as separate fields; first-year items are limited to those whose intervention window falls inside twelve months, with checks recorded separately from the works they may lead to.   Key signal

Separating consequence from timing keeps first-year capital credible: an important item may need investigation now and works later.

## Sources

Named sources consulted for this paper. Consequential claims link to their source in the text. Reviewed 3 November 2026; next review by 3 November 2027.
- [Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors](https://www.rics.org/), RICS. Accessed 3 November 2026.

## Questions

### What should be included in first-year capital expenditure?

Items whose intervention window genuinely falls within twelve months, such as failing or unsafe elements and current compliance obligations, plus investigations needed to resolve important uncertainty.

### Where does a high-consequence but sound item belong in a capital plan?

In the horizon that matches its condition and remaining life, with its impact rating showing why it matters, and with monitoring or testing in the near term if appropriate.

papers.title: Deferred Maintenance Is Debt Without a Statement
papers.question: Why is deferred maintenance described as a hidden liability in commercial buildings?
papers.answer: Deferring necessary work does not remove the cost; it moves it forward with interest in the form of further deterioration, consequential damage, construction inflation and compliance upgrades that larger works may trigger. Because none of this appears in accounts or valuations until it is discovered, deferred maintenance behaves like unrecorded debt.
papers.summary: Every postponed repair is a liability that accrues interest: deterioration, consequential damage, rising prices, triggered compliance. Unlike real debt, nobody sends a statement.
papers.limitations: A thesis that interprets external economic, policy and market developments through the physical reality of buildings. It is a view to test against individual assets, not a forecast or a finding from the Moyne Ross dataset.
papers.contentMarkdown:
When a company borrows, it records the debt. Interest accrues on a schedule. Lenders send statements. Analysts can see the liability and price it.

When a building owner defers necessary work, something similar happens with none of the paperwork. The obligation does not disappear. It sits in the building, growing, until someone discovers it, usually at the least convenient moment.  Research note

The debt analogy is a thesis. The mechanisms it describes, accelerated deterioration after protection fails, consequential damage, construction cost escalation and compliance triggered by larger works, are general building practice observations; their size varies widely between buildings and elements. Deepened 4 November 2026 with the NHS England backlog series and the published evidence on the 1:5:200 ratio and the law of fives.

## How the interest accrues

Deferred maintenance accrues interest in four ways. First, deterioration accelerates: a failing roof membrane lets water into insulation and structure, a cracked sealant lets air and water behind a facade, corrosion spreads once protection is lost. Second, consequential damage spreads the cost beyond the original element: the roof leak becomes a ceiling, a switchroom, a tenant’s stock.

Third, prices move. As [The Building That Has to Earn Its Hedge](/insights/the-building-that-has-to-earn-its-hedge) describes, construction costs can rise faster than general inflation. Fourth, larger works trigger compliance. Replacing a system late, as part of a bigger intervention, can bring upgrades into scope that a timely replacement might have avoided.

Deferred maintenance compounds. By the time it shows, the principal is larger and the interest has been running for years.

## The largest public example

The clearest published record of deferral accumulating is the NHS estate in England, which reports its maintenance backlog every year through the Estates Returns Information Collection. It is a public estate, not a commercial portfolio, but the mechanism is the same one this paper describes. NHS England estate: the cost to clear backlog maintenanceYearBacklogContext2018/19£6.5 billion2024/25£15.9 billionUp 15.7% in a year; high-risk backlog £3.5 billion, up 28%2025/26£17.3 billionNow above the £14.4 billion annual cost of running the estate; high-risk backlog £3.7 billion

NHS England Estates Returns Information Collection, as reported by BCIS (2024/25) and NHS England Digital (2025/26).

Two features matter for any owner. The backlog more than doubled in six years while investment continued, because deferred items degrade into more serious ones; the high-risk category grew fastest. And the backlog now exceeds the annual cost of running the estate. That is what a building’s statement looks like when the interest has been compounding for years.

## The ratios to avoid

Two numbers are often quoted to dramatise deferral, and neither should be relied on. The 1:5:200 ratio, said to relate a building’s construction cost to its maintenance cost and to the cost of the people in it, began as a passing remark in a 1998 Royal Academy of Engineering paper with no data behind it. When researchers at the University of Reading tested it against three office buildings in 2004, they found something closer to 1:0.4:12.

The law of fives, which holds that every pound of deferred maintenance becomes five of repair and then twenty-five of renewal, comes from 1984 work on concrete durability. It is a useful heuristic for reinforced concrete exposed to chlorides. It is not a measured ratio for roofs, plant or services. The honest version of the argument does not need either number: it needs the register to show what each deferral does to the item’s condition, timing and cost.

## Not all deferral is bad

Deferral is sometimes the right answer. A system may have more life than its age suggests. A building may be heading for redevelopment, making investment in some elements wasteful. An owner may choose to run a system to failure where failure is low-consequence and replacement is quick.

Deferral can be conscious or unconscious. Conscious deferral is a decision, recorded with its reason and its risk. Unconscious deferral is the absence of a decision. The first is asset management. The second is accumulating debt without knowing the balance.

## Recording a deferral properly

A conscious deferral can be recorded on the register in a few words: the item, the reason, the risk accepted, the monitoring in place and the trigger that would end the deferral. For example: chiller two beyond typical life; deferred because the tenant’s lease expires in eighteen months and the replacement specification depends on the next use; risk of failure accepted with temporary hire as contingency; monthly performance logging; replace on failure or at lease end, whichever comes first.

Five lines like that turn a hidden liability into a managed one. They also tell the next owner, lender or adviser exactly what was decided and why, which is what distinguishes asset management from neglect.

## Why the statement never arrives

Valuations rarely reflect deferred maintenance in detail. Income capitalisation, as [The Cap Rate Doesn’t See the Roof](/insights/the-cap-rate-does-not-see-the-roof) argues, does not see the physical building directly. Annual accounts record maintenance spent, not maintenance owed. Condition reports, where they exist, are often out of date. The liability shows up only when a buyer, lender, insurer or failure forces it into view.

This is why the backlog in ageing commercial stock is so hard to measure, and why it surprises owners so often.

## Writing the statement

The remedy is to write the statement yourself. A register that records, element by element, what work is due, when, at roughly what cost and with what confidence is, in effect, a schedule of the building’s physical liabilities. Items consciously deferred are recorded as such, with their reasons. Items unknown are recorded as uncertainty.

Once the debt is visible, it can be managed like debt: prioritised, scheduled, refinanced in time, or reflected in price. Invisible, it can only be discovered.  In the register

Deferred items appear as condition-driven rows with timing pulled toward the near term and impact reflecting consequential damage; conscious deferrals carry their reasoning in the action field.   Key signal

Deferred maintenance accrues interest through deterioration, consequential damage, cost inflation and compliance triggers, and it stays invisible until a register makes it a statement.

## Sources

Named sources consulted for this paper. Consequential claims link to their source in the text. Reviewed 3 November 2026; next review by 3 November 2027.
- [Royal Institution of Chartered Surveyors](https://www.rics.org/), RICS. Accessed 3 November 2026.
- [Cost to clear NHS backlog maintenance nears £16 billion](https://www.bcis.co.uk/news/cost-to-clear-nhs-backlog-maintenance-nears-16-billion/), BCIS. Accessed 3 November 2026.
- [Exposing the myth of the 1:5:200 ratio relating initial cost, maintenance and staffing costs of office buildings](https://www.arcom.ac.uk/-docs/proceedings/ar2004-0373-0381_Hughes_et_al.pdf), Hughes, Ancell, Gruneberg and Hirst, ARCOM 2004. Accessed 3 November 2026.
- [The cost of deferred maintenance: the law of fives](https://knottlab.com/cases/the-cost-of-deferred-maintenance-the-law-of-fives/), Knott Laboratory. Accessed 3 November 2026.

## Questions

### Is it ever sensible to defer building maintenance?

Yes, when the decision is conscious and recorded: for example where a system has more life than expected, where redevelopment is planned, or where failure is low-consequence. The problem is unrecorded deferral.

### Why do valuations miss deferred maintenance?

Income-based valuation methods focus on rent and market yields and usually include only general allowances for capital, so element-level backlog rarely appears until due diligence or failure reveals it.

papers.title: A Building Is Forty Decisions
papers.question: Why should a building’s capital plan be treated as a set of decisions rather than a report?
papers.answer: Each material line in a capital register represents a choice about whether to act, defer, investigate, stage, repair or replace, and these choices interact and change as evidence and plans change. Treating the register as a living set of decisions rather than a one-off report is where most of its value lies.
papers.summary: A typical Capital Register carries around forty material lines. Each is a decision waiting to be made. The value lies in making them well over time, not in the report that lists them.
papers.limitations: A thesis that interprets external economic, policy and market developments through the physical reality of buildings. It is a view to test against individual assets, not a forecast or a finding from the Moyne Ross dataset.

technicalPages.why: A chiller’s life as a distribution, not a date
Lift lives and the modernisation decision
Roof lives by covering and exposure

papers.contentMarkdown:
A Capital Strategy for a mid-sized commercial building commonly carries around forty material lines. Roof coverings, facade elements, windows, lifts, chillers, air handling, switchboards, fire detection and sprinklers, hydraulics, car park structure, common areas. Each line has a condition, an action, a cost basis, timing, impact and confidence.

It is tempting to read that as a report: here is what the building needs. We think it is better read as a set of forty decisions, most of which are still open.  Research note

The figure of around forty material lines is typical of Moyne Ross registers for mid-sized commercial buildings; the methodology reference shows registers of forty-six elements. Larger and more complex assets carry more. Deepened 4 November 2026 with published service lives (Menlo Park Fire Protection District, consistent with ASHRAE), ASHRAE’s public service life database and NBS. CIBSE’s 2026 economic life tables are a paid resource and were not reproduced. Deepened 11 November 2026 against the Technical Library: chiller lives as ranges with what moves them.

## Every line is a choice

For each line, an owner has real options. Act now or later. Investigate before committing. Repair rather than replace. Replace like for like or upgrade. Stage the work across years. Combine it with another item. Pass it to a tenant under the lease. Accept the risk and run the element to failure.

The register recommends a course for each, based on evidence and judgement. But the best course depends on things the register cannot know alone: the owner’s plans, hold period, tenants, appetite for disruption and capital availability. That is why [bringing the owner’s intentions to bear](/insights/bringing-the-owners-intentions-to-bear) changes the strategy without changing the building.

## Forty clocks

Each decision has a clock attached: the period over which an element typically lasts before it needs renewal. Published service lives give a starting point, though not a verdict on any particular building. Typical service lives of commercial building elementsElementTypical life (years)ElementTypical life (years)Single-ply roof membrane15 to 20Built-up asphalt roof18 to 25Metal roof panels25Metal curtain wall40Centrifugal chiller23 to 28Hot-water boiler (steel)24 to 25Packaged rooftop unit15Built-up air handling unit30VAV box17 to 25Building controls (digital)20Traction lift (gearless)50Lift controller20Switchboards and switchgear30Transformer30Fire detection and alarm15Sprinklers25Domestic water piping30Water heater10Car park structure, exposed30Car park structure, covered40

Menlo Park Fire Protection District facility condition assessment, Appendix 4 (US, consistent with ASHRAE service life data). UK practice uses the CIBSE Guide M11 economic life tables.

Laid side by side, the clocks explain why a building is forty decisions rather than one. A [roof](/technical/roof-coverings#service-life) membrane, a set of chillers and a fire panel installed in the same year will each want renewal at a different time, and a capital plan that bundles them into one event either spends too early on some or too late on others.

## Lives are distributions, not dates

A published life is an average, and averages hide a spread. ASHRAE’s public database illustrates it well. For centrifugal chillers, the units that had actually been replaced had a median life of 25 years, but most units in the sample were still running, so the median for all units could only be stated as more than 25. Survival depends on duty, maintenance and environment. The Technical Library gives the range rather than the point, with what moves a unit along it: twenty to thirty years for a water-cooled centrifugal chiller, fifteen to twenty for an air-cooled one, moved by water treatment, overhaul history and the refrigerant it runs on ([chiller lives](/technical/central-cooling-plant#service-life)).

NBS makes the same point for British practice: life expectancy tables give single figures, while research into component lives shows wide distributions, with most mechanical and electrical components averaging a little over 20 years. That is why the register records each element’s observed condition and evidence, not only its age. A [chiller](/technical/central-cooling-plant#service-life) at 26 years with a clean maintenance history is a different decision from one at 18 with repeated failures.

## Decisions interact

Many decisions depend on others. The roof should usually be renewed before solar goes on. The switchboard may need replacing before heating is electrified. Facade works and window replacement share access equipment, so doing them together saves money. A [lift](/technical/passenger-and-goods-lifts#service-life) modernisation may wait for a lobby refurbishment. Fire upgrades may be triggered by another project.

## Mapping the dependencies

A useful exercise is to draw the dependencies between the register’s lines. Roof before solar. Switchboard before electrified heating and charging. Hazardous materials survey before any works that disturb fabric. Facade inspection before facade allowance. Lobby refurbishment and lift modernisation together. Fire upgrades with any major refurbishment. Controls before plant optimisation.

Once drawn, most registers reduce to a handful of chains and a scattering of independent items. The chains are where sequencing creates or destroys value. The independent items can be timed on their own merits. Seeing the shape makes the decisions far easier to discuss with an owner than a list of forty rows.

## Decisions change

Decisions also change over time. A tenant announces it will leave. A survey resolves an uncertainty, up or down. A regulation tightens. A chiller performs better than expected. Each new piece of information reopens some decisions and closes others. A register that is updated as this happens remains useful. One that is not becomes a historical document within a year or two.

## Where the value sits

The most valuable part of capital advice is rarely the first document. It is the ongoing work of making these decisions well: which to make now, which to defer consciously, which to reopen when evidence changes. That is the argument of [The Living Record](/insights/the-living-record) and, in its fullest form, [Physical Assets Under Management](/insights/physical-assets-under-management).

It also suggests a question to ask of any building beyond what it needs: who is making its forty decisions, and how well.  In the register

Each row’s action field records the recommended choice; dependencies between rows, such as roof before solar or switchboard before heat pumps, are recorded in the cost basis and timing.   Key signal

A Capital Register is a network of interacting decisions that change with evidence, so its value lies in ongoing decision-making rather than in a one-off report.

## Sources

- [Service life data query: public database](https://weblegacy.ashrae.org/publicdatabase/system_service_life.asp?selected_system_type=2), ASHRAE. Accessed 3 November 2026.
- [How long will components and systems last?](https://www.thenbs.com/knowledge/how-long-will-components-and-systems-last), NBS. Accessed 3 November 2026.
- [Indicative economic life expectancy tool 2026](https://www.cibse.org/knowledge-research/knowledge-portal/indicative-economic-life-expectancy-tool-2026/), CIBSE. Accessed 3 November 2026.

## Questions

### How many items does a typical commercial building capital register contain?

It varies with size and complexity, but a mid-sized commercial building commonly carries a few dozen material lines, often around forty, across structure, envelope, services and space.

### Why does the order of capital works matter?

Many works depend on or share costs with others, such as renewing a roof before installing solar or upgrading a switchboard before electrifying heating. Good sequencing reduces cost, disruption and rework.

papers.title: The Cap Rate Doesn’t See the Roof
papers.question: How do commercial property valuations account for future capital expenditure?
papers.answer: Capitalisation and discounted cash flow valuations focus on income and market yields, and usually treat future capital expenditure through general allowances or deductions rather than an element-by-element view. As a result, two buildings with similar income can carry very different capital requirements that the headline valuation does not distinguish.
papers.summary: Income-based valuation is built to price rent, not concrete. Capital requirements enter as broad allowances, if at all, which leaves a gap between what a building is worth on paper and what it will cost to own.
papers.limitations: A thesis that interprets external economic, policy and market developments through the physical reality of buildings. It is a view to test against individual assets, not a forecast or a finding from the Moyne Ross dataset.

sections.heading: Where capital hides in a valuation
What the valuation standards now ask

technicalPages.why: What a roof’s condition and remaining life look like
Membrane lives by type

papers.contentMarkdown:
A capitalisation rate is a compact idea. Take a building’s net income, divide by a market yield, and you have a value. Discounted cash flow adds time: project income and costs, discount them, add an exit value. Both methods are sensible ways to price an income stream.

Neither is designed to see a roof. Physical condition enters these models indirectly, through rent, vacancy, a general allowance or a deduction for known works. The building itself is mostly invisible.  Research note

Valuation practice is governed by professional standards, including the RICS Valuation Global Standards (the Red Book) and International Valuation Standards, both in current editions effective from 31 January 2025. Valuers do consider condition and capital needs; the point here is that income-based methods usually reflect them through general allowances or deductions rather than an element-level programme. Practice varies by valuer, asset and market. Deepened 4 November 2026 with the 2025 valuation standards and a summary of how capital enters valuations. Deepened 11 November 2026 against the Technical Library: membrane and lift controller lives behind the worked comparison.

## Where capital hides in a valuation

Future capital needs enter valuations in a few ways. A deduction for known immediate works, often taken from a due diligence report. A general allowance in a cash flow, sometimes expressed per square metre or as a share of income. An adjustment to the yield to reflect a building’s age or grade. Each is a reasonable shortcut. None is a reading of what the building will actually need.

Two buildings with the same income, tenants and location can therefore be valued similarly while one faces a heavy programme of plant, facade and compliance works and the other does not.

The valuation says what the income is worth. The capital plan says what it will cost to keep earning it. Investors need both.

## What the valuation standards now ask

Valuation standards have been moving toward the building. The International Valuation Standards and the RICS Red Book Global Standards that incorporate them both took effect in their current editions on 31 January 2025. The Red Book edition added material on environmental, social and governance factors and on modelling, and valuers are expected to consider how such factors, including the physical characteristics of the asset, affect value.

What the standards do not do is supply the building evidence. A valuer can only reflect the capital position that is known to them, and in most valuations that evidence is a general allowance or a figure lifted from a due diligence report prepared for another purpose. How capital commonly enters a valuationMethodWhat it capturesWhat it tends to missDeduction for immediate worksKnown near-term costs from a reportAnything beyond the report’s horizon or scopeGeneral capital allowance in a cash flowA smoothed annual cost, often a share of incomeConcentration: a roof or facade falling due in one yearAdjusted yieldThe market’s view of risk in the asset classThe specific condition of this buildingBuilding-specific programmeTiming, size and uncertainty of each major itemLittle, if the evidence is current

Moyne Ross summary of common practice; valuation method varies by valuer, market and purpose.

## A worked comparison

Two neighbouring offices each produce two million dollars of net income on similar leases and are valued at a similar yield. The first had its central plant, [roof](/technical/roof-coverings) and lifts renewed six years ago; its ten-year capital requirement is modest and falls mostly late in the decade. The second has original plant, a membrane at the end of its life and lifts due for modernisation; the membrane, if exposed modified bitumen, will have had fifteen to twenty years in it ([membrane lives](/technical/waterproofing-membranes#service-life)), and the lift controllers lose parts support after fifteen to twenty; its ten-year requirement is several million dollars, mostly in years two to five.

A buyer pricing both on income and a general allowance pays nearly the same for each. A buyer who reads both registers sees that the present value of the second building’s programme is a material share of its price, and either negotiates or walks. The valuation answered a different question, and answered it correctly.

## The acquisition moment

The gap matters most at acquisition. A buyer who prices a building on income and a general allowance, then discovers a large capital requirement after settlement, has overpaid by roughly the present value of the difference. A seller whose building has a lighter programme than its age suggests may be underpaid unless that is demonstrated.

This is why technical due diligence exists, and why its quality matters. The approaches in Australia, Britain and the United States differ, as [Due Diligence Across Three Markets](/insights/due-diligence-across-three-markets) sets out, but each aims to bring physical condition into the price.

## A second number

We think every investment decision on a commercial building benefits from a second number beside the valuation: a ten-year capital requirement, built element by element, split by horizon, with its cost basis and confidence visible. The two numbers answer different questions. Together they give a far better picture of value than either alone.

The [Melbourne office study](/insights/when-the-building-is-not-the-asset) is an example. Its ten-year capital requirement, set beside its approved development pathway, changed the question from refurbishment to redevelopment. The valuation alone would not have shown that.

## Reading condition into value

Anyone relying on a valuation can ask how capital enters it, and whether that reflects the building or a generic assumption. Across a portfolio, buildings with similar yields may sit at very different points in their physical lives, and only the second number shows it.  In the register

A register’s ten-year total and its split across 1 yr, 2–5 yr and 6–10 yr horizons is the second number to read beside a valuation.   Key signal

Income-based valuations treat capital through broad allowances, so a separate element-level ten-year capital requirement is needed to see what the building will actually cost to own.

## Sources

## Questions

### Do property valuations include future capital expenditure?

Usually in a general way, through deductions for known works, allowances in cash flows or yield adjustments. They rarely reflect an element-by-element view of what the building will need.

### Why compare a valuation with a ten-year capital requirement?

The valuation prices the income; the capital requirement shows what it will cost to keep that income. Two buildings with similar values can carry very different capital needs.

papers.title: Three Kinds of Obsolescence
papers.question: What are the different types of building obsolescence and why do they matter for capital planning?
papers.answer: Physical obsolescence is wear and deterioration; functional obsolescence is when a building no longer suits how it is used, such as layout, floor-to-floor height or controls; and economic or external obsolescence comes from changes outside the building, such as regulation, energy markets or demand. Condition surveys mostly capture the first, so capital plans need deliberate judgement to capture the other two.
papers.summary: Buildings stop being useful in three different ways: they wear out, they stop fitting how people use them, and the world around them changes. Each needs a different response.
papers.limitations: A thesis that interprets external economic, policy and market developments through the physical reality of buildings. It is a view to test against individual assets, not a forecast or a finding from the Moyne Ross dataset.

sections.heading: Obsolescence shows up in vacancy first

technicalPages.why: Lifts: physical wear against functional fit
Controls that become obsolete before they wear out
What an office floor must provide to stay lettable

papers.contentMarkdown:
When people say a building is obsolete, they usually mean one of three different things. It may be worn out. It may no longer suit the way people want to use it. Or the world around it may have changed in a way that makes it less valuable, even if nothing inside it has.

These three kinds of obsolescence often arrive together, but they are not the same, and treating them as the same leads to poor decisions.  Research note

The three-way classification of physical, functional and economic obsolescence, called external obsolescence in American appraisal practice and the International Valuation Standards, is long established in valuation and asset management. Regulatory examples cited are current at the review date: the expected EPC B standard for larger let non-domestic buildings in England and Wales from 2031, and New York’s Local Law 97 emissions limits. Deepened 4 November 2026 with vacancy-by-grade evidence from Australia and South East England and CBRE’s estimate of UK stock below EPC B. Deepened 11 November 2026 against the Technical Library: the support clock, between physical and functional obsolescence.

## Physical: wearing out

Physical obsolescence is the familiar kind. Materials deteriorate, systems wear, components fail. A roof membrane loses waterproofing, a chiller loses efficiency and reliability, concrete spalls. This is what condition surveys measure and what most capital plans are built around.

Physical obsolescence is usually gradual and predictable within a range. Its response is maintenance, repair and replacement on a sensible schedule.

Condition surveys tend to miss a clock that sits between physical and functional obsolescence, which is manufacturer support. Lift controllers lose parts support after fifteen to twenty years, building management controllers after fifteen to twenty, switchboard breakers after twenty to twenty-five, and a fire panel when its vendor stops supplying it. The equipment still works but can no longer be repaired, which ends its useful life as surely as wear. The Technical Library records the support clock beside wear wherever it applies ([lifts](/technical/passenger-and-goods-lifts#service-life), [controls](/technical/building-management-and-control-system#service-life), [switchboards](/technical/main-electrical-supply#service-life), [fire panels](/technical/fire-detection-and-alarm-systems#service-life)).

## Functional: no longer fitting

Functional obsolescence happens when a building, or part of it, no longer does what its users need, even if it is in good condition. A low floor-to-floor height that cannot fit modern services. A deep floor plate in a world that values daylight. A building management system that cannot integrate with current controls. [Lifts](/technical/passenger-and-goods-lifts) that are reliable but too slow and too few for current occupancy patterns. A warehouse with insufficient clear height for modern racking.

A building can be in good repair and still be obsolete. Condition ratings alone will not show it.

Functional obsolescence is harder to see because it is relative to expectations, which change. Its responses are upgrade, reconfiguration or change of use, and sometimes acceptance that the building serves a different market than it once did.

## Economic: the world moves

Economic or external obsolescence comes from outside the building. Regulation tightens, as with minimum energy standards for letting in Britain or emissions limits in some American cities. Valuers in the United States and under the International Valuation Standards usually call this external obsolescence. Energy markets shift, making gas-dependent plant less attractive. Demand moves, as with secondary [office](/technical/commercial-office-areas) stock in some cities. Insurance reprices physical risk.

This kind of obsolescence can arrive quickly and without any change in the building’s physical state. It is the source of most talk about stranded assets, and it often shortens the economic life of systems that are physically sound, as [Energy Becomes a Building Function](/insights/energy-becomes-a-building-function) describes for gas.

## Obsolescence shows up in vacancy first

The three kinds of obsolescence leave different traces, but the market reads them together, and the clearest place to see that is vacancy by grade. The market’s reading of obsolescenceEvidenceBetter spaceOlder or lower-grade spaceSourceSydney CBD office vacancy, January 2026Prime 13.2%Secondary 14.9%Property Council of AustraliaSouth East England office vacancyGrade A 1.7%Grade B rising from 10.6% to 11%Knight Frank, via Property WeekUK city-centre office stock below EPC B60% by floor area (August 2025)CBREMelbourne CBD office vacancy, July 202618.9% overall, the highest of the Australian capitalsProperty Council of Australia

Vacancy definitions differ between sources; read for direction rather than direct comparison.

The South East figures are the starkest: Grade A space is almost fully let while Grade B vacancy is rising. Physical condition, functional fit and regulatory exposure tend to cluster in the same older buildings, which is why the gap between grades widens rather than closes as markets recover.

## Recording obsolescence on the register

On a Moyne Ross register, physical obsolescence lives in the condition field. Functional and economic obsolescence surface elsewhere: in the action, where an upgrade replaces a like-for-like renewal; in the timing, where a regulatory date or a refrigerant phase-out brings a sound item forward; and in the cost basis, where the reason is stated in words. A reader can therefore filter the register for items driven by a changing world rather than by wear, and see how much of the programme each accounts for.

In some older buildings that share is large. It is also the part of the programme most open to judgement and to the owner’s intentions, which is why it belongs in the conversation rather than in a formula.

## Reading all three

A capital plan that only reads physical condition will consistently misjudge timing for the other two. A chiller in fair condition may need replacement within five years because of its refrigerant. A sound office floor may need reconfiguration to remain lettable. A well-maintained building may need an energy upgrade to stay legally lettable.

In a Moyne Ross register, condition records physical state, while action, impact and timing carry the judgement about functional and economic obsolescence. Making that judgement explicit, with its reasoning in the cost basis, lets an owner see which lines are driven by wear and which by a changing world.  In the register

Physical obsolescence lives in the condition field; functional and economic obsolescence surface through action, impact and timing, with their reasoning recorded in the cost basis.   Key signal

Condition surveys mostly see physical obsolescence, but functional and economic obsolescence increasingly decide when systems and buildings stop earning their place.

Accessed 3 November 2026.

Accessed 3 November 2026.
