sections.heading: Types of accessibility lift
sections.markdown:
Accessibility lifts provide step-free access where a full passenger lift is impractical: vertical platform lifts over short rises, inclined platform lifts that travel along a stair, stair lifts with seats, low-rise passenger lifts, and home lifts in houses and small apartment buildings. They are the only accessible route between levels in many existing buildings, so when one fails, people who use wheelchairs or cannot manage stairs are excluded from part of the building.

These units are judged differently from other building equipment. A passenger lift out of service is an inconvenience shared by everyone; an accessibility lift out of service removes the building's only step-free route, and only for the people who cannot use the stairs. Its reliability is therefore an access question before it is a maintenance one, and in all three jurisdictions a persistently broken unit is a discrimination exposure as much as a repair item ([Disabled Access](https://moyneross.com/technical/disabled-access)).

| Type | Where it is found | Character |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Vertical platform lift (open or enclosed) | Entrances, mezzanines, stages, heritage buildings | Short rises; screw, chain or hydraulic drive; slow; hold-to-run controls |
| Inclined platform lift | Existing stairs in schools, churches, offices | Runs on the stair; folds away; restricts the stair |
| Stair lift with seat | Houses, small residential buildings | For people who can transfer to a seat |
| Low-rise passenger lift | Small apartment buildings, offices | Between a platform lift and a full lift |
| Home lift | Houses and townhouses | Domestic duty; often battery or screw driven |

Many units were installed to meet access requirements during refurbishments and then left without proper maintenance. Several are supplied by small manufacturers whose parts and support disappear. Battery-backed units depend on batteries that fail quietly.

They are also the one piece of lifting equipment commonly bought on price by a party who will never use it. Many were installed during a refurbishment to satisfy an access requirement, chosen for the smallest shaft and the lowest cost, then handed over with no maintenance contract. Where a full passenger lift could have been fitted instead, it would almost always have been the better long-term answer ([Passenger & Goods Lifts](https://moyneross.com/technical/passenger-and-goods-lifts)).

Drive type tells you most of what you need to know. Screw-driven platforms are slow but hold position mechanically and lower safely under battery. Chain-driven units stretch and need slack-chain protection. Hydraulic platforms leak and need emergency lowering that works without power. Battery-driven home lifts and stair lifts depend on batteries that fail silently in units that are seldom used.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Accessibility lifts have short-lived parts on a longer-lived structure: batteries last three to five years and safety edges five to ten, while the drive and platform last fifteen to thirty. A unit's life is decided as much by whether its maker still supplies parts as by wear.

| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Platform lift drive (screw, chain or hydraulic) | 15 to 25 years | Use; lubrication; exposure |
| Controls and safety circuits | 10 to 15 years | Manufacturer support; exposure |
| Batteries | 3 to 5 years | Charging; temperature |
| Safety edges and sensors | 5 to 10 years | Damage; exposure |
| Gates and doors | 10 to 20 years | Abuse; interlocks |
| Stair lift rails and carriages | 10 to 15 years | Use |
| Platform and carriage structure | 20 to 30 years | Corrosion on external units; impact |
| Hydraulic rams and seals | 15 to 20 years | Leaks; oil condition; cold |
| Emergency call equipment | 10 to 15 years | Network retirement rather than wear |
| Platform floor coverings and edging | 8 to 15 years | Wear; weather |

These units fail from two opposite causes, and which one applies depends entirely on the setting. In a house used by one person several times a day, components wear in the ordinary way. In a public building where the unit is used a few times a week by visitors, it fails from disuse: lubricant migrates, contacts corrode, batteries sulphate and die, and nobody discovers any of it until someone needs the lift.

What shortens life: external exposure: units at entrances get wet, corrode and suffer electrical faults; lack of use: seldom-used units seize and their batteries die; misuse and vandalism: gates forced, controls damaged; unsupported manufacturers, which leave units unrepairable.

Units used daily by the same person, such as in a house, wear differently from units used occasionally by many visitors in a public building; the second group often fails from neglect rather than wear.

What lengthens it: a real maintenance contract with scheduled visits, which many units simply do not have; battery replacement on a fixed cycle rather than on failure, since a dead battery usually strands someone; regular exercising of seldom-used units, ideally as part of a routine building check; weather protection for units at entrances: canopy, enclosure and drainage away from the pit; choosing a supported product with a national service presence, which matters more than specification; remote fault monitoring, so a failure is reported before a user finds it.

sections.heading: Reliability, support and the drive
sections.markdown:
Accessibility lifts are, as a class, the least reliable equipment in most buildings. Repeated breakdowns, long waits for parts from small suppliers, and units left out of service for months are routine. The consequence is not measured in downtime but in access: for as long as the unit is out, the building has no step-free route between those levels, and the people affected are precisely those with the fewest alternatives. Owners and occupiers who treat this as a maintenance backlog rather than a legal exposure tend to be corrected by a complaint.

Screw and nut drives wear, chains stretch, hydraulic systems leak and the batteries that provide travel or emergency lowering fail. The consequence is specific to this equipment: a unit that stops part way leaves a wheelchair user suspended between levels, unable to get off and often unable to reach a call point. Battery failure is the most common single cause, and the most preventable, because batteries are replaced on a known cycle and are almost never on one.

Control boards, limit switches and wiring in compact units are exposed to damp and dust; intermittent faults that clear when reset are common and usually precede a failure that leaves the unit out of service.

Platform lifts and stair lifts come from a long tail of small manufacturers, importers and installers. Companies close, change hands or withdraw from a market, and the unit becomes unrepairable: no boards, no proprietary controller tools, no one willing to take on maintenance of another maker's equipment. Unlike a passenger lift, there is rarely a modernisation path, because the whole unit is proprietary. The practical end of life is the day support ends, whatever condition the machinery is in.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unit stops part way or will not start | Battery, drive or safety circuit fault. Battery test; fault codes. | Test the battery and read the fault codes; replace the battery or repair the drive. |
| Frequent breakdowns and long waits for parts | Unsupported manufacturer or end of life. Parts support status. | Confirm the parts support position; hold spares on site, or plan replacement with a supported product. |
| Battery flat on a unit that is rarely used | Disuse and no replacement cycle. Battery date; charging circuit; usage frequency. | Replace the battery on a recorded cycle, whether or not it has failed. |
| No contractor will quote for maintenance | Orphaned product. Manufacturer trading status; parts and tools availability. | Plan replacement with a supported product, or a low-rise passenger lift or ramp where space allows. |
| Long outages but few recorded faults | Parts lead times, not reliability. Days out of service per fault, rather than fault count. | Measure days out of service; hold spares on site to shorten outages. |

sections.heading: Safety devices, entrapment and stairs
sections.markdown:
Platforms have safety edges and pans under them that stop travel if they touch an obstruction, and gates and doors with interlocks so they cannot open mid-travel. Damaged edges and bypassed interlocks expose users and bystanders to crushing and falls.

Users stranded on a stopped platform, often alone and with limited mobility, need a way to call for help and a means of emergency lowering. Many units have neither, or have a phone on a retired line.

Inclined platform lifts and stair lifts reduce stair width; when left unfolded or broken down they can obstruct an escape stair.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Platform continues when the edge is pressed | Safety edge fault. Test. | Take it out of service now; repair the safety edge and prove it by test. |
| Platform stops slightly below the landing | Levelling drift, worn drive or low battery voltage. Levelling measured loaded and unloaded at both landings, against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Measure the levelling loaded and unloaded; repair the drive and check the battery. |
| Gate closes but the unit will not move | Interlock contact or alignment. Each interlock tested individually; contacts inspected. | Test each interlock, and repair or realign the contacts. |

sections.heading: Usability, dignity and external siting
sections.markdown:
A unit can work perfectly and still fail its purpose. Hold-to-run controls that need sustained pressure defeat users with limited hand strength; keys held at a reception desk mean asking for help and waiting; call points out of reach from a wheelchair; signage that does not say how to summon assistance; a platform too small for a powered wheelchair. These are not maintenance faults and will not show in a breakdown record, but they are the reason many units go unused.

Hold-to-run controls that are hard to operate, keys that staff cannot find, and call points out of reach make units unusable even when they work.

Units at entrances and on external stairs are exposed to rain, wind-driven water and, at coastal sites, salt. Pits fill, control enclosures admit damp, safety edges and limit switches corrode, and intermittent electrical faults begin. External siting is the single strongest predictor of an unreliable accessibility lift.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unit works only with staff help | Key or call arrangements, not the lift. Observation. | Change the key or call arrangements so a visitor can use it unaided. |
| Corrosion and electrical faults at an entrance unit | Weather exposure. Inspection. | Add weather protection: a canopy or enclosure, pit drainage and sealed control cabinets. |
| Unit fails after rain or in cold weather | Water ingress or hydraulic oil viscosity. Enclosure and pit inspected; fault timing against weather. | Seal the enclosure and drain the pit; check the hydraulic oil for cold weather. |
| Unit works on test but users report it does not | A usability problem, not a fault. Watch a user operate it unaided, including summoning help. | Watch a user operate it unaided, and fix the controls, call points or signage that stop them. |
| Unit used only with a staff escort | Key control, or a policy rather than a fault. Observe whether a visitor could use it unaided. | Change the arrangement so a visitor can use it unaided. |
| Platform lift serving a rise of more than about a metre, or with no enclosure | Lift type used beyond its limits. Travel and speed against the limits for the lift type in the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Check the travel and type against the rules; replace with a suitable lift type where it exceeds them. |

sections.heading: Evacuation
sections.markdown:
Most accessibility lifts are not evacuation lifts and must not be used in a fire. That leaves the question of how a person who needed the lift to get up will get down, which is answered by the building's evacuation strategy, refuge areas and personal plans rather than by the lift. A building with an accessibility lift and no evacuation arrangement for its users has solved access and ignored egress ([Fire Detection & Alarm Systems](https://moyneross.com/technical/fire-detection-and-alarm-systems)).

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Platform lift the only way down from an upper level, with no evacuation plan for its users | Users who cannot leave in a fire. Fire strategy and personal evacuation plans; whether the lift is on an escape route or protected supply. | Agree an evacuation method for each user, with refuges, evacuation aids or an evacuation lift as the strategy requires. |
| Inclined platform lift folded across an escape stair | Stair width reduced on an escape route. Clear width with the platform folded, measured against the stair’s required width. | Confirm the folded width leaves the required clear width, or relocate the lift. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Safety edges, pans or interlocks failed or bypassed | safety · 4 Essential | Take out of service until proved. |
| No working emergency call from the platform, or no emergency lowering | safety · 4 Essential | Take out of service until restored. |
| Unit or its rail obstructing an escape stair | safety · 4 Essential | Clear now. |
| Unit out of service, leaving no step-free route between the levels | failure · 4 Essential | Restore now, or provide a managed alternative route in the meantime. |
| Repeated long outages amounting to a significant share of the year | failure · 4 Essential | Treat as an access failure; plan replacement. |
| Thorough examination or periodic inspection due | deadline · 4 Essential | At the prescribed interval. |
| Emergency call device on a network being retired | deadline · 4 Essential | Migrate before the line is withdrawn. |
| Worn drives, failing batteries, corrosion at an external unit | condition · 3 Important | Repair in the near term. |
| No maintenance contract in place | condition · 3 Important | Put one in place now. |
| Manufacturer no longer supports the unit | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Plan replacement; there is no modernisation path. |
| Unit works but users cannot operate it independently | condition · 4 Essential | Fix controls, keys, call points and signage. |
| No access audit; no evacuation arrangement for users | check · 3 Important | Assess with an access consultant and the fire strategy. |
| Cosmetic wear to platform finishes | nil · 1 Routine | Routine maintenance. |

Grading here follows consequence rather than cost. Almost every finding on an accessibility lift is cheap to fix relative to the building, and the reason they go unfixed is that nobody responsible encounters the problem. The grading should reflect who is affected and how completely, not the size of the repair.

The grading follows what a finding demands, not the size of the eventual bill.

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A lift consultant or accessibility lift specialist, ideally with an access consultant for usability. The checks below test the unit as a user would meet it, then its safety devices, its records and its parts support.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Function test | Over full travel with a typical load, including emergency lowering. |
| Safety tests | Safety edges, pans, gate and door interlocks, overspeed and slack chain protection. |
| Battery and drive inspection | Battery age and voltage under load, charging circuit, drive and motor condition, and emergency lowering on battery. |
| Communication test | Emergency call device and its line. |
| Usability review | Controls, reach, keys, signage and how users summon help. |
| Records review | Breakdowns, downtime, parts support, and statutory examinations against the intervals for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). |
| Stair review | For inclined units on escape stairs. |
| Downtime analysis | Total days out of service over two years, not the number of call-outs. |
| Manufacturer status check | Whether the maker still trades in the jurisdiction and will supply parts and tools. |
| Observed use | A user operating the unit unaided from arrival to arrival, including summoning help if it stops. |
| Alternatives review | Whether a ramp, a different route, or a low-rise passenger lift would provide more reliable access than repairing or replacing the existing unit. |
| Escape review | With the fire strategy, so a person using the lift can also leave the building in an emergency. |

The report should state safety, reliability, usability and remaining life, and whether a different solution (a low-rise lift or ramp) would serve better.

sections.heading: Maintaining, repairing or replacing
sections.markdown:
Many of these units have no maintenance contract at all, and putting one in place is often the most valuable step. Beyond that, the work turns on whether the maker still supports the unit, and on whether a problem is a fault to repair or a limitation of the design.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A maintenance contract | Scheduled visits, defined scope, response times and battery replacement included. | Wherever there is none; the single highest-value action available on this equipment. |
| Battery replacement on a cycle | Replace batteries on a recorded, diarised cycle. | Always, rather than waiting for a failure. |
| Safety device repair | Edges, pans, interlocks, slack chain and overspeed protection, each proved by test. | Wherever a device fails its test or has been bypassed. |
| Emergency communication | A digital or cellular connection with battery backup and a monitored answering arrangement, tested on a schedule. | Wherever the call device fails, reaches no one, or sits on a network being retired. |
| Weather protection | A canopy or enclosure, pit drainage and sealed control cabinets. | For external units. |
| Usability works | Accessible controls, call points within reach at both landings, removal of key-and-staff arrangements, and signage that says how to get help. | Wherever users cannot operate the unit on their own. |
| Remote monitoring | Faults reported to the contractor automatically. | So faults reach the contractor without a user having to report them. |
| Spares held on site | Critical spares kept at the building. | For units with long parts lead times; it turns a six-week outage into a same-week repair. |
| Replacement | A supported product or, better, a low-rise passenger lift or a ramp where space allows. | Where the maker no longer supports the unit, or the design does not suit its users; reliability over the next twenty years usually justifies the larger job. |
| Evacuation arrangements | Arrangements for the people who rely on the lift, recorded in the fire strategy and in personal plans where those are used. | In every building where people rely on the lift. |

Choosing between them starts with support. Where the manufacturer still trades, repair and a proper contract are almost always right, because the works are modest. Where the product is orphaned, money spent on repair buys nothing: there is no modernisation path and the next failure ends the unit. At that point the question is not which unit to buy but whether a different solution, usually a small passenger lift or a regraded approach with a ramp, would serve the building better for the next thirty years.

Interactions: replacing a platform lift with a low-rise passenger lift means structural work, a pit and a shaft, and usually touches the entrance, finishes and fire separation. Ramps change external levels and drainage ([Pavements & Hardstand](https://moyneross.com/technical/pavements-and-hardstand)). Both are the kind of work best done during a wider refurbishment.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Maintenance contracts recur. Batteries are replaced on a cycle. Repairs are itemised. Replacement is a lump sum per unit, with builders' work; replacing a platform lift with a low-rise lift or ramp is a larger project that may be justified by reliability. Downtime has an indirect cost in access complaints and legal risk.

What drives the cost: whether the product is supported, the rise and travel, external siting and the protection it needs, builders' work for any replacement, and parts lead times, which often cost more in downtime than in money. Commonly missed: putting a maintenance contract in place where there was none, the alternative access arrangements during an outage, usability works that are not strictly repairs, and the access and fire advice that should accompany any replacement decision.

Safety and accessibility rectification are code compliance; replacement is lifecycle; maintenance and batteries are repairs and maintenance.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a test on the day cannot: how long the unit has been out of service, whether its maker still supports it, and whether a trapped user can reach anyone. Ask for them before any work is specified.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Maintenance contract, if one exists, with scope, visit frequency and response times | Whether the unit is maintained at all, and how quickly faults are answered. |
| Breakdown history and total days out of service over the last two years | How long the building has been without step-free access, which matters more than how often. |
| Thorough examination or periodic inspection certificates | Whether statutory examinations are current. |
| Manufacturer and parts support position in writing, including whether the maker still trades locally | Whether the unit can still be repaired, and how quickly. |
| Battery replacement records and dates | Whether batteries are replaced before they fail. |
| Emergency call device line type, monitoring arrangement and test records | Whether a trapped user can reach someone. |
| Access complaints, discrimination correspondence and any claims | Whether people have already been excluded, and the risk that carries. |
| The building's access audit and any consultant recommendations | What has been recommended for the building's access. |
| Personal emergency evacuation plans for regular users, and the fire strategy's position on the unit | How people who rely on the lift would leave in an emergency. |
| Records of alternative access offered during past outages | What users were offered when the lift was out. |
| Any assessment of whether a passenger lift or ramp could replace the unit | Whether a passenger lift or ramp could replace the unit. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Accessibility lifts are misread when reliability is judged by how often they break, when an outage is treated as a maintenance matter, and when a design limitation is treated as a fault.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| A unit that rarely breaks is reliable | The measure that matters here is not how often the unit breaks but how long it stays broken. A unit failing twice a year and back in service the same day is serviceable; a unit failing twice a year and out for six weeks each time has made the building inaccessible for a quarter of the year. Ask for days out of service, not call-out counts. |
| An outage is a maintenance issue | An accessibility lift out of service means part of the building is not accessible. Treat repeated or prolonged outages as an accessibility failure, not just a maintenance issue. |
| Every problem is a fault to repair | Distinguish a fault from a design limitation before specifying anything. A platform too small for a powered wheelchair, a rise served at walking pace, or a unit sited where a user must cross a traffic route all work exactly as sold. They are reasons to reconsider the solution, not things a contractor can repair. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets access law, equipment standards for platform and stair lifts, and inspection rules. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Access law | The Disability (Access to Premises — Buildings) Standards 2010 and the National Construction Code set access requirements; the Disability Discrimination Act 1992 applies where access is not provided, and complaints about inaccessible buildings are made under it rather than through building control. | Approved Document M sets access requirements; the Equality Act 2010 requires reasonable adjustments, and the duty applies continuously, so a unit left out of service for long periods is a live exposure rather than a deferred repair. | The 2010 ADA Standards set where and how platform lifts may be used; ADA Title III complaints commonly cite broken or unavailable platform lifts, and a lift that requires staff assistance to operate may not meet the independent-use expectation. |
| Equipment standards | Low-rise platforms and lifts are covered by parts of the AS 1735 series, including AS 1735.14 and AS 1735.15 for low-rise platforms and stairway lifts. | BS EN 81-41 covers vertical lifting platforms, and BS EN 81-40 stair lifts and inclined platforms. | ASME A18.1 covers platform lifts and stairway chairlifts. |
| Inspection and evacuation | Platform lifts are plant under the work health and safety regulations. | LOLER requires thorough examination of lifting platforms; where a platform lift serves a means of escape, BS 9999 governs whether it may be used in an evacuation. | State elevator authorities inspect them. |

Discrimination complaints in all three countries commonly arise from broken accessibility lifts.

sections.heading: Worked example: an entrance platform lift that is often out
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 1970s office has a platform lift at its entrance, the only step-free way in. It broke down only twice in the past year, but each time it was out for about six weeks while parts were found. There is no maintenance contract, the maker has stopped trading, and a sign asks visitors to find staff for the key.

Two breakdowns sound reliable, but twelve weeks without step-free access is a failure finding and an accessibility failure, not a maintenance issue. The orphaned product explains the long outages. The key-and-staff arrangement is a finding in its own right: the route is not independent even when the lift works.

So the register carries the outages as a failure line, a maintenance contract with spares on site as a condition line now, removal of the key arrangement, and replacement with a supported product, or a ramp or low-rise lift if space allows, as a lifecycle line, with evacuation arrangements recorded meanwhile.

thresholds.rule: Low-rise platform lift: no more than 1000 mm; low-rise, low-speed constant pressure lift: no more than 2 m unenclosed or 4 m enclosed

source.title: NCC 2025 Volume One, Part E3 Lift installations

thresholds.rule: Rated speed no more than 0.15 m/s

source.title: Approved Document M, Volume 2: Buildings other than dwellings (with 2024 amendments)

thresholds.rule: At least every 6 months for equipment that lifts people; every 12 months for other lifting equipment, unless an examination scheme sets otherwise

source.title: Thorough examination of lifting equipment (INDG422)

thresholds.rule: Within 13 mm (1/2 in) of the landing from rated load to no load; no more than 32 mm between car sill and landing

source.title: 2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design

pages.title: Air Handling Units (AHUs)
pages.question: How do air handling units fail, what does each failure look like, and when do they affect health rather than just comfort?
pages.answer: Air handling units fail first at their wet parts: drain pans that do not drain, wet internal insulation and fouled coils grow microbes and cause the musty smell people notice when air conditioning starts. Seized outside air dampers starve buildings of fresh air and raise carbon dioxide. Fans wear at bearings and belts; old belt-driven fans waste energy. Rooftop casings corrode. Hygiene and outside air are health issues, not just comfort issues.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about air handling units (ahus); it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.

pages.searchTitle: Air handling units: hygiene, outside air, coils, fans and when to refurbish

questions.question: Why does the air conditioning smell musty when it starts?
questions.answer: Usually microbial growth in drain pans, coils or wet insulation. It is not cosmetic; a hygiene inspection should follow.

questions.question: Why are our meeting rooms stuffy?
questions.answer: Often too little outside air: the damper is closed or its minimum set too low. Measure the outside air, and consider carbon dioxide control.

questions.question: Can an old air handling unit be refurbished?
questions.answer: Often. Where the casing is sound and access is difficult, new internals can go into the existing casing.

questions.question: Is replacing belt-driven fans worthwhile?
questions.answer: Often. Direct-drive plug fans with electronically commutated motors are frequently a large energy saving.

questions.question: How long do air handling units last?
questions.answer: Indoor units 25 to 30 years and rooftop units 15 to 25, with fans 20 to 25, coils 15 to 25, motors 15 to 20 and belts 2 to 4.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Air handling unit problems show at the unit as water, rust and dirty coils, in the building as musty smells and stuffiness, and in maintenance logs and BMS trends. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| At the unit | Nameplate data: manufacturer, year, airflow, fan type | Coils, fans and casings |
| At the unit | Water on the plant room floor; corrosion at the base of casings; rust stains below rooftop units | Hygiene, humidifiers and intakes |
| At the unit | Drain pan condition: standing water, slime, rust; trap present and full | Hygiene, humidifiers and intakes |
| At the unit | Filters overloaded, missing, or bypassed around frames | Coils, fans and casings |
| At the unit | Coil fins dirty, flattened or corroded | Coils, fans and casings |
| At the unit | Noise and vibration; belt dust; hot bearings | Coils, fans and casings |
| At the unit | Dampers and actuators: position against what the controls show | Outside air, dampers and heat recovery |
| At the unit | Internal insulation wet, shedding or mouldy | Hygiene, humidifiers and intakes |
| In the building | Musty smells when air conditioning starts | Hygiene, humidifiers and intakes |
| In the building | Stuffiness, high carbon dioxide and complaints in meetings rooms | Outside air, dampers and heat recovery |
| In the building | Dust deposits around supply grilles | Coils, fans and casings |
| In the building | Temperature and humidity complaints | Outside air, dampers and heat recovery |
| In the records | Maintenance logs: filter changes, belt changes, coil cleaning | Investigation before the scope |
| In the records | Hygiene inspection reports | Hygiene, humidifiers and intakes |
| In the records | Indoor air quality monitoring | Outside air, dampers and heat recovery |
| In the records | BMS trends: fan status, damper position, supply temperature | Outside air, dampers and heat recovery |
| In the records | Energy consumption | Coils, fans and casings |

sections.heading: Types of air handling unit
sections.markdown:
An air handling unit conditions and moves air for a zone, a floor or a whole building. Inside its casing are fans, filters, heating and cooling coils, often heat recovery, sometimes humidification, dampers for outside, return and exhaust air, sound attenuators and a drain pan under the cooling coil. Units sit in plant rooms, on roofs or in ceiling voids, and serve the ductwork and terminal units downstream.

| Component | Job | What goes wrong |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Casing and panels | Contain air; insulate; keep out water on rooftop units | Corrosion; air leakage; wet or shedding internal insulation |
| Fans and motors | Move air | Bearing wear; belt wear; imbalance; motor failure; old forward-curved fans inefficient |
| Filters | Remove particles | Bypass around frames; overloaded filters; wrong grade |
| Cooling coils | Cool and dehumidify | Fouled fins; corrosion; leaks; freeze damage |
| Heating coils | Heat | Fouling; leaks; freeze damage |
| Drain pans | Collect condensate from cooling coils | Corrosion; standing water; microbial growth; overflow |
| Heat recovery (wheels, plates, run-around coils) | Recover energy from exhaust air | Seals; cross-leakage; fouling; drive failure |
| Humidifiers | Add moisture | Scale; water quality; microbial risk with adiabatic types |
| Dampers and actuators | Control outside air and economy cycle | Seized dampers; failed actuators; stuck positions |
| Attenuators | Reduce noise | Fibrous media degrading or wet |

Units vary from large site-built units in office plant rooms serving several floors, through packaged rooftop units on retail and industrial buildings (often with gas heating or direct expansion cooling built in), to dedicated outdoor air units supplying ventilation to fan coils or chilled beams. Hospitals, laboratories and cleanrooms have units built to stricter hygiene and filtration standards.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Indoor air handling units last twenty-five to thirty years and rooftop units fifteen to twenty-five, but their working parts turn over faster: motors fifteen to twenty years, humidifiers and damper actuators ten to fifteen, belts two to four. A sound casing can often be refurbished in place rather than replaced.

| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AHU casing (indoor) | 25 to 30 years | Condensation; drain pan leaks |
| AHU casing (rooftop) | 15 to 25 years | Weather; coastal exposure; panel seals |
| Fans | 20 to 25 years | Maintenance; balance |
| Fan motors (including EC motors) | 15 to 20 years | Run hours; heat |
| Belts | 2 to 4 years | Tension; alignment |
| Cooling and heating coils | 15 to 25 years | Cleaning; water treatment; coastal air |
| Heat recovery wheels | 15 to 20 years | Seals; drives |
| Humidifiers | 10 to 15 years | Water quality |
| Damper actuators | 10 to 15 years | Use; controls |
| Filters | Months to a year | Dust load; grade |

What shortens life: neglected filters, which let dust foul coils and fans and raise fan energy; blocked drains and standing condensate, which corrode drain pans and casings and grow microbes; coastal and industrial air on rooftop casings and coils; freezing in cold climates where frost protection fails; poor access inside units, so parts are never cleaned or inspected; running 24 hours when schedules have been lost or overridden.

sections.heading: Hygiene, humidifiers and intakes
sections.markdown:
Cooling coils produce condensate. If the drain pan does not drain because it is flat, corroded, or the trap is dry or the wrong depth for the fan pressure, water stands in the pan and grows bacteria and fungi. Wet fibrous insulation inside casings and attenuators does the same. Air carries spores and odours downstream. This is the commonest cause of musty smells from air conditioning and a recognised indoor air quality hazard.

Steam humidifiers scale; adiabatic (spray or pad) humidifiers can grow Legionella and other bacteria if water quality and maintenance lapse.

Outside air intakes near cooling towers, car park exhausts, kitchen exhausts, loading docks or flues draw contaminants into the building.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Musty smell at start-up | Microbial growth in drain pans, coils or wet insulation. Standing water and slime in the pan; wet insulation; swab results. | Commission a hygiene inspection; clean the pans and coils, and replace wet insulation. |
| Water on the floor or ceiling below | Blocked drain or dry trap. Drain flow; trap depth against fan pressure. | Clear the drain, and fix the trap depth and falls. |

sections.heading: Outside air, dampers and heat recovery
sections.markdown:
Outside air dampers seized shut starve the building of fresh air, raising carbon dioxide and complaints; seized open, they waste energy and can freeze coils. Economy cycle failures lose free cooling. Minimum outside air settings drift as controls change.

Wheels lose seals and leak exhaust air into supply; drives fail and wheels stop; plate heat exchangers foul. Recovery efficiency falls without obvious signs.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| High carbon dioxide in occupied spaces | Outside air damper closed or minimum set too low. Damper position; outside air flow measured against the design and the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Measure the outside air; repair the dampers and reset the minimum, with carbon dioxide control. |
| Heat recovery wheel or plate with frost, leaks or a seized bypass | Heat recovery not working, or exhaust air carried back into supply. Temperatures across the recovery device; damper and bypass operation. | Repair the bypass and seals, and confirm exhaust is not transferring to supply. |

sections.heading: Coils, fans and casings
sections.markdown:
Dust bypassing filters coats coil fins and cuts heat transfer; the coil then cannot cool or dehumidify fully and the chilled water system sees less temperature difference (low delta T). Coils corrode at fins and tube joints, and chilled water coils leak; heating and cooling coils burst when frozen.

Bearings wear and run hot; belts slip and shed; pulleys wear; fans lose balance and vibrate. Older forward-curved and belt-driven fans use far more energy than modern direct-drive plug fans with electronically commutated motors.

Panels corrode from condensation and drain pan leaks; seals harden; rooftop units let in rain. Leakage into a unit from the plant room or out of the unit wastes energy and bypasses filters.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cannot reach supply temperature; low chilled water delta T | Fouled cooling coil or failed valve. Coil pressure drop; air and water temperatures across the coil. | Clean the coil or repair the valve; replace a corroded coil. |
| Vibration and noise | Bearing wear, belt problems or imbalance. Vibration analysis. | Replace bearings and belts, or upgrade to a direct-drive fan. |
| Rising fan energy | Overloaded filters or fouled coils. Filter pressure drop. | Change the filters and clean the coils. |
| Water carried into ductwork | Coil face velocity too high or eliminators missing. Airflow measurement. | Measure the airflow; reduce face velocity or reinstate the eliminators. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Legionella risk from an adiabatic humidifier; heavy microbial growth in a unit serving a healthcare or occupied space; contaminated intake near a cooling tower or exhaust | safety · 4 Essential | Isolate or clean now; hygiene and engineer review. |
| Unit failed serving an occupied or critical space; major leaks | failure · 3 Important | Repair now. |
| Outside air below code minimum; failed dampers; corroded drain pans; fouled coils | condition · 3 Important | Repair in the near term. |
| Units at the end of their life; inefficient fans | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Plan replacement or refurbishment. |
| No hygiene inspection; outside air not measured | check · 2 Planned | Inspect and measure. |
| Normal wear | nil · 1 Routine | Routine maintenance. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A mechanical services engineer leads, with a hygiene specialist where microbial issues are suspected. The checks below open the unit to inspect its pans, coils and insulation, then measure the outside air it actually delivers.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Unit inspection | With panels open: casing, fans, motors, belts, filters, coils, drain pans and traps, humidifiers, heat recovery, dampers and actuators, attenuators. |
| Airflow measurement | Supply, return and outside air, against design and code minimums. |
| Coil performance | Air and water temperatures and flows; pressure drop. |
| Fan performance | Airflow, pressure, power, vibration. |
| Hygiene inspection | Visual, swabs and dust samples to AS/NZS 3666.2, BESA TR/19 or ASHRAE 180 practice. |
| Indoor air quality | Carbon dioxide, particulates, temperature and humidity in served spaces, against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). |
| Intake review | Distance to towers, exhausts, flues and docks. |
| Controls review | Schedules, setpoints, economy cycle, outside air control. |

The report should give the condition of each unit, airflow and outside air against requirements, hygiene status, and whether to repair, refurbish in place, or replace.

sections.heading: Cleaning, upgrading or replacing
sections.markdown:
Hygiene comes first: microbial growth and humidifier risks are dealt with before anything else. After that, upgrades to filters, fans and outside air control often pay for themselves, and a sound casing can take new internals rather than a whole new unit.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hygiene remediation | Clean coils, drain pans and casings; replace wet insulation with closed-cell or faced material; fix drain falls and traps. | Wherever drain pans, coils or insulation harbour growth. |
| Filter upgrade | Better grades and sealed frames to stop bypass. | Where filters are a poor grade or bypassed. |
| Fan upgrade | Replace belt-driven fans with direct-drive plug fans and electronically commutated motors, often a large energy saving. | Where belt-driven fans are worn or inefficient. |
| Coil replacement | Replace corroded or leaking coils, with coatings for coastal sites. | Where coils corrode or leak. |
| Dampers and outside air | Replace dampers and actuators, and control outside air with carbon dioxide sensors. | Where dampers fail or outside air falls below the minimum. |
| Heat recovery | Repair or add heat recovery. | Where it has failed or was never fitted. |
| Refurbishment in place | New internals within the existing casing. | Where the casing is sound and access is difficult. |
| Replacement | Replace the whole unit, sized to current loads and ventilation needs. | At the end of the unit's life. |
| Intake relocation | Move the intake. | Where contamination is the problem. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Inspection, airflow measurement and hygiene testing are lump sums. Component replacements (fans, motors, coils, dampers, humidifiers) are itemised per unit. Refurbishment in place is a lump sum per unit and avoids the cost of getting a new unit into a plant room. Replacement is a lump sum per unit including access (cranes for rooftop units, partial dismantling or wall openings for plant rooms), electrical and controls integration, and commissioning. Hygiene cleaning and filter changes recur.

Replacement and refurbishment are lifecycle; outside air and hygiene rectification can be code compliance; repairs are repairs and maintenance. Fan upgrades to direct-drive EC fans often pay back through energy savings and can sit in an energy line.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a look at the unit cannot: whether hygiene has been inspected, whether outside air has been measured, and how the unit behaves over time. Ask for them before replacing anything.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Maintenance logs: filter, belt and coil cleaning records | Whether filters, belts and coils are looked after. |
| Hygiene inspection reports and any microbial sampling | Whether microbial growth has been found. |
| Airflow and outside air test and balance reports | Whether the unit delivers the outside air it should. |
| Indoor air quality monitoring (CO₂, particulates) | Whether occupants get enough fresh air. |
| Installation dates and nameplate data for each unit | How old each unit is, and what it was built to do. |
| BMS trends for fans, dampers and supply temperatures | How the fans, dampers and supply temperatures actually behave. |
| Energy consumption data | Whether fan energy is rising. |
| Drawings showing intake locations relative to exhausts and towers | Whether intakes sit near exhausts or cooling towers. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Air handling units are misread when a musty smell is treated as a nuisance, and when a unit that runs is assumed to deliver enough outside air.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| A musty smell is cosmetic | Musty smells from air conditioning are not cosmetic. They are a sign of microbial growth in the unit, and a hygiene inspection should follow. |
| It runs, so the air is fine | High carbon dioxide and stuffiness in occupied rooms often mean the outside air damper is closed or its minimum set too low. Outside air has to be measured, not assumed. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets ventilation rates and standards for the hygiene and maintenance of air handling systems. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Ventilation | The National Construction Code calls up AS 1668.2 for ventilation. | Approved Document F sets ventilation; BS EN 16798-3 covers non-residential ventilation performance. | ASHRAE 62.1 sets ventilation rates, and the International Mechanical Code applies. |
| Hygiene and maintenance | AS/NZS 3666.1 and 3666.2 set design, installation and maintenance of air-handling systems for microbial control, and in several states maintenance of air-handling systems is an essential safety measure. NABERS Indoor Environment rates indoor air quality. | BESA TR/19 sets ventilation hygiene; air-conditioning systems over 12 kW need energy inspection at least every five years; healthcare follows HTM 03-01. | ASHRAE 180 sets inspection and maintenance practice, ASHRAE 241 the control of infectious aerosols, and ASHRAE 170 healthcare ventilation. |

Healthcare, laboratory and cleanroom units follow additional standards for filtration and hygiene in all three countries.

sections.heading: Worked example: a musty smell at start-up
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 1990s office has four air handling units. Occupants on two floors complain of a musty smell each morning when the air conditioning starts and of stuffiness in meeting rooms, and the BMS shows the outside air dampers on those units held at a fixed, low position. There is no hygiene inspection on record.

A musty smell at start-up points to microbial growth in the drain pans, coils or wet insulation, a hygiene finding that needs inspecting, not masking. Stuffiness with dampers held low points to too little outside air, which needs measuring against the code minimum.

So the register carries a hygiene inspection as a check line now, remediation of the pans, coils and insulation as a condition line, and outside air measured, with the dampers repaired and controlled by carbon dioxide sensors if it falls short.

thresholds.rule: 10 L/s per person

source.title: Approved Document F, Volume 2: Buildings other than dwellings

thresholds.rule: Below 800 ppm suggests good ventilation; consistently above 1500 ppm calls for action

source.title: Approved Document F, Volume 2: Buildings other than dwellings

pages.title: Ancillary Structures
pages.question: How do sheds, carports, shade structures and other minor structures fail, and which findings are hazards?
pages.answer: Minor structures fail at their bases and in wind. Timber posts rot at ground level and pergolas and carports lean; shade sails overload masts and fixings in storms when left up; flagpoles and signs crack by fatigue at their bases; car park canopy posts are struck by vehicles. Older sheds often hold weathered asbestos cement. Many were added without approval or engineering. Leaning or wind-damaged structures over people are falling hazards.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about ancillary structures; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Sheds, gazebos, monuments, water features

pages.searchTitle: Ancillary structures: sheds, carports, shade sails and flagpoles, and how they fail

questions.question: Why do pergolas and carports lean?
questions.answer: Usually because timber posts have rotted at ground level, or a vehicle has struck them. Probing or inspecting the posts at ground level shows which.

questions.question: Should shade sails come down in storms?
questions.answer: Shade sails have a design wind rating, and masts and fixings are overloaded when sails are left up in severe winds. Set procedures for taking them down before severe weather.

questions.question: Could an old shed contain asbestos?
questions.answer: Grey corrugated or flat cement sheeting on sheds and garages of the era may be asbestos cement. Only sampling confirms it; do not cut, drill or demolish it first.

questions.question: Do sheds and carports need approval?
questions.answer: It depends on size, use and location. In Australia minor structures may be exempt if they meet size and setback limits; in the United Kingdom they may be permitted development; in the United States permits are needed above set sizes.

questions.question: How long does shade sail fabric last?
questions.answer: Typically 8 to 12 years; the masts and fixings 20 to 30 years.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Ancillary structures show their problems at ground level and after storms: posts that lean, masts that bend, bases that rust. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On site | Leaning structures; posts loose, cracked or rotted at ground level | Wind, decay and impact |
| On site | Shade sails sagging, torn or with distorted masts; fixings pulling from walls | Wind, decay and impact |
| On site | Rust at flagpole and sign bases; cracking at welds and base plates | Wind, decay and impact |
| On site | Impact damage on carport and canopy posts | Wind, decay and impact |
| On site | Grey corrugated or flat cement sheeting on sheds and garages of the right era | Asbestos, fire and water features |
| On site | Bin enclosures built against walls and under eaves | Asbestos, fire and water features |
| On site | Water features with green water, slime, leaks or exposed electrics | Asbestos, fire and water features |
| In the records | Approvals and engineering for each structure | Unapproved structures |
| In the records | Shade sail installation certificates and wind instructions | Wind, decay and impact |
| In the records | Asbestos register entries for outbuildings | Asbestos, fire and water features |
| In the records | Inspection records for signs and flagpoles | Wind, decay and impact |
| In the records | Water feature maintenance records | Asbestos, fire and water features |

sections.heading: Types of structure
sections.markdown:
Ancillary structures are the minor buildings and structures on a site that are not part of the main building: sheds, garages and carports, bin and bike enclosures, pergolas and gazebos, shade sails and canopies over car parks and play areas, flagpoles, signage structures, monuments and memorials, and decorative water features. Individually small, they are numerous, often built without the scrutiny given to the main building, frequently altered or added informally, and sometimes contain the oldest and most hazardous materials on a site.

| Type | Where it is found | Main issues |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sheds, garages and outbuildings | Houses, schools, depots, older commercial sites | Asbestos cement sheeting; decayed timber; unapproved construction |
| Carports and car park shade structures | Apartments, retail, offices | Fixings and posts corroding; vehicle impact; wind |
| Shade sails | Play areas, schools, car parks, courtyards | Mast and fixing failure in wind; fabric degradation |
| Pergolas and gazebos | Residential and hospitality courtyards | Timber decay at post bases; connections |
| Bin and bike enclosures | Apartments and commercial sites | Damage; fire risk; vermin |
| Flagpoles and signage structures | Commercial and public sites | Fatigue cracking at the base; corrosion; wind |
| Monuments, memorials and sculptures | Public and institutional sites | Stability; heritage; materials |
| Water features | Lobbies, plazas, gardens | Leaks; Legionella; slips; electrical safety |

Because many of these were added after the main building, they may lack approval, engineering or proper foundations. They are usually exposed to weather on all sides, and their structural margins in wind are often smaller than the main building's.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Ancillary structures last as long as their bases and fixings. Steel sheds and carports last decades and shade sail fabric about a decade, while timber posts set in the ground decay first where they meet it.

| Structure | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Steel sheds and carports | 25 to 40 years | Coatings; coastal exposure; impact |
| Timber pergolas and structures | 15 to 30 years | Decay at post bases; treatment; maintenance |
| Shade sail fabric | 8 to 12 years | UV; tension; wind |
| Shade sail masts and fixings | 20 to 30 years | Corrosion; footing design |
| Flagpoles | 20 to 30 years | Fatigue; corrosion at the base |
| Asbestos cement sheds | Past life wherever weathered | Weathering; damage |
| Water feature equipment | 10 to 15 years | Water quality; pumps |

What shortens it: wind: shade sails, signs and flagpoles carry high wind loads relative to their size, and cyclic loading fatigues them; ground contact: timber posts set in soil or concrete rot at the base; vehicle impact on carport and canopy posts; coastal and industrial exposure; informal alterations: added roofs, enclosures and loads.

sections.heading: Wind, decay and impact
sections.markdown:
Shade sails act like sails: they load masts and fixings heavily in storms, and many are designed to be taken down before severe winds but are left up. Masts bend, footings pull out, and fixings to buildings tear out. Freestanding signs and flagpoles fail by fatigue cracking at welds and base plates after years of wind cycling, often without visible warning.

Timber posts embedded in soil or concrete stay wet at the base and rot from inside; the structure then leans or collapses, sometimes onto people. Steel posts corrode at ground level where water and debris collect.

Carport and canopy posts in car parks are struck by vehicles; bent or cracked posts and loosened base plates weaken the whole structure.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pergola or carport leaning | Post base decay or impact damage. Probe or inspect at ground level. | Exclude people if it stands over a used area; replace the decayed posts on stirrups or with steel. |
| Shade sail masts bent after a storm | Wind overload; sail not removed. Inspection; design wind rating. | Take the sail down; upgrade the masts and footings to an engineered design, and set take-down procedures. |
| Rust bleeding from a flagpole or sign base | Corrosion at the base and possible fatigue. Inspection; non-destructive testing of welds. | Inspect the base and welds; repair or replace a corroded base, and replace a pole with fatigue cracking. |
| Bin store, shed or carport roof sheets lifting | Fixings inadequate for wind. Fixing type and spacing; corrosion. | Refix the sheets with suitable fixings, and check the frame. |

sections.heading: Asbestos, fire and water features
sections.markdown:
Older sheds, garages and outbuildings are often clad or roofed in asbestos cement sheeting, which weathers, cracks and breaks. Damage and removal must be managed under asbestos rules.

Bin enclosures, storage sheds and combustible structures close to buildings are fire sources; bin fires against walls and under eaves spread into buildings.

Fountains and ponds leak, grow algae and Legionella, create slip hazards, and combine water with electrical equipment.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cracked cement sheeting on an old shed | Weathered asbestos cement. Sampling. | Sample it; plan licensed removal, or encapsulate it where it is sound and undisturbed. |
| Algae and slime in a water feature | Inadequate treatment. Water testing. | Test the water; treat it, or decommission the feature. |

sections.heading: Unapproved structures
sections.markdown:
Structures added informally may lack footings, engineering, fire separation from the main building or boundary setbacks. Their condition is often unknown and their compliance doubtful.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Structure with no record of approval | Informal addition. Council or authority records. | Check council or authority records; obtain retrospective approval or remove the structure. |
| Structure close to a boundary or another building, built of combustible materials | Possible fire spread. Distance to boundaries and buildings; materials. | Check against fire separation rules, and relocate or line the structure if required. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Leaning or damaged structures over occupied areas; damaged asbestos cement; water features with exposed electrics; bin stores against walls with fire risk | safety · 4 Essential | Exclude, make safe or remove now. |
| Structure collapsed or unusable | failure · 2 Planned | Remove or rebuild. |
| Approval or compliance required by an authority | deadline · 3 Important | By the required date. |
| Decay or corrosion starting; worn shade fabric | condition · 2 Planned | Repair in the near term. |
| Structures and fabrics at end of life | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Replace. |
| Unapproved structures; no engineering | check · 2 Planned | Assess. |
| Normal | nil · 1 Routine | Routine maintenance. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A building surveyor inspects; a structural engineer assesses structures that are leaning, damaged or carry significant wind loads; a licensed asbestos assessor samples suspect materials. The checks below start with an inventory, because these structures are often missing from the building's records, then look at bases, wind loads, approvals and hazards.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Inventory | Of every ancillary structure on the site, with type, age, material, location and use. |
| Condition inspection | Of posts, footings, connections, roofs and cladding, with probing of timber at ground level. |
| Wind-loaded structures | Shade sails, signs and flagpoles checked for masts, welds, base plates and fixings, with non-destructive testing of welds on tall poles and signs. |
| Approvals check | Against council or authority records. |
| Hazardous materials | Asbestos sampling of cement sheeting and other suspect materials in older structures. |
| Fire separation | Distance of bin stores, sheds and combustible structures from the main building. |
| Water features | Leaks, electrical safety, water treatment and Legionella risk. |

The report should list each structure with its condition, safety status, approval status and recommended action, including whether it should be kept, repaired, replaced or removed.

sections.heading: Repairing, protecting or removing
sections.markdown:
Most work on ancillary structures is at their bases and fixings, and much of it is cheap. The larger decisions are whether an unapproved or unsafe structure is worth keeping at all, and how to deal with an old shed that may contain asbestos.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Post base repairs | Replace decayed timber posts with posts on stirrups or galvanised bases above ground, or replace with steel. | Where posts are rotted or loose at ground level. |
| Impact protection | Bollards and post guards for carport and canopy posts in car parks. | Where carport and canopy posts stand in vehicle paths. |
| Shade sail works | Replace fabric on cycle, upgrade masts and footings to engineered designs, and set procedures for taking sails down before severe winds. | Fabric at the end of its life; masts and footings wherever they bend or were never engineered. |
| Sign and flagpole works | Repair or replace corroded bases, and replace poles with fatigue cracking. | Where bases rust or welds crack. |
| Asbestos removal | Licensed removal of weathered sheds and outbuildings, or encapsulation where sound and undisturbed. | Where cement sheet has weathered or cracked; encapsulation only where it is sound. |
| Removal | Remove redundant or unsafe structures. | Where a structure is unsafe, unused or not worth repairing. |
| Approvals | Obtain retrospective approval or remove non-compliant structures. | Where a structure has no record of approval. |
| Bin stores | Relocate bin stores, or build fire-rated enclosures, away from the building. | Where bin enclosures stand against walls or under eaves. |
| Water features | Treat the water, or decommission the feature. | Where water is untreated, the feature leaks, or electrics are exposed. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Inspection and engineering are lump sums. Repairs are itemised per structure or per post. Shade sail fabric is replaced on a cycle and is best carried as a recurring line; masts and footings are lump sums. Sign and flagpole replacement is per item. Asbestos removal is a lump sum per structure including licensed removal and clearance. Demolition of redundant structures is a lump sum.

Safety items are immediate; asbestos and approval issues are code compliance; replacement is lifecycle; maintenance is repairs and maintenance.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a walk around the site cannot: which structures were approved and engineered, what they are designed to withstand, and which contain asbestos. Ask for them before the inspection, because these structures are often missing from the building's main records.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Approvals, permits and engineering for each ancillary structure | Which structures were approved and engineered, and which were added informally. |
| Shade sail installation certificates, design wind ratings and take-down procedures | What wind each sail is designed for, and when it must come down. |
| Asbestos register entries for outbuildings | Which sheds and outbuildings contain asbestos, and in what condition. |
| Inspection records for signs, flagpoles and shade structures | Whether bases and welds have been checked, and when. |
| Water feature maintenance and water treatment records | Whether the water is treated and the equipment maintained. |
| Records of structures added after the main building was completed | What was added after the building was finished, which is where approvals are most often missing. |
| Incident records involving these structures | Whether anything has already failed or hurt someone. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Ancillary structures are easy to overlook because they are small and stand outside the main building. These are the misreadings that leave a hazard standing.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| A small structure is a small risk | Leaning structures, damaged shade sail masts and corroded sign or flagpole bases over areas people use are falling hazards. Exclude people until an engineer has assessed them. |
| A shade sail can stay up in any weather | Masts and fixings are designed for a wind rating, and sails left up in severe winds overload them. The take-down procedure matters as much as the structure. |
| An old shed is just a shed | Grey cement sheeting on sheds and garages of the era may be asbestos cement. Sample it before anyone cuts, drills or demolishes it. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Small structures are where planning and building rules give the most exemptions, and those exemptions differ by market. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out the approval rules, the wind standards and the asbestos rules.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Approvals | Minor structures may be exempt development under state planning rules if they meet size and setback limits; otherwise they need approval. | Outbuildings may fall under permitted development or need planning permission and building regulations approval, depending on size, use and location; signs may need advertisement consent. | Accessory structures follow local zoning and building codes, with permits above set sizes. |
| Wind | AS/NZS 1170.2 sets wind actions; shade structures in cyclonic regions need particular care. | BS EN 1991-1-4 (Eurocode 1), with its UK National Annex, sets wind actions on structures. | ASCE 7 sets wind loads; signs and flagpoles in high-wind areas need engineered foundations. |
| Asbestos | Asbestos in outbuildings is managed under work health and safety and state asbestos rules. | The Control of Asbestos Regulations 2012 govern asbestos in non-domestic premises. | Asbestos is regulated by the EPA and states for renovation and demolition. |

sections.heading: Worked example: a shopping centre car park after a storm
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. After a storm, a shade sail mast over a shopping centre's trolley bay is bent and the sail torn. Nearby, a timber pergola over the café seating leans, and an old cement-sheet shed at the loading dock has a cracked corner.

The bent mast and the leaning pergola stand over areas people use, so both are safety findings: exclude people until an engineer has assessed them. The mast points to wind overload, perhaps a sail left up in the storm; the pergola, to posts decayed at ground level. The cracked shed is a check finding until it is sampled for asbestos.

So the register carries two safety lines now, then shade sail works with engineered masts and take-down procedures, post base repairs or removal of the pergola, and a sampling line for the shed that becomes licensed removal or encapsulation once the result is in.

pages.title: Architectural & Decorative Features
pages.question: How do cornices, stone, terracotta and render ornament fail, how do you tell the causes apart, and when is it a public danger?
pages.answer: Ornament fails at the hidden metal that holds it on. Iron cramps and steel anchors rust, expand and split the stone or terracotta along their line, releasing the piece they were holding. Unprotected cornice tops feed water straight to those fixings. Crazed terracotta glaze lets water into hollow units. Cracks along a straight line with rust at the end, missing pieces and netting at street level mean the façade needs a close-up hammer survey now.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about architectural & decorative features; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Cornices, corbels, string courses, parapets, mouldings
