pages.searchTitle: Façade ornament: cornices, terracotta, stone decay, cramps and falling fragments

questions.question: Is falling stone from a façade serious?
questions.answer: Yes. Ornament falls in pieces, and a small piece from a high cornice is lethal; anything above a footpath that has not been tapped close up should be treated as unknown.

questions.question: Why is the stone cracking in a straight line?
questions.answer: Usually a corroding iron cramp or dowel inside the stone, expanding as it rusts. A metal detector finds it, and it is replaced in stainless steel.

questions.question: Why is the glaze coming off the terracotta?
questions.answer: Water in the body of the unit, then frost or salt, crazes and spalls the glaze. Stopping the water comes first, then consolidation or replacement units.

questions.question: Can heritage stonework be sandblasted clean?
questions.answer: No. Clean with low-pressure water, poultices or other methods suited to the material, not abrasive blasting.

questions.question: How long do iron cramps last in stonework?
questions.answer: 50 to 100 years before they jack the stone apart; stainless steel replacements do not.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Ornament problems show from the street as missing pieces, cracks along mouldings and vegetation on cornices, close up when units are tapped, and in records of fallen fragments. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Street or aerial | Missing pieces of moulding; fresh breaks lighter in colour than the weathered surface | Terracotta, stone and render |
| Street or aerial | Cracks along the line of mouldings and at the ends of units; rust staining from joints and cracks | Cramps and hidden metal |
| Street or aerial | Crazed, spalled or missing glaze on terracotta; replaced units in a different colour | Terracotta, stone and render |
| Street or aerial | Vegetation growing from cornices and parapets; birds nesting in projections | Cornices, projections and earlier repairs |
| Street or aerial | Netting over ornament, scaffolding sheds or hoardings at street level | Cornices, projections and earlier repairs |
| Street or aerial | Aerial imagery of the top surfaces of cornices and parapets: weatherings missing, vegetation, ponding | Cornices, projections and earlier repairs |
| Close up on site | Hollow sound when tapped; movement of units under hand pressure | Cramps and hidden metal |
| Close up on site | Sheet-like scaling and blistering of stone surfaces; black crusts | Terracotta, stone and render |
| Close up on site | Open joints on top surfaces; failed or missing lead and copper | Cornices, projections and earlier repairs |
| Close up on site | Previous cement patches debonding; corroded pins exposed | Cornices, projections and earlier repairs |
| In the records | Façade inspection reports and ordinance filings with unsafe findings, and make-safe records | Standards by country |
| In the records | Records of fragments falling, and insurance or council correspondence about them | Common misreads |
| In the records | Conservation management plans and heritage consents for previous repairs | Standards by country |

sections.heading: Types of ornament
sections.markdown:
Architectural and decorative features are the projecting and ornamental parts of a façade: cornices, string courses, parapet balustrades, pediments, window surrounds, columns and pilasters, finials, brackets and sculpture, in natural stone, terracotta and faience, cast stone, render on armatures, pressed metal and, more recently, glass-reinforced concrete and fibreglass. They are concentrated on buildings from the mid nineteenth century to about 1940, and on later buildings in the classical or art deco manner.

Two facts decide how they fail. First, most ornament is held in place by hidden metal: iron or steel cramps, dowels and armatures, or anchors tying hollow terracotta units back to a steel frame. Second, projections shed water poorly unless their top surfaces were protected, typically with lead, copper or a weathered top, so water sits exactly where the hidden metal is.

| Material | Typical period | What it implies |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sandstone and limestone with iron cramps and dowels | Nineteenth and early twentieth century | Cramp corrosion cracking and displacing stone; contour scaling and delamination of sandstone |
| Glazed architectural terracotta and faience | About 1880 to 1940, especially offices, banks, theatres and department stores | Hollow units on steel anchors; glaze crazing lets water in; anchor corrosion; frost spalling |
| Cast stone | 1900s to 1950s | Reinforcement close to the surface; cracking along bars |
| Render mouldings on armatures or brick cores | Victorian and Edwardian stock, interwar | Delamination from the backing; hidden armature corrosion |
| Pressed metal | Late nineteenth and early twentieth century | Corrosion from behind; fixing failure |
| GRC and fibreglass replacements | From the 1980s | Fixing condition; UV and coating wear |

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Natural stone lasts one to three hundred years and terracotta eighty to a hundred and twenty, but the iron cramps and anchors inside them last fifty to a hundred before they jack the stone apart, and lead weatherings and lime joints need renewing far sooner.

| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Natural stone | 100 to 300 years | Stone type and bedding; pollution; salts; water on top surfaces |
| Terracotta and faience | 80 to 120 years and more | Glaze integrity; anchor condition; joint maintenance |
| Iron cramps and anchors | 50 to 100 years before they jack the stone | Water at the fixing |
| Render ornament | 40 to 80 years | Bond; armature corrosion; water from above |
| Lead and copper weatherings | 50 to 100 years | Fixing and detailing; theft in some areas |
| Lime mortar joints in ornament | 30 to 60 years | Exposure; top surfaces |

What shortens life: missing weatherings on cornices and string courses, so water sits on the top surface and runs into joints; cement repairs and cement pointing, which trap moisture and force decay into the stone or terracotta beside them; impermeable coatings painted over stone and render; abrasive or acid cleaning, which removes the protective surface of stone and the glaze of terracotta; vegetation and birds: roots in joints, guano holding moisture; pollution, which forms sulfate crusts on limestone and marble.

sections.heading: Cramps and hidden metal
sections.markdown:
Iron cramps and dowels set in stone, and steel anchors holding terracotta, rust when water reaches them. The rust expands and splits the unit along the line of the fixing, often shearing off a corner or the front of a moulding. The fixing that was holding the piece in place is now what releases it. Cracks that follow the line of a hidden cramp, often with rust staining, are the signature.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Crack following a straight line through a stone unit, rust stain at its end, corner displaced | Cramp or dowel corrosion. Metal detector locates the cramp on the crack line; opening up shows rust. | Remove the corroded cramp, replace it in stainless steel, and repair the stone. |

sections.heading: Cornices, projections and earlier repairs
sections.markdown:
A cornice is a cantilever of stone or terracotta held in place by its own back weight and by cramps, sometimes by the parapet above. Water on the unprotected top surface penetrates the joints, corrodes the cramps and decays the backing. Removing or lowering a parapet above, often done in past alterations, reduces the weight holding the cornice in.

Cement patches and plastic repairs debond and fall; steel pins used in earlier repairs corrode in turn; resin repairs discolour.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cornice top with vegetation and open joints, staining below | Missing weathering; water at the cramps. Aerial imagery; joints open on top. | Clear the vegetation; add lead or copper weatherings, and repoint the top joints in lime. |
| Fragments found on the pavement below a cornice or parapet | An unsafe façade condition. Hammer survey of the feature from access; in New York City, owners of buildings taller than six storeys must file a critical examination of the façades every five-year cycle, and unsafe conditions call for immediate public protection (FISP Cycle 10 notice). | Protect the pavement now, remove anything loose, and pin, rebuild or replace the units before the protection comes down. |

sections.heading: Terracotta, stone and render
sections.markdown:
Terracotta units are hollow, fired clay with a glaze or slip on the face. Crazed or cracked glaze lets water into the body; the water freezes or carries salts, and the glaze and face spall off. Water inside the unit reaches the steel anchors and, often, the steel frame behind. Units were frequently filled with brick or mortar, which holds water.

Sandstone scales in sheets parallel to the surface (contour scaling) from salt crystallisation, and stone laid with its bedding planes parallel to the face (face-bedded) delaminates. Limestone and marble form black gypsum crusts in polluted air that blister and fall away taking the surface with them. Soft stone erodes, losing the detail of mouldings.

Render mouldings run on site or cast over brick cores and metal armatures lose their bond to the backing as water gets behind them. They sound hollow, crack around their perimeter, and can fall as a large piece.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sheets of stone lifting parallel to the face | Contour scaling from salts, or face-bedded stone. Salts in the debris; bedding planes visible parallel to the face. | Remove loose material safely; indent new stone, or repair with lime mortar. |
| Glaze crazed and spalled across terracotta units | Water in the body of the unit; frost or salt. Moisture in the unit; spalls concentrated on exposed and top surfaces. | Stop the water getting in; consolidate the glaze, or replace units from a specialist manufacturer. |
| Terracotta units cracking along joints with rust staining | Anchor corrosion behind the units. Opening shows corroded anchors or frame. | Open up; replace the anchors in stainless steel, and repair or replace the units. |
| Black crust blistering on limestone or marble | Gypsum crust from pollution. Sheltered areas worst; surface loss when crust falls. | Clean with a method suited to the stone, never abrasive blasting. |
| Hollow render moulding cracked around its edges | Delamination from the backing. Tapping; probing behind. | Make safe; re-fix with stainless pins, or replace the moulding. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Loose, cracked or displaced ornament over a public or occupied area; recent fragments fallen | safety · 4 Essential | Remove loose material and protect below immediately (netting, sidewalk shed, exclusion). |
| Ordinance finding of unsafe condition | deadline · 3 Important | Timing set by the ordinance; protection immediately. |
| Active cramp or anchor corrosion cracking units, without displacement; widespread terracotta spalling | condition · 2 Planned | Programme re-anchoring and repair in the near term. |
| Weatherings and joints at age; surface erosion without loss of detail | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Renewal on cycle with access for other façade work. |
| Heritage façade over a footpath with no close-up survey on record | check · 2 Planned | Close-up hammer survey before sizing works. |
| Surface soiling, minor erosion | nil · 1 Routine | Cleaning by appropriate method when warranted. |
| Stone, terracotta or render units detached or falling | failure · 4 Essential | Make safe now; public protection until repaired. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A façade engineer or building surveyor with conservation experience leads, with a conservator or stonemason. Where the building is listed or heritage-registered, a conservation architect advises on method and consents. The checks below hammer-tap every piece of ornament over a footpath or entrance, then locate hidden metal and read how each material is failing.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Close-up hammer survey | Of every unit over public areas and a sample elsewhere, removing anything loose at the time and recording it unit by unit on elevation drawings. |
| Metal detection | And ground-penetrating radar to locate cramps, dowels and anchors; borescope through joints. |
| Opening up | At representative locations to see anchor condition and the frame behind terracotta. |
| Material analysis | Stone identification, petrographic examination, mortar analysis, salt analysis. |
| Infrared thermography | To locate delamination in terracotta and render. |
| Review of past repairs | And their materials. |

The report should map defects unit by unit, distinguish make-safe items from repairs, and specify methods and materials appropriate to the fabric.

sections.heading: Making safe, re-anchoring and repairing
sections.markdown:
Anything loose over a footpath, entrance or courtyard is made safe first, with pieces stored for reinstatement. After that, the work removes the hidden cause, corroded metal and missing weatherings, before repairing the stone, terracotta and render in matching materials.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Make safe | Remove loose pieces and store them for reinstatement; netting or sidewalk sheds until repaired. | At once, wherever ornament is loose over people. |
| Re-anchoring | Remove corroded cramps and replace them with stainless steel; drilled stainless pins set in resin or grout through units into sound backing. | Where hidden metal is corroding or units are loose. |
| Weatherings | Lead or copper flashings over cornices and string courses, and repointing of top joints with lime mortar. | Where water reaches the top of projections. |
| Stone repair | Indents (new stone pieced in), lime mortar repairs for small losses, and replacement units cut to profile. | Where stone has decayed or broken. |
| Terracotta repair | Crack repair and glaze consolidation for minor damage; replacement units from a specialist manufacturer, or GRC or cast stone substitutes where approved. | Where terracotta has cracked or spalled. |
| Removal of harmful earlier repairs | Remove cement patches, impermeable coatings and corroded steel pins. | Wherever earlier repairs are causing damage. |
| Cleaning | Low-pressure water, poultices or other methods suited to the material, not abrasive blasting. | Where soiling or crusts need removing. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Survey is a lump sum plus access. Repairs are priced per unit, per anchor, per linear metre of cornice or string course, or by area for repointing and cleaning. Access, often by scaffold over a footpath, dominates. Protective netting and sidewalk sheds are recurring costs until the work is done. Replacement terracotta has long lead times.

Two-part lines are normal. Make-safe and ordinance repairs are code compliance or repairs and maintenance; re-anchoring and weatherings are lifecycle; conservation repairs follow the heritage approval process.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a look from the street cannot: what earlier surveys found, whether fragments have fallen, and what heritage consents govern any repair. Ask for them before the scaffolding goes up.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Façade inspection reports, ordinance filings and make-safe records | What earlier surveys found, and what was made safe. |
| Records of falling fragments and any incident reports | Whether fragments have already fallen, and where. |
| Heritage listing, conservation management plan and consents for past works | What consents and conservation policies govern any repair. |
| Specifications and records of previous repairs, with materials used | Which materials were used before, and whether they are causing harm. |
| Netting, shed or hoarding records and their duration | How long netting or sheds have been in place. |
| Records of cleaning methods used on the façade | Whether the façade has been cleaned in ways that damaged it. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Ornament is misread when what looks sound from the street is taken as sound, and when earlier cement repairs are taken as a fix rather than a cause.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| It looks sound from the street | Ornament falls in pieces, and a small piece from a high cornice is lethal. Any ornament above a footpath, entrance or courtyard that has not been hammer-tapped close up should be treated as unknown, not sound. |
| Patch it in cement | Cement patches, impermeable coatings and corroded steel pins from earlier repairs often cause the damage they were meant to stop. They are removed, and repairs made in lime and matching materials. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market controls works to heritage fabric, sets conservation practice for repair, and in some cities requires periodic inspection of ornament. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Heritage controls | State heritage legislation (for example the Heritage Act 2017 in Victoria and the Heritage Act 1977 in New South Wales) and local planning heritage overlays control works to listed fabric. | Works to listed buildings need listed building consent under the Planning (Listed Buildings and Conservation Areas) Act 1990. | Local landmarks commissions control listed buildings. |
| Conservation practice | The Burra Charter of Australia ICOMOS sets conservation practice. | BS 7913 guides the conservation of historic buildings, and BS 8221-1 and BS 8221-2 cover cleaning and repair; Historic England publishes technical guidance on stone, terracotta and lime. | The Secretary of the Interior's Standards for the Treatment of Historic Properties and the National Park Service Preservation Briefs (Brief 7 covers glazed architectural terra-cotta) set practice. |
| Inspection | There is no periodic façade inspection regime; the owner's duty to the public is general. | There is no national periodic façade inspection regime; the owner's duty of care to the public falls under the Occupiers' Liability Act 1957. | New York's FISP examines ornament on buildings over six storeys every five years, and its parapet rule requires annual observation of street-facing parapets; Chicago, Boston and San Francisco have similar regimes. |

sections.heading: Worked example: a fragment on the footpath
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 1910s stone-fronted building has a heavy cornice over a busy footpath. A small fragment of moulding was found on the footpath last month, its broken face lighter than the weathered surface around it. Vegetation grows from the top of the cornice, and there is no close-up survey on record.

A small piece from a high cornice is lethal, and a fresh break means more may follow. Ornament over a footpath that has not been hammer-tapped close up is unknown, not sound. Vegetation on top points to missing weatherings, and water reaching the cramps.

So the register carries the cornice as a safety line now, made safe with netting or a sidewalk shed and loose pieces stored, then a close-up tapping survey, weatherings, and re-anchoring in stainless steel, all within the heritage consents.

pages.title: Automatic Sprinkler Systems
pages.question: How do sprinkler systems fail, when is a system no longer adequate for a building, and which findings leave a building unprotected?
pages.answer: Sprinkler systems fail more often from what changes around them than from wear. Warehouses store more, higher or different goods than the design allows; fit-outs add rooms without heads and block spray patterns; valves closed for works stay closed. Internally, dry systems corrode where water is trapped, wet systems suffer microbial corrosion and pinhole leaks, and town main pressures fall. A perfect system can be inadequate for its current use.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about automatic sprinkler systems; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.

pages.searchTitle: Sprinkler systems: change of hazard, impairments, corrosion and testing

questions.question: Does a sprinkler system cover any change of storage?
questions.answer: No. A system is designed for a hazard, and storing more, higher or different goods can take the building beyond it. Check the design certificate against current storage.

questions.question: Why does the sprinkler pipework have pinhole leaks?
questions.answer: Often microbiologically influenced corrosion in wet pipework. A pipe section examination and water testing confirm it; affected pipe is replaced and the system treated.

questions.question: What happens if a sprinkler valve is left closed?
questions.answer: The area it serves has no sprinkler protection. Open and supervise the valve at once, and manage future impairments with permits and fire watches.

questions.question: How long do sprinkler heads last?
questions.answer: Standard heads are sample tested after 50 years and fast-response heads after 20, then periodically; recalled, painted or corroded heads are replaced sooner.

questions.question: How often must sprinklers be tested?
questions.answer: In Australia, AS 1851 sets weekly or monthly checks, annual flow tests and long-interval inspections; in the United Kingdom, weekly tests with periodic inspections; in the United States, NFPA 25 sets weekly to annual checks and five-yearly pipe assessments.

questions.question: We store more goods, and stack them higher, than when the warehouse was built. Are the sprinklers still adequate?
questions.answer: Not necessarily: the hazard may have changed beyond the design. Check the design certificate against current storage, and reduce the storage or redesign the system.

questions.question: How close to the sprinkler heads can we stack goods?
questions.answer: Storage close to the heads blocks the spray pattern. Bring it down below the clearance line, and mark the line on racking or walls so it stays clear.

questions.question: A new office fit-out has rooms with no sprinkler heads. Is that a problem?
questions.answer: It is a coverage gap. Add coverage to the standard, and have it certified.

questions.question: Why is the dry sprinkler system leaking at its low points?
questions.answer: Trapped water is corroding the pipe. Drain the low points, add auxiliary drains, and consider nitrogen inerting.

questions.question: The fire panel shows a sprinkler valve closed. What should happen?
questions.answer: An impairment has not been cleared. Open and supervise the valve now, and manage impairments with permits and fire watches.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Sprinkler problems show in the building as storage too close to heads, covered heads and new rooms without them, at the valves, and in the records of what the system was designed for. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| In the building | Storage within the clearance zone below heads; racking taller than the design; changed commodities | Changes of hazard, obstruction and coverage |
| In the building | Heads painted, taped, bagged, loaded with dust, or corroded | Changes of hazard, obstruction and coverage |
| In the building | New partitions, ceilings, ductwork and lights below or around heads; rooms without heads | Changes of hazard, obstruction and coverage |
| In the building | Signs of leaks and corrosion on pipework; drips and staining below | Corrosion, heads, CPVC and freezing |
| In the building | Spare head cabinet: stocked with heads matching those installed | Corrosion, heads, CPVC and freezing |
| In the building | Valve room: control valves open and secured; gauges reading; signage | Impairments and water supply |
| In the building | Booster or brigade inlet accessible and in good order | Impairments and water supply |
| In the records | Design certificate and hydraulic calculations, with the hazard classification and storage design | Changes of hazard, obstruction and coverage |
| In the records | Routine service records: weekly or monthly valve checks, alarm tests, flow tests | Investigation before the scope |
| In the records | Long-interval inspections: internal pipe inspections and head sampling | Corrosion, heads, CPVC and freezing |
| In the records | Impairment log | Impairments and water supply |
| In the records | Leak history | Corrosion, heads, CPVC and freezing |
| In the records | Changes of use or tenancy since design | Changes of hazard, obstruction and coverage |

sections.heading: Types of sprinkler system
sections.markdown:
An automatic sprinkler system discharges water onto a fire from heat-activated heads above it, controlling or extinguishing the fire before it spreads. It comprises a water supply (town main, storage tanks, fire pumps), control valves and alarm valve sets, pipework (risers, mains, branch lines), sprinkler heads, flow and tamper switches connected to the fire alarm, and a fire brigade booster or inlet. Each head opens independently when its glass bulb or fusible link reaches its rated temperature; only heads near the fire operate.

| Type | Where it is used | Character |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Wet pipe | Most heated buildings | Pipes full of water; simplest and most reliable |
| Dry pipe | Unheated spaces at risk of freezing: car parks in cold climates, loading docks, cold stores | Pipes full of air; water enters when a head opens; corrosion where water remains |
| Pre-action and deluge | Data rooms, heritage, special hazards | Covered on the specialist suppression page |
| Residential and domestic | Apartments, aged care, houses | Fast-response heads designed for life safety in dwellings |
| Storage protection (ESFR, in-rack) | Warehouses and logistics | Designed for a specific storage height, arrangement and commodity |

A sprinkler system is designed for a hazard: the building's use, ceiling heights, and in warehouses the commodity, packaging, storage height and racking. When the use changes, the system may no longer be adequate even though nothing in it has deteriorated. This is the most important and most overlooked sprinkler finding in industrial and retail buildings.

Codes in every market have extended sprinkler requirements over time, so older buildings of the same type are often unsprinklered; that is a fire safety strategy matter rather than a defect. Where each market now draws the line is set out under Thresholds by market.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Sprinkler systems last a long time if the water inside them is managed: wet steel pipework fifty years and more, dry galvanised pipework twenty to forty, and heads sample tested after fifty years, or twenty for fast-response types. What ends a system's usefulness sooner is usually a change in what the building stores.

| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Black steel wet pipework | 50 years and more | Water chemistry; microbiologically influenced corrosion |
| Galvanised dry pipework | 20 to 40 years | Water left in pipes; condensation |
| CPVC pipework | 30 to 50 years | Chemical incompatibility |
| Standard sprinkler heads | 50 years, then sample testing | Environment; corrosion; loading |
| Fast-response heads | 20 years, then sample testing | Environment |
| Alarm and dry pipe valves | 25 to 40 years with internal inspection | Water quality; maintenance |
| Control valves | 30 years and more | Exercising |
| Flow and tamper switches | 15 to 25 years | Electrical components |

What shortens life: water left in dry pipe systems after trip tests, which corrodes pipe from the inside; microbiologically influenced corrosion (MIC) in wet systems, producing pinhole leaks; oxygen introduced by frequent draining and refilling; corrosive atmospheres: car parks, swimming pools, cold stores, industrial processes; cPVC contact with incompatible products: some cable sheaths, sealants, spray foam and oils.

sections.heading: Changes of hazard, obstruction and coverage
sections.markdown:
A warehouse designed for low storage of ordinary goods that now holds high-piled plastics, or racking taller than the design height, overwhelms the system: too few heads open, too little water, and the fire outruns it. Retail and industrial tenancies change commodity and layout far more often than sprinkler systems are redesigned.

Storage stacked too close to heads, new ductwork, cable trays, lights and partitions below or beside heads, and ceilings lowered in fit-outs block the spray pattern or create unsprinklered areas. Heads painted, taped, bagged during works or loaded with dust and grease respond late or not at all.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Warehouse storing more, higher or different goods than designed | Hazard change beyond design. Design certificate against current storage. | Check the design certificate against current storage; reduce the storage or redesign the system. |
| Rooms without heads after fit-out | Coverage gap. Survey against layout. | Add coverage to the standard, and have it certified. |
| Storage stacked up close to the heads | Spray pattern blocked from above the goods. Measure from the deflectors to the top of the storage (Thresholds by market). | Bring the storage down below the clearance line, and mark the line on racking or walls so it stays clear. |

sections.heading: Impairments and water supply
sections.markdown:
Control valves closed for works and not reopened leave parts of a building unprotected. Supervised valves report closure to the fire panel; unsupervised valves do not.

Town main pressures fall as networks change; tanks lose capacity to sediment and corrosion; pumps deteriorate. A system that met its design at commissioning may not now, and only a flow test shows it.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Flow test below the design point | Water supply decline or obstruction. Flow test against design curve. | Find the obstruction or supply decline; improve the supply with pumps, tanks or a larger connection. |
| Fire panel shows valve closed | Impairment not cleared. Valve inspection. | Open and supervise the valve now, and manage impairments with permits and fire watches. |
| Main drain test pressure lower than at the last test | Supply decline, a partly closed valve or an obstruction. Static and residual pressures compared with the previous reading and the limits for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Confirm every control valve is fully open, then trace the supply; flow test the water supply where the fall is confirmed. |

sections.heading: Corrosion, heads, CPVC and freezing
sections.markdown:
Dry pipe systems corrode where trapped water sits at low points; wet systems suffer MIC, which produces tubercles and pinhole leaks and can block small pipes. Corrosion products can block heads. Leaks in occupied buildings cause damage and lead to systems being shut down.

Certain sprinkler heads have been subject to recalls; corroded heads and those in hot or corrosive areas can fail to open; heads replaced with the wrong temperature rating, response type or coverage break the design.

CPVC sprinkler pipe used in residential and light hazard buildings cracks when exposed to incompatible chemicals, sometimes years after installation.

Wet pipes in unheated spaces freeze and burst; dry systems with poor drainage freeze at low points.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pinhole leaks in wet pipework | Microbiologically influenced corrosion. Pipe section examination; water testing. | Examine a pipe section and test the water; replace affected pipe and treat for MIC. |
| Leaks at low points of a dry system | Trapped water corrosion. Drain and inspect low points. | Drain the low points, add auxiliary drains, and consider nitrogen inerting. |
| Cracked CPVC fittings | Chemical incompatibility. Products in contact. | Identify and isolate the incompatible products; replace the cracked sections. |
| Heads corroded, painted or loaded with dust or grease | Heads that may respond late or not at all. Head survey; sample heads removed and tested by a laboratory. | Replace affected heads like for like, and sample test heads of the same age and type. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Control valves closed; storage hazard beyond design; heads covered or obstructed over large areas; water supply below design | safety · 4 Essential | Restore protection or reduce the hazard now; fire watch until done. |
| Leaks causing damage; system out of service | failure · 4 Essential | Repair now with impairment management. |
| Routine and long-interval inspections due | deadline · 4 Essential | At the prescribed interval. |
| Corrosion, MIC, head defects, coverage gaps after fit-outs | condition · 4 Essential | Repair in the near term. |
| Pipework or heads at end of life; sample testing due | lifecycle · 3 Important | Plan replacement. |
| No design certificate; use changed; no recent flow test | check · 3 Important | Design review and testing. |
| Normal | nil · 1 Routine | Routine maintenance. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A fire services engineer leads, with the sprinkler maintenance contractor; for storage buildings, the review is against the storage design standards. The checks below compare the design basis with current use, then test the valves, the water supply and the pipework.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Design review | Design certificate, hazard classification, hydraulic calculations, storage design basis, against the building's current use, layout and storage (Thresholds by market). |
| Coverage and obstruction survey | Of all areas, including new rooms, ceilings and storage, with the clearance below heads measured against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). |
| Head survey | Type, temperature, response, condition, recalls, painting and loading; sample removal and laboratory testing at the age the standard sets. |
| Internal pipe inspection | Flushing, opening at representative points, internal camera inspection, and pipe sampling for MIC where leaks occur. |
| Water supply flow test | At the design point, with main drain results compared with the last test and the test intervals for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). |
| Valve inspection | Control valves open and supervised; alarm and dry pipe valves internally inspected. |
| Records review | Service history, impairments, leaks. |

The report should state whether the system matches the current hazard, coverage and obstruction issues, water supply adequacy, internal condition, and works needed.

sections.heading: Restoring, adapting or upgrading
sections.markdown:
Protection is restored first: valves opened and supervised, covers removed, storage cleared from below heads. After that, the work depends on whether the system still matches what the building stores, and on the state of its pipework and water supply.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Restore protection | Open and supervise valves, remove covers, clear storage from below heads, and manage impairments with permits and fire watches. | At once, wherever a valve is closed, a head covered or storage too close. |
| Match storage to the system | Reduce storage height or change commodities, or redesign the system with more water, larger heads or in-rack sprinklers. | Where storage exceeds the design basis. |
| Coverage additions | Add heads where fit-outs have left rooms or areas unprotected. | After every fit-out that changes the layout. |
| Head replacement | Replace recalled, painted, corroded or aged heads. | Wherever heads are defective, recalled or due on age. |
| Corrosion treatment | Replace corroded sections; nitrogen inerting of dry and pre-action systems; MIC treatment and replacement of affected pipe. | Where pipework leaks or internal inspection finds corrosion. |
| Water supply improvement | Pumps, tanks or larger connections. | Where flow tests fall below the design curve. |
| Dry system drainage | Auxiliary drains at low points. | Where water is trapped in dry systems. |
| CPVC protection | Identify and isolate incompatible products; replace cracked sections. | Wherever CPVC touches incompatible products, or has cracked. |
| Spare heads | Restock the spare head cabinet with heads matching each type installed, with the correct wrench. | Whenever the cabinet is short. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Routine and long-interval inspections are recurring contracts, with lump sums for internal pipe inspections, head sampling and flow tests. Head replacement is per head. Coverage additions per head with design. Redesign for storage is a lump-sum project, possibly with pumps and tanks. Pipework replacement is by length, with access and ceiling works dominating in occupied buildings.

Inspections and safety rectification are code compliance; pipework and heads at end of life are lifecycle; repairs are repairs and maintenance. A change of use that requires redesign is usually borne by the project that changes the use.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a walk-through cannot: what the system was designed for, whether the water supply still meets it, and when the system has been out of service. Ask for them before any change of use or storage.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Design certificate, hazard classification and hydraulic calculations | What the system was designed to protect, and against which storage. |
| Routine service records and annual certification | Whether the system is serviced and certified as required. |
| Flow test results against the design curve | Whether the water supply still meets the design. |
| Internal pipe inspection and head sampling reports | The state of the pipework inside, and of the oldest heads. |
| Impairment log | When the system has been out of service, and how that was managed. |
| Leak and repair history | Where corrosion is at work. |
| Storage arrangement and commodity description for warehouses | Whether what the warehouse now stores matches the design. |
| Insurer surveys and recommendations | What the insurer has asked for. |
| Records of recalled heads identified and replaced | Whether recalled heads have been found and replaced. |
| Fit-out records showing sprinkler alterations and who certified them | Whether alterations at fit-outs were designed and certified. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Sprinkler systems are misread when their condition is taken as proof that they protect the building, and when a closed valve is treated as a minor fault.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| A system in good condition protects the building | A sprinkler system can be in perfect condition and still be inadequate for what the building now stores. In warehouses and retail, the design basis against current use is the first thing to check. |
| A closed valve is a minor fault | A control valve left closed after works leaves the area it serves without sprinklers. Open and supervise it at once, and manage impairments with permits and fire watches. |
| Pinhole leaks are wear | In wet pipework they often point to microbiologically influenced corrosion, which spreads; a pipe section examination and water testing confirm it before pipe is simply patched. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets where sprinklers are required, how they are designed, and how often they are inspected and tested. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Where required | The National Construction Code sets where sprinklers are required, including newer requirements for apartment buildings. | Approved Document B sets where sprinklers are required, including new residential buildings over 11 metres. | The International Building and Fire Codes set where sprinklers are required. |
| Design | AS 2118.1 governs design and installation. | BS EN 12845 with the LPC Rules covers commercial systems, and BS 9251 residential systems; insurers often set additional requirements. | NFPA 13, 13R and 13D govern design. |
| Inspection and testing | AS 1851 sets routine service, including weekly or monthly checks, annual flow tests, and long-interval inspections and testing; sprinklers are essential safety measures with annual certification. | Weekly tests, quarterly to annual inspections, and long-interval inspections. | NFPA 25 sets inspection, testing and maintenance, including weekly to annual checks, five-yearly internal pipe assessments, and testing of sample heads at 50 years (20 for fast-response) and periodically thereafter. |

sections.heading: Worked example: a warehouse that now stores higher
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 1990s warehouse was sprinklered for palletised storage to a set height. A new tenant has installed taller racking and stores plastics, and the annual certificate is current. A flow test two years ago fell slightly below the design curve.

A system can be in perfect condition and still be inadequate for what the building now stores. Taller racking and plastics take the building beyond its design, a safety finding whatever the certificate says. The low flow test points to a supply decline or an obstruction that needs finding.

So the register carries the hazard change as a safety line now, managed by reducing the storage height or redesigning the system with in-rack sprinklers, and the water supply as a check line, becoming an upgrade if the supply is the cause.

thresholds.rule: Throughout a building where any part has an effective height of more than 25 m; new apartment buildings of four storeys and more since the 2019 amendments

source.title: NCC 2025 Volume One, Part E1 Fire fighting equipment

thresholds.rule: New residential buildings with a storey more than 11 m above ground, since 2020

source.title: Approved Document B: Fire safety, volumes 1 and 2

thresholds.rule: At least 457 mm (18 in) to the top of storage

source.title: 29 CFR 1910.159 Automatic sprinkler systems
source.publisher: US Occupational Safety and Health Administration

thresholds.rule: More than 10 per cent below the previous reading: evaluate immediately; more than 20 per cent: treat as an emergency

source.title: UFM 3-601-02 Fire protection systems inspection, testing, and maintenance (13 March 2026)

thresholds.rule: Main drain flow test every 12 months; inspector’s test valve opened at least every 2 years

pages.title: Basement, Cellars & Retaining Walls
pages.question: How do basements and retaining walls fail, and when is a leaning wall dangerous?
pages.answer: Basements leak at cracks, joints and penetrations; whether leaks follow rain or run all year separates surface water from groundwater. Retaining walls fail when drainage behind them blocks and water pressure builds: they rotate, bulge and crack, often after heavy rain. Timber sleeper walls rot at the posts below ground. Loads added behind walls overload them. A wall leaning or moving next to people, buildings or boundaries is a safety finding.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about basement, cellars & retaining walls; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Perimeter walls, structural integrity, damp-proofing, tanking

pages.searchTitle: Basements and retaining walls: leaks, leaning walls, drainage and radon

questions.question: Is a leaning retaining wall dangerous?
questions.answer: It can be. A wall leaning, bulging or moving beside a footpath, driveway, building or boundary is a safety finding: keep people and loads away and get an engineer's assessment.

questions.question: Why does my basement leak only when it rains?
questions.answer: Surface water is reaching the wall. Regrading, drainage channels and downpipe connections that carry rainwater away usually cure it; leaks all year round point to groundwater instead.

questions.question: Who is responsible for a retaining wall on a boundary?
questions.answer: It depends on who built it and whose land it supports. Establish ownership and approvals early, since failures often lead to disputes.

questions.question: Do retaining walls need council approval?
questions.answer: In Australia, councils require approval for walls above set heights, often around a metre.

questions.question: How long do sleeper retaining walls last?
questions.answer: Timber sleeper walls 10 to 25 years, against 50 years and more for blockwork and concrete walls.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Basement and retaining wall problems show as leaning or bulging walls, blocked weep holes and slumping ground outside, and damp, tide marks and busy pumps below ground. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On site | Retaining walls leaning forward, bulging or cracked; fence and handrail lines out of true | Pressure, rotation and surcharge |
| On site | Weep holes blocked or dry after rain; water seeping through the wall face | Pressure, rotation and surcharge |
| On site | Timber sleepers soft at the base; posts loose | Timber sleepers and anchors |
| On site | Ground cracking or slumping behind walls; loads placed close behind them | Pressure, rotation and surcharge |
| On site | Basement walls with damp patches, efflorescence, tide marks and mould | Water ingress and radon |
| On site | Water entering at joints and penetrations; sump pumps running constantly | Water ingress and radon |
| In the records | Waterproofing specification and warranty | Investigation before the scope |
| In the records | Retaining wall design and approvals | Standards by country |
| In the records | Leak and flood history | Water ingress and radon |
| In the records | Monitoring of wall movement | Pressure, rotation and surcharge |
| In the records | Radon test results in affected areas | Water ingress and radon |

sections.heading: Types of wall
sections.markdown:
Basements and cellars are rooms below ground, enclosed by walls that hold back soil and often groundwater. Retaining walls hold back soil at changes in level on a site: driveways, embankments, terraces, and the edges of basement excavations. Both resist earth pressure, and both must manage water, because water behind a wall both adds pressure and finds its way through.

| Form | Where it is found | Main issues |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Masonry cellar walls | Older houses and terraces | Damp and salts; no waterproofing; bowing under earth pressure |
| Reinforced concrete basement walls | Modern buildings and car parks | Leaks at cracks, joints and penetrations |
| Diaphragm, secant and contiguous pile walls | Deep basements in cities | Leaks between piles; joint seals |
| Cantilever concrete or blockwork retaining walls | Sites, driveways, landscaping | Rotation; cracking; blocked drainage |
| Timber sleeper walls | Australian residential sites | Decay of sleepers and posts; overturning |
| Crib, gabion and gravity walls | Embankments and landscaping | Movement; corrosion of gabion wire |
| Anchored and soil-nailed walls | Deep cuts and constrained sites | Anchor corrosion; monitoring |

Basement waterproofing follows three broad approaches, set out in Britain as Types A, B and C: a barrier applied to the structure (tanking), a structurally integral watertight concrete, and a drained cavity that accepts some water and pumps it away. Many buildings combine them. Which approach the building has decides how leaks are fixed.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Reinforced concrete basement walls last the life of the building, and block or concrete retaining walls fifty years and more, but timber sleeper walls last only ten to twenty-five. The drains behind a wall last fifteen to thirty years, and their failure is behind much of what goes wrong.

| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Reinforced concrete walls | Life of the building | Cracking; reinforcement corrosion |
| Applied tanking membranes | 20 to 40 years | Movement; installation quality |
| Drained cavity membranes and pumps | Membranes 30 years and more; pumps 10 to 15 | Pump maintenance |
| Timber sleeper retaining walls | 10 to 25 years | Treatment; drainage; soil contact |
| Blockwork and concrete retaining walls | 50 years and more | Drainage; reinforcement |
| Ground anchors | 25 to 50 years | Corrosion protection |
| Agricultural drains behind walls | 15 to 30 years | Silting; roots |

What shortens life: blocked drainage behind retaining walls and basement walls, which raises water pressure; surcharge loads: new structures, vehicles, fill and pools placed behind walls that were not designed for them; tree roots pushing on and through walls; rising groundwater and changed drainage on and around the site.

sections.heading: Water ingress and radon
sections.markdown:
Water enters basements through cracks, construction joints, tie holes, service penetrations and the junction between walls and floors. Leaks that run in wet weather point to surface water; leaks that run all year point to groundwater. Efflorescence, tide marks and mould follow, and stored goods and services are damaged.

Basements in radon-affected areas and on contaminated land collect radon or other ground gases through cracks and joints. Radon is a recognised cause of lung cancer; testing is advised in affected areas in Britain and the United States.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Basement leaks only in wet weather | Surface water reaching the wall. Correlation with rainfall; surface drainage. | Fix the surface drainage: regrading, channels and downpipe connections. |
| Basement leaks all year | Groundwater. Groundwater levels. | Inject cracks and joints; where external access is impossible, fit a drained cavity system with sumps and pumps. |
| High radon result in a basement or cellar | Ground gas entering through the floor and walls. A long-term test; the US EPA recommends fixing homes at 4 pCi/L (150 Bq/m³) or more (US EPA), and in the UK the risk is relatively low below 100 Bq/m³ (UKradon). | Seal entry points and fit a radon sump or ventilation, then retest. |

sections.heading: Pressure, rotation and surcharge
sections.markdown:
A wall designed for drained soil fails when its drainage blocks: water pressure adds to earth pressure and the wall rotates, bulges or cracks. Many retaining wall failures follow heavy rain on walls with blocked weep holes or failed drains.

Cantilever retaining walls rotate forward at the top; masonry cellar walls bow inward under earth pressure where floors do not restrain them. Movement that continues leads to collapse.

Driveways, car parking, new buildings, pools and fill placed close behind a wall add load it was never designed for.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Retaining wall leaning more after heavy rain | Blocked drainage and water pressure. Weep holes and drains inspected. | Clear the drains and open the weep holes; keep people and loads away, and get an engineer's assessment. |
| Wall cracked behind a new driveway or structure | Surcharge. Loads against design. | Remove the surcharge, or redesign the wall for it. |
| Inward bowing of cellar walls | Lack of restraint and earth pressure. Survey; restraint details. | Get an engineer's assessment; restraint, buttresses or anchors. |
| Cracks in a basement or retaining wall widening between readings | Movement still active. Crack widths read against fixed points over time, and graded on the asset’s market’s damage scale (Thresholds by market). | Keep reading the cracks, and have an engineer assess any crack that is still moving or has reached the moderate band. |

sections.heading: Timber sleepers and anchors
sections.markdown:
Timber sleepers and posts rot where they are in contact with wet soil, and walls lean and collapse, often after a decade or two. Posts rot below ground first, so a wall can look sound until it fails.

Ground anchors and soil nails lose capacity as their steel corrodes; reinforcement in walls corrodes where water penetrates cracks.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Timber wall leaning with soft posts | Decay below ground. Probe posts. | Replace the sleeper wall with a concrete or masonry system. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Retaining wall leaning or moving beside a public area, building or boundary; radon above action levels | safety · 4 Essential | Exclude people and loads, prop or remediate now. |
| Basement flooding; wall collapse | failure · 4 Essential | Repair now. |
| Seepage, efflorescence, blocked drainage, early rotation | condition · 3 Important | Repair in the near term. |
| Sleeper walls and pumps at end of life | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Replace. |
| Walls without design approval; radon untested in affected areas | check · 3 Important | Assess. |
| Minor damp | nil · 1 Routine | Monitor. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A structural or geotechnical engineer leads; a waterproofing specialist joins for basements. The checks below relate each leak or movement to rainfall and groundwater, then check the drainage and the loads behind the wall.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Wall survey | Verticality, bulging and cracking, with fixed survey points for monitoring over time and crack widths graded on the asset’s market’s damage scale (Thresholds by market). |
| Drainage inspection | Weep holes, drains behind walls by CCTV, outlets and surface drainage. |
| Leak tracing | Mapping wet areas, monitoring in wet and dry periods, and testing at joints and penetrations. |
| Timber probing | Of sleepers and posts at and below ground. |
| Load review | What sits behind the wall against its design. |
| Design and approval check | For retaining walls above the height that needs approval. |
| Radon testing | In affected areas, read against the action level that applies (4 pCi/L in the United States, US EPA). |

The report should state structural stability, the waterproofing approach and its failures, drainage condition, and remedies.

For basements, testing in both a dry and a prolonged wet period is often needed before the source of water can be confirmed and the right waterproofing repair chosen.

sections.heading: Draining, sealing or strengthening
sections.markdown:
Water is at the root of most findings, so drainage comes first: drains behind walls, weep holes and surface water. Sealing and tanking follow for basements, and strengthening or rebuilding for retaining walls that keep moving.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Restore drainage | Clear or replace drains behind walls, open weep holes, and fix surface drainage. | First, wherever drainage is blocked. |
| Crack and joint injection | Polyurethane or epoxy resins. | Where water enters through cracks and joints. |
| Drained cavity systems | Systems on the inside of the basement, with sumps and pumps. | Where external access is impossible. |
| External tanking | A membrane applied to the outside of the wall. | Where walls can be excavated. |
| Retaining wall strengthening | Buttresses, anchors or soil nails, or rebuilding. | Where a wall keeps moving. |
| Sleeper wall replacement | Concrete or masonry systems. | Where timber sleepers have decayed. |
| Surcharge | Remove surcharge loads, or redesign the wall for them. | Where loads have been placed behind a wall. |
| Radon mitigation | Sealing and sub-floor depressurisation. | Where radon testing shows a need. |
| Joint and penetration seals | Hydrophilic strips, injection hoses and puddle flanges at service penetrations, which are the commonest leak points. | Where water enters at joints and penetrations. |
| Surface water management | Regrading, drainage channels and downpipe connections so rainwater is carried away from basement and retaining walls. | Where leaks follow rain. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Investigation and monitoring are lump sums. Injection is priced by length of crack or joint; drained cavity systems by area with pumps; external tanking by area with excavation; retaining wall rebuilding by length and height. Drainage repairs by length. Pumps recur on cycle.

Rebuilding and new waterproofing are lifecycle; drainage and injection are repairs and maintenance; unsafe walls are immediate.

Basement leak repairs in occupied car parks and plant rooms often need out-of-hours access and protection of services, which can exceed the cost of the injection itself.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a walk past the wall cannot: how it was designed, whether it is still moving, and whose land it supports. Ask for them early, since responsibility for a boundary wall often decides what happens next.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Waterproofing specification, type and warranty | How the basement is meant to keep water out, and whether a warranty applies. |
| Retaining wall designs and approvals | Whether retaining walls were designed and approved. |
| Leak, flood and pump records | Whether leaks follow rain or persist, and how hard the pumps work. |
| Movement monitoring data | Whether walls are still moving. |
| Drainage drawings | Where the drains behind the walls run. |
| Radon test results in affected areas | Whether radon is a concern below ground. |
| Survey plans showing walls in relation to boundaries | Whose land each wall stands on and supports. |
| Geotechnical reports for the site | What the ground and groundwater are. |
| Records of loads or structures added behind walls | Whether walls carry loads they were not designed for. |
| Correspondence with neighbours about shared walls | Whether a shared wall is already in dispute. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Basements and retaining walls are misread when a leaning wall is treated as a slow maintenance item, and when every basement leak is taken to be the same problem.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| A leaning wall can wait | A retaining wall that is leaning, bulging or moving next to a footpath, driveway, building or boundary is a safety finding. Keep people and loads away and get an engineer's assessment. |
| Every basement leak is the same | Leaks only in wet weather point to surface water reaching the wall, which surface drainage cures; leaks all year point to groundwater, which needs sealing from inside or out. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets design standards for retaining walls and standards for keeping water and ground gases out of basements. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Design and approval | AS 4678 governs earth-retaining structures; councils require approval for retaining walls above set heights, often around a metre, and walls near boundaries can involve neighbours. | BS EN 1997 covers geotechnical design. | The International Building Code covers retaining walls (Section 1807). |
| Waterproofing and radon | The National Construction Code covers damp and weatherproofing. | BS 8102 sets the protection of below-ground structures against water, with grades of environment and Types A, B and C; the UK Health Security Agency maps radon-affected areas. | The International Building Code covers damp-proofing and waterproofing (Section 1805); the EPA recommends radon testing and mitigation above its action level. |

In all three jurisdictions, a retaining wall on or near a boundary can affect a neighbour's land, and responsibility depends on who built it and whose land it supports; failures often lead to disputes, so ownership and approvals should be established early. Strata and condominium buildings usually treat basement structure and waterproofing as common property.

sections.heading: Worked example: a sleeper wall leaning over a driveway
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 1990s house has a timber sleeper retaining wall about 1.2 metres high beside the neighbour's driveway. It leans visibly toward the driveway, its posts are soft at the base, and a carport slab was laid close behind it two years ago. Its weep holes are blocked.

A retaining wall leaning beside a driveway and a boundary is a safety finding: keep people and loads away and get an engineer's assessment. Soft posts point to decay below ground, the carport slab to surcharge, and the blocked weep holes to water pressure, and all three add to the lean.

So the register carries the wall as a safety line now, replacement with a concrete or masonry wall designed for the carport load, and ownership and approvals established early, since responsibility depends on who built the wall and whose land it supports.

thresholds.rule: Negligible under 0.1 mm; very slight under 1 mm; slight under 5 mm; moderate 5 to 15 mm; severe 15 to 25 mm

source.title: Standards and Tolerances Guide (December 2023), reproducing the AS 2870 damage categories

pages.title: Bathrooms & Wet Areas
pages.question: How do bathrooms and wet areas leak, how do you find the source, and when does resealing stop being enough?
pages.answer: Wet areas fail at the membrane nobody sees: gaps at wall-floor junctions, around the waste, at the threshold and at tap penetrations let every shower soak the substrate, and in apartments water appears in the ceiling below. Leaks that follow showering point to the membrane, screen or floor; constant leaks point to pipes. Regrouting stops water briefly but does not repair a failed membrane: strip and re-waterproof. Fans venting into the roof grow mould.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about bathrooms & wet areas; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
