pages.searchTitle: Bathrooms and wet areas: shower leaks, failed membranes, thresholds, mould and safety

questions.question: Will regrouting fix a leaking shower?
questions.answer: Not if the membrane has failed. Regrouting and resealing can stop water at the surface for a while; only stripping and re-waterproofing repairs a failed membrane.

questions.question: How do you find where a bathroom leak is coming from?
questions.answer: Separate leaks that follow showering from leaks that never stop. Flood test the floor and spray test the screen for the first; pressure test the pipes, or watch the meter, for the second.

questions.question: Why is the skirting outside the bathroom swelling?
questions.answer: Water is escaping at the threshold, usually through a missing or failed waterstop.

questions.question: Where should a bathroom exhaust fan discharge?
questions.answer: Outside. A fan discharging into the ceiling space causes condensation and mould there instead.

questions.question: How long does a bathroom last?
questions.answer: A refurbishment cycle of 15 to 25 years, with silicone renewed every 3 to 10 years and grout every 5 to 15; a well-installed membrane lasts the full cycle.

questions.question: Why does a stain appear on the ceiling below every time someone showers?
questions.answer: The membrane, screen or shower floor is failing. Flood test the floor and spray test the screen separately; strip and re-waterproof if the membrane has failed.

questions.question: Why is the ceiling under the bathroom wet all the time?
questions.answer: A stain that never dries points to a pressurised pipe or fitting, not the shower. Pressure test, find the leaking pipe or fitting, and repair it.

questions.question: Why is there mold on the bathroom ceiling?
questions.answer: The exhaust is inadequate, or the fan is not ducted outside. Fit a ducted fan discharging outside, with a run-on timer or humidity control.

questions.question: Why do the tiles around the shower drain sound hollow?
questions.answer: Water is under the tiles from a failed membrane or waste flange. Lift a tile; replace the waste flange and repair the membrane, or strip and re-waterproof.

questions.question: The hot water at the basin is scalding. What should be done?
questions.answer: It is a scald risk. Fit or repair the tempering or thermostatic mixing valve and retest.

questions.question: Why is the wall beside the shower tap damp even when nobody uses the shower?
questions.answer: A leaking mixer body or connection. Open the wall or tiles, and repair or replace the mixer.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Wet area problems show in the room as drummy tiles, failed grout and mould, around it as swollen joinery and stained ceilings below, and in the records of leaks and repairs. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| In the bathroom | Cracked, loose or drummy (hollow-sounding) tiles, especially near the shower and waste | Membranes, thresholds and falls |
| In the bathroom | Discoloured, missing or cracked grout; mouldy or split silicone at junctions | Membranes, thresholds and falls |
| In the bathroom | Water ponding on the floor after a shower; water crossing the threshold | Membranes, thresholds and falls |
| In the bathroom | Exhaust fan weak, noisy or discharging into the ceiling space | Mould and ventilation |
| In the bathroom | Mould on ceilings and around the shower | Mould and ventilation |
| In the bathroom | Moisture meter readings elevated at the base of walls and around the shower | Membranes, thresholds and falls |
| Around and below | Swollen skirtings, door frames and vanity bases near the bathroom door | Membranes, thresholds and falls |
| Around and below | Stained, bubbling or mouldy ceilings in the room or unit below | Membranes, thresholds and falls |
| Around and below | Damp carpet or lifting floor coverings outside the bathroom | Membranes, thresholds and falls |
| Around and below | Rot and termite damage in timber floors below, seen from the sub-floor | Plumbing leaks and substrate damage |
| In the records | Waterproofing certificates and installer details | Investigation before the scope |
| In the records | Leak complaints from neighbours below | Membranes, thresholds and falls |
| In the records | Previous repairs and resealing | Investigation before the scope |
| In the records | Building defect claims | Standards by country |

sections.heading: What the space does and what it contains
sections.markdown:
Bathrooms and wet areas are the bathrooms, ensuites, showers, toilets and laundries in homes and apartments. Functionally they must contain water, remove moisture, deliver safe hot water, drain properly and stay hygienic. Their most important component is one nobody sees: the waterproofing membrane under the tiles and behind the shower walls. Wet area leaks are among the most common and costly defects in residential buildings, especially apartments, where a failed shower floods the unit below and damages structure for years before it shows.

| Element group | Typical provision | What matters for the space |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Waterproofing membrane | Liquid or sheet membrane under tiles, turned up walls, over hobs and at door thresholds | Continuity at junctions, penetrations and wastes |
| Floor falls and wastes | Screed falling to floor wastes with puddle flanges | Water draining to the waste, not ponding or escaping |
| Tiles, grout and sealant | Ceramic or stone tiles with grout; flexible sealant at junctions | Not waterproof on their own; movement joints |
| Shower enclosure | Screen, hob or hobless step-down, waterstop at the entry | Containing spray and water flow |
| Fixtures and plumbing | WC, basin, bath, taps, mixers, wastes | Leaks at seals, connections and penetrations |
| Exhaust ventilation | Fan ducted to outside | Removing moisture, preventing mould |
| Substrate | Concrete slab, fibre cement or timber floor; wall sheets | Movement; rot if wet |

Era is a strong guide. Many bathrooms built before the 1980s have no membrane at all and rely on tiles and grout; later bathrooms have membranes of varying quality; current standards demand membranes with continuous upturns, flashing at thresholds, and floors falling to the waste. Timber-framed floors move and crack tiles and membranes more than concrete.

sections.heading: How long it stays fit for purpose
sections.markdown:
A bathroom is refurbished as a whole every fifteen to twenty-five years, but its parts run on shorter clocks: silicone three to ten years, grout five to fifteen, screen seals three to seven. A well-installed membrane lasts the full cycle; one that was not can fail within months, and then it decides when the cycle really ends.

| Component or quality | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Waterproofing membrane | 15 to 25 years if well installed; can fail within months if not | Installation quality; substrate movement |
| Grout | 5 to 15 years before cracking and staining | Cleaning; movement |
| Silicone sealant at junctions | 3 to 10 years | Mould; movement; cleaning |
| Tapware and mixers | 10 to 20 years | Water quality |
| Shower screens and seals | 10 to 20 years; seals 3 to 7 | Use; hardware |
| Exhaust fans | 10 to 15 years | Run hours; dust |
| Bathroom refurbishment cycle | 15 to 25 years | Leaks; wear; style |

What shortens fitness for purpose: poor membrane installation: thin coats, unreinforced junctions, membranes stopped short at walls and doors, and wastes without puddle flanges; substrate movement in timber floors and lightweight walls cracking tiles and membranes; hobless showers without adequate falls and waterstops, letting water flow across the floor; neglected sealant at junctions and around screens; weak or unused exhaust leaving moisture in the room.

sections.heading: Membranes, thresholds and falls
sections.markdown:
Water reaches the substrate through gaps in the membrane at wall-floor junctions, around the floor waste, at the shower entry and threshold, and where taps, mixers and pipes penetrate the wall. Grout and tiles are not waterproof; once the membrane fails, every shower soaks the substrate. In apartments water travels along the slab and appears in the ceiling below or in adjoining rooms, sometimes metres away.

At bathroom doors and shower entries, water flows along the floor or wicks under the tiles beyond the wet area. Missing or poorly sealed waterstop angles let water reach skirtings, carpets and timber floors outside the bathroom, which swell and rot.

Floors that do not fall to the waste, or fall the wrong way, leave water ponding against walls and doorways and push it toward weak points in the membrane.

The membrane is only as good as its weakest junction. In a failed shower the open floor is often intact; the failure sits at the internal corner where wall meets floor, at the flange around the waste, or at the step into the shower, where the membrane was not reinforced or not turned up far enough. That is why a leak is cured by finding and rebuilding the junction, not by coating the tiles.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ceiling stain below appears after showers and dries between | Membrane, screen or shower floor failure. Flood test of the shower floor; spray test of the screen. | Flood test the floor and spray test the screen separately; strip and re-waterproof if the membrane has failed. |
| Swollen skirting or door frame outside the bathroom | Water escaping at the threshold or waterstop. Moisture readings; flood test. | Fit or reseal the waterstop at the threshold, and replace the swollen joinery once it has dried. |
| Drummy tiles around the waste | Water under tiles from membrane or waste flange failure. Lift a tile; inspect the flange. | Lift a tile; replace the waste flange and repair the membrane, or strip and re-waterproof. |
| Water on the floor outside a hobless shower after use | Inadequate falls, or no waterstop at the entry. Water crosses the line of the screen; a level shows the floor falling away from the waste. | Re-form the falls, and fit a waterstop or a linear drain across the entry. |
| Tiles cracked in a straight line across a timber-framed floor | Floor movement cracking the tiles and the membrane beneath. The crack follows a joist or sheet joint, and the floor gives underfoot. | Stiffen the floor first; a new membrane on a floor that still moves fails again. |

sections.heading: Plumbing leaks and substrate damage
sections.markdown:
Leaking mixer bodies and connections inside walls, toilet pan seals, cistern connections, bath wastes and pipe joints leak constantly, unlike membrane leaks that follow showering.

Water in timber floors and framing causes rot and termite attack; in fibre cement and plasterboard, swelling and mould; in concrete slabs, corrosion of reinforcement over time.

Concealed plumbing leaks behave differently from shower leaks: the stain grows steadily whether or not anyone showers, the wall cavity stays damp, and the water meter moves with every outlet closed. Mixer bodies set into the wall behind the tiles, and their connections, are a common source, and reaching them means opening the wall or tiles from one side.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stain below that is wet all the time | Pressurised pipe or fitting leak. Pressure test; water meter with outlets closed. | Pressure test, find the leaking pipe or fitting, and repair it. |
| Stain below the WC | Pan seal or cistern connection leak. Dye test in the cistern and pan. | Replace the pan seal or cistern connection. |
| Damp in the wall beside the shower mixer, whether or not the shower is used | A leaking mixer body or connection. Moisture is constant and highest around the mixer; a pressure test confirms it. | Open the wall or tiles, and repair or replace the mixer. |

sections.heading: Mould and ventilation
sections.markdown:
Bathrooms without effective exhaust, or with fans discharging into the roof space, stay humid after showers; mould grows on ceilings, grout and sealant. Fans venting into roof spaces cause condensation and mould there too.

A fan that runs but discharges into the ceiling space moves the problem rather than removing it: moist air condenses on cold roof timbers and the underside of the roof, and mould appears there as well as in the bathroom. Following the duct to its end settles it.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mould on the ceiling | Inadequate exhaust or fan not ducted outside. Fan airflow; duct route (Thresholds by market). | Fit a ducted fan discharging outside, with a run-on timer or humidity control. |
| Mould on the roof timbers above the bathroom | Exhaust discharging into the roof space. The duct ends in the roof space, not at an outlet outside. | Duct the fan to outside, and treat or replace the mouldy materials. |

sections.heading: Slips and scalding
sections.markdown:
Two bathroom hazards hurt people directly rather than damaging the building: floors that are too slippery when wet, and hot water delivered hotter than people can safely bear. Both matter most where older people or young children use the room.

Smooth wet tiles cause falls, especially for older people. Hot water without tempering to safe temperatures scalds children and the elderly.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Very hot water at the basin or shower | Scald risk. Outlet temperature measured against the limits for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Fit or repair the tempering or thermostatic mixing valve and retest. |
| Lukewarm water at a little-used shower, or a long wait for hot water | Legionella risk from low temperatures or stagnation. Temperature at the outlet over time against the limits for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Flush little-used outlets weekly, remove dead legs, and restore temperatures. |
| Slips on a wet bathroom floor | Floor finish unsuitable when wet. Wet slip resistance test against the class for the use. | Treat the surface or replace it with a suitably slip-resistant finish. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Water damaging structure, electrical fittings or another dwelling; hot water above safe temperatures for vulnerable occupants | safety · 4 Essential | Stop use of the shower or fix now. |
| Active leak to the unit below; rotted floor | failure · 3 Important | Repair now. |
| Defect warranty or tribunal deadlines | deadline · 4 Essential | Act within the period. |
| Cracked grout, failed sealant, weak exhaust, mould | condition · 3 Important | Repair in the near term. |
| Bathroom at end of refurbishment cycle, or no membrane in an older bathroom | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Plan a full strip and re-waterproof. |
| Moisture readings elevated with no visible damage | check · 3 Important | Investigate further. |
| Normal | nil · 1 Routine | Routine resealing. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A building surveyor or wet area specialist leads; a plumber joins for pressure testing; in apartments, access to the unit below is essential. The checks below separate leaks that follow showering from leaks that never stop, then test each wet area on its own, with access to the room below.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Moisture mapping | With a meter around the shower, at wall bases, at the threshold and outside the door, and on the ceiling below. |
| Thermal imaging | To trace wet areas in walls and ceilings. |
| Flood test | Plug the waste and flood the floor or shower base for a set period, then check below and around for water. |
| Spray and use tests | Of screens and fixtures. |
| Dye tests | Of WC pans and cisterns. |
| Pressure test | Of hot and cold pipework, or a meter test with all outlets closed. |
| Invasive inspection | Lift a tile at the waste or threshold, or open the ceiling below, to see the membrane and substrate. |
| Exhaust check | Airflow and where the duct discharges. |
| Sub-floor inspection | Below timber-floored bathrooms for rot and termites. |

The report should identify the source of each leak with evidence, the extent of substrate damage, whether the membrane can be repaired or must be replaced, and in strata buildings whether the cause is common property or within the lot.

sections.heading: Maintaining, repairing or re-waterproofing
sections.markdown:
Water reaching structure, electrics or another home, and hot water hot enough to scald vulnerable people, come first. After that, the choice turns on the membrane: regrouting and resealing maintain a sound one, but only stripping and re-waterproofing repairs a failed one.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Regrout and reseal | Regrout and reseal as maintenance, where the membrane is sound. | Routinely, or as a short-term measure; it does not fix a failed membrane. |
| Penetrating sealers and coatings | Sealers and surface coatings applied over the tiles. | Only as a temporary measure; they rarely last. |
| Strip and re-waterproof | Remove tiles and screed, repair the substrate, install a compliant membrane with reinforced junctions, upturns, waste flanges and threshold waterstops, re-screed to falls and retile. This is the only lasting fix for a failed membrane. | Wherever the membrane has failed; the only lasting fix. |
| Plumbing repairs | Repair mixers, connections, pan seals and wastes. | Wherever a constant leak is traced to the plumbing. |
| Shower screen repair | New seals, adjustment or replacement. | Where screens leak in a spray test. |
| Exhaust | Replace weak fans with ducted fans discharging outside, with run-on timers or humidity control. | Wherever mould grows, or the fan discharges into the ceiling space. |
| Substrate repair | Replace rotted timber and swollen sheets; treat termite damage. | Where timber has rotted or sheets have swollen. |
| Safety | Slip-resistant floor tiles and tempering valves on hot water. | Where floors are slippery, or hot water is untempered. |
| Waterstops, hobs or linear drains at shower entries | A waterstop at the step-down, a hob, or a linear drain across the entry, with the floor re-formed to fall to it. | Where water escapes a hobless shower. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Regrouting and resealing are small items but recur. Strip and re-waterproof is priced per bathroom and is a significant project, with temporary loss of the bathroom and making good of adjoining finishes and the ceiling below. Plumbing repairs are itemised. Exhaust upgrades are per fan with ducting. In apartments, consequential damage below often costs as much as the bathroom itself.

Full re-waterproofing is lifecycle or a defect repair; leaks are failures; resealing is repairs and maintenance; in new buildings, claims may fall under statutory warranties.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a look at the tiles cannot: whether a membrane was installed and certified, whether water has already reached the home below, and who owns the membrane. Ask for them before any repair is priced.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Waterproofing certificates and installer details | Whether the membrane was installed and certified, and by whom. |
| Leak complaints from the unit below or neighbours | Whether water has already reached the home below. |
| Records of previous repairs, regrouting and resealing | Whether the surface has been patched over a failed membrane. |
| Building defect claims and warranty details for newer buildings | Whether the defect is still within a warranty or claim period. |
| Strata plan and by-laws defining membrane ownership | Whether the membrane is common property or part of the lot, which decides who pays. |
| Plumbing compliance certificates for renovations | Whether renovation plumbing was certified. |
| Moisture or thermal imaging reports from earlier investigations | What earlier investigations found. |
| Photographs of the membrane before tiling, where the installer took them | Whether junctions, upturns and flanges were done properly, without lifting a tile. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Wet area leaks are misread when resealing is taken for a repair, when the stain below is taken to mark the leak, and when a coating over the tiles is taken for waterproofing.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| Resealing fixes a leak | Leaks that follow showering point to the membrane, screen or floor; leaks that are constant point to pipes. Regrouting and resealing can stop water at the surface for a while, but they do not repair a failed membrane. |
| The leak is directly above the stain | In apartments, water travels along the slab before it appears, sometimes metres away, so the stain below does not mark the leak. Flood testing each wet area in turn, with moisture mapping, finds the source. |
| A sealer will waterproof the tiles | Grout and tiles are not waterproof, and sealers or coatings over them rarely last. The membrane beneath is what keeps water out. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets standards for waterproofing and ventilating wet areas, and its own rules on who owns the membrane in apartments. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Waterproofing, ventilation and responsibility | AS 3740 sets waterproofing of domestic wet areas, with a revised edition in 2021 tightening falls, upturns and threshold details; the National Construction Code requires exhaust from bathrooms and laundries to discharge to the outside in newer homes; state home building laws provide statutory warranties against defects (for example in New South Wales), and strata law decides whether the membrane is common property or part of the lot, which varies by plan. | BS 5385 covers wall and floor tiling, including wet areas; Approved Document F sets extract ventilation rates; NHBC Standards set warranty requirements for new homes; leasehold terms decide responsibility in flats. | The International Residential and Plumbing Codes set shower pan and wet area requirements, with membranes commonly to ANSI A118.10 and practice to the TCNA Handbook; exhaust fans must discharge outdoors; condominium declarations set responsibility. |

sections.heading: Worked example: a stain below an apartment shower
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. In a 2000s apartment building, a ceiling stain in one unit grows after the unit above uses its shower, and dries between. The shower above has a hobless entry, the tiles around its waste sound drummy, its silicone has been renewed twice, and the skirting outside the bathroom door is swollen.

A stain that follows showering and dries between points to the membrane, screen or floor, not the pipes. Drummy tiles at the waste and a swollen skirting point to water under the tiles, escaping at the threshold. Resealing stopped water at the surface for a while, but it does not repair a failed membrane.

So the register carries the active leak to the unit below as a failure line, a flood test and spray test to confirm the source, then a strip and re-waterproof with a waterstop or linear drain at the entry, and the strata plan checked to settle who pays.

thresholds.rule: No more than 45 °C in aged care, healthcare, early childhood centres and schools; 50 °C in most other buildings

source.title: NCC 2025 Volume Three (Plumbing Code), Part B2 Heated water services

thresholds.rule: At least 15 L/s run intermittently, or 8 L/s on a continuous system’s high rate

source.title: Approved Document F, Volume 1: Dwellings (2021 edition)

thresholds.rule: Stored at 60 °C or more; 50 °C at outlets within one minute (55 °C in healthcare)

source.title: HSG274 Legionnaires’ disease: Technical guidance, Part 2: Hot and cold water systems

pages.title: Building Maintenance Units (BMU)
pages.question: How do building maintenance units and façade access systems fail, how is their position established, and when are they unusable?
pages.answer: Façade access equipment carries people at height, so its position is set by certification as much as wear. An overdue inspection, missing logbook or uncertified anchors means it cannot be used and façade maintenance stops. The physical failures are fatigue cracks at welds and the slewing ring, worn brakes, degraded ropes, water in sockets and track fixings, and obsolete controls that keep a unit out of service for months. Units over ten years old need a major inspection.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about building maintenance units (bmu); it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Cradles, gantries, track/guide systems

pages.searchTitle: Building maintenance units and façade access: inspections, controls, anchors, coverage

questions.question: Can a BMU be used if its inspection is overdue?
questions.answer: No. Equipment with an overdue inspection or a missing logbook cannot lawfully be used until it is inspected and certified.

questions.question: Does an older BMU need a major inspection?
questions.answer: In Australia, regulators have issued safety alerts on major inspections for units more than ten years old; without one, the hidden structural condition is unknown.

questions.question: Why is our BMU out of service so often?
questions.answer: Often control obsolescence, with parts no longer available. Control modernisation on a sound structure is usually the main mid-life investment.

questions.question: How often must façade access equipment be examined?
questions.answer: In the United Kingdom, equipment lifting people needs a thorough examination at least every six months; in the United States, rope descent anchorages are inspected annually.

questions.question: How long does a BMU last?
questions.answer: Its structure, carriage and track 25 to 40 years, the cradle 20 to 30, controls, hoists and brakes 15 to 25, and wire ropes typically 5 to 10.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Façade access problems show on the roof as corrosion and obstructions, on the unit in its tags, ropes and controls, and above all in its logbook and inspection reports. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| From aerial imagery and the roof | Equipment present: track, carriage, monorail, davits, anchors; covered or uncovered | Ropes, hoists, controls and coverage |
| From aerial imagery and the roof | Corrosion on the unit, track and fixings; ponding around track fixings and sockets | Structure, stability and anchors |
| From aerial imagery and the roof | Rooftop plant or structures in the travel path of the unit | Ropes, hoists, controls and coverage |
| On site | Inspection tags and the logbook: current, overdue or missing | Structure, stability and anchors |
| On site | Rust at welds, connections and the slewing ring; oil leaks from hoists and gearboxes | Structure, stability and anchors |
| On site | Wire ropes with broken wires, corrosion or kinks | Ropes, hoists, controls and coverage |
| On site | Controls cabinet condition, water ingress, labels and warning signs | Ropes, hoists, controls and coverage |
| On site | Davit sockets full of water or debris; anchors loose or corroded | Structure, stability and anchors |
| On site | Façade restraint points present and usable | Structure, stability and anchors |
| In the records | Periodic and major inspection reports, with outstanding defects | Investigation before the scope |
| In the records | Plant registration, design registration and load test records | Standards by country |
| In the records | Maintenance contract and service reports; unit out of service for extended periods | Ropes, hoists, controls and coverage |
| In the records | Façade access strategy and whether it still covers every elevation | Ropes, hoists, controls and coverage |
| In the records | Anchor certification with dates; rescue plans | Structure, stability and anchors |

sections.heading: Types of façade access equipment
sections.markdown:
Building maintenance units and façade access equipment are the permanent systems used to reach the outside of a building for cleaning, inspection and repair. They are lifting equipment that carries people at height, so their condition is set by statutory inspection and certification as much as by wear, and a failed or uncertified system stops façade maintenance altogether.

| Form | Where it is found | Key components |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Roof-mounted BMU (track or rail mounted) | Towers and large offices | Carriage on rails or a track, slewing ring, jib or luffing arm, hoists, wire ropes, cradle, controls, counterweight |
| Monorail with trolley and cradle | Mid-rise offices, atria, curved façades | Monorail track fixed to the structure or parapet, trolley, hoist, cradle |
| Davit system | Mid-rise buildings | Fixed or portable davit arms in sockets along the roof edge; cradle or rope access from them |
| Parapet clamps and outriggers | Older and lower buildings | Temporary suspension points clamped to parapets |
| Rope access anchors | Most buildings over a few storeys | Permanent anchors for rope descent systems and abseil work |
| Atrium and internal gantries | Retail centres, atria, institutional buildings | Gantries or travelling platforms on rails |
| Façade restraint system | Tall buildings with cradles | Restraint rails, buttons or sockets on the façade that tie the cradle to the building in wind |

The system must reach every part of the façade that needs maintenance. A building's façade access strategy sets which equipment serves which elevation. Façade changes over time, such as new canopies, louvres, signs or balconies, can leave elevations that the equipment can no longer reach.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
A building maintenance unit's structure, carriage and track last twenty-five to forty years and its cradle twenty to thirty, while controls, hoists and brakes last fifteen to twenty-five, and wire ropes are replaced on condition, typically every five to ten. The controls usually decide the mid-life investment.

| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| BMU structure, carriage and track | 25 to 40 years | Coastal exposure; maintenance; fatigue at highly stressed welds |
| Slewing ring bearing | 20 to 30 years | Lubrication; use |
| Controls and electrical systems | 15 to 25 years | Obsolescence of parts; water ingress |
| Hoists and brakes | 15 to 25 years | Use; maintenance |
| Wire ropes | Replaced on condition, typically 5 to 10 years | Use, corrosion, damage; discard criteria |
| Cradle | 20 to 30 years | Corrosion; impact damage |
| Davit arms and sockets | 25 to 40 years | Water in sockets; coating |
| Rope access anchors | 20 to 30 years | Corrosion; roof works disturbing fixings; recertification |

What shortens life: infrequent use: equipment used once or twice a year seizes, corrodes and is neglected between uses; coastal and rooftop exposure: salt, UV and water on equipment stored uncovered on the roof; water in davit sockets and track fixings, which corrodes the base and leaks through the roof membrane; lapsed maintenance contracts and lapsed certification; obsolete controls, which turn a minor fault into a long outage.

sections.heading: Structure, stability and anchors
sections.markdown:
The jib, carriage and slewing assembly carry cyclic loads at high stress points. Fatigue cracks start at welds and section changes; corrosion reduces section at connections and fixings. Track and rail fixings corrode where water collects, and where they penetrate the roof, they leak.

Roof-mounted units rely on counterweight and rail clamps to stay on the roof under load and wind. Altered counterweights, worn clamps or modified units have led to instability incidents; regulators in Australia have issued safety alerts on BMU stability.

Davit sockets fill with water and corrode from the inside. Rope access anchors corrode at their base, and roof works that disturb the membrane around them can compromise their fixing. Anchors that are not inspected and recertified on schedule cannot be relied on.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Inspection overdue or logbook missing | Equipment cannot lawfully be used. Last inspection date against the required interval. | Take it out of use until inspected and certified, and restore the logbook. |
| Major inspection never done on a unit more than ten years old | Hidden structural condition unknown. Records; Australian guidance calls for a major inspection at that age. | Commission a major inspection before relying on the unit. |
| Corrosion at track fixings and leaks below them | Water at roof penetrations. Membrane condition at the fixings; leak log. | Refurbish the track and fixings, and renew the roof membrane at the penetrations. |
| Anchors without certification records | Anchors cannot be relied on. Certification records and intervals. | Take the anchors out of use; replace or recertify them. |
| Davit sockets or roof supports with no inspection in the last year | Support structure condition unknown. Inspection records for the supporting structure and the equipment, against the intervals for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Inspect the supports and sockets before the next use, and set a yearly regime. |

sections.heading: Ropes, hoists, controls and coverage
sections.markdown:
Ropes lose strength through broken wires, corrosion, abrasion and kinking. They are discarded against defined criteria; a rope that is not inspected to those criteria can fail.

Hoist brakes, gearboxes and drives wear with use and seize without it. Brake failure on a hoist carrying people is the critical mechanical failure.

Controls, limit switches and safety devices age, take in water and become unsupported. Parts become unavailable and the unit stays out of service while controls are re-engineered.

Façade alterations and new rooftop plant can block reach or travel, leaving elevations that can only be reached by hired equipment.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unit out of service for months, waiting on parts | Control obsolescence. Manufacturer support status; service reports. | Plan control modernisation on the sound structure. |
| Hired equipment used for some elevations | Coverage gap. Façade access strategy against the current façade. | Review the façade access strategy; add a monorail, davits or anchors to cover the gap. |
| Roof perimeter guard set well back from the parapet | Workers exposed at the roof edge while rigging. Guard position, setback and davit handling against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Have the edge protection and rigging arrangements reviewed against the rules that apply. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Structural crack, brake fault, failed safety device, or failed inspection item on equipment carrying people | safety · 4 Essential | Tag out of service immediately; repair before any use. |
| Equipment out of service with façade maintenance stopped; anchors uncertified | failure · 4 Essential | Restore now or arrange alternative access; façade inspections and cleaning depend on it. |
| Periodic inspection or certification due | deadline · 4 Essential | Timing set by the regulation or standard. |
| Corrosion, wear and leaks at fixings without a failed item | condition · 3 Important | Repair in the near term. |
| Controls approaching obsolescence; unit approaching end of structural life | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Plan modernisation or replacement. |
| Unit more than ten years old with no major inspection; coverage of the current façade unknown | check · 3 Important | Major inspection and coverage study. |
| Minor wear in a maintained, certified system | nil · 1 Routine | Routine servicing. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A competent person, usually the maintenance contractor or an independent lifting equipment inspector, carries out periodic and major inspections. A façade access consultant assesses coverage and strategy. The checks below start with the logbook and certificates, which decide whether the equipment can be used at all, then inspect the unit, track and anchors on the roof.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Records review | Logbook, inspection reports, registrations, load tests, maintenance reports. |
| Periodic inspection | Of the structure, mechanisms, ropes, brakes, controls and safety devices at the statutory interval for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). |
| Major inspection | Strip-down and non-destructive testing of welds, slewing ring and highly stressed components, with load testing, at the interval set by the standard or the inspector. |
| Wire rope examination | Against discard criteria. |
| Anchor and davit socket inspection | And proof load testing where required. |
| Coverage study | Mapping the reach of the equipment against the current façade, including additions since installation. |

The report should state whether the equipment is fit for use, defects by priority, the date of the next periodic and major inspection, remaining service life, and any elevations not covered.

sections.heading: Repairing, modernising or replacing
sections.markdown:
Equipment with a failed item, or whose inspection is overdue, is taken out of use first. Most of the rest follows the inspection reports: defects repaired, controls modernised on a sound structure, and the access strategy revised where the façade has changed.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Defect repair | Repair of defects found at inspection; rope replacement; brake and hoist overhaul. | Wherever inspection finds them. |
| Control modernisation | Replace controls and electrical systems on a sound structure. | Often the main mid-life investment. |
| Track and fixing refurbishment | Refurbish the track and fixings, renewing the roof membrane at penetrations. | Where fixings corrode or leak. |
| Unit replacement | A new unit, with crane lift, roof works and recommissioning. | At the end of the unit's structural life. |
| Strategy change | Replace a BMU with davits or rope access anchors where the façade allows, or add a monorail or davits to cover a gap. | Where the equipment no longer suits or covers the façade. |
| Façade restraint | Install restraint points. | Where the cradle has none. |
| Anchor replacement and recertification | Replace or recertify anchors. | Wherever anchors are corroded or uncertified. |
| Records | Restore the logbook, and keep it with the equipment. | Wherever it is missing. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Periodic inspection and servicing are a recurring contract per unit. Major inspections and control modernisation are lump sums. Replacement is a lump sum including crane hire, roof works and commissioning. Where equipment is out of service, hired access (swing stages, rope access or mobile platforms) is a recurring cost for each cleaning and inspection cycle.

Inspection and certification are code compliance; servicing is repairs and maintenance; modernisation and replacement are lifecycle. A major inspection is often the check line that sizes a replacement envelope.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a look at the unit cannot: whether it can lawfully be used, when its structure was last examined in depth, and whether it still reaches every elevation. Ask for them before anyone goes over the edge.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Logbook, current periodic inspection certificate and the last major inspection report | Whether the equipment can lawfully be used, and when its structure was last examined in depth. |
| Plant and design registration and load test records | Whether the design and unit are registered and load tested. |
| Maintenance contract and service reports for the last two years | How often the unit fails, and why. |
| Façade access strategy and any coverage study | Whether the equipment still reaches every elevation. |
| Anchor certification records and the rigging plan | Whether anchors are certified, and how they are to be used. |
| Manufacturer support status for the controls | Whether the controls can still be repaired. |
| Rescue plan for work at height on the façade | How someone would be rescued from the façade. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Façade access equipment is misread when it is judged by how it looks rather than by its records, and when a working unit is assumed to cover the whole façade.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| It looks fine, so it can be used | BMU problems are diagnosed more from records than from sight. The question is less "what is wrong" than "can this equipment be used, and for how long". |
| A working unit covers the façade | Hired equipment used for some elevations points to a coverage gap: the façade access strategy no longer matches the façade. A monorail, davits or anchors can close it. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets design standards for façade access equipment and requires it to be inspected at set intervals. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Design and registration | BMUs are designed to AS 1418.13, and their designs are registrable plant under the work health and safety regulations. | BS 6037-1 covers permanently installed suspended access equipment, and BS EN 1808 the safety requirements for suspended access equipment. | OSHA 29 CFR 1910.66 governs powered platforms for building maintenance; ANSI/IWCA I-14.1 and ASME A120.1 set further requirements for window cleaning and building maintenance platforms. |
| Inspection | AS 2550.13 governs use, inspection and maintenance, and sets the logbook and certificate formats; regulators have issued safety alerts on BMU stability and on major inspections for units more than ten years old. | Equipment lifting people needs a thorough examination at least every six months under the Lifting Operations and Lifting Equipment Regulations 1998, alongside PUWER 1998 and the Work at Height Regulations 2005. | 29 CFR 1910.27 requires rope descent anchorages to be inspected annually and certified at least every ten years. |

sections.heading: Worked example: a unit that has never had a major inspection
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 1990s office tower has a track-mounted BMU. Its periodic inspections are current, but it has never had a major inspection. Its controls have failed twice this year, each time leaving it out of service for months while parts were found, and window cleaning on one elevation now uses hired equipment.

BMU problems are diagnosed more from records than from sight. A unit of this age with no major inspection has a hidden structural condition that is unknown. The long outages point to control obsolescence, and the hired equipment to a gap in the access strategy.

So the register carries a major inspection as a check line now, control modernisation on the sound structure as a lifecycle line if the inspection supports it, and a review of the access strategy for the elevation the unit no longer serves.

thresholds.rule: Supporting building structure: at intervals not exceeding 12 months; equipment: at the manufacturer’s intervals, not exceeding 12 months

source.title: 1910.66 Powered platforms for building maintenance

thresholds.rule: Guard no more than 152 mm (6 in) inboard of the parapet or curb; setback no more than 457 mm (18 in); davits over 36 kg moved with their centre of gravity at or below 914 mm

pages.title: Building Management & Control System (BMCS)
pages.question: How do building management systems fail, how do you assess one, and when does obsolescence or cyber exposure force replacement?
pages.answer: A BMS fails quietly. Controllers and software lose vendor support; sensors drift; operators put points in manual and they stay there, so plant runs nights and weekends; sequences no longer fit the building; alarms are suppressed. Proprietary systems lock owners to one contractor. Internet-exposed systems with default passwords are a security risk. Assess a BMS by its trend data and overrides, not its hardware.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about building management & control system (bmcs); it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Central server, software, field controllers, sensors

sources.title: DA28 Building Management and Control Systems
CIBSE Guide H: Building control systems
Standard 135 BACnet
Industrial control systems
ISO 16484-1:2024 Building automation and control systems (BACS), Part 1
Approved Document F, Volume 2: Buildings other than dwellings

pages.searchTitle: Building management systems: overrides, drifted sensors, obsolescence and cyber risk

questions.question: Why does the plant run at night?
questions.answer: Usually schedules that have been overridden or lost. Trend data shows it, and recommissioning restores them.

questions.question: Is a sensor that reads the same value for weeks working?
questions.answer: Usually not. Sensors that read the same value for weeks are usually failed rather than steady.

questions.question: Is it a problem if only one contractor can work on our BMS?
questions.answer: Yes. Secure the licences, programs and passwords for the owner, and specify open protocols at the next upgrade.

questions.question: Should the BMS be reachable from the internet?
questions.answer: Not directly. Remove internet exposure, use secure remote access, and change default credentials.

questions.question: How long does a BMS last?
questions.answer: Head end hardware 5 to 8 years and software 5 to 10 before a major upgrade; plant controllers 15 to 20, and sensors 10 to 15 with calibration.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
BMS problems show at the head end as alarms, overrides and old versions, in the plant as disconnected actuators and night running, and in the records as missing documentation. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| At the head end | Software and operating system versions | Obsolescence, hardware and ownership |
| At the head end | Alarm list: number of active and suppressed alarms | Overrides, sequences and sensors |
| At the head end | Points in manual override | Overrides, sequences and sensors |
| At the head end | Trend data availability | Overrides, sequences and sensors |
| At the head end | Graphics matching the plant | Obsolescence, hardware and ownership |
| At the head end | Remote access arrangements and passwords | Cyber security |
| In the field | Controller models and ages; labels | Obsolescence, hardware and ownership |
| In the field | Sensors damaged, missing or in poor locations | Overrides, sequences and sensors |
| In the field | Actuators disconnected or held by cable ties | Overrides, sequences and sensors |
| In the building | Plant running at night and weekends | Overrides, sequences and sensors |
| In the building | Comfort complaints | Overrides, sequences and sensors |
| In the building | Energy use higher than benchmarks | Overrides, sequences and sensors |
| In the records | Points list, control narratives, network diagrams, as-built drawings | Investigation before the scope |
| In the records | Maintenance contract and contractor | Obsolescence, hardware and ownership |
| In the records | Software licences | Obsolescence, hardware and ownership |
| In the records | Calibration records | Overrides, sequences and sensors |
| In the records | Penetration tests or security assessments | Cyber security |
| In the records | No current backup of controller programs or the head end | Obsolescence, hardware and ownership |
| In the records | Licences and passwords held only by the contractor | Obsolescence, hardware and ownership |
| In the records | Several separate BMS in one building from different eras or tenants | Obsolescence, hardware and ownership |

sections.heading: Types of control system
sections.markdown:
A building management system (BMS, also called a building automation system) monitors and controls the building's mechanical plant and often lighting, metering, hydraulics and interfaces to fire, lifts and security. It is layered: a head end (server, software and operator workstations, now often cloud-hosted), a network, field controllers (direct digital controllers) in plant rooms and on floors, and sensors and actuators at the equipment. Its value lies in the control sequences it runs, the data it holds, and the people who can use it.

| Layer | What it includes | What goes wrong |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Head end | Server, software, graphics, alarms, trend logging | Unsupported operating systems and software; lost licences; single-vendor lock-in |
| Network | IP backbone, field buses (BACnet, Modbus, LonWorks, proprietary) | Old field buses; insecure connections to the internet |
| Field controllers | Plant controllers, unitary controllers on terminal units | Obsolescence; parts unavailable; proprietary programming |
| Sensors | Temperature, humidity, CO₂, pressure, flow, energy meters | Drift; failure; poor location |
| Actuators and outputs | Valve and damper actuators, drives, relays | Failure; overridden; disconnected |
| Integrations | Fire, lifts, lighting, metering, security, tenant systems | Undocumented; broken after changes |

Open protocols (BACnet in particular) allow equipment from different manufacturers to work together and allow more than one contractor to service the system. Many older systems are proprietary, so only one contractor can maintain or extend them, and that contractor sets the price of every change.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
A BMS ages at different speeds: head end hardware lasts five to eight years and its software five to ten before a major upgrade, while plant controllers last fifteen to twenty and sensors ten to fifteen with calibration. Vendor support, not wear, usually ends its life.

| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Head end software | 5 to 10 years before major upgrade | Operating system and vendor support |
| Head end hardware | 5 to 8 years | IT refresh |
| Plant controllers | 15 to 20 years | Vendor support; parts |
| Unitary controllers | 10 to 15 years | Vendor support |
| Sensors | 10 to 15 years with calibration | Drift; type |
| Actuators | 10 to 15 years | Use |
| Network infrastructure | 10 to 15 years | Protocol support |

What shortens life: vendor end of support for controllers and software; proprietary lock-in, which raises the cost of every repair and extension; lost documentation: points lists, control narratives, network diagrams; no calibration of sensors; cyber exposure that forces urgent replacement.

sections.heading: Overrides, sequences and sensors
sections.markdown:
Operators put points in manual to deal with complaints or faults, and they stay there. Plants run 24 hours because schedules were overridden; valves are held open; alarms are suppressed. Over time the building runs on overrides rather than sequences.

Sequences written for the original design no longer fit after fit-outs and plant changes; they were often never fully commissioned. Heating and cooling fight; outside air is wrong; chillers and boilers stage poorly.

Temperature, humidity, carbon dioxide and pressure sensors drift over years; a supply air sensor reading two degrees low makes the chiller work harder all year. Failed sensors default to values that hide the problem.

Trend logging is not set up, history is lost, meters are not connected. Without data, faults cannot be diagnosed and energy cannot be managed.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Plant running at night | Schedules overridden or lost. Schedule review; trends. | Restore the schedules and release the overrides. |
| Many points in manual | Workarounds for faults. Point list. | Fix the faults behind the overrides, then release them. |
| Hundreds of suppressed alarms | Alarm fatigue. Alarm list. | Rationalise the alarms so the real ones are seen. |
| Energy high despite modern plant | Poor sequences or drifted sensors. Trends; calibration. | Recommission: calibrate sensors and rewrite sequences to current loads. |
| Carbon dioxide trends that never move | Failed or uncalibrated sensor. Spot reading against the trend: outdoor air is around 400 ppm, and occupied spaces read higher. | Calibrate or replace the sensor, and check the ventilation it controls. |

sections.heading: Obsolescence, hardware and ownership
sections.markdown:
Controllers and software become unsupported: no spare parts, no security patches, no engineers who know the programming. Head ends running on unsupported operating systems are common. A single controller failure can then take plant out of automatic control for weeks.

Controller power supplies and batteries fail, losing programs or clocks; network switches and gateways fail; head end servers fail without backups. Without current backups of controller programs, recovery means reprogramming from scratch.

Programming tools, software licences, controller programs and administrator passwords are often held by the installing contractor rather than the owner. Changing contractor then means paying for access to the owner's own system, or replacing it.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Only one contractor can work on it | Proprietary system. Protocol and licensing. | Secure the licences, programs and passwords; specify open protocols at the next upgrade. |

sections.heading: Cyber security
sections.markdown:
BMS connected to the internet for remote access, with default passwords and unpatched software, can be found and controlled by attackers. Building systems have been used as entry points into corporate networks. National cyber security agencies publish guidance on securing building control systems.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| BMS reachable from the internet | Insecure remote access. Security assessment. | Remove direct internet exposure; secure remote access and change default credentials. |

sections.heading: Integration with fire and other systems
sections.markdown:
Interfaces to fire systems (for smoke mode and plant shutdown), lifts and metering are undocumented and break when either side changes. The first sign may be a failed fire test.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Air handling units keep running during a fire alarm test | Fire interface broken. Integrated test from the fire panel with the BMS logging each output. | Repair the interface, update the cause-and-effect matrix, and retest jointly with the fire contractor. |
| Meters and other systems missing from the BMS since an upgrade | Integration lost when one side changed. Points list against the field devices; protocol and gateway versions. | Reinstate the integration, and document it so the next change does not break it. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| BMS exposed to the internet with default credentials; fire interface failing | safety · 4 Essential | Isolate and secure now; test fire interfaces. |
| Head end or controllers failed, plant uncontrolled | failure · 3 Important | Restore now. |
| Unsupported controllers and software; drifted sensors; overrides | condition · 3 Important | Upgrade and recommission in the near term. |
| System at end of support | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Plan replacement, preferably open protocol. |
| No documentation or security assessment | check · 2 Planned | Audit. |
| Normal maintenance | nil · 1 Routine | Routine. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A controls engineer leads, independent of the incumbent contractor where possible, with a cyber security specialist for any system with remote access. The checks below start with several weeks of trend data, then the alarm list, overrides and controller versions, and finally who holds the licences and passwords.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Inventory | Of the head end, network devices, controllers, sensors and actuators, with manufacturer, model, firmware and software versions, and vendor support status. |
| Trend analysis | Over at least several weeks: plant start and stop times against occupancy, setpoints, simultaneous heating and cooling, outside air, chilled and hot water temperatures, chiller and boiler staging. |
| Override and alarm review | Points in manual, suppressed and standing alarms, and why. |
| Sensor calibration | Of key points (supply air, chilled water, outside air temperature and humidity, CO₂, static pressure, flow) against reference instruments. |
| Functional testing | Command actuators and confirm response at the equipment. |
| Documentation review | Points list, control narratives, network diagrams, as-built drawings, backups. |
| Ownership review | Who holds licences, programming tools, source programs and passwords. |
| Cyber security assessment | Remote access paths, internet exposure, credentials, patch levels, segmentation from corporate networks. |
| Integration testing | With fire (smoke mode, plant shutdown), lifts, metering and lighting. |

The report should give the support status of each layer, the operating faults found in the trends, the security position, the integration status, and a migration plan: recommission, upgrade in stages, or replace.

sections.heading: Recommissioning, upgrading or migrating
sections.markdown:
Recommissioning comes first and is often the best value: releasing overrides, restoring schedules and calibrating sensors. Upgrades and migration follow for unsupported systems, specified so that the owner holds the licences, programs and passwords.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Recommissioning | Release overrides, restore schedules, calibrate sensors, retune and rewrite sequences to current loads, rationalise alarms. Often the best value of any building services work. | First, wherever trends show overrides, lost schedules or drifted sensors. |
| Head end upgrade | Supported software and hardware, with proper backups. | Where the head end is unsupported. |
| Staged migration | Replace controllers plant by plant with open-protocol controllers, using gateways to keep old and new working together during the transition, rather than a single change-over. | Where controllers are unsupported and the plant cannot all change at once. |
| Specification | Specify the new system around open protocols, owner ownership of licences, programs and passwords, documentation deliverables and training, so that any competent contractor can service it. | Before any new system is bought. |
| Cyber security hardening | Remove direct internet exposure, use secure remote access, change default credentials, patch, segment the building network from corporate IT, log access. | Wherever the BMS can be reached from outside. |
| Analytics | Fault detection and diagnostics that read BMS data and flag faults automatically. | Where faults go unnoticed. |
| Integration repair | Repair and test integration with fire and other systems, documented. | Wherever interfaces fail their tests. |
| Documentation | Points lists, narratives and network diagrams brought up to date. | Wherever points lists, narratives or network diagrams are out of date. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Audits and trend analysis are lump sums. Recommissioning is priced per system or per plant item. Controller replacement is priced per controller or per point, with field wiring, sensors, actuators and programming. A head end upgrade is a lump sum. Analytics is a recurring subscription. Cyber hardening is a lump sum with recurring monitoring.

Replacement and staged migration are lifecycle; recommissioning and calibration are repairs and maintenance; cyber hardening and fire interface rectification are risk or code compliance driven. The usual shape is two-part: an audit first, then a migration envelope sized from it.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what the hardware cannot: how the plant actually runs, whether the owner can maintain the system without one contractor, and whether it is secure. Ask for several weeks of trend data first.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Points list, control narratives and network diagrams | What the system controls, and how it is meant to. |
| Head end, controller and firmware versions, with vendor support status | Whether the head end and controllers are still supported. |
| Backups of controller programs and the head end | Whether programs could be restored after a failure. |
| Who holds licences, programming tools and passwords | Whether the owner can use another contractor. |
| Maintenance contract and scope | What the contractor maintains, and what is excluded. |
| Several weeks of trend data for key plant | How the plant actually runs, night and day. |
| Any cyber security assessment or penetration test | Whether the system is secure. |
| Fire and lift interface test records | Whether fire and lift interfaces work. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
A BMS is misread when it is judged by its hardware rather than by what it does, and when a steady reading is taken as the sign of a working sensor.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| Inspect the hardware | A BMS is assessed by what it does, not what it is. Trend data over a few weeks usually reveals more than an inspection of the hardware. |
| A steady reading is a good reading | Sensors that read the same value for weeks are usually failed rather than steady. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market has guidance on specifying building controls, and increasingly treats control performance and cyber security as matters of compliance. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Guidance and specification | AIRAH DA28 is the industry guide to building management and control systems. | CIBSE Guide H covers building control systems; BSRIA publishes BMS specification and commissioning guidance. | ASHRAE 135 defines BACnet, ASHRAE Guideline 13 guides specifying building automation systems, and Guideline 36 sets high-performance sequences. |
| Security and performance | NABERS Energy ratings depend heavily on control performance; the Australian Signals Directorate's Australian Cyber Security Centre publishes guidance on operational technology security that applies to building systems; fire interfaces are tested as part of essential safety measures. | BS EN ISO 16484 covers building automation and control; the National Cyber Security Centre publishes operational technology guidance. | CISA publishes guidance on securing building and industrial control systems; building performance standards make control performance a compliance matter. |

sections.heading: Worked example: modern plant, high energy
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 2000s office has modern plant but energy use well above benchmarks. Trend data shows the air handling units running every night, 40 points held in manual, several temperature sensors reading the same value for weeks, and more than 300 suppressed alarms. Only the original contractor holds the passwords.

The trends say more than the hardware. Plant running at night points to lost or overridden schedules; points in manual are workarounds for faults; sensors that never change are usually failed, not steady; and suppressed alarms mean real faults go unseen. Passwords held only by the contractor are an ownership finding in their own right.

So the register carries recommissioning as a condition line, releasing overrides, restoring schedules, replacing failed sensors and rationalising alarms, and securing the licences, programs and passwords for the owner.

pages.title: Canopies & Awnings
pages.question: How do awnings and canopies fail, what are the warning signs, and when is an awning over a footpath unsafe?
pages.answer: Tied street awnings fail at the anchorages where their rods enter the masonry: corrosion inside the wall, cracked soft brick around the plate, then pull-out that can cascade along the frontage. A sagging fascia, one slack rod among taut ones, or rust bleeding where a rod enters the wall means closing the footpath. Blocked box gutters cause ponding collapse. Visual soundness of the frame does not clear the hidden anchorages.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about canopies & awnings; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
