pages.searchTitle: Shop awnings and canopies: slack tie rods, hidden anchorages, ponding and glass

questions.question: Is a sagging shop awning dangerous?
questions.answer: It can be. A tied awning over a footpath with any visible sag, slack rod or cracked anchorage is a public safety matter.

questions.question: Why is one awning rod slack?
questions.answer: Its anchorage has moved, or the rod has failed. Cracked masonry at that anchorage points to the anchorage.

questions.question: Do old awnings need inspecting?
questions.answer: In New South Wales, planning guidance advises that awnings over ten years old warrant inspection, and councils may require engineer certification.

questions.question: Can an awning be converted so it no longer relies on rods?
questions.answer: Yes. New beams fixed back into the floor structure turn it into a cantilever, so it no longer depends on ties.

questions.question: How long do awning tie rods last?
questions.answer: Tie rods, turnbuckles and clevises 30 to 60 years, as do their anchorages in masonry; the steel frame lasts 40 to 70.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Awning problems show from the street as a sagging fascia, slack rods and cracked masonry at anchorages, and close up at rods, fittings, gutters and glass. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Street or aerial | Fascia line sagging, out of level or stepped along the frontage | Ponding, cantilevers and posts |
| Street or aerial | Tie rods slack, bent, missing or at different angles; turnbuckles visibly adjusted on some rods and not others | Anchorages and tie rods |
| Street or aerial | Rust staining and cracking in the masonry where rods enter the wall | Anchorages and tie rods |
| Street or aerial | Signs, plant or lighting on or under the awning; evidence of people walking on the roof | Ponding, cantilevers and posts |
| Street or aerial | Vegetation, debris or ponding visible on the awning roof in aerial imagery; staining from overflowing gutters | Ponding, cantilevers and posts |
| Street or aerial | Damaged or leaning posts; soffit linings stained, sagging or missing | Ponding, cantilevers and posts |
| Close up on site | Rod condition at threads and fittings; section loss | Anchorages and tie rods |
| Close up on site | Masonry around anchorages: cracked, loose, previously repaired | Anchorages and tie rods |
| Close up on site | Anchorage plates inside the building where accessible, behind linings or in ceiling spaces | Anchorages and tie rods |
| Close up on site | Frame connections and fascia corrosion; gutter condition and outlet size | Ponding, cantilevers and posts |
| Close up on site | Glass canopy fittings: corrosion, missing caps, glass type markings | Glass canopies |
| In the records | Council awning inspection notices and engineer's certificates, with dates | Standards by country |
| In the records | Previous structural repairs, rod replacements or propping | Anchorages and tie rods |
| In the records | Gutter cleaning records | Ponding, cantilevers and posts |
| In the records | Approvals for signage on the awning | Ponding, cantilevers and posts |

sections.heading: Types of awning and canopy
sections.markdown:
Canopies and awnings are roofed projections from a façade that shelter entrances, footpaths, shopfronts and loading docks. Many project over public land, which makes their failures public safety failures, and the classic Australian street awning has a failure mode that is entirely hidden inside the wall.

| Form | Where it is found | How it is held up |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tied street awning | Retail strips and main streets, late nineteenth century to about the 1960s, Australia especially | Steel frame cantilevered from the façade, hung from tie rods angled up to anchorages in the wall above |
| Cantilevered awning | Retail and mixed use from the mid twentieth century | Steel or concrete beams fixed back into the structure with no ties; relies on the back-span and connection |
| Post-supported verandah awning | Heritage shopping streets | Posts at the kerb carrying a beam; posts in the footpath |
| Entrance canopy | Offices, apartments, institutions | Steel, concrete or glass, cantilevered or suspended on rods or cables |
| Glass canopy | Entrances from the 1990s | Laminated glass on point fixings or brackets, often with suspension rods |
| Loading dock canopy | Industrial and logistics | Steel portal extension or cantilever with sheet roof |
| Fabric and retractable awnings | Retail and hospitality | Frame and fabric; mechanical arms |

A tied awning carries its load through the tie rods into anchorages built into the masonry above: a plate, a bolt through the wall, or a hook built into a pier. The anchorage is inside the wall or behind internal finishes, it is often corroded, and the masonry around it is often old lime-mortared brick. The awning roof hides box gutters that, when blocked, add a large water load.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
A steel awning frame lasts forty to seventy years, but its tie rods, fittings and anchorages in masonry last thirty to sixty, roof sheeting and gutters twenty to forty, and fabric eight to fifteen. The anchorages decide an awning's strength, and they are hidden in the wall.

| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Steel awning frame | 40 to 70 years | Paint cycle; water at connections |
| Tie rods, turnbuckles and clevises | 30 to 60 years | Corrosion at threads and where rods enter the wall |
| Anchorages in masonry | 30 to 60 years | Water reaching the anchorage; masonry condition |
| Roof sheeting and box gutters | 20 to 40 years | Maintenance of gutters; coastal exposure |
| Soffit linings (pressed metal, fibre cement, timber) | 20 to 50 years | Water from above; hazardous materials in older linings |
| Glass canopy fittings | 25 to 40 years | Stainless grade; sealant at fittings |
| Fabric | 8 to 15 years | UV; wind damage |

What shortens life: blocked gutters on the awning roof, which add a water load the frame was never designed for and keep connections wet; added loads: illuminated signs, air conditioning units, people walking on the roof to reach signage or windows; water at the wall line through failed flashings, running down to the anchorages; vehicle impact on posts and low fascias; façade alterations that cut into the masonry around anchorages, or new shopfronts that remove the pier an anchorage sits in; coastal exposure and road salt in colder climates.

sections.heading: Anchorages and tie rods
sections.markdown:
The tie rod passes through or into the wall to a plate or hook. Water running down the façade reaches the point where the rod enters the wall and corrodes the rod and anchorage inside the masonry, out of sight. The masonry around the anchorage, often soft brick in lime mortar, cracks and loosens. When an anchorage pulls out or a rod snaps, the load transfers to neighbouring rods; if they are in similar condition, the failure progresses along the awning. The fatal Bathurst collapse in 1998 and later collapses in New South Wales followed this pattern.

Rods corrode at threads, turnbuckles and clevis pins, where section is thinnest and water sits. A rod that has lost tension because its anchorage has moved, or that has been adjusted to take up sag, signals a problem elsewhere.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| One slack rod among taut ones | Anchorage moved or rod failed. Masonry cracked at that anchorage; rod pulls out or turns freely. | Prop it, or close the footpath below; replace the anchorage and rod. |
| Local dip at one bay | Failed rod, anchorage or frame connection at that bay. Inspection of that bay's rod and fixings. | Prop that bay; repair the rod, anchorage or frame connection. |
| Rust bleeding from the wall at rod entry points | Anchorage corrosion inside the wall. Opening up exposes the plate or hook. | Open up the anchorage; replace it with through-bolted plates or chemical anchors into sound masonry. |
| Street awning more than ten years old with no engineer’s report | Structural adequacy unknown. Age and inspection record against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Commission an engineer’s inspection, opening up the tie-rod anchorages. |

sections.heading: Ponding, cantilevers and posts
sections.markdown:
A blocked box gutter turns the awning roof into a tank. The water load deflects the frame, deflection holds more water, and the awning can collapse in a single storm. Signs, plant and people on the roof add load the original design did not allow for.

Cantilevered awnings depend on the connection to the structure: bolts into a slab edge or beams built into the wall with a back-span inside. Corrosion of bolts, spalling of the slab edge, or decay of the back-span lets the awning rotate.

Posts at the kerb on post-supported awnings are struck by vehicles and corrode at the footpath line, where water and salt collect.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Uniform sag along the fascia | Connection rotation at the wall or general overload. All rods equally stretched; cracking along the wall line; added signage or water load. | Prop the awning; have an engineer assess the connections and loads. |
| Staining from the gutter line, deflection worst after rain | Blocked box gutter and ponding. Gutter full of debris; outlets undersized or blocked. | Clear the gutter; renew it with larger outlets and overflows. |
| Signage, plant or people now on an awning roof | Loads beyond what the awning was built for. Load check against the design actions: NSW structural engineers’ guidance applies 1.5 kPa with a 1.8 kN point load to awnings reachable from windows, roofs or balconies, and 1.0 kPa with 1.8 kN where access is only from the ground; older awnings were designed for as little as 0.25 kPa and 1.4 kN (Practice Note 18). | Remove the added load or keep people off; have an engineer check the awning for any load that must stay. |

sections.heading: Glass canopies
sections.markdown:
Point fittings and suspension rods corrode or loosen; glass breaks from impact, thermal stress or nickel sulphide inclusions where toughened glass is used without lamination.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Glass canopy panel cracked with no impact | Thermal stress or nickel sulphide inclusion. Glass type; fracture origin. | Make the area below safe; replace with laminated glass. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sag, slack or failed rod, cracked anchorage, damaged post, or glass breakage over a footpath or entrance | safety · 4 Essential | Close the footpath below or prop immediately; engineer within days. |
| Ponding on the roof with deflection | failure · 4 Essential | Clear and relieve the load now; engineer to assess. |
| Rod and frame corrosion without movement; cracked masonry around anchorages without displacement | condition · 2 Planned | Repair in the near term. |
| Roof sheeting, gutters and linings at age | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Renewal on cycle. |
| Council notice requiring certification | deadline · 3 Important | Timing set by the council. |
| Tied awning more than ten years old with no engineer's certificate on record | check · 2 Planned | Structural inspection with opening up of anchorages. |
| Fabric wear, minor coating wear | nil · 1 Routine | Routine care. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A structural engineer inspects every awning. For tied awnings, the method set out in Practice Note 18 of the Association of Consulting Structural Engineers of New South Wales, attached to NSW Planning Circular BS 13-001, is the benchmark: staged inspection, opening up, assessment, rectification and certification. The checks below read the fascia line and the rods from the street, then open up the anchorages, since a sound-looking frame does not clear them.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Visual inspection | Of the whole frame, every rod and fitting, the roof and gutters, and the soffit. |
| Opening up | Of every anchorage, or a representative sample where the same detail repeats, to expose the plate, bolt or hook inside the wall. |
| Masonry assessment | Around anchorages: mortar strength, cracking, the pier's capacity. |
| Measurement | Of fascia level and rod tension, recorded for comparison. |
| Load capacity check | Including signage, plant and any public access onto the roof, against 1.5 kPa where the awning can be reached from windows or balconies and 1.0 kPa where it cannot (Practice Note 18). |
| Glass canopies | Fitting inspection, glass identification, and assessment of post-breakage behaviour. |

The report should certify the awning as structurally adequate, or list the rectification needed and any propping or closure until it is done.

sections.heading: Propping, re-anchoring or replacing
sections.markdown:
Any awning over a footpath with sag, a slack rod or a cracked anchorage is propped, or the area below closed, first. Then the anchorages and rods are renewed, or the awning converted to a cantilever so it no longer depends on ties, or replaced where frame and anchorages are both at the end of their life.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Anchorage replacement | New through-bolted plates or chemical anchors into sound masonry, or a new anchorage in the floor structure where the masonry is poor. | Wherever anchorages have moved, cracked or corroded. |
| Rod replacement | New rods and fittings, galvanised or stainless. | Where rods are slack, bent or corroded. |
| Conversion to cantilever | New beams fixed back into the floor structure, so the awning no longer depends on ties. | Where the ties and anchorages cannot be relied on. |
| Frame repair | Treat corrosion, replace sections, and repaint. | Where the frame corrodes. |
| Roof and gutter renewal | Larger outlets and overflows, with debris and added loads removed. | Where water ponds on the awning roof. |
| Replacement | A new awning. | Where the frame and anchorages are both at the end of their life. |
| Glass canopies | Replace monolithic toughened glass with laminated glass, and renew fittings. | Wherever glass canopies use monolithic toughened glass, or fittings corrode. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Inspection is priced per awning, with opening up and making good as rates. Works are priced per awning bay or per linear metre of frontage, with anchorage replacement per anchorage. Footpath closure permits, traffic control, out-of-hours work and propping add materially. Certification recurs where a council regime applies.

Two-part lines are normal: inspection with opening up, then conditional rectification. Certification is code compliance; repairs are repairs and maintenance; replacement is lifecycle; propping and closure are immediate.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a look from the street cannot: whether the awning has been certified by an engineer, what has been repaired, and what has been added to it. Ask for them before relying on its appearance.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Engineer's certificates for the awning, current and previous | Whether an engineer has certified the awning, and when. |
| Council notices, approvals and correspondence | Whether the council has required anything. |
| Drawings of the awning and its anchorages | Where the anchorages are, and how the awning is held up. |
| Repair, rod replacement and propping records | What has been repaired, replaced or propped. |
| Gutter cleaning records | Whether the gutters are kept clear. |
| Approvals for signs and plant on the awning | Whether signs and plant on the awning were approved. |
| Records of people accessing the awning roof | Whether people walk on the awning roof. |
| Insurance notes on the awning | Whether the insurer has noted the awning. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Awnings are misread when a sound-looking frame is taken to mean a sound awning, and when the awning roof is treated as somewhere loads can be added freely.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| The frame looks sound | A tied awning over a footpath with any visible sag, slack rod or cracking at an anchorage is a public safety matter. The anchorages that decide its strength are hidden, and visual soundness of the frame does not clear them. |
| Anything can go on the awning roof | Signs, plant and people on the awning roof, and water ponding in a blocked gutter, add loads the awning was not designed for. Remove debris and added loads. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets design standards for awnings, requires approval for structures over the footpath or highway, and in some places periodic certification. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Design | Design follows AS/NZS 1170 for actions, AS 4100 for steel and AS 1288 for glass. | Design follows Approved Document A and the Eurocodes. | International Building Code Section 3105 governs awnings and canopies, with loads to ASCE 7. |
| Approval and inspection | NSW Planning Circular BS 13-001 records repeated awning collapses in New South Wales since 1998, advises that awnings over ten years old warrant inspection, and notes that councils may require engineer certification; several councils, including Wagga Wagga, run awning policies with periodic certification. Awnings over public land usually need council approval under local government legislation. | Structures over the highway need consent under the Highways Act 1980; the owner's duty of care to the public falls under the Occupiers' Liability Act 1957. | Façade ordinances in New York, Chicago and other cities include canopies, marquees and appurtenances in the periodic examination. |

sections.heading: Worked example: one slack rod on a shopfront awning
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 1920s shopfront awning over a busy footpath hangs from tie rods anchored into the brick wall above. One rod is slack while the others are taut, the masonry around its anchorage is cracked, and the fascia dips slightly at that bay. There is no engineer's certificate on record.

One slack rod among taut ones points to an anchorage that has moved or a rod that has failed, and the cracked masonry points to the anchorage. A tied awning over a footpath with a slack rod is a public safety matter; the hidden anchorages decide its strength.

So the register carries the awning as a safety line now, with the bay propped or the footpath below closed, opening up the anchorages as a check line, and new anchorages and rods, or conversion to a cantilever, with an engineer's certificate.

thresholds.measure: Awnings over public footways (New South Wales)
thresholds.rule: Awnings more than 10 years old inspected by a structural engineer

source.title: Planning Circular BS 13-001 Safety of awnings over public lands

pages.title: Central Cooling Plant
pages.question: How do chillers and central cooling plant fail, how do you read their operating data, and when does refrigerant rather than wear end their life?
pages.answer: Chillers often reach the end of their economic life on refrigerant before wear: R22 and R123 are almost gone, and HFCs are being phased down. Mechanically, condenser tubes foul without good water treatment, evaporator tubes rupture if flow fails, hermetic motors burn out and contaminate the circuit, and drives and controls lose parts support early. Rising approach temperatures, refrigerant top-ups and high purge run time are the early signs. Low delta T looks like a chiller problem but starts in the building.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about central cooling plant; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.

pages.searchTitle: Chillers and central cooling plant: refrigerant, tubes, low delta T and replacement

questions.question: Do we need a new chiller?
questions.answer: Not necessarily. Low delta T, failed valves and fouled coils produce the same symptoms at the plant as a failing chiller, and replacing the chiller will not fix them.

questions.question: Why does the chiller need refrigerant at every service?
questions.answer: It has a leak. A leak test locates it; repair it rather than topping up.

questions.question: What is low delta T?
questions.answer: Chilled water returning too cold from the building, usually from failed valves, three-way valves, bypasses or fouled coils. It forces more chillers and pumps to run than the load needs.

questions.question: Can an old chiller's refrigerant be changed?
questions.answer: Sometimes. Conversion to a lower-GWP alternative is possible where the manufacturer supports it for that machine.

questions.question: How long do chillers last?
questions.answer: Water-cooled centrifugal chillers 20 to 30 years, screw and absorption chillers 20 to 25, and air-cooled chillers 15 to 20.

questions.question: Why can't the air conditioning keep up on very hot days?
questions.answer: On an air-cooled chiller, usually corroded or fouled condenser coils, or hot air recirculating. Clean or recoat the coils, and clear anything that recirculates hot air.

questions.question: Why does the chiller trip out in hot weather?
questions.answer: Often the drive or starter overheating or failing. Check the fault log and switchroom temperature; improve cooling to the switchroom and plan drive replacement before parts run out.

questions.question: Why are all the chillers and pumps running when the building isn't busy?
questions.answer: Low delta T in the building, so the chillers cannot load. Fix the distribution: failed valves, three-way valves and bypasses, and fouled coils.

questions.question: Why is the chiller making a surging noise at quiet times?
questions.answer: An oversized centrifugal machine surging at low load. Review the load profile; a variable speed drive or a smaller machine suits light loads.

questions.question: The chiller works but the manufacturer no longer supports its control panel. What now?
questions.answer: Obsolete controls can strand a sound chiller. Get the support position in writing and plan a controls retrofit, keeping the machine if it is otherwise sound.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Cooling plant problems show in the plant room as leaks and wear, in the operating data as rising approaches and low delta T, in the building on hot afternoons, and in the records. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| In the plant room | Nameplates: manufacturer, model, serial, year and refrigerant. Year and refrigerant together fix most of the position | Refrigerant obsolescence and leaks |
| In the plant room | Oil stains under compressors and at fittings; refrigerant leak detector alarms; the smell of oil | Refrigerant obsolescence and leaks |
| In the plant room | Corrosion and condensation on chilled water pipework; damaged insulation | Low delta T and pumps |
| In the plant room | Pump seals weeping; noisy bearings; vibration on base frames | Low delta T and pumps |
| In the plant room | Number of chillers and pumps running against the load at the time | Low delta T and pumps |
| In the plant room | Plant room heat, ventilation, housekeeping, and refrigerant detection and alarm equipment | Refrigerant obsolescence and leaks |
| In operating data | Condenser approach (refrigerant condensing temperature minus leaving condenser water temperature) rising over time | Tubes, compressors and condensers |
| In operating data | Evaporator approach rising | Tubes, compressors and condensers |
| In operating data | Chilled water supply temperature drifting up on hot afternoons | Low delta T and pumps |
| In operating data | Low chilled water delta T across the building | Low delta T and pumps |
| In operating data | High purge run time on low-pressure machines | Refrigerant obsolescence and leaks |
| In operating data | Energy per unit of cooling rising | Tubes, compressors and condensers |
| In the building | Comfort complaints concentrated on hot afternoons | Low delta T and pumps |
| In the building | More chillers running than the load warrants | Low delta T and pumps |
| In the building | Temporary chillers hired in summer | Low delta T and pumps |
| In the records | Service reports with recurring faults and deferred recommendations | Investigation before the scope |
| In the records | Refrigerant log: additions and leak tests | Refrigerant obsolescence and leaks |
| In the records | Oil analysis, vibration analysis and eddy current tube test results | Tubes, compressors and condensers |
| In the records | Overhaul history against run hours | Tubes, compressors and condensers |
| In the records | Energy ratings and consumption trends | Standards by country |

sections.heading: Types of chiller
sections.markdown:
Central cooling plant produces chilled water for a whole building or campus: one or more chillers, their primary pumps, the chilled water pipework in the plant room, and the controls that sequence them. It works with the heat rejection plant (cooling towers, dry coolers or air-cooled condensers, which have their own page) and the air handling and terminal units that deliver the cooling to spaces.

| Type | Where it is found | Character |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Water-cooled centrifugal | Large offices, hospitals, campuses; 1960s onward | Most efficient at full load; surge at low load on older fixed-speed machines; longest life |
| Oil-free magnetic-bearing centrifugal | Retrofits and new plant from the 2000s | Excellent part-load efficiency; electronics-dependent; fewer mechanical wear parts |
| Water-cooled screw | Mid-size commercial and industrial | Robust; good part-load with variable speed; oil management matters |
| Air-cooled screw or scroll | Smaller offices, retail, apartments, where towers are unwanted | No cooling tower; condenser coils outdoors set the life |
| Absorption (lithium bromide) | Sites with waste heat or cheap gas; hospitals, tri-generation | Crystallisation and corrosion risks; vacuum must be maintained |
| Heat pump and heat recovery chillers | Electrification projects from the 2010s | Produce heating and cooling; replace boilers as well as chillers |
| Reciprocating | Older plant, 1970s to 1990s | Mostly replaced; spares scarce |

Distribution arrangements matter as much as the machines. Constant primary systems run fixed flow through each chiller. Primary-secondary systems decouple chiller flow from building flow through a bypass. Variable primary systems vary flow through the chillers themselves. Each has its own way of going wrong, and most chilled water problems that look like chiller problems start in the distribution system or at the coils.

Plant capacity is sized for a design load that may no longer exist. Tenancy changes, more efficient lighting, higher occupant densities, data rooms and longer hours all move the load, so a plant can be both old and wrongly sized.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Water-cooled centrifugal chillers last twenty to thirty years and air-cooled machines fifteen to twenty, while pumps last fifteen to twenty-five and their starters and drives ten to twenty. Refrigerant rules often end a machine's useful life before wear does.

| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Water-cooled centrifugal chiller | 20 to 30 years | Water treatment; overhaul history; refrigerant |
| Water-cooled screw chiller | 20 to 25 years | Oil management; run hours |
| Air-cooled chiller | 15 to 20 years | Condenser coil corrosion, especially near the coast |
| Absorption chiller | 20 to 25 years | Vacuum integrity; corrosion inhibitor |
| Primary pumps | 15 to 25 years; seals and bearings 5 to 10 | Run hours; alignment; water quality |
| Starters and variable speed drives | 10 to 20 years | Heat and dust in the plant room; harmonics |
| Plant controls and chiller panels | 10 to 15 years before parts support ends | Manufacturer support |
| Chilled water pipework (steel) | 40 to 60 years | Water treatment; external condensation and insulation |

Industry service-life tables (ASHRAE's service life database and CIBSE Guide M) give median lives in this range; the spread between a well-run and a neglected plant is wider than the spread between machine types.

What shortens life: poor water treatment on the condenser water side, which fouls and corrodes tube bundles; low flow and low temperature conditions that freeze and rupture evaporator tubes; oversizing after load reductions, which makes chillers cycle on and off at low load; refrigerant leaks that are topped up rather than repaired, bringing in moisture and air; deferred overhauls past the manufacturer's run-hour intervals; hot, dusty plant rooms that age drives and starters; coastal air on air-cooled condensers.

sections.heading: Refrigerant obsolescence and leaks
sections.markdown:
A chiller's economic life is often set by its refrigerant before its mechanical life. CFCs (R11, R12) went out of production in developed countries in 1996. HCFCs (R22, R123) are in the last stage of phase-out: R22 production and import ended in the United States in 2020 and servicing with it has been banned in Britain since 2015. HFCs (R134a, R410A, R407C) are being phased down under the Kigali Amendment, with Australia and the United States both stepping down to 15 per cent of baseline by 2036 and new high-GWP refrigerants restricted in new chillers. As a refrigerant becomes scarce, a leak or a compressor failure becomes a replacement decision.

Low-pressure centrifugal chillers (R11, R123) run below atmospheric pressure on the evaporator side, so leaks draw air and moisture in rather than letting refrigerant out. A purge unit removes them; high purge run time means a leak, and moisture forms acids that attack the motor and bearings.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Evaporator approach rising | Low refrigerant charge or fouled evaporator. Refrigerant log; leak test; evaporator inspection. | Leak test and repair; inspect the evaporator. |
| Refrigerant added at each service | Leak. Refrigerant log; leak test locates it; leak rate against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Find and repair the leak, rather than topping up. |
| High purge run time on an R123 or R11 machine | Air leak on the low-pressure side. Purge records; leak test under pressure. | Pressure leak test the low-pressure side, and repair it. |

sections.heading: Tubes, compressors and condensers
sections.markdown:
Condenser tubes carry tower water and foul with scale, biofilm and silt when water treatment lapses; fouling raises condensing pressure, power draw and wear. Corrosion and erosion thin the tubes, especially at the inlet ends. Evaporator tubes can freeze and rupture if water flow drops while the chiller is running, or during low-temperature operation; a rupture floods the refrigerant circuit with water and usually ends the machine.

Bearings wear, oil degrades and loses its lubricating properties, and oil migration leaves compressors running dry. In hermetic machines, where the refrigerant cools the motor, a winding failure burns the insulation and contaminates the whole refrigerant circuit with acid. Centrifugal compressors surge at low load: flow reverses briefly, with a characteristic noise, and repeated surge damages bearings and impellers.

Aluminium fins on copper tubes corrode quickly in salt air, separating from the tubes and losing heat transfer; capacity falls on the hottest days, when it is most needed.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Condenser approach rising over months | Fouled or scaled condenser tubes. Tube inspection; water treatment records; approach falls after cleaning. | Clean the tubes, and correct the water treatment. |
| Surging noise at light load | Oversized centrifugal at low load. Load profile; surge events in logs. | Review the load profile; a variable speed drive or a smaller machine suits light loads. |
| Acidic oil or refrigerant | Moisture or motor winding failure. Oil and refrigerant analysis. | Analyse the oil and refrigerant; overhaul the compressor or rewind the motor. |
| Capacity loss on hot days on an air-cooled unit | Condenser coil corrosion or fouling, or hot air recirculating. Coil condition; plant screen or wall blocking airflow. | Clean or recoat the coils, and clear anything that recirculates hot air. |

sections.heading: Low delta T and pumps
sections.markdown:
When chilled water returns from the building only a few degrees warmer than it left, chillers cannot load fully, so more chillers and pumps run to meet the same load. The cause is usually in the building: fouled or bypassing coils, failed control valves, three-way valves left from earlier systems, or bypasses open. The symptom appears at the plant and is often misread as a capacity shortfall.

Mechanical seals leak, bearings wear, couplings misalign, impellers erode and motors fail. Pumps running against throttled valves or at the wrong point on their curve wear faster. A pump failure without standby takes a chiller out of service.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Chillers cannot load; more chillers and pumps running than the load needs | Low delta T in the building. Supply and return temperatures; coil and valve condition. | Fix the distribution: failed valves, three-way valves and bypasses, and fouled coils. |

sections.heading: Starters, drives and controls
sections.markdown:
Starters, variable speed drives and chiller control panels fail with heat and age, and their parts stop being made long before the chiller is worn out. A ten-year-old drive or a twenty-year-old control panel can strand a sound machine.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Chiller tripping on drive or starter faults in hot weather | Drive or starter overheating or failing. Fault log; switchroom temperature; drive age and parts support. | Improve cooling to the switchroom and plan drive replacement before parts run out. |
| Control panel the manufacturer no longer supports | Obsolete controls stranding a sound chiller. Written support position from the manufacturer. | Plan a controls retrofit, keeping the machine if it is otherwise sound. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ammonia or large refrigerant leak; plant room without required refrigerant detection or ventilation; pressure relief discharging into the room | safety · 4 Essential | Isolate and ventilate now; plant room safety measures before restart. |
| Chiller failed with no standby capacity in a building that needs cooling (hospital, data, summer occupancy) | failure · 3 Important | Restore or hire temporary plant now. |
| Refrigerant service restrictions in force for the refrigerant used | deadline · 4 Essential | Plan replacement or conversion before the next major leak or repair. |
| Rising approaches, recurring leaks, worn pumps, unsupported drives or controls | condition · 3 Important | Repair, retube or upgrade in the near term. |
| Chiller approaching end of life on run hours and age with no current faults | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Plan replacement, sized to current load. |
| No tube testing, oil analysis or load study on record; capacity questioned after tenancy changes | check · 2 Planned | Plant condition and load assessment before sizing works. |
| Normal wear in a maintained plant | nil · 1 Routine | Routine maintenance. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A mechanical services engineer leads, with the chiller service contractor present. On large plant the investigation is planned around the cooling season so that machines can be opened. The checks below read the operating data first, approaches, delta T and refrigerant additions, then test the tubes, oil and vibration where the data points.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Records review | Service reports, refrigerant log, oil and vibration analysis, energy data, overhaul history, with the annual refrigerant added compared with the charge and the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). |
| Plant inspection | Of chillers, pumps, starters, drives, pipework and plant room safety equipment. |
| Eddy current testing | Of condenser and evaporator tubes to measure wall loss and find defects. |
| Oil and refrigerant analysis | For acids, moisture, metals and contaminants. |
| Vibration analysis | Of compressors and pumps. |
| Performance testing | Measured cooling output against power input across load. |
| Load assessment | Trended building load against installed capacity, to size any replacement correctly. |
| Refrigerant position | Current and forthcoming restrictions for the refrigerant in use. |
| Distribution check | Delta T, valves, bypasses and coil condition before blaming the chiller. |

The report should give remaining life for each machine and pump, the refrigerant position, whether to overhaul, retrofit or replace, and the correct size and configuration for any replacement.

sections.heading: Restoring, converting or replacing
sections.markdown:
Fix the system before the chiller: low delta T, failed valves and fouled coils look like a failing machine. Then the work follows the data, from tube cleaning and leak repair through overhauls and variable speed drives to replacement sized to today's load.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Water treatment and tube cleaning | Treat the condenser water and clean the tubes. | To restore condenser performance. |
| Leak repair | Find and repair leaks. | Rather than topping up. |
| Overhaul | Compressor rebuild, bearing and seal replacement, and motor rewind. | At run-hour intervals. |
| Retubing | Retube the bundles. | Where tubes show significant wall loss. |
| Variable speed drive retrofit | Drives on centrifugal and screw machines. | For part-load efficiency. |
| Controls upgrade | Supported chiller panels and plant sequencing. | Where panels are unsupported or the plant is poorly sequenced. |
| Refrigerant conversion | Convert to a lower-GWP alternative. | Where the manufacturer supports it for that machine. |
| Fix the distribution | Replace failed valves, remove three-way valves and bypasses, and clean coils. | To cure low delta T. |
| Replacement | Sized to the current load: often fewer or smaller machines, with variable speed, in a configuration that allows staged replacement. | At end of life; heat recovery or heat pump chillers where the building is electrifying. |

Interactions: chiller replacement involves rigging and access (often through roofs, façades or by crane), electrical supply works, temporary cooling, controls integration and sometimes heat rejection and pump replacement at the same time.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Assessment and testing are lump sums. Overhauls, retubing, drive retrofits and controls upgrades are lump sums per machine. Replacement is a lump-sum project including the machines, rigging and crane hire, pipework and electrical connection, controls integration, commissioning, and temporary cooling for the change-over, which can be a large share on occupied buildings.

Replacement and major overhaul are lifecycle; repairs and leak repair are repairs and maintenance; refrigerant-driven replacement and plant room safety measures carry code compliance elements. The usual shape where condition or load is uncertain is two-part: assessment first, then replacement or retrofit sized from it.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a walk through the plant room cannot: which refrigerant each machine uses, how the plant performs over a season, and what tests have found inside it. Ask for them before replacing a chiller.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Mechanical maintenance contract and two years of service reports with recommendations | What keeps recurring, and what has been recommended and deferred. |
| Refrigerant log, leak test records and refrigerant type for each machine | Which refrigerant each machine uses, and whether it leaks. |
| Installation and overhaul dates; run hours | How far through its life each machine is. |
| Eddy current, oil and vibration test results | The hidden condition of the tubes, compressors and bearings. |
| Water treatment reports for the condenser water system | Whether the condenser tubes are scaling or corroding. |
| Energy consumption data and energy ratings | Whether efficiency is falling, and what the building's rating relies on. |
| Comfort complaint log and records of temporary chiller hire | Whether the plant falls short on hot days. |
| Plant room refrigerant detection and alarm records | Whether the plant room is safe if refrigerant leaks. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Chiller problems are misread when the machine is blamed for faults in the building, and when a machine that runs well is assumed to have years left.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| The chiller is failing | Treat a chiller problem as a system problem until proven otherwise. Low delta T, failed valves and fouled coils produce the same symptoms at the plant as a failing chiller, and replacing the chiller will not fix them. |
| It runs, so it has years left | Refrigerant rules often end a machine's useful life before wear does. Check the refrigerant against the servicing restrictions in force, and the run hours against the overhaul history. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market restricts refrigerants, sets safety rules for refrigerating plant, and links energy performance to sale, letting or emissions limits. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Refrigerants | Refrigerants are controlled under the Ozone Protection and Synthetic Greenhouse Gas Management Act 1989, with HCFC imports reduced to a small servicing allowance that ends by 2030, HFC imports phased down to 15 per cent of baseline by 2036, and refrigerant handling licensed through the ARC scheme. | The GB fluorinated gas regulations restrict refrigerants by global warming potential and require leak checks at intervals set by the CO₂-equivalent charge; R22 servicing has been banned since 2015. | Refrigerant management follows Clean Air Act Section 608; the AIM Act phases HFCs down to 15 per cent of baseline by 2036, and EPA rules limit the global warming potential of refrigerants in new chillers from 2025. |
| Plant safety | Refrigerating system safety follows AS/NZS 5149, and pressure equipment in-service inspection AS/NZS 3788. | Refrigerating system safety follows BS EN 378; pressure systems need a written scheme of examination under the Pressure Systems Safety Regulations 2000. | ASHRAE 15 governs refrigerating system safety and ASHRAE 90.1 efficiency. |
| Energy | Offices of 1,000 m² and more need a current energy certificate under the Commercial Building Disclosure programme when sold or leased, and NABERS ratings drive lettability. | Air-conditioning systems over 12 kW need an energy inspection at least every five years, and let commercial buildings need an EPC of at least E under the minimum energy efficiency standards. | Building performance standards, such as New York City's Local Law 97, set emissions limits that drive plant replacement on a legislated timetable. |

sections.heading: Worked example: chillers that cannot carry a hot afternoon
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 1990s office has three water-cooled chillers. On hot afternoons all three run, yet the chilled water supply temperature drifts up and comfort complaints follow; the building's delta T is low, and a temporary chiller was hired last summer. One machine also needs refrigerant at each service.

Treat a chiller problem as a system problem until proven otherwise. Three chillers running against a low delta T point to failed valves, three-way valves or fouled coils in the building, which replacing a chiller would not fix. The machine needing refrigerant at each service has a leak to find and repair.

So the register carries fixing the distribution as a condition line, leak repair on the one machine, and a load study as a check line before any replacement, which would then be sized to the load the building actually has.

thresholds.rule: From 1 January 2020, bulk R22 imports may only service existing equipment, within about 45 tonnes (45,000 kg) a year until 2029; from 1 January 2030 imports are banned and servicing relies on reclaimed refrigerant

thresholds.rule: Appliances holding 50 lb (about 23 kg) or more of ozone-depleting refrigerant: repair when leaking more than 10 per cent a year for comfort cooling, 20 per cent for commercial refrigeration, 30 per cent for industrial process refrigeration

pages.title: Central Heating Plant
pages.question: How do boilers and heating systems fail, how do you read the signs, and when does fuel policy change the replacement decision?
pages.answer: Heating plant fails mostly through its water. Leaks topped up with fresh water bring in oxygen and minerals, corroding steel and iron, building magnetite sludge and blocking condensing boiler heat exchangers. Cast iron sections crack from thermal shock; non-condensing boilers corrode when run too cool. Combustion faults risk carbon monoxide. Gas restrictions and electrification policy now shape replacement: a like-for-like gas boiler may be stranded before it wears out.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about central heating plant; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Boilers (condensing/non-condensing), hydronic radiators, primary pumps

pages.searchTitle: Boilers and central heating plant: sludge, condensing performance, heat pump retrofit

questions.question: Why do our new condensing boilers keep locking out?
questions.answer: Often a blocked heat exchanger from old sludge, because the system was not cleaned before they went in. Clean and treat the system as well as the boiler.

questions.question: Why are the radiators cold at the bottom?
questions.answer: Magnetite sludge from oxygen getting into the system. Fix leaks, clean and flush, dose inhibitor and fit magnetic filtration.

questions.question: Can a heat pump replace our boilers?
questions.answer: Often, but heat pumps typically run at 45 to 55 °C, so emitters sized for higher temperatures may need upgrading, or a hybrid with boilers for the peaks.

questions.question: What temperature should stored hot water be?
questions.answer: At least 60 °C in calorifiers, to control Legionella; lower setpoints and cold water at the base of stores are findings.

questions.question: How long do boilers last?
questions.answer: Cast iron sectional boilers 25 to 35 years, steel shell boilers 25 to 30, and condensing boilers 15 to 20.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Heating problems show in the plant room as leaks, soot and a busy pressurisation unit, in the building as cold radiators and uneven heat, and in the records and operating data. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| In the plant room | Nameplates: type, year, output, fuel; pressure vessel registration plates and tags | Boilers, burners and combustion |
| In the plant room | Water on the floor; staining at boiler sections; weeping valves and pump seals | Water treatment, pressurisation and distribution |
| In the plant room | Make-up water meter readings rising; pressurisation unit running often | Water treatment, pressurisation and distribution |
| In the plant room | Relief valve discharge pipes with scale or water marks | Water treatment, pressurisation and distribution |
| In the plant room | Soot at burner and flue connections; smell of combustion products | Boilers, burners and combustion |
| In the plant room | Corroded pipework, damaged insulation, missing labels | Water treatment, pressurisation and distribution |
| In the building | Cold radiators or radiators cold at the bottom (sludge) or top (air) | Water treatment, pressurisation and distribution |
| In the building | Uneven heating; long warm-up times | Controls and heat pumps |
| In the building | Leaks at radiators and in ceilings | Water treatment, pressurisation and distribution |
| In the building | Hot water temperature complaints | Hot water |
| In the records | Service and combustion test reports | Boilers, burners and combustion |
| In the records | Water treatment analysis: pH, inhibitor level, iron, conductivity | Water treatment, pressurisation and distribution |
| In the records | Make-up water volumes | Water treatment, pressurisation and distribution |
| In the records | Pressure vessel inspection reports | Standards by country |
| In the records | Gas safety records and burner certification | Boilers, burners and combustion |
| In the records | Energy consumption and gas bills | Controls and heat pumps |
| In the records | Flue gas temperatures well above design: fouled heat exchangers | Boilers, burners and combustion |
| In the records | Return water temperature too high for condensing boilers to condense, which wastes their efficiency | Controls and heat pumps |
| In the records | Calorifier temperatures below 60 °C; cold water at the base of stores | Hot water |
| In the records | Boilers firing and stopping every few minutes in mild weather | Controls and heat pumps |

sections.heading: Types of heating plant
sections.markdown:
Central heating plant produces heat for space heating and often for domestic hot water: boilers or heat pumps, their burners and gas trains, primary pumps, pressurisation and expansion equipment, water treatment, calorifiers and plate heat exchangers, and the hydronic distribution to radiators, convectors, coils and underfloor circuits. The flues that serve boilers have their own page.

| Type | Where it is found | Character |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cast iron sectional boiler | Older offices, schools, apartment blocks | Long-lived; sections crack from thermal shock; low efficiency |
| Steel shell (fire-tube) boiler | Larger commercial and institutional plant | Robust; tube and furnace corrosion; pressure vessel |
| Condensing boiler (often modular or cascade) | Most plant installed since the 2000s | High efficiency if return water is cool; heat exchangers sensitive to water quality |
| Steam boiler | Hospitals, laundries, older US buildings, industrial | High-risk pressure plant; traps and condensate return corrode |
| Air-to-water heat pump | Electrification projects; new buildings | Lower flow temperatures; needs electrical capacity; refrigerant rules apply |
| District heat connection | Some campuses and city centres | Heat exchanger and metering only on site |
| Hydronic distribution | All wet systems | Pipework, valves, radiators, underfloor circuits; water quality decides life |

Fuel policy now shapes heating plant as much as condition. Victoria has barred gas connections to new homes needing a planning permit since 2024 and the ACT has barred new gas network connections since late 2023; Britain's policy is moving buildings off fossil-fuel heating; New York City's Local Law 154 requires all-electric new buildings. A gas boiler replaced like for like today may be a stranded asset before it wears out.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Cast iron and steel shell boilers last twenty-five to thirty-five years and condensing boilers fifteen to twenty, as do burners, pumps and air-to-water heat pumps. Water treatment is the cheapest life extension available for every part of the system.

| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cast iron sectional boiler | 25 to 35 years | Thermal shock; water quality |
| Steel shell boiler | 25 to 30 years | Water treatment; firing cycles |
| Condensing boiler | 15 to 20 years | Water quality; heat exchanger material |
| Burners and gas trains | 15 to 20 years | Maintenance; combustion tuning |
| Air-to-water heat pump | 15 to 20 years | Coastal exposure; cycling; refrigerant |
| Primary pumps | 15 to 20 years | Run hours; water quality |
| Pressurisation units and expansion vessels | 10 to 20 years | Diaphragm life; pressure setting |
| Calorifiers | 20 to 25 years | Water quality; temperature regime |
| Steel distribution pipework | 40 to 60 years | Oxygen ingress; water treatment |
| Radiators | 40 years and more | Internal corrosion from oxygenated water |

What shortens life: oxygen in the water, from leaks topped up with fresh water, from open vents, or from older plastic pipe without an oxygen barrier, which corrodes steel and iron and forms magnetite sludge; hard make-up water that scales heat exchangers; lapsed water treatment in closed systems; thermal shock from cold return water into hot cast iron boilers; non-condensing boilers running too cool, so flue gases condense and corrode them; short cycling of oversized boilers.

sections.heading: Water treatment, pressurisation and distribution
sections.markdown:
A closed heating system should hold the same water for years. When it leaks and is topped up, each fill brings fresh oxygen and minerals: steel and cast iron corrode, magnetite sludge accumulates in boilers, radiators and valves, and heat exchangers scale. Condensing boilers with narrow aluminium or stainless passages are particularly sensitive; blocked or corroded heat exchangers are the commonest reason they are replaced early.

Expansion vessel diaphragms fail and lose their gas charge; system pressure swings, relief valves discharge, and air is drawn in at high points. A relief valve that discharges regularly is a symptom, not a fault in itself.

Radiators pinhole from internal corrosion; valves seize; thermostatic radiator valves fail; pipes leak at joints in walls and ceilings; underfloor circuits lose flow from sludge. Older systems that were drained and refilled often are worst affected.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| High make-up water use; system pressure falling | Leaks. Make-up meter; inspection of pipework, radiators and boiler. | Find and fix the leaks, then restore water treatment. |
| Black water when radiators are bled; cold bottoms on radiators | Magnetite sludge from oxygen ingress. Water analysis shows high iron; filter catch. | Fix leaks, clean and flush, dose inhibitor, and fit magnetic filtration. |
| Relief valve discharging, pressure swinging | Failed expansion vessel. Vessel charge pressure; diaphragm. | Replace the expansion vessel or pressurisation unit. |

sections.heading: Boilers, burners and combustion
sections.markdown:
Burners drift out of adjustment, nozzles and heat exchangers soot up, and combustion becomes incomplete. The result is lower efficiency and, at worst, carbon monoxide production. Flame safeguards and gas valves age and must be tested.

Cast iron sections crack when cold water reaches a hot boiler, for example when a pump starts after a period off. A cracked section leaks into the combustion chamber.

Non-condensing boilers are designed to keep flue gases above their dew point. Run with low return temperatures, they condense acidic water inside, corroding tubes and furnaces. Steam boilers corrode at tubes and in the condensate return.

Steam traps fail open, wasting steam, or closed, flooding equipment; condensate pipework corrodes from carbonic acid; water hammer damages fittings. Steam boilers are high-hazard pressure equipment with inspection obligations.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Condensing boiler locking out, low flow faults | Blocked heat exchanger. Pressure drop across the boiler; water quality. | Clean the heat exchanger, and clean the system so it does not foul again. |
| Water in the combustion chamber of a cast iron boiler | Cracked section. Leak visible from inside; history of cold starts. | Replace the cracked section, or the boiler. |
| Corrosion inside a non-condensing boiler | Running too cool. Return temperature records. | Raise the return temperature with controls, or replace with a condensing boiler. |

sections.heading: Controls and heat pumps
sections.markdown:
Boiler plant is commonly much larger than the load it serves, because of conservative original design, later fabric improvements and changes of use. Oversized boilers fire and stop repeatedly (short cycling), which wastes fuel and wears burners and ignition systems. Lost weather compensation, failed optimum start and poor boiler sequencing waste energy and mask the real load.

Air-to-water heat pumps lose capacity in cold weather and defrost frequently; outdoor coils corrode near the coast; compressors fail from short cycling when the system volume is too small. They need lower flow temperatures than boilers, so radiators and coils sized for boilers may not heat the building.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Building cannot reach temperature after a heat pump retrofit | Emitters sized for higher flow temperatures. Heat loss vs emitter output at heat pump flow temperature. | Upgrade the emitters, improve the fabric, or carry the peaks with a boiler. |
| Boilers cycling every few minutes | Oversizing or poor controls. Load profile from gas data; burner run hours vs starts. | Sequence the boilers, or replace with modular boilers sized to the measured load. |
| Condensing boilers achieving non-condensing efficiency | High return temperatures from the building. Return temperature; bypasses; three-port valves. | Lower return temperatures with weather compensation and return temperature control. |

sections.heading: Hot water
sections.markdown:
Where the heating plant also heats domestic hot water through calorifiers or plate heat exchangers, the stored water must stay hot enough to control Legionella: stored at 60 °C or more and distributed hot enough that it does not fall into the growth range at outlets. Calorifiers that run cool to save energy, have cold stratified water at the base, or feed long dead legs carry a public health risk. Plate heat exchangers foul with scale on the hard-water side and lose output.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Calorifier stored below 60 °C | Setpoint lowered or plant undersized for hot water. Temperature records; Legionella sampling. | Restore the storage temperature, or upgrade the plant for the hot water demand. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gas leak, carbon monoxide or spillage, failed flame safeguard or safety valve, inadequate plant room ventilation | safety · 4 Essential | Isolate now; gas fitter and engineer before restart. |
| No heating in winter in residential, healthcare or education buildings; major leaks | failure · 3 Important | Restore now or provide temporary heat. |
| Pressure vessel inspection or gas safety check due | deadline · 4 Essential | Timing set by the regulation. |
| Sludge, corrosion, failed expansion vessel, poor combustion | condition · 3 Important | Repair and treat in the near term. |
| Boilers at the end of their life; fuel policy affecting replacement choice | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Plan replacement, including the electrification option. |
| No water treatment records; no assessment of heat pump readiness | check · 2 Planned | Assess before replacing. |
| Normal wear | nil · 1 Routine | Routine maintenance. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A mechanical services engineer leads, with a licensed gas fitter, the maintenance contractor and a water treatment specialist. The investigation is best done at the start of the heating season, when faults show and plant can still be taken offline. The checks below read the water treatment and make-up records first, then test combustion, pressurisation and return temperatures.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Records review | Service and combustion reports, water treatment logs, make-up water volumes, pressure vessel inspections, gas safety records, energy data. |
| Plant inspection | Of boilers, burners and gas trains, pumps, pressurisation units, expansion vessels, calorifiers, heat exchangers and pipework, with pressure vessel registration plates checked. |
| Combustion analysis | Of each burner at high and low fire: oxygen, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, flue temperature, efficiency. |
| System water analysis | To BSRIA BG 50 practice: pH, inhibitor concentration, total and dissolved iron, copper, conductivity, bacteria; a filter or strainer inspection to see what the water carries. |
| Make-up water metering | Over several weeks to quantify leaks. |
| Internal inspection | Of boilers and pressure vessels at the statutory interval, with ultrasonic thickness testing of shells and tubes where corrosion is suspected. |
| Pipework survey | Ultrasonic thickness readings on suspect runs; thermography of radiators and distribution. |
| Load assessment | Heating load derived from gas consumption against heating degree days, to size replacement plant to the real load rather than the nameplate. |
| Hot water review | Calorifier temperatures, dead legs, Legionella risk assessment. |
| Electrification readiness | Building heat loss, emitter output at heat pump flow temperatures, electrical supply capacity, outdoor space, structural capacity for plant, noise constraints. |

The report should give remaining life for each boiler and major component, water quality and its consequences, the safety position, the real heating load, and a replacement strategy that compares like-for-like gas, hybrid and full electric options against the building's fuel and emissions obligations.

sections.heading: Treating, repairing or electrifying
sections.markdown:
Water treatment comes first: it is the cheapest life extension for every component, and new boilers must not be fouled by old sludge. After that, the choice runs from repairs and controls to replacement, hybrid heat pumps or full electrification.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Water treatment programme | Find and fix leaks first, then clean and flush (chemically where sludge is heavy), dose with inhibitor, fit magnetic and side-stream filtration, add deaeration where air is a problem, and monitor quarterly. Water treatment is the cheapest life extension available for every component in the system. | First, in every system. |
| Component repairs | Expansion vessel and pressurisation unit replacement, pump replacement with variable speed, valve replacement, burner overhaul or replacement, heat exchanger cleaning. | Where individual components have failed. |
| Controls | Weather compensation, optimum start and stop, boiler sequencing, and return temperature control so condensing boilers condense. | Where boilers cycle, or condensing boilers do not condense. |
| Boiler replacement | Modular condensing boilers sized to the measured load, after the system has been cleaned so that new heat exchangers are not fouled by old sludge, with new flue, gas train and controls. | At the end of the boilers' life, after the system is cleaned. |
| Hybrid systems | Heat pumps carrying the base load with boilers for peaks and backup, which lowers emissions without a full emitter upgrade. | Where emissions must fall but not every emitter can be upgraded. |
| Full electrification | Heat pumps at flow temperatures typically in the 45 to 55 °C range, with emitter upgrades (larger radiators, fan convectors), buffer vessels, fabric improvements to reduce the load, electrical supply upgrade, and space for outdoor units with noise control. | Where policy, emissions limits or end of life make heat pumps the answer. |
| Hot water | Restore storage temperatures, remove dead legs, or move to point-of-use or heat pump hot water. | Where storage temperatures are low or demand has changed. |
| Distribution | Replace corroded pipework sections and pinholed radiators; replace non-barrier plastic pipe that admits oxygen. | Where pipework or radiators leak. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Assessment, combustion testing and water analysis are lump sums. Water treatment is a recurring contract, with a one-off clean and flush. Component repairs are itemised. Boiler replacement is a lump-sum project including boilers, flue system, gas train and supply, pumps, controls, commissioning and temporary heating where the building is occupied in winter.

Electrification adds lines that can exceed the plant cost: heat pumps and outdoor plant platforms, emitter upgrades through the building, electrical supply upgrade with the network operator, structural works for plant, and fabric improvements. Running cost and emissions comparisons belong in the strategy rather than in the register line.

Replacement is lifecycle; pressure vessel and gas safety obligations are code compliance; water treatment and repairs are repairs and maintenance; electrification driven by a building performance standard carries a deadline.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a walk through the boiler room cannot: whether the water is treated, whether the plant burns safely, and whether a heat pump retrofit has been assessed. Ask for them before replacing a boiler.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Service and combustion test reports for the last two years | Whether the plant burns safely and efficiently. |
| Water treatment reports and make-up water records | Whether the system leaks, and is protected from corrosion. |
| Pressure vessel registration, written scheme of examination and inspection reports | Whether pressure vessels are registered and examined. |
| Gas safety records and burner certification | Whether gas safety checks are current. |
| Gas and electricity consumption data for at least two heating seasons | How much the plant uses, and whether condensing boilers condense. |
| Legionella risk assessment and hot water temperature logs | Whether hot water is kept hot enough to control Legionella. |
| Installation dates for boilers, burners, pumps and calorifiers | How far through their lives the boilers, burners, pumps and calorifiers are. |
| Any electrification, decarbonisation or heat pump feasibility study | Whether heat pumps have been assessed for the building. |
| Obligations under any building performance standard that applies | Whether a building performance standard sets a deadline. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Heating plant is misread when new boilers are fitted to a dirty system, when condensing boilers are assumed to deliver their rated efficiency, and when a heat pump is treated as a straight swap.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| New boilers will fix it | Boilers replaced in a system full of sludge foul their new heat exchangers. Clean the system first, then size the boilers to the measured load. |
| Condensing boilers are efficient | Only if they condense. High return temperatures from the building leave them at non-condensing efficiency; return temperature control and weather compensation fix it. |
| A heat pump drops straight in | Emitters sized for higher flow temperatures can leave the building cold after a heat pump retrofit. Heat pumps typically run at 45 to 55 °C, so emitters, fabric or a hybrid arrangement need assessing first. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market regulates gas installations and pressure equipment, and has its own rules on water treatment, efficiency and the move away from gas. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Gas and pressure equipment | Gas installations follow AS/NZS 5601.1 and commercial gas appliances AS 3814; boilers and pressure vessels are classified by hazard level under AS 4343, built to AS/NZS 1200, registered under the work health and safety regulations and inspected in service to AS/NZS 3788. | The Gas Safety (Installation and Use) Regulations 1998 apply, with IGEM standards for non-domestic installations; pressure systems need a written scheme of examination under the Pressure Systems Safety Regulations 2000. | Boilers are built to the ASME Boiler and Pressure Vessel Code with controls to ASME CSD-1, and inspected by jurisdictional boiler inspectors under the National Board Inspection Code; NFPA 54 covers gas and NFPA 85 larger boiler combustion systems. |
| Water treatment, efficiency and fuel policy | Victoria and the ACT restrict new gas connections. | BSRIA BG 50 and BS 7593 guide water treatment; Approved Document L governs efficiency. | Local Law 97 and Local Law 154 in New York drive electrification. |

sections.heading: Worked example: new boilers that keep locking out
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 1970s school had its cast iron boilers replaced with condensing boilers three years ago. The new boilers lock out on low flow faults, radiators run black water when bled, and make-up water use is high. Gas use barely fell after the replacement.

Black water and high make-up point to leaks and magnetite sludge: the system was not cleaned before the new boilers went in, so their heat exchangers are fouling. Gas use barely falling points to high return temperatures, leaving the condensing boilers at non-condensing efficiency.

So the register carries leak repair and a full water treatment programme as condition lines, heat exchanger cleaning, and return temperature control and weather compensation, so the boilers condense.

pages.title: Chimney Stacks & Flues
pages.question: How do chimney stacks and flues fail, how do you read a leaning or stained chimney, and when is it dangerous?
pages.answer: Chimneys fail from exposure on all faces and from what goes up them. Stacks lean away from the weather as sulfates from flue gases swell the mortar on the wetter side; a large lean with open joints is a falling hazard. Brown stains on a breast mean tar or acid condensate through an unsuitable flue. Cracked liners leak carbon monoxide. Disused stacks still need capping, ventilation and support, and a breast removed below without support leaves the stack hanging.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about chimney stacks & flues; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Masonry condition, pointing, flashings, flue liners

questions.question: Why is my chimney stack leaning?
questions.answer: Usually sulfate attack: sulfates from flue gases swell the mortar on the wetter side, and the stack bends away from the weather. A large lean with open joints is a falling hazard and needs an engineer's assessment.

questions.question: What causes brown stains on a chimney breast?
questions.answer: Tar or acid condensate coming through an unsuitable or unlined flue, often after a new appliance was fitted. The flue needs relining with a liner matched to the fuel.

questions.question: Is it safe to use a fireplace or boiler if fumes come into the room?
questions.answer: No. A flue that leaks, or a carbon monoxide alarm activation, means the appliance comes out of use until the flue is tested.

questions.question: Does a removed chimney breast need support?
questions.answer: Yes, where the stack above remains. Gallows brackets, steel beams or corbelling, designed by an engineer and approved, carry it.

questions.question: How long does a chimney liner last?
questions.answer: Clay liners 50 to 80 years, stainless liners 15 to 30 years, and cast-in-place pumice liners 50 years and more, provided the liner suits the fuel.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Chimney problems show inside as staining, damp and fumes, from the street as lean and weathering, and in the roof space around the stack. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Inside | Brown staining and damp patches on chimney breasts that persist in dry weather: tar or acid condensate soaking through | Flues, liners, appliances and fire |
| Inside | Damp on breasts after rain only: water entering at the top of the stack or at the flashings | Flashings, water and staining |
| Inside | Smoke or fumes in rooms or adjoining homes when an appliance runs: liner failure | Flues, liners, appliances and fire |
| Inside | Carbon monoxide alarm activations, headaches or drowsiness when an appliance is on: stop using it and have the flue tested | Flues, liners, appliances and fire |
| Inside | Lower-floor chimney breasts missing, with upper breasts still in place | Removed breasts, shared stacks and asbestos flues |
| Inside | Smoke puffing back into the room when a fire is lit or the wind blows: poor draught, an obstruction such as a nest, or a stack too short for its surroundings | Flues, liners, appliances and fire |
| Inside | A sooty or acrid smell from a sealed fireplace in humid weather: salts and deposits in a disused flue | Flashings, water and staining |
| Street or aerial | Lean visible by sighting against vertical lines; cracks in stack joints | The stack: lean, weathering and wind |
| Street or aerial | Spalled bricks, eroded pointing, cracked flaunching, missing or loose pots | The stack: lean, weathering and wind |
| Street or aerial | Lifted flashings; vegetation on stacks | Flashings, water and staining |
| Street or aerial | Pots open on decommissioned stacks; cowls or caps present | Flashings, water and staining |
| Street or aerial | Stacks on party walls shared with neighbours; pots counted against the fireplaces in use | Removed breasts, shared stacks and asbestos flues |
| Street or aerial | Metal flues on commercial roofs discharging close to air intakes, windows or roof terraces | Kitchen exhaust and tall stacks |
| Roof space | Damp, efflorescence and staining on the stack where it passes through | Flashings, water and staining |
| Roof space | Mortar fallen from joints; holes in the masonry | The stack: lean, weathering and wind |
| Roof space | Chimney breast removed below with no support | Removed breasts, shared stacks and asbestos flues |

| In the records | Chimney sweep and CCTV inspection records | Investigation before the scope |
