sections.heading: Types of chimney and flue
sections.markdown:
Chimney stacks and flues carry combustion gases from appliances out of the building. The element covers masonry stacks with their pots, cappings, flaunching and flashings; flue liners (clay, concrete, pumice, stainless steel); prefabricated metal flues; boiler and generator flues on commercial buildings; kitchen exhaust ducts; and industrial stacks. It includes decommissioned stacks, which still stand above the roof and still need to be stable and weathertight.

| Form | Where it is found | Main risk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Masonry stack with unlined or parged flue | Houses and terraces before about 1950 | Gas leakage through the masonry; sulfate attack and lean |
| Masonry stack with clay or concrete liners | Houses from the mid twentieth century | Cracked liners; open joints |
| Stainless flexible or rigid liner in an old flue | Relined chimneys | Liner life; incorrect for the appliance |
| Twin-wall metal flue | Wood heaters, boilers, generators | Joints; support; clearances to combustibles |
| Commercial kitchen exhaust duct | Restaurants, institutions | Grease build-up and duct fires |
| Tall masonry or steel stack | Industrial and institutional | Banding and lightning protection; structural condition |
| Decommissioned stack | All older buildings | Damp from open pots; lean; removed breasts below |

Commercial and institutional buildings carry flues of their own: boiler flues rising through risers, generator exhausts, kitchen exhaust ducts, laboratory fume exhausts and, on older industrial and hospital sites, tall free-standing stacks. These follow appliance and fire codes as much as building codes, and their failures show up as fire, fume and condensation problems as well as fabric problems.

A stack can be read from the roof. Each pot usually marks one flue, so a stack with six pots serves six fireplaces, some of which may now be sealed, relined or connected to a boiler. Stacks on party walls are shared with the neighbour and so are their repairs. On commercial roofs, flues show as metal stacks with rain caps, often clustered above plant rooms and kitchens, and their height and position relative to air intakes and windows matters as much as their condition.

A chimney has two lives: as a structure, exposed on every face above the roof and built into the [roof structure](https://moyneross.com/technical/roof-structure) where it passes through, and as a flue, which must carry gases safely from whatever appliance is now connected to it. Appliances change far more often than chimneys, and many problems come from a modern appliance on an old flue, or an old flue left open when its appliance was removed ([Gas Services](https://moyneross.com/technical/gas-services), [Fireplaces](https://moyneross.com/technical/fireplaces)).

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
A chimney's parts wear at very different rates. The masonry stack can last a century, while flaunching, pointing and stainless liners need renewing within decades, and a liner suited to one appliance can fail quickly under the next.

| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Masonry stack | 80 to 120 years | Exposure on all faces; flue gases; frost |
| Flaunching and pointing | 20 to 40 years | Exposure |
| Lead flashings | 50 to 80 years | Fixing in chases |
| Clay liners | 50 to 80 years | Chimney fires; thermal shock |
| Stainless liners | 15 to 30 years | Fuel type; condensate; grade |
| Twin-wall flues | 20 to 30 years | Fuel; installation |
| Pumice and cast-in-place liners | 50 years and more | Chimney fires; installation quality |
| Pots, cowls and caps | 40 to 80 years; metal cowls 15 to 25 | Frost; fixing in the flaunching; corrosion |
| Commercial kitchen exhaust ducts | 20 to 30 years with cleaning | Grease build-up; access; fire history |
| Steel boiler and generator stacks | 20 to 40 years | Internal acid corrosion; insulation and cladding; support |

The stack above the roof ages much faster than the chimney below it: it is wet and cold on every face, and the top courses, flaunching, pots and flashings fail first. The flue's life depends on what has been burnt in it, and how wet and acidic its gases are.

What shortens life: exposure on all faces: stacks get wetter than walls, dry less and freeze more, so the top courses and pointing fail first; flue gases: sulfates from coal and oil, acid condensate from modern efficient appliances, and tar from smouldering wood all attack the lining and mortar from inside; cement repairs on lime-built stacks, which trap water and shift the weathering from the mortar into the brick; missing damp-proof trays where the stack passes through the roof, letting rain run down inside the stack to the rooms below; the wrong liner for the fuel, which fails in years rather than decades; neglected sweeping of working flues, which lets deposits build until they ignite.

What lengthens it: sweeping and inspection matched to the fuel, and a liner suited to the appliance connected; lime mortar for repairs to lime-built stacks, so the mortar, not the brick, takes the weathering; caps with ventilation on disused flues, so they neither take in rain nor stay damp; flashings and back gutters kept clear and sound.

sections.heading: The stack: lean, weathering and wind
sections.markdown:
Sulfates from flue gases condense in the flue lining and mortar, more on the wetter side of the stack. Mortar expands on that side, and the stack bends away from the prevailing weather. A leaning stack can be stable for decades, but a large lean, cracked joints and loose upper courses mean it may fall in a storm.

Frost and salts spall bricks on every face of the stack; pointing erodes fastest at the top courses and on the weather side; the flaunching, the mortar bed holding the pots, cracks and lets water into the flue and the stack; pots loosen in their flaunching and can be blown off. Once water is inside the stack it saturates the masonry from within, and frost damage accelerates.

Tall, slender stacks with weak mortar have little capacity to resist sideways load. In storms and earthquakes they are among the first parts of a building to fall, often through the roof below. Unreinforced masonry chimneys are a recognised hazard in seismic regions, and leaning or loose stacks are a hazard in any high wind.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stack bending away from the prevailing weather | Sulfate attack on mortar. Joints open on the weather side; mortar white and soft. | Have an engineer assess the lean; rebuild the upper courses, or the stack from the roof line, if it has gone too far for repointing. |
| Stack loose or cracked at roof level after a storm or earthquake | Lateral load on weak masonry. Cracks through bed joints at the roof line; movement by hand. | Make safe now: remove loose courses over paths and roofs, then rebuild. |
| Chimney ending below a nearby ridge or taller part of the building | Poor draught and fumes re-entering. Height of the terminal against the building around it and the limits for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Extend the flue or fit a suitable terminal, checked against the appliance’s requirements. |

sections.heading: Flashings, water and staining
sections.markdown:
Apron, step and back gutter flashings lift and pull from their chases as the mortar fails; lead is stolen; back gutters behind wide stacks fill with debris and overflow. Without a damp-proof tray through the stack at roof level, rain absorbed by the stack above the roof runs down inside it, past the flashings, and appears on chimney breasts and ceilings below, which is why new flashings alone often fail to stop chimney leaks ([Roof Coverings](https://moyneross.com/technical/roof-coverings)).

Wet tar from wood, and acid condensate from efficient gas boilers in unlined flues, soak through to the inside and stain chimney breasts brown; the staining is a sign of an unsuitable flue.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Damp on breasts after rain, dry otherwise | Water entry at the top or flashings. Flaunching, cap or flashing defects. | Repair the flaunching, cap or flashings. |
| Damp on breasts of a disused flue in all weather | Open pot and no ventilation. Pot open; fireplace sealed. | Cap the pot and ventilate the flue, with a vent at the base of the breast. |

sections.heading: Flues, liners, appliances and fire
sections.markdown:
Cracked or open-jointed liners, and unlined flues with decayed parging, let gases and smoke escape into rooms, roof spaces and, through shared stacks and party walls, into adjoining homes. A chimney fire or a single severe frost can crack clay liners along their length. Carbon monoxide leakage is the life-safety failure, and because it is invisible and odourless it is often discovered by alarms or by symptoms in a neighbour.

Modern condensing boilers and efficient wood heaters produce cooler, wetter gases than the open fires flues were built for. In an unlined or wrongly lined masonry flue the gases condense, and the acid condensate attacks the mortar and soaks through to the inside. An appliance change without a flue assessment is a common start to chimney failure and to carbon monoxide risk.

Creosote and soot build up in wood and coal flues and ignite. A chimney fire cracks liners and masonry and can spread to timbers built into or against the stack ([Roof Structure](https://moyneross.com/technical/roof-structure)).

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Brown staining on the chimney breast | Tar or acid condensate through an unsuitable flue. Appliance type; flue unlined. | Stop using the appliance on that flue; reline with a liner matched to the fuel. |
| Smoke or fumes in other rooms or adjoining dwellings | Liner failure. Smoke test; CCTV. | Take the appliance out of use now; smoke test and CCTV the flue, then reline. |
| Staining began after a new boiler or heater was fitted | Condensate from an appliance unsuited to the flue. Appliance date; flue unlined or wrong liner. | Reline with a liner suited to the new appliance's condensate. |
| Scorched timbers in the roof space next to the stack | Past chimney fire or timber built too close. Charring; timber against the flue; cracked liner (Thresholds by market). | Take the appliance out of use until timbers are separated from the flue and the liner is checked. |
| Smoke spilling into the room when the fire is lit | Poor draught: obstruction, cold flue, stack too short or downdraught from nearby buildings. Smoke test; obstruction in the flue; stack height relative to the roof and neighbours. | Clear any obstruction, then deal with what the smoke test shows, such as a cold flue or a stack too short for its position. |

sections.heading: Removed breasts, shared stacks and asbestos flues
sections.markdown:
Chimney breasts removed from lower floors to gain space, without supporting what remains above, leave the upper breasts and the stack hanging on the masonry of the wall. Gallows brackets, steel beams or corbelling are needed to carry the load; without them the remaining masonry can crack, settle and in the worst cases drop. Removals done decades ago without approval are common and are usually found only when someone looks in the roof space or the floor above.

Stacks on party walls serve both homes and usually belong to both. One owner's appliance can leak fumes into the other's rooms, one owner's removed breast can undermine the other's stack, and repairs need agreement and often a formal notice. On terraces, a single neglected stack can let water into two or three homes.

Many boiler, water heater and space heater installations from the 1950s to the 1980s used asbestos cement flue pipes, often running up through roof spaces and out through the roof. They become brittle and crack with age and heat, and must be identified before they are disturbed ([Hazardous Materials](https://moyneross.com/technical/hazardous-materials)).

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Chimney breast removed in a room below a stack that remains | Masonry above left without support. Inspection from the roof space and the room below for brackets or steelwork. | Have an engineer confirm the support, and add it where missing. |
| Grey fibrous flue pipe or cowl on an older heater or boiler | Possible asbestos cement flue. Asbestos register; sampling by a competent person. | Leave it undisturbed until sampled; remove it under asbestos controls when the appliance is replaced. |

sections.heading: Kitchen exhaust and tall stacks
sections.markdown:
Grease from cooking condenses on the walls of kitchen exhaust ducts and builds up between cleans. A flare-up on the cooking line can ignite it, and a duct fire spreads quickly along the duct and can break out wherever the duct passes through the building. Ducts with too few access panels cannot be cleaned along their full length, which is the usual root cause; cleaning frequency is set by the type and volume of cooking. ([Commercial Kitchens](https://moyneross.com/technical/commercial-kitchens))

Tall masonry stacks are held by steel bands that corrode and loosen; their tops weather fastest; lightning protection conductors corrode and detach. Steel stacks corrode internally from acid condensate. These are structural items needing periodic engineering inspection.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fumes from a commercial flue entering the building | Discharge too close to air intakes or windows. Flue position against intakes; wind direction when complaints occur. | Extend or relocate the flue away from intakes and windows. |
| Grease visible at kitchen duct joints or access panels | Cleaning frequency too low or ducts not fully accessible. Deposit depth and cleaning frequency against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market); cleaning records; access panel spacing. | Clean to the required frequency, and add access panels so the whole duct can be cleaned. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stack leaning with open joints or loose upper courses; loose pots; breast removed without support; flue gas leakage | safety · 4 Essential | Make safe now; appliance out of use. |
| Working flue with signs of leakage or carbon monoxide alarm activations | safety · 4 Essential | Take the appliance out of use until the flue is tested. |
| Stack over a roof, path or street loose or cracked after a storm or earthquake | safety · 4 Essential | Make safe now. |
| Timbers built into or touching a working flue; combustibles against an unlined flue | safety · 4 Essential | Take the appliance out of use until separated. |
| Water entering the building through the stack | failure · 3 Important | Repair now. |
| Cracked flaunching; eroded pointing; lifted flashings without leaks | condition · 3 Important | Repair in the near term. |
| Kitchen exhaust cleaning overdue against the required frequency | deadline · 4 Essential | Clean by the due date. |
| Liners and flashings at age | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Renew on cycle. |
| Gas safety check due under landlord rules | deadline · 4 Essential | Annual. |
| Working flue with no inspection record; appliance changed | check · 2 Planned | Inspect and test before use. |
| Minor weathering | nil · 1 Routine | Routine maintenance. |

A chimney carries two kinds of risk at once. Its structure can fall, which is graded on what is beneath it; its flue can poison or burn, which is graded on whether an appliance is connected and in use. A disused, capped stack in good order is nil; the same stack serving a boiler without a suitable liner is a check at best.

The grading follows what a finding demands, not the size of the eventual bill.

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A building surveyor inspects the stack; a structural engineer assesses lean; a licensed gas fitter, chimney sweep or flue specialist inspects the flue. The checks below cover the stack, its flashings, every working flue, and the roof space around each one.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| External inspection | From the roof or a platform, with the terminal height checked against the building around it and the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). |
| Plumb measurement | Of the stack. |
| CCTV inspection | Of the flue. |
| Smoke test | For leakage. |
| Appliance and flue compatibility check | Against the appliance's requirements. |
| Moisture and salts survey | Of chimney breasts, to separate rain entering at the top, condensate from appliances, and hygroscopic salts left by years of coal and wood burning, which draw moisture from the air and keep plaster damp after the source has stopped. |
| Support check | Wherever breasts have been removed: look in the roof space and the floor below for gallows brackets, steel beams or corbelling carrying the remaining masonry, and for approvals. |
| Carbon monoxide testing | In rooms served and in adjoining dwellings with appliances running, since leaking flues often affect neighbours first. |
| Kitchen exhaust inspection | Of the duct from hood to discharge through access panels, measuring grease deposits against the cleaning standard. |

The report should state stack plumb and condition, flashing condition, flue lining condition from CCTV, whether each flue suits the appliance connected to it, and the status of disused flues.

sections.heading: Making safe, repairing or relining
sections.markdown:
Chimney work divides between the stack, which must stand up and keep water out, and the flue, which must carry an appliance's gases safely. Making safe comes first wherever either has failed; the rest follows from what the inspection finds.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Make safe | Take appliances out of use; remove loose pots and upper courses over paths and roofs. | At once, wherever there is leakage, carbon monoxide or fire risk, or loose material above people. |
| Repoint and reflaunch | Lime-based mortar for lime-built stacks, so the mortar rather than the brick takes the weathering. | Where the stack is plumb and sound. |
| Rebuild | Rebuild the upper courses, or the stack from the roof line, with a damp-proof tray at roof level. | Where lean, sulfate attack or frost has gone too far for repointing. |
| Renew flashings | Lead or a durable alternative, with a back gutter behind wide stacks. | Where flashings have lifted or water enters at the roof line. |
| Reline | A liner matched to the fuel: suitable stainless grades for wood and oil, condensate-resistant liners for condensing gas appliances, and cast-in-place pumice or ceramic liners where an old stack needs structural support as well. | Wherever a working flue leaks, stains or serves a changed appliance. |
| Cap and ventilate | Cap decommissioned flues, with a vent at the base of the breast so the flue can dry. | On every disused flue. |
| Support | Gallows brackets, steel beams or corbelling under stacks over removed breasts, designed by an engineer and approved. | Wherever a breast has been removed below a stack that remains. |
| Remove redundant stacks | Take the stack down above the roof, with approvals, heritage consent and the neighbour's agreement where shared. | Where a stack serves nothing and has no heritage value. |
| Commercial flues and kitchen exhaust | Extend or relocate flues discharging near intakes, add access panels at every change of direction, and set cleaning frequency by cooking volume. | Wherever fumes reach intakes or windows, or ducts cannot be fully cleaned. |
| Tall stacks | Repair or replace bands, ladders and lightning protection, and inspect structurally on a cycle. | On industrial and boiler stacks, on a set cycle. |

Choosing between them starts with whether the flue is in use. A working flue must be safe for its appliance before anything else; a disused one needs only to stand up and keep water out. Where an old stack serves nothing and has no heritage value, removing it above the roof can cost less over time than keeping it.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Repairs are lump sums per stack; rebuilds by height; relining per flue. Scaffold dominates on roofs. Flue inspections and sweeping recur. What drives the cost: scaffold to the stack, the stack's height and the number of flues, heritage materials, relining and the appliance it must suit, and work to adjoining owners' shared stacks. Commonly missed: the damp-proof tray and flashings, capping disused flues, and support where breasts have been removed below.

Rebuild is lifecycle; repairs are repairs and maintenance; flue compliance is code compliance.

Where a stack is redundant, removal above the roof can be cheaper than repair over the long term, subject to heritage and planning controls.

A stack rebuild carries scaffold, demolition to below the defect, rebuild, new pots and flaunching, flashings and tray, and often relining in the same visit. Capping a disused flue is a small item per flue but needs the same access. Support for stacks over removed breasts is a structural lump sum and a safety item. Kitchen exhaust cleaning recurs at the frequency the standard sets for the cooking type.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what an inspection on the day cannot: which flue serves which appliance, what each liner is, and whether the flues have been swept, tested and kept clear. Ask for them before any appliance is used or changed.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Sweep and CCTV inspection records, and liner installation certificates | The condition of each flue inside, and what it is lined with. |
| Gas safety certificates and the appliance register, showing which flue serves which appliance | Which flue serves which appliance, and whether gas safety checks are current. |
| Details of any appliance changes and the flue assessment done at the time | Whether a changed appliance was checked against its flue. |
| Decommissioning records for disused flues | Which flues are disused, and whether they were capped and ventilated. |
| Approvals and engineering for any breast or stack removal | Whether a removed breast or stack was approved and supported. |
| Carbon monoxide alarm records, and any incidents or complaints, including from neighbours | Whether fumes have already reached people, including neighbours. |
| Records of chimney fires and the repairs that followed | Whether there has been a chimney fire, and what was repaired after it. |
| Kitchen exhaust cleaning certificates and the duct access plan | Whether kitchen exhaust has been cleaned as required, and can be reached throughout. |
| Party wall agreements or notices for shared stacks, and heritage listing where chimneys are protected | Who shares the stack, and whether heritage controls limit the work. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Chimney findings are misread when the stack and the flue are treated as one thing, or when damp on a breast is assumed to be rain.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| Damp on a chimney breast means the stack leaks | Damp on a chimney breast has three common causes that need different fixes: rain entering from above, condensate from the flue, and salts left by years of combustion that draw moisture from the air. Timing tells them apart: after rain, after the appliance runs, or in humid weather regardless of either. |
| The flue is fine if it draws well | Any flue serving a working appliance that shows signs of leakage, or where carbon monoxide alarms have activated, must be taken out of use until tested. |
| Fire risk is inside the flue | Fire risk in a working flue comes from what surrounds it as much as from the flue. Timbers built into the stack, roof framing touching it, and combustible material in the roof space next to an unlined flue are the paths by which a chimney fire becomes a house fire. Look at the roof space around every working flue, not just the flue itself. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets standards for appliances, flues and kitchen exhaust, and most require carbon monoxide alarms. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out the appliance and flue standards, kitchen exhaust, and alarms and checks.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Appliances and flues | Solid fuel appliances follow AS/NZS 2918, and gas appliances and flues AS/NZS 5601.1; fireplaces and flues in houses follow the National Construction Code's Housing Provisions for heating appliances. | Approved Document J covers combustion appliances and fuel storage; BS 5440 covers gas flues; HETAS registration covers solid fuel installations. | NFPA 211 governs chimneys and venting systems, with levels of inspection; NFPA 54 covers gas; International Building Code Chapter 21 covers masonry chimneys. |
| Kitchen exhaust | Commercial kitchen exhaust follows AS 1668.1, and is an essential safety measure in commercial buildings in some states. | Kitchen ventilation commonly follows BESA's DW/172 specification, and grease duct cleaning its TR19 Grease specification, which insurers commonly require. | NFPA 96 covers commercial kitchen exhaust and sets cleaning frequencies by cooking type. |
| Alarms and checks | In Victoria, rental providers must have a gas safety check done every two years by a licensed or registered gasfitter. | The Gas Safety (Installation and Use) Regulations 1998 require annual landlord gas safety checks; in England, rented homes with a fixed combustion appliance (other than a gas cooker) must have a carbon monoxide alarm. | Most states and the residential code require carbon monoxide alarms in homes with fuel-burning appliances. |

Removing a chimney breast or stack is structural work needing building approval in all three jurisdictions. In Britain, work to a stack shared with a neighbour usually needs a party wall notice under the Party Wall etc. Act 1996. Heritage controls in Australia, Britain and the United States frequently protect chimneys as part of a building's character, which can rule out removal and set the materials for repair.

sections.heading: Worked example: staining on a breast after a new boiler
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. In an 1890s terrace converted to flats, brown staining has appeared on a first-floor chimney breast since a condensing gas boiler was fitted to the old flue. From the street, the stack leans slightly away from the weather and its flaunching is cracked; a neighbour shares the stack.

The staining began with the new boiler, so the cause is condensate in an unlined or wrongly lined flue: the boiler comes out of use until the flue is tested, and the flue is relined for a condensing appliance. The lean needs an engineer's view: a slight lean with sound joints is a condition finding, a large one with open joints a falling hazard. The cracked flaunching is a repair.

So the register carries the flue as a safety line now, relining with it, an engineer's assessment of the lean as a check line, and reflaunching in the near term, with a party wall notice before any work to the shared stack.

thresholds.rule: At least 300 mm above any part of the building within 3.6 m horizontally

source.title: NCC 2025 Housing Provisions, Part 12.4 Heating appliances, fireplaces, chimneys and flues

thresholds.rule: At least 300 mm in front of the opening and 150 mm beyond each side

source.title: NCC 2025 Housing Provisions, Part 12.4 Heating appliances, fireplaces, chimneys and flues

thresholds.rule: Deposits of no more than 200 microns; cleaning every 3, 6 or 12 months for heavy, moderate or light use

pages.title: Cladding & Wall Systems
pages.question: How do cladding systems fail, what does each failure look like, and which findings are urgent?
pages.answer: Cladding fails in two ways. Most systems fail by water and fixings: face-sealed render, EIFS and sheet trap water against the frame and rot or corrode it unseen; precast and stone fail at corroding hidden anchors. Combustible systems fail a different test: an immaculate panel with a polyethylene or EPS core is a regulated remediation item regardless of condition. Know how the system manages water and what it is made of before judging its face.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about cladding & wall systems; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Precast concrete, ACP, stone/brick veneer, terracotta, weatherboards, renders

questions.question: Can a façade look fine and still have failed?
questions.answer: Yes. A face-sealed system on timber or light steel framing from the period of known failures can hide a decayed frame; its condition is unknown until it is probed or opened.

questions.question: How do I know if cladding is combustible?
questions.answer: By identification, not condition: records, panel labels or a sample identify the core. Composite panels in perfect condition can still have a combustible core.

questions.question: Why is stone cladding bowing?
questions.answer: Thin marble can bow thermally, uniformly across panels of the same stone; bowing at individual panels, or cracks at anchors, points to anchor failure.

questions.question: What does recladding involve?
questions.answer: Removing the system and replacing it with a drained and ventilated one, including new sheathing, membrane and flashings, with the frame repaired where decayed.

questions.question: How long does cladding last?
questions.answer: Precast panels the life of the building, stone 50 to 100 years, sandwich panels 25 to 40, EIFS and render on sheet 20 to 30, and face-sealed joint sealant 10 to 20.

questions.question: Why is there staining and cracking under the window corners on a rendered wall?
questions.answer: Water is getting in at the window perimeter of a face-sealed system. Probe the framing at the sills; reclad with a drained, ventilated system where the frame has decayed.

questions.question: Why are rust stains running from the joints of the concrete panels?
questions.answer: Concealed fixings are corroding. Open up at the fixing positions, and add stainless anchors or replace corroded hangers.

questions.question: The cladding looks perfect. Could it still be a fire risk?
questions.answer: Yes. Composite panels on apartment blocks of about 1995 to 2018 can have a combustible core with no visible defect. Identify the product from records, labels or a sample; replace it if combustible, with interim measures meanwhile.

questions.question: Why are the insulated metal wall panels rusting at the edges and bulging?
questions.answer: Cut-edge corrosion, with a wet or degraded core. Replace the affected panels, or the system where the core is wet or degraded.

questions.question: Why is the paint peeling and timber rotting at the bottom of the weatherboards?
questions.answer: End grain and ground-line wetting. Replace the decayed boards, seal the ends, restore ground clearance, and repaint.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Cladding problems show from the street as staining, spalling, bowing and fading, close up as soft render and moving panels, inside as damp at reveals, and in the records. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Street or aerial | Panel type and joint pattern: wide open joints suggest rainscreen; narrow sealed joints on every panel edge suggest face-sealed | Water behind the face |
| Street or aerial | Cracked, spalled or rust-stained precast, with staining in lines following reinforcement or at panel corners where fixings sit | Fixings, precast and stone |
| Street or aerial | Bowed stone panels visible in raking light; cracked stone at corners and anchor positions; missing or replaced panels in a different shade | Fixings, precast and stone |
| Street or aerial | Staining below window corners and sills on render and EIFS; cracks running from window corners; patched areas | Water behind the face |
| Street or aerial | Faded, chalked or peeling panel coatings; rust at sandwich panel laps and cut edges; dented panels at ground level | Panels, coatings and weatherboards |
| Street or aerial | Weatherboards with peeling paint, split boards, decay at ends and at ground line; boards close to or below paving | Panels, coatings and weatherboards |
| Street or aerial | Netting, hoarding or temporary covers on a façade, which mean someone has already found something | Fixings, precast and stone |
| Close up on site | Soft or bulging render and EIFS when pressed; hollow sound when tapped; cracks at sheet joints | Water behind the face |
| Close up on site | Moisture readings and soft spots in framing behind sheet systems, taken at sills, the bottom plate and below windows | Water behind the face |
| Close up on site | Movement of stone or precast panels when pushed; cracking at anchor positions; rust bleeding from joints | Fixings, precast and stone |
| Close up on site | Panel labels or markings on the back of composite panels where a panel can be removed; the core visible at cut edges | Combustible cladding |
| Close up on site | Cavity barriers present or absent at floor lines and around openings, where a panel can be lifted | Combustible cladding |
| Inside the building | Damp, mould and swelling at window reveals, at skirtings on external walls and at the base of walls under sills | Water behind the face |
| Inside the building | Stained ceilings below parapets and at slab edges; corrosion at exposed light steel framing in plant rooms or ceilings | Water behind the face |
| Inside the building | Musty smell in apartments with framed external walls, a common early sign of hidden decay | Water behind the face |
| In the records | Cladding audit, fire engineer report, regulator correspondence or registration on a state or national cladding programme | Combustible cladding |
| In the records | Insurance exclusions or loadings referring to the external walls or panel cores | Combustible cladding |
| In the records | Defect claims, expert reports and rectification orders on apartment buildings | Water behind the face |
| In the records | Repeated leak repairs at the same windows or elevations; sealant renewal history | Water behind the face |

sections.heading: Types of cladding
sections.markdown:
Cladding is any external wall system hung on or fixed to a structure rather than built up from the ground as masonry: precast concrete panels, metal composite and solid aluminium panels, stone veneer on brackets, terracotta and ceramic rainscreen, fibre cement and render systems on framing, exterior insulation and finish systems (EIFS), insulated sandwich panels, and timber or fibre cement weatherboards. Masonry has its own page. The system is more than the face: it includes the support framing or brackets, fixings, any insulation, the sheathing or sarking behind, cavity barriers, and the joints and flashings that make it weathertight.

Every system manages rain in one of three ways, and the way it manages rain decides how it fails. Face-sealed (barrier) systems stop water at the outer surface and rely entirely on sealant joints; when a joint fails, water is inside with no way out. Most precast of the 1960s to 1990s, early EIFS and much render on sheet are face-sealed. Drained and ventilated (rainscreen) systems accept that water passes the face, and drain it down a cavity to flashings and weep points, with a sealed line behind. Most modern panel, terracotta and weatherboard systems work this way. Mass systems absorb and release water, as solid masonry and thick render on masonry do.

| System | Typical era and use | What it implies |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Precast concrete panels, face-sealed joints, cast-in fixings | 1960s to 1990s offices, apartments, institutions | Joint sealant at or past its third renewal; reinforcement corrosion where cover is low; concealed fixing corrosion |
| Stone veneer on dowels, cramps or brackets | 1970s to 2000s offices and retail podiums | Fixing corrosion in carbon steel; thin marble panels bowing; anchor holes cracking |
| Metal composite panels (ACP) with polyethylene core | About 1995 to 2018, apartments, offices, hotels, retail | Combustibility, not condition, is the issue: a regulated rectification item |
| EIFS and render on foam or sheet | 1980s to 2000s in the United States; 1990s to 2010s apartments in Australia and New Zealand | Face-sealed versions trap water against framing; hidden decay of timber or steel frame and sheathing |
| Fibre cement or render on timber or light steel frame, no cavity | 1990s to 2010s apartments and townhouses | Same water-trapping risk; cracking at sheet joints; leaks at windows and parapets |
| Insulated sandwich panels (EPS, PIR, mineral wool core) | 1970s onward, industrial, cool stores, retail sheds | EPS cores are combustible and drive insurance and fire risk; delamination where cores get wet |
| Terracotta and ceramic rainscreen on aluminium rails | 2000s onward, commercial and institutional | Clip and rail fixings; cracked tiles at clips; generally durable |
| Timber and fibre cement weatherboards | Houses throughout; townhouses | Paint cycle drives life; decay at ends and ground contact; cracking at fixings in fibre cement |

Building class shapes the risk. Apartments carry the combustibility and water-trapping legacy of the 1995 to 2018 period and are the focus of the cladding regimes in all three jurisdictions. Offices carry precast and stone with ageing fixings. Industrial buildings carry sandwich panels whose core type matters more than their appearance. Houses carry weatherboards and render, where the paint and the ground line decide the life.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Cladding lives span a wide range: precast panels last the life of the building and stone fifty to a hundred years, while EIFS and render on sheet last twenty to thirty, and face-sealed joint sealants ten to twenty. Carbon steel fixings, hidden behind the face, last thirty to sixty years.

| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Precast concrete panel | Life of the building | Cover to reinforcement, carbonation, chloride exposure |
| Precast joint sealant (face-sealed) | 10 to 20 years | Exposure, joint design; see Sealants and Joints |
| Stone cladding | 50 to 100 years | Fixing material; thin marble bows; stone type |
| Carbon steel fixings and brackets | 30 to 60 years | Moisture at the fixing, coastal exposure |
| Stainless steel and aluminium fixings | Life of the building | Dissimilar metal contact, crevice corrosion in marine air |
| ACP and solid aluminium panel finish | 20 to 35 years | Coating type, UV, coastal exposure |
| EIFS and render on sheet | 20 to 30 years | Drained or face-sealed, impact, detailing at openings |
| Insulated sandwich panel | 25 to 40 years | Coating on the skins, cut-edge corrosion, core moisture |
| Timber weatherboards | 30 to 60 years with a maintained paint cycle | Paint cycle, ground clearance, end grain sealing |
| Fibre cement weatherboards and sheet | 40 to 60 years | Paint cycle, fixings, movement at joints |

What shortens life: face-sealed detailing on any system with framing behind it: one failed joint wets the frame with no route out; missing or reversed flashings at window heads, sills, floor lines and parapets; water directed into the wall rather than out of it; coastal and industrial exposure, which consumes coatings and corrodes carbon steel fixings and cut edges; dissimilar metals: aluminium rails on galvanised brackets, stainless fixings in aluminium without isolation, copper runoff; impact at ground level and on balconies, which opens EIFS and render and exposes sandwich panel cores; deferred sealant renewal on face-sealed systems; ground and paving too close to the bottom of weatherboards, render and sheet.

sections.heading: Water behind the face
sections.markdown:
Face-sealed EIFS, render on sheet and fibre cement without a cavity are only as good as their joints and their window details. When a sill or joint fails, water reaches the sheathing and frame and stays there. Timber frames rot; light steel frames corrode at the bottom track; oriented strand board and plywood sheathing delaminate. The face can look sound for years while the frame behind fails, which is how the leaky building crisis in New Zealand and the EIFS litigation in the United States unfolded.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Staining and cracking below window corners on render or EIFS; damp at reveals inside | Water entry at window perimeter in a face-sealed system. No head or sill flashing; moisture readings high at the sill and bottom plate; decay found on opening up. | Probe the framing at the sills; reclad with a drained, ventilated system where the frame has decayed. |

sections.heading: Fixings, precast and stone
sections.markdown:
Precast panels hang on cast-in ferrules, bearing angles and restraint fixings; stone hangs on dowels, cramps and kerf clips; panel systems hang on brackets and rails. Carbon steel fixings corrode where water reaches them. Expanding corrosion cracks the stone or concrete at the anchor and can release a section of panel. Section loss in hidden hangers is the most serious failure mode of heavy cladding because it gives little external warning.

Thin precast panels often have little concrete cover over the reinforcement, especially at edges, ribs and returns. Once carbonation reaches the steel, or chlorides from coastal air do, the steel corrodes and spalls the concrete face, usually in lines that follow the bars.

Thin marble panels lose strength and bow permanently under repeated heating and cooling (thermal hysteresis), dishing outward or inward. Sandstone and some limestones delaminate when laid face-bedded. Bowed and delaminated stone cracks at its anchors.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rust staining from precast joints; cracking at panel corners | Corrosion of concealed fixings. Staining at fixing positions per the panel drawings; cracks radiating from corners; openings expose corroded ferrules or angles. | Open up at the fixing positions; add stainless anchors or replace corroded hangers. |
| Spalling in lines across precast faces | Reinforcement corrosion from low cover. Covermeter shows low cover along the line; carbonation depth reaches the steel, the front marking a fall in pH from about 12.5 to 8.5 (Institute of Corrosion). | Repair the concrete to a recognised repair standard, or overclad where the substrate is sound. |
| Dished or bowed stone panels, cracks at anchors | Thermal bowing of thin marble, or anchor failure. Bowing uniform across panels of the same stone: hysteresis; local cracking at one anchor: anchor corrosion or overstress. | Check the anchors; add supplementary stainless anchors, or replace bowed panels. |
| Layers of stone flaking parallel to the face | Face-bedded stone, or salt crystallisation. Bedding planes parallel to the face; salts in the debris. | Replace the affected stone. |

sections.heading: Combustible cladding
sections.markdown:
Metal composite panels with a polyethylene core, EPS-cored sandwich panels, some high-pressure laminates and timber, foam insulation in cavities, and missing or misplaced cavity barriers can carry fire up and across a façade. This is a design and compliance issue, not a condition issue: an immaculate panel can be the most serious item on the building.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Immaculate composite panels on an apartment block of the 1995 to 2018 era | Possible combustible core; no condition defect. Product identified from records, panel labels or a core sample. | Identify the product from records, labels or a sample; replace it if combustible, with interim measures meanwhile. |
| Combustible cladding on a residential building above the height at which the asset’s market restricts it | External surface below the class now expected. Cladding classification against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Carry out a fire risk appraisal of the external wall to PAS 9980, and plan remediation where it is needed. |

sections.heading: Panels, coatings and weatherboards
sections.markdown:
Coated metal panels chalk and fade, then lose coating at edges and cut lines; composite panels can delaminate where skins debond from the core. Sandwich panels corrode from cut edges and fixings, and their cores degrade when wet. EIFS and render crack at sheet joints, around openings and from impact, and lose bond to the substrate.

Timber weatherboards decay where paint fails at end grain, at the ground line, and behind downpipes and gutters; boards cup and split as they cycle wet and dry. Fibre cement boards crack at fixings and lose coating; edges absorb water where unsealed.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sandwich panel skins rusting from laps and cut edges, panels bulging | Cut-edge corrosion; wet or degraded core. Corrosion starts at edges and fixings; panel soft or delaminated when pressed. | Replace affected panels, or the system where the core is wet or degraded. |
| Peeling paint and decay concentrated at weatherboard ends and the bottom courses | End grain moisture and ground-line wetting. Ends unsealed; boards close to paving or soil; sound boards higher up. Clearances to ground, paving and floor framing measured against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Replace decayed boards, seal the ends, restore ground clearance, and repaint. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Loose, cracked or displaced panel or stone over a footpath, entry or occupied area; anchor visibly failed | safety · 4 Essential | Make safe immediately: remove, net or hoard; engineer within days. |
| Combustible cladding identified where a regulator, scheme or order sets a remediation date | deadline · 4 Essential | Timing set by the regulator; interim fire safety measures until done. |
| Combustible cladding identified with no order yet | check · 2 Planned | External wall fire risk assessment by a fire engineer sets whether and how soon it must be remediated. |
| Decay or corrosion found in framing or sheathing behind a face-sealed system | failure · 3 Important | Remediation now; extent from opening up, often elevation by elevation. |
| Spalling precast from reinforcement corrosion; fixing corrosion without displacement; leaks at windows | condition · 3 Important | Programme repair in the near term; extent from investigation. |
| Coating faded and chalked; weatherboards due for repaint; sealant at age on a sound system | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Renewal on cycle. |
| Face-sealed system on framing of the at-risk era with no investigation on record | check · 2 Planned | Probe and open up before sizing works. |
| Isolated hairline cracks in render; minor coating wear | nil · 1 Routine | Routine care. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A façade engineer leads on panel and stone systems; a building surveyor can lead on houses and low-rise weatherboard and render. Combustibility is assessed by a fire engineer, and in Britain by an assessment under PAS 9980 for residential buildings in scope. The checks below identify each system and its era first, then probe or open the façade where the system type and era point.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Desk review | Of drawings, product certificates and any audit, to identify the system and its fixings before going on site. |
| Close-up survey | From rope access or a platform, every elevation over public areas, a representative sample elsewhere. |
| Opening up | At representative locations: sills and heads of windows, floor lines, parapets and the base of walls on framed systems; panel removal on rainscreen to see brackets, rails, insulation and cavity barriers; fixings exposed on precast and stone. |
| Moisture probing | Of framing behind sheet and EIFS systems at the high-risk points, with probes left in place for monitoring where the wall will not be stripped. |
| Concrete testing | On precast: cover survey, carbonation depth, chloride content at the depth of the steel. |
| Fixing testing | Pull-out tests on stone anchors and remedial fixings; section loss measured on exposed hangers. |
| Core identification | Of composite and sandwich panels by sample and laboratory test where records do not settle it. |
| Water testing | Of windows and joints to locate leak paths before remedial design. |

The report should state the system and how it manages water, what was found behind it, fixing condition, combustibility status, and remedial scope by elevation with measured extents.

sections.heading: Repairing, re-fixing or recladding
sections.markdown:
Anything loose over a footpath or entry is made safe first. After that, the choice runs from local repair through fixing remediation to recladding, and turns on what lies behind the face: a sound frame and fixings, or decay, corrosion and combustible materials.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Local repair | Reseal joints, repair precast concrete to a recognised repair standard, replace individual panels and boards, and repair render and recoat. | Where the system and what lies behind it are sound. |
| Fixing remediation | Supplementary stainless anchors drilled through panels or stone into the structure, and replacement of corroded hangers, which can require panels to be removed and rehung. | Where fixings corrode or anchors have failed. |
| Recladding | Remove the system and replace it with a drained and ventilated system, including new sheathing, membrane and flashings, with frame repair where decayed. | The usual answer for failed face-sealed systems on framing, and for combustible panels. |
| Overcladding | A new rainscreen fixed over an existing sound wall. | On precast and masonry, where the substrate is sound and the joints are not worth renewing. |
| Combustible cladding | Replace with non-combustible panels and insulation, reinstate cavity barriers, and keep interim measures (fire watch, alarms, a changed evacuation strategy) until complete. | Wherever combustible cladding is identified. |
| Weatherboards | Replace decayed boards, seal ends, restore ground clearance, and repaint on cycle. | Where boards decay or paint fails. |

Interactions: recladding carries window, sealant, flashing and balcony work with it; scaffolding or access dominates; on occupied apartment buildings the programme is often elevation by elevation; heritage listing can restrict materials.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Investigation is a lump sum with rates per opening, test and sample. Recladding and overcladding are measured by façade area, with separate lines for windows, flashings and frame repair found on opening up. Fixing remediation is priced per anchor or per panel. Panel replacement and board replacement are rate-based. Access is often the largest single component.

Combustible cladding rectification is a lump-sum project with consultant, approval and interim measure costs, coded as code compliance with its timing driven by the regulator. Recladding of a failed face-sealed system is lifecycle or repairs, with the frame repair a conditional line sized from opening up. The usual register shape is two-part: investigation first, then a conditional works envelope.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a sound-looking façade cannot: what each system and its core are made of, whether combustibility has been assessed, and whether framed walls have leaked. Ask for them before relying on the façade's appearance.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Façade drawings, specifications and product certificates naming each system, panel core and insulation | What each system is, and what its panels and insulation are made of. |
| Any cladding audit, fire engineer report, PAS 9980 assessment, EWS1 form, regulator correspondence or order | Whether combustibility has been assessed, and what the regulator or lender requires. |
| Façade inspection reports and ordinance filings | Whether periodic façade inspections are current, and what they found. |
| Records of panel replacement, fixing remediation, recladding or overcladding | What has already been replaced or re-fixed. |
| Leak logs, defect claims and expert reports on framed systems | Whether framed systems have leaked, and whether defects are in dispute. |
| Insurance terms referring to external walls | Whether the external walls affect insurance cover or premiums. |
| Repaint history for weatherboards and render | Where weatherboards and render are in their paint cycle. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Cladding is misread when a sound face is taken to mean a sound wall, and when immaculate panels are taken to mean there is nothing to find.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| A sound face means a sound wall | A sound-looking face-sealed system can hide a failed frame. Where the system is face-sealed, sits on timber or light steel framing, and was built in the period of known failures, condition of the frame is unknown until it is probed or opened. |
| Immaculate panels need nothing | Composite panels in perfect condition on an apartment building can still have a combustible core. That is a matter of identification, not condition: the product is identified from records, panel labels or a sample. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market restricts combustible materials in external walls, and has its own regime for remediation and periodic façade inspection. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Combustibility | The National Construction Code requires external walls of Type A and Type B construction to be non-combustible, tested to AS 1530.1, with performance solutions tested to AS 5113. | Approved Document B and regulation 7(2) prohibit combustible materials in the external walls of relevant buildings 18 m and over; PAS 9980:2022 sets the method for fire risk appraisal of external walls. | International Building Code Chapter 14 governs exterior walls, with NFPA 285 testing required for combustible components on most buildings of Types I to IV construction; EIFS follows ASTM E2568. |
| Remediation and inspection | State regimes act on combustible cladding: Cladding Safety Victoria administers rectification of high-risk buildings, New South Wales bans aluminium composite panels with more than 30 per cent polyethylene core on certain buildings under the Building Products (Safety) Act 2017 and runs Project Remediate, and Queensland ran a combustible cladding checklist programme. | The Building Safety Act 2022 places duties on accountable persons for higher-risk buildings, creates remediation orders and protects many leaseholders from remediation costs; the Cladding Safety Scheme and Building Safety Fund fund remediation of eligible buildings, and lenders rely on EWS1 forms. | Façade ordinances in New York, Chicago, Boston, San Francisco and others require periodic critical examination of cladding on taller buildings; New York's Cycle 10 runs from February 2025 to February 2029. |

In Australia, cladding on strata buildings is common property, and rectification and defect claims sit with the owners corporation.

sections.heading: Worked example: render on a 1990s apartment block
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 1990s apartment block is clad in render on sheet over timber framing, face-sealed at the windows. The render looks sound from the street, but there is staining below several window corners, and two apartments report musty smells and swelling at the window reveals.

A face-sealed system on timber framing from the period of known failures can hide a failed frame behind a sound face. Staining below window corners and swelling at the reveals point to water entering at the window perimeter. The frame's condition is unknown until it is probed or opened at the sills.

So the register carries probing and opening up at the sills as a check line now. If decay is found, recladding with a drained and ventilated system, with frame repair, becomes a failure line, and the owners corporation's defect position is checked alongside.

thresholds.rule: 150 mm to finished ground; 100 mm in low-rainfall or sandy, well-drained areas; 50 mm above paving that falls away; cladding taken 50 mm below the lowest floor framing

source.title: NCC 2025 Housing Provisions, Part 7.5 Timber and composite wall cladding

thresholds.rule: Class A2-s1, d0 or better where a storey is more than 11 m above ground

source.title: Approved Document B, Volume 1: Dwellings (2026 online version)

pages.title: Commercial Kitchens
pages.question: How do commercial kitchens fail, and which kitchen findings are fire and life-safety risks?
pages.answer: Kitchens fail on fire first: grease builds in hoods and ducts when cleaning is missed, suppression no longer covers moved appliances, and gas interlocks are bypassed. Exhaust without make-up air backdraughts gas appliances and produces carbon monoxide. Wet floors cause slips and leak into floors below; cool room releases fail and trap workers; damaged linings fail food inspections. Clean ducts to the cooking demand and keep suppression matched to the layout.

questions.question: Why does smoke spill out of the kitchen hood?
questions.answer: Too little exhaust capacity or make-up air for the cooking. Measure capture and make-up air, especially at peak.

questions.question: Does suppression need changing when appliances move?
questions.answer: Yes. Wet chemical suppression is designed for a set layout, and moved or added appliances may sit outside its nozzles.

questions.question: How often should kitchen exhaust ducts be cleaned?
questions.answer: At a frequency set by the cooking: NFPA 96 sets it in the United States and TR19 Grease sets the practice in the United Kingdom. Heavy frying and charcoal need far more frequent cleaning.

questions.question: Can someone be trapped in a cool room?
questions.answer: Yes, if the internal release fails. It must open from inside; test it, and fit an alarm and lighting.

questions.question: How long does a commercial kitchen fit-out last?
questions.answer: Fit-out and finishes 10 to 15 years, cooking equipment 8 to 15, and hoods 15 to 25.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Commercial kitchen problems show at the hoods, ducts and suppression nozzles, in doors that slam and smoke that spills, on wet floors and in cool rooms, and in cleaning and service records. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On site | Grease on hood surfaces, filters and duct access panels; cleaning certificates and dates | Grease, ducts and suppression |
| On site | Suppression nozzles against current appliance positions; service tags | Grease, ducts and suppression |
| On site | Doors slamming or hard to open; smoke escaping hoods | Make-up air and combustion |
| On site | Ponding water; cracked tiles and failed grout; floor wastes blocked | Floors, linings and hygiene |
| On site | Cool room internal release present and working; ice on panels; damaged seals | Cool rooms |
| On site | Gaps around services; damaged linings; pest evidence | Floors, linings and hygiene |
| In the records | Exhaust cleaning certificates | Grease, ducts and suppression |
| In the records | Suppression system service records | Grease, ducts and suppression |
| In the records | Gas interlock tests | Grease, ducts and suppression |
| In the records | Food safety inspection reports | Floors, linings and hygiene |
| In the records | Trade waste and grease arrestor records | Floors, linings and hygiene |
| In the records | Leak history below the kitchen | Floors, linings and hygiene |
| In the records | Charcoal, wok or high-volume frying equipment added since the kitchen was designed | Grease, ducts and suppression |

sections.heading: What the space does and what it contains
sections.markdown:
Commercial kitchens prepare food in restaurants, hotels, hospitals, aged care, schools, staff canteens and food courts. They concentrate hazards in one room: open flames and hot oil under grease-laden exhaust hoods, gas, wet slippery floors, heavy electrical loads, cool rooms that people can be trapped in, and food safety requirements for every surface. Functionally the kitchen must cook safely, exhaust heat, smoke and grease, stay hygienic and pass inspection. Whether the operator or the building owner is responsible varies: in leased restaurants the tenant usually owns the fit-out but the building carries the exhaust riser, grease waste and gas supply.

| Element group | Typical provision | What matters for the space |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Exhaust hoods and ducts | Canopy hoods, grease filters, ducts to roof, exhaust fan | Capture; grease accumulation; fire |
| Fire suppression | Wet chemical systems over cooking appliances; extinguishers and blankets | Coverage of current appliances; servicing |
| Make-up air | Supply air to replace exhaust | Negative pressure, draughts, combustion problems |
| Gas | Supply, isolation valves, interlocks to exhaust | Shut-off when exhaust fails or fire |
| Floors and drainage | Non-slip floors falling to drains, floor wastes, grease arrestor | Slips; leaks; grease |
| Wall and ceiling finishes | Smooth, impervious, cleanable surfaces | Food safety; pest harbourage |
| Cool rooms and freezers | Insulated panels, doors, refrigeration | Entrapment release; ice; seals |
| Electrical | Heavy power supply, RCD protection | Capacity; wet environment |

sections.heading: How long it stays fit for purpose
sections.markdown:
A commercial kitchen's fit-out lasts ten to fifteen years and its cooking equipment eight to fifteen, while hoods and cool room panels last fifteen to twenty-five. Menu and equipment changes usually end its fitness for purpose before anything wears out.

| Component or quality | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Kitchen fit-out and finishes | 10 to 15 years | Use; cleaning; operator changes |
| Exhaust hoods and filters | 15 to 25 years; filters cleaned weekly | Grease; cleaning |
| Exhaust fans | 10 to 15 years | Grease; run hours |
| Cooking equipment | 8 to 15 years | Use; maintenance |
| Cool room panels and refrigeration | 15 to 25 years; refrigeration 10 to 15 | Ice damage; refrigerant rules |
| Floors | 10 to 20 years | Traffic; chemicals; water |

What shortens fitness for purpose: grease in hoods, ducts and fans when cleaning is missed; water and chemicals attacking floors, junctions and substrates; menu and equipment changes outgrowing the exhaust, suppression and power; electrification of cooking replacing gas with heavier electrical loads.

sections.heading: Grease, ducts and suppression
sections.markdown:
Grease builds up in filters, hoods, ducts and exhaust fans. A flare-up ignites it, and fire travels along the duct, sometimes through floors to the roof. Infrequent cleaning, missing access panels and ducts without fire-rated enclosures turn kitchen fires into building fires.

Wet chemical suppression is designed for a set appliance layout. When fryers and ranges are moved or added, nozzles no longer cover them; fusible links not replaced and gas interlocks bypassed stop the system working.

A certificate saying the exhaust was cleaned does not settle whether the duct was. Cleaning that reaches only the hood and the first part of the duct leaves grease where a flare-up can find it, so the evidence is grease depth measured at access points along the whole route to the fan.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Suppression nozzles over empty bench | Appliances moved since design. Layout against design. | Redesign the suppression to the current layout, and interlock it to gas and power. |
| Thick grease at duct access panels, or no access panels at all | Cleaning too infrequent for the cooking, or parts of the duct unreachable. Grease depth measured at access points; certificates cover the hood but not the duct run. | Clean the full duct at a frequency set by the cooking, and add access panels. |
| Gas still flowing in a suppression or interlock test | An interlock bypassed or failed. Gas does not shut off on discharge, or when the exhaust stops. | Restore and test the interlock before cooking continues. |

sections.heading: Make-up air and combustion
sections.markdown:
Exhaust without adequate make-up air puts the kitchen under negative pressure: doors slam, draughts pull smoke out of hoods, and gas appliances and flues backdraught, producing carbon monoxide.

The balance is the point. A kitchen should run slightly negative, so smells and heat stay in the kitchen, but not starved: once exhaust far outstrips make-up air, the hoods stop capturing, and gas appliances and flues can backdraught carbon monoxide into the room.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Smoke escaping canopies at busy times | Exhaust capacity or make-up air shortfall. Airflow measurements. | Measure capture and make-up air; rebalance, or upgrade the hood and fan for the cooking now done. |
| Doors slamming, flues backdraughting | Negative pressure. Pressure and CO measurement (Thresholds by market). | Stop using the affected gas appliances until make-up air is restored, and measure carbon monoxide. |

sections.heading: Floors, linings and hygiene
sections.markdown:
Wet, greasy floors cause slips. Floors without falls to drains hold water; failed floor junctions and wastes leak into substrates and floors below, rotting timber and corroding steel.

Damaged wall linings, open joints, gaps around services and dead spaces behind equipment harbour pests and fail food safety inspections.

Equipment changes are the usual trigger: a new fryer bank, wok station or charcoal grill changes exhaust, suppression, power and gas loads all at once.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stains below the kitchen | Floor membrane or waste failure. Flood test. | Flood test; renew the membrane and wastes, with falls to drains. |
| Food safety non-compliances for linings | Damaged or unsuitable finishes. Inspection report. | Replace with impervious, cleanable linings, and seal the penetrations. |
| Water ponding away from the floor wastes | A floor without falls to drains. A level shows the ponding; tiles crack where water sits. | Re-form the floor to fall to drains, with a slip-resistant finish. |
| Hot water at hand basins slow to arrive or barely warm | Hot water not reaching temperature. Temperatures at the outlets against the limits for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Rebalance or repair the hot water circulation, and fit tempering at hand basins where required. |

sections.heading: Cool rooms
sections.markdown:
Cool room doors must open from inside; failed internal releases have trapped workers. Ice build-up damages panels, failed door seals waste energy and corrupt food safety, and refrigeration faults lose stock.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No working release on the inside of a cool room door | An internal release missing, broken or iced up. Test the release from inside, with the door held. | Repair or fit the release, with an alarm and lighting, before the room is used again. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Grease build-up in ducts; suppression not covering appliances; gas interlocks bypassed; cool room releases failed; CO from backdraught | safety · 4 Essential | Rectify before cooking continues. |
| Exhaust or refrigeration failed | failure · 3 Important | Repair now. |
| Duct cleaning, suppression servicing or food inspection due | deadline · 4 Essential | At the prescribed interval. |
| Floor, lining and drainage defects | condition · 3 Important | Repair in the near term. |
| Fit-out and equipment at end of life | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Refurbish. |
| Services capacity unknown for the current menu | check · 2 Planned | Assess. |
| Normal | nil · 1 Routine | Routine. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A building services engineer experienced in kitchen ventilation leads, with the suppression and gas contractors, a hydraulic engineer for floors and drainage, and the operator's food safety lead. The checks below start with fire and life safety, the exhaust, suppression, gas interlocks and cool room releases, then measure capacity against the cooking the kitchen now does.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Exhaust inspection | Hoods, filters, ducts from hood to fan and the fan itself, with grease depth measured at access points against the limit for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market), and the duct route checked for access panels and fire-rated enclosure through floors. |
| Airflow measurement | Of hood capture and make-up air, and observation at peak cooking. |
| Suppression review | Nozzle positions against the appliances now installed, service tags, link replacement dates, manual release, and gas and power shut-off on discharge. |
| Gas safety check | Appliances, connections, isolation, interlock to exhaust, and carbon monoxide levels with appliances running. |
| Floor and drainage inspection | With flood tests and checks below the kitchen for leaks. |
| Cool room safety check | Internal releases, alarms, lighting, panels and seals. |
| Food safety review | Against recent inspection findings. |

The report should list fire and life safety items first, then capacity against the current menu and equipment, and a refurbishment plan.

sections.heading: Making safe, cleaning, upgrading or refurbishing
sections.markdown:
Grease in the ducts, suppression that misses the appliances, bypassed gas interlocks and failed cool room releases come first, before cooking continues. After that, the work matches exhaust, make-up air, suppression and power to the current menu, and repairs floors and linings.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Exhaust cleaning | Clean at a frequency matched to the cooking type, with access panels added so the whole duct can be cleaned. | In every kitchen; heavy frying and charcoal need far more frequent cleaning. |
| Duct fire protection | Fire-rated enclosures where ducts pass through other floors and spaces. | Where ducts pass through other floors and spaces. |
| Suppression redesign | Redesign to the current appliance layout, serviced and interlocked to gas and power. | Whenever appliances are moved or added. |
| Make-up air | Balance make-up air to exhaust, so the kitchen is slightly negative but not starved. | Where doors slam, hoods spill or flues backdraught. |
| Floors | Falls to drains, slip-resistant finishes, coved junctions and new membranes where leaks occur. | Where floors pond, are slippery or leak. |
| Linings | Impervious, cleanable surfaces with sealed penetrations to deny pests harbourage. | Where linings fail food safety inspection. |
| Cool rooms | Internal releases, alarms, seals, panels and refrigeration on cycle. | In every cool room and freezer. |
| Electrification planning | Power capacity for induction and electric equipment where gas is being phased out. | Where gas cooking is being phased out. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Exhaust cleaning and suppression servicing recur, and are often the operator's cost. Exhaust, make-up air and duct fire protection upgrades are lump sums. Kitchen refurbishment is a lump sum including closure time, which in hotels and hospitals needs temporary kitchens. Floors and linings are priced by area. In leased premises, the lease decides who pays for base-building items such as the exhaust riser and grease waste.

Fire safety items are immediate; servicing is recurring compliance; refurbishment is lifecycle.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a walk through the kitchen cannot: whether the whole duct is cleaned, whether suppression covers today's appliances, and who pays for each part. Ask for them before the kitchen changes its menu or its operator.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Exhaust and duct cleaning certificates | Whether the whole duct is cleaned, and how often. |
| Suppression system service records | Whether suppression is serviced and covers the appliances now installed. |
| Gas compliance and interlock test records | Whether gas shuts off when the exhaust stops or the suppression fires. |
| Food safety inspection reports | What food safety inspectors have found. |
| Leak history below the kitchen | Whether the kitchen floor leaks into spaces below. |
| Lease allocation of kitchen responsibilities | Who pays for what, between operator and owner. |
| Equipment schedule and layout as currently installed | What the kitchen now cooks with, against what it was designed for. |
| Insurance requirements for kitchen fire protection | What the insurer requires as evidence. |
| Pest control contract and reports | Whether pests are controlled. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Commercial kitchens are misread when a kitchen fire is assumed to stay in the kitchen, when the item that failed is fixed without asking why, and when a cleaning certificate is taken as proof.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| A fire in the kitchen stays in the kitchen | Grease in exhaust ducts, suppression that no longer covers the appliances, and gas without interlocked shut-off are fire and life-safety findings. |
| Fix the item that failed | Most kitchen findings trace to a mismatch between the kitchen as designed and the cooking it now does. A new fryer bank, wok station or charcoal grill changes the exhaust, suppression, power and gas loads all at once, so each change needs all four checked. |
| The certificate shows it was cleaned | A cleaning certificate that does not say how much of the duct was cleaned settles little. Grease depth measured at access points along the whole duct is the evidence. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets standards for kitchen exhaust and fire protection, wet chemical suppression, gas interlocks and food premises. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Exhaust, suppression, gas and food premises | AS 1668.1 and AS 1668.2 cover kitchen exhaust and fire requirements; AS 4674 covers the design and fit-out of food premises; the Food Standards Code sets premises requirements; gas installations follow AS/NZS 5601.1. | BESA DW/172 sets kitchen ventilation specification and TR19 Grease sets duct cleaning practice; food hygiene regulations apply; gas interlocks follow BS 6173. | NFPA 96 governs commercial cooking ventilation, including duct cleaning frequencies; UL 300 lists wet chemical suppression; the FDA Food Code and state health codes govern food premises. |

Insurers in all three countries commonly require evidence of exhaust cleaning and suppression servicing, and may decline claims for kitchen fires without it.

Health authorities can close premises that fail food safety inspections.

sections.heading: Worked example: a wok station added to a café kitchen
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A café in a mixed-use building added a wok station and a second fryer when its menu changed. The suppression nozzles still point at the old layout, the exhaust certificate covers the hood but not the duct to the roof, smoke spills from the canopy at lunch, and the back door slams when the exhaust runs.

The findings trace to one mismatch: the kitchen as designed against the cooking it now does. Suppression that misses the new appliances, and a duct that may hold grease, are fire and life-safety findings. Smoke spilling and a slamming door point to too little make-up air, which can also backdraught the gas appliances.

So the register carries the suppression and the duct as safety lines before cooking continues, a full duct clean with access panels, a carbon monoxide check, make-up air rebalanced, and the exhaust and power checked against the new menu, with the lease settling who pays.

pages.title: Commercial Office Areas (Base-Build)
pages.question: How do office floors fail as working space, and how do you tell base-building problems from fit-out drift?
pages.answer: An office floor fails as a workplace before its parts wear out. Built-in limits (low ceilings, deep plates, few toilets) cap how far it can be repositioned; comfort fails where zoning no longer matches partitions, outside air is low, or the perimeter overheats; repeated fit-outs leave abandoned services and break sprinkler, detection and egress coverage. Separate base-building performance from tenant drift: the remedies and who pays differ. Time refurbishment to lease expiry.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about commercial office areas (base-build); it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
