pages.searchTitle: Office floors: comfort complaints, fit-out drift, sprinkler coverage, grade and refurbishment

questions.question: Who fixes sprinkler coverage after a tenant fit-out?
questions.answer: Usually the tenant who changed the layout, through the fit-out approval or make-good. Compliance problems on office floors almost always trace back to fit-outs.

questions.question: Why are perimeter offices hot in the afternoon?
questions.answer: Façade heat gain and glare. Blinds, films or glazing upgrades, with perimeter zoning that matches the layout, treat it.

questions.question: Why is the meeting room stuffy after lunch?
questions.answer: Low outside air or high density. Measure carbon dioxide and outside air, and upgrade where the rates fall short.

questions.question: Why will a sound office floor not lease?
questions.answer: Often market grade or functional limits rather than condition. Compare it with the buildings tenants could choose instead.

questions.question: How long does an office fit-out last?
questions.answer: Usually a lease term of 7 to 12 years; base-building carpet lasts 10 to 15, and ceiling grids 20 to 30.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Office floor problems show in the ceiling and its tiles, in lighting, diffusers, carpet and closed blinds, in partitions that cut across services, and in complaint, fit-out and leasing records. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On a floor walk | Ceiling height and how crowded the ceiling void is with ducts, cables and abandoned services when tiles are lifted | Functional limits and energy |
| On a floor walk | Stained, sagging, cut or mismatched ceiling tiles, showing leaks and repeated fit-out changes | Fit-out residue and compliance drift |
| On a floor walk | Lighting type and evenness; dark patches or glare at screens; fluorescent fittings remaining | Comfort, air and light |
| On a floor walk | Diffusers capped, blocked by partitions or blowing onto desks; supplementary split systems added by tenants | Comfort, air and light |
| On a floor walk | Carpet worn in traffic routes, frayed at tile edges, or patched with mismatched tiles | Wear and damage |
| On a floor walk | Partitions or joinery cutting across sprinkler and detector coverage; exit signs not visible from new rooms | Fit-out residue and compliance drift |
| On a floor walk | Toilet and end-of-trip provision against apparent occupancy | Functional limits and energy |
| On a floor walk | Blinds closed all day at the perimeter, a sign of glare and heat problems | Comfort, air and light |
| In the records | Comfort complaint logs by floor and zone | Comfort, air and light |
| In the records | Fit-out approvals and as-built drawings for each tenancy | Fit-out residue and compliance drift |
| In the records | Make-good schedules and lease terms | Fit-out residue and compliance drift |
| In the records | Air and light measurements from commissioning or audits | Comfort, air and light |
| In the records | Energy and indoor environment ratings | Functional limits and energy |
| In the records | Vacancy and leasing feedback | Functional limits and energy |

sections.heading: What the space does and what it contains
sections.markdown:
Commercial office areas are the lettable floors where tenants work: the open floor, ceilings, lighting, floor finishes, the air conditioning outlets and controls, power and data distribution, and the core services that reach each floor. As a functional space, an office floor is judged on whether it does its job for a tenant and holds its place in the market, not only on the condition of its parts. A floor can be in good condition and still fail if its ceiling is too low for current services, its air supply is below current expectations, its lighting is uneven, its toilets are too few for modern densities, or its energy rating keeps tenants away.

Responsibility is split, and the split decides who pays. The base building (sometimes called shell and core, or in Britain Category A fit-out) is the owner's: raised floors or slab finishes, suspended ceilings, base lighting, air conditioning to the floor, fire services, core toilets and amenities. The tenant fit-out (Category B in Britain) is the tenant's: partitions, meeting rooms, kitchens, joinery, specialist lighting and supplementary cooling. At lease end, make-good clauses decide what returns to base build and at whose cost.

| Element group | Typical base-building provision | What matters for the space |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ceilings | Suspended grid with tiles, or exposed soffits in newer and refurbished floors | Height, acoustic performance, access to services, appearance |
| Lighting and controls | LED panels or older fluorescent troffers on a regular grid, with controls | Even light at the desk, glare, energy, flexibility for layouts |
| Air conditioning outlets | VAV boxes, fan coils or chilled beams with diffusers and zones | Outside air, temperature control by zone, noise, draughts |
| Floor finishes | Carpet tiles on raised floor or screed; some exposed concrete | Wear, acoustic performance, flexibility for cabling |
| Power and data | Floor boxes, raised floor cabling, or ceiling and pole distribution | Capacity and flexibility for tenant layouts |
| Fire and life safety | Sprinklers, detection, warning, emergency lighting, exit signs | Coverage that follows the fit-out |
| Amenities | Core toilets, showers and end-of-trip facilities, tea points | Ratios for current occupancy; quality |
| Façade interface | Perimeter glazing, blinds, perimeter heating or cooling | Glare, heat gain, daylight, comfort at the perimeter |

Market grading formalises fitness for purpose. In Australia the Property Council's guide to office building quality grades buildings from Premium to D against floor plate, services, amenities and sustainability; in Britain the British Council for Offices guide to specification sets market expectations; in the United States, buildings are commonly classed A, B or C. These grades move: a floor that was A grade at completion can slide as expectations for air, light, amenities and energy rise.

sections.heading: How long it stays fit for purpose
sections.markdown:
A tenant fit-out lasts seven to twelve years, usually a lease term, while base-building carpet lasts ten to fifteen, ceiling grids twenty to thirty and LED lighting fifteen to twenty. A floor's fitness for purpose is set as much by its market grade as by the condition of anything on it.

| Component or quality | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tenant fit-out | 7 to 12 years, usually a lease term | Lease events; tenant needs; workplace trends |
| Base-building carpet tiles | 10 to 15 years | Traffic; quality; make-good practice |
| Suspended ceiling tiles and grid | 20 to 30 years; tiles sooner where damaged | Water leaks; services works; appearance |
| Base-building lighting | 15 to 20 years for LED; fluorescent now obsolete | Technology; energy rating |
| Terminal units and diffusers | 15 to 25 years | Air conditioning page; controls |
| Base-building refurbishment cycle | 15 to 25 years for a major floor refurbishment | Market grade; vacancy; energy targets |
| Market grade | Drifts down a grade over 15 to 25 years without investment | Competing stock; rising expectations |

What shortens fitness for purpose: rising market expectations for outside air, daylight, amenities, end-of-trip facilities, wellness ratings and energy performance, which age a floor faster than its materials wear; repeated fit-outs that leave behind abandoned cabling, patched ceilings, unbalanced air systems and fire services altered piecemeal; higher occupant densities than the floor was designed for, overloading air conditioning, toilets and lifts; water leaks from above that stain ceilings and damage carpets; energy and emissions rules that push older floors below letting or rating thresholds.

sections.heading: Functional limits and energy
sections.markdown:
Some limits are built in: floor-to-ceiling height that leaves little room for modern services and lighting, deep floor plates with poor daylight away from the façade, close column grids that constrain layouts, and cores with too few toilets or lifts for today's densities. These cannot be fixed by refurbishing finishes and decide how far a floor can be repositioned.

Floors with fluorescent lighting, poor controls, old terminal units and single glazing drag down whole-building ratings, which affect leasing and in some places the right to let.

Some limits cannot be repaired: a low floor-to-ceiling height, a deep plan far from the windows, a tight column grid. They are matters of grade and positioning, judged by comparison with the buildings tenants could choose instead, not by condition.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Floor hard to lease despite good condition | Market grade drift or functional limits. Grade assessment; leasing feedback. | Assess the grade against the market, and plan base-building refurbishment at lease expiry. |
| Tenants asking for amenities the floor cannot offer | Amenities and end-of-trip below current expectations. Ratios and facilities compared with competing buildings. | Upgrade amenities and end-of-trip at the next base-building refurbishment. |

sections.heading: Comfort, air and light
sections.markdown:
Hot and cold complaints concentrated at the perimeter, in meeting rooms and in corner offices point to zoning that no longer matches the layout, failed terminal units, or façade heat gain and glare. Stuffiness and afternoon fatigue point to low outside air. Uneven light and glare follow fit-outs that moved desks without moving fittings.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Complaints at the perimeter in afternoons, blinds always down | Façade heat gain and glare. Orientation; glazing type; perimeter temperatures. | Add solar control, with blinds, films or glazing upgrades, and check the perimeter zoning. |
| Complaints in meeting rooms and enclosed offices | Zoning that no longer matches partitions. Terminal unit zoning against layout. | Rezone and rebalance the air conditioning to the current layout. |
| Stuffiness and complaints after lunch | Low outside air or high density. CO₂ readings; outside air measurement (Thresholds by market). | Measure outside air and carbon dioxide; upgrade the outside air where it falls short. |
| Dark patches between desks, or glare on screens | Lighting laid out for an earlier layout, or old fittings. Light levels at desks measured against the current layout and the limits for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Upgrade to LED designed for even desk light and low glare, with controls. |
| Staff complaining of cold first thing in winter | Start-up too late or heating short. Temperature logging from start of occupancy against the limits for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Bring start times forward or rebalance heating. |

sections.heading: Fit-out residue and compliance drift
sections.markdown:
Each tenancy leaves traces: cabling abandoned in ceilings and floors, ceiling tiles cut and patched, diffusers capped, sprinkler heads moved, detectors added or removed, and air systems rebalanced for a layout that no longer exists. Over several tenancies the base building no longer matches its design or drawings, and services perform poorly even though each component works.

Fit-outs create new rooms and paths that must still meet egress travel distances, fire detection and sprinkler coverage, emergency lighting, exit signs and accessibility. Compliance problems on office floors almost always trace back to fit-out changes.

Every tenancy changes a floor, and few put it back. Over two or three leases a floor accumulates cabling no one owns, sprinkler heads in the wrong places and air balanced for walls that have gone, which is why the as-built drawings for each fit-out matter more than the original base-building drawings.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ceiling void crowded with abandoned cabling and capped ducts | Fit-out residue from previous tenancies. Ceiling inspection. | Remove abandoned cabling and services, and replace damaged tiles. |
| Rooms without sprinkler or detector coverage | Fit-out compliance drift. Survey against the layout. | Add or relocate sprinklers, detectors, emergency lights and exit signs to suit the layout. |
| A partition or joinery unit cutting across a sprinkler head's spray | Fit-out added after the sprinkler layout. The clearance between the head and the obstruction, measured. | Relocate the head, or add one to cover the new room. |

sections.heading: Wear and damage
sections.markdown:
Carpet tiles wear in traffic routes and fray at edges; ceiling tiles sag, stain and crack; grid bends where services workers lean on it; corner protection and wall finishes in corridors are damaged. Wear matters most in multi-tenant floors and common areas where the owner is responsible.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stained tiles in a line | Leak from services or the floor above. Trace the line to a pipe, riser or wet area. | Trace the line to its source and repair it, then replace the tiles. |
| Ceiling grid bent near risers and service access points | Services workers leaning on the grid. Damage concentrated around access points. | Straighten or replace the grid, and provide proper access to the services above. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rooms without required sprinkler, detection, emergency lighting or exit coverage; egress paths blocked by the fit-out | safety · 4 Essential | Rectify before occupation continues. |
| Leaks damaging finishes and services; air conditioning failed on a floor | failure · 3 Important | Repair now. |
| Rating, letting standard or lease obligation requiring upgrade by a date | deadline · 3 Important | By the required date. |
| Comfort complaints; worn finishes in common areas; fit-out residue affecting services | condition · 2 Planned | Repair or rebalance in the near term. |
| Floor at the end of its refurbishment cycle; market grade sliding | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Plan a base-building refurbishment, ideally at lease expiry. |
| Grade, air, light and amenities never assessed against the market | check · 2 Planned | Assess fitness for purpose. |
| Normal tenant wear within a lease | nil · 1 Routine | Recovered through make-good. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A building surveyor or leasing-focused building consultant leads, with a services engineer for air, light and controls and an access and fire consultant where fit-outs have changed layouts. The checks below walk every floor, separating base-building elements from tenant fit-out, then measure air, light and coverage against the current layout.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Floor walk | Of every floor, recording base-building elements, condition, fit-out residue and compliance coverage, with ceiling tiles lifted at representative points. |
| Fitness-for-purpose assessment | Against the relevant market guide: floor-to-ceiling height, floor plate depth and daylight, column grid, lighting, outside air, zoning, density capacity, amenities and end-of-trip ratios, and energy rating. |
| Environmental measurements | Temperature by zone over a working day, CO₂ as a proxy for outside air, light levels at desks, and noise from services. |
| Coverage check | Of sprinklers, detection, emergency lighting and exit signs against the current layout, and egress distances. |
| Base-build versus fit-out split | From leases, fit-out approvals and make-good schedules, so findings are allocated correctly. |
| Services integration review | Terminal unit zoning, controls, power and data capacity per floor. |
| Leasing evidence | Vacancy, feedback from agents and tenants, and competing stock. |

The report should grade each floor for condition, compliance and market fitness, separate base-building items from tenant obligations, and set out a floor-by-floor programme timed to lease events.

sections.heading: Rectifying, upgrading and repositioning
sections.markdown:
Rooms left without sprinkler, detection, emergency lighting or exit signs after a fit-out come first. After that, the work keeps base-building performance apart from fit-out drift, since the remedy and who pays differ, and times repositioning with lease expiries.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Compliance rectification | Add or relocate sprinklers, detectors, emergency lights and exit signs, and correct egress paths. | After every fit-out that changes rooms or paths. |
| Rezoning and rebalancing | Rebalance and rezone air conditioning to the current layout; replace failed terminal units and controls. | Where complaints follow the partitions. |
| Outside air upgrades | Outside air upgrades where measured rates fall below current standards or market expectations. | Where rooms are stuffy or carbon dioxide runs high. |
| Lighting upgrade | Lighting upgrade to LED with daylight and occupancy controls, designed for even desk light and low glare. | Where lighting is fluorescent, uneven or glaring. |
| Ceiling works | Remove abandoned services, replace damaged tiles, or open up to exposed soffits where height is limited and acoustics can be managed. | Where voids hold abandoned services, or tiles are damaged. |
| Floor finishes | Carpet tile replacement in common areas and at refurbishment; make-good recovery for tenant areas. | In common areas, at refurbishment, and at make-good. |
| Amenities and end-of-trip | Amenities and end-of-trip upgrades to current ratios and expectations. | Where provision lags the occupancy or the market. |
| Base-building refurbishment | Category A refurbishment at lease expiry, often with speculative fitted suites to attract smaller tenants. | At lease expiry, where the floor's grade is sliding. |
| Façade and solar control | Blinds, films or glazing upgrades where perimeter comfort fails. | Where perimeter comfort fails. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Office floor costs are usually measured by lettable area per floor. Compliance rectification is itemised per device. Rebalancing and controls are lump sums per floor. Lighting and ceiling replacement are priced by area, usually done together. Carpet is by area. Base-building refurbishment is a lump sum per floor or by area, and is most economical on vacant floors at lease expiry. Amenities upgrades are lump sums per core or per floor.

Make-good recoveries from outgoing tenants offset some costs, and lease incentives, rather than capital works alone, often decide leasing outcomes. Compliance items are code compliance; refurbishment is lifecycle or repositioning capital; tenant-caused damage is recoverable; rating-driven upgrades can carry deadlines.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what one floor walk cannot: what each tenant changed and must reinstate, where comfort complaints concentrate, and how the floor compares with the market. Ask for them before deciding whether a problem belongs to the base building or the tenant.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Floor-by-floor tenancy schedule with lease expiries and make-good terms | Which leases end when, and what each tenant must reinstate. |
| Fit-out approvals and as-built drawings for each tenancy | What each tenant changed, and whether it was approved. |
| Comfort complaint logs and any indoor environment measurements | Where comfort complaints concentrate, and what was measured. |
| Energy and indoor environment ratings and certificates | How the building rates for energy and indoor environment. |
| Base-building specification and any market grade assessment | What the base building was specified to provide, and its grade. |
| Records of base-building refurbishments by floor | When each floor was last refurbished. |
| Leasing agent feedback and vacancy history | Why tenants choose other buildings. |
| Fire services and egress certification after the latest fit-outs | Whether fire services and egress were certified after the latest fit-outs. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Office floors are misread when base-building problems and fit-out drift are handled together, when a floor that is hard to lease is assumed to need repair, and when the original drawings are trusted after several fit-outs.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| It is all one problem | Separate what the base building must fix from what the tenant changed. Most office-floor problems are either base-building performance (air, light, amenities, energy) or fit-out drift (coverage, zoning, residue); the remedy and who pays are different. |
| It will not lease, so it needs repair | A floor that is hard to lease despite good condition points to market grade drift or functional limits, which are matters of positioning, not repair. A grade assessment and leasing feedback settle it. |
| The base-building drawings show the floor | After several fit-outs the base-building drawings no longer show the floor. The as-built drawings for each tenancy, and a survey against the current layout, do. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets rules that fit-outs must keep meeting, for fire, egress and access, and links office energy performance to sale, letting or emissions. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Fit-out compliance, energy and grade | The Property Council's guide to office building quality sets market grading; fit-outs need building approval under the National Construction Code, which governs egress, fire services and access; AS 1668.2 sets ventilation and AS/NZS 1680 lighting; NABERS Energy and Indoor Environment ratings and Commercial Building Disclosure affect leasing; leases commonly include make-good and green lease clauses. | The British Council for Offices guide to specification sets market expectations and the Category A and B fit-out convention; fit-outs need building regulations approval and must keep fire safety and access; the Workplace (Health, Safety and Welfare) Regulations 1992 set minimum standards for workplaces; EPC minimum standards apply to letting; dilapidations practice governs lease-end obligations. | Buildings are commonly classed A, B or C by market convention, and floor area is measured to BOMA standards; tenant improvements need permits under the International Building Code and must meet the 2010 ADA Standards; ASHRAE 55 and 62.1 set comfort and ventilation; city benchmarking and building performance standards affect older office stock. |

sections.heading: Worked example: a floor after its third tenant
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 1990s office floor is vacant after its third tenant. The ceiling void is crowded with abandoned cabling, two enclosed offices built by the last tenant have no sprinkler heads, perimeter blinds were kept closed all day, and leasing agents say the floor shows poorly against newer buildings nearby.

Separate the base building from what tenants changed. The uncovered offices are fit-out drift and a safety finding, and the abandoned cabling is residue that make-good should have cleared. The closed blinds point to façade heat gain and glare, a base-building performance issue, and the leasing feedback to market grade.

So the register carries the sprinkler coverage as a safety line, a make-good claim for the residue, solar control for the perimeter, and a base-building refurbishment with LED lighting and rezoned air conditioning, timed for the next letting.

thresholds.rule: Below 800 ppm suggests good ventilation; consistently above 1500 ppm calls for action

thresholds.rule: Average 200 lux, with no point below 100 lux

pages.title: Common Circulation Areas
pages.question: How do corridors and lift lobbies fail, and when do they stop being safe escape routes?
pages.answer: Corridors are escape routes first. They fail when stored furniture, bins and bikes narrow them, when fire and smoke doors are wedged open or apartment doors replaced with unrated ones, when smoke vents do not open, and when emergency lighting or exit signs fail. Then wear: trolleys gouge walls, carpets wear in traffic paths, odours spread through poorly ventilated corridors. Storage and doors that do not close are safety findings, not housekeeping.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about common circulation areas; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Finishes, wall protection, wayfinding, lighting in corridors and lift lobbies

pages.searchTitle: Corridors and lift lobbies: blocked escape routes, fire doors, smoke vents and wear

questions.question: Can residents keep bikes in the corridor?
questions.answer: No. Items stored in corridors narrow the escape route and add fire load; they are safety findings, so storage is needed elsewhere.

questions.question: Can corridor fire doors be held open?
questions.answer: Not by wedging. Hold-open devices linked to the fire alarm let them stand open and close when the alarm sounds.

questions.question: Are flat entrance doors part of the fire protection?
questions.answer: Yes. They protect the corridor from a fire in the flat, and owner-replaced doors may not be fire-rated.

questions.question: How often must communal fire doors be checked?
questions.answer: In England, quarterly in residential buildings over 11 metres, with flat entrance doors checked annually; AS 1851 sets inspection in Australia and NFPA 80 in the United States.

questions.question: How long does corridor carpet last?
questions.answer: 8 to 15 years, depending on traffic and quality; hard floors 15 to 25.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Corridor problems show on a walk-through as stored items, wedged doors, worn carpet and gouged walls, dark spots and failed signs, and in fire door and complaint records. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On a walk-through | Items stored in corridors and lift lobbies | Escape routes, layout and storage |
| On a walk-through | Fire doors wedged or propped; doors not closing fully; seals damaged | Fire doors, smoke doors and smoke vents |
| On a walk-through | Apartment entrance doors of mixed designs or with added hardware | Fire doors, smoke doors and smoke vents |
| On a walk-through | Worn carpet paths; gouged walls and corners | Wear, lighting, signs and odour |
| On a walk-through | Dark spots; emergency lights or exit signs failed | Wear, lighting, signs and odour |
| On a walk-through | Smoke vents blocked or closed | Fire doors, smoke doors and smoke vents |
| On a walk-through | Dead-end corridors created by new partitions | Escape routes, layout and storage |
| In the records | Fire door inspection records | Fire doors, smoke doors and smoke vents |
| In the records | Fire safety statements | Standards by country |
| In the records | Complaints about storage and odours | Escape routes, layout and storage |
| In the records | Refurbishment history | Wear, lighting, signs and odour |
| In the records | Strata or building rules on corridor use | Escape routes, layout and storage |
| In the records | Hold-open devices on fire doors, and whether they release when the alarm is tested | Fire doors, smoke doors and smoke vents |
| In the records | Lift lobby finishes worn at the lift doors, where traffic concentrates | Wear, lighting, signs and odour |

sections.heading: What the space does and what it contains
sections.markdown:
Common circulation areas are the corridors, lift lobbies and passages on each floor that connect lifts, stairs, tenancies, apartments and amenities. Functionally they are escape routes as much as access routes: they must stay clear, lit, signed and protected from smoke, while taking constant wear from people, trolleys, cleaning machines and furniture moves. In apartment buildings they are common property and among the most visible indicators of how a building is managed.

| Element group | Typical provision | What matters for the space |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Floor finishes | Carpet, vinyl, tiles, timber | Wear, trips, cleaning, acoustics |
| Wall finishes and protection | Paint, wall coverings, corner guards, kick plates | Damage from trolleys and moves |
| Doors | Fire and smoke doors, apartment entry doors, hold-open devices | Closing, sealing, fire rating |
| Lighting | Corridor lighting with emergency lighting | Levels, controls, emergency coverage |
| Signage and wayfinding | Exit signs, floor numbers, unit numbers | Egress and finding destinations |
| Ventilation | Corridor supply, smoke vents in residential corridors | Odour, smoke control |
| Ceilings and services | Suspended ceilings carrying services | Access, fire rating where required |

sections.heading: How long it stays fit for purpose
sections.markdown:
Corridor carpet lasts eight to fifteen years and paint and wall coverings five to ten, while hard floors last fifteen to twenty-five and door hardware ten to fifteen. Corridors are usually refurbished every ten to twenty years.

| Component or quality | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Corridor carpet | 8 to 15 years | Traffic; quality; cleaning |
| Vinyl and hard floors | 15 to 25 years | Traffic; maintenance |
| Paint and wall coverings | 5 to 10 years | Damage; style |
| Fire and smoke door hardware | 10 to 15 years | Use; abuse |
| Corridor refurbishment | 10 to 20 years | Wear; market |
| Lighting | 15 to 20 years for LED | Technology |

What shortens fitness for purpose: furniture moves and trolleys damaging walls and corners; storage and bins left in corridors; door abuse: wedging, propping, slamming; fit-outs that change corridor layouts.

Corridors look worn long before any element fails, because they take every trip people and goods make through the building. Their fitness for purpose is mostly about escape safety and presentation rather than material life.

sections.heading: Escape routes, layout and storage
sections.markdown:
Corridors fill with stored furniture, bins, bicycles, prams and deliveries, narrowing escape widths and adding fire load. In apartment buildings, residents' items in corridors are a persistent fire safety problem.

Fit-outs and reconfigurations can create dead-end corridors longer than permitted or remove alternative escape routes.

A corridor's width is a safety allowance, not spare floor space. A bike, a pram or a stack of boxes narrows the route people use to escape and adds fuel to a fire in the place they must pass, which is why stored items are graded as safety findings rather than housekeeping.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Corridors cluttered on residential floors | Storage shortage or poor management. Building rules; storage provision. | Provide storage, clear the corridor, and enforce the rules. |
| A corridor that now ends at a new partition | A dead end created by a fit-out. Travel distance to an exit measured against the fire strategy (Thresholds by market). | Have the egress reviewed, and remove or rearrange the partition. |

sections.heading: Fire doors, smoke doors and smoke vents
sections.markdown:
Corridor fire and smoke doors are wedged open, closers fail, hold-open devices are not linked to the alarm, and seals are damaged. Apartment entrance doors, which protect the corridor from a flat fire, are replaced or altered by residents. Each failure lets smoke into the escape route.

In residential buildings, corridor smoke vents and shaft systems must open on alarm; failed actuators and blocked vents leave corridors filling with smoke.

Every door onto a corridor is part of its protection. A fire door wedged open, a flat entrance door that does not close, or a smoke vent that stays shut each lets smoke into the route people use to escape; a corridor is only as protected as its weakest door.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Doors wedged open on every floor | Doors used for convenience; no hold-open devices. Inspection; use patterns. | Fit hold-open devices linked to the alarm where doors need to stand open, and stop the wedging. |
| Smoke spread in a minor fire or alarm test | Failed doors, seals or vents. Door survey; smoke vent test. | Survey every door, repair closers and seals, and test the smoke vents. |
| Flat entrance doors of mixed designs | Owner-replaced doors that may not be fire-rated. No evidence of a rating, with gaps and missing closers. Gaps are measured against the door’s evidence and the limits for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Survey them, and replace non-compliant doors with self-closing, fire-rated doorsets. |
| A smoke vent still shut during an alarm test | A failed actuator, or a blocked vent. The vent does not open when the alarm is triggered (Thresholds by market). | Repair the actuator, clear the vent, and retest. |

sections.heading: Wear, lighting, signs and odour
sections.markdown:
Carpets wear in traffic paths and at lift lobbies; walls and corners are gouged by trolleys and moves; doors and frames are chipped. Damage accumulates quickly in hotels, aged care, hospitals and apartment buildings.

Dark corridors from failed or poorly controlled lighting, emergency lights not working, and exit signs hidden or wrong after layout changes compromise both daily use and escape.

Poor corridor ventilation spreads cooking and garbage odours in apartment buildings and hotels.

In mixed-use and hotel buildings, corridors also carry trolleys and housekeeping, multiplying wear and door damage.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Walls damaged at a consistent height | Trolleys or bins. Wall protection review. | Fit corner guards, rails or impact-resistant finishes at that height. |
| Odours along corridors | Inadequate ventilation or unbalanced pressure. Airflow check. | Rebalance the corridor ventilation, and renew the door seals. |
| Exit signs hidden, or pointing the wrong way | Signs not updated after a layout change. From some points no sign leads to an exit. | Renew and reposition the signs to suit the layout. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Obstructed escape routes; fire doors not closing; failed emergency lighting; smoke vents not opening | safety · 4 Essential | Rectify now. |
| Corridor lighting failed | failure · 3 Important | Repair now. |
| Fire door checks and certification due | deadline · 3 Important | At the prescribed interval. |
| Worn finishes; wall damage; odours | condition · 2 Planned | Repair in the near term. |
| Corridors at end of refurbishment cycle | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Refurbish. |
| No fire door register; layout changes unreviewed | check · 2 Planned | Survey. |
| Normal | nil · 1 Routine | Routine. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A building surveyor leads, with a fire safety consultant for doors, egress and smoke systems, and the building manager for use and rules. The checks below walk every floor at different times of day, survey every door, and test the smoke vents and lighting against the current layout.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Floor-by-floor walk | At different times of day, recording obstructions, stored items, door positions, finishes, lighting and signage. |
| Fire door survey | Of every corridor, lobby and apartment entrance door: closing from fully open, gaps, seals, hardware, glazing, labels. |
| Egress review | Corridor widths, travel distances, dead ends and alternative routes against the current layout and fire strategy (Thresholds by market). |
| Smoke vent and ventilation test | In residential corridors, triggered from the fire alarm, with the free area of each vent measured against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). |
| Lighting check | Levels, controls and emergency lighting coverage. |
| Management review | Building rules, storage provision and how breaches are dealt with. |

The report should give safety items floor by floor, a fire door defect register, and a refurbishment and management plan.

sections.heading: Clearing, repairing or refurbishing
sections.markdown:
Obstructions, fire doors that do not close, failed emergency lighting and smoke vents that do not open come first. After that, the work protects walls where damage concentrates, gives stored items somewhere else to go, and refurbishes finishes floor by floor.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Clear and manage | Remove stored items, provide storage, and enforce rules. | Wherever corridors hold stored items. |
| Fire doors | Repair closers and seals; fit hold-open devices linked to the alarm; replace non-compliant apartment doors. | Wherever doors do not close or seal, or lack a rating. |
| Wall protection | Corner guards, rails and impact-resistant finishes where damage concentrates. | Where damage concentrates. |
| Floor finishes | Replace worn carpet with durable products suited to traffic. | Where carpet wears in traffic paths. |
| Lighting | LED with occupancy dimming that never leaves corridors dark. | Where corridors are dark or the lighting is outdated. |
| Smoke vents | Repair and test. | Wherever vents fail to open on alarm. |
| Refurbishment | Refurbish the finishes and signage. | At the end of the corridor's cycle. |
| Storage provision | Resident and tenant storage cages, bin rooms and bike parking so items have somewhere to go besides corridors. | Where residents and tenants have nowhere else to put things. |
| Signage and wayfinding | Renew signs with layout changes, including exit signs visible from every point. | After every layout change. |
| Acoustic and odour control | Corridor ventilation rebalanced and door seals renewed. | Where odours or noise travel along corridors. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Corridor works are usually priced per floor. Fire door works are per door. Finishes by area. Lighting per fitting. Refurbishment per floor, often staged. Management measures are operating costs. Safety items are code compliance; refurbishment is lifecycle.

Fire door remediation in apartment buildings can be large because every flat entrance door may need replacement or upgrading, often with owners sharing costs. Corridor refurbishments are best staged floor by floor to keep the building in use, with access to apartments and tenancies coordinated. Management measures such as storage and rule enforcement cost little and fix the most common safety problem.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what one walk-through cannot: whether doors are checked on schedule, who owns the flat entrance doors, and whether fit-outs have changed the escape routes. Ask for them before refurbishing finishes.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Fire door register and inspection records | Whether every fire door is checked, and what was found. |
| Fire safety statements | Whether the fire safety measures were certified. |
| Building or strata rules on corridors | What the rules allow in corridors. |
| Complaints and incident records | Whether incidents or complaints point to a pattern. |
| Refurbishment history | When the corridors were last refurbished. |
| Flat entrance door ownership and replacement records in apartment buildings | Who owns the flat entrance doors, and which were replaced. |
| Smoke vent test records | Whether the smoke vents open on alarm. |
| Egress and layout drawings after fit-outs | Whether fit-outs have changed the escape routes. |
| Records of items removed from corridors and notices issued | Whether storage in corridors has been enforced. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Corridors are misread when stored items and propped doors are treated as housekeeping, when a corridor is judged by its finishes, and when the doors survey stops at the corridor doors.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| It is a housekeeping matter | A corridor is an escape route. Storage in it and fire doors that do not close are safety findings, not housekeeping issues. |
| Worn carpet is the main problem | Corridors look worn long before any element fails, but their fitness for purpose is mostly about escape safety: doors, clear widths, lighting and smoke vents come before finishes. |
| The corridor doors close, so the doors are fine | Flat entrance doors protect the corridor from a fire in a flat, and residents often replace them. Survey every one, not just the corridor doors. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets egress widths and travel distances, requires fire and smoke doors to be kept closing and inspected, and assigns corridors to the owners corporation. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Egress, fire doors and inspection | The National Construction Code sets egress widths and travel distances, and fire and smoke door requirements; fire doors are inspected under AS 1851; strata by-laws control corridor use. | The Fire Safety (England) Regulations 2022 require quarterly checks of communal fire doors and annual checks of flat entrance doors in residential buildings over 11 metres; Approved Document B sets requirements. | NFPA 101 and the International Fire Code require egress paths kept clear and fire doors maintained, with NFPA 80 inspection. |

In strata and condominium buildings in all three countries, corridors are common property and their fire safety is the owners corporation's duty, while flat entrance doors may belong to individual owners, which complicates remediation.

Hotel and aged care corridors carry additional operator and accreditation requirements.

sections.heading: Worked example: an apartment corridor
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 2000s apartment building's corridors hold bikes, prams and boxes outside several doors. The corridor fire door on most floors is wedged open, a third of the flat entrance doors have been replaced by owners with doors of different designs, and in the last alarm test one floor's smoke vent stayed shut.

A corridor is an escape route, so the stored items and wedged doors are safety findings, not housekeeping. Replaced entrance doors may not be fire-rated, and a vent that stays shut leaves that corridor to fill with smoke. Doors wedged on every floor point to doors people need open, with no hold-open devices.

So the register carries the obstructions, the wedged doors and the smoke vent as safety lines now, hold-open devices linked to the alarm, a survey of every flat entrance door with owner replacement where needed, and storage cages and bike parking so items have somewhere to go.

thresholds.rule: No more than 20 m to an exit or point of choice, and no more than 40 m to one of two exits

source.title: NCC 2025 Volume One, Part D2 Provision for escape

thresholds.measure: Apartment entry doors to an exit
thresholds.rule: Within 6 m of an exit or point of choice

source.title: NCC 2025 Volume One, Part D2 Provision for escape

thresholds.rule: 3 mm at the top and sides; no more than 10 mm at the bottom

source.title: Fire door intumescent seal regulations (quoting AS 1905.1 clearances)

thresholds.rule: No more than 4 mm, except at the bottom

pages.title: Common Internal Areas
pages.question: How do shared areas in apartment buildings fail, and what makes them a collective risk?
pages.answer: Residential common areas fail through residents' alterations, storage and deferred decisions. Flat entrance doors replaced or stripped of closers compromise the corridor escape route; bikes, furniture and charging e-bikes fill corridors, stairs and storerooms; intercoms and lift phones stop when networks are switched off; moves damage walls and lifts. Collective funding delays refurbishment until defects or orders force it. A funded capital works plan and enforced by-laws are the main controls.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about common internal areas; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.

pages.searchTitle: Apartment common areas: flat entrance doors, e-bike charging, intercoms and funding

questions.question: Who pays to replace non-compliant flat entrance doors?
questions.answer: It depends on who owns them under the strata plan or lease. Settle the cost allocation between owners and the building before the work starts.

questions.question: Can residents charge e-bikes in the bike room?
questions.answer: Not in escape routes or general storage. A designated charging room with detection, and enforced rules, manage the fire risk.

questions.question: Why did our intercom stop working?
questions.answer: Often because the network it depended on was switched off, such as Australia's 3G networks in late 2024.

questions.question: What is a capital works plan?
questions.answer: A long-term plan of the common area works due and how they will be funded, prepared from a condition survey and reviewed regularly.

questions.question: How long do intercom systems last?
questions.answer: 10 to 15 years, though network shutdowns and the end of vendor support can end them sooner.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Common area problems show on a walk-through as stored items and charging bikes, altered entrance doors, failing intercoms and worn lobbies, and in the plan, fund, by-laws and minutes. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On a walk-through | Items stored in corridors, stairs and lobbies; e-bikes charging in common areas | Flat entrance doors, storage and charging |
| On a walk-through | Flat entrance doors of mixed designs, without closers, or with added openings | Flat entrance doors, storage and charging |
| On a walk-through | Intercom panels faulty or replaced piecemeal; parcels piled in lobbies | Intercoms, access and security |
| On a walk-through | Entry doors not closing or latching | Intercoms, access and security |
| On a walk-through | Damaged walls, doors and lift interiors from moves | Defects, funding and wear |
| On a walk-through | Worn carpets and dated lobbies | Defects, funding and wear |
| In the records | Capital works or maintenance plan and fund balance | Defects, funding and wear |
| In the records | Annual fire safety certification | Standards by country |
| In the records | By-laws on storage, moves and alterations | Flat entrance doors, storage and charging |
| In the records | Defect reports and claims | Defects, funding and wear |
| In the records | Intercom and access control contracts | Intercoms, access and security |
| In the records | Notices about defects, special levies or compliance orders on lobby noticeboards | Defects, funding and wear |

sections.heading: What the space does and what it contains
sections.markdown:
Common internal areas are the shared interior spaces of apartment buildings: the entrance lobby with mailboxes and intercom, corridors and lift lobbies on each floor, stairs, and shared rooms such as bike stores, parcel rooms, gyms and residents' lounges. They are common property, owned and maintained collectively through the owners corporation, body corporate, residents' management company or landlord, and funded from levies or service charges. Functionally they must give residents safe, secure access and escape, present the building well, and stay affordable to maintain. This page draws together the residential aspects; the entrance, corridors and stairs each have their own space page.

| Element group | Typical provision | What matters for the space |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Entry and intercom | Entry doors, intercom panel, access control, mailboxes, parcel lockers | Security; reliability; network dependence |
| Corridors and lift lobbies | Finishes, lighting, fire doors, smoke vents | Escape route; appearance; wear |
| Stairs | Fire-isolated or open stairs | Escape; storage; propped doors |
| Shared rooms | Bike stores, gyms, lounges, bin rooms | Fire load; batteries; hygiene; misuse |
| Fire and life safety | Detection, warning, emergency lighting, sprinklers, flat entrance doors | Compliance; resident alterations |
| Security | CCTV, fobs, access control to car parks and floors | Obsolescence; privacy; lost fobs |

Because costs are shared, decisions are collective and often deferred. Many owners corporations have long-term maintenance or capital works plans that are not followed, or none at all, and common areas then deteriorate until a defect or compliance order forces action.

sections.heading: How long it stays fit for purpose
sections.markdown:
Corridor carpet lasts eight to fifteen years, paint seven to twelve and CCTV seven to ten, while intercoms and access control last ten to fifteen and lobbies are refurbished every fifteen to twenty. Network shutdowns and collective decisions end their fitness for purpose as often as wear does.

| Component or quality | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Corridor carpet | 8 to 15 years | Traffic; moves |
| Paint and wall finishes | 7 to 12 years | Damage from moves |
| Intercom and access control | 10 to 15 years | Technology; network shutdowns; vendor support |
| Lobby refurbishment | 15 to 20 years | Market; wear |
| Lighting | 15 to 20 years for LED | Technology |
| CCTV | 7 to 10 years | Technology |

What shortens fitness for purpose: furniture moves without protection, damaging walls, doors and lifts; resident storage in corridors, stairs and bike rooms; network changes: older intercoms, lift phones and alarm diallers depended on networks that have been switched off, such as Australia's 3G networks in late 2024 and copper lines being retired in Britain and the United States; deferred maintenance from collective decision-making.

sections.heading: Flat entrance doors, storage and charging
sections.markdown:
Each flat's entrance door protects the corridor escape route from a fire in that flat. Residents replace doors with non-rated ones, remove closers, add cat flaps and letterboxes, and fit hardware that defeats the seals. Responsibility for these doors is often contested between owners and the building.

Bikes, prams, furniture and e-bikes left in corridors, stairs and lobbies obstruct escape and add fire load; e-bikes and scooters charging in common areas and storage rooms are a growing fire source.

In an apartment building, each flat's entrance door is part of the common fire protection even when the flat's owner owns it. That split is why door remediation stalls: the corridor is the owners corporation's duty, the door may be the owner's, and the cost allocation has to be settled before the work can start.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Flat doors without closers | Resident alterations. Door survey; by-law enforcement. | Survey every door, enforce the by-laws, and replace non-compliant doors, settling the cost allocation first. |
| Storage throughout corridors | Insufficient storage and weak enforcement. Storage provision; enforcement records. | Provide storage and charging rooms, and enforce the rules. |
| E-bikes or scooters charging in a corridor, stair or bike room | No designated charging room. Chargers plugged into common area outlets, with batteries left overnight. | Stop charging in escape routes, and provide a charging room with detection. |
| Flat entrance doors with wide or uneven gaps at the edges | Fire doors no longer sealing. Gap measurement against the door’s evidence and the asset’s market (Thresholds by market); check records against the inspection intervals the market sets. | Adjust or replace the doors, renew seals, and set up the checks the market requires. |

sections.heading: Intercoms, access and security
sections.markdown:
Intercoms and access systems depending on retired mobile networks or copper lines stop working; proprietary fob systems tie buildings to one supplier; lost fobs compromise security.

Doors that do not close and latch, tailgating, and unmonitored CCTV allow intrusions, parcel theft and vandalism.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Intercom stopped working | Network shutdown or obsolete equipment. Network type; vendor. | Upgrade to a supported system on current networks, with open fob formats. |
| An entry door that does not close and latch behind people | A failed closer or latch, or a door propped for deliveries. The door stays ajar when released. | Restore the closer and latch, and add parcel lockers to reduce propping. |

sections.heading: Defects, funding and wear
sections.markdown:
Newer apartment buildings often carry construction defects in common areas, such as waterproofing, fire separation and façade issues. Owners corporations must pursue them within statutory warranty periods, and the funds and expertise to do so are often lacking.

Without a funded long-term plan, common area refurbishments and compliance works are deferred until they become urgent and more costly.

Moves, deliveries and heavy use damage lobbies, corridors, lift cars and doors; damage is often not recovered from residents.

Common areas belong to everyone, and so to no one in particular. Costs are shared and decisions collective, which tends to defer them; the capital works plan and its fund are how a building turns that deferral into a schedule, and an assessment should test whether the plan matches the building's actual condition.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Common areas dated despite sound fabric | Deferred refurbishment. Capital works plan; fund balance. | Fund and schedule the refurbishment through the capital works plan. |
| A capital works fund far short of the works the plan shows due | A plan not based on condition, or levies set too low. Plan items compared with a condition survey and the fund balance. | Update the plan from a condition survey, and set levies to fund it. |
| Defects in a newer building with the warranty period running | Construction defects not yet pursued. Defect reports, and the date the warranty period ends. | Commission an expert report, and pursue the claim within the period. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Non-compliant flat entrance doors; storage and charging in escape routes; failed emergency lighting | safety · 4 Essential | Rectify now. |
| Intercom or entry security failed | failure · 3 Important | Restore now. |
| Fire safety certification or capital works plan due | deadline · 3 Important | As required. |
| Worn finishes; security weaknesses | condition · 2 Planned | Improve in the near term. |
| Lobby and corridors at end of refurbishment cycle | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Refurbish from the capital works fund. |
| No capital works plan or door survey | check · 2 Planned | Prepare. |
| Normal | nil · 1 Routine | Routine. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A building surveyor leads, with fire safety and security specialists, working through the strata manager, managing agent or landlord so residents can be notified and flats accessed. The checks below walk every common area, survey every flat entrance door with its ownership, and test the plan and fund against the building's actual condition.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Common area walk-through | Of every floor, stair, lobby and shared room at different times, recording storage, doors, finishes, lighting, signage and security. |
| Flat entrance door survey | Of every door: rating labels, closers, seals, gaps, hardware, glazing and alterations, with ownership noted. |
| Intercom and access control review | Technology, the network it depends on, vendor support, fob management and integration with lifts and car park gates. |
| Storage and battery review | Where residents store bikes and e-bikes, where they charge them, and what rooms exist for this. |
| Capital works plan review | Whether the plan reflects actual condition and whether the fund can pay for what is due. |
| By-law and enforcement review | Rules on storage, moves, door alterations and renovations, and how breaches are dealt with. |

The report should list safety items, a funded refurbishment and compliance plan, and recommended by-law changes.

sections.heading: Making safe, enforcing, funding and refurbishing
sections.markdown:
Non-compliant flat entrance doors, and storage or charging in escape routes, come first. After that, the building needs rules that are enforced, supported intercoms and access control, and a capital works plan and fund that match its condition.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Flat entrance doors | Complete a survey, enforce by-laws on alterations, and replace non-compliant doors, settling cost allocation between owners and the building first. | Wherever doors are non-compliant. |
| Storage and charging rules | Designated bike and storage rooms, battery charging rooms with detection, and enforcement. | Wherever items or chargers sit in escape routes. |
| Intercom and access upgrades | Supported systems using current networks or the internet, with open fob formats so the building is not locked to one vendor. | Where systems depend on retired networks or a single vendor. |
| Move management | Booking, lift and wall protection, and recovery of damage costs from residents. | In every building where residents move in and out. |
| Security | Door closers and latches restored, CCTV reviewed, parcel lockers to reduce theft. | Where doors fail to latch, or parcels are stolen. |
| Refurbishment | Refurbish lobbies and corridors, funded and scheduled through the capital works fund. | At the end of the cycle. |
| Capital works plan | A plan prepared from a condition survey and reviewed regularly. | Wherever there is none, or it no longer matches the building. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Common area works are paid for by levies or service charges and, for larger items, special levies. Flat entrance doors are priced per door, often the largest compliance cost in older apartment buildings. Intercom and access control upgrades are lump sums per building. Refurbishment is priced per floor or for the lobby. Planning and surveys are modest costs that reduce the risk of sudden special levies.

Safety items are code compliance; refurbishment is lifecycle and the core of the capital works plan.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a walk-through cannot: whether the works due are planned and funded, whether defects are being pursued in time, and what the owners have decided. Ask for them before advising on any levy or major work.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Capital works or maintenance plan and current fund balance | Whether the works due are planned and funded. |
| Annual fire safety certification and any orders | Whether the fire safety measures are certified, and whether orders are outstanding. |
| By-laws and records of enforcement | Whether the rules exist, and are enforced. |
| Defect reports and claims | What defects have been found, and whether claims are within time. |
| Intercom and access control contracts and network details | Whether the intercom depends on a retired network or a single vendor. |
| Flat entrance door survey results | Which flat entrance doors comply, and who owns them. |
| Minutes of owners corporation meetings on major works | What the owners have decided, deferred or rejected. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Common areas are misread when resident behaviour is treated as a building defect or a defect as behaviour, and when a building with sound fabric is assumed to be well planned.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| It is the residents' problem | Flat entrance doors that do not self-close and seal, and storage or battery charging in corridors and stairs, are fire safety findings for the whole building. |
| Fix the building and the behaviour follows | Separate common property defects from resident behaviour: the first needs funding and works, the second needs by-laws and enforcement. Many common area problems combine both. |
| Sound fabric means a sound plan | Common areas that look dated despite sound fabric point to deferred refurbishment. Check the capital works plan and the fund balance against the building's actual condition. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market places duties on the body that runs an apartment building, sets rules for flat entrance doors and fire safety, and in places requires reserves or plans for future works. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Strata duties, fire doors and reserves | State strata legislation requires owners corporations to maintain and repair common property, with New South Wales requiring a ten-year capital works fund plan and Victoria requiring maintenance plans for larger owners corporations; annual fire safety certification applies to essential safety measures; by-laws control storage, moves and alterations. | The Building Safety Act 2022 creates duties for higher-risk residential buildings, and the Fire Safety (England) Regulations 2022 require quarterly checks of communal fire doors and annual checks of flat entrance doors in buildings over 11 metres; leasehold law and the Landlord and Tenant Act 1985 govern service charge consultation. | State condominium and homeowners association laws govern common elements and reserves; Florida requires milestone inspections and structural integrity reserve studies for condominium buildings of three or more storeys; local fire codes require corridors and stairs kept clear. |

sections.heading: Worked example: an apartment building with a thin fund
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 2005 apartment building's intercom stopped working when the 3G network closed, e-bikes charge overnight in the bike room, a dozen flat entrance doors have been replaced by owners, and the lobby looks twenty years old. The capital works plan dates from handover and was never updated, and the fund covers less than a third of what it shows due.

Separate common property from behaviour. The doors and the e-bike charging are fire safety findings for the whole building, needing enforcement as well as works. The intercom failed with its network, and a supported system on current networks with open fobs fixes it. The dated lobby and thin fund point to a plan that no longer matches the building.

So the register carries the flat entrance doors and the e-bike charging as safety lines, with by-law enforcement and a charging room with detection, an intercom upgrade as a failure line, and a new capital works plan from a condition survey, with levies set to fund it.

pages.title: Communications, Security & Specialist Systems
pages.question: How do communications, security and specialist building systems fail, and which failures are safety issues?
pages.answer: These systems turn over faster than buildings. The urgent issue is copper line retirement: lift emergency phones, alarm diallers and intercoms on copper lines can go silent, and Britain's network is retired on 31 January 2027. Access-controlled escape doors that do not release on fire alarm are a life-safety failure. Analogue CCTV and proprietary access control lose support; internet-exposed cameras are compromised; nurse call gaps put residents at risk.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about communications, security & specialist systems; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: CCTV, Access Control, Intercom, MATV, AV, Nurse Call
