pages.searchTitle: Communications and security: copper retirement, lift phones, access control, CCTV

questions.question: Will our lift phones work after the copper network is switched off?
questions.answer: Not if they still run on copper. Check them before the line is retired and migrate them to 4G/5G or IP with battery backup; a lift phone that cannot call out is a life-safety failure.

questions.question: When is the UK analogue phone network switched off?
questions.answer: On 31 January 2027, affecting lift phones, alarm diallers and telecare.

questions.question: Why do controlled doors stay locked in a fire test?
questions.answer: A broken fire interface. Fix it and test it; doors must release when the alarm sounds.

questions.question: Why can only one company add access cards?
questions.answer: The access control is proprietary. At replacement, choose an open-standard system with the owner holding the licences and databases.

questions.question: How long does building network equipment last?
questions.answer: Network switches and comms equipment 5 to 10 years, IP cameras and recorders 7 to 10, copper structured cabling 15 to 25, and fibre backbones 25 and more.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Communications and security problems show as old cameras, readers and intercoms, propped doors, weak reception and crowded comms rooms, and in line types and test records. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On site | Analogue cameras (coaxial cable) and old recorders; cameras pointing at walls or obscured | Obsolescence and cyber exposure |
| On site | Access control readers of an old proprietary type; doors propped open | Obsolescence and cyber exposure |
| On site | Lift car emergency phones; label or test showing the line type | Copper retirement and fire interfaces |
| On site | Comms rooms: temperature, cable congestion, labelling, equipment age | Coverage and cabling |
| On site | Intercom panels faded or failing | Obsolescence and cyber exposure |
| On site | Weak mobile reception in basements and cores | Coverage and cabling |
| In the records | Lift emergency phone and alarm monitoring line types and test records | Copper retirement and fire interfaces |
| In the records | Access control and CCTV vendor, version and support status | Obsolescence and cyber exposure |
| In the records | Fire interface test records for access-controlled doors | Copper retirement and fire interfaces |
| In the records | Cabling test results and documentation | Coverage and cabling |
| In the records | Privacy policies and signage for CCTV | Standards by country |
| In the records | Nurse call test and maintenance records | Obsolescence and cyber exposure |

sections.heading: Types of system
sections.markdown:
This element covers the low-voltage building systems that connect, secure and serve occupants: structured cabling and communications rooms; the incoming carrier and fibre connections; CCTV; access control and intercoms; master antenna and satellite television (MATV); audio-visual systems; public address; in-building mobile and emergency services radio coverage; and specialist systems such as nurse call in healthcare and aged care, and lift emergency telephones. Fire detection and warning systems have their own page.

| System | Where it is found | What goes wrong |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Structured cabling and comms rooms | All commercial and multi-residential buildings | Obsolete cabling categories; congested risers; undocumented patching; hot rooms |
| Carrier lead-in (fibre, copper) | All buildings | Copper networks being switched off; single lead-in with no diversity |
| CCTV (analogue and IP) | Commercial, residential, retail, car parks | Analogue obsolescence; poor coverage; cyber exposure; privacy compliance |
| Access control | Commercial and residential entries, car parks, lifts | Proprietary lock-in; controller obsolescence; failure to release on fire alarm |
| Intercoms | Apartment entries, car parks, lifts | Analogue systems failing; dependence on copper lines |
| MATV and satellite | Apartments, hotels, hospitals | Amplifiers and distribution ageing; changing broadcast standards |
| Lift emergency telephones and alarm diallers | Every lift; alarm monitoring | Copper line switch-off leaves them silent |
| In-building coverage (DAS, emergency radio) | Large and below-ground buildings | Coverage gaps; required for emergency services in some jurisdictions |
| Nurse call | Hospitals, aged care | Life safety for residents; obsolescence; coverage gaps |
| Audio-visual and public address | Commercial, education, assembly | Technology obsolescence |

These systems turn over faster than the building fabric: technology changes, vendors withdraw support, and the networks they rely on change. The biggest current change is the retirement of copper telephone networks, which affects every device that still dials out over a copper line.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Network switches and comms equipment last five to ten years and IP cameras and recorders seven to ten, while copper structured cabling lasts fifteen to twenty-five and fibre backbones twenty-five and more. Network retirements, not wear, often set the deadline.

| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Structured cabling (copper) | 15 to 25 years | Category standards; bandwidth needs |
| Fibre backbone | 25 years and more | Physical damage |
| Network switches and comms equipment | 5 to 10 years | Vendor support |
| IP CCTV cameras and recorders | 7 to 10 years | Technology; firmware support |
| Analogue CCTV | At end of life | Replace |
| Access control controllers | 10 to 15 years | Vendor support |
| Intercoms | 10 to 15 years | Technology; line dependence |
| MATV amplifiers and distribution | 10 to 20 years | Standards changes |
| Nurse call systems | 10 to 15 years | Vendor support |

What shortens life: vendor end of support, especially for proprietary access control and nurse call; network changes: copper switch-off, new broadcast standards; cyber security requirements that retire insecure devices early; hot, undocumented comms rooms.

sections.heading: Copper retirement and fire interfaces
sections.markdown:
Copper telephone networks are being retired: Britain's analogue network is retired on 31 January 2027, Australia has largely replaced copper with the NBN, and United States carriers are retiring copper lines. Lift emergency telephones, alarm and fire monitoring diallers, intercoms, door entry systems and some building management connections that depend on copper lines can go silent without warning. Lift emergency phones are the most serious: people trapped in a lift must be able to call for help.

Access-controlled doors on escape routes must release on fire alarm or power failure; interfaces broken by upgrades or rewiring can lock people in. Lifts with access control must still respond to fire service controls.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lift phone silent on test | Copper line retired or disconnected. Line type; carrier notice. | Take the lift out of service; migrate the phone to 4G/5G or IP with battery backup. |
| Alarm monitoring signals not received | Dialler on a retired line. Monitoring centre test. | Migrate the dialler off copper, with battery backup and monitoring. |
| Doors stay locked in a fire alarm test | Broken fire interface. Interface test. | Fix the fire interface, and retest. |
| Fire alarm, lift phone or monitoring dialler still on a copper service | Service due to be switched off by the carrier. Line audit of every safety-critical connection; carrier notices. | Move each service to a supported path, and test it end to end with the monitoring centre. |

sections.heading: Obsolescence and cyber exposure
sections.markdown:
Analogue CCTV, proprietary access control and older nurse call systems lose spare parts and support; a single controller failure can disable a system. Proprietary access control ties the building to one integrator for cards, readers and changes.

IP cameras, access controllers and intercoms connected to the internet with default passwords and unpatched firmware are commonly compromised. Governments in all three countries have restricted certain camera and equipment manufacturers in government facilities, which affects buildings with government tenants.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Only one company can add a card | Proprietary access control. Vendor; licensing. | Replace with an open-standard system, with the owner holding licences and databases. |
| Cameras visible from the internet | Insecure configuration. Security assessment. | Segregate the network, change credentials and update firmware. |

sections.heading: Coverage and cabling
sections.markdown:
CCTV blind spots after fit-outs; access control bypassed by propped doors; weak mobile and emergency radio coverage in basements and large buildings; nurse call points missing in new rooms.

Older cabling categories cannot carry modern bandwidth or power-over-Ethernet loads; risers fill with abandoned cable; comms rooms overheat; patching is undocumented, so faults take days to trace.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Network faults take days to trace | Undocumented cabling and patching. Documentation. | Document the cabling and patching, and remove redundant cable. |
| No mobile or radio signal in basements, stairs or plant rooms | Coverage gap for occupants and emergency services. Signal survey; fire brigade radio requirements. | Fit an in-building coverage system where people work or the brigade needs radio. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lift emergency phones or alarm diallers not working; access-controlled escape doors not releasing; nurse call failures | safety · 4 Essential | Rectify now. |
| Copper line retirement scheduled for devices still on copper | deadline · 4 Essential | Migrate before the switch-off date. |
| System failed (CCTV, access control, intercom) | failure · 3 Important | Repair now. |
| Unsupported systems; cyber exposure; coverage gaps | condition · 3 Important | Upgrade in the near term. |
| Systems at end of life | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Replace on cycle. |
| Line types unknown; no security assessment | check · 2 Planned | Audit. |
| Normal | nil · 1 Routine | Routine. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A communications and security systems consultant, with the lift contractor for emergency phones and a cyber security specialist. The checks below build an inventory of systems and line types first, then test lift phones, diallers and the fire interfaces on access-controlled doors.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Inventory | Of every system with vendor, model, version, age and support status. |
| Line audit | Every device that dials out (lift phones, alarm diallers, intercoms, BMS modems) and the line type it uses. |
| Testing | Lift phones, alarm monitoring, nurse call, intercoms. |
| Fire interface testing | Of access-controlled doors and lifts. |
| Coverage review | CCTV, access control, mobile and emergency radio. |
| Cyber security assessment | Of IP devices and remote access. |
| Cabling and comms room survey | Categories, capacity, documentation, cooling. |
| Compliance review | Privacy for CCTV, emergency radio coverage where required, procurement restrictions for government tenants. |

The report should give the inventory, the copper migration list, safety failures, support status, security risks and a replacement programme.

sections.heading: Migrating, securing or replacing
sections.markdown:
Lift phones and alarm diallers on copper come first, since a phone that cannot call out is a life-safety failure, and so do doors that stay locked in a fire. After that, the work replaces locked-in and insecure systems and documents the cabling.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Migrate devices off copper | Lift phones and diallers to 4G/5G or IP with battery backup and monitoring. | Before each line is retired. |
| Fix fire interfaces | Repair the interfaces and test them. | Wherever doors stay locked in a fire alarm test. |
| Replace analogue CCTV | IP systems, designed for coverage and privacy. | Where analogue cameras and recorders are at the end of their life. |
| Replace proprietary access control | Open-standard systems, with the owner holding licences and databases. | Where only one company can maintain the system. |
| Harden cyber security | Segregated networks, changed credentials, firmware updates, removal of restricted equipment where required. | Wherever systems can be reached from outside. |
| Improve coverage | Distributed antenna systems or emergency responder radio systems. | Where mobile or emergency radio coverage is weak. |
| Upgrade cabling | Upgrade cabling and comms rooms, remove redundant cable, and document patching. | Where faults take days to trace. |
| Replace nurse call | Supported systems with full coverage. | Where nurse call is unsupported or has gaps. |
| Battery backup | Battery backup for digital lift phones and diallers. | So they work during power failures. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Audits are lump sums. Copper migration is priced per device with monitoring contracts recurring. CCTV, access control and intercom replacement are priced per device plus head end. Cabling upgrades are per outlet or per floor. In-building coverage systems are lump sums. Nurse call is per bed or room.

Safety rectification and copper migration are code compliance or deadline-driven; replacement is lifecycle; maintenance contracts recur.

Digital line migration often needs new equipment in lift cars and panels as well as a new service.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a look at the equipment cannot: which lines each lift phone and dialler uses, which systems are still supported, and whether the fire interfaces work. Ask for the line types first, since retirement dates are fixed.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Inventory of systems with vendors, versions and support status | Which systems the building has, and which are still supported. |
| Line types for lift phones, alarm diallers and intercoms, and carrier notices | Which devices still rely on copper lines, and when they will be cut off. |
| Fire interface test records | Whether access-controlled doors release in a fire. |
| Cabling documentation and test results | What the cabling is, and where it goes. |
| CCTV privacy policy and signage | Whether CCTV meets privacy law. |
| Nurse call test records | Whether nurse call works everywhere it should. |
| Any cyber security assessment | Whether the systems are secure. |
| Lift emergency phone test records | Whether lift phones actually connect. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Communications systems are misread when lift phones and diallers are assumed to keep working after the copper network goes, and when a working system is assumed to be a secure one.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| The lift phone will keep working | Lift emergency telephones and alarm diallers on copper lines must be checked before the line is retired. A lift phone that cannot call out is a life-safety failure. |
| It works, so it is secure | Cameras visible from the internet point to insecure configuration. Segregate the networks, change default credentials and keep firmware current. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market regulates cabling work, lift emergency communication and CCTV privacy, and is retiring its copper telephone network. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cabling, lifts, privacy and network retirement | Cabling work requires registered cablers under the communications cabling rules; AS/NZS 3080 and related standards cover structured cabling; lift emergency communication requirements follow the lift standards; state privacy and surveillance laws govern CCTV; the copper network has largely been replaced by the NBN. | The analogue telephone network is retired on 31 January 2027, with all users to be migrated by then, affecting lift phones, alarm diallers and telecare; BS EN 81-28 covers remote alarms on lifts; UK GDPR and the Surveillance Camera Code govern CCTV. | Carriers are retiring copper lines under FCC rules; ASME A17.1 requires two-way communication in lifts; the International Fire Code and NFPA 1225 require emergency responder radio coverage in many buildings; federal procurement rules restrict certain telecommunications and video equipment. |

sections.heading: Worked example: lift phones on a retiring network
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. An office building's lift emergency phones and fire alarm dialler still run over copper lines, and the carrier has given notice of retirement. Access control was added by a tenant and only its installer can add cards, and in a recent fire test two controlled doors stayed locked.

A lift phone that cannot call out is a life-safety failure, so the phones and dialler must move off copper before the line goes. Doors that stay locked in a fire test point to a broken fire interface, also a safety finding. The locked-in access control is an ownership finding.

So the register carries the lift phones and dialler as deadline lines, migrated to 4G/5G or IP with battery backup, the fire interface repaired and retested as a safety line, and open-standard access control at replacement.

pages.title: Disabled Access (DDA)
pages.question: How do buildings fall short on access, and which access findings create safety or discrimination risk?
pages.answer: Access findings fall into three kinds. Older buildings predate current requirements: steps at entries, narrow doors, no accessible toilets or lifts. Alterations can trigger upgrades to the path of travel the owner did not plan for. And features fail in use: tactile indicators lift into trip hazards, closers make doors too heavy, accessible toilets become storerooms, lifts stay out of service. Missing evacuation provision for people with disability is a safety finding.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about disabled access (dda); it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Ramps, handrails, tactile indicators, accessible amenities

sources.title: Disability (Access to Premises — Buildings) Standards 2010
Approved Document M
2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design
AS 1428.1:2021 Design for access and mobility, Part 1: General requirements for access, new building work
BS 8300-2:2018 Design of an accessible and inclusive built environment: Buildings
Approved Document M, Volume 2: Buildings other than dwellings (with 2024 amendments)
2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design

pages.searchTitle: Disabled access in existing buildings: what fails and what triggers upgrades

questions.question: Does an older building have to meet current access standards?
questions.answer: Not automatically. Older buildings predate current requirements, but new work must meet them and, in Australia, so must the affected part and path of travel in an alteration. A building can still carry discrimination risk where barriers remain.

questions.question: What triggers an access upgrade?
questions.answer: Alterations. In Australia the Premises Standards apply to new work and to the affected part and path of travel; in the United States, alterations must improve the path of travel up to a proportion of the alteration cost.

questions.question: Why can't some people open the doors?
questions.answer: The closer force is usually too high, or there is no automatic operator. Measure the opening force; adjusting the closer or fitting an operator fixes it.

questions.question: Are lifted tactile indicators serious?
questions.answer: Yes. Lifted indicators are a trip hazard and are graded as a safety finding, to be rectified now.

questions.question: What is an access action plan?
questions.answer: A staged programme setting priorities and dates where full compliance is impractical at once. In Australia it can be lodged with the Human Rights Commission, which helps manage discrimination risk.

questions.question: What records show whether a building is accessible?
questions.answer: Access audits and reports, alteration approvals with their access conditions, complaints, evacuation plans, lift downtime records and any access action plan.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Access problems show on the route a person takes: the entry, the doors, the toilet, the way out. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On site | Steps or steep ramps at entries; level changes along routes | Older buildings and alterations |
| On site | Doors that are narrow, heavy, or have high thresholds | Wear, doors and lost features |
| On site | Accessible toilets cluttered, locked or used as storage; missing grab rails or wrong layouts | Management and evacuation |
| On site | Tactile indicators lifted, missing or in the wrong places; worn contrast strips | Wear, doors and lost features |
| On site | Signs without braille or tactile lettering where required | Wear, doors and lost features |
| On site | Lifts and platform lifts out of service | [Accessibility Lifts](https://moyneross.com/technical/accessibility-lifts) |
| On site | No hearing augmentation signage in meeting rooms and auditoria | Wear, doors and lost features |
| In the records | Access audits | Investigation before the scope |
| In the records | Building approvals for alterations, with access reports | Older buildings and alterations |
| In the records | Complaints and discrimination claims | Older buildings and alterations |
| In the records | Personal emergency evacuation plans | Management and evacuation |

sections.heading: What access covers
sections.markdown:
Disabled access covers the features that let people with disability reach, enter, use and leave a building: a continuous accessible path of travel from the street and car park, ramps and step-free entries, doors that are wide enough and light enough to open, lifts, accessible toilets and showers, handrails, tactile ground surface indicators that warn of hazards, luminance contrast so edges and doors can be seen, signage in braille and tactile form, hearing augmentation, accessible parking, and provision for evacuation. Requirements depend on the building's use and age, and on whether it is being altered.

| Provision | Where it applies | What commonly fails |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Accessible path of travel and entry | Public and commercial buildings, apartment common areas | Steps at entries; steep ramps; gaps and level changes |
| Ramps, kerb ramps and landings | Entries and changes of level | Too steep; no landings; no handrails; slippery |
| Doors and doorways | Throughout the accessible path | Too narrow; too heavy; poor circulation space; thresholds |
| Accessible toilets and showers | Public and commercial buildings | Wrong dimensions; used as storage; fittings missing |
| Tactile ground surface indicators | Stairs, ramps, kerbs, platform edges | Lifting and missing; wrong placement |
| Luminance contrast and signage | Doors, edges, stairs, wayfinding | Faded; missing braille and tactile signs |
| Hearing augmentation | Meeting rooms, auditoria, counters | Absent or not working |
| Accessible lifts and platform lifts | Multi-level buildings | Out of service; not compliant |
| Accessible parking | Car parks | Wrong size; no shared zone; not signed |

Era is a strong guide. Australian buildings designed before the Disability (Access to Premises — Buildings) Standards took effect in 2011, British buildings before Approved Document M was extended in the 1990s and 2000s, and American buildings before the Americans with Disabilities Act (1990) often fall well short of current requirements, and alterations to them can trigger upgrades.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Access features wear at different rates. Ramps and paths last decades, while the fittings and finishes along the route need renewing far sooner. Typical lives are a guide; traffic, cleaning and use move them.

| Element | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ramps and paths | 30 to 50 years | Surface wear; settlement |
| Tactile indicators (adhesive or discrete) | 5 to 15 years | Traffic; adhesive failure; cleaning |
| Accessible toilet fittings | 15 to 25 years | Use; vandalism |
| Door closers and automatic door operators | 10 to 15 years | Use; adjustment |
| Hearing augmentation systems | 10 to 15 years | Technology; maintenance |
| Signage | 10 to 20 years | UV; damage |

What shortens it: heavy traffic lifting and wearing tactile indicators; door closers adjusted too strong for fire or security, making doors too heavy to open; fit-outs that block circulation space or remove features; poor management: accessible toilets used for storage, ramps blocked, lifts left out of service.

sections.heading: Older buildings and alterations
sections.markdown:
Older buildings have steps at entries, narrow doors, no accessible toilets, no lift between levels, and no tactile or contrast provisions. These are not defects in the ordinary sense, but they expose owners and occupiers to discrimination complaints and limit who can use the building.

New work must generally meet current requirements, and in Australia and the United States, alterations can extend obligations to the path of travel serving the altered area. A fit-out or refurbishment can therefore bring an access upgrade obligation the owner did not plan for.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Steps at the only entry | Building predates access requirements. Era; approvals. | Plan a ramp, platform lift or regraded path; if it cannot be done at once, set it in an access action plan. |
| New fit-out with an accessible toilet but steps at the entry | Path of travel not upgraded with the alteration. Approval documents; access report. | Upgrade the path of travel as the approval requires, and check the access report's conditions. |
| Doorways too narrow for a wheelchair on the accessible route | Clear width below current standards. Clear opening measured with the door at 90 degrees, against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Widen the opening or rehang the door at the next alteration. |
| Ramp that feels steep, or a lip at its top or bottom | Ramp gradient or level change outside the rules. Gradient and level change measured against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Regrade the ramp or fix the lip; add handrails where required. |

sections.heading: Wear, doors and lost features
sections.markdown:
Doors on accessible routes must be openable by people with limited strength. Closers set strong for fire, smoke or wind, and heavy external doors without automatic operators, make doors effectively impassable.

Tactile indicators lift and become trip hazards or are removed; luminance contrast strips fade; signage is damaged; handrails loosen; ramp surfaces become slippery.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tactile indicators lifting at stairs | Adhesive failure from traffic and cleaning. Inspection. | Replace the lifted indicators now; they are a trip hazard. |
| Doors that people in wheelchairs cannot open | Closer force too high or no automatic operator. Door force measurement against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Adjust the closer to the required force, or fit an automatic operator. |

sections.heading: Management and evacuation
sections.markdown:
Accessible toilets used as storerooms or cleaners' rooms, ramps and accessible parking obstructed, lifts and platform lifts out of service for long periods, and hearing loops not switched on all remove access that exists on paper.

Many buildings provide accessible entry but no plan for getting people with disability out in an emergency: no refuges, evacuation lifts, communication systems or personal evacuation plans.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Accessible toilet full of boxes | Management practice. Observation. | Clear it, and put a procedure in place to keep it available. |
| No refuge or evacuation plan | Egress for people with disability not addressed. Fire strategy; plans. | Review the fire strategy and prepare evacuation plans for people who need assistance. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lifted tactile indicators or damaged ramps creating trip hazards; no means of evacuation for people with disability | safety · 4 Essential | Rectify now. |
| Only accessible route unavailable (lift out of service, ramp blocked) | failure · 3 Important | Restore now. |
| Upgrade required by an alteration approval or a complaint resolution | deadline · 4 Essential | By the required date. |
| Heavy doors, faded contrast, missing signage, accessible toilets misused | condition · 3 Important | Fix in the near term. |
| Access features at end of life | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Renew. |
| No access audit; alterations planned | check · 2 Planned | Audit. |
| Normal | nil · 1 Routine | Routine. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
An accredited access consultant leads; in California, a Certified Access Specialist. The checks below follow the route a person takes, from the boundary to the facilities and out again in an emergency.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Access audit | Against current requirements, covering the path of travel from the boundary and car park through entries, circulation, lifts, sanitary facilities, signage and egress. |
| Measurements | Ramp gradients, door widths and opening forces, circulation spaces, toilet layouts and luminance contrast, against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). |
| Alteration review | Which areas have been altered since access requirements took effect and what obligations followed. |
| Management review | How accessible facilities are kept available. |
| Egress review | With the fire strategy for people with disability. |
| User consultation | Where practicable: people who use the building can identify barriers that measurements miss, such as confusing wayfinding or doors that only staff can unlock. |

The report should separate safety items, compliance obligations triggered by alterations, discrimination risks, and good-practice improvements, with priorities.

sections.heading: Upgrading access
sections.markdown:
Access work ranges from adjusting a door closer to rebuilding an entry, and much of it is cheap. What sets the scope is the kind of finding: wear or management that can be fixed quickly, a requirement triggered by an alteration, or a historic shortfall that carries discrimination risk. The kind decides urgency and who pays.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Entries | Ramps, platform lifts or regraded paths; automatic doors. | Where steps or steep ramps stand at the entry, especially the only one. |
| Doors | Closer adjustment, automatic operators, wider doors, threshold ramps. | Where opening force, width or thresholds stop people using the door. |
| Accessible sanitary facilities | New or upgraded rooms; clearing storage. | Where none are on the accessible route or the layout is wrong; clearing storage costs nothing. |
| Tactile indicators and contrast | Replace lifted indicators, renew contrast strips. | Lifted indicators at once, since they are a trip hazard; worn contrast in the near term. |
| Signage | Signs in braille and tactile form; wayfinding. | Where signs lack braille or tactile lettering where required. |
| Hearing augmentation | Systems in meeting rooms and at service counters. | Where meeting rooms, auditoria or counters have none. |
| Lifts | Reliability and accessibility upgrades. | Where a lift is the only step-free route and is often out of service. |
| Evacuation provisions | Refuges, communication, evacuation plans. | Where the fire strategy does not provide for people who need assistance to leave. |
| Management | Procedures to keep features available. | Always; many findings are management, not fabric. |
| Accessible parking | Bays resized and marked with shared zones and signage, close to the accessible entry. | Where accessible bays are missing, undersized or far from the accessible entry. |
| Wayfinding | Consistent signage, contrast and lighting so people with low vision can find entries, lifts and toilets. | Where people with low vision cannot find their way. |
| Staged programme | An access action plan setting priorities and dates, which in Australia can be lodged with the Human Rights Commission and helps manage discrimination risk. | Where full compliance is impractical at once. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Audits are lump sums. Minor works (tactile indicators, signage, closers) are itemised. Ramps and automatic doors are lump sums per entry. New accessible toilets are lump sums per room. Lifts are major projects. Path of travel upgrades triggered by alterations sit with the alteration project.

Safety items are immediate; alteration-triggered upgrades are code compliance; discrimination risk reduction is a strategic choice; renewals are lifecycle.

An access action plan spreads cost over time while showing commitment, which matters in discrimination disputes.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a walk-through cannot: what was approved and on what conditions, what people have complained about, and what the owner has committed to fix. Ask for them before the audit, so the auditor knows where to look.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Access audits and access reports for approvals | Which barriers are already known, and what was agreed when the building was last approved. |
| Building approvals for alterations, with access conditions | Whether past alterations triggered path-of-travel upgrades, and whether they were done. |
| Complaints and discrimination claims | Where people have already been excluded, and the risk that carries. |
| Personal emergency evacuation plans | Whether people who need assistance can leave in an emergency. |
| Lift and platform lift downtime records | How often the only step-free route is lost. |
| Management procedures for accessible facilities | Whether accessible toilets, routes and parking are kept clear and working. |
| Any access action plan | Which upgrades are committed, in what order and by when. |
| Accessible parking layout and signage records | Whether accessible bays meet the size, marking and location required. |
| Door opening force measurements on the accessible route | Whether the doors on the accessible route can be opened by the people it serves. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Access findings are often read as all or nothing: either the building complies or it needs rebuilding. Most findings are neither, and reading them that way either inflates the scope or leaves real risk untouched.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| The building was approved, so it is accessible | Approval reflects the rules of its time. Older buildings predate current requirements, and a building can still carry discrimination risk where barriers remain. |
| An accessible toilet in the fit-out makes the tenancy accessible | Not if the path of travel from the entry still has steps. Alterations can trigger upgrades to the path of travel, not only to the area altered. |
| Access problems mean major works | Many are wear and management: lifted indicators, heavy closers, a toilet used for storage. They are quick and cheap to fix. |
| Evacuation is a matter for the fire systems | Getting people with disability out needs refuges, communication and personal evacuation plans as well. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Access needs are the same everywhere; the laws that require them are not. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out the law that creates the duty, the standards for new and altered work, and what applies to existing buildings.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| The duty | The Disability Discrimination Act 1992 and the Disability (Access to Premises — Buildings) Standards 2010. | The Equality Act 2010 requires reasonable adjustments to remove barriers. | The Americans with Disabilities Act and the 2010 ADA Standards; the Fair Housing Act covers multifamily housing. |
| Design standards | The National Construction Code sets access requirements, calling up AS 1428.1 and related parts, including tactile indicators. | Approved Document M sets access for new and altered buildings; BS 8300 sets design guidance for accessible buildings. | ICC A117.1 is adopted in building codes. |
| Existing buildings and alterations | The Premises Standards apply to new work and to the affected part and path of travel in alterations. | Approved Document M applies to altered buildings. | Existing public accommodations must remove barriers where readily achievable, and alterations must improve the path of travel up to a proportion of the alteration cost. |

sections.heading: Worked example: a fit-out that stopped at the front door
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 1980s two-storey office in Australia has a newly fitted ground-floor tenancy with an accessible toilet. The only entry from the street has three steps, the entry door has a heavy closer, and the tactile indicators at the internal stair are lifting at the edges.

The lifted indicators are a trip hazard and the first line on the register: graded safety, rectified now. The heavy closer is a condition finding, fixed by adjusting the closer or fitting an operator. The steps are the larger question: the fit-out approval may have required the path of travel to be upgraded, and if it did, the ramp or platform lift carries a deadline.

So the register carries three lines, not one access upgrade. The check that settles the largest of them is the approval and its access report: whether the path of travel was in scope decides whether the entry is a deadline now or a historic shortfall for an access action plan.

thresholds.measure: Opening force at the leading edge (England)

thresholds.rule: At least 815 mm with the door open 90 degrees

source.title: 2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design

thresholds.rule: No more than 22.2 N

source.title: 2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design

pages.title: Dock Levellers & Goods Hoists
pages.question: How do dock levellers and goods hoists fail, and which faults put people at risk?
pages.answer: Dock equipment fails by overload, impact and lost safety devices. Heavier battery-electric forklifts overload levellers rated for older machines, cracking lips and decks; worn bumpers let trailers hit the building; hydraulic leaks let decks sink. The dangerous failures are free-fall protection that does not stop a deck when a trailer pulls away, trailers creeping without restraints, open dock edges, and goods hoist doors that open with no car behind them.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about dock levellers & goods hoists; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Platforms, hydraulic systems, controls

sources.title: Loading docks and vehicle safety
Powered industrial trucks
Lifting equipment at work (LOLER)
BS EN 1398:2009 Dock levellers: Safety requirements
ASME A17.1/CSA B44 Safety Code for Elevators and Escalators
Thorough examination of lifting equipment (INDG422)

pages.searchTitle: Dock levellers and goods hoists: free fall, trailer creep, interlocks and dock safety

questions.question: Why does one dock have most of the incidents?
questions.answer: Something local: its levels, lighting, restraint or approach. Compare that dock's geometry, equipment and lighting with the others; a general equipment survey will miss it.

questions.question: How do you stop trailers pulling away during loading?
questions.answer: Vehicle restraints, interlocked with the dock door or leveller where possible, with driver signal lights inside and outside. They are the most effective engineering control against creep and early departure.

questions.question: Why do the leveller's hydraulic seals keep failing?
questions.answer: Usually contamination: water and grit entering through a damaged pit or a failed breather destroy each new set of seals within months. The pit is the fix, not the cylinder.

questions.question: Is a goods hoist door that opens without the car serious?
questions.answer: Yes. It is a life-safety failure; take the hoist out of use until the interlock is repaired and proved at every landing.

questions.question: How long do dock levellers last?
questions.answer: Hydraulic levellers 15 to 25 years and mechanical ones 10 to 20, with bumpers replaced every 3 to 8 years and seals and shelters every 5 to 10.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Dock problems show while the dock is working: how trailers are held, how forklifts cross the lip, where people wait, and whether anyone rides the hoist. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What you notice watching the dock work | Trailers chocked, restrained, or neither; whether the restraint is engaged before loading starts | Trailer creep, levels and the dock face |
| What you notice watching the dock work | Forklifts crossing the lip at an angle, or bouncing as they cross | Trailer creep, levels and the dock face |
| What you notice watching the dock work | Drivers waiting in or near the dock area rather than in a designated place | Pedestrians, open edges and lighting |
| What you notice watching the dock work | Dock doors left open with no trailer and no edge protection across the opening | Pedestrians, open edges and lighting |
| What you notice watching the dock work | Levellers left raised or lips extended between vehicles | Pedestrians, open edges and lighting |
| What you notice watching the dock work | Staff riding a goods hoist, or stacking goods against its landing doors | Goods hoists |
| What you notice watching the dock work | How dark the inside of a trailer is compared with the warehouse | Pedestrians, open edges and lighting |
| On site | Cracks at deck welds, lip hinges and support beams, inspected from beneath the deck with the leveller propped on its maintenance stand | Levellers: free fall, structure and hydraulics |
| On site | Free-fall protection tested, not just inspected: velocity fuses on hydraulic units, safety legs or stops on mechanical ones | Levellers: free fall, structure and hydraulics |
| On site | Oil beneath levellers and around power packs; decks that drift down under load | Levellers: free fall, structure and hydraulics |
| On site | Lips that do not extend fully, do not sit flat on the trailer bed, or are bent at the ends | Trailer creep, levels and the dock face |
| On site | Bumpers: worn, missing, loose or already crushed flat, and impact damage to the dock face behind them | Trailer creep, levels and the dock face |
| On site | Vehicle restraints present, functional, and interlocked with doors or levellers where fitted | Trailer creep, levels and the dock face |
| On site | Pit edges and curb angles broken out; pit floors holding water; drainage blocked | Levellers: free fall, structure and hydraulics |
| On site | Goods hoist landing doors tested individually to confirm they cannot open with the car elsewhere | Goods hoists |
| On site | Rider prohibition signage on goods hoists, and whether it is being ignored | Goods hoists |
| On site | Dock lighting levels at the dock face and inside a trailer | Pedestrians, open edges and lighting |
| In the records | Maintenance and service records for each leveller, restraint and hoist, individually rather than as a site total | Investigation before the scope |
| In the records | Free-fall and interlock test records, with dates | Levellers: free fall, structure and hydraulics |
| In the records | Incident and near-miss reports at the docks, including vehicle departures during loading | Trailer creep, levels and the dock face |
| In the records | Forklift fleet list with weights, including battery-electric machines, against each leveller's rating plate | Levellers: free fall, structure and hydraulics |
| In the records | Vehicle movements per dock, which gives the real duty | Trailer creep, levels and the dock face |
| In the records | Plant registration and inspection records for goods hoists | Goods hoists |
| In the records | The lease, showing who is responsible for dock equipment maintenance and renewal | Standards by country |
| In the records | Hazardous materials register for the dock structure | Asbestos in the dock structure |

sections.heading: Types of dock equipment
sections.markdown:
Dock levellers bridge the gap and height difference between a loading dock floor and a truck bed, so forklifts and pallet jacks can drive between them. Goods hoists and service lifts move goods, not people, between levels: dumbwaiters in kitchens and hospitals, material hoists in retail and industrial buildings, and scissor lift tables at docks. Dock equipment works with dock doors, seals and shelters, vehicle restraints, bumpers, dock lighting and the dock edge itself, and its failures injure people and damage buildings and vehicles.

A loading dock is a place where a four-tonne machine drives across a moving bridge onto a vehicle that is not attached to the building, over a drop of more than a metre, many times an hour. Almost every serious dock incident comes from one of those three facts: the bridge drops, the vehicle moves, or someone goes over the edge. The equipment on this page exists to prevent exactly those three things, and its condition is read against them.

| Type | Where it is found | Character |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hydraulic dock leveller | Logistics, retail, industrial docks | Hydraulic cylinders raise the deck and extend the lip; velocity fuses stop free fall |
| Mechanical (spring) dock leveller | Older and lighter-duty docks | Springs and hold-downs; more manual adjustment and wear |
| Air-bag dock leveller | Some logistics docks | Air bag lifts the deck; fan and bag condition |
| Edge-of-dock leveller | Light-duty docks | Small height range; mounted at the dock face |
| Vehicle restraints | Busy docks | Hold the trailer to the dock so it cannot creep or drive away during loading |
| Scissor lift tables | Docks without raised floors, mezzanines | Hydraulic scissor mechanism; pinch points |
| Goods hoists and dumbwaiters | Retail, hospitals, kitchens, warehouses | Small lifts for goods only; door interlocks critical |

Loading docks are among the most dangerous areas of logistics and retail buildings: trailers creep away from docks under forklift braking, people fall from open dock edges, forklifts fall through gaps, and levellers drop under load. Equipment condition, the surrounding dock structure and site management together decide the risk.

The dock is also a structure, not just a set of machines. The pit the leveller sits in, the curb angle at its edge, the slab the forklifts brake on, the bumpers, the doors and the apron outside all take the same punishment and fail together. Assessing levellers without the structure around them misses most of the cost ([Slab on Ground](https://moyneross.com/technical/slab-on-ground), [Pavements & Hardstand](https://moyneross.com/technical/pavements-and-hardstand)).

Goods hoists belong here rather than with passenger lifts because they are goods-only equipment, often unregistered, frequently ridden by staff despite prohibition, and maintained, if at all, by the tenant's general contractor rather than a lift company. Their landing door interlocks are the whole of their safety, and nobody checks them ([Passenger & Goods Lifts](https://moyneross.com/technical/passenger-and-goods-lifts)).

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Dock equipment works hard and wears fast. Bumpers last three to eight years and dock seals five to ten, levellers ten to twenty-five, and goods hoists twenty to thirty, but the real measure is the duty: vehicle movements per dock, and the weight of the forklifts crossing each lip.

| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hydraulic dock leveller | 15 to 25 years | Cycles; load ratings; impact |
| Mechanical dock leveller | 10 to 20 years | Spring and hinge wear |
| Hydraulic power packs and cylinders | 10 to 15 years | Seals; contamination |
| Lip hinges and deck plates | 10 to 20 years | Impact; fatigue cracking |
| Vehicle restraints | 10 to 15 years | Impact; controls |
| Dock seals and shelters | 5 to 10 years | Abrasion; UV |
| Dock bumpers | 3 to 8 years | Truck impacts |
| Goods hoists | 20 to 30 years; controls 15 to 20 | Duty; door abuse |
| Dock doors and door tracks | 10 to 20 years | Impact; cycles; wind |
| Dock pit concrete and curb angle | 20 to 30 years | Impact; water; forklift braking |
| Scissor lift tables | 15 to 20 years | Cycles; hydraulics; pit drainage |
| Dock lighting and signal systems | 10 to 15 years | Impact; weather; lamp type |

Cycles rather than years set the life of dock equipment. A leveller at a dock handling forty trailers a day works through its design cycles in a fraction of the calendar life quoted for a leveller used twice a week, and a facility that has intensified since it was built, as most logistics buildings have, is running equipment far past its intended duty. Where the operator records vehicle movements per dock, that number predicts leveller condition better than age.

What shortens life: overload: forklifts heavier than the leveller rating, especially with battery-electric forklifts that weigh more than older models; impact from trailers backing into docks without bumpers, and from forklifts dropping onto lips; lack of planned maintenance, with repairs only after breakdown; weather at external docks, corroding pits, hinges and hydraulics.

What lengthens it: bumpers replaced before they are gone, since a worn bumper transfers every trailer impact into the dock structure; ratings matched to the actual forklift fleet, including the weight of battery-electric machines; vehicle restraints, which stop the impact loads and the creep that crack lips and hinges; planned maintenance with free-fall testing rather than repair on breakdown; pit drainage kept clear at external docks, so hydraulics and hinges are not standing in water; driver and forklift operator discipline: chocks or restraints every time, no departure before the signal.

sections.heading: Levellers: free fall, structure and hydraulics
sections.markdown:
If a trailer pulls away while the leveller lip is resting on it, the deck loses its far support and drops. Hydraulic levellers rely on a velocity fuse in the cylinder to sense the rate of fall and lock; mechanical levellers rely on safety legs or stops under the deck. Both are single devices that are rarely tested, easily adjusted out during a repair, and invisible in normal operation. When they fail, the deck falls with a loaded forklift on it, which is the most serious failure this equipment has and the one that most often kills.

Deck plates, lip hinges and support beams crack from fatigue and overload. Cracks begin at welds and hinge points, where stress concentrates, and propagate slowly until a lip fails under a forklift or a deck deforms permanently. The usual underlying cause is a fleet that has outgrown the equipment: battery-electric forklifts are substantially heavier than the internal-combustion machines many docks were rated for, and the combined weight of truck and load can exceed the leveller's capacity on every single crossing.

Seals leak, oil contaminates, power packs fail and cylinders drift, so levellers do not rise, lips do not extend, or decks sink under load.

Pit edges and curb angles break up under repeated impact; bumpers wear away, letting trailers strike the building; dock walls and slabs crack.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Deck sinks slowly under load | Hydraulic leak or failed holding valve. Drift test; oil leaks. | Drift test it, and repair the holding valve or leak; check the free-fall protection while it is open. |
| Cracks at lip hinges and deck welds | Fatigue and overload. Inspection; forklift weight against rating. | Take it out of use if it is cracked under load; repair or replace it, rated for the current fleet. |
| Deck does not stop when tested for free fall | Failed velocity fuse or safety leg. Free-fall test. | Take it out of use now; restore the velocity fuse or safety leg, and retest. |
| Lip hinges cracking repeatedly after repair | Rating exceeded by the current fleet. Forklift and load weight against the rating plate. | Replace the leveller with one rated for the current fleet. |
| Water in the pit at an external dock | Apron falls or blocked pit drainage. Levels surveyed at the apron; drain traced. | Correct the apron falls and clear the pit drainage. |

sections.heading: Trailer creep, levels and the dock face
sections.markdown:
Trailers move away from the dock in two ways. They creep, walking forward a few centimetres at a time under the braking and acceleration of a forklift entering and leaving, until the gap is wide enough to drop a wheel into. And they depart early, when a driver believes loading is finished and pulls away with a forklift still on board or the lip still resting on the deck. Wheel chocks depend on someone placing them and nobody moving them; vehicle restraints engage the trailer's rear impact guard mechanically and, where interlocked with the dock door or leveller, make early departure physically difficult rather than merely prohibited.

A dock is built for a particular trailer bed height. Vans, rigid trucks, refrigerated trailers and container chassis all present different heights, and a fleet that has changed since the dock was built leaves levellers working at the ends of their range, lips meeting at steep angles, and forklifts climbing gradients they were not meant to cross. Steep approach angles ground long-wheelbase forklifts and overstress lips.

Open docks and dock aprons collect water, which runs into pits, corrodes hinges, frames and hydraulics, and freezes in cold climates. Aprons that fall towards the building send trailer run-off into the pit. Wind catches raised dock doors. Dock seals and shelters degrade under ultraviolet and abrasion, which is an energy and product-integrity issue in temperature-controlled buildings as much as a maintenance one ([Stormwater Drainage](https://moyneross.com/technical/stormwater-drainage)).

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Trailers moving during loading | No vehicle restraints or poor procedures. Observation; incident reports. | Fit vehicle restraints interlocked with the door or leveller, with driver signal lights. |
| Dock walls and doors damaged | Bumpers worn or missing. Inspection. | Replace the bumpers, steel-faced at heavy-use docks, on a cycle. |
| Forklifts bouncing or grounding on the lip | Trailer bed height outside the leveller's range. Bed heights of the current vehicle mix measured. | Measure the bed heights of the current fleet; adjust the dock levels or the leveller's range. |
| Incidents clustered at one dock of several | Something local: levels, lighting, restraint or approach. Compare that dock's geometry, equipment and lighting with its neighbours. | Compare that dock's levels, lighting, restraint and approach with the others. |
| Bumpers crushed flat and dock face damaged | Bumper replacement cycle too long. Bumper thickness remaining; impact marks above the bumper line. | Shorten the bumper replacement cycle. |

sections.heading: Goods hoists
sections.markdown:
Goods hoists and dumbwaiters rely on landing door interlocks so that a door cannot be opened unless the car is at that landing. That single device is the whole of their safety. Failed or deliberately bypassed interlocks leave an open shaft at floor level in a working area, and because these hoists are goods-only, nobody treats them as lifting equipment for people. Staff ride them anyway, in kitchens, retail stockrooms and hospitals, which turns a goods hoist with a defeated interlock into the most dangerous machine in the building.

Goods hoists frequently sit outside every maintenance regime in a building. They are too small to interest the lift contractor, not covered by the passenger lift contract, and often not on any asset register. In leased buildings neither party believes they own them. The result is equipment with no inspection history, no interlock testing and no certification, discovered only when someone is hurt or when a due diligence inspection asks for its records.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Goods hoist door opens without car | Interlock fault or bypass. Interlock test. | Take the hoist out of use; repair the interlock and prove it at every landing. |
| Goods hoist with no inspection records at all | Equipment outside every maintenance regime. Asset register and lease checked; hoist registration status. | Bring it into a maintenance and inspection regime, and register it where required. |

sections.heading: Pedestrians, open edges and lighting
sections.markdown:
Docks mix forklifts, delivery drivers, warehouse staff and sometimes visitors in a confined space with blind corners and reversing vehicles. Separation of pedestrian routes from vehicle routes, barriers, marked walkways and dock-edge gates are as much a part of dock safety as the levellers, and are commonly eroded by racking changes and storage creep.

Docks without doors closed, without edge barriers, or with levellers left raised leave drops of over a metre where people and forklifts can fall.

Forklift operators drive from bright warehouse light into the dark interior of a trailer, across a gap they cannot see clearly. Poor dock lighting, failed trailer lights and glare at external docks are contributing factors in a large share of dock incidents, and the fix is inexpensive compared with everything else on this page ([Lighting](https://moyneross.com/technical/lighting)).

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Open dock edges with no door closed or barrier when no trailer is present | Fall from the dock face. Observation of the dock between loadings; door and barrier use. | Keep dock doors closed or fit barriers or gates when no vehicle is docked, and mark the edge. |
| Pedestrians walking through the dock apron or behind reversing trailers | No separation of people and vehicles. Route observation during a loading peak. | Mark separate pedestrian routes, add barriers, and control access to the apron. |

sections.heading: Asbestos in the dock structure
sections.markdown:
Dock structures in buildings from before the 1990s can carry asbestos in roof sheeting, wall cladding, flue and service penetrations around the dock area. Impact damage from trailers and forklifts is a common way for it to be disturbed ([Hazardous Materials](https://moyneross.com/technical/hazardous-materials)).

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Old dock with fibre-cement panels, pit linings or bitumen-coated board | Possible asbestos in the dock structure. The asbestos register; sampling by a competent person. | Check the register before drilling, cutting or removing; manage or remove under asbestos controls. |
| Old leveller with brake linings or gaskets of unknown type | Possible asbestos in friction materials. Equipment age and records; sampling before maintenance. | Treat as asbestos-containing until sampled; replace with asbestos-free parts. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Free-fall protection failed or absent on a leveller in use | safety · 4 Essential | Take out of use now; this is the failure that kills. |
| Goods hoist landing door opening without the car present | safety · 4 Essential | Take out of use until the interlock is proved. |
| Cracked lips, decks or hinges under load | safety · 4 Essential | Take out of use now. |
| Open dock edges with no barrier, gate or closed door | safety · 4 Essential | Protect now. |
| No vehicle restraint or chocking in use at an operating dock | safety · 4 Essential | Stop loading until a restraint procedure is in place. |
| Staff riding a goods hoist | safety · 4 Essential | Stop now; signage alone is not a control. |
| Leveller or hoist inoperable at a dock still in use | failure · 4 Essential | Repair now or take the dock out of service. |
| Leveller rating below the weight of the current forklift fleet | failure · 4 Essential | Restrict the fleet or replace the leveller. |
| Goods hoist registration, inspection or thorough examination due | deadline · 4 Essential | At the prescribed interval. |
| Hydraulic leaks, deck drift, worn bumpers, broken pit edges, failed dock seals | condition · 3 Important | Repair in the near term. |
| No maintenance regime for the goods hoists; no free-fall testing record | condition · 3 Important | Put a regime in place now. |
| Equipment at the end of its life, or dock levels unsuited to the current vehicle mix | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Plan replacement. |
| Forklift weights unknown; vehicle movements unknown; asbestos status unknown | check · 3 Important | Establish before sizing works. |
| Scuffing and cosmetic damage to dock doors and finishes | nil · 1 Routine | Routine maintenance. |

Dock findings sit closer to the safety end of the scale than most building equipment, because the failure modes are sudden and the people exposed are working rather than passing through. A leveller with no proven free-fall protection is graded on what it will do the next time a trailer pulls away, not on whether it has done so yet.

The grading follows what a finding demands, not the size of the eventual bill.

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A dock equipment specialist or mechanical engineer, with a lift consultant for goods hoists. The checks below start from the incident record, dock by dock, then test the safety functions.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Inventory | Of every leveller, restraint, seal, bumper and hoist, with ratings and ages. |
| Rating check | Current forklift weights, including battery-electric models, against leveller capacity. |
| Structural inspection | Of decks, lips, hinges, beams and pit frames for cracks. |
| Function tests | Raise, lip extension, free-fall protection, restraint engagement and interlocks. |
| Hydraulic inspection | Leaks, drift, oil condition. |
| Dock structure | Pit edges, walls, bumpers, doors and lighting. |
| Goods hoists | Door interlocks, controls, signage, registration, and statutory examinations against the intervals for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). |
| Operations review | Of incidents and loading procedures with the site operator. |
| Free-fall testing of every leveller | Which is the one test that matters most and the one most often absent from records. |
| Vehicle bed height survey | Across the current fleet mix against each dock's range. |
| Lighting measurement | At the dock face and inside a trailer. |
| Pedestrian and vehicle route observation | During a loading peak. |
| Lease and asset register review | To establish who owns and maintains each item, since unowned equipment is unmaintained equipment. |

The report should list each dock with its safety status, condition, rating adequacy and recommended works.

Inspections are best scheduled with the operator so docks can be taken out of service in turn without stopping operations.

sections.heading: Making safe, repairing or replacing
sections.markdown:
Free-fall protection and hoist interlocks come before anything else, because their failure can kill. After that, the work follows the duty: restraints against trailer creep, repairs rated for the current fleet, and a maintenance regime that covers every item, hoists included.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Free-fall protection | Velocity fuses, safety legs and stops restored and tested on every leveller, with maintenance stands provided and their use trained. | First, before anything else on this list. |
| Goods hoist interlocks | Interlocks repaired or replaced and proved at every landing, the hoist brought into a maintenance and inspection regime, and riding physically prevented rather than only prohibited. | Wherever a landing door opens without the car, or staff ride the hoist. |
| Vehicle restraints | Restraints interlocked with the dock door or leveller where possible, with driver signal lights inside and outside. | At every operating dock; the single most effective engineering control against creep and early departure. |
| Structural repair or replacement | Repair or replace cracked lips and decks, rated for the actual fleet rather than the historic one. | Wherever lips, decks or hinges crack. |
| Bumper replacement | Bumpers on a cycle, steel-faced at heavy-use docks. | Before they crush flat; cheap, and it protects the structure behind. |
| Pit and curb repair | New curb angles and concrete, with drainage corrected at external docks. | Where pit edges break out or pits hold water. |
| Hydraulic overhaul | Seals, hoses, power packs and oil, with contamination addressed rather than topped up. | Where decks drift or oil leaks. |
| Edge protection | Gates or barriers at open dock doors, and procedures so levellers are stored level and doors closed when no trailer is present. | Wherever dock doors stand open without a trailer. |
| Dock lighting | Lighting at the dock face and adjustable trailer lights, with glare controlled at external docks. | Where trailer interiors are dark against the warehouse. |
| Pedestrian separation | Marked routes, barriers, and a designated waiting area for drivers away from the vehicle path. | Wherever drivers and staff share the dock with forklifts. |
| Dock seals and shelters | Renewed seals and shelters. | At the end of their life; in temperature-controlled buildings they matter for energy and product integrity as well as weather. |
| Maintenance regime | A regime covering every item, hoists included, with free-fall and interlock testing scheduled and recorded. | Wherever any item sits outside one. |

Choosing between them is unusually simple here, because the hierarchy is set by consequence rather than condition. Free-fall protection, hoist interlocks and restraint against vehicle movement come first whatever else is outstanding. Structural repair follows, then the equipment that protects the structure, then everything else.

The question behind most dock programmes, though, is whether the dock suits what the building now does. A facility handling heavier forklifts, different trailers and several times the movements it was designed for will keep cracking lips and breaking pit edges whatever is repaired. At that point the answer is a rebuilt dock with current ratings and geometry, programmed dock by dock so the operation continues.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Maintenance contracts recur. Bumpers and seals are recurring replacements. Leveller replacement is per dock, including pit frame repairs, and needs the dock out of service. Vehicle restraints are per dock with electrical and control work. Pit edge repairs are per dock. Goods hoist modernisation is a lump sum per hoist.

What drives the cost: the number of docks, whether the operation can release them one at a time, pit and structural repairs hidden until the leveller is lifted out, the rating required for the current fleet, electrical and control work for restraints and interlocks, and out-of-hours working to avoid stopping the operation. Commonly missed: the pit frame and curb angle, apron drainage, dock door repairs disturbed by the works, temporary loading arrangements, and the goods hoists, which are routinely left out of dock scopes altogether.

Safety rectification is code compliance; replacement is lifecycle; bumpers, seals and repairs are repairs and maintenance. In logistics leases, tenants commonly maintain dock equipment and owners replace it at end of life.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what watching a shift cannot: which docks have incidents, whether the life-safety functions have been tested, and whether the levellers are rated for today's fleet. The lease decides who acts on what they show.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Maintenance and service records for each dock leveller, restraint, scissor table and goods hoist, individually | Whether each leveller, restraint and hoist is maintained, item by item. |
| Free-fall protection test records and landing door interlock test records, with dates | Whether the life-safety functions have actually been tested. |
| Leveller rating plates and the current forklift fleet list with machine and load weights | Whether the levellers are rated for the forklifts now crossing them. |
| Vehicle movements per dock, and the mix of vehicle types and bed heights | The real duty on each dock, and whether the levels suit the vehicles. |
| Incident and near-miss reports at the docks, including any vehicle departure during loading | Which docks have problems, and why. |
| Goods hoist registration, inspection and thorough examination certificates | Whether the goods hoists are registered and examined as required. |
| Loading procedures, including how restraints or chocks are applied and who signals departure | How trailers are held at the dock, and who signals departure. |
| The asset register, to establish which items are recorded at all | Which items are recorded at all. |
| Lease terms allocating maintenance, inspection and replacement of dock equipment between owner and tenant | Who must maintain, inspect and replace the dock equipment. |
| Hazardous materials register entries for the dock structure and cladding | Whether the dock structure or cladding contains asbestos. |
| Any dock safety audit or insurer survey and its outstanding recommendations | What has already been recommended, and what is outstanding. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Dock equipment is misread when the machines are surveyed without the incident record, when repeated repairs are blamed on the wrong part, and when nobody is sure who owns the equipment.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| Survey the equipment first | Start from the incident and near-miss record, dock by dock. Dock equipment faults are mechanical and visible, but which dock has them, and why, is usually about geometry, vehicle mix or management rather than the machine. A site where one dock of eight produces most incidents has a local cause that a general equipment survey will miss. |
| It is just a mechanical fault | A dock leveller that does not stop when its lip loses support, or a goods hoist door that opens with no car behind it, is a life-safety failure. Take it out of use until repaired. |
| The seals keep failing, so replace the cylinder | Two findings are regularly misattributed. Repeated hydraulic repairs on one leveller are usually contamination rather than seals: water and grit entering through a damaged pit or a failed breather destroy each new set of seals within months, so the pit is the fix, not the cylinder. And a leveller that will not sit flat on a trailer bed is more often a levels problem than a lip problem, because the lip was designed for a narrower range of bed heights than the fleet now presents. |
| Nobody maintains it, so nobody can afford to | Where responsibility is split between owner and tenant, the diagnosis has to include the lease. Equipment nobody believes they own shows the same symptoms as equipment nobody can afford to fix, and the remedy is entirely different. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market treats dock equipment and goods hoists as plant or work equipment with duties to maintain and examine it, and each has rules on holding trailers and separating people from vehicles. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Equipment duties | Dock equipment and goods hoists are plant under the work health and safety regulations, which require risk management, maintenance and, for some hoists, registration; goods hoists are registrable plant in several states. | PUWER 1998 requires work equipment to be maintained, inspected and suitable for the use to which it is put, which a leveller underrated for the current fleet falls foul of; BS EN 1398 covers dock levellers. | OSHA requires dock boards and levellers to be strong enough for their loads and secured to prevent displacement; ANSI MH30.1 covers dock leveling devices, and ASME A17.1 dumbwaiters and material lifts. |
| Lifting and examination | Powered mobile plant duties cover the forklifts that use the docks. | LOLER 1998 requires thorough examination of goods hoists, and of dock levellers where they lift loads. | OSHA covers powered industrial truck operation at docks. |
| Vehicles and people | Safe Work Australia and state regulators publish guidance on loading dock and forklift safety; where the dock is a workplace shared between the owner's contractors and the tenant's staff, consultation duties fall on both. | The HSE publishes guidance on loading bay safety and vehicle movement, and its workplace transport guidance covers dock design, restraint and pedestrian separation. | OSHA requires trailers to be chocked or restrained against movement. |

In all three jurisdictions, landlords and tenants should agree in the lease who maintains and inspects dock equipment.

sections.heading: Worked example: one dock of eight with most of the incidents
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 2000s distribution centre has eight docks with hydraulic levellers. Dock 3 has produced most of the near misses in the incident log, including a trailer that pulled away during loading; its leveller's hydraulic seals have been replaced three times in two years, and water stands in its pit after rain.

One dock of eight with most of the incidents has a local cause. The repeated seal failures point to contamination from the wet pit, not to the cylinder, so the pit drainage is the fix. The early departure points to restraint: none is fitted, and chocks are used inconsistently. The free-fall protection on every leveller is tested before anything else.

So the register carries free-fall testing as a check line now, vehicle restraints as a safety line, pit drainage and a hydraulic overhaul at Dock 3 as condition lines, and the lease checked to settle who pays.

thresholds.rule: At least every 6 months for equipment that lifts people; every 12 months for other lifting equipment, unless an examination scheme sets otherwise

source.title: Thorough examination of lifting equipment (INDG422)

pages.title: Ductwork & Air Distribution
pages.question: How does ductwork fail, what are the warning signs, and when is it a fire safety issue?
pages.answer: Ductwork lasts decades, but what is attached to it does not. Torn vapour barriers on chilled ducts sweat and drip; joints leak; dirt accumulates and grows microbes; flexible ducts kink and sag; fit-outs unbalance the system. The serious finding is fire and smoke dampers missing, obstructed, painted shut, never connected or untested: they are life-safety devices on fixed testing regimes, and an untested damper should be treated as non-functional.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about ductwork & air distribution; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Insulated ductwork, grilles, diffusers
