pages.searchTitle: Ductwork and air distribution: fire dampers, condensation, dirty ducts and balance

questions.question: Why are there water stains along the ducts in summer?
questions.answer: Condensation from a torn vapour barrier on chilled ductwork. Repair the insulation and vapour barrier, sealing every joint.

questions.question: How often must fire dampers be tested?
questions.answer: Commonly annually; in the United States, NFPA 80 and 105 require a test one year after installation and then every four years, or six in hospitals.

questions.question: Is an untested fire damper a problem?
questions.answer: Yes. A damper that has not been tested, cannot be accessed, or is obstructed should be treated as non-functional until tested.

questions.question: Why are some rooms short of air after a fit-out?
questions.answer: Lost balance or kinked flexible duct. Rebalance, relocate diffusers to suit the partitions, and keep flex runs short and straight.

questions.question: How long does ductwork last?
questions.answer: Galvanised ductwork 30 to 50 years and more, insulation 20 to 30, sealants and internal lining 15 to 25, and flexible duct 15 to 20.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Ductwork problems show in the ceiling as torn insulation, sagging flex and damper access, in occupied space as dust, draughts and stains, and in the damper and balance records. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| In ceiling voids and risers | Torn or missing insulation; wet insulation; condensation drips; rust on ducts and hangers | Condensation, leakage and wet exhaust |
| In ceiling voids and risers | Flexible ducts sagging, kinked, crushed or disconnected | Balance, flexible duct and noise |
| In ceiling voids and risers | Dust and debris visible inside open ducts and at grilles | Dirt, linings and hazardous materials |
| In ceiling voids and risers | Fire dampers: access panels, fusible links, obstruction, painted blades | Fire and smoke dampers |
| In ceiling voids and risers | Older materials: flexible connectors and lagging of the asbestos era | Dirt, linings and hazardous materials |
| In occupied spaces | Dust streaks around supply diffusers | Dirt, linings and hazardous materials |
| In occupied spaces | Draughts, noise, whistling | Balance, flexible duct and noise |
| In occupied spaces | Hot and cold spots after fit-outs | Balance, flexible duct and noise |
| In occupied spaces | Water stains from condensation on ceilings | Condensation, leakage and wet exhaust |
| In the records | Test and balance reports | Investigation before the scope |
| In the records | Duct cleaning and hygiene inspection reports | Dirt, linings and hazardous materials |
| In the records | Fire damper inspection and test records | Fire and smoke dampers |
| In the records | Fit-out records | Balance, flexible duct and noise |
| In the records | Asbestos register | Dirt, linings and hazardous materials |

sections.heading: Types of ductwork
sections.markdown:
Ductwork carries air between air handling units, fans and the spaces they serve: supply, return, outside air and exhaust. Air distribution includes the grilles, registers and diffusers at each end, the balancing dampers that set airflows, the flexible connections to terminal units, the insulation and vapour barrier on chilled ducts, internal acoustic lining, and the fire and smoke dampers where ducts pass through fire-rated walls and floors.

| Form | Where it is found | Character |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Galvanised sheet steel, rectangular and spiral | Most commercial and institutional buildings | Long-lived; joints and seals age; corrodes in wet or chemical exhaust |
| Stainless steel | Kitchen exhaust, laboratories, wet areas | Durable; welded for grease ducts |
| Fibreglass ductboard | Some commercial and residential systems | Self-insulated; fibres erode; hard to clean |
| Flexible duct | Final connections to diffusers; houses | Kinks, sags and tears; short life |
| Internally lined duct | Acoustic sections near fans | Lining erodes and harbours dirt and microbes |
| Pre-insulated panel duct | Some modern commercial systems | Light; joints and damage |
| Builder's work shafts | Older buildings, risers | Masonry or plaster ducts; leaky and dirty |

Fire and smoke dampers close when heat or a fire alarm signal is detected, to stop fire and smoke travelling through the ductwork. They are life-safety devices with their own inspection and testing regimes, and they are commonly found missing, painted shut, obstructed or never connected to the fire alarm.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Galvanised ductwork lasts thirty to fifty years and more, but its insulation lasts twenty to thirty, its sealants and linings fifteen to twenty-five, and flexible duct fifteen to twenty. Fit-outs and fire damper testing usually decide the work long before the metal wears out.

| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Galvanised ductwork | 30 to 50 years and more | Moisture; corrosive exhaust |
| Duct sealants and gaskets | 15 to 25 years | Temperature; age |
| Flexible duct | 15 to 20 years | Damage; UV in roof spaces |
| External insulation and vapour barrier | 20 to 30 years | Damage; condensation |
| Internal lining | 15 to 25 years | Air velocity; moisture |
| Grilles and diffusers | 20 to 30 years | Fit-out changes |
| Fire dampers | 20 to 30 years with testing | Corrosion; obstruction; fusible link age |

What shortens life: torn vapour barriers on chilled ductwork; corrosive and greasy exhausts; fit-outs that cut, reroute and kink ductwork without rebalancing; poor filtration upstream, which loads ducts with dust; rodents and pests in older systems.

sections.heading: Fire and smoke dampers
sections.markdown:
Dampers corrode, seize, are obstructed by cables or debris, are painted or taped shut, or were never installed or connected. A damper that does not close lets fire and smoke through a fire-rated wall or floor.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fire damper blades painted or obstructed | Poor installation or maintenance. Inspection. | Clear and test the dampers, and fit access panels. |
| No damper test records, or dampers that cannot be reached | Fire dampers of unknown condition. Records and access survey, against the test intervals for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Add access panels, test every damper, and repair or replace failures. |

sections.heading: Condensation, leakage and wet exhaust
sections.markdown:
Supply ducts carrying cold air sweat if their insulation or vapour barrier is torn, compressed or missing. Water wets the insulation, drips onto ceilings, and corrodes the duct and its supports.

Joints and seams leak as sealants age, wasting fan energy and delivering less air than designed. Leaky return ductwork in ceilings draws in dust and fibres.

Exhausts from pools, laundries, kitchens and laboratories carry moisture and chemicals that corrode galvanised ductwork from the inside; corrosion shows first at the lowest points and joints where condensate collects.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Water stains on ceilings along duct runs, in summer | Condensation from torn vapour barrier. Insulation inspection. | Repair the insulation and vapour barrier, sealing every joint. |
| Rust and drips at duct joints near cold plant | Joint leakage and condensation. Leakage test of the section; insulation and vapour barrier inspection. | Seal the joints and reinstate the vapour barrier. |

sections.heading: Dirt, linings and hazardous materials
sections.markdown:
Dust, debris and construction residue accumulate inside ducts, particularly where filtration has been poor. In humid conditions, microbes grow on the dirt. Internal acoustic lining erodes and sheds fibres into the airstream.

Older ductwork can contain asbestos in flexible connectors, gaskets, duct lagging and some insulation.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dust streaks around diffusers | Dirty ductwork or poor filtration. Duct inspection; filter condition. | Fix the filtration, then clean the ductwork to the hygiene standard. |
| Fibres at diffusers | Eroding internal lining or fibreglass ductboard. Inspection. | Replace the lining with faced lining, or move attenuation to dedicated attenuators. |
| Grease in a kitchen extract duct beyond the hood | Fire risk from grease. Deposit thickness against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Clean the full duct to the specification, adding access panels where needed. |

sections.heading: Balance, flexible duct and noise
sections.markdown:
Fit-outs add, remove and relocate diffusers and adjust dampers without rebalancing. Some areas get too much air, others too little, and the system no longer matches its design.

Long, sagging, kinked or crushed flexible duct restricts airflow; it tears and leaks; in roof spaces it degrades with heat.

High air velocities, throttled dampers near outlets and poorly selected diffusers generate noise and dump cold air onto occupants. Fit-outs that move partitions without moving diffusers create draughty and stuffy spots.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Zones short of air after a fit-out | Loss of balance or kinked flex. Airflow measurement. | Rebalance, relocate diffusers, and replace kinked flex with short, straight runs. |
| Noise and draughts at diffusers after a fit-out | Airflow redistributed by the new layout. Airflow at each diffuser against design. | Rebalance the system, and replace kinked or crushed flexible duct. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fire or smoke dampers missing, obstructed, failed or untested; deteriorating asbestos in duct materials | safety · 4 Essential | Rectify now; fire engineer and licensed asbestos removal. |
| Fire damper testing due | deadline · 4 Essential | At the interval the standard sets. |
| Condensation damaging ceilings; disconnected ducts | failure · 3 Important | Repair now. |
| Dirty ductwork, poor balance, torn insulation | condition · 3 Important | Clean, rebalance and repair in the near term. |
| Ductwork, insulation and flex at end of life | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Replace with major plant or fit-out works. |
| No hygiene inspection; fire damper register incomplete | check · 2 Planned | Inspect. |
| Minor dust | nil · 1 Routine | Routine cleaning. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A mechanical services engineer leads, with a ventilation hygiene specialist and a fire damper inspector. The checks below start with the fire damper register, then open the ductwork where stains, dust and complaints point.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Visual inspection | Of a representative sample of ductwork, insulation, vapour barrier, flexible connections and supports, prioritising risers, plant rooms and areas with complaints. |
| Hygiene inspection | By camera and access panels, with dust samples, to AS/NZS 3666, BESA TR/19 or NADCA ACR practice, to decide whether cleaning is needed. |
| Airflow measurement | At a sample of diffusers and grilles against design, and a review of the latest test and balance report. |
| Fire and smoke damper survey | Location against every fire-rated wall and floor the ductwork passes, access panel present, blade and spring condition, fusible link, release and drop test, connection to the fire alarm where required. |
| Leakage testing | Of sections to DW/143 or SMACNA methods where energy use or airflow shortfalls warrant. |
| Asbestos sampling | Of flexible connectors, gaskets, lagging and older insulation. |
| Noise survey | Where complaints exist. |

The report should give a fire damper register with location, type, access and test result for every damper; hygiene condition; airflow and balance findings; insulation condition; hazardous materials; and prioritised works.

sections.heading: Testing, cleaning, sealing or rebalancing
sections.markdown:
Fire and smoke dampers come first, as life-safety devices. After that, the work fixes the cause before the symptom: filtration before cleaning, vapour barriers before ceilings, and rebalancing after every fit-out.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fire and smoke dampers | Install missing dampers, replace failed or corroded units, remove obstructions and paint, fit access panels, connect motorised dampers to the alarm, and test and register every damper. | Wherever dampers are missing, failed, obstructed or untested. |
| Cleaning | By brushing, air washing and vacuum to the hygiene standard; cleaning is pointless without fixing the filtration or moisture problem that dirtied the ducts. | Where ductwork is dirty, after fixing the cause. |
| Lining replacement | Replace eroding internal lining with faced or perforated-metal-faced lining, or move attenuation to dedicated attenuators. | Where internal linings erode. |
| Insulation and vapour barrier repair | Repair the insulation and vapour barrier on chilled ductwork, sealing every joint. | Where condensation stains ceilings. |
| Flexible duct replacement | Short, straight, supported runs. | Where flex sags, kinks or disconnects. |
| Sealing | Reseal joints; aerosol internal sealing for inaccessible sections. | Where ducts leak. |
| Rebalancing | Rebalance, with diffusers relocated to suit the partitions. | After fit-outs. |
| Corrosion | Replace corroded wet-exhaust sections in stainless steel with drainage at low points. | Where wet exhaust ductwork corrodes. |
| Asbestos removal | Removal by licensed contractors. | Where connectors or lagging contain asbestos. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Inspection and testing are lump sums with rates per damper tested. Fire damper rectification is priced per damper, with access panels and ceiling and wall making good, which can exceed the damper cost. Cleaning is priced by length or per system. Insulation repair is by length. Rebalancing is per floor or per system. Replacement of ductwork is usually carried in a fit-out or major plant project.

Fire damper works and testing are code compliance and recur; cleaning and repairs are repairs and maintenance; replacement is lifecycle; asbestos removal is code compliance.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a look into the ceiling cannot: whether every fire damper has been tested, whether the system was rebalanced after fit-outs, and whether asbestos is present. Ask for the damper register first.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Fire and smoke damper register with test records and dates | Whether every fire and smoke damper has been tested, and when. |
| Annual essential safety measures or fire safety statements covering dampers | Whether dampers were certified at the last annual review. |
| Test and balance reports, original and after recent fit-outs | Whether the system was rebalanced after fit-outs. |
| Duct hygiene inspection and cleaning records | Whether ductwork has been inspected or cleaned. |
| Asbestos register | Whether connectors or lagging contain asbestos. |
| Mechanical as-built drawings showing ductwork and damper locations | Where the ducts and dampers are. |
| Fit-out records showing changes to ductwork | What fit-outs changed. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Ductwork is misread when an untested fire damper is assumed to close in a fire, and when dirty ducts are cleaned without fixing what made them dirty.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| An untested damper will close | Fire and smoke dampers are life-safety devices. A damper that has not been tested, cannot be accessed, or is obstructed should be treated as non-functional until tested. |
| Clean the ducts and the dust goes | Cleaning is pointless without fixing the filtration or moisture problem that dirtied the ductwork in the first place. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets standards for ductwork, for fire and smoke dampers and their testing, and for duct hygiene. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Ductwork | AS 4254.1 and 4254.2 cover flexible and rigid ductwork. | BESA DW/144 specifies sheet metal ductwork. | SMACNA standards for ductwork; NFPA 90A for air conditioning systems. |
| Fire and smoke dampers | AS 1668.1 covers fire and smoke control in ductwork; fire dampers are inspected and tested under AS 1851 as essential safety measures. | Fire dampers follow BS EN 15650 and are tested at least annually under BS 9999 guidance; Approved Document B applies. | NFPA 80 and NFPA 105 require fire and smoke dampers to be tested one year after installation and then every four years (six in hospitals). |
| Hygiene and cleaning | AS/NZS 3666 covers hygiene. | BESA TR/19 sets ductwork hygiene. | NADCA ACR for duct cleaning. |

Fire damper testing is commonly an annual certification item in all three countries.

sections.heading: Worked example: ceiling stains after a fit-out
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. An office floor was refitted last year. Since then, water stains have appeared on ceilings along the chilled supply ducts each summer, two new meeting rooms are short of air, and the fire damper register has not been updated for the fit-out.

Stains along chilled duct runs in summer point to condensation from a vapour barrier torn during the works. Rooms short of air after a fit-out point to lost balance or kinked flexible duct. Dampers moved or added in the fit-out are untested, and so non-functional until tested.

So the register carries testing every damper on the floor as a safety line now, insulation and vapour barrier repair as a condition line, and rebalancing, with the flexible ducts replaced in short, straight runs.

thresholds.rule: Deposits of no more than 200 microns

source.title: Ventilation hygiene standards (TR19)

thresholds.rule: One year after construction, then every 6 years

source.title: UFM 3-601-02 Fire protection systems inspection, testing, and maintenance (13 March 2026)

pages.title: Electric Vehicle (EV) Charging
pages.question: How does EV charging fail in existing buildings, and what limits how many chargers a building can take?
pages.answer: EV charging in existing buildings is mostly a capacity problem. A few uncontrolled chargers can overload a car park board or the main supply, so load management or a supply upgrade comes first. Faults come from shared circuits, missing protection and poor terminations; extension-lead charging is a fire and shock risk. Unmetered charging on common supply causes disputes, and proprietary software can strand chargers. Enclosed car parks raise fire questions regulators are still settling.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about electric vehicle (ev) charging; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.

pages.searchTitle: EV charging in existing buildings: capacity, safety and what fails

questions.question: Can our building's supply handle EV chargers?
questions.answer: It depends on measured maximum demand against the supply and the board ratings. A few uncontrolled chargers can overload a car park board; load management shares capacity and often avoids an upgrade.

questions.question: Why do our chargers trip when several cars charge?
questions.answer: Capacity is exceeded or there is no load management. Load measurement and maximum demand data confirm it.

questions.question: Is charging from a normal power outlet safe?
questions.answer: Charging from general-purpose outlets with extension leads is a fire and shock risk. Stop the practice and provide approved charging after a capacity check.

questions.question: How long do EV chargers last?
questions.answer: AC chargers and load management systems typically last 8 to 12 years; the cabling and distribution behind them 25 to 40 years. Software support, which depends on the vendor, often ends a charger's useful life first.

questions.question: Who pays for charging in an apartment building?
questions.answer: Unmetered charging on a common supply causes disputes. Meter each charger or user, and set billing and cost sharing in the strata by-laws.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Charging problems show in the car park, at the switchboard, and in disputes over who pays. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On site | Chargers on circuits shared with other loads; distribution boards with no spare capacity | Capacity and load management |
| On site | Damaged cables and connectors; chargers out of service | Installation, damage and fire safety |
| On site | Extension leads running from outlets to vehicles in car parks, an unsafe workaround where chargers are not available | Installation, damage and fire safety |
| On site | Chargers without bollards or wheel stops in vehicle paths | Installation, damage and fire safety |
| On site | Chargers located near exits or fire stairs in enclosed car parks | Installation, damage and fire safety |
| In the records | Electrical capacity study and maximum demand data | Capacity and load management |
| In the records | Charger installation certificates and test results | Installation, damage and fire safety |
| In the records | Load management settings | Capacity and load management |
| In the records | Strata by-laws or agreements for EV charging | Software, billing and fairness |
| In the records | Charger fault and downtime logs | Software, billing and fairness |

sections.heading: Types of charger
sections.markdown:
Electric vehicle charging infrastructure supplies power to vehicles parked at a building: wall-mounted and pedestal AC chargers for overnight and workplace charging, DC fast chargers for rapid top-ups, the cabling and distribution boards that feed them, load management systems that share limited supply between chargers, and the software, payment and billing systems that run them. It is increasingly expected by tenants and residents and required for new buildings in some places, and retrofitting it into existing buildings is mostly an electrical capacity and cost-allocation problem.

| Type | Where it is found | Character |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Single-phase AC wall chargers | Houses, apartment car spaces, workplaces | Slow overnight charging; modest load each |
| Three-phase AC chargers | Workplaces, apartments, commercial car parks | Faster; higher load; needs three-phase supply |
| DC fast chargers | Retail, service stations, fleet depots | High power; large supply upgrades; cooling |
| Load-managed networks | Apartment and office car parks | Share available capacity among many chargers |
| Shared-bay or common chargers | Apartments without individual circuits | Billing and booking systems |

In apartment buildings, the questions are as much legal as technical: who owns the car spaces and the cabling routes, how capacity is shared, who pays for the backbone, and how each user is billed. Strata and condominium law in several jurisdictions has been changed recently to make approval easier.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Charging equipment is short-lived against the building around it. Chargers and load management last around a decade, the cabling and distribution behind them last decades, and software support often decides when a charger becomes obsolete.

| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AC chargers | 8 to 12 years | Use; weather; software support |
| DC fast chargers | 8 to 12 years; modules sooner | Heat; use; manufacturer support |
| Cabling and distribution | 25 to 40 years | Installation quality; loading |
| Load management systems | 8 to 12 years | Software and communications support |
| Charger software and back-end services | Depends on vendor | Protocol support; vendor viability |

What shortens it: weather and vandalism at external and public chargers, damaging cables and connectors; vendor failure: networked chargers can be stranded if the operator or software platform disappears, unless they use open protocols; heat in enclosed car parks and around high-power DC chargers; poor installation, which causes nuisance tripping and earth faults.

sections.heading: Capacity and load management
sections.markdown:
Each charger is a large continuous load. A few uncontrolled chargers can exceed the spare capacity of a car park distribution board or the building's main supply. Without load management or a supply upgrade, adding chargers causes tripping, overheating and, at worst, overloaded cables. Capacity, not chargers, is usually the limiting factor.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Chargers trip when several vehicles charge | Capacity exceeded or no load management. Load measurement; maximum demand. | Measure maximum demand; add load management before more chargers, or upgrade the supply. |
| Car park with no dedicated distribution board or spare capacity for charging | Not ready for charging demand. Boards and capacity against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Plan board and supply upgrades before chargers are requested. |

sections.heading: Installation, damage and fire safety
sections.markdown:
Chargers need dedicated circuits, correct earthing and protection against specific faults such as loss of the supply neutral and DC fault currents. Chargers installed on shared circuits, without the required protection, or with poor terminations overheat, trip and create shock risks.

Cables run over, connectors dropped and damaged, and chargers struck by vehicles cause faults and hazards.

Electric vehicle fires are not more frequent than petrol vehicle fires on current evidence, but they burn differently, can reignite and are harder to extinguish. In enclosed and basement car parks, location of chargers, detection, ventilation and fire brigade access are under active review by regulators.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Charger warm at terminals, faults recorded | Poor terminations or undersized cabling. Thermography; inspection. | Isolate the charger; remake the terminations and check the cabling and protection. |
| Residents charging from general outlets with extension leads | Lack of approved charging. Observation. | Stop the practice now, and provide approved charging after a capacity check. |
| Chargers mounted where vehicles strike them, or blocking escape routes | Damage and egress risk. Layout review; impact protection; escape route widths. | Relocate or protect the chargers with bollards or wheel stops. |

sections.heading: Software, billing and fairness
sections.markdown:
Networked chargers depend on back-end software for access, billing and load management. Proprietary systems can strand chargers if the vendor fails or ends support; open protocols allow switching providers.

In shared buildings, chargers on common supply without metering shift costs to other owners; disputes follow. Sub-metering and billing systems solve this but must meet legal metrology rules where users are charged.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Chargers offline and unusable | Back-end or communications failure. Network status; vendor. | Check the network and the vendor contract; prefer open-protocol chargers at replacement. |
| Disputes over electricity costs | Unmetered charging on common supply. Metering arrangement. | Meter each charger or user, and set billing in the by-laws or lease. |
| No metering of individual charging circuits | Costs cannot be allocated. Metering arrangement against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Fit sub-meters or networked chargers that record use per user. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Overloaded circuits or boards; unsafe installations; extension-lead charging | safety · 4 Essential | Isolate and rectify now. |
| Chargers out of service | failure · 2 Planned | Repair. |
| New-building or approval requirements for EV provision | deadline · 4 Essential | As required. |
| Unmetered charging; poor load management; ageing chargers | condition · 2 Planned | Improve in the near term. |
| Chargers at end of life | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Replace. |
| No capacity study; tenant or resident demand rising | check · 2 Planned | Assess capacity. |
| Working, metered, managed | nil · 1 Routine | Routine. |

Most EV findings in existing buildings are capacity and fairness issues rather than defects; the safety grade is reserved for overloaded circuits, missing protection and informal charging.

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
An electrical engineer leads, with an EV infrastructure specialist and, for strata buildings, advice on by-laws and cost sharing. The checks below establish how much capacity is left, how the existing chargers were installed, and how charging is shared and paid for.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Capacity study | Measured maximum demand against supply and car park board ratings, and the number of chargers that can be supported with and without load management. |
| Installation inspection | Of existing chargers: circuits, protection, earthing, terminations and test results. |
| Demand forecast | Likely uptake among residents, tenants or fleet, and charger types needed. |
| Layout and fire review | Charger locations, vehicle protection, ventilation, detection and brigade access in enclosed car parks. |
| Metering and billing review | How energy is measured and charged. |
| Software review | Protocols, vendor support and data access. |

The report should give a staged infrastructure plan from current capacity to future demand, safety rectification, and cost allocation options.

sections.heading: Building the charging network
sections.markdown:
The order matters more than the charger. Establish capacity first, then the backbone and load management that let chargers be added cheaply, then the chargers, metering and rules. Adding chargers one at a time without a capacity check is how car parks end up overloaded.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Backbone infrastructure | A dedicated distribution board and cable tray serving the car park, sized for future chargers, so individual chargers can be added cheaply later. | When more than a few chargers are expected, before adding them one by one. |
| Load management | Sharing available capacity dynamically among chargers. | Where capacity is limited; it often avoids a supply upgrade. |
| Supply upgrade | A larger supply, coordinated with the network. | Where demand exceeds what load management can handle. |
| Rectification of unsafe installations | Dedicated circuits, correct protection and earthing, new terminations. | At once, wherever circuits are shared, protection is wrong or terminations overheat. |
| Metering and billing | Metering and billing for each charger or user. | Wherever charging runs on a common supply. |
| Open-protocol chargers | Chargers that do not tie the building to one operator. | At every new installation or replacement. |
| Vehicle protection | Bollards and wheel stops at chargers. | Wherever chargers stand in vehicle paths. |
| Fire safety measures | Location away from exits, and reviews of detection and ventilation. | In enclosed car parks, as guidance requires. |
| Strata by-laws | By-laws setting standards, approval processes and cost sharing. | In apartment buildings, before owners install chargers. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Capacity studies are lump sums. Backbone infrastructure is a lump sum per car park level; individual chargers are priced per charger with connection to the backbone. Load management is a lump sum plus subscription. Supply upgrades are large lump sums with network contributions and long lead times. Software, billing and maintenance are recurring.

Safety rectification is immediate; new-building requirements are code compliance; backbone and chargers are improvements often funded by users or tenants; replacement is lifecycle.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a look at the car park cannot: how much capacity is left, how the chargers were installed, and who pays for the electricity. Ask for them before adding chargers, so the next ones are planned rather than squeezed in.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Electrical capacity study and maximum demand data | How many chargers the supply can take, with or without load management. |
| Charger installation certificates and test results | Whether each charger was installed and tested to the standard. |
| Load management system details and settings | How capacity is shared, and whether the settings match the supply. |
| Metering and billing arrangements | Who pays for the electricity each charger uses. |
| Strata by-laws or lease clauses on EV charging | What owners or tenants may install, and how costs are shared. |
| Charger fault and downtime records | How reliable the chargers are, and whether faults repeat. |
| Vendor and software contracts | Whether the chargers are tied to one operator, and for how long. |
| Records of any EV-related incidents or fire brigade advice for the car park | What has happened in the car park, and what the fire brigade has advised. |
| Network operator correspondence on supply upgrades | Whether a supply upgrade is possible, and on what terms. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
EV charging problems are easily read as faulty chargers, when the cause sits in the building's supply or in how charging is shared and paid for.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| The chargers keep tripping, so they are faulty | A capacity problem shows when many vehicles charge at once (evenings in apartments, mornings at workplaces); an installation problem shows at one charger regardless of how many are in use. |
| A general outlet will do for charging | Charging from general-purpose outlets with extension leads, and chargers added without a capacity check, are fire and shock risks. Stop the practice and assess capacity before adding more chargers. |
| More chargers need a bigger supply | Load management shares available capacity among chargers and often avoids a supply upgrade. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Charging installations follow electrical rules in every market, but the requirements to provide charging differ widely. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out the installation standards, the rules on provision, and those on apartments and public charging.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Installation | Installations follow AS/NZS 3000 and the charging equipment standards. | BS 7671 Section 722 sets installation requirements, including protection against loss of the supply neutral; the IET Code of Practice guides installation. | NFPA 70 Article 625 governs EV charging installations. |
| Provision in buildings | Some planning schemes require EV-ready car parks; the Australian Building Codes Board has published advice on EV charging in buildings. | Approved Document S requires charge points or cable routes in new and majorly renovated residential and non-residential buildings with parking. | Several states and cities require EV-ready parking in new buildings. |
| Apartments | New South Wales and other states have amended strata law to ease approval of charging in apartment buildings. | Leaseholders and tenants generally need the freeholder's or landlord's consent under the lease. In October 2026 the government opened a consultation for England on an 'ability to charge', under which consent could not be unreasonably refused. | Several states have 'right to charge' laws limiting how condominium and homeowner associations may restrict chargers; California's bars associations from prohibiting or unreasonably restricting a charger in an owner's unit or designated parking space. |
| Equipment and public charging | Charging equipment follows Australian adoptions of IEC 61851 and IEC 62196, the international standards for charging systems and connectors. | Smart charge point regulations apply. | Federal funding programmes set standards for public chargers; accessibility guidance applies to accessible charging spaces. |

sections.heading: Worked example: an apartment car park with tripping chargers
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 2000s apartment building has eight owner-installed chargers in its basement car park, all on the common supply. Chargers trip most weekday evenings, two residents charge from general outlets with extension leads, and owners dispute the electricity costs.

The extension leads are the first line: a safety finding, stopped now. The evening trips, with many vehicles charging at once, point to capacity rather than faulty chargers: a capacity study measures maximum demand, and load management may avoid a supply upgrade. The cost dispute comes from unmetered charging on the common supply.

So the register carries a safety line now, a capacity study as a check line, and backbone infrastructure, load management and metering as condition lines once the study is in, with by-laws setting the rules for future chargers.

thresholds.measure: EV charging readiness in car parks
thresholds.rule: Dedicated EV boards on each storey, sized for future 7 kW (32 A) chargers in 10 per cent of spaces (Class 5 and 6) or 20 per cent (Class 3, 7b, 8 and 9)

thresholds.rule: At least 36 mm of DIN rail per circuit

pages.title: Electrical & Communications Risers
pages.question: How do service risers fail, and why are they a fire safety and capacity issue?
pages.answer: Risers fail at the floors and in their capacity. Every cable and pipe added breaks the fire stopping unless reinstated, so older risers often let fire and smoke reach every floor. Trays fill with abandoned cables, leaving no room for new services and adding fire load; enclosed risers overheat; water reaches electrical equipment; riser cupboards become storerooms. Open riser penetrations are a safety finding; exhausted capacity limits tenants and electrification.

questions.question: Why is there light coming through the riser floor?
questions.answer: The fire stopping is missing. Every open penetration lets fire and smoke reach the floor above; reinstate it with a tested system.

questions.question: Our riser is full: do we need a new one?
questions.answer: Not necessarily. Removing abandoned cable often frees enough space, and is far cheaper than a new riser.

questions.question: Who should fire stop after a new cable is installed?
questions.answer: The contractor who made the penetration, under a permit that requires a tested seal and a photograph.

questions.question: Can riser cupboards be used for storage?
questions.answer: No. Storage in risers is a safety finding; lock them, and manage the keys.

questions.question: How long does fire stopping last?
questions.answer: Until it is next disturbed, which in a busy riser can be a matter of months.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Riser problems show on each floor as open penetrations, overfull trays, storage, heat, water and missing labels, and in drawings, fire stopping records and capacity schedules. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On a riser walk, every floor | Open or poorly sealed slab penetrations; foam around cables | Fire stopping |
| On a riser walk, every floor | Overfull trays; cables hanging free; abandoned cables | Congestion and capacity |
| On a riser walk, every floor | Storage and rubbish in riser cupboards | Access, labelling and safe isolation |
| On a riser walk, every floor | Warm air on opening the door; equipment fans running hard | Heat and water |
| On a riser walk, every floor | Water staining, drips or corrosion | Heat and water |
| On a riser walk, every floor | Unlabelled boards and cables; doors unlocked or without fire rating labels | Access, labelling and safe isolation |
| In the records | Riser drawings and capacity schedules | Congestion and capacity |
| In the records | Fire stopping records with photographs | Fire stopping |
| In the records | Cabling records and carrier agreements | Congestion and capacity |
| In the records | Maximum demand data per riser | Congestion and capacity |
| In the records | Riser doors without fire rating labels or closers | Fire stopping |
| In the records | Carrier equipment installed without approval or records | Access, labelling and safe isolation |

sections.heading: What the space does and what it contains
sections.markdown:
Risers are the vertical shafts and cupboards that carry services between floors: electrical risers with sub-mains, busducts and distribution boards; communications risers with backbone cabling, fibre and carrier equipment; and hydraulic and mechanical shafts with pipes and ducts. Functionally a riser must give services a protected route, give maintenance staff safe access, keep fire and smoke from spreading between floors, stay cool and dry, and have room for future services. Risers are where capacity for new tenants, electrification and EV charging is decided, and where fire separation between floors most often breaks down.

| Element group | Typical provision | What matters for the space |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Access doors | Fire-rated doors or panels on each floor | Rating, locking, signage |
| Floor fire stopping | Fire-stopped slab penetrations at every floor | Integrity after every new cable |
| Cable support | Trays, ladders, conduits, busducts | Capacity, segregation, support |
| Distribution equipment | Floor distribution boards, comms racks, carrier equipment | Clearance, heat, labelling |
| Ventilation | Natural or mechanical cooling | Heat build-up from equipment |
| Lighting and power | Lighting and outlets for maintenance | Safe work |
| Spare capacity | Space on trays and in the shaft | Future services |

Because risers are behind locked doors, their condition is often unknown to owners and only discovered when a fire engineer or new tenant opens them.

sections.heading: How long it stays fit for purpose
sections.markdown:
A riser's structure lasts the life of the building and its cable trays thirty to fifty years, while communications cabling lasts fifteen to twenty-five and door hardware ten to twenty. Its fire stopping lasts only until the next contractor disturbs it, and its spare capacity until the next tenancy uses it up.

| Component or quality | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Riser structure and doors | Life of the building; door hardware 10 to 20 years | Use; alterations |
| Fire stopping | Until next disturbed | Every new cable or pipe |
| Cable trays and support | 30 to 50 years | Overloading |
| Communications cabling | 15 to 25 years | Technology |
| Spare capacity | Consumed by each tenancy and upgrade | Demand growth |

What shortens fitness for purpose: abandoned cables left in place when tenants and carriers change; new services squeezed in without fire stopping or support; storage in riser cupboards; demand growth from electrification, data and EV charging.

Risers are long-lived structurally; their usefulness is consumed by each tenancy, carrier and upgrade that adds services without removing old ones.

sections.heading: Fire stopping
sections.markdown:
Every cable or pipe added through a riser floor breaks the fire stopping unless it is reinstated with a tested system. Over years, riser floors become a series of holes packed with foam, mineral wool or nothing, letting fire and smoke travel between all floors. This is one of the most common serious fire defects in existing buildings.

A riser joins every floor of the building, so its fire stopping is what keeps a fire on one floor from travelling up the shaft. The damage accumulates: each contractor who adds a cable breaks a little of the seal and moves on, which is why risers are surveyed floor by floor, from both sides of each slab.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Light visible through slab penetrations | Fire stopping missing. Inspection from both sides. | Reinstate the fire stopping with a tested system, and record it with photographs. |
| A riser door without a closer or a rating label | A fire door that no longer protects the riser. The door stays open when released, or has been replaced. Gaps are measured against the door’s evidence and the limits for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Repair it, or replace it as a self-closing fire door. |

sections.heading: Congestion and capacity
sections.markdown:
Cable trays fill with abandoned cables that nobody dares remove, leaving no space for new services, overloading supports, adding fire load and smoke from burning insulation, and making tracing faults slow.

Risers without spare space or electrical capacity limit what tenants and new uses can do; adding a new riser later is expensive.

A riser that looks full may not be. Trays packed with abandoned cable can hide space for years of new services, and removing that cable is far cheaper than building a new riser, so the survey has to tell missing capacity from wasted capacity.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Trays bowed or collapsed | Overloading with cables. Inspection. | Remove abandoned cables, and add trays and supports. |
| New tenant cannot connect | Space or capacity exhausted. Capacity survey. | Survey capacity; remove abandoned cables first, then add risers, busducts or backbone if still needed. |
| Carrier equipment no one has a record of | Equipment installed without approval or records. No agreement or drawing matches the equipment. | Identify the owner, regularise or remove it, and record it in the riser register. |

sections.heading: Heat and water
sections.markdown:
Risers are closed cupboards stacked one above another, so heat from the equipment inside builds up, and water from any pipe or roof penetration above finds its way down onto the boards.

Distribution boards, busducts and comms equipment in enclosed risers generate heat; without ventilation, temperatures rise, shortening equipment life and causing faults.

Risers next to plumbing shafts and wet areas, or below roof penetrations, get water on electrical and communications equipment.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Equipment faults on hot days | Riser overheating. Temperature logging. | Log temperatures, and add ventilation or cooling. |
| Corrosion on boards | Water ingress. Leak tracing. | Trace the leak; add drip trays and upstands, or relocate the pipes. |

sections.heading: Access, labelling and safe isolation
sections.markdown:
When boards and cables in risers are unlabelled or labels are out of date after fit-outs, electricians cannot be sure what they are isolating. Work on live circuits and accidental outages to other tenants follow.

Riser doors left unlocked, used as cleaners' cupboards or storage, or locked with keys no one can find; equipment unlabelled so isolations are unsafe.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A riser cupboard used for cleaning gear or storage | Unmanaged access. Mops, chemicals or boxes stand against the boards. | Clear it, lock it, and manage the keys. |
| Breakers labelled for tenants who left years ago | Labels not updated after fit-outs. Circuits traced do not match the schedule. | Trace and relabel every circuit, and keep a riser register updated after every job. |
| Cables, trays or stored items in the space in front of a board | Working space lost. The clear space in front of each board measured against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Clear the working space, reroute trays that intrude, and keep it marked and free of storage. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unsealed riser floors; storage in risers; water on electrical equipment | safety · 4 Essential | Rectify now. |
| Riser equipment failed from heat or water | failure · 4 Essential | Repair now. |
| Fire stopping certification due with annual statements | deadline · 4 Essential | At the prescribed interval. |
| Congestion; overheating; poor labelling | condition · 3 Important | Improve in the near term. |
| Capacity exhausted for planned uses | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Plan new capacity. |
| No capacity or fire stopping records | check · 2 Planned | Survey. |
| Normal | nil · 1 Routine | Routine. |

A single riser floor without fire stopping can compromise compartmentation for the whole building, so riser findings should be graded on what they connect, not how small the gap looks.

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
An electrical and communications engineer leads, with a passive fire specialist for penetrations and the carriers for their equipment. The checks below walk the riser on every floor, looking at each slab penetration from both sides, then compare the capacity left with the loads planned for the building.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Riser walk on every floor | Penetrations through slabs and walls, fire stopping type and condition, doors and their ratings and locks, trays and supports, distribution equipment, labelling, housekeeping, water and temperature, with photographs; the working space in front of each board and the riser door gaps measured against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). |
| Capacity survey | Free space on trays and in the shaft, electrical capacity of submains and busducts against maximum demand, and fibre and copper backbone capacity. |
| Abandoned cable identification | By tracing and carrier records, to free space and reduce fire load. |
| Temperature logging | In risers holding active equipment through a hot period. |
| Records review | Riser drawings, fire stopping records and carrier agreements. |

The report should list fire stopping defects floor by floor, capacity remaining for planned uses, and works needed.

sections.heading: Fire stopping, clearing and adding capacity
sections.markdown:
Unsealed riser floors, storage in risers and water on electrical equipment come first. After that, removing abandoned cable usually frees more space than expected, and permits and a riser register stop the next contractor undoing the work.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fire stopping | Tested systems at every floor and wall penetration, recorded with photographs and product data. | Wherever penetrations are open, or packed with untested materials. |
| Abandoned cable removal | Remove abandoned cable, which frees space, reduces fire load and makes faults easier to trace. | Wherever trays hold cable no longer in use. |
| Cable management | New or additional trays and supports, segregation of power and data, and labelling of every cable and board. | Where trays are overloaded, or power and data are mixed. |
| Ventilation or cooling | Ventilation or cooling where equipment heat builds up. | Where risers overheat. |
| Water protection | Drip trays, upstands and relocation of pipes away from electrical equipment. | Wherever water can reach electrical equipment. |
| Access control and housekeeping | Locked doors with managed keys and no storage. | Wherever risers are unlocked or used for storage. |
| Penetration permits | Permits, so every new service is fire stopped and recorded. | In every building with shared risers. |
| New capacity | Additional risers, busducts or backbone where demand will exceed what exists. | Where demand will exceed what exists, once wasted space is recovered. |
| Riser register | A floor-by-floor record of services, capacity and fire stopping, updated after every job. | In every building with shared risers. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown: Fire stopping is priced per penetration or per riser floor, and a whole-building remediation can be substantial in older buildings. Cable removal is priced per riser. Trays by length. Cooling per riser. New risers are major projects involving slab penetrations on every floor, so preserving and recovering capacity in existing risers is usually far cheaper. Fire stopping is code compliance; capacity is lifecycle or tied to the project needing it.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a walk up the riser cannot: what each floor's fire stopping is and when it was last disturbed, how much capacity is left, and what new loads are coming. Ask for them before any tenant connects a new service.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Riser drawings and capacity schedules | What each riser holds, and how much capacity is left. |
| Fire stopping records with photographs and products | Whether each penetration was sealed with a tested system. |
| Cabling records and carrier agreements | Which cables belong to whom, and which carriers have rights. |
| Maximum demand data by riser | How close each riser is to its electrical limit. |
| Riser temperature records | Whether the risers overheat. |
| Penetration permit records | Whether new penetrations are controlled. |
| Fire safety certification noting riser fire stopping | Whether riser fire stopping was certified. |
| Records of electrical and communications works by tenants and carriers, with approvals | What tenants and carriers have added, and whether it was approved. |
| Planned loads such as EV charging and electrification that will use riser capacity | What new loads the risers will have to carry. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Risers are misread when an open penetration is treated as untidy rather than unsafe, when it is blamed on a single contractor, and when a full tray is taken for a full riser.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| It is just untidy | Open penetrations in riser floors let fire and smoke reach every floor. Treat them as safety findings, and reinstate fire stopping with tested systems. |
| Someone made a mistake | Fire stopping failures are almost always cumulative: each contractor breaks a little and nobody reinstates it. |
| The riser is full | Distinguish missing capacity (no space or electrical headroom) from wasted capacity (abandoned cables, poorly organised trays); the second is far cheaper to fix. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets rules for fire stopping service penetrations, for electrical and communications cabling, and for who may work on them. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Fire stopping, cabling and installation | The National Construction Code requires service penetrations through fire-rated floors and walls to be protected, with AS 4072.1 setting penetration systems and AS 1530.4 testing; fire stopping is an essential safety measure in annual certification; communications cabling must be done by registered cablers; AS/NZS 3000 governs electrical installations in risers. | Approved Document B requires fire stopping of penetrations through compartment floors and walls; BS 7671 governs electrical installations; the Building Safety Act 2022 adds golden thread information duties for higher-risk buildings, including records of fire stopping. | The International Building Code and NFPA 101 require fire-rated shafts and tested firestop systems; NFPA 70 governs electrical installations and requires removal of accessible abandoned communications cables in many cases; local fire marshals inspect firestopping. |

sections.heading: Worked example: a riser after twenty years of tenants
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 2000s office's communications riser has been worked on by a dozen tenants and three carriers. On most floors light shows through gaps around newer cables, some packed with foam; the trays are bowed and packed with cable, much of it from tenants long gone; and a new tenant has been told there is no room to connect.

Open penetrations let fire and smoke reach every floor, and are safety findings; the foam points to successive contractors who never reinstated a tested seal. The full trays may be wasted rather than missing capacity, since abandoned cable is far cheaper to remove than a new riser is to build.

So the register carries fire stopping on every floor as a safety line now, abandoned cable removal and new trays as a condition line, a capacity survey before any new riser, and penetration permits and a riser register so it does not happen again.

pages.title: Emergency Lighting
pages.question: How does emergency lighting fail, how do you test it, and when is it a life-safety defect?
pages.answer: Emergency lighting fails at the battery: fittings that light on a quick test go dark before the rated duration. Fit-outs cause the other failures: fittings rewired to the wrong circuit so they stay dark when local lights fail, new corridors without coverage, exit signs pointing to doors that no longer lead out. Self-test systems help only if someone reads their reports. It is a life-safety system, and its test records establish its position.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about emergency lighting; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
