questions.question: How often should emergency lighting be tested?
questions.answer: Monthly short tests and an annual full-duration test in the United Kingdom and the United States; six-monthly discharge tests for at least the rated duration in Australia.

questions.question: Why do emergency lights pass short tests but fail full ones?
questions.answer: Their batteries have lost capacity. Replace all the batteries of an age together, not fitting by fitting.

questions.question: Do fit-outs affect emergency lighting?
questions.answer: Often. New partitions leave dark sections of escape routes, and fittings get wired to the wrong circuits; check coverage after every fit-out.

questions.question: Is self-testing emergency lighting worth it?
questions.answer: Yes, if someone reads the reports. Monitoring that shows no faults for years may itself have stopped testing.

questions.question: How long do emergency lighting batteries last?
questions.answer: Nickel-cadmium and nickel-metal hydride 4 to 6 years, and lithium iron phosphate 8 to 10.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Emergency lighting problems show on escape routes as unlit indicators, hidden or missing fittings and wrong signs, in the battery room, and in the test logbook. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On site | Charge indicators off on fittings; exit signs unlit or dim | Batteries, chargers and central systems |
| On site | Fittings damaged, missing, painted over or hidden by fit-out | Wiring, coverage and exit signs |
| On site | Escape routes, stairs, changes of direction and final exits without fittings | Wiring, coverage and exit signs |
| On site | Exit signs pointing the wrong way, or to doors now locked or removed | Wiring, coverage and exit signs |
| On site | Test labels and dates on fittings; key switches for testing | Testing and monitoring |
| On site | Central battery room: temperature, battery condition, alarms | Batteries, chargers and central systems |
| In the records | Test logbook with each fitting, its result and date | Investigation before the scope |
| In the records | Annual fire safety statement or essential safety measures report | Standards by country |
| In the records | Monitoring system reports and fault lists | Testing and monitoring |
| In the records | Battery replacement records | Batteries, chargers and central systems |
| In the records | Emergency lighting layout drawings against the current fit-out | Wiring, coverage and exit signs |

sections.heading: Types of emergency lighting
sections.markdown:
Emergency lighting lights the way out when normal lighting fails. It has three jobs: escape route lighting along corridors, stairs and to final exits; open-area (anti-panic) lighting in large rooms so people can reach a route; and high-risk task lighting where a process must be shut down safely. Exit signs, lit at all times or photoluminescent, show the direction to exits. It is a life-safety system with prescribed design, testing and record-keeping in all three jurisdictions.

| Type | Where it is found | Character |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Self-contained luminaires and exit signs | Most buildings | Battery, charger and lamp in each fitting; every fitting must be tested |
| Central battery systems | Larger buildings, hospitals, theatres, some towers | Batteries and inverter in one room; sub-circuit monitoring; wiring must survive fire |
| Monitored or addressable systems | Larger buildings from the 2000s | Fittings test themselves on schedule and report faults to a panel or software |
| Maintained fittings | Exit signs; theatres, cinemas, public spaces | Lit at all times, and stay lit in a failure |
| Non-maintained fittings | Most escape lighting | Off normally, on when the local supply fails |
| Photoluminescent signs and markings | Stairs and exit signs where permitted | Glow after charging by normal light; no wiring |

Fittings must be placed at every exit door, every change of direction and intersection, on every stair flight, near fire alarm call points and fire-fighting equipment, and outside final exits, with enough light along the route. Fittings must also sense the failure of the local lighting circuit they serve: a fitting wired to a different circuit will not come on when the lights around it fail.

Era tells you the likely state. Fluorescent self-contained fittings with nickel-cadmium batteries dominate installations of the 1980s to 2000s and are at end of life; LED fittings with nickel-metal hydride or lithium iron phosphate batteries are the current generation, often with self-test.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Nickel-cadmium and nickel-metal hydride batteries last four to six years and lithium iron phosphate eight to ten, while LED emergency luminaires and exit signs last fifteen to twenty. The batteries decide most of the work, and they fail quietly until a full-duration test.

| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Nickel-cadmium and nickel-metal hydride batteries | 4 to 6 years | Heat in ceiling spaces; charging |
| Lithium iron phosphate batteries | 8 to 10 years | Heat; battery management |
| LED emergency luminaires and exit signs | 15 to 20 years | Driver and charger; heat |
| Fluorescent emergency fittings | 10 to 15 years | Lamp availability ending |
| Central battery systems | 15 to 20 years; batteries 5 to 10 | Battery room temperature |
| Monitoring panels and software | 10 to 15 years | Vendor support |
| Photoluminescent signs | 20 to 25 years | Fading; charging light levels |

What shortens life: heat: fittings in hot ceiling spaces, near plant or in roof spaces lose battery life fastest; missed testing: batteries never discharged lose capacity unnoticed; fit-outs that disconnect fittings, rewire them to the wrong circuits, or hide them behind new partitions; damage in car parks, plant rooms and stairs.

sections.heading: Batteries, chargers and central systems
sections.markdown:
Batteries are the commonest failure. They lose capacity with age and heat until the fitting cannot run for its rated duration, which each market sets (Thresholds by market). A fitting that lights on a quick switch test can fail a full-duration test, which is why the duration test is required.

Chargers fail and leave batteries flat; fluorescent tubes and early LED modules fail; indicators fail so faults are not seen.

Central battery systems fail as one: a battery, inverter or changeover fault darkens a whole area. Sub-circuit monitoring must detect local lighting failures, and wiring to fittings must be fire-resisting so it survives long enough to be useful.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fittings pass a short test but go dark within the duration | Battery capacity lost. Full-duration discharge test against the duration for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Replace the batteries, all of an age together. |
| Charge indicators off | Charger, supply or indicator failure. Inspection and test. | Check the supply, charger and indicator; repair or replace the fitting. |

sections.heading: Wiring, coverage and exit signs
sections.markdown:
Non-maintained fittings must be fed from the same unswitched circuit as the normal lighting in that area so that they detect its failure. Fit-outs often rewire them to another circuit or to a switched supply; the fitting then stays dark when the local lights fail, or drains its battery every time the lights are switched off.

New partitions create corridors, dead ends and changes of direction the original layout did not cover; exit signs end up pointing to doors that no longer lead out, or are hidden behind signage and joinery.

Photoluminescent signs need enough normal light to charge; in dim stairs and plant areas they may not glow brightly enough when needed.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fitting works on test switch but stays dark when local lights fail | Wired to the wrong circuit. Circuit check against local lighting. | Rewire the fitting to the local lighting circuit. |
| Batteries flat each morning | Fed from a switched supply. Circuit check. | Rewire it to an unswitched supply. |
| Dark sections of escape routes after a fit-out | Coverage gap. Layout review against current partitions. | Add fittings designed to the standard, and verify by measurement. |
| Corridors or large rooms with no emergency lighting at all | Coverage below the market’s rules. Rooms and paths of travel without fittings, against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Add fittings to cover the gaps, designed to AS/NZS 2293.1. |

sections.heading: Testing and monitoring
sections.markdown:
Self-test and addressable systems only help if someone reads their reports. Communication faults, unsupported software and disabled schedules leave a building believing it is tested when it is not.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Monitoring shows no faults for years | Monitoring not working or not testing. Manual test of a sample. | Test the monitoring itself, and make someone responsible for its reports. |
| Self-test fittings showing fault lights that nobody reads | Faults detected but not acted on. Walk-round of indicators; monitoring reports and who receives them. | Assign someone to read and act on the reports, and log repairs. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Escape routes, stairs or exits without working emergency lighting or exit signs; fittings that will not operate on local failure | safety · 4 Essential | Rectify now. |
| Periodic testing due | deadline · 4 Essential | Six-monthly duration test in Australia; monthly functional and annual duration tests in Britain and the United States. |
| Batteries failing duration tests across the installation | condition · 4 Essential | Replace batteries or fittings in the near term. |
| Fluorescent fittings and old batteries at end of life | lifecycle · 3 Important | Replace with LED, ideally with self-test. |
| No test records; layout not checked after fit-outs | check · 3 Important | Test every fitting and review coverage. |
| Isolated faults found and fixed at testing | nil · 1 Routine | Routine maintenance. |
| Emergency lighting failing its full-duration test across a circuit, floor or central battery | failure · 4 Essential | Repair now; interim measures until done. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
An electrical contractor licensed for fire safety systems carries out testing; a lighting designer or fire engineer reviews coverage where layouts have changed. The checks below start with the logbook and the last full-duration test, then walk every escape route against the current fit-out.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Full-duration test | Of every fitting by simulating failure of the normal supply, recording each result. |
| Circuit check | That each non-maintained fitting is fed from the local lighting circuit it protects. |
| Coverage survey | Against the current layout: every exit, change of direction, stair flight, call point and final exit; light levels along routes where doubtful. |
| Exit sign review | Visibility, direction, legibility, correct pictograms. |
| Central battery inspection | Batteries, charger, inverter, changeover, sub-circuit monitoring, room ventilation and temperature, fire-resisting wiring. |
| Monitoring check | Manual test of a sample against what the system reports. |
| Records review | Logbooks, annual statements, battery dates. |

The report should list every fitting with its result, coverage gaps, wiring faults, and the works needed to certify the system.

sections.heading: Replacing, rewiring or monitoring
sections.markdown:
Dark escape routes, stairs and exits come first, since the building cannot be certified until they are fixed. After that, batteries are replaced as a programme, fittings upgraded to LED, and testing made automatic with someone reading the reports.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Battery replacement programme | Replace all batteries of an age together rather than fitting by fitting. | Where batteries fail duration tests, or reach their age. |
| Fitting replacement | LED fittings with long-life batteries, which cut energy and maintenance. | At the end of the fittings' life. |
| Self-test or addressable monitoring | Automatic testing with faults reported, and someone responsible for reading the reports. | Wherever testing is manual or records are thin. |
| Rewiring | Rewire fittings fed from the wrong circuits. | Where fittings will not operate when the local lighting fails. |
| Coverage additions | Additional fittings designed to the standard. | After fit-outs. |
| Exit sign updates | Current pictograms and positions. | Where signs are outdated or point the wrong way. |
| Central battery refurbishment | Batteries, chargers, monitoring, or replacement with distributed fittings. | Where central battery systems are failing. |
| Records | A logbook or digital record for every fitting, with test dates, results and actions. | Always. |
| Escape route lighting design | Verify the design by measurement. | After major fit-outs. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Testing is a recurring contract at the prescribed interval. Battery replacement is priced per fitting and recurs on battery life. Fitting replacement is priced per fitting, with ceiling access in occupied areas. Monitoring systems are priced per fitting plus a panel. Coverage additions are per fitting with design. Central battery refurbishment is a lump sum.

Testing and safety rectification are code compliance; battery replacement is repairs and maintenance on a cycle; fitting replacement is lifecycle.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a walk-through cannot: whether every fitting passed its last full-duration test, when the batteries were replaced, and whether the layout matches the current fit-out. Ask for the logbook first.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Emergency lighting test logbook with every fitting and result | Whether every fitting passed its last full-duration test. |
| Annual fire safety statement or essential safety measures report | Whether the system was certified at its last annual review. |
| Monitoring system reports and fault history | Whether faults are reported, and acted on. |
| Battery replacement records and dates | How old the batteries are. |
| Emergency lighting and exit sign layout drawings | Where the fittings and signs are meant to be. |
| Fit-out records since the last layout review | Whether fit-outs have changed the escape routes. |
| Monitoring system access and reports | Whether anyone can read the monitoring. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Emergency lighting is misread when a fitting that lights on a short test is taken to be working, when failures are left to the next service, and when years of fault-free monitoring are taken at face value.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| It lit on test, so it works | Fittings that pass a short test can still go dark within the required duration when their batteries have lost capacity. Only a full-duration test shows it. |
| It can wait for the next service | Emergency lighting that fails its duration test, is wired so it will not operate, or is missing from escape routes is a life-safety defect. Buildings cannot be certified for their annual fire safety obligations until it is fixed. |
| No faults means no problems | Monitoring that shows no faults for years may itself have stopped working or testing. Test the monitoring, and make someone responsible for reading its reports. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market requires emergency lighting and exit signs, sets standards for their design, and sets testing intervals, including a full-duration test. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Requirements, testing and certification | The National Construction Code requires emergency lighting and exit signs (Part E4); AS/NZS 2293.1 covers design, AS/NZS 2293.3 luminaires and exit signs, and AS/NZS 2293.2 inspection and maintenance, including a six-monthly discharge test for at least the rated duration. Emergency lighting is an essential safety measure under state building regulations, certified annually. | BS 5266-1 sets the code of practice, with BS EN 1838 for lighting levels and BS EN 50172 for systems: monthly functional tests and an annual full-duration test, with a logbook. The Regulatory Reform (Fire Safety) Order 2005 places the duty on the responsible person. | NFPA 101 Section 7.9 requires emergency lighting with monthly 30-second tests and an annual 90-minute test, or approved self-testing equipment; Section 7.10 covers exit marking; UL 924 lists equipment; the International Building and Fire Codes adopt equivalent requirements. |

sections.heading: Worked example: fittings that pass a short test
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. An office's emergency lighting passes its monthly short tests, but the last full-duration test, two years ago, recorded several fittings going dark early. The batteries are original to a 2014 fit-out, and a recent refit added meeting rooms along an escape corridor without new fittings.

Fittings that pass a short test but go dark within the duration have lost battery capacity, and batteries of that age are past a four-to-six-year life. Dark sections of an escape route after a fit-out are a coverage gap. Both are life-safety defects, and the building cannot be certified until they are fixed.

So the register carries the escape corridor as a safety line now, a battery replacement programme for every fitting of that age, a full-duration test, and self-testing monitoring so the next failure is reported automatically.

thresholds.rule: Typically 90 minutes

source.title: AS/NZS 2293.1:2026 Emergency lighting and exit signs for buildings, Part 1: System design, installation and operation

thresholds.rule: Every path of travel on a storey over 300 m²; rooms over 100 m² that do not open to a lit corridor or open space; rooms over 300 m²

source.title: NCC 2025 Volume One, Part E4 Visibility in an emergency, exit signs and warning systems

thresholds.rule: Designed for 1 to 3 hours, most often 3 hours where premises may be re-occupied straight after a failure

source.title: Fire safety risk assessment: offices and shops

thresholds.rule: Battery units run for at least 90 minutes each year

source.title: UFM 3-601-02 Fire protection systems inspection, testing, and maintenance (13 March 2026)

pages.title: Emergency Power
pages.question: How do standby generators and UPS systems fail, and how do you know they will work in an outage?
pages.answer: Emergency power fails when it is needed. Generators most often fail to start: flat batteries, failed chargers or heaters, contaminated fuel. Diesels run unloaded in weekly tests wet stack and lose power. UPS batteries fail silently and drop the load the instant mains fails. Loads added over the years can exceed capacity, stalling the generator when fire pumps start. A generator not tested under load recently is unproven.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about emergency power; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.

pages.searchTitle: Standby generators and UPS: load testing, wet stacking, fuel, batteries and capacity

questions.question: Does a weekly generator run prove it works?
questions.answer: No. Weekly no-load runs do not show whether it will carry the building; only a test under load does.

questions.question: Why does our generator leak oil and smoke?
questions.answer: Often wet stacking from running at light load. Exercise it under meaningful load, with periodic load bank tests.

questions.question: Why did the generator stall when the fire pump started?
questions.answer: Too much load, or no starting sequence. Remove non-essential loads, sequence large motors, or increase capacity.

questions.question: How often should a standby generator be tested?
questions.answer: In the United States, NFPA 110 requires monthly exercise under load for at least 30 minutes and a four-hour test every three years for Level 1 systems.

questions.question: How long do generator batteries last?
questions.answer: Starting batteries 3 to 5 years and UPS VRLA batteries 3 to 7; the generator set itself 25 to 30 years.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Emergency power problems show at the generator as old batteries, cold engines, soot and stale fuel, at the UPS as alarms, and in the test logs and outage history. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| In the generator and UPS rooms | Nameplates: rating, year, run hours | Starting, wet stacking and fuel |
| In the generator and UPS rooms | Battery dates and condition; charger status | Starting, wet stacking and fuel |
| In the generator and UPS rooms | Coolant heater working (engine block warm) | Starting, wet stacking and fuel |
| In the generator and UPS rooms | Fuel tank level, gauges, water in sight glasses; bund condition and contents | Starting, wet stacking and fuel |
| In the generator and UPS rooms | Exhaust soot and oil leaks | Starting, wet stacking and fuel |
| In the generator and UPS rooms | Louvres clear; room temperature | Rooms, exhaust and permits |
| In the generator and UPS rooms | UPS alarms; battery room temperature | Transfer switches, UPS and capacity |
| In the records | Test logs: weekly or monthly runs, with load and duration | Investigation before the scope |
| In the records | Load bank test reports | Starting, wet stacking and fuel |
| In the records | Fuel test results | Starting, wet stacking and fuel |
| In the records | Battery test and replacement records | Starting, wet stacking and fuel |
| In the records | Transfer switch tests | Transfer switches, UPS and capacity |
| In the records | List of loads on emergency supply and the load study | Transfer switches, UPS and capacity |
| In the records | Records of real outages and how the system performed | Transfer switches, UPS and capacity |

sections.heading: Types of emergency supply
sections.markdown:
Emergency power keeps essential loads running when the normal supply fails: standby generators with their fuel systems, automatic transfer switches and exhaust; uninterruptible power supplies (UPS) with their batteries; and the distribution that carries emergency power to the loads. Some loads are life safety (fire pumps, smoke control fans, fire-fighting lifts, emergency lighting central systems); others are business continuity (data rooms, refrigeration, critical tenants). Healthcare buildings combine both, with the strictest requirements.

| Component | Job | What goes wrong |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Diesel standby generator | Supply essential loads after a mains failure | Fails to start (batteries, fuel, heaters); fails under load; wet stacking from light running |
| Gas generator | As above, on mains gas | Gas supply may fail in the same event |
| Fuel system: bulk tank, day tank, pumps, pipework | Store and deliver fuel | Fuel degradation, water and microbial growth; leaks; bund failures |
| Automatic transfer switch (ATS) | Switch loads between mains and generator | Mechanism failure; incorrect settings |
| Static UPS | Bridge the gap until the generator starts; condition power | Battery failure; capacitor and fan ageing |
| UPS batteries (VRLA, lithium) | Stored energy | Short life; heat sensitivity; thermal runaway in some chemistries |
| Load bank connection | Testing under load | Absent, so generators are never properly tested |

The question that matters is not whether a generator exists but which loads it actually supports, whether it can carry them, and whether it has been proven to start and run under load recently. Load growth, tenant additions and changes to fire systems often put loads on the emergency supply that the generator was never sized for.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
A diesel generator set lasts twenty-five to thirty years, or by run hours, and transfer switches twenty to thirty, but starting batteries last three to five years and UPS batteries three to seven. Batteries are the first thing to check when a generator fails to start.

| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Diesel generator set | 25 to 30 years (or by run hours) | Maintenance; exercising under load |
| Starting batteries | 3 to 5 years | Heat; charger condition |
| Automatic transfer switches | 20 to 30 years | Operation; maintenance |
| Static UPS | 10 to 15 years | Heat; capacitor and fan replacement |
| VRLA batteries | 3 to 7 years | Temperature; cycling |
| Lithium batteries | 10 to 15 years | Temperature; management system |
| Fuel tanks | 20 to 40 years | Corrosion; water; bund integrity |
| Stored diesel fuel | 1 to 2 years without treatment | Water; microbial growth; oxidation |

What shortens life: running unloaded during weekly tests, which causes wet stacking in diesels; hot battery rooms: every 10 °C above about 20 to 25 °C roughly halves lead-acid battery life; water in fuel from condensation and tank breathing; lack of exercise: generators that never run under load fail when needed; deferred battery replacement.

sections.heading: Starting, wet stacking and fuel
sections.markdown:
The commonest reason a generator fails in an emergency is that it does not start: flat or failed starting batteries, failed charger, failed coolant heater in cold climates, air in the fuel system, or a fault in the controller. Each is cheap to prevent and invisible without testing.

Diesels run at light load do not reach operating temperature; unburnt fuel and carbon build up in the exhaust and cylinders. The engine then smokes, loses power and may fail when asked to take full load. Weekly no-load runs cause it; regular load bank testing prevents it.

Diesel stored for long periods takes up water, grows microbes at the fuel-water interface (diesel bug), oxidises and forms sludge. Filters block in the first hours of running, exactly when the generator is needed. Biodiesel blends degrade faster.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Black smoke and oil at exhaust joints | Wet stacking. Test logs showing no-load running. | Run a load bank test, and exercise the generator under meaningful load. |
| Generator failed to start in a test or outage | Batteries, charger, fuel or heater. Battery test; charger output; fuel filters. | Replace the batteries; check the charger, fuel and heater, and fit monitoring. |
| Filters blocking during runs | Fuel contamination. Fuel sample. | Test, polish and treat the fuel, and remove water. |
| Generator run each week but never on load | Wet stacking and an untested set. Test records against the routine runs the asset’s market expects (Thresholds by market), and a periodic load test to show whether it can carry the building. | Run a load bank test, and add load to routine runs. |

sections.heading: Transfer switches, UPS and capacity
sections.markdown:
Transfer switches that are rarely operated can stick, and settings changed during maintenance can stop them transferring or prevent return to mains. A transfer switch failure looks like a generator failure to the building.

UPS batteries fail first, usually without warning unless monitored; a UPS with failed batteries drops its load the instant the mains fails. Capacitors and cooling fans age and need replacement at mid-life. Lithium battery systems introduce fire risks that need separation and detection.

Loads added to emergency boards over the years can exceed the generator's capacity; large motor loads such as fire pumps and smoke fans starting together can stall it. Life-safety loads must be given priority and the generator must carry them.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| UPS dropped load on mains failure | Failed batteries. Battery test. | Replace the batteries, with monitoring. |
| Generator stalls when fire systems start | Capacity or load sequencing. Load study. | Remove non-essential loads and sequence large motors, or increase capacity. |
| UPS batteries past their design life | Battery failure on the next outage. Battery dates; impedance or discharge test. | Replace the battery strings, and test under load. |

sections.heading: Rooms, exhaust and permits
sections.markdown:
Generator rooms need combustion and cooling air; blocked louvres and recirculated exhaust cause overheating. Exhaust discharge near air intakes and windows brings fumes into the building. Noise and air emission limits constrain where and how long generators can run.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fumes inside the building during tests | Exhaust re-entry. Discharge location. | Extend the exhaust away from intakes. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Generator serving life-safety loads fails to start or carry load; fuel leak; lithium battery fire risk without separation | safety · 4 Essential | Rectify now; interim measures. |
| Generator or UPS failed | failure · 4 Essential | Repair now. |
| Mandatory testing due | deadline · 4 Essential | At the prescribed interval. |
| Batteries at end of life; fuel contaminated; wet stacking; capacity tight | condition · 4 Essential | Repair in the near term. |
| Generator or UPS at end of life | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Replace on cycle. |
| No load bank test or load study | check · 3 Important | Test and study. |
| Normal | nil · 1 Routine | Routine. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
An electrical engineer leads, with the generator and UPS maintenance contractors. The checks below start with the test logs and load bank reports, then the batteries, fuel and transfer switch, and the loads the system must carry.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Records review | Test logs, load bank reports, fuel analysis, battery records, maintenance, outage history. |
| Inspection | Of generator, fuel system, transfer switches, UPS and batteries, rooms and exhaust. |
| Load bank test | At or near rated load for a sustained period. |
| Black-start test | Simulated mains failure with transfer of real loads. |
| Fuel sampling | For water, microbes and contamination. |
| Battery testing | By impedance or discharge. |
| Load study | What is on emergency supply, life-safety priority, starting sequence, capacity. |
| Transfer switch test | Transfer, retransfer and timing, with settings recorded. |

The report should state whether the system is proven to carry its loads, the life-safety position, condition and remaining life, and works needed.

Tests are planned with the building so critical tenants and life-safety systems are covered throughout.

sections.heading: Testing, servicing or replacing
sections.markdown:
A generator serving life-safety loads that fails to start or carry its load comes first. After that, a testing regime under real load proves the system, and batteries, fuel and load management keep it working.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Testing regime | Exercise generators monthly under meaningful load, run periodic load bank tests at or near rated load, and run full black-start tests transferring real loads; record every test. | Always, for every emergency system. |
| Starting system | Replace starting batteries on a fixed cycle, check chargers and coolant heaters, and fit monitoring that alarms on battery or charger faults. | Wherever generators fail to start, or batteries are old. |
| Fuel management | Test fuel periodically; polish and treat it; remove water; turn fuel over; maintain tanks, bunds, vents and leak detection. | Wherever fuel is stored. |
| Generator overhaul | Overhaul at run-hour or age intervals, or replacement where parts and controls are no longer supported. | At run-hour or age intervals. |
| UPS maintenance | Replace batteries on a cycle with monitoring; replace capacitors and fans at mid-life; replace the UPS at end of life. | Wherever a UPS supports critical loads. |
| Load management | Remove non-essential loads from emergency boards, sequence the starting of large motors such as fire pumps and smoke fans, and increase capacity where the life-safety load needs it. | Where the generator stalls, or loads have grown. |
| Load bank connection point | A connection so testing can be done without disconnecting the building. | Where load bank testing is impractical. |
| Room and exhaust works | Clear louvres, extend exhaust away from intakes, add acoustic treatment. | Where louvres are blocked or exhaust re-enters. |
| Battery safety | Separation, ventilation and detection for lithium and large lead-acid installations. | For lithium and large lead-acid installations. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Testing, fuel management and maintenance are recurring contracts; load bank tests and fuel polishing are recurring lump sums. Starting and UPS batteries are replaced on a cycle and are best carried as recurring allowances. Generator replacement is a lump-sum project including the generator set, crane lift, fuel system, exhaust and acoustic works, switchboard and transfer switch changes, and commissioning, with temporary generation where life-safety loads must remain covered. UPS replacement is similar.

Life-safety testing and rectification are code compliance; batteries and fuel management are repairs and maintenance on a cycle; replacement is lifecycle; capacity increases sit with the project that adds load.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a weekly run cannot: whether the generator has carried real load recently, how it performed in actual outages, and what it must carry. Ask for the load bank reports first.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Generator and UPS test logs with load and duration | Whether the generator and UPS are exercised, and under what load. |
| Load bank test reports | Whether the generator can carry its rated load. |
| Fuel analysis results and fuel management records | Whether the fuel is fit to use. |
| Starting and UPS battery test and replacement records | Whether the batteries will start the engine and hold the UPS. |
| Load study and the list of loads on each emergency board | What the system must carry, and whether it can. |
| Outage history and how the system performed | How the system performed when it was really needed. |
| Maintenance contracts and service reports | What the contractors found and recommended. |
| Generator run hours, installation date and overhaul history | How far through its life the generator is. |
| Environmental permits for the generator where required | Whether permits limit running hours for testing. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Emergency power is misread when a generator that starts every week is taken to be proven, and when loads are added to emergency boards without checking what the generator can carry.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| It runs every week, so it works | A standby generator that has not been tested under load recently should be treated as unproven. Weekly no-load runs do not show whether it will carry the building. |
| It will carry whatever is connected | A generator that stalls when fire pumps and smoke fans start has more load than it can carry, or no starting sequence. Remove non-essential loads, sequence large motors, or increase capacity. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets standards for generating sets and emergency supplies, and in some cases for how often they are tested under load. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Generating sets and testing | AS/NZS 3010 covers generating sets, AS/NZS 3009 emergency power in hospitals, and AS 1940 fuel storage; generators supporting fire systems are maintained as essential safety measures. | BS 7698 and BS ISO 8528 cover generating sets; BS 9999 and BS 5839 set life-safety supply requirements; healthcare follows HTM 06-01. | NFPA 110 sets testing for emergency and standby power systems, including monthly exercise under load for at least 30 minutes and a four-hour test every three years for Level 1 systems; NFPA 111 covers stored energy systems; NFPA 70 Articles 700, 701 and 702 cover emergency, legally required and optional standby systems. |

Environmental permits also apply in all three jurisdictions to larger diesel generators, limiting running hours and emissions, which affects testing regimes.

sections.heading: Worked example: a generator that only ever runs light
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. An office tower's diesel generator runs weekly for fifteen minutes with no load. There is black smoke and oil at the exhaust joints, the starting batteries are six years old, and the fuel has not been tested since installation. In a recent outage the generator stalled when the fire pump started.

A generator not tested under load is unproven: weekly no-load runs do not show whether it will carry the building. The oil and smoke point to wet stacking from running light; six-year-old batteries are past their life; and stalling on the fire pump points to capacity or load sequencing.

So the register carries the generator as a safety line now, with a load bank test, new starting batteries, fuel testing and polishing, and load sequencing so the fire pump and smoke fans start in turn.

thresholds.rule: Standby diesel engines run for 30 minutes each week

source.title: Fire safety risk assessment: offices and shops

pages.title: Energy Efficiency Upgrades
pages.question: How do energy efficiency upgrades underperform, and when does efficiency become a compliance deadline?
pages.answer: Energy upgrades fail in operation more than equipment: drives bypassed, LED without controls, efficient plant sequenced badly, recommissioning savings drifting back within a few years. Fabric upgrades without moisture control cause condensation and mould; electrification hits supply and emitter limits. Ratings, minimum letting standards and building performance limits now turn efficiency into a deadline and value issue regardless of physical condition. Measure, or savings disappear.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about energy efficiency upgrades; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: LED retrofits, VSD installations, high-efficiency plant

pages.searchTitle: Energy efficiency upgrades: why savings fail and what to fix first

questions.question: Why didn't our energy upgrade save anything?
questions.answer: Usually because of operation, not equipment: drives left in bypass, LED without controls, efficient plant sequenced badly. Check the controls and trend data before blaming the equipment.

questions.question: Why are our energy savings fading?
questions.answer: Savings drift as controls are overridden, schedules lost and setpoints changed. Recommissioning restores them; monitoring and fault detection keep them.

questions.question: Can insulation upgrades cause problems?
questions.answer: Yes. Insulation without vapour control or ventilation can cause condensation and mould, which is a safety finding where it affects health.

questions.question: What is the minimum energy rating for letting commercial property in England?
questions.answer: In England and Wales, let non-domestic property must meet a minimum EPC rating of E, with proposals to raise the minimum further.

questions.question: What should be done first to cut a building's energy use?
questions.answer: Recommissioning: remove overrides, restore schedules, reset setpoints and tune sequences. It is usually the best value measure, and comes before new equipment.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Energy upgrades show their problems in the data more than on site: use that does not fall, or falls and climbs back. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On site or in data | Energy use not falling after upgrades, or rising again after a year or two | The performance gap and drift |
| On site or in data | Drives in bypass or hand mode; plant running at night | The performance gap and drift |
| On site or in data | LED lighting on in empty spaces | The performance gap and drift |
| On site or in data | Condensation and mould after fabric upgrades | Quality and unintended consequences |
| On site or in data | Ratings below market expectations or legal minimums | Rules, tenants and load growth |
| In the records | Energy bills and interval data | The performance gap and drift |
| In the records | Ratings and certificates with expiry dates | Rules, tenants and load growth |
| In the records | Energy audits and upgrade business cases | The performance gap and drift |
| In the records | Measurement and verification reports | The performance gap and drift |
| In the records | Building performance standard filings | Rules, tenants and load growth |
| In the data | Ratings drifting down at each renewal despite upgrades, a sign of operational drift or load growth | The performance gap and drift |
| In the records | Tenants unaware of the building's rating or their own consumption | Rules, tenants and load growth |

sections.heading: Types of upgrade
sections.markdown:
Energy efficiency upgrades are works that cut a building's energy use and emissions: LED lighting and controls, variable speed drives on fans and pumps, high-efficiency chillers, boilers and heat pumps, building management system tuning, insulation and glazing improvements, air sealing, heat recovery, and on-site renewable generation. They are increasingly driven by regulation and the market rather than by savings alone: ratings and disclosure schemes affect leasing and value, minimum standards restrict letting in some places, and building performance standards set emissions limits with penalties.

| Upgrade | Typical effect | Watch points |
| --- | --- | --- |
| LED lighting with controls | Large cut in lighting energy | Driver quality; controls commissioning |
| Variable speed drives on fans and pumps | Large cut in fan and pump energy at part load | Harmonics; drives bypassed; poor sequencing |
| High-efficiency chillers and boilers | Lower plant energy | Sizing to current load; low delta T; return temperatures |
| Heat pumps replacing gas | Electrification; lower emissions | Flow temperatures; emitters; electrical capacity |
| BMS recommissioning and analytics | Often the cheapest saving | Overrides creeping back |
| Insulation, glazing and air sealing | Lower heating and cooling loads | Condensation; ventilation |
| Heat recovery ventilation | Lower ventilation energy | Maintenance; cross-leakage |
| Solar PV and batteries | On-site generation | Roof; connection limits |

The market tools differ by country: NABERS ratings and Commercial Building Disclosure in Australia; Energy Performance Certificates, the minimum energy efficiency standards and Display Energy Certificates in Britain; ENERGY STAR benchmarking and city building performance standards in the United States.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
An upgrade's life is set less by wear than by how long its savings last. Equipment typically lasts ten to twenty years or more, but the savings from recommissioning can drift within a few years unless they are monitored.

| Upgrade | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| LED fittings | 15 to 20 years | Drivers; heat |
| Variable speed drives | 10 to 15 years | Heat; harmonics |
| Heat pumps and efficient plant | 15 to 25 years | Maintenance; sizing |
| BMS recommissioning savings | 2 to 5 years before drift | Overrides; staff changes |
| Insulation and glazing upgrades | Life of the building | Moisture; installation |
| Solar PV | 25 to 30 years; inverters 10 to 15 | Inverters; roof |

What shortens it: drift: controls overridden, schedules lost, setpoints changed; poor commissioning so upgrades never deliver their designed savings; load growth and longer hours offsetting savings; lack of measurement, so nobody notices when savings disappear.

sections.heading: The performance gap and drift
sections.markdown:
Upgrades often save less than predicted: drives installed but bypassed, LED retrofits without controls, efficient chillers sequenced badly, heat pumps undersized. The gap between predicted and actual savings is usually commissioning and operation, not equipment.

Savings from recommissioning and controls fade over two to five years as overrides accumulate and staff change. Without monitoring, buildings slide back to old performance.

Without sub-metering and a baseline, savings cannot be proved, incentives cannot be claimed, and failures go unnoticed.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No saving after a drive retrofit | Drive bypassed or controls not changed. Drive status; trend data. | Take the drive out of bypass and change the control sequence so it varies speed. |
| Savings fading after recommissioning | Overrides and drift. BMS overrides; trend data. | Remove the overrides, restore schedules, and add fault detection so drift is caught early. |
| Savings claimed but no measured before-and-after data | Unverified result. Interval data across the change, adjusted for weather and occupancy. | Set up measurement and verification for future projects. |

sections.heading: Quality and unintended consequences
sections.markdown:
Insulation and air sealing without ventilation and moisture control cause condensation and mould; electrification without electrical capacity planning hits supply limits; heat pumps on emitters sized for boilers leave buildings cold.

Low-quality LED drivers, drives with harmonic problems, and poorly installed insulation fail early or underperform.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Condensation after insulation upgrade | No vapour control or ventilation. Inspection; humidity. | Add vapour control and ventilation; treat mould now where it affects health. |
| Heat pump building cold in winter | Undersized heat pump or emitters. Heat loss vs output. | Compare the heat loss with the heat pump and emitter output; resize or add capacity. |
| Overheating after glazing film, insulation or air sealing | Comfort traded for energy. Temperature logging; ventilation and shading. | Add shading or ventilation; review the upgrade design. |

sections.heading: Rules, tenants and load growth
sections.markdown:
Rising minimum standards and emissions limits can make a building unlettable or liable to penalties regardless of its physical condition, turning efficiency into a compliance and value issue.

In leased buildings, owners pay for upgrades while tenants often receive the savings, and tenants control lighting, equipment and hours. Without green lease clauses and shared data, worthwhile upgrades are not made and savings are not sustained.

Savings are eroded when buildings run longer hours, add equipment, densify occupancy or add data and EV charging loads, which can make an upgrade appear to have failed when it is working.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rating below the letting minimum | Regulatory shortfall. Certificate. | Plan the upgrades that reach the minimum by the regulatory date. |
| Main switchboard near capacity before electrification | Electrical capacity will limit heat pumps and chargers. Maximum demand against supply; for larger buildings, NCC J9D3 time-of-use meters on major services help size this (NCC J9D3). | Model the electrified load and plan supply upgrades. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fabric upgrade causing condensation and mould affecting health | safety · 4 Essential | Rectify now. |
| Building below a legal minimum for letting or facing performance standard penalties | deadline · 4 Essential | By the regulatory date. |
| Upgrades underperforming; savings drifting | condition · 2 Planned | Recommission in the near term. |
| Plant at end of life: an opportunity to upgrade | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Replace with efficient, low-emission plant. |
| No audit; ratings unknown | check · 2 Planned | Audit. |
| Upgrades performing | nil · 1 Routine | Monitor. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
An energy auditor or building services engineer leads, with the controls contractor and, for fabric work, a building physics specialist. The checks below establish what the building actually uses, what past upgrades delivered, and where the controls have drifted.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Energy audit | To a recognised standard (AS/NZS 3598 in Australia, ESOS requirements in Britain for large organisations, ASHRAE 211 in the United States), breaking consumption down by end use and identifying measures with costs and savings. |
| Interval data analysis | Base load, night and weekend consumption, start-up times and weather response, which reveal waste faster than any site visit. |
| Ratings and compliance review | Current ratings and certificates, their expiry, legal minimums for letting or sale, and any building performance standard limits and dates that apply. |
| Controls review | Overrides, schedules, setpoints, sequences and drives in bypass. |
| Verification of past upgrades | Whether installed measures are operating as designed. |
| Electrification and capacity review | Electrical supply headroom for heat pumps and EV charging. |
| Fabric and moisture review | Before insulation, glazing or air sealing work. |

The report should rank measures by cost and saving, state regulatory deadlines and exposure, and include a measurement and verification plan so savings can be proved and held.

sections.heading: Choosing and keeping upgrades
sections.markdown:
The cheapest saving is usually in the controls and operation of what is already installed, so the order is to recommission first, upgrade equipment at the end of its life, and measure the result. Savings that are not measured tend to drift away.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Recommissioning | Remove overrides, restore schedules, reset setpoints and tune sequences. | First, before new equipment; usually the best value measure. |
| LED with controls | LED lighting and its controls installed together, so light is efficient and switched off when not needed. | When lighting is replaced. |
| Variable speed drives | Drives on fans and pumps, with control sequences changed so they actually vary speed. | On fans and pumps running at fixed speed. |
| Plant replacement at end of life | Efficient, right-sized and lower-emission plant, including heat pumps where the building and supply suit them. | When plant reaches the end of its life. |
| Fabric upgrades | Insulation, glazing and air sealing designed with vapour control and ventilation. | Where heat loss or gain is high, and never without vapour control. |
| Heat recovery | Heat recovery on ventilation systems. | Where outdoor air rates are high. |
| On-site generation and storage | Solar and batteries. | Where the roof, the connection and the tariffs suit. |
| Monitoring and analytics | Sub-metering and automated fault detection so drift is caught early. | Wherever savings have drifted before, or upgrades need verifying. |
| Tenant engagement | Green lease clauses and shared data. | In tenanted buildings, since tenants control much of the energy use. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Audits and recommissioning are lump sums with quick paybacks. Equipment upgrades are lump sums per measure, often timed with end-of-life replacement so only the efficiency premium is attributed to energy. Fabric upgrades are larger and slower to pay back but can be essential for ratings. Monitoring and analytics are recurring subscriptions. Incentives can offset costs, such as state energy saving schemes in Australia and federal tax incentives for efficient commercial buildings in the United States.

Upgrades required to meet letting minimums or performance standards carry deadlines and penalties; otherwise they are lifecycle or improvement items justified by savings, value and tenant demand.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a walk-through cannot: what the building actually uses, what past upgrades delivered, and where it stands against the rules. Ask for two years of data before judging any upgrade.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Energy bills and interval data for at least two years | How much energy the building uses, and whether past upgrades saved anything. |
| Current ratings, certificates and their expiry dates | Where the building stands against letting minimums and disclosure rules. |
| Energy audits and upgrade business cases | What has been recommended, and what was expected of it. |
| Measurement and verification reports for past upgrades | Whether past upgrades delivered their savings. |
| Building performance standard filings and any penalties | Whether the building meets its legal limits, and what missing them costs. |
| Green lease clauses and tenant energy data | What tenants use, and what they have agreed to share or do. |
| Electrical capacity information for electrification | Whether the supply can take heat pumps and other electrified plant. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Energy upgrades are often judged by the equipment installed rather than by what it saves in use, and by raw bills rather than normalised ones. Both readings mislead the next decision.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| New equipment will cut the bills | The cheapest energy saving is usually in the controls and operation of what is already installed. Check those before buying new equipment. |
| The bills went up, so the upgrade failed | Normalising for weather and occupancy is essential before judging an upgrade: raw bills mislead when the climate or use of the building has changed. |
| Once savings are made, they stay made | Savings drift as controls are overridden, schedules lost and setpoints changed, often within two to five years. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Energy rules are where the three markets differ most, and they change often. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out ratings and disclosure, minimum standards and penalties, the rules for new and altered work, and audits and support.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Ratings and disclosure | NABERS ratings are widely used in commercial leasing; Commercial Building Disclosure requires a current energy certificate when offices of 1,000 m² or more are sold or leased. | Energy Performance Certificates are required on sale and letting; Display Energy Certificates apply to larger public buildings. | Many cities and states require energy benchmarking through ENERGY STAR Portfolio Manager. |
| Minimum standards and penalties | There is no national minimum energy rating for letting existing commercial buildings; Commercial Building Disclosure requires disclosure, not a minimum. For rental homes, the ACT has required ceiling insulation of at least R2 since 1 April 2023, and Victoria phases in minimum energy efficiency standards from 1 March 2027. | In England and Wales, let non-domestic property must meet a minimum EPC rating of E, with proposals to raise the minimum further. | Building performance standards such as New York City's Local Law 97 set emissions limits with penalties. |
| New and altered work | The National Construction Code Section J sets energy efficiency for new and altered work. | Approved Document L governs work to existing buildings. | ASHRAE 90.1 and the IECC govern new work. |
| Audits and support | State schemes in Victoria and New South Wales fund many upgrades. | Large organisations must carry out ESOS assessments. | Federal tax incentives support efficient commercial buildings. |

sections.heading: Worked example: an office whose savings faded
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 1990s office was recommissioned three years ago and its rating improved. Since then, energy use has crept back up, two supply air fans run in bypass, and the plant runs most nights.

Before anything else, the data should be normalised for weather and occupancy. If use is still up, the pattern is savings drift: overrides, lost schedules and drives in bypass. That is a condition finding, fixed by recommissioning again and by fault detection that catches drift early.

So the register carries a recommissioning line now and a monitoring line to keep it, not a plant replacement. The chillers and boilers become lifecycle lines when they reach the end of their life, the point at which to replace them with efficient, lower-emission plant.

pages.title: Escalators & Moving Walks
pages.question: How do escalators and moving walks fail, and which faults are safety-critical?
pages.answer: Escalators wear at step chains, drives and handrails, and fail most dangerously at the edges: broken comb teeth and skirt gaps trap feet and fingers, handrails running at a different speed from the steps cause falls, brakes that stop too hard throw passengers, and safety devices bypassed in maintenance remove protection. Controllers lose support like lift controllers, and units are usually modernised or replaced whole.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about escalators & moving walks; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Drive motors, step chains, handrails, control systems
