questions.question: Why do people fall at the top of the escalator?
questions.answer: Usually a handrail speed out of step with the steps, or crowding at the discharge. Measure the handrail speed on both sides, and watch the landing at peak.

questions.question: What causes escalator entrapments?
questions.answer: Broken comb teeth, step-to-skirt gaps beyond their limit, and missing skirt deflectors. They are entrapment hazards, and the unit is stopped until they are fixed.

questions.question: Is an escalator that keeps stopping faulty?
questions.answer: Not necessarily. It may be protecting itself exactly as designed, or tripping on a defective device; only testing each device and reading the controller's fault log tells them apart.

questions.question: Should an old escalator be modernised or replaced?
questions.answer: Modernised within its truss where the truss is sound, which is far cheaper. Full replacement is for a corroded truss, the wrong duty class for the traffic, or geometry that no longer suits the building.

questions.question: How long do escalator parts last?
questions.answer: Handrails 5 to 10 years, controllers 15 to 20, step chains 15 to 25, drive machines and steps 20 to 30, and the truss 40 years and more.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Escalator problems show first to passengers, as a handrail out of step, uneven steps or crowding at a landing, then on site at the combs, skirts and pits, and above all in the injury record. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What you notice as a passenger | The handrail creeping ahead of or behind your hand as you ride: a speed mismatch, and a common cause of falls | Handrails, brakes and safety devices |
| What you notice as a passenger | Noticeable vibration, clicking or a rhythmic bump underfoot: chain or roller wear | Chains, obsolescence, maintenance and asbestos |
| What you notice as a passenger | Steps that do not sit level with each other, or a visible gap opening between them | Combs, skirts and steps |
| What you notice as a passenger | Missing yellow demarcation lines at the step edges, which is what tells people where to stand | Combs, skirts and steps |
| What you notice as a passenger | A gap you can see between the step and the panel beside it along the incline | Combs, skirts and steps |
| What you notice as a passenger | Crowding at the top or bottom because the landing has nowhere for people to go | Landings, water, fire and access |
| What you notice as a passenger | Frequent stoppages, or a unit standing idle behind barriers for weeks at a time | Chains, obsolescence, maintenance and asbestos |
| On site | Comb plates at both landings: broken or missing teeth, and the mesh between comb and step cleats | Combs, skirts and steps |
| On site | Step to skirt gaps measured along the incline, and skirt deflector brushes present, intact and correctly set | Combs, skirts and steps |
| On site | Handrail speed against step speed on both sides, measured rather than judged | Handrails, brakes and safety devices |
| On site | Handrail inlet guards and their switches at all four inlets | Handrails, brakes and safety devices |
| On site | Step condition: cracks, broken cleats, missing demarcation, and any step that has been replaced with a non-matching one | Combs, skirts and steps |
| On site | Emergency stop buttons at both landings: present, accessible, labelled and not obstructed by retail fit-out | Handrails, brakes and safety devices |
| On site | Upper and lower pits during maintenance: water, debris, corrosion, lubrication condition, drainage on outdoor units | Landings, water, fire and access |
| On site | Truss condition beneath the steps, which is the one thing that decides repair against replacement | Chains, obsolescence, maintenance and asbestos |
| On site | Evidence of bypassed safety devices: jumpered switches, taped contacts, devices disconnected and left | Handrails, brakes and safety devices |
| In the records | Breakdown, entrapment and injury records with location on the unit and cause | Landings, water, fire and access |
| In the records | Maintenance contract scope and hours, and attendance records against it | Chains, obsolescence, maintenance and asbestos |
| In the records | Safety device test records and stopping distance test results | Handrails, brakes and safety devices |
| In the records | Periodic inspection certificates and outstanding defects | Standards by country |
| In the records | Modernisation or replacement history and recommendations | Chains, obsolescence, maintenance and asbestos |
| In the records | Running hours and duty data where the controller or building system logs them | Chains, obsolescence, maintenance and asbestos |
| In the records | Insurance claims and legal correspondence arising from escalator incidents | Landings, water, fire and access |

sections.heading: Types of escalator and moving walk
sections.markdown:
Escalators and moving walks carry large numbers of people between levels or along concourses in shopping centres, transport interchanges, airports, offices and institutions. Each comprises a steel truss, a drive machine and brake, step or pallet chains carrying steps or pallets, handrails driven in step with the treads, comb plates where people step on and off, skirt panels beside the steps, and a set of safety devices that stop the unit when something goes wrong.

An escalator is closer to a continuously running machine than to a lift. It carries its full design load every minute it operates, cannot be taken slowly out of service without stranding a route, and its passengers stand on moving machinery with no attendant and no instruction. That combination is why its failures are weighted so heavily towards injury rather than inconvenience.

| Type | Where it is found | Character |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Commercial escalator | Shopping centres, offices | Designed for moderate duty cycles |
| Heavy-duty (public service) escalator | Transport interchanges, airports, stadiums | Designed for continuous heavy use; heavier components |
| Moving walk (pallet type) | Airports, large retail | Flat or inclined pallets; trolley use in retail |
| Outdoor escalator | Transport and public realm | Weather exposure; drainage; corrosion |

Escalators are among the most heavily used and most injury-prone pieces of building equipment; most injuries involve falls, often linked to handrail speed mismatches, abrupt stops or passenger behaviour, and entrapments at comb plates and skirts.

Duty is fixed at purchase and is the single most consequential fact about any escalator. A commercial-duty unit and a public-service unit can look identical from the landing and differ entirely in chain, step, drive and truss specification. Where a building's use has changed since the escalator was chosen, or where a developer specified to price, the unit wears out years early and no maintenance regime will prevent it ([Passenger & Goods Lifts](https://moyneross.com/technical/passenger-and-goods-lifts)).

The truss is the part that decides the economics. It is a steel structure built into the building and supported at both landings, and replacing it means opening floors or roofs and bringing a new truss in by crane. While the truss is sound, almost everything else can be renewed inside it; when the truss has corroded, the unit is effectively at the end of its life whatever the condition of its machinery ([Structural Frame](https://moyneross.com/technical/structural-frame)).

Moving walks differ enough to be read separately. Pallet-type walks run flat or on a shallow incline, often over long distances in airports, and their failures concentrate in pallet chains, the long runs of tracking and the comb at each end rather than in the step geometry that dominates escalator injuries. Inclined walks in retail take trolleys, which brings castor locks, trolley-specific pallets and magnetic braking into the picture, and a trolley released on an incline is a hazard an escalator never has.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
An escalator is renewed in parts around a long-lived truss. Handrails last five to ten years and step chains fifteen to twenty-five, while the truss lasts forty years and more, and its condition decides whether a unit is modernised or replaced.

| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Truss | 40 years and more | Corrosion; water |
| Drive machine and gearbox | 20 to 30 years | Duty; lubrication |
| Step chains | 15 to 25 years | Load; lubrication; wear |
| Steps and pallets | 20 to 30 years | Damage; wear |
| Handrails | 5 to 10 years | UV; cracking; tension |
| Controllers | 15 to 20 years | Manufacturer support |
| Comb plates | Replaced as teeth break | Damage |
| Balustrade panels and decking | 20 to 30 years | Impact; vandalism; style |
| Step rollers and tracks | 10 to 20 years | Duty; lubrication; alignment |
| Safety devices and switches | 15 to 20 years | Testing regime; moisture |
| Lighting and demarcation | Renewed with steps | Damage; visibility requirements |

Hours run, not years, set the clock. An escalator in a shopping centre open twelve hours a day and one in a transport interchange running twenty hours carry very different mileage in the same calendar year, and manufacturers quote lives against duty hours for exactly that reason. Where a building management system or the controller logs running hours, that figure predicts chain and step wear far better than the installation date.

What shortens life: duty beyond what the unit was designed for; outdoor exposure; poor lubrication; trolleys and luggage.

The duty an escalator was designed for matters as much as its age. A commercial escalator moved into a transport interchange, or a shopping centre escalator running longer hours than designed, wears through chains, steps and drives years early. Heavy-duty units built for public transport have heavier components and longer intervals between major overhauls.

What shortens it: excess duty: more hours, more passengers or heavier loads than designed; outdoor and semi-outdoor exposure: rain, dust and salt corrode trusses, chains and steps, and water collects in the pit; poor lubrication of chains and drives, which accelerates wear and noise; trolleys, prams and luggage on units not designed for them, which damage steps and combs.

What lengthens it: matching duty to use, replacing commercial-duty units with public-service units where traffic has grown rather than repairing them repeatedly; lubrication on schedule, which is the cheapest single protection for chains, tracks and drives; keeping pits dry and clean, with drainage maintained on outdoor and semi-outdoor units; shutting down outside trading hours where traffic allows, or running on slow-speed or standby operation, which cuts duty hours substantially; trolley management in retail: trolleys only on units designed for them, with the right castors and locks; prompt step and comb replacement, since one damaged step or broken comb accelerates damage to everything it passes.

sections.heading: Combs, skirts and steps
sections.markdown:
The comb plate is where passengers step on and off, and its teeth mesh into the cleats of each step. Teeth break when objects are caught, and a missing tooth leaves a gap that catches shoes, laces and small fingers. Alongside it, the skirt panel runs beside the steps for the whole length of the incline; where the gap between step and skirt is too wide, or the skirt is dished by impact, feet and clothing are drawn in. Soft-soled shoes, loose laces, long clothing and small children are the recurring factors in entrapment injuries, which is why skirt deflector brushes, correct gaps and intact combs matter more than almost anything else on the unit.

Cracked or broken steps, missing demarcation lines, and damaged cleats cause trips and entrapments.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Broken comb teeth | Impact from objects or wear. Inspection. | Stop the unit and replace the comb plate. |
| Entrapments at the step edge along the incline | Skirt gap or missing deflector brushes. Gap measured against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market); deflectors checked for full length. | Bring the skirt gaps within limits, and fit deflector brushes along the full length. |

sections.heading: Handrails, brakes and safety devices
sections.markdown:
Handrails are driven separately from the steps, and the two must run at the same speed. As a handrail stretches and its drive slips, it lags behind the steps; a passenger holding it is slowly pulled off balance, which is a common cause of falls at the top of an incline. Handrails also crack, lose their surface and become slippery with age and ultraviolet exposure. Where the rail enters the balustrade at each landing there is an inlet, and inlets are a finger entrapment point for children, guarded by a switch that should stop the unit.

An escalator's brake must stop a fully loaded descending unit without throwing the people standing on it. Too fierce and passengers fall forwards down the incline, which is how a single stop can injure many people at once; too weak and the brake cannot hold the load. Stopping distance is therefore specified between limits and tested, loaded where it can be arranged. Auxiliary brakes are required on taller and heavier units, and a unit whose brake has drifted out of adjustment gives no warning before the day it matters.

An escalator is protected by a set of devices that stop it: comb plate impact switches, handrail inlet switches, missing step detection, overspeed and reversal protection, skirt switches, broken chain detection and emergency stops at both landings. None of them is apparent to a passenger, and a unit with several bypassed will run normally for years. Devices are sometimes disabled during fault-finding and not reinstated, which is the single most serious thing that can be found on an escalator inspection, because the unit looks and feels entirely normal.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Passengers stumbling at the top | Speed too high. Step speed against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Measure handrail speed against step speed, and adjust the drive or replace the handrail. |
| Unit stops abruptly | Brake or safety device fault. Stopping distance test. | Test the stopping distance; adjust or repair the brake and the safety devices. |
| Unit running normally but several devices do not stop it on test | Safety devices bypassed. Each device tested individually; look for jumpers and taped contacts. | Stop the unit; reinstate every bypassed device and prove each one. |
| Passengers stumbling as they step on a fast escalator | Speed too high. Step speed against the limits for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Reduce the speed where the unit allows. |

sections.heading: Chains, obsolescence, maintenance and asbestos
sections.markdown:
Step chains carry every step and every passenger, and they elongate as their pins and bushes wear. Elongation shows as uneven step running, growing gaps between steps, noise and vibration, and it is measured against a discard limit rather than judged by eye. As the chain lengthens, tensioning takes up the slack until the adjustment runs out. Drive chains and gearboxes wear in parallel, accelerated by heavy duty and thin lubrication. A broken step or drive chain on a unit whose protection devices are not working can let a loaded escalator run backwards, which is the most dangerous single failure an escalator has.

Controllers lose manufacturer support like lift controllers; escalators are usually replaced or modernised as a whole rather than in many small stages.

Water and debris in the lower pit also corrode chains and drive components and can short electrical equipment, especially on outdoor and semi-outdoor units.

As with lifts, the most common hidden failure is the contract. Escalator maintenance is labour-intensive, requires steps to be lifted and the unit taken out of service, and is easy to under-deliver without it showing. Rising call-outs with no component explanation, lubrication that looks dry, and safety test records that are complete but suspiciously quick are the signs.

Escalators installed before the 1990s can contain asbestos in brake linings and in truss and landing fire protection. It is safe in place but must be identified before modernisation, which disturbs exactly those components ([Hazardous Materials](https://moyneross.com/technical/hazardous-materials)).

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Steps running unevenly with noise | Step chain and roller wear. Chain elongation measurement. | Measure the chain elongation; replace the chains, with rollers and tracks, at the limit. |
| Rising breakdowns and long parts waits | Controller obsolescence. Parts support status. | Get the parts support position; plan modernisation within the existing truss. |
| Chains tensioned repeatedly with no adjustment left | Chain elongation at its discard limit. Elongation measured against the manufacturer's limit. | Replace the chains, with rollers and tracks; they are at the discard limit. |
| Noise and wear far ahead of the unit's age | Duty beyond design. Running hours and passenger numbers against the specified duty class. | Compare running hours and passenger numbers with the duty class; a heavier-duty unit may be needed at replacement. |

sections.heading: Landings, water, fire and access
sections.markdown:
A large share of escalator injuries involve behaviour rather than component failure: running, carrying luggage, prams and trolleys, standing on the comb, children playing on the balustrade, and crowding at the exit so that passengers pile up when those ahead cannot move away. Landing design matters here as much as the machine, and an escalator discharging into a congested space is a hazard the unit itself cannot fix.

Outdoor and semi-outdoor escalators live in conditions nothing else in the building endures. Rain enters the truss, drainage blocks, and water sits in the lower pit where it corrodes chains, tracks, the truss itself and electrical equipment. Salt near the coast and de-icing salt at entrances accelerate it. Corrosion of the truss is slow, hidden beneath the steps, and is the one defect that turns a repairable unit into a replacement ([Stormwater Drainage](https://moyneross.com/technical/stormwater-drainage)).

An escalator makes a permanent hole between storeys. The fire strategy for that opening, whether by smoke curtains, sprinkler protection, a fire shutter or the building's smoke management, is part of the installation and is commonly disturbed by modernisation or by fit-out works around the landings ([Smoke Management Systems](https://moyneross.com/technical/smoke-management-systems), [Passive Fire Protection](https://moyneross.com/technical/passive-fire-protection)).

No accessibility standard in any of the three jurisdictions treats an escalator as an accessible route. A building that relies on escalators between levels still needs a lift serving those levels, and that lift becomes a single point of failure for every person who cannot use the escalator ([Accessibility Lifts](https://moyneross.com/technical/accessibility-lifts), [Disabled Access](https://moyneross.com/technical/disabled-access)).

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Falls concentrated at the top of an up escalator | Handrail lag, or crowding at the discharge. Handrail speed measured; landing observed at peak. | Measure the handrail speed and watch the landing at peak; clear the discharge area. |
| Injuries clustered on one unit of several identical ones | Something specific to that unit or its landing. Compare components, gaps and landing layout against its neighbours. | Compare that unit's components, gaps and landing with its neighbours. |
| Rust staining or water in the lower pit | Drainage failure or weather ingress. Pit inspection; drainage traced; truss examined beneath steps. | Restore the drainage and weather protection, and examine the truss beneath. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Safety devices bypassed, disconnected or failing on test | safety · 4 Essential | Stop the unit until every device is proved. |
| Broken comb teeth; step to skirt gaps beyond limit; missing skirt deflectors | safety · 4 Essential | Stop until fixed. |
| Brake out of its stopping distance limits, or auxiliary brake defective | safety · 4 Essential | Stop until adjusted and retested. |
| Handrail speed mismatch, cracked handrail or missing inlet guard | safety · 4 Essential | Stop or restrict until corrected. |
| Cracked or broken steps, or missing demarcation lines | safety · 4 Essential | Stop until replaced. |
| Chain elongation at or beyond the discard limit | failure · 4 Essential | Replace now; the unit should not run on. |
| Unit out of service, or stopping unpredictably in service | failure · 4 Essential | Repair now. |
| Truss corrosion found beneath the steps | failure · 4 Essential | Assess structurally; plan replacement. |
| Periodic inspection or statutory test due | deadline · 4 Essential | At the prescribed interval. |
| Chain and roller wear short of the limit; handrail wear; noisy drives; water in the pit | condition · 3 Important | Repair in the near term. |
| Maintenance delivered below the contracted scope | condition · 3 Important | Enforce or re-tender now. |
| Unit at the end of its life, or its duty class unsuited to current traffic | lifecycle · 3 Important | Plan modernisation in the truss, or replacement. |
| No audit, no injury analysis, duty unknown, asbestos status unknown | check · 3 Important | Audit before sizing works. |
| Cosmetic damage to balustrade panels and decking | nil · 1 Routine | Routine maintenance. |

Escalators carry a higher proportion of safety findings than any other building element, and the reason is that their dangerous faults are invisible to passengers. A unit with bypassed devices, a drifted brake or an out-of-limit skirt gap runs smoothly and feels entirely normal until the day it injures someone, so these findings are graded on what they could do rather than on any distress they are currently showing.

The grading follows what a finding demands, not the size of the eventual bill.

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
An independent lift and escalator consultant leads, with the maintenance contractor operating the unit; testing needs the unit out of service and landings protected. The checks below start from the injury record, then test every safety device and inspect the unit from comb to pit.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Records review | Breakdowns, entrapments and injuries over several years, maintenance hours and scope, inspection findings. |
| Component inspection | With steps removed: step chains and rollers (elongation measured), steps and pallets, drive chain and machine, brake, truss, tracks and lubrication. |
| Safety device testing | Comb plate, handrail inlet, missing step, overspeed and reversal protection, emergency stops, skirt switches. |
| Stopping distance tests | Against the limits for the unit, unloaded and where possible loaded, with speed checked against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). |
| Handrail speed | Measured against step speed on both sides. |
| Gap measurements | Between steps, skirts and combs, with step-to-skirt gaps against 4 mm on either side and 7 mm in total (Smith). |
| Duty assessment | Of current traffic against design, and controller parts support. |
| Truss inspection beneath the steps | With steps lifted, which is the only way to see the component that decides repair against replacement. |
| Injury and incident mapping | Each recorded incident placed on the unit, to show whether the pattern is combs, skirts, handrails, stopping or the landing. |
| Running hours and passenger counts | Against the unit's specified duty class. |
| Landing observation at peak | Watching how people arrive and discharge, since crowding at the exit is an escalator hazard the machine cannot show. |
| Hazardous material survey | Before modernisation is specified. |

The report should state safety defects, component condition and remaining life, whether the unit suits its duty, and whether to repair, modernise in the existing truss or replace.

Escalator testing is intrusive: steps are lifted, the unit is out of service for a day or more, and both landings must be barricaded. In retail and transport buildings this is planned around trading and service hours well in advance, and the cost of the outage often exceeds the cost of the inspection.

sections.heading: Restoring safety, modernising or replacing
sections.markdown:
Safety restoration comes first and waits for no programme. After that, most escalators are kept going by recurring replacement of combs, steps, handrails and chains, then modernised within the existing truss; full replacement is for a corroded truss or the wrong duty class.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Immediate safety restoration | Every bypassed device reinstated and proved, broken combs and steps replaced, skirt gaps brought within limits, deflectors fitted, and brakes adjusted and retested. | At once; none of this waits for a programme. |
| Comb plate and step replacement | Replace combs and steps, with demarcation lines renewed. | As recurring maintenance rather than a project. |
| Handrail replacement | New handrails, with drive adjustment so speed matches the steps on both sides. | On the handrail's cycle. |
| Step chain replacement | New chains, usually with step rollers and tracks, since worn tracks destroy a new chain. | When elongation reaches the limit. |
| Safety upgrades | Skirt deflectors, handrail inlet guards, missing step detection, broken chain protection, and auxiliary brakes where the unit's rise requires them. | On older units built to weaker requirements. |
| Modernisation within the existing truss | New drive, brake, controller, chains, steps, handrails and balustrades, leaving the truss and the building openings untouched. | Where the truss is sound; usually several weeks per unit and far cheaper than replacement. |
| Full replacement | A new unit. | Where the truss is corroded, the duty class is wrong for the traffic, or the geometry no longer suits the building. |
| Weather protection and drainage | Canopies, heating where appropriate, pit drainage and corrosion protection. | For outdoor and semi-outdoor units. |
| Landing and crowd management | Clear the discharge area, move retail fit-out away from the comb, and keep emergency stops visible and unobstructed. | Where crowding at the landings causes incidents. |
| Maintenance contract reset | Defined scope, hours, lubrication schedules, safety device testing, and reporting coded by cause. | Where maintenance falls short of its contract. |

Choosing between them turns on the truss and on duty. A sound truss carrying a unit of the right duty class can be modernised repeatedly over decades. A corroded truss, or a commercial-duty unit in a public-service location, is a replacement however good its machinery looks, because the underlying mismatch returns within a few years.

Interactions: escalator works almost always touch the floor openings, balustrades and finishes around the landings, the fire protection of the opening, and the lighting; and because an escalator is not an accessible route, a lift serving the same levels should not be out of service at the same time ([Accessibility Lifts](https://moyneross.com/technical/accessibility-lifts)).

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Maintenance is a recurring contract, and handrails, combs and steps are replaced as recurring repairs. Modernisation in the truss is a lump sum per unit with a planned outage of several weeks. Full replacement is a larger lump sum that includes removal and installation through building openings or by crane, structural and finishes works, and a longer outage; in shopping centres and stations the disruption cost to tenants and operators often shapes timing.

What drives the cost: duty class and size, the number of units, access for removal and installation (crane lifts, opening roofs or floors, overnight road closures), structural and finishes works at the landings, fire protection of the opening, and above all the cost of the outage itself. In shopping centres and stations, lost trade and the cost of managing people around a closed route commonly exceed the price of the works and are what actually sets the programme. Commonly missed: steps and combs consumed during commissioning, temporary barriers and wayfinding, out-of-hours working premiums, hazardous material removal, and the independent consultant's fee.

Modernisation and replacement are lifecycle; safety upgrades are code compliance; component replacement is repairs and maintenance.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a ride cannot: where incidents happen on each unit, whether the safety devices and brakes have been tested, and how hard each unit works. Ask for them before any safety work or modernisation is specified.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Breakdown, entrapment and injury records with the location on the unit and the cause of each | Where on the unit incidents happen, which points to the component. |
| Maintenance contract scope and hours, and attendance records against it | Whether the contractor delivers what was promised. |
| Safety device test records and stopping distance test results, loaded where available | Whether the brakes and safety devices work as they should. |
| Step chain elongation measurements and their trend over time | How close the chains are to their discard limit. |
| Periodic inspection certificates and any outstanding defects or notices | Whether statutory inspections are current, and what is outstanding. |
| Modernisation or replacement history per unit, with dates and scope | What has been renewed on each unit, and when. |
| Manufacturer's parts support position for the controller and drive | Whether the controller and drive can still be repaired. |
| Running hours, passenger counts and the specified duty class of each unit | Whether each unit works harder than it was built for. |
| Insurance claims and legal correspondence arising from incidents on the units | What incidents have cost, and what is in dispute. |
| Hazardous materials register entries for the escalator equipment and truss enclosure | Whether the equipment or truss enclosure contains asbestos. |
| The fire strategy for the floor openings the escalators pass through | How the floor openings the escalators pass through are protected in a fire. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Escalators are misread when the machine is inspected before the injury record is read, when frequent stops are taken as faults, and when noise is taken as wear.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| Start with the machine | Escalator diagnosis starts from the injury record rather than the machine. Where on the unit each incident happened, and to whom, separates the three failure families: falls point to handrail speed, stopping and step irregularity; entrapments point to combs, skirts and inlets; crush and crowding incidents point to landing design rather than the escalator at all. |
| It is just a breakdown | Broken comb teeth, excessive skirt gaps and bypassed safety devices are entrapment and fall hazards. Stop the unit until fixed. |
| An incident is an incident | Falls usually point to handrail speed, abrupt stopping or step irregularities; entrapments point to combs, skirts and inlets. Recording the location and cause of each incident shows which component needs attention. |
| A unit that keeps stopping is faulty | Two diagnoses are commonly confused. An escalator that stops frequently may be protecting itself exactly as designed, with a device detecting a real fault each time, or it may be tripping on a defective device. The two look identical from the landing and are separated only by testing each device and reading the controller's fault log. |
| A noisy unit is a worn one | Equally, a noisy unit is not necessarily a worn one. Noise from a dry chain, a flat roller or a damaged step is a maintenance matter; noise accompanied by measured chain elongation at its limit is the end of a component's life. Measurement separates them, and without it a unit can be either over-maintained or run past its discard point. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market registers or inspects escalators, sets standards for new units and for improving the safety of old ones, and places duties on whoever controls them. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Registration and duties | Escalators and moving walks are registered plant under state work health and safety regulations, with periodic inspection where state rules require it; the duties fall on the person with management or control, which in a leased building is often contested between owner and tenant. | PUWER 1998 requires maintenance and inspection; the HSE treats escalators as work equipment, with duties on the person in control of the premises, and has issued guidance on escalator safety. | Periodic inspections and tests, including brake tests, are set by state and city elevator authorities; several jurisdictions have tightened escalator inspection after incidents in transport buildings. |
| Design and existing units | Design and modernisation follow the AS 1735 series, now aligned with EN and ISO standards. | BS EN 115-1 governs design and installation, and BS EN 115-2 the improvement of safety of existing units, the usual reference for bringing older units up to current safety expectations. | ASME A17.1 governs escalators and moving walks, requiring brake and safety device testing at set intervals, and A17.3 covers existing units. |

Accessibility rules in all three jurisdictions do not treat escalators as an accessible route, so a lift must be available wherever an escalator links levels; taking a lift out of service at the same time as an escalator modernisation can break that requirement. In Australia, where an escalator is the only means between levels for most users, the Disability (Access to Premises) Standards still require an accessible route, which in practice means a lift.

sections.heading: Worked example: falls at the top of one escalator
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A shopping centre has four escalators between two floors. The injury log shows six falls in a year, five of them at the top of one up escalator and none on its identical neighbour. A kiosk was recently placed close to that escalator's top landing.

Falls clustered at the top of one up unit point to handrail speed or crowding at the discharge, not to the escalators in general. Measuring the handrail speed against the steps on both sides, and watching the landing at peak, separates the two; the kiosk makes crowding likely. A handrail speed mismatch is a safety finding; crowding is fixed by clearing the landing.

So the register carries the handrail speed as a safety line if the measurement confirms it, relocation of the kiosk as landing management, and an injury analysis across all four units as a check line.

pages.title: External Coating Systems
pages.question: How do external paints, renders and protective coatings fail, what does each failure mean, and when does it matter beyond appearance?
pages.answer: Most coating failures are water or preparation problems, not product problems. Peeling to bare substrate at sills and wall bases means moisture behind; peeling between coats means poor preparation or incompatible layers; chalking is normal ageing and the cue to recoat. What matters most is what the coating protects: rust stains through a concrete coating mean the reinforcement is already corroding, and hollow render over a footpath is a falling hazard. Old layers may contain lead.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about external coating systems; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Paint systems on concrete, masonry, metal substrates; adhesion, weathering, protective function

questions.question: Why does paint peel off at the bottom of the wall?
questions.answer: Usually moisture behind the coating. Fix the water source first, or the new coating will fail the same way.

questions.question: What does chalky paint mean?
questions.answer: Normal UV ageing. A coating that is chalked but sound can be washed and recoated.

questions.question: Is old paint likely to contain lead?
questions.answer: Layers from before about 1970 may. Test before preparation, and work under lead controls where it is present.

questions.question: Can I paint over rust stains on concrete?
questions.answer: No. Rust stains emerging through a coating on concrete mean the reinforcement beneath is corroding; repair the concrete first.

questions.question: How often does a building need repainting?
questions.answer: Paint on timber every 5 to 10 years, acrylic on masonry and render every 8 to 15, and elastomeric and anti-carbonation coatings every 10 to 20.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Coating problems show from the street as fading, peeling and cracked render, close up as chalk, blisters and hollow render, inside as damp, and in the repaint history. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Street or aerial | Faded and patchy colour; mismatched patches from local repairs | Chalking, adhesion, blistering and cracking |
| Street or aerial | Peeling and flaking, worst at sills, the base of walls, under gutters and on the most exposed elevations | Chalking, adhesion, blistering and cracking |
| Street or aerial | Cracked and bulging render; missing render patches exposing the masonry | Render, concrete and steel |
| Street or aerial | Rust staining through coatings on concrete; rust at edges and fixings of coated steel | Render, concrete and steel |
| Street or aerial | Mould, algae and dark staining on shaded elevations | Chalking, adhesion, blistering and cracking |
| Close up on site | Chalk on a finger wiped across the surface | Chalking, adhesion, blistering and cracking |
| Close up on site | Peeling to bare substrate or between coats; thickness of the paint stack at a peeled edge | Chalking, adhesion, blistering and cracking |
| Close up on site | Blisters: dry or water-filled | Chalking, adhesion, blistering and cracking |
| Close up on site | Hollow sound of render when tapped; cracks following sheet joints | Render, concrete and steel |
| Close up on site | Coating cracks tracking cracks in the concrete beneath; spalling under coatings | Render, concrete and steel |
| Inside the building | Damp at the inside face of walls with failed coatings, and blistering of internal paint on external walls | Chalking, adhesion, blistering and cracking |
| In the records | Repaint history with dates, products and preparation specifications | Investigation before the scope |
| In the records | Hazardous materials register and lead testing | Lead paint |
| In the records | Coating warranties and concrete repair records | Investigation before the scope |

sections.heading: Types of coating
sections.markdown:
External coating systems are the paints, renders, texture coatings and protective coatings on the outside of a building. Some are decorative, but most do a job: keeping water out of masonry and render, stopping carbonation reaching reinforcement in concrete, protecting steel from corrosion and timber from decay. When a protective coating fails, the element beneath starts to fail.

| Coating | Where it is used | What it protects |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Acrylic paint | Render, masonry, fibre cement, timber | Appearance; water shedding; timber and sheet substrates |
| Alkyd and oil-based enamel | Older timber joinery and metalwork | Timber and steel; becomes brittle with age |
| Texture and membrane coatings | Render, fibre cement, concrete, apartments from the 1980s | Water resistance; bridging fine cracks |
| Elastomeric coatings | Concrete and render prone to cracking | Crack bridging and water resistance |
| Anti-carbonation coatings | Concrete frames and precast | Slowing carbonation to protect reinforcement |
| Mineral (silicate) paints and limewash | Masonry, heritage render | Breathable protection compatible with lime and stone |
| Cement and polymer renders | Masonry walls, sheet systems | Weather barrier and finish; see Cladding and Wall Systems for render on sheet |
| Protective coatings on steel | Exposed steel frames, balustrades, awnings, plant | Corrosion protection, often over galvanising |

Older buildings carry many layers. In Australia, paint applied before about 1970 commonly contains lead; in the United States, the cut-off for housing is 1978; in Britain, lead paint was common until the 1960s and in some uses later. Thick stacks of old paint crack and peel as a unit, and their removal is a hazardous materials operation.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Coatings are short-lived by design: paint on timber lasts five to ten years, acrylic on masonry and render eight to fifteen, and protective coatings on steel ten to twenty-five to first major maintenance. Render itself lasts thirty to sixty years, so most coating work is a recurring cycle.

| Coating | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Acrylic on masonry and render | 8 to 15 years | Exposure; preparation; colour (dark colours age faster) |
| Paint on timber | 5 to 10 years | Exposure; end grain sealing; timber movement |
| Texture and elastomeric coatings | 10 to 20 years | Film thickness; substrate movement |
| Anti-carbonation coatings | 10 to 20 years | Product; film thickness; UV |
| Mineral paints and limewash | 10 to 20 years (limewash 3 to 7 years) | Exposure; substrate |
| Render | 30 to 60 years | Bond to substrate; cracking; water from above |
| Protective coatings on steel | 10 to 25 years to first major maintenance | Corrosivity of the site; system specification |

What shortens life: preparation: coating applied over dust, chalk, mould, loose old paint or damp substrates fails early, whatever the product; exposure: UV on north and west elevations in Australia, wind-driven rain, coastal salt, industrial atmospheres; moisture behind the coating: rising damp, leaking gutters, failed flashings and sills; incompatible layers: acrylic over gloss enamel without preparation; impermeable paint over lime render or soft brick; substrate movement: cracking sheet joints, moving timber, cracking concrete; too many coats: thick stacks crack and peel as a unit.

sections.heading: Chalking, adhesion, blistering and cracking
sections.markdown:
UV breaks down the binder at the surface, leaving loose pigment that wipes off as a powder. It is the normal ageing of exterior paint and the usual cue for a recoat.

Paint peels from the substrate when moisture builds up behind it or it was applied over a poor surface; it peels between coats when a new coat was applied over a glossy, dirty or incompatible older coat.

Blisters form when moisture vapour from inside the wall pushes against an impermeable film, or when solvent or water is trapped during application. Blisters full of water point to moisture behind.

Brittle old alkyd and oil paints crack in a fine pattern as they age (checking, alligatoring). Coatings crack along lines that follow joints in sheet substrates and cracks in concrete or render below.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Powder on the finger, colour faded | Normal UV ageing. Even across the elevation; worst on the sunniest faces. | Wash and recoat while the coating is sound. |
| Peeling to bare substrate at sills, wall bases and under gutters | Moisture behind the coating. Source of water at that location; damp readings behind. | Fix the water source first, then prepare and recoat. |
| Peeling between coats in sheets | Intercoat adhesion failure: incompatible or poorly prepared coats. Cross-cut adhesion test fails between layers; glossy layer beneath. | Remove the incompatible layers, and recoat with a compatible system. |
| Water-filled blisters | Moisture vapour or water from behind. Damp substrate; impermeable coating on a wall that needs to breathe. | Find and fix the moisture source; use a breathable coating. |
| Fine crazing in a mud-crack pattern on old paint | Embrittled thick alkyd or oil paint. Paint stack thick; age. | Remove and recoat in full, under lead controls where lead is present. |

sections.heading: Render, concrete and steel
sections.markdown:
Render loses its bond to masonry when water gets behind it or when it is stronger than the backing; it sounds hollow, bulges and falls. Fine map cracking is drying shrinkage; cracks along regular lines follow the substrate.

Where an anti-carbonation or protective coating fails, carbonation advances to the reinforcement, which corrodes and spalls the concrete. Rust staining through a coating is the sign that it is already happening.

Coatings on steel break down at edges, welds, bolts and damage points first, then rust spreads under the film. Galvanising under the coating extends life until it too is consumed.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cracks in straight lines at regular spacing | Substrate joints in sheet or panel. Joint locations match. | Address the joints in the sheet or panel beneath before recoating. |
| Hollow, bulging render | Render debonded from masonry. Tapping; render lifts at the edges. | Cut out and replace the debonded render, or strip and re-render. |
| Rust staining through a coating on concrete | Reinforcement corrosion beneath. Cover survey; carbonation depth at the steel, the front marking a fall in pH from about 12.5 to 8.5, and chloride content where the threshold of 0.2 to 0.4 per cent by mass of cement may be exceeded (Institute of Corrosion). | Repair the concrete and treat the reinforcement, then apply an anti-carbonation coating. |

sections.heading: Lead paint
sections.markdown:
Deteriorating lead paint chalks, flakes and sheds lead dust and chips onto the ground and into interiors, which is a health hazard, particularly to children.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Old paint being sanded, scraped or burnt off | Lead dust and fumes. Test the paint first, against the definition of lead paint for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Stop the work, contain the area, and resume only with lead-safe methods and clean-up. |
| Flaking paint and chips in the soil along the base of an older building | Lead paint shedding into the ground. Paint and soil sampling. | Stabilise or remove the paint under lead controls, and assess the soil where children play. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Loose render over a public or occupied area; deteriorating lead paint where children live or play | safety · 4 Essential | Remove loose render and protect below; stabilise lead paint under controls immediately. |
| Coating failure with concrete spalling and exposed reinforcement | failure · 3 Important | Concrete repair and recoat now. |
| Widespread peeling, blistering or render debonding without loss; coating failure on steel with spreading rust | condition · 3 Important | Repair and recoat in the near term. |
| Chalking and fading; coating at the end of its cycle | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Recoat on cycle. |
| Lead-safe work requirements on pre-1978 housing in the United States before works | deadline · 3 Important | Works must follow the rule; timing set by the works. |
| Pre-1970 paint layers with unknown lead content; coating on concrete with unknown carbonation depth | check · 2 Planned | Test before specifying works. |
| Isolated scuffs, minor mould on shaded walls | nil · 1 Routine | Clean and touch up. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A coatings inspector or building surveyor leads; a concrete repair specialist joins where reinforcement corrosion is suspected. The checks below read where and how the coating is failing, then test the substrate beneath, since a fresh coat hides what is underneath.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Condition rating | Of chalking, cracking, flaking, blistering and rusting against the ISO 4628 series. |
| Adhesion testing | By cross-cut (ISO 2409 or ASTM D3359) or pull-off (ISO 4624 or ASTM D4541). |
| Film thickness | Measurement on steel and on concrete coatings. |
| Render tapping survey | To map hollow areas. |
| Carbonation depth | Testing with phenolphthalein, and cover survey, on coated concrete. |
| Lead testing | By laboratory analysis of paint chips or by XRF on buildings of the relevant era, against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). |
| Moisture investigation | Where peeling or blistering points to water behind. |

The report should state the coating system and its condition, the cause of failures, substrate repairs needed, hazardous content, and a specification for preparation and recoating.

sections.heading: Recoating, stripping or repairing the substrate
sections.markdown:
Water is fixed first, or the new coating will fail the same way. After that, the choice runs from washing and recoating a sound coating to full removal, and turns on whether the problem lies in the coating or in the render, concrete or steel beneath.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Wash and recoat | Wash the surface and apply a new coat. | Where the coating is chalked but sound. |
| Spot preparation and recoat | Prepare and recoat the failed areas. | Where failure is local. |
| Full removal and recoat | Remove the whole stack and recoat, under lead controls where lead is present. | Where the stack has failed or is incompatible. |
| Fix the water first | Gutters, sills, flashings and damp sources. | Always, or the new coating will fail the same way. |
| Render | Cut out and replace debonded areas, or strip and re-render, with a mix compatible with the substrate. | Where render is hollow, bulging or cracked. |
| Concrete | Repair spalls and treat reinforcement to a recognised concrete repair standard, then apply an anti-carbonation coating. | Where rust stains or spalling show through the coating. |
| Steel | Blast or mechanically clean, then apply a protective system specified for the site's corrosivity category. | Where rust spreads beneath coatings on steel. |
| Heritage masonry | Remove impermeable paints, and use mineral paints or limewash. | On traditional masonry. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Recoating is priced by area with preparation rated separately; substrate repairs (render, concrete) are priced by area or per repair. Access often dominates on multi-storey buildings. Lead removal adds containment, waste disposal and clearance testing. Recoating recurs on a cycle set by the coating and exposure.

Recoating is lifecycle; patching is repairs and maintenance; lead management is code compliance; concrete repair before recoating is repairs or lifecycle depending on extent.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what the surface cannot: what has been applied before and when, whether old paint contains lead, and whether coated concrete has been tested. Ask for them before specifying preparation.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Repaint history with dates, products and specifications | What has been applied before, when, and to what specification. |
| Coating warranties | Whether a coating warranty still applies. |
| Hazardous materials register and lead test results | Whether old paint contains lead. |
| Concrete repair and carbonation testing records for coated concrete | Whether coated concrete has been tested or repaired. |
| Records of damp and leak repairs on affected walls | Whether damp and leaks behind the coating have been fixed. |
| Colour and product schedule for the current coating | What the current coating is, so new work is compatible. |
| Heritage constraints on colours and materials | Which colours and materials heritage controls allow. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Coatings are misread when a fresh coat is taken to mean a sound wall, and when peeling is treated as a paint problem rather than a water problem.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| A fresh coat means a sound wall | A fresh coat of paint hides what is underneath. On concrete, an apparently sound coating with rust stains emerging, or on render, a sound surface that sounds hollow, means the problem is in the substrate. |
| Peeling means poor paint | Peeling to bare substrate at sills, wall bases and under gutters points to moisture behind the coating. Fix the water first, or the new coating will fail the same way. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets standards for painting buildings and protecting steel and concrete, and rules for work on lead paint. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Painting and protection | AS/NZS 2311 guides the painting of buildings, and AS/NZS 2312 the protection of structural steel. | BS 6150 guides the painting of buildings, BS EN ISO 12944 the protection of steel, BS EN 1504 concrete repair and protection, and BS EN 13914-1 external render. | AMPP (formerly SSPC and NACE) standards govern protective coatings on steel. |
| Lead paint | AS/NZS 4361.2 guides the management of lead paint in residential, public and commercial buildings. | The Control of Lead at Work Regulations 2002 govern work on lead paint. | The EPA Renovation, Repair and Painting Rule (40 CFR Part 745) requires lead-safe work practices on housing and child-occupied facilities built before 1978; OSHA 29 CFR 1926.62 covers worker exposure. |

In Australia, external repainting on strata buildings is common property and a regular sinking-fund item.

sections.heading: Worked example: peeling at the base of a rendered wall
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 1950s rendered house was repainted three years ago. The paint is now peeling to bare render along the base of the walls and under one gutter, and the render behind sounds hollow in places. The original paint layers have never been tested for lead.

Peeling to bare substrate at the base of walls and under a gutter points to moisture behind the coating, not poor paint: the gutter and ground-level damp are the cause. The hollow render is a substrate problem a fresh coat would hide. Layers from before 1970 of unknown lead content need testing before any preparation.

So the register carries lead testing as a check line, the gutter and damp sources fixed first, the debonded render cut out and replaced, and then preparation and recoating, under lead controls if lead is present.

thresholds.rule: Lead at or above 1.0 mg/cm² by XRF, or 0.5 per cent by weight in a laboratory sample

source.title: 24 CFR 35.86 Definitions (lead-based paint)
source.publisher: US Department of Housing and Urban Development

pages.title: Fencing, Gates & Signage
pages.question: How do fences, powered gates and signs fail, and which failures put lives at risk?
pages.answer: The life-safety risks here are powered gates and pool barriers. Powered sliding and swing gates crush and trap people when force limitation, safety edges and beams fail or are set wrongly, and gates that leave their tracks can fall. Pool gates that do not self-close and latch, gaps and climbable objects defeat child barriers. Fences rot at their posts and boundary walls lean. Exit and safety signs that are missing or wrong mislead people.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about fencing, gates & signage; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Perimeter fencing, gates (including operators), wayfinding, statutory signage

pages.searchTitle: Fencing, gates and signage: powered gate safety, pool barriers and boundary walls

questions.question: How do I know if a powered gate is safe?
questions.answer: It must stop and reverse when it meets an obstruction. Force measurement and a test of the safety edges and photoelectric beams confirm it; a gate that fails should be disabled until fixed.

questions.question: What makes a pool gate non-compliant?
questions.answer: A gate that does not self-close and latch from any position, a latch at the wrong height, gaps, or climbable objects within the non-climbable zone. Close the pool until it is fixed.

questions.question: Why is the fence leaning?
questions.answer: Usually because the posts have decayed at the base; probing them confirms it. A boundary wall leaning with a tree nearby may be root pressure or foundation movement.

questions.question: Who is responsible for a boundary fence?
questions.answer: It depends on the market and any agreement. In Australia, disputes follow state dividing fences legislation; in the United Kingdom, party wall and boundary law apply. Boundary surveys and fencing agreements settle it.

questions.question: How long do gate operators last?
questions.answer: Typically 10 to 15 years, with their safety devices, such as photo-eyes and safety edges, lasting 5 to 10.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
The serious problems here show at powered gates and pool gates; the rest show as leaning fences, damaged bollards and signs that no longer match the building. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On site | Powered gates: safety edges, photoelectric beams, force settings, warning signs, manual release, tracks and stops | Powered gates and pool barriers |
| On site | Pool gates: self-closing and latching from any position; latch height; gaps; climbable objects within the non-climbable zone | Powered gates and pool barriers |
| On site | Fences leaning, posts rotted or loose, panels missing | Fences, walls and boundaries |
| On site | Boundary walls cracked or leaning | Fences, walls and boundaries |
| On site | Bollards and barriers damaged by vehicles | Fences, walls and boundaries |
| On site | Signs: present, legible, correct and visible | Signage |
| In the records | Gate maintenance and safety test records | Powered gates and pool barriers |
| In the records | Pool barrier certificates and registration | Powered gates and pool barriers |
| In the records | Boundary agreements and surveys | Fences, walls and boundaries |
| In the records | Signage schedules | Signage |
| On site | Children or the public able to reach powered gate mechanisms, rollers and racks without guards | Powered gates and pool barriers |
| On site | Signs for car park height clearance that do not match the actual lowest point | Signage |

sections.heading: What this covers
sections.markdown:
Fencing, gates and signage cover the boundary and security elements of a site and the signs that guide and warn people: perimeter fences and walls, pool and play area fencing, security fencing, pedestrian and vehicle gates, powered sliding and swing gates, boom gates and bollards, and wayfinding, statutory, safety and accessibility signs. The serious risks are in powered gates and barriers, which have killed and injured people, and in safety barriers such as pool fences, where a failure lets children reach water.

| Element | Where it is found | Main issues |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Timber, steel and masonry boundary fences | All sites | Decay, corrosion, lean; boundary responsibility |
| Pool and play area fences | Residential, hotels, schools, childcare | Gates not self-closing and latching; gaps; climbable objects |
| Security fencing | Industrial, commercial, utilities | Damage; breaches; corrosion |
| Powered sliding and swing gates | Apartments, commercial and industrial sites | Crushing and impact hazards; safety device failure |
| Boom gates and barriers | Car parks | Impact on people and vehicles |
| Bollards | Building frontages, car parks | Impact damage; inadequate protection |
| Statutory and safety signs | All buildings | Missing, faded or inaccurate signs; non-compliance |
| Wayfinding and accessibility signs | Larger buildings and public sites | Legibility, tactile and braille requirements |

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Fences and walls last decades, but the parts that keep people safe do not: gate operators last ten to fifteen years and their safety devices five to ten. On any powered gate, the safety devices are the first thing to check.

| Element | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Timber fences | 15 to 25 years | Post decay; treatment |
| Steel and aluminium fences | 25 to 40 years | Coatings; coastal exposure |
| Masonry boundary walls | 50 years and more | Foundations; roots; lean |
| Gate operators and controls | 10 to 15 years | Use; weather; maintenance |
| Gate safety devices (photo-eyes, edges) | 5 to 10 years | Damage; alignment; weather |
| Boom gates | 10 to 15 years | Use; impact |
| Signs | 10 to 20 years | UV fading; vandalism |

What shortens it: ground contact at post bases; vehicle impact on gates, barriers and fences; heavy use of powered gates without maintenance; uV fading signs and degrading plastics; tree roots pushing over boundary walls.

sections.heading: Powered gates and pool barriers
sections.markdown:
Powered sliding and swing gates and barriers create crushing points at closing edges, shearing points where gates pass posts, and drawing-in points at rollers and racks. Gates without working force limitation, safety edges and photoelectric beams, or with them set wrongly, can crush people, especially children. Gates that come off their tracks or hinges can fall. Deaths and serious injuries have led to specific safety standards in all three countries.

Pool gates that do not self-close and self-latch from any open position, gaps under or through fences, and climbable objects such as chairs, pot plants and barbecues placed next to fences defeat the barrier. Most child drownings in home and apartment pools happen where barriers have failed or been propped open.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Powered gate does not reverse when it meets an obstruction | Force limitation or safety edge failure. Force measurement; device test. | Disable the gate now; restore force limitation and safety edges, and test them. |
| Gate jerks, jumps or leaves the track | Worn rollers, track or stops. Inspection. | Replace worn rollers, track or stops before the gate derails. |
| Pool gate stays open from some positions | Hinge tension or latch fault. Test from several open positions, and measure the barrier against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Close the pool until fixed; adjust the hinge tension or replace the latch, and retest from every position. |
| Pedestrian gate on an accessible route too narrow or heavy to open | Access barrier. Clear width and opening force against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Widen the gate, adjust the closer, or fit a powered operator. |

sections.heading: Fences, walls and boundaries
sections.markdown:
Timber fence posts rot at ground level and fences lean or fall in wind; steel corrodes at bases and welds; masonry walls crack and lean from tree roots, poor foundations and retained soil.

Damaged fences and gates that do not close or lock leave sites open; access control on gates fails or is bypassed.

Fences and walls on boundaries are often shared, and responsibility for repair or replacement depends on law and agreement; leaning walls toward a neighbour create liability.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fence leaning in sections | Post base decay. Probe posts. | Replace the posts on galvanised stirrups or with steel. |
| Boundary wall leaning with a tree nearby | Root pressure or foundation movement. Inspection; engineer. | Have an engineer assess it; repair or rebuild it with the neighbour's agreement. |

sections.heading: Signage
sections.markdown:
Exit, fire, safety and accessibility signs go missing, fade, become hidden behind fit-outs, or point the wrong way after layout changes. Car park signs for height clearance and speed are damaged. Signs that are wrong are worse than none, because people rely on them.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Exit signs pointing to a removed door | Layout changed without updating signs. Walkthrough against plans. | Walk the routes against the plans and update the signs. |
| Safety signs faded, missing or inconsistent | Signs no longer effective. Signage audit against the site’s hazards. | Replace with signs to the relevant standard. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Powered gate safety devices failing; pool barrier non-compliant; boundary wall leaning toward a public area; exit signs wrong or missing | safety · 4 Essential | Disable, close or rectify now. |
| Gate or fence failed; site insecure | failure · 2 Planned | Repair now. |
| Pool barrier inspection or registration due | deadline · 3 Important | By the required date. |
| Decay, corrosion, worn operators, faded signs | condition · 2 Planned | Repair in the near term. |
| Fences and operators at end of life | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Replace. |
| No gate safety test records; signage not reviewed after changes | check · 2 Planned | Inspect. |
| Normal | nil · 1 Routine | Routine maintenance. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A gate and automation specialist for powered gates; a pool barrier inspector where required; a building surveyor for fences, walls and signage. The checks below begin with the powered gates and pool barriers, where the life-safety risks are, then the fences, walls and signs.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Powered gate safety assessment | Identify crushing, shearing and drawing-in points; test force limitation with a force meter; test safety edges, photoelectric beams, stop and reverse functions, manual release and warning devices. |
| Pool barrier inspection | Against the applicable standard: height, gaps, gates and latches, non-climbable zones and nearby objects. |
| Fence and wall survey | Lean, post condition, corrosion, foundations and tree influence. |
| Boundary check | Position against title and survey, and any agreements with neighbours. |
| Signage audit | Against the current layout, fire strategy and accessibility requirements. |
| Bollard and barrier check | For damage and adequacy where vehicles approach buildings and pedestrians. |

The report should give the safety status of gates and barriers, required rectification, and a renewal plan.

sections.heading: Making gates, fences and signs safe
sections.markdown:
The order of work follows the risk: powered gate safety devices and pool barriers first, because a failure there can kill, then fences, walls and signs. Most of the safety work is upgrading devices and hardware, not replacing whole gates.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Powered gate safety upgrades | Force limitation, safety edges, photoelectric beams at the right heights, guards over rollers and racks, end stops and anti-derailment, warning lights, manual release, and a documented risk assessment. | Wherever a gate does not stop and reverse on contact, or its devices are missing or untested. |
| Gate operator replacement | A new operator, with controls meeting current standards. | At the end of the operator's life. |
| Pool barrier rectification | Gate hardware, latch heights, gap closures, removal of climbable objects, and certification. | Wherever the gate does not self-close and latch from every position, or the barrier fails inspection. |
| Fence repairs | Replace posts with galvanised stirrups or steel, replace panels, or rebuild. | Where posts are rotted or loose, or panels are missing. |
| Boundary wall repairs | Repair or rebuild, with the neighbour's agreement. | Where walls crack or lean. |
| Bollards | Bollards protecting entrances, gates and pedestrians from vehicles. | Where vehicles threaten entrances, gates or pedestrians. |
| Signage renewal | Signs renewed to current standards, including tactile and braille signs where required. | Where signs are faded, wrong after a fit-out, or lack tactile and braille forms where required. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Gate maintenance and safety testing recur. Safety upgrades are lump sums per gate. Operator replacement is per gate. Fences are priced by length. Boundary walls by length and height, often shared with neighbours. Pool barrier rectification is usually a modest lump sum. Signage is priced per sign or as an audit-based package.

Safety rectification is code compliance and immediate; replacement is lifecycle; maintenance is repairs and maintenance.

Disabling an unsafe powered gate has an operational cost in security and access that should be weighed against the speed of repair.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what an inspection on the day cannot: whether gate safety devices have been tested, whether the pool barrier is certified, and who owns the boundary. Ask for them before the inspection, so the inspector tests what has not been tested.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Powered gate risk assessments, maintenance and safety test records | Whether the gate's safety devices have been assessed and tested, and when. |
| Gate operator make, model and age | How old the operator is, and whether its controls meet current standards. |
| Pool barrier certificates and registration | Whether the pool barrier is certified and registered where that is required. |
| Boundary surveys and fencing agreements with neighbours | Where the boundary is, and who is responsible for the fence or wall on it. |
| Signage schedule and records of signage updates after fit-outs | Whether the signs still match the building after its last change. |
| Incident records involving gates and barriers | Whether a gate or barrier has already hurt someone or failed. |
| Pool barrier inspection reports and records of gate hardware replacement | When the barrier was last inspected, and whether its gate hardware has been kept up. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Gates and fences are easy to treat as a matter of security and appearance, when the powered gates and pool barriers among them are life-safety equipment.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| The gate works, so it is safe | A powered gate that does not stop and reverse on contact is a life-safety failure, however well it opens and closes. Disable it until it is fixed. |
| The pool gate closes, so the barrier is compliant | It must self-close and latch from any position. A pool gate that stays open from some positions is a life-safety failure; close the pool until it is fixed. |
| A leaning fence is a fencing problem | Decayed posts are the usual cause, but a boundary wall leaning with a tree nearby may be root pressure or foundation movement, which needs an engineer. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market treats powered gates as machinery and pool barriers as life-safety equipment, but under different standards. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out the rules for powered gates, pool barriers, boundaries and signs.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Powered gates | Powered gates follow AS/NZS 60335.2.103 for drives and manufacturer safety requirements. | Powered gates follow BS EN 12453 and BS EN 12604, and the Machinery Directive principles under the Supply of Machinery (Safety) Regulations; the Health and Safety Executive has issued alerts on powered gate deaths. | Gate operators follow UL 325, and gate construction ASTM F2200. |
| Pool barriers | Pool barriers follow AS 1926.1, with state registration and certification. | There is no national pool barrier standard for private pools. Pool operators control access, barriers included, under the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974, with HSE guidance in HSG179. | Pool barriers follow the International Swimming Pool and Spa Code and local codes. |
| Boundaries | Fencing disputes follow state dividing fences legislation. | Party wall and boundary law apply. | Boundary fences are a matter of state law and local ordinance: local codes set fence heights and positions, and some states have statutes on shared division fences. |
| Signs | Exit and safety signs follow the National Construction Code and AS 1319. | Safety signs follow the Health and Safety (Safety Signs and Signals) Regulations 1996. | Exit signs follow NFPA 101 and the International Building Code; accessible signage follows the 2010 ADA Standards. |

sections.heading: Worked example: an apartment gate that did not reverse
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 2000s apartment building has a powered sliding gate to its car park and a pool behind a glass barrier. The gate's safety edge is split and the gate does not reverse when pushed against; the pool gate stays open when opened fully; the timber boundary fence leans in two sections.

The gate and the pool barrier are both life-safety failures: disable the gate and close the pool until each is fixed. The gate needs its safety edge replaced and its force limitation tested; the pool gate needs its hinge tension or latch put right and retesting from every position. The leaning fence points to decayed posts, a condition finding.

So the register carries two safety lines now, a gate safety assessment as a check line, since there are no test records, and fence post repairs in the near term. If the operator is near the end of its life, replacement with controls meeting current standards follows.

thresholds.rule: At least 1200 mm high; no more than 100 mm under the barrier; a 900 mm non-climbable zone; 300 mm clear inside

source.title: Pool fences: requirements for pool barriers

thresholds.measure: Doors and gates on accessible routes
thresholds.rule: At least 815 mm clear; no more than 22.2 N to open (interior)

source.title: 2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design

pages.title: Fire Detection & Alarm Systems
pages.question: How do fire detection and alarm systems fail, when are they at the end of their life, and which findings leave a building unprotected?
pages.answer: Detection systems pass their tests until they cannot be supported. An unsupported panel is end of life because the next fit-out cannot be programmed in. The dangerous failures are quieter: zones isolated after works or nuisance alarms, detectors left covered, fit-outs without coverage, interfaces to lifts, doors and smoke control that no longer work, and signalling that stops when copper lines are retired. Isolations and failed interfaces mean the building is unprotected now.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about fire detection & alarm systems; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
