pages.searchTitle: Fire detection and alarm systems: unsupported panels, isolations and unwanted alarms

questions.question: Does a current annual fire safety statement mean the system is fine?
questions.answer: It establishes compliance at its date, not remaining life. A compliant system on an unsupported panel is at the end of its life, and isolated zones leave parts of the building unprotected.

questions.question: Why does our fire alarm keep going off?
questions.answer: Usually the wrong detector for the space, contamination, or a detector next to a supply diffuser. The event log shows where; heat or multi-sensor detectors suit kitchens and areas near bathrooms.

questions.question: When does a fire alarm panel need replacing?
questions.answer: When its manufacturer stops supporting it, or it cannot take new devices, typically after 15 to 20 years.

questions.question: What happens to the brigade connection when copper lines are retired?
questions.answer: Signalling over a retired line stops reaching the brigade. Upgrade to supported, preferably dual-path, communications before the line goes.

questions.question: How long do smoke detectors last?
questions.answer: Point smoke and heat detectors 10 to 15 years, domestic smoke alarms 10 years, and standby batteries 3 to 5.

questions.question: Parts of the fire alarm have been switched off for weeks. Is that acceptable?
questions.answer: No. Zones are usually left isolated after works or nuisance alarms. Clear the isolations now, and manage future ones with a permit and a daily check.

questions.question: Why can't the fire alarm be heard in some parts of the building?
questions.answer: There are too few sounders or speakers, often after fit-outs. Add sounders or speakers, or a voice system where intelligibility is required.

questions.question: The smoke alarms in the apartments are more than ten years old. Do they need replacing?
questions.answer: Yes. They are past their built-in life. Replace them with interconnected photoelectric alarms, hard-wired or with sealed ten-year batteries.

questions.question: Why can't a new tenant be connected to the fire alarm panel?
questions.answer: The panel is unsupported or at capacity. Confirm vendor support and panel loading, and plan replacement with a supported addressable system.

questions.question: The fire brigade was not called when the alarm was tested. Why?
questions.answer: A signalling failure, often a retired telephone line. Test with the monitoring centre, and upgrade to supported, preferably dual-path, signalling.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Detection problems show at the panel, in its event log, and in the building as covered detectors, uncovered rooms and silent sounders. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| At the panel | Panel make, model and age; vendor support status | Panels, isolations and coverage |
| At the panel | Faults, isolations and disabled devices on the display or event log | Panels, isolations and coverage |
| At the panel | Battery dates; standby charge indication | Panels, isolations and coverage |
| At the panel | Zone block plan or graphics matching the building as it now is | Panels, isolations and coverage |
| At the panel | Logbook entries for tests, faults and false alarms | Unwanted alarms and domestic alarms |
| In the building | Detectors covered with caps, bags or tape; painted detectors | Panels, isolations and coverage |
| In the building | Rooms and voids without detectors; detectors next to supply diffusers | Panels, isolations and coverage |
| In the building | Smoke detectors in kitchens, bathrooms and dusty areas | Unwanted alarms and domestic alarms |
| In the building | Call points obstructed or missing at exits | Panels, isolations and coverage |
| In the building | Sounders and speakers absent from new rooms | Interfaces, warning and signalling |
| In the building | Domestic alarms missing, beeping or dated more than ten years ago | Unwanted alarms and domestic alarms |
| In the records | Routine service records at each required frequency | Investigation before the scope |
| In the records | Annual fire safety statement or essential safety measures report | Standards by country |
| In the records | Unwanted alarm history and brigade charges | Unwanted alarms and domestic alarms |
| In the records | Cause-and-effect matrix and the last full interface test | Interfaces, warning and signalling |
| In the records | Alarm signalling contract and the line or network it uses | Interfaces, warning and signalling |
| In the records | Fire engineering report or fire strategy | Interfaces, warning and signalling |

sections.heading: Types of system
sections.markdown:
A fire detection and alarm system detects fire, warns occupants, calls the fire brigade and drives the building's fire responses. It comprises detectors and manual call points; the fire indicator or control panel; occupant warning, from simple sounders to emergency warning and intercommunication systems (EWIS) with voice messages and wardens' phones; alarm signalling to a monitoring centre or brigade; and the interfaces that shut down or switch air handling to fire mode, home lifts, release doors, start smoke control and signal sprinkler and suppression status.

| Type | Where it is used | Character |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Photoelectric point smoke detector | Most occupied spaces | Best for smouldering fires; affected by dust and steam |
| Ionisation smoke detector | Older installations | Contains a small radioactive source; being replaced; disposal rules apply |
| Heat detector (fixed or rate-of-rise) | Kitchens, car parks, plant rooms, dusty areas | Slower; used where smoke detectors would false alarm |
| Multi-sensor detector | Modern offices, hotels | Combines smoke and heat to reduce false alarms |
| Optical beam detector | Atria, warehouses, large open volumes | Needs stable mounting and alignment |
| Aspirating smoke detection | Data rooms, heritage buildings, high ceilings, prisons | Very sensitive; pipe network must stay clear |
| Flame detector | Fuel stores, hangars, industrial | Line of sight to the hazard |
| Domestic smoke alarms | Houses and apartments | Self-contained or interconnected, mains or long-life battery; 10-year life |

Systems are conventional (detectors grouped in zones, so the panel knows only the zone) or addressable (each device reported individually, with drift compensation and fault reporting). Large buildings network several panels. What a system must include depends on building class and height under each jurisdiction's building code; what it must do in an alarm is set out in the cause-and-effect matrix, which is the document most often out of date.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Detection systems last as long as their panels stay supported: fifteen to twenty years for a panel, ten to fifteen for detectors, ten for domestic smoke alarms, and three to five for standby batteries. A system can be fully compliant and still at the end of its life.

| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Control and indicating panel | 15 to 20 years before manufacturer support ends | Vendor support; programming tools |
| Point smoke and heat detectors | 10 to 15 years | Contamination; environment; manufacturer advice |
| Domestic smoke alarms | 10 years | Built-in end of life |
| Aspirating systems | 15 to 20 years; filters and fans sooner | Pipe condition; environment |
| Beam detectors | 10 to 15 years | Mounting stability |
| EWIS amplifiers and speakers | 15 to 20 years | Heat; vendor support |
| Standby batteries | 3 to 5 years | Temperature; charger |
| Fire-rated cabling | Life of the building | Damage; alterations |

What shortens life: contamination: dust, steam, insects and construction dust drift detectors toward false alarms; fit-outs that cover, remove, relocate or add detectors and change zones without reprogramming; panel obsolescence that stops the system being extended or reprogrammed; neglected batteries in panels and EWIS; building works during which detectors are covered or zones isolated and never restored.

sections.heading: Panels, isolations and coverage
sections.markdown:
A panel keeps passing its routine tests until the day it cannot be repaired, extended or reprogrammed because its maker no longer supports it. That day usually comes with a tenancy change: a fit-out needs new devices and new cause-and-effect programming, and the panel cannot take them. Unsupported panels are therefore end of life whatever their test results.

Detectors are covered and zones isolated during building works and cleaning, then forgotten. A building can run for months with floors effectively unprotected. Addressable panels show isolations; the question is whether anyone reads them.

Fit-outs add rooms, partitions, ceilings and voids without adding detectors; concealed spaces above ceilings and below floors are left unprotected where required; detectors end up too close to air supply diffusers, which blow smoke away from them.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Zones isolated for weeks | Isolation after works or nuisance alarms. Event log; works records. | Clear the isolations now, and manage future ones with a permit and a daily check. |
| New tenancy cannot be connected | Panel unsupported or at capacity. Vendor advice; panel loading. | Confirm vendor support and panel loading; plan replacement with a supported addressable system. |
| Detectors with no sensitivity readings for years | Detectors drifting out of their range. Sensitivity readings from an addressable panel, or tests on site; US Department of Defense guidance tests smoke detector sensitivity every five years (UFM 3-601-02). | Read or test sensitivity, and clean or replace detectors outside their marked range. |

sections.heading: Unwanted alarms and domestic alarms
sections.markdown:
Contaminated detectors, the wrong detector type for the space (smoke detectors in kitchens and near showers), cooking, steam, dust from works, and insects cause unwanted alarms. Brigades charge for repeated unwanted alarms in many jurisdictions; occupants learn to ignore alarms; and the response to repeated false alarms is often to isolate zones, which leaves areas unprotected.

Smoke alarms in dwellings are removed, painted over, disconnected after nuisance alarms, or simply past their ten-year life; interconnection between alarms fails; tenancies change without checks.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Repeated unwanted alarms from one area | Wrong detector type or contamination. Event log; detector type against the space. | Fit the right detector for the space, clean or replace contaminated detectors, and move detectors away from diffusers. |
| Smoke alarms in flats with a date more than ten years old | Alarms past their built-in life. Manufacture or expiry date on the alarm base. | Replace them with interconnected photoelectric alarms, hard-wired or with sealed ten-year batteries. |

sections.heading: Interfaces, warning and signalling
sections.markdown:
Over the years the interfaces the panel drives change: air handling units replaced, lifts modernised, access control upgraded, smoke control added. Unless the cause-and-effect matrix and interfaces are updated and tested together, lifts do not home, doors do not release, and smoke control does not start in a real fire.

Sounders and speakers that are inaudible in parts of the building, EWIS amplifiers with failed batteries, and messages that are unintelligible in noisy or reverberant spaces leave occupants unwarned.

Alarm signalling equipment that dials out over a copper line stops working when the line is retired; monitoring contracts lapse; dual-path signalling is reduced to one path. The panel alarms locally but nobody is called.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lifts did not home or doors did not release in a test | Interface or cause-and-effect fault. Interface test; matrix review. | Update the cause-and-effect matrix and run a full integrated test. |
| Brigade not called in a test | Signalling failure, often a retired line. Monitoring centre test; line type. | Test with the monitoring centre; upgrade to supported, preferably dual-path, signalling. |
| Alarm inaudible in parts of the building | Insufficient sounders or speakers after fit-outs. Sound level and intelligibility test against the limits for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Add sounders or speakers, or a voice system where intelligibility is required. |
| Alarm faint inside apartments with the entry door shut | Too little sound reaching the units. Sound level at the unit entry doors, or inside the units, against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Measure at the entry doors, and add sounders in the common areas or inside units where the level falls short. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Zones isolated or detectors covered in occupied areas; alarm signalling not reaching the brigade; inaudible warning; failed interfaces to lifts, doors or smoke control | safety · 4 Essential | Restore protection now; fire watch until done. |
| Panel failed or out of service | failure · 4 Essential | Restore now with interim fire watch. |
| Routine service, annual certification or domestic alarm requirements due | deadline · 4 Essential | At the prescribed interval or date. |
| Contaminated or aged detectors; repeated unwanted alarms; coverage gaps; matrix out of date | condition · 4 Essential | Repair and recommission in the near term. |
| Unsupported panel; detectors at end of life | lifecycle · 3 Important | Plan replacement before the next tenancy change. |
| No interface test on record; system not reviewed after fit-outs | check · 3 Important | Audit and full integrated test. |
| Isolated faults found and fixed at service | nil · 1 Routine | Routine maintenance. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A fire services engineer or fire safety consultant leads, with the maintenance contractor and, for complex buildings, a fire engineer. The checks below start at the panel and its event log, then walk the building and test the interfaces.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Records review | Service records against the required frequencies, annual statements, event logs, unwanted alarm history, cause-and-effect matrix, fire strategy and any performance solutions. |
| Panel inspection | Make, model, firmware, vendor support, spare capacity, isolations, faults, battery age and standby test. |
| Coverage survey | Against the current layout, including ceiling and floor voids where detection is required, detector types against spaces, and call points at exits. |
| Detector sampling | Sensitivity and contamination readings from the panel for addressable systems; functional tests of a sample. |
| Occupant warning test | Sound levels and, for voice systems, speech intelligibility in representative spaces, against the levels for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). |
| Signalling test | End to end with the monitoring centre, and identification of the communication path. |
| Full integrated test | Of the cause-and-effect matrix with every interface operating: air handling, smoke control, lifts, doors, sprinkler and suppression signals. |
| Domestic alarms | Type, power, interconnection and age in a sample of dwellings, or all where the law requires. |

The report should state compliance, coverage gaps, unwanted alarm causes, interface results, signalling path, panel support status, and a plan for repair or replacement.

sections.heading: Restoring, upgrading or replacing
sections.markdown:
Protection is restored first: covers removed and isolations cleared. After that, the work follows what the event log and the interface tests show, from cutting unwanted alarms to replacing an unsupported panel.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Restore protection | Remove covers, clear isolations, and manage future isolations through a permit and daily check. | At once, wherever detectors are covered or zones isolated. |
| Reduce unwanted alarms | The right detector for each space (heat or multi-sensor in kitchens and near bathrooms), clean or replace contaminated detectors, relocate detectors away from diffusers, and manage hot works. | Where unwanted alarms repeat from one area. |
| Coverage additions | Additions designed to the standard, with the zone plan and graphics updated. | Wherever fit-outs have left rooms or voids without detection. |
| Cause-and-effect update | Update the matrix and run full integrated testing. | Whenever any interfaced system changes. |
| Panel replacement | A supported addressable system, reusing compatible cabling where possible, with temporary protection during changeover. | Where the panel is unsupported or at capacity. |
| Detector replacement programme | Replace detectors on age, by floor or zone. | As detectors reach the end of their life. |
| Occupant warning upgrade | Additional sounders or speakers, or a voice system where intelligibility is required. | Where the alarm is inaudible or unintelligible in parts of the building. |
| Signalling upgrade | Supported, preferably dual-path, communications. | Before copper lines are retired, and wherever the brigade is not called in a test. |
| Domestic alarms | Interconnected photoelectric alarms, hard-wired or with ten-year sealed batteries. | Where required, and wherever alarms are missing or more than ten years old. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Routine servicing and annual certification are recurring contracts. Detector replacement is priced per device. Coverage additions per device, with design and reprogramming. Panel replacement is a lump-sum project including the panel, reprogramming, interfaces, commissioning and full integrated testing, with temporary fire watch or temporary panels during changeover. Signalling upgrades are a lump sum plus a recurring monitoring fee. Unwanted alarm charges are an operating cost that the remedies reduce.

Servicing, rectification and signalling are code compliance; detector and panel replacement are lifecycle; the integrated test is the check line that sizes the rest.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a look at the panel cannot: whether the system has been serviced and certified, what the event log shows, and whether the interfaces and signalling still work. Ask for them before relying on the annual statement.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Routine service records for the last twelve months against the required frequencies | Whether the system is serviced as often as required. |
| Current annual fire safety statement or essential safety measures report, with any qualifications | Whether the system was compliant at its last certification, and with what qualifications. |
| Panel make, model, firmware and vendor support status | Whether the panel can still be supported. |
| Event log extract showing faults, isolations and unwanted alarms | Where faults, isolations and unwanted alarms occur. |
| Cause-and-effect matrix and the latest full integrated test report | Whether the alarm still triggers everything it should. |
| Alarm signalling contract and communication path | Whether the brigade will be called, and over what line. |
| Zone block plan and as-built drawings | Whether the zones on the panel match the building as it now is. |
| Fire strategy or fire engineering report, and any performance solutions | What the system is relied on to do. |
| Domestic smoke alarm records for residential buildings | Whether homes in the building have working alarms. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Fire detection is misread when the annual statement is taken as proof of remaining life, when isolations are treated as temporary, and when unwanted alarms are blamed on the system as a whole.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| A current annual statement means the system is sound | A current annual statement establishes compliance at its date; it does not establish remaining life. A compliant system on an unsupported panel is at the end of its life, and isolated zones mean parts of the building are unprotected regardless of what the paperwork says. |
| Isolations are temporary | Zones isolated after works or nuisance alarms are often left for weeks, and leave parts of the building unprotected. Manage isolations through a permit and a daily check. |
| Unwanted alarms mean a faulty system | They usually come from the wrong detector for the space, contamination, or a detector next to a supply diffuser. The event log shows where, and the fix is the right detector in the right place. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market places duties on whoever controls a building's fire safety, sets standards for detection, warning and testing, and has rules for homes and for unwanted alarms. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Duties and certification | The National Construction Code sets required detection and warning by building class; systems are essential safety measures with annual certification (the Annual Fire Safety Statement in New South Wales and the annual essential safety measures report in Victoria). | The Regulatory Reform (Fire Safety) Order 2005 places duties on the responsible person; the Building Safety Act 2022 and the Fire Safety (England) Regulations 2022 add duties for higher-risk residential buildings. | NFPA 101 and the International Fire Code set where systems are required. |
| Design and testing | AS 1670.1 covers detection system design, AS 1670.4 emergency warning and intercommunication, and AS 1851 routine service at monthly, six-monthly and yearly frequencies. | BS 5839-1 covers non-domestic systems, with weekly call point tests and periodic servicing, and every device tested annually; BS 7273 covers interfaces. | NFPA 72 governs installation, inspection and testing, including annual functional testing of initiating devices and periodic smoke detector sensitivity testing; NFPA 4 covers integrated system testing. |
| Homes and unwanted alarms | Brigades charge for unwanted alarms; Queensland requires interconnected photoelectric smoke alarms in all dwellings by 1 January 2027. | BS 5839-6 covers dwellings; rented homes must have smoke alarms under the smoke and carbon monoxide alarm regulations. | Many jurisdictions charge for false alarms. |

sections.heading: Worked example: a compliant system on a panel nobody supports
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 2000s office has a current annual fire safety statement. Its panel's manufacturer no longer supports the model, two zones on the third floor have been isolated since a fit-out two months ago, and the alarm signal goes to the brigade over a copper line due to be retired.

The statement establishes compliance at its date, not remaining life. The isolated zones leave part of the building unprotected now, whatever the paperwork says: a safety finding. The unsupported panel is at the end of its life, and the copper line has a retirement date that the signalling must beat.

So the register carries the isolations as a safety line now, a signalling upgrade as a deadline line, panel replacement as a lifecycle line, and a cause-and-effect test after the fit-out as a check line.

thresholds.measure: Alarm level at unit entry doors (Class 2 and 3)
thresholds.rule: 85 dB(A) at the entry door with a smoke alarm system, or 100 dB(A) with a smoke detection system, in place of measuring inside the unit

source.title: NCC 2025 Volume One, Specification 20 Smoke detection and alarm systems

thresholds.rule: 75 dB(A) at the bedhead

source.title: Fire safety risk assessment: sleeping accommodation

thresholds.rule: At least 15 dB above the average ambient level; 75 dB(A) at the pillow in sleeping rooms

source.title: Audibility vs. intelligibility of fire alarm systems (FPE Extra, issue 69)

pages.title: Fire Pumping Systems
pages.question: How do fire pumps fail, how do you prove a pump will deliver in a fire, and which findings leave sprinklers and hydrants without enough water?
pages.answer: Fire pumps fail to start (flat diesel batteries, fuel problems, controllers left in manual, power isolated) or fail to deliver (worn impellers, blocked strainers, falling town main pressure). Only an annual flow test against the pump curve proves performance; many pumps have no usable test arrangement. A jockey pump starting constantly is masking a leak. Electric pumps fed after the main switch can lose power when the building is isolated in a fire.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about fire pumping systems; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Electric and diesel fire pumps, controllers

pages.searchTitle: Fire pumps: failure to start, performance decline, flow testing and power supply

questions.question: If the fire pump runs every week, does it work?
questions.answer: Not necessarily. A pump that starts and runs on weekly tests can still be unable to deliver the flow the sprinklers and hydrants need; only a flow test against its rating proves it.

questions.question: Why does the jockey pump keep starting?
questions.answer: Usually a leak or a passing valve somewhere in the system. A pressure decay test with the pumps isolated finds it.

questions.question: Why won't the diesel fire pump start reliably?
questions.answer: Usually the batteries, the fuel or the engine heater. A battery test and a fuel sample show which; starting batteries last 3 to 5 years.

questions.question: Where should a fire pump's power come from?
questions.answer: From ahead of the building's main switch, in fire-rated cable, so that switching off the building does not switch off the pump.

questions.question: How long do fire pumps last?
questions.answer: Pump casings and impellers 25 to 35 years, diesel engines 25 to 30, electric motors 20 to 30, controllers 15 to 20, and jockey pumps 10 to 15.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Fire pump problems show in the pump room, at the controller and the gauges, and in the test records, above all the flow test against the pump curve. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| In the pump room | Nameplates: rating, year; pump curve displayed | Performance, supply and relief |
| In the pump room | Controllers showing alarms or manual mode; selector switches in off | Starting, power and controllers |
| In the pump room | Diesel batteries, fuel level, engine heater, exhaust condition | Starting, power and controllers |
| In the pump room | Packing gland or seal leaks; corrosion; vibration | Performance, supply and relief |
| In the pump room | Jockey pump run counter; frequent starts | Jockey pumps and the pump room |
| In the pump room | Pressure gauges; test header and flow meter presence | Performance, supply and relief |
| In the pump room | Room temperature, ventilation, flooding signs, storage | Jockey pumps and the pump room |
| In the records | Weekly run test records | Investigation before the scope |
| In the records | Annual flow test results plotted against the pump curve | Performance, supply and relief |
| In the records | Diesel battery and fuel records | Starting, power and controllers |
| In the records | Tank inspection and cleaning records | Performance, supply and relief |
| In the records | Water authority pressure and flow information | Performance, supply and relief |
| In the records | Power supply arrangement for electric pumps | Starting, power and controllers |
| In the records | Controller status signalled to the fire panel | Starting, power and controllers |
| In the records | Relief valve discharge during weekly runs | Performance, supply and relief |
| In the records | Pump room access for the brigade and its signage | Jockey pumps and the pump room |

sections.heading: Types of fire pump
sections.markdown:
Fire pumps boost water pressure and flow to sprinklers, hydrants and hose reels where the town main cannot supply enough on its own. A pumpset comprises one or more duty pumps driven by electric motors or diesel engines, a small jockey (pressure maintenance) pump that keeps the system pressurised, controllers that start pumps automatically when pressure falls, test and flow measurement arrangements, and the suction supply from the main or from storage tanks. Diesel pumps also have fuel, batteries, cooling and exhaust systems.

| Component | Job | What goes wrong |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Electric duty pump and controller | Primary fire pump in many buildings | Supply not protected; controller faults; motor failure |
| Diesel duty pump | Independent of mains power; standby or duty | Fails to start (batteries, fuel); cooling; exhaust |
| Jockey pump | Keeps pressure up so duty pumps start only in a real demand | Runs constantly when the system leaks; masks leaks |
| Controllers | Start and supervise pumps; report to fire panel | Electronics; settings; obsolescence |
| Suction supply: town main, break tank, storage tanks | Water source | Low main pressure; tank sediment, corrosion, failed level controls |
| Test header and flow meter | Annual performance testing | Absent or unusable, so pumps are never flow tested |
| Pump room | Housing | Freezing; flooding; ventilation; access |

The power supply to an electric fire pump must keep it running in a fire: it is connected ahead of the main switch or from a protected supply, and its cables are fire-rated, so isolating the building does not stop the pump. Pump rooms are often separately fire-rated, with access for the brigade.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
A fire pump's casing and impeller last twenty-five to thirty-five years and its engine or motor twenty to thirty, while controllers last fifteen to twenty and starting batteries three to five. A pump that is never flow tested can lose performance for years without anyone noticing.

| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fire pumps (casing and impeller) | 25 to 35 years | Water quality; run time; cavitation |
| Electric motors | 20 to 30 years | Run time; damp |
| Diesel engines | 25 to 30 years | Exercise; maintenance |
| Controllers | 15 to 20 years | Vendor support |
| Jockey pumps | 10 to 15 years | Cycling |
| Starting batteries | 3 to 5 years | Temperature; charger |
| Steel tanks | 20 to 30 years | Internal corrosion; coatings |
| Concrete tanks | 40 years and more | Joints; leaks |

What shortens life: missed weekly runs, which leave seals dry, batteries flat and faults undetected; a leaking system that makes the jockey pump cycle constantly; cold pump rooms in winter; water quality and sediment drawn from tanks; cavitation from poor suction conditions.

sections.heading: Starting, power and controllers
sections.markdown:
Diesel pumps fail to start for the same reasons as standby generators: flat batteries, failed chargers, fuel problems, failed engine heaters. Electric pumps fail to start when their supply has been isolated, a controller fault is present, or settings have changed. A pump that does not start on a pressure drop leaves the sprinklers and hydrants on town main pressure alone.

Electric fire pumps connected after the main switch, or with non-fire-rated cabling, can lose power when the building is isolated in a fire, or when the cable burns. This is a design defect found in older buildings and after switchboard replacements.

Controllers left in manual or off after maintenance, start pressures set wrongly, and pumps set to stop automatically when they should run until manually stopped are common findings after service visits. The controller's status should be supervised by the fire alarm panel.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Diesel slow to start or fails | Batteries, fuel or heater. Battery test; fuel sample. | Test the batteries and sample the fuel; restore batteries, chargers, heater and fuel management. |
| Pump supply after the main switch | Design defect. Single-line diagram. | Reconnect the supply ahead of the main switch with fire-rated cable. |
| Run log shows short or missed pump runs | Runs too short to prove the pump and its driver. Run log against the required run and the limits for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Run each pump for the full period, recording start time, suction and discharge pressures, temperatures and fuel level. |

sections.heading: Performance, supply and relief
sections.markdown:
Impellers wear and erode, wear rings open up, and suction strainers block; the pump delivers less flow and pressure than its rating. Only an annual flow test against the pump's rated curve shows the decline. Pumps whose test arrangements were never installed or have become unusable are often never flow tested.

Town main pressures fall as utilities manage networks; break tanks and storage tanks lose capacity to sediment, corrosion and failed inlet valves; suction pipes blocked or undersized cause cavitation. The pump can only boost what reaches it.

Pumps running against closed outlets (churn) heat the water in the casing; circulation relief valves and pressure relief valves prevent damage and over-pressure. Stuck or wrongly set relief valves either waste water continuously or let pressures exceed what pipework and fittings are rated for.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Flow test below the rated curve | Impeller wear, blocked strainer, or suction restriction. Suction pressure during test; strainer inspection. | Check suction pressure and the strainer; overhaul the pump, or replace it where performance cannot be restored. |
| Cavitation noise during tests | Low suction pressure or blocked suction. Suction gauge; tank level. | Check suction pressure and tank level, and clear the suction. |
| No flow tests on record | No usable test arrangement. Inspection. | Install a flow meter or test header so the pump can be tested. |
| Supply pressure lower than at the last test | Town main or tank supply decline. Flow test results compared with the previous and acceptance readings and the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Trace the decline with the water authority or by tank inspection, and confirm the pump can still meet the design with the supply it now has. |
| Boosted hydrant outlets below pressure in a test | Pump or relay pump short of its duty. Pressure at the most disadvantaged outlet in each zone, against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Test at the most disadvantaged outlets; overhaul or re-select the pump, or correct the pipework. |

sections.heading: Jockey pumps and the pump room
sections.markdown:
A jockey pump that starts frequently is replacing water lost through a leak or a passing valve. It wears out quickly, and the leak it masks may be corroding pipework or wasting water.

Pump rooms freeze in cold climates, flood in basements, overheat in summer, and are used for storage. Diesel exhaust leaks and fuel spills create further hazards.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Jockey pump starts every few minutes | System leak or passing valve. Pressure decay test with pumps isolated. | Pressure decay test with the pumps isolated; find and repair the leak or passing valve. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pump fails to start; controller in off or manual; pump supply unprotected; performance well below design | safety · 4 Essential | Restore now; fire watch and brigade notification. |
| Pump failed or out of service | failure · 4 Essential | Repair now with impairment management. |
| Weekly runs and annual flow tests due | deadline · 4 Essential | At the prescribed interval. |
| Performance decline; jockey cycling; battery or fuel issues; tank deterioration | condition · 3 Important | Repair in the near term. |
| Pumps or controllers at end of life | lifecycle · 3 Important | Replace. |
| No flow test record; town main pressure not checked recently | check · 3 Important | Flow test and supply check. |
| Normal | nil · 1 Routine | Routine. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A fire services engineer with the pump maintenance contractor. The checks below start in the pump room, then compare the flow test record with the pump curve.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Records review | Weekly run logs against the run times for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market), annual flow tests, battery and fuel records, tank inspections. |
| Inspection | Of pumps, motors, engines, controllers, jockey pump, pipework, valves, tanks and pump room. |
| Flow test | At churn, rated flow and peak flow, plotted against the manufacturer's curve and the system's design requirement. |
| Supply check | Town main pressure and flow, tank capacity and condition. |
| Power supply review | For electric pumps: connection point and cable rating. |
| Leak investigation | Where the jockey pump cycles frequently. |
| Controller testing | Automatic start on pressure drop, alarm signals to the fire panel, and phase reversal and power failure alarms on electric controllers. |

The report should state whether pumps deliver the required performance, the reliability of starting and power, the adequacy of the water supply, and works needed.

sections.heading: Restoring, overhauling or replacing
sections.markdown:
Starting reliability and supervision come first, because a pump that does not start, or whose fault nobody sees, gives no protection. After that, the work follows what the flow test shows against the pump curve.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Overhaul | Impeller and wear ring replacement, seals, bearings and alignment. | Where performance has declined but can be restored. |
| Starting reliability | A battery replacement cycle, chargers, engine heaters and fuel management. | Wherever a diesel pump is slow to start or fails. |
| Controller replacement | A new controller. | Where the controller is faulty or at the end of its life. |
| Test arrangements | A flow meter or test header so annual testing is possible. | Wherever the pump cannot be flow tested. |
| Power supply correction | Reconnect ahead of the main switch with fire-rated cable. | Wherever the pump's supply could be switched off with the building's. |
| Leak repair | Repair the leak or passing valve. | Where the jockey pump cycles. |
| Tank works | Clean, recoat, reline or replace tanks, and repair level controls. | Where tanks corrode, leak or lose capacity. |
| Pump replacement | A new pump sized to current design requirements. | Where performance cannot be restored. |
| Pump room | Heating, drainage, ventilation and clearance. | Where the room is cold, wet, poorly ventilated or used for storage. |
| Relief valves | Reset or replace circulation and pressure relief valves, and pipe the discharges to drain. | Where relief valves discharge wrongly or the pump overheats on churn. |
| Supervision | Signal controller mode, pump running and power failure to the fire panel. | So faults are seen as they happen. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Weekly and annual testing are recurring. Overhauls are lump sums per pump. Controller and pump replacement are lump-sum projects with temporary measures during the outage. Power supply correction is a lump sum. Tank cleaning recurs; relining and replacement are lump sums.

Testing and safety rectification are code compliance; overhaul and replacement are lifecycle; repairs are repairs and maintenance.

Pump room works and tank relining often require the system to be impaired; temporary pumps, fire watches and brigade notification are part of the project cost.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a weekly run cannot: whether the pump still delivers its rated flow, whether a diesel will start, and whether a fault would be noticed. Ask for them before relying on the pump.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Weekly pump run records | Whether the pump starts and runs every week. |
| Annual flow test reports plotted against the pump curve | Whether the pump still delivers its rated flow. |
| Diesel battery and fuel records | Whether a diesel pump will start when it is needed. |
| Tank inspection and cleaning records | Whether the stored water is sound and sufficient. |
| Single-line diagram showing the fire pump power supply | Whether the pump's power could be switched off with the building's. |
| Pump and controller installation dates | How old the pump and controller are. |
| Water supply pressure and flow data | Whether the town main still supplies what the design assumed. |
| Controller alarm and supervision test records | Whether pump faults reach the fire panel. |
| Impairment records for pump outages | When the pump has been out of service, and how that was managed. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Fire pumps are misread when a weekly run is taken as proof of performance, when a cycling jockey pump is blamed on the pump, and when the pump's power supply is never traced.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| It runs every week, so it works | A fire pump that has not been flow tested against its rating is unproven. A pump that starts and runs on weekly tests can still be unable to deliver the flow the sprinklers and hydrants need. |
| The jockey pump is faulty | A jockey pump that starts every few minutes is usually responding to a leak or a passing valve in the system. A pressure decay test with the pumps isolated finds it. |
| The pump's power is secure | A pump supplied from after the building's main switch can be switched off with the building in a fire. Its supply belongs ahead of the main switch, in fire-rated cable. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets standards for fire pump installations and for testing them, including flow tests against the pump curve. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Installation | AS 2941 governs fire pump installations; water authorities publish main pressure information for design. | BS EN 12845 and the LPC Rules set sprinkler pump requirements; BS 9990 covers wet rising mains. | NFPA 20 governs installation. |
| Testing and certification | AS 1851 sets routine service, including weekly pumpset tests and annual flow tests; fire pumps are essential safety measures with annual certification. | Weekly automatic start tests apply, and insurers often set additional pump testing requirements. | NFPA 25 sets testing, including weekly no-flow runs for diesel pumps, monthly for electric pumps (or weekly where required), and annual flow tests against the pump curve. |

In all three jurisdictions, insurers and the fire brigade commonly need notice before a fire pump is taken out of service, and impairment procedures apply until it is restored.

sections.heading: Worked example: a pump that starts but has never been flow tested
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 1990s warehouse has a diesel fire pump that starts and runs on its weekly test. There is no flow test on record because the installation has no test header, the jockey pump starts every few minutes, and the engine's starting batteries are six years old.

A pump that starts and runs every week is still unproven: without a flow test, nobody knows whether it delivers the flow the sprinklers need. The cycling jockey pump points to a leak or a passing valve. Six-year-old batteries are past their three-to-five-year life, which threatens the one thing the weekly run does prove.

So the register carries the batteries as a condition line now, a test header and flow test as a check line that may become an overhaul or replacement, and the leak behind the jockey cycling found and repaired.

pages.title: Fireplaces
pages.question: How do fireplaces and heaters fail, and which findings mean stop using them?
pages.answer: The main risks are carbon monoxide and fire. Flued gas heaters with cracked heat exchangers or blocked flues, and fires that spill under negative pressure, put carbon monoxide into homes; unflued heaters release combustion products indoors. Wood heaters too close to combustibles or on small hearths ignite surroundings; creosote causes flue fires. Any sign of spillage or carbon monoxide means stop use until tested; service gas heaters regularly and fit carbon monoxide alarms.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about fireplaces; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Ornamental, decorative and functional fireplaces \u2014 period-stock feature element

pages.searchTitle: Fireplaces and heaters: carbon monoxide, spillage, clearances, flues and unflued heaters

questions.question: What should I do if my gas heater leaves soot?
questions.answer: Stop using it until a licensed gas fitter has tested it. Soot points to incomplete combustion or spillage, and so to carbon monoxide.

questions.question: Can exhaust fans make a heater dangerous?
questions.answer: Yes. Rangehoods, bathroom fans and dryers can depressurise a tight home and pull combustion products down the flue into the room.

questions.question: How close can a wood heater be to timber?
questions.answer: No closer than its clearances allow; scorched timber nearby means it is too close.

questions.question: Are unflued gas heaters safe in bedrooms?
questions.answer: No. They release combustion products and moisture into the room, and are restricted in schools and some jurisdictions.

questions.question: How long do wood heaters last?
questions.answer: 15 to 25 years; gas heaters and log fires last 10 to 20.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Fireplace problems show as soot, yellow flames, scorched timber and cracked glass, fans and joinery near the appliance, and in service, installation and sweeping records. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On site | Soot staining above fireplaces or heaters | Carbon monoxide, spillage and unflued heaters |
| On site | Heaters close to combustible walls or mantels; small hearths | Clearances and alterations |
| On site | Gas heaters without service tags; yellow flames | Carbon monoxide, spillage and unflued heaters |
| On site | No carbon monoxide alarm | Carbon monoxide, spillage and unflued heaters |
| On site | Cracked fireboxes and door glass | Flues, conversions and emissions |
| In the records | Gas heater service records | Carbon monoxide, spillage and unflued heaters |
| In the records | Installation certificates | Clearances and alterations |
| In the records | Chimney sweeping records | Flues, conversions and emissions |
| In the records | Doors and windows sealed tightly in a home with an open fireplace or gas heater, limiting combustion air | Carbon monoxide, spillage and unflued heaters |
| In the records | Exhaust fans near heaters, which can cause spillage | Carbon monoxide, spillage and unflued heaters |
| In the records | Timber mantels and shelving installed close to fireboxes | Clearances and alterations |
| In the records | Smoke smell in the house after the fire has burned down | Flues, conversions and emissions |
| In the records | Heaters with dated or missing compliance plates | Clearances and alterations |
| In the records | Wet or painted timber stored for burning, which builds creosote quickly | Flues, conversions and emissions |

sections.heading: Types of fireplace and heater
sections.markdown:
Fireplaces and heaters with flues include open masonry fireplaces, enclosed wood heaters (slow combustion stoves), gas log fires and flued gas space heaters. They combine fire, combustion products and a flue, so their risks are fire spreading to the building, carbon monoxide entering living spaces, and smoke and emissions. Chimneys and flues are covered on their own page; this page covers the appliance, hearth, surrounds and the room.

| Type | Where it is found | Main risks |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Open fireplaces | Older houses | Sparks and embers; poor draw; heat loss |
| Wood heaters | Houses, especially rural | Clearances to combustibles; flue fires; emissions |
| Gas log fires | Houses and apartments | Flue spillage; servicing |
| Flued gas space heaters | Houses | Carbon monoxide from cracked heat exchangers or blocked flues |
| Unflued gas heaters | Older homes | Combustion products indoors; banned or restricted in some places |
| Decorative and ethanol fireplaces | Apartments | Fuel handling fires |

Many older homes have fireplaces that are no longer used but remain open to the flue, while others have been converted to gas or fitted with inserts; the condition of each, and whether the flue still suits the appliance, is often unknown.

For assessment, fireplaces are graded by the risk they pose to occupants as much as by their condition; a sound-looking heater can still spill carbon monoxide.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Wood heaters last fifteen to twenty-five years and gas heaters and log fires ten to twenty, while door seals and glass last five to ten and hearths and surrounds the life of the building. Changes around an appliance, such as fans, airtightness and new joinery, can make it unsafe long before it wears out.

| Item | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Wood heaters | 15 to 25 years | Use; firebox wear |
| Gas heaters and log fires | 10 to 20 years | Servicing |
| Hearths and surrounds | Life of the building | Cracking; alterations |
| Door seals and glass | 5 to 10 years | Heat |

What shortens life: no servicing of gas heaters; burning wet or treated timber; alterations that bring combustible materials close.

Appliance life depends heavily on use and servicing. Gas heaters that are serviced regularly last much longer and stay safer than those left for years; wood heater fireboxes, baffles and bricks wear with heavy use and wet fuel. Hearths and surrounds last as long as the building unless cracked by heat or altered. The useful life of wood heating is also being shortened by emissions rules and by electrification, which make replacement with heat pumps more attractive than like-for-like renewal.

sections.heading: Carbon monoxide, spillage and unflued heaters
sections.markdown:
Gas space heaters with cracked heat exchangers or blocked flues, and fires whose flues spill under negative pressure from exhaust fans, put carbon monoxide into homes. Deaths from unserviced gas heaters have led to safety campaigns and servicing advice.

Kitchen rangehoods, bathroom fans and clothes dryers depressurise tightly sealed homes, pulling combustion products down flues and into rooms. Spillage is worst when several fans run together, which is why testing must be done under worst-case conditions.

Unflued gas heaters release combustion products and moisture into rooms; they are restricted in schools and some jurisdictions.

Carbon monoxide gives no warning people can rely on. A heater that looks and sounds normal can spill it because its heat exchanger has cracked, its flue is blocked, or the house's exhaust fans are pulling air down the flue. When there is any sign of spillage, the only safe assumption is that the appliance is unsafe until tested.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Soot above a gas heater | Incomplete combustion or spillage. Service; CO test. | Stop using it; have a licensed gas fitter service it and test for carbon monoxide. |
| Headaches when the heater runs | Carbon monoxide. CO test (Thresholds by market). | Stop using the heater, ventilate the room, and have the heater tested before it runs again. |
| An open fire or open-flued heater near a strong exhaust fan | Negative pressure pulling combustion products down the flue. A spillage test with the fans running together. | Interlock or balance the fans, or replace with a room-sealed appliance. |
| An unflued gas heater in a bedroom | Combustion products and moisture released into a sleeping room. The heater's type and location. | Remove it from the bedroom, and give the owners guidance on unflued heaters. |

sections.heading: Clearances and alterations
sections.markdown:
Renovations bring new timber mantels, shelving, cabinetry and wall linings close to fireplaces and heaters, often without anyone checking clearances, and new airtightness reduces the combustion air an appliance needs.

Wood heaters and fireplaces installed too close to timber framing, linings, furniture or mantels, or on inadequate hearths, ignite nearby materials over time.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Scorched timber near a wood heater | Inadequate clearance. Measurement. | Correct the clearance with a heat shield, a larger hearth, or relocation. |
| A new timber mantel or shelving close to the firebox | A renovation without a clearance check. The distance measured against the appliance's clearances. | Remove or shield the combustible material. |
| Hearth small, cracked or level with a timber floor | Hearth too small for the opening. Hearth extent measured against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Extend or replace the hearth in non-combustible material. |

sections.heading: Flues, conversions and emissions
sections.markdown:
Gas log fires and inserts fitted into old masonry fireplaces depend on flues that may be cracked or unsuited, and on correct flue liners and terminations.

Creosote from slow-burning wet wood builds up and ignites in flues; nests and debris block flues; see the chimney page.

Wood heaters produce fine particle pollution indoors and outdoors; regulations restrict emissions and, in some areas, use.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Smoke into the room | Poor draw or blocked flue. Flue inspection. | Inspect and sweep the flue, fit a bird guard, and check for negative pressure. |
| A gas log fire in an old masonry fireplace with no visible liner | A conversion relying on an unsuited flue. A flue inspection for cracks, the liner and the termination. | Fit a correct liner and termination, or decommission the fire. |
| Chimney ending below the ridge or a nearby taller part of the building | Poor draught and smoke re-entry. Terminal height measured against the building around it and the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Extend the flue or fit a suitable terminal. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Carbon monoxide or spillage; inadequate clearances; unflued heaters in bedrooms | safety · 4 Essential | Stop use now. |
| Appliance failed | failure · 4 Essential | Repair or replace. |
| Gas safety checks due in rented homes | deadline · 4 Essential | At the prescribed interval. |
| Worn seals and glass | condition · 4 Essential | Repair. |
| Appliance at end of life | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Replace or decommission. |
| Service history unknown | check · 3 Important | Service and test. |
| Normal | nil · 1 Routine | Routine. |

Carbon monoxide findings are always graded as safety regardless of how old or new the appliance is, because the consequence is death; clearance and flue defects follow closely because they cause house fires.

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A licensed gas fitter for gas appliances and a qualified installer or chimney sweep for solid fuel, with the building surveyor. The checks below test each gas appliance for carbon monoxide spillage with the house's fans running, measure clearances to anything combustible, and inspect the flues.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Gas appliance service | With carbon monoxide spillage testing under worst-case conditions (exhaust fans running, doors closed). |
| Clearance check | Of wood heaters and fireplaces to combustible materials and hearth size against the installation standard. |
| Flue inspection | And sweeping. |
| Carbon monoxide alarm check | . |
| Compliance check | Of installation certificates and emissions ratings. |
| Occupant interview | Symptoms when appliances run, smoke or smells, and how often appliances are used and serviced. |

The report should state whether each appliance is safe to use, and repairs, replacement or decommissioning.

Testing should be repeated after any renovation that changes airtightness or adds exhaust fans.

Record results for each appliance separately.

sections.heading: Testing, correcting and replacing
sections.markdown:
Any sign of carbon monoxide or spillage comes first: stop using the appliance until a licensed gas fitter has tested it. After that, the fix depends on whether the fault is in the appliance, its installation or the house around it, since each needs a different remedy.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Servicing | Service gas heaters at the recommended interval, commonly every two years. | On every gas heater. |
| Replacement | Replace cracked or unsafe appliances, including older flued gas heaters that fail testing. | Wherever an appliance fails testing. |
| Clearances | Correct clearances with heat shields, larger hearths or relocation. | Wherever combustibles are too close. |
| Flue sweeping | Sweep flues and fit bird guards. | On a regular cycle for wood fires. |
| Carbon monoxide alarms | Carbon monoxide alarms in rooms with fuel-burning appliances. | In every such room. |
| Unflued heaters | Remove unflued heaters from bedrooms and sensitive buildings. | Wherever they remain. |
| Decommissioning | Decommission unused fireplaces and seal and ventilate their flues, or convert to electric heating as part of electrification. | Where fireplaces are unused, or the home is electrifying. |
| Combustion air | Provide dedicated air supply to appliances in airtight homes, or replace with room-sealed appliances. | In airtight homes with fuel-burning appliances. |
| Spillage controls | Interlock or balance exhaust fans in homes with open-flued appliances. | In homes with open-flued appliances and exhaust fans. |
| Owner guidance | Owner guidance on dry firewood, flue cleaning intervals and never running unflued heaters in closed bedrooms. | In every home with a fireplace or heater. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Servicing and sweeping recur. Appliance replacement is per unit. Clearance corrections are itemised. Decommissioning is a small lump sum per fireplace. Safety items are immediate; servicing is recurring; replacement is lifecycle.

Carbon monoxide alarms and servicing are inexpensive compared with the risk they control. Replacing an older flued gas heater or wood heater with a heat pump may cost more up front but removes the carbon monoxide and flue risks, and often qualifies for energy incentives.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a look at the heater cannot: when it was last serviced and tested, whether a licensed fitter installed it, and what has changed around it. Ask for them before the heater is used again.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Gas heater service records | When each gas heater was last serviced and tested. |
| Installation certificates | Whether the appliance was installed and certified properly. |
| Chimney sweeping records | When the flue was last swept. |
| Carbon monoxide alarm details | Whether carbon monoxide alarms are fitted and working. |
| Emissions ratings of wood heaters | Whether wood heaters meet emissions rules. |
| Records of renovations near heaters or fireplaces | Whether renovations brought combustibles close to the appliance. |
| Electrification or heater replacement plans | Whether the heater is due to be replaced. |
| Any incidents involving smoke, soot or carbon monoxide | Whether there have been smoke, soot or carbon monoxide incidents. |
| Wood heater emissions compliance plates and model details | Which wood heater model is installed, and whether it complies. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Fireplaces are misread when signs of carbon monoxide are put down to an old heater's quirks, when every fault is blamed on the appliance, and when an appliance is assumed to stay as safe as when it was installed.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| It always smells like that | Any sign of carbon monoxide or flue spillage means stop using the appliance until a licensed gas fitter has tested it. |
| The heater is faulty | Separate appliance faults (servicing, cracked heat exchangers, worn seals) from installation faults (clearances, flues, combustion air) and from house effects (negative pressure from fans and airtightness), because each needs a different fix. |
| It was safe when it was installed | Renovations bring timber mantels and joinery close to fireplaces, new airtightness reduces combustion air, and new exhaust fans pull combustion products down flues. An appliance can become unsafe without anything happening to it. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets rules for installing and servicing gas and solid fuel appliances, their clearances and flues, carbon monoxide alarms, and wood heater emissions. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Installation, safety checks and emissions | AS/NZS 2918 covers installation of solid fuel heating appliances; AS/NZS 4012 and 4013 set wood heater efficiency and emissions; AS/NZS 5601.1 covers gas appliances; state gas regulators recommend regular servicing of gas heaters. | The Gas Safety (Installation and Use) Regulations 1998 require annual gas safety checks in rented homes; Approved Document J covers combustion appliances; smoke control areas and Ecodesign rules restrict wood burning; carbon monoxide alarms are required with fixed combustion appliances in many homes. | NFPA 211 covers chimneys, fireplaces and vents; the EPA sets new wood heater emissions standards; the International Residential and Fuel Gas Codes cover installation; many states require carbon monoxide alarms. |

Rental minimum standards in several places also set heater requirements.

sections.heading: Worked example: a gas heater after a renovation
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 1980s house was renovated with new windows, a powerful kitchen rangehood and a timber mantel around its flued gas heater. Since then, soot has appeared above the heater, the occupants report headaches on cold evenings, and the heater has no service record for six years.

Soot and headaches point to carbon monoxide: stop using the heater until a licensed gas fitter has tested it. Then separate the causes. The heater may have a cracked heat exchanger after six years without service; the house now pulls air down the flue through a tighter envelope and a stronger rangehood; and the new mantel may sit inside the clearance.

So the register carries the heater as a safety line, out of use until tested, a spillage test with the rangehood running, the mantel's clearance checked, carbon monoxide alarms, and a room-sealed or electric replacement if the heater fails.

pages.title: Flooring
pages.question: How do floor finishes fail, and which flooring findings are safety or neighbour issues?
pages.answer: Flooring fails mostly from moisture and movement. Slabs without vapour barriers or not dried debond vinyl and resin and cup timber; tiled floors without movement joints crack and tent; hard floors in apartments without acoustic underlays cause noise disputes. Polished and glazed floors become slippery when wet, and lifted tiles and carpet edges trip people. Test older vinyl tiles for asbestos before removing them.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about flooring; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
