pages.searchTitle: Flooring: lifting vinyl, cupped timber, tenting tiles, noise, slips and asbestos tiles

questions.question: Why is new vinyl lifting?
questions.answer: Usually moisture rising through the slab. Test the slab's relative humidity, and dry it or lay a surface membrane before new flooring.

questions.question: Do old vinyl floor tiles contain asbestos?
questions.answer: Often. They are safe in place but release fibres when broken up or sanded; test before any work.

questions.question: Why are the floor tiles lifting in a ridge?
questions.answer: No movement joints. Cut joints at the edges and across large areas, and relay the lifted tiles.

questions.question: Do hard floors in apartments need acoustic underlay?
questions.answer: Usually, under strata by-laws; without it, footsteps carry to the unit below.

questions.question: How long does flooring last?
questions.answer: Timber and tiles 30 to 50 years, vinyl 15 to 25, laminate 10 to 20, and carpet 8 to 15.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Flooring problems show as cupped, bubbling, cracked or ridged finishes, worn paths and slippery entries, old vinyl tiles, and in moisture tests, approvals and incident records. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On site | Timber boards cupped or gapped; vinyl bubbling or lifting | Moisture and substrates |
| On site | Tiles cracked, hollow-sounding or ridged | Tile cracking and tenting |
| On site | Worn carpet paths and frayed tile edges | Noise, wear and cleaning |
| On site | Hard floors in upper apartments with complaints below | Noise, wear and cleaning |
| On site | Older vinyl tiles of small square formats | Slips, trips and asbestos |
| On site | Slippery entries and wet areas | Slips, trips and asbestos |
| In the records | Moisture test results before flooring | Moisture and substrates |
| In the records | Strata approvals and by-laws for hard floors | Noise, wear and cleaning |
| In the records | Asbestos register | Slips, trips and asbestos |
| In the records | Slip incidents | Slips, trips and asbestos |
| In the records | Cracks in vinyl or tiles following a straight line, reflecting a joint or crack in the slab below | Moisture and substrates |
| In the records | Dark discolouration or adhesive bleeding at vinyl seams, signs of moisture | Moisture and substrates |
| In the records | Gaps between timber boards widening in dry weather and closing in wet | Moisture and substrates |
| In the records | Grit and water tracked inside entries, wearing and dulling floors | Noise, wear and cleaning |

sections.heading: Types of flooring
sections.markdown:
Flooring is the finish layer people walk on: carpet, vinyl sheet and tiles, timber (solid, engineered and parquet), laminate, ceramic and stone tiles, polished concrete and resin floors, laid over screeds, underlays and the structural floor. Flooring is judged on wear and appearance, but its failures also include slips and trips, acoustic complaints between apartments, moisture-driven failures that start in the slab below, and hazardous materials in older vinyl tiles and adhesives.

| Type | Where it is found | What commonly fails |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Carpet | Offices, apartments, hotels | Wear, stains, trips at joins |
| Vinyl sheet and tiles | Healthcare, kitchens, apartments | Moisture debonding; seams; older tiles may contain asbestos |
| Solid and engineered timber | Homes, apartments, offices | Cupping and gapping from moisture; acoustic complaints |
| Laminate | Homes and apartments | Swelling at joints; acoustic |
| Ceramic and stone tiles | Entries, wet areas, kitchens | Cracking, tenting, slips when wet |
| Polished concrete and resin | Commercial and modern homes | Cracking; slips; coating wear |

In offices the base-building floor finish usually belongs to the owner and tenant flooring to the tenant; in apartments flooring is usually the owner's, with by-laws controlling changes.

The engine should treat flooring by space: the same finish can be fine in a bedroom and a hazard in a wet entry.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Timber floors last thirty to fifty years with refinishing and tiles thirty to fifty, while vinyl lasts fifteen to twenty-five, laminate ten to twenty and carpet eight to fifteen. Moisture from below and poor substrates end more floors early than wear does.

| Type | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Commercial carpet tiles | 10 to 15 years | Traffic; quality |
| Residential carpet | 8 to 12 years | Use; tenancy turnover |
| Vinyl | 15 to 25 years | Traffic; moisture below |
| Timber | 30 to 50 years with refinishing | Moisture; wear |
| Laminate | 10 to 20 years | Moisture |
| Ceramic and stone tiles | 30 to 50 years | Movement; installation |

What shortens life: moisture from slabs without vapour barriers, leaks and wet cleaning; missing movement joints in tiled floors; heavy traffic and grit; poor substrate preparation.

Floor life depends on traffic, grit control at entries, cleaning practices and moisture in the substrate. A good floor laid on a damp slab can fail within months, while a modest floor on a dry, well-prepared substrate with good matting can last decades.

sections.heading: Moisture and substrates
sections.markdown:
Moisture rising through concrete slabs debonds vinyl and resin, swells and cups timber, and causes adhesives to fail; old slabs without vapour barriers and new slabs not dried before flooring are the usual causes. Timber also cups from leaks and humidity.

Self-levelling compounds that crack or debond, screeds that are weak or uneven, and timber subfloors that move transmit their defects through the finish: cracks reflect through vinyl and tiles, and uneven substrates cause trips and premature wear.

Moisture rising through a slab is invisible until it lifts the floor. Slabs without vapour barriers, and new slabs covered before they dried, both carry it, and a new floor laid on such a slab fails the same way as the last unless the slab is tested and the moisture dealt with first.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Vinyl or resin lifting across a slab | Moisture vapour from the slab. In-situ relative humidity test. | Test the slab's relative humidity; dry it, or lay a surface membrane before new flooring. |
| Timber cupping | Moisture from below or a leak. Moisture readings. | Find and stop the moisture or leak, then let the boards settle before refinishing or replacing them. |
| Cracks in vinyl or tiles running in a straight line | A crack or joint in the substrate reflecting through. The line matches a slab joint or screed crack. | Repair the substrate before replacing the finish. |
| Dark staining or adhesive bleeding at vinyl seams | Moisture attacking the adhesive. Discoloured seams, with high in-situ humidity readings. | Test the slab, and lay a surface membrane before relaying. |

sections.heading: Tile cracking and tenting
sections.markdown:
Tiled floors laid without movement joints at perimeters and across large areas crack, debond and lift in a ridge (tenting) as the slab and tiles move with temperature and shrinkage.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tiles ridging along a line | No movement joints. Joint inspection. | Cut movement joints, and relay the lifted tiles. |

sections.heading: Slips, trips and asbestos
sections.markdown:
Floors hurt people in two ways: by tripping or slipping them, and, in older buildings, by releasing asbestos fibres when old vinyl tiles and their adhesives are broken up. Both are safety findings.

Older vinyl floor tiles and their adhesives commonly contain asbestos; they are safe in place but release fibres when broken up or sanded.

Polished and glazed surfaces become slippery when wet; lifted tiles, curled carpet edges and changes in level trip people.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Slips on entry tiles | Low wet slip resistance. Slip test. | Apply a slip treatment or replace the finish, and add entry matting. |
| Small square vinyl tiles in an older building | Possible asbestos in the tiles or adhesive. The asbestos register, and testing before any work. | Test first; have a licensed contractor remove them, or encapsulate them under new flooring. |
| Lips at thresholds, transitions or lifted boards | Trip hazard. Level change measured against the limits for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Fit a transition strip or ramp, or relay the floor. |

sections.heading: Noise, wear and cleaning
sections.markdown:
Hard floors in apartments, especially timber and tile laid over carpet areas without acoustic underlays, transmit footsteps to the unit below, generating complaints and by-law disputes.

Traffic paths wear carpet, scratch timber and wear through coatings; grit tracked in accelerates wear.

Wrong cleaning chemicals strip coatings, polish stone, soften adhesives and leave slippery residues.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Noise complaints after a renovation | Hard floor without acoustic underlay. Floor construction; acoustic test (Thresholds by market). | Require a tested acoustic underlay under hard floors, as the by-laws allow. |
| Coatings stripped, or stone polished slippery, after cleaning | The wrong cleaning chemicals. The damage follows a change of products or contractor. | Change the cleaning specification, and restore the finish. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Trip hazards; slippery floors with incidents; damaged asbestos-containing tiles | safety · 4 Essential | Make safe now. |
| Floor failed (lifting, tenting) | failure · 3 Important | Repair now. |
| By-law or tribunal orders on noise | deadline · 3 Important | As required. |
| Wear; minor cupping; stains | condition · 2 Planned | Repair in the near term. |
| Flooring at end of life | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Replace. |
| Moisture or asbestos status unknown | check · 2 Planned | Test before works. |
| Normal | nil · 1 Routine | Routine. |

Flooring findings rarely reach safety grade except for trip and slip hazards and disturbed asbestos tiles; most are condition and lifecycle items, but moisture-driven failures recur until the cause is fixed.

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A building surveyor or flooring specialist leads, with an asbestos assessor for older floors and an acoustic consultant where noise is the issue. The checks below map failures by area, since where they sit points to the cause, test the slab for moisture and old tiles for asbestos, and test entry floors wet.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Condition survey | Of flooring by area: wear, lifting, cracking, cupping and trip edges. |
| Moisture testing | Of slabs by in-situ relative humidity probes before new flooring, and of timber floors where cupping occurs. |
| Tile inspection | Tapping for hollow tiles, checking for movement joints. |
| Slip resistance testing | Of floors at entries, wet areas and ramps. |
| Acoustic testing | Of impact sound between apartments where complaints exist. |
| Asbestos sampling | Of older vinyl tiles and adhesives before removal. |

The report should give causes of failure, safety items, and replacement or repair recommendations.

Before replacing a failed floor, establish the cause, or the replacement will fail the same way.

For apartment noise disputes, test the floor as built rather than relying on product data, because installation details such as perimeter isolation decide the result.

sections.heading: Repairing, preparing and replacing
sections.markdown:
Trip hazards, slippery floors with incidents and damaged asbestos-containing tiles come first. After that, the cause beneath the floor is dealt with, whether moisture, substrate or missing movement joints, before any new finish goes down, or it fails the same way.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Moisture mitigation | Moisture mitigation with surface membranes or proper drying before new flooring. | Wherever the slab tests wet. |
| Movement joints | Movement joints cut into tiled floors, with lifted tiles relaid. | Where tiles crack or tent. |
| Acoustic underlays | Acoustic underlays under hard floors in apartments, required by by-laws. | Wherever hard floors are laid over homes. |
| Slip treatments | Slip treatments or replacement finishes in wet and entry areas, with entry matting. | Where floors are slippery when wet. |
| Trip hazard repair | Relay lifted tiles, restretch or replace carpet, fit transition strips. | Wherever tiles lift, carpet curls or levels change. |
| Refinishing timber | Refinishing timber floors rather than replacing them. | Where timber is worn but sound. |
| Asbestos removal or encapsulation | Licensed removal of asbestos-containing tiles and adhesives, or leaving them encapsulated under new flooring. | Wherever old tiles test positive. |
| Replacement | Replacement on cycle with products suited to the traffic and moisture conditions. | At the end of the floor's life. |
| Substrate repair | Remove failed screeds and levelling compounds before new flooring. | Where screeds or levelling compounds have failed. |
| Entry matting | Entry matting long enough to remove grit and water, protecting floors throughout the building. | At every entrance. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Flooring is priced by area. Moisture membranes add to the cost of new flooring but prevent repeat failures. Acoustic underlays add modestly. Asbestos removal adds licensed removal and clearance. Replacement in occupied buildings is staged, with furniture moves.

Safety items are immediate; replacement is lifecycle; repairs are repairs and maintenance; tenant-caused damage is recoverable.

Investigating moisture costs little compared with replacing a floor that fails twice.

Replacement in rental and hotel stock is timed with vacancies.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a walk across the floors cannot: whether the slab was tested before the floor went down, whether old tiles contain asbestos, and what was approved in apartments. Ask for them before any floor is replaced.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Moisture test results for recent flooring | Whether the slab was dry enough when the floor was laid. |
| Strata approvals and by-laws on hard flooring | Whether hard floors in apartments were approved, and on what conditions. |
| Asbestos register covering floor tiles | Whether old floor tiles contain asbestos. |
| Slip and trip incident records | Where people slip and trip. |
| Flooring warranties | Whether a failing floor is still under warranty. |
| Cleaning specifications | Whether cleaning is damaging the floors. |
| Substrate preparation records | How the substrate was prepared. |
| Noise complaints from neighbours | Whether neighbours have complained of noise. |
| Moisture records for the substrate | Whether the substrate has a history of moisture. |
| Records of leaks affecting floors | Whether leaks have damaged the floors. |
| Product data for installed floors | What the installed products are, and their limits. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Floors are misread when old tiles are ripped up before testing, when the finish is blamed for a failure that started beneath it, and when a new floor is laid on the problem that failed the old one.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| Just rip it up | Do not sand, grind or rip up older vinyl tiles and adhesives until they have been tested for asbestos. |
| The flooring was faulty | Flooring failures concentrated near external walls, wet areas or at ground level point to moisture; failures across the whole floor point to substrate preparation or the product. |
| A new floor will fix it | A new finish laid on a wet slab, a weak screed or a floor without movement joints fails the same way as the old one. Deal with the cause beneath before replacing the finish. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets standards for slab moisture before flooring, slip resistance, sound insulation between homes, and work on asbestos. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Moisture, slip resistance, sound and asbestos | Slip resistance classification follows AS 4586 with guidance in Standards Australia handbook HB 198; resilient flooring installation follows AS 1884; strata by-laws commonly require approval and acoustic underlays for hard floors; the National Construction Code sets sound insulation for apartment floors. | BS 8203 covers resilient floor coverings and BS 8204 screeds; Approved Document E covers sound insulation; the HSE slip assessment approach guides floor safety. | ASTM F2170 sets slab moisture testing; ANSI A326.3 slip resistance; the International Building Code sets impact insulation class for floors between dwellings; condominium rules often regulate hard floors. |

In all three countries, apartment by-laws or rules often require owners to obtain approval and use acoustic underlays before laying hard floors.

sections.heading: Worked example: vinyl lifting along an outside wall
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. In a ground-floor office of a 1970s building, sheet vinyl laid three years ago is bubbling and lifting along the external wall, with dark staining at the seams. The floor beneath was not tested before laying, and in a store room nearby, small square vinyl tiles from the original fit-out remain.

Failures concentrated at ground level and along an outside wall point to moisture from the slab rather than the product, and the stained seams to adhesive attacked by it. The old square tiles may contain asbestos and must be tested before anyone disturbs them.

So the register carries asbestos testing of the old tiles as a check line, an in-situ humidity test of the slab, and relaying the vinyl over a surface membrane rather than relaying it as before.

thresholds.rule: New build: airborne at least 45 dB, impact no more than 62 dB; conversions: 43 dB and 64 dB

source.title: Approved Document E (2003 edition incorporating 2004, 2010, 2013 and 2015 amendments)

thresholds.rule: Up to 6.4 mm may be vertical; 6.4 to 13 mm bevelled no steeper than 1:2

source.title: 2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design

pages.title: Foundations
pages.question: How do foundations fail, how do you tell subsidence from heave or settlement, and when is underpinning needed?
pages.answer: Foundations rarely wear out; the ground moves them. Trees drying clay cause subsidence, worst at the corner nearest the tree and seasonal at first; tree removal and leaks cause heave; leaking drains wash soil away; timber piles rot when groundwater falls; stumps decay. Read the crack taper and distortion, then monitor for a full wet and dry season: progressive movement matters more than width. Remove the cause before underpinning.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about foundations; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Concrete footings, piles, pile caps, slabs, strip footings, pad foundations

pages.searchTitle: Foundations: subsidence, heave, settlement, stumps and when to underpin

questions.question: Is a wide crack in my wall serious?
questions.answer: Width alone does not decide severity. Progressive movement is more serious than a wide crack that has stopped; on reactive clay, twelve months of monitoring is usually needed to tell them apart.

questions.question: Does foundation movement mean underpinning?
questions.answer: Often not. Remove the cause first, such as leaking drains, poor drainage or a tree; many buildings then stabilise and need only crack repair.

questions.question: Can removing a tree damage my house?
questions.answer: On clay, yes: removing a large tree can cause heave as the ground rewets and swells. Assess the heave risk before removal, and phase it.

questions.question: Why are the floors uneven in a house on stumps?
questions.answer: Usually decayed or sunken stumps. A sub-floor inspection confirms it, and restumping with concrete or steel stumps re-levels the floors.

questions.question: How long do house stumps last?
questions.answer: Timber stumps 30 to 60 years, and concrete stumps 50 years and more.

questions.question: Why do the cracks open in summer and close in winter?
questions.answer: Seasonal movement of clay soil. Monitor for twelve months; manage trees and drainage, and repair the cracks once stable.

questions.question: Why is there a crack between the extension and the original building?
questions.answer: Different foundations moving differently. Establish both foundation depths and monitor; underpin only if movement continues.

questions.question: Why has the ground suddenly dropped near a drain?
questions.answer: A washout from a leaking drain. Repair the drain, then stabilise the ground, by underpinning or resin injection if needed.

questions.question: Why are the floors lifting in the middle after a tree was removed?
questions.answer: Heave after tree removal or leaks. Survey the levels and stop any leaks, and assess heave before any further tree removal.

questions.question: Why are there cracks at one corner of the building near a large tree?
questions.answer: Subsidence from clay shrinkage. Find the cause, usually a tree or a leak; remove it, then monitor before deciding on underpinning.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Foundation movement shows outside as tapering cracks and distorted openings, inside as sticking doors and sloping floors, and in the records as soil reports and past repairs. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Outside | Tapering diagonal cracks in masonry, usually starting at openings and running through bricks and mortar | Subsidence and heave on clay |
| Outside | Distorted window and door heads; gaps between frames and walls | Subsidence and heave on clay |
| Outside | Cracks continuing below the damp-proof course into the footing | Settlement, washout and chemical attack |
| Outside | Trees within a distance of the building comparable to their height, especially on clay | Subsidence and heave on clay |
| Outside | Paths and paving sloping toward walls; downpipes discharging at the wall base | Settlement, washout and chemical attack |
| Outside | Gaps opening between extensions and the original building | Settlement, washout and chemical attack |
| Inside | Doors and windows sticking or swinging open; floors sloping noticeably | Subsidence and heave on clay |
| Inside | Cracks at the corners of openings and between walls and ceilings | Subsidence and heave on clay |
| Inside | Skirting boards pulling away from floors; tiled floors cracking along a line | Subsidence and heave on clay |
| In the records | Soil and site classification; geotechnical reports | Investigation before the scope |
| In the records | Previous underpinning or restumping | Removing the cause, monitoring or underpinning |
| In the records | Insurance subsidence claims | Standards by country |
| In the records | Crack monitoring data | Investigation before the scope |
| In the records | Drain CCTV surveys | Settlement, washout and chemical attack |
| In the records | Mine subsidence or coal mining reports | Mine subsidence and earthquakes |

sections.heading: Types of foundation
sections.markdown:
Foundations transfer the building's weight to the ground. Their form depends on the soil and the load: strip footings under walls, pad footings under columns, raft slabs over the whole footprint, piles taken down to firmer strata, and in older Australian houses, timber or concrete stumps supporting suspended floors. A foundation's behaviour is governed as much by the ground as by the concrete: reactive clays that swell and shrink with moisture, fill, soft alluvium, groundwater, mine workings and earthquakes all move foundations that are themselves sound.

| Type | Where it is found | Main vulnerabilities |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Strip and pad footings | Most low-rise buildings of all eras | Shallow; affected by soil moisture change, trees and leaking drains |
| Raft and stiffened raft slabs | Houses and low-rise on reactive clays (Australia, parts of the US) | Edge movement and dishing or doming with soil moisture |
| Bored and driven piles | Larger buildings, poor ground | Defects at construction; corrosion; negative skin friction in settling fill |
| Timber piles | Older buildings in waterfront cities (Boston, parts of Europe) | Decay where the water table drops and exposes the timber |
| Timber and concrete stumps | Australian houses with suspended floors | Timber stumps rot and sink; concrete stumps crack and lean |
| Screw piles and mini-piles | Underpinning and light structures | Corrosion; installation quality |

In Australia, sites are classified by soil reactivity under AS 2870, from stable sand and rock through moderately, highly and extremely reactive clays to problem sites; the classification sets how much movement a house footing must tolerate. In Britain, shrinkable clays in the south-east and trees drive most subsidence. In the United States, expansive soils in Texas, Colorado and California, and seismic hazard on the west coast, dominate.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Concrete footings and piles last the life of the building, and timber piles last indefinitely while they stay below the water table; timber stumps last thirty to sixty years. What shortens a foundation's life is usually something around it: a tree, a leaking drain, or falling groundwater.

| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Concrete footings and piles | Life of the building | Soil movement; sulfates; construction quality |
| Timber piles below the water table | Indefinite while saturated | Exposure when groundwater falls |
| Timber stumps | 30 to 60 years | Moisture, termites, species, treatment |
| Concrete stumps | 50 years and more | Reinforcement corrosion; lean |
| Underpinning | Life of the building if the cause is addressed | Recurrence of the original cause |

Foundations rarely wear out; they move. What shortens their effective life is a change in the ground around them:

What shortens it: trees drawing moisture from clay, which shrinks and lets footings drop, most in dry seasons and droughts; tree removal, which lets clay rewet and swell over years (heave); leaking drains and water pipes, which soften soil and wash fines away; poor site drainage: water ponding against footings, downpipes discharging at the wall base; excavation nearby: neighbouring basements, trenches and dewatering; falling groundwater, which exposes timber piles to decay; mine workings collapsing below the site.

sections.heading: Subsidence and heave on clay
sections.markdown:
Clay soils lose volume as they dry. Tree roots and drought dry the soil beneath part of a building, which then drops relative to the rest. Movement is seasonal at first, opening in summer and closing in winter, and can become progressive as the tree grows. Damage concentrates at the corner or side nearest the tree.

Clay swells as it wets. Removing large trees, leaking pipes and changed drainage let clay rewet under a building; the affected part rises, sometimes over many years. Heave lifts floors and cracks walls in patterns opposite to subsidence.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Diagonal cracks widening toward the top at one corner, near a large tree | Subsidence from clay shrinkage. Seasonal crack opening; soil moisture and root analysis; crack widths graded on the asset’s market’s damage scale (Thresholds by market). | Find the cause, usually a tree or a leak; remove it, then monitor before deciding on underpinning. |
| Cracks widening in summer and closing in winter | Seasonal clay movement. Twelve months of crack monitoring. | Monitor for twelve months; manage trees and drainage; repair the cracks once stable. |
| Floors lifting in the middle, cracks wider at the top of internal walls | Heave after tree removal or leaks. Level survey; history of tree removal. | Survey the levels and stop any leaks; assess heave before any further tree removal. |

sections.heading: Settlement, washout and chemical attack
sections.markdown:
New loads compress the ground beneath them. Most settlement happens early in a building's life; continuing settlement points to fill that is still consolidating, soft soils, or an extension on a shallower foundation pulling away from the original.

Leaking drains and broken stormwater pipes wash fine soil from beneath footings, leaving voids that let them drop locally, often suddenly.

Sulfates in soil and groundwater attack concrete; acid sulfate soils and contaminated land corrode reinforcement and steel piles.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sudden local drop near a drain run | Washout from a leaking drain. Drain CCTV; void detection. | Repair the drain, then stabilise the ground, by underpinning or resin injection if needed. |
| Crack between extension and original building | Different foundations moving differently. Foundation depths; level survey. | Establish both foundation depths and monitor; underpin only if movement continues. |
| Floors out of level across an internal wall line | Differential movement of the footings. Level survey with a straight edge, graded on the asset’s market’s floor scale (Thresholds by market). | Map the levels and find the cause, then monitor before deciding on underpinning. |

sections.heading: Timber piles and stumps
sections.markdown:
Timber piles last as long as they stay saturated. When groundwater falls, through dewatering or changed drainage, the tops dry and rot, and the structure above settles. Timber stumps rot at ground level and are attacked by termites, and the floor sinks unevenly.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Uneven floors in a house on timber stumps | Decayed or sunken stumps. Sub-floor inspection. | Restump with concrete or steel stumps, and re-level the floors. |

sections.heading: Mine subsidence and earthquakes
sections.markdown:
Collapse of old coal and mineral workings beneath a site produces settlement troughs and tilt. Mining regions in New South Wales, Britain and parts of the United States carry this risk and have notification or compensation schemes.

Earthquakes can cause loose saturated sands to liquefy, so foundations lose support. Older foundations not designed for seismic loads can fail to hold buildings together in a quake.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Building tilting slowly over a wide area | Mine subsidence or regional settlement. Mining records; survey. | Check the mining records and survey; in mine subsidence districts, claim through the relevant scheme. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rapid or large movement with wide cracks, distorted openings that threaten egress, or loss of bearing to walls and columns | safety · 4 Essential | Prop and engineer now. |
| Progressive movement with cracks of 5 to 15 mm or more | failure · 4 Essential | Stabilise now: fix the cause and underpin where needed. |
| Seasonal movement causing repeated cracking; decaying stumps | condition · 3 Important | Address causes and repair in the near term. |
| Mine subsidence or heritage obligations requiring action by a date | deadline · 4 Essential | By the required date. |
| Cracks of unknown cause; trees near a building on clay | check · 3 Important | Monitor for twelve months and investigate. |
| Hairline cracks shown stable | nil · 1 Routine | Cosmetic repair. |
| Timber stumps or piles at the end of their life | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Plan restumping or replacement. |

Crack widths map to damage categories under BRE Digest 251 in Britain and Appendix C of AS 2870 in Australia; see the masonry page. A lifecycle grade rarely applies to foundations themselves; it applies to stumps and other replaceable elements.

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A structural or geotechnical engineer leads, with an arborist where trees are involved and a drainage contractor for drain surveys. The checks below read the crack pattern first, then trace it to a cause, and monitor long enough to see whether it is moving.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Crack mapping and monitoring | Record every crack with width and taper, fit tell-tales or gauge studs, and read them monthly for at least a year, grading each crack against the AS 2870 categories (QBCC guide) or BRE Digest 251 in the UK. |
| Level survey | Of floors and brick courses to show the shape of movement, with straight-edge offsets graded against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). |
| Drain investigation | CCTV and pressure testing of drains and water pipes near the affected area. |
| Trial pits and boreholes | Foundation type and depth, soil type, moisture content and plasticity, roots. |
| Tree survey | Species, height, distance and water demand; root identification from samples. |
| Groundwater monitoring | Where timber piles or dewatering are involved. |
| Records review | Original foundation design, previous repairs, insurance claims, mining reports. |

The report should identify the cause of movement with the evidence for it, whether movement is seasonal or progressive, and the remedy, starting with removing the cause.

sections.heading: Removing the cause, monitoring or underpinning
sections.markdown:
Remove the cause first: leaking drains, poor site drainage, trees, and downpipes discharging at the wall base. Many buildings then stabilise and need only crack repair; underpinning is for movement that continues once the cause is gone.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Remove the cause | Repair leaking drains and pipes, fix site drainage, manage or remove trees (assessing heave risk before removal), and stop downpipes discharging at the wall base. | First, wherever a cause is found. |
| Monitor after removing the cause | Crack monitoring through a full wet and dry season. | Many buildings stabilise and need only crack repair. |
| Underpinning | Mass concrete underpinning, mini-piles, screw piles, or resin injection to stiffen and lift soils, selected for the ground and access. | Where movement continues after the cause is removed. |
| Restumping | Concrete or steel stumps in place of decayed timber stumps, with floors re-levelled. | For houses on decayed timber stumps. |
| Root barriers | Barriers between trees and buildings. | Where trees must stay. |
| Crack repair | Stitching with helical bars, repointing, and replacement of damaged bricks. | After stabilisation. |
| Heave precautions | Phased removal, monitoring and flexible repairs. | Where trees are removed from clay sites. |
| Pile remediation | Underpinning to new piles, or raising groundwater where possible. | For decayed timber piles. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Monitoring and investigation are lump sums spread over a year. Drain repairs are priced by length or per defect. Underpinning is priced per metre of wall or per pile, with access, excavation and reinstatement of floors and finishes inside often doubling the cost. Restumping is priced per stump or per house. Crack repairs are itemised after stabilisation.

Underpinning and restumping are lifecycle or major repair items; drain and drainage works are repairs and maintenance; monitoring is the check line that decides whether underpinning is needed at all. In Britain, subsidence is commonly an insurance matter, and insurers manage the investigation and repair.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what one inspection cannot: what the ground is, whether movement is progressive or seasonal, and whether trees, drains or old workings are to blame. Ask for them before anyone specifies underpinning.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Geotechnical reports and the site or soil classification | What the ground is, and how reactive. |
| Foundation drawings and design | What the building stands on, and how deep. |
| Crack monitoring records and engineer's reports on movement | Whether movement is progressive or seasonal. |
| Underpinning, restumping or previous repair records, with warranties | What has been done before, and whether it is still warranted. |
| Insurance claims for subsidence or heave | Whether movement has been claimed, and what was accepted. |
| Drain CCTV surveys and repair records | Whether leaking drains are softening the ground. |
| Tree removal records and arborist reports | Whether trees are drying the clay, or were removed, which raises the risk of heave. |
| Mine subsidence or mining reports where relevant | Whether the site lies over old mine workings. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Foundation movement is misread when the width of a crack is taken as its severity, when underpinning is reached for before the cause is removed, and when removing a tree is taken as the cure.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| A wide crack is a serious crack | Width alone does not decide severity. Progressive movement is more serious than a wide crack that has stopped. Twelve months of monitoring, covering a full wet and dry season, is usually needed to tell them apart on reactive clay. |
| Movement means underpinning | Remove the cause first: repair leaking drains, fix site drainage, manage trees, and stop downpipes discharging at the wall base. Many buildings then stabilise and need only crack repair. |
| Removing the tree solves it | On clay, removing a large tree can cause heave as the ground rewets and swells. Assess the heave risk before removal, phase it, and monitor. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets design codes for foundations, requires approval for underpinning, and has its own arrangements for mining and groundwater. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Design and codes | AS 2870 governs residential slabs and footings, including site classification and damage categories; AS 2159 covers piling; the National Construction Code calls these up. | Approved Document A governs structure; BS 8004 and BS EN 1997 cover foundations; NHBC Standards Chapter 4.2 sets building near trees. | The International Building and Residential Codes (Chapter 18 of the IBC) govern foundations, with special provisions for expansive soils; ASCE 7 sets seismic design. |
| Repairs and approvals | Restumping and underpinning need building approval. | Underpinning needs building regulations approval and often party wall notices; subsidence is usually handled through buildings insurance. | The International Existing Building Code governs repairs. |
| Mining and groundwater | In New South Wales, Subsidence Advisory NSW manages mine subsidence districts and compensation. | The Coal Authority provides mining reports. | Boston's Groundwater Conservation Overlay District protects timber piles from falling groundwater. |

sections.heading: Worked example: a crack at the corner nearest a tree
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 1960s brick house on reactive clay has a diagonal crack running up from the corner of a window at the end nearest a large gum tree. The crack is about 4 mm at the top, tapering to almost nothing at the base, and the owner says it opens each summer.

A crack that tapers and widens toward the top at the corner nearest a tree points to subsidence from clay shrinkage. Width alone does not decide severity: a crack that opens in summer and closes in winter is seasonal, and twelve months of monitoring is needed to tell it from progressive movement. The cause is the tree, and possibly the drainage at that corner.

So the register carries crack monitoring as a check line now, management of the tree and drainage as the first remedy, with heave risk assessed before any removal, and underpinning only if movement continues once the cause is dealt with.

thresholds.rule: Negligible under 0.1 mm; very slight under 1 mm; slight under 5 mm; moderate 5 to 15 mm; severe 15 to 25 mm

pages.title: Gas Services
pages.question: How do building gas services fail, and when do they become a safety or decommissioning question?
pages.answer: Gas services fail by leaks, corrosion and alteration. Joints and regulators leak; buried and damp steel corrodes; pipes in car parks are struck; appliances removed without capping leave live open ends; emergency shut-offs seize or lose their interfaces. Any smell of gas is a leak until proven otherwise. Gas restrictions and electrification mean many installations now face decommissioning within the building's life, which changes repair decisions.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about gas services; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Supply pipework, metering

pages.searchTitle: Gas services: leaks, corroded pipes, emergency shut-offs, LPG and decommissioning

questions.question: What should I do if I smell gas?
questions.answer: Treat it as a leak until proven otherwise: isolate the supply, ventilate, avoid ignition sources, and call the gas network or a licensed gas fitter.

questions.question: Why does the gas meter move with everything off?
questions.answer: A leak in the consumer piping. A tightness test finds it.

questions.question: Does a kitchen gas shut-off need testing?
questions.answer: Yes. It should cut the gas on a fire alarm; one that does not is a safety finding.

questions.question: How often are gas safety checks needed?
questions.answer: In the United Kingdom, rented homes need an annual landlord gas safety check by a Gas Safe registered engineer.

questions.question: How long does gas pipework last?
questions.answer: Copper and polyethylene 50 years and more, steel above ground 40 to 60, buried steel 20 to 40, and regulators 15 to 25.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Gas problems show as a smell of gas, corrosion and unprotected pipes, open ends, untested shut-offs and detectors, and in compliance certificates, tightness tests and consumption. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On site | Smell of gas around meters, regulators, plant rooms and appliances | Leaks, corrosion and damage |
| On site | Corrosion on steel pipe, especially at penetrations and near the ground | Leaks, corrosion and damage |
| On site | Pipes in vehicle areas without impact protection | Leaks, corrosion and damage |
| On site | Capped and uncapped open ends; redundant pipework | Shut-offs, alterations and CSST |
| On site | Emergency shut-off valves: location, labelling, accessibility | Shut-offs, alterations and CSST |
| On site | Gas detectors in plant rooms and kitchens, and their test labels | Shut-offs, alterations and CSST |
| On site | LPG cylinders and tanks: separation, signage, condition | LPG |
| In the records | Gas compliance certificates for installations and alterations | Standards by country |
| In the records | Gas safety records for rented homes | Standards by country |
| In the records | Tightness test results | Investigation before the scope |
| In the records | Gas consumption data | Leaks, corrosion and damage |
| In the records | Network or supplier notices | Standards by country |
| In the records | Appliances with yellow or sooty flames, scorching around burners, or condensation and staining near flues, which point to combustion problems rather than piping, but share the same inspection | Common misreads |

sections.heading: Types of gas installation
sections.markdown:
Gas services bring natural gas or LPG from the network or storage to appliances: the meter and regulator set, consumer piping through the building, isolation valves, emergency shut-off valves, and connections to boilers, water heaters, cookers, kitchens and process equipment. LPG installations add cylinders or bulk tanks with their own separation and safety rules. Appliances, flues and combustion air are covered on their own pages.

| Material | Where it is found | What goes wrong |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Black or galvanised steel | Older commercial and residential piping, risers | Corrosion, especially where buried or in damp areas; thread leaks |
| Copper | Residential and light commercial, especially Australia and Britain | Mechanical damage; leaks at joints |
| Polyethylene | Buried service and site mains | Third-party damage; must be protected where it emerges |
| Corrugated stainless steel tubing (CSST) | US houses and light commercial | Lightning can perforate it unless bonded |
| Multilayer composite | Newer installations | Correct fittings and tools essential |

Gas policy is changing what these systems are worth. Victoria bars gas connections to new homes needing planning permits from 2024, the ACT bars new gas network connections, Britain is moving buildings off fossil-fuel heating, and New York City requires new buildings to be all-electric. Existing gas services may face decommissioning within the life of the building, which changes whether to repair or retire them.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Copper and polyethylene gas piping last fifty years and more and steel above ground forty to sixty, but buried steel lasts twenty to forty and regulators fifteen to twenty-five. In many buildings, electrification now decides the end of the gas system before wear does.

| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Steel piping above ground | 40 to 60 years | Damp; coating |
| Buried steel | 20 to 40 years | Soil corrosivity; cathodic protection |
| Copper piping | 50 years and more | Damage |
| Polyethylene | 50 years and more | Third-party damage |
| Regulators | 15 to 25 years | Network conditions; debris |
| Emergency shut-off valves | 15 to 25 years | Testing |
| LPG tanks | 20 to 30 years with periodic inspection | Corrosion; certification |

What shortens life: damp and buried environments without protective coatings or cathodic protection; mechanical damage in car parks, loading docks and plant rooms; unauthorised alterations by unlicensed people; lightning on unbonded CSST.

Gas piping rarely wears out above ground in dry conditions; its life is set by corrosion where it is buried or damp, by damage, and increasingly by whether the building will keep using gas at all.

sections.heading: Leaks, corrosion and damage
sections.markdown:
Leaks occur at threaded joints, unions, valves and where pipes have been damaged or corroded. Small leaks waste gas and can be found by smell or tightness testing; larger leaks in confined spaces create explosion risk. Gas detectors in plant rooms and kitchens give warning only if they work.

Buried steel without coating or cathodic protection corrodes, particularly in wet or aggressive soils; above-ground steel corrodes where it passes through walls and floors, where condensation sits, or in coastal air.

Gas pipes in car parks and loading docks are struck by vehicles; pipes in plant rooms are used as supports or damaged during works. Unprotected meters and regulators at ground level are vulnerable.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gas smell near the meter | Leaking regulator or meter connection. Leak detection. | Isolate, and call the network or a licensed gas fitter; repair the regulator or connection. |
| Gas consumption with appliances off | Leak in consumer piping. Tightness test. | Tightness test; find and repair the leak. |
| Rust and pitting at wall penetrations | Corrosion where moisture is trapped. Inspection. | Replace the corroded sections, with coatings or materials suited to the environment. |

sections.heading: Shut-offs, alterations and CSST
sections.markdown:
Kitchens and plant rooms need accessible manual isolation and often automatic shut-off on fire alarm or loss of ventilation. Valves that are seized, inaccessible or disconnected from their controls do not stop gas in an emergency.

Pipes extended to new appliances by unlicensed people, redundant pipes left live, or open ends left uncapped when appliances were removed create direct leak paths.

In the United States, corrugated stainless steel tubing can be perforated by nearby lightning strikes, causing fires, unless it is bonded as its manufacturers and codes require.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Kitchen gas not cutting off on alarm test | Shut-off valve or interface fault. Function test. | Repair the shut-off valve or interface, and retest. |
| Uncapped pipe ends | Appliances removed without capping. Inspection. | Cap them now, and remove redundant pipework. |
| Gas pipework added or altered with no compliance certificate | Unverified work. Records of alterations; tightness test and inspection of the new work. | Test and certify the work, or have it redone by a licensed gasfitter. |

sections.heading: LPG
sections.markdown:
LPG cylinders and tanks must be separated from openings, drains, ignition sources and boundaries; LPG is heavier than air and collects in low places. Encroachment by later buildings, fences and drains often breaks separation distances.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| LPG cylinders beside doors, windows, drains or ignition sources | Cylinder location against the separation rules. Distances to openings, drains and ignition sources measured against AS/NZS 1596. | Relocate the cylinders, or change the openings or ignition sources nearby. |
| LPG tank or cylinders with no inspection or test record | Pressure equipment of unknown condition. Supplier records; tank test and inspection dates. | Have the supplier inspect and test the installation, and keep the records. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gas leak; uncapped live pipe; failed emergency shut-off; LPG separation breached | safety · 4 Essential | Isolate and rectify now. |
| Supply disconnected by the network for safety | failure · 4 Essential | Repair and recommission now. |
| Landlord gas safety checks or periodic inspections due | deadline · 4 Essential | At the prescribed interval. |
| Corrosion; unprotected pipes; redundant pipework | condition · 3 Important | Repair in the near term. |
| Piping at end of life; gas phase-out planned | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Replace or decommission. |
| Installation never tested; alterations unrecorded | check · 3 Important | Tightness test and inspection. |
| Normal | nil · 1 Routine | Routine. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A licensed gas fitter or gas engineer; for large and commercial installations, a gas engineer with the relevant competence. The checks below start with compliance certificates and tightness test results, then walk the pipework from meter to appliance and test the emergency shut-offs.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Tightness test | Of the installation, and pressure tests after alterations. |
| Visual inspection | Of meters, regulators, piping, supports, penetrations, isolation and shut-off valves. |
| Function test | Of emergency shut-off valves and their interfaces with fire alarms and ventilation. |
| Gas detector test | In plant rooms and kitchens. |
| Bonding check | Of CSST in the United States and of metallic gas piping generally. |
| LPG separation review | . |
| Consumption review | And decommissioning options. |
| Ventilation check | Of plant rooms, kitchens and meter enclosures, since gas safety depends on combustion air and on dispersing small leaks. |
| Records reconciliation | Compare compliance certificates with the appliances and pipework actually present to find unrecorded alterations. |

The report should state safety defects, the tightness test result, condition of piping and valves, compliance, and whether to repair, replace or decommission.

sections.heading: Repairing, protecting or decommissioning
sections.markdown:
Any smell of gas comes first: isolate, ventilate, and call the network or a licensed gas fitter. After that, the work repairs and protects the pipework, caps what is redundant and, where the building is electrifying, decommissions it safely with the network.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Leak repairs | Repairs and recommissioning by licensed gas fitters. | Wherever a leak is found. |
| Pipe replacement | Replace corroded sections, with coatings or materials suited to the environment. | Where pipes corrode. |
| Impact protection | Protect pipes, meters and regulators. | In vehicle areas. |
| Capping and removal | Cap and remove redundant pipework. | Wherever appliances have been removed. |
| Emergency shut-off upgrades | Shut-offs with interfaces to fire alarms and kitchen ventilation. | Where shut-offs fail or are missing. |
| Gas detection | Detection in plant rooms and commercial kitchens. | Where none is fitted. |
| CSST bonding | Bond corrugated stainless steel tubing. | Wherever CSST is installed. |
| Decommissioning | Decommission with electrification, including safe disconnection and removal of meters by the network. | When the building moves off gas. |
| Meter and regulator relocation | Move them, arranged with the network operator. | Out of enclosed spaces, car parks or vehicle paths. |
| Labelling | Label isolation valves and pipework. | So emergency services and maintenance staff can find and shut off gas quickly. |
| Ventilation upgrades | Upgrade ventilation to plant rooms and kitchens. | Where combustion air or leak dispersal is inadequate. |
| Network coordination | When decommissioning, have the network remove the meter and disconnect the service so no live gas remains at the property boundary. | When decommissioning. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Inspections and gas safety checks recur. Repairs are itemised. Pipe replacement is by length with access. Shut-off and detection systems are lump sums per area. Decommissioning is a lump sum, usually part of an electrification project that also carries appliance replacement and electrical upgrades.

Safety rectification and inspections are code compliance; replacement is lifecycle; decommissioning sits with electrification.

Work on gas services must be done by licensed or registered gas fitters and certified, so even small items carry call-out, testing and certification costs. Network charges apply to meter relocation and disconnection.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a walk along the pipework cannot: whether the installation is certified and tight, whether the shut-offs work, and whether the building is moving off gas. Ask for them before any alteration.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Gas compliance certificates for the installation and alterations | Whether the installation and alterations were certified. |
| Landlord gas safety records for rented homes | Whether rented homes have current gas safety records. |
| Tightness test results | Whether the pipework holds pressure. |
| Emergency shut-off and gas detector test records | Whether shut-offs and detectors work. |
| Gas consumption data | Whether gas is being used, or lost, when appliances are off. |
| LPG installation and inspection records | Whether LPG storage is installed and inspected properly. |
| Electrification plans affecting gas | Whether the building is moving off gas, and when. |
| Ventilation design for plant rooms and kitchens | Whether plant rooms and kitchens are ventilated as designed. |
| Network operator correspondence about the supply and meters | What the network has said about the supply and meters. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Gas installations are misread when a smell of gas is treated as anything other than a leak, and when a fault at one appliance is blamed on the supply.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| It is probably nothing | Any smell of gas is treated as a leak until proven otherwise: isolate the supply, ventilate, avoid ignition sources and call the gas network or a licensed gas fitter. |
| The supply is the problem | Distinguish a supply problem from an installation problem: low pressure across all appliances points to the regulator or network; a problem at one appliance points to its branch, valve or the appliance itself. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market governs gas installations and LPG, licenses the people who work on them, and in places restricts new gas. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Installation, safety checks and fuel policy | AS/NZS 5601.1 governs gas installations and AS/NZS 1596 LPG storage; gas fitters are licensed and issue compliance certificates; state gas safety regulators oversee installations; Victoria and the ACT restrict new gas connections. | The Gas Safety (Installation and Use) Regulations 1998 require Gas Safe registered engineers, annual landlord gas safety checks in rented homes, and maintenance; IGEM standards cover non-domestic installations. | NFPA 54 (the National Fuel Gas Code) and the International Fuel Gas Code govern installations, including CSST bonding; NFPA 58 covers LPG; local jurisdictions and utilities set permits and inspection; some cities require all-electric new construction. |

In strata, condominium and leasehold buildings in all three jurisdictions, common gas piping is usually the owners corporation's or landlord's responsibility up to each dwelling's meter or isolation valve, with appliances and internal piping the occupant's; responsibility for decommissioning shared gas supplies needs to be settled before electrification projects start.

sections.heading: Worked example: gas use with the kitchen closed
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A building with a ground-floor restaurant shows gas consumption overnight while the kitchen is closed. The kitchen's emergency shut-off did not cut the gas in the last fire alarm test, an uncapped pipe end remains where a fryer was removed, and the meter sits in an unprotected corner of the car park.

Consumption with appliances off points to a leak in the consumer piping. An uncapped end and a shut-off that fails are safety findings, as is any smell of gas, which is treated as a leak until proven otherwise. The meter in the car park needs impact protection or relocation.

So the register carries a tightness test and leak repair, capping of the open end, and the shut-off repaired and retested as safety lines now, with impact protection or relocation of the meter arranged with the network.

pages.title: Glazing Systems
pages.question: How do windows, curtain walls and glazed façades fail, what does each failure look like, and when is it urgent?
pages.answer: Glazing fails at seals, drainage and glass before frames. IGUs fog when edge seals fail, usually where water sits in blocked sills; leaks recur at predictable joints: sill ends, curtain wall splices, stack joints. Toughened glass can break with no impact from nickel sulphide inclusions, which at height is a safety issue. Structural silicone holds glass on and must be tested, not trusted. Frames usually outlast all of these.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about glazing systems; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
