pages.searchTitle: Windows, curtain walls and glazing: leaks, misted units, glass breakage, SSG

questions.question: Why did a toughened glass pane break on its own?
questions.answer: Usually a nickel sulphide inclusion, with the break starting inside the pane rather than at an edge. Glass that was not heat-soaked can break again.

questions.question: Why are my double-glazed windows misted between the panes?
questions.answer: The unit's edge seal has failed. The mist cannot be wiped from either face; the unit is replaced, or the elevation reglazed where failure is widespread.

questions.question: Why does the curtain wall leak at the same place on every floor?
questions.answer: Usually a splice or stack joint failure. Water testing at the joint reproduces the leak and confirms it.

questions.question: Do leaking windows always need resealing?
questions.answer: No. Clearing weep holes and reinstating baffles and end dams often stops leaks without resealing.

questions.question: How long do window seals last?
questions.answer: Wet perimeter and cap seals 10 to 20 years, gaskets and insulating glass unit edge seals 20 to 30, and structural silicone 25 years and more.

questions.question: Why do the windows only leak in heavy wind and rain?
questions.answer: The drainage is overwhelmed or pressure equalisation has failed, often with blocked weep holes or missing baffles. Clear the weep holes and reinstate the baffles.

questions.question: Why did a window crack from the edge with nothing hitting it?
questions.answer: Thermal stress, usually where an edge is damaged or partly shaded, or blinds or film sit close to the glass. Replace the pane and check the edges, shading, blinds and film.

questions.question: Why is water coming in at the bottom corners of the windows?
questions.answer: Missing or failed end dams and sill flashing. Water test at the sill ends, and reinstate the end dams and sill flashing.

questions.question: A glass panel on the facade feels loose. Is that serious?
questions.answer: Yes. On a structurally glazed façade it can mean the silicone has lost adhesion. Make the area below safe, then add mechanical retention or reglaze.

questions.question: Why are the old steel windows cracking their glass?
questions.answer: Rust at the glazing rebate is jacking the glass. Strip, treat and repaint the frames, and reglaze.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Glazing problems show from the street as misted, replaced or broken panes, close up as failed seals and blocked weeps, inside as wet sills and condensation, and in the logs. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Street or aerial | Misted or hazy panes in a pattern across an elevation: IGU seal failure, often concentrated on the most exposed faces | Misted insulating glass units |
| Street or aerial | Replaced panes visible as a different tint or reflection, a record of breakage or seal failure | Glass breakage and structural silicone |
| Street or aerial | Broken or taped panes; netting or protection below a curtain wall | Glass breakage and structural silicone |
| Street or aerial | Gaskets visibly shrunk at corners, caps missing or displaced, black streaking below gaskets | Water infiltration and seals |
| Street or aerial | Staining or efflorescence at sills and on the slab edge below window walls | Water infiltration and seals |
| Street or aerial | Rusting steel windows with cracked panes; cracked masonry at window jambs | Anchors and steel windows |
| Close up on site | Blocked or absent weep holes in sills and transoms | Water infiltration and seals |
| Close up on site | Wet seals hard, cracked or peeling; gaps at gasket corners; gaps at the perimeter seal | Water infiltration and seals |
| Close up on site | On SSG, a visible change in the silicone line, staining behind glass, or glass that moves when pressed | Glass breakage and structural silicone |
| Close up on site | Glass type markings in the corner of each pane (toughened, laminated, heat-soak); absence of markings on panes required to be safety glass | Glass breakage and structural silicone |
| Close up on site | Hardware loose, corroded or failing; doors and sashes not closing | Anchors and steel windows |
| Inside the building | Water staining, swollen floor finishes and mould at sills and at the base of window walls | Water infiltration and seals |
| Inside the building | Condensation on frames and glass on cold days, more than the glass type should allow; draughts at sashes and joints | Misted insulating glass units |
| Inside the building | Corrosion at accessible anchors in ceiling voids at the slab edge | Anchors and steel windows |
| In the records | Breakage log, especially repeated spontaneous breakage of toughened glass | Glass breakage and structural silicone |
| In the records | Leak logs that recur at the same floor or the same mullion line | Water infiltration and seals |
| In the records | Glass schedule, heat-soak certificates, SSG adhesion test records and warranties | Glass breakage and structural silicone |
| In the records | Façade inspection reports and ordinance filings | Standards by country |

sections.heading: Types of glazing system
sections.markdown:
Glazing systems are the framed and frameless glass in a building's envelope: windows, sliding and hinged doors, shopfronts, window walls, curtain walls, structural silicone glazing and point-fixed glass. Skylights and atrium roofs have their own page. A system is the glass, the frame, the gaskets and seals that hold the glass and keep water out, the internal drainage, the anchors to the structure, and the perimeter seal to the surrounding wall.

| System | Where it is used | How it keeps water out |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Framed windows: timber, steel, aluminium, uPVC | Houses, older apartments and offices, institutions | Frame seals and drained sill; perimeter sealant and flashing to the wall |
| Window wall (slab to slab) | Apartments from the 1990s | Units span floor to floor, set on the slab edge; depends on sill drainage, end dams and the perimeter seal |
| Stick curtain wall | Offices, 1960s onward | Mullions and transoms assembled on site; pressure-equalised drainage; splice and transom joints are the weak points |
| Unitised curtain wall | Offices and towers from the 1990s | Factory-made units with interlocking stack and mullion joints; quality more consistent, joints still critical |
| Structural silicone glazing (SSG) | Offices from the 1980s | Glass bonded to the frame with silicone instead of caps; adhesion is the structural fixing |
| Point-fixed (spider) and fin glazing | Entrances, atria, retail | Bolted fittings through holes in toughened or laminated glass; weather seal is sealant between panes |
| Shopfronts | Retail at ground level | Simple frames and large panes; impact and security dominate |

Glass type matters to safety and to how glass breaks. Annealed (float) glass breaks into large sharp shards. Heat-strengthened glass is about twice as strong and breaks into larger pieces that tend to stay in the frame. Toughened (tempered) glass is four to five times as strong and breaks into small cubes; it can break spontaneously from nickel sulphide inclusions unless heat-soak tested. Laminated glass holds together when broken. Insulated glass units (IGUs) are two or three panes sealed around the edge with a dry air or gas space; the edge seal is their life. Double glazing became standard in British housing from the 1980s, in Australian commercial work through the 2000s, and more widely in Australian housing after the energy provisions tightened.

Era tells the story: steel windows with putty glazing in pre-war and mid-century buildings; single-glazed aluminium in Australian and American stock of the 1960s to 1990s; stick curtain walls with captured glass in offices of the 1970s and 1980s; four-sided SSG in the late 1980s and 1990s; unitised systems and IGUs from the 2000s.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Glazing systems outlast their seals: aluminium framing lasts forty to sixty years and steel windows sixty and more, but wet seals last ten to twenty years, gaskets and insulating glass units twenty to thirty, and hardware ten to twenty-five. Most glazing work is renewing the parts that age inside a sound frame.

| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Aluminium framing | 40 to 60 years | Anodising or powder coat condition; coastal exposure; thermal breaks |
| Steel windows | 60 years and more with maintenance | Paint cycle; rust jacking at glass and in masonry |
| Timber windows | 30 to 60 years | Paint cycle; sill decay |
| uPVC windows | 25 to 35 years | UV, hardware |
| IGU edge seal | 20 to 30 years | Water standing in the glazing rebate; sealant quality; UV on exposed seals |
| EPDM gaskets | 20 to 30 years | UV; shrinkage at corners |
| Wet perimeter and cap seals | 10 to 20 years | Exposure; joint design |
| Structural silicone | 25 years and more | Original adhesion and cure; never assumed without testing |
| Hardware: hinges, stays, rollers, locks | 10 to 25 years | Use; coastal corrosion |

What shortens life: water held in the glazing rebate because weep holes are blocked or omitted, which destroys IGU edge seals from below; west and north elevations in Australia (west and south in the northern hemisphere), where UV and thermal cycling age seals and gaskets fastest; coastal air on aluminium finishes, steel anchors and stainless fittings; missing sill flashings and end dams on window walls, sending water into the slab edge and the unit below; frame deflection under wind and building movement on long spans, which works seals loose; poor cleaning practice: abrasive cleaning and scrapers scratch glass and damage coatings and seals.

sections.heading: Water infiltration and seals
sections.markdown:
Glazing leaks at a small number of predictable places: the perimeter seal between frame and wall, the sill where it meets the slab or opening below, end dams at sill ends, splice joints in stick curtain wall mullions, transom-to-mullion joints, stack joints in unitised systems, and glazing pockets that cannot drain. Most systems are designed to let some water past the outer seal and drain it out again; leaks occur when the drainage path is blocked, missing or overwhelmed.

Dry gaskets shrink back from corners, leaving gaps where water enters the glazing pocket. Wet seals harden and lose adhesion. On capped systems, the cap can loosen as pressure plates relax.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Leak at the same mullion on every floor | Splice or stack joint failure in the curtain wall. Water test at the joint reproduces the leak. | Water test the splice or stack joint, then reseal it. |
| Leak at sill ends and at the slab below window walls | Missing or failed end dams and sill flashing. Water test at sill ends; water found on the slab edge on opening up. | Reinstate the end dams and sill flashing. |
| Leak only in heavy wind-driven rain | Overwhelmed drainage or pressure equalisation failure. Weep holes blocked or baffles missing; water rises in the sill under pressure. | Clear the weep holes and reinstate the baffles. |

sections.heading: Misted insulating glass units
sections.markdown:
Moisture enters the cavity of an insulated unit through a failed edge seal. The first sign is fogging or condensation between the panes, then a white bloom or residue on the inner faces, and on low-emissivity units, a hazy or corroded coating. Thermal performance falls and the unit cannot be repaired, only replaced.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fogging or white bloom between panes | IGU edge seal failure. Cannot be wiped from either face; units at the bottom of the elevation or with blocked weeps worst affected. | Replace the unit; reglaze the elevation where failure is widespread. |

sections.heading: Glass breakage and structural silicone
sections.markdown:
Thermal stress breaks annealed and some heat-strengthened glass when part of a pane heats faster than the rest: shading from deep frames, internal blinds close to tinted glass, and edge damage concentrate the stress. Nickel sulphide inclusions break toughened glass spontaneously, often years after installation and without any load; non-heat-soaked toughened glass at height can release a whole pane of fragments. Impact and edge damage from installation or building movement account for most other breaks.

On SSG, the silicone bond is what holds the glass on. Poor surface preparation, incompatible materials, inadequate bite (bond width) or cure at installation can leave bonds that pass a visual check but have little strength. Loss of adhesion lets glass move, leak and in the worst case detach.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Break in toughened glass with no impact, small fragments, a characteristic butterfly-shaped pair of fragments at the origin | Nickel sulphide inclusion. Origin inside the pane, not at an edge; glass not heat-soaked; other spontaneous breaks in the same batch. | Protect the area below; assess the remaining risk, and replace with heat-soaked or laminated glass where warranted. |
| Single crack starting at an edge at right angles, wandering across the pane | Thermal stress in annealed or heat-strengthened glass. Edge damaged or partly shaded; blinds or film close to the glass; tinted or coated glass. | Replace the pane; check the edges, shading, and any blinds or film close to the glass. |
| Cracks radiating from a point | Impact. Point of contact visible; often at low level. | Replace the pane. |
| Glass loose or moving on an SSG façade | Structural silicone adhesion loss. Hand pull adhesion test fails at the substrate; bond width less than design. | Make the area below safe; add mechanical retention, or reglaze. |
| Clear glass low in a window or beside a door with no safety glass mark | Glass that may break dangerously on impact. Glass type in the locations the asset’s market treats as critical (Thresholds by market). | Identify the glass from its marks; replace it with safety glass or protect it. |

sections.heading: Anchors and steel windows
sections.markdown:
Curtain wall and window wall anchors fix the system to the slab edge. Water reaching them through failed perimeter seals or slab edge joints corrodes carbon steel components, and dissimilar metal contact corrodes aluminium. They are concealed behind ceiling and floor finishes.

Steel windows rust where paint fails, and rust at the glazing rebate jacks the glass and cracks it. Steel frames built into masonry rust at the sill and jamb and crack the surrounding brick or stone.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cracked glass and rust at steel windows | Rust jacking at the glazing rebate. Rust visible at the rebate; putty or glazing compound failed. | Strip, treat and repaint the frames, and reglaze. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Broken or loose glass at height over a public or occupied area; SSG glass moving; spontaneous breakage of non-heat-soaked toughened glass above a footpath | safety · 4 Essential | Make safe immediately: remove, protect below, restrict access; engineer and glazier within days. |
| Active leaks damaging slab edges, finishes or units below; corroded anchors with displacement | failure · 4 Essential | Repair now; locate the leak path by water testing first. |
| Widespread gasket shrinkage, failed perimeter seals, IGU failure across an elevation, hardware failing | condition · 2 Planned | Programme repair or replacement in the near term. |
| Seals and IGUs at age without failure; single-glazed system below current energy expectations | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Plan renewal or upgrade, often combined with a façade programme. |
| Façade ordinance finding of unsafe or safe with repair | deadline · 4 Essential | Timing set by the ordinance. |
| SSG with no adhesion test record; toughened glass at height with no heat-soak record; recurring leaks of unknown path | check · 2 Planned | Test before sizing works. |
| Isolated misted unit; minor hardware wear | nil · 1 Routine | Replace or adjust in routine maintenance. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A façade engineer leads; a glazier assists with glass identification and opening of glazing pockets. The checks below map leaks and breakages by location first, since where they recur points to the cause, then water test the suspect joints.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Visual survey | Of every elevation, close up from building maintenance units or rope access where defects are suspected, recording broken, misted and replaced units and seal condition. |
| Glass identification | From markings and with a polarising filter or edge-stress viewer to confirm toughened glass; heat-soak status from records, with safety glass confirmed in the critical locations for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). |
| Field water testing | To locate leak paths: a nozzle test under AAMA 501.2 or a chamber test under ASTM E1105 in the United States, and test methods under AS/NZS 4284 practice in Australia, done before any remedial design. |
| Adhesion testing | Of sealants and structural silicone by the hand pull method in ASTM C1521, with bond width and depth measured. |
| Opening up | Of glazing pockets, sill drainage and a sample of slab-edge anchors behind ceilings and floor finishes. |
| Thermography | To show air leakage, failed IGUs and thermal bridging at frames. |

The report should identify the system and glass types, leak paths found by testing, IGU and seal condition by elevation, SSG adhesion results, anchor condition, and any glass that must be made safe.

sections.heading: Draining, resealing or reglazing
sections.markdown:
Broken or loose glass at height is made safe first. Most leaks then yield to restoring drainage, which often stops them without resealing; resealing, reglazing and full replacement follow as seals, units and frames reach the end of their lives.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Drainage restoration | Clear weeps, and reinstate baffles and end dams. | First, for most leaks; it often stops them without resealing. |
| Reseal and regasket | Replace perimeter seals, cap seals and gaskets; on stick curtain walls, a wet-sealed overlay of joints can extend life. | Where seals and gaskets have shrunk, hardened or failed. |
| IGU replacement | Unit by unit, or reglazing of whole elevations. | Unit by unit for isolated failures; whole elevations where failure is widespread. |
| SSG remediation | Supplementary mechanical retention (toggles or caps), or full reglazing. | Where adhesion of the structural silicone is doubtful. |
| Toughened glass risk | Replace with heat-soaked or laminated glass, with interim protection below. | Where breakage history or location warrants. |
| Anchor repair | Replace or supplement corroded anchors, which requires access through finishes. | Where anchors corrode. |
| Replacement or overclad | Full replacement of the system, or a new system over the old on curtain walls. | When frames, seals and glass are all at the end of their life, or an energy upgrade is wanted. |
| Steel windows | Strip, treat and repaint, reglaze with matching sections, or install secondary glazing on heritage frames. | Where steel windows corrode. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Investigation is a lump sum with rates per water test and adhesion test. Resealing and regasketing are measured by linear metre; IGU replacement per unit; reglazing and replacement by façade area. Access by building maintenance unit, rope access or swing stage, and out-of-hours work in occupied buildings, are often the largest components.

Two-part lines are normal: testing first, then works sized from the results. Reseal and regasket are repairs and maintenance; IGU and system replacement are lifecycle; safety glazing upgrades and ordinance findings are code compliance; make-safe is immediate.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a look from the street cannot: what glass is installed where, whether toughened glass was heat-soaked, and where breakages and leaks recur. Ask for them before replacing a broken pane or chasing a leak.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Shop drawings and the glass schedule, with glass types by location | What glass is where, and whether it is toughened, heat-soaked or laminated. |
| Heat-soak certificates for toughened glass, and SSG adhesion test and compatibility records | Whether toughened glass was heat-soaked, and whether structural silicone has been tested. |
| Breakage log and leak log by location | Where breakages and leaks recur, which points to the cause. |
| Previous water testing, façade inspection reports and ordinance filings | What earlier tests and inspections found. |
| Warranties for IGUs, sealants and systems, with dates | Whether units, sealants and systems are still under warranty. |
| Window maintenance and hardware service records | Whether hardware is serviced. |
| Façade access strategy and the certification of the equipment that serves it | How the façade can be reached for inspection and repair. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Glazing is misread when a spontaneous breakage is treated as a maintenance matter, and when a leak is resealed without asking where along the system it recurs.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| Replace the broken pane and move on | Spontaneous breakage of toughened glass at height is a safety matter, not a maintenance one. A building with non-heat-soaked toughened glass over public areas and a history of breakage needs an assessment of the remaining risk, not just replacement of the broken pane. |
| Every leak needs resealing | Clearing weeps and reinstating baffles and end dams often stops leaks without resealing. Where a leak recurs, at the same mullion on every floor or at the sill ends, points to the joint or detail at fault. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets standards for glass, windows and insulating units, and for curtain walls, energy performance and periodic inspection. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Glass and units | The National Construction Code calls up AS 1288 for glass selection and installation and AS 2047 for windows and external glazed doors; insulated glass units are made to AS 4666. | Approved Document K covers safety glazing and protection from impact; glazing follows the BS 6262 series, toughened glass BS EN 12150, heat-soaked toughened glass BS EN 14179 and insulating glass units BS EN 1279. | International Building Code Chapter 24 governs glass and glazing; ASTM E1300 sets load resistance, ASTM C1048 heat-treated glass and ASTM E2190 insulating glass units; safety glazing follows 16 CFR 1201. |
| Curtain walls, energy and inspection | Section J sets energy performance for glazing. | Curtain walling follows BS EN 13830, with working standards published by the Centre for Window and Cladding Technology; Approved Documents L (energy), B (fire) and Q (security in dwellings) also apply. | ASTM C1401 covers structural sealant glazing; façade ordinances include windows and curtain walls in the periodic examination, and New York's Cycle 10 runs from February 2025 to February 2029. |

In Australia, windows on strata buildings are commonly lot property and the façade common property, which complicates whole-building replacement.

sections.heading: Worked example: toughened glass breaking over an entrance
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 2000s office has a glazed canopy and curtain wall over its main entrance. Two toughened panes have broken in three years with no sign of impact, each shattering into small fragments, and there are no heat-soak certificates in the records. Leaks also recur at the same mullion on several floors.

Spontaneous breakage of toughened glass at height over an entrance is a safety matter, not a maintenance one: breaks that start inside the pane point to nickel sulphide inclusions, and without heat-soak certificates more panes may follow. Leaks at the same mullion on every floor point to the splice or stack joint.

So the register carries the glass over the entrance as a safety line now, with interim protection below and an assessment of the remaining risk, replacement with heat-soaked or laminated glass, and water testing and resealing of the stack joint as a condition line.

thresholds.rule: Framed side panels within 300 mm of a doorway: Grade A safety glass

source.title: NCC 2025 Housing Provisions, Part 8.4 Glazing: human impact

thresholds.rule: Below 800 mm in windows; up to 1500 mm in doors and in side panels within 300 mm of a door

source.title: Approved Document K (2013 edition incorporating 2016 and 2020 amendments)

pages.title: Hazardous Materials
pages.question: Which hazardous materials should be presumed in a building, and when do they become a safety or capital issue?
pages.answer: Hazardous materials are mostly safe while sound and undisturbed; the risk is works and deterioration. Asbestos is presumed in buildings of the relevant era until a register says otherwise, and a register that did not inspect an area clears nothing there. Weathered asbestos cement, damaged friable lagging, flaking lead paint and leaking PCB capacitors are safety findings. Removal is usually costed with the works that will disturb the material.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about hazardous materials; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.

questions.question: Does a building need an asbestos register?
questions.answer: In Australia, workplaces built before the end of 2003 need an asbestos register and management plan, reviewed at least every five years and after works. In the United Kingdom there is a duty to manage asbestos in non-domestic premises.

questions.question: Is asbestos dangerous if it is left alone?
questions.answer: Mostly not while it is sound and undisturbed. The risk comes when works disturb it or it deteriorates, as weathered cement sheet and damaged lagging do.

questions.question: Can I rely on the asbestos register?
questions.answer: As a starting point. Its age, scope and any areas not accessed decide how much reliance it deserves; where an area was not inspected, treat suspect materials there as asbestos until sampled.

questions.question: What is the oily residue in old light fittings?
questions.answer: Possibly leaking PCB capacitors. Sampling confirms it, and the capacitors are removed as hazardous waste.

questions.question: Should asbestos be removed before a refurbishment?
questions.answer: Materials the works will disturb need a refurbishment and demolition survey and licensed removal first. Sound materials outside the works can be managed in place.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Hazardous materials rarely announce themselves: the signs are the materials of the era, their condition, and what the records do and do not cover. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On site | Grey cement sheeting on roofs, eaves, walls and fences in buildings of the relevant era | Deterioration, leaks and ground hazards |
| On site | Lagged pipework and boilers in plant rooms; sprayed coatings on steel and soffits | Deterioration, leaks and ground hazards |
| On site | Vinyl floor tiles of older sizes and patterns; textured ceiling coatings | Where hazardous materials are found |
| On site | Asbestos labels or warning stickers; areas marked "not accessed" in registers | Registers and surveys |
| On site | Flaking paint on older window frames, doors and railings | Deterioration, leaks and ground hazards |
| On site | Old fluorescent fittings with capacitors; oily residue | Deterioration, leaks and ground hazards |
| In the records | Asbestos register and management plan with dates | Registers and surveys |
| In the records | Refurbishment and demolition surveys | Works, fire and storms |
| In the records | Removal and clearance certificates | Works, fire and storms |
| In the records | Lead and PCB test results | Registers and surveys |
| In the records | Radon results in affected areas | Deterioration, leaks and ground hazards |
| On site | Debris, dust or broken fragments of suspect materials on floors, in ceiling voids or around plant, a sign that materials have already been disturbed | Works, fire and storms |

sections.heading: Where hazardous materials are found
sections.markdown:
Hazardous materials are building materials and components that can harm people when they deteriorate or are disturbed: asbestos, lead paint, polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), synthetic mineral fibres, mercury in lamps and controls, ozone-depleting substances in plant, and ground hazards such as radon and contaminated land. Most are not a hazard while sound and undisturbed. They become a capital issue when they deteriorate, when works disturb them, and when the building is refurbished or demolished.

| Material | Typical era and use | Hazard |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Asbestos (cement sheet, vinyl tiles, insulation, lagging, sprayed coatings, gaskets, textured coatings) | Buildings before about 1990 in Australia and Britain (banned 2003 and 1999); US legacy materials of similar eras | Fibres cause mesothelioma, lung cancer and asbestosis when disturbed |
| Friable asbestos (sprayed insulation, lagging, loose fill) | Commercial buildings, plant rooms, some houses | Releases fibres readily; highest risk |
| Lead paint | Buildings painted before about 1970 (Australia), the 1960s (Britain), 1978 (US housing) | Lead poisoning from dust and chips, especially children |
| PCBs | Fluorescent light capacitors, transformers, sealants, 1950s to 1980 | Toxic and persistent; contaminate surroundings |
| Synthetic mineral fibres | Insulation, ceiling tiles, from mid-century | Skin and respiratory irritation; older types more hazardous |
| Mercury | Fluorescent lamps, thermostats, switches | Toxic if broken or disposed of incorrectly |
| Ozone-depleting substances | Halon fire systems, older refrigerants | Regulated; require recovery |
| Radon and ground gases | Buildings on certain geologies and contaminated land | Lung cancer; explosion risk from methane |

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Hazardous materials do not wear out on a schedule; they change condition. Bonded materials stay safe while sound and undisturbed, and weathering, damage and works turn them into a hazard, so condition and disturbance matter more than age.

| Material | What happens over time | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bonded asbestos cement | Weathers, erodes and cracks; becomes friable at the surface | Exposure; lichen; impact |
| Friable asbestos | Deteriorates and releases fibres | Vibration; water; disturbance |
| Vinyl tiles and adhesives | Stable unless sanded or removed | Works |
| Lead paint | Chalks, flakes and peels | Weather; friction at windows and doors |
| PCB capacitors | Leak as they age | Age; heat |
| Asbestos registers | Become outdated after works and with time | Review cycles |

What shortens it: works: refurbishment, services installation, drilling and demolition disturbing materials that were stable; deterioration from weather, water and vibration; out-of-date registers that do not reflect what is there; contractors who are not told what they may disturb.

sections.heading: Works, fire and storms
sections.markdown:
Most exposure happens when trades drill, cut, sand or remove materials without knowing they contain asbestos or lead: electricians in ceiling voids, plumbers in risers, painters preparing old surfaces, flooring contractors lifting tiles. The register exists to prevent this, and the refurbishment survey before works is the critical step.

Fire, storms and impact can break asbestos materials and spread debris across a site and neighbouring land, turning a managed material into an emergency clean-up.

Hazardous materials turn refurbishments and demolitions into licensed removal projects, often with significant cost and programme effects, especially where friable asbestos is extensive.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Drilling, cutting or demolition started without a refurbishment survey | Asbestos disturbed without knowing where it is. Survey records against the work area; the HSE survey guide expects a refurbishment and demolition survey before such work (HSG264). | Stop the work, isolate the area, survey, and decontaminate if needed. |
| Fire or storm damage to an older building with cement sheet or lagging | Asbestos debris spread by the event. Visual inspection; sampling of debris; air monitoring. | Restrict access and arrange licensed clean-up before repairs. |
| Sanding or stripping old paint | Lead dust released. Paint testing before work, against the definition of lead paint for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Use lead-safe methods and clean-up, and keep occupants away. |

sections.heading: Deterioration, leaks and ground hazards
sections.markdown:
Weathered asbestos cement roofs and walls shed fibre and cannot be safely cleaned or coated; friable lagging and sprayed insulation deteriorate with vibration and water; lead paint flakes and chalks around windows and doors, contaminating soil and interiors.

Capacitors in old light fittings and transformers leak oily PCB fluid as they age, contaminating fittings, ceilings and the surrounding fabric.

Radon enters buildings through floors in affected areas; contaminated land and landfill gas affect basements and ground floors.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cement sheet roof weathered with exposed fibres | Asbestos cement weathering. Sampling; register. | Sample if not already identified; plan removal or encapsulation, and keep people off the roof. |
| Damaged lagging in a plant room | Friable asbestos deteriorating. Sampling; air monitoring. | Isolate the area now; licensed removal with air monitoring. |
| Flaking paint on a pre-1970 building | Possible lead paint. Paint testing. | Test the paint; stabilise or remove it under lead-safe work practices. |
| Oily residue in old light fittings | Leaking PCB capacitors. Sampling. | Isolate the fittings and remove the capacitors as hazardous waste. |

sections.heading: Registers and surveys
sections.markdown:
Registers that are out of date, incomplete, marked "not accessed" for large areas, or not shown to contractors give false assurance. A register that says "no asbestos detected" in areas that were never inspected is a common trap.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Register shows large areas not accessed | Incomplete survey. Register review. | Survey those areas before any works; treat suspect materials there as asbestos until sampled. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Damaged friable asbestos in accessible areas; deteriorating lead paint where children are present; leaking PCBs | safety · 4 Essential | Isolate and remediate now. |
| Asbestos released by works | failure · 4 Essential | Stop work, decontaminate and clear now. |
| Register review or management plan update due; no register in a workplace of the relevant era | deadline · 4 Essential | At the required interval. |
| Bonded asbestos weathering; lead paint flaking | condition · 4 Essential | Manage or remove in the near term. |
| Removal planned with refurbishment or replacement | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Plan with the works. |
| Areas not accessed; refurbishment planned | check · 3 Important | Survey before works. |
| Sound and managed materials | nil · 1 Routine | Manage in place. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A licensed or accredited asbestos assessor or surveyor; lead and PCB specialists as needed. The checks below decide what is present, in what condition, and what the works will disturb, before anything is priced.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Management survey | To identify accessible materials for the register. |
| Refurbishment and demolition survey | Intrusive, before any works that will disturb the fabric. |
| Sampling and laboratory analysis | Of suspect materials. |
| Condition assessment | And risk scoring of each material. |
| Lead paint testing | By laboratory or XRF. |
| PCB identification | Of capacitors and sealants. |
| Air monitoring | Where release is suspected. |
| Radon testing | In affected areas. |

The report should give a register with locations, materials, condition and risk, actions, and the removal scope linked to planned works.

Surveys must be matched to purpose: a management survey supports day-to-day safety but is not enough for refurbishment or demolition, which needs intrusive sampling of the areas to be disturbed.

sections.heading: Managing, encapsulating or removing
sections.markdown:
Most hazardous materials can stay where they are while they are sound and undisturbed. The choice between managing them in place, sealing them, or removing them turns on their condition and on whether works will disturb them, not on their presence alone.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Manage in place | Label, protect from damage and inspect sound materials on a schedule, recording condition in the register. | While the material is sound and no works will disturb it. |
| Encapsulation | Seal sound bonded materials with sealants or enclosures. | Where sound bonded material needs protecting but removal is not yet needed. |
| Licensed removal | Enclosures, air monitoring, decontamination, disposal and clearance certificates. | Before works that would disturb the material, and where friable material is damaged. |
| Lead paint | Stabilise or remove under lead-safe work practices, with clean-up and clearance testing. | Where paint is flaking, or before works that would disturb it. |
| PCB removal | Remove capacitors, transformers and sealants as hazardous waste, and clean contaminated fabric. | Where fittings or sealants contain or leak PCBs, usually with their replacement. |
| Register updates | Update the register after every removal or change, and review the management plan. | After every removal or change, and at each scheduled review. |
| Contractor controls | Permits requiring register checks before any work that drills, cuts or removes materials. | Always, before any such work. |
| Radon mitigation | Sealing and sub-floor depressurisation. | Where tests exceed action levels. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Surveys and register reviews recur. Removal is priced per area or per item, with containment, air monitoring, disposal and clearance. Friable removal costs much more than bonded. Removal is usually carried in the works line that disturbs it.

Register, management and safety items are code compliance; removal with refurbishment is lifecycle; emergency remediation is immediate.

Removal discovered mid-project costs far more than removal planned from a refurbishment survey, through delays, re-sequencing and decontamination.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what an inspection cannot: what has been sampled, what has been removed and cleared, and whether anyone checks the register before drilling. Ask for them before any works are scoped, so the survey covers what the records do not.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Asbestos register and management plan | What has been identified, where, in what condition, and how it is managed. |
| Refurbishment and demolition surveys | What lies in areas a management survey does not reach, before works disturb it. |
| Removal and clearance certificates | Which materials have gone, and that the areas were cleared afterwards. |
| Lead paint and PCB testing | Whether paint, fittings and sealants of the era contain lead or PCBs. |
| Radon results | Whether ground gas needs mitigation in affected areas. |
| Contractor permit procedures | Whether trades check the register before they drill or cut. |
| Air monitoring results after removals | That removals left the air clear. |
| Records of incidents involving disturbed materials | Where materials have already been disturbed, and how it was handled. |
| Lead paint disclosure documents for residential property | What has been disclosed about lead paint at sale or lease. |
| Hazardous waste disposal records | That removed material went to an approved facility. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Hazardous materials are misread in both directions: a material missing from the register is assumed absent, or a material that is present is assumed to need removal at once. Both lead to the wrong scope.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| It is not on the register, so it is not asbestos | Never assume a material is free of asbestos because it is not on the register. If the register did not inspect an area, treat suspect materials there as asbestos until sampled. |
| The building has a register, so the asbestos is known | Treat the register as a starting point, not a conclusion: its age, scope and any areas not accessed decide how much reliance it deserves. |
| Asbestos must be removed as soon as it is found | Sound, undisturbed material is mostly safe and can be managed in place. The risk comes with works and deterioration. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Hazardous materials are the same in each market; the duties around them are not. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out the rules on managing and removing asbestos, and on lead.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Asbestos | The model work health and safety regulations require an asbestos register and management plan for workplaces built before the end of 2003, reviewed at least every five years and after works; removal is licensed. The Asbestos and Silica Safety and Eradication Agency coordinates national strategy. | The Control of Asbestos Regulations 2012 impose a duty to manage asbestos in non-domestic premises; HSG264 sets survey practice. | OSHA regulates asbestos exposure; EPA rules govern renovation and demolition notification and, since 2024, ban ongoing uses of chrysotile asbestos. |
| Lead | AS/NZS 4361.2 covers lead paint. | The Control of Lead at Work Regulations 2002 apply. | The Renovation, Repair and Painting Rule governs lead in pre-1978 housing. |

Disclosure obligations at sale and lease vary, but commonly include known asbestos in all three countries.

sections.heading: Worked example: a register with gaps before a refurbishment
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 1970s office in Australia is to be refurbished floor by floor. Its asbestos register is six years old, lists the plant room as "not accessed", and records vinyl floor tiles and a cement sheet roof as asbestos-containing and in good condition.

The register is past its five-yearly review, a deadline finding, and it has a gap where the risk is highest: plant rooms of the era often hold lagging. Before anything else, that makes a review of the register and a refurbishment and demolition survey of the floors and the plant room. The floor tiles are sound and can be managed in place until the works remove them.

So the register carries a survey line now and a licensed removal allowance timed with each floor's works, sized once the survey is in. If the plant room survey finds damaged lagging, that becomes a safety finding: isolate and remediate now.

thresholds.rule: Lead at or above 1.0 mg/cm², or 0.5 per cent by weight

pages.title: Heat Rejection Plant
pages.question: How do cooling towers, dry coolers and condensers fail, and what makes a cooling tower a public health item?
pages.answer: Cooling towers are first a public health item: Legionella grows in warm, dirty, stagnant water and towers spread it as aerosols, so registration, risk management, sampling and prescribed responses are law in all three jurisdictions. Mechanically, towers scale, corrode and foul; fill collapses under deposits; fans and gearboxes wear. Dry coolers and air-cooled condensers lose capacity to coil corrosion near the coast and to hot air recirculating behind screens and walls.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about heat rejection plant; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.

pages.searchTitle: Cooling towers and heat rejection: Legionella, water treatment, fill and recirculation

questions.question: What happens after a positive Legionella result in a cooling tower?
questions.answer: The response the regulation prescribes, typically immediate disinfection, re-testing and notification. It is not a maintenance item.

questions.question: Why are standby cooling tower cells a risk?
questions.answer: Water left stagnant in standby cells and dead legs grows bacteria. Drain standby cells or circulate them.

questions.question: Do cooling towers need registering?
questions.answer: Yes. Australian states require registration and a risk management plan, the United Kingdom requires notification to the local authority, and New York City requires registration and sampling.

questions.question: Why do air-cooled condensers struggle on hot days?
questions.answer: Often hot air recirculating from screens or walls around them, or fouled coils.

questions.question: How long do cooling towers last?
questions.answer: Galvanised steel towers 15 to 20 years, stainless or fibreglass 20 to 30, and concrete 30 to 40; fill and drift eliminators 10 to 15.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Heat rejection problems show at the tower as scale, corrosion, drift and stagnant cells, around it in its siting, and above all in its registration and sampling records. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| From aerial imagery and the roof | Tower type and material; visible corrosion and staining | Corrosion, scale, fill and mechanicals |
| From aerial imagery and the roof | Drift and staining on surrounding roof and plant | Legionella, stagnation and drift |
| From aerial imagery and the roof | Proximity of towers to air intakes, windows and occupied areas | Legionella, stagnation and drift |
| From aerial imagery and the roof | Condensers boxed in by walls or screens | Hot air recirculation |
| On site | Scale and biofilm on fill and basin; sludge in basins | Corrosion, scale, fill and mechanicals |
| On site | Damaged or missing drift eliminators | Legionella, stagnation and drift |
| On site | Corrosion of basin, casing and supports; white rust | Corrosion, scale, fill and mechanicals |
| On site | Fan and gearbox noise, oil leaks, vibration | Corrosion, scale, fill and mechanicals |
| On site | Water treatment dosing equipment working, chemicals in date | Legionella, stagnation and drift |
| On site | Coil fins corroded, flattened or blocked | Hot air recirculation |
| In the records | Tower registration and risk management plan | Standards by country |
| In the records | Legionella and bacterial count sampling results | Legionella, stagnation and drift |
| In the records | Water treatment reports | Investigation before the scope |
| In the records | Independent audit reports where required | Standards by country |
| In the records | Maintenance and cleaning records | Corrosion, scale, fill and mechanicals |
| In the records | Basin overflowing or make-up valve running constantly | Corrosion, scale, fill and mechanicals |
| In the records | Algae on exposed wet surfaces in sunlight | Legionella, stagnation and drift |
| In the records | Visible plume or drift wetting nearby surfaces | Legionella, stagnation and drift |
| In the records | Standby cells left full and stagnant; isolated pipework branches | Legionella, stagnation and drift |

sections.heading: Types of heat rejection plant
sections.markdown:
Heat rejection plant takes heat out of a building's cooling system and releases it to the outside air. Water-cooled chillers reject heat through cooling towers or dry coolers; air-cooled chillers and refrigeration plant reject it through condenser coils on the machine itself. The choice of system decides the risks: cooling towers are efficient but carry a Legionella risk that is regulated in all three jurisdictions; dry and air-cooled systems avoid that risk but are larger, noisier and lose capacity on hot days.

| Type | How it works | Main risk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Open-circuit cooling tower | Condenser water sprayed over fill; part evaporates, cooling the rest | Legionella; scale, corrosion and biofouling; structural corrosion |
| Closed-circuit cooler (fluid cooler) | Condenser water stays in a coil; a separate spray circuit evaporates over it | Legionella in the spray circuit; coil corrosion |
| Evaporative condenser | Refrigerant condenses in a coil wetted by spray | Legionella; coil corrosion; refrigerant leaks |
| Dry cooler | Water or glycol through finned coils, fans blowing air across | Coil corrosion; reduced capacity in heat |
| Adiabatic cooler | Dry cooler with pre-cooling pads or sprays used on hot days | Water quality in pads and sprays; pad decay |
| Air-cooled condenser (on chillers and split plant) | Refrigerant condenses in finned coils | Coil corrosion; hot air recirculation |

Towers sit on roofs or at ground level and are built in galvanised steel, stainless steel, fibreglass or concrete. Inside are the fill (the surface over which water spreads), drift eliminators (which catch water droplets before they leave), the basin, distribution system, fans with motors and gearboxes or belts, and the water treatment and bleed equipment.

Every cooling tower has a water treatment system that is as important as the tower: chemical dosing (corrosion and scale inhibitors, biocides), controlled bleed-off to limit how far dissolved solids concentrate, often side-stream filtration, and monitoring. Treatment is usually provided by a specialist contractor under a service agreement, and the regulated records are theirs to keep but the owner's to hold.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Galvanised steel cooling towers last fifteen to twenty years, stainless or fibreglass twenty to thirty, and concrete thirty to forty, while fill and drift eliminators last ten to fifteen. Water treatment decides how long all of them actually last.

| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Galvanised steel cooling tower | 15 to 20 years | Water treatment; white rust; basin corrosion |
| Stainless or fibreglass cooling tower | 20 to 30 years | UV on fibreglass; structural supports |
| Concrete tower | 30 to 40 years | Concrete deterioration |
| Fill | 10 to 15 years | Fouling; collapse under weight of deposits |
| Drift eliminators | 10 to 15 years | UV; damage; fouling |
| Fans, motors, gearboxes | 15 to 20 years | Vibration; lubrication |
| Dry coolers | 20 to 25 years | Coil corrosion; fan motors |
| Air-cooled condenser coils | 15 to 20 years; 5 to 10 unprotected near the coast | Salt air; coating |

What shortens life: water treatment failures: scale, corrosion and biofouling all follow; coastal and industrial air on coils and steel; debris and nearby sources: leaves, dust from construction, exhausts drawn into towers; poor siting: towers and condensers too close to walls or screens, so hot air recirculates; intermittent operation with stagnant water.

sections.heading: Legionella, stagnation and drift
sections.markdown:
Legionella bacteria multiply in warm water with sediment, biofilm and stagnation, and cooling towers produce aerosols that can carry them to people nearby. Outbreaks of Legionnaires' disease have been traced to towers in all three countries, which is why towers are registered, risk-managed and tested by law. Risk rises with poor water treatment, dead legs and stagnant pipework, damaged drift eliminators, intermittent operation, and dirty fill and basins.

Towers that run intermittently, standby cells left full, and pipework branches that no longer carry flow hold warm stagnant water where biofilm and Legionella grow. Plant changes over the years often leave dead legs behind.

Drift eliminators catch water droplets before they leave the tower. Damaged, displaced or poorly fitted eliminators release more aerosol, and towers placed near air intakes, openable windows, roof terraces or public areas expose people to it.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| High bacterial counts | Treatment failure, dead legs, stagnation. Records; system inspection; counts against the action levels for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Disinfect and resample; restore treatment and remove dead legs. |
| Drift visible from the tower, or a tower close to air intakes or windows | Aerosol reaching people. Drift eliminator condition; distances to intakes, windows and public areas. | Replace or refit eliminators, and review siting with the risk assessment. |

sections.heading: Corrosion, scale, fill and mechanicals
sections.markdown:
Galvanised towers develop white rust when the zinc is attacked by poorly balanced water, especially in the first months; steel basins and supports then corrode. Fibreglass degrades under UV. Coils on dry coolers and condensers corrode, especially aluminium fins in salt air.

As water evaporates, dissolved minerals concentrate. Without enough bleed-off and treatment, they deposit as scale on fill and in condenser tubes, cutting heat transfer and raising chiller energy use.

Biofilm and sediment build up on fill, adding weight until the fill sags and collapses, and providing habitat for Legionella.

Fan blades crack, gearboxes leak and wear, belts slip, motors fail, and vibration switches fail to act. A fan or gearbox failure takes a cell out of service.

Towers consume water through evaporation, drift and bleed. Uncontrolled bleed, overflowing basins and leaks waste water and dilute treatment chemicals.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rising condenser approach on the chillers | Scaled or fouled tower and tubes, or tower capacity lost. Tower inspection; water treatment records. | Clean the tower and tubes, and check the tower's capacity. |
| White powder on galvanised surfaces | White rust from unbalanced water. Water chemistry. | Rebalance the water treatment. |
| Fill sagging or collapsed | Biofouling and deposits. Visual; fill weight. | Replace the fill, and correct the water treatment. |
| Standby cell or tower left idle for weeks | Stagnant water and biofilm. Operating records; water treatment in the idle cell. | Run or drain idle cells, and disinfect before returning them to service. |

sections.heading: Hot air recirculation
sections.markdown:
Air-cooled condensers and dry coolers placed too close together, against walls or behind solid plant screens, draw in their own hot discharge air. Capacity falls on hot days and head pressures rise.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Head pressure high on hot days, air-cooled plant | Hot air recirculation or fouled coils. Temperature at coil inlet higher than ambient. | Clean the coils, and remove the screens or walls that recirculate hot air. |
| Plant screens added around air-cooled condensers | Hot air trapped and recirculated. Coil inlet temperature compared with ambient. | Open the screen, add baffles, or move the units. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Legionella above the action levels in the regulation; tower near air intakes or public areas with damaged drift eliminators | safety · 4 Essential | Disinfect and follow the prescribed response now. |
| Tower not registered, no risk management plan, sampling or audit overdue | deadline · 4 Essential | Comply immediately. |
| Tower out of service; fill collapsed; fan failure | failure · 3 Important | Repair now. |
| Corrosion, scale, worn mechanicals | condition · 3 Important | Repair in the near term. |
| Tower at end of life | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Replace; consider dry or adiabatic alternatives. |
| Condenser capacity in doubt on hot days | check · 2 Planned | Assess. |
| Normal wear | nil · 1 Routine | Routine. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A mechanical services engineer and the water treatment contractor; an independent auditor where regulation requires one. The checks below start with the registration, risk management plan and sampling results, then inspect the basin, fill, eliminators and mechanicals.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Records review | Registration, risk management plan, sampling results and trends, treatment logs, cleaning and disinfection records, audit reports. |
| Tower inspection | With the tower drained and isolated: fill, eliminators, distribution, basin, casing, structure, access. |
| Water sampling | For Legionella (laboratory culture to AS/NZS 3896 in Australia, or an equivalent accredited method) and heterotrophic plate count, with chemistry for conductivity, pH, inhibitor and biocide levels. |
| System survey | For dead legs, stagnant branches and standby cells. |
| Siting review | Distance to air intakes, windows and occupied areas; recirculation around condensers. |
| Mechanical checks | Fan, gearbox and motor vibration, oil condition, belt tension. |
| Capacity check | The tower's ability to deliver design condenser water temperature on a hot day, against the chillers' needs; a performance test to the Cooling Technology Institute method where capacity is in doubt. |
| Structural check | Of supports and the roof under the tower. |

The report should state compliance status, the Legionella risk position, tower condition and remaining life, capacity, siting risks, and whether to refurbish, replace like for like, or move to a dry or adiabatic system.

sections.heading: Restoring compliance, repairing or replacing
sections.markdown:
Compliance comes first: registration, a current risk management plan, and sampling and disinfection on the regulated schedule. After that, the work restores water treatment and the tower's parts, or replaces it, with a new tower or with dry or adiabatic coolers.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Compliance | Register, write or update the risk management plan, restore sampling and audit schedules, keep records. | Wherever registration, the plan, sampling or records have lapsed. |
| Clean and disinfect | Clean and disinfect the tower. | On the regulated schedule, and after positive results. |
| Water treatment | Automatic dosing and conductivity-controlled bleed, side-stream filtration, and monitoring. | In every tower. |
| Remove dead legs | Remove dead legs, and drain standby cells or circulate them. | Where water stagnates. |
| Replace fill and drift eliminators | New fill and eliminators, with high-efficiency eliminators where the tower is near people. | Where fill sags or eliminators are damaged. |
| Mechanical repairs | Fans, gearboxes, motors, variable speed drives. | Where fans, gearboxes or motors wear. |
| Basin and casing repair | Coatings, stainless basins, structural repairs. | Where basins and casings corrode. |
| Relocation or screening | Move or screen the tower. | Where it sits near intakes or occupied areas. |
| Replacement | A new tower in stainless or fibreglass, or dry or adiabatic coolers. | At the end of the tower's life. |

| Option | Advantages | Trade-offs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| New cooling tower | Most efficient chiller operation; compact | Legionella regime continues; water use |
| Dry cooler | No Legionella regime; no water use | Larger, heavier, noisier; chiller efficiency lower on hot days |
| Adiabatic cooler | Near tower efficiency on hot days with much less water; lower Legionella risk | Pads and sprays need water management; still regulated in some jurisdictions |
| Air-cooled chillers replacing water-cooled plant | Removes the tower and condenser water system | Lower efficiency; space and noise on the roof |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Water treatment, sampling and audits are recurring contracts and compliance costs. Fill and eliminator replacement are lump sums per cell. Mechanical repairs are itemised. Tower replacement is a lump-sum project including crane lift, structural works, pipework and electrical connection, controls, water treatment equipment and commissioning, with temporary heat rejection where the building cannot be without cooling.

Moving to dry or adiabatic cooling can change chiller selection and roof structure, and is usually part of a wider plant strategy rather than a like-for-like line.

Legionella compliance is code compliance and recurs; replacement is lifecycle; repairs are repairs and maintenance; a positive result is immediate.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a look at the tower cannot: whether it is registered, whether sampling has found Legionella, and how it has been treated and cleaned. Ask for them first, since they decide whether the tower is compliant.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Tower registration and the current risk management plan | Whether the tower is registered, and how its risk is managed. |
| Legionella and heterotrophic plate count results for at least two years, with the responses taken to any positive results | Whether Legionella has been found, and how it was handled. |
| Water treatment service reports and chemical dosing records | Whether the water is treated as it should be. |
| Cleaning and disinfection records | Whether cleaning and disinfection are on schedule. |
| Independent audit reports where required | Whether independent audits found problems. |
| Maintenance records for fans, gearboxes and motors | Whether fans, gearboxes and motors are maintained. |
| Installation date and materials of the tower | How old the tower is, and what it is made of. |
| Drawings showing tower location relative to air intakes and occupied areas | Whether the tower sits near intakes or occupied areas. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Cooling towers are misread when a positive Legionella result is treated as routine maintenance, and when condenser problems are blamed on the chillers they serve.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| A positive result is a maintenance item | A positive Legionella result above regulatory action levels requires the response the regulation prescribes, typically immediate disinfection, re-testing and notification. It is not a maintenance item. |
| The chillers are struggling | A rising condenser approach on the chillers often points to a scaled or fouled tower and tubes, or a tower short of capacity. Check the tower before the chillers. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market regulates cooling towers for Legionella control, through registration or notification, risk management and sampling. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Registration, Legionella control and maintenance | States regulate cooling towers under public health legislation, typically requiring registration, a risk management plan, independent audit and routine Legionella and heterotrophic plate count sampling with prescribed responses (for example the Public Health and Wellbeing Regulations 2019 in Victoria and the Public Health Regulation 2022 in New South Wales). AS/NZS 3666 sets design, maintenance and performance-based maintenance of cooling water systems. | The Notification of Cooling Towers and Evaporative Condensers Regulations 1992 require towers to be notified to the local authority; the HSE Approved Code of Practice L8 and HSG274 Part 1 set the control regime. | ASHRAE 188 sets the risk management standard for building water systems; New York City's Local Law 77 requires cooling tower registration, inspection and Legionella sampling; the Cooling Technology Institute publishes standards for tower performance and maintenance. |

sections.heading: Worked example: a positive Legionella result
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. An office's cooling towers returned a Legionella count above the regulatory action level in routine sampling. One cell is kept as standby, full and stagnant; the drift eliminators are damaged, and the towers sit near a fresh air intake.

A result above the action level requires the response the regulation prescribes, typically immediate disinfection, re-testing and notification; it is not a maintenance item. The stagnant standby cell is a likely source, and damaged eliminators near an intake raise the exposure.

So the register carries the response as a safety line now, the standby cell drained or circulated, high-efficiency eliminators, and a review of the risk management plan, with relocation or screening from the intake considered.

thresholds.rule: Under control up to 10,000 cfu/ml; corrective action above 100,000 cfu/ml

source.title: HSG274 Legionnaires’ disease: Technical guidance, Part 1: Evaporative cooling systems

thresholds.rule: Review above 100 cfu/litre; immediate action above 1,000 cfu/litre

source.title: HSG274 Legionnaires’ disease: Technical guidance, Part 1: Evaporative cooling systems

pages.title: Hot & Warm Water Plant
pages.question: How do hot water systems fail, and how do you balance Legionella risk against scalding?
pages.answer: Hot water plant sits between two hazards: water must be stored at 60 °C and kept hot through the loop to control Legionella, yet delivered cool enough not to scald. Failures sit at both ends: cool storage, failed circulation pumps, dead legs and little-used outlets grow Legionella; failed or bypassed TMVs scald vulnerable people. Tanks corrode when anodes are spent; relief valves seize. Electrification is reshaping replacement choices.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about hot & warm water plant; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
