pages.searchTitle: Hot water systems: Legionella, scalding, TMVs, loop temperatures and heat pumps

questions.question: What temperature should hot water be stored at?
questions.answer: At least 60 °C, to control Legionella, with lower delivery temperatures at personal hygiene outlets; in Australia no more than 50 °C, or 45 °C in healthcare, aged care and childcare.

questions.question: Why is the hot water loop not hot enough?
questions.answer: Usually a failed circulating pump or an unbalanced loop. Repair and rebalance it; a loop below 50 °C is a Legionella risk.

questions.question: What is a TMV, and why does it matter?
questions.answer: A thermostatic mixing valve, which limits the delivered temperature to prevent scalding. A failed TMV where vulnerable people bathe is a safety finding.

questions.question: Why is the relief valve on our water heater dripping?
questions.answer: Often a failed thermostat, or high mains pressure.

questions.question: How long do water heaters last?
questions.answer: Storage water heaters 8 to 15 years, heat pump and continuous-flow heaters 10 to 15, and calorifiers 20 to 25.

questions.question: Why does it take so long for hot water to arrive at some taps?
questions.answer: Dead legs, or the circulating loop not reaching that branch. Remove dead legs, extend the loop, or heat at the point of use.

questions.question: Why is there water under the hot water tank?
questions.answer: The tank has corroded through, or the relief valve is discharging. Replace the tank, or correct the relief valve discharge.

questions.question: The hot water tested positive for Legionella. What now?
questions.answer: It usually follows low storage or loop temperatures and stagnation. Disinfect and retest; restore storage and loop temperatures, and flushing.

questions.question: The water heater has no relief valve, or it has been plugged. Is that dangerous?
questions.answer: Yes. There is no protection against over-pressure or flash steam. Replace the relief valve and drain line, and test it.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Hot water problems show at heaters as rust, water and relief valve discharge, at outlets as long waits or very hot water, and in temperature records, TMV logs and test results. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On site | Water heater nameplates, ages and anode service tags | Heaters, relief valves and combustion |
| On site | Rust and water staining at the base of tanks; damp in cupboards and ceilings below roof-space heaters | Heaters, relief valves and combustion |
| On site | Relief valve drain lines: present, discharging, terminating safely | Heaters, relief valves and combustion |
| On site | Thermometers at calorifier outlets and returns; temperature at the far end of the loop | Legionella and the loop |
| On site | TMV locations, service tags and dates | Scalding and TMVs |
| On site | Long waits for hot water at outlets; very hot water at sinks in sensitive areas | Legionella and the loop |
| On site | Gas heater flues and cupboard ventilation | Heaters, relief valves and combustion |
| In the records | Water temperature monitoring records | Legionella and the loop |
| In the records | Legionella risk assessment and test results | Legionella and the loop |
| In the records | TMV service records | Scalding and TMVs |
| In the records | Heater replacement history | Heaters, relief valves and combustion |
| In the records | Scald incident reports | Scalding and TMVs |

sections.heading: Types of hot water plant
sections.markdown:
Hot and warm water plant heats water for washing, bathing and kitchens: storage water heaters (gas, electric, heat pump, solar), continuous-flow (instantaneous) heaters, central plant with calorifiers or plate heat exchangers and a heated flow-and-return loop, and the thermostatic mixing valves (TMVs) and tempering valves that limit outlet temperatures to prevent scalding. It sits between two hazards that pull in opposite directions: water must be kept hot enough to control Legionella, and delivered cool enough not to scald.

| Type | Where it is found | Character |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gas storage water heater | Houses, small commercial | Anode protection, burner and flue; 8 to 12 year life |
| Electric storage water heater | Houses and apartments | Element and thermostat; anode; off-peak operation |
| Heat pump water heater | Houses and apartments, electrification retrofits | Lower storage temperatures; boost cycles for Legionella control |
| Solar water heater | Houses in sunny climates | Collectors on roof; frost and overheating protection; booster |
| Continuous-flow (instantaneous) gas or electric | Houses, apartments, small commercial | No storage; flow and pressure dependent |
| Central plant with flow and return loop | Apartments, hotels, hospitals, offices | Calorifiers or heat exchangers, circulating pumps, balancing valves |
| Thermostatic mixing valves | Healthcare, aged care, childcare, schools, accessible bathrooms | Blend hot and cold to a safe temperature at the outlet; need annual testing |

Required temperatures differ by jurisdiction but follow the same logic: store at 60 °C or more; keep circulating water hot throughout the loop; deliver to outlets at a temperature that will not scald, lower still in buildings for children, the elderly and people with disabilities. Fuel policy is changing hot water as it is changing heating: gas restrictions and electrification push heat pump and electric systems.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Storage water heaters last eight to fifteen years and heat pump and continuous-flow heaters ten to fifteen, while calorifiers last twenty to twenty-five. Replacing a heater is routine; keeping the water hot enough, and safe at the tap, is the harder part.

| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Storage water heaters | 8 to 15 years | Anode replacement; water hardness; temperature |
| Heat pump water heaters | 10 to 15 years | Compressor; coastal exposure |
| Solar collectors | 15 to 25 years | Frost; overheating; seals |
| Continuous-flow heaters | 10 to 15 years | Scale; flow |
| Calorifiers | 20 to 25 years | Water quality; inspection |
| Circulating pumps | 10 to 15 years | Run hours; scale |
| Thermostatic mixing valves | 10 to 15 years with annual service | Scale; debris; maintenance |
| Copper hot water pipework | 40 to 60 years | Water chemistry; velocity |

What shortens life: hard water, which scales heat exchangers, elements and valves and reduces efficiency; neglected anodes: once the sacrificial anode is consumed, the tank corrodes from inside and fails; high velocity in hot water pipes, which erodes copper at bends; poor maintenance of TMVs, which drift and fail.

sections.heading: Legionella and the loop
sections.markdown:
Legionella grows between about 20 and 45 °C. Storage that runs cool to save energy, stratified tanks with cold water at the base, loops that fall below temperature at their far ends, dead legs, and little-used outlets all create growth sites. Showers then aerosolise the bacteria. Healthcare and aged care buildings, with vulnerable occupants, carry the highest risk.

Central systems depend on circulating pumps and balancing valves to keep the whole loop hot. Failed pumps, seized or unbalanced valves, and branches added in fit-outs leave parts of the system cool, wasting water while people run taps and growing Legionella.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Return loop running cool | Circulating pump failure or imbalance. Temperature mapping and pump status, against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Repair the circulating pump, and rebalance the loop. |
| Long waits for hot water at certain outlets | Dead legs or loop not reaching that branch. Temperature at outlet over time. | Remove dead legs, extend the loop, or heat at the point of use. |
| Positive Legionella result | Low storage or loop temperatures, stagnation. Temperature records; outlet use patterns. | Disinfect and retest; restore storage and loop temperatures, and flushing. |

sections.heading: Scalding and TMVs
sections.markdown:
Water at storage temperatures causes serious burns within seconds, especially to children, the elderly and people with reduced sensation. TMVs that fail, drift or are removed, and tempering valves missing from outlets that need them, expose occupants to scalding.

TMVs scale and foul and their thermostatic elements drift. They can fail hot (scald risk) or cold. They must be tested and serviced, typically annually, and after any work on the system.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Very hot water at basins in an aged care home | Failed or bypassed TMV. TMV test. | Service or replace the TMV now. |
| Hot water too hot at basins in a school, childcare centre or aged care home | Scald risk. Delivery temperature at each outlet against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Fit or repair tempering or thermostatic mixing valves and retest every outlet. |

sections.heading: Heaters, relief valves and combustion
sections.markdown:
Storage tanks are protected by sacrificial anodes. When anodes are spent, tanks rust through and leak, often without warning, causing water damage in roof spaces, cupboards and ceilings.

Temperature and pressure relief valves protect tanks from explosion. Valves that are never operated seize, and discharge pipes that are blocked, run to unsafe places or are missing put people and buildings at risk.

Gas water heaters in poorly ventilated cupboards or with blocked flues can produce carbon monoxide; flues disconnected in renovations are a recurring finding.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Water under a storage tank | Tank corroded through or relief valve discharging. Inspection. | Replace the tank, or correct the relief valve discharge. |
| Relief valve discharging continuously | Thermostat failure or high mains pressure. Temperature and pressure checks. | Replace the thermostat, or fit pressure control. |
| Storage heater with no working relief valve, or a valve that has been plugged | No protection against over-pressure or flash steam. Relief valve and setting against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Replace the relief valve and drain line, and test it. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Failed TMVs in healthcare, aged care, childcare or accessible bathrooms; positive Legionella; relief valve blocked; gas heater flue spillage | safety · 4 Essential | Isolate, disinfect or rectify now. |
| Heater failed; no hot water | failure · 3 Important | Replace now. |
| TMV servicing and Legionella testing due | deadline · 4 Essential | At the prescribed interval. |
| Loop below temperature; scale; corroding tanks | condition · 3 Important | Repair in the near term. |
| Heaters at end of life | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Replace, considering electrification. |
| No risk assessment or temperature records | check · 2 Planned | Assess. |
| Normal | nil · 1 Routine | Routine. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A hydraulic engineer or licensed plumber, with a water hygiene specialist for Legionella risk. The checks below start with the temperature records and the Legionella risk assessment, then measure temperatures at the far end of the loop and at the TMVs.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Legionella risk assessment | Of the whole system: storage, loop, dead legs, little-used outlets, vulnerable occupants. |
| Temperature mapping | At storage outlets, loop returns and sentinel outlets nearest and furthest from the plant, recorded over at least a day. |
| TMV testing | Of a sample or all valves in sensitive buildings: outlet temperature, fail-safe on cold supply loss, condition of strainers and checks. |
| Heater inspection | Age, anode, relief valves and drains, flues, ventilation, scale. |
| Water sampling | For Legionella where risk or history warrants. |
| Circulation check | Pumps, balancing valves and their settings. |
| Energy review | Heat loss from loops, fuel type and electrification options. |

The report should state Legionella and scald risks, temperature performance, plant condition and remaining life, and an upgrade or replacement plan.

sections.heading: Controlling temperature, servicing or replacing
sections.markdown:
Failed TMVs where vulnerable people bathe, and loops that cannot stay above 50 °C, come first. After that, the work keeps storage hot, removes dead legs, extends tank life with anodes, and replaces heaters, increasingly with heat pumps.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Temperature control | Restore storage to at least 60 °C, fix circulation, rebalance loops, add pipe insulation. | Wherever storage or the loop runs below temperature. |
| Dead leg removal | Remove dead legs, and set flushing regimes for little-used outlets. | Where water stagnates. |
| TMV servicing | Service annually, replace failing valves, and install them where codes now require. | In every building with TMVs. |
| Anode replacement | Replace anodes to extend tank life; replace tanks on failure or age. | On storage heaters. |
| Relief valve testing | Test relief valves and correct discharge pipes. | On every storage heater. |
| Disinfection | Thermal or chemical disinfection, followed by re-testing. | After positive results. |
| Electrification | Heat pump water heaters or electric systems replacing gas, with boost cycles for Legionella control and electrical capacity checked. | Where gas heaters reach the end of their life, or policy favours electric. |
| Water treatment | Treatment for scale. | In hard water areas. |
| Point-of-use heating | Local heaters for remote outlets. | Where the loop cannot keep them hot economically. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
TMV servicing and Legionella testing recur annually. Heaters are replaced per unit, often on a recurring allowance in residential buildings. Central plant replacement is a lump sum with temporary hot water. Loop rebalancing and dead leg removal are lump sums. Electrification adds electrical capacity, space and possibly roof or external plant locations.

Safety and testing are code compliance; replacement is lifecycle; repairs and anode replacement are repairs and maintenance.

Legionella remediation after a positive result carries disinfection, re-testing and sometimes temporary closures.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a look at the heaters cannot: whether the water stays hot enough to control Legionella, whether TMVs are serviced, and whether anyone has been scalded. Ask for the temperature records first.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Legionella risk assessment and water management plan | How Legionella risk is assessed and managed. |
| Temperature monitoring records | Whether storage and the loop stay hot enough. |
| Legionella test results and actions taken | Whether Legionella has been found, and what was done. |
| TMV register and service records | Whether every TMV is serviced. |
| Water heater register with ages and service records | How old each heater is. |
| Scald incident reports | Whether anyone has been scalded. |
| Gas compliance certificates for gas heaters | Whether gas heaters are certified safe. |
| Records of outlet flushing for little-used fixtures | Whether little-used outlets are flushed. |
| Drawings of the hot water loop showing balancing valves | How the loop is meant to be balanced. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Hot water is misread when a failed TMV or a cool loop is treated as routine maintenance, and when a long wait at the tap is treated as only an inconvenience.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| It is a maintenance item | A failed TMV in a building for vulnerable people is a scald risk, and a hot water system that cannot keep its loop above 50 °C is a Legionella risk. Both are safety findings, not maintenance items. |
| A long wait is only an inconvenience | Long waits for hot water at certain outlets point to dead legs or a loop that does not reach that branch, and water standing lukewarm is where Legionella grows. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets storage and delivery temperatures for hot water, requirements for TMVs, and a framework for managing Legionella. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Temperatures, TMVs and Legionella | AS/NZS 3500.4 governs heated water, requiring storage at 60 °C and delivery to personal hygiene outlets at no more than 50 °C, or 45 °C in healthcare, aged care, childcare and similar buildings; TMVs are maintained to AS 4032.3; state health departments regulate Legionella in some building types; gas appliances follow AS/NZS 5601.1. | The HSE Approved Code of Practice L8 and HSG274 Part 2 require storage at 60 °C and distribution at 50 °C (55 °C in healthcare) within a minute, with monthly temperature checks; TMVs to TMV2 or TMV3 schemes in care settings; Approved Document G sets safety requirements for hot water systems. | ASHRAE 188 sets a risk management standard for Legionella in building water systems, and many healthcare facilities are required to have water management programmes; plumbing codes require mixing valves listed to ASSE standards at certain fixtures. |

sections.heading: Worked example: hot water in an aged care home
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. An aged care home's hot water loop returns at 46 °C, residents' basins in one wing deliver water well above 50 °C, and the TMV register has no service entries for two years. A recent Legionella sample returned positive.

A failed TMV in a building for vulnerable people is a scald risk, and a loop below 50 °C is a Legionella risk; both are safety findings. The positive result shows the loop temperature matters now, not at the next service.

So the register carries the TMVs in that wing as a safety line, serviced or replaced now, disinfection and re-testing, and the circulation repaired and the loop rebalanced, with annual TMV servicing set up.

thresholds.rule: No more than 45 °C in aged care, healthcare patient areas, early childhood centres and schools; 50 °C in most other cases

source.title: NCC 2025 Volume Three (Plumbing Code), Part B2 Heated water services

thresholds.rule: Rated working pressure, or 1400 kPa if lower, not exceeded; water kept below 99 °C

source.title: NCC 2025 Volume Three (Plumbing Code), Part B2 Heated water services

thresholds.rule: Stored at 60 °C or more; 50 °C at outlets within one minute (55 °C in healthcare); return to the calorifier no less than 50 °C

source.title: HSG274 Legionnaires’ disease: Technical guidance, Part 2: Hot and cold water systems

pages.title: Hydrant & Hose Reel Systems
pages.question: How do hydrant, rising main and hose reel systems fail, and when are they unusable by fire-fighters?
pages.answer: Hydrant systems fail where fire-fighters meet them. Boosters and hydrants are hidden by planting, parking and hoardings; caps go missing and valves seize. Flow and pressure at remote outlets fall as mains pressures drop and pipes corrode, which only a flow test shows. Dry risers leak when charged. Hose reels crack and leak. A booster the brigade cannot find or connect to is a failed system however well it was built.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about hydrant & hose reel systems; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.

pages.searchTitle: Hydrants, hose reels and rising mains: access, pressure and testing

questions.question: What makes a hydrant system fail for the brigade?
questions.answer: A booster or hydrant that fire-fighters cannot find, reach or connect to is a failed system, however well it was built.

questions.question: Why is pressure low only at some hydrant outlets?
questions.answer: Low pressure only at remote outlets or in one zone points to pipework, valves or a pressure-reducing valve in that part of the system; low pressure everywhere points to the supply or pumps.

questions.question: How often are dry risers tested?
questions.answer: In the United Kingdom, BS 9990 calls for six-monthly inspection and annual pressure testing; in the United States, NFPA 25 sets periodic hydrostatic tests of dry standpipes.

questions.question: Does an extension need more hydrants?
questions.answer: Often. Extensions can leave areas without hydrant or hose reel coverage, so the system needs checking against the building as it now is.

questions.question: How long do hose reels last?
questions.answer: The hoses 10 to 15 years and the reel units 20 to 30.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Hydrant problems show from the street, as a booster the brigade cannot see or reach, and inside at landing valves, risers and hose reels. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On site | Booster and hydrants visible and accessible from the street; signage; caps present | Access, boosters and extensions |
| On site | Landing valves in stairs: caps, wheels, leaks, signage | Valves, dry risers, hose reels and freezing |
| On site | Dry riser inlets: doors, caps, damage | Valves, dry risers, hose reels and freezing |
| On site | Hose reels: hose condition, nozzle, isolating valve open, obstruction | Valves, dry risers, hose reels and freezing |
| On site | Corrosion and leaks on pipework | Flow, pressure and pressure-reducing valves |
| In the records | Routine service records | Investigation before the scope |
| In the records | Flow and pressure test results | Flow, pressure and pressure-reducing valves |
| In the records | Dry riser pressure test records | Valves, dry risers, hose reels and freezing |
| In the records | Backflow device test records | Flow, pressure and pressure-reducing valves |
| In the records | Block plan at the booster | Access, boosters and extensions |
| In the records | Pressure-reducing valve settings and tags at landing valves in tall buildings | Flow, pressure and pressure-reducing valves |
| In the records | Booster block plan present, legible and matching the building | Access, boosters and extensions |
| In the records | Areas of extensions without hydrant or hose reel coverage | Access, boosters and extensions |

sections.heading: Types of system
sections.markdown:
Hydrant systems give fire-fighters water at the building: external hydrants in the grounds, internal hydrant landing valves in stairs and on floors, rising mains (wet or dry) that carry water up tall buildings, and a booster or fire brigade inlet where fire appliances can pump into the system. Hose reels are fixed hoses for occupants to tackle small fires. In the United States the equivalent internal system is the standpipe, in Classes I to III.

| Type | Where it is found | Character |
| --- | --- | --- |
| External pillar or below-ground hydrants | Sites, campuses, industrial estates | Must be accessible and visible to fire appliances |
| Internal hydrant landing valves | Fire stairs and floors of larger buildings | Valves, outlets and caps; fire-fighters bring hoses |
| Booster assembly or brigade inlet | Building frontage | Where appliances connect; must be accessible and signed |
| Dry rising main | Mid-rise buildings, especially in Britain | Empty pipe charged by fire appliances |
| Wet rising main | Tall buildings | Permanently charged, usually with pumps |
| Hose reels | Australian commercial and industrial buildings; less common elsewhere | Occupant use; hose and nozzle deteriorate |
| Standpipes (US) | US multi-storey buildings | Class I for fire service; II and III with occupant hose |

In tall buildings the system is divided into pressure zones, with pumps, intermediate tanks or pressure-reducing valves keeping outlet pressures within the range fire-fighters' hoses and nozzles can handle. Booster assemblies carry a block plan showing the system, zones and pressures for the brigade. The system must suit the local brigade's couplings and procedures, which differ between jurisdictions and sometimes between brigades.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Hydrant systems are long-lived: galvanised pipework thirty to fifty years, booster assemblies twenty-five to forty, and valves twenty to thirty, while hose reel hoses last ten to fifteen. A system can outlast its usefulness, though, when the building grows around it or access to it is lost.

| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hydrant valves and landing valves | 20 to 30 years | Operation; corrosion; vandalism |
| Booster assemblies | 25 to 40 years | Damage; corrosion; caps stolen |
| Galvanised pipework | 30 to 50 years | Internal corrosion; MIC |
| Dry riser inlets and valves | 20 to 30 years | Vandalism; corrosion |
| Hose reel hoses | 10 to 15 years | UV; abrasion |
| Hose reel units | 20 to 30 years | Corrosion; damage |

What shortens life: vandalism and theft: caps, couplings and brass fittings; seldom operated valves that seize; landscaping, parking and construction that obstruct access; freezing of exposed wet pipework; internal corrosion.

Hydrant systems are rarely used in earnest, so their condition is established only by testing; a valve that has not been operated for years is likely to stick when the brigade needs it.

sections.heading: Access, boosters and extensions
sections.markdown:
Hydrants and boosters must be reachable by fire appliances and visible on arrival. Planting, parking bays, bins, fences and construction hoardings block them; signage fades or is removed; booster cabinets are locked with the wrong key.

Building extensions, new mezzanines and subdivided tenancies put parts of the building beyond hose reach from existing outlets; the original design no longer covers the building.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Booster hidden from the street | Access obstruction. Site inspection. | Clear and protect the access, with signage and lighting, or relocate the booster. |
| Fire main inlet far from where an appliance can park | Access shortfall for the fire service. Distance from where an appliance can park to each inlet, against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Provide hardstanding within reach, or move the inlet. |

sections.heading: Flow, pressure and pressure-reducing valves
sections.markdown:
Hydrant systems must deliver a set flow at a set pressure at the most remote outlets. Falling town main pressures, corroded or partly blocked pipes, failed pumps and closed valves leave outlets short. Only a flow test shows it.

Pressure-reducing valves at landing valves or zone boundaries in tall buildings drift, stick or are adjusted wrongly. Outlets then deliver pressure too high for fire-fighters to control a hose safely, or too low to fight a fire. Their settings are only proven by flow testing at each zone.

Galvanised and black steel hydrant mains corrode internally; microbiologically influenced corrosion causes pinhole leaks; corrosion products and debris block valves and reduce flow at remote outlets.

Backflow prevention devices protect drinking water from fire system water; they need annual testing and can restrict flow if poorly selected or failing.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Flow test below requirement at remote outlets | Supply decline, corrosion or closed valves. Pressure readings along the system (Thresholds by market). | Take pressure readings along the system; clear blockages, open closed valves and replace corroded pipe. |
| Street feed hydrant low in the annual test | Town main below requirement. Residual pressure at the feed hydrant under flow, against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Raise it with the water authority, and add tanks or pumps where the main cannot meet it. |

sections.heading: Valves, dry risers, hose reels and freezing
sections.markdown:
Wet pipework in unheated car parks, external areas and roof spaces freezes and splits in cold climates; dry systems are used in these locations for that reason.

Hydrant and landing valves seize, leak or are vandalised; caps and blank flanges go missing, letting debris in; dry riser inlets are damaged; non-return valves stick.

Dry risers leak when charged because joints, valves and drain valves have deteriorated unseen; inlets and landing valves are vandalised; air release valves stick.

Hoses crack and leak from UV and age; nozzles go missing; reels jam; isolating valves are closed; reels are obstructed by storage.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dry riser loses pressure on test | Leaking valves or joints. Pressure test and inspection. | Pressure test and inspect; repair the valves and joints. |
| Hose reel leaks when pressurised | Aged hose. Inspection. | Replace the hose and service the reel. |
| Hose reels that no longer reach parts of a floor after a fit-out | Coverage lost. Hose lay against the current layout (Thresholds by market). | Add or move reels to restore coverage. |
| No standpipe flow test in the last five years | Capacity unproven. US Department of Defense guidance flow tests standpipes every five years for flow and minimum discharge pressure, and hydrostatically tests dry standpipes (UFM 3-601-02). | Flow test at the most remote outlets, and pressure test dry systems. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Booster or hydrants inaccessible or inoperable; dry riser failing pressure test; flow well below requirement | safety · 4 Essential | Restore now; notify the brigade. |
| Routine service and flow testing due | deadline · 4 Essential | At the prescribed interval. |
| Leaks; seized valves; missing caps; aged hoses | condition · 3 Important | Repair in the near term. |
| Pipework and valves at end of life | lifecycle · 3 Important | Replace. |
| No flow test on record | check · 3 Important | Flow test. |
| Normal | nil · 1 Routine | Routine. |
| Main burst or leaking under test; riser or hydrant system out of service | failure · 4 Essential | Repair now; notify the brigade and manage the impairment. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A fire services engineer or the hydrant maintenance contractor, coordinated with the brigade where its equipment is used for testing. The checks below start at the street, as a fire-fighter arrives, then test flow and pressure at the remote outlets.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Access and signage inspection | From the brigade's arrival point: booster and hydrant visibility, clear hardstand, signage, lighting, block plan, cabinet keys. |
| Coverage check | Of every part of the building against hose reach from the outlets, especially after extensions and fit-outs. |
| Valve inspection and operation | Hydrant valves, landing valves, isolating valves (open and secured), non-return valves, caps and couplings. |
| Flow and pressure test | At the most hydraulically remote outlets, and at each pressure zone in tall buildings, against the design requirement; pressure-reducing valve settings confirmed under flow. |
| Dry riser pressure test | And inlet, valve and drain inspection. |
| Hose reel test | Flow, hose condition, nozzle, reel operation. |
| Backflow device test | Of the backflow prevention device on the hydrant supply, to AS/NZS 2845.1 and the water authority’s requirements. |
| Pipework inspection | For corrosion, leaks, supports and frost protection. |

The report should state whether the system delivers required flow and pressure at every outlet and zone, whether the brigade can find and connect to it, coverage gaps, and failed components.

sections.heading: Restoring access, repairing or extending
sections.markdown:
Access comes first: a booster or hydrant that fire-fighters cannot find, reach or connect to gives no protection. After that, the work follows the flow and pressure tests, the condition of valves and risers, and whether the system still covers the building.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Clear and protect access | Relocate parking, bins and planting; bollards against vehicle damage; signage, lighting and updated block plans. | At once, wherever a booster or hydrant is hidden or blocked. |
| Replace valves | Valves, caps and couplings, with anti-theft and anti-vandal fittings where theft is common. | Where valves seize or leak, or caps are missing. |
| Pressure-reducing valves | Recalibrate or replace them, and confirm by flow test. | Where pressure at landing valves is wrong in tall buildings. |
| Restore performance | Clear blockages, replace corroded pipe, add or upgrade pumps, and increase supply connections. | Where flow or pressure falls below the requirement. |
| Dry riser repairs | Inlet boxes, valves, drains, joints and air release valves. | Where a dry riser loses pressure on test. |
| Extend coverage | Additional outlets. | Where extensions leave areas uncovered. |
| Hose replacement | New hoses, with the reels serviced. | Where hoses leak or reach the end of their life. |
| Frost protection | Protect exposed wet pipework. | Where pipework is exposed to freezing. |
| Booster relocation | Move the booster to where the brigade can reach it. | Where it cannot be made accessible where it is. |
| Cabinet keys | Standardise cabinet keys to brigade keys, and leave cabinets unlocked where permitted. | Wherever the brigade could be locked out. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Routine servicing and flow testing recur; dry riser pressure tests recur annually where required. Valve, coupling and hose replacement are priced per item. Pipework replacement is by length, with access and making good. Pressure-reducing valve replacement is per valve. Additional outlets are priced per outlet with pipework. Booster relocation is a lump sum with civil works.

Testing, access and safety rectification are code compliance; pipework and valve replacement at end of life is lifecycle; repairs are repairs and maintenance.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a walk-around cannot: whether the remote outlets get enough water, whether dry risers hold pressure, and whether the system still covers the building as it has grown. Ask for them before any extension.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Routine service records and annual certification | Whether the system is serviced and certified as required. |
| Flow and pressure test reports for remote outlets and each pressure zone | Whether the remote outlets and each pressure zone get enough water. |
| Dry riser pressure test records | Whether the dry risers hold pressure. |
| Pressure-reducing valve settings and test records | Whether pressure-reducing valves are set correctly. |
| Backflow prevention device test records | Whether the backflow devices protect the water supply. |
| Booster block plan and hydrant system drawings | Whether the brigade can find its way around the system. |
| Records of extensions and fit-outs since the system was designed | Whether the system still covers the whole building. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Hydrant systems are misread when a well-built system is assumed to work for the brigade, when low pressure is blamed on the wrong part of the system, and when extensions are assumed to be covered.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| A well-built system works | A booster or hydrant that fire-fighters cannot find, reach or connect to is a failed system, however well it was built. |
| Low pressure means weak pumps | Two patterns are often confused. Low pressure at every outlet points to the supply or pumps; low pressure only at remote outlets or one zone points to pipework, valves or a pressure-reducing valve in that part of the system. |
| The extension is covered | Extensions often leave areas without hydrant or hose reel coverage, and need additional outlets designed to the brigade's requirements. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets standards for hydrants, hose reels and rising mains, and for how often they are inspected and tested. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Design | AS 2419.1 governs hydrant installations, AS 2441 hose reels, and AS/NZS 2845.1 backflow prevention. | BS 9990 covers rising mains; Approved Document B sets requirements for fire-fighting access and water. | NFPA 14 governs standpipes, and NFPA 24 private hydrants and mains. |
| Inspection and testing | AS 1851 sets routine service and flow testing; hydrants and hose reels are essential safety measures with annual certification. | BS 9990 calls for six-monthly inspection and annual pressure testing of dry risers. | NFPA 25 sets inspection and testing, including periodic flow tests and hydrostatic tests of dry standpipes. |

Brigade requirements also apply in all three jurisdictions: couplings, booster locations and block plans must suit the local fire service, which may inspect and comment on hydrant arrangements during approvals and after changes.

sections.heading: Worked example: a booster behind the bins
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 1980s office was extended at the rear some years ago. Its hydrant booster now sits behind a row of waste bins in the car park, out of sight from the street, and the block plan at the booster shows the building before the extension. The last flow test was satisfactory at the original outlets.

A booster that fire-fighters cannot find or reach is a failed system, however well it was built: a safety finding. The out-of-date block plan and the extension raise the question of coverage, since the flow test covered only the original outlets.

So the register carries clearing and protecting the booster as a safety line now, with an updated block plan, and a coverage and flow test of the extension as a check line that may become additional outlets.

thresholds.measure: Boosted hydrant pressure (AS 2419.1:2021, as applied in New South Wales)
thresholds.rule: 700 kPa at the most disadvantaged outlet

source.title: Position statement summary: FRNSW pump performance for high rise buildings

thresholds.measure: Unassisted residual pressure at a feed hydrant flowing 10 L/s (AS 2419.1)
thresholds.rule: 150 kPa in New South Wales; 200 kPa in the other states and territories

pages.title: Insulation
pages.question: How does roof insulation fail, how do you tell condensation from a leak, and which insulation findings are hazards?
pages.answer: Insulation fails by gaps, wetting and condensation. Drips across a ceiling in cold weather with no rain are condensation, not a leak; mould in lines follows thermal bridges at framing. Wet insulation in a warm flat roof must come out. Some findings are hazards rather than performance problems: batts over downlights, foil on damaged wiring, loose-fill asbestos and vermiculite. Spray foam on rafters hides the structure and can trap moisture.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about insulation; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Thermal and acoustic performance and condition

questions.question: Why is my ceiling dripping on cold mornings with no rain?
questions.answer: That is condensation, not a leak. Warm, moist air reaches a cold surface in the roof. The cure is vapour control and ventilation; adding insulation without them makes it worse.

questions.question: Why is there mould in lines on my ceiling?
questions.answer: The lines follow the framing above: thermal bridging, where the joists or rafters are colder than the insulated areas between them.

questions.question: Is it safe to cover downlights with insulation?
questions.answer: Only with fittings rated for insulation contact, or with downlight covers. Batts over or against downlights and transformers are a fire hazard.

questions.question: Can loose grey insulation in an Australian roof contain asbestos?
questions.answer: Yes. Loose grey or blue fluffy material, especially in the ACT or New South Wales, may be loose-fill asbestos. Do not disturb it; it needs immediate expert assessment.

questions.question: How long does roof insulation last?
questions.answer: Bulk batts kept dry and undisturbed 30 to 50 years, loose fill 20 to 40, and rigid boards in warm roofs 25 to 50, though performance falls long before the material wears out.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Insulation problems show as condensation, mould in lines, rooms too hot or too cold, and frost that melts in stripes; in the roof space they show as gaps and wet batts. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Inside | Drips across a ceiling on cold mornings with no rain: condensation within the roof | Condensation, wetting and ventilation |
| Inside | Mould in lines on ceilings, matching the framing above: thermal bridging | Condensation, wetting and ventilation |
| Inside | Mould in the corners where ceilings meet external walls: insulation missing at the edges | Gaps, bridging and vermin |
| Inside | Rooms under the roof much hotter in summer or colder in winter than the rest of the building: gaps or missing insulation | Gaps, bridging and vermin |
| Inside | A musty smell from the roof space, or dark staining on rafters near the eaves: blocked ventilation | Condensation, wetting and ventilation |
| Inside | Higher heating and cooling bills than similar buildings, or plant running hard to hold temperatures in top-floor spaces | Gaps, bridging and vermin |
| Roof space | Gaps, displaced and compressed batts; insulation missing over areas | Gaps, bridging and vermin |
| Roof space | Batts over or against downlights and transformers | Fire, electrical hazards and spray foam |
| Roof space | Wet, stained or mouldy insulation; water marks on the underside of sheeting | Condensation, wetting and ventilation |
| Roof space | Foil laminates sagging onto wiring | Fire, electrical hazards and spray foam |
| Roof space | Loose fluffy grey-blue material or granular vermiculite | Fire, electrical hazards and spray foam |
| Roof space | Spray foam on the underside of the covering or rafters | Fire, electrical hazards and spray foam |
| Roof space | Insulation stopping short of the wall plate, leaving a cold strip around the ceiling edge | Gaps, bridging and vermin |
| Roof space | Droppings, nests and tunnelling through batts | Gaps, bridging and vermin |
| Roof space | Loose fill thinned or drifted, with ceiling joists showing through | Gaps, bridging and vermin |
| Outside | On frosty or snowy mornings, roofs where the frost melts first or in stripes: heat escaping through gaps or along framing | Gaps, bridging and vermin |
| Outside | Drone or thermal imagery showing warm patches across a roof | Gaps, bridging and vermin |
| Outside | Eaves vents covered, painted over or blocked from inside | Condensation, wetting and ventilation |
| In the records | Insulation type and R-values; installation certificates | Investigation before the scope |
| In the records | Energy ratings: NABERS, EPC, ENERGY STAR | Standards by country |
| In the records | Mr Fluffy register (ACT and New South Wales) and asbestos register | Fire, electrical hazards and spray foam |
| In the records | Spray foam installation records and manufacturer documentation | Fire, electrical hazards and spray foam |
| In the records | Records of electrical, data and plumbing works through the roof space, which usually disturb insulation | Gaps, bridging and vermin |

sections.heading: Types of insulation
sections.markdown:
Roof and ceiling insulation limits heat flow through the roof. It is bulk (glasswool, rockwool, polyester, cellulose, natural wool), reflective (foil laminates and foil-faced blankets), rigid board (PIR, PUR, XPS, EPS, mineral fibre) or sprayed foam. It works with vapour control layers, sarking, ventilation and the airtightness of the ceiling to manage condensation.

| Arrangement | Where it is found | Main risk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Batts or loose fill on the ceiling, ventilated roof space | Houses and low-rise | Gaps, compression, displacement by trades; downlight clearances |
| Blanket under metal sheeting | Industrial and commercial sheds; Australian houses | Condensation where the blanket and foil are damaged |
| Warm flat roof: boards above the deck, under the membrane | Commercial and apartment flat roofs | Saturation by leaks; combustibility of boards on tall buildings |
| Inverted roof: boards above the membrane under ballast | Commercial roofs and podiums | Rainwater cooling below the boards; ballast displaced |
| Cold flat roof: insulation between joists below the deck | Older flat roofs, extensions | Interstitial condensation and deck decay |
| Spray foam to the underside of roof sheeting or rafters | Retrofits, especially in Britain from the 2010s | Hides the roof structure; condensation and decay behind it; lender acceptance |
| Blown loose fill (cellulose, mineral wool) over ceilings | Houses and low-rise, often as a top-up | Settlement and drifting; covering of downlights and junction boxes |
| Insulated sandwich panels (PIR, EPS or mineral fibre core) | Cold stores, food factories, warehouses, modular buildings | Core combustibility; joints; condensation at panel joints in chilled spaces |

Insulation never works alone. It needs a continuous layer with no gaps, a vapour control layer on the warm side in cold climates so that moist air cannot reach cold surfaces, ventilation or a vapour-open layer on the cold side so that any moisture can escape, and a dry roof above it. Where any of these is missing, the insulation itself becomes the place water collects ([Roof Coverings](https://moyneross.com/technical/roof-coverings), [Waterproofing Membranes](https://moyneross.com/technical/waterproofing-membranes)).

What is labelled is not what is installed. Insulation is rated by its R-value (U-value for the whole roof in Britain), but the rated value assumes full thickness, no gaps, no compression and a dry material. In practice a roof space can hold the right product everywhere and deliver much less than its label, which is why depth, coverage and continuity matter more in an inspection than the product data.

Some older insulation is hazardous: loose-fill asbestos (the Mr Fluffy homes in the ACT and New South Wales), vermiculite that may contain asbestos, and foil laminates stapled over live wiring under the 2009 and 2010 Australian Home Insulation Program.

Which side is warm depends on the climate and the building. In heating climates the warm, moist side is inside, and condensation forms on the underside of the roof; in hot, humid climates, and in cooled buildings such as cold stores, the drive can reverse, and a vapour barrier in the wrong place traps water within the build-up. A roof designed for one climate and copied into another is a common source of hidden condensation.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Insulation rarely wears out; it stops working. Bulk batts can last fifty years if dry and undisturbed, but gaps, wetting, dust and vermin cut their performance long before the material itself fails.

| Insulation | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bulk batts and blankets, dry and undisturbed | 30 to 50 years | Compression, wetting, vermin |
| Loose fill | 20 to 40 years | Settlement; displacement |
| Rigid boards in warm roofs | 25 to 50 years | Water from leaks |
| Reflective foil | 20 to 40 years | Dust on the reflective face; damage |
| Spray foam | 30 years and more | Adhesion; shrinkage; what it hides |
| Insulated sandwich panels | 25 to 40 years | Joint seals; facing corrosion; damage; condensation in chilled spaces |
| Extruded polystyrene in inverted roofs | 30 years and more | Water absorption over time; displacement |
| Vapour-permeable sarking and underlays | Life of the roof covering if undamaged | Tearing by trades; UV before the covering went on |

Life is uneven across a roof space. Insulation near the access hatch, along service runs, at the eaves and under past leaks is disturbed, compressed or wetted first, while areas no one visits may be close to their installed condition decades later. An inspection that looks only near the hatch overstates the problem in one place and misses it in others.

What shortens life: disturbance by trades running cables, ducts and downlights; leaks and condensation; poor vapour control on the warm side; vermin nesting in batts; dust on foil, which defeats its reflectivity.

Performance falls long before the material wears out. Batts compressed to half their depth lose much of their insulating value; foil covered in dust loses most of its reflective benefit; loose fill settles and blows into drifts. A roof can have insulation throughout and still deliver a fraction of the labelled value.

What lengthens it: keeping trades out of it, or requiring them to restore it: electricians, plumbers and data installers are the main cause of displaced insulation; boards and walkways in roof spaces that are used, so insulation is not trodden flat; downlight covers and clearances maintained, so insulation is not cut back from fittings; leaks fixed promptly and condensation designed out before insulation is added or upgraded; vermin control, since nesting animals displace and foul batts.

sections.heading: Gaps, bridging and vermin
sections.markdown:
Small gaps cut performance out of proportion to their area, because heat takes the easiest path: a roof with a few per cent of its area uninsulated can lose a large share of its insulating effect. Batts pushed aside by trades, compressed under boards and storage, cut back from downlights or never fitted tight to the wall plate leave cold spots on the ceiling below, which then attract condensation and mould. Loose fill settles over the years and drifts in roof-space wind, thinning at the eaves where it matters most.

Rafters, purlins, steel framing, roof-to-wall junctions and slab edges carry heat past the insulation. They show as lines on thermal images and as pattern staining or mould on ceilings, and steel bridges in particular can create local condensation even where the insulation is continuous.

Rats, mice, possums and birds nest in insulation, flatten and soil it, and chew wiring within it. Infested insulation is unhygienic as well as ineffective, and usually has to be removed rather than topped up.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mould on ceilings in lines | Thermal bridging at framing. Lines follow joist or rafter spacing. | Insulate the bridging framing where the build-up allows, and control vapour. |
| Mould near external walls and corners | Missing insulation at the ceiling edge. Insulation stops short of the wall plate. | Refit the insulation tight to the wall plate. |
| Hot or cold rooms | Gaps or missing insulation. Thermal imaging. | Refit and top up where thermal imaging shows gaps. |
| Frost or snow melting early, or in stripes along the framing | Heat loss through gaps or bridging. Thermal imaging from inside confirms the pattern. | Confirm with thermal imaging from inside, then refit or top up. |
| Droppings, nests and flattened insulation | Vermin. Activity in the roof space; damaged wiring nearby. | Pest control first, then remove, clean and replace the insulation. |

sections.heading: Condensation, wetting and ventilation
sections.markdown:
Warm air holds more moisture than cold air. When warm, moist air from inside the building reaches a surface colder than its dew point, the underside of metal sheeting, the deck of a cold flat roof, or sarking with low vapour permeability, the moisture condenses. The water wets the insulation, drips on ceilings, corrodes metal and decays timber. Tightly sealed modern roofs in cold and alpine climates are more prone than older draughty ones, which is why codes in all three countries now include condensation provisions. Humid activities below, such as pools, kitchens, laundries, showers and unflued heaters, multiply the risk.

Bulk insulation that gets wet loses most of its value and holds water against the ceiling and structure, staining and weakening plasterboard until it sags. In warm flat roofs, wet boards spread water across the roof, keep leaks running long after the original defect is repaired, and must be removed ([Waterproofing Membranes](https://moyneross.com/technical/waterproofing-membranes)).

Adding insulation moves the cold point. Thicker insulation above a ceiling makes the roof space colder, so moisture that once escaped harmlessly now condenses on sarking, battens and the underside of the covering. Insulating between rafters without a ventilated gap or a vapour-open underlay can rot rafters within a few years. Upgrades that look simple are where most new condensation problems begin.

Cold roofs depend on air moving from eaves to ridge. Insulation pushed into the eaves, boarded-over vents and sealed roof spaces stop that flow, and moisture builds up through winter. The first signs are often mould on the underside of the sarking or roof boards, and damp, dark staining on rafters at the eaves.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Water drips across a ceiling in cold weather with no rain | Condensation. Uniform pattern; underside of sheeting wet; humid space below; no vapour control. | Add vapour control and ventilation; more insulation alone will not help. |
| Water stain under one point after rain | Leak. Defect in the covering above. | Find and fix the leak above; see Roof Coverings. |
| Mould on sarking or roof boards and dark rafters at the eaves | Blocked roof-space ventilation. Insulation packed into the eaves; vents covered; humidity high in winter. | Clear the eaves, with baffles to keep ventilation paths open. |
| New condensation after insulation was added or upgraded | Cold point moved into the roof. Timing follows the upgrade; no vapour control or ventilation provided. | Assess the build-up; add vapour control on the warm side and ventilate the roof space. |
| Wet, heavy boards found in a warm flat roof | Leak or condensation spreading through the build-up. Cores and moisture survey; see Waterproofing Membranes. | Remove the wet insulation and fix the cause; see Waterproofing Membranes. |

sections.heading: Inverted roofs and sandwich panels
sections.markdown:
In inverted roofs, rainwater running beneath the insulation boards carries heat away from the membrane and reduces the roof's performance unless a water-flow-reducing layer is used; boards float or blow away where ballast is light; and boards absorb water over time if not of a closed-cell type.

Insulated panels fail at their joints, where seals perish and let moist air into the core, and at their facings, which corrode at cut edges and fixings. In cold stores, warm moist air leaks inward through failed joints and condenses or freezes within the panel, delaminating facings and eventually distorting panels. Damage from forklifts and racking is common at low level ([Cladding & Wall Systems](https://moyneross.com/technical/cladding-and-wall-systems)).

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ice, frost or delaminated facings inside cold store panels | Moist air entering through failed panel joints. Joint seals perished; moisture or ice within the panel. | Reseal the joints and replace damaged panels, with vapour sealing on the warm side. |

sections.heading: Fire, electrical hazards and spray foam
sections.markdown:
Batts over downlights and transformers can overheat and ignite; foil laminates stapled over damaged or poorly terminated wiring can become live, as Australia's 2009 to 2010 Home Insulation Program showed. Combustible insulation boards and sandwich panel cores add fuel to a roof fire and can spread it through concealed spaces; their use on tall buildings and in some occupancies is now restricted.

Foam applied to the underside of roof coverings or rafters makes the structure impossible to inspect, can trap moisture against timber, and makes covering repairs harder because the covering is glued to the foam. In Britain, many lenders and surveyors will not accept it without evidence that it was correctly specified and installed, and removal is disruptive.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Scorching or discolouration of insulation around a light fitting | Insulation in contact with a heat source. Fitting type and clearance; no cover or barrier. Keep the clearance the fitting and the wiring rules require, and allow for the cleared area as lost insulation (Thresholds by market). | Clear insulation from the fitting now; fit a cover or a fitting rated for insulation contact. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Loose-fill asbestos; foil over damaged wiring; batts over downlights or transformers | safety · 4 Essential | Isolate and assess now; do not disturb. |
| Saturated insulation; active condensation decaying the structure | failure · 2 Planned | Remove wet insulation and fix the cause now. |
| Mould growth in the roof space or on ceilings from condensation | condition · 2 Planned | Correct ventilation and vapour control in the near term. |
| Insulation upgrade planned without a condensation risk assessment | check · 2 Planned | Assess the build-up before the work is specified. |
| Gaps and compression across large areas; condensation without damage yet | condition · 2 Planned | Repair in the near term. |
| Let commercial premises in England or Wales below the minimum energy efficiency standard, where insulation is part of the fix | deadline · 4 Essential | Improve before the letting restrictions apply. |
| Insulation below current standards, with roof works planned that will require an upgrade | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Upgrade with the works. |
| Vermin-infested insulation | condition · 2 Planned | Remove, clean and replace after pest control. |
| Possible vermiculite or spray foam with no records | check · 2 Planned | Identify and assess first. |
| Small gaps | nil · 1 Routine | Top up in routine maintenance. |

Insulation findings are usually about what the insulation is doing to the building rather than the insulation itself. Missing insulation is an energy cost; wet or condensing insulation is a building defect that grows; hazardous insulation is a safety matter whatever its thermal performance.

The grading follows what a finding demands, not the size of the eventual bill.

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A building surveyor or energy consultant leads, with a hygrothermal assessment where condensation is suspected. The checks below cover the type, depth and coverage of the insulation, where moisture comes from, and any hazards in the roof space.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Roof space inspection | Of coverage, depth, condition and clearances. |
| Thermal imaging | From inside in cold weather. |
| Core samples | Through flat roof build-ups. |
| Condensation risk analysis | Of the build-up (BS EN ISO 13788 or dynamic modelling). |
| Sampling | Of suspect materials for asbestos. |
| Electrical inspection | Where foil is near wiring. |
| Humidity and surface temperature logging | In the roof space through a cold spell, where condensation is suspected but not seen. |
| Inspection beyond the hatch | Walk boards or a borescope to reach the eaves, valleys and far corners, not just the area near the access point. |
| Depth and coverage | Measured on a grid across the roof space and compared with the labelled R-value, with thickness and laps checked against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). |
| Sarking and membrane identification | From labels or product data, to establish vapour permeability. |
| Ventilation check | Eaves, ridge and gable openings, and whether insulation blocks them. |
| Hygrothermal modelling | Before retrofitting insulation into cold or tightly sealed roofs. |

The report should state insulation type, coverage and depth, any wet areas, condensation risk in the build-up, any hazardous materials, and what an upgrade would require.

sections.heading: Refitting, replacing or upgrading
sections.markdown:
What to do turns on moisture before anything else. A dry roof space with gaps needs refitting and topping up; a roof with condensation needs vapour control and ventilation first; a leaking roof needs the roof fixed; and some insulation is a hazard to be removed by a specialist.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Top up and refit | Refit displaced batts tight to each other and to the wall plate, top up to current depth, and fit downlight covers or downlights rated for insulation contact. | Where the roof space is dry and accessible; cheap and effective. |
| Remove and replace wet insulation | Remove the wet insulation and replace it. | Only after the leak or condensation source is fixed; replacing it first only repeats the problem. |
| Vapour control and ventilation | A vapour control layer on the warm side, sealed ceiling penetrations, eaves and ridge ventilation with baffles to keep paths open, and vapour-permeable sarking. | The cure for most condensation. |
| Convert cold flat roofs to warm roofs | Move the insulation above the deck so the structure stays warm and dry. | When the membrane is renewed. |
| Remove spray foam | Remove it and reinstate a ventilated build-up. | Where it hides decay, traps moisture or blocks a sale or mortgage. |
| Replace damaged sandwich panels | Replace panels and reseal joints, with vapour sealing on the warm side in cold stores. | Where joints have failed or panels are damaged; consider fire performance when replacing combustible cores. |
| Hazardous insulation | Licensed removal of asbestos-containing insulation; in the ACT and New South Wales, confirmed loose-fill asbestos homes fall under the government purchase and demolition programmes. | Wherever asbestos-containing insulation is confirmed. |
| Loose-fill top-ups | Top up loose fill, with depth markers so coverage can be checked later. | Where loose fill has thinned or drifted. |

Choosing between them starts with moisture. If the roof space or build-up is dry and the problem is gaps or depth, top up and refit. If there is condensation, fix vapour control and ventilation first, then insulate. If there is a leak, fix the roof first. Insulating a wet or condensing roof makes it worse.

Interactions: re-roofing and membrane replacement are the natural time to upgrade insulation, and in some jurisdictions the work triggers an upgrade. Any upgrade needs the condensation risk checked first, and may need electrical work around downlights and cables ([Main Electrical Supply](https://moyneross.com/technical/main-electrical-supply), [Energy Efficiency Upgrades](https://moyneross.com/technical/energy-efficiency-upgrades)).

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Inspection is a lump sum. Top-up and replacement are priced by area. Wet insulation removal adds strip-out and disposal. Asbestos removal is licensed, with clearance testing. Upgrades triggered by roof works are carried in the roof line.

What drives the cost beyond area: access to low or obstructed roof spaces, making electrical installations safe first, strip-out and disposal of wet or hazardous material, and in flat roofs whether the membrane must come off. Commonly missed: vapour control and ventilation works, downlight replacement, and remediation of mould or decay found during the work.

Upgrades triggered by works are code compliance; replacement is lifecycle; top-ups are repairs and maintenance; hazardous insulation is code compliance.

Top-ups are inexpensive where access is easy; costs rise sharply in low or obstructed roof spaces and where downlights and cabling must be made safe first. Flat roof insulation upgrades are carried in the membrane replacement line, not separately.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a look into the roof space cannot: what the insulation is, whether hazardous materials have been identified, and whether condensation risk was checked before any upgrade. Ask for them before anyone disturbs the insulation.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Insulation type, R-value and installation records | What is installed, and how well it should perform. |
| Energy ratings | How the building rates, and how much the roof contributes. |
| Asbestos register; loose-fill asbestos register status in the ACT and New South Wales | Whether asbestos-containing insulation has been identified. |
| Spray foam installation documentation | What spray foam was used, and how it was applied. |
| Records of condensation, mould and leaks under the roof | Where moisture has already appeared under the roof. |
| Pest control records for the roof space | Whether vermin have nested in the insulation. |
| For cold stores, panel inspection and repair records | The condition of cold store panels and their joints. |
| Photographs of the roof space | What the roof space looked like before anyone climbed in. |
| Any hygrothermal or condensation assessment | Whether condensation risk in the build-up has been assessed. |
| Electrical safety inspection of the roof space where foil insulation is present | Whether foil insulation has been checked for contact with damaged wiring. |
| Records of any insulation upgrade and whether a condensation risk assessment was done | Whether a past upgrade was checked for condensation risk. |
| Roof-space ventilation details and any changes made to them | Whether ventilation paths have been changed or blocked. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Insulation findings are misread when moisture is blamed on the wrong source, or when more insulation is taken to be the answer to damp under a roof.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| Drips on the ceiling mean the roof leaks | Condensation and leaks are easily confused. A leak follows the rain and appears under one point; condensation follows the temperature, appears on cold mornings and spreads evenly. Re-roofing a building with a condensation problem, or adding insulation without addressing vapour, leaves the problem where it was. |
| More insulation will fix the damp | When a building has mould or damp under the roof, the first question is whether the moisture comes from outside (a leak), from inside (condensation), or from the ground or walls below. The answer decides the remedy: a leak needs the roof fixed, condensation needs vapour control and ventilation, and neither is helped by more insulation alone. |
| Grey fluffy insulation is just old insulation | Loose grey or blue fluffy material in an Australian roof space, especially in the ACT or New South Wales, may be loose-fill asbestos. Do not disturb it; it requires immediate expert assessment. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets thermal requirements for insulation and rules on condensation and ventilation, and each has its own hazardous products to watch for. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each, with the energy rules that affect letting.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Thermal requirements | The National Construction Code sets energy requirements in Section J and the Housing Provisions; insulation materials follow AS/NZS 4859.1 and installation AS 3999. | Approved Document L sets thermal requirements and triggers upgrades on renovation; the Future Homes and Buildings Standards are tightening thermal requirements further for new work. | The International Energy Conservation Code and ASHRAE 90.1 set requirements; required R-values vary by climate zone under the energy code. |
| Condensation and ventilation | The Housing Provisions include condensation management, requiring vapour-permeable sarking and roof-space ventilation in the colder climate zones. | Approved Document C and BS 5250 govern moisture and condensation. | International Building Code Section 1202 covers attic ventilation; the residential code (Section R806) sets roof-space ventilation. |
| Hazards and electrical | Downlight clearances follow AS/NZS 3000; the ACT and New South Wales maintain registers of loose-fill asbestos (Mr Fluffy) homes. | RICS has published guidance on spray foam insulation. | International Building Code Chapter 26 covers foam plastics; the EPA publishes guidance on vermiculite that may contain asbestos. |
| Energy rules for letting and sale | Offices of 1,000 square metres or more need a NABERS Energy rating when sold or leased under the Commercial Building Disclosure programme, and roof insulation can affect it. | Commercial lettings in England and Wales are subject to the Minimum Energy Efficiency Standards, which set a minimum EPC rating for letting, and roof insulation is often part of meeting them. | Benchmarking laws and building performance standards in many cities, such as New York City's Local Law 97, can make roof insulation part of compliance. |

Insurance and lending can turn on insulation type in all three markets: spray foam on rafters and asbestos-containing products affect mortgage, insurance and sale decisions.

sections.heading: Worked example: drips in a warehouse office on winter mornings
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. The first-floor office inside a 1990s warehouse has drips across its ceiling on cold mornings in winter, with no rain. The roof space above has new batts laid last year over the old ones, packed into the eaves, and several downlights sit buried under them.

Drips spread across a ceiling on cold mornings with no rain are condensation, and they began after the upgrade: the new batts moved the cold point and blocked the eaves ventilation. More insulation would make it worse. The buried downlights are a separate finding, a fire hazard to clear now.

So the register carries the downlights as a safety line now, vapour control and the reopening of the eaves ventilation as a condition line, and any wet insulation removed once the cause is fixed.

thresholds.rule: About 20 downlights with 50 mm clearance, or 3 with 200 mm, use up 0.5 per cent of a 200 m² ceiling

source.title: NCC 2025 Housing Provisions, Part 13.2 Building fabric

thresholds.rule: Bulk insulation kept at full thickness; reflective sheets lapped at least 150 mm or taped

source.title: NCC 2025 Housing Provisions, Part 13.2 Building fabric

pages.title: Integrated Building Systems
pages.question: How do the interfaces between building systems fail, and why can a building pass every test and still fail in a fire?
pages.answer: Critical functions live in the interfaces: fire alarms shutting down air handling, starting smoke control, homing lifts, releasing doors and cutting gas. Each system passes its own tests while the links between them go untested, and every new fire panel, lift controller or BMS can break them. Documentation is lost, proprietary gateways lock buildings in, and shared networks expose systems to attack. Only full integrated testing proves a building in a fire.
