questions.question: Why did the lifts not return in the fire drill?
questions.answer: Usually an interface broken when the lift controller or fire panel changed and never re-tested.

questions.question: What is a cause-and-effect matrix?
questions.answer: The record of what every connected system should do in a fire or outage. Without a current one, faults cannot be recognised.

questions.question: How often should integrated fire testing happen?
questions.answer: At least annually, and after any change to the fire panel, smoke control, lifts, access control or BMS, with all contractors present.

questions.question: Can building systems be hacked?
questions.answer: Yes, where they share networks or face the internet with default passwords and unpatched software.

questions.question: How long does building systems integration last?
questions.answer: Interface hardware 10 to 20 years and software 5 to 15, but the matrix is valid only until a connected system changes.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Integration problems show as systems of different ages and vendors talking through gateways, communication alarms, unlabelled relays and bypassed outputs, and in the matrix, test reports and network records. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On site | Systems of very different ages and vendors connected together | Documentation and lock-in |
| On site | BMS graphics or alarms showing communication failures with other systems | Untested interfaces and changes |
| On site | Interface panels and relays without labels | Documentation and lock-in |
| On site | Building network equipment in unsecured cupboards; no network diagram | Cyber exposure |
| In the records | Cause-and-effect matrix and its date | Documentation and lock-in |
| In the records | Full integrated test reports | Untested interfaces and changes |
| In the records | Integration specifications and protocols | Documentation and lock-in |
| In the records | Network diagrams and access controls | Cyber exposure |
| In the records | Cyber security assessments | Cyber exposure |
| In the records | Bypass switches or disabled outputs on fire panels for air handling, lifts or doors | Untested interfaces and changes |
| In the records | Contractors who each say an interface is someone else's responsibility | Untested interfaces and changes |
| In the records | Fire drills where some systems responded and others did not | Untested interfaces and changes |

sections.heading: What is integrated
sections.markdown:
Integrated building systems are the interfaces between services: the links that make the fire alarm shut down air handling, start smoke control, release doors and home lifts; the building management system reading meters and controlling plant; access control talking to lifts and car park gates; and the networks that now carry most of this data. Each system has its own page; this page covers what happens between them. In modern buildings, many critical functions exist only in the interfaces, so a building can have every system working on its own and still fail in a fire or an outage.

| Interface | What it does | What commonly fails |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fire alarm to air handling and smoke control | Shut down or switch AHUs; start fans and dampers | Interfaces broken by upgrades; cause-and-effect out of date |
| Fire alarm to lifts | Home lifts; enable fire-fighter control | Lift modernisation without re-testing |
| Fire alarm to access control and doors | Release locks; close fire doors | Locks that stay locked |
| Fire alarm to gas and kitchen systems | Shut off gas; stop exhaust or start suppression | Bypassed interlocks |
| BMS to plant and meters | Control, schedule and monitor | Overrides; lost points; unsupported software |
| Access control to lifts and car parks | Floor and gate access by credential | Vendor lock-in; failed integration after upgrades |
| Building networks | Carry BMS, security, lighting and metering data | Cyber exposure; no ownership; flat networks |

The record of how these systems are supposed to work together (the cause-and-effect matrix, the integration specification and the network design) is often the first document lost, and the last one updated.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Interface hardware lasts ten to twenty years, integration software and protocols five to fifteen, and network equipment five to ten. The cause-and-effect matrix lasts only until a connected system changes, which is why integration is proven by testing after every change, not judged by its age.

| Item | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cause-and-effect matrix | Valid until any connected system changes | Upgrades, fit-outs, modernisations |
| Interface hardware (relays, modules, gateways) | 10 to 20 years | Panel and system replacement |
| Integration software and protocols | 5 to 15 years | Vendor support; security updates |
| Network equipment | 5 to 10 years | Vendor support; security |
| Documentation | Out of date at the first change | Discipline of updating |

What shortens validity: replacing one system (fire panel, lift controller, BMS) without re-testing the others connected to it; fit-outs that add zones, doors and plant without updating the matrix; proprietary protocols that stop working when one vendor changes; unmanaged networks that no one owns.

Integration lasts only as long as every connected system stays unchanged.

sections.heading: Untested interfaces and changes
sections.markdown:
Systems are routinely tested on their own: fire alarms, smoke fans, lifts and locks each pass their checks. The interfaces between them are tested only in full integrated tests, which are often skipped. Faults then appear only in a real fire: air handlers keep running, lifts do not home, doors stay locked.

A new fire panel, lift controller, access control system or BMS breaks interfaces unless every connected function is re-tested. Each modernisation is a point of failure for the others.

Interfaces cross the responsibilities of several contractors; each maintains its own system and none owns the links. Faults fall between them.

Interfaces are also lost quietly during routine maintenance, when relays are bypassed to stop nuisance shutdowns and never restored.

Each system in a building can pass its own test while the building as a whole fails. In a fire, the alarm must stop air handlers, start smoke control, home the lifts, release the doors and shut off gas; those links are proven only by a full integrated test with every contractor present, and every change to any connected system puts them back in doubt.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lifts did not home in a real alarm | Interface broken after lift or fire panel change. Integrated test. | Repair the interface, then run a full integrated test of every connected function. |
| Doors stayed locked in a drill | Access control interface failure. Interface test. | Repair the access control interface so the doors release on alarm, and re-test. |
| Bypass switches on, or fire panel outputs to air handlers disabled | Interfaces bypassed during maintenance and never restored. The fire panel log shows disabled outputs, or bypass keys left on. | Restore the outputs, and re-test the functions they drive. |
| Contractors each saying an interface belongs to someone else | No one owns the links between systems. Maintenance contracts that each stop at their own system. | Appoint a single point of responsibility for the interfaces and their testing. |
| Stair doors hard to open, or alarms faint, after a change to another system | One system’s change upsetting another. Stair door forces and alarm sound levels measured after any change to air handling, doors or fit-out, against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Retest the affected interfaces together, and record the result in the cause-and-effect matrix. |

sections.heading: Documentation and lock-in
sections.markdown:
Without a current cause-and-effect matrix and integration records, nobody knows what the building should do in a fire or outage, so faults cannot be recognised.

Integrations built on proprietary gateways depend on vendors who may withdraw support, raise prices or disappear, leaving the building unable to change any one system without disturbing the rest.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| BMS shows plant offline | Gateway or protocol failure. Network diagnostics. | Diagnose the gateway and protocol; plan migration to open protocols if support has ended. |
| No one can say what the building does in a fire | Matrix lost or out of date. Records review. | Rebuild the cause-and-effect matrix from the fire strategy and the current systems, then test against it. |
| A gateway from a vendor that no longer supports it | Integration locked to an unsupported platform. The vendor's support status and the protocol used. | Plan replacement with open protocols, so systems can be changed independently. |

sections.heading: Cyber exposure
sections.markdown:
Building systems connected to shared or internet-facing networks, with default passwords and unpatched software, can be attacked, and an attack on one system can reach others. Building networks often have no owner and no security monitoring.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unknown devices on the building network | Unmanaged network. Network audit. | Audit the network, segment building systems, and control remote access. |
| Building controllers reachable from the internet with default passwords | An exposed building network. A scan of the building network, and its remote access arrangements. | Change default passwords, patch, segment the network and control remote access. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fire interfaces failing (AHUs, smoke control, lifts, doors, gas) | safety · 4 Essential | Rectify now; fire watch if needed. |
| Integration failure stopping plant or access | failure · 3 Important | Restore now. |
| Integrated testing due under standards or certification | deadline · 4 Essential | At the prescribed interval. |
| Cyber exposure; poor documentation | condition · 3 Important | Improve in the near term. |
| Integration platforms unsupported | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Plan replacement. |
| No integrated test since major changes | check · 2 Planned | Test. |
| Normal | nil · 1 Routine | Routine. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A building services engineer experienced in systems integration leads, with the fire, mechanical, lift, security and controls contractors present and a cyber security specialist for networks. The checks below start with the records, the matrix and the last integrated test, then test every interface together with all contractors present, and audit the building network.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Records review | Cause-and-effect matrix, integration specifications, protocols, network diagrams, and the dates of every change to connected systems. |
| Full integrated test | Of fire functions: initiate alarms by zone and confirm every connected response, including air handling, smoke control, lifts, doors, gas and suppression. |
| BMS and access integration check | Communications, points, and functions across systems. |
| Network and cyber review | Segmentation, remote access, credentials, patching and ownership. |
| Responsibility map | Who maintains each interface. |

The report should state which interfaces work, which fail, who owns each, and what must be fixed or documented.

The integrated test is the single most informative check of a building's life-safety systems, and it is usually the one most overdue.

sections.heading: Proving, documenting and securing
sections.markdown:
Failing fire interfaces, whether to air handlers, smoke control, lifts, doors or gas, come first, with every connected function re-tested. After that, the building needs a current matrix, a single owner for the interfaces, open protocols and a secured network.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Interface rectification | Rectify failed interfaces and re-test every connected function, not just the one that failed. | Wherever an interface fails. |
| Matrix and records | Update the cause-and-effect matrix and integration records, and make updating them a condition of every contract that touches a connected system. | Wherever the matrix is lost or out of date. |
| Integrated testing | Integrated testing at least annually and after any change to the fire panel, smoke control, lifts, access control or BMS, with all contractors present. | In every building with connected fire systems. |
| Open protocols | Open protocols in new integrations, so systems can be replaced independently. | In every new integration. |
| Network segmentation | Separate building systems from corporate and guest networks, control remote access, change default credentials and patch. | Wherever building systems share networks or allow remote access. |
| Single point of responsibility | Appoint one contractor or engineer to own the interfaces and coordinate testing. | Wherever several contractors share the interfaces. |
| Golden thread of information | A maintained record of how systems connect, kept with the building. | In every building with connected systems. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Full integrated testing is a recurring lump sum, larger than the sum of individual tests because several contractors must attend together out of hours. Interface repairs are itemised and usually modest. Replacing an integration platform is a lump sum that should be timed with the replacement of a major connected system. Network security works are lump sums with recurring monitoring. Documentation is a small cost that saves large ones.

Fire interface items are code compliance; integration platforms are lifecycle; cyber measures are risk management.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what no single system's test can: what the building should do in a fire, whether that has been proven since the last change, and who owns the links. Ask for the matrix and the last integrated test first.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Current cause-and-effect matrix with its date and author | What the building should do in a fire or outage, and how current that is. |
| Full integrated test reports since the last major change | Whether the interfaces have been proven since the last major change. |
| Integration specifications, protocols and gateway details | How the systems are connected, and on what platforms. |
| Network diagrams and remote access arrangements | Who can reach the building systems remotely, and how. |
| Cyber security assessments | Whether the building network has been assessed for cyber risk. |
| Contracts showing who maintains each interface | Who is responsible for each interface. |
| Records of bypassed or disabled fire panel outputs | Whether fire panel outputs have been bypassed or disabled. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Integrated systems are misread when each system's own test is taken to prove the whole, when a change to one system is assumed to leave the others alone, and when an interface fault is pinned on a single contractor.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| Every system passed its test | A building whose fire interfaces have not been proven by a full integrated test since its last major change should be treated as unproven in a fire, even if every system passes its own checks. |
| We only changed the lift controller | A new fire panel, lift controller, access control system or BMS breaks interfaces unless every connected function is re-tested. Upgrading one system can break its interfaces with the rest. |
| It is the fire contractor's job | Interfaces cross the responsibilities of several contractors; each maintains its own system and none owns the links. A single point of responsibility, with integrated testing, closes the gap. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets requirements for testing fire systems together, for keeping information about how a building's systems connect, and in places for securing building networks. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Integrated testing, records and security | AS 1851 sets routine service of fire protection systems and their interfaces, and AS 1670.1 and AS 1668.1 define fire alarm and smoke control interfaces; annual fire safety certification depends on those interfaces working; performance solutions often rely on them. | BS 7273 covers the interface between fire detection and other systems such as door locks and gas shut-off; BS 9999 sets testing; the Building Safety Act 2022 requires a golden thread of accurate building information, including how systems connect, for higher-risk buildings. | NFPA 4 sets integrated testing of fire protection and life safety systems, including after changes; NFPA 72 covers interfaces; local fire codes and authorities having jurisdiction require re-acceptance testing after modifications. |

sections.heading: Worked example: a drill after a lift modernisation
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. An office's lifts were modernised last year. In this year's evacuation drill the alarm sounded and the smoke fans started, but the lifts did not return to the ground floor and two access-controlled doors stayed locked. The fire, lift and security contractors each say the fault is in someone else's system, and the cause-and-effect matrix dates from 2009.

Each system passes its own checks; the failures are in the links, broken when the lift controller changed and never re-tested. With no current matrix and no one owning the interfaces, nobody can say what the building should do in a fire, and until a full integrated test proves it, the building is unproven.

So the register carries the lift and door interfaces as safety lines, repaired and re-tested with every contractor present, a new cause-and-effect matrix, one party appointed to own the interfaces, and integrated testing after every future change.

pages.title: Internal Doors & Hardware
pages.question: How do internal doors and hardware fail, and which door findings are life-safety failures?
pages.answer: Doors usually outlast their hardware. Closers leak and lose adjustment so fire doors stay open or doors become too heavy for people with disability; hinges wear and frames distort so doors bind and do not latch; seals are painted over or lost. The life-safety failures are on escape routes: keyed locks and chains on exit doors, wrong exit devices, and electronic locks that do not release on fire alarm or power loss.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about internal doors & hardware; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.

pages.searchTitle: Internal doors and hardware: locked exits, failed closers, fire doors held open, access

questions.question: Can an exit door be locked?
questions.answer: It must open from the inside without a key, and electronic locks on escape routes must release on fire alarm and on power failure.

questions.question: Why won't the fire door close properly?
questions.answer: A failed or badly adjusted closer, or a door binding on worn hinges or a distorted frame.

questions.question: Can fire doors be held open?
questions.answer: Only with hold-open devices that release on alarm, never with wedges, hooks or kick-down stops.

questions.question: What makes a door accessible?
questions.answer: Lever handles, low opening forces, enough clear width and space beside the door, and no high thresholds.

questions.question: How long do door closers last?
questions.answer: 10 to 15 years; locks and latches last 10 to 20, and hinges 15 to 30.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Door problems show as doors propped, binding or not latching, locks and chains on exits, knobs on accessible routes, missing seals and markings, and in schedules, inspections and interface tests. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On site | Doors propped, wedged or not closing; closers leaking oil or disconnected | Closers, binding and seals |
| On site | Doors binding, sagging or not latching; worn hinges | Closers, binding and seals |
| On site | Keyed locks or chains on exit doors; magnetic locks on escape routes | Escape hardware, security and alterations |
| On site | Round knobs and heavy doors on accessible routes | Accessibility and automatic doors |
| On site | Damaged leaves and frames; missing seals | Closers, binding and seals |
| On site | Glazed doors without manifestation | Accessibility and automatic doors |
| In the records | Door and hardware schedule | Investigation before the scope |
| In the records | Fire door inspection records | Closers, binding and seals |
| In the records | Access control and fire alarm interface tests | Escape hardware, security and alterations |
| In the records | Keying and master key records | Escape hardware, security and alterations |
| In the records | Access audit | Accessibility and automatic doors |
| In the records | Kick-down stops, hooks or wedges on fire doors | Escape hardware, security and alterations |
| In the records | Decorative hardware on doors that need certified fire-rated hardware | Escape hardware, security and alterations |
| In the records | Automatic doors reopening repeatedly or closing too fast | Accessibility and automatic doors |

sections.heading: Types of door and hardware
sections.markdown:
Internal doors and hardware control movement, privacy, security, sound and fire between spaces: the door leaves and frames, and the hardware that makes them work, including hinges, locks and latches, handles, closers, exit devices (panic bars), door stops, seals, electric strikes and magnetic locks for access control, and hold-open devices. Doors occur in every space, and their failures cut across fire safety, security, accessibility and acoustics. Fire doors are covered in detail on the passive fire protection page; this page covers doors and hardware generally.

| Type | Where it is found | What commonly fails |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hollow-core timber doors | Residential and light commercial | Damage; poor sound and fire performance |
| Solid-core timber doors | Offices, apartments, fire and acoustic doors | Swelling, binding, seal loss |
| Steel doors and frames | Plant rooms, stairs, back-of-house | Corrosion; frame damage |
| Glazed doors | Offices, lobbies, meeting rooms | Unsafe glass; missing manifestation |
| Door closers | Fire doors, entry doors, corridors | Oil leaks; wrong force settings |
| Exit devices and egress hardware | Exit doors, stairs, assembly areas | Wrong type; locked without release |
| Electronic locking | Access-controlled doors | Fail-secure on egress routes; interface faults |
| Hinges, locks and handles | All doors | Wear; sagging; non-accessible handles |

Hardware wears much faster than doors. A building with sound doors can still fail on egress, accessibility and fire safety because of its closers, locks and exit devices.

For the engine, doors are best assessed by function rather than by count: a building with a few non-compliant exit doors has a more serious finding than one with many worn but compliant internal doors.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Door leaves last twenty-five to fifty years and frames the life of the building, but their hardware turns over much faster: closers ten to fifteen years, locks and latches ten to twenty, hinges fifteen to thirty, and exit devices fifteen to twenty.

| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Door leaves | 25 to 50 years | Use; damage; moisture |
| Frames | Life of the building if undamaged | Impact; movement |
| Closers | 10 to 15 years | Cycles; adjustment |
| Hinges | 15 to 30 years | Door weight; cycles |
| Locks and latches | 10 to 20 years | Cycles; abuse |
| Exit devices | 15 to 20 years | Use |
| Electronic locks | 10 to 15 years | Electronics; vendor support |
| Seals | 5 to 15 years | Damage; painting |

What shortens life: high traffic in corridors, entries and amenities; abuse: doors kicked, wedged, slammed and struck by trolleys; moisture swelling timber doors near wet areas and entrances; building movement that distorts frames.

Hardware on high-traffic doors may need replacing several times within the life of the door.

sections.heading: Escape hardware, security and alterations
sections.markdown:
Doors on escape routes must open easily in the direction of travel without keys or special knowledge. Keyed deadlocks on exit doors, magnetic locks that do not release on fire alarm or power loss, chained doors, and exit devices of the wrong type for the occupancy trap people.

Worn locks, lost master keys and unmanaged key systems, and access-controlled doors that do not latch compromise security.

Tenants and residents replace hardware with decorative or non-compliant items, add bolts and chains, fit kick-down stops to hold fire doors open, and remove closers they find inconvenient.

A door on an escape route has one job in an emergency: to open from the inside, at once, for anyone. Keyed locks, chains, bolts, and electronic locks that hold when the alarm sounds or the power fails all defeat that, which is why each is a life-safety finding wherever it sits on an escape route.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Exit door locked when the alarm sounds | Electronic lock not released. Interface test. | Repair the interface, and make the lock fail safe on alarm and on power loss. |
| A kick-down stop, hook or wedge on a fire door | A fire door held open by its users. The door stays open when released. | Remove it, and fit a hold-open device that releases on alarm where the door must stay open. |
| Decorative or unlabelled hardware on a fire door | Hardware replaced by a tenant or resident. Hinges, closer or lock without the certification the door needs. | Replace it with certified hardware, and set hardware standards for occupants. |
| Master keys that cannot be accounted for | Unmanaged keying. Key records show losses, or there are none. | Renew the keying system with key control. |

sections.heading: Closers, binding and seals
sections.markdown:
Closers leak oil, lose adjustment, and are disconnected or removed. Fire and smoke doors then stay open; entry doors slam; doors set too strong cannot be opened by people with limited strength.

Heavy doors on worn hinges sag, frames distort from building movement, and timber swells, so doors bind, do not latch, and are left open.

Seals painted over, damaged or removed let sound and smoke through, undermining meeting room privacy and smoke compartments.

A door that does not close and latch is no longer a fire door, a smoke door or a secure door. Closers, hinges, frames and seals all play a part, and the test is the same for all of them: release the door from fully open, and watch it close and latch on its own.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Doors not closing fully | Closer adjustment or failure, or binding. Test from fully open. | Adjust or replace the closer, and free any binding, so the door closes and latches from fully open. |
| Door rubs at the head on the lock side | Hinge wear or frame distortion. Inspection. | Repair or replace the hinges, and correct the frame. |
| Noise through meeting room doors | Missing or damaged seals. Inspection. | Replace the seals, and stop them being painted over. |
| Fire doors with uneven or wide gaps at the edges | Leaf dropped, warped or badly hung. Gap measurement against the door’s evidence and the limits for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Adjust or rehang the leaf, renew the seals, and replace doors that cannot meet the limits. |

sections.heading: Accessibility and automatic doors
sections.markdown:
Doors on accessible routes are judged by whether anyone can use them: whether a person with limited strength, using a wheelchair or a walking aid, can open the door and pass through it without help.

Round knobs, high opening forces, narrow clear widths, high thresholds and insufficient space beside the door make doors impassable for many people with disability.

Automatic swing and sliding doors inside buildings, common at accessible entries and amenities, fail when sensors drift or operators wear, either closing on people or refusing to open.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Door hard to open | Closer set too strong or stack effect. Opening force measurement against the limits for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Reduce the closer force or treat the stack effect; fit an automatic operator where needed. |
| Glazed doors with no markings | Missing manifestation. Clear glass with nothing at eye level. | Add manifestation so the glass can be seen. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Exit doors locked or with wrong hardware; electronic locks not releasing; fire doors not closing | safety · 4 Essential | Rectify now. |
| Doors failed or security breached | failure · 3 Important | Repair now. |
| Fire door and egress hardware inspections due | deadline · 3 Important | At the prescribed interval. |
| Worn hardware, binding doors, heavy doors on accessible routes | condition · 2 Planned | Repair in the near term. |
| Hardware at end of life; obsolete keying | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Replace. |
| No door schedule or interface test | check · 2 Planned | Survey. |
| Normal | nil · 1 Routine | Routine. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A door hardware specialist or building surveyor, with fire, access and security consultants. The checks below test every door on an escape route, every fire door and every door on an accessible route: from fully open, from the inside, and with the alarm running.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Door survey | Of doors on escape routes, fire doors, accessible routes and secure areas: leaf, frame, hardware, operation, closing, latching and seals, with fire door gaps measured (gov.uk; LookUpStrata; FCIA). |
| Egress hardware check | Type and operation of exit devices and locks against the occupancy. |
| Interface testing | Of electronic locks with the fire alarm and on power failure. |
| Opening force measurement | On accessible routes, against the limits for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). |
| Keying review | Of the master key system, the key register and recorded losses. |
| Automatic door safety check | Of sensors, speeds and forces. |

The report should give a door schedule with defects and a hardware replacement plan.

Doors are best surveyed with a hardware schedule in hand, so each door's function (fire, egress, access, security, acoustic) is known before it is judged.

Check doors in both directions of travel.

sections.heading: Making doors open, close and latch
sections.markdown:
Exit doors that are locked or carry the wrong hardware, and electronic locks that do not release, come first. After that, the work gets every fire and smoke door closing and latching, makes doors on accessible routes usable, and sets standards so occupants' replacements comply.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Egress hardware | Replace keyed locks on exit doors with compliant exit devices; fail-safe electronic locks on escape routes. | Wherever exit doors carry keyed locks, or electronic locks that hold. |
| Closers | Closers replaced and adjusted to balance closing and opening force. | Where doors do not close, slam, or are too heavy. |
| Hinges and frames | Hinges and frames repaired so doors close and latch. | Where doors sag, bind or rub. |
| Accessible hardware | Lever handles, lower forces, automatic operators. | On accessible routes. |
| Seals | Seals replaced. | Where seals are missing, damaged or painted over. |
| Keying | Keying system renewed with key control. | Where keys cannot be accounted for. |
| Hold-open devices | Remove hold-open hooks and wedges, replacing them with hold-open devices that release on alarm where doors need to stay open. | Wherever fire doors are held open. |
| Hardware standards | Hardware standards for tenants and residents so replacements comply. | Wherever occupants replace hardware. |
| Automatic door servicing | Automatic door servicing to the standard. | On every automatic door. |
| Door protection | Door protection plates and frame guards where trolleys and bins strike doors. | Where doors are struck. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Hardware is priced per door and per item, and most hardware renewal is far cheaper than door replacement. Door replacement is priced per door, more for fire-rated and acoustic doorsets with frames and certification. Keying systems are priced per building. Automatic operators are priced per door with power and controls. Interface works for electronic locks are lump sums with fire alarm programming.

Egress and fire door items are code compliance; hardware renewal is lifecycle; adjustments and repairs are repairs and maintenance. Accessibility upgrades may be triggered by alterations.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what testing one door at a time cannot: which doors are fire-rated, whether locks release on alarm, and what occupants have replaced. Ask for the door schedule first.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Door and hardware schedule with fire ratings | Which doors are fire-rated, and what hardware each needs. |
| Fire door inspection records | Whether every fire door is checked, and what was found. |
| Access control and fire alarm interface test records | Whether locks release on alarm and power failure. |
| Keying and master key records, including lost keys | Whether keys are controlled. |
| Access audit covering doors on accessible routes | Whether doors on accessible routes meet requirements. |
| Records of door replacements by tenants or residents | What occupants have replaced. |
| Automatic door service records | Whether automatic doors are serviced. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Doors are misread when locks on escape routes are treated as a security decision, when a door that nearly closes is passed, and when replacement hardware is assumed to match what it replaced.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| Locking it is a security decision | Any door on an escape route that cannot be opened from the inside without a key, or that stays locked in a fire alarm or power failure, is a life-safety failure. |
| It nearly closes | A fire or smoke door that does not close and latch from fully open does not hold back smoke. Adjust or replace the closer, and free the binding. |
| Hardware is hardware | Decorative or unlabelled hinges, closers and locks on a fire door can undo its rating. Replacements need the certification the door requires. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets rules for hardware on escape routes, for fire doors and their inspection, and for doors on accessible routes. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Egress hardware, fire doors and access | The National Construction Code sets egress door hardware and swing requirements; AS 1905.1 covers fire doors; AS 1428.1 sets accessible door requirements; AS 5007 covers powered doors. | BS EN 1125 covers panic exit devices and BS EN 179 emergency exit devices; BS EN 1154 covers closers; Approved Documents B and M and BS 8300 apply. | NFPA 101 and the International Building Code govern egress doors and locking; NFPA 80 covers fire doors; ANSI/BHMA A156 standards cover hardware; the 2010 ADA Standards set accessible door requirements. |

In all three countries, a single non-compliant lock on an exit door can lead to orders or prosecution after an incident, so egress hardware is a priority in any audit.

sections.heading: Worked example: the doors on a refurbished floor
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. On a refurbished office floor, the exit door to the stair has a magnetic lock that stayed locked in the last alarm test. Several fire doors to meeting rooms are held open with kick-down stops, the meeting room doors leak sound through painted-over seals, and the doors on the accessible route have round knobs.

An exit door that stays locked in an alarm is a life-safety failure. Kick-down stops defeat fire doors, and painted seals let both sound and smoke through. Round knobs make the accessible route impassable for many people.

So the register carries the magnetic lock and the held-open doors as safety lines now, a fail-safe interface and hold-open devices that release on alarm, new seals, and lever handles on the accessible route, with hardware standards for future tenants.

pages.title: Internal Stairwells
pages.question: How do stairwells fail as daily stairs and escape routes, and which findings are life-safety failures?
pages.answer: Stairs fail in daily use through falls: worn and slippery nosings, edges that cannot be seen, uneven risers, missing handrails, dark landings. As escape routes they fail when doors are propped or closers broken, when storage fills the enclosure, when security locks doors without release or re-entry, when emergency lighting fails, and when final exits are blocked. Propped doors, storage, failed emergency lighting and locked exits are life-safety failures.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about internal stairwells; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Treads, risers, handrails, balustrades, wall finishes, lighting, safety systems

pages.searchTitle: Fire stairs: propped doors, locked re-entry, storage, falls and blocked final exits

questions.question: Can fire stair doors be locked from the stair side?
questions.answer: Only under conditions such as release on fire alarm or designated re-entry floors, so people in a smoke-filled stair can leave it.

questions.question: Can stair doors be propped open?
questions.answer: Not by wedging. A propped stair door lets smoke into the escape route for every floor above.

questions.question: Why do people keep falling on one flight?
questions.answer: Usually uneven risers, worn nosings or poor light on that flight. Measure the risers and check the nosings.

questions.question: Can anything be stored under the stairs?
questions.answer: No. Storage in a fire-isolated stair narrows the route and adds fire load inside the protected enclosure.

questions.question: How long do stair nosings last?
questions.answer: 10 to 25 years, depending on traffic and material.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Stair problems show as propped and locked doors, storage, worn nosings, missing handrails, dark landings and blocked final exits, and in fire door, incident and locking records. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On site, flight by flight | Doors propped, wedged or held by hooks; closers and latches not working | Stair doors, locking and re-entry |
| On site, flight by flight | Storage, bikes or rubbish in stairs and under flights | Storage, separation and smoke |
| On site, flight by flight | Worn, polished or loose nosings; no contrast strips | Falls, nosings and lighting |
| On site, flight by flight | Handrails missing, loose or on one side only | Falls, nosings and lighting |
| On site, flight by flight | Dark landings; emergency lights failed | Falls, nosings and lighting |
| On site, flight by flight | Floor level signs missing | Final exits |
| On site, flight by flight | Locked stair doors with no indication of release | Stair doors, locking and re-entry |
| On site, flight by flight | Final exits blocked or locked | Final exits |
| In the records | Fire door inspection records | Stair doors, locking and re-entry |
| In the records | Annual fire safety certification | Standards by country |
| In the records | Fall incidents on stairs | Falls, nosings and lighting |
| In the records | Smoke control test records | Storage, separation and smoke |
| In the records | Security locking arrangements and fire alarm interfaces | Stair doors, locking and re-entry |
| In the records | Cigarette butts and furniture on landings, a sign the stair is used as a break area | Storage, separation and smoke |

sections.heading: What the space does and what it contains
sections.markdown:
Internal stairwells are the vertical escape routes and everyday stairs of a building: fire-isolated stairs enclosed in fire-rated construction, open stairs between floors, and feature stairs in lobbies and atria. Functionally a stair must be safe to use every day (even risers, slip-resistant nosings, handrails, good light), and, if it is an escape stair, must stay clear, protected from fire and smoke, lit when the power fails, and lead people out to safety. Fire-isolated stairs are the most important life-safety space in a multi-storey building and the one most often misused for storage, smoking and shortcuts.

| Element group | Typical provision | What matters for the space |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Treads, risers and nosings | Concrete, steel or timber stairs with nosings | Even geometry; slip resistance; visible edges |
| Handrails and balustrades | Handrails on one or both sides; balustrades at open sides | Height, continuity, grip, openings |
| Enclosure and doors | Fire-rated walls and self-closing fire doors | Fire and smoke separation |
| Smoke control | Stair pressurisation or vents in taller buildings | Keeping smoke out |
| Lighting and emergency lighting | Lighting on every flight and landing | Visibility when power fails |
| Signage | Exit signs, floor level identification, re-entry signs | Orientation in an emergency |
| Discharge | Exit to open space or a protected route | Clear path to safety |

sections.heading: How long it stays fit for purpose
sections.markdown:
A stair's structure lasts the life of the building, while nosings last ten to twenty-five years, tread and landing finishes ten to twenty, door hardware ten to fifteen and paint seven to fifteen. Its fitness for purpose is mostly about escape: doors that close, a clear route, and light to see by.

| Component or quality | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stair structure | Life of the building | Corrosion of steel stairs; alterations |
| Nosings | 10 to 25 years | Traffic; product |
| Floor finishes on treads and landings | 10 to 20 years | Traffic; cleaning |
| Fire door hardware | 10 to 15 years | Use; abuse |
| Paint and wall finishes | 7 to 15 years | Damage; appearance |
| Stair lighting | 15 to 20 years for LED | Technology |

What shortens fitness for purpose: use as storage, smoking areas or shortcuts, with doors propped open; worn nosings that become slippery and hard to see; security measures that lock stair doors without proper release; penetrations by services through stair walls.

Stair condition is less a matter of age than of how the stair is used.

sections.heading: Falls, nosings and lighting
sections.markdown:
Falls on stairs are among the most common serious injuries in buildings. Worn or slippery nosings, edges that cannot be seen, uneven risers, missing handrails, poor lighting and wet treads from leaks all contribute. Older stairs often have handrails on one side only and nosings without contrast.

Falls on stairs come from what the foot cannot judge: a nosing worn smooth, an edge that blends into the tread, a riser a little taller than the rest, a landing in shadow. Measuring the risers and looking at the nosings flight by flight usually shows why falls concentrate on one flight rather than another.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Falls on one flight | Uneven risers, worn nosings or poor light. Riser and going measurement against the limits for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market), and nosing condition. | Measure the risers; replace worn nosings with slip-resistant, contrasting nosings, and improve the lighting. |
| Water on treads | Roof or services leak into the stair. Leak tracing. | Trace and repair the leak, and keep the treads dry. |
| A handrail on one side only, or stopping at landings | Handrails short of what the stair needs. Gaps in the rail through landings, or one side bare. Height, extent and continuity checked against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Fit handrails on both sides where required, continuous through landings. |
| A low balustrade, or open risers on a stair | Barrier or treads that will not stop a fall. Barrier height, and the openings between treads and balusters, checked against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Raise or extend the barrier, and close the open risers. |

sections.heading: Stair doors, locking and re-entry
sections.markdown:
Stair doors are propped for convenience, ventilation or deliveries, and closers and latches fail. A propped stair door lets smoke into the escape route for every floor above and defeats stair pressurisation.

Security often locks stair doors from the stair side to stop people moving between floors. Rules in each jurisdiction allow this only under conditions such as release on fire alarm or re-entry floors, so that people in a smoke-filled stair can leave it. Locks fitted without those conditions can trap people.

A stair door does two jobs that pull against each other. Security wants it locked from the stair side; escape wants anyone in a smoke-filled stair to be able to leave it. The rules allow locking only on conditions, such as release on fire alarm or designated re-entry floors, and the test is to try the doors from inside the stair with the alarm running.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Doors propped on several floors | Stair used for circulation between floors. Use patterns. | Fit hold-open devices linked to the alarm where doors must stand open, and repair the closers and latches. |
| People unable to leave the stair on a floor | Locked re-entry without release. Security interface test. | Bring the locking into line with release-on-alarm and re-entry rules, and sign it. |
| Stair doors that do not latch, or show daylight at the edges | Fire doors no longer sealing the stair. Gap measurement against the door’s test evidence and the limits for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Adjust the hinges and closer, renew the seals, and replace doors that cannot meet the limits. |

sections.heading: Storage, separation and smoke
sections.markdown:
A fire-isolated stair is a protected enclosure, and three things undo it from the inside: goods stored in it, breaches in its walls, and pressurisation that lets smoke in or holds the doors shut.

Furniture, boxes, bicycles and rubbish stored in stairs, especially under the lowest flight, narrow the route and add fire load inside the protected enclosure.

Service penetrations, unrated access panels and glazing replaced with ordinary glass compromise the stair enclosure.

Pressurisation that has failed or is unbalanced either lets smoke in or makes doors too hard to open; see the smoke management page.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Smoke in the stair during a drill | Doors propped or pressurisation failed. Door survey; smoke test. | Survey and repair the doors, and test the pressurisation. |
| Ordinary glass or an unrated access panel in the stair enclosure | Separation lost to a later change. No rating marks on the glass or panel. | Replace them with rated glazing or panels, and fire stop the penetrations. |
| Cigarette butts and chairs on a landing | The stair being used as a break area. Litter and furniture on one landing, with the door near it propped. | Clear it, enforce the rules, and give people somewhere else to go. |

sections.heading: Final exits
sections.markdown:
Stairs that discharge into car parks, loading docks or locked yards, or whose final exit doors are blocked or chained, fail at the last step.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A final exit door chained, or opening onto a locked yard | An escape route that fails at the last step. The door cannot be opened without a key, or the yard is closed. | Keep final exits openable without keys, and the route beyond them clear. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Propped or failed stair doors; storage in stairs; failed emergency lighting; locked final exits; unsafe locking | safety · 4 Essential | Rectify now. |
| Stair unusable through damage or leaks | failure · 4 Essential | Repair now. |
| Fire door and emergency lighting checks due | deadline · 3 Important | At the prescribed interval. |
| Worn nosings; missing handrails; dark landings | condition · 3 Important | Repair in the near term. |
| Finishes at end of life | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Refurbish. |
| No review of locking and re-entry | check · 2 Planned | Assess. |
| Normal | nil · 1 Routine | Routine. |

Most stair findings are cheap to fix, so there is rarely a reason to defer them.

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A building surveyor with a fire safety consultant; a security consultant where stairs are locked. The checks below go flight by flight through every stair, test the doors from both sides with the alarm running, and follow each stair to its final exit.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Flight-by-flight inspection | Of every stair: doors, closers and latches, storage, treads and nosings, handrails, lighting, signage, enclosure penetrations and discharge. |
| Riser and going measurement | Where falls occur or stairs look irregular, against the riser and going limits for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). |
| Slip resistance testing | Of nosings and landings to AS 4586, against the classification the NCC lists for stair treads and nosing strips in Table D3D15 (NCC Part D3). |
| Locking and re-entry test | Security doors released by the fire alarm and on power failure. |
| Smoke control and emergency lighting tests | Of stair pressurisation, smoke vents and emergency lighting, triggered from the fire alarm and on mains failure. |
| Use review | Why doors are propped and stairs used for storage. |

The report should list life-safety items by stair and floor, and stair improvements.

Stairs are best inspected at different times of day, because propped doors and storage often appear outside business hours.

Night and weekend checks are often revealing.

sections.heading: Clearing, repairing and securing safely
sections.markdown:
Propped or failed stair doors, storage in stairs, failed emergency lighting and locked final exits come first, as life-safety failures. After that, the work makes every step visible and every rail continuous, and brings security locking into line with the rules.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Door repair | Closers, latches and seals restored so every stair door closes and latches from fully open; hold-open devices linked to the fire alarm where stairs are genuinely used for circulation between floors. | Wherever stair doors do not close and latch. |
| Clear storage | Clear storage from every stair and enforce building rules, with regular checks recorded. | Wherever stairs hold stored items. |
| Nosings | Slip-resistant nosings with contrasting edges on every tread and landing edge, so each step can be seen and gripped. | Wherever nosings are worn or loose, or lack contrast. |
| Handrails | Handrails on both sides where required, continuous through landings, at the right height and graspable. | Where rails are missing, short or one-sided. |
| Lighting | Even lighting on every flight with emergency lighting tested to the standard, and occupancy-dimmed lighting that never leaves a flight dark. | Where flights or landings are dark. |
| Locking | Bring security locking into line with release-on-alarm and re-entry rules, with signage on the stair side. | Wherever stair doors are locked from the stair side. |
| Fire separation | Fire stopping of service penetrations and replacement of any unrated panels or glazing in the enclosure. | Wherever the enclosure has been breached. |
| Final exits | Final exits kept clear and openable without keys, with signage outside to stop obstruction. | Wherever final exits are blocked or locked. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Stair works are priced per flight or per stair. Nosings and handrails are priced by length; door works per door; lighting per fitting; locking changes per door with fire alarm interface. Most items are code compliance and low in cost relative to their safety value; the main cost driver is doing the work without closing escape routes, which usually means one stair at a time and out-of-hours work.

Keeping stairs clear costs only management time.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what one walk down the stairs cannot: whether every door is checked, whether locked doors release on alarm, and where people have fallen. Ask for them before changing any security arrangement.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Fire door inspection records for every stair door | Whether every stair door is checked, and what was found. |
| Annual fire safety certification and any qualifications on stairs | Whether the stairs were certified, and with what qualifications. |
| Stair fall incident records | Where people have fallen. |
| Security locking and fire alarm interface test records | Whether locked stair doors release on alarm. |
| Smoke control and emergency lighting test records | Whether smoke control and emergency lighting work. |
| Building rules on stair use and storage, with records of enforcement | Whether the rules on stair use are enforced. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Stairs are misread when propped doors and storage are treated as housekeeping, when locking a stair door is treated as a security decision alone, and when falls are blamed on the people who fall.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| It is only housekeeping | Fire-isolated stairs must stay clear, closed, lit and able to discharge to safety. Storage, propped doors, failed emergency lighting and locked final exits are life-safety failures. |
| Locking the stair doors is a security matter | Locked re-entry is allowed only under conditions such as release on fire alarm or designated re-entry floors, so that people in a smoke-filled stair can leave it. Test the doors from inside the stair with the alarm running. |
| Falls are people's own fault | Falls concentrated on one flight point to uneven risers, worn nosings or poor light. Measure the risers and check the nosings flight by flight. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets requirements for stair construction, handrails and nosings, and for keeping fire stairs closed, clear and openable, including when doors may be locked. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Stairs, doors and re-entry | The National Construction Code sets stair geometry, handrails, fire-isolated stairs and door requirements, with fire doors maintained under AS 1851; slip resistance follows AS 4586; strata and building rules prohibit storage in stairs. | Approved Document B governs escape stairs and Approved Document K stair geometry and guarding; the Fire Safety (England) Regulations 2022 require checks of fire doors in residential buildings; the responsible person must keep escape routes clear. | NFPA 101 and the International Building Code govern exit stairs, including re-entry rules for locked stair doors; NFPA 80 covers stair door inspection; OSHA requires exit routes kept clear. |

Insurers and fire services in all three countries treat obstructed or compromised escape stairs as serious breaches and can require immediate action or issue orders.

sections.heading: Worked example: a fire stair used between floors
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. In a 1990s office, staff use one fire stair to move between their three floors. Its doors are propped open on those floors, the doors on other floors are locked from the stair side for security, chairs and cigarette butts sit on one landing, and two falls have been recorded on the same flight, where the nosings are worn smooth.

Propped doors let smoke into the escape route for every floor above. Doors locked from the stair side may trap people in a smoke-filled stair unless they release on alarm. The landing is being used as a break area, and falls on one flight point to the worn nosings.

So the register carries the propped and locked doors as safety lines, hold-open devices linked to the alarm and locking brought into line with the re-entry rules, the landing cleared, and slip-resistant, contrasting nosings on the worn flight.

pages.title: Internal Wall & Ceiling Finishes
pages.question: How do wall and ceiling finishes fail, and when is a ceiling dangerous?
pages.answer: Most finish failures are cosmetic, but some are not. Old lath and plaster ceilings lose their keys and sag, and plasterboard ceilings with failed fixings or soaked by leaks bow and can fall without warning. Textured coatings and older plasters may contain asbestos and older paints lead, which are safe until disturbed. Hairline cracks at joints are normal; tapering and recurring cracks can signal structural movement. Mould points to condensation.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about internal wall & ceiling finishes; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
