pages.searchTitle: Ceilings and wall finishes: sagging plaster, cracks, mould, asbestos and suspended ceilings

questions.question: Is a sagging ceiling dangerous?
questions.answer: It can be. An old lath and plaster ceiling, or plasterboard bowing between supports, can fall without warning; keep people out from under it until it is assessed.

questions.question: Why does mould come back after painting?
questions.answer: The moisture cause has not been fixed. Improve the ventilation before repainting.

questions.question: Are ceiling cracks serious?
questions.answer: Most are shrinkage and seasonal movement. Wide, tapering or growing cracks, especially above doors and windows, may point to structural movement.

questions.question: Can I drill into a textured ceiling?
questions.answer: Not until it has been tested. Textured coatings in older buildings can contain asbestos.

questions.question: How long does a lath and plaster ceiling last?
questions.answer: 80 to 120 years; plasterboard lasts the life of the building if it is kept dry and well fixed.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Finish problems show as sagging and cracked ceilings, nail pops, stains and mould, textured and flaking older surfaces, and missing or stained tiles, and in asbestos, leak and repair records. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On site | Ceilings sagging, bulging or with cracks running along battens; cornices pulling away | Sagging, collapse and water |
| On site | Nail pops and cracks at plasterboard joints | Cracking |
| On site | Stains, softness and mould on ceilings | Sagging, collapse and water |
| On site | Textured ceilings and walls in older buildings | Asbestos and lead |
| On site | Flaking paint on older surfaces | Asbestos and lead |
| On site | Missing, stained or sagging suspended ceiling tiles | Suspended and fire-rated ceilings |
| In the records | Asbestos register | Asbestos and lead |
| In the records | Leak history | Sagging, collapse and water |
| In the records | Previous ceiling repairs | Sagging, collapse and water |
| In the records | Cracks running parallel at regular spacing on ceilings, following battens or joists | Cracking |
| In the records | Ceiling fans and heavy fittings fixed to plasterboard alone | Sagging, collapse and water |
| In the records | Patched and mismatched suspended ceiling tiles after services works | Suspended and fire-rated ceilings |
| In the records | Bulges in ceilings below wet areas or roof leaks | Sagging, collapse and water |
| In the records | Mould returning on ceilings soon after repainting | Sagging, collapse and water |
| In the records | Old ceilings with fine cracks and slight bulges | Sagging, collapse and water |

sections.heading: Types of finish
sections.markdown:
Internal wall and ceiling finishes are the visible surfaces of rooms: lath and plaster in older buildings, plasterboard on timber or steel framing, suspended ceiling grids and tiles in commercial buildings, paint, wall coverings, textured coatings, timber panelling, wall tiles and acoustic panels. They are judged on appearance, but some failures are structural in effect: old lath and plaster ceilings and poorly fixed plasterboard ceilings can collapse, and textured coatings and paints in older buildings may contain asbestos or lead.

| Type | Where it is found | What commonly fails |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lath and plaster | Houses and buildings before about 1940 | Plaster keys break and ceilings sag and fall |
| Plasterboard | Most buildings since the 1950s | Cracks at joints, nail pops, sagging ceilings, water damage |
| Suspended ceilings | Commercial buildings | Stained and sagging tiles; grid damage; missing tiles |
| Textured coatings | Ceilings and walls from the mid twentieth century | May contain asbestos in older buildings |
| Paint | Everywhere | Flaking; lead in older paint; mould |
| Wall tiles | Wet areas, kitchens | Cracking, debonding, grout failure |
| Wall coverings and panelling | Offices, hotels, older homes | Peeling, damage, fire performance |

Finishes are assessed by space, since ceilings over beds, desks and corridors carry more consequence if they fall than those over storage.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Plasterboard lasts the life of the building if it stays dry and well fixed, and lath and plaster eighty to a hundred and twenty years, while suspended ceiling grids last twenty-five to forty years, their tiles fifteen to twenty-five, and paint five to ten. Water and age, not wear, bring ceilings down.

| Finish | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Paint | 5 to 10 years | Wear; moisture; style |
| Plasterboard | Life of the building if dry and well fixed | Water; movement; fixing |
| Lath and plaster | 80 to 120 years | Vibration; water; loss of key |
| Suspended ceiling tiles | 15 to 25 years | Water; services works; appearance |
| Suspended ceiling grid | 25 to 40 years | Corrosion; damage |
| Wall coverings | 10 to 15 years | Damage; style |

What shortens life: water from leaks and condensation; building movement cracking joints and cornices; services works that cut and patch ceilings; vibration and roof works loosening old plaster.

Ceilings in older buildings deserve particular attention because their age, not their appearance, often decides whether they are safe.

sections.heading: Sagging, collapse and water
sections.markdown:
Lath and plaster ceilings hang by plaster keys pushed through the laths; as keys break with age, vibration and water, the ceiling sags and can fall in large sections. Plasterboard ceilings fixed with failing adhesive, too few fasteners or undersized battens, or soaked by leaks, sag and can drop without warning. Sagging ceilings are a safety finding.

Leaks from roofs, wet areas and services stain, soften and collapse ceilings; condensation in bathrooms and cold rooms grows mould on ceilings and walls.

Old ceilings rarely fall without warning to someone who knows what to look for: a sag in the middle of a room, cracks along the line of the battens, a bulge below a wet area. Plaster keys break with age, vibration and water; once enough have gone, a section can come down at once, which is why a sagging ceiling is a safety finding until it has been looked at from above.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Old ceiling sagging in the middle of the room | Lath and plaster keys failing. Inspection from above. | Keep people out from under it; refix or replace the ceiling. |
| Plasterboard ceiling bowing between battens | Fixing or adhesive failure, or water. Inspection from the roof space. | Refix with additional fasteners, or replace water-damaged boards after fixing the leak. |
| Mould on bathroom ceiling | Condensation from poor exhaust. Fan and humidity check. | Improve the exhaust, treat the mould, then repaint. |
| A ceiling fan or heavy fitting fixed to plasterboard alone | A fitting pulling the ceiling down over time. No framing behind the fixing. | Refix it to the framing. |

sections.heading: Cracking
sections.markdown:
Cracks at plasterboard joints, cornices and corners come from timber shrinkage, seasonal movement and structural movement. Most are cosmetic; cracks that are wide, recurring or tapering may reflect foundation or structural movement.

Most cracks in plasterboard and plaster are shrinkage and seasonal movement, harmless and recurring. The ones that matter are wide, tapering or growing, or sit above doors and windows; they point to movement in the structure, which has to be dealt with before any repair will hold.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hairline cracks at joints and cornices | Normal shrinkage and movement. Pattern; stability. | Repair the cracks, with flexible joints where movement will recur. |
| Tapering cracks above doors and windows | Structural or foundation movement. See foundations page. | Treat it as possible structural movement; see [Foundations](https://moyneross.com/technical/foundations). |

sections.heading: Asbestos and lead
sections.markdown:
Textured coatings and some plasters, ceiling tiles and wall boards in older buildings contain asbestos; older paint contains lead. They are safe while intact but release fibres or dust when sanded, drilled or removed.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A textured ceiling in an older building about to be drilled for new lights | Possible asbestos about to be disturbed. The asbestos register, and testing before work. | Test first; leave intact material undisturbed, or have licensed contractors remove it. |
| Old painted walls or ceilings about to be sanded or stripped | Lead in older paint. Paint testing before work, against the definition of lead paint for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Test first; use lead-safe methods and clean-up, and keep occupants away during the work. |

sections.heading: Suspended and fire-rated ceilings
sections.markdown:
Tiles stain from leaks and sag from humidity; grids are bent by trades; tiles are left out after works, breaking fire, acoustic and smoke performance where the ceiling is part of a system.

Heavy fittings such as light fittings, fans and speakers hung from plasterboard without proper support also pull ceilings down over time.

Fire-rated ceilings lose rating when cut for services.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stained suspended tiles in a line | Leak from services or the floor above. Trace the line. | Trace the line to its source and repair it, then replace the tiles. |
| Tiles left out, or mismatched, after services works | A ceiling system with gaps in it. Openings in a ceiling that forms part of a fire, smoke or acoustic system. | Replace the tiles, and restore the ceiling system. |
| Services cut through a fire-rated ceiling | Rating lost to penetrations. Openings above the ceiling without fire stopping. | Fire stop the penetrations with tested systems. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sagging ceilings; damaged asbestos-containing finishes; flaking lead paint where children are present | safety · 4 Essential | Exclude, make safe and remediate now. |
| Ceiling collapsed or water-damaged | failure · 3 Important | Repair now. |
| Asbestos register review due | deadline · 3 Important | At the prescribed interval. |
| Cracking, mould, stained tiles, worn paint | condition · 2 Planned | Repair in the near term. |
| Finishes at end of cycle | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Refurbish. |
| Hazardous content unknown in older finishes | check · 2 Planned | Sample before works. |
| Normal | nil · 1 Routine | Routine. |

A sagging ceiling is graded as safety even if it has not moved recently, because collapse gives little warning and falls on people below.

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A building surveyor inspects, with a licensed asbestos assessor before any sampling or works on older finishes. The checks below inspect ceilings from below and, where they can be reached, from above, test older finishes for asbestos and lead before any work, and trace stains to their source.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Ceiling inspection | From below and, where accessible, from the roof space or ceiling void, checking fixings, keys, battens and adhesives. |
| Crack mapping | With widths and patterns to separate cosmetic from structural cracking. |
| Moisture and mould assessment | Where stains or mould appear. |
| Hazardous materials sampling | Of textured coatings, older plasters, ceiling tiles and paints before work. |
| Suspended ceiling survey | Where the ceiling forms part of a fire, smoke or acoustic system. |

The report should identify any collapse risk, hazardous content, the cause of cracking and staining, and a repair or refurbishment plan.

Where ceilings are old and inaccessible from above, a small inspection opening can confirm their fixing.

Record which rooms sit under old or sagging ceilings, so that the most occupied rooms are made safe first and the others are scheduled.

sections.heading: Securing, repairing and redecorating
sections.markdown:
Sagging ceilings, damaged asbestos-containing finishes and flaking lead paint come first. After that, every repair waits for its cause to be fixed, whether the leak, the movement or the ventilation, or the damage returns.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ceiling securing | Refix plasterboard with additional fasteners, or replace sagging lath and plaster ceilings, after propping where needed. | Wherever ceilings sag or bow. |
| Crack repair | Crack repair after any movement is resolved, with flexible joints where movement will recur. | Where cracks are stable or seasonal. |
| Leak and moisture fixes | Leak and moisture fixes before redecorating, then repair or replacement of damaged boards. | Wherever ceilings are stained or softened. |
| Mould treatment | Mould treatment and improved ventilation. | Where mould grows. |
| Hazardous materials | Leave intact asbestos-containing finishes undisturbed and recorded, or remove by licensed contractors before works; stabilise or remove lead paint safely. | Wherever older finishes contain asbestos or lead. |
| Suspended ceilings | Replace stained and missing tiles and straighten grids; restore ceiling systems that form part of fire or acoustic designs. | Where tiles are stained, missing or sagging. |
| Redecoration | Redecoration on cycle. | At the end of the paint cycle. |
| Heavy fittings | Support heavy fittings from framing, not plasterboard. | Wherever fans, lights or speakers hang from plasterboard. |
| Ventilation improvements | Ventilation improvements in bathrooms and laundries so ceilings do not grow mould again after repainting. | Where mould returns after repainting. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Ceiling repairs and replacements are priced by area, with propping and access, and in occupied buildings the cost of temporary relocation. Hazardous materials removal adds licensed removal, air monitoring and clearance. Suspended tiles are priced per tile or by area. Redecoration is by area on a cycle.

Collapse risks are immediate; hazardous materials are code compliance when disturbed; redecoration and ceiling replacement are lifecycle.

Ceiling refixing is far cheaper than repairs after a collapse.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a look at the ceiling cannot: whether older finishes contain asbestos or lead, where water has come through before, and what has been repaired. Ask for them before anyone drills, sands or removes a finish.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Asbestos register covering finishes | Whether finishes contain asbestos. |
| Lead paint test results for older buildings | Whether older paint contains lead. |
| Leak history and repairs | Where water has come through before. |
| Previous ceiling repairs or replacements | Which ceilings have already been repaired or replaced. |
| Records of works that disturbed finishes | Whether earlier works disturbed hazardous finishes. |
| Mould complaints | Where mould recurs. |
| Records of heavy fittings installed on ceilings | Which ceilings carry heavy fittings. |
| Building age and renovation history | How old each finish is likely to be. |
| Records of ceiling repairs after leaks | Whether ceilings were properly repaired after leaks. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Wall and ceiling finishes are misread when a sagging ceiling is treated as cosmetic, when mould is simply painted over, and when every crack is treated alike.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| It is only a sag | A sagging ceiling, particularly an old lath and plaster ceiling or a plasterboard ceiling bowing between supports, can fall without warning. Keep people out from under it until it is assessed. |
| Paint over the mould | Recurring mould after repainting means the moisture cause has not been fixed. |
| All cracks are cosmetic | Hairline cracks at joints and cornices are normal shrinkage and movement; tapering cracks above doors and windows may reflect structural or foundation movement, which must be dealt with first. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets rules for work on asbestos and lead paint, and standards for plasterboard, ceilings and fire-rated ceiling systems. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Hazardous finishes and ceiling systems | Plasterboard installation follows AS/NZS 2589; lead paint management follows AS/NZS 4361.2; asbestos-containing finishes are managed under work health and safety laws. | Plastering and drylining follow BS 8212 and BS EN 520; asbestos-containing textured coatings are managed under the Control of Asbestos Regulations 2012; lead paint follows HSE guidance. | Gypsum board application follows ASTM C840 and GA-216; lead-safe practices under the EPA Renovation, Repair and Painting Rule apply in pre-1978 housing; asbestos is regulated by OSHA and the EPA. |

In all three countries, work that disturbs asbestos-containing finishes must follow asbestos rules, and in rental housing, landlords must keep ceilings and walls safe and free of hazards such as mould and lead dust under housing standards.

sections.heading: Worked example: an old house with a sagging ceiling
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. In a 1920s house, the living room's lath and plaster ceiling sags in the middle with cracks along the line of the battens, the bathroom ceiling grows mould a few months after each repaint, and the owner plans to fit downlights in a textured hallway ceiling.

A sagging lath and plaster ceiling can fall without warning, so the living room is kept clear underneath until it is assessed from above. Mould that returns after repainting means the moisture is still there. The textured hallway ceiling may contain asbestos and must be tested before it is drilled.

So the register carries the living room ceiling as a safety line, refixed or replaced, a ducted exhaust fan for the bathroom before it is repainted, and asbestos testing of the hallway ceiling before the downlights go in.

thresholds.rule: Lead at or above 1.0 mg/cm² by XRF, or 0.5 per cent by weight in a laboratory sample

source.title: 24 CFR 35.86 Definitions (lead-based paint)
source.publisher: US Department of Housing and Urban Development

pages.title: Kitchen
pages.question: How do residential kitchens fail, and which kitchen findings are safety issues?
pages.answer: Kitchens are usually refurbished for style before they fail, but the real defects are hidden. Slow leaks under sinks and dishwashers swell cabinet bases and floors; aged flexible hoses burst and flood apartments below; recirculating or ceiling-ducted rangehoods leave moisture and combustion products indoors; gas cooktops too close to combustibles or fitted without certification are fire risks; new appliances overload old circuits. Replace hoses on a cycle and duct extraction outside.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about kitchen; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Cabinetry, benchtops, appliances, joinery, butler\u2019s pantry

sources.title: Engineered stone ban

pages.searchTitle: Residential kitchens: hidden leaks, flexible hoses, gas clearances, extraction and safety

questions.question: How often should kitchen flexible hoses be replaced?
questions.answer: Every 5 to 10 years, with accessible isolation valves; burst hoses are a leading cause of residential water damage claims.

questions.question: Why is the cabinet under the sink swollen?
questions.answer: A slow leak at the waste or tap connections. Empty the cabinet to find it, repair the connection, and replace the base.

questions.question: Does a rangehood need to vent outside?
questions.answer: It should. Recirculating hoods, and hoods ducted into the ceiling, leave moisture, grease and combustion products indoors.

questions.question: Is a gas cooktop near a timber splashback a problem?
questions.answer: Yes. Clearances to combustible materials are set by the gas rules, and scorch marks mean it is too close.

questions.question: Is engineered stone dangerous?
questions.answer: Not in place. Cutting it releases silica dust, and Australia has banned new installations since 1 July 2024.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Kitchen problems hide behind the doors: swollen cabinet bases, old hoses, scorch marks and recirculating hoods, and in the records of certificates, leaks and appliance ages. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| In the kitchen | Swollen, stained or soft cabinet bases under the sink and dishwasher | Leaks under the sink and appliances |
| In the kitchen | Flexible hoses that are kinked, rusted or past their date | Leaks under the sink and appliances |
| In the kitchen | Rangehood type and where it discharges; greasy filters | Extraction and moisture |
| In the kitchen | Gas cooktop clearances to splashbacks and cabinets | Gas, fire and electrical safety |
| In the kitchen | Power boards running appliances; tripping | Gas, fire and electrical safety |
| In the kitchen | Swollen laminate at joints; cracked stone at cut-outs | Benchtops, cabinets and heavy use |
| In the kitchen | Mould on ceilings or in cupboards | Extraction and moisture |
| In the records | Gas compliance certificates | Gas, fire and electrical safety |
| In the records | Appliance ages and warranties | Benchtops, cabinets and heavy use |
| In the records | Leak and insurance claims | Leaks under the sink and appliances |
| In the records | Electrical certificates for renovations | Gas, fire and electrical safety |
| In the records | No isolation valves under the sink, or valves that cannot be turned | Leaks under the sink and appliances |
| In the records | Fire blanket and smoke alarm near the kitchen absent | Gas, fire and electrical safety |

sections.heading: What the space does and what it contains
sections.markdown:
The residential kitchen is the room where water, gas or high electrical loads, heat, grease and heavy daily use come together: cabinetry and benchtops, sink and tapware, dishwasher and laundry connections where present, cooktop and oven, rangehood, refrigerator, splashbacks and the floor beneath. Functionally it must work, stay dry, extract cooking moisture and fumes, and be safe from fire, gas and electrical hazards. Kitchens are usually refurbished for style long before they fail, but hidden leaks under sinks and dishwashers, and gas and ventilation issues, are real defects.

| Element group | Typical provision | What matters for the space |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cabinetry | Particleboard or MDF carcasses with laminate or two-pack doors | Moisture swelling, hinges, drawers |
| Benchtops | Laminate, stone, engineered stone, timber, stainless steel | Damage, joints, sealing at the sink |
| Sink and tapware | Sink, mixer, waste, under-sink connections | Leaks into cabinets and floors |
| Appliances | Cooktop, oven, dishwasher, rangehood, refrigerator | Age, safety, energy, connections |
| Rangehood and exhaust | Ducted to outside or recirculating | Moisture, grease and combustion products |
| Gas or electric cooking | Gas cooktop with flexible connection; induction or ceramic | Gas safety; electrical capacity |
| Splashback and clearances | Tiles, glass, stone | Heat clearances near burners |

sections.heading: How long it stays fit for purpose
sections.markdown:
A residential kitchen is usually refurbished every fifteen to twenty-five years, often for style before it fails. Its working parts turn over faster: dishwashers eight to twelve years, cooktops, ovens and rangehoods ten to fifteen, and flexible hoses five to ten, which is why hose age matters more than how the kitchen looks.

| Component or quality | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Kitchen refurbishment cycle | 15 to 25 years | Style; wear; leaks |
| Cabinetry | 15 to 25 years | Moisture; hardware |
| Laminate benchtops | 10 to 20 years | Heat; moisture at joints |
| Stone and engineered stone benchtops | 25 years and more | Impact; sealing |
| Cooktops and ovens | 10 to 15 years | Use |
| Dishwashers | 8 to 12 years | Use; water quality |
| Rangehoods | 10 to 15 years | Grease; motors |
| Flexible hoses | 5 to 10 years | Burst risk with age |

What shortens fitness for purpose: slow leaks under sinks and dishwashers swelling cabinetry and floors; ageing flexible hoses that burst; recirculating rangehoods that leave moisture and combustion products in the home; heavy use in rented and shared homes.

sections.heading: Leaks under the sink and appliances
sections.markdown:
Waste connections, tap connections and braided flexible hoses leak slowly into the cabinet base, which swells, delaminates and grows mould; dishwasher inlet and outlet hoses leak into the floor. Burst flexible hoses flood whole apartments and the units below, and are a leading cause of residential water damage insurance claims.

Kitchen leaks are slow and hidden, or sudden. A drip at a waste joint or hose fitting soaks the cabinet base for months before anyone empties the cupboard, while a burst hose floods in minutes. Both are found only by emptying the cabinet, looking behind the dishwasher, and checking the dates on the hoses.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Swollen cabinet base under the sink | Slow leak at waste or tap connections. Inspection with the cabinet emptied. | Repair the connection, replace the swollen base and kickboard, and fit isolation valves. |
| Water on the floor in front of the dishwasher | Hose or door seal leak. Run a cycle and inspect. | Replace the hose or door seal, and check the floor beneath. |
| Braided hoses with rust spots, kinks or no date tag | Hoses near the end of their life. Corrosion at the crimped ends, and an installation date unknown or more than five to ten years ago. | Replace them with quality hoses and accessible isolation valves. |
| Floor beside the refrigerator lifting or stained | A leak at the refrigerator's water connection. Moisture readings are highest behind the refrigerator, and the supply line weeps when it is pulled out. | Repair or replace the connection, and fit an isolation valve. |
| Hot water too hot at the kitchen tap | Temperature control failed or absent. Outlet temperature against the limits for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Fit or repair tempering at the heater or outlet. |

sections.heading: Extraction and moisture
sections.markdown:
Recirculating rangehoods or hoods ducted into the ceiling space leave moisture, grease and, with gas cooking, nitrogen dioxide and other combustion products indoors. Condensation and mould follow in poorly ventilated homes.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Condensation and mould after cooking | Rangehood recirculating or ducted into the ceiling. Duct route inspection (Thresholds by market). | Duct the rangehood to outside, sized for the cooktop. |
| Grease film on cupboards and the ceiling near the cooktop | Extraction too weak, or filters clogged. Saturated filters and little airflow at the hood. | Clean or replace the filters; duct or upgrade the hood. |

sections.heading: Gas, fire and electrical safety
sections.markdown:
Most kitchen safety findings are cheap to fix and serious to miss: an aged hose, a cooktop too close to a combustible splashback, a cooktop fitted without a compliance certificate, appliances run off power boards. Each can cause a flood, a fire or a gas leak without warning.

Flexible gas connections deteriorate; burners placed too close to combustible splashbacks or cabinets are a fire risk; cooktops fitted by unlicensed people may leak.

Cooking is the leading cause of house fires. Grease-laden rangehood filters, combustible materials near cooktops and the absence of fire blankets or alarms in kitchens of older homes raise the risk.

Induction cooktops and more appliances need circuits older kitchens do not have; overloaded circuits and power boards trip or overheat.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Scorch marks behind the cooktop | Clearance to combustible materials too small. Measurement against gas rules. | Have a licensed gas fitter correct the clearance, or replace the splashback with non-combustible material. |
| Circuit trips when cooking | Overloaded circuit. Load assessment. | Add dedicated circuits for the cooktop, oven and dishwasher, with RCD protection. |
| Smoke alarm missing or disabled near the kitchen | An alarm removed after nuisance alarms from cooking. An empty alarm base, or the battery taken out. | Refit alarms positioned to avoid nuisance alarms, and add a fire blanket near the cooktop. |

sections.heading: Benchtops, cabinets and heavy use
sections.markdown:
Laminate swells at sink cut-outs and joints, stone chips and cracks at cut-outs, hinges and drawer runners fail. Engineered stone in place is not a hazard, but cutting it releases silica dust; Australia has banned new engineered stone installations.

In rented homes and shared housing, heavy use and slow reporting of leaks accelerate damage.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Benchtop edges chipped, swollen or delaminating near the sink | Water reaching the core of a laminate or timber top. Edges and joints at the sink and cooktop. | Reseal or replace the affected sections. |
| Engineered stone benchtop to be cut or modified | Silica dust hazard. Product type; current rules on engineered stone. | Do not cut or modify it on site; replace with a permitted material if changes are needed. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gas leaks or unsafe clearances; aged flexible hoses; overloaded circuits | safety · 4 Essential | Rectify now. |
| Active leaks damaging floors or units below | failure · 3 Important | Repair now. |
| Tenancy or sale requirements for gas or electrical safety | deadline · 3 Important | As required. |
| Swollen cabinetry; weak extraction; worn appliances | condition · 2 Planned | Repair or replace in the near term. |
| Kitchen at end of refurbishment cycle | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Refurbish. |
| Gas and electrical compliance unknown | check · 2 Planned | Inspect. |
| Normal | nil · 1 Routine | Routine. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A building surveyor or building inspector leads, with a licensed gas fitter for gas cooking and an electrician where circuits are in doubt; in apartments, access to the unit below helps trace leaks. The checks below open what cannot be seen, the cabinet under the sink, the hose behind the dishwasher and the duct above the rangehood, then check gas and electrical safety.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Under-sink and appliance inspection | With cabinets emptied: waste and tap connections, flexible hoses and their dates, isolation valves, cabinet bases and the floor beneath. |
| Moisture readings | In floors, walls and kickboards around the sink, dishwasher and refrigerator water connection. |
| Dishwasher test | Run a cycle and inspect for leaks at hoses, seals and the floor. |
| Rangehood check | Type, airflow, filter condition and where the duct actually discharges. |
| Gas safety check | By a licensed fitter: connection condition, leak test, burner clearances to splashbacks and cabinets. |
| Electrical check | Number and rating of circuits, RCD protection, use of power boards, tripping history. |
| Condition survey | Of cabinetry, benchtops, splashbacks and appliances, with ages. |

The report should list safety items, leaks and damage with their extent, and when the kitchen is due for renewal.

sections.heading: Making safe, repairing or refurbishing
sections.markdown:
Gas leaks, unsafe clearances, aged hoses and overloaded circuits come first, and most are inexpensive. After that, the work stops water and moisture, by repairing leaks and ducting extraction outside, and refurbishment follows on its cycle, with moisture-resistant carcasses and sealed cut-outs.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Flexible hose replacement | Quality braided hoses on a cycle, with accessible isolation valves. | Every five to ten years; a cheap measure against flooding. |
| Leak repairs | Repair wastes and connections, replace swollen cabinet bases and kickboards, and repair damaged floors. | Wherever a leak is found. |
| Ducted extraction | A rangehood ducted to the outside, sized for the cooktop, with filters cleaned regularly. | Where the rangehood recirculates or discharges into the ceiling. |
| Gas safety works | Certified connections and compliant clearances, or conversion to induction cooking where electrification is planned. | Wherever connections are uncertified or clearances are too small. |
| Electrical upgrades | Dedicated circuits for cooktops, ovens and dishwashers, with RCD protection. | Where circuits trip or appliances run off power boards. |
| Fire safety | Smoke alarms positioned to avoid nuisance alarms, and a fire blanket near the cooktop. | In every kitchen. |
| Leak detection | Water sensors under sinks and dishwashers, especially in apartments. | Under sinks and dishwashers, especially in apartments. |
| Refurbishment | Refurbish on cycle, with moisture-resistant carcasses and sealed benchtop cut-outs. | At the end of the kitchen's cycle. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Hose replacement, leak repairs and leak sensors are small items with large avoided costs. Rangehood ducting is a lump sum, harder in apartments where ducts must reach the façade. Electrical upgrades are lump sums, sometimes requiring switchboard work. Induction conversion is a lump sum including the appliance and circuit. Kitchen refurbishment is priced per kitchen and in rented stock timed with vacancies.

Safety items are immediate; refurbishment is lifecycle; leak repairs are repairs and maintenance. In strata, water damage to other units from kitchen leaks usually falls to the owner whose fittings failed.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a look at the doors and benchtops cannot: whether gas and electrical work was certified, how old the hoses and appliances are, and whether the kitchen has leaked before. Ask for them before judging the kitchen on its finishes.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Gas compliance certificates for cooktops and ovens | Whether gas appliances were fitted and certified by a licensed fitter. |
| Electrical certificates for kitchen renovations | Whether renovation circuits were certified. |
| Appliance ages and warranties | How far through their lives the appliances are. |
| Leak and insurance claims, including damage to units below | Whether the kitchen has already leaked, and damaged homes below. |
| Strata approvals for kitchen renovations | Whether a renovation had the approvals it needed. |
| Records of flexible hose replacement | Whether the hoses are past their life. |
| Records of any kitchen fires or near misses | Whether there have been fires or near misses. |
| Electrification plans affecting gas cooking | Whether gas cooking is due to be replaced. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Kitchens are misread when they are judged on their finishes, when an old hose is treated as too minor to report, and when an existing engineered stone benchtop is treated as a hazard.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| Judge it by the finishes | Kitchens are judged mostly on what cannot be seen: the cabinet base under the sink, the hose behind the dishwasher and the duct above the rangehood. Open them before forming a view. |
| An old hose is a minor item | Flexible hoses past their life, gas cooktops too close to combustible materials, and gas connections fitted without certification are safety findings. |
| The engineered stone benchtop is a hazard | Engineered stone in place is not a hazard; cutting it releases silica dust. Australia's ban on new installations matters for a refurbishment, not for an existing benchtop left alone. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets rules for gas cooking appliances and their clearances, for kitchen extraction and circuits, and in places for the materials used. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Gas, ventilation, electrical work and materials | AS/NZS 5601.1 sets gas appliance installation and clearances, and gas work must be done by licensed fitters with compliance certificates; the National Construction Code requires kitchen exhaust to discharge to the outside in newer homes; work health and safety law has banned new engineered stone installations since 1 July 2024; strata by-laws often control kitchen renovations. | Approved Document F sets extract ventilation rates for kitchens; the Gas Safety (Installation and Use) Regulations 1998 require Gas Safe registered engineers and annual gas safety checks in rented homes; electrical work must comply with BS 7671 and Part P. | The International Residential Code covers range hoods, kitchen circuits and GFCI protection; the International Fuel Gas Code covers gas cooking appliances and clearances; some cities restrict gas in new buildings. |

sections.heading: Worked example: a tired kitchen in a rented apartment
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 1990s apartment kitchen looks tired but works. Emptying the sink cabinet shows a swollen, mouldy base; the braided hoses have rust at their crimped ends and no date; the gas cooktop sits close to a timber splashback with scorch marks; and the rangehood recirculates. The tenant runs the microwave and kettle from a power board.

The finishes put this kitchen at the end of its cycle, but the findings that matter are hidden. Aged hoses and a cooktop too close to combustible material are safety findings; the swollen base points to a slow leak; recirculation leaves moisture and combustion products indoors; and the power board points to too few circuits.

So the register carries the hoses and the cooktop clearance as safety lines now, the leak repair and new base as a condition line, ducted extraction and an extra circuit, and refurbishment on its cycle, with moisture-resistant carcasses.

thresholds.rule: No more than 45 °C in aged care, healthcare, early childhood centres and schools; 50 °C in most other buildings

source.title: NCC 2025 Volume Three (Plumbing Code), Part B2 Heated water services

thresholds.rule: At least 30 L/s through a cooker hood ducted outside, 60 L/s from a fan elsewhere, or 13 L/s on a continuous system’s high rate

source.title: Approved Document F, Volume 1: Dwellings (2021 edition)

pages.title: Landscaping & Irrigation
pages.question: How does landscaping affect the building, and which landscape findings are safety issues?
pages.answer: Landscaping matters most where it meets the building. Trees drop limbs and fall, and their roots cause subsidence on clay, block drains and lift paving; podium and roof planters leak through membranes into car parks and apartments; irrigation sprays onto walls and lacks backflow protection; garden beds bridge damp-proof courses and termite barriers. Defective trees over occupied areas are a safety finding.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about landscaping & irrigation; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Hard and soft landscaping, retaining walls, irrigation systems

sources.title: ANSI A300 Tree Care Standards
AS 3959:2018 Construction of buildings in bushfire-prone areas
AS 4373-2007 Pruning of amenity trees
AS 4970:2025 Protection of trees on development sites
BS 5837:2012 Trees in relation to design, demolition and construction

pages.searchTitle: Landscaping and irrigation: trees, roots, podium planters and damage to buildings

questions.question: Can a tree damage a building's foundations?
questions.answer: On clay soils, roots draw moisture from the ground and can cause subsidence; they also block drains and lift paving. Damage that follows the line of the roots and worsens in dry seasons points to the tree.

questions.question: Should a tree near a building be removed?
questions.answer: Not without assessing heave first: on clay, removing a tree near a building can cause the ground to swell. Pruning, root barriers or replacement may be better.

questions.question: Why does a podium planter leak?
questions.answer: Through a failed membrane or blocked drainage. A flood test and a drainage inspection tell which.

questions.question: Can garden beds cause damp?
questions.answer: Yes, where beds and mulch are heaped against walls and bridge the damp-proof course, or irrigation sprays onto them. They also give termites hidden access over barriers.

questions.question: How long does podium planter waterproofing last?
questions.answer: Typically 20 to 30 years.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Landscaping matters most where it meets the building, and that is where its problems show: limbs over paths, roots near walls and drains, water through planters. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On site | Trees with dead limbs, cracks, cavities, fungal fruiting bodies, lean or root lifting | Trees and roots |
| On site | Large trees close to buildings on clay soils | Trees and roots |
| On site | Leaks and staining under podium planters; plants growing from drainage outlets | Planters, irrigation and the building's edge |
| On site | Irrigation spraying onto walls, windows and paving; wet patches and leaks | Planters, irrigation and the building's edge |
| On site | Garden beds above damp-proof courses and vents; mulch against walls | Planters, irrigation and the building's edge |
| On site | Green walls with dead plants, leaks and staining below | Planters, irrigation and the building's edge |
| In the records | Arborist reports and tree management records | Trees and roots |
| In the records | Landscape maintenance contracts | Planters, irrigation and the building's edge |
| In the records | Irrigation drawings and backflow tests | Planters, irrigation and the building's edge |
| In the records | Leak history under planters | Planters, irrigation and the building's edge |
| On site | Soil levels raised around tree trunks, or trenches cut close to trees, signs of root damage | Trees and roots |

sections.heading: What landscaping covers
sections.markdown:
Landscaping covers the planted and hard-landscaped external areas of a site: trees, garden beds, lawns, planters, podium and roof gardens, green walls, landscape walls and features, and the irrigation systems that water them. Landscaping interacts with the building more than its cost suggests: trees damage foundations, drains and pavements; planters on podiums and roofs load the structure and test waterproofing; irrigation leaks soak walls and membranes; and in bushfire areas vegetation sets fire risk.

| Element | Where it is found | Main issues |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Trees | All sites | Limb and tree failure; roots affecting foundations, drains and paving |
| Planters on podiums and roofs | Apartments, offices, retail | Membrane leaks; root penetration; load |
| Green walls | Commercial buildings from the 2000s | Irrigation leaks; plant loss; fixings |
| Irrigation systems | Most landscaped sites | Leaks; overspray onto buildings; backflow; controllers |
| Garden beds against buildings | All buildings | Bridging damp-proof courses and termite barriers |
| Landscape walls and edging | All sites | Movement; drainage |

Landscape works also carry statutory and planning obligations: tree preservation controls, landscape conditions on development approvals, and bushfire vegetation management, all of which constrain what an owner can change.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Landscaping lasts as long as it is maintained. Trees can outlive the building, while irrigation controllers last around a decade and podium planter waterproofing twenty to thirty years, with the structure below at risk when it fails.

| Element | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Trees | Decades to centuries | Species; site; maintenance |
| Shrubs and planting | 5 to 20 years | Species; care; water |
| Irrigation controllers | 8 to 12 years | Technology; weather |
| Irrigation pipework and emitters | 10 to 20 years | UV; damage; water quality |
| Green wall systems | 10 to 20 years; plants sooner | Irrigation; plant selection; maintenance |
| Podium planter waterproofing | 20 to 30 years | Root barriers; drainage |

What shortens it: poor plant selection for the site: large trees near buildings, vigorous roots near drains; lack of maintenance: unpruned trees, untended irrigation; drainage failures in planters; construction damage to tree roots.

Trees outlast most building elements but change constantly: a sapling planted near a wall becomes a large tree within the life of the building, and its effect grows with it.

sections.heading: Trees and roots
sections.markdown:
Trees with decay, cracks, weak forks, root damage or dieback drop limbs or fall in storms. Trees damaged by construction often decline years later. Failures over car parks, footpaths and play areas cause injuries and damage.

Roots draw moisture from clay soils, causing foundation subsidence; they enter and block drains through joints; they lift pavements and walls. Removing trees on clay can cause heave.

Trenching, excavation, compaction and level changes within a tree's root zone kill roots and destabilise trees, often with decline appearing years later when the link is forgotten.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cracks in a building near a large tree on clay | Subsidence from root moisture uptake. See foundations page. | Assess the foundations before acting on the tree; on clay, removing it can cause heave. |
| Repeated drain blockages near trees | Root intrusion. CCTV. | Survey by CCTV, clear and repair the drain, and fit a root barrier. |
| Dead branches in a tree crown | Decline, decay or root damage. Arborist assessment. | Get an arborist's assessment and act on it; exclude people below if the tree is over an occupied area. |
| Tree works planned near a building or new construction | Root damage or removal affecting the tree or the building. Tree protection zone set by an arborist. | Fence the protection zone before works start. |

sections.heading: Planters, irrigation and the building's edge
sections.markdown:
Planters over occupied space depend on waterproofing, root barriers and drainage. Roots penetrate unprotected membranes, drains block with soil and roots, and leaks appear in car parks and apartments below. Saturated planters can also exceed the structure's design load.

Irrigation leaks and overspray wet walls, footings and windows, causing damp, efflorescence and decay; systems run in rain; connections to drinking water lack backflow protection.

Garden beds and mulch heaped against walls cover vents, bridge damp-proof courses and give termites hidden access over barriers.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Leaks in a car park under a planter | Membrane failure or blocked drainage. Flood test; drainage inspection. | Flood test the planter and clear its drainage; replace the membrane, with a root barrier, if it has failed. |
| Damp walls behind garden beds | Bridged damp-proof course or irrigation. Inspection. | Lower the beds, pull mulch back from walls, vents and barriers, and redirect any irrigation. |

sections.heading: Vegetation and bushfire
sections.markdown:
In bushfire-prone areas, the planting around a building is part of its fire risk, and what is required of the building and its surroundings follows from the level of exposure it is assessed at.

In bushfire-prone areas, vegetation and mulch close to buildings carry fire to the walls, decks and roof gutters.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dense vegetation or mulch against the building in a bushfire-prone area | Fuel at the building edge. Bushfire attack level assessment; vegetation and separation. | Manage vegetation to the assessed level, and keep a clear zone around the building. |
| Gutters full of leaves and timber decks against the building | Ember ignition points. Inspection of gutters, decks and openings. | Clear gutters, fit guards and ember screens, and replace combustible items near the building. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Defective trees over occupied areas; vegetation creating bushfire risk | safety · 4 Essential | Prune, remove or exclude now. |
| Planter leaks damaging structure or units | failure · 2 Planned | Repair now. |
| Irrigation backflow testing due | deadline · 3 Important | At the prescribed interval. |
| Roots affecting drains and paving; bridged damp-proof courses; irrigation overspray | condition · 2 Planned | Address in the near term. |
| Planting, irrigation and green walls at end of life | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Renew. |
| No tree risk assessment | check · 2 Planned | Assess. |
| Normal | nil · 1 Routine | Routine maintenance. |

Tree findings are graded by consequence as well as defect: the same decay in a tree over a car park, a footpath or a play area is a higher grade than in a tree in an unused corner of the site.

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A qualified arborist for trees; a landscape architect or contractor for landscaping; a waterproofing specialist for planters. The checks below start where landscaping meets the building: trees near it or over occupied areas, planters over occupied space, and beds against its walls.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Tree risk assessment | Using a recognised method, prioritising trees near people and buildings. |
| Root and foundation review | Where trees are near buildings on clay. |
| Planter investigation | Drainage, root barriers, membrane condition, saturated weight against design loads. |
| Irrigation audit | Leaks, overspray, controllers, backflow devices. |
| Building interface check | Beds, mulch and paving against walls, vents and barriers. |
| Bushfire assessment | Where relevant. |

The report should give tree risks, building interactions, planter and irrigation issues, and a maintenance and renewal plan.

Tree risk is judged by the likelihood of failure and the consequence: a defective tree over an empty field is less urgent than a sound-looking tree with a structural defect over a children's play area or a busy entrance.

sections.heading: Managing trees, planters and irrigation
sections.markdown:
The costly failures are where landscaping meets the building, so the work starts there: trees near it or over occupied areas, planters over occupied space, and beds and irrigation against the walls. Removing a tree is not always the answer; near a building on clay, it can cause heave.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tree work | Pruning, removal, cabling or replacement with suitable species, with heave assessed before removing trees near buildings. | Where an arborist finds defects, or a tree is damaging the building; assess heave first. |
| Root barriers | Barriers between trees and buildings or drains. | Where roots threaten foundations, drains or paving and the tree is to stay. |
| Planter rectification | New membranes with root barriers, drainage cells and clear outlets. | Where planters leak into the structure below. |
| Irrigation repair | Redirect sprays, fix leaks, rain sensors, smart controllers, backflow devices. | Where irrigation sprays walls and windows, leaks, or runs in rain. |
| Clearances | Lower beds and remove mulch from walls, vents and barriers. | Where beds or mulch bridge damp-proof courses, cover vents or cross termite barriers. |
| Vegetation management | Keep vegetation and mulch back from walls, decks and roof gutters. | In bushfire-prone areas. |
| Green wall renewal | Renew the planting and the system. | Where plants have died or the system leaks. |
| Tree protection | Fencing and root protection zones around trees. | During any works near trees. |
| Water-efficient landscaping | Drought-tolerant planting and drip irrigation, reducing water use and leaks. | When planting or irrigation is renewed. |
| Maintenance programme | A programme setting pruning, irrigation checks, planter drainage clearing and mulch control. | Always, so drainage, irrigation and mulch are kept in check. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Landscape maintenance is a recurring contract. Arborist assessments recur. Tree work is per tree. Planter rectification is a lump sum with soil removal and reinstatement. Irrigation upgrades are lump sums.

Safety tree work is immediate; planter rectification is lifecycle or failure; maintenance is repairs and maintenance.

Tree removal near buildings on clay can require phased work and monitoring to manage heave. Podium planter rectification usually means removing soil and plants by hand or crane, which often costs more than the waterproofing itself.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a walk around the grounds cannot: which trees have known defects or protection, how the planters were waterproofed, and what the approval requires to be kept. Ask for them before any tree work, because protected trees cannot simply be removed.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Arborist reports and tree management records | Which trees have known defects, and what has been done about them. |
| Tree preservation orders or controls | Which trees cannot be pruned or removed without consent. |
| Landscape maintenance contracts | What is maintained, how often, and by whom. |
| Irrigation drawings and backflow test certificates | Where the irrigation runs, and whether backflow testing is current. |
| Planter waterproofing records and leak history | How the planters were waterproofed, and where they have leaked. |
| Bushfire assessments | Whether the site is in a bushfire-prone area, and what that requires. |
| Planning approval landscape conditions | Which planting must be kept or replaced under the approval. |
| Records of works near trees | Whether roots may have been damaged by trenching or level changes. |
| Strata by-laws on planting | What owners may plant on balconies and in courtyards over shared structures. |
| Bushfire attack level assessments where relevant | The level of exposure the building and its surroundings are assessed at. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Landscaping is easily read as gardening, when its worst failures are structural: limbs over people, roots under foundations, and water through planters into the building.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| Cracks near a tree mean the tree must go | Root problems are distinguished from other causes by position and timing: damage that follows the line of a tree's roots, worsens in dry seasons and is worst nearest the tree points to the tree; damage unrelated to tree positions points elsewhere. Even then, removing a tree on clay can cause heave. |
| A healthy-looking tree is a safe tree | Decay, cracks, weak forks and root damage can be read by an arborist before a limb drops. A tree with significant defects over an occupied area, car park, road or footpath is a safety risk. |
| Irrigation only affects the garden | Leaks and overspray wet walls, footings and windows, causing damp, efflorescence and decay, and beds heaped against walls bridge damp-proof courses. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market has standards for tree work, controls on removing trees, and rules for vegetation in fire-prone areas. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Tree work and construction | AS 4970 covers protection of trees on development sites, and AS 4373 pruning. | BS 5837 covers trees in relation to construction. | ANSI A300 sets tree care standards. |
| Controls on trees | Tree preservation controls apply in many council areas. | Tree preservation orders and conservation areas restrict work on trees; occupiers owe a duty of care for tree safety. | Local tree ordinances apply. |
| Bushfire and wildfire | AS 3959 sets construction in bushfire-prone areas. | The Building Regulations carry no wildfire-specific requirements; fire and rescue services publish local wildfire guidance. | Wildland-urban interface codes set vegetation clearances in fire-prone areas. |

In all three jurisdictions, landscape conditions attached to planning approvals can require planting to be kept or replaced, and trees on boundaries create shared liability with neighbours. Strata and condominium landscaping is common property, with by-laws on what owners may plant on balconies and in private courtyards over shared structures.

sections.heading: Worked example: a leak beneath a podium garden
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 2000s apartment building has a landscaped podium over its car park. Water drips into the car park below one planter after rain, plants grow from the planter's drainage outlet, and a large tree on the boundary stands over the residents' entry path with dead branches in its crown.

The tree comes first: a tree with significant defects over a path people use is a safety risk, so it needs an arborist's assessment and pruning, or exclusion beneath it, at once. The planter leak is a failure finding if it is damaging the structure: plants in the outlet point to blocked drainage, and a flood test shows whether the membrane has also failed.

So the register carries the tree as a safety line now, the planter as a failure line, with the drainage cleared first and a new membrane with a root barrier if the test fails, and a maintenance programme so the outlets are cleared before they block again.

pages.title: Lift Cars & Machine Rooms
pages.question: How do lift cars, machine rooms and pits fail as spaces, and what does the building control?
pages.answer: Lift spaces fail through heat, water, wear and missing accessibility features. Hot machine rooms make controllers fail, so breakdowns cluster in hot weather; water in pits corrodes buffers and safety gear; car interiors are battered by goods and moves; older cars lack braille, tactile and audio features. Machine rooms become storerooms. The building usually controls these space issues even when the lift contractor maintains the machinery.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about lift cars & machine rooms; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Interior finishes, lighting, ventilation, architectural integration

sources.title: ASME A17.1 Safety Code for Elevators and Escalators
AS 1735.1.1:2022 Lifts, escalators and moving walks, Part 1.1: General requirements
2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design
