pages.searchTitle: Lift cars and machine rooms: worn interiors, accessibility, heat, water in pits

questions.question: Why do our lifts break down in hot weather?
questions.answer: Often the machine room overheats. Log its temperature, and add cooling or ventilation before replacing components.

questions.question: Why is there water in the lift pit?
questions.answer: After storms, groundwater or a failed sump; after cleaning, washdown entering the shaft. Drain and waterproof the pit, with an alarmed sump pump.

questions.question: Who is responsible for a lift machine room?
questions.answer: Usually the building for the room's heat, water, access and housekeeping; the lift contractor for the machinery.

questions.question: What accessible features should lift cars have?
questions.answer: Braille and tactile buttons, audible and visual indicators, handrails, and enough room for a wheelchair; they are usually corrected at modernisation.

questions.question: How long do lift car interiors last?
questions.answer: Finishes 10 to 20 years and flooring 5 to 15; landing frames last 15 to 25.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Lift space problems show in the cars as damage, heat and missing accessible features, at landings, in hot or cluttered machine rooms and wet pits, and in breakdown and temperature records. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On site | Car interiors dented, scratched or with protective blankets permanently fitted | Car interiors, accessibility and landings |
| On site | Buttons without braille or tactile marking; no audible announcements | Car interiors, accessibility and landings |
| On site | Hot, dark or stuffy cars | Car interiors, accessibility and landings |
| On site | Machine rooms hot, unlocked, or used for storage | Machine rooms: heat, access and storage |
| On site | Water or oil in pits | Water in pits and shafts |
| On site | Damaged landing frames and sills | Car interiors, accessibility and landings |
| In the records | Lift breakdown records, especially in hot weather | Machine rooms: heat, access and storage |
| In the records | Machine room temperature records | Machine rooms: heat, access and storage |
| In the records | Pit inspection notes from the lift contractor | Water in pits and shafts |
| In the records | Modernisation history | Car interiors, accessibility and landings |
| In the records | Control cabinets at landings in machine-room-less installations, with their locks and ventilation | Machine rooms: heat, access and storage |
| In the records | Roof leaks or staining in rooftop machine rooms | Machine rooms: heat, access and storage |
| In the records | Trapped passenger incidents and how long they lasted | Car interiors, accessibility and landings |

sections.heading: What the space does and what it contains
sections.markdown:
Lift cars and machine rooms are the spaces of the lift installation: the car interior that passengers ride in, the landing entrances on each floor, the machine room or control space, and the shaft and pit. The machinery itself is on the lifts page; this page covers the spaces. Functionally the car must be safe, accessible, lit, ventilated and presentable; the machine room must keep equipment cool, dry, secure and reachable; and the pit and shaft must stay dry and clear.

| Space | Typical provision | What matters |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Car interior | Wall panels, floor, ceiling, lighting, handrails, mirror, ventilation fan | Finish condition, accessibility, lighting, air |
| Car fixtures | Buttons, indicators, audio, emergency phone, CCTV | Accessibility, function, communication |
| Landing entrances | Door frames, sills, indicators and buttons on each floor | Damage, sill trip edges, fire rating |
| Machine room | Controller, drive, machine; ventilation, lighting, access | Temperature, security, housekeeping |
| Pit | Buffers, ladder, lighting, drainage or sump | Water, debris, access |
| Shaft | Fire-rated enclosure, venting where required | Fire separation, water ingress |

In buildings with several lifts, the condition of cars and landings is a daily signal of building quality to every occupant and visitor, and dated cars can undermine an otherwise refurbished lobby.

sections.heading: How long it stays fit for purpose
sections.markdown:
Car interior finishes last ten to twenty years and car flooring five to fifteen, while landing frames last fifteen to twenty-five and machine room cooling fifteen to twenty. Interiors date before they wear out, and are best renewed with the controls at modernisation.

| Component or quality | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Car interior finishes | 10 to 20 years | Use; goods carried in passenger lifts |
| Car flooring | 5 to 15 years | Traffic; trolleys |
| Landing door frames and finishes | 15 to 25 years | Impact; cleaning |
| Car ventilation fans and lighting | 10 to 15 years | Run hours |
| Machine room ventilation and cooling | 15 to 20 years | Heat load; maintenance |

What shortens fitness for purpose: goods and furniture carried in passenger lifts without protective blankets; hot machine rooms shortening controller life; water in pits and shafts; machine rooms used for storage.

Car interiors are usually refurbished with controls modernisation, so their timing is tied to the lift cycle.

sections.heading: Car interiors, accessibility and landings
sections.markdown:
Car walls are dented and scratched by trolleys, furniture and building materials; floors wear at the entrance; handrails loosen; mirrors crack. The car interior is the lift's face to users and dates the building quickly.

Older cars lack braille and tactile buttons, audible announcements, handrails, adequate size for wheelchairs, and visual indicators; these are usually corrected at modernisation.

Failed car fans and lights make cars hot and dark, and trapped passengers distressed.

Worn landing sills and poor levelling leave trip edges at entrances; see the lifts page for causes.

In machine-room-less lifts, the control equipment sits in a cabinet at a landing or in the shaft, so access and heat problems move into corridors and shafts.

Machine rooms on roofs also suffer roof leaks that drip onto controllers.

Lift lobbies and landing areas also suffer damage when goods are wheeled to the lift, so landing frames and nearby walls wear at the same rate as the car.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Car walls repeatedly damaged | Goods and moves in passenger lifts. Protection practices. | Use protective pads for moves, or direct goods to a goods lift; refurbish with impact-resistant finishes. |
| Complaints from vision-impaired users | Missing tactile and audio features. Accessibility audit. | Fit braille and tactile buttons, and audible and visual indicators. |
| A hot, dark car | A failed car fan or lights. Fan and lights checked with the contractor (Thresholds by market). | Repair or replace the car fan and lighting. |
| A trip edge at a landing entrance | Worn sills or poor levelling. The step measured at each landing against the limits for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Repair the sills, and have the contractor adjust the levelling; see [Passenger & Goods Lifts](https://moyneross.com/technical/passenger-and-goods-lifts). |
| Car too small for a wheelchair user to enter and use | Car below current access sizes. Car dimensions against the limits for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Record the gap for the next modernisation. |

sections.heading: Machine rooms: heat, access and storage
sections.markdown:
The machine room is the lift's plant room, and the building, not the lift contractor, usually controls it. Heat, water, storage and access there cause breakdowns that look like lift faults but are fixed by building work.

Machine rooms without adequate ventilation or cooling overheat; electronic controllers and drives fail or trip, causing breakdowns concentrated in hot weather.

Machine rooms used as storerooms, left unlocked, or reached only by unsafe ladders and roofs expose workers and equipment to risk.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Breakdowns cluster on hot days | Machine room overheating. Temperature logging. | Log machine room temperatures; add cooling or ventilation, with temperature alarms, before replacing components. |
| A machine room used for storage, or left unlocked | Poor housekeeping and access control. Stored items beside the equipment, and no lock. | Clear it, lock it, and light the access route. |
| Drips onto controllers in a rooftop machine room | Roof leaks. Staining above the controllers, and leaks after rain. | Repair the roof, and waterproof the machine room. |

sections.heading: Water in pits and shafts
sections.markdown:
Groundwater, failed sumps, cleaning water and leaks reach pits, corroding buffers, rails and safety gear and causing electrical faults; flooding can take lifts out of service for long periods.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Corrosion of pit equipment | Water in the pit. Pit inspection; sump. | Drain and waterproof the pit, with a sump pump and alarm where groundwater is present. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Water in pits affecting safety equipment; machine rooms with unsafe access or storage | safety · 4 Essential | Rectify now. |
| Lifts out of service from heat or flooding | failure · 4 Essential | Restore now. |
| Statutory lift inspections | deadline · 4 Essential | At the prescribed interval. |
| Worn interiors; hot cars; accessibility gaps | condition · 4 Essential | Improve in the near term. |
| Interiors at end of life | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Refurbish, ideally with modernisation. |
| Machine room conditions unknown | check · 3 Important | Assess. |
| Normal | nil · 1 Routine | Routine. |

Most findings in these spaces are building responsibilities that reduce breakdowns and entrapments when fixed, and they are often cheaper than the breakdowns they cause.

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A lift consultant leads with the building surveyor, coordinating with the lift contractor for access to machine rooms, shafts and pits. The checks below inspect every car and landing, the machine room and the pit, keeping the building's items apart from the lift contractor's.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Car inspection | Of every car: walls, floor, ceiling, lighting, ventilation fan, handrails, mirrors, fixtures, braille and tactile buttons, audible announcements and visual indicators. |
| Machine room inspection | Temperature against equipment limits, ventilation and cooling, lighting, access route and ladders, security, housekeeping, lifting beams and fire separation. |
| Pit inspection | With the contractor: water, sump and pump, debris, lighting, ladder. |
| Landing survey | On each floor: door frames, sills, indicators, buttons and fire rating labels. |
| Records review | Breakdowns by season and cause, inspection reports, modernisation history, and statutory examinations against the intervals for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). |

The report should separate building items (heat, water, finishes, access and housekeeping) from lift contractor items, and align refurbishment with modernisation.

Where the lift contractor has already reported building-side defects, start from their reports, which often list heat, water and access problems repeatedly over years.

sections.heading: Refurbishing, cooling, draining and securing
sections.markdown:
Water in pits reaching safety equipment, and machine rooms with unsafe access, come first. After that, the building fixes what it controls, heat, water, storage and finishes, and car refurbishment is timed with controls modernisation.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Car refurbishment | Car refurbishment with durable, impact-resistant finishes, ideally timed with controls modernisation so accessibility features are upgraded at the same time. | When interiors are worn or dated. |
| Protection for moves and deliveries | Protective pads and procedures for moves and deliveries in passenger lifts, or directing goods to a goods lift. | Wherever passenger lifts carry goods. |
| Machine room cooling | Machine room cooling and ventilation sized to the equipment heat, with temperature alarms. | Where breakdowns cluster in hot weather. |
| Pit drainage and waterproofing | Pit drainage and waterproofing, with sump pumps and alarms where groundwater is present. | Wherever water reaches the pit. |
| Accessible fixtures | Braille and tactile buttons, audible and visual indicators, handrails. | Where cars lack tactile, audible or visual features. |
| Machine room access and housekeeping | Safe access routes, locks, lighting and removal of storage. | Wherever machine rooms are unlocked, cluttered or hard to reach. |
| Landing repairs | Landing repairs to frames and sills. | Where frames are damaged or sills worn. |
| Roof and shaft waterproofing | Roof and shaft waterproofing for rooftop machine rooms and shafts. | Where water reaches controllers or the shaft. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Car interiors are priced per car and are best done with modernisation to avoid two disruptions. Machine room cooling is a lump sum per room; pit works per pit; landing repairs per floor. Interior refurbishment is lifecycle; accessibility and access safety items are code compliance; heat and water works are condition items that cut breakdowns.

Heat and water fixes in machine rooms and pits are usually cheap relative to the breakdowns and damaged equipment they prevent, and should not wait for modernisation. In strata buildings, these spaces are common property and their costs fall to the owners corporation.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what one inspection cannot: whether breakdowns follow the weather, whether water reaches the pit, and what the lift contractor has reported about the building's side. Ask for them before replacing lift components.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Breakdown records by season and cause | Whether breakdowns follow heat, water or particular causes. |
| Machine room temperature records | Whether the machine rooms overheat. |
| Pit inspection notes and sump records | Whether water reaches the pits. |
| Accessibility audit of lifts | Whether the cars meet accessibility requirements. |
| Modernisation history and plans | What has been modernised, and what is planned. |
| Car interior refurbishment history | When the car interiors were last refurbished. |
| Entrapment records with durations and causes | How often and for how long passengers are trapped. |
| Lift contractor reports noting building-side defects such as heat, water and access | What the contractor has asked the building to fix. |
| Records of roof or shaft leaks affecting lift equipment | Whether roof or shaft leaks have reached lift equipment. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Lift spaces are misread when the building's problems are handed to the lift contractor, when water in the pit is treated as a single cause, and when summer breakdowns are fixed by replacing parts.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| It is the lift contractor's problem | Separate space issues (heat, water, finishes, accessibility features) from machinery issues; the lift contractor handles the second but the building usually controls the first. |
| Water in the pit is water in the pit | Water in a pit after every storm points to groundwater or a failed sump; water after cleaning points to washdown entering the shaft. |
| Replace the failing controller | If breakdown records show controllers and drives failing mainly in summer, check machine room temperatures before replacing components; cooling is often the cheaper and lasting fix. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets accessibility requirements for lift cars, and rules for machine rooms, pits and the safety of people who work in them. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Lift cars, machine rooms and access | The AS 1735 series governs lifts and the Disability (Access to Premises — Buildings) Standards set accessibility for new and upgraded lifts, including car size, controls and indicators; work health and safety laws govern safe access to machine rooms and pits. | BS EN 81-20 covers lift construction including machine spaces, and BS EN 81-70 accessibility; LOLER requires thorough examination; the Workplace Regulations and Work at Height Regulations govern access. | ASME A17.1 sets machine room and pit requirements, including temperature limits, lighting and access; the 2010 ADA Standards govern car accessibility; state elevator authorities inspect. |

In all three countries, machine rooms and pits are restricted spaces that only authorised lift workers may enter.

Accessibility upgrades usually follow modernisation.

sections.heading: Worked example: lifts that fail every summer
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 1990s office's two lifts break down several times each summer, and the contractor has replaced a drive twice. The rooftop machine room has one small fan, a water stain above a controller, and boxes stored against the wall. The cars are dented from moves, with no tactile buttons or audible announcements.

Breakdowns in summer, after component replacements, point to an overheating machine room rather than faulty parts, and the stain points to a roof leak onto the controllers. The cars' damage and missing accessible features are building items, best fixed together at modernisation.

So the register carries machine room cooling with temperature alarms and the roof leak as failure lines, the storage cleared and the room locked, protective pads for moves, and car refurbishment with accessible fixtures timed with modernisation.

thresholds.rule: At least 1100 mm wide and 1400 mm deep

thresholds.rule: At least every 6 months for equipment that lifts people

pages.title: Lighting Control System
pages.question: How do lighting control systems fail, and how do you tell if they are working?
pages.answer: Lighting controls fail by being defeated rather than broken. Sensors are covered, time clocks bypassed, daylight dimming disabled, and car parks lit at full output all night. Fit-outs leave sensors in the wrong places. Proprietary networked systems lose vendor support and programming tools. The test is simple: walk the building at night and read the interval meter. A good system that has been overridden saves nothing.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about lighting control system; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: BMS integration, time clocks, motion/daylight sensors, networked systems

pages.searchTitle: Lighting controls: lights on all night, overridden sensors, daylight dimming, DALI

questions.question: Why are the lights on all night?
questions.answer: Usually lost schedules or overrides. A walk at night and the interval meter show it, and recommissioning fixes it.

questions.question: Why do the lights switch off while we are in the room?
questions.answer: Time delays that are too short, or sensors badly placed for the layout. Lengthen the delays and move the sensors.

questions.question: Should car park lights switch off when empty?
questions.answer: Better to dim them to a background level when unoccupied, so drivers are never in the dark and minimum levels for safe movement are kept.

questions.question: What if no one can change the lighting programming?
questions.answer: Recover the tools and passwords, and at replacement specify an open-protocol system such as DALI-2 with programming held by the owner.

questions.question: How long do lighting control sensors last?
questions.answer: Occupancy and daylight sensors 10 to 15 years, as do DALI controllers and gateways; time clocks and contactors 15 to 20.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Lighting control problems show at night as lights left on, by day as perimeter lights at full output, in sensors covered or bypassed, and in interval meter data and complaints. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On site | Lights on in empty areas after hours; car parks at full output all night | Commissioning, overrides and sensors |
| On site | Sensors covered, disconnected or missing; switches added to bypass controls | Commissioning, overrides and sensors |
| On site | Perimeter lights at full output on bright days | Commissioning, overrides and sensors |
| On site | Controllers and gateways in plant rooms with fault lights | Obsolescence, integration and security |
| On site | Complaints of lights switching off in meeting rooms or toilets | Commissioning, overrides and sensors |
| In the records | Programming backups, group schedules and documentation | Obsolescence, integration and security |
| In the records | Vendor, software and firmware versions; support status | Obsolescence, integration and security |
| In the records | Interval meter data showing night-time lighting load | Commissioning, overrides and sensors |
| In the records | Complaint records about lighting | Commissioning, overrides and sensors |
| In the records | Wireless sensors with flat or low battery warnings | Commissioning, overrides and sensors |
| In the records | Emergency lighting test logs that stop at a date | Egress and emergency lighting |
| In the records | Time clocks showing the wrong time | Commissioning, overrides and sensors |

sections.heading: Types of lighting control
sections.markdown:
A lighting control system decides when lights are on and how bright: time clocks and astronomical timers, photocells, occupancy and absence sensors, daylight sensors that dim lights near windows, switches and scene controllers, and networked systems that address each luminaire individually, such as DALI and proprietary wired and wireless platforms, often linked to the building management system. In common areas and car parks, controls cut most of the lighting energy; in offices they are part of how a tenancy works.

| Type | Where it is found | Character |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Time clocks and contactors | Common areas, external lighting, older buildings | Simple; lose schedules after power failures or daylight saving changes |
| Photocells and astronomical timers | External and façade lighting | Photocells get dirty or shaded; timers need correct location |
| Occupancy and absence sensors | Corridors, stairs, toilets, car parks, offices | Placement and time delay decide success |
| Daylight dimming | Perimeter zones of offices and atria | Often never commissioned, or later disabled |
| DALI and DALI-2 | Offices and commercial from the 2000s | Open standard; needs programming, documentation and gateways |
| Proprietary networked and wireless systems | Offices, retail and campuses from the 2010s | Flexible; vendor lock-in; software support; cyber exposure |
| Integration with BMS, security and emergency lighting tests | Larger buildings | Interfaces break when either side changes |

Energy codes in all three jurisdictions require automatic controls in new and substantially altered buildings, and energy ratings reward them. A good system that has been overridden or never commissioned saves nothing.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Sensors, controllers and gateways last ten to fifteen years and time clocks and contactors fifteen to twenty, while proprietary networked systems often last only eight to fifteen before support ends. Commissioning, not hardware, usually decides whether a system saves anything.

| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Time clocks and contactors | 15 to 20 years | Contact wear; battery backup |
| Occupancy and daylight sensors | 10 to 15 years | Technology; damage; dirt |
| DALI controllers and gateways | 10 to 15 years | Vendor support |
| Proprietary networked systems | 8 to 15 years | Vendor support; software and app support |
| Wall controllers and scene plates | 15 to 20 years | Use |

What shortens life: vendor end of support for proprietary hardware, software and apps; lost programming, passwords and documentation; fit-outs that move partitions without moving sensors or regrouping fittings; overrides left in place after complaints.

Software and apps age faster than hardware: a system with sound sensors can become unmanageable when the commissioning software stops running on supported computers.

sections.heading: Commissioning, overrides and sensors
sections.markdown:
Daylight dimming set too conservatively or switched off; time delays too short (lights going off on people) or too long (saving little); groups that no longer match the floor layout after fit-outs; time clocks that lost their schedule after a power failure or never adjusted for daylight saving.

Occupants and facilities staff defeat controls that annoy them: sensors taped over, time clocks bypassed with a switch, lighting held on through the BMS. Car parks then run at full output 24 hours a day, and common areas stay lit all night.

Sensors behind partitions, too far from desks, aimed at corridors or above glazed walls switch lights off on occupants or on for passers-by. Car park sensors that cannot see along aisles leave drivers in the dark.

Daylight sensors drift and collect dust, so they read less daylight than there is and keep lights brighter than needed. Battery-powered wireless sensors stop reporting when batteries run flat, and systems may default to lights on.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| High night-time electricity use | Lighting not switching off. Interval meter data; night visit. | Reset the schedules and remove the overrides. |
| Lights switching off on occupants | Short time delays or poor sensor placement. Settings; sensor locations against layout. | Lengthen the time delays, and move sensors to suit the layout. |
| Perimeter lights at full output in daylight | Daylight dimming disabled or never set up. Settings; light level measurement. | Set up and enable daylight dimming. |
| One switch or sensor controlling a whole open floor | Control zones too large. Area served by each control against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Divide the floor into smaller control zones at the next upgrade. |
| Perimeter lights switched with the core of a large office | Daylight zone not separately controlled. Perimeter circuits against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Separate the perimeter circuits and add daylight sensors. |
| Time switch holding lights on in rooms that are rarely used | Override where occupancy does not justify it. Occupancy against the conditions the asset’s market sets for time switches (Thresholds by market). | Return the room to occupancy control. |

sections.heading: Obsolescence, integration and security
sections.markdown:
Proprietary systems depend on the vendor's gateways, software and commissioning tools. When support ends, faults cannot be fixed and layouts cannot be changed without replacing the system.

Links to the BMS, security system and automatic emergency lighting tests break when either side is upgraded; automated tests stop silently.

Networked lighting systems on the building or corporate network, with default passwords or unpatched gateways, can be a route into other systems.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No-one can change programming | Proprietary lock-in or lost tools and passwords. Vendor; documentation. | Recover the tools and passwords; specify an open-protocol system at replacement. |

sections.heading: Egress and emergency lighting
sections.markdown:
Many DALI and networked systems run automatic emergency lighting tests and log results. When the integration breaks, tests stop running, but the building may still believe it is compliant.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Emergency lighting tests not running | Integration failure. Test logs. | Repair the integration, and run the tests. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stairs or egress paths left dark by sensor faults or settings | safety · 4 Essential | Fix now. |
| System failed, lights stuck on or off | failure · 3 Important | Repair now. |
| Overrides, drift and poor commissioning | condition · 3 Important | Recommission in the near term. |
| System unsupported or proprietary at end of life | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Plan replacement, preferably open protocol. |
| No documentation; energy data not reviewed | check · 2 Planned | Audit. |
| Minor adjustments | nil · 1 Routine | Routine. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
An electrical or lighting controls specialist. The checks below start with a walk through the building at night and the interval meter, then the programming, documentation and who holds the tools.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Night audit | Walk the building after hours and note what is on and why. |
| Interval meter analysis | Of lighting loads by time of day and day of week. |
| Controls inventory | Types, vendors, versions, gateways and support status. |
| Sensor and setting review | Against current layouts: placement, time delays, daylight levels, groups. |
| Safety check | Stairs and egress paths stay lit when occupied. |
| Integration testing | With the BMS, security and emergency lighting test systems. |
| Documentation and ownership review | Programming backups, tools, passwords, who holds them. |
| Car park check | Lighting levels in dimmed mode against the minimum for safe movement. |

The report should quantify energy wasted by poor control, list safety issues, give support status, and recommend recommissioning or replacement.

sections.heading: Recommissioning, relocating or replacing
sections.markdown:
Dark stairs and egress paths come first, wherever sensors or settings leave them unlit. After that, recommissioning is usually the cheapest energy saving available, and replacement goes to an open-protocol system the owner controls.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Recommissioning | Reset schedules, time delays and daylight levels; regroup to current layouts; remove overrides. Usually the cheapest energy saving in the building. | First, wherever lights run after hours or switch off on occupants. |
| Sensor relocation and replacement | Relocate and replace sensors to suit the layout. | After fit-outs, or where sensors switch lights off on occupants. |
| Car park controls | Dim to a background level when unoccupied rather than switching off, so drivers are never in the dark. | In car parks. |
| Replacement | An open-protocol system such as DALI-2, with programming, tools and passwords held by the owner. | Where the system is unsupported or locked to one vendor. |
| Integration repair | Repair the integration with the BMS and emergency lighting tests. | Where scheduled tests have stopped. |
| Network security | Segregate lighting networks and change default credentials. | Wherever lighting networks connect to the building network. |
| Documentation | Groups, schedules, settings and backups. | Always. |
| Training | Training for facilities staff. | So settings are changed properly rather than overridden. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Audits and recommissioning are lump sums and usually pay back quickly in energy. Sensor replacements are per unit. System replacement is per floor or per area, often combined with LED conversion so both are done once with ceilings open.

Recommissioning is repairs and maintenance; replacement is lifecycle or an energy upgrade; safety fixes on egress paths are immediate.

Combining control upgrades with LED conversion avoids paying twice for ceiling access.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what the hardware cannot: how the system is programmed, who can change it, and whether it actually switches lights off. Ask for the interval meter data first.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Programming backups, group and schedule documentation | How the system is programmed, and whether it could be restored. |
| Vendor, software and firmware details and support status | Whether the system is still supported. |
| Interval meter data for lighting | Whether lights actually switch off at night. |
| Complaint records | Where lighting bothers occupants. |
| Who holds programming tools and passwords | Whether the owner can change the programming. |
| Energy ratings and disclosure certificates | What the building's energy rating relies on. |
| Records of fit-outs that changed lighting groups | Whether groups still match the layout after fit-outs. |
| Commissioning reports for the original installation | How the system was set up originally. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Lighting controls are misread when the controllers are inspected rather than their effect, and when a control that dims egress lighting is assumed to keep people safe.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| Inspect the controllers | The fastest assessment of lighting controls is a walk through the building at night and a look at the interval meter. Both show whether the controls are doing anything. |
| Dimming is always safe | Controls that dim or switch egress lighting must still meet the minimum levels for safe movement in every state. Car parks are best dimmed to a background level when unoccupied rather than switched off, so drivers are never in the dark. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market requires automatic lighting controls in new and refurbished buildings, and rewards effective control through its energy rating schemes. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Controls and energy | NCC Section J requires automatic lighting controls in many spaces in new and altered buildings; NABERS Energy ratings reward effective control. | Approved Document L requires lighting controls in new and refurbished buildings; BS EN 15193 sets methods for lighting energy. | ASHRAE 90.1 and the IECC set mandatory controls (occupancy, daylight, scheduling); California Title 24 adds further requirements. |

Energy rating and disclosure schemes in all three countries make lighting energy a lettability and compliance issue: NABERS and Commercial Building Disclosure in Australia, Energy Performance Certificates and minimum standards in Britain, and building performance standards in several United States cities. Controls are usually the cheapest way to improve these ratings.

Where controls dim or switch egress lighting, the minimum levels for safe movement in each jurisdiction still apply in every control state, including car parks and stairs.

sections.heading: Worked example: a building that never goes dark
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 2000s office has a networked lighting control system. A walk at night finds most floors lit, the car park at full output, and sensors in two meeting rooms taped over after complaints. The interval meter shows almost no drop in load overnight, and only the installer holds the programming tools.

The walk and the meter answer the question: the controls are doing almost nothing. Lights on at night point to lost schedules or overrides; taped sensors point to time delays too short or sensors badly placed; and tools held only by the installer are an ownership finding.

So the register carries recommissioning as a condition line, resetting schedules, delays and daylight levels, car park dimming to a background level, and recovering the programming tools and passwords for the owner.

thresholds.rule: No more than 250 m² of lighting per demand-operated control, other than in a single functional space

thresholds.rule: Separate control of the natural lighting zone in Class 5, 6 or 8 buildings over 250 m²

source.title: NCC 2025 Volume One, Part J7 Artificial lighting and power

thresholds.rule: Only where a space is regularly occupied: more than 1 person per 40 m², or used more than once every 15 minutes

pages.title: Lighting
pages.question: How do lighting installations fail, and when does obsolescence or safety force replacement?
pages.answer: Lighting is being pushed to LED: fluorescent, metal halide and other mercury lamps are being withdrawn and replacements are scarce. LED fittings fail at their drivers, from heat and surges. The safety findings are elsewhere: steel lighting columns corrode at the ground line and fall in wind, suspended fittings hang from corroded fixings, stairs and car parks are lit below standard, and pre-1980 fittings may hold leaking PCB capacitors.

questions.question: Is a rusty lighting column dangerous?
questions.answer: It can be. A column with visible corrosion or damage at its base is a falling hazard; treat it as unsafe until tested.

questions.question: Should we retrofit LED tubes or replace the fittings?
questions.answer: New fittings rather than retrofit tubes, designed to the required levels and usually combined with controls.

questions.question: Why are our LED fittings failing in groups?
questions.answer: Usually driver failure from heat or surges. Replace the drivers, and add surge protection on external circuits.

questions.question: Are fluorescent lamps being phased out?
questions.answer: Yes. Australia is phasing out mercury lamps under the Minamata Convention, and several US states have banned fluorescent lamps.

questions.question: How long do LED lights last?
questions.answer: LED luminaires 15 to 20 years, or 50,000 hours or more to 70 per cent output; their drivers 10 to 15.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Lighting problems show as dim stairs, car parks and paths, failed and flickering fittings, corroded columns and fixings, and in the inventory, lux surveys and test records. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |

| On site | Corrosion at column bases, missing or loose access doors, cracked bases, leaning columns | Columns, fixings and PCBs |
| On site | Suspended fittings with corroded fixings; fittings hanging by cables | Columns, fixings and PCBs |
| On site | Old fluorescent fittings in plant rooms and car parks; oily residue at capacitors | Columns, fixings and PCBs |
| In the records | Lighting inventory and maintenance records; failure rates | Investigation before the scope |
| In the records | Lux surveys | Light levels, glare and spill |
| In the records | LED retrofit records and product data | Lamp obsolescence and LED quality |
| In the records | Column inspection and testing records | Columns, fixings and PCBs |
| In the records | Hazardous materials register | Columns, fixings and PCBs |
| In the records | Energy data for common area lighting | Lamp obsolescence and LED quality |

sections.heading: Types of lighting
sections.markdown:
Lighting here covers the luminaires the building owner is responsible for: lobbies, corridors, stairs, toilets, car parks, plant rooms, loading docks, external areas, façade and landscape lighting, and lighting columns on site. Tenant lighting is usually part of fit-outs but may revert to the owner at lease end. Emergency lighting and lighting controls have their own pages.

| Type | Where it is found | What it implies |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Linear fluorescent (T8, T5) with magnetic or electronic ballasts | Offices, car parks, corridors, plant rooms from the 1970s | Lamps being withdrawn under mercury rules; ballasts failing |
| Compact fluorescent | Downlights, common areas | Being withdrawn |
| Metal halide and high-pressure sodium | Car parks, external areas, warehouses, sports | Inefficient; slow to restrike; lamps and ballasts scarce |
| Halogen and incandescent | Downlights, displays, older common areas | Inefficient; hot; general lamps restricted in many markets |
| LED | Most new and retrofit installations since the 2010s | Long life; drivers fail first; early products varied in quality |
| Fluorescent fittings with PCB capacitors | Fittings made before about 1980 | Leaking capacitors are hazardous |
| Lighting columns (steel, aluminium, concrete) | Car parks, campuses, external areas | Base corrosion can fell a column |
| Suspended and high-bay fittings | Warehouses, atria, car parks | Fixing corrosion; falling fittings |

Required light levels vary by space: stairs, car parks and external paths have minimums for safe movement and security; offices and work areas have task levels. Many older car parks and stairs fall short because fittings have failed or been removed, lamps have depreciated, or layouts have changed.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
LED luminaires last fifteen to twenty years and their drivers ten to fifteen, against twenty to twenty-five for fluorescent fittings, which the phase-out of mercury lamps is retiring sooner. Steel columns corrode at the ground line, out of sight, long before anyone notices.

| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| LED luminaires | 50,000 hours or more to 70 per cent output; 15 to 20 years | Heat; driver quality |
| LED drivers | 10 to 15 years | Heat; surges |
| Fluorescent fittings | 20 to 25 years | Ballasts; lamp supply ending |
| External luminaires | 15 to 20 years | Ingress protection; coastal exposure |
| Steel lighting columns | 25 to 40 years | Base corrosion; impact |
| Aluminium columns | 30 to 50 years | Base corrosion in salt and soil |
| Concrete columns | 30 to 50 years | Reinforcement corrosion |

What shortens life: heat in enclosed fittings and hot ceiling spaces; water ingress where seals and glands fail; coastal and road-salt exposure on fittings and columns; surges from lightning and switching, especially on long external circuits; vehicle impact in car parks and on columns; poor-quality retrofits.

sections.heading: Lamp obsolescence and LED quality
sections.markdown:
Fluorescent, compact fluorescent, metal halide and other mercury-containing lamps are being withdrawn under the Minamata Convention and related rules: most fluorescent tubes left the European Union and British markets in 2023, several United States states have banned them, and Australia is phasing mercury lamps out. Inefficient general-service lamps are also restricted. Buildings still lit by these lamps face rising lamp costs and scarcity and are converting to LED.

LED chips age slowly; their drivers fail from heat and surges. Early-generation and low-cost LED products suffered colour shift, flicker, poor dimming and early failure. Retrofit LED tubes in fluorescent fittings can be unsafe if the fitting was rewired incorrectly or the tube is unsuited to the ballast.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| LED fittings failing in clusters on one circuit | Driver failure from heat or surges. Driver type, location and circuit history. | Replace the drivers, and add surge protection on external circuits. |
| Fluorescent lamps hard or costly to source | Mercury lamp withdrawal. Supplier advice. | Convert to LED with new fittings. |
| Flicker or colour shift in LED fittings | Driver or product quality. Product data; replacement history. | Replace the driver, or the product with a better-quality one. |

sections.heading: Light levels, glare and spill
sections.markdown:
Stairs, car parks, loading docks and external paths lit below the required level create trip, vehicle and security risks. Causes include failed fittings left unreplaced, lamp depreciation, dirty or yellowed diffusers, fittings removed in fit-outs, and new layouts.

External lighting that spills onto neighbours, the night sky or habitat can breach planning conditions and invite complaints; glare from poorly aimed floodlights reduces visibility rather than improving it.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dark stairs or car park zones | Failed or removed fittings, or depreciation. Lux survey against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Replace or reinstate fittings, and bring levels to standard. |
| Offices or workshops dim at desks and benches | Light levels below what the work needs. Lux survey at the task against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Replace or add fittings, or relamp to recover the design level. |

sections.heading: Columns, fixings and PCBs
sections.markdown:
Steel columns corrode from the inside and outside at and just below ground level, where water and salt collect, and at the access door opening, which weakens the section. They fall without warning in wind. Columns struck by vehicles are cracked or bent at the base. Concrete columns spall when reinforcement corrodes.

Suspended fittings in car parks and warehouses hang from fixings that corrode in damp, exhaust-laden air; fittings on façades and soffits corrode at their brackets. Falling fittings are a safety finding.

Fluorescent and high-intensity discharge fittings made before about 1980 often contain capacitors filled with PCBs. As they age they leak an oily residue, and they must be removed and disposed of as hazardous waste.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rust and section loss at a column base or door | Ground-line corrosion. Ultrasonic wall thickness test. | Treat it as unsafe; test it, then replace the column or sleeve the base. |
| Oily residue in old fittings | Leaking PCB capacitor. Sampling; date of manufacture. | Remove the PCB capacitor, and dispose of it as hazardous waste. |
| External lighting spilling into windows or neighbouring property | Light spill or glare. Complaint locations; aiming and shielding of fittings. | Re-aim or shield the fittings, or replace with better-controlled optics. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Columns corroded or damaged at the base; suspended fittings with failed fixings; leaking PCB capacitors | safety · 4 Essential | Remove, secure or isolate now. |
| Stairs, car parks or paths unlit | failure · 3 Important | Restore now. |
| Widespread failures; levels below standard | condition · 3 Important | Repair and relamp in the near term. |
| Fluorescent and HID lighting due for LED conversion | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Plan conversion, often with controls. |
| No column testing; PCB status unknown; no lux survey | check · 2 Planned | Inspect and survey. |
| Isolated failures | nil · 1 Routine | Routine maintenance. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
An electrical contractor or lighting engineer; a structural engineer or specialist for column testing. The checks below count fittings by type and area, then measure light levels on stairs, car parks and paths, and test columns where their bases show corrosion.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Inventory | Of luminaires by type, wattage, area and age, with failure counts. |
| Lux survey | On a grid in stairs, car parks, loading docks and external areas, against the relevant standard. |
| Column inspection | Visual check of base, door and foundation; ultrasonic wall thickness testing at the ground line; tests at intervals set by an inspection regime. |
| Fixing inspection | Of suspended and façade fittings. |
| Hazardous materials | Identify pre-1980 fittings and sample capacitors where needed. |
| Energy review | Installed load and hours, savings from LED and controls. |
| External lighting review | Against planning conditions and spill limits. |

The report should give the inventory, light levels against standards, column and fixing safety, hazardous materials, and an LED conversion plan with energy savings.

sections.heading: Converting, upgrading or making safe
sections.markdown:
Corroded columns and suspended fittings come first, as falling hazards, then dark stairs, car parks and paths. After that, most lighting work is conversion to LED with new fittings, designed to the required levels and usually combined with controls.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| LED conversion | New LED fittings rather than retrofit tubes, designed to the required levels, usually combined with controls. | Where fluorescent or HID lighting is due for replacement. |
| Car park and stair upgrades | Bring light levels to standard. | Where stairs, car parks or paths are dim. |
| Column replacement | Replace the column, or sleeve and repair the base where testing shows limited loss, with impact protection in car parks. | Where columns corrode or are damaged. |
| Fixing replacement | Corrosion-resistant fixings, and secondary safety chains on suspended fittings. | Where fixings corrode. |
| PCB removal | Remove PCB capacitors and dispose of them as hazardous waste. | Where old fittings leak an oily residue. |
| Surge protection | Protect external lighting circuits. | Where LED fittings fail in clusters outdoors. |
| External lighting redesign | Redesign to control spill and glare. | Where light spills onto neighbours or dazzles. |
| Maintenance factor | Design new lighting with realistic allowance for dirt and depreciation, and schedule cleaning. | In every new design. |
| Car park protection | Guards on low-mounted fittings exposed to vehicles. | Where low fittings are exposed to vehicles. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
LED conversion is priced per fitting or per area, with access (high-bay and car park work), design, and disposal of old fittings. Columns are priced per column including foundation where needed. Fixing works are per fitting. PCB removal is per fitting with hazardous waste disposal. Lux surveys and column testing are lump sums, with testing recurring.

LED conversion is lifecycle or an energy upgrade with payback; column safety, levels below standard and PCB removal are code compliance; relamping and repairs are repairs and maintenance.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a walk at night cannot: how many fittings of each type there are, what light levels were measured, and whether columns have been tested. Ask for them before specifying an LED conversion.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Lighting inventory and maintenance records | How many fittings of each type there are, and how often they fail. |
| Lux surveys of stairs, car parks and external areas | Whether stairs, car parks and paths are lit to standard. |
| Lighting column inspection and test records | Whether columns have been tested. |
| LED retrofit records and product warranties | What was retrofitted, and whether the products are under warranty. |
| Hazardous materials register | Whether old fittings contain PCBs. |
| Common area lighting energy data | What the common area lighting costs to run. |
| Planning conditions on external lighting | What planning conditions say about external lighting. |
| Lighting design reports for recent upgrades | What recent upgrades were designed to achieve. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Lighting is misread when a corroded column or fitting is treated as ordinary wear, and when LED retrofit tubes are taken to have solved the problem.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| A rusty column is ordinary wear | A lighting column with visible corrosion or damage at its base, or a suspended fitting with corroded fixings, is a falling hazard. Treat it as unsafe until tested. |
| LED tubes solve it | Retrofit tubes keep the old fittings, and LED fittings that fail in clusters on one circuit point to drivers failing from heat or surges. New fittings designed to the required levels, with surge protection outdoors, are the lasting answer. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets light levels for interiors, car parks and public areas, limits lighting energy, and is phasing out inefficient and mercury lamps. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Light levels | AS/NZS 1680 sets interior lighting, including safe movement in stairs and circulation; AS/NZS 1158 sets public and pedestrian area lighting, applied to car parks and external paths. | BS EN 12464-1 and 12464-2 set indoor and outdoor workplace lighting, BS 5489-1 road and public area lighting; the Institution of Lighting Professionals' TR22 sets inspection and testing of lighting columns; most fluorescent lamps were withdrawn from sale in 2023. | Illuminating Engineering Society recommended practices set levels (including parking facilities). |
| Energy and lamp phase-out | NCC Section J limits lighting energy in new and altered work; Australia is a party to the Minamata Convention and is phasing out mercury lamps. | Approved Document L limits energy. | ASHRAE 90.1 and the IECC limit lighting power; federal efficiency rules restrict inefficient general-service lamps, and several states have banned fluorescent lamps. |

sections.heading: Worked example: a dim car park with rusting columns
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 1990s shopping centre's open car park has steel lighting columns, several with rust and section loss at the base and one with its access door missing. Its fluorescent fittings are increasingly hard to source, and parts of the car park are dim at night.

A column with visible corrosion at its base is a falling hazard, unsafe until tested. Dim zones point to failed or removed fittings, or to depreciation. The fluorescent lamps face withdrawal, so conversion is a matter of when, not whether.

So the register carries the corroded columns as safety lines now, tested and replaced or sleeved, a lux survey of the car park, and conversion to new LED fittings designed to the required levels, with surge protection.

thresholds.rule: Average 20 lux, with no point below 5 lux

source.title: Lighting at work (HSG38)

thresholds.rule: Offices: average 200 lux, minimum 100 lux; fine work: average 500 lux, minimum 200 lux

source.title: Lighting at work (HSG38)

pages.title: Lightning Protection
pages.question: How do lightning protection systems fail, and how do you know a system still protects the building?
pages.answer: Lightning protection fails by losing continuity and coverage rather than wearing out. Roof works detach conductors and nobody reinstates them; new plant, solar and antennas are left unbonded and outside the protected zone; copper is stolen at low level; earth resistance rises as electrodes corrode; surge protection devices are exhausted after storms. Only continuity and earth testing show whether the system still works. ESE terminals rely on coverage claims the main standards do not recognise.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about lightning protection; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Air terminals, down-conductors, earthing systems

sources.title: AS 1768:2021 Lightning protection (formerly AS/NZS 1768:2007)
AS/NZS 3000:2018 Electrical installations (Australian/New Zealand Wiring Rules)
BS 7430:2011+A1:2015 Code of practice for protective earthing of electrical installations
BS EN 62305-1:2011 Protection against lightning: General principles
NFPA 70 National Electrical Code
NFPA 780 Standard for the Installation of Lightning Protection Systems

pages.searchTitle: Lightning protection: broken conductors, unbonded plant, earthing and surge protection

questions.question: Does adding solar panels affect lightning protection?
questions.answer: Yes. New plant, solar arrays and antennas need bonding to the system, and its coverage may need extending.

questions.question: Why are lightning conductors missing at ground level?
questions.answer: Usually theft. Replace them with less attractive materials or concealed routes.

questions.question: How often should lightning protection be tested?
questions.answer: At intervals set by the standard; in the United Kingdom, BS EN 62305 sets visual inspection and full testing at intervals that depend on the protection level.

questions.question: What does storm damage say about a lightning system?
questions.answer: Burns at joints point to poor connections; damage to equipment inside points to missing bonding or surge protection; damage to masonry points to side flashing or a broken conductor.

questions.question: How long does lightning protection last?
questions.answer: Conductors and air terminals 30 to 50 years, earth electrodes 20 to 40, and test joints and clamps 20 to 30.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Lightning protection problems show on the roof as loose or missing conductors and unbonded plant, at ground level as missing down conductors and test joints, and in the test records. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On the roof and façade | Conductors loose, detached, cut or missing; fixings broken | Continuity, coverage and earthing |
| On the roof and façade | Plant, solar and antennas without bonding connections | Side flashing, bonding and surge protection |
| On the roof and façade | Corrosion at joints, especially between dissimilar metals | Continuity, coverage and earthing |
| On the roof and façade | Test joints at the base of down conductors missing, damaged or painted over | Continuity, coverage and earthing |
| On the roof and façade | Down conductors stolen at low level | Continuity, coverage and earthing |
| In the records | Design, risk assessment and drawings | Investigation before the scope |
| In the records | Inspection and test reports with earth resistance readings | Continuity, coverage and earthing |
| In the records | Records of roof works and plant additions | Continuity, coverage and earthing |
| In the records | Surge protection device status checks | Side flashing, bonding and surge protection |
| In the records | Burn marks or melted fixings near air terminals after storms | Side flashing, bonding and surge protection |
| In the records | Equipment failures after storms | Side flashing, bonding and surge protection |
| In the records | Air terminals bent or missing after roof works | Continuity, coverage and earthing |

sections.heading: Parts of a lightning protection system
sections.markdown:
A lightning protection system intercepts lightning strikes and conducts the current safely to earth, so it does not pass through the building fabric, start a fire or damage equipment. External protection comprises air terminals or a mesh of conductors on the roof, down conductors on the façade or within the structure, and an earth termination network. Internal protection comprises equipotential bonding of metal services and surge protection devices on power, data and communications lines.

| Component or type | Where it is found | Character |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Conventional air terminals and roof mesh | Most protected buildings | Recognised by all main standards; coverage designed by the rolling sphere or mesh method |
| Down conductors | Façades, within columns, or using the steel frame | Must be continuous and bonded; test joints at the base |
| Earth electrodes and earth network | Below ground around the building | Corrode; resistance rises; disturbed by excavation |
| Bonding to metal roof plant, railings and services | Roofs and service entries | Lost when plant is added or replaced |
| Surge protection devices | Main boards, data and communications entries | Absorb surges and wear out |
| Early streamer emission (ESE) terminals | Some buildings, marketed as covering wider areas | The enhanced coverage claimed is not recognised by IEC and BS EN 62305, and NFPA 780 does not cover them |

Not every building needs a system; the decision comes from a risk assessment considering height, exposure, construction, contents, occupants and the consequence of a strike. Tall buildings, buildings on exposed sites, hazardous stores, heritage buildings, hospitals and buildings with sensitive electronics usually do.

Design follows a lightning protection level chosen from the risk assessment. There are four levels (I is the most demanding), each with its own rolling sphere radius, mesh size and down conductor spacing (Thresholds by market). Natural components such as a continuous steel frame, reinforcing steel or a metal roof can form part of the system if they are electrically continuous and thick enough, which is common in modern framed buildings and must be confirmed rather than assumed.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Copper and aluminium conductors and air terminals last thirty to fifty years and earth electrodes twenty to forty, while test joints and clamps last twenty to thirty. Roof works and theft can break a system long before age does.

| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Copper and aluminium conductors | 30 to 50 years | Fixings; theft; dissimilar metals; coastal exposure |
| Air terminals | 30 to 50 years | Fixings; damage |
| Earth electrodes | 20 to 40 years | Soil corrosivity; excavation |
| Test joints and clamps | 20 to 30 years | Corrosion; tampering |
| Surge protection devices | Until they absorb enough surges; often 5 to 15 years | Lightning activity; switching surges |

What shortens life: roof works that detach conductors and do not reinstate them; new rooftop plant, solar arrays and antennas added without bonding or coverage; copper theft of down conductors and earth tapes; dissimilar metals: aluminium against copper or lead, causing corrosion at joints; excavation that damages earth electrodes.

sections.heading: Continuity, coverage and earthing
sections.markdown:
Conductors detach from their fixings, are cut during roof works, or are stolen. A break in the path means a strike looks for another way to earth: through the fabric, services or people.

New plant, solar arrays, antennas, telecommunications masts and roof extensions sit outside the original protected zone or are left unbonded.

Earth electrodes corrode, soil dries, and connections loosen. Higher resistance means higher voltages during a strike and a greater chance of side flashing to services.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Conductor ends hanging free near new plant | Roof works without reinstatement. Continuity test. | Reinstate and refix the conductors, and bond the new plant. |
| Missing down conductors at low level | Theft. Inspection. | Replace them, with less attractive materials or concealed routes. |
| High earth resistance readings | Corroded electrodes or dry soil. Test against previous readings. | Add or replace earth electrodes. |
| ESE terminal with few down conductors | Design relying on unrecognised coverage claims. Design review against the standard. | Redesign to a recognised standard where the risk requires. |

sections.heading: Side flashing, bonding and surge protection
sections.markdown:
Where metal services, plant or people are too close to a down conductor, the strike current can jump across the gap (side flashing). Near down conductors at ground level, people can be exposed to dangerous touch and step voltages; insulation, barriers or bonding control this.

Metal pipes, cable trays, handrails and plant that are not bonded can flash over to the protection system or to each other, causing fire or damage.

Surge protection devices sacrifice themselves to protect equipment; after enough surges they no longer protect, often without obvious indication unless status indicators are checked.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Equipment damage after storms | Surge protection absent or exhausted. Device status; coordination. | Replace exhausted surge devices, and coordinate them across boards and data entries. |
| New rooftop plant or solar not bonded to the system | Side-flash risk. Inspection of bonds and separation distances. | Bond or separate the new plant, and add surge protection to its supply. |

sections.heading: Natural components
sections.markdown:
Systems that rely on the steel frame or reinforcement as down conductors depend on continuity that was meant to be confirmed at construction. Later alterations, cut reinforcement and replaced roof sheeting can break that continuity without anyone noticing.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Steel frame or metal roof counted as part of the system, with no continuity record | Natural component unproven. Continuity test across joints and to earth; design records. | Test and record continuity, and bond across any breaks. |
| Reinforcement relied on as down conductors in a refurbished building | Continuity possibly broken by alterations. Design records; continuity test from roof to earth. | Test each path, and add dedicated down conductors where continuity is lost. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Loose conductors at height over public areas; protection missing on hazardous stores | safety · 4 Essential | Secure or rectify now. |
| System broken (continuity lost) | failure · 4 Essential | Repair now. |
| Inspection and testing due | deadline · 4 Essential | At the interval the standard sets. |
| High earth resistance; corrosion; unbonded plant | condition · 3 Important | Repair in the near term. |
| System at end of life | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Replace, often with re-roofing. |
| No risk assessment; ESE system; no records | check · 3 Important | Assess. |
| Normal | nil · 1 Routine | Routine. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A lightning protection specialist or electrical engineer. The checks below walk the roof and every down conductor, then compare the earth resistance readings with earlier tests and the system with what is now on the roof.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Risk assessment | To confirm whether protection is required and to what level. |
| Visual inspection | Of air terminations, conductors, fixings, joints, bonding and test points. |
| Continuity testing | Of conductors and bonds. |
| Earth resistance testing | Of each electrode and the whole network. |
| Coverage check | Of new plant, solar and antennas against the design. |
| Surge protection review | Devices present, status, coordination. |

The report should give the system status, test readings against previous results, gaps, and works needed.

Inspection intervals under BS EN 62305 depend on the protection level: for levels I and II, a visual inspection every year and a complete inspection every two years; for levels III and IV, every two and four years. Critical structures such as those with explosive or flammable contents are inspected more often. Earth resistance is measured by fall-of-potential or clamp methods and compared with previous readings rather than judged alone.

sections.heading: Reinstating, extending or redesigning
sections.markdown:
Loose conductors over public areas, and systems broken by roof works or theft, come first. After that, the work keeps the system matched to the roof: new plant bonded, coverage extended, electrodes improved and surge protection renewed.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Reinstate and refix | Reinstate and refix conductors, replacing stolen sections with less attractive materials or concealed routes. | Wherever conductors are loose, cut or stolen. |
| Bond new plant | Bond new plant, solar arrays and antennas. | Whenever anything is added to the roof. |
| Extend coverage | Extend the system to new roof elements. | Where the roof has changed. |
| Earth improvement | Additional or replacement electrodes. | Where earth resistance has risen. |
| Surge protection | Replace exhausted devices and coordinate across boards and data entries. | Where devices are exhausted, or equipment fails after storms. |
| Redesign | Redesign ESE-based systems to a recognised standard. | Where the risk requires. |
| Coordinate with re-roofing | Reinstate and test the system as part of the roof works. | At every re-roofing. |
| Test joints | Reinstate test joints at the base of every down conductor. | So future testing is possible. |

Interactions: lightning protection must be bonded to new solar arrays, plant and antennas, coordinated with surge protection at the main switchboard, and reinstated after every re-roofing; heritage buildings may need conductor routes approved.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Inspection and testing are recurring lump sums. Repairs are itemised by length of conductor or per bond. Earth improvements are per electrode. Full replacement is a lump sum, often carried with re-roofing. Surge protection is per device.

Testing and safety rectification are code compliance; repairs are repairs and maintenance; replacement is lifecycle.

Theft-prone sites may justify concealed or less valuable conductor materials despite higher installation cost. Inspections are best combined with roof access for other work.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a walk on the roof cannot: what the system was designed to protect, how its earth resistance has changed, and what has been added to the roof since. Ask for them before the next roof works.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Risk assessment and design drawings | What the system was designed to protect, and how. |
| Inspection and test reports with earth resistance readings | Whether the system is continuous, and how its earth resistance has changed. |
| Records of roof works and plant additions | Whether roof works left the system broken. |
| Surge protection device schedule | Which surge devices protect which boards. |
| Insurer requirements and inspection records | What the insurer requires. |
| Records of strikes and storm damage | Where the building has been struck, and what was damaged. |
| Heritage constraints on conductor routes | Which routes heritage controls allow. |
| Records of plant, antennas and solar added to the roof since the last inspection | What has been added to the roof since the last inspection. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Lightning protection is misread when a system installed once is assumed to stay complete, and when storm damage is repaired without asking where the current went.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| Once installed, it stays complete | Roof works, new plant and theft break or bypass lightning protection: conductor ends left hanging near new plant, unbonded solar arrays and antennas, and missing down conductors at low level. Reinstate, bond and test after every change to the roof. |
| Just repair the storm damage | After a strike, damage tells you where the current went: burns at joints and fixings point to poor connections; damage to equipment inside points to missing bonding or surge protection; damage to masonry points to side flashing or a broken conductor. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets standards for assessing the risk, designing and inspecting lightning protection, and for surge protection. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Design, inspection and surge protection | AS/NZS 1768 sets lightning protection, including risk assessment, design and inspection; surge protection follows AS/NZS 1768 and AS/NZS 3000. | BS EN 62305 sets risk assessment, design and inspection, with visual inspection and full testing at intervals set by the protection level (more often for higher levels); BS 7430 covers earthing. | NFPA 780 sets installation requirements; UL 96A covers installation and certification; NFPA 70 covers surge protection devices. |

Insurers in all three jurisdictions may require lightning protection for high-risk buildings and evidence of inspection. Heritage buildings often have historic systems that need repair rather than replacement, with routes agreed with heritage authorities.

Explosives and flammable stores carry stricter protection and inspection requirements in all three jurisdictions under their hazardous materials rules.

sections.heading: Worked example: a roof that has changed since it was protected
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. An office tower's lightning protection was installed with the building. Since then, a solar array and new antennas have been added, re-roofing has left conductor ends hanging near new plant, two down conductors are missing at street level, and the last test report is six years old.

Each change has broken or bypassed the system: the hanging ends break continuity, the solar array and antennas are unbonded, and the missing down conductors point to theft. A system broken in these ways cannot be relied on, whatever it was designed for.

So the register carries reinstating continuity as a failure line, bonding of the solar array and antennas, replacement of the stolen conductors with less attractive materials, and a full inspection and test, with test joints reinstated.

thresholds.measure: Rolling sphere radius by protection level (BS EN 62305)
thresholds.rule: 20 m, 30 m, 45 m and 60 m for levels I to IV

pages.title: Load-Bearing Masonry
pages.question: How do load-bearing masonry walls fail, and when do alterations or bowing make them unsafe?
pages.answer: Load-bearing masonry rarely fails on its own; it fails when it loses support or restraint. Walls and chimney breasts removed without engineering, steel beams on inadequate bearings, floors not tied to walls so gables bow, rubble-cored stone faces separating, and rotted timber lintels behind arches are the common causes. Bowing walls and crushed bearings need urgent engineering. Unreinforced masonry is the most vulnerable construction in earthquakes.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about load-bearing masonry; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Solid brick, stone, or blockwork walls, lintels, arches
