pages.searchTitle: Load-bearing masonry: bowing walls, removed walls, lintels and restraint

questions.question: Is it safe to remove a load-bearing wall or chimney breast?
questions.answer: Only with engineering and approval. Unengineered alterations are a common cause of structural failure in older buildings; where walls or breasts have been removed, find out what now carries the load.

questions.question: Why is my gable wall bowing?
questions.answer: Usually because it is not tied to the floors and roof. Straps, tie rods or helical ties restrain it, with propping while the work is designed.

questions.question: Why has the brickwork dropped over a window?
questions.answer: A failed lintel or a spreading arch. Prop the opening, then replace the lintel or repair the arch.

questions.question: Should old brickwork be repaired with cement?
questions.answer: No. Lime-based repairs move and breathe with traditional masonry, avoiding the damage hard cement causes.

questions.question: How long do lintels last?
questions.answer: Timber lintels 50 to 150 years and steel lintels 40 to 80; brick arches last the life of the building.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Masonry problems show as walls out of plumb, cracks under beam ends and over openings, bulging stone faces, and in the records of what has been altered. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On site | Walls bowing outward or out of plumb, especially gables and tall walls | Restraint, bowing and rubble cores |
| On site | Cracks below beam ends; crushed or cracked masonry at bearings | Alterations, overload and lintels |
| On site | Cracks and dropped brickwork over openings; arches cracked at the crown or separating at the springing | Alterations, overload and lintels |
| On site | Bulging stone faces; loose stones | Restraint, bowing and rubble cores |
| On site | Rooms opened up by removing walls or chimney breasts, with new beams | Alterations, overload and lintels |
| On site | Vertical cracking in piers between openings | Alterations, overload and lintels |
| In the records | Building approvals and engineering for alterations | Investigation before the scope |
| In the records | Previous structural reports | Investigation before the scope |
| In the records | Restraint or strapping works | Restraint, bowing and rubble cores |
| In the records | Seismic evaluations in seismic regions | Earthquake and settlement |
| In the records | Doors and windows in upper storeys that bind or have been planed repeatedly, often the first sign of a wall moving out of plumb | Restraint, bowing and rubble cores |

sections.heading: Types of masonry wall
sections.markdown:
Load-bearing masonry walls carry floors and roofs as well as enclosing the building. They are solid brick, stone or blockwork, sometimes cavity walls where the inner leaf carries the load, with arches, lintels and piers over and between openings. Most pre-war houses, terraces, warehouses and institutional buildings in Australia, Britain and the United States are load-bearing masonry, as are many low-rise apartment blocks of later eras. The façade aspects of masonry (ties, pointing, spalling) are covered on the masonry and brickwork page; this page covers how masonry carries load and how that fails.

| Form | Where it is found | Main vulnerabilities |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Solid brick walls | Pre-war houses, terraces, warehouses | Removed walls and breasts; lack of restraint; settlement |
| Stone walls with rubble cores | Older buildings, especially in Britain and colonial Australia | Separation of faces from cores; bulging |
| Cavity walls with load-bearing inner leaf | Mid twentieth century onward | Ties; inner leaf alterations |
| Concrete blockwork | Low-rise residential and commercial | Shrinkage cracking; reinforcement where present |
| Unreinforced masonry in seismic regions | Older buildings in California and other seismic areas | Collapse in earthquakes |

Masonry is strong in compression and weak in tension and bending. It depends on being held in line by the floors and roof it supports, on arches and lintels spanning openings, and on not being weakened by holes and removed walls. Most structural failures in masonry buildings come from alterations or loss of restraint rather than from the masonry itself.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Solid brick and stone walls last centuries if kept dry and restrained, and lime mortar fifty to a hundred years between repointing; timber lintels last fifty to a hundred and fifty years and steel lintels forty to eighty. What cuts a wall's life short is usually an alteration, or the loss of the floors and roof that hold it in place.

| Element | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Solid brick and stone walls | Centuries if dry and restrained | Water; alterations; foundation movement |
| Lime mortar joints | 50 to 100 years | Exposure; hard repointing |
| Timber lintels and bond timbers | 50 to 150 years | Decay; insects |
| Steel lintels | 40 to 80 years | Corrosion |
| Brick arches | Life of the building | Spreading; abutment movement |
| Wall restraint straps and ties | 50 years and more | Corrosion |

What shortens life: alterations: walls removed, openings widened, chimney breasts taken out; loss of restraint: floors and roofs not tied to walls, or ties removed; water washing out mortar and rotting embedded timbers; foundation movement; hard cement repairs and impermeable coatings.

sections.heading: Restraint, bowing and rubble cores
sections.markdown:
Walls that are not tied to the floors and roof they support can bow outward, especially tall gable walls and walls where floor joists run parallel and so do not bear on them. Removal of internal walls that braced external ones has the same effect.

Stone walls with rubble cores separate as the core mortar washes out; the outer faces bulge and can collapse.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Wall bowing outward with floors running parallel | Lack of restraint. Plumb survey; inspection of floor-to-wall connections. | Tie the wall to the floors and roof with straps, tie rods or helical ties; prop it meanwhile. |
| Bulging stone face with cracks | Separation from the rubble core. Tapping; endoscope into the core. | Grout the rubble core and pin the stone face, or rebuild badly bulged sections. |

sections.heading: Alterations, overload and lintels
sections.markdown:
Load-bearing walls removed to open up rooms, openings widened, chimney breasts removed and walls chased for services remove support or concentrate load. Steel beams inserted without adequate bearings, padstones or engineering crush the masonry at their ends.

New loads such as storage, roof plant, added storeys and heavier roof coverings can exceed the capacity of slender or weakened walls, which crush, crack vertically or bow.

Timber lintels behind arches and timber bond courses in old walls rot; steel lintels corrode; arches spread when their abutments move or when nearby openings remove their support. Masonry above drops and cracks.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cracks below the ends of a new beam | Inadequate bearing or padstone. Opening up at the bearing. | Open up the bearing; add a padstone or spreader beam. |
| Dropped brickwork over an opening | Failed lintel or spreading arch. Inspection of lintel or abutment. | Prop the opening; replace the lintel or repair the arch. |
| Vertical cracks in a heavily loaded pier | Overload or crushing. Load review. | Review the loads with an engineer; relieve or strengthen the pier. |
| Masonry building being extended upward or converted to flats | A change of consequence class. In England, flats and offices of more than 4 and up to 15 storeys fall in Class 2b, which needs horizontal and vertical ties or a check that the loss of any one wall does not cause disproportionate collapse (Approved Document A, Table 11). | Have the robustness assessed before the change, and add ties or strengthening where the new class requires it. |

sections.heading: Earthquake and settlement
sections.markdown:
Unreinforced masonry is the most vulnerable common construction in earthquakes: walls fall outward, parapets and chimneys collapse, and floors pull out of their bearings. Seismic regions require or encourage retrofit.

Foundation movement cracks masonry walls diagonally through openings; see the foundations page.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Diagonal cracks through openings | Foundation movement. See the foundations page. | Treat it as foundation movement; see Foundations. |
| Cracks wider at one end and opening over months | Progressive movement. Crack monitoring, with widths graded on the asset’s market’s damage scale (Thresholds by market). | Monitor and find the cause before repair; have an engineer assess cracks in the moderate band or above. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Walls bowing significantly; crushed bearings under beams; bulging stone faces; unreinforced masonry parapets in seismic areas | safety · 4 Essential | Prop and engineer now. |
| Failed lintels with dropped masonry; unsupported loads after alterations | failure · 4 Essential | Support and repair now. |
| Seismic retrofit required by ordinance | deadline · 4 Essential | By the ordinance date. |
| Early bowing; cracked arches; decaying lintels | condition · 3 Important | Repair in the near term. |
| Lintels at end of life | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Replace. |
| Alterations with no engineering on record | check · 3 Important | Assess. |
| Stable minor cracks | nil · 1 Routine | Monitor. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A structural engineer experienced with masonry and, for heritage buildings, conservation. The checks below read the shape of each wall first, then open up bearings, lintels and floor-to-wall connections where the shape points.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Plumb and bulge survey | Of walls, with monitoring where movement is suspected and crack widths graded against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). |
| Restraint check | How floors, roofs and walls are connected, by opening up at representative points. |
| Alteration review | Identify removed walls and breasts and check what supports the load, with approvals. |
| Bearing inspection | At beam ends and lintels. |
| Wall construction | Solid, cavity or rubble-cored, by endoscope or opening. |
| Load review | Against current use. |
| Seismic evaluation | In seismic regions. |

The report should state stability, the cause of movement, safety measures and repairs.

Movement is judged over time: fixed survey targets on bowing walls, read several times over a year, show whether a bow is historic and stable or still growing, which decides between monitoring and immediate restraint.

sections.heading: Restraining, repairing or rebuilding
sections.markdown:
Propping comes first wherever a wall is bowing or a lintel has failed, so nothing can collapse while repairs are designed. The repairs then follow the cause: restraint for bowing, bearings and lintels for alterations, and lime-based materials throughout traditional masonry.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Restraint | Straps tying floors and roofs to walls, tie rods with pattress plates across buildings, and helical ties into walls. | Where walls bow because they are not tied to the structure. |
| Bearings | Padstones and spreader beams under beam ends. | Where masonry cracks or crushes under beams. |
| Lintel replacement and arch repair | New lintels, or arches repaired. | Where lintels have failed or arches have spread. |
| Crack stitching | Helical bars across the crack. | After the cause has been addressed. |
| Grouting and pinning | Grout rubble cores and pin stone faces. | Where stone faces separate from the core. |
| Rebuilding | Rebuild badly bowed or failed sections. | Where sections cannot be restrained or repaired. |
| Seismic retrofit | Anchor walls to floors, brace parapets, and add frames or walls. | In seismic regions, and wherever an ordinance requires it. |
| Retrospective engineering and approval | Engineering and approval for past alterations. | Wherever alterations have none on record. |
| Temporary propping and shoring | Props and shores while permanent repairs are designed. | So that a bowing wall or failed lintel cannot collapse in the meantime. |
| Lime-based repairs | Lime mortars and repairs in traditional masonry. | So repairs move and breathe with the original, avoiding the damage hard cement causes. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Investigation is a lump sum. Restraint and stitching are priced per tie or per metre. Lintel replacement per opening with propping. Rebuilding by area. Seismic retrofit is a lump-sum project. Propping is an immediate cost.

Repairs to stop movement are condition items; ordinance retrofits are deadlines; safety items are immediate.

Propping and shoring can run for months while designs and approvals are prepared, and their hire is a recurring cost until the permanent repair is complete. Work to party walls adds surveyors' fees and agreement with neighbours. Heritage approval can extend programmes and require specialist materials and trades.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a look at the walls cannot: which alterations were engineered and approved, what now carries the load where walls were removed, and whether bowing walls are still moving. Ask for them before any sale, refinancing or further alteration.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Building approvals and engineering for alterations | Whether alterations were engineered and approved. |
| Previous structural reports | What earlier engineers found. |
| Restraint and strengthening records | What restraint and strengthening has already been done. |
| Seismic evaluations and retrofit orders | Whether a seismic retrofit is required, and by when. |
| Heritage listing | Whether heritage controls govern any repair. |
| Records of chimney breast or wall removals, with what now supports the load | What now carries the load where walls or chimney breasts were removed. |
| Monitoring data for bowing walls | Whether bowing walls are still moving. |
| Party wall awards for work to shared walls | What was agreed for work to shared walls. |
| Strata or landlord consents for alterations within units | Whether alterations within units had the consent they needed. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Load-bearing masonry is misread when an alteration is assumed to have been engineered, and when a bowing or cracked wall is treated as a matter for crack repair alone.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| The opening was done properly | Alterations to load-bearing walls without engineering are a common cause of structural failure in older buildings. Where walls or chimney breasts have been removed, find out what is now carrying the load. |
| Stitch the crack and move on | Crack stitching with helical bars follows dealing with the cause. A wall bowing because it is not tied to its floors needs restraint first, or the crack returns. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets design standards for masonry, requires approval for alterations to load-bearing walls, and in seismic regions sets rules for older unreinforced walls. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Design | AS 3700 and AS 4773 govern masonry; AS 1170.4 sets earthquake actions. | BS EN 1996 governs masonry; Approved Document A covers structure and restraint. | TMS 402 governs masonry design. |
| Alterations, heritage and seismic | Alterations to load-bearing walls need building approval; heritage controls often apply. | Alterations need building regulations approval and often party wall notices; heritage buildings need listed building consent. | The International Existing Building Code Appendix A1 covers seismic strengthening of unreinforced masonry; several California cities require unreinforced masonry and soft-storey retrofits. |

In all three jurisdictions, past alterations without approval can create disclosure, insurance and certification issues at sale or refinancing, and may require retrospective approval or rectification before a building can be certified. Strata and leasehold buildings treat load-bearing walls as common or landlord structure even where they sit within a unit, so owners cannot alter them without consent.

sections.heading: Worked example: a chimney breast removed downstairs
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A Victorian terrace had its ground-floor chimney breast removed some years ago to open up the living room. The breast above, in the bedroom, remains. There are cracks in the bedroom ceiling near the breast, and no engineering or approval for the removal is on record.

Where a chimney breast has been removed below but remains above, the question is what now carries it. With no engineering on record, the alteration is at least a check finding; if opening up shows the upper breast is unsupported, or bearing on inadequate steelwork, it is a failure finding and needs propping at once.

So the register carries opening up the removal as a check line now, propping and properly designed support if the breast is unsupported, and retrospective engineering and approval, since unapproved alterations raise issues at sale or refinancing.

thresholds.rule: Negligible under 0.1 mm; very slight under 1 mm; slight under 5 mm; moderate 5 to 15 mm; severe 15 to 25 mm; limits half as wide again for plasterboard partitions

pages.title: Loading Docks & Goods Handling
pages.question: How do loading docks fail as working spaces, and which dock findings are safety-critical?
pages.answer: Docks fail first on safety: forklifts, reversing trucks and pedestrians mixing without segregation; roller shutters with failed springs or safety edges; open dock edges; fumes from idling vehicles entering the building. Then on condition and capacity: columns and doors struck repeatedly, slab joints broken by heavy forklifts, depressed docks flooding when pumps fail, and waste rooms overflowing with odour, vermin and fire risk.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about loading docks & goods handling; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.

pages.searchTitle: Loading docks: vehicle and pedestrian safety, dock doors, impact, flooding and waste

questions.question: How should pedestrians be kept safe in a loading dock?
questions.answer: Physically segregated walkways with barriers, marked crossings, mirrors, good lighting, and a traffic management plan that is enforced.

questions.question: Why does the dock roller shutter keep getting damaged?
questions.answer: Usually it sits in a vehicle or forklift path. Protect it with bollards and guide protection, or move it.

questions.question: Is a roller shutter with a broken spring dangerous?
questions.answer: Yes. A door whose spring fails can drop suddenly; take it out of use until the springs and cables are replaced.

questions.question: Why does the loading dock flood?
questions.answer: Usually blocked grates or failed pumps in the depressed dock. Clean them regularly, and fit pump alarms.

questions.question: How long do dock roller shutters last?
questions.answer: 15 to 20 years, with springs and motors replaced sooner.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Dock problems show at peak times as people among vehicles, struck doors and columns, flooding, waste and fumes, and in traffic plans, incident reports and maintenance records. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On site | Pedestrian routes absent or crossed by forklift paths; worn line marking; no barriers at doors | Vehicles, pedestrians and dock edges |
| On site | Damaged roller shutters, guide rails and safety edges; doors held open | Dock doors and impact damage |
| On site | Gouged columns and walls; missing bollards; damaged sprinkler pipes | Dock doors and impact damage |
| On site | Broken slab joints and potholes in the dock floor | Dock doors and impact damage |
| On site | Ponding and blocked grates; pump alarms | Drainage, waste and fumes |
| On site | Overflowing waste rooms; odour; vermin evidence | Drainage, waste and fumes |
| On site | Fumes in the dock and adjoining corridors | Drainage, waste and fumes |
| In the records | Traffic management plan | Vehicles, pedestrians and dock edges |
| In the records | Incident and near-miss reports | Vehicles, pedestrians and dock edges |
| In the records | Door and leveller maintenance records | Dock doors and impact damage |
| In the records | Waste contracts and complaints | Drainage, waste and fumes |
| In the records | Pump and drainage maintenance | Drainage, waste and fumes |
| In the records | Trucks queuing on public roads or footpaths waiting for a bay | Vehicles, pedestrians and dock edges |

sections.heading: What the space does and what it contains
sections.markdown:
Loading docks and goods handling areas are where vehicles deliver and collect goods and waste: truck bays and hardstand, dock levellers and doors, the dock floor, goods lifts and hoists, waste and recycling rooms, bin wash areas and the corridors that lead into the building. Functionally the dock must let vehicles, forklifts, trolleys and people move without colliding, keep weather and fumes out of the building, carry heavy loads, drain properly, and handle waste hygienically. In shopping centres, hospitals, hotels and mixed-use buildings it is shared by many tenants and operators and is often the most abused space in the building.

| Element group | Typical provision | What matters for the space |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dock doors | Roller shutters, sectional doors, high-speed doors | Safe operation; weather and security |
| Dock levellers and restraints | Hydraulic levellers, vehicle restraints, bumpers | Free-fall protection; trailer creep |
| Dock floor and hardstand | Heavy-duty concrete, joints, drainage | Loads, joints, falls to drains |
| Traffic management | Line marking, barriers, pedestrian paths, mirrors, lighting | Segregation of people and vehicles |
| Waste and recycling rooms | Bin rooms, compactors, bin wash | Hygiene, vermin, fire, ventilation |
| Goods lifts and hoists | Goods lifts serving floors and tenancies | Reliability; door damage |
| Ventilation | Exhaust for vehicle fumes in enclosed docks | Diesel fumes and carbon monoxide |
| Impact protection | Bollards, column guards, wall protection | Protecting structure and services |

sections.heading: How long it stays fit for purpose
sections.markdown:
Roller shutters and dock doors last fifteen to twenty years, with springs and motors replaced sooner, levellers fifteen to twenty-five, and floor joints ten to twenty before major repair, while line marking lasts only two to five. Changes in the vehicles and volumes delivering often end a dock's fitness for purpose before wear does.

| Component or quality | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Roller shutters and dock doors | 15 to 20 years; springs and motors sooner | Cycles; impact; maintenance |
| Dock levellers | 15 to 25 years | Loads; impact |
| Dock floor joints and surfaces | 10 to 20 years before major repair | Wheel loads; impact |
| Line marking and signage | 2 to 5 years | Traffic |
| Compactors and waste equipment | 10 to 15 years | Use; maintenance |
| Bollards and guards | 10 to 20 years | Impact |

What shortens fitness for purpose: larger vehicles than the dock was designed for, scraping canopies and turning over kerbs; heavier forklifts, including battery-electric models, overloading levellers and slab joints; more tenants and deliveries than the dock was sized for, causing congestion; poor waste management that spills into circulation and drains.

sections.heading: Vehicles, pedestrians and dock edges
sections.markdown:
Docks mix reversing trucks, forklifts and pedestrians. Without segregated walkways, barriers, lighting and rules, people are struck; this is among the most serious workplace hazards in buildings with docks.

Open dock edges without doors closed or barriers, and levellers left raised, create drops for people and forklifts. Trailers pulling away early or creeping are covered on the dock leveller page.

The safest dock separates people from vehicles physically, not with paint alone. Marked walkways that forklifts cross freely, drivers who wait beside their trucks, and staff who take the shortest route all put people where vehicles reverse; watching the dock at peak shows where that happens.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Near misses between forklifts and people | No segregation or traffic plan. Observation; incident records. | Segregate walkways with barriers, mark crossings, and write and enforce a traffic management plan. |
| Dock doors open with no trailer and no barrier | An open edge that people and forklifts can fall from. Doors left open between deliveries, and levellers left raised. | Keep doors closed or barriers in place when no trailer is docked, and store levellers level. |

sections.heading: Dock doors and impact damage
sections.markdown:
Roller shutters and sectional doors are struck by vehicles and forklifts; counterbalance springs and cables fail; safety edges and photo-eyes are damaged or bypassed. A door whose spring fails can drop suddenly.

Columns, walls, services, sprinkler pipes and door frames in docks are struck repeatedly; unprotected columns can be weakened, and struck sprinkler pipes flood docks.

A dock door is a heavy machine at the end of a traffic route. Its safety devices, the edges and photo-eyes that stop it closing on people, are what get damaged or bypassed, and its springs, if they fail, can let it drop. Repeated damage at the same height points to the traffic, not the door.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Door damaged repeatedly at the same height | Vehicle or forklift impact. Door location against traffic paths. | Protect the door with bollards and guide protection, or move it out of the traffic path. |
| Canopy and services damaged at the dock entry | Vehicles taller than the dock was designed for. Clearance against vehicle fleet. | Check clearances against the vehicles now delivering; add height warnings, or raise the canopy and services. |
| A roller shutter that drops quickly or stops part-way | A failing counterbalance spring or cable. The door is heavy to lift by hand, or the spring shows wear or breakage. | Take the door out of use, and replace the springs and cables. |

sections.heading: Drainage, waste and fumes
sections.markdown:
Depressed truck docks drain to pits and pumps; blocked grates and failed pumps flood the dock in storms. Oil and waste wash into stormwater without interceptors.

Overflowing bins, broken compactors and poor washdown attract vermin and odour; waste rooms are also a common fire origin when bins are stored against walls or under combustible linings.

Vehicles idling in enclosed docks fill them with diesel fumes and carbon monoxide that can be drawn into the building through doors and air intakes.

Congestion compounds every hazard: when more deliveries arrive than bays allow, trucks wait on access roads and footpaths and drivers take shortcuts.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dock floods in storms | Blocked grates or failed pumps. Inspection; pump tests. | Clean the grates and pits, and maintain the pumps with alarms. |
| Odour and vermin in the dock | Waste room management. Inspection; contract review. | Right-size the waste room, add a compactor and washdown, and vermin-proof it. |
| Bins stacked against walls under combustible linings | A waste room set up to become a fire origin. Linings not fire-rated, and bins against the walls. | Enclose the waste room in fire-rated construction, and keep bins off the walls. |
| A diesel smell in corridors next to the dock | Vehicles idling in an enclosed dock. Fumes strongest at delivery times, with carbon monoxide readings to match. | Ventilate the dock with fans interlocked to carbon monoxide detection, and enforce no-idling. |
| Drivers or staff with headaches after vehicles idle in an enclosed dock | Exhaust building up. Carbon monoxide readings at workstations while vehicles run, against the exposure limits for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Stop engines idling, improve extract, and add monitoring if the readings are high. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No pedestrian segregation; dock doors with failed safety devices or springs; open edges; fumes entering the building | safety · 4 Essential | Rectify now. |
| Dock unusable through door, leveller or flooding failure | failure · 3 Important | Repair now. |
| Statutory inspections of doors, lifts or equipment due | deadline · 3 Important | At the prescribed interval. |
| Impact damage; slab joints; waste hygiene | condition · 2 Planned | Repair in the near term. |
| Doors, levellers and finishes at end of life | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Replace. |
| No traffic management plan or capacity review | check · 2 Planned | Assess. |
| Normal | nil · 1 Routine | Routine. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A building surveyor leads, with a workplace transport or safety specialist, the dock equipment and door contractors, and the centre or facilities manager who runs the dock. The checks below observe the dock at peak delivery times, then check doors, edges, drainage and waste rooms, and compare clearances with the vehicles now delivering.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Operations observation | At peak delivery times, recording vehicle movements and sizes, reversing manoeuvres, forklift and trolley paths, pedestrian routes, and where people wait. |
| Traffic management review | Whether there is a written plan, whether it matches what happens, and whether segregation, crossings, barriers, mirrors and lighting support it. |
| Door and leveller safety checks | Springs, cables, safety edges, photo-eyes, free-fall protection and restraints, against maintenance records. |
| Impact damage survey | Of columns, walls, door frames, sprinkler pipes and services, with a structural engineer where columns are damaged. |
| Floor, drainage and pump survey | Joints, surface, falls, grates, pits, pumps and interceptors. |
| Waste room review | Capacity against tenants, equipment, washdown, vermin control, fire separation and sprinkler coverage. |
| Air quality check | For diesel fumes and carbon monoxide in enclosed docks and adjoining spaces. |

The report should rank safety measures first, then capacity and condition, with a staged plan that keeps deliveries running.

sections.heading: Segregating, protecting and managing
sections.markdown:
Pedestrian segregation, dock door safety devices and dock edge protection come first, before any condition item. After that, the work protects what vehicles keep striking, keeps the dock drained and the waste room clean, and manages deliveries so the dock is not overwhelmed.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Traffic management | Physically segregated walkways with barriers, marked crossings, convex mirrors, good lighting and a written plan briefed to drivers and staff. | Wherever vehicles and people share the dock. |
| Dock door safety | Replace failed springs and cables, restore safety edges and photo-eyes, add guide protection and fast-acting doors where traffic is heavy. | Wherever springs, safety edges or photo-eyes have failed. |
| Impact protection | Bollards at doors and corners, column guards, and protection for sprinkler pipes and services in vehicle paths. | Wherever vehicles strike doors, columns or services. |
| Floor and joint repair | Repair floors and joints, with armoured joints in forklift routes. | Where joints break up or potholes form. |
| Drainage | Regular grate and pit cleaning, pump maintenance with alarms, oil interceptors where vehicles wash or leak. | Where the dock floods, or oil reaches stormwater. |
| Waste rooms | Right-sized rooms, compactors, washdown with drainage, vermin proofing, fire-rated enclosure and sprinkler coverage. | Where waste rooms overflow, smell or attract vermin. |
| Ventilation | Ventilate enclosed docks, interlocked with carbon monoxide detection, with no-idling rules. | Where fumes build up in enclosed docks. |
| Delivery scheduling | Schedule deliveries to reduce conflicts. | Where docks are congested; it avoids building works. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Traffic management works, bollards and guards are itemised and modest, and among the best value safety spending in a building. Doors and levellers are priced per bay; floor repairs by length of joint or area; waste room upgrades and ventilation are lump sums. Works in operating docks are usually done at night or in stages, adding cost. Tenants and operators often share dock costs through outgoings.

Safety items are code compliance; equipment replacement is lifecycle; repairs are repairs and maintenance.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what one visit cannot: where near misses happen, whether the doors' safety devices are maintained, and whether the dock still suits the vehicles and volumes it now handles. Ask for them before any capacity decision.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Traffic management plan | How vehicles and people are meant to move through the dock. |
| Incident and near-miss reports at the dock | Where near misses and incidents happen. |
| Dock door and leveller maintenance and safety records | Whether dock doors and levellers are maintained and their safety devices tested. |
| Waste contracts and complaint records | Whether waste is collected often enough, and what people complain about. |
| Drainage and pump maintenance records | Whether the dock's drainage is maintained. |
| Delivery schedules and vehicle sizes | How many deliveries arrive, when, and in what vehicles. |
| Planning conditions on delivery hours and vehicle sizes | What planning conditions allow. |
| Records of structural damage from vehicle impacts | Whether vehicles have damaged the structure. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Docks are misread when safety and condition items are handled together, when repeated damage is treated as wear, and when congestion is answered only with building works.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| Fix the dock floor first | Vehicle-pedestrian segregation, dock door safety devices and dock edge protection are life-safety matters. Fix them before condition items. |
| The door just keeps wearing out | A door damaged repeatedly at the same height points to vehicle or forklift impact along that path. Protect it or move it; replacing it in place only resets the count. |
| We need more docks | Where docks are congested, delivery scheduling reduces conflicts without building works, and is the first answer to test. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market places duties on whoever runs a workplace to manage vehicle and pedestrian traffic, and sets rules for powered doors and loading areas. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Workplace traffic, doors and loading areas | Work health and safety laws require traffic management where vehicles and people interact, with Safe Work Australia guidance on traffic management in workplaces; powered garage and industrial door drives follow AS/NZS 60335.2.95; waste room requirements are set by councils and the National Construction Code. | The Health and Safety Executive's workplace transport guidance and the Workplace Regulations 1992 require safe traffic routes; powered industrial doors follow BS EN 13241 and BS EN 12453; Approved Document H covers refuse storage. | OSHA requires safe walking-working surfaces, forklift operation and dock safety measures; industrial doors follow UL 325 for operators; local codes set waste room and ventilation requirements. |

Planning approvals in all three countries often limit delivery hours and vehicle sizes, constraining how docks can operate.

sections.heading: Worked example: a dock at peak time
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A shopping centre's loading dock has painted walkways that forklifts cross at will, and drivers wait beside their trucks. One roller shutter has been struck so often that its guide rail is bent and its safety edge no longer works, the dock floods in heavy rain, and trucks queue on the street at the morning peak.

Vehicle and pedestrian segregation and dock door safety are life-safety matters to fix before anything else. A shutter struck at the same point points to the traffic path, not the door. Flooding points to blocked grates or pumps, and the queue to more deliveries than the bays can take.

So the register carries segregated walkways with barriers, and the shutter's safety edge, as safety lines now, bollards and guide protection, drainage maintenance with pump alarms, and delivery scheduling before any expansion of the dock.

thresholds.rule: 50 ppm averaged over 8 hours

pages.title: Lobbies & Atria
pages.question: How do lobbies and atria fail, and what makes a large open volume unsafe?
pages.answer: Atria are judged on what can fall, what can burn and what can be reached. Older overhead glass that is not laminated can fall; upper-level balustrades below current heights or with climbable rails create fall risks; smoke control fails when fans and make-up air fail or the volume is infilled. Then comfort and maintenance: atria stratify and overheat at the top, condense on cold glass, echo, and leave lights and detectors at height unmaintained for lack of access.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about lobbies & atria; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.

pages.searchTitle: Lobbies and atria: overhead glass, open edges, smoke control, comfort and access at height

questions.question: Can we add a mezzanine or bridge in an atrium?
questions.answer: Only after the fire engineer has reviewed it. Any change that encloses, infills or alters an atrium can invalidate its smoke control design.

questions.question: Is old atrium roof glass dangerous?
questions.answer: It can be. Overhead glass must hold together when broken; older monolithic toughened or wired glass can fall.

questions.question: Why is the top of the atrium so hot?
questions.answer: Stratification: hot air collects at the top. High-level exhaust or destratification fans, and solar control, help.

questions.question: Why are lights at the top of the atrium never fixed?
questions.answer: Usually there is no practical way to reach them. Gantries, monorails or winches, or moving the equipment within reach, solve it.

questions.question: How long do atrium glazing seals last?
questions.answer: 15 to 25 years; smoke control equipment lasts 20 to 25, and balustrades 30 to 50.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Atrium problems show at the edges and overhead as low balustrades and glass types, as drips and heat at upper levels, as dead high-level lights, and in smoke control and glass records. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On site | Balustrade heights and climbability at upper levels; furniture or planters against them | Overhead glass and open edges |
| On site | Glass type markings in atrium roofs and balustrades; cracked panes | Overhead glass and open edges |
| On site | Leak staining on atrium floors and walls; condensation marks | Comfort, condensation and acoustics |
| On site | Failed high-level lights and fittings left in place | Maintenance at height |
| On site | Upper walkways noticeably hotter than the ground floor | Comfort, condensation and acoustics |
| On site | Smoke curtains, vents and fans present; obstructions around them | Smoke control |
| On site | Infilled floors or new enclosures within the atrium | Smoke control |
| In the records | Fire engineering report and atrium smoke control design | Smoke control |
| In the records | Integrated smoke control test reports | Smoke control |
| In the records | Glass schedules for roof and balustrades | Overhead glass and open edges |
| In the records | Maintenance access strategy | Maintenance at height |
| In the records | Leak history | Comfort, condensation and acoustics |
| In the records | Furniture, planters or display stands placed against upper-level balustrades | Overhead glass and open edges |
| In the records | Echo making announcements hard to understand | Comfort, condensation and acoustics |

sections.heading: What the space does and what it contains
sections.markdown:
Lobbies and atria are the large internal volumes that organise a building: ground floor lobbies leading to lifts, and multi-storey atria that bring daylight into deep plans and connect floors visually. They combine architectural finishes, high-level glazing and lighting, open edges at upper levels, and in atria, smoke control systems that make the open volume safe in a fire. Functionally they must be safe to stand under and beside, comfortable, maintainable at height, and controllable in a fire.

| Element group | Typical provision | What matters for the space |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Overhead glazing and roofs | Glazed atrium roofs, skylights, clerestories | Overhead glass safety; leaks; heat gain; cleaning |
| Edges and balustrades | Balustrades on upper-level walkways and bridges | Fall protection; climbability; glass safety |
| Smoke control | Atrium smoke exhaust, make-up air, smoke curtains | Keeping smoke above people in a fire |
| Finishes | Stone floors, feature walls, high ceilings | Durability, slip, acoustics |
| High-level lighting and equipment | Feature lighting, speakers, detectors at height | Maintenance access |
| Climate control | Air conditioning, perimeter heating, natural ventilation | Stratification, solar gain, draughts |

sections.heading: How long it stays fit for purpose
sections.markdown:
Atrium glazing seals and gaskets last fifteen to twenty-five years, smoke control equipment twenty to twenty-five and high-level lighting fifteen to twenty, while balustrades last thirty to fifty. Height makes every renewal expensive, so access usually decides when the work is done.

| Component or quality | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Finishes refurbishment | 15 to 25 years | Market; wear |
| Atrium glazing seals and gaskets | 15 to 25 years | UV; movement |
| Atrium glass | 25 to 40 years | Breakage; coatings |
| Smoke control equipment | 20 to 25 years | Testing; controls |
| High-level lighting | 15 to 20 years | Technology; access |
| Balustrades | 30 to 50 years | Fixings; code changes |

What shortens fitness for purpose: maintenance access that was never designed, so high-level items are neglected; solar gain and stratification that make atria hot at upper levels; alterations that enclose or infill the volume and undermine smoke control; acoustic problems as hard finishes reflect noise.

Atria are often the oldest-looking part of a refurbished building, because their height makes them the hardest and most expensive area to refresh.

sections.heading: Overhead glass and open edges
sections.markdown:
Atrium roofs and high glazing overhang occupied floors. Overhead glass must hold together when broken; older monolithic toughened or wired glass can fall. High-level fittings, signs and decorations can also fall if fixings corrode or are disturbed.

Atria create open edges on every upper floor. Balustrades below current heights, with climbable rails or furniture placed against them, and glass panels that can break and fall, create fall risks to people above and impact risks to people below. Some buildings have needed screens to prevent deliberate falls.

An atrium is judged first on what can fall. Overhead glass that is not laminated, fittings with corroded fixings, and people at open edges all sit above others, so the questions are what the glass is, how the balustrades compare with current heights and climbability, and what stands against them.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Planters, furniture or displays against upper-level balustrades | Edges made climbable by what stands against them. Items within reach of the top rail on an upper level. | Move the items away, and set rules and fixings that keep them away. |
| A cracked overhead pane with no sign of impact | Possible spontaneous breakage of toughened glass. The glass marking and fracture origin, and the glass schedule. | Protect the area below now, and replace with laminated glass. |
| An upper-level balustrade that seems low, or with gaps a child could pass through | Barrier that may not prevent a fall. Height and openings measured against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Raise or infill the barrier, and keep climbable furniture away from it. |

sections.heading: Smoke control
sections.markdown:
An atrium connects floors that would otherwise be separate compartments. In a fire, smoke rises into the atrium and must be exhausted fast enough to stay above people. Failed fans, blocked make-up air, enclosed floors and untested systems turn the atrium into a smoke chimney.

An atrium joins floors that would otherwise be separate compartments, so its smoke control is what keeps a fire on one floor from filling the others. That design rests on the atrium's geometry: infilling a floor, enclosing a space or adding a bridge changes how smoke moves, and the design must be checked again.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Smoke test fails to clear the atrium | Exhaust or make-up air shortfall, or changed geometry. Integrated test; layout review. | Repair fans and dampers, restore make-up air, or have the fire engineer redesign for the changed geometry. |
| A new floor infill, bridge or enclosure inside the atrium | An alteration that may invalidate the smoke design. The geometry compared with the fire engineering report. | Have the fire engineer review it before approval, and retest the system. |

sections.heading: Comfort, condensation and acoustics
sections.markdown:
Atria stratify: hot air collects at the top, making upper walkways uncomfortable, while the ground floor is cold and draughty. Glazed roofs gain heat in summer and lose it in winter, and condensation drips from cold glass and frames.

Large volumes with hard finishes echo, making announcements unintelligible and lobbies noisy.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Drips onto the floor in cold weather without rain | Condensation on cold glass or frames. Weather correlation; humidity. | Control the condensation with warm air over the glazing, thermally broken frames, or humidity control. |
| Drips in rain | Glazing seal or gutter failure. Water test. | Water test, and renew the seals and gutters. |
| Upper levels hot, ground floor draughty | Stratification and stack effect. Temperature profile. | Add high-level exhaust or destratification fans, solar control, and draught lobbies at entries. |
| Announcements hard to understand | Echo from a large volume with hard finishes. Reverberation measured, or obvious to the ear. | Add absorptive panels, baffles or finishes. |

sections.heading: Maintenance at height
sections.markdown:
Lights, detectors, speakers and glazing at height that can only be reached by scaffold or large lifts go unmaintained, and failed lights and detectors are left in place.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Many failed high-level lights | No practical maintenance access. Access strategy. | Provide gantries, monorails or winches, or move equipment within reach. |
| Dim circulation routes at night or in winter | Failed fittings or lighting designed for the space when new. Lux survey of the routes against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Replace failed fittings and add lighting where the survey falls short. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Non-laminated overhead glass over occupied areas with breakage history; low or climbable balustrades at upper levels; smoke control failing tests | safety · 4 Essential | Protect, restrict access or rectify now. |
| Leaks damaging finishes; lights and detectors failed at height | failure · 3 Important | Repair now. |
| Smoke control testing due | deadline · 3 Important | At the prescribed interval. |
| Comfort and acoustic problems; worn finishes | condition · 2 Planned | Improve in the near term. |
| Finishes and glazing seals at end of life | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Refurbish. |
| Glass types and smoke design unknown | check · 2 Planned | Assess. |
| Normal | nil · 1 Routine | Routine. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A building surveyor or façade engineer with a fire engineer and services engineer. The checks below start at the edges and overhead, then test the smoke control against its design, and plan how every high-level item will be reached.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Overhead glazing survey | Glass types, seals, gutters, cracked or loose panes, from access equipment. |
| Edge survey | Balustrade heights, openings, climbability, glass type and fixings at every upper level. |
| Smoke control review | Against the fire engineering report, with integrated testing. |
| Comfort survey | Temperature profile by level, draughts, solar gain, condensation. |
| Acoustic assessment | Where announcements or noise are a problem. |
| Maintenance access review | How every high-level item is reached. |
| Alteration review | Changes to the volume since design. |

The report should state safety items, smoke control status, comfort and acoustic issues, and a maintenance access and refurbishment plan.

Inspection of high-level elements is best combined with scheduled glazing cleaning or smoke testing, when access equipment is already in place.

sections.heading: Making safe, restoring smoke control or refurbishing
sections.markdown:
Overhead glass that can fall, unsafe edges and smoke control that fails its test come first. After that, the work treats comfort and acoustics, provides access so high-level items are maintained, and refurbishes in one high-level campaign rather than piecemeal.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Overhead glass | Replace with laminated glass or add protective screens; renew seals and gutters. | Wherever overhead glass is not laminated, or seals leak. |
| Balustrades | Raise heights, close climbable rails, replace monolithic glass, add screens where risk warrants. | Wherever balustrades are low, climbable or glazed with monolithic glass. |
| Smoke control | Repair fans and dampers, restore make-up air, redesign after alterations. | Wherever smoke control fails its test, or the atrium has been altered. |
| Comfort | High-level exhaust or destratification fans, solar control glazing or films, draught lobbies at entries. | Where upper levels overheat, or the ground floor is draughty. |
| Acoustic treatment | Absorptive panels, baffles and finishes. | Where announcements are hard to understand. |
| Maintenance access | Gantries, monorails, winches for lights, or relocation of equipment to reachable positions. | Wherever high-level items cannot be reached. |
| Refurbishment | Refurbish the finishes and lighting. | At the end of the cycle, in one high-level campaign. |
| Edge management | Rules and fixings that keep furniture, planters and display items away from balustrades so they cannot be climbed. | Wherever furniture or displays stand near balustrades. |
| Condensation control | Thermally broken frames, warm air washes over glazing, or humidity control where drips recur. | Where drips recur in cold weather. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
High-level work in atria is dominated by access: scaffolds over occupied floors, specialist lifts and out-of-hours work. Glazing and balustrade works are per pane or per metre plus access. Smoke control works and redesign are lump sums. Maintenance access installations are lump sums that reduce future costs. Refurbishment is a lump sum.

Safety items are immediate or code compliance; smoke testing recurs; refurbishment is lifecycle; access installations are improvements with operating savings.

Because access is the main cost, inspection, cleaning, lamp replacement and glazing repairs should be bundled into a single high-level campaign every few years rather than done piecemeal.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a look upward cannot: what the overhead glass is, what the smoke design assumes, and whether anything has changed since. Ask for them before approving any works inside the volume.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Fire engineering report and atrium smoke design | What the smoke control is designed to do, and on what geometry. |
| Integrated smoke control test reports | Whether the smoke control works as a whole. |
| Glass schedules for roof and balustrades | Whether overhead and balustrade glass is laminated. |
| Maintenance access strategy and equipment certification | How high-level items are reached, and whether the equipment is certified. |
| Leak and condensation history | Whether drips come from leaks or condensation. |
| Records of alterations within the atrium | Whether the volume has changed since it was designed. |
| Balustrade and edge protection certificates | Whether the edges were certified. |
| Comfort and condensation complaints by level | Where comfort problems concentrate. |
| High-level lighting and detector maintenance records | Whether high-level lights and detectors are maintained. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Atria are misread when works within the volume are treated as ordinary fit-out, when their problems are handed to a single specialist, and when every drip is taken for a leak.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| It is only a fit-out | Any change that encloses, infills or alters an atrium can invalidate its smoke control design. Check the fire engineering basis before approving works within the volume. |
| One consultant can cover it | Problems in atria are usually of three kinds: safety at the edges and overhead, smoke behaviour in a fire, and comfort and maintenance. Each needs its own specialist, and the smoke question is the one most often left untested after alterations. |
| Drips mean a leak | Drips onto the floor in cold weather without rain are condensation on cold glass or frames; drips in rain point to seals or gutters. Weather correlation separates them before anyone reseals. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market treats atria as a special case for fire and smoke, and sets rules for overhead glass and guarding at open edges. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Atria, glazing, guarding and smoke control | The National Construction Code treats atria as a special case, with smoke hazard management, sprinklers and separation requirements; AS 1288 governs overhead and barrier glass and AS 1668.1 smoke control; changes to an atrium generally need fire engineering review and building approval. | Approved Document B and BS 9999 cover atria, including when they may connect floors and what smoke control they need, with smoke control components to the BS EN 12101 series; Approved Document K covers guarding and glazing; higher-risk residential atria fall under the Building Safety Act 2022. | International Building Code Section 404 governs atriums, requiring sprinklers and smoke control designed and tested under Section 909 and NFPA 92; guards follow Section 1015 and overhead glazing Chapter 24; alterations need fire department review. |

sections.heading: Worked example: an atrium with a new bridge
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 1990s office atrium had a link bridge and a meeting pod added on two upper levels during a refurbishment. Several high-level lights have been out for a year, drips fall onto the lobby floor on cold mornings, planters stand against an upper balustrade, and the glass schedule for the roof cannot be found.

The bridge and pod change the atrium's geometry, so the smoke design may no longer hold until the fire engineer has reviewed it and the system has been retested. Planters against a balustrade make the edge climbable. Drips on cold, dry mornings point to condensation, and the dead lights point to no practical access.

So the register carries the smoke control review and integrated test as a check on a safety system, the planters moved now, glass identification as a check line, condensation control, and a maintenance access solution with the lights replaced in one high-level campaign.

pages.title: Localised HVAC
pages.question: How do split systems, VRF, rooftop units and heat pumps fail, and when does refrigerant or electronics end their life?
pages.answer: Localised systems end their life on electronics, outdoor coils and refrigerant. Inverter boards fail after power disturbances and parts for older models disappear; outdoor coils corrode in salt air; flare joints leak; R22 units are almost unserviceable and R410A faces rising costs. VRF puts large refrigerant charges in occupied rooms and needs concentration limits and leak detection. Gas rooftop units risk carbon monoxide from cracked heat exchangers.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about localised hvac; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.

pages.searchTitle: Split systems, VRF and packaged units: leaks, refrigerant, noise and replacement

questions.question: Is it worth repairing an old split system?
questions.answer: Repairs to drains, fans and sensors usually are; a failed compressor or main board on a unit more than about ten years old, or on R22, usually means replacement.

questions.question: Why does my air conditioner keep needing gas?
questions.answer: It has a refrigerant leak. Pressure test and repair it rather than regassing.

questions.question: Why is water dripping from the indoor unit?
questions.answer: A blocked condensate drain, or a failed condensate pump.

questions.question: Can air conditioners be too noisy for neighbours?
questions.answer: Yes. Australian state noise regulations restrict air conditioner noise at neighbouring residences, particularly at night, and in the United Kingdom noise limits apply to air-source heat pumps on dwellings.

questions.question: How long do split systems last?
questions.answer: Wall-mounted splits 10 to 15 years, ducted reverse-cycle 12 to 18, and VRF and packaged rooftop units 15 to 20.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Local system problems show outdoors as corroded coils and crowded units, indoors as water stains and dirty filters, around the building as noise, and in the repair records. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Outdoor units | Nameplate data: year and refrigerant | Refrigerant, VRF and compressors |
| Outdoor units | Coil corrosion; fins flattened or missing | Outdoor units, coils and electronics |
| Outdoor units | Units crowded together or against walls | Outdoor units, coils and electronics |
| Outdoor units | Oil stains at pipe joints (refrigerant leaks) | Refrigerant, VRF and compressors |
| Outdoor units | Pipe insulation degraded by UV | Outdoor units, coils and electronics |
| Outdoor units | Rust on casings and mounting frames | Outdoor units, coils and electronics |
| Indoor units | Water stains below indoor units | Ducted systems and condensate |
| Indoor units | Dust and mould on filters and coils | Ducted systems and condensate |
| Indoor units | Noise; error codes on controllers | Outdoor units, coils and electronics |
| In the records | Installation dates; refrigerant type and charge | Investigation before the scope |
| In the records | Service and repair records; repeated regassing | Refrigerant, VRF and compressors |
| In the records | Strata by-laws on air conditioning | Standards by country |
| In the records | Energy rating labels | Refrigerant, VRF and compressors |
| In the records | Outdoor units on balconies or roofs added piecemeal, with pipes and cables run across façades | Outdoor units, coils and electronics |
| In the records | Noise from outdoor units near bedroom windows of neighbours | Outdoor units, coils and electronics |
| In the records | Condensate discharged onto roofs, balconies or footpaths | Ducted systems and condensate |
