sections.heading: Types of local system
sections.markdown:
Localised HVAC is heating and cooling equipment that serves a room, a dwelling or a tenancy rather than a whole building: split systems and multi-head splits, ducted reverse-cycle systems, variable refrigerant flow (VRF) systems, packaged rooftop units, heat pumps for space and water heating, evaporative coolers, and hydronic or electric underfloor heating. It is the dominant system in Australian houses and apartments, in smaller offices and retail everywhere, and in much of the United States.

| Type | Where it is found | Character |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Wall-mounted split system | Houses, apartments, small offices | Cheap, short-lived; electronics and outdoor coils fail |
| Multi-head split | Apartments, small offices | One outdoor unit, several indoor; whole system fails together |
| Ducted reverse-cycle | Australian houses and townhouses | Indoor unit in the roof space; ductwork and zoning |
| Variable refrigerant flow (VRF/VRS) | Offices, hotels, apartments from the 2000s | Large refrigerant charges piped through the building; branch boxes; proprietary controls |
| Packaged rooftop unit | Retail, industrial, US commercial | Self-contained; often gas heating; exposed to weather |
| Air-source heat pump | Houses and small commercial; replacing boilers | Space heating and hot water; refrigerant rules apply |
| Evaporative cooler | Australian houses in dry climates | Pads, pump and fan on the roof; water quality |
| Underfloor heating | Houses, apartments, some commercial | Hydronic pipes or electric mats in slabs; long life, hard to repair |

Ownership is often split. In strata buildings, indoor units belong to the lot, outdoor units sit on common property roofs or balconies, and refrigerant pipework passes through common property. In offices, tenants may own and maintain their own units. Replacement, access and refrigerant leaks then involve several parties.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Split systems last ten to fifteen years, ducted reverse-cycle twelve to eighteen, and VRF and packaged rooftop units fifteen to twenty. Units installed together tend to fail together, so a building's local systems are best planned as a population rather than one by one.

| Equipment | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Wall-mounted split | 10 to 15 years | Electronics; coastal exposure |
| Ducted reverse-cycle | 12 to 18 years | Run hours; roof space heat |
| VRF outdoor units | 15 to 20 years | Compressor; coastal exposure |
| VRF indoor units and branch boxes | 15 to 20 years | Electronics; fans |
| Packaged rooftop units | 15 to 20 years | Weather; coil corrosion; heat exchanger |
| Air-source heat pumps | 15 to 20 years | Cycling; coastal exposure |
| Evaporative coolers | 10 to 15 years | Water quality; pads; corrosion |
| Underfloor heating pipe in slab | 40 years and more | Pipe type; oxygen barrier |
| Underfloor electric mats | 20 to 30 years | Damage at installation |

What shortens life: coastal air on outdoor coils and casings; poor installation: refrigerant flare joints that leak, pipework not pressure tested, condensate drains without fall; outdoor units crammed together or boxed in, recirculating hot air; electrical supply problems: surges and voltage dips damage inverter electronics; no maintenance: filters and coils never cleaned; obsolete refrigerants.

sections.heading: Refrigerant, VRF and compressors
sections.markdown:
Splits leak at flare joints and brazed connections; VRF systems, with long runs and many joints, can lose large charges. Equipment on R22 is now hard to service anywhere, and units on R410A face rising refrigerant costs as HFCs are phased down; newer units use R32 and other lower-GWP refrigerants that are mildly flammable (A2L) and need different installation rules.

VRF systems put a large refrigerant charge into pipework running through occupied spaces. Codes limit how much refrigerant may be in a room relative to its volume, and require leak detection and other measures for small rooms. Systems are proprietary: controls, branch boxes and parts tie the building to one manufacturer.

Compressors fail from low refrigerant charge (overheating), liquid refrigerant returning to the compressor (slugging), short cycling on oversized units, and electrical faults. In inverter units the compressor is usually outlived by the electronics; in older fixed-speed units it is usually the end.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unit regassed repeatedly | Refrigerant leak. Leak test; larger systems are also held to leak-rate triggers in some markets (Thresholds by market). | Pressure test and repair the leak, rather than regassing. |
| Unit runs continuously and never reaches setpoint | Undersized, low refrigerant, or fouled coils. Load calculation; refrigerant pressures; coil condition. | Check the charge, coils and sizing; repair or resize. |
| Unit starts and stops every few minutes | Oversized or controls fault. Load; thermostat location. | Check the controls; replace oversized units at renewal. |
| Many units of the same age failing together | End of life across the population. Installation dates; parts availability. | Replace the units as one programme, or consolidate them into VRF or a central system. |

sections.heading: Outdoor units, coils and electronics
sections.markdown:
Aluminium fins corrode and separate from tubes in salt air; capacity falls on the hottest and coldest days. Units within a few hundred metres of surf can fail in under ten years without coated coils.

Inverter boards, sensors and communication boards fail, often after power disturbances. Parts for older models stop being available, and a single board failure can make a ten-year-old unit uneconomic to repair.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Capacity loss on hot days | Coil corrosion or hot air recirculation. Coil condition; siting. | Clean the coils or replace them with coated coils, and clear any recirculation. |
| Unit dead after a storm | Electronics failure. Error codes; board replacement availability. | Repair the board, or replace an older unit. |

sections.heading: Ducted systems and condensate
sections.markdown:
Ducted reverse-cycle systems in roof spaces suffer from the same ductwork faults as larger systems: flexible ducts kink, tear and disconnect, roof space heat degrades insulation, and zone dampers fail. A failing ducted system often has a sound unit and failed ductwork.

Indoor unit drains block or lose fall; condensate pumps fail; water leaks onto walls, ceilings and floors.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Water stains below indoor unit | Blocked drain or failed pump. Drain inspection. | Clear the drain or replace the condensate pump. |
| Ducted system weak in some rooms | Disconnected or kinked flexible duct. Roof space inspection. | Reconnect and straighten the flexible ducts. |

sections.heading: Rooftop units, evaporative coolers and other systems
sections.markdown:
Gas-fired rooftop units have heat exchangers that crack with age, risking carbon monoxide entering the supply air; economisers seize; casings leak water into the building.

Pads clog with minerals; pumps fail; water stagnates in the tank; casings corrode; drains and bleed fail. Water must be managed to limit scale and microbial growth.

Hydronic underfloor circuits lose flow from sludge, especially where older plastic pipe without an oxygen barrier lets oxygen into the system; pipe damaged by later fixings leaks into the slab. Electric mats fail where damaged at installation, and the fault must be located before the floor is lifted.

Heat pump water heaters store water at lower temperatures than gas or electric units; they rely on periodic boost cycles to control Legionella. Units with failed boost elements or controls set too low carry that risk.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Carbon monoxide alarm near a rooftop unit supply | Cracked heat exchanger. Combustion inspection. | Shut the unit down; replace the heat exchanger or the unit. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cracked heat exchanger on a gas rooftop unit; refrigerant leak in a small room without detection | safety · 4 Essential | Isolate now. |
| Unit failed serving a critical space | failure · 3 Important | Repair or replace now. |
| R22 equipment where servicing is restricted | deadline · 4 Essential | Replace before the next major repair. |
| Coil corrosion, leaks, drain faults | condition · 3 Important | Repair in the near term. |
| Units at end of life | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Replace on cycle. |
| Refrigerant type unknown; VRF compliance unknown | check · 2 Planned | Inspect. |
| Normal wear | nil · 1 Routine | Routine maintenance. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A mechanical services contractor or engineer; for strata and multi-tenant buildings, the inventory is the most important output because ownership is fragmented. The checks below build an inventory first, of units, ages, refrigerants and owners, then inspect a sample and read the repair records.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Inventory | Of every indoor and outdoor unit: type, make, model, year, refrigerant and charge, capacity, location, area served, and owner (lot, tenant or common property). |
| Sample condition inspection | Of outdoor coils, casings, pipe insulation, mounting frames, electrical isolators, indoor units, drains and filters. |
| Refrigerant review | Repeated regassing in service records, leak testing, and the refrigerant's servicing and supply outlook. |
| VRF assessment | System charges against the smallest rooms served, leak detection and alarms where required, branch box and controller support, refrigerant pipework condition. |
| Combustion inspection | Of gas-fired rooftop units, including heat exchanger inspection. |
| Noise assessment | Where outdoor units are near neighbouring dwellings. |
| Electrical capacity | Where heat pumps are replacing gas heating. |
| Siting review | Recirculation, access for maintenance, roof and balcony loads, waterproofing penetrations. |

The report should give a full inventory with condition and remaining life, refrigerant position, safety items, ownership, and a replacement strategy (like for like, consolidation, or a central system).

sections.heading: Repairing, replacing or consolidating
sections.markdown:
Safety comes first: a cracked heat exchanger on a gas rooftop unit, or refrigerant concentrations above the limits in small rooms. After that, the choice between repair and replacement turns on each unit's age and refrigerant, and many scattered units may be better consolidated.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Repair or replace | Repair is usually worthwhile for drains, fans and sensors; a failed compressor or main board on a unit more than about ten years old, or on R22, usually means replacement. | For every failed unit. |
| Leak repair | Leak repair with pressure testing. | Rather than repeated regassing. |
| Coil protection | Factory-coated or treated coils near the coast; relocation away from salt spray where possible. | Near the coast. |
| Replacement | Current refrigerants (R32 and other A2L refrigerants, or natural refrigerants), installed to the safety requirements for A2L equipment, with higher efficiency units. | At the end of a unit's life, or where R22 servicing is restricted. |
| VRF compliance | Leak detection and alarms, or reconfiguration to reduce charges, where refrigerant concentration limits are exceeded in small rooms. | Where refrigerant concentration limits are exceeded in small rooms. |
| Rooftop units | Heat exchanger replacement or unit replacement where cracks are found; economiser repairs. | Where heat exchangers crack or economisers fail. |
| Consolidation | Replacing many individual splits with VRF or a central system, which also clears façades and balconies. | Where many individual splits clutter the building. |
| Noise control | Acoustic enclosures, relocation, or quieter units where neighbours are affected. | Where neighbours are affected. |
| Strata coordination | By-laws setting standards for units on common property and a planned replacement programme. | In strata buildings. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Replacement is priced per unit for splits and ducted systems, per system for VRF, and per unit for rooftop units, with crane hire for rooftop and high-level outdoor units. Refrigerant recovery and disposal, electrical upgrades, structural support for new plant, roof and waterproofing works at penetrations, and making good to finishes add to each replacement. In strata buildings, costs split between lot owners and the owners corporation according to ownership.

Individual unit replacement is lifecycle and, for small units, often treated as a recurring allowance rather than discrete lines. Safety items are immediate; refrigerant-driven replacement can carry a deadline.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a walk around the units cannot: how old each unit is, what refrigerant it uses, and who owns it. Ask for an inventory first, since the population matters more than any one unit.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Inventory of units with installation dates, refrigerants and owners | How many units there are, how old, on which refrigerants, and who owns each. |
| Service and repair records, including regassing | Which units leak, and how often they have been regassed. |
| VRF design documents, refrigerant charges and leak detection details | Whether VRF systems meet the refrigerant concentration limits. |
| Combustion inspection records for gas rooftop units | Whether gas rooftop units have been checked for cracked heat exchangers. |
| Strata by-laws and approvals for units on common property | Whether units on common property were approved. |
| Noise complaints | Whether neighbours have complained about noise. |
| Electrical supply capacity records where heat pumps are planned | Whether the supply can take more heat pumps. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Local systems are misread when a unit is regassed rather than repaired, when each unit is judged alone, and when a major failure on an old unit is repaired as a matter of course.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| Top it up | A unit regassed repeatedly has a refrigerant leak. Pressure test and repair it, rather than regassing. |
| Fix each unit as it fails | Many units of the same age failing together are at the end of their life across the population. Plan replacement as a programme, or consolidate into VRF or a central system. |
| A big failure is worth repairing | A failed compressor or main board on a unit more than about ten years old, or on R22, usually means replacement rather than repair. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market licenses refrigerant work and sets safety rules for equipment, and each sets efficiency, noise and approval rules. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Refrigerants and equipment safety | Refrigerant work requires an Australian Refrigeration Council licence; equipment safety follows AS/NZS 5149 and, for A2L refrigerants, AS/NZS 60335.2.40; energy labelling and minimum efficiency are set under the Greenhouse and Energy Minimum Standards (GEMS) scheme. | The GB fluorinated gas regulations govern refrigerants and leak checks; heat pumps installed for government grants need MCS certification. | EPA Section 608 governs refrigerant handling; A2L equipment follows UL 60335-2-40 and the model mechanical codes. |
| Efficiency, noise and approvals | State noise regulations restrict air conditioner noise at neighbouring residences, particularly at night. In strata schemes, by-laws govern outdoor units on common property. | Approved Document L sets efficiency; permitted development rules and noise limits apply to air-source heat pumps on dwellings. | Department of Energy minimum efficiency standards apply; the Technology Transitions rule restricts higher-GWP refrigerants in new residential and light commercial equipment. |

sections.heading: Worked example: thirty split systems in a strata building
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 2000s apartment building has around thirty wall-mounted split systems, installed piecemeal by owners over several years, with outdoor units on balconies and the roof. Several have been regassed repeatedly, some use R22, a neighbour complains about night-time noise, and the strata has no by-law on units.

Repeated regassing points to leaks, and the R22 units face servicing restrictions. Units of a similar age will fail together, so they are planned as a population, not one by one. Noise near bedroom windows and units on common property are matters for the strata.

So the register carries the R22 units as a deadline line, leak repair, a by-law and a planned replacement programme for the strata, noise control for the complaint, and consolidation into a central system considered at renewal.

thresholds.rule: Appliances holding 50 lb (about 23 kg) or more of ozone-depleting refrigerant: repair when leaking more than 10 per cent a year for comfort cooling, 20 per cent for commercial refrigeration, 30 per cent for industrial process refrigeration

source.title: 40 CFR 82.157 Appliance maintenance and leak repair

pages.title: Main Electrical Supply
pages.question: How do main switchboards, transformers and supply equipment fail, and when does capacity rather than condition decide replacement?
pages.answer: Main supply equipment fails invisibly until it fails catastrophically. Terminations loosen and overheat; breakers seize when never operated and lose maker support; HV insulation degrades by partial discharge; transformer oil breaks down. Open-bus and fused boards expose workers to arc flash. Thermography under load and breaker testing find the faults. Capacity often decides replacement first: electrification, cooling and EV charging run out of supply before the board wears out.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about main electrical supply; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: HV and LV switchgear, transformers, main switchboards

pages.searchTitle: Main switchboards and supply: hot spots, breakers, arc flash and capacity

questions.question: Is a switchboard that works safe?
questions.answer: Not necessarily. Overheating, water exposure and missing covers are safety findings, and the faults that matter are invisible until the board fails.

questions.question: What does a hot spot on thermography mean?
questions.answer: Usually a loose or overloaded connection. Re-terminate and torque it, then re-survey to confirm.

questions.question: Can our building take EV chargers and heat pumps?
questions.answer: Check a year of maximum demand against the supply agreement first. Network upgrades have long lead times, so apply early and manage demand meanwhile.

questions.question: Why does the main breaker trip for small faults?
questions.answer: Loss of discrimination. A protection review resets or replaces devices so the nearest breaker trips first.

questions.question: How long do main switchboards last?
questions.answer: LV main switchboards 30 to 40 years, though their air and moulded case breakers reach the end of support after 20 to 25.

questions.question: The electricity network says we can't add more load. What can we do?
questions.answer: The supply capacity has been reached. Apply to the network early for an upgrade, and manage demand meanwhile.

questions.question: Is it a problem that the switch room is used for storage?
questions.answer: Yes. There is no safe working space in front of the equipment. Clear the room and mark the working space.

questions.question: A circuit breaker did not trip when it was tested. Is that serious?
questions.answer: Yes. A seized mechanism or failed trip unit means the breaker cannot be relied on. Replace or retrofit it.

questions.question: Why is the neutral running hot?
questions.answer: Harmonics or an unbalanced load. Measure harmonics and balance, then filter or rebalance the load.

questions.question: Why is a whole circuit showing hot on the thermal imaging survey?
questions.answer: A hot spot across a whole circuit is overload, not a loose connection. Measure the load against the rating; redistribute it, or upgrade the circuit.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Main supply problems show at the switchboard as heat, burn marks and missing covers, in the switchroom as water and storage, and in thermography, test and demand records. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| In the switchroom | Board type and era from the nameplate; open busbars; fuses; asbestos labels | Protective devices and arc flash |
| In the switchroom | Discolouration, burn marks or melted insulation at terminations | Connections, insulation and transformers |
| In the switchroom | Warm surfaces; hum or buzzing; smell of hot insulation | Connections, insulation and transformers |
| In the switchroom | Water staining, pipes overhead, damp; storage in front of the board | Capacity and switchroom conditions |
| In the switchroom | Missing covers, unlabelled circuits, open escutcheons | Protective devices and arc flash |
| In the switchroom | Surge protection status indicators | Protective devices and arc flash |
| In the switchroom | Transformer oil leaks; bund condition | Connections, insulation and transformers |
| In the records | Thermographic surveys and their findings | Connections, insulation and transformers |
| In the records | Breaker testing and maintenance records | Protective devices and arc flash |
| In the records | Periodic inspection and test reports | Investigation before the scope |
| In the records | Maximum demand data and the supply agreement | Capacity and switchroom conditions |
| In the records | Transformer oil tests; HV partial discharge tests | Connections, insulation and transformers |
| In the records | Single-line diagrams; protection studies; arc-flash study | Protective devices and arc flash |
| In the records | Asbestos and PCB registers | Connections, insulation and transformers |

sections.heading: Parts of the main supply
sections.markdown:
The main electrical supply brings power into the building and splits it to the sub-mains: the network connection, any high-voltage switchgear and transformers the owner is responsible for, the low-voltage main switchboard with its main switch and protective devices, metering, power factor correction, surge protection and the main earthing arrangement. Distribution beyond the main switchboard, emergency power and solar have their own pages.

| Component | Where it is found | What goes wrong |
| --- | --- | --- |
| HV switchgear (ring main units, circuit breakers) | Buildings with their own substation: large offices, hospitals, campuses, industrial | Insulation breakdown (partial discharge); oil-filled units leak; SF₆ units leak a potent greenhouse gas; mechanisms seize |
| Transformers (oil-filled or dry-type) | Owner-operated substations | Insulation ageing; oil degradation; leaks; older units may contain PCBs |
| LV main switchboard | Every building | Hot terminations; ageing breakers; unsupported devices; inadequate arc-fault containment; water in the switchroom |
| Air circuit breakers and moulded case breakers | Main and large sub-main protection | Mechanisms seize when never operated; trip units drift |
| Metering | Network meters; check meters; embedded network meters | Ownership and accuracy disputes |
| Power factor correction | Commercial and industrial | Capacitor failure and fire; older units may contain PCBs |
| Earthing and bonding | Every building | Corroded electrodes; disconnected bonds |
| Surge protection | Main and critical boards | Devices reach end of life after surges and stop protecting |

Era tells a lot. Boards from before the 1980s often have open busbars, rewireable or cartridge fuses, and asbestos-based arc shields or backing boards. Boards from the 1980s and 1990s have breakers whose makers no longer support them. Modern boards are built to defined forms of separation and with arc-fault containment. Capacity is the other dimension: a board in good order can still be the constraint on electrification, cooling upgrades and electric vehicle charging.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Main switchboards last thirty to forty years and transformers twenty-five to fifty, but their breakers reach the end of manufacturer support after twenty to twenty-five. Long before anything wears out, electrification and EV charging can make the supply too small.

| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| LV main switchboard | 30 to 40 years | Switchroom environment; loading; maintenance |
| Air and moulded case breakers | 20 to 25 years before support ends | Operation and testing; manufacturer support |
| Oil-filled transformers | 30 to 50 years | Loading; oil condition; cooling |
| Dry-type transformers | 25 to 35 years | Heat; dust |
| HV switchgear | 30 to 40 years | Insulation; type (oil, SF₆, vacuum) |
| Power factor correction capacitors | 10 to 15 years | Harmonics; heat |
| Surge protection devices | Until they absorb enough surges; check indicators | Surge exposure |
| Incoming cables | Life of the building | Overload; damage |

What shortens life: heat, damp and dust in switchrooms; switchrooms used as storerooms; water pipes over boards; loose terminations, which heat, oxidise and get worse; breakers that are never operated, whose mechanisms seize; load growth past ratings; harmonics from electronic loads, which overheat neutrals, transformers and capacitors.

sections.heading: Connections, insulation and transformers
sections.markdown:
Bolted connections at busbars, breakers and cable lugs loosen with thermal cycling, vibration and poor installation; resistance rises, the joint heats, oxidises and loosens further. Aluminium conductors are especially prone. Overheating ends in an arc fault or fire, and the early stage is visible only on a thermographic survey under load.

Insulation in HV switchgear, transformers and cables degrades with heat, moisture and electrical stress. In HV equipment, partial discharge (small sparks within voids in insulation) erodes it from within until it fails. It can be detected by testing long before failure.

Transformer oil absorbs moisture and breaks down; insulation paper ages; overheating and internal faults generate gases in the oil that can be measured. Leaks are an environmental and fire risk. Transformers made before about 1980 may contain PCBs.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hot spot at a termination on thermography | Loose or overloaded connection. Temperature rise against adjacent phases; torque check after isolation. | Re-terminate and torque the connection, then re-survey to confirm. |
| Hot neutral | Harmonics or unbalanced load. Harmonic measurement. | Measure harmonics and balance; filter or rebalance the load. |
| Rising gases in transformer oil | Internal overheating or arcing. Dissolved gas analysis pattern. | Retest, and plan oil treatment or transformer replacement. |
| Partial discharge readings on HV gear | Insulation deterioration. Repeat testing; trend. | Monitor it, and plan replacement of the switchgear. |

sections.heading: Protective devices and arc flash
sections.markdown:
Breakers protect against overload and fault; if they do not open, a fault becomes a fire. Mechanisms seize when never exercised; electronic trip units drift; and breakers whose makers have stopped supporting them cannot be repaired. Changes to the installation over the years can leave devices that no longer discriminate, so a minor fault trips the main supply.

Older open-bus boards and boards without arc-fault containment expose anyone working on or near them to arc flash: an explosive release of energy during a fault. This is a direct hazard to electricians and the reason for de-energised working rules and arc-flash studies.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Main breaker trips for faults on final circuits | Loss of discrimination. Protection study. | Review the protection settings to restore discrimination. |
| Breaker fails to trip on test | Seized mechanism or failed trip unit. Primary or secondary injection test. | Replace or retrofit the breaker; it cannot be relied on. |

sections.heading: Capacity and switchroom conditions
sections.markdown:
Maximum demand may already be close to the supply rating. Electrification of heating, larger cooling plant, data loads and electric vehicle charging all add load, and network supply upgrades take months to years. The main switchboard is often where capacity runs out first.

Basement switchrooms flood, and pipes or gutters above boards leak. Water on a switchboard is an immediate hazard and a common cause of long outages.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hot spot across a whole circuit | Overload. Load measurement against rating. | Measure the load; redistribute it, or upgrade the circuit. |
| Network refuses additional load | Supply capacity reached. Maximum demand; supply agreement. | Apply to the network early, and manage demand meanwhile. |
| Switchroom used for storage, or boards blocked by furniture | No safe working space. Clearances in front of the equipment against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Clear the room and mark the working space. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Exposed live parts; burning or overheating; water on or above the board; PCB oil leaking | safety · 4 Essential | Isolate or protect now. |
| Main board or transformer failed; building without supply | failure · 4 Essential | Restore now; temporary supply. |
| Periodic inspection and testing due | deadline · 4 Essential | At the interval set by the regulation or standard. |
| Thermographic hot spots; breakers failing tests; unsupported devices; partial discharge | condition · 3 Important | Repair in the near term. |
| Board at end of life; open-bus or fused boards | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Plan replacement. |
| Capacity unknown for electrification or EV charging; no recent thermography | check · 2 Planned | Assess. |
| Normal maintenance | nil · 1 Routine | Routine. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
An electrical engineer or licensed electrical contractor leads; HV equipment needs an HV-qualified specialist. The checks below start with thermography, breaker test results and the single-line diagram, then look at capacity against the loads planned for the building.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Records review | Single-line diagrams, supply agreement, maximum demand data, maintenance and test records, previous inspection reports. |
| Visual inspection | Of the switchroom and boards, covers off where safe to do so. |
| Thermographic survey | Under significant load. |
| Breaker testing | Operation and trip testing by primary or secondary injection. |
| Insulation resistance and earth testing | . |
| HV testing | Partial discharge, insulation, oil analysis including dissolved gases and PCB content. |
| Protection and discrimination study | ; arc-flash study where the board is worked on live. |
| Capacity assessment | Measured maximum demand against supply and board ratings, with planned loads added. |
| Hazardous materials | Asbestos and PCB sampling. |

The report should state whether each component is to be maintained, modernised or replaced, the capacity headroom, safety items, and any supply upgrade needed.

sections.heading: Maintaining, upgrading or replacing
sections.markdown:
Exposed live parts, burning and water near boards come first. After that, most of the work is maintenance that testing has found; board replacement and supply upgrades need early planning, since shutdowns and network lead times are long.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Re-terminate and torque | Re-terminate and torque hot connections, then re-survey to confirm. | Wherever thermography finds hot connections. |
| Breaker maintenance | Exercise, clean and test breakers on a cycle; retrofit unsupported breakers with supported units designed to fit the existing board. | On a cycle, and where breakers are unsupported. |
| Protection review | Reset or replace devices to restore discrimination. | Where faults trip the wrong breaker. |
| Arc-flash mitigation | Arc-flash studies and labelling, remote operation and racking, arc-fault detection, maintenance switches that speed tripping during work, or board replacement. | Where people operate or maintain boards live or nearby. |
| Switchroom works | Remove water pipes from above boards, clear storage, add bunding, drainage and flood protection, ventilate or cool the room, restrict access. | Where water, storage or heat threaten the boards. |
| Board replacement | A staged changeover, with temporary supply or generators and out-of-hours shutdowns, often sized for future electrification. | At the end of the board's life. |
| Transformer works | Oil filtering and drying, gasket and bushing repairs, replacement where tests show advanced deterioration, and PCB removal under hazardous waste rules. | Where oil tests show deterioration, or PCBs are present. |
| HV works | Replacement of oil-filled switchgear with vacuum or SF₆-free alternatives; partial discharge monitoring. | Where oil-filled switchgear is ageing, or partial discharge is rising. |
| Supply upgrade | Application to the network early, since lead times are long; demand management, load shifting, batteries and solar as interim measures. | Where planned loads exceed the supply. |
| Surge protection | Renew and coordinate surge protection at main and critical boards. | Where indicators show it has failed, or it is absent. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Testing, thermography and studies are lump sums, with thermography and breaker testing recurring. Repairs and breaker retrofits are itemised per device. Board replacement is a lump-sum project including temporary supply, out-of-hours shutdowns, cabling changes and commissioning, and can be large relative to the board itself. Transformer and HV works are lump sums, with oil disposal and PCB handling where relevant. Supply upgrades carry network contributions and long lead times, and belong with the electrification, cooling or EV charging project that needs them.

Replacement is lifecycle; safety, periodic testing and arc-flash compliance are code compliance; repairs are repairs and maintenance. Where capacity is uncertain, the usual shape is two-part: a capacity and condition assessment first, then a conditional board and supply upgrade envelope.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a look at the board cannot: what thermography and breaker tests have found, how close the building is to its supply limit, and what loads are coming. Ask for them before any electrification is planned.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Single-line diagram and switchboard drawings | How the supply is arranged, and what each board feeds. |
| Supply agreement, network capacity and maximum demand data for at least a year | How close the building is to its supply limit. |
| Thermographic surveys and maintenance records for the main switchboard | Whether hot spots have been found and fixed. |
| Breaker test records | Whether the breakers trip when they should. |
| Periodic inspection and test reports | What the last periodic inspection found. |
| Transformer oil test results and HV partial discharge test records | Whether transformers and HV gear are deteriorating. |
| Arc-flash study and protection coordination study | How dangerous the boards are to work on, and whether protection is coordinated. |
| Asbestos and PCB registers | Whether boards or transformers contain asbestos or PCBs. |
| Planned load additions: electrification, cooling, EV charging, tenant loads | What new loads the supply will have to carry. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Main switchboards are misread when a board that works is taken to be a sound one, and when capacity is checked only after new loads have been promised.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| It works, so it is sound | A switchboard with signs of overheating, water exposure, or missing covers over live parts is a safety finding. Do not judge a board as sound because it is working: the faults that matter are invisible until it fails. |
| There is plenty of capacity | Electrification, cooling, EV charging and tenant loads can exceed the supply. Check a year of maximum demand against the supply agreement before loads are promised, and apply to the network early, since lead times are long. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets standards for electrical installations and their maintenance, periodic verification, and safe work near live equipment. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Installation, maintenance and safe work | Installations follow AS/NZS 3000, which includes arc-fault containment requirements for larger switchboards; assemblies are built to AS/NZS 61439; periodic verification follows AS/NZS 3019; safe work on low-voltage equipment follows AS/NZS 4836 and the work health and safety regulations, which restrict live work; customer-owned HV installations carry additional obligations under state electrical safety laws; supply upgrades follow the distribution network service provider's connection rules. | BS 7671 governs installations and periodic inspection produces an Electrical Installation Condition Report; the Electricity at Work Regulations 1989 require systems to be maintained safe and restrict live work; switchgear follows BS EN 61439. | NFPA 70 (the National Electrical Code) governs installations; NFPA 70B, now a mandatory standard, sets maintenance intervals and condition assessment; NFPA 70E sets electrical safety and arc-flash requirements, including labelling; OSHA enforces electrical safety at work. |

In the United Kingdom, SF₆ is a regulated fluorinated gas, and supply upgrades follow the distribution network operator's process. In the United States, PCB transformers are regulated by the EPA.

sections.heading: Worked example: a hot spot on the main board
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 1980s office's main switchboard works without trouble. A thermographic survey found a hot spot at one termination, two breakers failed to trip on test last year, a chilled water pipe runs above the board, and the owner plans to add EV charging in the car park.

A working board is not a sound one: the faults that matter are invisible until it fails. The hot termination needs re-terminating; breakers that fail to trip cannot be relied on; water overhead is a safety finding. And the EV charging raises the question of capacity before it is promised.

So the register carries the pipe over the board as a safety line, re-termination and re-survey, breaker replacement or retrofit, and a capacity check against a year of maximum demand before the EV charging is committed.

thresholds.rule: At least 762 mm (30 in) wide and, at the lowest voltage class, 0.9 m (3 ft) deep

pages.title: Main Entrance & Reception Areas
pages.question: How do building entrances and reception areas fail, and which entrance findings are safety issues?
pages.answer: Entrances fail first on safety and access, then on image. Wet polished floors with short or worn matting make the entry the building's main slip location; automatic and revolving doors hurt people when sensors drift; heavy doors, revolving-only entries and high desks exclude people with disability; security turnstiles that do not release on alarm block escape. Then finishes date long before they wear out, and a tired entrance drags down the whole building's market position.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about main entrance & reception areas; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Finishes, joinery, reception desks, wayfinding, architectural features

pages.searchTitle: Building entrances and receptions: slips, door safety, access, security and draughts

questions.question: Why do people slip just inside the entrance?
questions.answer: Usually matting too short or worn, so wet shoes reach polished stone, or a finish slippery when wet. Test the floor wet, and lengthen the matting.

questions.question: Does a revolving door need an accessible door beside it?
questions.answer: Yes. People using wheelchairs, prams or walking aids need an adjacent swing or sliding door.

questions.question: Must security turnstiles release in a fire?
questions.answer: Yes. Turnstiles and access-controlled doors must release on fire alarm and on power failure.

questions.question: Why is the reception area draughty?
questions.answer: No draught lobby, or stack effect in a tall building. A draught lobby or air curtain treats the cause.

questions.question: How often are building entrances refurbished?
questions.answer: Usually every 10 to 15 years, for market positioning more than wear.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Entrance problems show on a walk-through as worn matting and dull floors, doors that strike or stall, barriers to access, draughts at the desk and dated finishes, and in incident records. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On a walk-through | Matting worn, curled, undersized or missing; water and grit marks on floors beyond it | Slips and matting |
| On a walk-through | Scratched, dull or patchy stone floors; slip incidents reported | Slips and matting |
| On a walk-through | Automatic doors that close quickly on people, revolving doors without a working stop, door sensors misaligned | Doors, access and security |
| On a walk-through | A revolving door with no adjacent accessible swing or sliding door | Doors, access and security |
| On a walk-through | Reception desk without a lowered section; no hearing loop signage | Doors, access and security |
| On a walk-through | Turnstiles without a wide accessible gate or fire release; queues at peak | Doors, access and security |
| On a walk-through | Draughts felt at the desk; staff heaters under the reception counter | Draughts and weather |
| On a walk-through | Dated finishes, lighting and directories | Market dating and wayfinding |
| In the records | Slip and trip incident records | Slips and matting |
| In the records | Automatic and revolving door maintenance and safety checks | Doors, access and security |
| In the records | Access control fire release tests | Doors, access and security |
| In the records | Access audit | Doors, access and security |
| In the records | Refurbishment history | Market dating and wayfinding |

sections.heading: What the space does and what it contains
sections.markdown:
The main entrance and reception is where people arrive: the entry doors and any draught lobby, entry matting, the reception or concierge desk, security turnstiles and access control, seating, wayfinding, and the finishes that set the building's first impression. Functionally it has to admit people safely and easily in all weather, control who goes further, welcome visitors and people with disability, and let everyone out fast in an emergency. It is the most heavily used and most visible space in most buildings, and its condition shapes how tenants, buyers and visitors judge the whole asset.

| Element group | Typical provision | What matters for the space |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Entry doors | Automatic sliding, swing or revolving doors; glazed manual doors | Safe operation, accessibility, weather control, egress |
| Draught lobby and matting | Double doors with a lobby; recessed entrance matting | Keeping wind, rain and grit out; slip prevention |
| Reception and concierge | Desk joinery with a lowered section, seating | Accessibility, presentation, security sightlines |
| Security | Turnstiles, access control, CCTV, intercom | Control without blocking escape |
| Floor and wall finishes | Stone, terrazzo, timber, feature walls | Slip resistance, durability, appearance |
| Lighting | Feature and general lighting | Welcome, visibility for security, transition from daylight |
| Wayfinding and signage | Directories, lift signage, statutory signs | Finding lifts, tenancies and exits |

Entrances are refurbished more often than any other base-building space because they carry a building's market position. A tired entrance in an otherwise sound building is one of the most common reasons owners refurbish ahead of the services cycle.

sections.heading: How long it stays fit for purpose
sections.markdown:
An entrance's finishes, desk and lighting are usually renewed every ten to fifteen years, while automatic door operators and turnstiles last ten to fifteen, matting five to ten, and stone floors thirty to fifty with honing and sealing. Market expectations, not wear, usually end the cycle.

| Component or quality | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Entrance refurbishment (finishes, desk, lighting) | 10 to 15 years | Market positioning; wear |
| Automatic door operators | 10 to 15 years | Cycles; maintenance; weather |
| Revolving doors | 20 to 30 years with overhaul | Use; maintenance |
| Entrance matting | 5 to 10 years | Traffic; cleaning |
| Stone and terrazzo floors | 30 to 50 years with honing and sealing | Traffic; grit; cleaning |
| Turnstiles and access control | 10 to 15 years | Technology; vendor support |
| Reception joinery | 10 to 20 years | Use; style |

What shortens fitness for purpose: market expectations for hospitality-style lobbies, end-of-trip access and amenity, which date older entrances quickly; grit and water tracked in when matting is undersized or worn, which scratches floors and makes them slippery; door cycles: automatic doors in busy entrances open thousands of times a day; security upgrades retrofitted without regard to egress, access or appearance; weather exposure where there is no draught lobby or canopy.

sections.heading: Slips and matting
sections.markdown:
Polished stone, terrazzo and glazed tiles become slippery when wet, and entrances are where rain arrives. Undersized or worn matting, no draught lobby, cleaning products that leave residues, and sealers that polish the surface turn the entrance into the building's most common slip location.

Matting works by length. People need several steps on matting to leave water and grit behind before they reach a hard floor; a mat one stride long removes little, and the first metres of polished stone take the rest. That is why slips concentrate just inside the door on wet days.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Slips concentrated inside the entry on wet days | Matting too short or worn; slippery finish. Wet slip resistance test; matting length. | Lengthen and recess the matting; test the floor wet, and treat or replace the finish in the wet zone. |
| Floor dull in a path from the door | Grit tracked past inadequate matting. Matting review. | Extend the matting so grit is removed before the hard floor, and hone the stone. |
| A floor slippery even when dry after cleaning | Cleaning products leaving residue, or a sealer that polishes the surface. Slip resistance improves once the residue is stripped. | Change the cleaning products, strip the sealer, and retest. |
| A lip at the threshold or matwell | Trip at the change of level. Level change measured against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Reset the mat flush, or bevel or ramp the threshold. |

sections.heading: Doors, access and security
sections.markdown:
Automatic doors that close on people, swing doors without safeguarding, and revolving doors that do not stop when obstructed injure people, especially children and older users. Sensors drift out of adjustment, safety beams fail and doors are left on settings that suit throughput rather than safety.

Heavy manual doors, revolving doors without an adjacent accessible door, steps or thresholds, reception desks with no lowered section, and no hearing augmentation exclude people with disability from the first space they meet.

Turnstiles, locked doors and access-controlled entries must release on fire alarm and power failure. Security added after construction often fails this, or creates queues and pinch points in an evacuation.

Every device added to an entrance for security must still let people out. Turnstiles, locked doors and access-controlled entries are tested by releasing them on fire alarm and on power loss; a device that holds in either test is a safety finding, however secure it makes the building.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Door strikes reported | Sensors or safety settings out of adjustment. Door safety check against the standard. | Reset sensors, safety beams and closing speeds to the standard, and record the check. |
| Turnstiles stay locked in an alarm test | Fire interface fault. Interface test. | Repair the fire interface, and test release on alarm and on power loss. |
| A revolving door with no swing or sliding door beside it | No accessible alternative to the revolving door. People using wheelchairs, prams or walking aids cannot pass. | Add an adjacent accessible door. |
| An accessible gate at the turnstiles that is locked, or none at all | Security added without an accessible route. The only wide gate needs staff to open it. | Provide a wide accessible gate that opens without staff and releases on alarm. |
| Entrance door heavy to open, or narrow for a wheelchair | Door force or width short of access needs. Opening force and clear width measured against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Adjust or replace the closer, fit a powered operator, or widen the opening. |

sections.heading: Draughts and weather
sections.markdown:
Entrances without draught lobbies let wind and cold or hot air in, chilling reception staff, wasting energy and driving revolving or air curtain retrofits. Stack effect in tall buildings can make doors hard to open and lobbies draughty.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Draughts and doors hard to open in winter | Stack effect or no draught lobby. Pressure and airflow observation. | Add a draught lobby or air curtain, and review stack effect with the mechanical engineer. |
| Heaters under the reception desk | Draughts reaching the desk. Staff report cold in winter, and the desk faces the doors. | Treat the cause with a draught lobby or air curtain, rather than heaters. |

sections.heading: Market dating and wayfinding
sections.markdown:
Finishes, lighting and joinery date long before they wear out. An entrance that looks old signals an old building, regardless of the condition of the services behind it.

Directories that are out of date, lifts hidden from the entry, and missing signs for accessible routes and amenities confuse visitors and undermine the welcome.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Visitors unable to find lifts or tenants | Wayfinding and sightlines. Observation; directory currency. | Update the directories, and open sightlines to the lifts. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unsafe automatic or revolving doors; slippery entry with incidents; security that does not release on alarm | safety · 4 Essential | Rectify now. |
| Entry doors failed, building insecure or inaccessible | failure · 3 Important | Repair now. |
| Access or security requirements triggered by works or a complaint | deadline · 3 Important | By the required date. |
| Worn matting and floors; draughts; outdated directories | condition · 2 Planned | Repair in the near term. |
| Entrance at the end of its refurbishment cycle or below market | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Plan refurbishment with leasing strategy. |
| No access audit; door safety unchecked | check · 2 Planned | Assess. |
| Normal | nil · 1 Routine | Routine. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A building surveyor or interior consultant leads, with an access consultant, a door specialist and security and fire consultants as needed. The checks below watch the entrance at peak, test the floor wet and the doors against their standard, and test every security device for release on alarm.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Walk-through at peak times | To see queues, door behaviour, matting performance and wayfinding in use. |
| Slip resistance testing | Of floors wet and dry, against the classification needed for an entrance. |
| Door safety check | Of automatic, swing and revolving doors against the relevant standard: sensors, safety beams, closing speeds and forces, stop functions. |
| Access audit | Of the entry sequence: approach, doors, thresholds, desk, hearing augmentation and signage. |
| Security and egress review | Turnstiles and access-controlled doors tested for release on alarm and power loss, and evacuation capacity. |
| Comfort review | Draughts, temperatures and stack effect at the desk and doors. |
| Market review | Against competing buildings and the building's target grade. |

The report should separate safety and access items from presentation and market items, and give a programme for both.

sections.heading: Making safe, improving access or refurbishing
sections.markdown:
Unsafe doors, a slippery entry and security that does not release come first, whatever the budget. Access improvements follow, and refurbishment of finishes, lighting and joinery is timed with the building's leasing strategy.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Matting | Recessed entrance matting long enough to remove water and grit before people reach hard floors. | Wherever matting is short, worn or missing. |
| Floor treatment | Hone and treat stone for wet slip resistance, change cleaning products, or replace finishes in the wet zone. | Where the floor fails a wet slip test. |
| Door safety upgrades | Sensors and safety beams to current standards, closing speeds reset, revolving door stops and an adjacent accessible door. | Wherever doors fail their safety check. |
| Draught lobby or air curtain | A draught lobby or air curtain, to control wind, stack effect and energy loss. | Where draughts reach the desk, or doors are hard to open. |
| Accessible reception | Lowered desk section, hearing loops, seating, clear signage. | Where the desk, hearing augmentation or signage falls short. |
| Security integration | Wide accessible gates, fire release on all locked devices, and evacuation capacity checked. | Wherever security devices are added, or fail to release. |
| Wayfinding | Updated digital or fixed directories and clear sightlines to lifts. | Where visitors cannot find lifts or tenancies. |
| Refurbishment | Refurbish the finishes, lighting and joinery to reposition the building. | At the end of the cycle, timed with leasing. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Matting, door safety upgrades, signage and desk modifications are itemised and relatively modest. Draught lobbies and revolving door installations are lump sums with façade work. Floor treatment is by area; replacement by area with weekend or overnight work in occupied buildings. A full entrance refurbishment is a lump-sum project, often the most visible capital spend in a leasing strategy.

Safety and access items are code compliance; door operators and matting are lifecycle on short cycles; refurbishment is repositioning capital timed with leasing.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a walk-through cannot: where people have slipped or been struck, whether doors and security devices are checked, and what the entrance offers people with disability. Ask for them before any refurbishment is designed.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Slip, trip and door incident records | Where people slip, trip or are struck by doors. |
| Automatic and revolving door maintenance and safety check records | Whether door safety is checked against the standard. |
| Access audit for the entrance sequence | Whether the entrance works for people with disability. |
| Access control and turnstile fire release test records | Whether security devices release on alarm. |
| Entrance refurbishment history and any repositioning plans | When the entrance was last refurbished, and what is planned. |
| Cleaning specifications for entrance floors | Whether cleaning is making the floor slippery. |
| Visitor and tenant feedback on arrival experience | How visitors and tenants experience arriving. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Entrances are misread when safety and image are budgeted together, when a slip is blamed on the person, and when a security upgrade is judged only on how secure it is.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| Do it all in the refurbishment | Entrance problems are usually either safety and access (doors, slips, egress) or market and image. Fix the first regardless of budget; time the second with leasing strategy. |
| Slips are the walker's fault | Slips concentrated just inside the entry on wet days point to matting that is too short or worn, or a finish slippery when wet. A wet slip test and the matting length settle it. |
| Secure means safe | Turnstiles and locked doors must release on fire alarm and power failure, with a wide accessible gate. Security added after construction often fails this. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets standards for powered doors, access to entrances and counters, slip resistance, and egress through security devices. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Doors, access, slip resistance and egress | AS 5007 covers powered doors for pedestrian access and egress; the National Construction Code and AS 1428.1 set access requirements for entrances, doors and counters; AS 4586 classifies slip resistance; security doors on egress paths must meet the code's egress provisions. | BS EN 16005 covers safety in use of power-operated pedestrian doors; Approved Document M and BS 8300 set access; the Workplace (Health, Safety and Welfare) Regulations 1992 require doors and floors to be safe; the Equality Act 2010 requires reasonable adjustments. | ANSI/BHMA A156.10 covers power-operated pedestrian doors and A156.27 revolving doors; the 2010 ADA Standards govern accessible entrances, doors and counters; NFPA 101 and the International Building Code govern egress through security devices. |

sections.heading: Worked example: a stone lobby on a wet morning
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 1990s office entrance has polished granite floors, a single short mat inside revolving doors, and no swing door beside them. Slips cluster just inside the door on wet days, reception staff keep heaters under the desk, and turnstiles installed last year have one narrow accessible gate that needs a guard to open.

Slips just inside the door on wet days point to matting too short for the traffic and a finish slippery when wet. The revolving door with no accessible alternative, and an accessible gate that needs staff, are access findings, and the gate must also release on alarm. Heaters under the desk point to draughts, probably stack effect through the revolving door.

So the register carries the slips and the turnstile release as safety lines now, longer recessed matting and a wet slip test of the stone, an adjacent accessible door and an accessible gate that opens without a guard, and a draught review, with the finishes refurbished in step with leasing.

pages.title: Maintenance Access Areas
pages.question: How do ceiling voids, hatches, platforms and confined spaces fail, and why does poor access matter?
pages.answer: Maintenance access fails dangerously or silently. Workers fall through ceilings and roof spaces with no walkways, through open hatches and from unsafe ladders; confined spaces kill when entered without testing and controls; hidden asbestos, wiring and heat injure people in voids. Where access is poor, maintenance is skipped and equipment fails. Identify confined spaces, guard hatches and provide catwalks to every item needing service.

pages.searchTitle: Maintenance access: ceiling voids, roof spaces, hatches, confined spaces and safe routes

questions.question: Is it safe to walk on a suspended ceiling?
questions.answer: No. Suspended ceilings and plasterboard cannot carry people; workers need catwalks, walkway boards or access panels.

questions.question: What is a confined space?
questions.answer: A tank, pit, sump or duct where the air can be toxic or short of oxygen. Entry needs testing, ventilation, a permit and a rescue plan.

questions.question: Why does maintenance keep getting skipped on some equipment?
questions.answer: Often because it cannot be reached safely. Skipped tasks on the same items point to access, not the contractor.

questions.question: Is foil insulation near wiring dangerous?
questions.answer: It can be. Foil in contact with damaged wiring can electrocute workers in ceiling and roof spaces.

questions.question: How long do roof access platforms last?
questions.answer: Steel platforms, ladders and guardrails last 25 to 40 years.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Access problems show as plant with no route to it, unguarded hatches and ladders, unsigned pits and hidden hazards in voids, and in skipped maintenance and incident records. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |

| On site | Plant above ceilings with no catwalks or access panels; footprints or damage on ceiling tiles | Ceilings, hatches and platforms |
| On site | Roof spaces without walkway boards; insulation over joists | Ceilings, hatches and platforms |
| On site | Hatches without guardrails or with damaged ladders | Ceilings, hatches and platforms |
| On site | Fixed ladders without cages or fall arrest | Ceilings, hatches and platforms |
| On site | Corroded platforms and missing guardrails | Ceilings, hatches and platforms |
| On site | Confined spaces without signs or locks | Confined spaces |
