| In the records | Maintenance records showing skipped tasks | Neglect from poor access |
| In the records | Footprints on insulation or damage to plasterboard ceilings below roof spaces | Ceilings, hatches and platforms |
| In the records | Foil insulation near wiring; old rubber-insulated wiring in roof spaces | Hidden hazards, wiring and heat |
| In the records | Hatches painted shut or blocked by furniture | Neglect from poor access |

sections.heading: What the space does and what it contains
sections.markdown:
Maintenance access areas are the spaces people enter only to maintain the building: ceiling voids, roof spaces, crawl ways, plant platforms and catwalks, access hatches, fixed ladders, service walkways and confined spaces such as tanks and pits. Functionally they must let maintenance be done safely and conveniently. When they do not, maintenance is skipped or done dangerously: people fall through ceilings, off platforms and from ladders, are overcome in confined spaces, or disturb asbestos they did not know was there.

| Type | Where it is found | Main hazards |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ceiling voids | Above suspended ceilings in most buildings | Falls through ceilings; asbestos; live wiring |
| Roof spaces | Pitched roofs in houses and low-rise | Falls between joists; heat; insulation hazards |
| Access hatches | Ceilings, roofs, floors | Falls through open hatches; unsafe ladders |
| Fixed ladders and stairs | Plant platforms, roofs, pits | Falls; non-compliant geometry |
| Platforms, catwalks and walkways | Plant rooms, atria, roofs | Missing guardrails; corrosion |
| Confined spaces | Tanks, pits, ducts, sumps, voids | Toxic or oxygen-deficient atmospheres |

Good access is designed in from the start; most problems arise in older buildings and wherever plant was added later.

sections.heading: How long it stays fit for purpose
sections.markdown:
Steel platforms, ladders and guardrails last twenty-five to forty years, walkway boards twenty to forty, and hatches twenty to thirty. Fitness for purpose changes whenever plant is added somewhere no one planned access to, which is the usual way these spaces fall short.

| Component or quality | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Steel platforms and ladders | 25 to 40 years | Corrosion; damage |
| Access hatches | 20 to 30 years | Hinges; seals; damage |
| Walkway boards in roof spaces | 20 to 40 years | Decay; damage |
| Guardrails | 25 to 40 years | Fixings; corrosion |
| Fitness for current plant locations | Changes when plant is added | Plant added without access |

What shortens fitness for purpose: plant added in places with no designed access; corrosion of ladders and platforms on roofs and in damp plant areas; insulation and services covering walkways and joists; locked or lost access, so people improvise.

Access provisions rarely wear out first; they become inadequate because plant is added or moved without access being designed, and because equipment in voids multiplies over decades of fit-outs.

sections.heading: Ceilings, hatches and platforms
sections.markdown:
Suspended ceilings and plasterboard cannot carry people. Workers in ceiling voids and roof spaces step between supports or onto ceilings and fall through, often onto occupied spaces below. Roof spaces filled with insulation hide joists.

Open ceiling and roof hatches without guarding are fall holes; portable ladders used to reach hatches slip; fixed ladders without cages or fall arrest, or with wrong geometry, injure users.

Platforms and walkways without guardrails, with corroded grating or loose fixings, and plant placed close to roof edges without protection create fall hazards.

Ceilings and plasterboard look like floors from above, and are not. A worker reaching plant across a ceiling void, or crossing a roof space where insulation hides the joists, is one misstep from falling through onto the room below, which is why every item needing maintenance needs a defined route to it.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Broken ceiling tiles under plant | People standing on the ceiling to reach equipment. Access review. | Provide catwalks or access panels below the equipment, so no one stands on the ceiling. |
| Workers using portable ladders to roofs | No fixed access. Observation. | Install fixed access with fall protection, or a guarded hatch. |
| Footprints on insulation, and no walkway boards | People walking on joists hidden by insulation. Damage to the ceiling below, and insulation crushed in a line. | Lay walkway boards to every item needing maintenance, with lighting. |
| Fixed ladder or platform to plant with uneven rungs or no guardrail | Access unsafe for regular use. Rung spacing and width, and guardrail height, measured against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Repair or replace the ladder and add guardrails, or provide a stair where access is frequent. |

sections.heading: Confined spaces
sections.markdown:
Tanks, pits, sumps and some ducts can contain toxic gases or lack oxygen. Entering without testing, ventilation, permits and rescue arrangements kills workers and rescuers.

A confined space is defined by its hazard, not its size: a tank, pit, sump or duct where the air can be toxic or short of oxygen. Rescuers die as well as the workers they try to reach, which is why entry needs testing, ventilation, a permit and a rescue plan every time.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unsigned pits and tanks | Confined spaces not identified. Register review. | Identify, sign and lock every confined space, and set entry procedures and rescue plans. |
| A sump or tank with a lid anyone can lift | A confined space with no control on entry. No sign, no lock, and no entry in the register. | Sign and lock it, and add it to the register with an entry procedure. |
| Workers entering a pit or tank without a gas test | Confined space entered without controls. Gas monitoring before and during entry, against the exposure limits for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Stop entry until there is a permit, testing and rescue arrangements. |

sections.heading: Hidden hazards, wiring and heat
sections.markdown:
Ceiling voids and roof spaces may contain asbestos, loose-fill insulation, live and damaged wiring, hot surfaces and vermin. Workers who do not know they are there disturb them.

Damaged cables, unprotected joints, old wiring and foil insulation in contact with wiring can electrocute workers in ceiling and roof spaces.

Roof spaces in hot climates reach temperatures that cause heat stress within a short time, especially in insulated and poorly ventilated roofs; work is unsafe in the middle of the day in summer.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Foil insulation lying on old wiring in a roof space | A risk of electrocution. Foil in contact with cables, or rubber-insulated wiring nearby. | Have an electrician isolate and assess before anyone works in the space, and separate or remove the foil. |
| A roof space too hot to work in by midday | Heat stress in an insulated, poorly ventilated roof. Temperatures measured during the working window. | Schedule roof space work for the cooler part of the day. |

sections.heading: Neglect from poor access
sections.markdown:
Equipment nobody can reach is equipment nobody maintains. The signs are in the records and the ceilings rather than in the plant itself: tasks skipped for the same items, and damage below them where workers improvise.

Equipment that is hard to reach is not maintained: filters, dampers, valves and lights in difficult voids are left until they fail.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Filters and dampers neglected above ceilings | No practical access. Maintenance records. | Provide practical access, or relocate the plant at replacement. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unidentified confined spaces; unguarded hatches; no safe access to plant above ceilings or on roofs | safety · 4 Essential | Rectify before next access. |
| Access equipment damaged or unusable | failure · 4 Essential | Repair now. |
| Certification of anchors, ladders or platforms due | deadline · 3 Important | At the prescribed interval. |
| Corrosion; missing walkways; poor lighting | condition · 2 Planned | Repair in the near term. |
| Access equipment at end of life | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Replace. |
| No access audit | check · 2 Planned | Audit. |
| Normal | nil · 1 Routine | Routine. |

Access findings are graded on the consequence if someone uses the access as it stands today: a fall through a ceiling or a confined space entry without controls is a safety grade even if nobody has been hurt yet.

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A health and safety consultant or building surveyor with the maintenance contractors. The checks below follow the route to every item of plant needing maintenance, record the hazards on the way, and compare them with the confined space and asbestos registers.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Access audit | Of every item of plant and service needing maintenance: how it is reached and what protection exists. |
| Confined space survey | And register. |
| Hatch, ladder and platform inspection | Against standards. |
| Hazard check | In voids: asbestos, wiring, insulation, heat. |
| Maintenance record review | For skipped tasks. |
| Roof space survey | Walkways, clearances, hazards, ventilation and temperature. |
| Electrical safety check | Of wiring and insulation contact in voids. |
| Contractor interviews | Maintenance staff know which items are hard or dangerous to reach. |

The report should list hazards and a plan for safe access.

The audit should start from the maintenance schedule: for every task, ask where the equipment is and how someone gets to it safely.

sections.heading: Identifying, guarding and providing access
sections.markdown:
Unidentified confined spaces, unguarded hatches and ceilings people stand on come first, before the next maintenance visit. After that, the work gives every item of plant a safe route, removes hidden hazards, and records the routes for every contractor.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Catwalks and walkways | Catwalks and walkways in ceiling voids and roof spaces to every item needing maintenance, with lighting. | Wherever plant sits above ceilings or in roof spaces. |
| Access panels | Panels located under equipment so it can be reached from below. | Where equipment can be serviced from below. |
| Hatch guarding and fixed ladders | Guard the hatches, and fit compliant fixed ladders with fall protection. | Wherever hatches are open holes or ladders are unsafe. |
| Platforms and guardrails | Platforms and guardrails on roofs and in plant rooms. | Wherever plant sits near edges or on unprotected structure. |
| Confined space controls | Signs, locks, register, entry procedures and rescue plans. | Wherever tanks, pits, sumps or ducts can be entered. |
| Plant relocation | Move plant to accessible positions at replacement. | When hard-to-reach plant is replaced. |
| Hazard removal | Asbestos, damaged wiring, loose insulation. | Wherever voids hold asbestos, damaged wiring or loose insulation. |
| Work scheduling | Schedule work to avoid roof spaces in the heat of the day. | In hot climates and insulated roofs. |
| Access documentation | Drawings showing access points, routes and hazards for each item of plant, given to every contractor. | In every building with plant above ceilings or on roofs. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Access works are itemised: catwalks by length, hatches, ladders and platforms per item. Confined space controls are low cost. Plant relocation is part of replacement projects. Safety items are code compliance and prevent costly incidents.

Access works are modest compared with the cost of a fall or confined space incident, and they also reduce maintenance time and missed tasks, so they often pay for themselves. Relocating plant to accessible positions is cheapest when done as part of a planned replacement. Confined space signage, locks and procedures cost little.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a walk through the voids cannot: which spaces are confined, where asbestos is, and which tasks get skipped because no one can reach the plant. Ask for them before the next maintenance visit.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Confined space register and procedures | Which spaces are confined, and how entry is controlled. |
| Asbestos register covering ceiling voids and roof spaces | Where asbestos is in voids and roof spaces. |
| Access equipment certification | Whether anchors, ladders and platforms are certified. |
| Incident and near-miss records | Whether there have been falls, near misses or injuries. |
| Maintenance records showing skipped tasks | Which tasks are skipped, and on which equipment. |
| Drawings showing access to plant above ceilings and on roofs | How each item of plant is meant to be reached. |
| Contractor feedback on access difficulties | Where contractors find access hard or unsafe. |
| Work at height and confined space procedures | How work at height and confined space entry are controlled. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Access is misread when unguarded hatches and confined spaces are treated as maintenance details, when skipped tasks are blamed on the contractor, and when one visit is taken to show the condition.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| It is a maintenance detail | Confined spaces, unguarded hatches and ceilings that people stand on are serious fall and life hazards. Identify, sign and control them before the next maintenance visit. |
| The contractor is skipping tasks | If maintenance records show tasks skipped or delayed for the same equipment, the cause is often access, not the contractor. If damage to ceilings and finishes appears below the same equipment repeatedly, workers are improvising their own access. |
| One visit shows the condition | Record the time and conditions of each observation, because the condition of these spaces changes with operations and the worst state is the one that matters for safety. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market places duties on whoever controls a building to provide safe access for maintenance, and sets rules for work at height and confined spaces. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Work at height, confined spaces and access | Work health and safety regulations govern falls and confined spaces, with codes of practice; AS 1657 covers fixed platforms, walkways, stairways and ladders; AS/NZS 2865 covers confined spaces. | The Work at Height Regulations 2005 and Confined Spaces Regulations 1997 apply; BS 5395 and BS EN ISO 14122 cover fixed access. | OSHA 29 CFR 1910 Subpart D covers walking-working surfaces and ladders, and 1910.146 permit-required confined spaces. |

In all three countries, duties for safe access fall on whoever controls the building as a workplace, including when the work is done by contractors; designers also have duties to provide safe maintenance access in new work and alterations (for example under the UK Construction (Design and Management) Regulations 2015 and Australian work health and safety duties for designers). Incidents involving falls or confined spaces lead to regulator investigation and prosecution.

sections.heading: Worked example: plant above an office ceiling
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. An office's fan coil units sit above a suspended ceiling with no catwalks or access panels. Ceiling tiles below several units are cracked, maintenance records show filter changes skipped for two years on those units, and a pump pit in the basement has an unmarked lid.

Skipped tasks on the same units, and cracked tiles below them, point to access, not the contractor: workers are standing on the ceiling, or not going at all. The unmarked pit is an unidentified confined space, a serious life hazard.

So the register carries the pit and the ceiling as safety lines before the next visit, the pit signed, locked and registered with an entry procedure, access panels or catwalks to the units, and access drawings for every contractor.

pages.title: Masonry/Brickwork
pages.question: What goes wrong with brick and block façades, what does each defect look like, and how serious is it?
pages.answer: Masonry façades fail at the hidden steel and at the joints, not in the brick. Corroding ties crack the outer leaf horizontally at regular tie courses; corroding lintels and shelf angles crack brickwork over openings and at floor lines; brick growing against a shrinking concrete frame bows the panels between floors. Even-width cracks near corners are usually movement and benign; tapering cracks through openings point to the ground. Read the crack pattern first, then its width.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about masonry façades; it describes how these walls behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Pointing, cracking, efflorescence, structural stability

pages.searchTitle: Brickwork: reading cracks, wall ties, lintels, shelf angles, damp and repointing

questions.question: Why are there horizontal cracks every few courses in my brick wall?
questions.answer: Regular horizontal cracks about every sixth course, in the outer leaf only, point to wall tie corrosion. Remedial stainless ties are the usual repair.

questions.question: Does an uncracked wall mean the ties are sound?
questions.answer: No. Wire ties corrode by thinning and can fail without cracking the wall; on a cavity wall of the right era in an exposed position, the ties still need investigating.

questions.question: Why is the brickwork cracked above my window?
questions.answer: A stepped crack rising from a lintel end, often with rust at the bearing, points to lintel corrosion. The brickwork is propped and the lintel replaced.

questions.question: Should old brickwork be repointed with cement?
questions.answer: Repoint in a mortar no stronger than the brick, and in lime mortar for lime-built walls.

questions.question: How long do wall ties last?
questions.answer: Galvanised mild-steel ties from before about 1980 last 30 to 60 years, and as little as 15 to 25 in marine exposure; stainless steel ties last the life of the building.

questions.question: Why is there a diagonal crack running through the bricks and down past the damp course?
questions.answer: That pattern points to foundation movement, often with sticking doors and sloping floors. Address the cause and monitor; see Foundations.

questions.question: Why is the brick crumbling and salty at the bottom of the wall?
questions.answer: Rising damp with salt attack, usually where the damp-proof course is bridged or absent. Remove the bridging, fit a new damp-proof course if the old one has failed, and replaster in a salt-resistant system.

questions.question: Why is there a straight vertical crack near the corner of a long brick wall?
questions.answer: Clay brick expansion or thermal movement in a long run without movement joints. Saw-cut and seal a movement joint, and tie across where panels have been freed.

questions.question: Why are brick faces flaking off high up on the wall and chimney?
questions.answer: Frost damage, or hard cement pointing on soft brick. Repoint in a mortar no stronger than the brick, and replace the spalled bricks.

questions.question: Why is the brickwork bulging at each floor level?
questions.answer: On a framed building, the frame has shortened and there is no soft joint under the shelf angle. Form a soft joint under each shelf angle, and treat or replace the angles.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Brickwork problems show from the street as cracks, bulges and spalls, close up in the mortar and at lintels, inside as damp and matching cracks, and in repeated repairs. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Street or aerial | Horizontal cracks at regular vertical spacing across an elevation; on a veneer or cavity wall this is the tie signature | Wall ties and sulfate attack |
| Street or aerial | Bulging or bowing panels, best seen by sighting along the wall at a low angle or in raking light; floor-line bowing on framed buildings | Wall ties and sulfate attack |
| Street or aerial | Brickwork lifted at eaves or verges, or a gap opening under the roof edge | Wall ties and sulfate attack |
| Street or aerial | Stepped cracks rising from the ends of lintels, rust staining below lintels and shelf angles, dropped arches | Lintels, shelf angles and embedded steel |
| Street or aerial | Diagonal tapering cracks through openings; distorted window heads | Movement and foundation cracking |
| Street or aerial | Spalled brick faces, mortar eroded or proud of the brick, mismatched patch repairs and repointing in a different colour | Damp, frost and salts |
| Street or aerial | Vegetation in joints, overflowing gutter staining, white salt deposits and lime runs below defective details | Damp, frost and salts |
| Street or aerial | Weep holes buried by paving or garden beds; render carried down over the damp-proof course | Damp, frost and salts |
| Close up on site | Mortar that is soft enough to rake out with a key or crumbles to the touch; white, swollen mortar in most joints (sulfate) | Wall ties and sulfate attack |
| Close up on site | Hollow sound or movement when brick faces are tapped; loose bricks at parapets and corners | Wall ties and sulfate attack |
| Close up on site | Crack width and whether it tapers; whether the crack passes through bricks or follows joints; displacement across the crack face | Movement and foundation cracking |
| Close up on site | Rust at lintel bearings, compressed or missing sealant under shelf angles, spalling along the angle line | Lintels, shelf angles and embedded steel |
| Close up on site | A salt tide line and eroded brick just above ground; damp-proof course visible or bridged | Damp, frost and salts |
| Inside the building | Damp, blown plaster and salt bloom on the inside face of external walls, highest at the base (rising) or random and weather-related (penetrating) | Damp, frost and salts |
| Inside the building | Cracks on the internal face on the same line as external cracks: this points to movement of the whole wall, not only the outer leaf | Movement and foundation cracking |
| Inside the building | Sticking doors and windows, floor slopes and cornice gaps on the same line as external cracking: foundation movement | Movement and foundation cracking |
| Inside the building | Decayed skirting and floor timbers against external walls | Damp, frost and salts |
| In the records | Repeated repointing or crack repair on the same elevation, which means the cause was never addressed | Movement and foundation cracking |
| In the records | Leak logs concentrated on one elevation, at window heads, or at each floor line | Damp, frost and salts |
| In the records | Previous façade inspections with unsafe or safe-with-repairs findings, and make-safe hoarding or netting invoices | Standards by country |
| In the records | Original specifications naming the tie type and lintel material; an absent tie specification on a building of the right era | Wall ties and sulfate attack |

sections.heading: Types of brick wall
sections.markdown:
Masonry walls take four main forms, and the form decides what can go wrong. Solid walls, one to two bricks thick and bonded with headers, dominate pre-1930 stock in Britain and Australia and early twentieth-century buildings in the United States. They have no cavity and rely on thickness and soft lime mortar to absorb and release moisture. Cavity walls, two leaves with a gap between them held together by metal ties, became standard in Britain from the 1920s and in Australian multi-storey and commercial work through the mid twentieth century. Brick veneer, a single outer leaf tied back to a timber or steel frame, has been the dominant Australian house and low-rise form since the 1950s. On framed buildings, masonry is cladding: an outer leaf carried at each floor on steel shelf angles or on the slab edge and tied back to the frame.

Bond pattern tells you the form from the street. Header courses (bricks laid end-on, showing their short face, in Flemish or English bond) mean a solid wall. Stretcher bond with no headers means a cavity or veneer, and therefore ties, which are the commonest hidden failure in masonry. Snapped half-bricks laid to imitate headers in stretcher work are a known trap; the rhythm is usually too regular and the heads often look slightly short.

| Era | Typical form | What it implies |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Before about 1920 | Solid brick or stone, lime mortar, timber or iron lintels behind arches, slate or no damp-proof course | Rising damp and salt attack at the base; decayed timber lintels; cement repointing damaging soft brick |
| 1920s to 1970s | Cavity walls with galvanised mild-steel ties: flat fishtail or vertical-twist strip, wire butterfly; black ash mortar in parts of Britain | Tie corrosion now advanced in exposed and coastal positions; strip ties crack the wall as they rust, wire ties thin silently; black ash mortar accelerates both |
| 1950s to 1980s | Concrete-framed buildings clad in brick on shelf angles or slab edges, often with no compressible joint under the angle | Bowing, spalling and horizontal cracking at floor lines as the frame shortens and the brick grows |
| 1900s to 1940s, United States | Steel frame encased in solid masonry with no cavity or drainage | Rust jacking of spandrel beams and columns, cracking and displacement along floor and column lines |
| 1980s onward | Stainless or exposure-rated ties, cavity trays, weep holes, movement joints | Lower risk; failures are mostly workmanship: missing or misplaced ties, mortar-bridged cavities, omitted joints |

Brick type governs movement. Fired clay bricks expand permanently as they take up moisture after leaving the kiln, quickly in the first months and slowly for decades after. Calcium silicate and concrete bricks and blocks do the opposite and shrink. A wall of either needs movement joints, sized and spaced for its material, and the two must not be mixed in one panel without allowing for the difference. Mortar governs durability. Lime mortar is softer and more permeable than the brick, so the joint weathers and is renewed while the brick survives. Cement mortar is harder and less permeable; laid against soft brick it forces moisture and salts out through the brick face and the brick fails instead of the joint.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Fired clay brick lasts a hundred to a hundred and fifty years and more, but what holds it in place does not: galvanised ties from before about 1980 last thirty to sixty years, and as little as fifteen in marine exposure, while galvanised lintels and shelf angles last forty to eighty.

| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fired clay brick | 100 to 150 years and more | Shortened by salt crystallisation, frost and hard cement pointing |
| Lime mortar joints | 50 to 100 years sheltered; 30 to 50 years exposed | Exposure, roof drainage, rising damp |
| Cement mortar joints | 40 to 70 years | Cracking at movement rather than erosion; sulfate attack where wet |
| Galvanised mild-steel ties (before about 1980) | 30 to 60 years; as little as 15 to 25 years in marine exposure or black ash mortar | Zinc consumed once the mortar carbonates and stays damp |
| Stainless steel ties | Life of the building | Workmanship: omitted, misplaced or bridged ties |
| Galvanised steel lintels and shelf angles | 40 to 80 years | Coastal exposure, water held behind them, missing cavity trays |
| Bitumen or polymer damp-proof course | 50 years and more | Bridging by raised ground, paving, render or garden beds, rather than material failure |
| Injected chemical damp-proof course | 20 to 30 years | Product, installation and salt loading |

What shortens life: exposure. Elevations facing the prevailing rain, sites within a few kilometres of surf, and industrial atmospheres keep walls wetter and consume galvanising faster. The same building can have ties failing on one elevation and sound on another; water management faults. Overflowing gutters, missing copings and sills without drips, blocked weep holes and absent cavity trays put water exactly where ties and lintels sit; missing movement joints. Long runs of clay brick without joints, and brick cladding on concrete frames without soft joints under the shelf angles, crack and bow as the materials move against each other; hard repointing and impermeable coatings. Cement pointing on lime-built walls, and paints or renders that trap moisture, move decay into the brick; bridged damp-proof courses. Raised paths and garden beds, render taken down over the damp-proof course, and debris in the cavity carry ground moisture past the barrier; cavity wall insulation retrofits. Fill injected into cavities in exposed locations can carry rain across to the inner leaf and keep ties wet.

sections.heading: Wall ties and sulfate attack
sections.markdown:
Ties hold the outer leaf to the inner leaf or frame. Galvanised mild-steel ties lose their zinc once the surrounding mortar carbonates and stays damp, then the steel rusts. Rust occupies several times the volume of the steel it replaces. In the outer leaf bed joint that expansion lifts the brickwork above, and because ties are laid at regular vertical spacing (about every sixth course) the wall cracks horizontally in a regular pattern. Strip ties (fishtail and vertical twist) jack and crack the wall. Wire ties mostly thin and snap with little expansion, so they can lose restraint with no visible sign. The end result in both cases is an outer leaf free to bulge, and under wind suction, to fall.

Soluble sulfates from clay bricks, ground water or flue gases react with cement in wet mortar and render, forming expansive compounds. Mortar swells, softens and whitens; the wall grows vertically and cracks along most bed joints, not only at tie courses. Chimneys, parapets, rendered walls and walls in wet ground are the usual places.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Horizontal cracks at regular intervals, about every sixth course, outer leaf only | Wall tie corrosion. Worst on exposed elevations and higher up, where less load resists the lift; ties located by metal detector coincide with the cracks; inner face uncracked. | Survey the ties; install stainless remedial ties, removing or cutting back strip ties that are expanding. |
| Horizontal cracks in most bed joints, white swollen mortar, wall growth | Sulfate attack. Every course affected, not only tie courses; chimneys, parapets, rendered or wet walls; can affect both leaves; mortar soft when probed. | Confirm by mortar analysis, and get an engineer's advice on repair or rebuilding. |

sections.heading: Lintels, shelf angles and embedded steel
sections.markdown:
Steel lintels over openings and shelf angles carrying cladding at each floor corrode where water reaches them, usually because cavity trays and stop ends are missing or weep holes are blocked. Corrosion lifts the brickwork over the lintel and opens a crack along its bearing; as the flange thins the brickwork drops and the opening head deflects. Behind the arches of older buildings, timber lintels rot unseen until the arch drops.

A concrete frame shortens over its first decades through creep and shrinkage. Clay brick grows. Where brick cladding is built tight to the underside of each shelf angle or slab edge, with no compressible joint, the frame unloads onto the brick panel below. The brick at the angle line crushes and spalls, panels bow outward between floors, and corners crack where the two elevations push against each other.

In early steel-framed buildings the columns and spandrel beams are wrapped in solid masonry with no drainage. Water reaching the steel rusts it, and the rust pushes the masonry outward along column and floor lines, cracking corners and displacing brick and stone, often first at parapets where exposure is greatest.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Horizontal crack and outward bow repeated at each floor line of a framed building | Frame shortening; no soft joint under the shelf angle. Repeats floor by floor; brick spalled at the angle; no sealant line, or crushed sealant, under the angle. | Form a soft joint under each shelf angle, and treat or replace the angles. |
| Stepped crack rising from a lintel end, horizontal crack along the lintel, brick lifted or dropped over the opening | Lintel corrosion. Rust at the bearing; crack widest at the lintel; opening frame itself square. | Prop the brickwork and replace the lintel, with a cavity tray, stop ends and weep holes. |
| Cracking and displacement along column and floor lines of an early steel-framed building | Rust jacking of embedded steel. Rust staining at the crack; corners and parapets first; brick pushed outward rather than dropped. | Open up, treat or replace the steel, and rebuild with flashing and drainage. |

sections.heading: Movement and foundation cracking
sections.markdown:
Long runs of clay brickwork without movement joints expand and push past corners and returns, producing vertical cracks near corners, cracks at short returns and brickwork sliding outward on the damp-proof course at the base (oversailing). Concrete block and calcium silicate shrink and crack vertically at openings and mid-panel. These cracks are usually even in width and stop growing once the material has stabilised.

Settlement, subsidence and the seasonal swelling and shrinking of reactive clay soils distort the wall. Cracks run diagonally through brick and mortar, taper (wider at one end), pass through openings, and are accompanied by sticking doors and windows, sloping floors and cracking internally on the same line. On reactive clay they open and close with the seasons; trees, leaking drains and changes to garden watering are the usual triggers.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Diagonal crack tapering wider at top or bottom, through openings, continuing below the damp-proof course | Foundation movement. Crack passes through bricks in a continuous line; sticking doors, floor slopes, matching internal cracks; seasonal movement on reactive clay; nearby trees or leaking drains. | Address the cause and monitor; see Foundations. |
| Vertical crack of even width near a corner or at a short return; brickwork oversailing at the base | Clay brick expansion or thermal movement. Long run without movement joints; no distortion of openings; width does not change across seasons. | Saw-cut and seal a movement joint, and tie across where panels have been freed. |
| Vertical cracks at openings and mid-panel in blockwork or calcium silicate brick | Drying shrinkage. Material type; cracks widest early in life and then stable. | Repair once the cracks have stabilised; add movement joints where runs are long. |

sections.heading: Damp, frost and salts
sections.markdown:
Rising damp is ground moisture drawn up a wall without a working damp-proof course, carrying salts that deposit in a band up to about a metre high. Penetrating damp is rain driven through solid walls, defective pointing, or across a cavity bridged by mortar droppings, debris on ties or retrofit insulation. Both decay plaster, timber in contact with the wall, and embedded steel.

Water freezing in saturated brick, and salts crystallising as walls dry, break off brick faces (spalling) and turn surfaces powdery. Salt damage dominates in Australian stock at the base of walls with failed damp-proof courses and in coastal walls; frost damage dominates in Britain and the colder United States in parapets, chimneys and exposed copings. Hard cement pointing concentrates both in the brick.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Powdery brick, eroded mortar and salts in a band at the base | Rising damp with salt attack. Tide line up to about a metre; bridged or absent damp-proof course; worse behind garden beds and paving. | Remove the bridging, then a new damp-proof course if the old one has failed; replaster in a salt-resistant system. |
| Spalled faces high on exposed walls, parapets and chimneys | Frost damage, or hard cement pointing on soft brick. Cold climate; mortar proud of recessed brick; damage concentrated next to hard pointing. | Repoint in a mortar no stronger than the brick, and replace spalled bricks. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator, ordinance or order sets the date, as façade inspection ordinances do), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Loose, displaced or bulging brickwork over a footpath, entrance or occupied area; parapet or chimney out of plumb; outer leaf detached from ties | safety · 4 Essential | Make safe immediately (exclusion zone, netting or take-down), engineer within days, repair within months. |
| Displaced lintel with dropped brickwork; cracks 15 mm and wider; active water entry damaging the structure behind | failure · 4 Essential | Repair now; propping where load-bearing. |
| Tie corrosion cracking; lintel corrosion cracking over openings; floor-line bowing on a framed building; cracks 5 to 15 mm; persistent penetrating damp | condition · 2 Planned | Programme repair in the near term, ahead of the next façade inspection cycle where one applies. |
| Mortar eroded or friable over large areas; scattered spalling; damp-proof course bridged without salt damage yet; galvanised ties of the at-risk era with no cracking | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Renewal on a planned cycle; combine with access for other façade work. |
| Tie-era cavity wall in exposed or marine position with no record of tie condition; cracks of unknown cause; damp of unknown source | check · 2 Planned | Investigate first; size the works from what the investigation finds. |
| Hairline to 1 mm cracks of even width; historic movement shown stable; efflorescence on new work | nil · 1 Routine | Monitor; cosmetic repair once shown stable. |

Crack width scales are a useful second step. Each market grades damage into categories by crack width (Thresholds by market). Category 0 to 1 is normally cosmetic, 2 is moderate and usually repairable, 3 and above indicates significant movement needing structural attention.

> Width is not the whole answer. A 3 mm crack from tie corrosion is more serious than a 3 mm expansion crack, because the first keeps opening and the second does not. Grade the cause, then use width to set urgency within it.

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A building surveyor leads the survey; a structural engineer joins where there is bulging, lean or suspected foundation movement; a façade engineer leads on framed buildings and on buildings under a façade ordinance. In New York the inspection must be made by a Qualified Exterior Wall Inspector. The checks below read the crack pattern first, then open up or test where the pattern points: at ties, lintels, shelf angles and the damp-proof course.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Visual survey of every elevation | Close up from access where defects or public areas warrant it, with a crack map recording location, pattern, width and taper. |
| Tie inspection. | Locate ties with a metal detector, drill and inspect by borescope, and remove a brick or tie at representative positions to examine the embedded section, where corrosion is worst. Weight sampling to the most exposed elevations and upper storeys; extend it when corrosion is found. BRE Digest 401 sets out the approach in British practice. |
| Mortar analysis | Where sulfate attack is suspected, or to specify matching repointing mortar. |
| Plumb and bulge survey | By laser or plumb line where panels look out of line; record for comparison. |
| Crack monitoring | With tell-tales or gauge studs for at least twelve months, covering a full wet and dry season on reactive clay, before concluding a crack is stable, with widths graded against the AS 2870 damage categories (QBCC guide) or BRE Digest 251. |
| Lintels and shelf angles: | Covermeter to locate, opening up at bearings to see section loss and tray detail. |
| Hammer tapping | Of faces and parapets over public areas, removing anything loose at the time. |
| Moisture: | Calcium carbide or gravimetric samples at depth. Electrical moisture meters read salt as water and overstate rising damp; they show distribution, not diagnosis. |
| Thermography | To show wet zones, cavity fill voids and bridged areas. |

The report should state the form of wall, the tie type and condition by elevation and height, lintel and shelf angle condition, crack causes with the evidence for each, anything made safe, and repairs by priority with extents measured, not estimated.

sections.heading: Re-tying, repairing or rebuilding
sections.markdown:
Anything loose over a footpath, entrance or occupied area is made safe first. After that, each repair follows the cause the crack pattern points to: remedial ties, new lintels, soft joints at shelf angles, movement joints, or the bridging removed from a damp-proof course.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Remedial ties | Stainless helical or resin-anchored ties drilled through the outer leaf into the inner leaf or frame, at the spacing the standard requires, with extra ties at openings, corners and the top of walls; expanding strip ties are removed or cut back from the outer leaf, or the jacking continues, while wire ties can usually be left in place. | Wherever ties have corroded. |
| Rebuilding | Take the panel down and rebuild it on new ties. | Where panels are bulged beyond what ties can restrain, or bricks are displaced. |
| Lintels | Replace in stainless steel or galvanised to the exposure class, with a cavity tray, stop ends and weep holes over, propping the brickwork above during the work. | Where lintels corrode or have displaced. |
| Shelf angles and floor lines | Cut out the mortar bed beneath each angle and form a soft joint of compressible filler and sealant; inspect and treat the angle and its fixings, and replace angles that have lost section, which requires propping the cladding. | Where brickwork bows at each floor line of a framed building. |
| Movement joints | Saw-cut and seal joints at corners and in long runs, and tie across where panels have been freed. | Where expansion or thermal movement cracks long runs. |
| Repointing | Rake out to about twice the joint width, and repoint in a mortar no stronger than the brick; lime mortar for lime-built walls. | Where mortar is eroded or friable. |
| Damp | Remove the bridging first (lower ground and paving, cut render back above the damp-proof course, clear debris from cavities); then a new damp-proof course where the old one has failed, sawn-in or injected, and internal replastering in salt-resistant systems. | Where damp rises or penetrates. |
| Embedded steel | Open up along the affected lines, clean or replace and protect the steel, and rebuild with the flashing and drainage the original lacked. | Where rust jacking cracks an early steel-framed building. |
| Foundation movement | Address the cause (drains, trees, watering) and monitor. | Underpinning is reserved for movement that continues after the cause is removed. |

Interactions: tie and lintel work, repointing and shelf angle joints share the same access and are best packaged by elevation; cavity insulation may need to be extracted where it bridges; older renders and paints may hold hazardous materials that set the method.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Investigation is a lump sum with a rate for each probe or opening. Remedial ties and repointing are measured by wall area; lintels by opening; soft joints, damp-proof courses and movement joints by linear metre; rebuilding by area. Access is often the largest single component on multi-storey façades, which is why works are packaged elevation by elevation. Make-safe protection recurs until the repair is done.

The usual register shape is two-part: the investigation as a check line, and a conditional works envelope sized from what it finds. Ties, lintels and shelf angles are lifecycle items; repointing is repairs and maintenance on a long cycle; ordinance inspections and make-safe works are code compliance.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what the crack pattern alone cannot: what ties and lintels the wall relies on, what has been repaired before, and whether movement is continuing. Ask for them before specifying repairs.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Previous façade inspection reports and any ordinance filings, with their unsafe and repair findings | What earlier inspections found, and what is outstanding. |
| Drawings and specifications showing the wall form, tie type, lintels and shelf angles | What the wall is, and what ties, lintels and shelf angles it relies on. |
| Records of tie replacement, lintel replacement, repointing and crack repairs, with dates, extents and warranties | What has already been replaced or repaired, and whether the cause was dealt with. |
| Any crack monitoring data and engineer's reports on movement or foundations | Whether movement is continuing. |
| Damp-proof course installation records and guarantees, and any cavity insulation retrofit records | Whether damp has been treated before, and whether cavity insulation was added. |
| Leak and damp logs by elevation, and make-safe hoarding or netting records | Where damp and leaks concentrate, and where brickwork has been made safe. |
| Heritage listing and conservation constraints, which set materials and methods | Which materials and methods a repair must use. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Brickwork is misread when a crack is judged by its width, when the absence of cracking is taken to clear the ties, and when two cracks of similar shape are given the same cause.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| The widest crack is the serious one | Most masonry defects show as cracks, and the pattern of the crack identifies the cause far more reliably than its width. Read the pattern first, then the width. |
| No cracks, so the ties are fine | Wire ties corrode by thinning with little expansion, so they can fail without cracking the wall. On a cavity wall or veneer of the right era in a marine or exposed position, the absence of tie cracking does not clear the ties; it sends the item to investigation. |
| Similar cracks have the same cause | Two patterns are often confused. Tie cracking and sulfate cracking are both horizontal: tie cracks repeat only at tie courses and only in the outer leaf; sulfate cracks appear in most joints and the mortar itself is changed. Foundation cracks and movement cracks can both start at openings: foundation cracks taper and distort the opening; movement cracks are even and leave it square. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets design and material standards for masonry, has its own working references for repair, and its own arrangements for façade inspection and ownership. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Design and materials | The National Construction Code calls up AS 3700 Masonry structures and AS 4773 Masonry for small buildings; wall ties are rated to exposure classes under AS/NZS 2699.1, and masonry units are tested to AS/NZS 4456. | Approved Documents A and C set structural and moisture requirements; design follows BS EN 1996 with PD 6697 guidance on movement joints, and workmanship BS 8000-3. | The International Building Code calls up TMS 402/602 for masonry. |
| Repair references | AS 2870 governs residential footings and gives the crack damage categories. | Cleaning and repair follow BS 8221-1 and BS 8221-2; BRE Digests 251 (crack classification) and 401 (replacing wall ties) are the working references. | The Brick Industry Association's Technical Notes are the standard practice references for ties, movement and repair. |
| Inspection and ownership | There is no periodic façade inspection regime; on strata buildings the façade is common property and belongs in the capital works plan. | On leasehold blocks the works are service-charge items subject to section 20 consultation; higher-risk buildings sit under the Building Safety Act 2022. | ASTM E2270 sets the practice for periodic façade inspection; New York City's Façade Inspection and Safety Program requires a critical examination of buildings over six storeys every five years, with Cycle 10 filing windows running from February 2025 to February 2029 across three sub-cycles, and Chicago, Boston, San Francisco and several other cities run comparable ordinances. |

sections.heading: Worked example: horizontal cracks on a 1960s cavity wall
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 1960s block of flats near the coast has cavity walls. Its exposed elevation shows horizontal cracks at regular intervals, about every sixth course, in the outer leaf only and worst near the top. The mortar between the cracks is sound, and the sheltered elevations show no cracks.

Horizontal cracks repeating at tie courses, in the outer leaf only, point to wall tie corrosion rather than sulfate attack, which would affect most joints and change the mortar itself. The sheltered elevations are not cleared by their lack of cracks: wire ties can fail without cracking, so the ties there need investigating too.

So the register carries remedial ties on the exposed elevation as a condition line, removal or cutting back of any strip ties that are expanding, a tie survey of the sheltered elevations as a check line, and a safety check of the parapets and the top of the walls, where the cracking is worst.

thresholds.rule: Category 0 under 0.1 mm; 1 under 1 mm; 2 under 5 mm; 3 from 5 to 15 mm; 4 from 15 to 25 mm

source.title: Standards and Tolerances Guide (December 2023), reproducing the AS 2870 damage categories

thresholds.rule: Category 0 under 0.1 mm; 1 up to 1 mm; 2 up to 5 mm; 3 from 5 to 15 mm; 4 from 15 to 25 mm; 5 above 25 mm

pages.title: Occupational Health & Safety (OHS)
pages.question: Which safety provisions in a building protect occupants and workers, and which gaps are serious hazards?
pages.answer: Workplace safety in a building rests on safe access to plant, sound stairs, slip-resistant floors, safe glazing, controlled confined spaces, and records that tell people what they are working on. The serious gaps are plant reached by climbing or portable ladders, unidentified confined spaces, slippery entries and wet areas, unmarked or unsafe glass doors, and contractors working without registers or permits. Falls on stairs and floors are the most common serious injuries.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about occupational health & safety (ohs); it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Safe access provisions, handrails, statutory signage

pages.searchTitle: Workplace safety in buildings: plant access, stairs, slips, glazing and confined spaces

questions.question: Who is responsible for workplace safety in a building?
questions.answer: In Australia, the model work health and safety laws place duties on persons conducting a business or undertaking and on those with management or control of the workplace. In the United Kingdom the duties sit under the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974 and its regulations.

questions.question: Is a portable ladder acceptable access to rooftop plant?
questions.answer: Plant reachable only by portable ladder or climbing is a safety finding. Fixed access, a caged ladder, a ladder with fall arrest or a platform with guardrails, is the remedy.

questions.question: Why do people keep slipping at the entrance?
questions.answer: Usually because the floor finish is unsuitable when wet. A slip resistance test confirms it; an anti-slip treatment, a new finish or recessed matting fixes it.

questions.question: What does a confined space in a building need?
questions.answer: Pits, tanks and voids that could be entered need signs, locked covers, a register and entry procedures.

questions.question: What is a health and safety file?
questions.answer: In the United Kingdom, the Construction (Design and Management) Regulations 2015 require one for the building. It holds the information needed to maintain and work on the building safely.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Workplace hazards in a building show in how plant is reached, how stairs and floors wear, and in the incident log. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On site | Plant reachable only by portable ladder or climbing; roof hatches without guardrails | Access to plant and confined spaces |
| On site | Stairs with worn nosings, uneven risers, missing handrails or contrast | Stairs, floors and glazing |
| On site | Polished or glazed floors at entries and wet areas; mats curling | Stairs, floors and glazing |
| On site | Glass doors without manifestation; cracked or annealed glass in doors | Stairs, floors and glazing |
| On site | Pits, tanks and voids without confined space signs or locks | Access to plant and confined spaces |
| On site | Missing or faded safety signs at plant and hazards | Records and contractors |
| In the records | Asbestos, plant and confined space registers | Records and contractors |
| In the records | Health and safety file or building manual | Records and contractors |
| In the records | Contractor induction and permit records | Records and contractors |
| In the records | Incident and injury records | Stairs, floors and glazing |
| In the records | Slip resistance test results | Stairs, floors and glazing |

sections.heading: What workplace safety covers
sections.markdown:
This element covers the safety provisions built into the fabric of a building and its management that protect occupants, workers and contractors: safe access to plant and roofs, stairs and handrails, slip-resistant surfaces, safety glazing and manifestation on glass, confined space identification, statutory and safety signage, the health and safety records that must be kept for the building, and the systems for managing contractors. It sits behind many other elements: roof safety, balustrades, lifts, plant and hazardous materials each have their own pages, and this page covers what ties them together and the provisions not covered elsewhere.

| Provision | Where it applies | What commonly fails |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Access to plant and services | Plant rooms, roofs, risers, ceiling voids | Ladders without cages or fall protection; plant reached by climbing |
| Stairs and handrails | All buildings | Uneven risers; worn or slippery nosings; missing handrails; low balustrades |
| Floor slip resistance | Entries, wet areas, ramps, external paving | Polished or wet surfaces; wrong finishes for the location |
| Glazing safety | Doors, sidelights, low-level glass | Ordinary glass in critical locations; no manifestation on glass doors |
| Confined spaces | Tanks, pits, ducts, voids | Not identified, signed or controlled |
| Safety signage | Plant, hazards, emergency equipment | Missing, faded or wrong |
| Building safety records | All workplaces and managed buildings | Missing or out of date: registers, manuals, the health and safety file |
| Contractor management | All managed buildings | No induction, permits or hazard information |

Duties sit with whoever manages or controls the building as a workplace, in Australia the person conducting a business or undertaking and those with management or control of a workplace, in Britain the employer and those in control of premises, and in the United States the employer under OSHA. Owners of tenanted buildings usually retain duties for common areas, plant and structure.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
The physical safety measures in a building wear with traffic and time, and the records that support them go out of date as soon as the building changes. Typical lives are a guide; traffic, cleaning and alterations move them.

| Element | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stair nosings and treads | 10 to 25 years | Traffic; cleaning |
| Anti-slip treatments | 1 to 5 years | Traffic; cleaning products |
| Fixed ladders and platforms | 25 to 40 years | Corrosion; damage |
| Glass manifestation | 5 to 15 years | Cleaning; damage |
| Safety signs | 10 to 20 years | UV; damage |
| Records and registers | Must be kept current | Changes to the building |

What shortens it: heavy traffic wearing stairs and floors; cleaning regimes that polish floors or strip treatments; changes to the building without updating records and signs; plant added without safe access.

Records have no wear life but go out of date every time the building changes, which is the commonest way they fail.

sections.heading: Access to plant and confined spaces
sections.markdown:
Plant installed on roofs, high walls and in ceiling voids without fixed ladders, platforms and fall protection is reached by portable ladders or climbing, which causes falls. New plant is often added without access being designed.

Tanks, pits, sumps, ducts and voids with limited entry and poor ventilation can hold toxic or oxygen-deficient atmospheres. Deaths occur when people enter unidentified confined spaces without controls, and when rescuers follow them.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ladder marks on walls near plant | No designed access to plant. Inspection. | Install fixed access: a caged ladder, a ladder with fall arrest, or a platform with guardrails. |
| Fixed ladder to plant with uneven rungs or no cage or fall arrest | Ladder unsafe for regular use. Rung spacing and width measured against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Repair or replace the ladder, and add fall protection or a stair where access is frequent. |
| Roof edges or plant platforms with no guardrail | Fall from height. Guardrail height and condition against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Install guardrails or edge protection before further access. |

sections.heading: Stairs, floors and glazing
sections.markdown:
Uneven risers, worn and slippery nosings, missing contrast on edges, missing handrails, and balustrades below current heights cause falls, the most common serious injury in buildings.

Polished stone, glazed tiles and smooth finishes at entries, in wet areas and on ramps become slippery when wet or contaminated; cleaning products and sealers make them worse. Slip resistance can be measured and compared with the level needed for the location.

Glass doors and full-height glazing without manifestation are walked into; ordinary annealed glass in doors and low-level panels breaks into dangerous shards. Older buildings often have glass that would not meet current safety glazing rules.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Repeated slips at an entry | Floor finish unsuitable when wet. Slip resistance test. | Test the slip resistance; treat or replace the finish and add recessed matting. |
| Falls on one stair | Uneven risers or worn nosings. Measurement against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Measure the risers and nosings; replace worn nosings and correct the flight. |
| People walking into glass doors | Missing manifestation. Inspection. | Apply manifestation at the right heights, and check the glass is safety glass. |

sections.heading: Records and contractors
sections.markdown:
Asbestos registers, plant registers, confined space registers, operation and maintenance manuals, and the health and safety file (in Britain) are needed for anyone working safely on the building. Where they are missing or out of date, contractors work blind.

Contractors without induction, permits or hazard information disturb asbestos, enter confined spaces, work at height without protection and isolate systems unsafely.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Contractors unaware of hazards | No induction or registers. Records. | Set up inductions, permits and registers, and make them available to contractors. |
| No asbestos register, plant risk assessments or confined space register on site | Contractors working without the information they need. Records review. | Assemble the registers and include them in contractor induction. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unprotected access to plant at height; unidentified confined spaces; dangerous glazing; slippery entries | safety · 4 Essential | Rectify now. |
| Injury-causing defects | failure · 4 Essential | Repair now. |
| Register reviews and statutory inspections due | deadline · 4 Essential | At the required interval. |
| Worn stairs, faded signs, ageing treatments | condition · 4 Essential | Repair in the near term. |
| Stair finishes and fittings at end of life | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Replace. |
| No registers or building safety file | check · 3 Important | Compile. |
| Normal | nil · 1 Routine | Routine. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A health and safety consultant or building surveyor with safety expertise leads, with specialists for slip testing, glazing and confined spaces. The checks below cover how plant is reached, the condition of stairs, floors and glazing, and the records contractors rely on.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Access audit | Of every plant item, roof area, riser and ceiling void that needs maintenance, recording how it is reached and what protection exists. |
| Stair survey | Consistency of risers and goings, nosing condition and contrast, handrails on both sides where required, balustrade heights and openings. |
| Slip resistance testing | Of floors at entries, wet areas, ramps and external paving, wet and dry, against the classification needed for each location. |
| Glazing survey | Safety glass markings in doors and low-level panels, and manifestation on glass doors and full-height glazing. |
| Confined space survey | Identify every tank, pit, sump, duct and void that meets the definition, and record entry points, hazards and controls. |
| Records review | Asbestos, plant and confined space registers, operation and maintenance manuals, the health and safety file, and their currency. |
| Contractor management review | Inductions, permits to work, isolation procedures and hazard information. |
| Incident review | Where and how injuries and near misses have occurred. |

The report should list hazards by risk, compliance gaps, missing records, and a prioritised programme.

sections.heading: Making the building safe to work in
sections.markdown:
Most fixes are physical and modest: a fixed ladder, a contrasting nosing, a strip of manifestation. Records and a contractor system cost little more and prevent the next incident. The order of work follows the safety findings first.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fixed access to plant | Caged ladders or ladders with fall arrest, platforms with guardrails, walkways and roof hatches with guardrails. | Wherever plant at height is reached by portable ladder or climbing. |
| Stair repairs | Replace worn nosings with slip-resistant, contrasting nosings, add handrails, raise balustrades where people are at risk. | Where nosings are worn, risers uneven or handrails missing, and wherever falls cluster on one flight. |
| Slip remedies | Anti-slip treatments, replacement finishes in wet and entry areas, recessed entry matting, and cleaning that does not polish floors. | Where floors are slippery when wet, above all at entries and wet areas. |
| Glazing | Replace annealed glass in critical locations with safety glass; apply manifestation at the right heights. | Where annealed glass sits in doors and low panels, or people walk into glass doors. |
| Confined spaces | Signs, locked covers, a register and entry procedures. | Wherever pits, tanks and voids could be entered. |
| Signage | Signs at plant, hazards and emergency equipment. | Where signs are missing or faded. |
| Records | Compile and maintain registers, manuals and the safety file, and make them available to contractors. | Where registers or the safety file are missing or out of date. |
| Contractor system | Inductions, permits to work and isolation procedures. | Wherever contractors work on plant or in hazardous areas. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Audits and slip testing are lump sums, with slip testing recurring where floors are treated. Fixed access works are priced per item: ladders, platforms, walkways and guardrails. Stair works per flight; floor treatments and replacement finishes by area; glazing per pane; signage per sign. Compiling registers and a safety file is a lump sum, then a recurring update cost. Contractor management systems are an operating cost.

Most items are code compliance; worn stairs and finishes are lifecycle; treatments and signage are repairs and maintenance; serious hazards are immediate.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a walk-through cannot: where incidents have happened, which hazards are registered, and whether contractors are told about them. Ask for them before the inspection, so the inspector knows where to look.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Asbestos, plant and confined space registers | What hazards are known, and where. |
| Health and safety file or building manual, with operation and maintenance manuals | How the building is meant to be accessed, maintained and worked on safely. |
| Contractor induction, permit and isolation procedures | Whether contractors are told about hazards before they start. |
| Incident and injury records, including slips and falls | Where incidents cluster, which points to the surface or stair to fix. |
| Slip resistance test results | Whether floors meet the slip resistance their use needs. |
| Roof and plant access records and safety system certificates | Whether access to roofs and plant is designed and certified. |
| Glazing schedules for doors and low-level panels | Whether the glass in doors and low panels is safety glass. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Workplace safety findings are often blamed on people rather than on the building, or dismissed because nothing has happened yet. Both readings leave the hazard in place.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| People keep slipping because they are careless | Several slips at one entrance, or falls on one flight, point to that surface or stair rather than to the people using it. |
| No-one has been hurt, so the access to plant is fine | Unidentified confined spaces and plant reachable only by climbing are serious hazards. Identify, sign and control them before anyone next needs access. |
| Safety records are paperwork, not condition | Missing registers and an incomplete safety file leave contractors unaware of hazards, and are findings in their own right. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market places the duty for a safe workplace on those who run or control it, but through different laws. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out the general duties and the rules on falls, floors, glazing, confined spaces and records.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| General duties | The model work health and safety laws place duties on persons conducting a business or undertaking and those with management or control of workplaces. | The Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974, and the Workplace (Health, Safety and Welfare) Regulations 1992, which cover floors, stairs and glazing. | The OSH Act and OSHA standards. |
| Falls, stairs and access | A code of practice covers managing the risk of falls; AS 1657 covers fixed platforms, walkways, stairways and ladders. | The Work at Height Regulations 2005; Approved Document K covers stairs and guarding. | OSHA's walking-working surfaces standard (29 CFR 1910 Subpart D); building codes govern stairs. |
| Floors and glazing | AS 4586 classifies slip resistance; AS 1288 covers glazing. | Approved Document K covers glazing. | ANSI A326.3 sets dynamic slip resistance testing of hard surface flooring; building codes govern safety glazing. |
| Confined spaces | A code of practice covers confined spaces. | The Confined Spaces Regulations 1997. | OSHA's permit-required confined spaces standard (1910.146). |
| Records and facilities | A code of practice covers the work environment and facilities. | The Construction (Design and Management) Regulations 2015 require a health and safety file for the building. | OSHA's recordkeeping rule (29 CFR 1904) requires many employers to record work-related injuries and illnesses; 29 CFR 1910.141 sets sanitation facilities. |

sections.heading: Worked example: rooftop plant reached by ladder
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 1990s warehouse has rooftop air conditioning units reached through a ceiling hatch by portable ladder. There are scuff marks on the wall below the hatch, and the incident log records two slips at the main entrance in wet weather last winter.

The roof access is the first line: plant at height reached by climbing is graded safety, rectified now with a fixed ladder with fall arrest or a platform, and a guardrail at the hatch. The slips point to the entrance floor, not to the people: a slip resistance test confirms whether the finish is the cause.

So the register carries the access as a safety line now and the entrance floor as a check line, becoming a condition line for treatment or replacement once the test result is in. The records to ask for are the plant register, the safety file and the contractor induction procedure.

pages.title: Partitioning Systems
pages.question: How do internal partitions fail, and when does a partition matter for fire safety?
pages.answer: Partitions carry no structural load but may carry fire and acoustic ratings, which they lose when services penetrate them or when they stop at the ceiling instead of the slab. Partitions built tight to deflecting slabs crack; meeting rooms leak sound over ceilings; full-height glass without manifestation is walked into; operable walls wear their tracks and jam or drop. Check the fire strategy before removing or penetrating any partition.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about partitioning systems; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Fixed and operable partitions, performance requirements
