pages.searchTitle: Partitions: lost fire and acoustic rating, cracking, glazed walls and operable walls

questions.question: Can we remove a partition wall?
questions.answer: Only after checking the fire strategy. Partitions forming compartments, corridors or risers are fire-safety elements.

questions.question: Why can people in the next meeting room hear us?
questions.answer: Usually the partition stops at the ceiling, or sound passes around services and outlets. Seal above the ceiling, or add a ceiling barrier.

questions.question: Why is the top of the partition cracking?
questions.answer: The slab above is deflecting onto a wall built tight to it. A deflection head lets them move independently.

questions.question: Do glass partitions need markings?
questions.answer: Yes. Full-height glass without manifestation is walked into, and older glazed partitions may not use safety glass.

questions.question: How long do operable walls last?
questions.answer: 15 to 25 years with servicing, as do glazed partitions and toilet partitions.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Partition problems show above the ceiling as walls that stop short and unsealed penetrations, and below it as cracks, damage, unmarked glass and dragging operable walls, and in fire strategy and fit-out records. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On site | Partitions stopping at the ceiling when tiles are lifted | Fire rating, acoustic leakage and services |
| On site | Unsealed penetrations through walls above ceilings | Fire rating, acoustic leakage and services |
| On site | Cracks at partition heads under long spans | Movement, damage and glazing |
| On site | Glass without manifestation | Movement, damage and glazing |
| On site | Operable walls hard to move, leaning or with damaged seals | Operable walls |
| On site | Damaged and patched plasterboard | Movement, damage and glazing |
| In the records | Fire strategy showing rated walls | Fit-out alterations |
| In the records | Fit-out drawings and approvals | Fit-out alterations |
| In the records | Acoustic complaints | Fire rating, acoustic leakage and services |
| In the records | Operable wall service records | Operable walls |
| In the records | Back-to-back power outlets in walls between apartments or meeting rooms | Fire rating, acoustic leakage and services |
| In the records | Corridor and riser walls altered by fit-outs | Fit-out alterations |
| In the records | Water staining and swelling at the base of plasterboard near wet areas | Movement, damage and glazing |
| In the records | Toilet partitions swollen or with broken hardware | Movement, damage and glazing |

sections.heading: Types of partition
sections.markdown:
Partitioning systems divide space within a building: plasterboard on steel or timber studs, demountable and glazed office partitions, operable walls in meeting and function rooms, toilet cubicle partitions, and non-loadbearing masonry walls. Partitions carry no structural load, but they can be fire-rated, acoustically rated, or both, and they decide how well a space works for privacy, sound and layout flexibility. Most partitions in commercial buildings belong to tenant fit-outs and change at every lease.

| Type | Where it is found | What commonly fails |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Plasterboard stud walls | Offices, apartments, all building types | Damage; cracking at joints; acoustic leakage |
| Fire-rated plasterboard walls | Compartment and corridor walls, risers | Penetrations; walls not to slab |
| Acoustic partitions | Meeting rooms, apartments, hotels | Gaps above ceilings; services penetrations |
| Glazed and demountable partitions | Offices | Glass safety; manifestation; acoustic seals |
| Operable walls | Meeting and function rooms, schools, hotels | Track and mechanism failure; seals; safety |
| Toilet cubicle partitions | Amenities | Moisture swelling; hardware |
| Masonry internal walls | Older buildings | Cracking; alterations |

For assessment, the important question about any partition is its role: dividing space only, separating sound, or separating fire. The answer decides whether a defect is cosmetic, a comfort issue or a life-safety issue.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Plasterboard partitions last the life of the fit-out or longer, and glazed partitions, operable walls and toilet partitions fifteen to twenty-five years. Their fire and acoustic performance lasts only until the next penetration, which is why it is checked after every round of works.

| Type | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Plasterboard partitions | Life of the fit-out or longer | Damage; alterations |
| Glazed partitions | 15 to 25 years | Fit-out changes; hardware |
| Operable walls | 15 to 25 years with servicing | Use; track wear |
| Toilet partitions | 15 to 25 years | Moisture; abuse |
| Acoustic and fire performance | Until next penetration or alteration | Services works; fit-outs |

What shortens life, or performance: services penetrations that break fire and acoustic ratings; fit-out changes that remove or alter walls without understanding their role; slab deflection crushing or cracking partitions without deflection heads; moisture in plasterboard near wet areas.

In offices, partitions are usually removed and rebuilt with each fit-out, so their life is the lease term rather than their material life.

Rated partitions in the base building, such as corridor and riser walls, last as long as the building but lose performance with each penetration.

sections.heading: Fire rating, acoustic leakage and services
sections.markdown:
Rated partitions only perform if they run to the slab or a rated ceiling and every penetration is sealed. Cables, pipes and ducts added later, and walls stopped at the suspended ceiling, let fire, smoke and sound pass. Partitions are often assumed to be rated, or assumed not to be, without checking.

Meeting rooms and apartments leak sound through gaps above ceilings, around services, under doors and through back-to-back outlets.

Power, data and plumbing inside stud walls are cut into during alterations, and back-to-back outlets create sound and fire paths.

A partition's role decides how much a defect matters. The same hole above the ceiling is a nuisance in a plain dividing wall, a privacy complaint in a meeting room wall, and a fire safety finding in a corridor or riser wall, so the first step is identifying which partitions the fire strategy and acoustic design rely on.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Conversations audible between meeting rooms | Gap above ceiling or services penetration. Ceiling void inspection. | Seal the gap above the ceiling and around services, or add ceiling barriers. |
| Rated wall with open penetrations | Services works without fire stopping. Inspection. | Fire stop every penetration with tested systems. |
| Back-to-back power outlets in a wall between apartments or meeting rooms | A sound and fire path through the wall. Outlets aligned on both faces of the same cavity. | Offset the outlets, or seal behind them. |
| Neighbours heard through a wall between apartments | Separating wall short of its sound insulation. Field sound test against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market); flanking paths and penetrations checked. | Seal penetrations and flanking paths, or add an independent lining. |

sections.heading: Fit-out alterations
sections.markdown:
Fit-outs sometimes remove or alter partitions that are part of the base building's fire or acoustic design, such as corridor walls and riser enclosures, without realising their role. The loss only shows in a fire or in neighbour complaints.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A corridor or riser wall altered or removed during a fit-out | A base-building fire or acoustic wall lost without review. The fire strategy plans compared with the walls on site. | Reinstate the wall, and require fire and acoustic review before base-building walls are altered. |

sections.heading: Movement, damage and glazing
sections.markdown:
Partitions are light walls fixed between a moving slab and a busy floor. They crack when the slab above deflects, are damaged by furniture and moves, swell where water reaches them and, where glazed, can be walked into.

Partitions built tight to slabs above crack and bow when the slab deflects; deflection heads that allow movement are missing or jammed.

Plasterboard is damaged by furniture, trolleys and moves, and swells and grows mould where it gets wet.

Full-height glass without manifestation is walked into; older glazed partitions may not use safety glass.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cracking at the partition head | Slab deflection without a deflection head. Head detail inspection. | Fit or free a deflection head. |
| Full-height glass with nothing at eye level | Glazing people walk into. No manifestation; check whether the glass is safety glass. | Add manifestation, and replace any glass that is not safety glass. |
| Swelling and staining at the base of plasterboard near wet areas | Water reaching standard plasterboard. Moisture readings at the base of the wall. | Fix the water source, and replace with moisture-resistant board. |
| People walking into glass screens or doors | Glazing not marked. Manifestation heights and contrast against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Add manifestation at the required heights, contrasting with the background. |

sections.heading: Operable walls
sections.markdown:
Operable walls are heavy, moving panels on overhead tracks. Tracks and carriers wear, panels drop or jam, seals fail so rooms leak sound, and panels have injured people when moved improperly.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Operable wall dragging or dropping | Track or carrier wear. Service inspection. | Service the tracks and carriers, or replace failing panels; stop using the wall if a panel drops. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fire-rated partitions breached; unsafe glazing; operable walls with failing tracks | safety · 4 Essential | Rectify now. |
| Partitions damaged or unusable | failure · 3 Important | Repair. |
| Fire certification requiring rectification | deadline · 3 Important | As required. |
| Acoustic leakage; cracking; damage | condition · 2 Planned | Repair in the near term. |
| Partitions at end of fit-out life | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Replace with fit-out. |
| Rated partitions not identified | check · 2 Planned | Survey. |
| Normal | nil · 1 Routine | Routine. |

The same open penetration is a safety finding in a compartment wall, a condition finding in an acoustic wall between meeting rooms, and nil in a plain dividing wall; grade by role, not appearance.

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A building surveyor leads, with a fire engineer to identify rated partitions and an acoustic consultant where privacy or noise is the issue. The checks below first identify which partitions are rated, from the fire strategy and acoustic design, then lift ceiling tiles along them to check the heads and penetrations.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Identify rated partitions | From the fire strategy, fire engineering report and acoustic design, and mark them on plans, since fit-outs often blur which walls matter. |
| Ceiling void inspection | Along rated partitions to check they run to the slab and that every penetration is sealed with a tested system. |
| Head detail inspection | Where partitions crack, to check for deflection heads. |
| Acoustic testing | Between rooms where complaints exist, with flanking paths traced. |
| Glazing check | For safety glass marks and manifestation. |
| Operable wall inspection | By the manufacturer or a specialist: tracks, carriers, panels, seals and safe operation. |

The report should give a plan of rated partitions, defects in each, and a remediation plan coordinated with fit-out cycles.

Where drawings are missing, ratings may need to be inferred from construction, which takes opening up and specialist judgement.

sections.heading: Sealing, restoring and repairing
sections.markdown:
Breached fire-rated partitions, unsafe glazing and operable walls with failing hardware come first. After that, the work restores acoustic separation, lets partitions move with the slab, and controls fit-outs so base-building walls are not altered without review.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fire stopping and extension | Fire stopping of every penetration in rated partitions with tested systems, and extension of partitions to the slab where they stop at the ceiling. | Wherever a rated partition is breached or stops short. |
| Acoustic sealing | Acoustic sealing above ceilings, around services and at outlets, with ceiling barriers where walls cannot be extended. | Where sound leaks between rooms. |
| Deflection heads | Deflection heads fitted or freed where slab movement cracks partitions. | Where partition heads crack. |
| Glazing safety | Safety glass and manifestation on glazed partitions. | Wherever glazed partitions lack either. |
| Operable wall servicing | Operable wall servicing on a schedule, with replacement where tracks or panels are failing. | On every operable wall. |
| Labelling | Labelling of rated partitions above ceilings so trades know what they are penetrating. | Wherever rated partitions run above ceilings. |
| Plasterboard repairs | Repairs to damaged plasterboard, with moisture-resistant board near wet areas. | Where boards are damaged or swollen. |
| Fit-out controls | Fit-out controls requiring fire and acoustic review before base-building walls are altered. | In every building with tenant fit-outs. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Fire and acoustic sealing is priced per penetration or by length of partition, with access above ceilings driving cost. Partition replacement is priced by area and usually coincides with fit-outs, when it is cheapest. Operable wall servicing recurs; replacement is a lump sum per wall. Labelling of rated walls is inexpensive and prevents future breaches.

Fire safety items are code compliance; acoustic and finish repairs are condition items; replacement is lifecycle and often a tenant cost.

Identifying rated walls once, on plans and on site, avoids repeated investigation at every fit-out.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a look at the walls cannot: which partitions are rated, what fit-outs have done to them, and whether operable walls are serviced. Ask for the fire strategy plans before any wall is cut or removed.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Fire strategy and plans showing rated partitions | Which partitions are rated, and for what. |
| Fit-out drawings and approvals | What fit-outs changed, and whether it was approved. |
| Acoustic reports and complaints | Where sound leaks, and what was measured. |
| Operable wall service records | Whether operable walls are serviced. |
| Fire stopping records for partition penetrations | Whether partition penetrations were fire stopped. |
| Glazing schedules for partitions | Whether glazed partitions use safety glass. |
| Tenant fit-out guide and rules on altering walls | What tenants may and may not do to walls. |
| Records of neighbour noise complaints | Whether noise between neighbours is a pattern. |
| Strata approvals for wall alterations | Whether wall alterations in apartments were approved. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Partitions are misread when a wall is removed or cut without checking its role, and when every defect is graded the same whatever the wall is for.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| It is just a wall | Before removing or penetrating any partition, check the fire strategy: partitions forming compartments, corridors or risers are fire-safety elements. |
| A hole is a hole | Decide first whether a partition is a fire, acoustic or plain dividing wall, because the same defect matters very differently depending on its role. |
| The crack is a defect in the wall | Cracks at the head of partitions under long spans come from the slab deflecting onto a wall built tight to it. Fit or free a deflection head; patching the crack alone will not hold. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets requirements for fire-rated and acoustic separation, for glazing in partitions, and for keeping rated walls intact through alterations. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Fire and acoustic separation, and glazing | The National Construction Code sets fire resistance levels and sound insulation requirements, including between apartments and between units and corridors; AS 1530.4 sets fire testing; AS 1288 governs glazing including manifestation; fit-outs that alter partitions need approval. | Approved Document B governs fire separation and Approved Document E sound insulation, including pre-completion testing in new homes; BS EN 1364 covers fire testing of non-loadbearing walls; Approved Document K covers glazing manifestation. | The International Building Code sets fire partitions and fire barriers and sound transmission requirements in dwelling units; ASTM E90 and E336 cover sound testing; tenant improvements need permits and fire review. |

Tenancy fit-out guides should identify which walls tenants may not alter.

Strata by-laws restrict wall changes.

sections.heading: Worked example: meeting rooms that overhear each other
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. On an office floor, conversations carry between two new meeting rooms. Lifting a ceiling tile shows the partition between them stops at the ceiling, and the corridor wall beside them, which the fire strategy shows as rated, has new cables passing through it unsealed. The glass fronts of the rooms have no markings.

First decide what each wall is for. The meeting room partition is acoustic: the gap above the ceiling explains the complaint. The corridor wall is a fire-safety element, so its unsealed cables are a safety finding. Unmarked full-height glass is walked into.

So the register carries fire stopping of the corridor wall as a safety line, an acoustic barrier or extension above the meeting room partition, manifestation on the glass, and labelling of rated walls above the ceiling.

pages.title: Passenger & Goods Lifts
pages.question: How do lifts fail, when do they need modernisation rather than maintenance, and which faults are safety-critical?
pages.answer: Lifts are modernised in stages: controls, drives and doors at 15 to 20 years, machines and ropes at 25 to 35. Unsupported controllers are the usual trigger, shown by rising breakdowns and long waits for parts. Doors cause most breakdowns. The safety faults are door interlocks, brakes and unintended movement, levelling trip hazards, and emergency phones that no longer connect as copper lines are retired. Buried hydraulic cylinders corrode and leak.

pages.searchTitle: Passenger and goods lifts: breakdowns, modernisation, safety failures and inspections

questions.question: When does a lift need modernising?
questions.answer: When its controller and drive lose parts support, or breakdowns rise and outages lengthen. Age alone is a poor guide: a well-maintained thirty-five-year-old lift with supported controls can outperform a neglected fifteen-year-old one.

questions.question: Why does our lift keep breaking down at the doors?
questions.answer: Door equipment takes more wear and abuse than any other part. Where doors dominate the breakdown record and the controller is still supported, a door package is worth doing on its own.

questions.question: Is an emergency lift phone that doesn't connect serious?
questions.answer: Yes. An emergency phone that does not connect is a safety failure; take the lift out of service until it is fixed.

questions.question: How often must lifts be inspected?
questions.answer: In the United Kingdom, LOLER requires thorough examination of passenger lifts at least every six months. In Australia and the United States, intervals are set by state, or state and city, regulators.

questions.question: How long do lift parts last?
questions.answer: Controllers, drives and door equipment 15 to 20 years, suspension ropes 10 to 20, geared machines 25 to 35, gearless machines 30 to 40, and hydraulic cylinders 25 to 30.

questions.question: Why are our lifts so slow at busy times when they rarely break down?
questions.answer: That is usually traffic capacity, not condition. Measure waiting times against the people and floors served; group or destination control may be enough before an extra lift.

questions.question: Why does the elevator stop a little above or below the floor?
questions.answer: Usually a drive, brake or valve problem. Measure levelling at each floor and repair the cause; a trip step at a landing is a safety finding.

questions.question: Why does the lift keep faulting when the engineer finds nothing wrong?
questions.answer: Often power quality, phase loss or an unstable generator supply rather than a component. Log the supply at the lift and correct the power quality or phase problem.

questions.question: Why is the lift out of service for weeks waiting for parts?
questions.answer: Usually controller obsolescence: the manufacturer no longer supports the controls. Get the parts support position in writing, and plan modernisation of the controls and drive.

questions.question: Why is our hydraulic lift slower in winter?
questions.answer: Hydraulic oil thickens in the cold. Check the oil and its temperature range with the maintenance contractor.

questions.question: Why does the lift fault after heavy rain?
questions.answer: Water in the pit is reaching the equipment. Inspect the pit and sump pump; waterproof the pit, and renew the sump and pump.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Lift problems show first to passengers, as waits, door faults and steps at landings; then on site, from machine room to pit; and above all in the breakdown record. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What you notice as a passenger | Long waits at the start and end of the day, or several lifts arriving together while one floor is never served promptly | Traffic capacity |
| What you notice as a passenger | Doors that reopen repeatedly, close too slowly, or nudge shut against people | Doors, ropes, brakes and levelling |
| What you notice as a passenger | A step up or down into the car at a landing, which is a trip hazard and a levelling fault | Doors, ropes, brakes and levelling |
| What you notice as a passenger | Vibration, lateral sway, banging or scraping during travel, or a jolt at each start and stop | Doors, ropes, brakes and levelling |
| What you notice as a passenger | Buttons worn blank, indicators dark, no audible floor announcement and no braille on the controls | Obsolescence, maintenance and power |
| What you notice as a passenger | A handwritten out-of-service notice, which usually means an outage long enough for someone to make a sign | Obsolescence, maintenance and power |
| On site | Controller nameplate, manufacturer and date in the machine room or control cabinet, and whether anything about it looks aftermarket | Obsolescence, maintenance and power |
| On site | Machine room: temperature, ventilation, oil leaks, housekeeping, storage of unrelated items, and whether the room is secure | Obsolescence, maintenance and power |
| On site | Ropes at the machine: broken wires, red dust, uneven groove wear on the sheave | Doors, ropes, brakes and levelling |
| On site | Pit: water, oil, debris, corrosion of buffers and guide shoes, sump pump condition | Hydraulic lifts and the pit |
| On site | Doors at every landing, not just the ground floor: damage, gaps, sensors, interlock condition | Doors, ropes, brakes and levelling |
| On site | Levelling measured at each floor, loaded and unloaded if possible | Doors, ropes, brakes and levelling |
| On site | Emergency phone tested from inside the car at every lift, listening for who answers and whether they identify the building | Emergency communication and fire functions |
| On site | Fire service recall tested with the fire contractor, including fire-fighter control where provided | Emergency communication and fire functions |
| In the records | Call-out and breakdown history per lift over two to three years, coded by cause if the contractor provides it | Obsolescence, maintenance and power |
| In the records | Entrapment records, which are the clearest measure of how a lift is actually performing | Obsolescence, maintenance and power |
| In the records | Maintenance contract: scope, attendance hours, response times, what is excluded and who holds the controller codes | Obsolescence, maintenance and power |
| In the records | Modernisation history and any outstanding recommendations, with dates | Obsolescence, maintenance and power |
| In the records | Registration and periodic inspection or thorough examination certificates | Standards by country |
| In the records | Rope and safety gear test results | Doors, ropes, brakes and levelling |
| In the records | Manufacturer's written parts support position for the controller and drive | Obsolescence, maintenance and power |
| In the records | Traffic or waiting-time analysis, if one has ever been done | Traffic capacity |
| In the records | Hazardous materials register entries for the machine room and lift equipment | Hydraulic lifts and the pit |

sections.heading: Types of lift
sections.markdown:
Passenger and goods lifts move people and goods between floors. A lift comprises the drive machine and brake, the controller, suspension (steel ropes or coated belts), car and counterweight, guide rails, landing and car doors with their operators and interlocks, safety gear and overspeed governor, buffers in the pit, the car interior and fixtures, emergency communication, and interfaces to fire systems. In apartment buildings the lifts are usually the largest single sinking fund item; in offices they shape tenant experience every day.

A lift is read as three things at once. It is plant, with a machine, brake, ropes and safety gear that are tested and certified like any other lifting equipment. It is a control system, whose electronics date faster than any mechanical part and usually decide when money must be spent. And it is the building's accessible route, so when it stops, parts of the building become unreachable for anyone who cannot use the stairs.

| Type | Where it is found | Character |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Geared traction | Offices and apartments, 1950s to 1990s | Worm or helical gear between motor and sheave; gearbox wear; oil |
| Gearless traction | Taller and newer buildings | Efficient; long-lived machines; controllers set the modernisation cycle |
| Machine-room-less (MRL) | Most new buildings from the 2000s | Machine in the shaft; access for maintenance is the constraint |
| Hydraulic | Low-rise buildings, goods lifts | Cylinder in the ground or beside the car; oil leaks; slow in cold |
| Goods and service lifts | Retail, hospitals, hotels, industrial | Heavy use; door and floor damage |
| Fire-fighting and evacuation lifts | Tall buildings | Protected power, controls and lobbies; additional testing |

Type can usually be established without opening anything. A machine room above the shaft with a visible gearbox and sheave means geared traction; a machine room with a compact gearless machine means gearless; no machine room at all, with a control cabinet beside the top landing, means machine-room-less. A pit with an oil tank and a ram beneath or beside the car means hydraulic, and hydraulic lifts rarely serve more than five or six floors. Speed, floors served and the number of lifts in a group together tell you whether the installation was ever sized for the building's traffic ([Plant Rooms](https://moyneross.com/technical/plant-rooms)).

Lifts are modernised in stages rather than replaced: controls, drives and door operators at 15 to 20 years; car interiors when the building is refurbished; machines, ropes, guides and safety gear at 25 to 35 years. Each stage brings the components it touches up to the current standard, which often adds work such as unintended car movement protection or accessibility features.

How the lifts are grouped matters as much as their condition. Two lifts serving fifteen floors with separate controls behave worse than two under group control, and a single lift in an apartment building means every repair takes the building's only accessible route out of service. In tall buildings some lifts carry extra duties: fire-fighting lifts with protected power and controls, evacuation lifts, and goods lifts taking trolley and pallet traffic that passenger lifts were never built for ([Emergency Power](https://moyneross.com/technical/emergency-power), [Fire Detection & Alarm Systems](https://moyneross.com/technical/fire-detection-and-alarm-systems)).

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
A lift's parts age at very different rates: controllers, drives and door equipment fifteen to twenty years, ropes ten to twenty, machines twenty-five to forty, and guide rails and safety gear longer still. What usually ends a controller's life is the end of parts support rather than wear.

| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Controllers and drives | 15 to 20 years | Manufacturer support; electronics |
| Door operators and equipment | 15 to 20 years | Traffic; abuse; maintenance |
| Geared machines | 25 to 35 years | Gear wear; lubrication |
| Gearless machines | 30 to 40 years | Bearings; brake |
| Suspension ropes | 10 to 20 years | Trips; sheave condition; lubrication |
| Hydraulic cylinders | 25 to 30 years | Corrosion of buried cylinders; seals |
| Car interiors | 10 to 20 years | Use; style |
| Guide rails, buffers and safety gear | 30 to 40 years | Rarely limiting; must be tested |
| Landing and car door interlocks | 20 to 30 years | Traffic; abuse; alignment |
| Overspeed governor and safety gear | 30 to 40 years, subject to testing | Test results; pit conditions; corrosion |
| Fixtures, buttons and indicators | 10 to 20 years | Use; vandalism; parts support |
| Emergency communication equipment | 10 to 15 years | Network retirement rather than wear |
| Shaft wiring and travelling cables | 25 to 35 years | Flexing; heat; rodents |

Lifts do not reach the end of their life as a whole. Each part has its own clock, and the earliest clock to run out is almost always the controller, because support for its electronics ends long before anything mechanical wears out. A lift is therefore modernised in stages through a long life rather than replaced once, and a building that defers the first stage usually finds the second and third arriving together.

What shortens life: heavy traffic, especially goods and hospital lifts and lifts serving car parks; door abuse: doors forced, struck by trolleys and held open; water in the pit from groundwater or failed sumps, corroding buffers, rails and safety gear; hot, dusty machine rooms that age electronics; call-out-only maintenance instead of planned preventive maintenance.

What lengthens it: planned preventive maintenance with defined scope and hours, rather than a contract that only responds to call-outs; a dry, clean, cool machine room or control space, with the pit kept free of water and oil; door protection: full-height light curtains, trolley guards on goods lifts, and management of how doors are used; modernising in planned stages while parts are still supported, which costs less and avoids emergency work; an independent condition audit every five years, so the programme is set by evidence rather than by the maintenance contractor's recommendations.

sections.heading: Obsolescence, maintenance and power
sections.markdown:
Controllers and drives are the usual trigger for modernisation, and the failure is commercial rather than mechanical. When a manufacturer stops making boards, and the programming tools and codes are proprietary to that manufacturer, a single component failure can stop a lift for weeks while a board is found on the second-hand market. Proprietary controls also lock the building into one maintenance contractor, since no one else can adjust the lift. Installations from the 1980s to the early 2000s are commonly in this position now, and the symptom is not breakdown frequency alone but the length of each outage.

The most common hidden failure is the contract itself. Lifts under a call-out-only or minimum-scope contract receive no preventive work, so wear is found when it stops the lift. Hours attended, tasks performed and parts replaced are rarely checked against what the contract promises, and a building can pay for planned maintenance for years without receiving it. Rising call-outs on a lift with no mechanical explanation is often this.

Lift drives are sensitive to the quality of the supply. Voltage dips, phase loss, harmonics from other equipment and unstable generator supplies cause lifts to trip and reset, which shows as intermittent faults with no component defect behind them. Lifts on standby generators need the generator's capacity and waveform checked, since a lift starting is a large, sudden load ([Main Electrical Supply](https://moyneross.com/technical/main-electrical-supply), [Emergency Power](https://moyneross.com/technical/emergency-power)).

In residential, retail and public buildings, lifts take damage that has nothing to do with wear: burnt or prised buttons, graffiti, forced doors, liquids in the car, and objects dropped down the shaft. The consequence is not only cosmetic. Objects in the pit foul safety gear, and liquids reach shaft wiring.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Breakdowns rising each year, long waits for parts | Controller obsolescence. Parts support status; call-out records. | Get the parts support position in writing; plan modernisation of the controls and drive. |
| Intermittent faults with no component defect found | Power quality, phase loss or generator supply. Supply logging at the lift; recent electrical works. | Log the supply at the lift, and correct the power quality or phase problem. |
| Rising call-outs with no mechanical explanation | Preventive maintenance not being performed. Attendance records against contract scope and hours. | Check attendance against the contract; reset it with a defined preventive scope and hours. |
| Only one contractor will quote, and parts take weeks | Proprietary controls with no open access. Written parts and tools position from the manufacturer. | Get the parts and tools position in writing; prefer open access at modernisation. |

sections.heading: Doors, ropes, brakes and levelling
sections.markdown:
Doors cause most breakdowns and most injuries, because they are the only part of a lift that moves every time it is used and the only part passengers touch. Operators, tracks, rollers, gibs and interlocks wear; doors are struck by trolleys and beds, forced by passengers and held open by people loading; door sensors go out of alignment or fail, so doors close on people. A landing door whose interlock lets it open without the car present is the most serious of all lift faults, because it opens a shaft at floor level.

Steel ropes wear from running over sheaves and from the loads they carry. Wear shows as broken wires, loss of diameter, and rouge, the fine red dust produced by wire rubbing on wire inside the rope. Sheave grooves wear unevenly, which grips some ropes harder than others, accelerates rope wear and eventually causes slip. Coated steel belts on newer machine-room-less lifts fail differently again, and are monitored electronically rather than by eye. Ropes and belts are replaced on measured condition, not on age.

Brakes wear and their linings contaminate; a failed brake can let a car move with doors open. Newer standards require protection against unintended car movement, and modernising the controls usually brings this requirement with it.

Cars that stop above or below the floor create trip hazards, a common cause of injury to elderly passengers and a sign of drive, brake or hydraulic valve problems.

Guide rails are aligned to fine tolerances on installation. Building settlement, shrinkage of a concrete frame over its first years, and seismic or wind movement in tall buildings pull them out of line. The symptom is ride quality: vibration, lateral sway and noise that worsen over years and that no amount of maintenance fixes, because the cause is the shaft rather than the lift.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Most call-outs for doors | Door equipment wear or abuse. Call-out coding; door inspection. | A door package: operators, tracks, rollers, interlocks and full-height light curtains. |
| Car stops above or below floor level | Drive, brake or valve problems. Levelling measurements. | Measure levelling at each floor; repair the drive, brake or valve. A trip step at a landing is a safety finding. |
| Red dust on ropes | Internal rope wear. Rope inspection and measurement. | Measure the ropes against the discard criteria, and replace them with the sheave regrooved or renewed. |
| Vibration and sway that worsen over years | Guide rail alignment or building movement. Ride quality measurement; rail alignment survey. | Measure ride quality and survey the rail alignment; realign the rails. |
| Doors reopening repeatedly for no obvious reason | Door sensor misalignment or failure. Light curtain test across the full opening height. | Test the light curtain across the full opening height; realign or replace it. |

sections.heading: Hydraulic lifts and the pit
sections.markdown:
Buried hydraulic cylinders corrode from the outside where groundwater reaches them, and nothing about that corrosion is visible from inside the building. Seals leak oil, which escapes into the ground around the cylinder and becomes a contamination problem as well as a lift problem. Older single-bottom cylinders can fail without warning, dropping the car, which is why current standards require double-bottom or protected designs. Hydraulic oil also thickens in the cold, so hydraulic lifts in unheated buildings run noticeably slower in winter.

Pits are the lowest point of the building and collect groundwater, water from firefighting and testing, and water from leaking risers. Standing water corrodes buffers, guide shoes, safety gear and the bottom of the shaft wiring, and the damage is slow, hidden and expensive. Sump pumps fail unnoticed because nobody looks in a pit between inspections ([Stormwater Drainage](https://moyneross.com/technical/stormwater-drainage)).

Lift installations from before the 1990s can contain asbestos in brake and clutch linings, in machine room gaskets and electrical arc chutes, in shaft and machine room fire protection and in some car fittings. It is safe in place but must be identified before modernisation work begins, because a controller or brake change disturbs exactly these components ([Hazardous Materials](https://moyneross.com/technical/hazardous-materials)).

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Oil in the pit or ground near a hydraulic lift | Seal or cylinder leak. Oil consumption; cylinder test. | Check oil consumption and test the cylinder; plan replacement with a protected design. |
| Lift noticeably slower in cold weather | Hydraulic oil viscosity. Hydraulic lift; speed varies with temperature; oil heater absent. | Check the oil and its temperature range with the maintenance contractor. |
| Faults appearing after rain or firefighting tests | Water in the pit reaching equipment. Pit inspection; sump pump condition; tide marks. | Waterproof the pit, and renew the sump and pump. |

sections.heading: Emergency communication and fire functions
sections.markdown:
Trapped passengers must be able to reach help at any hour, and the equipment that lets them do so is failing for a reason that has nothing to do with lifts. Lift phones were wired to copper telephone lines, and those networks are being retired worldwide; a line that is withdrawn leaves a phone that rings nowhere. Batteries in autodiallers fail silently, phones are disconnected during maintenance or refurbishment and not reconnected, and the monitoring centre contract lapses. The fault is invisible until someone is trapped.

Fire service recall and fire-fighter control must work with the fire alarm and protected power supply. Interfaces broken by fire panel or lift upgrades leave lifts that do not home or cannot be used by fire-fighters.

Fire service recall, fire-fighter control and fire-fighting lift functions depend on wiring and logic shared with the fire alarm, the protected power supply and the lobby doors. Each of those systems is upgraded on its own cycle, and interfaces are routinely broken by a fire panel replacement or a lift modernisation. Lifts that fail to home on alarm, or a fire-fighting lift that cannot be taken under fire-fighter control, are failures of the building's fire strategy rather than of the lift ([Fire Detection & Alarm Systems](https://moyneross.com/technical/fire-detection-and-alarm-systems), [Passive Fire Protection](https://moyneross.com/technical/passive-fire-protection)).

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Phone silent on test | Line retired, disconnected or battery failed. Line type; test. | Take the lift out of service; upgrade to a digital or cellular autodialler with monitored answering. |
| Lift does not home on fire alarm | Fire interface broken by a panel or lift upgrade. Joint test with the fire contractor; dates of recent works. | Restore the fire interface, test it jointly with the fire contractor, and record it. |
| No stretcher-sized lift in a taller building | Emergency access short of the market’s rules. Car size against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Check the car against the requirement at the next modernisation, with the fire strategy. |

sections.heading: Traffic capacity
sections.markdown:
A lift installation can be in good order and still be failing the building. Changes of use, denser fit-outs, new floors or a shift in how a building works can push demand past what the lifts were sized for, and the symptom is long waits at peak with few breakdowns. Lifts cannot be made much faster, so the remedies are different from any other fault: better group or destination control, changes to how floors are served, or in the worst cases an additional lift.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Long waits at peak but few breakdowns | Traffic capacity, not condition. Waiting-time measurement against the population served; floors and lift count. | Measure waiting times; group or destination control may be enough before an extra lift. |
| Small car that a wheelchair user cannot turn in | Car below current access sizes. Car dimensions and car lighting against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Record the gap for the next modernisation, and check whether the building needs a larger car. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Landing door openable without the car present; car moves with doors open; brake or safety gear defect | safety · 4 Essential | Remove from service until fixed. |
| Emergency communication not working, or reaching no one who answers | safety · 4 Essential | Remove from service until restored. |
| Levelling errors creating a trip step at a landing | safety · 4 Essential | Correct now; restrict use if significant. |
| Fire-fighting or evacuation lift not performing its fire functions | safety · 4 Essential | Restore now; notify the fire strategy owner. |
| Lift out of service, or entrapments recurring | failure · 4 Essential | Repair now. |
| The only lift in a building with occupants who depend on it out of service | failure · 4 Essential | Repair now and make interim arrangements for residents. |
| Periodic inspection, thorough examination or registration due | deadline · 4 Essential | At the prescribed date. |
| Emergency phone on a network being retired | deadline · 4 Essential | Migrate before the line is withdrawn. |
| Rising breakdowns, worn doors, rope wear approaching discard criteria, hydraulic leaks | condition · 3 Important | Repair or modernise in the near term. |
| Maintenance delivered below the contracted scope | condition · 3 Important | Enforce or re-tender the contract now. |
| Controls, drives or machines at the end of their life; parts support ended | lifecycle · 3 Important | Plan staged modernisation. |
| Waiting times materially worse than the building needs | lifecycle · 3 Important | Traffic study, then control or capacity works. |
| No condition audit; modernisation history unknown; asbestos status unknown | check · 3 Important | Audit before sizing works. |
| Cosmetic wear to car interiors and fixtures | nil · 1 Routine | Routine maintenance. |

Lift findings separate cleanly into two kinds, and they should not be traded against each other. Safety defects stop the lift today whatever they cost. Everything else is a programme: obsolescence, wear and capacity are planned, staged and budgeted, and deferring them raises cost and risk but harms nobody immediately.

The grading follows what a finding demands, not the size of the eventual bill.

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
An independent lift consultant leads, with the maintenance contractor present; independence matters because the contractor may also bid for the modernisation. The checks below start with the breakdown record, then test the safety functions and inspect each lift from machine room to pit.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Records review | Breakdowns and entrapments per lift over two to three years, maintenance scope and hours, modernisation history, inspection certificates. |
| Machine room or control cabinet inspection | Controller, drive, machine, brake, governor, ropes and sheaves. |
| Shaft and pit inspection | From the car top and pit: guides, doors, interlocks, counterweight, buffers, water and oil. |
| Performance testing | Door times, levelling accuracy, ride quality, waiting times at peak, with levelling read against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). |
| Safety testing | As the standard requires: safety gear, governor, buffers, brake, unintended movement protection, at the examination interval for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). |
| Parts support | Written advice from the manufacturer on controller and drive support. |
| Code gap review | Accessibility, fire service functions, communications and unintended movement against current standards. |
| Traffic analysis | Where waiting times are in question: measured waiting and journey times at peak against the population and floors served. |
| Ride quality measurement | With an accelerometer, which gives a comparable number rather than an opinion and identifies guide and rope problems. |
| Supply quality logging | At the lift where intermittent faults are unexplained. |
| Hazardous material survey | Of the machine room and lift equipment before modernisation is specified. |

The report should give a staged modernisation scope and timing per lift, safety defects, and whether the maintenance contract is adequate.

Two practical points. Full safety testing takes a lift out of service for a day or more, so it is planned around the building rather than done on arrival; and in a single-lift building the audit itself needs arrangements for residents who cannot use the stairs.

sections.heading: Repairing, modernising or replacing
sections.markdown:
Most lifts are renewed in stages rather than replaced. Safety failures come first; then the work follows the breakdown record and the parts support position, from a maintenance contract reset and a door package to modernising the controls and drive.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Controls and drive modernisation | A new controller and drive, normally with door operators and fixtures, bringing current requirements such as unintended car movement protection, accessible fixtures and regenerative drives. | Where parts support has ended or breakdowns are rising; the stage that cures most reliability problems. |
| Door package | Operators, tracks, rollers, gibs, interlocks and full-height light curtains. | Where doors dominate the breakdown record and the controller is still supported. |
| Rope or belt replacement | New ropes or belts, with sheave regrooving or replacement. | On measured condition against the discard criteria. |
| Machine replacement | Usually a gearless machine, quieter and more efficient, which may need machine room and structural alterations. | At the end of a geared machine's life. |
| Hydraulic cylinder replacement | A protected or holeless design, or conversion to traction where travel and shaft allow; cylinder work means excavating the pit and dealing with any contaminated ground. | Where a cylinder leaks or reaches the end of its life. |
| Traffic and control works | Group control, destination control, changes to which floors are served, or an additional lift. | Where capacity is the problem; control changes are far cheaper than a new shaft and often enough. |
| Car interior refurbishment | New interiors, taken as the opportunity for accessible controls, audible announcements, braille and handrails. | When interiors and fixtures are worn. |
| Emergency communication upgrade | A digital or cellular autodialler with battery backup and a monitored answering arrangement, tested on a schedule. | Wherever the phone fails, reaches no one, or sits on a network being retired. |
| Fire interface restoration | Restore the interface, test it jointly with the fire contractor, and record it against the fire strategy. | Wherever a lift does not perform its fire function. |
| Pit and shaft works | Waterproofing, sump and pump renewal, cleaning, and renewal of corroded buffers and guide components. | Where water or debris reaches the pit. |
| Maintenance contract reset | A defined preventive scope and hours, response and repair times, parts and tools availability, and reporting coded by cause. | Where maintenance falls short of its contract; often the highest-value change available, and it costs nothing but attention. |

Choosing between them starts with the parts support position. Where controls are supported, targeted repairs and a door package buy years at modest cost. Where support has ended, piecemeal repair becomes a trap: each outage lengthens, and money spent on an obsolete controller is lost at modernisation. Where capacity rather than condition is the complaint, no amount of modernisation will shorten the queue.

Full replacement rather than staged modernisation is justified in narrow cases: a shaft or machine room that cannot accommodate compliant equipment, a hydraulic installation at the end of its cylinder life where conversion is cheaper than renewal, or a building being refurbished so thoroughly that the lift is rebuilt with it.

In multi-lift buildings the programme is staggered so one lift is always in service, which lengthens the works but keeps the building usable. In single-lift buildings the opposite applies: the works are compressed, planned well ahead, and accompanied by arrangements for residents who cannot use the stairs.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Maintenance contracts recur. Modernisation is priced per lift per stage, and is usually programmed lift by lift. Builders' work (machine room alterations, electrical supply, fire interfaces, pit works) adds to each stage. Rope replacement recurs on condition. Hydraulic cylinder replacement includes excavation. Temporary loss of service in single-lift buildings can require temporary arrangements for residents with limited mobility.

What drives the cost: the number of lifts and floors served, the stage being undertaken, whether the controls are proprietary (which limits who can bid), machine room access and craneage, builders' work in the shaft and pit, electrical supply upgrades, fire interface works, and the cost of keeping the building usable while a lift is out. Commonly missed: hazardous material removal, pit waterproofing, structural work for a heavier or different machine, temporary access arrangements for residents, and the independent consultant's fee, which is small against the works and usually pays for itself in the tender.

Modernisation stages are lifecycle; safety items and inspections are code compliance; ropes and repairs are repairs and maintenance; communication migration carries a deadline where lines are being retired.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what an inspection on the day cannot: how each lift has actually performed, what the contractor promised and delivered, and whether the controller can still be supported. Ask for them before any modernisation is specified.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Breakdown, call-out and entrapment records per lift for the last two to three years, coded by cause | Whether a lift is unreliable, unsafe or simply too small for the building. |
| Maintenance contract with its scope, attendance hours, response times, exclusions, and who holds the controller codes and tools | What the contractor has promised, and what is excluded. |
| Attendance records against that scope, so delivery can be checked against the promise | Whether the contractor delivers what was promised. |
| Registration, periodic inspection and thorough examination certificates, and any outstanding notices | Whether statutory inspections are current, and what they asked for. |
| Modernisation history per lift, with dates, scope and outstanding recommendations | Which parts have been renewed, and what is still outstanding. |
| Manufacturer's written parts and tools support position for the controller and drive | Whether the controller and drive can still be repaired. |
| Rope, safety gear, governor and brake test results, and the date of the last full load test | Whether the safety-critical parts have been tested, and when. |
| Emergency phone line type, monitoring arrangement and test records | Whether a trapped passenger can reach someone. |
| Fire interface test records, and the fire strategy showing which lifts carry fire-fighting or evacuation duties | Which lifts carry fire functions, and whether they work. |
| Any traffic or waiting-time study, and tenant or resident complaints about lift service | Whether the lifts are too few or too slow for the building. |
| Hazardous materials register entries for lift equipment and machine rooms | Whether the machine rooms and equipment contain asbestos. |
| Sinking fund or reserve fund forecast for the lifts, in strata and leasehold buildings | Whether money is set aside for the lifts in strata and leasehold buildings. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Lifts are misread when they are judged on their age, when the lift is inspected before its record is read, and when a safety failure is treated as a fault to schedule.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| An old lift needs replacing | Age alone is a poor guide. A well-maintained geared lift of thirty-five years with supported controls can be more reliable than a neglected installation of fifteen. What settles it is the parts support position, the breakdown and entrapment record, and the safety test results. |
| Start by inspecting the lift | Begin with the breakdown record rather than the lift. Counting call-outs by cause over two or three years separates the three questions that matter: whether the lift is unreliable, whether it is unsafe, and whether it is simply too small for the building. Doors dominating the record points to door equipment; long individual outages point to parts support; a thin record with long waits points to capacity. |
| It is only a fault | A landing door that can be opened without the car present, a car that moves with its doors open, or an emergency phone that does not connect are safety failures. Take the lift out of service until fixed. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market registers or inspects lifts, sets standards for new lifts and modernisation, and requires emergency communication and fire functions. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each, with accessibility.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Registration and inspection | Lifts are registered plant under state work health and safety regulations, with design and item registration requirements, and routine and major inspection intervals set by state regulators. | The Lifting Operations and Lifting Equipment Regulations 1998 require thorough examination of passenger lifts at least every six months, by a competent person independent of the maintenance contractor, and reports must be acted upon. | Annual inspections and periodic load tests, including five-year full load safety tests, are set by state and city elevator authorities rather than nationally, so obligations differ between jurisdictions in the same country. |
| Design and modernisation | The AS 1735 series, now adopting the ISO 8100 and EN 81 based standards, governs design and modernisation. | BS EN 81-20 and 81-50 govern new lifts and modernisation, including unintended car movement protection; BS EN 81-80 guides improving existing lifts. | ASME A17.1 governs new lifts and A17.3 existing lifts. |
| Communication, fire and evacuation | Emergency communication must reach an answering service at all times, which has made the retirement of copper and 3G networks a live compliance issue. | BS EN 81-28 covers remote alarms; fire-fighting lifts follow BS EN 81-72, and evacuation lifts BS 9999 and BS EN 81-76. | Fire service recall and fire-fighter operation are required. |
| Accessibility | The Disability (Access to Premises — Buildings) Standards 2010 set accessibility for new and upgraded lifts. | Approved Document M and BS 8300 govern accessibility. | The 2010 ADA Standards set accessibility. |

sections.heading: Worked example: a 1990s lift with rising breakdowns
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 1990s six-storey office has two traction lifts. Call-outs have risen each year for three years, most coded to doors, and the last two breakdowns each took three weeks while controller parts were sourced. The emergency phones are on a copper line due for retirement.

The record answers the questions. Doors dominate the call-outs, which points to door equipment; long individual outages point to the controller's parts support, which the manufacturer confirms has ended. Age alone would not settle it, but the parts position does: modernising the controls and drive, with a door package, is the stage that cures both. The phones need upgrading before the line is retired.

So the register carries the emergency phones as a deadline line, controls and drive modernisation with the door package as a lifecycle line, staggered so one lift is always in service, and a maintenance contract reset in the meantime.

thresholds.rule: Where lifts serve storeys above an effective height of 12 m, at least one takes a raised stretcher in a space 600 mm by 2000 mm by 1400 mm high

source.title: NCC 2025 Volume One, Part E3 Lift installations

thresholds.measure: Passenger lift car size (England, new lifts)
thresholds.rule: At least 1100 mm wide and 1400 mm deep

source.title: Approved Document M, Volume 2: Buildings other than dwellings (with 2024 amendments)

thresholds.rule: At least every 6 months for equipment that lifts people; every 12 months for other lifting equipment, unless an examination scheme sets otherwise

source.title: Thorough examination of lifting equipment (INDG422)

thresholds.rule: Within 13 mm (1/2 in) of the landing from rated load to no load; no more than 32 mm between car sill and landing

source.title: 2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design

thresholds.rule: At least 54 lux at the car controls, platform and threshold

pages.title: Passive Fire Protection
pages.question: How does passive fire protection fail, how do you find the breaches, and which findings put lives at risk?
pages.answer: Passive protection fails by alteration and use, not age. Every cable, pipe and duct added through a fire wall is a potential breach; risers and ceiling voids above corridors are the worst. Fire doors fail when closers break, doors are wedged open, seals are painted over, and residents replace flat entrance doors with unrated ones. Walls that stop at the ceiling and damaged steel protection are found only by looking above ceilings and behind linings.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about passive fire protection; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Fire-rated doors, walls, ceilings, structural protection
