pages.searchTitle: Passive fire protection: fire stopping, fire doors and compartment walls

questions.question: Is expanding foam a fire seal?
questions.answer: Usually not. Foam in fire walls is generally untested for fire; identify the product, and replace it with a tested sealing system.

questions.question: Can a fire door be propped open?
questions.answer: Not wedged. Where a door needs to stay open in use, a hold-open device linked to the fire alarm releases it when the alarm sounds.

questions.question: How often must fire doors be checked?
questions.answer: In England, residential buildings over 11 metres need quarterly checks of communal fire doors and annual best-endeavour checks of flat entrance doors; NFPA 80 requires annual inspection in the United States; AS 1851 sets inspection in Australia.

questions.question: Why does smoke spread between floors?
questions.answer: Usually through breached riser penetrations or walls not built to the slab. A survey of the risers and ceiling voids shows where.

questions.question: How long do fire door seals and closers last?
questions.answer: Door closers and hardware 10 to 15 years, intumescent seals 10 to 20, and fire doors 20 to 30 years with maintenance.

questions.question: The fire doors don't close properly. What needs doing?
questions.answer: Usually a failed or disconnected closer, binding or an obstruction. Repair or replace the closer, free the binding, and clear the obstruction.

questions.question: Residents have fitted their own front doors to their flats. Is that a fire problem?
questions.answer: It can be. Survey the doors, and replace non-compliant ones with certified doorsets.

questions.question: The fire protection on the steel beams has been knocked off in places. Does it matter?
questions.answer: Yes. It is usually damage by trades. Repair the protection with compatible products, and control trades with permits.

questions.question: There are gaps around the edges of the fire doors. Is that a problem?
questions.answer: Gaps of several millimetres come from wear, distortion or poor installation. Adjust or repair the door, or replace it where it cannot meet the standard.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Passive fire protection problems show in risers, ceiling voids and on escape routes: holes around services, foam in fire walls, and doors that do not close. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| In the building | Holes and unsealed gaps around services in risers, plant rooms and above ceilings | Penetrations, walls and cavity barriers |
| In the building | Expanding foam around pipes and cables in fire walls | Penetrations, walls and cavity barriers |
| In the building | Fire doors propped or wedged open; closers disconnected; doors not closing fully into the frame | Fire doors and glazing |
| In the building | Gaps at door edges; seals painted, damaged or missing; non-rated hardware | Fire doors and glazing |
| In the building | Fire door labels or tags missing or illegible | Fire doors and glazing |
| In the building | Ordinary glass in fire-resisting screens and doors | Fire doors and glazing |
| In the building | Walls stopping at the ceiling line when tiles are lifted | Penetrations, walls and cavity barriers |
| In the building | Damaged spray protection on steel; chipped intumescent coatings | Structural protection and unverified products |
| In the records | Fire strategy or fire engineering report, including performance solutions | Investigation before the scope |
| In the records | Compartmentation drawings | Penetrations, walls and cavity barriers |
| In the records | Fire door register and inspection records | Fire doors and glazing |
| In the records | Fire stopping records, with photographs and product details | Penetrations, walls and cavity barriers |
| In the records | Annual fire safety statements or essential safety measures reports | Standards by country |
| In the records | Asbestos register | Structural protection and unverified products |

sections.heading: What passive protection covers
sections.markdown:
Passive fire protection is the fabric of the building that contains fire and smoke and keeps the structure standing long enough for people to escape and fire-fighters to work: fire-resisting walls, floors and ceilings that divide the building into compartments; fire doors and their hardware; fire-resisting glazing; protection of penetrations where services pass through; cavity barriers and fire stopping in concealed spaces; and fire protection of the structure itself. It does nothing until a fire, and it is broken every time a building is altered.

| Element | Job | What goes wrong |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fire-resisting walls and floors | Divide the building into compartments; protect stairs, shafts and escape routes | Holes cut for services; walls stopped at the ceiling instead of the slab |
| Penetration seals | Restore fire resistance where pipes, cables and ducts pass through | Missing, unrated or damaged seals; new services added |
| Fire doors and doorsets | Close openings in fire-resisting walls | Gaps, failed closers, damaged seals, propped open, wrong hardware, replaced with non-rated doors |
| Fire-resisting glazing | Light and visibility through fire-resisting elements | Replaced with ordinary glass; frames and beads changed |
| Fire-resisting ceilings and shafts | Protect structure and voids | Tiles removed, access panels unrated |
| Cavity barriers | Stop fire spreading through concealed cavities, including façades | Missing, misplaced or open |
| Structural fire protection | Keep steel and other structure from losing strength | Spray-applied coatings damaged; intumescent paint chipped or overcoated |
| Fire dampers | Close ducts at compartment walls | Covered on the ductwork page |

A building's passive fire protection is defined by its fire strategy or fire engineering report, which sets the compartments, fire-resistance levels and escape routes. Without that document, nobody knows which walls and doors matter. Many older buildings have no current strategy, and many performance solutions rely on passive elements that later works have undone.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Passive fire protection lasts the life of the building if nobody breaches it. Masonry walls and floors, plasterboard walls and spray-applied protection all last as long as the building while intact, but penetration seals, fire doors and their hardware wear and are disturbed far sooner.

| Element | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Masonry and concrete compartment walls and floors | Life of the building | Penetrations; alterations |
| Plasterboard fire-resisting walls | Life of the building if intact | Damage; services penetrations |
| Penetration seals | 20 to 30 years if undisturbed | Further works; product |
| Fire doors | 20 to 30 years with maintenance | Use; abuse; maintenance |
| Door closers and hardware | 10 to 15 years | Use |
| Intumescent seals | 10 to 20 years | Painting over; damage |
| Intumescent coatings on steel | 15 to 25 years | Damage; moisture; overcoating |
| Spray-applied fire protection | Life of the building if undisturbed | Damage; water |

What shortens life: alterations: every cable, pipe and duct installed after construction is a potential breach; fit-outs that move walls, add doors and remove ceilings; daily use: doors wedged open, closers disconnected, seals damaged by trolleys; maintenance by trades who do not know which elements are fire-rated; water on spray-applied and intumescent protection.

sections.heading: Penetrations, walls and cavity barriers
sections.markdown:
The most common passive fire defect in existing buildings is an unsealed or improperly sealed penetration: cables pushed through holes in fire walls, pipes surrounded by expanding foam that is not fire-rated, ducts without dampers, holes left after services were removed. Risers, plant rooms and ceiling voids above corridors are the worst areas. Each breach lets fire and smoke move between compartments.

Fire-resisting walls must run from floor slab to floor slab or to a fire-rated ceiling. Walls that stop at the suspended ceiling, or that had their top sections removed for services, leave a path for fire over the top. This is often found only by lifting ceiling tiles.

Concealed spaces in walls, floors, roofs and façades need barriers to stop fire travelling unseen. Missing or misplaced cavity barriers in façades and in timber-framed construction have allowed fire to spread rapidly through buildings.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Smoke spread between floors in a fire or drill | Breached riser penetrations or walls not to slab. Riser and ceiling void survey. | Survey every riser and ceiling void; fire stop each breach with a tested system, and complete walls to the slab. |
| Foam in penetrations | Untested sealing. Product identification. | Identify the product; replace untested foam with a tested sealing system. |

sections.heading: Fire doors and glazing
sections.markdown:
Fire doors fail through use: closers disconnected or broken so doors do not close; doors wedged or propped open; gaps at edges larger than allowed; intumescent and smoke seals painted over, damaged or missing; non-rated hinges, locks and vision panels; doors cut down to clear new floor finishes; and, in apartment buildings, flat entrance doors replaced by residents with non-rated doors. A fire door that does not close fully is not a fire door.

Broken fire-resisting glazing replaced with ordinary glass, or beads and frames replaced with untested parts, loses its fire resistance entirely.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Doors do not close fully | Failed or disconnected closer, binding, obstruction. Door inspection. | Repair or replace the closer, free the binding, and clear the obstruction. |
| Gaps of several millimetres at door edges | Wear, distortion or poor installation. Gap measurement against the door’s evidence and the limits for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Adjust or repair the door, or replace it where it cannot meet the standard. |
| Flat entrance doors of different designs | Resident replacements. Door survey. | Survey them; replace non-compliant doors with certified doorsets. |
| Smoke doors with hollow-core or thin leaves | Not a smoke door. Leaf construction and seals against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Replace the leaves with compliant ones, and fit smoke seals. |
| No record of fire door checks in a block of flats | Checks not being carried out. Check records against the intervals for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Start a check regime, and record each door’s gaps, closer and seals. |

sections.heading: Structural protection and unverified products
sections.markdown:
Spray-applied fire protection on steel is knocked off by later trades, fixings and services; intumescent coatings are chipped, overpainted with incompatible paint, or weathered where exposed. Unprotected steel loses strength quickly in fire.

Fire stopping and door products must be installed as tested. Untested combinations, products used outside their tested range, and missing certification leave the protection unproven. Older protection may contain asbestos.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Exposed steel with patches of protection | Damage by trades. Structural protection survey. | Repair the protection with compatible products, and control trades with permits. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stair or escape route doors not closing; breached riser or stair penetrations; fire doors wedged open; flat entrance doors not fire-rated in apartment buildings | safety · 4 Essential | Rectify now; fire watch or interim measures where needed. |
| Fire door checks and annual certification due | deadline · 4 Essential | At the prescribed interval. |
| Widespread penetration breaches; walls not to slab; damaged structural protection | condition · 4 Essential | Remediation programme in the near term. |
| Doors and hardware at end of life | lifecycle · 3 Important | Replace on cycle. |
| No fire strategy; compartmentation unknown | check · 3 Important | Fire strategy and compartmentation survey. |
| Minor door adjustments | nil · 1 Routine | Routine maintenance. |
| Fire-resisting construction or doors damaged by fire, water or impact and no longer intact | failure · 4 Essential | Repair now; interim measures until done. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A fire engineer or passive fire specialist leads, working from the fire strategy; where there is no strategy, the investigation begins by establishing one. The checks below cover every riser, stair and escape route in full, rather than by sample.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Strategy review | Compartments, fire-resistance levels, escape routes and performance solutions. |
| Compartmentation survey | Above ceilings, in risers and plant rooms, recording every penetration and its seal, with photographs. |
| Fire door survey | Of every door on escape routes and compartment lines, including all flat entrance doors in residential buildings: closing, gaps, seals, hardware, glazing, labels, with gaps measured against the limits for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). |
| Structural protection survey | Of exposed and concealed steel. |
| Product identification | Against tested systems and certification. |
| Asbestos sampling | Of older protection. |
| Escape route check | Door closing, glazing and wall integrity on every stair and protected corridor. |

The report should give a register of defects by location with photographs, prioritised by risk, and the strategy those defects affect.

sections.heading: Restoring compartments and doors
sections.markdown:
Escape routes come first: stair doors that do not close and breached risers let smoke reach every floor. After that, the work is to make good every breach with tested products, and to prevent the next one with permits and labelling.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fire stopping | Seal every breach with tested systems, recorded with photographs and product data. | Wherever services pass through fire-rated walls and floors unsealed or with untested products. |
| Fire door repair | Closers, seals, hardware and adjustment; replacement of doors that cannot be repaired; certified doorsets for flat entrances. | Wherever doors do not close fully, gaps are too large, or seals and hardware are wrong. |
| Hold-open devices | Devices linked to the fire alarm. | Where doors need to stay open in use, rather than being wedged. |
| Wall completion to slab | Complete fire-resisting walls up to the slab. | Where walls stop at the ceiling. |
| Glazing replacement | Tested fire-resisting glass and frames. | Where ordinary glass has been fitted in fire-resisting screens or doors. |
| Structural protection repair | Repair with compatible products. | Where spray protection or intumescent coatings are damaged. |
| Fire strategy update | Update the fire strategy and the compartmentation drawings. | Where there is none, or the building has changed. |
| Management | Permits for works that penetrate fire-rated elements, and regular door checks. | Always; it prevents the next breach. |
| Labelling | Identify fire-resisting walls above ceilings and in risers. | So trades know what they are penetrating. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Surveys are lump sums. Fire stopping is priced per penetration or per riser floor. Door repair and replacement per door. Structural protection repair by area. Fire strategy preparation is a lump sum. Access above ceilings and in risers, and work in occupied buildings, drive cost.

Safety rectification and certification are code compliance; door and hardware replacement is lifecycle; ongoing door checks are repairs and maintenance.

Fire door surveys of whole apartment buildings are lump sums priced per door.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a sample inspection cannot: where the compartments are meant to be, what has been sealed and with what, and whether doors are checked. Ask for them before the survey, so it covers every riser and escape route.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Fire strategy or fire engineering report, including performance solutions | What the compartments and doors are relied on to do. |
| Compartmentation drawings | Where the fire-resisting walls and floors are. |
| Fire door register and inspection records | Whether fire doors are checked, and what was found. |
| Fire stopping records with photographs | What has been sealed, and with which products. |
| Annual fire safety statements or essential safety measures reports | Whether passive elements were certified at their last review. |
| Asbestos register | Whether existing protection or seals contain asbestos. |
| Permits for works that penetrated fire-rated elements | Whether works that breached fire-rated elements were controlled. |
| Fire door certification for replaced doors | Whether replacement doors are certified. |
| Records of resident door replacements in apartment buildings | Whether flat entrance doors have been replaced with doors of unknown rating. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Passive fire protection is misread when a sample survey is taken to represent the building, when expanding foam is taken for a fire seal, and when a door that nearly closes is taken as good enough.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| A sample survey shows the building's condition | Passive fire protection is only as good as its weakest breach. A single unsealed riser or a fire door that does not close can let smoke reach every floor, so surveys must be thorough rather than representative in risers, stairs and escape routes. |
| Foam seals the penetration | Expanding foam in fire walls is generally untested for fire. Identify the product, and replace it with a tested sealing system. |
| A door that nearly closes is fine | A fire door that does not close fully, or has gaps of several millimetres at its edges, will not hold back smoke. Adjust, repair or replace it. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets fire-resistance requirements, tests the products that provide them, and requires fire doors to be inspected. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Requirements | The National Construction Code sets fire-resistance levels and compartmentation; AS 4655, now withdrawn, covered fire safety audits. | Approved Document B sets requirements; the Fire Safety Act 2021 brings flat entrance doors and external walls into the responsible person's duties. | International Building Code Chapter 7 governs fire-resistance-rated construction. |
| Testing and products | AS 1530.4 sets fire-resistance testing, AS 4072.1 penetration seals and AS 1905.1 fire doors. | BS 8214 covers fire doors. | Firestop systems are tested to ASTM E814 and UL 1479. |
| Inspection | AS 1851 sets fire door inspection; passive elements are essential safety measures with annual certification. | The Fire Safety (England) Regulations 2022 require quarterly checks of communal fire doors, and annual best-endeavour checks of flat entrance doors, in residential buildings over 11 metres. | NFPA 80 requires annual inspection of fire doors, and NFPA 105 covers smoke doors. |

sections.heading: Worked example: an apartment riser opened for new cabling
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 2000s apartment building had new data cabling run up its riser last year. The riser walls now have holes around the new cables, some packed with expanding foam, and the stair door on two floors is wedged open. Several residents have replaced their flat entrance doors with doors of different designs.

A single unsealed riser can let smoke reach every floor, so the riser is surveyed in full, not sampled. The holes and the foam are breaches, the wedged stair doors defeat the stair's protection, and the replaced entrance doors are of unknown rating.

So the register carries the stair doors and the riser breaches as safety lines now, fire stopping with tested systems recorded with photographs, a survey of the flat entrance doors as a check line, and permits for any future work through fire-rated elements.

pages.title: Pavements & Hardstand
pages.question: How do car parks, driveways and paving fail, and how do you tell surface wear from structural failure?
pages.answer: Pavements fail when water gets in. Asphalt oxidises and block-cracks, then water through the cracks softens the base and potholes form. Alligator cracking in wheel paths means the base has failed and surface treatments will not fix it. Concrete panels step at joints when subgrade pumps out; pavers sink where bedding washes out. Trip hazards in pedestrian areas are the safety finding. Crack sealing and resealing are far cheaper than rebuilding.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about pavements & hardstand; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Car parks, driveways, pedestrian paving (asphalt/concrete/pavers)

pages.searchTitle: Pavements and hardstand: cracking, potholes, trip hazards and when to reseal or rebuild

questions.question: Why does the car park keep getting potholes?
questions.answer: Water gets through cracks into the base, softens it, and potholes form. Patch full depth, seal the cracks and fix the drainage, or they return.

questions.question: Can cracked asphalt just be resealed?
questions.answer: Only where the cracking comes from age and runs across the whole surface. Cracking in wheel paths means the base has failed, and resealing over it wastes money.

questions.question: When does a trip edge need fixing?
questions.answer: Australian councils and owners often intervene at around 20 millimetres; British highways authorities use intervention levels; in the United States the ADA Standards limit changes in level on accessible routes. A trip edge on a pedestrian route is a safety finding.

questions.question: How long does an asphalt car park last?
questions.answer: The wearing course 15 to 20 years, with resealing every 7 to 10; the pavement structure 20 to 40 years.

questions.question: Why do pavers sink near pits and edges?
questions.answer: The bedding washes out or the edge restraint fails. Lifting the pavers shows which; relay them on new bedding with edge restraints.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Pavement problems show on the surface, but the pattern matters more than any one crack: where the cracking runs, where water ponds, where people trip. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On site | Greyed, ravelled asphalt; block cracking; alligator cracking in wheel paths | Asphalt: ageing, cracking and potholes |
| On site | Potholes, patches, ruts and ponding after rain | Asphalt: ageing, cracking and potholes |
| On site | Concrete panels cracked, spalled at joints, or stepped | Concrete and paved surfaces |
| On site | Pavers rocking, sunken or lifted, with weeds and open joints | Concrete and paved surfaces |
| On site | Trip edges on footpaths and around services pits | Trip hazards |
| On site | Faded line marking and missing wheel stops | Sealing, patching or rebuilding |
| On site | Tree roots lifting surfaces | [Landscaping & Irrigation](https://moyneross.com/technical/landscaping-and-irrigation) |
| In the records | Pavement design and construction records | Investigation before the scope |
| In the records | Resurfacing and resealing history | Asphalt: ageing, cracking and potholes |
| In the records | Trip and fall incident claims | Trip hazards |
| In the records | Drainage drawings | Asphalt: ageing, cracking and potholes |
| On site | Water ponding against kerbs and in low spots for hours after rain, showing where the base is being saturated | Asphalt: ageing, cracking and potholes |
| On site | Patches of different ages and materials, recording where the pavement has failed before | Asphalt: ageing, cracking and potholes |

sections.heading: Types of pavement
sections.markdown:
Pavements and hardstand are the external trafficked surfaces of a site: car parks, driveways, loading and truck hardstand, service roads, footpaths and plazas. They are asphalt, concrete or segmental pavers over a base course and subgrade, with kerbs, edge restraints, line marking, wheel stops, and the drainage that keeps water out of the structure. Suspended car park decks are structure and have their own page; this page covers pavements on the ground.

| Type | Where it is found | Character |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Asphalt (flexible) pavement | Car parks, roads, driveways | Ages by oxidation; cracks; rutting under heavy loads; needs resealing |
| Concrete (rigid) pavement | Truck hardstand, loading areas, service roads | Long life; joints and cracking; settlement |
| Segmental pavers (concrete, clay, stone) | Footpaths, plazas, driveways, residential | Settlement and rocking; edge restraint; weeds |
| Permeable pavements | Newer sites with stormwater controls | Clogging reduces infiltration |
| Sprayed seal and gravel | Rural and industrial yards | Stone loss; potholes |

Water is the main enemy of pavements: once it gets through cracks into the base and subgrade, the pavement loses support and fails under traffic. Drainage, crack sealing and resealing protect the investment far more cheaply than rebuilding.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
A pavement has two lives: the surface, which needs resealing every seven to ten years, and the structure beneath, which lasts decades if the surface keeps the water out. Keeping water out decides which fails first.

| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Asphalt wearing course | 15 to 20 years, with resealing at 7 to 10 | Traffic; sun; water |
| Asphalt pavement structure | 20 to 40 years | Base condition; drainage; loads |
| Concrete pavement | 30 to 40 years | Joints; subgrade; loads |
| Segmental pavers | 25 to 40 years | Bedding; edge restraint; traffic |
| Line marking | 2 to 5 years | Traffic; product |
| Kerbs and edge restraints | 30 to 50 years | Impact; settlement |

What shortens it: water entering cracks and saturating the base and subgrade; heavy vehicles on pavements designed for cars, such as trucks, garbage trucks and cranes; poor drainage and ponding; tree roots lifting pavements and pavers; deferred resealing, which lets asphalt oxidise and crack.

sections.heading: Asphalt: ageing, cracking and potholes
sections.markdown:
Asphalt binder hardens and becomes brittle in sun and air. The surface greys and ravels, then cracks in blocks. Once cracks open, water enters and accelerates failure.

Interconnected cracking in wheel paths, like crocodile skin, means the pavement structure is failing under repeated loads, usually because the base is weak or wet. It cannot be fixed by surface treatment.

Heavy or slow-moving loads, and soft asphalt in heat, push the surface into ruts and ripples, which hold water.

Potholes form where water and traffic break out cracked asphalt and pump out base material. They grow quickly in wet weather.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Block cracking across the whole surface | Asphalt ageing. Age; no wheel-path pattern. | Seal the cracks and reseal the surface; the base is sound. |
| Alligator cracking in wheel paths | Structural failure of the base. Cores; deflection testing. | Repair the base full depth; resealing over it wastes money. |
| Ruts in truck routes | Overloading or weak asphalt. Traffic type; asphalt mix. | Rebuild the truck routes for the traffic, in concrete where trucks turn and stand. |
| Potholes after rain | Water through cracks into base. Crack pattern; drainage. | Patch full depth, seal the cracks, and fix the drainage that lets water in. |

sections.heading: Concrete and paved surfaces
sections.markdown:
Joints spall and lose sealant; panels crack across corners; panels settle and fault (step) at joints where the subgrade has softened or been pumped out.

Pavers settle where bedding washes out or the base was inadequate; they rock, spread and lose joints where edge restraints fail; roots lift them; weeds grow in joints.

Unsupported pavement edges break away where vehicles run off them, and broken kerbs let edges crumble and water enter the base.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stepped concrete panels | Subgrade softening or pumping. Water at joints; voids. | Find and stop the water at the joints; lift slabs by grout or replace panels. |
| Sunken pavers near pits or edges | Bedding washout or edge failure. Lift pavers; inspect. | Relay on new bedding with edge restraints. |

sections.heading: Trip hazards
sections.markdown:
Steps between slabs, lifted pavers, broken edges and potholes in pedestrian areas trip people, especially the elderly and people with impaired vision. Many public liability claims start here.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lifted pavers, slab edges or tree-root heave on a footpath | Trip hazard. Level change measured against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Grind, relay or ramp the lip, and record the repair. |
| Accessible parking bays narrow or with no shared zone | Bay layout below current requirements. Bay and aisle widths against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Remark the bays to current layout. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Trip hazards in pedestrian routes; large potholes in traffic areas | safety · 4 Essential | Make safe now: patch, grind or barricade. |
| Pavement failure in operational truck areas | failure · 3 Important | Repair now. |
| Accessible parking or routes not compliant | deadline · 3 Important | Rectify as required. |
| Cracking, ruts and ponding without failure | condition · 2 Planned | Repair in the near term. |
| Surface at end of life; resealing due | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Reseal or resurface on cycle. |
| Pavement capacity for current traffic unknown | check · 2 Planned | Assess. |
| Minor wear | nil · 1 Routine | Routine maintenance. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A civil or pavement engineer for larger pavements; a building surveyor for small sites. The checks below read the pattern of cracking first, because it decides between sealing and rebuilding, then the base, the drainage and the trip hazards.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Condition survey | Mapping distress types and extent, scored using a pavement condition index method so areas can be ranked and tracked. |
| Trip hazard survey | Of pedestrian routes, measuring height differences and recording each level change against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). |
| Cores and test pits | To measure asphalt thickness, base quality and subgrade. |
| Deflection testing | On heavy-duty pavements to measure structural capacity. |
| Drainage review | Falls, pits, ponding and subsoil drains. |
| Traffic review | Vehicle types and loads now using the pavement. |
| Accessibility check | Of accessible parking, kerb ramps and routes. |

The report should give a condition map, priorities, recommended treatments by area, and a resurfacing programme.

Pedestrian trip surveys are best repeated annually on busy sites, so that hazards are found before they cause claims.

sections.heading: Sealing, patching or rebuilding
sections.markdown:
The pattern of the damage decides the work. Cracking from age across a whole area can be sealed; cracking in wheel paths and truck areas means the base has failed and needs repair or reconstruction, and sealing over it wastes money.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Crack sealing | Seal the cracks to keep water out. | Where the pavement is sound and the cracking comes from age. |
| Resealing | Seal coats or thin overlays on the asphalt. | On a cycle, every seven to ten years, while the base is sound. |
| Patching | Full-depth repair of failed areas, including base. | Where areas have failed, potholes included. |
| Mill and overlay | Mill off the worn surface and lay new asphalt. | Where the surface is worn but the base is sound. |
| Reconstruction | Rebuild the pavement, designed for current traffic. | Where the base has failed. |
| Concrete joint repair | Joint repair and panel replacement; slab lifting by grout. | Where concrete panels crack, spall at joints or step. |
| Relaying pavers | Lift and relay pavers on new bedding, with edge restraints. | Where pavers rock, sink or lift. |
| Trip hazard removal | Grind, lift or replace the raised edge. | Wherever a trip edge stands on a pedestrian route; at once. |
| Drainage improvements | Pits, falls and outlets that clear water from the pavement and its edges. | Where water ponds against kerbs or in low spots after rain. |
| Line marking | Renew the line marking. | When markings have faded, typically every two to five years. |
| Kerb and edge repair | Repair kerbs and edges, with new edge restraints. | Where pavements are breaking away at the edge. |
| Heavy-duty sections | Rebuilt in concrete where trucks turn and stand, the zones that fail first in asphalt car parks. | Where trucks turn and stand on asphalt. |
| Permeable pavement maintenance | Vacuum sweeping to restore infiltration. | Where permeable paving has clogged. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Surveys are lump sums. Crack sealing is priced by length; resealing, overlays and reconstruction by area; patching by area and depth; pavers by area; line marking by length or per bay. Traffic management and night work in operating sites add cost.

Resealing and resurfacing are lifecycle on a cycle; patching and crack sealing are repairs and maintenance; trip hazards are immediate; accessibility rectification is code compliance.

Resurfacing in a busy car park is usually staged so parking remains available.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a walk across the car park cannot: what the pavement was built to carry, when it was last renewed, and where people have fallen. Documented inspection and repair is also the main defence to a trip claim.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Pavement design and construction records | What the pavement was built for, and how it was built. |
| Resurfacing, resealing and repair history | When the surface was last renewed, and where it keeps failing. |
| Trip and fall incident and claim records | Where people have fallen, and the claims that followed. |
| Drainage drawings | Where water is meant to go, and why it ponds where it does. |
| Traffic and vehicle use, especially heavy vehicles | Whether the pavement carries more, or heavier, traffic than it was built for. |
| Accessibility audit for external routes and parking | Whether accessible routes and parking meet the requirements. |
| Trip hazard survey records and repair actions | Whether trip hazards are found and fixed, the main defence to a claim. |
| Permeable pavement maintenance records where present | Whether permeable paving has been swept to keep it draining. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Pavements are misread when every crack is treated the same way. The pattern of cracking tells age from structural failure, and the treatment that suits one wastes money on the other.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| Cracks can be sealed and resurfaced over | Fatigue cracking in wheel paths means the pavement structure has failed. Resealing or overlaying it without repairing the base wastes money; the cracks return quickly. |
| All cracking is the same problem | The pattern of cracking is the key to treatment: random block cracking across a whole area is age and can be sealed; cracking confined to wheel paths, truck turning areas and loading zones is structural and needs the base repaired; cracks along the line of a buried service or near a tree point to those causes. |
| Potholes are a surface problem | They come from water getting through cracks into the base. Patching without sealing the cracks and fixing the drainage lets them return. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market has its own standards for pavement design and condition, and its own threshold for when a trip edge must be fixed. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out the design standards, the access rules and liability for trips.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Design and condition | Austroads guides cover pavement design and maintenance; AS/NZS 2890.1 covers parking facilities. | BS 7533 covers paving with pavers and flags. | ASTM D6433 sets the pavement condition index method; AASHTO guides pavement design. |
| Access | AS 1428 covers access. | The Equality Act 2010 and Approved Document M set access. | The 2010 ADA Standards set accessible routes and parking, including limits on changes in level. |
| Trips and liability | Councils and owners carry public liability for trip hazards, often using a threshold of around 20 millimetres for intervention. | Highways authorities use intervention levels for trips; occupiers have duties under the Occupiers' Liability Acts. | Liability for trips falls under state premises liability law, and many cities require adjoining owners to repair sidewalks. |

In all three jurisdictions, owners and occupiers owe a duty of care to people using their pavements, and documented inspection and repair is the main defence to trip claims; strata and condominium car parks and driveways are typically common property.

sections.heading: Worked example: a truck yard that keeps potholing
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 1990s distribution centre has an asphalt car park and truck yard. The car park is grey and block-cracked across its whole area; the truck turning area has alligator cracking and potholes that have been patched twice; and water ponds against the kerb by the loading dock after rain.

The two areas need different answers. The car park's block cracking is age: seal the cracks and reseal the surface. The alligator cracking where trucks turn means the base has failed, which is why the patches keep failing; it needs reconstruction for the traffic, and the turning area is the place for a heavy-duty concrete section. The ponding points to drainage that lets water into the base.

So the register carries crack sealing and resealing as a lifecycle line for the car park, reconstruction of the truck area as a failure line if operations are affected, and a drainage fix with it. Any trip edges on the pedestrian routes come first, as safety lines.

thresholds.rule: Up to 6.4 mm may be vertical; 6.4 to 13 mm bevelled no steeper than 1:2; higher changes are treated as a ramp or step

source.title: 2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design

thresholds.rule: At least 2440 mm wide, with an adjacent access aisle

pages.title: Plant Rooms
pages.question: How do plant rooms fail as spaces, and why do replacement routes matter so much?
pages.answer: Plant rooms fail around the equipment as much as in it. Storage blocks access, exits and switchboard clearances; refrigerant and gas detection lapses; switch rooms overheat; basement rooms flood, often with water pipes over switchboards; access by ladder and hatch injures staff. The costliest failure appears at replacement: plant boxed in by later walls and services must be cut out. Plan the route before the plant reaches end of life.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about plant rooms; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.

pages.searchTitle: Plant rooms: replacement routes, refrigerant detection, flooding, heat and storage

questions.question: Can plant rooms be used for storage?
questions.answer: No. Storage blocks access and escape, adds fire load and obstructs the working clearance at switchboards; it is a safety finding.

questions.question: How will we get the old chiller out?
questions.answer: Plan the route before replacement is due: knock-out panels, removable louvres, roof hatches, lifting beams or floor strengthening, measured against the plant's dimensions and weight.

questions.question: Do chiller rooms need refrigerant detection?
questions.answer: Yes. Leaking refrigerant can displace oxygen or be toxic or flammable; detection, alarms and emergency ventilation are required.

questions.question: Why does the switch room trip in summer?
questions.answer: Often the room overheats. Log temperatures, then restore the ventilation or add cooling.

questions.question: How often should plant room gas detectors be calibrated?
questions.answer: Annually, with the detectors themselves replaced every 5 to 10 years.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Plant room problems show as storage and redundant equipment, heat, water and missing bunds, detectors and exits, and in drawings, registers and flood history. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On site | Storage, rubbish and redundant equipment in plant rooms | Flooding, heat and storage |
| On site | Equipment that could not be removed without demolition: no doors, hatches or lifting points large enough | Replacement routes, access and noise |
| On site | Temperature high in switch rooms; ventilation louvres blocked | Flooding, heat and storage |
| On site | Refrigerant and gas detectors present, calibrated and alarming to the BMS | Refrigerant, gas and detection |
| On site | Water pipes over switchboards; flood marks; sump alarms | Flooding, heat and storage |
| On site | Bunds missing under oil and chemical stores | Flooding, heat and storage |
| On site | Dark corners; emergency lighting failures; missing signage | Replacement routes, access and noise |
| In the records | Plant room drawings and replacement routes | Replacement routes, access and noise |
| In the records | Refrigerant registers and leak detection calibration | Refrigerant, gas and detection |
| In the records | Flood history | Flooding, heat and storage |
| In the records | Lifting equipment certification | Replacement routes, access and noise |
| In the records | Noise complaints | Replacement routes, access and noise |
| In the records | Rooftop plant without walkways or edge protection | Replacement routes, access and noise |

sections.heading: What the space does and what it contains
sections.markdown:
Plant rooms house the equipment that runs the building: chiller and boiler rooms, pump rooms, switch rooms and substations, generator rooms, tank rooms, air handling plant rooms, and open roof plant areas. Each element of equipment has its own page; this page covers the room as a space. Functionally a plant room must let equipment run safely, let people maintain it, and let equipment be replaced at the end of its life. The last point is often forgotten: plant rooms built around equipment that later cannot be removed turn a routine replacement into demolition.

| Provision | Why it matters | What commonly fails |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Access and egress | Safe entry and escape; restricted access | Single doors; blocked exits; poor stairs and ladders |
| Replacement route | Getting equipment in and out | Plant boxed in by later walls, services or equipment |
| Ventilation and temperature | Combustion air, cooling, refrigerant and gas safety | Overheating; refrigerant accumulation; CO |
| Drainage and bunding | Water, oil and chemicals contained and drained | No bunds; blocked drains; flooding |
| Fire separation | Contain fires in boiler and switch rooms | Penetrations; doors propped |
| Lighting and emergency lighting | Safe work and escape | Dark rooms; failed emergency lights |
| Clearances and housekeeping | Safe working space around equipment | Storage; restricted clearances at switchboards |
| Noise and vibration control | Protect neighbours and structure | Failed isolators; complaints |
| Signage and safety equipment | Hazard warning and response | Missing signs, gas detection, eyewash |

sections.heading: How long it stays fit for purpose
sections.markdown:
A plant room's fabric lasts the life of the building, while ventilation fans and louvres last fifteen to twenty-five years, bunds and drainage twenty to thirty, and gas detection five to ten with annual calibration. What usually ends a plant room's fitness for purpose is the day its largest item needs replacing and cannot get out.

| Provision | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Room fabric and floors | Life of the building | Water; chemicals; alterations |
| Ventilation fans and louvres | 15 to 25 years | Run hours; corrosion |
| Refrigerant and gas detection | 5 to 10 years; sensors calibrated annually | Sensor drift |
| Bunds and drainage | 20 to 30 years | Corrosion; damage |
| Lifting beams and equipment | Life of the building with periodic inspection | Certification |
| Floor coatings | 5 to 15 years | Traffic; spills |

What shortens fitness for purpose: equipment added over time until there is no space or route left; storage of materials, chemicals and redundant equipment; water from leaks, floods and condensation; refrigerant changes that bring new safety requirements.

sections.heading: Refrigerant, gas and detection
sections.markdown:
Refrigerants leaking in chiller rooms can displace oxygen or be toxic or flammable depending on type; leak detection, alarms and emergency ventilation are required. Boiler rooms without adequate combustion air or with flue leaks accumulate carbon monoxide.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Refrigerant alarms or low charge | Leaks in a poorly ventilated room. Leak detection records (Thresholds by market). | Find and repair the leak, and check the room's detection and emergency ventilation. |
| A gas or carbon monoxide detector with a lapsed calibration label | Detection not calibrated. Calibration records have lapsed, and the detector does not alarm on test gas. | Calibrate or replace the detectors, and test the alarm to the building management system. |

sections.heading: Flooding, heat and storage
sections.markdown:
Basement plant rooms flood from burst pipes, failed sumps and storms, putting switchboards, pumps and generators out of action at once. Water pipes above switchboards are a recurring defect.

Switch rooms, communications rooms and plant rooms with inadequate ventilation overheat, shortening equipment life and causing trips.

Plant rooms used as storerooms block access to equipment and escape, add fire load and violate working clearances at switchboards.

Plant rooms concentrate risk: one burst pipe above a switchboard, or one blocked louvre, can take out power, pumps and the generator together. Keeping these room problems apart from the condition of the equipment inside matters, because the fixes sit in different budgets.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Trips and failures of electrical equipment in summer | Overheated switch room. Temperature logging. | Log temperatures; restore the ventilation, or add cooling to the switch room. |
| Equipment corroded at low level | Flooding or chronic damp. Flood history. | Reroute water pipes away from electrical equipment, and add upstands, sumps and alarms. |
| Boxes, furniture and redundant equipment in front of a switchboard | A plant room used as a storeroom. The working clearance at the switchboard is obstructed; clearances measured against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Clear the room, remove redundant equipment, and set housekeeping rules. |
| No bund under a fuel tank or chemical store | Spill containment never provided. Staining on the floor, with no upstand or drain. | Install a bund and drainage for the store. |

sections.heading: Replacement routes, access and noise
sections.markdown:
Chillers, boilers, switchboards and generators were often lifted in before walls and floors were completed, and later services, partitions and equipment block the way out. At replacement, owners face cutting openings in walls and slabs, crane lifts or breaking equipment down, adding cost and time that a route plan would have avoided.

Plant reached by fixed ladders without cages, through ceiling hatches, or across roofs without edge protection injures maintenance staff; single exits from large plant rooms trap people in emergencies.

Failed vibration isolators and inadequate acoustic treatment transmit noise and vibration to occupied spaces and neighbours.

Rooftop plant areas add exposure: corrosion, weather damage to equipment and access hazards at roof edges.

The question to ask of every plant room is how its largest item leaves the building. Chillers, boilers and switchboards were often lifted in before walls and floors were finished; later services, partitions and equipment close the route, and a replacement then needs openings cut, floors strengthened and cranes booked. Planning the route ahead of the replacement costs a fraction of discovering it during one.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No route for a chiller replacement | Plant boxed in after installation. Dimensions against openings. | Plan a route now: knock-out panels, removable louvres, roof hatches, lifting beams or floor strengthening. |
| Noise complaints from occupied floors | Failed isolators or acoustic breaches. Vibration measurements. | Replace failed isolators, and add acoustic linings or enclosures. |
| One exit from a large plant room | No second exit. Travel distance to the single door from the far corner. | Provide a second exit where the room's size requires it. |
| Fixed ladder to a plant platform with uneven or narrow rungs | Unsafe access. Rung spacing and width against the limits for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Repair or replace the ladder, or provide a stair where access is frequent. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Failed refrigerant or gas detection; blocked exits; storage at switchboards; water over switchboards | safety · 4 Essential | Rectify now. |
| Plant room flooded or overheated causing outages | failure · 3 Important | Restore now. |
| Detector calibration and lifting equipment certification due | deadline · 4 Essential | At the prescribed interval. |
| Poor housekeeping; noise; worn floors and coatings | condition · 3 Important | Improve in the near term. |
| No replacement route for major plant | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Plan the route before the next replacement. |
| Plant room conditions never assessed | check · 2 Planned | Assess. |
| Normal | nil · 1 Routine | Routine. |

A missing replacement route is not urgent today but becomes a major cost and delay at the next replacement, so it belongs in the capital plan now.

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A building services engineer leads, with the mechanical, electrical and fire maintenance contractors, and a structural engineer where replacement routes need openings or lifting. The checks below go room by room for exits, clearances, detection, ventilation and flood risk, then trace how each major item would leave the building.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Room-by-room inspection | Access and second exits, clearances at switchboards and plant, housekeeping, ventilation openings, drainage, bunding, lighting, emergency lighting, signage and safety equipment. |
| Replacement route study | For each major item: dimensions and weights against doors, corridors, lifts, hatches, floor capacity and crane access, recording what would need to be removed. |
| Detection testing | Refrigerant, gas and carbon monoxide sensors calibrated and alarming to the building management system, with emergency ventilation triggered. |
| Temperature logging | In switch rooms, communications rooms and enclosed plant rooms through a hot period. |
| Flood risk review | Pipes over electrical equipment, sumps and pumps, floor levels against flood paths. |
| Noise and vibration measurement | Where neighbours or occupants complain. |

The report should list safety items, give a replacement route for each major item with any enabling works, and set out room improvements.

sections.heading: Making safe, protecting and planning replacement
sections.markdown:
Failed refrigerant or gas detection, blocked exits and storage at switchboards come first. After that, the work protects equipment from water and heat, makes access safe, and plans the route out for every major item before it is needed.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Housekeeping rules | No storage in plant rooms, regular checks, and removal of redundant equipment. | Wherever plant rooms are used for storage. |
| Replacement routes | Knock-out panels, removable louvres, roof hatches, lifting beams and floor strengthening, built before the replacement is due. | Before any major item reaches the end of its life. |
| Detection and emergency ventilation | Detection and emergency ventilation for refrigerants, gas and carbon monoxide, with alarms to the building management system. | Wherever refrigerant or combustion plant is installed. |
| Cooling | Cooling for switch and communications rooms. | Where switch or communications rooms overheat. |
| Flood protection | Reroute water pipes away from electrical equipment, add upstands, sumps and alarms. | Wherever water can reach electrical plant. |
| Bunds and drainage | Bunds and drainage for oil, fuel, chemicals and water. | Wherever liquids are stored or plant can leak. |
| Safe access | Stairs instead of ladders where practicable, caged ladders and platforms, second exits from large rooms. | Wherever plant is reached by ladders, hatches or unprotected roofs. |
| Acoustic and vibration treatment | Isolator replacement, acoustic linings and enclosures. | Where noise or vibration reaches occupied spaces. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Housekeeping and signage cost little. Detection, ventilation, cooling and flood protection are lump sums per room. Replacement route works are lump sums that are far cheaper before a replacement than during one, and should be carried in the capital plan alongside the plant they serve. Access improvements are itemised.

Safety items are code compliance; route provision is lifecycle planning tied to major plant replacement.

Flood damage to a basement switch room typically costs far more than the protection that would have prevented it.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a walk through the plant rooms cannot: how each major item would leave the building, whether detection is calibrated, and how earlier replacements were done. Ask for them before any major plant is due.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Plant room drawings and replacement route studies | How each major item would leave the building. |
| Refrigerant registers and detection calibration records | Whether refrigerant and gas detection is calibrated and working. |
| Flood and leak history | Whether the plant rooms have flooded, and why. |
| Lifting equipment certificates | Whether lifting equipment is certified for use. |
| Noise complaints | Whether plant noise reaches occupants or neighbours. |
| Plant room housekeeping and access procedures | Whether plant rooms are kept clear and access controlled. |
| Weights and dimensions of major plant | What the largest items weigh and measure. |
| Records of past plant replacements and how they were done | How earlier replacements got equipment in and out. |
| Insurer survey reports on plant rooms | What the insurer has found and recommended. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Plant rooms are misread when storage and detection are treated as housekeeping, when room problems are mixed up with the condition of the equipment, and when the way in is assumed to be the way out.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| It is only housekeeping | Plant rooms with refrigerant or combustion hazards must have working detection and ventilation. Storage in plant rooms and blocked exits are safety findings. |
| The equipment is the problem | Separate room problems (access, ventilation, flooding, storage) from equipment problems, which belong on each equipment page. |
| It came in, so it can go out | Major plant was often lifted in before walls and floors were completed. Measure the route out against the plant's dimensions and weight before replacement is due, not during it. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets rules for refrigerating plant rooms, working clearances at switchboards, and safe access to plant. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Plant rooms, refrigerants, clearances and access | AS/NZS 5149 governs refrigerating systems safety including machinery rooms; AS/NZS 3000 sets switchboard clearances; AS 1657 covers fixed ladders and platforms; work health and safety laws govern plant room access. | BS EN 378 governs refrigerating system safety; BS 7671 sets switchgear access; the Work at Height Regulations and Workplace Regulations apply; gas safety regulations cover boiler rooms. | ASHRAE 15 governs refrigerant safety in machinery rooms; NFPA 70 sets working clearances; OSHA governs access; the International Mechanical Code covers boiler room ventilation. |

In all three countries, workplace safety law places duties on whoever controls plant rooms to keep them safe for maintenance workers, including contractors.

Insurers also inspect plant rooms and may set conditions on housekeeping and flood protection.

sections.heading: Worked example: a basement plant room
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 1980s office's basement plant room holds two chillers, the main switchboard and the fire pumps. A chilled water pipe crosses above the switchboard, archive boxes are stacked in front of it, the refrigerant detector's calibration lapsed two years ago, and the chillers were lifted in before the ground floor slab was poured.

Storage at the switchboard and an uncalibrated refrigerant detector are safety findings. The pipe above the switchboard means one leak could take out power and the fire pumps together. And the chillers, nearing the end of their life, have no way out without cutting the slab, a planning finding that should not wait for the replacement.

So the register carries the storage and the detector as safety lines now, rerouting the pipe with upstands and alarms, and a replacement route study for the chillers as a lifecycle line, ahead of their replacement.

pages.title: Plant Screens & Parapets
pages.question: How do parapets and plant screens fail, how do you read a leaning parapet, and when is it a falling hazard?
pages.answer: Parapets are exposed on every face and lean when frost and sulfate attack swell one face, or when a concrete roof slab expands and pushes them out, cracking the wall at roof level and the corners. Open coping joints and a missing damp-proof course send water down into the wall. Plant screens fail at fixings through the membrane and in wind. A parapet out of plumb or with loose copings over a street is a falling hazard until assessed.
