pages.searchTitle: Parapets and plant screens: lean, loose copings, ornament and roof edge protection

questions.question: Why is my parapet leaning?
questions.answer: The direction tells you. Sulfate and frost attack lean it towards the drier side, often away from the weather; slab expansion pushes it outward with a horizontal crack at the slab line; a lean inward over the roof may mean lost ties.

questions.question: Is a leaning parapet dangerous?
questions.answer: Over a street or public area, yes: a parapet out of plumb, or with loose copings, is a falling hazard until an engineer has assessed it.

questions.question: Can a parapet serve as roof edge protection?
questions.answer: Only if it is high enough: guardrails are typically 900 to 1,100 mm in Australia, at least 950 mm in the United Kingdom, and 42 inches under OSHA. Many older parapets fall short once the roof has been raised.

questions.question: Why does terracotta ornament fail?
questions.answer: The iron cramps and anchors behind it corrode, showing as rust staining at joints, and units crack or loosen. Only tapping each unit and opening sample joints shows the real condition.

questions.question: How long does a parapet last?
questions.answer: A masonry parapet 60 to 100 years and its copings 40 to 80, while the copings keep water out; metal cappings 20 to 40.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Parapet problems show inside as damp and cracks at the top of the walls, from the street as lean and loose copings, and on the roof as open joints and corroded screen bases. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Inside | Damp, staining and blistered paint at the top of external walls on the top floor, worst after wind-driven rain: copings, upstands or the parapet itself | Copings and the roof junction |
| Inside | Horizontal cracks in top-floor walls at slab level, or along the ceiling line at external walls: roof slab expansion pushing the parapet | Lean, slab expansion, ties and movement |
| Inside | Water arriving at the head of a wall only in storms: overflowing box gutters or parapet outlets, not the parapet | Copings and the roof junction |
| Inside | Vibration or rattling from roof plant and screens in high wind | Plant screens |
| Inside | Pieces of masonry, render or terracotta found on the roof, the footpath or balconies below | Ornament and concrete parapets |
| Inside | Water running down the inside face of walls in the top-floor stairwell or plant room | Copings and the roof junction |
| Street or aerial | Parapets visibly out of plumb; bowing along the roof line | Lean, slab expansion, ties and movement |
| Street or aerial | Horizontal cracks in the wall just below roof level; cracks at corners at the top of the building | Lean, slab expansion, ties and movement |
| Street or aerial | Copings displaced, open joints, vegetation; missing cappings | Copings and the roof junction |
| Street or aerial | Loose or missing louvres; screens added since construction | Plant screens |
| Street or aerial | Rust staining at joints in cornices and ornament; cracked or missing terracotta units | Ornament and concrete parapets |
| Street or aerial | Netting, sheds or hoardings over the footpath below, a sign of known falling-masonry risk | Ornament and concrete parapets |
| On the roof | Cracks and open joints in parapet masonry on the roof side | Lean, slab expansion, ties and movement |
| On the roof | Membrane upstand height and termination; flashings pulled away | Copings and the roof junction |
| On the roof | Screen post bases corroded; bolts loose; louvre blades rattling | Plant screens |
| On the roof | Copings that rock or slide when pushed; joints open or filled with vegetation | Copings and the roof junction |
| On the roof | Height of the parapet above the finished roof, measured, wherever people access the roof | Parapets as roof edge protection |
| On the roof | Signs, antennas and services fixed into the parapet | Plant screens |
| In the records | Parapet observation reports where required | Standards by country |
| In the records | Screen engineering | Plant screens |
| In the records | Coping and flashing repair records | Copings and the roof junction |
| In the records | Façade ordinance filings and repair orders where the city requires them | Standards by country |
| In the records | Engineering for acoustic screens and any screen extensions | Plant screens |

sections.heading: Types of parapet and screen
sections.markdown:
Parapets are the low walls that rise above the roof at its edge: masonry, concrete or framed, finished with a coping. Plant screens are the walls, louvres and panels that hide rooftop plant and are usually steel framed and fixed to the roof structure. Both are exposed on every face, both carry high wind loads at the edge of the building, and both stand over the street or a public area on many buildings.

A parapet does several jobs: it terminates the roof membrane and supports its flashing, it can serve as the guardrail for roof access if it is high enough, and on many buildings it is a fire separation or carries ornament. Its coping sheds water off the top; a damp-proof course under the coping stops water going down into the wall.

| Form | Where it is found | Main risk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Solid masonry parapet with stone or brick coping | Pre-war commercial, residential and institutional | Lean, frost and sulfate attack, loose copings |
| Cavity or veneer parapet | Mid twentieth century onward | Tie corrosion, water into the cavity from the coping |
| Concrete parapet | Concrete-framed buildings | Reinforcement corrosion at low cover; cracks at movement joints |
| Framed parapet with metal capping | Modern commercial and residential | Capping fixings; water into framing |
| Plant screen on steel posts | Offices, retail, apartments | Fixings through the membrane; wind |
| Acoustic screen | Buildings near residences | Heavy panels; fixings and wind |

Parapets also carry the building's ornament on many older façades: cornices, pediments, balustrades, finials and terracotta or cast stone units, fixed back with iron cramps and dowels that corrode out of sight ([Architectural & Decorative Features](https://moyneross.com/technical/architectural-and-decorative-features)). Some are fire parapets, rising above the roof at a boundary or a fire wall to stop fire spreading across the roof, and must keep their height and integrity. And on most roofs they are the only thing between people working on the roof and the edge.

Their era is readable from the street. Solid brick or stone parapets with heavy cornices belong to buildings before about 1940; thin cavity or veneer parapets with precast or metal copings to the mid twentieth century; concrete upstands to concrete-framed buildings of the 1960s onward; and framed parapets with metal cappings, and the plant screens above them, to the last few decades.

Because a parapet sits at the meeting of wall, roof and edge, its problems belong to several pages at once: the masonry it is built of ([Masonry/Brickwork](https://moyneross.com/technical/masonry-brickwork)), the membrane that turns up its inside face ([Waterproofing Membranes](https://moyneross.com/technical/waterproofing-membranes)), the gutters and overflows that drain the roof it encloses ([Rainwater Systems](https://moyneross.com/technical/rainwater-systems)) and the edge protection it may be relied on to provide ([Roof Safety Systems](https://moyneross.com/technical/roof-safety-systems)). A repair that addresses only one of these usually fails at the others.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Parapets and screens wear at very different rates. Masonry parapets last sixty to a hundred years and copings forty to eighty, while metal cappings, screen framing and louvres need renewing within twenty to forty.

| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Masonry parapet | 60 to 100 years | Two-sided exposure; damp-proof course under coping |
| Stone and concrete copings | 40 to 80 years | Joints; fixings |
| Metal cappings | 20 to 40 years | Coastal exposure; fixings |
| Plant screen framing | 25 to 40 years | Coatings; fixings through the membrane |
| Louvres and cladding on screens | 20 to 30 years | Fixings; wind |
| Terracotta and cast stone ornament | Century material; iron cramps and dowels 50 to 100 years | Cramp corrosion; open joints; frost |
| Lead and zinc cappings | 40 to 80 years | Fixing; thermal movement; theft of lead |
| Acoustic screen panels | 20 to 30 years | Panel weight on fixings; wind; vibration |

Parapets age fastest on the elevations facing the prevailing weather and at corners, where exposure is greatest and movement is restrained in two directions. Copings and their joints are the first line of defence, and their failure sets the life of the masonry below.

The coping sets the clock. While copings and their joints keep water out, a parapet can last as long as the wall below it; once they fail, frost, sulfates and corrosion work down from the top, and the parapet ages several times faster than the wall it sits on.

What shortens life: two-sided exposure: parapets are wetted and frozen from both faces and the top, so they get wetter and colder than any part of the wall below; no damp-proof course under the coping and open coping joints, which let water run down into the wall and the cavity; expansion of the roof slab on concrete-roofed buildings, which pushes parapets and corners outward; fixings through the membrane for screens, cappings, signs and antennas, each a new leak path and corrosion point; screens added without engineering for wind loads at the edge of the building; cement repairs to lime-built parapets, which trap water and push the damage into the brick and stone.

What lengthens it: copings kept tight: joints repointed or resealed and fixings checked before water reaches the wall below; movement joints maintained in long parapet runs and at corners on concrete-roofed buildings; screens fixed to independent frames rather than through the membrane and parapet; roof works that respect the upstand: new insulation and membranes that do not reduce the upstand or the parapet's guarding height.

sections.heading: Lean, slab expansion, ties and movement
sections.markdown:
Parapets lean when frost, sulfate attack and wetting expand one face more than the other, and when the roof slab or structure behind pushes or pulls them. A parapet is a cantilever from roof level with little weight on top to hold it, so its stability depends on its mortar, its thickness and any restraint back to the roof; tall, thin, unrestrained parapets with soft or sulfate-attacked mortar are the ones that fail in wind, often onto the street below.

A concrete roof slab heats and expands in the sun far more than the shaded walls below it, and it shrinks and creeps over its life. Where the parapet and wall are built tight against the slab with no slip joint, the slab pushes them outward, cracking the wall horizontally at roof level, opening stepped cracks at the corners, and displacing the parapet. The cracks are often worst on the longest elevations and at corners where expansion meets restraint in two directions.

Cavity parapets are wet on both leaves and the ties in them corrode first. With little load on top to hold the outer leaf, it lifts and leans more readily than the wall below, and the horizontal cracks of tie corrosion appear at the top of the building before anywhere else ([Masonry/Brickwork](https://moyneross.com/technical/masonry-brickwork)).

Long runs of parapet expand and contract with heat and moisture more than the walls below, which are shaded and restrained. Without movement joints they crack vertically at regular intervals and at corners, and the cracks let water into the wall.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Parapet leaning, joints open on one face | Differential frost or sulfate expansion. Mortar soft and white on the wet face. | Exclude people below if it stands over a public area; have an engineer assess it, then restrain or rebuild. |
| Horizontal crack at roof level, parapet pushed out, corners cracked | Roof slab expansion. Concrete roof slab bearing on the wall; no slip joint. | Form a slip joint between slab and wall, and repair the cracked masonry. |
| Vertical cracks at regular spacing along a parapet | Missing movement joints. Crack spacing regular; no joints in the run; worst at corners. | Form movement joints so the cracks do not simply reopen. |

sections.heading: Copings and the roof junction
sections.markdown:
Coping joints open as mortar fails, and water runs down into the wall below. Copings without dowels or with corroded iron cramps loosen and slide; stone copings crack where their fixings rust and expand; concrete copings without drips throw water down the face; metal cappings lift in wind when their fixings corrode or were too few, and once a length lifts it acts like a sail. Copings without a damp-proof course or tray beneath them let every joint failure soak the wall.

The membrane turns up the inside face of the parapet; where the upstand is low, the termination fails or the flashing pulls out, water enters at the roof edge and appears inside at the top of external walls. Outlets and overflows through the parapet leak around their sleeves where the membrane meets them ([Waterproofing Membranes](https://moyneross.com/technical/waterproofing-membranes), [Rainwater Systems](https://moyneross.com/technical/rainwater-systems)).

Each re-roofing, insulation upgrade or new walkway raises the roof surface inside the parapet. The membrane upstand ends up lower than the water that can pond against it, and the parapet's height above the roof falls below what edge protection requires. Parapets that were adequate when built are often neither watertight nor safe as guarding after two generations of roof works.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Damp at the top of walls inside | Coping joints, missing damp-proof course or roof junction. Water test at copings and upstand. | Water test the copings and upstand; reset the copings with a damp-proof course or tray. |
| Damp at wall head appearing only in heavy storms | Roof drainage overflowing against the parapet. Box gutter or outlet capacity; no overflow through the parapet. | Check the box gutter and outlet capacity, and add overflows through the parapet; see Rainwater Systems. |
| Membrane upstand now below the roof surface or ponding line | Roof raised by later works. Records of re-roofing or insulation added; upstand height measured. | Renew the upstands and flashings, raised to suit the roof. |
| Coping lifted or missing after a storm | Fixings corroded or too few. Remaining copings move by hand; fixings rusted. | Make safe; reset the copings with new dowels and sound fixings. |

sections.heading: Ornament and concrete parapets
sections.markdown:
Cornices, balustrades and terracotta or cast stone ornament are held by iron cramps, dowels and anchors set into the masonry behind. Water entering through open joints corrodes them; the rust expands, cracks the units and eventually releases them. Terracotta that looks sound can be held by little more than its mortar. Falls of ornament from parapets onto streets are the reason many cities now require regular façade inspection.

Concrete upstands and parapets carry reinforcement close to both faces and are exposed on three sides, so carbonation and chlorides reach it quickly. Spalling follows the bars, corner cracks open where the parapet has no movement joints, and pieces of concrete fall from the outer face.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rust staining at cornice or terracotta joints; cracked units | Corroding cramps and anchors behind the ornament. Cramps exposed at sample positions; units loose when tested. | Make safe now; remove units, replace corroded cramps with stainless steel, and repair or replicate. |

sections.heading: Plant screens
sections.markdown:
Screen posts are bolted through the membrane to the structure or to plant platforms. Corroded bases, loose bolts and fixings designed for less wind than the screen now carries let louvres and panels loosen and blow off. Plant vibration loosens fixings over time, and acoustic panels, which are heavy, overload fixings designed for lighter louvres. Screens extended or clad after construction often have no engineering for the extra wind load at all.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Loose louvres after storms | Screen fixing or design for wind. Fixings corroded or undersized. | Secure or remove loose panels; re-engineer the fixings for current wind loads. |
| Screen panels vibrating or rattling | Fixings loosened by plant vibration or overloaded by heavy panels. Bolts loose; panel type heavier than the original design. | Retighten or replace the fixings, and check the panels against the original design load. |

sections.heading: Parapets as roof edge protection
sections.markdown:
A parapet is often the only thing between people working on a roof and the edge. Whether it protects them depends on its height above the finished roof, which later roof works can quietly reduce.

Where people work on the roof, a parapet often serves as the guardrail. Many older parapets are lower than fall protection rules require, and some have been lowered or capped down in past repairs; they then need guardrails added.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Parapet top within reach of falling from the roof | Parapet too low to serve as guarding. Height above the finished roof measured against edge protection rules and the limits for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Add guardrails on top of or behind the parapet before further roof access. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Parapet leaning or bowing over a public area; loose copings; screens loose | safety · 4 Essential | Make safe now: remove, restrain or exclude below. |
| Loose copings or screen panels over a street or entrance | safety · 4 Essential | Secure or remove now. |
| Terracotta or ornament with corroded cramps, units loose or cracked, over a street | safety · 4 Essential | Make safe now: remove loose units, net or hoard below. |
| Annual parapet observation due (New York) | deadline · 4 Essential | Annual. |
| Façade inspection under a city ordinance due or overdue | deadline · 4 Essential | Inspect and file by the due date. |
| Leaks at the roof junction or copings | failure · 3 Important | Repair now. |
| Open coping joints; cracked masonry without lean; corroded screen bases | condition · 2 Planned | Repair in the near term. |
| Parapet too low to serve as edge protection where people work on the roof | condition · 2 Planned | Add guardrails before further roof access. |
| Copings, cappings and screens at age | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Renew on cycle. |
| Screens with no engineering; parapet used as roof edge protection with unknown height | check · 2 Planned | Assess. |
| Minor weathering | nil · 1 Routine | Routine maintenance. |

Parapets over streets, entrances and neighbours are graded on what could fall and who is beneath it. The same crack or loose coping on a parapet facing an inaccessible light well may be a condition finding; facing a busy footpath it is a safety finding.

The grading follows what a finding demands, not the size of the eventual bill.

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A façade or structural engineer inspects close up. The checks below are made close up and from the roof side, because a survey from the street understates the risk.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Plumb survey | Of parapets. |
| Close inspection | Of copings, joints and the roof face. |
| Opening up | Under copings to find the damp-proof course. |
| Screen fixing inspection | And wind load check. |
| Water testing | Of the roof junction. |
| Hammer sounding of ornament and copings | Unit by unit, from access equipment. |
| Borescope inspection | Into the cavity and behind cornices to see ties, cramps and anchors without removing units. |
| Wind load check | Of screens, signs and antennas against current codes, including any extensions. |
| Coping removal | At sample positions to inspect the damp-proof course, dowels and fixings, and the wall head below. |
| Height measurement | Of parapets wherever people access the roof, against the edge protection rules for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). |
| Moisture readings | On internal walls below the parapet to map water entry. |
| Cover and carbonation testing | On concrete parapets. |

The report should state parapet height and plumb by elevation, coping condition, the presence of a damp-proof course and ties, screen fixing adequacy against current wind loads, and any parapets that do not meet edge protection height.

sections.heading: Making safe, restraining or rebuilding
sections.markdown:
Parapet and screen work starts with whatever could fall: loose copings, ornament and panels over a street or entrance are made safe before anything else. The options then run from resetting copings and adding restraint to rebuilding, with screens and edge protection alongside.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Make safe | Remove or restrain loose copings, ornament and screen panels, and protect the footpath with hoarding or netting while repairs are designed. | At once, wherever anything loose stands over a street, entrance or balcony. |
| Reset copings | New dowels, a damp-proof course or tray, and sealed or lead-covered joints; or weathered, throated copings that throw water clear of the face. | Where copings rock, joints are open or water reaches the wall head. |
| Rebuild leaning parapets | Rebuild from sound masonry, with a damp-proof course beneath the coping, restraint ties back to the roof structure, and lime mortar where the original was lime. | Where sulfate attack, failed ties or lean have gone beyond what restraint can hold. |
| Restraint without rebuilding | Stainless ties, brackets or posts connecting the parapet back to the roof. | Where the parapet is sound but unrestrained. |
| Slip joints and movement joints | Joints that let the roof slab and the masonry move. | Where slab expansion or long runs are the cause, so the crack does not simply reopen. |
| Ornament repair | Remove units, replace corroded cramps with stainless steel, repair or replicate terracotta and cast stone, and repoint. | Wherever cramps are corroding or units are loose or cracked. |
| Concrete repair | Repair spalled concrete, with cover restored and an anti-carbonation coating. | On concrete parapets that are spalling. |
| Renew upstands and flashings | New upstands and flashings, raised where the roof has been raised. | Where flashings have pulled away, or later works have buried the upstand. |
| Re-engineer screens | New fixings designed for current wind loads, or independent frames bearing on the structure rather than through the parapet and membrane. | Where screens have no engineering, rattle, or have loosened in storms. |
| Guardrails | Guardrails on top of or behind low parapets. | Wherever roof access needs edge protection and the parapet is too low. |

Choosing between them depends on whether the parapet is sound and merely unrestrained or wet, or whether its fabric has failed. Restraint and new copings save a sound parapet; a parapet with sulfate-attacked mortar, failed ties or lean beyond what restraint can hold has to be taken down and rebuilt.

Interactions: parapet work shares scaffold and street protection with façade repairs and roof membrane works, and is cheapest combined with them; heritage parapets and ornament need consent for materials and methods.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Parapet and coping work is priced by linear metre; screens per bay or as a lump sum. Scaffold or access dominates. Observations recur annually where required.

What drives the cost: access and street protection, the length of parapet affected, coping material and heritage constraints, opening up to inspect the damp-proof course and ties, and coordination with roof membrane works. Commonly missed: making good the membrane upstand, guardrails where the parapet is too low, and permits for work over the public way.

Rebuild is lifecycle; make-safe and observations are code compliance; repairs are repairs and maintenance.

Parapet works over a street need scaffold or edge access with footpath protection and permits, which can exceed the cost of the masonry itself. Screen re-engineering is usually a lump sum per screen with crane hire. Restraint ties are priced per tie. Annual parapet observations, where required, are a small recurring compliance cost.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a close inspection cannot: whether required inspections and filings are current, what the screens were designed for, and whether later roof works raised the surface or disturbed the junction. Ask for them before scaffold goes up.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Parapet observation and façade inspection reports | What inspections have found, and whether required filings are current. |
| Screen engineering | Whether the screens were designed for the loads they carry. |
| Coping and flashing repair records | Where water has got in before, and what was done. |
| Records of any make-safe works, hoardings or netting over the street | Whether a falling hazard is already known and being managed. |
| Fire strategy where parapets act as fire separation | Whether a parapet is part of the building's fire separation and must be kept. |
| Wind load design for screens | What the screens and their fixings were designed to withstand. |
| Roof access and edge protection records | Whether people working on the roof rely on the parapet for protection. |
| Heritage listing | Whether materials and methods for repairs are controlled. |
| Records of roof works that disturbed parapet flashings | Where later works may have opened the roof junction. |
| Council or insurer notices about falling masonry | Whether an authority or insurer has already required action. |
| Previous coping repairs and the materials used | Whether earlier repairs suit the parapet, such as cement on a lime-built wall. |
| Records of re-roofing or insulation works that raised the roof surface | Whether the parapet and its upstands are now too low. |
| Roof drainage design, including overflows through the parapet | Whether water at the wall head comes from the drainage rather than the parapet. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Parapets are misread when the direction of lean is ignored, when ornament is judged from the street, and when water at the top of a wall is blamed on the wrong source.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| A parapet that has stood for a century is safe | A parapet over a street that is out of plumb, or has loose copings, is a falling hazard. Treat it as unsafe until an engineer has assessed it. |
| A lean is a lean | Reading the direction of lean helps. Sulfate and frost attack lean the parapet towards the drier side, often away from the weather. Slab expansion pushes outward, with a horizontal crack at the slab line and stepped cracks at the corners. A parapet leaning inward over the roof may have lost its ties to the structure behind. |
| Ornament that looks sound is sound | Ornament can look sound and not be. Hammer sounding and tapping each unit, and opening up at sample joints to see the cramps, is the only reliable way to judge it; a visual survey from the street understates the risk. |
| Damp at the wall head is the parapet | Water at the top of a wall is often blamed on the parapet when it comes from the roof drainage, and the reverse. Test the coping and the wall above the termination separately from the gutter and outlets, and start from the top. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets standards for parapet masonry and wind loads, sets heights for parapets used as edge protection, and in some places requires parapets to be inspected. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Structure and wind | Masonry follows AS 3700 and wind actions AS/NZS 1170.2, called up by the National Construction Code. | Approved Document A and the Eurocodes (BS EN 1996, BS EN 1991-1-4) apply. | ASCE 7 sets wind loads; International Building Code Section 705.11 covers fire parapets, which must generally rise at least 30 inches above the roof. |
| Edge protection | Where a parapet is the roof edge protection, its height must meet the fall protection requirements under the work health and safety regulations and AS 1657; guardrails under AS 1657 are typically 900 to 1,100 mm high, which many older parapets do not reach once the roof has been raised. | Parapets used as edge protection fall under the Work at Height Regulations 2005, which require guardrails of at least 950 mm; BS 6180 covers barriers in and about buildings. | OSHA guardrails must be 42 inches (plus or minus 3) high. |
| Inspection and orders | Councils and building authorities can issue emergency or building orders requiring dangerous parapets and masonry to be made safe. | Local authorities can act on dangerous structures under the Building Act 1984 (sections 77 and 78), including emergency measures to make them safe. | New York requires annual observation of parapets facing a public right of way under 1 RCNY 103-15, with a plumbness check; its Façade Inspection and Safety Program (Local Law 11) requires façades of buildings over six storeys to be inspected every five years, and other cities, including Chicago, have similar ordinances. |

Rebuilding heritage parapets and their ornament needs heritage consent in all three jurisdictions, which sets materials and methods.

sections.heading: Worked example: a leaning parapet over a shopfront
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 1920s three-storey brick building has a parapet along its street frontage, with rooftop air conditioning behind a louvred screen added in the 1990s. From the street the parapet leans outward slightly, with a horizontal crack just below roof level and stepped cracks at the corners; two louvre blades rattle in wind.

The parapet stands over a footpath, so it is a falling hazard until an engineer has assessed it, with hoarding or netting below in the meantime. An outward lean with a crack at the slab line and stepped corner cracks points to roof slab expansion rather than sulfate attack, which means a slip joint as well as repair. The screen has no engineering on record, so its fixings are a check, once the loose blades are secured.

So the register carries the parapet as a safety line now, restraint or rebuilding with a slip joint once the engineer reports, securing the louvres now, and a screen assessment as a check line, all best combined with any façade works that share the scaffold.

thresholds.rule: At least 1 m high where a roof with general access is 1 m or more above the surface below

source.title: NCC 2025 Volume One, Part D3 Construction of exits

thresholds.rule: At least 1100 mm high

source.title: Approved Document K (2013 edition incorporating 2016 and 2020 amendments)

thresholds.rule: 1070 mm (42 in) high, plus or minus 75 mm; resisting 890 N

pages.title: Portable Fire Equipment
pages.question: How does portable fire equipment fail, and what does it say about a building's fire safety management?
pages.answer: Portable equipment fails by being missing, discharged, out of date or wrong for the hazard: water extinguishers next to switchboards, no wet chemical or blanket at commercial cooking, units hidden behind furniture. Older foam units contain PFAS and are being withdrawn. Each item is cheap, but the pattern is telling: a building with lapsed extinguisher servicing and wrong types usually has gaps elsewhere in its fire safety.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about portable fire equipment; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.

questions.question: Does it matter which extinguisher is where?
questions.answer: Yes. A water extinguisher beside a switchboard is dangerous, and commercial cooking needs wet chemical and a fire blanket. Types must match the hazard nearby.

questions.question: What do out-of-date extinguisher tags tell you?
questions.answer: Many out-of-date tags point to a lapsed service contract, and a building with neglected extinguishers usually has gaps elsewhere in its fire safety management.

questions.question: Are e-bike and scooter batteries a fire risk?
questions.answer: Yes. Lithium-ion batteries charged indoors need designated, separated charging locations, with detection and clear procedures.

questions.question: Should PFAS foam extinguishers be replaced?
questions.answer: Yes, with fluorine-free or other types.

questions.question: How long do fire extinguishers last?
questions.answer: Stored-pressure extinguishers 10 to 20 years with periodic pressure testing, carbon dioxide extinguishers 20 years and more, and fire blankets 7 to 10.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Portable equipment problems show at each location: an empty bracket, a gauge in the red, an out-of-date tag, or the wrong type beside the hazard. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On site | Extinguisher at each required location, mounted, signed and unobstructed | Missing, damaged and obstructed units |
| On site | Gauge in the green; tamper seal and pin intact | Missing, damaged and obstructed units |
| On site | Service tag with the last date and the next due | Missing, damaged and obstructed units |
| On site | Type matched to the hazard nearby | Wrong types, coverage gaps and PFAS |
| On site | Blankets in kitchens; wet chemical at commercial cooking | Wrong types, coverage gaps and PFAS |
| On site | Corrosion, damaged hoses, faded labels | Missing, damaged and obstructed units |
| In the records | Routine service records and register by location | Investigation before the scope |
| In the records | Pressure testing dates | Missing, damaged and obstructed units |
| In the records | Annual fire safety certification | Standards by country |
| In the records | Fire risk assessment (Britain) | Standards by country |
| In the records | Extinguishers moved from their signed locations | Missing, damaged and obstructed units |
| In the records | Missing fire blankets in staff kitchens | Wrong types, coverage gaps and PFAS |
| In the records | Equipment near charging areas for e-bikes and scooters | Lithium-ion battery hazards |

sections.heading: Types of portable equipment
sections.markdown:
Portable fire equipment is the first-attack equipment occupants use on a small fire: fire extinguishers, fire blankets, and the signage and mountings that make them findable. It is selected for the fire risks in each area, placed at set travel distances and near exits, and serviced on prescribed intervals. It is cheap, numerous and easily neglected, and in many buildings its records are the most reliable indicator of how fire safety is managed overall.

| Type | Suited to | Not suited to |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Water | Paper, wood, textiles (Class A) | Electrical equipment; cooking oils; flammable liquids |
| Foam (AFFF and fluorine-free) | Class A and flammable liquids (Class B) | Cooking oils; live electrical equipment in some types; older AFFF contains PFAS |
| Carbon dioxide | Electrical equipment; flammable liquids | Class A fires (no cooling); confined spaces |
| Dry powder (ABE) | Most fires including electrical | Cooking oils; indoor use where powder damages equipment and visibility |
| Wet chemical | Cooking oil and fat fires (Class F/K) | Most other uses |
| Fire blankets | Small cooking fires; clothing fires | Larger fires |

Placement follows the hazard: wet chemical and blankets in kitchens, carbon dioxide near switchboards and electrical equipment, water or foam for general areas, powder in car parks and workshops. In Australia, extinguishers are common in all commercial buildings; in Britain they are part of the responsible person's risk assessment; in the United States they are required by the fire code in most occupancies.

Extinguishers are rated by the fire classes they can tackle, and the classes differ slightly by jurisdiction: Class A ordinary combustibles, Class B flammable liquids, Class C flammable gases in Australia and Britain (electrical fires in the United States), electrical fires as Class E in Australia, and cooking oils and fats as Class F in Australia and Britain and Class K in the United States. Labels show the classes and ratings, and selection should follow them rather than colour alone.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Portable equipment is short-lived and easily overlooked: stored-pressure extinguishers last ten to twenty years with periodic pressure testing, fire blankets seven to ten, and hoses five to ten. Its condition is a quick guide to how fire safety is managed in the rest of the building.

| Equipment | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stored-pressure extinguishers | 10 to 20 years with periodic pressure testing | Corrosion; damage; test results |
| Carbon dioxide extinguishers | 20 years and more with pressure testing | Cylinder testing |
| Hoses and horns | 5 to 10 years | Cracking; UV |
| Fire blankets | 7 to 10 years | Damage; packaging |
| Signage and mounting | 10 to 20 years | Fading; damage |

What shortens life: exposure: outdoor, car park and coastal locations corrode cylinders and fittings; tampering and misuse: extinguishers used as door stops or discharged; missed servicing, which leaves discharged or depressurised units in place.

Units in sheltered indoor positions last much longer than those in car parks, loading docks and external areas; marine environments corrode cylinders and fittings within a few years.

sections.heading: Missing, damaged and obstructed units
sections.markdown:
Extinguishers are moved, stolen, used and not replaced, or slowly lose pressure. Gauges in the red, broken tamper seals and missing units are the commonest findings.

Cylinders corrode, hoses crack, pins and seals go missing, and labels fade. Pressure testing at set intervals catches cylinders that are no longer safe.

Extinguishers behind furniture, in cupboards, without signage, or mounted too high are not used in an emergency.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gauge in the red | Discharged or leaking. Weight or pressure check. | Replace or recharge the unit. |
| Service tags out of date | Servicing lapsed. Records. | Restore the service contract, covering every unit. |
| Empty brackets | Missing or used unit. Register. | Replace the missing unit, and update the register. |
| Extinguishers on the floor or mounted high | Not readily usable. Mounting heights against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Mount units on brackets or stands at the right height, beside the exits and hazards they serve. |

sections.heading: Wrong types, coverage gaps and PFAS
sections.markdown:
Water extinguishers next to switchboards, powder in kitchens without wet chemical, and no blanket at cooking areas leave occupants with equipment that is dangerous or ineffective for the likely fire. Fit-outs that change the use of rooms rarely change the extinguishers.

Travel distances grow when layouts change; new hazards (battery charging, kitchens, workshops) arrive without equipment.

Older foam extinguishers contain PFAS and are being withdrawn; disposal must follow environmental rules.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Water extinguisher beside a switchboard | Wrong type for the hazard. Hazard review. | Re-select the type to match the hazard. |
| Kitchen without blanket or wet chemical | Coverage gap. Hazard review. | Add a fire blanket, and a wet chemical extinguisher at commercial cooking. |
| Extinguishers far apart on a large floor | Travel distance too long. Distance to the nearest extinguisher against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Add or move units so every point is within distance. |

sections.heading: Lithium-ion battery hazards
sections.markdown:
E-bikes, scooters, tools and battery storage bring lithium-ion battery fires, which reignite and release toxic gases and are not reliably controlled by ordinary extinguishers. Charging areas in car parks, bike stores and apartments need hazard-specific measures: separation, detection, and guidance on what to do, rather than more extinguishers.

Misuse also matters: extinguishers used as door stops, moved to where staff find them convenient, or partly discharged and replaced on the bracket without being serviced.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| E-bikes and scooters charged in corridors, stairs or plant rooms | Battery fire risk on an escape route. Fire risk assessment; where charging actually happens. | Move charging off escape routes, to a separated, supervised area with detection. |
| Swollen, damaged or hot battery packs | Cell failure that can lead to thermal runaway. Inspection of the pack. | Stop charging it, isolate it away from combustibles, and have it removed safely. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Wrong type at a high hazard (water at switchboards, none at commercial cooking); discharged units in high-risk areas | safety · 4 Essential | Replace now. |
| Routine service due | deadline · 4 Essential | Six-monthly in Australia; annually in Britain and the United States, with monthly checks. |
| Missing, damaged or depressurised units | condition · 3 Important | Replace in the near term. |
| Units at end of life or failing pressure tests | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Replace on cycle. |
| No register; placement not reviewed after fit-outs | check · 3 Important | Survey. |
| Normal | nil · 1 Routine | Routine. |
| Extinguisher failed to discharge in use, or cylinder corroded or damaged | failure · 4 Essential | Remove from service and replace now. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A fire equipment contractor or fire safety consultant. The checks below cover every location on the register, then compare each type with the hazard nearby.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Location survey | Against requirements and the travel distances for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). |
| Hazard match | Of each unit to the hazards nearby. |
| Condition check | Gauge, seals, hose, cylinder, mounting, signage, service tag. |
| Records review | Service and pressure test dates; in the United States, monthly visual inspection, annual maintenance, and hydrostatic tests every five years for water and carbon dioxide units and every twelve for stored-pressure dry chemical (OSHA 1910.157). |
| PFAS foam identification | Of foam extinguishers, from labels and product data, so PFAS foam can be replaced. |
| Records cross-check | Compare the register with what is on site, unit by unit. |
| Hazard review | Of new uses since the last survey: kitchens, battery charging, workshops, storage. |

The report should list each location with its status, missing or wrong units, and the next service and test dates.

Where lithium-ion charging is present, the survey should also identify charging locations and whether the fire risk assessment or fire strategy addresses them.

Survey results are best recorded on floor plans so gaps in coverage are visible at a glance.

sections.heading: Replacing, re-selecting and managing
sections.markdown:
Most of the work is inexpensive: replacing missing or failed units, matching types to hazards, and a service contract that covers every unit. The larger decisions are about new hazards, such as lithium-ion battery charging, and phasing out PFAS foam.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Replace units | Replace missing, discharged, damaged and failing units. | Wherever a unit is missing, empty, damaged or fails its test. |
| Re-select types | Match each type to the hazard nearby. | Where the wrong type stands at a hazard. |
| Relocate and sign | Place units so they are visible and within travel distance, and sign them. | Where units are hidden, moved or too far apart. |
| Replace PFAS foam units | Fluorine-free or other types. | Wherever foam extinguishers contain PFAS. |
| Register and service contract | A register and contract covering every unit. | Wherever servicing has lapsed or units are unrecorded. |
| Lithium-ion charging areas | Designated, separated charging locations with detection and clear procedures. | Wherever e-bikes, scooters or batteries are charged indoors. |
| Training | Wardens and staff taught which extinguisher to use, and when not to. | In every occupied building. |
| Mounting and protection | Brackets at the right height, and cabinets in exposed or vandal-prone locations. | Where units stand on the floor, are exposed, or are tampered with. |
| Signage | Signage to current standards, so units can be found in smoke. | Where signs are missing or faded. |
| Fire risk review | Review the equipment after any change of use, so it follows the hazard. | After every fit-out or change of use. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Servicing is a recurring contract priced per unit. Replacement is per unit. Pressure testing recurs per unit at set intervals. These are small individually and often carried as a recurring allowance. Servicing and safety replacements are code compliance; replacement at end of life is lifecycle.

Replacing units in bulk at the end of their life is usually cheaper than piecemeal replacement after failed pressure tests. Disposal of PFAS foam units adds a hazardous waste cost.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a walk-through cannot: whether every unit is registered and serviced, whether the equipment was reviewed after the building changed, and how battery charging is controlled. Ask for them early, since they say a good deal about fire safety management generally.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Register of extinguishers and blankets by location and type | Where every unit is, and what type. |
| Service and pressure test records | Whether units are serviced and tested as required. |
| Annual fire safety certification or fire risk assessment | Whether the equipment was reviewed against the building's risks. |
| Foam extinguisher product data and PFAS status | Whether foam units contain PFAS. |
| Records of fit-outs or changes of use that added new hazards | Whether new hazards have arrived without new equipment. |
| Policies for e-bike, scooter and battery charging | Whether battery charging is controlled. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Portable equipment is misread when it is treated as a minor item, when single units are fixed without asking why the pattern arose, and when any extinguisher is assumed to suit any fire.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| Extinguishers are a minor item | Portable equipment is a reliable indicator of fire safety management: a building where extinguishers are out of date, missing or wrongly placed usually has gaps elsewhere. |
| Fix the units that are wrong | Patterns matter more than single units: many out-of-date tags point to a lapsed contract; many wrong types point to fit-outs that changed uses without a fire risk review. |
| Any extinguisher will do | Types must match the hazard: water beside a switchboard is dangerous, and commercial cooking needs wet chemical and a fire blanket. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets where portable equipment is required, how it is selected, and how often it is serviced and tested. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Requirements and selection | The National Construction Code requires portable fire extinguishers in many building classes; AS 2444 governs selection and location. | The Regulatory Reform (Fire Safety) Order 2005 requires appropriate fire-fighting equipment based on the fire risk assessment; BS 5306-8 covers selection and positioning. | The International Fire Code sets where extinguishers are required; NFPA 10 governs selection and installation. |
| Service and testing | AS 1851 sets six-monthly service and periodic pressure testing; extinguishers are essential safety measures with annual certification. | BS 5306-3 covers maintenance, with an annual basic service and extended services or overhauls at five or ten years depending on type. | NFPA 10 sets monthly visual inspection, annual maintenance, six-yearly internal maintenance for stored-pressure dry chemical units, and hydrostatic testing at five or twelve years depending on type. |

sections.heading: Worked example: a fit-out that changed the hazards
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. An office floor was refitted as a co-working space with a commercial kitchen and an e-bike store. Water extinguishers still stand where the old layout put them, one beside the new switchboard; the kitchen has no wet chemical extinguisher or blanket; and half the service tags are a year out of date.

The pattern says more than any one unit: wrong types point to a fit-out that changed uses without a fire risk review, and lapsed tags to a lapsed contract. The water unit beside the switchboard and the kitchen without wet chemical are safety findings. The e-bike store is a new hazard with nothing to manage it.

So the register carries the switchboard and the kitchen as safety lines now, a service contract covering every unit, a designated charging area with detection for the e-bikes, and a fire risk review of the floor as a check line.

thresholds.rule: An ABE extinguisher of at least 2.5 kg within 10 m of each unit’s entry door

source.title: Fire safety risk assessment: offices and shops

thresholds.rule: About 1 m for larger extinguishers and 1.5 m for smaller ones

pages.title: Power Distribution
pages.question: How does power distribution fail, what are the warning signs, and when is rewiring needed?
pages.answer: Distribution fails by insulation, connections and alteration. Rubber-insulated wiring from before the 1960s perishes to bare conductors and must be replaced; aluminium branch wiring in some US houses of 1965 to 1973 overheats at devices. Missing or untested RCDs leave people unprotected from shock. Tenant fit-outs add unrecorded circuits and breach fire stopping. Harmonics from electronic loads overheat shared neutrals.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about power distribution; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Distribution boards, sub-mains cabling, tenant/sub-metering

questions.question: Is old rubber wiring dangerous?
questions.answer: Yes. Rubber-insulated wiring is past its life wherever it is found, and crumbling insulation at fittings and switches is a safety finding.

questions.question: Why is my power outlet warm or scorched?
questions.answer: A loose terminal, overload, or aluminium wiring. Isolate the circuit and have it repaired.

questions.question: Do all circuits need RCD protection?
questions.answer: New and altered circuits do in Australia, and BS 7671 requires it on socket circuits in the United Kingdom; adding it to older circuits is the usual remedy where it is missing.

questions.question: How often should an electrical installation be inspected?
questions.answer: Periodically; in the United Kingdom, at least every five years for privately rented homes. The inspection's coded observations show what needs doing.

questions.question: How long does wiring last?
questions.answer: PVC wiring 40 to 60 years and distribution boards 25 to 40; rubber-insulated wiring is past its life wherever it is found.

questions.question: Why does the power keep tripping when nothing new is plugged in?
questions.answer: An RCD that trips intermittently points to earth leakage from an appliance or damp, or an ageing RCD. Test the circuit and appliances, and find the leakage.

questions.question: Why do the breakers trip under normal use?
questions.answer: The circuit has been overloaded by added equipment. Measure the load, then add circuits or redistribute it.

questions.question: The insulation on the old wiring is crumbling at the light fittings. Is that a problem?
questions.answer: Yes. That is perished rubber-insulated cable. Rewire the affected circuits.

questions.question: None of the breakers in the electrical panel are labelled. Does that matter?
questions.answer: It shows undocumented alterations. Trace and label the circuits, and update the drawings.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Distribution problems show at the boards as missing schedules and covers, in the wiring as perished insulation, at outlets as heat and scorching, and in the periodic inspection report. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| At distribution boards | Board type, age and maker; rewireable fuses, cartridge fuses or breakers; RCDs present on which circuits | Busducts, alterations and harmonics |
| At distribution boards | Circuit schedules present and accurate; boards added by tenants | Busducts, alterations and harmonics |
| At distribution boards | Discolouration, burn marks, melted insulation, a smell of hot plastic | Insulation, connections and RCDs |
| At distribution boards | Missing blanks and covers exposing live parts | Insulation, connections and RCDs |
| In ceilings, risers and occupied spaces | Rubber-insulated cables, especially at light fittings and old switches | Insulation, connections and RCDs |
| In ceilings, risers and occupied spaces | Unsupported cables draped over ceilings; damaged sheathing | Insulation, connections and RCDs |
| In ceilings, risers and occupied spaces | Unsealed cable penetrations in risers and walls | Fire stopping in risers |
| In ceilings, risers and occupied spaces | Scorched or warm outlets and switches; flickering lights | Insulation, connections and RCDs |
| In ceilings, risers and occupied spaces | Daisy-chained power boards and extension leads, signs that circuits are too few | Busducts, alterations and harmonics |
| In the records | Periodic inspection and test reports with observations and their codes | Investigation before the scope |
| In the records | RCD test records | Insulation, connections and RCDs |
| In the records | Circuit schedules and as-built drawings | Busducts, alterations and harmonics |
| In the records | Thermographic surveys of boards and busducts | Busducts, alterations and harmonics |
| In the records | Metering arrangements and any embedded network documents | Busducts, alterations and harmonics |

sections.heading: Parts of the distribution
sections.markdown:
Power distribution takes electricity from the main switchboard to the points of use: sub-main cables and busducts in risers, distribution boards on each floor or tenancy, final circuits to outlets, lighting and equipment, residual current devices (RCDs) and other protection, metering for tenants and services, and the trays, ladders and conduits that carry cables. It is the most altered part of a building's electrical system, because every fit-out touches it.

| Era | Typical wiring | What it implies |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Before about 1950 | Vulcanised India rubber (VIR) insulated cables; lead-sheathed cables; knob-and-tube in the United States | Rubber insulation perishes and crumbles off the conductor; replacement is the only remedy |
| 1950s to 1960s | Tough rubber sheathed (TRS) cables; early PVC | Brittle sheathing; lighting circuits often without an earth conductor |
| 1965 to 1973, United States | Aluminium branch circuit wiring in some houses | Connections at outlets and switches overheat; a recognised fire risk |
| 1960s onward | PVC insulated and sheathed cables; steel conduit in commercial work | Long-lived if not overheated or damaged |
| 1990s onward | Low-smoke zero-halogen cables in some buildings; RCD protection on socket circuits | Current practice |

| Component | Where it is found | What goes wrong |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sub-main cables | Risers, basements, ceiling spaces | Overload; damage; joints; fire stopping where they pass compartments |
| Busducts (busways) | Riser distribution in towers and industrial buildings | Joints loosen and overheat; tap-off units disturbed |
| Distribution boards | Each floor, tenancy and plant area | Ageing devices; no RCDs; unlabelled alterations; added sub-boards |
| Final circuits and accessories | Throughout | Loose terminals; damaged outlets; overload |
| RCDs and RCBOs | Distribution boards | Absent in older installations; failing to trip if never tested |
| Sub-metering | Tenancies, plant, embedded networks | Inaccurate or unread meters; recharge disputes |
| Cable support systems | Ceiling spaces, risers | Overloaded trays; unsupported cables draped on ceilings |

Metering and ownership vary by building type. In multi-tenant commercial buildings the owner may meter tenants with check meters or recharge by area. In apartment buildings, residents are either supplied by the network directly or through an embedded network owned by the building, which carries its own regulatory and consumer obligations.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
PVC wiring lasts forty to sixty years and distribution boards twenty-five to forty, while RCDs and RCBOs last fifteen to twenty-five. Rubber-insulated wiring is past its life wherever it is found.

| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| PVC wiring | 40 to 60 years | Heat; overload; damage |
| Rubber-insulated wiring | Past its life wherever found | Replace |
| Distribution boards | 25 to 40 years | Device support; alterations; environment |
| Busducts | 30 to 40 years | Joint maintenance; loading |
| RCDs and RCBOs | 15 to 25 years | Testing; surges |
| Socket outlets and switches | 20 to 30 years | Use; loose terminals |
| Sub-meters | 15 to 25 years | Technology; communications |

What shortens life: heat: cables bundled together, run through insulation or in hot ceiling spaces and plant rooms lose capacity and age faster; overload from added equipment, power boards and extension leads; alterations by tenants and contractors without records or proper protection; harmonics from electronic loads overheating shared neutrals; mechanical damage by other trades in ceilings and risers; moisture in basements, car parks and external areas.

sections.heading: Insulation, connections and RCDs
sections.markdown:
Rubber insulation hardens, cracks and falls away with age and heat, leaving bare conductors in light fittings, switches and ceiling spaces. Disturbing old cables during renovation accelerates the breakdown. PVC insulation that has been overheated becomes brittle and discoloured around terminations and in bundles.

Terminals at outlets, switches, joint boxes and boards loosen with thermal cycling and poor workmanship; resistance and heat rise until the accessory scorches or ignites. Aluminium branch wiring in United States houses of 1965 to 1973 does this at devices not rated for aluminium; remediation with approved connectors or rewiring is the accepted fix.

RCDs disconnect a circuit when current leaks to earth, protecting people from electric shock. Older installations often have none, or only on some circuits; devices that are never tested can fail to trip. Wet areas, outdoor circuits and portable equipment circuits are where the absence matters most.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Crumbling insulation at light fittings and switches | Perished rubber-insulated cable. Inspection; era of the building or rewiring. | Rewire the affected circuits. |
| Warm or scorched outlets and switches | Loose terminal, overload, or aluminium wiring. Thermography; inspection of terminals. | Isolate the circuit; repair the terminal, reduce the load, or remediate the aluminium wiring. |
| RCD trips intermittently | Earth leakage from appliances or damp, or an ageing RCD. Insulation resistance test; RCD test. | Test the circuit and appliances, and find the leakage. |
| No RCD test records, or test buttons never pressed | Shock protection unverified. Records and test, against the intervals for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Test every RCD, replace those that fail, and set a test schedule. |

sections.heading: Busducts, alterations and harmonics
sections.markdown:
Busduct sections are joined with bolted connections that must be torqued and checked. Loose joints overheat and fail; tap-off units opened or moved by tenants are a common source of faults.

Fit-outs add circuits and sub-boards, remove or bypass protection, reuse old cables, and leave boards without circuit schedules. Over time nobody knows what a breaker controls, and isolation for maintenance becomes unsafe.

Computers, LED drivers and variable speed drives draw distorted current. On three-phase circuits that share a neutral, some harmonic currents add rather than cancel, so the neutral can carry more current than the phases and overheat, particularly in older installations with reduced neutrals.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Breakers trip under normal load | Circuit overloaded by added equipment. Load measurement. | Add circuits or redistribute the load. |
| Neutral hotter than phases | Harmonics. Harmonic measurement. | Upgrade the neutral, or add harmonic filtering. |
| Unlabelled breakers and added boards | Undocumented alterations. Inspection against drawings. | Trace and label the circuits, and update the drawings. |

sections.heading: Fire stopping in risers
sections.markdown:
Every time cables are pulled through fire-rated walls, floors and riser slabs, the fire stopping is disturbed. Unsealed penetrations let fire and smoke spread between compartments; risers in older buildings are often riddled with them.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Smoke spread between floors in a fire drill or fire | Unsealed riser penetrations. Riser inspection. | Fire stop every riser penetration with tested systems. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Perished rubber wiring; exposed live parts; scorched accessories; no RCD on wet area or outdoor circuits; aluminium branch wiring without remediation | safety · 4 Essential | Isolate, make safe or rewire now. |
| Circuits or boards failed | failure · 4 Essential | Repair now. |
| Periodic inspection and testing due | deadline · 4 Essential | At the interval set by the regulation or standard. |
| Overheating terminations; unsupported devices; unsealed penetrations; missing schedules | condition · 4 Essential | Repair in the near term. |
| Wiring and boards at the end of their life | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Plan rewiring floor by floor or with fit-outs. |
| No periodic inspection on record; wiring type unknown | check · 3 Important | Inspect and test. |
| Minor defects | nil · 1 Routine | Routine maintenance. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A licensed electrical contractor or electrical engineer carries out a periodic inspection and test. The checks below start with the periodic inspection report and its coded observations, then look at boards, riser penetrations and the outlets occupants use.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Visual inspection | Of boards, a sample of accessories and accessible wiring, with covers off where safe. |
| Testing | Of a representative sample of circuits: insulation resistance, earth continuity, polarity, earth fault loop impedance, and RCD operation times, with RCD tests at the intervals for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). |
| Wiring type survey | To identify rubber-insulated, aluminium or other at-risk wiring. |
| Thermographic survey | Of distribution boards and busduct joints under load. |
| Load and harmonic measurement | Where overload or neutral heating is suspected. |
| Fire-stopping survey | Of risers and penetrations. |
| Documentation review | Circuit schedules, drawings, metering. |

The report should list observations by severity code, sample results extrapolated to the installation, wiring types and extent, boards needing replacement, fire-stopping breaches, and the next inspection date.

sections.heading: Rewiring, protecting or documenting
sections.markdown:
Perished wiring, exposed live parts and scorched outlets come first. After that, the work follows the periodic inspection: RCD protection, board replacement, rewiring floor by floor, fire stopping, and the documentation that alterations left behind.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rewiring | Rewire rubber-insulated and other end-of-life circuits, usually floor by floor or tenancy by tenancy. | Wherever wiring has perished or reached the end of its life. |
| Aluminium wiring remediation | Approved connectors at every device, or rewiring. | Where aluminium branch wiring is found. |
| RCD protection | Add RCD protection to circuits without it, or upgrade boards to RCBOs. | Wherever circuits lack it. |
| Board replacement | New boards. | Where devices are unsupported or boards are unsafe. |
| Busduct maintenance | Torque checks and joint replacement. | On a cycle, and where joints overheat. |
| Neutral upgrades | Upgrade the neutrals, or add harmonic filtering. | Where neutrals overheat. |
| Fire stopping | Fire stop every penetration with tested systems, recorded with photographs. | Wherever risers and walls have unsealed penetrations. |
| Documentation | Circuit schedules, labelling and as-built drawings. | Wherever schedules and drawings are missing or wrong. |
| Additional circuits | New circuits. | Where loads have outgrown the installation. |
| Load management | Redistribute circuits and add submains where boards are overloaded. | Where boards are overloaded. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Periodic inspection and testing is a recurring lump sum. Rewiring is priced per circuit, per floor or per tenancy, with ceiling access and making good often the largest component. Boards are priced per board. RCD upgrades per circuit or per board. Fire stopping per penetration or per riser. Busduct joint work per joint.

Testing and safety rectification are code compliance; rewiring and board replacement are lifecycle; repairs are repairs and maintenance. Rewiring is usually best timed with fit-outs, when ceilings are open.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a working installation cannot: what the last periodic inspection found, whether the RCDs have been tested, and what tenants have altered. Ask for them before any fit-out or change of use.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Periodic inspection and test reports with observations | What the last periodic inspection found, and how urgent each item is. |
| RCD test records | Whether RCDs trip when they should. |
| Circuit schedules and electrical as-built drawings | What each circuit feeds. |
| Thermographic surveys of boards and busducts | Whether boards and busducts are overheating. |
| Rewiring records and dates | Which parts have been rewired, and when. |
| Fire-stopping records for risers | Whether riser penetrations are fire stopped. |
| Metering and embedded network arrangements | How the building is metered, and who supplies the residents. |
| Records of electrical fires, scorching or tripping incidents | Whether there have been fires, scorching or repeated tripping. |
| Tenant fit-out electrical certificates | Whether tenant works were certified. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Power distribution is misread when a working installation is taken to be a safe one, and when power boards and extension leads are treated as a convenience rather than as evidence.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| It works, so it is safe | A working installation is not a safe one. Periodic inspection and testing exist because insulation breakdown, failed RCDs and loose terminals give no warning until they cause a shock or a fire. |
| Extension leads are a convenience | Daisy-chained power boards and extension leads are a sign that there are too few circuits for the loads. Add circuits or redistribute the load, rather than adding more leads. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets standards for electrical installations, protection against shock, and periodic inspection. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Installation, protection and inspection | Installations follow AS/NZS 3000, with periodic verification to AS/NZS 3019; RCD protection is required on new and altered circuits; electrical safety regulators in each state set licensing and notification. Embedded networks in residential buildings are regulated by the Australian Energy Regulator and state rules. | BS 7671 governs installations and requires RCD protection on socket circuits; periodic inspection results in an Electrical Installation Condition Report, required at least every five years for privately rented homes in England; the Electricity at Work Regulations 1989 require installations to be maintained safe. | NFPA 70 (the National Electrical Code) governs installations, including GFCI and AFCI protection; NFPA 70B sets maintenance; the Consumer Product Safety Commission publishes guidance on aluminium branch wiring remediation. |

sections.heading: Worked example: rubber wiring in a 1950s block
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 1950s apartment block's common areas still have rubber-insulated wiring, crumbling at the light fittings. Several tenants run daisy-chained power boards, one outlet in the laundry is scorched, the circuits have no RCD protection, and there is no periodic inspection on record.

A working installation is not a safe one. Perished rubber wiring and a scorched outlet are safety findings; circuits without RCDs give no protection against shock; and the power boards point to too few circuits for the loads.

So the register carries the rubber wiring and the scorched outlet as safety lines now, a periodic inspection as a check line, RCD protection, and rewiring of the common areas, with additional circuits where loads have grown.

thresholds.rule: Push-button test every 6 months; operating-time test every 12 months in high and medium risk areas, every 2 years in low risk areas

source.title: Electrical safety (inspection and testing timeframes)

pages.title: Public Amenities
pages.question: How do shared toilets and end-of-trip facilities fail, and when are there too few?
pages.answer: Amenities fail on water, numbers and management. Membranes and wastes leak into the floor below; dry traps and scaled urinals cause odour; little-used showers become Legionella risks. Densified floors outgrow fixture numbers and end-of-trip demand outstrips bikes, lockers and showers. Accessible toilets turned into storerooms leave people without facilities. Refurbish as a whole block, with membranes, every 15 to 20 years.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about public amenities; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Floor/wall finishes, partitions, fixtures, vanities, accessories in toilets and end-of-trip
