BS 6465-1:2006+A1:2009 Sanitary installations: Design of sanitary facilities and scales of provision
NCC 2025 Volume Three (Plumbing Code), Part B2 Heated water services
HSG274 Legionnaires’ disease: Technical guidance, Part 2: Hot and cold water systems

pages.searchTitle: Shared toilets and end-of-trip: leaks, odour, fixture numbers, Legionella and access

questions.question: How many toilets does an office floor need?
questions.answer: As many as the code ratio requires for the people now on the floor. A floor densified since it was built can fall short without any fixture changing.

questions.question: Why do the toilets smell in a lightly used room?
questions.answer: Usually a dry floor waste trap. Trap primers or water-based seals keep it wet.

questions.question: Are rarely used showers a health risk?
questions.answer: Yes. Little-used showers become dead legs where Legionella can grow; flush them on a recorded schedule.

questions.question: Is a locked accessible toilet a problem?
questions.answer: Yes. Accessible facilities that are locked, used for storage or outdated leave people without facilities, and are graded as safety findings.

questions.question: How long do amenities last before refurbishment?
questions.answer: Usually 15 to 20 years, though refurbishment is often brought forward for leasing.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Amenity problems show as stains on the ceiling below, odours, queues and full bike racks, damaged partitions and blocked-off accessible toilets, and in call-out and complaint records. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On site | Ceiling stains below amenities on the floor beneath | Leaks, blockages, odour and wear |
| On site | Odour on entry; dry floor wastes; scaled urinals | Leaks, blockages, odour and wear |
| On site | Queues at peak; complaints about numbers | Fixture numbers and end-of-trip |
| On site | Swollen or corroded partitions; broken locks | Leaks, blockages, odour and wear |
| On site | Accessible toilets cluttered or locked | Legionella and accessible facilities |
| On site | End-of-trip bike racks and lockers full; showers queued | Fixture numbers and end-of-trip |
| On site | Cracked tiles and failed grout around wastes | Leaks, blockages, odour and wear |
| In the records | Leak and plumbing call-out history | Leaks, blockages, odour and wear |
| In the records | Occupancy figures against fixture numbers | Fixture numbers and end-of-trip |
| In the records | Cleaning and hygiene complaints | Leaks, blockages, odour and wear |
| In the records | Legionella management for showers | Legionella and accessible facilities |
| In the records | Refurbishment history | Investigation before the scope |
| In the records | Water marks around WC pans and at floor wastes, showing leaks or overflows | Leaks, blockages, odour and wear |
| In the records | Tenant or visitor complaints about cleanliness and odour | Leaks, blockages, odour and wear |

sections.heading: What the space does and what it contains
sections.markdown:
Public amenities are the shared toilets, accessible toilets, showers, change rooms, end-of-trip facilities, parents' rooms and tea points in commercial, institutional and mixed-use buildings. They are among the most heavily used and most judged spaces in a building: tenants rate buildings on their amenities, codes set how many fixtures are needed for the occupancy, and failures (leaks, odour, broken fixtures, shortages) are noticed immediately. Functionally they must provide enough fixtures for the people in the building, stay hygienic, be accessible, and not leak into the floors below.

| Element group | Typical provision | What matters for the space |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sanitary fixtures | Toilets, urinals, basins, showers | Numbers for the occupancy; reliability; water use |
| Wet area waterproofing | Membranes under floors and up walls | Leaks to floors below |
| Partitions and cubicles | Toilet partitions, doors and hardware | Corrosion, damage, privacy |
| Finishes | Tiles, vanities, mirrors, accessories | Hygiene, durability, appearance |
| Ventilation | Exhaust to every room | Odour and moisture removal |
| Accessible facilities | Accessible toilets and showers, ambulant cubicles | Compliance, availability |
| End-of-trip | Bike parking, lockers, showers, drying rooms | Capacity against demand |

sections.heading: How long it stays fit for purpose
sections.markdown:
Amenities are refurbished every fifteen to twenty years, while tapware and flush valves last ten to fifteen and membranes fifteen to twenty-five. Rising occupancy and rising expectations end their fitness for purpose as often as wear does.

| Component or quality | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Amenities refurbishment | 15 to 20 years | Wear; market; leaks |
| Wet area membranes | 15 to 25 years | Installation; movement |
| Tapware and flush valves | 10 to 15 years | Water quality; use |
| Toilet partitions | 15 to 25 years | Moisture; damage |
| Exhaust fans | 10 to 15 years | Run hours |
| End-of-trip lockers and fittings | 10 to 15 years | Use |

What shortens fitness for purpose: higher occupancy densities than the amenities were designed for; rising market expectations for end-of-trip and quality; water leaks through membranes and around fixtures; vandalism and heavy use in public buildings.

Amenities are among the first spaces tenants judge, and their refurbishment is often brought forward for leasing reasons even when fixtures still work.

sections.heading: Leaks, blockages, odour and wear
sections.markdown:
Amenities leak through failed floor membranes, around floor wastes, at wall junctions, from cisterns, flush valves and pipework in ducts, and from overflowing urinals and blocked drains. Leaks show on ceilings of the floor below and damage tenancies.

Toilets and urinals block from paper, wipes and scale, overflowing onto floors and into the floor below. Recurrent blockages in one block often point to a defect in the stack or branch rather than misuse.

In shared buildings, amenities on one floor often serve several tenants, so a single failure affects many people.

Odours come from failed exhaust, dry floor waste traps in little-used rooms, blocked or scaled urinals, sealant and grout harbouring bacteria, and leaks soaking substrates.

Partitions swell and corrode, hardware breaks, tiles crack, grout discolours, and accessories go missing.

In a shared building, the floor below pays for a leak in the amenities above: its ceiling, its fit-out and its tenant's patience. That is why leaks are graded as failures, and why the damage below often costs more than the repair.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stain on the ceiling below a toilet block | Membrane failure or pipe leak. Flood test; dye test; duct inspection. | Flood test the floor and dye test the fixtures; repair the membrane, joint or duct pipework found. |
| Odour in a lightly used room | Dry floor waste trap. Trap inspection. | Fit trap primers or water-based seals to dry wastes. |
| Odour near urinals | Scale and blockage or failed waterless cartridges. Inspection. | Descale or clear the urinals, or replace failed waterless cartridges on a schedule. |
| Cubicle partitions swelling at the base | Moisture and cleaning water. Material type. | Replace with moisture-resistant partitions. |
| Toilets in one block blocking again and again | A defect in the stack or branch, rather than misuse. Blockages recur in the same block; a CCTV survey of the branch shows the defect. | CCTV the branch and stack, and repair the defect. |

sections.heading: Fixture numbers and end-of-trip
sections.markdown:
Codes set fixture numbers by occupancy. When floors are densified, queues and complaints follow, and the building no longer meets the occupancy it is let for. End-of-trip facilities sized for a few cyclists are overwhelmed as commuting changes.

Fixture numbers are a calculation, not a judgement. Count each floor's toilets, urinals and basins, including accessible and ambulant facilities, against the code ratios for the people now on the floor, not the occupancy the building was designed for. A floor densified since it was built can fall short without a single fixture changing.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Queues at peak | Fixtures below the occupancy now on the floor. Count against code ratios. | Count fixtures against the code ratios for the current occupancy; add fixtures or convert space. |
| Bike racks, lockers and showers full at peak | End-of-trip demand beyond what was provided. Counts at peak and usage data. | Expand the end-of-trip facilities to match demand. |

sections.heading: Legionella and accessible facilities
sections.markdown:
Two amenity findings affect people's health and rights rather than the building: showers and outlets left unused long enough to grow Legionella, and accessible facilities that cannot be used by the people who need them. Both are graded as safety findings.

Showers in end-of-trip facilities and accessible bathrooms that are rarely used become dead legs where Legionella can grow, then aerosolise when used.

Accessible toilets used as storerooms, locked with keys staff cannot find, or with layouts and fittings that do not meet requirements leave people with disability without facilities.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| An end-of-trip shower unused for weeks | A dead leg where Legionella can grow. Temperature checks and flushing records show water standing. | Flush it on a recorded schedule, and disinfect if testing warrants. |
| An accessible toilet used for storage, or locked | A management failure, not a fabric one. Cleaning gear or boxes inside, or no one can find the key. | Clear it, keep it available, and make the access arrangement known. |
| Hand basin water too hot to keep hands under | Tempering failed or absent. Outlet temperature against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Fit or repair tempering or thermostatic mixing valves and retest every outlet. |
| Hot water slow to arrive or lukewarm at little-used outlets | Legionella risk from low temperature or stagnation. Temperatures at the outlets over time, and the flushing record, against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Restore temperatures, flush little-used outlets, and remove dead legs. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Legionella risk from little-used showers; accessible facilities unavailable | safety · 4 Essential | Flush, disinfect, restore now. |
| Leaks damaging floors below; amenities closed | failure · 3 Important | Repair now. |
| Fixture numbers below code for current occupancy | deadline · 3 Important | Before occupancy increases or as required. |
| Worn fixtures and finishes; odour; partition damage | condition · 2 Planned | Repair in the near term. |
| Amenities at end of refurbishment cycle | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Refurbish. |
| Occupancy against fixtures unknown | check · 2 Planned | Assess. |
| Normal | nil · 1 Routine | Routine. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A building surveyor leads, with a hydraulic engineer for leaks and drainage, an access consultant, and the cleaning contractor for hygiene issues. The checks below trace each leak to its source, count fixtures against the current occupancy, and review little-used outlets and accessible facilities.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Leak investigation | Flood tests of floors, dye tests of fixtures and wastes, and inspection of service ducts for leaking cisterns, valves and joints. |
| Fixture count | Against the code ratios for current and planned occupancy, floor by floor, including accessible and ambulant facilities. |
| End-of-trip review | Bike spaces, lockers, showers and drying against current use and market expectations. |
| Ventilation check | Of exhaust rates to every room. |
| Legionella review | Of little-used showers and outlets, with temperature checks and flushing records. |
| Access audit | Of accessible toilets and showers. |
| Condition survey | Of fixtures, tapware, partitions, finishes and accessories. |

The report should give the cause of each leak, capacity against occupancy, safety items, and a staged refurbishment plan.

sections.heading: Repairing, expanding or refurbishing
sections.markdown:
Little-used showers and unavailable accessible facilities come first. After that, leaks are repaired before the floor below suffers more, capacity is matched to the occupancy now on each floor, and refurbishment follows floor by floor, keeping other amenities open.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Leak repair | Re-membrane floors with correct falls and waste flanges, repair joints and replace cisterns and valves in ducts. | Wherever amenities leak to the floor below. |
| Capacity increases | Add fixtures or convert space, often as part of a whole-floor or core refurbishment. | Where fixtures fall short of the occupancy now on the floor. |
| End-of-trip expansion | More bike spaces, lockers and showers to match demand. | Where bike racks, lockers and showers are full. |
| Odour control | Trap primers or water-based seals for dry wastes, exhaust repairs, urinal maintenance regimes. | Wherever odour persists. |
| Flushing regimes | Flush little-used showers and outlets on a schedule, with records. | Wherever showers or outlets go unused for days. |
| Accessible facilities | Clear them, upgrade them to current layouts, and keep them available. | Wherever accessible facilities are cluttered, locked or outdated. |
| Refurbishment | Durable, water-efficient fixtures and moisture-resistant partitions. | At the end of the cycle, or earlier for leasing. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Amenities are refurbished as lump sums per block or per floor, including membranes, finishes, fixtures and partitions, with out-of-hours work. Leak repairs are itemised. End-of-trip facilities are lump sums. Refurbishment is lifecycle; capacity upgrades for occupancy can be code compliance; leaks are failures.

Leaks often cost more in damage to the floor below than in the repair itself, so early repair is economical. Refurbishments are usually carried out floor by floor while other floors' amenities remain available.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a walk through the amenities cannot: how many people each floor's fixtures serve, where leaks recur, and what the leases promise. Ask for them before any change to occupancy.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Leak and plumbing call-out history | Where leaks and blockages recur. |
| Occupancy figures by floor | How many people each floor's amenities now serve. |
| End-of-trip usage data | Whether end-of-trip facilities meet demand. |
| Legionella management records | Whether little-used outlets are flushed and tested. |
| Access audit | Whether accessible facilities meet requirements. |
| Refurbishment history | When each block was last refurbished. |
| Fixture schedules by floor | How many fixtures each floor has. |
| Cleaning specifications and complaint records | Whether cleaning matches use, and what users complain about. |
| Flood test results after previous repairs | Whether earlier repairs were proved by testing. |
| Lease clauses on amenities and end-of-trip provision | What the leases promise about amenities. |
| Plumbing maintenance contract and response times | How quickly faults are fixed. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Amenities are misread when every problem is treated as a plumbing fault, when queues are blamed on the users, and when recurring blockages are blamed on misuse.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| It is a plumbing problem | Amenities problems usually come down to water (leaks, traps, Legionella), numbers (ratios, end-of-trip demand) or management (cleaning, storage). Each needs a different fix. |
| Queues mean people are slow | Queues at peak usually mean fixtures below the code ratio for the occupancy now on the floor. Count them against the current occupancy, not the original design. |
| Blockages mean misuse | Recurrent blockages in one block often point to a defect in the stack or branch rather than misuse. A CCTV survey settles it. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets the number of sanitary fixtures by occupancy and the design of accessible facilities, and workplace law adds its own duties. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Fixture numbers, access and wet areas | The National Construction Code sets sanitary facility numbers by building class and occupancy, and accessible facilities under AS 1428.1; wet areas follow the code's waterproofing provisions. | BS 6465 sets the scale of sanitary provision; Approved Documents G and M apply; the Workplace Regulations 1992 require suitable facilities. | The International Plumbing Code sets minimum fixture counts by occupancy; the 2010 ADA Standards set accessible facilities. |

Lease terms in all three countries often promise amenities to a standard or ratio, so shortfalls can be a leasing issue as well as a code one.

In all three countries, workplace health and safety law also requires employers to provide adequate, clean and accessible facilities for workers, independent of building code fixture counts, and health authorities may have additional requirements for shower hygiene and Legionella in public buildings.

sections.heading: Worked example: a densified office floor
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 1990s office floor was refitted at a higher density, and its amenities now have queues at lunch. The ceiling below the toilet block is stained, the end-of-trip showers sit unused on weekends, the accessible toilet stores cleaning trolleys, and one urinal smells despite cleaning.

The findings fall into the three groups that need different fixes. Water: the stain needs a flood test and dye tests to find its source, and the smell points to scale or a failed cartridge. Numbers: the queues point to fixtures below the ratio for the new occupancy. Management: the idle showers are a Legionella risk, and the accessible toilet is unavailable.

So the register carries the showers and the accessible toilet as safety lines now, the leak as a failure line, a fixture count against the current occupancy as a deadline line, and added fixtures in the next refurbishment of the block.

thresholds.rule: No more than 45 °C in aged care, healthcare, early childhood centres and schools; 50 °C in most other buildings

source.title: NCC 2025 Volume Three (Plumbing Code), Part B2 Heated water services

thresholds.rule: Stored at 60 °C or more; 50 °C at outlets within one minute (55 °C in healthcare)

source.title: HSG274 Legionnaires’ disease: Technical guidance, Part 2: Hot and cold water systems

thresholds.rule: Flushed at least every 7 days, or as the risk assessment sets

source.title: HSG274 Legionnaires’ disease: Technical guidance, Part 2: Hot and cold water systems

pages.title: Pumping Systems
pages.question: How do booster, sump and sewage pumping systems fail, and when do they threaten the building?
pages.answer: Pumping systems fail at their controls and power. Floats tangle and foul, pumps ragging with wipes trip out, and most sump and sewage pumps have no backup power, so they stop in the same storm that floods the basement, often reaching switchboards, lifts and fire pumps. Booster sets fail when pressure vessels lose their charge. A sump without a monitored alarm or backup power is a flood waiting to happen.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about pumping systems; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Domestic cold/hot water booster pumps, sump pumps

pages.searchTitle: Sump, sewage and booster pumps: basement flooding, alarms, backup power

questions.question: What happens if the basement sump pump fails in a storm?
questions.answer: Without a monitored alarm and backup power, the basement floods, and the water often reaches the main switchboard, lifts and fire pumps.

questions.question: Why do the booster pumps start every few seconds?
questions.answer: A failed pressure vessel or diaphragm. Replace or recharge the vessel.

questions.question: Why does the sewage pump keep tripping?
questions.answer: Usually ragging from wipes and rags. Vortex or cutter pumps, screens and signage help.

questions.question: Should duty and standby pumps alternate?
questions.answer: Yes, so both share run hours and a failed standby is found before it is needed.

questions.question: How long do sump pumps last?
questions.answer: Submersible stormwater pumps 10 to 15 years and sewage pumps 8 to 15; booster pumps 15 to 20.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Pumping problems show in basements as water marks and silt, at pits and pumps as odour, wear and alarm panels, upstairs as low pressure, and in maintenance and flood records. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On site | Water marks and silt lines on basement walls; corrosion at the base of switchboards and equipment | Sumps, controls and backup power |
| On site | Pit lids: condition, odour, ventilation | Sewage pits and gases |
| On site | Pumps: duty and standby both present; run hours; noise | Sumps, controls and backup power |
| On site | Alarm panels: high-level alarm, monitoring connection | Sumps, controls and backup power |
| On site | Booster set: number of pumps running, pressure gauges, vessel condition | Booster sets and pressure vessels |
| On site | Low pressure complaints on upper floors | Booster sets and pressure vessels |
| In the records | Pump maintenance and pit cleaning records | Investigation before the scope |
| In the records | Flood incident history | Sumps, controls and backup power |
| In the records | Alarm monitoring arrangements | Sumps, controls and backup power |
| In the records | Backup power arrangements | Sumps, controls and backup power |
| In the records | Pump and pit design capacities | Sumps, controls and backup power |
| In the records | Silt, leaves and litter on car park ramps and grates feeding the sump, and the condition of silt traps | Sumps, controls and backup power |
| In the records | Odour around sewage pits and corrosion of fittings near them, signs of hydrogen sulphide | Sewage pits and gases |

sections.heading: Types of pumping system
sections.markdown:
Hydraulic pumping systems move water where gravity and mains pressure cannot: domestic water booster sets that raise pressure to upper floors, stormwater sump pumps that keep basements and car parks dry, sewage ejectors that lift waste from below the sewer, lift pit pumps, and the pits, controls, alarms and rising mains that go with them. Fire pumps have their own page.

| Type | Where it is found | Consequence of failure |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Domestic water booster set (multiple pumps, variable speed, pressure vessels) | Apartment and office towers | Low or no water pressure on upper floors |
| Stormwater sump pumps | Basements, car parks, below-ground loading docks, lift pits | Basement flooding, often reaching switchrooms and plant |
| Sewage ejectors and pump stations | Basement toilets, kitchens and plant below the sewer | Sewage overflow; health hazard; odour |
| Groundwater dewatering pumps | Basements below the water table | Uplift and flooding; structural risk |
| Lift pit pumps | Lift pits | Water damage to lift equipment |

Many sump and sewage pumps have no backup power, so they stop in the same storm that knocks out the mains supply and floods the basement. In basement car parks and plant rooms, a failed sump pump can put the main switchboard, lifts and fire pumps under water.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Booster pumps last fifteen to twenty years, while pressure vessels, variable speed drives and submersible stormwater pumps last ten to fifteen and sewage pumps eight to fifteen. A pump's age matters less than whether anyone will know when it stops.

| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Booster pumps | 15 to 20 years | Run hours; water quality |
| Variable speed drives | 10 to 15 years | Heat; surges |
| Pressure vessels | 10 to 15 years | Diaphragm life; charge pressure |
| Submersible stormwater pumps | 10 to 15 years | Silt and debris; run hours |
| Sewage pumps | 8 to 15 years | Rags and wipes; H2S corrosion |
| Float switches and level controls | 5 to 10 years | Fouling; tangling |
| Concrete pits | 30 to 50 years | H2S attack in sewage pits |
| Control panels and alarms | 15 to 20 years | Damp; vendor support |

What shortens life: silt, debris and rags drawn into pumps; hydrogen sulphide in sewage pits corroding concrete, steel and electrical equipment; short cycling from failed pressure vessels or poor level settings; no maintenance because pumps are out of sight.

sections.heading: Sumps, controls and backup power
sections.markdown:
Float switches tangle, stick or foul with grease and debris; level sensors drift. The pump either does not start, letting the pit overflow, or runs dry and burns out. A high-level alarm is the last line of defence, and it is often not monitored.

Sump and sewage pumps without generator or battery backup fail in power outages, which often coincide with storms. Basements then flood exactly when the drainage is most needed.

Sewage pumps block with wet wipes, rags and fats; stormwater pumps block with silt, leaves and litter washed down ramps. Pumps trip on overload and the pit fills.

Pits and pumps sized for the original catchment are overwhelmed when ramps, courtyards or new connections are added, or when rainfall intensities increase.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Basement flooded after a storm with a power outage | Sump pumps without backup power. Power arrangement; incident timeline. | Provide backup power for critical sumps, with a monitored high-level alarm. |
| Basement flooded in rain with power on | Blocked pumps, failed floats or undersized pit. Pump inspection; capacity check. | Clear the pumps, replace floats with level sensors, and check the pit's capacity. |
| Sewage pump tripping repeatedly | Ragging from wipes and rags. Pump inspection. | Fit vortex or cutter pumps, with screens or signage about wipes. |

sections.heading: Booster sets and pressure vessels
sections.markdown:
Pressure vessels lose their charge and diaphragms fail, so pumps start and stop constantly; drives fail; one pump fails and the others cannot meet peak demand; controls lose their settings. Upper floors get low pressure or none.

Check valves on rising mains stick open, letting water run back into the pit, so pumps cycle continuously; or stick closed, so pumps run against a closed valve.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Booster pumps starting every few seconds | Failed pressure vessel or diaphragm. Vessel charge pressure. | Replace or recharge the pressure vessel. |
| Upper floors low pressure at peak times | Booster capacity or a failed pump. Pressure logging and pump status, against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Repair the failed pump, or upgrade the booster set. |
| Pumps cycling with no inflow | Check valve letting water run back. Valve inspection. | Replace the check valve. |

sections.heading: Sewage pits and gases
sections.markdown:
Sewage in pits produces hydrogen sulphide, which corrodes concrete and metal and is lethal in confined spaces. Pits need ventilation, and entering them is confined space work.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rotten-egg smell at a sewage pit or in a plant room | Hydrogen sulfide from septic sewage. Gas monitoring before entry, against the exposure limits for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Ventilate the pit, seal the covers, shorten retention time, and treat entry as a confined space. |
| Pit lids corroded, unsealed or not rated for the traffic over them | Odour escape and a fall or collapse risk. Lid condition, seals and load rating. | Replace with sealed lids of the right load class. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sump serving switchrooms or lift pits with failed pumps or alarms; sewage pit with no ventilation or failed lid | safety · 4 Essential | Restore now; temporary pumping. |
| Pumps failed; flooding or no water to upper floors | failure · 3 Important | Repair now. |
| Worn pumps, failed pressure vessels, fouled floats | condition · 3 Important | Repair in the near term. |
| Pumps at end of life | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Replace on cycle. |
| No backup power or alarm monitoring; capacity unknown | check · 2 Planned | Assess. |
| Normal | nil · 1 Routine | Routine maintenance. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A hydraulic engineer or pump contractor; confined space procedures for pit entry. The checks below start with the alarm monitoring and backup power, then inspect pits, pumps and booster sets, and test a drawdown where capacity is in doubt.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Inventory | Of every pumping system, pit, pump, control and alarm. |
| Function test | Start and stop levels, duty and standby changeover, high-level alarm and its monitoring. |
| Pump condition | Insulation resistance of motors, impeller wear, run hours. |
| Pit inspection | Silt, grease, concrete condition, H2S levels, ventilation. |
| Booster testing | Pressures at top floors at peak demand, vessel charge, drive faults. |
| Capacity review | Catchment, rainfall intensity and pump capacity. |
| Power review | Backup supply for critical pumps. |
| Drawdown test | Measure how quickly each pump empties the pit against its rated capacity, which shows wear and blockage that a simple start test misses. |

The report should list each system with its condition, flood risk, alarm and power arrangements, and works needed.

sections.heading: Monitoring, backing up or replacing
sections.markdown:
Sumps that protect switchrooms, lift pits and fire pumps come first: a monitored high-level alarm and backup power. After that, the work keeps pumps sharing their run hours, pits clean, vessels charged, and capacity matched to the catchment.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Controls | Replace floats with reliable level sensors; set alarms to a monitored system. | Wherever floats foul or alarms sound only locally. |
| Backup power | Generator connection or battery backup for critical sumps. | For sumps protecting switchrooms, lifts and fire pumps. |
| Pump replacement | Vortex or cutter pumps for sewage. | Where pumps fail or rag up. |
| Pit cleaning | Clean pits on a schedule, with silt traps on ramps. | Wherever silt and debris reach the pit. |
| Pressure vessel replacement | Replace or recharge the vessel. | Where booster pumps cycle rapidly. |
| Check valve replacement | A new check valve. | Where pumps cycle with no inflow. |
| Pit refurbishment | H2S-resistant linings, ventilation, lockable lids. | Where sewage pits corrode or smell. |
| Capacity upgrade | Larger pumps, additional pumps, bigger pits. | Where pits or pumps cannot keep up with the catchment. |
| Flood protection | Protect switchrooms below ground. | Wherever a switchroom sits near a sump. |
| Duty and standby alternation | Alternate the pumps. | So both share run hours and a failed standby is found before it is needed. |
| Education and screening | Signage about wipes and fats, and macerators or screens where ragging recurs. | For sewage systems. |
| Variable speed booster sets | Variable speed sets with correctly sized pressure vessels. | In place of fixed-speed pumps, to cut energy and pressure fluctuation. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Maintenance and pit cleaning recur. Pump replacement is per pump. Controls and alarms per system. Backup power per system or as part of a generator project. Pit refurbishment and capacity upgrades are lump sums. Booster set replacement is a lump sum with temporary supply.

Replacement is lifecycle; repairs and cleaning are repairs and maintenance; flood protection works and alarms may be risk-driven or code compliance.

Temporary pumping during replacement is a separate line where the pit cannot be left unattended.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a look at the pumps cannot: whether anyone would know if a pump stopped, whether it has power when the mains fails, and whether the basement has flooded before. Ask for the alarm and flood history first.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Pump maintenance and pit cleaning records | Whether pumps are serviced and pits cleaned. |
| Flood incident history | Whether the basement has flooded, and why. |
| Alarm monitoring arrangements | Whether anyone is told when a pump fails. |
| Backup power arrangements | Whether pumps have power when the mains fails. |
| Pump and pit design data | Whether pits and pumps are sized for the catchment. |
| Upper floor pressure complaints | Whether upper floors get enough pressure. |
| Insurance claims for basement flooding | What flooding has cost. |
| Drawdown or capacity test results | Whether pumps can keep up with inflow. |
| Hydraulic drawings showing pits, catchments and rising mains | Where pits and rising mains are, and what drains to them. |
| Pressure vessel charge records and booster set service reports | Whether booster sets and vessels are serviced. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Pumping systems are misread when a sump that has never flooded is assumed to be safe, and when a standby pump is assumed to be ready.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| It has never flooded | A basement sump with no monitored high-level alarm and no backup power is a flood waiting for the right storm. The consequence often reaches the main switchboard, lifts and fire pumps. |
| The standby pump will cover it | A standby pump that never runs may fail unnoticed. Alternate duty and standby so both share run hours, and a failed standby is found before it is needed. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets standards for boosters, sanitary and stormwater pumps, and rules for entering pits and confined spaces. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Pumps and confined spaces | AS/NZS 3500.1 covers water boosters, AS/NZS 3500.2 sanitary pumps and AS/NZS 3500.3 stormwater pumps; confined space entry follows AS/NZS 2865 and the work health and safety regulations. | Approved Document H covers drainage; BS EN 12056-4 covers wastewater lifting plants; the Confined Spaces Regulations 1997 govern pit entry. | The International and Uniform Plumbing Codes cover sumps, ejectors and booster pumps; OSHA 29 CFR 1910.146 governs permit-required confined spaces. |

In all three jurisdictions, sewage pumping into the public sewer may also be subject to the utility's connection conditions, and flooding of basements from failed pumps is commonly excluded from or limited under insurance where maintenance cannot be shown. Strata and leasehold buildings usually treat sump and booster systems as common property, maintained by the owners corporation or landlord.

sections.heading: Worked example: a sump beside the switchroom
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. An office's basement sump drains the car park ramp and sits beside the main switchroom. Its high-level alarm sounds only locally, it has no backup power, its floats are fouled with silt, and the standby pump has not run in years.

A sump with no monitored alarm and no backup power is a flood waiting for the right storm, and here the consequence reaches the main switchboard. Fouled floats and an untested standby pump make it more likely.

So the register carries the sump as a safety line now, with a monitored alarm and backup power, level sensors in place of floats, pit cleaning with silt traps on the ramp, and duty and standby alternation.

thresholds.rule: Working pressure at least 50 kPa at outlets; static pressure no more than 500 kPa within the building

source.title: NCC 2025 Volume Three (Plumbing Code), Part B1 Cold water services

thresholds.rule: Ceiling of 20 ppm; a single peak of 50 ppm for no more than 10 minutes

source.title: 29 CFR 1910.1000 Air contaminants (Table Z-1)
source.publisher: US Occupational Safety and Health Administration

pages.title: Rainwater Systems
pages.question: How do gutters, box gutters and downpipes fail, and how do you tell a maintenance problem from a capacity problem?
pages.answer: Rainwater goods are small in cost and large in consequence. Box gutters and internal outlets that overflow spill inside the building, so the overflow is as important as the gutter. Leaks only in heavy storms are capacity problems that cleaning will not fix; leaks in any rain are perforation or joints. Gutters rust along the sole where debris and water stand; the cleaning regime sets their life. Roofs extended or re-roofed often carry goods sized for a smaller catchment.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about rainwater systems; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Gutters, downpipes, scuppers, overflow systems, rainwater heads

pages.searchTitle: Gutters, box gutters and downpipes: storm leaks, overflows and when to resize

questions.question: Why does the box gutter leak only in heavy storms?
questions.answer: Leaks only in the heaviest storms are a capacity problem, not a maintenance one. Clearing the gutters will not stop them; the outlets and overflows must be resized.

questions.question: Does every box gutter need an overflow?
questions.answer: It should have one, discharging visibly outside the building and sized to carry the full flow if the outlet blocks. On an older building it is often the single most valuable change.

questions.question: Why is water coming through the ceiling away from the gutter?
questions.answer: Internal stacks carry water through the building, and water can run along purlins or the top of a wall before it drips. Trace the path from the roof down before cutting into ceilings.

questions.question: How often should gutters be cleaned?
questions.answer: On a cycle matched to the trees: quarterly or more where trees overhang, and always before the wet season.

questions.question: How long do gutters last?
questions.answer: Zinc-aluminium coated steel eaves gutters 20 to 30 years, coated steel box gutters 15 to 30, stainless steel box gutters 40 years and more, and lead-lined gutters 50 to 80.

questions.question: Why is there a dirty streak down the wall under the gutter?
questions.answer: The gutter is blocked or corroded and overflowing at that point. Clear the gutter, and repair or replace it where perforated.

questions.question: Why is the ground washing away at the bottom of the downpipe?
questions.answer: The downpipe is disconnected from the drain, or the drain is blocked. Reconnect the downpipe and clear the drain, directing discharge away from footings.

questions.question: Why did the roof start leaking after it was re-roofed or new plant was added?
questions.answer: The catchment changed or the outlet level was raised. Recheck the drainage against the changed catchment, and lower or add outlets.

questions.question: Why is the gutter pulling away from the building?
questions.answer: The weight of debris, snow or ice, or corroded brackets. Clear the gutter, and replace corroded brackets at the right spacing.

questions.question: Why is the gutter rusting along the bottom?
questions.answer: Water is standing in it from poor fall or blockage. Correct the falls and clear debris; replace the run where the sole is perforated.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Rainwater problems show inside along gutter lines and below outlets, from the street as staining and debris, and on the roof as corrosion, ponding and missing overflows. When a leak appears relative to the rain matters most. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Inside | Water along the line of a box gutter in heavy rain only, dry in light rain: capacity or overflow, not a hole | Capacity, overflows and changed catchments |
| Inside | Water along the same line in any rain, however light: a perforated gutter or a failed joint | Corrosion, joints and movement |
| Inside | Ceilings stained below sumps and outlets; drips in risers and service cupboards where internal stacks run, sometimes far from any gutter | Corrosion, joints and movement |
| Inside | Damp at the base of external walls, and mould inside behind them, where downpipes discharge against the building or into a blocked drain | Blockage, ponding and ice |
| Inside | Gurgling or rumbling stacks in storms, then a sudden surge or overflow: a siphonic or full-bore system struggling | Capacity, overflows and changed catchments |
| Inside | Water appearing at the head of walls on the top floor in storms: a parapet gutter or outlet overflowing inward | Capacity, overflows and changed catchments |
| Street or aerial | Vegetation, moss and debris in gutters and box gutters; ponding at sumps; trees overhanging the roof | Blockage, ponding and ice |
| Street or aerial | Staining on walls below gutter lines and at downpipe joints; tide marks on fascias where gutters overflow | Blockage, ponding and ice |
| Street or aerial | Downpipes disconnected, crushed, missing or discharging onto walls, paths or lower roofs; missing lead hoppers | Blockage, ponding and ice |
| Street or aerial | Overflows absent from box gutters and parapet roofs, or overflows that discharge where no one would see them | Capacity, overflows and changed catchments |
| Street or aerial | Gutters sagging between brackets or pulling away from the fascia | Blockage, ponding and ice |
| On the roof | Corrosion along gutter soles, at laps, rivets and sumps; perforations; patches of sealant over past leaks | Corrosion, joints and movement |
| On the roof | Falls in box gutters: water standing after rain, especially away from the outlet | Corrosion, joints and movement |
| On the roof | Outlet size against the gutter and catchment; overflow presence, size and level relative to the outlet | Capacity, overflows and changed catchments |
| On the roof | Leaf guards clogged; outlet grates missing; siphonic outlet baffles damaged | Blockage, ponding and ice |
| On the roof | Buckling and open joints at the ends of long gutter runs; missing expansion joints | Corrosion, joints and movement |
| In the records | Gutter cleaning contract and log, with frequency matched to the trees | Blockage, ponding and ice |
| In the records | Leak register, noting which leaks occur only in heavy storms | Capacity, overflows and changed catchments |
| In the records | Drawings or a hydraulic report showing design rainfall, catchments, outlets and overflows | Capacity, overflows and changed catchments |
| In the records | Records of roof extensions, re-roofing, insulation upgrades and plant decks added since construction | Capacity, overflows and changed catchments |

sections.heading: Types of rainwater system
sections.markdown:
Rainwater systems collect water from the roof and carry it to the [stormwater drainage](https://moyneross.com/technical/stormwater-drainage): eaves gutters, box gutters, valley gutters, sumps, rainwater heads, scuppers, overflows, downpipes and internal stacks, siphonic systems, and the connections at ground level. On large metal roofs, box gutters run the length of the building between bays or behind parapets, inside the building envelope; on apartment and office buildings with flat roofs, outlets feed internal downpipes in risers.

Every system is designed for a rainfall intensity and a catchment. Its weak point is what happens when it is overwhelmed. An eaves gutter that overflows spills outside the building. A box gutter or internal outlet that overflows spills inside it, unless it has an overflow sized to take the full flow. Buildings extended, re-roofed or fitted with larger plant decks often have rainwater systems sized for the original roof, and rainfall intensities used in design have increased in many regions.

Each system is sized for a rainfall intensity and a catchment. Systems whose failure stays outside the building are designed for more frequent storms; those whose failure comes inside, box gutters, internal outlets and siphonic systems, are designed for rarer ones and should always have an overflow sized to carry the flow if the outlet blocks. Each market sets its own design storms (Thresholds by market). Published design intensities have been revised upward in many places since older buildings were designed, so a system that met its original design may be undersized today.

| Form | Where it is found | Main risk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Eaves gutters and external downpipes | Houses, low-rise, older buildings | Corrosion, blockage, overflow at the wall |
| Box gutters | Industrial and commercial metal roofs; parapeted roofs | Overflow and leaks inside the building |
| Valley gutters | Pitched roofs | Debris and overflow under the covering |
| Internal outlets and stacks | Flat roofs, apartments, offices | Leaks in risers and ceilings; blockage |
| Siphonic systems | Large commercial roofs from the 1990s | Blockage changes the hydraulics; design-dependent |
| Cast iron and lead rainwater goods | Heritage buildings | Cracking, joint failure, theft of lead |
| Asbestos cement downpipes and gutters | Mid-century buildings | Hazardous material on replacement |

Overflows take several forms: rainwater heads with an overflow lip, sump overflows that discharge through the wall, weirs cut into the side of a box gutter, scuppers through parapets, and secondary outlets set slightly higher than the primary ones. What matters is that the overflow discharges where it can be seen, outside the building, and is big enough. Where a roof is enclosed by parapets, the rainwater system and the parapet are one problem ([Plant Screens & Parapets](https://moyneross.com/technical/plant-screens-and-parapets)); where it is pitched, the gutters work with the covering ([Roof Coverings](https://moyneross.com/technical/roof-coverings)).

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Rainwater goods range from uPVC eaves gutters, lasting twenty-five to forty years, to copper and lead, lasting fifty years and more, with coated steel box gutters at the short end. Material matters, but so does how the system is kept clear.

| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Zinc-aluminium coated steel eaves gutters | 20 to 30 years | Cleaning regime; leaf litter; coastal exposure; ponding at joints |
| Galvanised or coated steel box gutters | 15 to 30 years | Falls; water standing; foot traffic; debris at sumps |
| Stainless steel box gutters | 40 years and more | Weld quality at joints and sumps; chlorides; contact with mild steel swarf |
| Lead-lined box and parapet gutters | 50 to 80 years | Bay length and fixing; underside condensation; theft |
| Cast iron gutters and downpipes | 100 years and more with painting | Paint cycle; joint failure; frost; impact |
| Aluminium gutters | 30 to 50 years | Contact with copper or steel; coastal exposure |
| Copper gutters | 50 to 100 years | Thickness; joints; theft |
| uPVC eaves gutters and downpipes | 25 to 40 years | UV embrittlement; joint seals; impact |
| Internal stacks and outlets | 30 to 50 years | Joint type; outlet clamping rings; movement in tall buildings |
| Siphonic outlets and pipework | 30 to 50 years for pipework; outlets need regular maintenance | Blockage; air baffles damaged; changes to the roof |
| Asbestos cement gutters and downpipes | Past their life on most buildings | Brittleness; impact; licensed removal when replaced |

Life varies along a single run. Sumps, stop ends, the low points where water stands, the lengths under trees and the gutter beneath a valley or a copper roof fail first, while the rest of the gutter often has years left when the first perforation appears. That is why gutters are usually replaced in sections, and why a gutter that is sound at the ends may be perforated in the middle where debris collects.

What shortens life: no cleaning regime, especially with trees over the roof: the single largest determinant of gutter life; flat or back falls in box gutters, keeping them wet; dissimilar metals and copper or lead run-off; foot traffic in box gutters used as walkways to plant; undersized outlets and missing overflows, which turn every blockage into an internal flood; ground-level damage to downpipes from vehicles and trolleys.

What lengthens it: a cleaning regime matched to the trees: quarterly or more where trees overhang, with outlet grates and leaf guards cleared, not just the gutter; correct falls in box gutters so they drain dry between storms; walkways beside box gutters, so people do not walk in them to reach plant; isolating dissimilar metals and protecting gutter soles beneath copper and lead; protecting downpipes at ground level where vehicles and trolleys pass.

sections.heading: Capacity, overflows and changed catchments
sections.markdown:
Gutters, outlets and downpipes sized for a smaller catchment or a lower rainfall intensity overflow in heavy storms, and the overflow goes wherever the water finds the lowest point. For eaves gutters that is outside, down the face of the wall. For box gutters, valley gutters and outlets within parapets it is inside, along the line of the gutter and into ceilings, walls and services. Box gutters without overflows, or with overflows smaller than the outlet they protect, are the commonest cause of storm leaks in commercial and apartment buildings. Many older systems were sized to rainfall intensities that have since been revised upward, so a system that met its design when built can be short of capacity today.

Roofs change after they are designed. Extensions, plant decks, screens, new parapets and roof-mounted solar add catchment, redirect flow or block overflows, while the outlets stay as they were. Re-roofing and insulation upgrades raise the roof surface against an outlet or a weir, so that water must pond before it drains. Many storm leaks in older buildings trace to an alteration rather than to age ([Solar Photovoltaic Systems](https://moyneross.com/technical/solar-photovoltaic-systems)).

Siphonic systems run pipes full of water under suction, so they can drain a large roof through few, small pipes laid nearly level. They work only when every outlet is clear and its air baffle is intact: a blocked or damaged outlet admits air, the siphon breaks, and the remaining outlets cannot carry the flow. They depend on maintenance and on overflows more than any other system, and their design must be checked whenever the roof or the published rainfall data changes.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Leaks inside along the box gutter line, only in heavy storms | Overflow: undersized outlet or no overflow. Overflow absent or small; outlet capacity below the catchment's design flow. | Add or enlarge overflows, and resize the outlets against current rainfall data. |
| Leaks after re-roofing or adding plant, where there were none before | Catchment changed or outlet level raised. Alteration dates match; outlets now above the roof or gutter surface. | Recheck the drainage against the changed catchment, and lower or add outlets. |
| Overflow discharging regularly in moderate rain | Outlet partly blocked or undersized. Debris in the outlet; capacity check against the catchment. | Clear the outlet; if it is clear, it is undersized and needs resizing. |
| Storm leaks on a siphonic roof with clean gutters | Siphon breaking at one outlet; design intensity exceeded. Outlet condition and design calculations against current rainfall data. | Restore the outlets and re-verify the design as a whole against current rainfall data. |

sections.heading: Blockage, ponding and ice
sections.markdown:
Leaves, flowering and seeding trees, sediment from tiles and membranes, bird nests, tennis balls and wind-blown litter collect at outlets and sumps. Blockage is seasonal: it peaks with leaf fall and after storms that strip trees, often exactly when heavy rain follows. Leaf guards help only if they are themselves maintained; guards clogged with fines can stop water reaching the outlet entirely. A blocked outlet holds water in the gutter, which overflows, ponds against laps and joints, and corrodes the sole.

Water held on a roof by blocked outlets adds weight: a few centimetres over a large roof is many tonnes. On light steel and timber roofs the structure deflects, the low point deepens, and more water collects. This ponding instability can end in collapse, and it is why codes in all three jurisdictions now require roofs enclosed by parapets to have secondary drainage and to be designed for the water that would build up if the primary drains were blocked.

In cold climates, ice blocks outlets and gutters while meltwater backs up under the roof covering at the eaves (ice damming). The weight of snow and ice tears eaves gutters from their brackets, and freezing water splits cast iron and stresses joints. Trace heating, snow guards and heated outlets are the usual responses where this is routine.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Staining down a wall from an eaves gutter | Blocked or corroded gutter overflowing at that point. Debris or perforation above the stain. | Clear the gutter, and repair or replace it where perforated. |
| Damp and washouts at the base of a wall | Downpipe disconnected from the drain. Pipe ends above ground; drain blocked. | Reconnect the downpipe and clear the drain, directing discharge away from footings. |
| Gutter pulling away from the fascia, brackets bent | Weight of debris, snow or ice; corroded brackets. Bracket spacing and condition; water held in the gutter. | Clear the gutter, and replace corroded brackets at the right spacing. |
| Ponding on a lower roof below a downpipe | Downpipe discharging onto the roof without a spreader. Erosion and staining at the discharge point. | Fit a spreader, or carry the downpipe to a gutter. |

sections.heading: Corrosion, joints and movement
sections.markdown:
Steel gutters corrode from the inside, along the sole where water and debris stand, at laps and rivets, and at sumps and stop ends. Gutters beneath copper roofs or lead flashings corrode faster where the run-off lands. Box gutters perforate first at sumps, joints and the low points of sagging soles, and because they sit over the building every perforation leaks inside. Cast iron corrodes from the joints outward once paint has gone, and lead-lined gutters corrode from the underside where condensation forms in an unventilated void.

Internal stacks run through ceilings, risers and occupied space, and their joints are out of sight until they leak: solvent-welded PVC joints crack, rubber ring joints displace, cast iron collars corrode, and expansion joints in tall stacks fail where movement was not allowed for. Outlet clamping rings loosen from the membrane they hold, letting water track around the outlet into the roof build-up. At ground level, downpipes disconnect from the drain or the drain beneath them blocks, and water discharges against footings and walls.

Long runs of metal gutter expand and contract with every change in temperature. Without expansion joints, or with joints that have failed, the gutter buckles, rivets and laps work loose and sealant cracks, and the same positions leak year after year. Box gutters fixed rigidly to the structure at both ends are particularly prone.

Cast iron gutters and downpipes crack from frost and impact and leak at their joints once the paint has gone. Lead rainwater heads, hoppers and gutters are stolen for their scrap value, often leaving water discharging straight onto the wall, which then saturates.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Leaks inside along the box gutter line in any rain | Perforated gutter or failed joint. Corrosion or open joint at the leak position. | Repair the joint or replace the perforated run. |
| Leaks at an internal stack in a riser | Joint failure or outlet clamp loose. Water test at the outlet; joint inspection. | Water test the outlet, then remake the joint or tighten the clamp. |
| Rust along the gutter sole, sound elsewhere | Water standing from poor fall or blockage. Water present after rain; debris. | Correct the falls and clear debris; replace the run where the sole is perforated. |
| Water standing at one end of a box gutter after rain | Back fall or sagging sole. Level check along the gutter; water collects away from the outlet. | Re-lay the sole to the correct fall, or replace the gutter. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator, ordinance or order sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ponding on a light roof with visible deflection; blocked outlets with water building against a parapet | safety · 4 Essential | Clear and relieve now; stop access. |
| Gutters, brackets or cast iron loose over entrances and paths | safety · 4 Essential | Secure or remove now. |
| Perforated box gutters or failed internal joints leaking into the building | failure · 3 Important | Repair now; replace the failed runs. |
| Siphonic system failing in storms, with water inside | failure · 3 Important | Restore outlets now; check the design. |
| Internal stack or gutter leaking near switchboards, risers or electrical equipment | safety · 4 Essential | Isolate and repair now. |
| Box gutters or parapet roofs without adequate overflows | condition · 3 Important | Add or enlarge overflows in the near term. |
| Gutter soles corroding where water stands; poor falls | condition · 3 Important | Programme repair or replacement of the affected runs. |
| Gutters and downpipes at the end of their life, no current leaks | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Replace with the roof covering where possible. |
| Lead goods stolen; water discharging against the wall | condition · 3 Important | Replace the goods (often in a non-lead material) in the near term. |
| Storm-only leaks of unknown cause; roof altered since design | check · 3 Important | Capacity check against current rainfall data before sizing works. |
| Siphonic system with no maintenance records | check · 3 Important | Inspect outlets and verify the design before relying on it. |
| Asbestos cement gutters or downpipes of unknown status | check · 3 Important | Identify before any work. |
| Debris in gutters, minor staining | nil · 1 Routine | Cleaning regime. |

A box gutter without an adequate overflow is graded on what will happen at the next blockage, not on whether it has leaked yet. One blocked outlet in a storm puts water inside the building, which is why missing overflows are a condition finding even on a roof with no leak history.

The grading follows what a finding demands, not the size of the eventual bill.

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A roof plumber inspects condition; a hydraulic engineer checks capacity where the roof has changed or storm leaks occur. The checks below test capacity as well as condition, because storm-only leaks are rarely fixed by repairs.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Visual inspection | Of every gutter, sump, outlet and downpipe, with falls checked after rain or by level, and falls and bracket spacing against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). |
| Capacity check | Of box gutters, outlets and overflows against the catchment and current design rainfall intensity. |
| Water testing | Of internal outlets and stacks. |
| CCTV | Of internal stacks and the connections to stormwater. |
| Hazardous material check | On asbestos cement goods before removal. |
| Drone survey | Of gutters and outlets on large or fragile roofs, rather than walking them. |
| Overflow testing | Confirm each overflow discharges outside and is clear, and sized for the flow the asset’s market requires (Thresholds by market). |
| Design check | Against current published rainfall intensities (the Bureau of Meteorology's design rainfalls in Australia, NOAA Atlas 14 in the United States) where the system is old or the roof has changed. |
| Box gutter measurement | Falls, sole width and depth against the catchment. |
| Rainfall data | Current published design intensity for the location, which may exceed what the system was designed for. |
| Riser inspection | Of internal stacks through access panels. |

The report should list runs needing replacement, any capacity shortfall and the fix, and the cleaning cadence the roof needs.

sections.heading: Cleaning, repairing or upgrading
sections.markdown:
The work depends on the kind of leak. Leaks in any rain are holes and joints, repaired or replaced; leaks only in heavy storms are capacity, fixed with overflows and larger outlets rather than cleaning; and every system needs a cleaning regime matched to its trees.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cleaning regime | Gutters, sumps, outlets and leaf guards cleared on a cycle matched to the trees, quarterly or more where trees overhang, and always before the wet season. | Always; the cheapest protection a roof has, and the first thing to restore. |
| Repairs | Reseal joints, replace short sections, rivet and seal laps, refix brackets, fit expansion joints. | Where the run is otherwise sound; repeated repairs at the same positions signal replacement. |
| Overflows | Add or enlarge overflows so every box gutter and parapet outlet has one, discharging visibly outside the building and sized to carry the full flow if the outlet blocks. | Wherever box gutters or parapet roofs lack them; often the single most valuable change on an older building. |
| Capacity upgrades | Additional outlets and downpipes, larger sumps and rainwater heads, and wider or deeper box gutters, designed against current published rainfall intensities. | Where leaks occur only in heavy storms, or the catchment has changed. |
| Box gutter replacement | New gutters with correct falls, sumps and stop ends, in stainless steel or a heavier coated steel, with walkways alongside so the gutter is not used as a path. | Where box gutters are perforated, sag or hold water. |
| Replacement of eaves gutters and downpipes | New goods in materials suited to the exposure, with spreaders where downpipes discharge onto lower roofs. | Usually with the roof covering. |
| Siphonic system remediation | Outlets and baffles repaired, the system re-verified against the roof and current rainfall data, and a maintenance contract put in place. | Where storms cause leaks on a siphonic roof; redesigned as a whole, not outlet by outlet. |
| Ground connections | Reconnect downpipes, clear or repair drains, and direct discharge away from footings. | Wherever downpipes discharge against walls or onto the ground. |
| Snow and ice measures | Trace heating, heated outlets and snow guards. | In cold regions. |
| Asbestos cement goods | Licensed removal and replacement. | Wherever gutters or downpipes are asbestos cement. |

Interactions: gutters and box gutters are best replaced with the roof covering, when access is already in place; capacity upgrades may need parapets altered for overflows, new downpipes through the building, and changes at ground level to the [stormwater drainage](https://moyneross.com/technical/stormwater-drainage). Roof alterations, plant decks and solar arrays should come with a drainage check, since they change the catchment the system was designed for.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Replacement is rate-based on linear metre and profile, with sumps, rainwater heads and overflows itemised. Capacity upgrades are lump-sum design-and-construct items. Cleaning is a recurring maintenance contract. Gutters are often replaced with the roof covering and may sit inside that register line.

What drives the cost: access to gutters at height and over occupied areas, the number of sumps, rainwater heads and overflows, internal stacks that run through finished spaces and risers, alterations to parapets and walls for new overflows, and connections at ground level. Commonly missed: the overflow provision, outlet changes when the roof level changes, and repairs to finishes damaged by past leaks.

Replacement is lifecycle; capacity upgrades are lifecycle or code compliance where overflows are missing; cleaning and minor repairs are repairs and maintenance.

Where trees overhang a roof, cleaning may need to be quarterly; it is still the cheapest protection the roof has.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a dry-day inspection cannot: when leaks happen relative to the rain, what the system was designed for, and whether the roof has changed since it was designed. Ask for them before sizing any works.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Gutter cleaning contract and log, with frequency and the date of the last clean | Whether the gutters are cleaned often enough for the trees, and when they were last done. |
| Leak register, noting which leaks occur only in heavy storms and where | Whether leaks follow storms, which points to capacity, or any rain, which points to holes. |
| Roof drainage drawings or a hydraulic design report, including the design rainfall intensity the system was sized for | What rainfall the system was designed for, and where the overflows are meant to be. |
| Records of roof extensions, re-roofing, insulation upgrades, plant decks and solar arrays added since construction, and any drainage check that accompanied them | Whether the catchment has changed since the system was designed. |
| Roof plumber, leak investigation and CCTV reports on internal stacks and ground connections | The condition of internal stacks and ground connections. |
| Siphonic system commissioning report and maintenance records | Whether a siphonic system was commissioned and is maintained. |
| Tree management records for trees near the roof | How much debris the gutters must cope with. |
| Insurance claims for water damage, and any exclusions applied to the roof or drainage | What leaks have cost, and whether insurers have limited cover. |
| For strata and leasehold buildings, the maintenance responsibilities for gutters and stacks that pass through private lots | Who maintains gutters and stacks that pass through private lots. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Rainwater leaks are misread when every leak is treated as a maintenance problem, or when water inside is assumed to come from the roof directly above it.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| Cleaning the gutters will stop the storm leaks | Leaks that occur only in the heaviest storms are capacity problems, not maintenance problems. Clearing the gutters will not stop them; outlets and overflows must be resized. |
| Water appears under its source | Water inside does not always appear beneath its source. Internal stacks carry water through the building, so a joint failing in a riser can stain a ceiling floors below the roof, and water entering at a sump can run along purlins or the top of a wall before it drips. Trace the path from the roof down before cutting into ceilings. |
| Water at a gutter line means the roof leaks | The common misreading is a roof covering leak for a gutter problem. Water arriving along the line of a gutter, a sump or the head of a wall almost always comes from the rainwater system; re-sheeting the roof will not stop it. |

Timing is the most useful evidence. Note when each leak appears relative to the rain: only in intense downpours points to capacity or overflow; in any rain points to a hole or a failed joint; days after the rain points to water held somewhere, in insulation, a sagging gutter or a blocked sump. A leak log that records the weather alongside each leak will often solve the problem without opening anything up.

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sizes roof drainage to a design storm, but sets that storm and the overflow rules differently. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out design, overflows and loads, and what applies when the roof changes.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Design | Roof drainage follows AS/NZS 3500.3, called up by the National Construction Code, using the Bureau of Meteorology's design rainfalls (revised in 2016); Standards Australia's handbook HB 114 guides the design of eaves and box gutters. | Approved Document H (part H3) covers rainwater drainage, and BS EN 12056-3 sets the layout and calculation of roof drainage, with design rainfall chosen according to the risk the building can tolerate. | The International Plumbing Code (Chapter 11) sizes roof drains and leaders on the 100-year, one-hour rainfall rate; NOAA Atlas 14 is the usual source of rainfall data. |
| Overflows and loads | Eaves gutters are typically designed for a 5 per cent annual exceedance probability storm, and box gutters, internal gutters and their overflows for a 1 per cent storm. | BS 8490 guides siphonic roof drainage. | Secondary (emergency) drains or scuppers are required where parapets or other construction would trap water; the International Building Code (Section 1611) and ASCE 7 set rain loads assuming the primary drains are blocked, including ponding; ASPE 45 covers siphonic roof drainage. |
| Changes and constraints | A change of roof area, plant deck or outlet arrangement means the system should be rechecked. | Sustainable drainage requirements can apply where discharge arrangements change, and listed buildings carry constraints on replacing cast iron and lead goods. | Added roof area, plant or new drains are work under the local plumbing and building codes, and the drainage is sized again for the area it serves. |

Gutters and downpipes on common property are owners corporation items in Australian strata schemes and service-charge items on British leasehold blocks.

sections.heading: Worked example: storm leaks along a warehouse box gutter
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 1980s warehouse has a central box gutter draining to two internal outlets. Water comes through the ceiling along the gutter line in heavy summer storms, but not in ordinary rain; the gutters were cleaned a month ago, and a plant deck was added on the roof last year.

Leaks only in the heaviest storms, with clean gutters, are a capacity problem, and cleaning will not stop them. The plant deck changed the catchment the system was designed for, and with no overflows, water that the outlets cannot take has nowhere to go but inside.

So the register carries a capacity check against current rainfall data as a check line, overflows as a condition line, and larger or additional outlets once the check is in. Water reaching switchboards or electrics would come first, as a safety line.

thresholds.rule: Eaves gutters: 5 per cent annual chance (1 in 20); box gutters: 1 per cent annual chance (1 in 100)

source.title: AS/NZS 3500.3:2025 Plumbing and drainage, Part 3: Stormwater drainage

thresholds.rule: Fall at least 1:500 unless designed to AS/NZS 3500.3; brackets at no more than 1.2 m centres

source.title: NCC 2025 Housing Provisions, Part 7.4 Gutters and downpipes

thresholds.measure: Eaves gutter overflow on houses, at 150 mm/h
thresholds.rule: 0.17 L/s per metre of gutter for a 4 m ridge-to-gutter length; 0.25 L/s for 6 m; 0.33 L/s for 8 m

source.title: NCC 2025 Housing Provisions, Part 7.4 Gutters and downpipes

pages.title: Recreational Facilities
pages.question: How do playgrounds, courts and shared recreation facilities fail, and which findings are safety issues?
pages.answer: Recreation facilities fail first on safety. Most playground injuries are falls, so surfacing displaced, compacted or worn under equipment is the key finding; entrapment gaps, protrusions and broken parts are next. Courts crack through to trip lines as their bases move; gym cables fray; barbecues leak gas and build up grease. Close unsafe equipment until fixed; renew surfaces and equipment on predictable cycles.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about recreational facilities; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Swimming pools, tennis courts, playgrounds

sources.title: Public Playground Safety Handbook
