pages.searchTitle: Recreational facilities: playground safety, surfacing, courts and gyms

questions.question: How deep should playground surfacing be?
questions.answer: Deep enough for the fall height of the equipment above it. Loose fill must be topped up and raked to that depth across the full fall zone; bare ground under swings and slides means it has been displaced.

questions.question: How often should a playground be inspected?
questions.answer: BS EN 1176 sets routine, operational and annual inspections, and the Australian standards are commonly followed the same way. Insurers commonly require evidence of regular inspection.

questions.question: Why do tennis court cracks keep coming back?
questions.answer: Cracks that repeat through new surfaces usually come from base movement or shrinkage. Map them; if they are structural, the base needs rebuilding, not another resurfacing.

questions.question: When should playground equipment be closed?
questions.answer: When it stands over inadequate surfacing, has entrapment gaps or broken parts, or wobbles. It stays closed until fixed.

questions.question: How long does playground equipment last?
questions.answer: Typically 10 to 20 years; rubber surfacing 7 to 15, with loose fill topped up every year.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Recreation facilities show their problems under the equipment and on the surfaces people use: bare ground beneath swings, cracks in courts, frayed cables, gates left open. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On site | Loose fill displaced or thin under equipment; worn or hard rubber surfacing | Playgrounds: surfacing, entrapment and wear |
| On site | Broken, worn or missing parts; exposed bolts; rust at bases; splintered timber | Playgrounds: surfacing, entrapment and wear |
| On site | Court cracks, puddles, moss and damaged nets and fences | Courts and gyms |
| On site | Gym equipment with frayed cables or out of service | Courts and gyms |
| On site | Barbecues with grease build-up and damaged hoses | Lighting, barbecues and shade |
| On site | Missing signage on age groups and use | Playgrounds: surfacing, entrapment and wear |
| In the records | Playground inspection records | Investigation before the scope |
| In the records | Equipment manufacturer and installation certificates | Playgrounds: surfacing, entrapment and wear |
| In the records | Court resurfacing history | Courts and gyms |
| In the records | Gym service contracts | Courts and gyms |
| In the records | Incident records | Playgrounds: surfacing, entrapment and wear |
| On site | Play area gates that do not self-close or latch | Playgrounds: surfacing, entrapment and wear |
| On site | Hot metal and plastic surfaces in direct sun | Lighting, barbecues and shade |
| On site | Play equipment designed for older children installed where toddlers play, with no signage on age groups | Playgrounds: surfacing, entrapment and wear |

sections.heading: Types of facility
sections.markdown:
Recreational facilities are the shared amenities on a site: playgrounds, tennis and multi-sport courts, gyms, barbecue areas, outdoor fitness equipment, and swimming pools and spas (whose water systems are covered on the specialist hydraulics page). In apartment buildings and retirement villages they are common property and a significant part of the sinking fund; in schools, hotels and public sites they carry public safety obligations.

| Facility | Where it is found | Main hazards |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Playgrounds | Apartments, schools, childcare, parks, shopping centres | Falls onto inadequate surfacing; entrapment; equipment failure |
| Tennis and multi-sport courts | Apartments, schools, clubs | Surface cracking and trips; fencing; lighting |
| Gyms | Apartments, offices, hotels | Equipment failure; flooring; ventilation |
| Barbecue and outdoor kitchen areas | Apartments, parks | Gas safety; burns; hygiene |
| Outdoor fitness equipment | Parks, apartments | Wear; surfacing |
| Pools and spas | Apartments, hotels, schools | See specialist hydraulics |

Each facility type has its own safety standard and inspection expectations, and many sites are inspected only when something breaks. In shared residential buildings, the duty of care for these facilities sits with the owners corporation, landlord or operator, and the condition of play equipment and courts is often the first thing residents and buyers notice.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Recreation equipment wears quickly against the building around it. Play equipment lasts ten to twenty years and rubber surfacing seven to fifteen, while loose fill needs topping up every year, and the surfacing most often decides whether a playground is safe.

| Element | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Playground equipment | 10 to 20 years | Use; materials; weather |
| Impact-absorbing surfacing | Loose fill topped up yearly; rubber 7 to 15 years | Wear; displacement |
| Tennis court surfaces | 7 to 15 years; resurfacing more often | Surface type; cracking |
| Court fencing and nets | 15 to 25 years; nets 2 to 5 | Corrosion; damage |
| Gym equipment | 7 to 12 years | Use; maintenance |
| Barbecues | 8 to 15 years | Use; cleaning |

What shortens it: heavy use and vandalism; weather and coastal exposure; lack of inspection and maintenance; ground movement under courts.

Facilities used by the public or by many residents wear far faster than identical equipment in a private garden, and coastal and hot climates shorten the life of plastics, rubber and coatings.

sections.heading: Playgrounds: surfacing, entrapment and wear
sections.markdown:
Most playground injuries are falls. Loose fill (bark, sand) displaces away from under equipment and compacts; rubber surfacing wears and hardens. Surfacing that is too thin or hard for the fall height turns falls into serious head injuries.

Gaps of certain sizes between parts trap heads, fingers and clothing; protruding bolts and broken parts snag and cut. Standards set the dimensions that avoid them.

Bearings, chains, swing hangers and moving parts wear; timber rots; steel corrodes at the base; fixings loosen. Failures happen under load.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bare ground under swings and slides | Loose fill displaced. Depth measurement. | Close the equipment until the loose fill is topped up to the depth its fall height needs. |
| Rubber surfacing hard to the touch | Aged surfacing. Impact attenuation test. | Test the impact attenuation; replace surfacing that fails. |
| Equipment wobbling | Loose fixings or rotted posts. Inspection. | Close it; tighten the fixings or replace rotted posts. |

sections.heading: Courts and gyms
sections.markdown:
Asphalt and concrete court bases crack from shrinkage and ground movement; cracks reflect through acrylic surfaces and create trip lines; drainage problems leave puddles and moss.

Cables, pulleys and weight stacks wear; treadmills fail; poor ventilation and hygiene affect users; heavy equipment on upper floors may exceed floor loads.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cracks repeating through court surfaces | Base movement or shrinkage. Crack mapping. | Map the cracks; treat and resurface, or rebuild the base if the cracking is structural. |
| Frayed gym cables | Wear. Inspection. | Take the machine out of use and replace the cable. |

sections.heading: Lighting, barbecues and shade
sections.markdown:
Poorly lit courts and play areas used in the evening cause falls and security problems; gates on play areas that do not self-close let small children reach roads, pools and car parks.

Gas leaks, faulty ignition and grease build-up cause fires and burns; poor cleaning creates hygiene issues.

Shade sails and canopies over play areas fail at fixings and masts in high winds, and unshaded equipment in hot climates gets hot enough to burn.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Barbecue gas bottles or hoses damaged, or no gas isolation | Gas leak or fire risk. Inspection and leak test of the gas installation. | Repair to the gas installation standard, and fit an isolation valve. |
| Shade sail sagging or fixings corroded | Wind failure risk. Fixings and masts; wind rating; storm removal practice. | Replace the fixings and set a storm procedure. |
| Dark paths and play areas at night | Failed or inadequate lighting. Night inspection; lux readings. | Repair or add lighting. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Inadequate surfacing; entrapment hazards; broken equipment; gas leaks | safety · 4 Essential | Close and fix now. |
| Facility out of use | failure · 4 Essential | Repair. |
| Periodic inspections due | deadline · 4 Essential | At the prescribed interval. |
| Worn equipment; court cracking | condition · 4 Essential | Repair in the near term. |
| Equipment and surfaces at end of life | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Replace. |
| No inspection records | check · 2 Planned | Inspect. |
| Normal | nil · 1 Routine | Routine. |

Closing a facility is often the right immediate response: a play unit taped off for a week while surfacing is topped up is far better than a serious fall onto compacted ground.

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A qualified playground inspector leads on play equipment; court and sports surface contractors, gym equipment servicers and licensed gas fitters cover their areas. The checks below start with the playgrounds, where the safety risk is, then the courts, gyms and amenities.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Playground inspection | Against the current standard: free height of fall, surfacing type, depth and impact attenuation (tested in place where rubber surfacing is old), entrapment and finger traps, protrusions and sharp edges, structural integrity of posts and fixings, and wear of moving parts. |
| Court inspection | Cracking pattern and its cause, surface wear and slip resistance, drainage, fencing, nets and posts, and lighting levels. |
| Gym inspection | Equipment condition and service history, flooring, ventilation and floor loading for heavy equipment. |
| Barbecue and outdoor kitchen inspection | Gas connections and appliances, electrical safety, grease and hygiene. |
| Shade structure check | Fixings, masts and fabric. |
| Records review | Inspection frequency, incidents and complaints. |

The report should list immediate safety actions, items to close, and a renewal programme by facility.

sections.heading: Repairing, replacing or closing
sections.markdown:
Safety comes first: equipment over inadequate surfacing, or with entrapment gaps or broken parts, is closed until fixed. After that, the question is whether equipment is worn and can be repaired, or no longer meets the standard by design and needs replacing.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Surfacing | Top up and rake loose fill to the depth needed for the fall height; replace hardened or torn rubber surfacing; extend surfacing to the full fall zone. | Wherever fill is thin or displaced, rubber has hardened, or surfacing stops short of the fall zone. |
| Equipment | Replace broken and worn parts, tighten and cap fixings, remove items that cannot be made compliant, and replace whole play units at the end of their life. | Where parts are broken or worn, or equipment cannot be made compliant. |
| Courts | Treat cracks, resurface, rebuild bases where cracking is structural, and repair fencing, nets and lighting. | Where courts crack, hold water or lose their fencing, nets or lighting. |
| Gyms | Service and replace equipment, and check floors for heavy items. | On a service contract, and wherever equipment is worn or out of service. |
| Barbecues | Clean, service and replace units; check gas compliance. | Where units are greasy, hoses damaged, or gas compliance is due. |
| Gates and shade | Self-closing gates, shade structures engineered for wind. | Where play area gates do not self-close or latch, or shade is missing or not engineered. |
| Inspection regime | Routine visual checks, operational inspections and an annual comprehensive inspection, recorded. | Always; insurers commonly require evidence of it. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Inspections recur at routine, operational and annual intervals. Loose fill top-ups recur yearly; rubber surfacing is replaced on its cycle. Play equipment replacement is a lump sum per play area including surfacing; court resurfacing is per court, with base reconstruction a larger lump sum. Gym equipment is replaced per item on a rolling cycle. In strata buildings these are common property sinking fund items.

Safety items are immediate; replacement is lifecycle; maintenance is repairs and maintenance.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a look at the equipment cannot: whether it has been inspected as required, whether the surfacing still absorbs a fall, and where injuries have happened. Insurers commonly ask for the same evidence.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Playground inspection reports at each required frequency | Whether the playground has been inspected as often as required, and what was found. |
| Equipment manufacturer certificates and installation records | Whether the equipment was certified and installed to the standard. |
| Surfacing impact test results | Whether the surfacing still absorbs a fall from the equipment's height. |
| Court resurfacing and repair history | When the courts were last resurfaced, and whether cracking keeps returning. |
| Gym equipment service contracts and records | Whether the gym equipment is serviced, and by whom. |
| Barbecue gas compliance certificates | Whether the gas barbecues are certified as safe. |
| Incident and complaint records | Whether injuries repeat at one item, which points to its design or surfacing. |
| Insurance requirements for recreation facilities | What inspections the insurer expects. |
| Shade structure engineering certificates | Whether the shade structures are engineered for wind. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Recreation facilities are misread when worn equipment and equipment that no longer meets the standard are treated as the same problem, or when every incident is put down to bad luck.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| The equipment is fine, so the playground is safe | Playground equipment over inadequate surfacing, or with entrapment gaps or broken parts, should be closed until fixed. Most serious playground injuries come from falls and entrapment. |
| Worn equipment just needs repair | Separating wear from design is important: equipment that is worn needs repair; equipment whose design no longer meets the standard (for example, fall heights above what the surfacing can absorb) needs replacement or redesign. |
| Incidents are bad luck | Incident records are a useful guide: repeated injuries at one item point to its design or surfacing, while scattered minor incidents usually reflect normal use. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market has its own standards for playground equipment and the surfacing beneath it, and its own inspection practice. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out the equipment and surfacing standards, inspection, and gas and access rules.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Equipment | AS 4685 sets requirements for playground equipment. | BS EN 1176 covers playground equipment. | ASTM F1487 covers public playground equipment. |
| Surfacing | AS 4422 sets requirements for impact-attenuating surfacing. | BS EN 1177 covers impact-attenuating surfacing. | ASTM F1292 covers surfacing impact attenuation. |
| Inspection and guidance | Councils, schools and owners corporations commonly follow the standards' inspection regimes. | BS EN 1176 sets routine, operational and annual inspections; the Royal Society for the Prevention of Accidents and others carry out annual inspections; occupiers' liability law applies. | The Consumer Product Safety Commission's Public Playground Safety Handbook is widely used. |
| Gas and access | Barbecues on gas follow AS/NZS 5601.1. | The Equality Act 2010 requires service providers, including those running play areas, to make reasonable adjustments for disabled people. | The 2010 ADA Standards set the accessibility of play areas. |

Insurers in all three countries commonly require evidence of regular inspection of play and recreation facilities.

sections.heading: Worked example: an apartment playground with no inspection records
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. An apartment complex has a playground with a climbing frame and swings over bark mulch, a tennis court, and a gas barbecue area. The mulch under the swings is worn to bare ground, the court has cracks that return after each resurfacing, and there are no inspection records.

The swings come first: bare ground under them is inadequate surfacing, a safety finding, so they are closed until the fill is topped up to the depth their fall height needs. Court cracks that keep returning suggest base movement rather than surface wear, so mapping them comes before another resurfacing. The missing records are a check finding, and insurers commonly ask for them.

So the register carries the surfacing as a safety line now, an inspection regime as a check line, and a court investigation that may become a base rebuild, with the barbecue's gas compliance certificate to ask for.

pages.title: Residential Units/Guest Rooms
pages.question: How do apartments and guest rooms fail as places to live, and who is responsible in strata buildings?
pages.answer: Units fail on safety, health and neighbours. Missing or non-interconnected smoke alarms and entry doors that do not close are safety findings; weak exhaust and indoor drying cause condensation and mould; bathroom and laundry leaks damage the unit below; hard floors laid over carpet cause noise complaints. Units also slide below rental minimums or brand standards. In strata, establish whether each defect is common property or the owner's before deciding who pays.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about residential units/guest rooms; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Kitchens, bathrooms, living areas, bedrooms — all finishes and fixtures

pages.searchTitle: Apartments and guest rooms: leaks between units, mould, noise, smoke alarms and who pays

questions.question: Who pays for a leak between apartments?
questions.answer: It depends on the source: common property falls to the owners corporation, the owner's fixtures to the owner. Establish the cause before repair.

questions.question: Why is there mould in the apartment every winter?
questions.answer: Usually condensation from weak or unused exhaust, cold surfaces and clothes dried indoors, rather than a leak.

questions.question: Do apartment smoke alarms need to be interconnected?
questions.answer: Increasingly, yes. Queensland, for example, requires interconnected photoelectric alarms in all dwellings by 1 January 2027.

questions.question: Why can I hear my upstairs neighbour walking?
questions.answer: Often a hard floor laid without acoustic underlay. Strata by-laws commonly require tested underlays.

questions.question: How often are hotel rooms refurbished?
questions.answer: Soft goods every 5 to 7 years, and case goods and bathrooms every 10 to 15, set by brand standards.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Unit problems show in a sample of units as mould, stains, worn finishes, alarms and doors that fall short, and in leak, noise, mould and compliance records. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| In a sample of units | Mould on ceilings, reveals and wardrobe backs; exhaust fans weak or switched off | Leaks, windows and mould |
| In a sample of units | Water staining on ceilings from the unit above | Leaks, windows and mould |
| In a sample of units | Hard floors in upper units, with noise complaints below | Noise between units |
| In a sample of units | Smoke alarm type, date and interconnection | Smoke alarms and fire separation |
| In a sample of units | Entry door closers and seals | Smoke alarms and fire separation |
| In a sample of units | Leaks and draughts at windows and balcony doors | Leaks, windows and mould |
| In a sample of units | Worn kitchens, bathrooms and carpets | Minimum and brand standards |
| In the records | Leak and defect history by unit | Leaks, windows and mould |
| In the records | Noise complaints and by-law breaches | Noise between units |
| In the records | Smoke alarm compliance records | Smoke alarms and fire separation |
| In the records | Mould complaints and remediation | Leaks, windows and mould |
| In the records | Brand audits and property improvement plans for hotels | Minimum and brand standards |
| In the records | Rental standard compliance records | Minimum and brand standards |

sections.heading: What the space does and what it contains
sections.markdown:
Residential units and guest rooms are where people live and sleep: apartments in strata, build-to-rent and student buildings, and rooms in hotels, serviced apartments and aged care. As a functional space, a unit must be safe to sleep in, healthy (dry, ventilated, warm or cool enough), quiet enough to live beside neighbours, and of a standard that suits the market or brand. For capital planning, the key question is who is responsible: in strata buildings most of the unit interior belongs to the owner, while structure, external walls, windows and shared services may be common property; in rented and hotel buildings, the operator carries everything.

| Element group | Typical provision | What matters for the space |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Kitchen | Cabinetry, benchtop, appliances, exhaust | Function, condition, ventilation |
| Bathroom and laundry | Fixtures, waterproofing, exhaust | Leaks to units below; mould |
| Living and bedrooms | Floor and wall finishes, joinery, doors | Wear, acoustics, condition |
| Windows and balcony doors | Framed glazing, seals | Leaks, draughts, condensation, security |
| Heating and cooling | Split systems, ducted systems, heaters | Comfort, ownership, refrigerant |
| Smoke alarms and fire separation | Interconnected alarms, fire-rated entry door and walls | Life safety |
| Hot water | Individual or central | Temperature control, Legionella |

Hotels refresh rooms on brand-driven cycles: soft furnishings every five to seven years and case goods and bathrooms every ten to fifteen, set out in brand standards and property improvement plans. Build-to-rent operators turn units over between tenancies. Strata owners refurbish their own units on their own timing, which leaves shared issues such as noise and wet area leaks between neighbours.

sections.heading: How long it stays fit for purpose
sections.markdown:
A unit's parts run on different clocks: paint five to ten years, carpet eight to twelve, appliances ten to fifteen, and kitchens and bathrooms fifteen to twenty-five. Hotels refresh soft goods every five to seven years, and rising rental and brand standards can end a unit's fitness for purpose without any single failure.

| Component or quality | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Kitchen cabinetry and benchtops | 15 to 25 years | Use; moisture; style |
| Appliances | 10 to 15 years | Use |
| Bathroom refurbishment | 15 to 25 years | Waterproofing; wear |
| Carpet | 8 to 12 years | Use; tenancy turnover |
| Hard floors | 20 to 30 years | Wear; acoustics |
| Paint | 5 to 10 years | Tenancy turnover |
| Hotel soft goods | 5 to 7 years | Brand standards |
| Hotel case goods and bathrooms | 10 to 15 years | Brand standards |

What shortens fitness for purpose: moisture from cooking, showers and drying clothes indoors without adequate exhaust; tenancy turnover and guest use; owner alterations in strata buildings, especially hard floors and bathroom renovations; rising standards for rental minimums, energy and brand quality.

sections.heading: Smoke alarms and fire separation
sections.markdown:
Smoke alarms missing, disconnected, out of date or not interconnected leave sleepers unwarned. Entry doors that do not close or have been replaced, and penetrations through walls between units, let fire and smoke spread.

Smoke alarm laws change more often than buildings do. A unit that complied when it was built can fall short of current law, which may now require interconnected photoelectric alarms in every bedroom and hallway, so the check is against current law, not the original approval.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A unit entry door that does not close by itself, or a replacement door of a different design | A failed closer, or an owner-fitted door that is not fire-rated. The door stays open when released, and there is no evidence of its fire rating. | Repair the closer, or replace the door with a self-closing, sealed, fire-rated door. |
| Smoke alarms that sound only in the room where they are tested | Alarms that are not interconnected. Testing one alarm does not set off the others. | Interconnect them, or replace them with interconnected photoelectric alarms where required. |

sections.heading: Leaks, windows and mould
sections.markdown:
Bathroom, laundry and kitchen leaks through failed membranes, shower screens, wastes and appliance connections are the most common source of damage between units. In strata, determining whether the cause is common property or the owner's fixture decides who pays.

Units with weak or unused bathroom and kitchen exhaust, clothes dried indoors, poor heating and cold window frames grow mould on ceilings, window reveals and wardrobes. It is a health issue, and in rented housing a legal one.

Window and sliding door seals, sills and tracks leak and let draughts in, damaging floors and finishes.

Mould in a unit is usually condensation, not a leak, and the difference decides who acts. Condensation grows on the coldest surfaces of the dampest rooms, worst in winter and where washing is dried indoors; a leak grows from a source and follows rain or the unit above. Humidity logging over a week tells them apart.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mould on ceilings in bathrooms and bedrooms | Condensation from inadequate exhaust and heating. Fan airflow; humidity logging; occupant habits. | Increase the exhaust and get it running, with humidity or run-on controls; address heating and indoor drying. |
| Stain below a bathroom after showers | Membrane or shower screen leak. Flood and dye tests. | Flood and dye test; re-waterproof, or replace the screen and seals. |
| Stain below a bathroom constantly | Pipe leak. Pressure test; inspection. | Pressure test, and repair the pipe. |
| Water at window sills in storms | Seal or sill failure. Water test. | Water test; replace the seals and repair the sill. |
| Mould behind wardrobes on outside walls | Cold surfaces and still air behind furniture. Thermal imaging shows the cold spot, and the mould stops where air moves. | Improve ventilation and heating, move furniture off the wall, and treat the mould. |

sections.heading: Noise between units
sections.markdown:
Impact noise from hard floors laid over carpet, plumbing noise, and airborne noise through party walls generate complaints. Hard floor replacements without acoustic underlay are a common cause, and strata by-laws often regulate them.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Impact noise complaints after a renovation | Hard floor without acoustic underlay. Floor construction; acoustic test. | Test the floor; require a tested acoustic underlay, or remediate where the complaint is upheld. |
| Plumbing noise heard in the unit next door | Pipes fixed to party walls without isolation. The noise follows flushing or taps next door. | Fit acoustic clips or lagging where the pipes can be reached. |

sections.heading: Minimum and brand standards
sections.markdown:
Rental minimum standards, housing quality regimes and hotel brand standards set requirements for heating, ventilation, security and condition. Units can fall below them without any single failure.

In aged care and student buildings, intensive use and occupants with particular needs accelerate wear and raise safety expectations further.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bathroom or kitchen with no working extract fan | Ventilation below what the market expects. Fan airflow measured against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Repair or fit a fan ducted outside. |
| Hot water too hot at the basin or bath | Temperature control failed or absent. Outlet temperature against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Fit or repair tempering and retest. |
| A unit short of the operator’s brand or the jurisdiction’s minimum standard | Specification below the standard the unit is let or sold against. Checklist of the brand standard or the local minimum standard, room by room. | Prioritise items that affect safety and habitability, then brand items at refurbishment. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Missing or failed smoke alarms; entry doors not self-closing in apartment buildings; severe mould | safety · 4 Essential | Rectify now. |
| Leaks damaging neighbours | failure · 3 Important | Repair now. |
| Rental minimum standards, smoke alarm laws or brand deadlines | deadline · 3 Important | By the required date. |
| Mould, noise complaints, worn finishes | condition · 2 Planned | Repair in the near term. |
| Kitchens, bathrooms and soft goods at end of cycle | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Refurbish on cycle. |
| No unit sample inspected | check · 2 Planned | Inspect. |
| Normal | nil · 1 Routine | Routine. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A building surveyor inspects a representative sample of units, with acoustic, mould, leak and fire specialists as needed; for hotels, the brand's quality auditor's findings are a key input. The checks below inspect a sample of units, weighted to those with complaints, then test leaks, ventilation, sound and alarms, and settle who owns each item.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Unit sample inspection | Kitchens, bathrooms, laundries, floors, windows and balcony doors, smoke alarms, entry doors and ventilation, in units of each type, floor and orientation, weighted to those with complaints. |
| Leak investigations | With flood tests of showers and floors, dye tests of fixtures, and pressure tests of pipework, to separate common property from owner causes. |
| Ventilation and moisture assessment | Measured exhaust airflows, humidity logging over a week, and thermal imaging of cold spots. |
| Acoustic testing | Of impact and airborne sound where complaints exist, against the code at the time and current standards. |
| Smoke alarm and entry door compliance check | Against current law, which may be stricter than when the building was built. |
| Ownership review | Strata plan, by-laws and lot boundaries, or lease and management agreements. |

The report should separate owner, common property and operator items, state safety and health findings, and give a refurbishment plan by unit type.

sections.heading: Making safe, repairing or refurbishing
sections.markdown:
Smoke alarms, entry doors and severe mould come first, since they affect people sleeping in the unit. After that, the work stops water and moisture, controls noise, and refurbishes on cycle, with each item allocated to the owner, the owners corporation or the operator.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Smoke alarms | Interconnected photoelectric alarms in every bedroom and hallway where required, hard-wired or with ten-year sealed batteries. | Wherever alarms are missing, expired or not interconnected. |
| Entry doors | Self-closing, sealed fire-rated doors where the building requires them, replacing owner-fitted doors that do not comply. | Wherever entry doors do not self-close or are not fire-rated. |
| Ventilation | Stronger ducted exhaust in bathrooms, laundries and kitchens, with humidity or run-on controls so it actually runs. | Where mould or condensation grows. |
| Wet area rectification | Re-waterproof bathrooms and laundries, replace shower screens and seals, repair wastes. | Where wet areas leak to neighbours. |
| Acoustic controls | By-laws requiring tested underlays for hard floors, and acoustic remediation where complaints are upheld. | Where hard floors or services carry noise between units. |
| Windows and doors | Replace seals and rollers, repair sills, and adjust or replace balcony doors. | Where windows and balcony doors leak or draught. |
| Refurbishment cycles | Kitchens, bathrooms, flooring and paint on planned cycles in rented and hotel stock, timed with vacancies. | In rented and hotel stock, timed with vacancies. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Unit works are priced per unit and grouped by type. In hotels, rooms are refurbished floor by floor to keep revenue flowing, with soft goods and case goods on separate cycles. In build-to-rent, works are timed with tenancy turnover. In strata, common property items fall to the owners corporation and lot items to owners, and leaks often lead to cost recovery between them.

Smoke alarms and doors are code compliance with deadlines; leaks are failures; refurbishment is lifecycle; mould remediation is condition or safety depending on extent.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a sample of units cannot: where leaks and complaints recur, whether alarms meet current law, and who owns each item. Ask for them before any repair is allocated.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Leak and defect records by unit, with causes and who paid | Where leaks recur, and who paid for them. |
| Noise complaints and by-law breaches | Whether noise is a pattern, and whether by-laws are enforced. |
| Smoke alarm compliance records | Whether alarms meet current law. |
| Mould complaints and remediation records | Whether mould recurs, and how it was dealt with. |
| Strata plan, by-laws and lot boundary definitions | Which items are the owner's and which are common property. |
| Brand audits and property improvement plans for hotels | What the hotel brand requires, and by when. |
| Refurbishment history by unit type | Where each unit type is in its cycle. |
| Rental minimum standard compliance records, for rented units | Whether rented units meet the minimum standards now in force. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Units are misread when a defect is repaired before anyone establishes who owns it, when mould is blamed on a leak, and when compliance at completion is taken as compliance today.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| Repair it first, sort out who pays later | In strata buildings, the cause of a defect decides who pays, so investigation must establish whether the source is common property or within the owner's lot before repair. |
| Mould means a leak | Mould in a unit is usually condensation from weak exhaust, indoor drying and cold surfaces, not a leak. Humidity logging over a week, and measured fan airflows, tell them apart. |
| It complied when it was built | Smoke alarm and rental standard laws change. Check alarms and entry doors against current law, which may be stricter than when the building was approved. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets smoke alarm and habitability requirements for homes, rules for rented housing, and the boundary between a unit and common property. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Safety, habitability and ownership | State laws set smoke alarm requirements (Queensland requires interconnected photoelectric alarms in all dwellings by 1 January 2027), rental minimum standards (for example Victoria's), and strata management; the National Construction Code sets fire separation, sound insulation and ventilation for apartments; strata legislation defines lot and common property boundaries. | The Housing Health and Safety Rating System assesses hazards in homes; the Homes (Fitness for Human Habitation) Act 2018 gives tenants rights; Awaab's Law sets timescales for social landlords to deal with damp and mould; smoke and carbon monoxide alarm regulations apply to rented homes; leasehold law sets landlord and leaseholder responsibilities. | The International Property Maintenance Code and local housing codes set habitability standards; HUD inspects assisted housing under its national standards; condominium law and declarations define unit and common element boundaries; hotel brands set property improvement plans. |

sections.heading: Worked example: mould and complaints in a build-to-rent block
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 2010s build-to-rent block has mould complaints from units on its south side every winter, a stain below one bathroom after showers, impact noise complaints below a unit whose carpet was replaced with timber, and battery smoke alarms in hallways only.

The south-side mould, worst in winter, points to condensation: weak or unused exhaust, cold surfaces and indoor drying. The stain after showers points to the membrane or screen, the noise to a hard floor without acoustic underlay, and hallway-only battery alarms may fall short of current law.

So the register carries the smoke alarms as a safety line, ventilation upgrades with humidity controls as a condition line, flood and dye tests on the leaking bathroom, and acoustic remediation of the hard floor.

thresholds.rule: 75 dB(A) at the bedhead

pages.title: Retail Tenancies (Base-Build)
pages.question: How do retail tenancies fail as lettable space, and which tenancy findings belong to the landlord?
pages.answer: Retail tenancies fail on fit more than condition. Food, fitness and service tenants need exhaust risers, grease waste, power and water that many shells lack, and retrofitting them is costly. Repeated fit-outs breach demising walls and alter sprinkler and detection coverage. Food tenancies leak, smell and block drains. Poor make-good hands shells back in bad order. Separate landlord provision, tenant obligations and market fit: each has a different fix and payer.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about retail tenancies (base-build); it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Base-building elements, services integration, structural finishes

pages.searchTitle: Retail tenancies: services for the tenant type, fire separation, make-good and vacancy

questions.question: Why can't a food tenant take this shop?
questions.answer: Usually there is no kitchen exhaust riser, grease waste connection or enough power, and retrofitting them is costly and sometimes impossible.

questions.question: Who fixes fire separation after a tenant leaves?
questions.answer: The outgoing tenant, through make-good, where the lease is clear; condition reports at entry and exit support the claim.

questions.question: Why do fire alarm faults follow new tenancies?
questions.answer: Fit-outs alter detection without proper reprogramming. Test and sign off each fit-out.

questions.question: Why is a shop in good condition still empty?
questions.answer: Often configuration, trade area or rent, rather than condition.

questions.question: How long does a retail fit-out last?
questions.answer: 5 to 10 years; shopfronts last 15 to 25, and base-building service provisions 25 to 40.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Retail problems show in vacant shells and the services they lack, in penetrations and altered fire services, in stains and odours, and in the tenancy schedule, fit-out records and leasing history. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On site | Vacant tenancies and the kinds of tenants that have left; types now trading nearby | Make-good and centre obsolescence |
| On site | Service provisions visible in shell tenancies: exhaust risers, grease waste points, power boards, condenser water connections | Service provision for the tenant type |
| On site | Penetrations through demising walls and ceilings; altered sprinkler heads and detectors | Fire separation after fit-outs |
| On site | Water staining on slabs and ceilings below food tenancies | Grease, odour and leaks |
| On site | Odour in malls or neighbouring premises | Grease, odour and leaks |
| On site | Redundant equipment and damage left in vacated tenancies | Make-good and centre obsolescence |
| In the records | Tenancy schedule with leases, expiries and make-good terms | Make-good and centre obsolescence |
| In the records | Fit-out guides and design criteria for tenants | Service provision for the tenant type |
| In the records | Fit-out approvals and fire services certification after each fit-out | Fire separation after fit-outs |
| In the records | Trade waste agreements for food tenants | Grease, odour and leaks |
| In the records | Complaints about odour and leaks | Grease, odour and leaks |
| In the records | Vacancy and leasing history | Make-good and centre obsolescence |

sections.heading: What the space does and what it contains
sections.markdown:
Retail tenancies are the shops, food outlets, gyms and service premises let to tenants in shopping centres, high streets, office podiums and mixed-use buildings. As a functional space, a retail tenancy is judged on whether the base building provides what the current and likely future tenants need: the right shell, frontage and depth, and service connections for power, water, drainage, grease waste, exhaust, gas and air conditioning. The landlord usually provides the shell and service stubs; the tenant fits out within it and must make good at lease end. Many problems arise where that boundary is unclear or where the base building was set up for a different kind of tenant.

| Provision | Typical base-building scope | What matters for the space |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Shell | Slab, walls, ceiling or soffit, demising walls | Condition, fire separation, flatness |
| Shopfront | Glazed frontage, doors, signage zone (landlord or tenant) | Weather, security, presentation |
| Power and data | Supply to a tenancy board, metered | Capacity for the tenant type |
| Water and drainage | Water and sewer stubs; grease waste for food | Location and capacity; grease treatment |
| Exhaust and ventilation | Kitchen exhaust riser for food; general exhaust | Whether food tenants can operate |
| Air conditioning | Base supply, condenser water, or space for tenant units | Capacity and connection points |
| Fire services | Sprinklers, detection and warning extended into the tenancy | Coverage after each fit-out |
| Gas | Metered supply for food tenants | Capacity; future electrification |

The retail mix has shifted toward food, health, gyms and services, which need more power, exhaust, grease waste, water and structural capacity than the fashion shops many centres were designed around. Tenancies without these provisions are harder to let.

sections.heading: How long it stays fit for purpose
sections.markdown:
A retail fit-out lasts five to ten years and a shopfront fifteen to twenty-five, while base-building service provisions last twenty-five to forty and centres are refurbished every ten to fifteen. Tenant mix and trade usually end a tenancy's fitness for purpose before its fabric does.

| Component or quality | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tenant fit-out | 5 to 10 years | Lease term; brand refits |
| Shopfronts | 15 to 25 years | Damage; centre refurbishment |
| Base-building service provisions | 25 to 40 years | Tenant mix changes |
| Demising walls and fire separation | Life of the building if maintained | Penetrations by fit-outs |
| Centre or precinct refurbishment | 10 to 15 years | Competing centres; retail trends |

What shortens fitness for purpose: changes in tenant mix, especially toward food and fitness, which need services the tenancy lacks; repeated fit-outs that penetrate demising walls and alter fire services; poor make-good that leaves services, ceilings and floors in poor order for the next tenant; water damage from tenant equipment and leaks.

sections.heading: Service provision for the tenant type
sections.markdown:
A tenancy without a kitchen exhaust riser, grease waste connection, adequate power or water cannot take a food tenant, and retrofitting these through floors above, roofs or common areas is costly and sometimes impossible. Gyms need structural capacity and acoustic separation; medical tenants need specialised services. The lack of provisions shows up as vacancy and lower rents.

A shell is worth what tenants can do in it. A tenancy without an exhaust riser, a grease waste connection or enough power can only take tenants who need none of them, and retrofitting those services through floors above or across common areas is costly where it is possible at all. The fit-out guide should say plainly what each tenancy provides.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Food tenants unable to take vacant shops | No exhaust riser, grease waste or capacity. Services survey against fit-out guide. | Survey services against the fit-out guide, and add exhaust risers, grease waste and power where the market needs them. |

sections.heading: Fire separation after fit-outs
sections.markdown:
Each fit-out penetrates demising walls and ceilings for services, relocates sprinkler heads and detectors, and changes layouts. Fire separation between tenancies and from common areas degrades unless every fit-out is checked; sprinkler and detection coverage may not follow the new layout.

Retail fire separation fails one fit-out at a time. Each new tenant cuts through demising walls for services, moves sprinkler heads and detectors, and builds new ceilings; unless each fit-out is checked and signed off, the separation between tenancies and from the mall degrades quietly.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fire alarm faults after each new tenancy | Fit-outs altering detection without proper reprogramming. Fire services records. | Reprogram and test after each fit-out, and enforce sign-off through fit-out approval. |
| Unsealed penetrations through a demising wall | Fit-out services run through the separation without fire stopping. Open holes or foam around services between tenancies. | Fire stop with tested systems, and check every fit-out before sign-off. |
| Sprinkler heads boxed in by a tenant's ceiling or signage | Coverage lost to a fit-out. Heads above a new ceiling, or blocked by bulkheads. | Relocate or add heads to cover the tenancy as it is fitted out. |
| Stock or signage close below sprinkler heads | Spray pattern obstructed. Clearance from the deflectors to the top of stock measured against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Lower the storage or relocate the signage, and brief the tenant. |

sections.heading: Grease, odour and leaks
sections.markdown:
Food tenancies without adequate grease treatment block drains; inadequate exhaust spreads odour into malls and neighbouring premises and causes complaints from residents in mixed-use buildings.

Food tenancies, salons and gyms use water heavily; leaking equipment, floor wastes and wet floors damage the slab, adjacent tenancies and floors below.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Odour complaints in a mall | Exhaust inadequate or discharging near intakes. Exhaust survey. | Upgrade the exhaust, and move its discharge away from intakes. |
| Blocked drains downstream of food court | Grease treatment inadequate. See trade waste page. | Upgrade the grease treatment; see [Trade Waste Systems](https://moyneross.com/technical/trade-waste-systems). |
| Stains on the slab below a salon, gym or food tenancy | Leaking equipment, floor wastes or wet floors. Stains below the tenancy's wet zones. | Repair the source, and require waterproofing and floor wastes in the fit-out guide. |
| Grease deposits in food court extract ducts | Cleaning not keeping up with use. Deposit depth against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market); cleaning records. | Clean the full duct run and set the frequency to the use. |
| A food court drain run that blocks repeatedly on a flat section | Gradient too shallow for the flow and grease load. Levels and invert survey against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Relay the run to fall, add access, and enforce arrestor maintenance. |

sections.heading: Make-good and centre obsolescence
sections.markdown:
Tenants leaving without proper make-good leave behind redundant equipment, damaged floors and ceilings, capped services and altered fire services; disputes are common where lease terms are vague.

Tenancies can be in good condition but in a centre or street that has lost trade. Configuration matters too: very deep, narrow tenancies, or poor frontage and visibility, are hard to let regardless of condition.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Shells handed back in poor order | Weak make-good clauses or enforcement. Lease review; condition reports. | Tighten the make-good clauses, record condition at entry and exit, and claim where needed. |
| Long vacancy in good condition shells | Configuration, trade area or rent. Leasing evidence. | Test configuration, trade area and rent; merge or split tenancies if demand supports it. |
| Disputes over outgoings between landlord and tenants | Shared or estimated metering. Tenancies that are not separately metered. | Separately meter power, water and gas to every tenancy. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fire separation breached between tenancies; sprinkler or detection coverage missing after fit-out | safety · 4 Essential | Rectify before trading continues. |
| Leaks damaging adjacent tenancies or structure | failure · 3 Important | Repair now. |
| Lease, health or trade waste obligations requiring works | deadline · 3 Important | By the required date. |
| Service provisions inadequate for current market; make-good shortfalls | condition · 2 Planned | Upgrade at vacancy or lease renewal. |
| Shopfronts and centre finishes at end of cycle | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Refurbish with centre strategy. |
| Services capacity per tenancy unknown | check · 2 Planned | Survey. |
| Normal | nil · 1 Routine | Routine. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A building surveyor or retail building consultant leads, with services and fire engineers and the centre's leasing team. The checks below survey the services each tenancy provides against the fit-out guide, check fire separation and coverage after each fit-out, and read the leasing history.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Tenancy services survey | Power, water, drainage, grease waste, exhaust, gas and air conditioning provision to each tenancy, against the fit-out guide and the tenant types sought. |
| Fire separation and services review | Of a sample of tenancies and every vacant one: demising wall penetrations, sprinkler and detection coverage, egress. |
| Make-good inspections | At each lease end against the lease, with photographs. |
| Leak and odour investigation | Where complaints exist. |
| Leasing review | Vacancy, tenant mix trends and why tenancies are hard to let. |
| Lease review | Base-building and tenant responsibilities, make-good and fit-out obligations. |

The report should separate landlord capital, tenant obligations and market repositioning, and identify tenancies needing services upgrades to be lettable.

sections.heading: Providing services, rectifying and repositioning
sections.markdown:
Fire separation and sprinkler or detection coverage lost to fit-outs come first. After that, the work separates what the landlord must supply, what the tenant must return and what the market wants, since each is paid for by a different party.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Services upgrades | Kitchen exhaust risers, grease waste connections, larger power supplies and condenser water, installed when tenancies are vacant and ideally for groups of tenancies at once. | Where tenancies cannot take the tenants the market wants. |
| Fire rectification after fit-outs | Fire separation and services rectification after each fit-out, enforced through fit-out approval and sign-off. | After every fit-out. |
| Fit-out guide | Fit-out guide updated so tenants know what is provided and what they must do. | Wherever the guide is out of date. |
| Make-good enforcement | Clear lease clauses, condition reports at entry and exit, and claims where needed. | At every lease expiry. |
| Reconfiguration | Merging or splitting tenancies to suit demand. | Where demand favours larger or smaller tenancies. |
| Shopfront and centre refurbishment | Shopfront and centre refurbishment as part of a repositioning strategy. | Where the centre is losing trade. |
| Separate metering | Separate metering of power, water and gas to every tenancy so outgoings are recovered accurately. | Wherever tenancies share or estimate meters. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Services upgrades are lump sums per tenancy or per group, often justified by higher rents from food and service tenants. Fire separation rectification is itemised. Reconfiguration is a lump sum with demolition and new demising. Make-good shortfalls are recoverable from outgoing tenants where leases allow. Centre refurbishment is a large lump-sum repositioning project.

Fire safety items are code compliance; services upgrades and reconfiguration are repositioning capital; shopfronts are lifecycle; tenant damage is recoverable.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a walk through the centre cannot: what each tenancy provides, what tenants have changed and must return, and why shops stand empty. Ask for them before deciding who pays for each finding.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Tenancy schedule with leases, expiries and make-good terms | Which leases end when, and what each tenant must return. |
| Fit-out guide and tenant design criteria | What the landlord provides, and what tenants must do themselves. |
| Services provision schedule per tenancy | What services each tenancy has. |
| Fit-out approvals and fire services certificates after each fit-out | Whether each fit-out was approved and its fire services certified. |
| Trade waste agreements and odour complaints | Whether food tenants' waste and odour are controlled. |
| Vacancy history and leasing agent feedback | Why shops stand empty, and what tenants want. |
| Make-good condition reports | What condition tenancies were handed back in. |
| Planning conditions on uses, hours and extraction | What planning conditions allow each tenancy to do. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Retail is misread when landlord, tenant and market problems are handled together, when an empty shop is assumed to be in poor condition, and when an approved fit-out is assumed to have left the fire separation intact.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| It is all the landlord's problem | Separate base-building provision (what the landlord must supply), tenant condition (what the tenant must return) and market fit (what tenants want). Each is fixed by a different party and budget. |
| An empty shop needs work | Long vacancy in a sound shell points to configuration, trade area or rent rather than condition. Leasing evidence, not a condition survey, settles it. |
| The fit-out was approved, so it is compliant | Each fit-out penetrates demising walls and moves sprinklers and detectors. Unless every fit-out is checked at sign-off, fire separation and coverage degrade one tenant at a time. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets rules for fire separation between tenancies, for food premises and trade waste, and for the leases that allocate obligations. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Separation, food premises and leases | State retail leases legislation (for example in New South Wales and Victoria) governs disclosure, outgoings and some fit-out and make-good matters; fit-outs need approval under the National Construction Code; food premises must meet the Food Standards Code premises requirements; trade waste agreements apply to food tenants. | Fit-outs need building regulations approval; food premises must meet food hygiene regulations and local authority requirements for extraction and odour; dilapidations practice governs lease-end obligations; planning use classes affect which tenants can trade. | Tenant improvements need permits under the International Building Code (mercantile occupancy); food establishments follow state health codes based on the FDA Food Code; the 2010 ADA Standards apply to public accommodations. |

Mixed-use buildings add residential neighbours, so odour, noise and hours conditions in planning approvals often constrain food and entertainment tenants in all three countries.

sections.heading: Worked example: a vacant shell in a neighbourhood centre
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A neighbourhood centre has a shop vacant for a year after a clothing tenant left. Food operators have looked at it, but there is no exhaust riser or grease waste connection. The previous tenant left a bulkhead ceiling that boxes in two sprinkler heads, and the demising wall has unsealed holes where cables ran.

Separate the three questions. The boxed-in heads and unsealed holes are fire findings the tenant should have rectified at make-good. The missing exhaust and grease waste are base-building provision, which decides who can lease the shop. Whether a food tenant is the right market is a leasing question.

So the register carries the sprinkler coverage and the demising wall as safety lines, a make-good claim against the outgoing tenant, and a services upgrade for food use if leasing evidence supports it, with the fit-out guide updated.

pages.title: Roof Coverings
pages.question: How do roof coverings fail, what does each failure look like, and when does a covering need repair rather than replacement?
pages.answer: Roof coverings fail at their edges, laps, fixings and junctions, not in the field. Coated steel rusts from laps and the bottom metre above the gutter; underside rust with a sound top means condensation. Tile roofs fail at ridge bedding, valleys and fixings; scattered slipped slates mean the nails have rusted through. Asbestos cement weathers to exposed fibre and is fragile at any age. Most leaks start at flashings and penetrations, so find the junction before condemning the sheet.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about roof coverings; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Slate, tiles, flagstones, shingles, sheet metal (copper, zinc, lead, steel)
