pages.searchTitle: How roof coverings fail: leak or condensation, repair or replace

questions.question: Why is my ceiling dripping when it hasn't rained?
questions.answer: Drips spread evenly under a metal roof on cold, clear mornings, dry by the afternoon, are condensation, not a leak. Warm, moist air from the space below condenses on the cold underside of the sheet. The answer is vapour control and ventilation, not a new roof.

questions.question: Where do most roof leaks start?
questions.answer: At the junctions, not in the field of the roof: flashings at walls and parapets, penetrations, valleys, box gutters and ridge cappings. Find the junction before condemning the sheet.

questions.question: How long does a metal roof last?
questions.answer: Zinc-aluminium coated steel lasts 40 years and more in a benign inland setting and 15 to 25 years within about a kilometre of surf; galvanised iron lasts 30 to 50 years. Life is a property of each zone of a roof, not of the roof as a whole.

questions.question: How long do roof tiles and slates last?
questions.answer: Concrete tiles last 50 years and more and terracotta 80 years and more, but their bedding and pointing last 20 to 30. Natural slate lasts 80 to 150 years and its nails 50 to 100; fibre cement slate lasts 25 to 40 years.

questions.question: Why are slates slipping off my roof?
questions.answer: Scattered slipped slates usually mean nail sickness: the iron nails have rusted through. A line of slipped slates points to a failed batten. Isolated slips can be refixed; slippage that keeps spreading means re-slating is near.

questions.question: How can I tell if a roof is asbestos cement?
questions.answer: Grey, lichen-covered corrugated or deep-profile sheet on an industrial or farm building of the 1920s to 1980s should be treated as asbestos cement until a sample says otherwise. Only sampling by an accredited assessor confirms it, and it sets the method and the cost of any work.

questions.question: How do I know if hail has damaged my roof?
questions.answer: Hail damage sits in patches on the exposed slopes: dented sheet with the coating split at the dent, and fractured tiles and slates. It is often invisible from the ground and appears as leaks weeks later, so the exposed slopes need a close inspection after the storm.

questions.question: What are the black streaks on my shingle roof?
questions.answer: Algae. It affects appearance only. Moss is different, because it lifts the edges of the shingles. Neither should be pressure washed.

questions.question: Can a roof be repaired instead of replaced?
questions.answer: Repair is right while the field is sound; repeated repair of the same zones signals that replacement is near. Partial replacement of the failed bays is sensible when the rest of the roof has years left and the junction between old and new can be detailed properly.

questions.question: Can a new roof go over the old one?
questions.answer: Over-roofing puts a new covering on a support frame over the existing one, where regulation, the structure and the existing material allow. It is common for sound but ageing metal and some asbestos cement roofs, and is limited by building codes on the number of layers.

questions.question: Why is the metal roof rusting along the bottom edge and at the overlaps?
questions.answer: That is the normal edge and lap corrosion of coated steel, where water lingers. Treat and coat where the metal is intact, and replace the lower run above the gutter where it is not.

questions.question: Why is there mortar from the roof on the ground and in the gutters?
questions.answer: The ridge bedding and pointing has failed, and the cappings are loose. Rebed and repoint the ridges and hips.

questions.question: Why are tiles cracking near the air conditioning units and solar panels?
questions.answer: Foot traffic to plant and solar, or plant sitting directly on the covering. Replace the broken tiles, and put walkways and plant platforms on separate supports.

questions.question: Why is there a rust streak on the roof below a copper pipe or flue?
questions.answer: Run-off from copper or lead attacks coated steel. Isolate the dissimilar metals, route the run-off away, and replace the affected sheets.

questions.question: Is it safe to walk on an old corrugated grey roof?
questions.answer: No. Treat it as a fragile asbestos cement roof: no access without staging, covers or guardrails, and manage the asbestos.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Roof problems usually show first inside, from the street or in aerial imagery. Start with what you see, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Inside | Ceiling stains that grow after rain, under a junction, a penetration or a valley | Where roofs actually leak |
| Inside | Drips spread evenly under a metal roof on cold, clear mornings, dry by the afternoon, with no rain | Condensation under metal roofs |
| Inside | Damp or staining along the top of an external wall | Box gutters and parapets |
| Inside | Rust flakes or fibre falling from the underside of sheeting in a warehouse or plant room | Metal sheet or Asbestos cement |
| Street or aerial | Rust at laps and along the bottom edge of metal sheets; patches in a different material | Metal sheet |
| Street or aerial | Slipped, missing or broken tiles and slates; ridge cappings out of line | Tiles and slates |
| Street or aerial | Grey, lichen-covered corrugated or deep-profile sheet on an industrial or farm building of the 1920s to 1980s | Asbestos cement |
| Street or aerial | Missing shingles or tabs folded back after a storm; damage concentrated on one slope | After hail or a storm |
| Street or aerial | Sagging ridgelines and dished roof planes | [Roof Structure](https://moyneross.com/technical/roof-structure): the structure, not the covering |
| On the roof | Fixings backed out, flashings lifted, cracked tiles along the routes people walk to plant and solar | Metal sheet, Tiles and slates |
| In the records | A leak register that repeats the same locations, or call-outs clustered after storms | Where roofs actually leak |

sections.heading: Start by identifying the covering
sections.markdown:
A roof covering is the weathering layer on a pitched or low-pitched roof. It is one layer of a system: battens or purlins below it, sarking or underlay beneath that, flashings where it meets walls and penetrations, ridge and hip cappings, valleys, and the gutters it drains to ([Rainwater Systems](https://moyneross.com/technical/rainwater-systems)). Flat roof membranes have their own page, [Waterproofing Membranes](https://moyneross.com/technical/waterproofing-membranes). The material sets the failure, the fragility and the cost of renewal, so identify it first, and record each part of a mixed roof separately.

| Covering | Where it is found | How to tell | Character |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Coated steel sheet (zinc-aluminium, pre-painted) | Industrial and commercial roofs everywhere; Australian houses since the 1960s | Profiled sheet, corrugated or with trapezoidal ribs, with lines of screw heads along the purlins; a factory colour or a dull silver-grey metallic finish. | Light, fast; life set by coating and exposure; fails at laps, cut edges and fixings |
| Galvanised corrugated iron | Australian houses and sheds before about 1970 | Galvanised corrugated iron on Australian houses. | Zinc consumed; rust at laps and nail holes |
| Asbestos cement sheet (corrugated and Super Six) | Industrial, agricultural and some housing, 1920s to 1980s | Grey, lichen-covered corrugated or deep-profile sheet on an industrial or farm building of the 1920s to 1980s should be treated as asbestos cement until a sample says otherwise ([Hazardous Materials](https://moyneross.com/technical/hazardous-materials)). | Fragile; weathers to exposed fibre; replacement is licensed removal |
| Concrete tiles | Houses and townhouses from the 1950s | Thick interlocking tiles of one moulded profile; the colour is a surface layer that weathers towards grey, with sandy aggregate showing as the surface erodes. | Durable body; surface erodes; ridge bedding and pointing fail first |
| Terracotta tiles | Houses throughout; heritage stock | Fired clay with its colour through the body, usually orange to red, glazed or unglazed; older roofs show variation from tile to tile. | Very durable; glazed or unglazed; frost damage in cold climates |
| Natural slate | Heritage stock in Britain, Australia and the north-eastern United States | Scattered slipped slates point to natural slate on iron nails. | Century material; nails and battens fail first |
| Fibre cement slate | Housing from the 1970s in Britain; earlier types contain asbestos | Uniform, slightly curled grey slates of the 1970s to 1990s are often fibre cement. | Shorter life; delamination and curling |
| Asphalt shingles | Most United States houses | Overlapping strips with a surface of mineral granules, laid in courses: flat three-tab strips or thicker laminated ones. | Granule loss, curling and wind damage; insurers drive replacement |
| Lead, copper and zinc | Heritage roofs, domes, bays, flashings everywhere | Standing-seam terne or copper on American civic buildings; lead on British bays, dormers and parapet gutters. | Long life if detailed correctly; fail by fatigue, creep and underside corrosion |
| Standing-seam metal | Commercial and architectural roofs | Flat pans between raised seams running from ridge to eave, with no fixings in view. | Concealed fixings; clips and thermal movement |

The same parts go by different names in each market:

| Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Roof sheeting, roof cladding | Profiled sheeting | Metal roofing, metal panels |
| Sarking | Underlay, roofing felt | Underlayment |
| Ridge capping | Ridge tiles | Ridge cap |
| Barge | Verge | Rake |
| Asbestos cement, fibro | Asbestos cement | Asbestos cement, transite |
| Re-roofing | Re-roofing, re-covering | Reroofing: tear-off (replacement) or re-cover |

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Life is a property of each zone of a roof, not of the roof as a whole. The bottom metre of sheet above the gutter, the slope facing the prevailing weather or the sea, the area under a tree, and the bays below plant or a copper flue all reach the end of their life first; a roof is usually renewed when its worst zones fail, while the rest still has years left.

| Covering | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Zinc-aluminium coated steel, benign inland | 40 years and more | Coastal exposure halves it; industrial air; ponding at laps |
| Coated steel within about a kilometre of surf | 15 to 25 years | Unwashed areas under eaves and laps corrode first |
| Galvanised iron | 30 to 50 years | Zinc thickness; exposure |
| Asbestos cement sheet | 40 to 60 years before it weathers to fibre | Exposure; lichen; foot traffic |
| Concrete tiles | 50 years and more; bedding and pointing 20 to 30 | Surface erosion; frost |
| Terracotta tiles | 80 years and more; bedding and pointing 20 to 30 | Frost; poor-quality batches |
| Natural slate | 80 to 150 years; nails 50 to 100 | Slate quality; nail material |
| Fibre cement slate | 25 to 40 years | Product generation |
| Asphalt shingles | 15 to 30 years | Heat, UV, hail, wind |
| Lead | 80 to 100 years when bays are sized correctly | Bay size, fixing, underside condensation |
| Copper | 70 to 100 years | Thickness; acid run-off |
| Zinc | 40 to 80 years | Underside ventilation |
| Standing-seam steel, unpainted zinc-aluminium coated | 60 years and more | Sealant and fixing renewal within that life; debris; no inspection Building Enclosure, reporting the Metal Construction Association |

Life is shortened by coastal, industrial and geothermal air on surfaces rain never washes, low pitch and ponding at laps, copper and lead run-off onto coated steel, condensation under metal roofs over humid spaces, foot traffic to plant and solar, heavier coverings on structures designed for lighter ones, and gutters and valleys left to block. Washing the unwashed areas, keeping water off the laps, isolating dissimilar metals, putting walkways and plant on separate supports, and repairing ridges and fixings as a programme all extend it; most coating warranties depend on the washing.

sections.heading: Where roofs actually leak
sections.markdown:
Most leaks arrive at the junctions, not through the field of the roof. Wherever the covering meets a wall, a penetration, a valley or a gutter, water has to be turned, and that is where it gets in, so a roof with many junctions deserves a closer look than a plain one. Find the junction before condemning the sheet.

| Where | What goes wrong | What you see |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Flashings at walls and parapets | Flashings pull out of their chases, apron and step flashings lift, mortar fillets crack away | Damp or staining where the roof meets a wall |
| Penetrations: flues, pipes, plant, solar | Flashings crack around the penetration, and are disturbed each time plant or panels are added ([Solar Photovoltaic Systems](https://moyneross.com/technical/solar-photovoltaic-systems)) | A stain below one point that grows after rain |
| Valleys | Valley irons corrode, and debris backs water up under the covering | Stains near the internal corners of the roof |
| Box gutters and parapet gutters | Blocked outlets or no overflow provision send water into the building ([Rainwater Systems](https://moyneross.com/technical/rainwater-systems), [Plant Screens & Parapets](https://moyneross.com/technical/plant-screens-and-parapets)) | Damp along the wall head; sudden heavy leaks in storms |
| Ridge and hip cappings | Bedding and pointing fail and cappings work loose | Damp along the line of the ridge after storms |
| Laps on a low-pitched roof | Wind-driven rain is pushed up the laps where the pitch is at or below the product's minimum | Leaks only in rain from one direction |

Each covering is designed for a minimum pitch. Short-lapped products such as corrugated sheet and most tiles rely on gravity and overlap to shed water and need a steeper roof; trapezoidal, concealed-fix and standing-seam sheet carry longer, sealed laps and run down to a degree or two; manufacturers publish the limits for each profile and tile. A covering laid below its rated pitch, or a roof that has flattened as its structure deflected, leaks at the laps in wind-driven rain long before the material itself has aged.

To trace a leak, test the suspect junctions with water, working upward from the lowest, and use thermal imaging after rain to find wet insulation. Water on a ceiling is not always a leak: see Common misreads.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Leak that appears well away from any visible defect | Water travelling along the structure or sarking. Trace from inside upslope of the stain; hose test working upward from the lowest point. | Find the entry point before replacing anything. |

sections.heading: Metal sheet: laps, fixings and condensation
sections.markdown:
Sheet steel corrodes from the edges and laps inward. The coating chalks and loses gloss, then cut edges, end laps and fixing holes show red rust, then the sheet perforates where water and debris sit: the bottom metre above the gutter, end laps and the low side of penetrations. Zinc-aluminium coatings resist corrosion well in the open but poorly where salt or acid is never rinsed off, which is why the protected surfaces under eaves and laps fail before the exposed ones.

Over humid spaces (pools, kitchens, laundries, cool rooms, food processing, unheated sheds with wet processes) warm, moist air meets the cold underside of the sheet on clear nights and condenses. It drips back as an apparent leak and corrodes the sheet from beneath, so a roof can perforate from the underside while the top looks sound.

Screws back out under thermal cycling, washers perish and holes elongate; lifting sheets admit water and can be peeled off in wind. Long sheet runs move substantially between a hot afternoon and a cold night, and without expansion joints or oversized holes, fixings shear, sheets buckle and laps open. Concealed clips on standing-seam roofs can bind and tear seams for the same reason.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rust at laps and the bottom metre of sheets, the field sound | Normal edge and lap corrosion of coated steel. Corrosion concentrated where water lingers; coating chalked. | Programme repair or partial replacement in the near term: treat and coat where the metal is intact; replace the lower run above the gutter where it is not. |
| Holes along the gutter edge or at end laps; daylight from the roof space | Corrosion through the sheet where water and debris sit. Holes through the metal on close inspection, with red rust around them. | Repair now; replace the failed bays. |
| Even drips on cold, clear mornings, no rain | Condensation. Humid space below; no vapour control; uniform pattern; underside corrosion while the top is sound. | Correct the cause (vapour control, ventilation) before renewing the covering. |
| A rust stripe below a copper pipe, flue or lead flashing | Dissimilar metal run-off. Source above the stripe. | Isolate the dissimilar metals and route copper and lead run-off away from coated steel; replace the affected sheets. |
| Staining in a line along a purlin; fixings backed out or washers perished | Fixings leaking or backing out. Fixings loose, washers perished, holes elongated on that line. | Replace failed fixings with oversized screws and new washers. |
| Sheets buckled between purlins on a long run | Thermal movement where expansion joints or oversized holes were not provided. Long sheet runs with no provision for expansion; damage repeats at fixings and laps. | Replace the buckled sheets and refix with expansion joints or oversized holes. |
| Torn seams or pans distorted at the clips (standing seam) | Concealed clips binding, so the pans cannot move with temperature. Damage repeats at the clip positions along the seam. | Free or replace the bound clips and repair the torn seams. |
| Waves in the flat pans, seams closed, no leak | Oil canning: stress in the flat sheet. Pans wave but the seams are closed and the fixings sound; no leak. | Routine maintenance; a matter of appearance. |
| Rust spots across a new roof within weeks | Swarf from cutting and drilling. Small orange spots; no pitting beneath when cleaned. | Routine maintenance: remove the swarf before it marks the coating. |

sections.heading: Tiles and slates
sections.markdown:
Tile bodies rarely fail. What fails is the system around them: ridge and hip cappings lose their bedding and pointing, valley irons corrode, tiles slip when nails or battens fail, and broken tiles go unreplaced. Concrete tiles erode at the surface and become porous; poor-quality terracotta spalls in frost. Slates fail by "nail sickness": the iron nails rust through and slates slip, usually scattered across the roof rather than in lines. Fibre cement slates curl, crack and delaminate.

Beneath tiles and slates, the underlay is the second line of defence. Older bitumen felts become brittle, tear and sag; foil sarking tears where trades have worked in the roof space. Once it has gone, driven rain reaches the battens, and the batten fixings that hold the covering on begin to decay.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Loose ridge cappings, mortar on the ground and in gutters | Ridge bedding and pointing failure. Cappings move by hand. | Rebed and repoint the ridges and hips. |
| Slipped slates scattered across the roof | Nail sickness. Nails rusted through on slates lifted. | Refix or replace the slipped slates; where slippage keeps spreading, plan re-slating with stainless steel or copper nails. |
| A line of slipped tiles or slates | Batten failure. Batten decayed or broken below. | Lift the affected courses, renew the battens and underlay beneath, and reuse the sound slates and tiles. |
| Cracked tiles along the routes people walk to plant and solar | Foot traffic to plant and solar arrays; plant mounted directly on the covering. Damage follows the access routes and the equipment positions. | Replace the broken tiles; put walkways and plant platforms on separate supports. |
| Concrete tiles weathered to a rough grey surface across whole slopes | Concrete tiles erode at the surface and become porous. Erosion uniform across the slopes; tile bodies still whole. | Plan replacement by zone, worst first. |
| Uniform, slightly curled grey slates | Age: fibre cement slates curl, crack and delaminate. Distortion uniform across the slopes, not scattered. | Plan replacement by zone, worst first. In the United Kingdom, test slates laid before 2000 for asbestos first. Health and Safety Executive |

sections.heading: Asbestos cement and fragile roofs
sections.markdown:
Grey, lichen-covered corrugated or deep-profile sheet on an industrial or farm building of the 1920s to 1980s should be treated as asbestos cement until a sample says otherwise ([Hazardous Materials](https://moyneross.com/technical/hazardous-materials)). The cement matrix erodes and lichen roots into it, exposing fibre on the surface; sheets become brittle and crack at fixings. Coating can extend the life of sound sheet but not of eroded sheet, and pressure cleaning is prohibited.

> Every asbestos cement roof and most translucent sheets are fragile at any age. Their condition is a fall-through hazard before it is a weathertightness issue, and no-one should walk on them.

In a workplace in Australia, or a non-domestic building in the United Kingdom, an asbestos cement roof brings a duty to keep an asbestos register and management plan Safe Work Australia. Access to fragile roofs needs walkways, mesh or edge protection Health and Safety Executive. Replacement is licensed removal, usually with lighter metal sheet.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Corrugated grey sheets on an older building, or translucent sheets between them | Fragile roof. Material identified from age, profile and records; asbestos register. | Treat as fragile: no access without staging, covers or guardrails, and manage the asbestos. |

sections.heading: Shingles, lead, copper and zinc
sections.markdown:
Asphalt shingles, the covering of most United States houses, lose their granules, curl, crack and lose wind resistance as their sealant strips age. The strip bonds each shingle to the course below, and field surveys and wind tunnel tests reported by the National Roofing Contractors Association found that it loses adhesion in service: partly unsealed shingles appeared on 22 of 27 roofs surveyed, and on one roof more than 20 years old almost 86 per cent of the strips. Wind damage begins at those shingles, so an old roof loses shingles in a wind a new one would resist.

Ridges and waves in a shingle roof come from below: the Asphalt Roofing Manufacturers Association attributes buckling most often to wrinkled underlayment or a moving wood deck. Dark streaks are algae and affect appearance only; moss can lift the leading edges. Neither should be pressure washed. Under the International Residential Code, a roof that already has two layers must be stripped, not re-covered.

Lead creeps and cracks by thermal fatigue when bays are oversized or fixed too rigidly, and corrodes from the underside where condensation forms, showing white carbonate at laps (Historic England). Zinc corrodes from the underside where unventilated. Copper weathers to a protective brown, then green, patina that is left in place, but its run-off attacks other metals.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Short end laps or open joints on a sheet roof at low pitch | Laps too short for the pitch. End laps measured against the limits for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Relay or seal the laps to suit the pitch. |

sections.heading: After hail or a storm
sections.markdown:
Suction on a roof is greatest at the edges, corners and ridge, so wind failures start there: a lifted ridge capping or a peeled barge flashing gives the wind purchase on the sheets behind. Roofs re-sheeted with fewer fixings than the original design, or fixed into decayed battens, are the usual victims; in cyclonic regions the fixings and the batten-to-rafter tie-down are what keep the roof on.

Hail dents metal and can split its coating at the dent, fractures tiles and slates in patches across the exposed slopes, bruises shingles and shatters ageing translucent sheeting. The damage is often invisible from the ground and appears as leaks weeks later, so the exposed slopes need a close inspection after the storm, with photographs before anything is moved. In the United States, insurers increasingly set the replacement point for shingle and metal roofs through age-based terms and roof inspections.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sarking torn, sagging or missing under a tiled roof after a storm | Second line of defence lost. Sarking condition from the roof space against the limits for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Repair or replace the sarking when the covering is lifted. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fragile roof (asbestos cement, translucent sheet) reached without walkways, mesh or edge protection | safety · 4 Essential | Stop access until controls are in place. |
| Loose sheets, tiles, cappings or flashings above a footpath or entrance | safety · 4 Essential | Secure or remove now. |
| Active leak wetting structure, insulation, electrics or occupied space | failure · 3 Important | Repair now; find the junction before condemning the sheet. |
| Perforated sheets | failure · 3 Important | Repair now; replace the failed bays. |
| Slates or tiles already falling, slippage spreading | failure · 3 Important | Repair now; plan re-slating or re-battening. |
| Shingles creased, torn or missing after wind | failure · 3 Important | Repair now: replace the damaged shingles and check that the shingles around them are sealed. |
| Lap and edge corrosion short of perforation | condition · 3 Important | Programme repair or partial replacement in the near term: treat and coat where the metal is intact; replace the lower run above the gutter where it is not. |
| Condensation corroding sheets from beneath | condition · 3 Important | Correct the cause (vapour control, ventilation) before renewing the covering. |
| Fixings leaking or backing out | condition · 3 Important | Replace failed fixings with oversized screws and new washers. |
| Loose ridge and hip cappings | condition · 3 Important | Rebed and repoint the ridges and hips. |
| Isolated slipped slates | condition · 3 Important | Refix or replace the slipped slates; where slippage keeps spreading, plan re-slating with stainless steel or copper nails. |
| Covering near the end of its life, no current leaks | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Plan replacement by zone, worst first. |
| Asbestos cement weathered to exposed fibre | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Plan replacement by licensed removal; coating can extend the life of sound sheet but not of eroded sheet. |
| Shingles curled, granules in the gutters | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Plan replacement; the end is usually determined by an insurance inspection rather than a leak. |
| Asbestos cement roof with no register: a workplace in Australia, a non-domestic building in the United Kingdom | deadline · 4 Essential | The duty applies now; register and plan before any roof work. |
| Sheet that may be asbestos cement, with no register entry | check · 3 Important | Identify by sampling before any work; it sets the method and the cost. |
| Water entering at a point not yet found | check · 3 Important | Investigate before sizing works. |
| Chalking, minor lichen, swarf, algae streaks, a single cracked tile | nil · 1 Routine | Routine maintenance. |

The grading follows what a finding demands, not the size of the eventual bill. A modest repair to a loose capping over an entrance is a safety finding; the replacement of a large but sound roof reaching the end of its life is lifecycle, however much it costs.

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A roof plumber, roofing contractor or building surveyor with safe access inspects. On large metal roofs, asbestos cement and any roof with translucent sheeting, the inspection is planned around fragility and edge protection, often from a mobile platform or with a drone rather than on foot ([Roof Safety Systems](https://moyneross.com/technical/roof-safety-systems)).

| Check | What it tells you |
| --- | --- |
| Aerial imagery and drone survey | Extent, material, patching, the pattern of corrosion across bays, and hail damage on the exposed slopes. |
| Close inspection | The state of laps, fixings, flashings, penetrations, valleys and the gutter edge, with sample fixings removed and their holes checked. |
| Underside inspection | From the roof space or plant deck: corrosion, condensation, daylight, and the state of the underlay and battens. |
| Thermal imaging | After rain or at dusk: wet insulation, and the extent of a leak path. |
| Coating thickness readings | Whether enough metal is left for a coating or restoration to be worthwhile. |
| Tile and slate sampling | Lifting courses shows the nails, battens and underlay, and checks that replacements match the original weight. |
| Hazardous material sampling | Whether sheeting, felts, mastics and gutter linings contain asbestos, where the era warrants it; by an accredited assessor. |
| Water testing | Which junction is leaking, working upward from the lowest suspect. |

The report should give an extent plan, remaining life by zone, the junctions needing work now, condensation findings, the fragile areas and how they are to be accessed, and the hazardous materials position.

sections.heading: Repair, restoration, over-roofing or replacement
sections.markdown:
These are different jobs, and quotes often blur them. A repair fixes a defined defect; a coating treats a surface that is still sound; partial replacement renews the zones that have failed; full replacement renews the covering with its flashings and gutters. The choice turns on the condition of the field and the junctions, not on the age of the roof.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Repairs | Replace failed fixings with oversized screws and new washers, reseal laps, replace individual sheets or tiles, rebed and repoint ridges and hips, renew flashings and chases. | While the field is sound. Repeated repair of the same zones signals that replacement is near. |
| Coating or restoration | Clean, treat corrosion, prime and coat sound but weathered metal sheet. | Only where the metal is intact. It is not an answer to perforation, failed fixings or underside corrosion. |
| Partial replacement | Replace the failed bays: often the lower run above the gutter, the slope facing the weather, or the bays below plant. | When the rest of the roof has years left and the junction between old and new can be detailed properly. |
| Full replacement | A new covering, with new battens or purlins where needed, underlay or sarking, flashings, cappings, gutters and the roof safety system. | When the worst zones have failed and the rest is near the end of its life. Replacing the covering without the flashings and gutters usually returns the leaks within a few years. |
| Re-slating and re-tiling | Relay with new stainless steel or copper nails and new battens and underlay, reusing sound slates and tiles. | When nail sickness or batten failure keeps spreading. Match heritage material where listing requires it. |
| Over-roofing | A new covering on a support frame over the existing one. | Sound but ageing metal and some asbestos cement roofs, where regulation, the structure and the existing material allow. Codes limit the number of layers (Standards by country). |
| Asbestos cement replacement | Licensed removal, with edge protection, safety mesh and air monitoring during the works; usually replaced with lighter metal sheet. | When the sheet has weathered to exposed fibre, or when the roof is renewed. |
| Condensation control | Vapour control layers and insulation beneath metal roofs over humid spaces, and ventilation of the roof void. | Wherever condensation is found, before or with any re-roofing. |

Interactions: re-roofing is the natural point to upgrade insulation (and in some jurisdictions it is required; see [Insulation](https://moyneross.com/technical/insulation)), to renew roof safety systems, gutters and flashings, and to rationalise solar mounting and plant penetrations. Heavier coverings replacing lighter ones need a structural check; lighter ones replacing heavier ones change the wind design.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Inspection is a lump sum. Repairs are itemised per sheet, per tile area, per linear metre of ridge or flashing. Replacement is priced by roof area for the covering, with separate lines for battens or purlins, sarking, flashings, safety systems and gutters. Asbestos cement replacement adds licensed removal, air monitoring and disposal. Access and edge protection are significant on any roof.

What drives the cost beyond area: height and access (scaffold, mobile platforms or crane lifts), edge protection and safety mesh, pitch, the number of junctions and penetrations, working over an occupied building with temporary weather protection, heritage materials and listing constraints, and licensed removal for asbestos cement. Items commonly left out of first estimates are flashings, gutters and downpipes, the roof safety system, removal and reinstatement of solar panels and plant, and any insulation upgrade the work triggers.

Where condition is unverified, the usual shape is two-part: inspection first, then a replacement envelope that falls away if the inspection finds the covering sound. Replacement is lifecycle; repairs are repairs and maintenance; asbestos removal carries a code compliance element.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what an inspection cannot: when the roof was last renewed and with what, whether its warranties still hold, where it has leaked before, and whether asbestos has been identified. Ask for them before the inspection, so the inspector knows where to look.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Last re-roofing or sectional replacement: date, extent, product and invoice | How old each zone of the roof really is, and what it is made of. |
| Coating and workmanship warranties, with their conditions | Whether a warranty still holds. Most depend on washing and maintenance, so ask for evidence the conditions were met. |
| Roof maintenance and gutter cleaning records | Whether gutters, valleys and fixings have been looked after, or left to block and spread. |
| Leak register, call-out records, leak investigations and thermal surveys | Where the roof has leaked before. The same locations repeating, or call-outs clustered after storms, point to a failing junction or zone. |
| Hazardous materials register and management plan | Whether the sheeting, felts, mastics or gutter linings contain asbestos, which sets the method and cost of any work. |
| Roof plan: penetrations, plant, solar, walkways and the safety system, with its certification | Where the junctions are, and whether the roof can be reached and worked on safely. |
| Structural sign-off for solar arrays or plant added since construction | Whether the structure was checked for the added load. |
| Insurance roof inspections, storm claims and exclusions | Past storm damage, and any limits an insurer has already placed on the roof. |
| Heritage listing or conservation-area constraints | Whether the material must be matched on renewal, which shapes the scope and the cost. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Water on a ceiling, damp at the head of a wall and an old roof all invite the wrong conclusion, and the wrong conclusion usually means the wrong scope: a new roof where a flashing, a gutter or the ventilation was the problem. These are the commonest.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| Water on the ceiling means the roof leaks | Condensation puts water on the ceiling too. A leak follows the rain and sits under a junction; condensation follows the temperature, appears on cold clear mornings and spreads evenly. Re-sheeting a roof that is suffering condensation leaves the problem where it was. |
| Damp at the head of a wall is a roof leak | It usually comes from an overflowing box gutter, a parapet capping or a wall flashing, not the covering. |
| A coating will rescue an old roof | A coating extends life only where the metal is intact. It is not an answer to perforation, failed fixings or underside corrosion, or to a failed valley or flashing. |
| The roof is old, so it needs replacing | A roof is usually renewed when its worst zones fail, while the rest still has years left. Partial replacement of the failed bays is often the right scope. |
| Shingles blew off, so the wind must have been severe | Wind damage begins at shingles whose sealant strip had already lost its bond with age. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
A roof fails the same way in each market; the rules that govern its repair do not. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out the standards for coverings and their fixing, the rules on asbestos and on working at height, and when re-roofing brings wider requirements with it.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Coverings, fixing and wind | The National Construction Code calls up AS 1562.1 for metal roof cladding, AS 2050 for roof tiles and AS 4200.1 and AS 4200.2 for sarking. Wind actions follow AS/NZS 1170.2, with much heavier fixing and tie-down in cyclonic regions. | BS 5534 governs slating and tiling for pitched roofs, including wind uplift and fixing. Lead sheet follows the rolled lead industry's guidance and BS EN 12588. | International Building Code Chapter 15 governs roof assemblies. Asphalt shingles follow ASTM D3462 and wind uplift ratings; hail resistance is rated under UL 2218. |
| Asbestos | Under the model Work Health and Safety Regulations, a workplace must keep an asbestos register and management plan, and removal above set quantities is licensed. Pressure cleaning of asbestos roofs is banned in several states. | The Control of Asbestos Regulations 2012 place a duty to manage asbestos in non-domestic buildings. | Asbestos-containing roofing is regulated during renovation and demolition by EPA rules and OSHA's asbestos standard. |
| Working on the roof | The Code of Practice on managing the risk of falls at workplaces. | The Work at Height Regulations 2005, and HSE guidance on roof work (HSG33), especially for fragile roofs. | OSHA's construction fall protection rules. |
| When re-roofing triggers more | State building regulations decide when re-roofing needs a permit. In Victoria, replacing tiles with tiles or sheeting with sheeting is exempt; changing the material, or replacing structural battens, needs a building permit. | In England, renovating more than half of the roof's area is controlled work: regulation 23 of the Building Regulations 2010 requires its thermal performance to be brought up to standard so far as that is technically, functionally and economically feasible, with Approved Document L as guidance. | The International Residential Code (R908.3.1.1) does not permit a re-cover where the existing roof is water soaked or too deteriorated to act as a base, is slate, clay, cement or asbestos-cement tile, or already has two or more applications. The International Building Code sets the equivalent rule for other buildings. |
| Heritage and insurance | Heritage listings and heritage overlays under state planning law can require a permit to change a roof's material or appearance. | Listed and conservation-area roofs carry material constraints. | Insurers increasingly set the replacement point for shingle and metal roofs through age-based underwriting and roof inspections. |

sections.heading: Worked example: a warehouse roof that drips in winter
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A distribution warehouse built in the early 1990s has a zinc-aluminium coated steel roof. The tenant reports water dripping onto stock on winter mornings. Aerial imagery shows rust along the bottom edge of the sheets above the gutter on one slope, and no patching.

The drips fall evenly across two bays on cold, clear mornings, with no rain. That pattern is condensation, and a new roof would not stop it. The edge rust is a separate finding: lap and edge corrosion short of perforation.

So the register carries two lines, not one roof replacement: condensation control for the affected bays, and treatment or partial replacement of the lower run on that slope, both graded condition, with the rest of the roof a lifecycle line further out. An inspection of the underside is the check that could change this: corrosion on the hidden face would move those bays to replacement.

thresholds.rule: At least 150 mm above 15 degrees; 200 mm from 5 to 15 degrees

source.title: NCC 2025 Housing Provisions, Part 7.2 Sheet roofing

thresholds.rule: Laps at least 150 mm; fixed at no more than 300 mm centres; sags no deeper than 40 mm

source.title: NCC 2025 Housing Provisions, Part 7.3 Roof tiles and shingles

pages.title: Roof Safety Systems
pages.question: How do roof safety systems fail, how do you judge whether a roof can be safely accessed, and what findings stop access?
pages.answer: Roof safety systems fail first on paper: anchors and lines past their inspection date cannot be used, however sound they look. Physically, anchors pull from thin sheeting, corroded purlins and soft membranes; static lines lose tension; a deployed energy absorber means the system has been shock loaded. The commonest real gap is coverage: plant and gutters near unprotected edges or fragile roof lights. Guardrails and walkways come before harness systems everywhere.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about roof safety systems; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Fall arrest anchors, static lines, access walkways

questions.question: How often must roof anchors be inspected?
questions.answer: In Australia, AS/NZS 1891.4 requires inspection by a competent person at intervals not exceeding 12 months; in the United Kingdom, BS 7883 calls for at least annual inspection. A system out of inspection cannot be used.

questions.question: Is a certified anchor system enough?
questions.answer: Not if it does not reach the work. A clean, certified system that does not reach the plant serviced every quarter is still a finding.

questions.question: Should a roof have guardrails or anchors?
questions.answer: Guardrails and walkways first on routine routes: they need no training and protect everyone. Anchors and lines suit infrequent access to places guardrails cannot reach.

questions.question: What is a rescue plan for fall arrest?
questions.answer: A procedure, equipment and trained people to recover someone who has fallen and is held by the system. A fall arrest system without one is incomplete.

questions.question: How long do roof anchors last?
questions.answer: Stainless anchors and static lines 20 to 30 years and galvanised anchors 15 to 25, but each must be inspected at least annually, and an energy absorber replaced after any deployment.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Roof safety problems show at the access point, in the tags on each anchor, and most of all in how people actually work on the roof. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What you notice at the access point | No rigging plan or signage where people get onto the roof | Coverage, clearance and the wrong system |
| What you notice at the access point | Access by portable ladder over the gutter, with nothing to hold at the top | Access, fragile surfaces and guardrails |
| What you notice at the access point | A roof hatch that opens onto an unguarded roof, or has no handholds | Access, fragile surfaces and guardrails |
| What you notice at the access point | Tags on anchors and lines that are missing, unreadable or past their date | Certification and the hardware |
| What you notice at the access point | Contractors working at the edge without being attached to anything | Coverage, clearance and the wrong system |
| What you notice at the access point | Plant serviced on a schedule (monthly or quarterly) but no walkways or guardrails, only anchors | Coverage, clearance and the wrong system |
| From aerial imagery | Guardrails, walkways and anchors visible; plant, gutters and roof lights close to edges with no edge protection | Access, fragile surfaces and guardrails |
| From aerial imagery | Fragile roof lights with no mesh, covers or guardrails | Access, fragile surfaces and guardrails |
| From aerial imagery | Roof hatch location and whether a guardrail surrounds it | Access, fragile surfaces and guardrails |
| On the roof | Inspection tags: current, overdue or missing on each anchor and line | Certification and the hardware |
| On the roof | Rigging plan displayed at the roof access point showing anchors, routes and restrictions | Coverage, clearance and the wrong system |
| On the roof | Corrosion at anchors, terminations and fixings; slack static lines; deployed energy absorbers | Certification and the hardware |
| On the roof | Guardrail heights, mid-rails, toe boards and fixings; freestanding guardrail feet and weights | Access, fragile surfaces and guardrails |
| On the roof | Ladder rungs, cages or lifelines; hatch handholds and opening protection | Access, fragile surfaces and guardrails |
| On the roof | Anchor positions relative to edges, plant and roof lights | Coverage, clearance and the wrong system |
| On the roof | Walkway surfaces worn smooth or clogged, and walkway supports damaging the roof covering | Access, fragile surfaces and guardrails |
| On the roof | Edge protection that relies on a parapet lower than the guarding height required | Access, fragile surfaces and guardrails |
| When work is under way | Workers unclipping to pass plant, intermediates or level changes, because the system does not continue past them | Coverage, clearance and the wrong system |
| When work is under way | Temporary guardrails or elevating work platforms brought in for routine visits: the permanent system does not suit the work | Coverage, clearance and the wrong system |
| When work is under way | No one on the roof able to describe how a fallen worker would be recovered | Rescue |
| In the records | Anchor register with each item's location, type, installation date and inspection history | Certification and the hardware |
| In the records | Installation certificates, load test records and design documentation | Certification and the hardware |
| In the records | Rigging plan and rescue plan | Rescue |
| In the records | Contractor permits and safe work method statements for roof access | Recertifying, extending or redesigning |

sections.heading: Types of system
sections.markdown:
Roof safety systems let people reach and work on roofs without falling: anchor points, horizontal static lines, guardrails and edge protection, walkways and platforms, fixed ladders and stairs, roof hatches, and protection over fragile surfaces. They are how an owner meets the duty to provide safe access for maintenance of the roof, gutters, plant and façade, and they are only useful if they are certified, inspected, matched to the work that needs doing, and backed by a rigging plan.

All three jurisdictions apply the same order of control: avoid work at height where possible; prevent falls with collective measures that need no user skill (guardrails, walkways, platforms, covers); then use work restraint, which stops a person reaching the edge; and only then fall arrest, which stops a fall after it starts. Fall arrest needs trained users, enough clearance below the anchor, and a rescue plan, because a person suspended in a harness must be recovered quickly.

| Component | What it does | Typical forms |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Single-point anchors | Attachment point for restraint or fall arrest | Cast-in or through-bolted to concrete; purlin-mounted on metal roofs; clamp-on to standing seam; deadweight on membranes |
| Horizontal static lines | Continuous attachment along a route | Stainless cable with terminal anchors, intermediates and an energy absorber |
| Guardrails | Collective edge protection | Fixed through the roof, clamped to parapets or standing seams, or freestanding counterweighted |
| Walkways and platforms | Safe route over the roof; protection over fragile areas; level standing at plant | Aluminium or GRP grating on supports; with handrails at edges |
| Fixed ladders and stairs | Access between levels | Caged ladders, ladders with vertical lifelines or rails, ship ladders, stairs |
| Roof hatches | Access from inside to the roof | Hatch with handholds, guardrail around the opening on the roof |
| Fragile surface protection | Prevent falls through roof lights and sheets | Mesh under sheets, covers, guardrails around |

A system is designed around the work, not the roof. Every item that needs routine attention (gutters and outlets, plant, roof lights, the façade cleaning cradle or rope access points) should be reachable by a safe route, with the edges, fragile surfaces and openings on the way protected. On metal roofs anchors depend on the [roof structure](https://moyneross.com/technical/roof-structure) they fix to; on flat roofs, on the [membrane](https://moyneross.com/technical/waterproofing-membranes) they pass through; and fragile surfaces such as roof lights and asbestos cement sheet need their own protection ([Skylights, Dormers & Glazed Atria](https://moyneross.com/technical/skylights-dormers-and-glazed-atria), [Roof Coverings](https://moyneross.com/technical/roof-coverings)).

Frequency decides the right protection. A roof visited once a year to clear a gutter may be served by a well-placed anchor and trained users; a roof where plant is serviced monthly needs guardrails, walkways and platforms that anyone can use without equipment. Systems designed for occasional access and then used for routine maintenance are one of the commonest mismatches found.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Roof safety systems last decades, but their certification lasts a year. Stainless anchors and static lines last twenty to thirty years and fixed guardrails up to forty, while an energy absorber is replaced after any deployment, and a system out of inspection cannot be used however sound it looks.

| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stainless anchors and static lines | 20 to 30 years | Fixing substrate; coastal exposure; certification |
| Galvanised anchors | 15 to 25 years | Coastal exposure |
| Energy absorbers | Replace after any deployment; otherwise with the system | Shock loading |
| Fixed guardrails | 25 to 40 years | Coatings; fixings through the roof |
| Freestanding guardrails | 20 to 30 years | Counterweight and feet condition; movement |
| Aluminium walkways | 25 to 40 years | Supports; slip resistance |
| Fixed ladders | 25 to 40 years | Corrosion of rungs and fixings |
| Deadweight anchors | 15 to 25 years | Membrane condition beneath; roof slope; movement |
| Ladder safety systems (rail or cable) | 20 to 30 years | Corrosion; carriers and sleeves wearing; certification |
| Roof hatches | 25 to 40 years | Seals; hinges and stays; corrosion |
| Safety mesh under roof lights | Life of the roof covering | Corrosion of mesh and fixings; disturbed at re-roofing |
| Parapet-clamped and counterweighted edge protection | 20 to 30 years | Clamp fixings; parapet condition |

A system's usable life ends on two clocks: the physical life of its parts, and its certification. A sound anchor with an expired tag cannot be used, and a certified system that no longer reaches the plant has stopped doing its job even if every part is in order.

Wear follows use. Anchors and lines on a roof visited weekly see far more loading, abrasion and accidental damage than those on a roof visited once a year, and walkway surfaces and hatch hinges on busy routes wear out first. The anchor register should record not only age and inspection, but how hard each part is used.

What shortens life: lapsed inspection, which makes a sound system unusable on the day it lapses; roof works: re-roofing or membrane replacement that disturbs or removes anchors and does not recertify them; coastal and industrial exposure on fixings and lines; substrate deterioration: anchors into corroded purlins or thin sheeting, or deadweights on deteriorated membranes; plant added without extending the system.

What lengthens it: an anchor register kept current, with each item's next inspection date and the inspector booked ahead of it; the system redesigned whenever the roof changes: new plant, solar, roof lights or a re-roof; stainless steel and isolated fixings in coastal and industrial air; a permit and induction process so contractors use the system as designed and report damage.

sections.heading: Certification and the hardware
sections.markdown:
Anchors, static lines and fall arrest equipment must be inspected by a competent person at set intervals, typically every twelve months, and some must be proof-load tested on installation and whenever they are disturbed. A system past its inspection date cannot lawfully be used, however sound it looks. This is the commonest failure, it gives no physical sign, and it is often found only when a contractor arrives to service the plant and refuses to go onto the roof.

Anchors are only as strong as what they are fixed to. Anchors fixed only to roof sheeting, or to purlins that have lost section, can pull out under a fall; clamp-on anchors loosen on standing seams that have moved; deadweight anchors slide on wet or soft membranes and are only rated for specified roof slopes and surfaces. Through-fixed anchors leak and corrode at the penetration.

Cable tension falls, intermediates detach, terminations corrode, and energy absorbers deploy after a shock load. A deployed absorber means the system has arrested a fall or been overloaded and must be withdrawn until replaced and recertified.

Static lines, rails and anchors are designed for specific connectors, travellers and lanyards. Users arriving with their own equipment may not be able to pass intermediate brackets, may connect in a way that overloads the system, or may use a lanyard too long for the available fall clearance. The rigging plan should state what equipment the system requires.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tags overdue or missing | System cannot be used. Last inspection date against the required interval. | Withdraw it from use until inspected; recertify, and book the next inspection before this one lapses. |
| Energy absorber extended or indicator showing | System has been shock loaded. Indicator; withdraw from use. | Withdraw it from use now and replace the deployed parts. |
| Anchors fixed to sheeting only | Anchorage capacity doubtful. Installation records; inspection of fixing. | Have the fixing inspected; replace anchors on inadequate substrates. |
| Anchors removed or covered after re-roofing | System disturbed. Re-roofing date against recertification records. | Reinstate and recertify the anchors before anyone relies on them. |
| Contractors bring their own lanyards and connectors | Possible incompatibility with the installed system. Rigging plan silent on required equipment; travellers do not pass brackets. | State the compatible equipment on the rigging plan, and check it at induction. |

sections.heading: Coverage, clearance and the wrong system
sections.markdown:
Plant, gutters, roof lights and roof edges that need maintenance lie outside the reach of the system, or require a worker to pass an unprotected edge to reach it. Plant added after the system was designed is the usual cause.

A fall arrest system needs enough clear distance below the anchor for the lanyard, the absorber, the harness stretch and the person's height. Anchors placed too far back from an edge create a swing fall into the building or the ground; anchors too low leave insufficient clearance on low roofs. These are design faults visible only on a site plan.

Fall arrest relies on trained users, correct equipment, adequate clearance and a rescue plan, every time. Where people visit a roof often, or where the people visiting are contractors whose training is unknown, a system that depends on all of these is the least reliable choice. Restraint, which stops people reaching the edge, and collective protection, which needs nothing from the user, are more dependable for routine work.

Many older buildings have no roof safety system at all, and their roofs are reached by a portable ladder over the gutter. Maintenance on these roofs is either done unsafely, done expensively with temporary edge protection or elevating work platforms each time, or not done, and the roof deteriorates as a result.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No rigging plan at the access point | Users cannot use the system correctly. Absent or out of date against the current roof. | Prepare a rigging plan for the roof as it is now, and display it at the access point. |
| Plant or gutters near an edge outside the system's reach | Coverage gap. Site plan against maintenance needs. | Extend the system to reach every maintained item, or add guardrails along the route. |
| Anchors set back from an edge with a long drop | Swing fall or clearance problem. Fall clearance calculation. | Calculate the fall clearance; prefer restraint, or move or add anchors. |
| Rigging plan does not match the roof | Roof changed since the system was designed. New plant, solar or roof lights not on the plan. | Redesign the system for the roof as it is now, and update the plan. |
| Routine plant servicing reliant on fall arrest only | System type mismatched to access frequency. Maintenance schedule against system design; no collective protection on the route. | Add guardrails or walkways along the routine route. |

sections.heading: Access, fragile surfaces and guardrails
sections.markdown:
Falls cluster at the transitions: stepping from a ladder onto the roof over a gutter, climbing through a hatch with nothing to hold, crossing from one roof level to another. A system that protects the roof but leaves these moments unprotected leaves the most common fall unaddressed.

Roof lights, ageing translucent sheeting and asbestos cement roofs will not bear a person's weight, at any age and often without warning. Falls through fragile surfaces are among the most common fatal falls in roof work. They need permanent mesh, covers or guardrails, or a walkway that keeps people away from them.

Guardrails are too low, lack mid-rails or toe boards, or have loose fixings; freestanding guardrails shift on membranes; walkways lose slip resistance and their supports damage the membrane; ladders corrode and lose rungs; hatches lack handholds or protection around the opening at the top.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Access by portable ladder over the gutter | No designed access. No fixed ladder, stairs or hatch; no ladder bracket or tie-off. | Provide a fixed ladder, stairs or a hatch, or at least a ladder bracket or tie-off point. |
| Roof lights or translucent sheets without mesh, covers or guardrails | Fragile surface hazard. Material identified; no protection on the route to plant. | Fit mesh, covers or guardrails on the route, and mark the fragile surfaces. |
| Parapet used as edge protection | Parapet may be too low after roof works. Parapet height above the finished roof against guarding requirements and the limits for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Measure the parapet above the finished roof; add guardrails where it falls short. |

sections.heading: Rescue
sections.markdown:
A person arrested in a harness must be recovered quickly, because hanging in a harness becomes dangerous within minutes. A fall arrest system without a rescue plan, the equipment to carry it out and people trained to do so is incomplete.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fall arrest anchors with no rescue plan | System incomplete. No rescue procedure, equipment or trained users on record. | Write a rescue plan, provide the equipment, and train the users. |
| Fall arrest system with no clearance or rescue calculation | Arrest may not stop a fall in time, or a user may be left suspended. (Thresholds by market). | Calculate the clearance below each anchor, and plan and equip a prompt rescue. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator, ordinance or order sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Plant, gutters or roof lights maintained near an unprotected edge or fragile surface | safety · 4 Essential | Stop access until protected. |
| Fragile roof lights or sheeting on access routes with no mesh, covers or guardrails | safety · 4 Essential | Protect or bar access now. |
| Anchors or lines uncertified, failed inspection, or energy absorbers deployed | failure · 4 Essential | Withdraw from use; repair and recertify. |
| Periodic inspection or recertification due | deadline · 4 Essential | Inspect by the due date. |
| Fixed ladders above the height at which the asset’s market requires ladder safety or personal fall arrest, without either | deadline · 4 Essential | Fit ladder safety systems before 18 November 2036, sooner when replaced. |
| No rescue plan for a fall arrest system in use | condition · 4 Essential | Prepare the plan and equipment before the next use. |
| Fall arrest relied on for frequent routine access | condition · 3 Important | Add collective protection along the routes in the near term. |
| Corrosion without failure; loose guardrail fixings; rigging plan out of date | condition · 3 Important | Programme repair and update in the near term. |
| System at the end of its service life | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Plan replacement, ideally with re-roofing. |
| No system on a roof that needs maintenance access | check · 3 Important | Design the system to the work on the roof. |
| Minor wear, faded signage | nil · 1 Routine | Routine maintenance. |

Findings on roof safety systems are about people, not the building, so they are graded on the work that will next take place on the roof. A gap on a route used monthly is a safety finding; the same gap on a roof visited once a decade under a specific method statement may be a condition finding.

The grading follows what a finding demands, not the size of the eventual bill.

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A competent height safety inspector inspects; a height safety engineer designs new systems and assesses coverage. The checks below start from the work done on the roof, then test the hardware against it.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Records review | Anchor register, certificates, load tests, rigging plan. |
| Item-by-item inspection | Of anchors, lines, guardrails, walkways, ladders and hatches, with pass or fail recorded and tags updated. |
| Proof load testing | Of anchors where the standard requires it, on installation and after disturbance. |
| Coverage assessment | Every item that needs maintenance mapped against the system, with routes from the access point. |
| Fall clearance check | For fall arrest anchors. |
| Substrate check | Purlins, decks and membranes under anchors. |
| Route walk | From each access point to each item that needs maintenance, noting every edge, fragile surface and transition passed on the way. |
| Access frequency review | Maintenance schedules for plant, gutters, façade and roof lights, to match the protection to how often each route is used. |
| Access procedures | Contractor permits, inductions and the record of who accesses the roof and why. |

The report should give a site plan with every item and its status, the next inspection date, coverage gaps, and a recommended design hierarchy for new work.

sections.heading: Recertifying, extending or redesigning
sections.markdown:
The options run from keeping a sound system certified to redesigning one that no longer fits the roof. Which applies turns on what work is done on the roof, how often, and by whom, more than on the condition of the anchors.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Recertify | Recertify items that pass inspection, update tags and the anchor register, and book the next inspection before the current one lapses. | Wherever the system is sound but its inspection is due. |
| Replace failed parts | Anchors that fail load testing or are fixed to inadequate substrates, deployed energy absorbers, and corroded lines, terminations and fixings. | Wherever inspection finds them. |
| Collective protection first on routine routes | Guardrails at edges near plant and gutters, walkways and platforms at plant, and covers, mesh or guardrails at roof lights and hatches. | On routes used routinely; more expensive to install than anchors, but usable by anyone and nearly maintenance-free. |
| Extend or redesign anchor and line systems | Reach every maintained item, preferring restraint (which stops people reaching the edge) over arrest (which stops a fall once it starts), with fall clearance checked for every arrest anchor. | Where the system does not reach the work, or the roof has changed. |
| Access points | Fixed ladders with ladder safety systems or cages to current rules, hatches with guardrails and handholds, and ladder brackets or tie-offs where portable ladders remain. | Wherever getting on and off the roof is unprotected. |
| Plans and procedures | Rigging and rescue plans displayed at each access point, a permit and induction process for contractors, and rescue equipment on site. | On every roof with a fall arrest or restraint system. |
| Coordination with roof works | Reinstate and recertify anchors, walkways and mesh after re-roofing, and extend the system whenever plant or solar is added. | With every re-roofing and every addition to the roof. |

Choosing between them turns on how often each route is used and by whom. Routes used regularly by contractors get collective protection; occasional access by a trained in-house team can rely on restraint anchors; fall arrest is the last resort, for places that cannot be protected any other way, and always comes with clearance checks, compatible equipment and a rescue plan.

Interactions: re-roofing and membrane replacement disturb anchors and walkways, which must be reinstated and recertified afterwards; adding plant or solar should come with an extension of the system; and replacing fixed ladders is the time to bring cages and ladder safety systems up to current rules.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Inspection is a recurring cost per item. Replacement is priced per anchor, per metre of static line or guardrail, per metre of walkway, and per ladder or hatch. New systems are lump-sum design-and-install items. Re-roofing usually carries a line for reinstatement and recertification.

What drives the cost: the number of items needing access and how spread out they are, the substrate (anchors through membranes need waterproofed bases, anchors on metal roofs need sound purlins), coastal-grade materials, and access for installation. Commonly missed: recertification after roof works, rescue equipment and training, rigging plan updates, and protection of fragile roof lights.

Inspection, recertification and new systems are code compliance; replacement at end of life is lifecycle; repairs are repairs and maintenance.

Preparing and updating the rigging plan is a small lump sum each time the system or roof changes.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a walk across the roof cannot: whether each item is certified, what the system was designed for, and who goes on the roof and how often. Ask for them before anyone next goes up.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Anchor register and inspection certificates with dates | Which items are certified, and when each is next due. |
| Installation certificates and load test records | Whether the anchors were installed and tested to carry a fall. |
| Rigging plan and rescue plan | How the system is meant to be used, and how a fallen worker would be recovered. |
| Records of re-roofing and plant changes since the system was installed | Whether the roof has changed since the system was designed. |
| Contractor access procedures for the roof | Whether people who go on the roof are told how to use the system. |
| Training records for people who use fall arrest systems | Whether users are trained in fall arrest. |
| Plant maintenance schedules showing who accesses the roof and how often | Who goes on the roof, how often and to what, which decides the right system. |
| Fragile surface register or roof plan marking roof lights and fragile sheeting | Where the fragile surfaces are. |
| Records of any falls, near misses or deployed absorbers | Whether the system has already been loaded, and parts need replacing. |
| Façade access arrangements where the roof serves rope access or a cradle | Whether the roof also carries rope access or a cradle, with their own requirements. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Roof safety systems are misread when the hardware is judged on its own, rather than against the work people actually do on the roof each day.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| A certified system is a safe system | A roof safety system is assessed against the work done on the roof. A clean, certified system that does not reach the plant that is serviced every quarter is still a finding. |
| Start with the anchors | Start from the work, not the hardware. List every item on the roof that someone must reach, how often and by whom, then walk each route from the access point. Every edge, fragile surface, opening and level change passed without protection is a finding, whatever the condition of the anchors. |
| Anchors are the answer for every roof | Guardrails and walkways need no training and protect everyone, which is why the hierarchy puts them first. A roof that relies only on anchors for frequent, routine access, such as quarterly plant servicing, is often better served by guardrails along that route. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets a duty to manage the risk of falls with a hierarchy that puts collective protection first, and each requires anchors to be inspected regularly. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out the duty, the equipment standards, inspection and ladders.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Duty and hierarchy | The model work health and safety regulations and the Safe Work Australia code of practice on managing the risk of falls set the duty and the hierarchy. | The Work at Height Regulations 2005 set the duty and hierarchy, including identification and protection of fragile surfaces; the Construction (Design and Management) Regulations 2015 require designers to provide for safe maintenance access. | OSHA 29 CFR 1910 Subpart D governs walking-working surfaces in general industry, with 1910.28 setting where fall protection is needed; 1926 Subpart M covers construction work. On low-slope roofs, 1910.28 allows designated areas and work rules in place of fall protection only for infrequent, temporary work set back from the edge; routine work near the edge needs guardrails, restraint or arrest. |
| Anchors and equipment | AS/NZS 5532 covers single-point anchor devices, and AS 1657 fixed platforms, walkways, stairways and ladders. | BS 7883 covers the design, installation and inspection of anchor systems, BS EN 795 anchor devices, and BS 8610 anchor system specification. | 1910.29 covers guardrails and ladder safety systems, and 1910.140 personal fall protection; ANSI/ASSP Z359 sets fall protection standards. |
| Inspection | AS/NZS 1891.4 requires anchors and fall arrest equipment to be inspected by a competent person at intervals not exceeding 12 months. | BS 7883 calls for anchor systems to be inspected at least annually. | 1910.27 requires rope descent anchorages to be inspected annually and certified at least every ten years. |
| Fixed ladders | AS 1657 covers fixed ladders, with cages or ladder safety systems where required. | BS 4211 covers permanently fixed ladders. | Fixed ladders over 24 feet must have ladder safety or personal fall arrest systems, with cages phased out by 2036. |

sections.heading: Worked example: quarterly plant servicing on a warehouse roof
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 2000s warehouse has rooftop air conditioning serviced quarterly, reached by portable ladder over the gutter. The roof has a static line installed with the building; its tags expired two years ago, a row of plant added later sits beyond the line's reach near the edge, and the translucent roof lights on the route have no mesh.

Starting from the work rather than the hardware, the quarterly route passes unprotected roof lights and ends at plant near an unprotected edge: both safety findings, whatever the line's condition. The expired tags mean the line cannot be used until recertified. Access every quarter is better served by a walkway and guardrails along the route than by fall arrest.

So the register carries the fragile roof lights and the unprotected plant as safety lines now, recertification as a failure line, a fixed access point, and collective protection along the routine route, with the rigging plan redrawn for the roof as it now is.

pages.title: Roof Structure
pages.question: How do roof structures fail, what are the warning signs, and when is a sagging or altered roof dangerous?
pages.answer: Roof structures fail from water, alteration and added load. Pitched cut roofs spread at the eaves when ties are missing or a heavier covering goes on: the ridge dips and wall tops crack and lean out. Trusses fail where webs are cut or plates back out. Cold-formed purlins corrode along gutter lines and buckle under added plant. RAAC planks can fail suddenly. A gap between ceiling and internal walls that opens seasonally is usually truss uplift, not a structural defect.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about roof structure; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Primary framing (trusses, rafters), substrate, sarking
