pages.searchTitle: Roof structure: spread, sagging, truss defects, overload, RAAC and tie-down

questions.question: Why does the ridge of my roof dip?
questions.answer: A dipped ridge with walls pushed out at the eaves points to roof spread: the rafter feet have moved on the plate because ties are missing or detached. Restoring the ties is often the whole cure.

questions.question: Can I put solar panels or plant on my roof?
questions.answer: Only after a structural check. Plant, solar arrays and tanks on light steel and timber roofs are a common cause of overload, and the roof can look normal until it is not.

questions.question: Why do ceiling gaps open in winter and close in summer?
questions.answer: That is truss uplift, a seasonal movement of the trusses. It is graded nil: a matter of finishes, not structure.

questions.question: What is RAAC and why does it matter?
questions.answer: Reinforced autoclaved aerated concrete: lightweight planks used in flat roofs, designed for about 30 years and now past it. Where planks are distressed they need propping at once.

questions.question: How long does a roof structure last?
questions.answer: Dry timber framing 80 to 120 years and more, steel portal frames 50 to 80, cold-formed purlins 30 to 60, and concrete roof slabs 60 to 100.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Roof structure problems show in the shape of the roof from outside, in cracks and sags inside, and in the roof space itself. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Inside | Cracks along the line where ceilings meet external walls, and walls leaning out at the top: roof spread | Spread, trusses and decay |
| Inside | Gaps opening between ceilings and internal walls in winter and closing in summer: truss uplift, usually harmless | Spread, trusses and decay |
| Inside | Ceilings sagging under a stored load, water tank or added services: overloaded ceiling joists | Overload, snow and ponding |
| Inside | Rust flakes falling from purlins, or purlins visibly twisted, in warehouses and plant rooms | Steel: corrosion, bracing and connections |
| Inside | Creaking and movement in high wind; doors in the top storey binding after a storm | Wind tie-down and fire damage |
| Inside | Spalling, rust staining and sagging on the soffit of a concrete roof slab, often in lines following the reinforcement | Concrete slabs and RAAC |
| Street or aerial | Ridgeline dipping or roof plane sagging between trusses or rafters | Spread, trusses and decay |
| Street or aerial | Walls bowing out at eaves level; cracks at the top of external walls near the corners | Spread, trusses and decay |
| Street or aerial | Plant, solar arrays and tanks added on roofs; ponding | Overload, snow and ponding |
| Street or aerial | Ridge and hip lines that wave or step between trusses, rather than running straight | Spread, trusses and decay |
| Street or aerial | Damage concentrated along the edges and corners of roofs after a storm | Wind tie-down and fire damage |
| Roof space | Nail plates lifted; webs or braces cut or missing; trusses out of plumb | Spread, trusses and decay |
| Roof space | Decay at wall plates, valleys and under leaks; termite workings and mud leads; borer holes and frass | Spread, trusses and decay |
| Roof space | Rafters spreading at the wall plate; collar ties or ceiling joists detached | Spread, trusses and decay |
| Roof space | Corrosion of purlins, cleats and bolts; buckled or twisted purlins | Steel: corrosion, bracing and connections |
| Roof space | Hung services, storage and water tanks on ceiling joists | Overload, snow and ponding |
| Roof space | Rod bracing slack, turnbuckles loose, fly braces missing on steel rafters | Steel: corrosion, bracing and connections |
| Roof space | Charred timber or distorted steel from a past fire | Wind tie-down and fire damage |
| In the records | Truss design certificates and layouts; structural drawings | Investigation before the scope |
| In the records | Engineering for plant, solar and tanks added to the roof | Overload, snow and ponding |
| In the records | Termite inspection and treatment records | Spread, trusses and decay |
| In the records | Records of re-covering, alterations and loft conversions | Spread, trusses and decay |
| In the records | RAAC surveys where the building is of the relevant era and type | Concrete slabs and RAAC |

sections.heading: Types of roof structure
sections.markdown:
The roof structure carries the covering, the plant and services on and under it, wind and snow, and in some buildings ceilings and people. It includes the primary framing (trusses, rafters, portal frames, beams, slabs), secondary members (purlins, battens, ceiling joists), bracing and tie-downs that resist wind uplift and racking, and the connections between them.

Loads travel down through the roof in a chain: covering to battens or purlins, purlins to rafters, trusses or portal frames, and those to the walls, columns and [frame](https://moyneross.com/technical/structural-frame) below. Wind does the opposite, lifting the roof, so the same chain must also hold it down: every connection from the covering fixing to the foundation is part of the tie-down. A roof is only as strong as its weakest link in either direction, and that link is usually a connection, not a member.

| Form | Where it is found | Critical points |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cut timber roof: rafters, ridge, purlins, collar ties, ceiling joists | Houses before about 1970; heritage stock | Rafter spread where ties are missing; decay at wall plates; heavier re-covering |
| Nail-plated timber trusses | Australian houses and low-rise from the 1970s; widespread elsewhere | Nail plates backing out; webs cut by trades; bracing and tie-downs |
| Steel portal frame with cold-formed purlins | Industrial and logistics; retail sheds | Purlin corrosion at eaves and gutters; bolted connections; bracing; overload by plant |
| Steel trusses | Older industrial, institutional and commercial | Corrosion at bearings and gutters; riveted connections |
| Concrete roof slab | Apartments and offices | Waterproofing over it; deflection; reinforcement corrosion; plant loads |
| Precast and lightweight planks, including RAAC | Britain especially, 1950s to 1990s; some elsewhere | Low bearing, cracking, moisture; reinforced autoclaved aerated concrete can fail with little warning |
| Timber and steel decks to flat roofs | Commercial and residential flat roofs | Decay or corrosion from leaks; deflection causing ponding |

The form can usually be read from outside. Hipped and gabled roofs on houses are cut timber or trusses; regular lines of fixings across a metal roof at a metre or two apart mark purlins on a steel or timber frame, with portal frames at the bay spacing; sawtooth roofs on older factories sit on steel or timber trusses with glazing on one face; flat roofs behind parapets on apartments and offices are usually concrete slabs, or timber and steel decks on lighter buildings. The era narrows it further: cut roofs before about 1970 in Australia and earlier in Britain, nail-plated trusses after, RAAC in British public and commercial buildings of the 1950s to 1990s.

Most roof structures are hidden behind ceilings and coverings, so their condition is read indirectly: from the shape of the roof, from cracks where the roof meets the walls, from the roof space where it can be reached, and from the history of what has been added to the roof since it was built ([Roof Coverings](https://moyneross.com/technical/roof-coverings), [Solar Photovoltaic Systems](https://moyneross.com/technical/solar-photovoltaic-systems)).

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
A dry, unaltered roof structure usually outlasts everything on it: timber framing eighty years and more, steel portal frames fifty to eighty. Its life is cut short by water, by alterations that cut or overload members, and by materials such as RAAC that were never designed to last.

| Structure | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Timber roof framing, dry | 80 to 120 years and more | Leaks, condensation, termites and borers |
| Nail-plated trusses | Life of the building if dry and unaltered | Moisture at plates; alterations |
| Steel portal frames | 50 to 80 years | Coatings; corrosion at bases and eaves |
| Cold-formed purlins | 30 to 60 years | Coating mass; condensation; coastal exposure; gutter leaks |
| Concrete roof slabs | 60 to 100 years | Membrane maintenance; cover; chlorides |
| RAAC planks | Designed for 30 years and now past it | Moisture; bearing length; cracking |
| Steel trusses with riveted or bolted connections | 80 to 100 years and more if kept dry and painted | Corrosion at bearings, gutters and connections |
| Glued laminated timber | Life of the building if dry | Moisture at bearings and exposed ends; adhesive in very old glulam |
| Timber and plywood flat roof decks | 30 to 60 years | Leaks and condensation; ventilation |

Members rarely wear out; connections and bearings do. Nail plates, bolts, cleats, straps and the ends of members sitting on walls or in gutters are where water collects, where load concentrates and where alterations are made, so the life of a roof structure is effectively the life of its connections.

A sound roof structure in a dry roof space lasts the life of the building. Its life is set by water and by alteration: members at bearings, valleys and box gutter lines and under past leaks, and anything cut or loaded after it was built, are where life runs out.

What shortens life: water: leaking coverings, gutters and membranes, and condensation in unventilated roofs; alterations: webs and braces cut for ducts and loft conversions, chimney breasts removed below, hatches cut through members; added load: plant, solar arrays, water tanks, heavier replacement coverings, hung services and storage on ceiling joists; termites and borers in timber in Australia, and furniture beetle and death-watch beetle in old British oak and softwood; coastal exposure on purlins, cleats and bolts.

What lengthens it: keeping the roof space dry: leaks fixed promptly, condensation controlled, ventilation maintained; an engineering check before anything is added to the roof or hung from it; trades kept away from structural members: no cutting of webs, braces or bridging for services; regular timber pest inspection in termite areas, and protecting steel bases from wet ground; recoating exposed steel before corrosion takes section.

sections.heading: Spread, trusses and decay
sections.markdown:
A pitched cut roof pushes outward at the eaves under load. Ceiling joists or collar ties restrain it; where they are missing, too high, poorly fixed or removed, the rafters spread, the ridge drops and the tops of the walls are pushed out. Re-covering a roof designed for slate with heavier concrete tiles is a common trigger.

Nail plates back out where timber shrinks, gets wet or was poorly pressed in at manufacture; webs cut by trades for ducts, flues and access take a member out of the truss and redistribute its load onto members not designed for it; missing or loose bracing lets a whole run of trusses lean like dominoes; and tie-downs that stop at the top plate rather than reaching the wall frame fail under uplift. Truss roofs are engineered systems, and a single altered member can matter far more than its size suggests.

Timber at wall plates, valleys, box gutter lines and under leaks decays; termites attack from the ground up through walls into the roof; borers attack sapwood. Decay concentrates at bearings, where loss of section is most serious.

Trusses with their bottom chords in a cold, dry roof space and their top chords in sun and weather move differently with the seasons, and the bottom chord can lift off internal walls by several millimetres. It opens gaps between ceilings and internal walls, typically in winter, and closes them again. It is a cosmetic nuisance, not a defect, and is managed by fixing ceilings to the walls rather than to the trusses at the junction.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ridge dipped, walls pushed out at the eaves, cracks at wall tops | Roof spread. Rafter feet moved on the plate; ties missing or detached; heavier covering. | Restore the ties: new collar or ceiling ties, and steel straps across the plate. |
| Ceiling cracks along the wall line on top floors | Truss uplift or roof spread. Spread if walls lean out; uplift if seasonal and walls plumb. | Tell spread from uplift: if the walls lean out, restore the ties; if the gaps are seasonal, it is truss uplift. |
| Ceiling gaps that open in winter and close in summer | Truss uplift. Seasonal; no cracking in external walls; ridge straight. | No structural repair is needed: it is a seasonal movement, graded nil. |
| Termite mudding in the roof space or on wall plates | Active or past termite attack. Timber pest inspection; damaged timber sounds hollow. | Get a timber pest inspection; replace damaged timber and install a management system. |

sections.heading: Steel: corrosion, bracing and connections
sections.markdown:
Purlins and cleats corrode at the eaves and along box gutter lines, under translucent sheets and where condensation drips. Portal frame bases corrode where they sit in wet ground or are buried by raised floor levels. Section loss in cold-formed purlins, which are thin to start with, quickly reduces capacity.

Bolted cleats corrode and loosen at purlin-to-rafter connections; rod and cable bracing goes slack, so the frame sways and racks in wind; fly braces that stop rafters buckling under uplift are removed for services or never installed. These parts are small and easy to overlook, but they are what keep a light steel roof stable.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Purlins twisted or buckled near plant | Overload or missing bracing. Plant added; bridging missing. | Restore the bridging and bracing, and carry the plant on an independent frame. |
| Corrosion along the box gutter line | Gutter leaks. Staining continues to the gutter above. | Fix the gutter leak above, then treat or replace the corroded steel; see Rainwater Systems. |
| Portal frame bases rusting at ground level | Wet ground or raised ground level around the base. Base plates buried or below slab level; section loss measured. | Expose the base; clean, treat and recoat it, and keep ground and water away from it. |
| Frame swaying in wind; bracing rods slack or loose | Bracing tension lost or bracing removed. Rods slack by hand; turnbuckles or connections loose. | Retension or replace the rod bracing. |

sections.heading: Overload, snow and ponding
sections.markdown:
Plant, solar arrays and tanks added without checking the structure overload purlins and slabs. Cold-formed purlins buckle sideways when their bridging or fly bracing is removed or never installed. Ponding from blocked gutters loads light roofs past capacity.

In snow regions, drifts against parapets, plant and higher roofs concentrate load well above the average for the roof. On flat and low-slope roofs, water held by blocked outlets deflects the structure, which holds more water: on light steel and timber decks this ponding instability can end in collapse. Codes now design for both, but older roofs and later alterations often were not.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Roof plane sagging between supports | Undersized or overloaded rafters or purlins. Covering weight; member sizes; added loads. | Have the members checked against the loads now on the roof, and strengthen them. |
| Ceiling sagging under storage, tanks or services | Overloaded ceiling joists. Load placed on the ceiling structure rather than the roof frame. | Take the load off the ceiling, and carry tanks and services on the roof structure. |
| Roof plane dished beneath a solar array or plant | Added load on members not designed for it. No engineering for the addition; deflection measured. | Have the addition engineered, and carry it on an independent frame bearing on the primary structure. |

sections.heading: Concrete slabs and RAAC
sections.markdown:
Roof slabs deteriorate when their membrane fails: water and chlorides reach the reinforcement, which corrodes, expands and spalls the soffit, usually in lines following the bars. Long-term creep deflection makes the slab sag between supports, which causes ponding, which accelerates membrane failure and adds load. Plant loads on slabs that were not designed for them, and new penetrations cored through slabs for services, cut reinforcement and reduce capacity.

Reinforced autoclaved aerated concrete planks are light, weak and permeable, with little reserve of strength. Where they get wet, where their bearings are short or poorly built, where they were cut on site, or where their reinforcement corrodes, they can crack, deflect and fail suddenly with little warning. Planks are commonly found in flat roofs, and sometimes floors and walls, of British schools, hospitals, offices and public buildings of the 1950s to 1990s. Where present they are a structural safety matter regardless of how they look.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rust staining and spalls in lines on slab soffits | Reinforcement corrosion from membrane failure. Membrane defect above; cover low. | Fix the membrane first, then repair the concrete and reinstate cover. |
| Cracks or sag in flat roof panels of a 1950s to 1990s building | RAAC planks. Plank identification from below; bearing length; moisture. | Treat it as RAAC until identified; prop now where planks are distressed, and restrict access below. |

sections.heading: Wind tie-down and fire damage
sections.markdown:
In high winds the roof is lifted, not pushed down. Roofs fail when the tie-down chain breaks: battens pulling from rafters, trusses from wall plates, or wall plates from the walls. Older roofs often have far less tie-down than current codes require, and alterations such as new openings in walls or cut top plates can break the chain. In cyclonic regions this is the dominant risk to the structure.

Fire chars timber, reducing its section, and distorts or softens steel, which can lose much of its strength and not fully recover. A roof that has been through a fire, even a small one confined to the roof space, needs an engineer's assessment before it is relied on; char depth and steel distortion are measurable, but reused members are often left unassessed.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Roof damage concentrated at edges and corners after a storm | Tie-down or connection failure. Battens or trusses lifted at their fixings; tie-down below current requirements. | Repair, and upgrade the tie-down, most economically when the covering is off. |
| Charred or blackened members in the roof space | Past fire. Char depth measured; steel distortion; no assessment on record. | Have an engineer assess the members: char depth for timber, distortion for steel. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator, ordinance or order sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Visible sag with cracking, buckled members or failed connections; RAAC planks showing cracking, deflection or wet | safety · 4 Essential | Prop and restrict use now. |
| Ponding on a light roof with visible deflection | safety · 4 Essential | Relieve the water and restrict access now. |
| Rafter spread pushing walls out; members decayed or corroded through at bearings | failure · 4 Essential | Repair or strengthen now. |
| Plant, solar or tanks overloading members, with visible deflection | failure · 4 Essential | Relieve the load; strengthen or relocate. |
| Cut webs, missing bracing or bridging; corrosion taking section; termite damage short of failure | condition · 3 Important | Programme repair in the near term. |
| Fire-damaged members never assessed | check · 3 Important | Engineer's assessment before reliance. |
| Bracing slack or removed; fly braces missing | condition · 3 Important | Restore before the next high-wind season. |
| Tie-down well below current requirements in a cyclonic or high-wind region | condition · 3 Important | Upgrade at the next re-roofing, sooner if exposed. |
| Coatings on steel portal frames and purlins at the end of their life | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Plan recoating. |
| Plant or solar added with no engineering; RAAC possible from the building's era and type | check · 3 Important | Assess before sizing works. |
| Truss uplift gaps; minor surface rust | nil · 1 Routine | Routine maintenance. |

Because roof structures are hidden, the grade often depends on what cannot yet be seen. A sound-looking roof with unrecorded plant on it, or planks of a suspect era, is a check, not a nil: the assessment decides whether it becomes safety or nothing at all.

The grading follows what a finding demands, not the size of the eventual bill.

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A structural engineer leads, with a timber pest inspector for timber roofs in termite areas. The checks below read the shape of the roof first, then confirm the cause in the roof space and measure how far it has gone.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Roof space inspection | Of all accessible members, connections, bearings and bracing. |
| Level survey | Of ridges and roof planes; plumb of walls at eaves. |
| Section measurement | On corroded steel; probing of timber for decay. |
| Load assessment | Of existing and proposed plant, solar and tanks against capacity. |
| Concrete testing | Of slab soffits: cover, carbonation, chlorides. |
| RAAC identification | And assessment to the Institution of Structural Engineers guidance where planks may be present. |
| Timber pest inspection | To AS 4349.3 in Australia. |
| Drone and roof survey | Of the roof shape, ridge lines and areas of ponding or deflection before entering the roof space. |
| Opening up | At sample bearings, valleys and box gutter lines where ceilings or coverings hide them. |
| Truss identification | From manufacturer marks and layout drawings, to compare what is there with what was designed. |
| Moisture readings | In timber at bearings and under leaks. |
| Tie-down inspection | In cyclonic regions. |
| Deflection measurement | Under plant against design limits. |

Sampling is weighted to bearings, valleys, box gutter lines and areas under plant, where decay, corrosion and overload concentrate.

sections.heading: Tying, strengthening or replacing
sections.markdown:
Much of the cure is modest: restoring ties and bracing often settles spread and sway on its own. Strengthening and replacing members follow where they are undersized, overloaded, decayed or corroded, always after the cause has been dealt with, and propping holds the roof while that is designed.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Restore ties and bracing | New collar or ceiling ties, steel straps across the plate, reinstated truss webs and bracing, and retensioned or replaced rod bracing. | For spread and sway; often the whole cure, and modest in cost. |
| Strengthen members | Sister rafters and purlins, add intermediate purlins, and plate or replace truss members, designed by an engineer for the loads now on the roof. | Where members are undersized or overloaded. |
| Replace decayed or corroded members | Replace them after treating the cause (leak, condensation, termites); in termite areas, install a management system and inspect annually. | Where decay, insects or corrosion have taken section. |
| Steel repair | Clean, treat and recoat; replace corroded purlins, cleats and bolts; restore fly bracing and bridging. | Where steel corrodes or its coatings are at the end of their life. |
| Independent plant frames | Frames bearing on the primary structure, so plant, tank and solar loads bypass purlins and decks. | Wherever plant, tanks or solar sit on members not designed for them. |
| Concrete slab repair | Break out, treat or replace reinforcement, and reinstate cover. | After the membrane above has been fixed. |
| RAAC | Immediate propping where planks are distressed, then additional bearings, strengthening or replacement of the planks, guided by the IStructE assessment. | Wherever RAAC is identified. |
| Tie-down upgrade | Upgrade the connections that hold the roof down. | In high-wind and cyclonic regions, most economically when the covering is off. |
| Propping | Temporary props, with access restricted below. | As an interim measure while strengthening is designed. |

Choosing between them starts with the cause. Where the structure is sound but restraint has been lost, restoring ties, bracing and tie-down is enough; where members have lost section to decay or corrosion, they are repaired or replaced; where the load has changed, the structure is strengthened or the load carried on its own frame. Strengthening a roof without removing the cause of decay or overload only resets the clock.

Interactions: re-roofing is the natural time to restore ties, bracing and tie-down, replace corroded purlins and check the structure for any new covering, solar array or plant; a heavier covering, or one with different wind performance, needs the structure checked before it goes on ([Roof Coverings](https://moyneross.com/technical/roof-coverings)). Repairs inside occupied buildings need ceilings opened and services moved, and in termite areas the treatment must cover the whole building, not only the roof.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Engineering assessment is a lump sum. Repairs are itemised per member or connection; strengthening and plant frames are lump sums; purlin replacement is by length and usually done with re-roofing. Termite management recurs annually. RAAC remediation is a lump-sum project with propping as an immediate cost.

What drives the cost: access to the roof space and the members (ceilings opened, services moved), the number of members and connections affected, propping while work proceeds, work over occupied space, and whether the covering must come off. Commonly missed: making good ceilings and finishes, termite treatment and its ongoing management, and engineering for every item added to the roof.

On large industrial roofs, purlin and fixing replacement is usually combined with re-sheeting, since the covering must come off to reach them; on occupied buildings, the cost of access, temporary works and making good can exceed the cost of the structural work itself.

Strengthening for added loads is code compliance; repairs are repairs and maintenance; recoating steel is lifecycle; the assessment is the check line that sizes everything else.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what the roof space cannot: what the roof was designed to carry, what has been added or cut since, and whether past damage was assessed. Ask for them before anything else goes on the roof.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Structural drawings and truss certificates | How the roof was designed, and for what loads. |
| Engineering for plant, solar arrays and tanks on the roof | Whether additions to the roof were checked before they went on. |
| Termite inspection and treatment records | Whether termites have been found, and how the building is protected. |
| Records of re-covering, alterations and loft or roof-space conversions | Whether members have been cut, or heavier coverings added. |
| RAAC survey for buildings of the relevant type and era | Whether RAAC is present, and its condition. |
| Leak history, since leaks drive most decay and corrosion | Where decay and corrosion are most likely, since leaks drive most of both. |
| Records of any fire, and assessments made afterwards | Whether fire-damaged members were assessed. |
| Truss layouts and manufacturer documentation, where trusses are used | How the trusses were meant to be braced and loaded. |
| Wind classification and tie-down details for the roof, especially in cyclonic regions | Whether the roof is tied down for its wind exposure. |
| Structural assessments after storms, fires or alterations | What earlier engineers found, and what they recommended. |
| Records of services and storage installed in the roof space | Whether ceiling joists carry loads they were not designed for. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Roof structure findings are misread when the roof space is opened before the roof's shape is read, or when cracks at the top of walls are blamed on the wrong cause.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| Start in the roof space | Read the shape of the roof first. A dipped ridge with walls pushed out at the eaves points to spread; a straight ridge with dished roof planes points to undersized or overloaded rafters or purlins; a dish beneath a particular piece of plant points to that plant; damage concentrated at the edges and corners after a storm points to tie-down. The roof space then confirms which, and measurement settles how much. |
| The roof looks fine, so the addition is fine | Additions to a roof need a structural check before they go on, not after. Plant, solar arrays and tanks on light steel and timber roofs are a common cause of overload, and the roof can look normal until it is not. |
| Cracks at the top of walls mean the foundations | Cracks at the top of walls can come from the roof or from the walls themselves. Roof spread pushes the top of the wall out and the crack runs along the wall plate; foundation movement cracks walls diagonally from openings. Read the shape of the roof first. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets design standards for timber, steel and loads, and rules for when an alteration or added load needs the structure checked. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each, with wind, snow and termites.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Design standards | The National Construction Code calls up AS 1684 for timber framing, AS 1720.1 for timber structures, AS 4440 for nail-plated trusses, AS 4100 and AS/NZS 4600 for steel, and AS/NZS 1170 for actions. | Approved Document A and the Eurocodes (BS EN 1995 for timber, BS EN 1993 for steel, BS EN 1991 for actions) apply. | International Building Code Chapters 16 (loads), 22 (steel) and 23 (wood), with ASCE 7 for actions and ANSI/TPI 1 for trusses. |
| Alterations and added loads | Queensland and other cyclone-prone jurisdictions have guidance on upgrading older roofs at re-roofing. | Alterations that add load or cut members are building work requiring approval, and listed buildings need consent for structural interventions in historic roofs; BS 7913 guides the conservation of historic buildings, including their roof structures. | The International Existing Building Code governs alterations and added loads: alterations that increase gravity loads on a member by more than about 5 per cent require that member to be shown adequate, and additions such as rooftop solar must be checked for wind and dead load. |
| Wind, snow and termites | Wind classification for housing follows AS 4055, and cyclonic regions C and D require continuous tie-down from roof to foundation; termite management follows AS 3660.1 and inspections AS 4349.3. | Wind and snow actions follow BS EN 1991-1-4 and BS EN 1991-1-3, with their UK National Annexes. | In snow regions, drift loads against parapets, plant and higher roofs set by ASCE 7 govern many older roof failures. |

In the United Kingdom, the Institution of Structural Engineers publishes guidance on identifying and assessing RAAC, and the government has published guidance for building owners.

sections.heading: Worked example: a warehouse roof dished under new plant
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 1990s steel portal-framed warehouse had two large air conditioning units and a solar array added to its roof five years ago. The roof plane is now visibly dished beneath one of the units, the purlins near it are twisted, and there is no engineering on record for either addition.

A dish beneath a particular piece of plant points to that plant. With visible deflection and twisted purlins, the overload is a failure finding, and the absence of engineering makes the solar array a check finding, even where the roof looks normal. Strengthening is designed by an engineer for the loads now on the roof, and the units go on an independent frame bearing on the portal frames.

So the register carries the overloaded area as a failure line, with propping and restricted access below in the meantime if the engineer advises it, an independent plant frame, and a structural check of the solar array as a check line.

pages.title: Sanitary & Drainage Systems
pages.question: How do sanitary plumbing and drains fail, and how do you tell a blockage from a defect?
pages.answer: Drainage fails by roots, ground movement and corrosion. Roots enter clay joints and crack pipes; ground movement displaces joints and leaks undermine footings; cast iron stacks corrode from inside along the crown; pitch fibre collapses. Repeated blockages at one place mean a defect, which CCTV finds. Wet area waterproofing fails at wastes and junctions. Missing backflow protection lets sewer surcharge flood basements.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about sanitary & drainage systems; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Pipework, fixtures, fittings

sources.title: Approved Document H
AS 3740:2021 Waterproofing of domestic wet areas
AS/NZS 3500.2:2025 Plumbing and drainage, Part 2: Sanitary plumbing and drainage
BS EN 12056-2:2000 Gravity drainage systems inside buildings: Sanitary pipework
BS EN 752:2017 Drain and sewer systems outside buildings: Sewer system management
Approved Document H: Drainage and waste disposal (2015 edition)

pages.searchTitle: Drains, stacks and wet areas: repeated blockages, sewer odour, leaks and relining

questions.question: Why does the same drain keep blocking?
questions.answer: Usually root intrusion, a belly or a collapse. A CCTV survey is cheaper than a year of call-outs, and shows whether to reline or replace.

questions.question: Why does the bathroom smell of sewer gas?
questions.answer: A dry trap, a failed vent, or a cracked pipe.

questions.question: Can drains be fixed without digging?
questions.answer: Often. Cured-in-place relining avoids excavating under slabs and opening finishes, where the drain has not collapsed.

questions.question: Why does sewage come up in the basement in heavy rain?
questions.answer: The sewer surcharges with no backflow protection. Overflow relief gullies at the right level and backflow valves on low fixtures prevent it.

questions.question: How long do drains last?
questions.answer: Cast iron 50 to 75 years, clay 50 to 100 if undisturbed, and PVC 50 and more; pitch fibre is past its life wherever found.

questions.question: Why do the floor drains smell in dry weather?
questions.answer: The traps are drying out. Fit trap primers or waterless seals, or add the fixtures to a flushing routine.

questions.question: Why is the ground sinking along the line of the drain?
questions.answer: A leaking or collapsed drain is undermining the soil. CCTV the drain, repair or replace it, and reinstate the ground.

questions.question: Why are the old cast iron waste pipes leaking?
questions.answer: Internal corrosion along their length. Test the wall thickness, and reline or replace the stack, riser by riser.

questions.question: Why does a long drain keep blocking when there are no roots or breaks?
questions.answer: The gradient is too shallow for the flow. Relay the run to fall, or add flushing points and access.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Drainage problems show indoors as odours, slow drains and damp around showers, outdoors as wet patches and subsidence over drain runs, and in call-out history and CCTV surveys. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On site | Pipe materials in risers, ceilings and plant rooms; cracks and rust on cast iron | Cast iron stacks and venting |
| On site | Odour of sewer gas in bathrooms and corridors | Cast iron stacks and venting |
| On site | Slow drains and gurgling fixtures | Roots, collapse and blockages |
| On site | Damp, stained or swollen skirtings and floors around showers and toilets | Wet areas and sewer surcharge |
| On site | Cracked tiles and failed grout at shower floors | Wet areas and sewer surcharge |
| On site | Wet patches, subsidence or lush growth over drain runs outside | Roots, collapse and blockages |
| On site | Inspection openings and chambers: accessible, covers intact | Roots, collapse and blockages |
| In the records | CCTV drain surveys | Investigation before the scope |
| In the records | Blockage and plumber call-out history by location | Roots, collapse and blockages |
| In the records | Defect claims for wet areas | Wet areas and sewer surcharge |
| In the records | Sewer authority correspondence | Standards by country |
| In the records | As-built drainage drawings | Roots, collapse and blockages |
| In the records | Repeated plumber visits to the same stack or drain run, recorded by unit or tenancy | Roots, collapse and blockages |

sections.heading: Types of drainage
sections.markdown:
Sanitary and drainage systems carry waste water from fixtures to the public sewer: sanitary fixtures (toilets, basins, sinks, showers, urinals), traps, above-ground pipework and stacks, vents that protect trap seals, in-ground drainage, inspection openings and access chambers, and the connection to the sewer. Wet area waterproofing in bathrooms and showers is included because its failure presents as a drainage problem. Stormwater drainage, trade waste and pumped systems have their own pages.

| Material | Typical era | What it implies |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cast iron | Before about 1970 in all three countries; later in some US buildings | Internal corrosion, especially at the crown of horizontal pipes; cracking; joint failure |
| Galvanised steel waste | Mid twentieth century | Corrosion and blockage |
| Vitrified clay with mortar or rubber joints | Below ground, before about 1980 | Root intrusion and joint displacement; cracking |
| Asbestos cement | Below ground and stacks, mid century | Cracking; hazardous on removal |
| Pitch fibre (Orangeburg in the US) | Below ground, 1950s to 1970s | Deforms and collapses |
| uPVC and HDPE | From the 1970s | Long-lived; joints and supports; noise |

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Cast iron stacks and drains last fifty to seventy-five years, clay drains fifty to a hundred if undisturbed, and PVC fifty and more, while pitch fibre drains are past their life wherever they are found. Tree roots and ground movement end many drains early.

| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cast iron stacks and drains | 50 to 75 years | Water chemistry; hydrogen sulphide |
| Clay drains | 50 to 100 years if undisturbed | Trees; ground movement |
| Pitch fibre drains | Past life wherever found | Replace |
| PVC drains | 50 years and more | Ground movement; installation |
| Sanitary fixtures | 20 to 40 years | Use; vandalism; style |
| Tapware and cisterns | 10 to 20 years | Water quality; wear |
| Wet area membranes | 15 to 25 years | Installation; movement |

What shortens life: tree roots seeking water through joints in clay and older pipes; ground movement from reactive clays, settlement and nearby excavation; fats, oils, wipes and debris flushed into the system; hydrogen sulphide corroding cast iron and concrete from inside; poor wet area waterproofing installed with the building.

sections.heading: Roots, collapse and blockages
sections.markdown:
Roots enter through joints in clay and older pipes, grow into mats that catch debris, and crack and displace pipes as they thicken. Joints displaced by ground movement leak into the ground, undermining foundations and paving, and let roots in.

Pitch fibre pipes deform into ovals and collapse; asbestos cement and clay crack under load or ground movement. Collapsed drains cause blockages, leaks into the ground and subsidence.

Fats, wipes, sanitary products and debris block drains, especially at bellies (sags) where water and solids sit. Repeated blockages at the same place usually point to a defect in the pipe.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Repeated blockages at the same place | Root intrusion, belly or collapse. CCTV survey. | CCTV the drain; reline or replace it rather than clearing it again. |
| Subsidence over drain lines | Leaking or collapsed drain undermining soil. CCTV. | CCTV the drain, repair or replace it, and reinstate the ground. |
| Long, flat drain runs blocking with no root or collapse found | Gradient too shallow for the flow. Levels and invert survey against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Relay the run to fall, or add flushing points and access. |

sections.heading: Cast iron stacks and venting
sections.markdown:
Cast iron corrodes from the inside, worst along the crown of horizontal pipes where hydrogen sulphide gas collects, and along the invert where water runs. Pipes crack lengthwise and leak in ceilings and walls; many mid-century apartment buildings are now replacing cast iron stacks.

Vents protect trap seals from being siphoned. Blocked, removed or undersized vents let traps empty, bringing sewer gas and odour into the building; air admittance valves fail closed or open.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sewer gas odour in a bathroom | Dry trap, failed vent or cracked pipe. Smoke test. | Refill or replace the trap, repair the vent, or find the cracked pipe. |
| Cast iron stacks leaking along their length | Internal corrosion. Inspection; pipe section. | Test the wall thickness; reline or replace the stack, riser by riser. |
| Floor wastes and little-used traps smelling in dry weather | Traps drying out. Trap seal depth; how often each fixture is used. | Fit trap primers or waterless seals, or add the fixtures to a flushing routine. |

sections.heading: Wet areas and sewer surcharge
sections.markdown:
Bathroom and shower waterproofing fails at floor wastes, wall-floor junctions and around penetrations; water soaks into floors and walls, rots timber, corrodes steel, and leaks into the floor below. In apartment buildings it is among the most common defects.

When the public sewer surcharges in heavy rain, sewage can back up into the lowest fixtures. Overflow relief gullies and backflow valves protect against this; where they are missing or below floor levels set incorrectly, basements and ground floors flood with sewage.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Leaks from ceilings under bathrooms | Wet area membrane failure or pipe leak. Flood test; dye test. | Flood test to separate the membrane from the pipes; rectify the wet area or repair the pipe. |
| Sewage in the basement in heavy rain | Sewer surcharge without backflow protection. Event timing; relief gully levels. | Fit overflow relief gullies at the right level, and backflow valves on low fixtures. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sewage leaking into occupied spaces; sewer gas in occupied rooms; no backflow protection in flood-prone basements | safety · 4 Essential | Rectify now. |
| Collapsed drains; blocked stacks; wet area leaks damaging structure | failure · 3 Important | Repair now. |
| Root intrusion, corrosion, displaced joints | condition · 3 Important | Repair in the near term. |
| Cast iron and clay at end of life; pitch fibre | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Plan replacement or relining. |
| No CCTV; repeated blockages of unknown cause | check · 3 Important | Survey. |
| Normal | nil · 1 Routine | Routine. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A licensed plumber or drainage contractor leads; a hydraulic engineer joins for larger buildings, stack replacement programmes and where drainage is implicated in subsidence. The checks below start with the call-out history and a CCTV survey of the drains, then trace odours, leaks and wet areas inside.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| CCTV survey | Of in-ground drains and the main stacks, with each defect coded to the industry system the asset’s market uses, located by distance and depth, and recorded on a plan, with gradients read against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). |
| Smoke testing | Of stacks and vents to locate leaks, dry traps and the source of sewer odours. |
| Dye and flood testing | Of bathrooms and showers to separate membrane failure from pipe leaks. |
| Cast iron sampling | Remove a short section from representative stacks to measure remaining wall thickness, which sets the replacement horizon for the whole building. |
| Backflow review | Levels of overflow relief gullies and the lowest fixtures against the sewer, and the presence of backflow valves. |
| Fixture survey | For condition, water efficiency and accessibility. |

The report should give the condition of each drain run and stack with defects located, the cause of recurring blockages, wet area findings, backflow risk, and options for relining, repair or replacement.

sections.heading: Relining, repairing or replacing
sections.markdown:
Sewage or sewer gas in occupied spaces comes first. After that, a CCTV survey decides the work: relining avoids excavating under slabs and opening finishes, patch repairs suit isolated defects, and collapsed or pitch fibre drains need replacing.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Relining | Drains and stacks with cured-in-place liners, which avoids excavating under slabs and opening finishes in occupied apartments, provided the host pipe is still round and continuous. | Where the drain has not collapsed. |
| Patch repairs | Repairs at isolated defects, such as a single displaced joint or root entry point. | Where defects are isolated. |
| Excavation and replacement | Dig up and replace the drain. | Where drains have collapsed, are badly displaced, or are pitch fibre. |
| Root management | Cutting and jetting as interim measures, followed by relining or replacement to stop recurrence. | Where roots enter the drains. |
| Stack replacement | Replace stacks riser by riser, with temporary arrangements for residents. | In apartment buildings with failing stacks. |
| Wet area rectification | Strip tiles and screed, re-waterproof with correct falls, upturns and waste flanges, and retile. | Where wet areas leak. |
| Vent repairs | Repair vents, including replacing failed air admittance valves. | Where traps empty or sewer gas escapes. |
| Backflow protection | Overflow relief gullies at the right level and backflow valves on low fixtures. | Where low fixtures or basements can flood from the sewer. |
| Fixture replacement | Water-efficient fittings, reducing water use and sometimes drain loading. | When fixtures are replaced. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
CCTV surveys and smoke tests are lump sums per building or per run. Relining is priced by length and diameter; excavation and replacement by length and depth, with surface reinstatement (paving, landscaping, slabs) often the largest part. Stack replacement is priced per stack or per floor, with access through apartments and making good of finishes. Wet area rectification is priced per bathroom. Blockage clearing is reactive maintenance whose frequency tells you where capital is needed.

Replacement and relining are lifecycle; patch repairs and clearing are repairs and maintenance; backflow protection and wet area rectification can be code compliance or defect items.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a look at the fixtures cannot: where the drains are defective, how often they block, and who is responsible for each part. Ask for the CCTV surveys and call-out history first.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| CCTV drain surveys with coded defect reports and plans | Where the drains are defective, and how badly. |
| Blockage and plumber call-out history by location | Where blockages recur. |
| Wet area defect claims, flood test results and rectification records | Whether wet areas have leaked, and how they were fixed. |
| As-built drainage drawings and sewer connection details | Where the drains run and connect to the sewer. |
| Sewer authority or utility correspondence, including lateral inspection notices | Whether the sewer authority has required action. |
| Records of relining, stack replacement or excavation repairs | What has already been relined or replaced. |
| Cast iron wall thickness test results where stacks are cast iron | How much wall is left in cast iron stacks. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Drainage is misread when repeated blockages are cleared one at a time, and when a leak below a bathroom is blamed on the membrane without testing.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| Clear it again | Repeated blockages are a symptom, not the problem. A CCTV survey of the drain is cheaper than a year of call-outs. |
| The leak below is the shower membrane | Leaks from ceilings under bathrooms can come from a failed wet area membrane or from a pipe. A flood test of the wet area, separate from the pipes, settles which. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market governs sanitary plumbing, drainage and wet areas, and draws a line between the owner's drains and the utility's sewer. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Drainage and wet areas | AS/NZS 3500.2 governs sanitary plumbing and drainage, including overflow relief gullies; AS 3740 governs wet area waterproofing in houses and the National Construction Code in other buildings; plumbing is licensed and certified; wet areas are a leading strata defect. | Approved Document H governs drainage; BS EN 12056 covers gravity drainage inside buildings and BS EN 752 drains outside; private sewers transferred to water companies in 2011 changed responsibility for shared drains. | The International and Uniform Plumbing Codes govern drainage; some regions require sewer lateral inspection and repair on sale or renovation; NASSCO sets pipeline condition coding. |

Ownership. In all three jurisdictions the boundary between owner and utility responsibility matters: in Australia the sewer connection point and boundary trap; in Britain, the 2011 transfer of private sewers and lateral drains to water companies; in the United States, private laterals up to the main. Strata and condominium buildings treat stacks and shared drains as common property, while fixtures and wet areas within units are often the owner's.

sections.heading: Worked example: a stack that keeps blocking
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 1970s apartment building has cast iron stacks. Plumbers have been called to the same stack eleven times in two years, ground-floor residents report sewer odour, and a ceiling below one bathroom is stained. No CCTV survey has been done.

Repeated blockages are a symptom, not the problem: a CCTV survey is cheaper than a year of call-outs. Cast iron of this age corrodes internally, and a cracked or corroded stack can let sewer gas escape. The stained ceiling needs a flood test to tell a membrane failure from a pipe leak.

So the register carries a CCTV survey and wall thickness testing as check lines now, relining or replacement of the stack riser by riser, and a flood test of the bathroom above the stain.

thresholds.rule: 100 mm drain serving at least one WC: 1:80 or steeper; 150 mm drain serving at least five: 1:150; 75 mm or 100 mm drains with peak flow below 1 L/s: 1:40

source.title: Approved Document H: Drainage and waste disposal (2015 edition)

pages.title: Sealants & Joints
pages.question: How do façade sealant joints fail, how do you read a failed joint, and when does it need a programme rather than patching?
pages.answer: Sealants are the shortest-lived element on most façades and set the weathertightness of every panel and window. Read the failure: sealant peeled clean from one face is an adhesion problem from preparation; a split down the middle is over-extension or age; a skin of substrate pulled off means the substrate is weaker than the sealant. Original sealant on a panel façade past 15 years is due for a full programme, whatever it looks like from the ground.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about sealants & joints; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.

questions.question: Why does the sealant keep failing after repairs?
questions.answer: Often because new sealant has been patched over old. Sealant that peels cleanly from one face has lost adhesion; the joint needs full removal, cleaning and priming.

questions.question: How can you tell why a joint failed?
questions.answer: Where it failed tells you why: peeled from one face is adhesion, split down the middle is over-extension or age, and a skin of substrate pulled off calls for a lower-modulus sealant.

questions.question: Does old caulk contain PCBs?
questions.answer: It can, in buildings built or renovated between 1950 and 1979. The hazardous materials register, or testing, confirms it before removal.

questions.question: Can fire-rated joints be resealed with ordinary sealant?
questions.answer: No. Joints at slab edges and through fire-separating walls need a tested fire-rated system matched to the joint.

questions.question: How long do façade sealants last?
questions.answer: Silicone 15 to 25 years on well-designed joints, hybrid polymer 10 to 20, polyurethane 8 to 15, and acrylic 5 to 10 in exposed positions.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Sealant problems show inside as damp and draughts at window heads and joints, from the street as staining and patched sealant, and close up in how each joint has failed. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Inside | Damp, staining and mould at window heads, sills and panel joints, worst after wind-driven rain from one direction | Ageing, wet substrates and staining |
| Inside | Leaks that appear on one elevation and not others: exposure, not workmanship | Ageing, wet substrates and staining |
| Inside | Leaks that recur after each patch repair: the sealant has been patched over old material, or the joint itself is wrong | Adhesive, cohesive and substrate failure |
| Inside | Draughts and whistling at window perimeters in wind | Adhesive, cohesive and substrate failure |
| Street or aerial | Dark staining or efflorescence below joints; streaking down panels from horizontal joints | Ageing, wet substrates and staining |
| Street or aerial | Sealant in several colours and ages, which means patching rather than a programme | Ageing, wet substrates and staining |
| Street or aerial | Visible gaps at panel corners and window perimeters; daylight through joints from inside | Adhesive, cohesive and substrate failure |
| Close up on site | Gaps between sealant and substrate along one face (adhesive failure) or splits down the centre of the bead (cohesive failure) | Adhesive, cohesive and substrate failure |
| Close up on site | Crazing, chalking, cracking and hardness: an aged bead does not spring back when pressed | Ageing, wet substrates and staining |
| Close up on site | Bead dimensions: very thin or very thick beads, sealant smeared over the face rather than in the joint | Adhesive, cohesive and substrate failure |
| Close up on site | Sealant bonded to old sealant rather than the substrate; patching over failed joints | Adhesive, cohesive and substrate failure |
| Close up on site | Fluid staining on stone and concrete beside silicone joints | Ageing, wet substrates and staining |
| Close up on site | Fire-rated joints at slab edges and through walls: missing, gapped or replaced with non-rated material | Fire-rated joints |
| In the records | Date of the last sealant programme and the product used; no programme on a panel façade older than 15 years is itself a finding | Investigation before the scope |
| In the records | Leak log by elevation and location; repeated patching at the same spots | Ageing, wet substrates and staining |
| In the records | Hazardous materials register entries for sealants on buildings of the PCB era | Hazardous sealants |

sections.heading: Types of sealant and joint
sections.markdown:
Sealant joints are the weathertight line between every panel, every window frame and every movement joint in a façade, and between the façade and the roof, balconies and podium. A joint is designed to move: panels expand and contract with temperature, frames deflect under wind, and concrete structures shorten. The joint is a system of a sealant bead, a backing rod that sets its depth and shape, and a bond breaker so the sealant sticks only to the two sides of the joint and not to the back.

| Type | Typical use and era | Character |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Polysulphide | Precast and curtain wall joints, 1950s to 1980s | Durable when young, hardens with age; early products in some buildings contain PCBs |
| Oil-based mastic and butyl | Older window perimeters and glazing | Hardens and cracks; low movement capacity |
| Polyurethane | Concrete and precast joints from the 1970s | Good adhesion to concrete; UV sensitive; can soften or chalk |
| Silicone | Glazing, curtain wall, panel joints from the 1970s | Excellent UV and movement durability; can stain porous stone; does not take paint |
| Hybrid (silyl-modified polymer) | General façade use from the 2000s | Paintable, good adhesion; durability between polyurethane and silicone |
| Acrylic | Internal and low-movement joints | Low movement capacity; not for exposed movement joints |
| Preformed seals and gaskets | Curtain walls, expansion joints, precast | Compression seals; life set by material and compression set |
| Fire-rated sealants | Joints in fire-separating walls and floors, slab edges | Part of the fire separation; tested as a system |

Joint geometry decides life as much as product. A good movement joint has a bead roughly half as deep as it is wide, an hourglass profile thinner at the centre, adhesion on two faces only, and a width sized for the movement the joint must take. Joints made too narrow, too deep, or bonded to the back (three-sided adhesion) fail early whatever the product.

On most façades the sealant is the first line of defence and the cheapest component, so it is often the most neglected. Behind a well-designed façade there is a second line: a drained and vented cavity, flashings and weep holes that collect what gets past the sealant. Where there is no second line, as with face-sealed panels and many older precast and curtain wall façades, every failed joint is a leak ([Cladding & Wall Systems](https://moyneross.com/technical/cladding-and-wall-systems), [Glazing Systems](https://moyneross.com/technical/glazing-systems), [Masonry/Brickwork](https://moyneross.com/technical/masonry-brickwork)).

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Sealants are among the shortest-lived parts of a façade: silicone lasts fifteen to twenty-five years on well-designed joints, polyurethane eight to fifteen, and acrylic five to ten in exposed positions. Most surviving polysulphide is past its life, so an older façade with original joints is usually due.

| Sealant | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Silicone on well-designed joints | 15 to 25 years | Joint design; surface preparation; exposure |
| Polyurethane | 8 to 15 years | UV exposure; joint movement |
| Hybrid polymer | 10 to 20 years | Product grade; exposure |
| Polysulphide | 15 to 25 years originally; most surviving examples are past life | Age-hardening |
| Acrylic | 5 to 10 years in exposed positions | Not a façade movement sealant |
| Preformed compression seals | 15 to 25 years | Compression set; UV |

Sealant life varies by elevation more than any other façade element: joints facing the sun and weather may need replacing in half the time of those on sheltered faces, and horizontal joints and the tops of panels fail before vertical ones.

What shortens life: exposure: north and west elevations in Australia, south and west in the northern hemisphere, and any elevation with heavy wind-driven rain; poor joint design: joints too narrow for the movement, beads too thick, no backing rod or bond breaker; poor preparation: dust, release agents on precast, old sealant residue, wet or cold substrates, missed primer; incompatibility between new sealant and old, or between sealant and coatings, gaskets or stone; horizontal joints that hold water, and joints at the bottom of sloped surfaces; patching new sealant over old, which bonds to the old bead rather than the substrate.

What lengthens it: joints designed for the movement, with backing rod or bond breaker and the right width and depth; full cut-out and replacement, with primer and compatibility testing, rather than patching over old sealant; a planned resealing cycle by elevation, combined with façade inspection and cleaning access; products matched to the substrate: non-staining sealants on stone and porous concrete.

sections.heading: Adhesive, cohesive and substrate failure
sections.markdown:
The sealant peels away from one face of the joint, leaving a clean substrate. It is caused by poor surface preparation, missing primer, contamination such as precast release agents or old sealant residue, or a substrate that was wet or dusty at installation. Adhesive failure usually starts early in the life of the joint and appears along long runs.

The bead splits along its middle while staying bonded to both faces. It means the joint has moved more than the sealant can take, the bead is too thin at its centre, or the sealant has aged and lost elasticity. Cohesive failure late in life is the expected end of a well-installed joint.

The sealant stays intact but pulls a skin of concrete, render or stone off the joint face. The substrate is weaker than the sealant, often because a high-modulus sealant was used on a weak or carbonated surface.

Without a bond breaker or backing rod, sealant bonds to the back of the joint as well as its sides. It cannot stretch, so it tears at the first opening of the joint, often within a few years.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sealant peeled cleanly from one face | Adhesive failure: preparation, primer or contamination. New sealant needs full removal of old material, cleaning and priming; test adhesion before the programme. | Test adhesion at sample joints, then cut out and replace the joint completely. |
| Split down the middle, bonded both sides | Cohesive failure: over-extension or ageing. Check joint width against movement; if the joint is too narrow, a different sealant or joint design is needed. | Widen the joint, or change to a sealant suited to its movement. |
| Sealant intact, skin of substrate pulled off | Substrate failure. Lower-modulus sealant; substrate repair; possibly a bridge seal over the joint. | Repair the substrate, then fit a bridge seal or a lower-modulus sealant. |
| Torn across the back as well as split | Three-sided adhesion. Reinstate backing rod or bond breaker in the new joint. | Cut out and replace, with a backing rod or bond breaker. |

sections.heading: Ageing, wet substrates and staining
sections.markdown:
UV and heat drive out plasticisers and break down the surface. The bead hardens, crazes and cracks, loses the ability to stretch, and eventually splits at the first big movement. Polysulphides and older polyurethanes harden most; silicones least.

Sealant applied to damp, cold or freshly cleaned surfaces, or in hot sun, cures poorly and bonds badly. Whole elevations sealed in poor conditions fail together within a few years, and the pattern of failure by date and elevation often traces the original programme.

Some silicones bleed fluid into porous stone and concrete, leaving a dark band either side of the joint. Dirt pick-up darkens soft sealants. Incompatible sealants soften, discolour or fail to cure when applied over or next to another product.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hard, crazed bead with fine cracks | Age and UV. Full replacement on cycle. | Plan a cut-out-and-replace programme. |
| Failure concentrated on one or two elevations | Exposure. Programme can be staged by elevation. | Stage the programme by elevation, starting with the most exposed. |
| Failure everywhere within a few years of a programme | Workmanship or product. Warranty claim; test adhesion; review specification. | Claim under the warranty; test adhesion and review the specification. |
| Whole elevation failing within a few years of resealing | Poor application conditions or preparation. Failure dates and pattern match the programme; adhesive failure throughout. | Pursue the contractor and warranty; adhesion testing supports the claim. |
| Leak persists after the visible joint was resealed | Second line of defence missing or blocked. Cavity drainage and weep holes blocked; flashings absent. | Clear the cavity drainage and weep holes, and add flashings. |

sections.heading: Fire-rated joints
sections.markdown:
Joints at slab edges, through fire walls and around fire doors carry fire-stopping as well as weathering. They are often replaced with ordinary sealant during façade programmes, losing their fire rating unseen ([Passive Fire Protection](https://moyneross.com/technical/passive-fire-protection)).

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ordinary sealant in joints at slab edges or fire walls | Fire-rated joints replaced like for like with weathering sealant. No fire-rated product or certificate; joint in a fire-separating line. | Replace with a tested fire-rated system matched to the joint. |

sections.heading: Hazardous sealants
sections.markdown:
Polysulphide and some other sealants applied from the 1950s to about 1980 may contain polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), which also migrate into adjacent concrete and masonry. Removal is then a hazardous materials operation.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Hard, dark sealant on a building of the 1950s to 1970s | Possible PCB sealant. Sampling before removal; PCB sealant can contaminate the concrete or masonry next to it (Thresholds by market). | Sample before any removal; if PCBs are found, treat the work as hazardous materials removal, including the adjacent substrate. |
| Sealant residue and stained masonry beside joints already cut out | PCBs left in the substrate. Sampling of the adjacent concrete or masonry. | Sample the substrate, and remove or encapsulate contaminated material. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sealant or panels so failed that cladding or glazing is loose | safety · 4 Essential | Make safe now. |
| Failed fire-rated joints at slab edges or through fire-separating walls | condition · 2 Planned | Repair with a tested system in the near term; it is a fire compliance item. |
| Failed joints with water entering and damaging finishes, fixings or framing | failure · 3 Important | Repair now; locate leaks by water testing. |
| Widespread adhesive or cohesive failure with no damage yet | condition · 2 Planned | Programme replacement in the near term, by elevation. |
| Original sealant past 15 years on a panel or precast façade, no programme on record | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Full programme due; test a sample to confirm timing. |
| Sealants on a building of the PCB era with no hazardous materials survey | check · 2 Planned | Test before any removal; sets the method of the programme. |
| Isolated failures at a few joints | nil · 1 Routine | Local repair in routine maintenance. |

The grading follows what a finding demands, not the size of the eventual bill.

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A façade engineer or sealant consultant leads, using rope access or building maintenance units for close access. The checks below read how each joint has failed, which tells you why, then test adhesion at a sample before anyone decides the façade is sound.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Close-up survey | Of a representative sample of joints on every elevation, recording failure mode, hardness, bead size and the percentage of joint length failed. |
| Adhesion testing | By the hand pull method in ASTM C1521 at a sample of joints on each elevation and substrate. |
| Joint measurement | Width, depth and movement, compared with the movement capacity of the proposed product. |
| Compatibility and adhesion test patches | Of the proposed sealant on each substrate, left to cure and pulled before the programme starts. |
| PCB sampling | Of sealants on buildings of the 1950s to 1980 era before any removal. |
| Water testing | Where leaks are being traced. |

The report should state the sealant type and age, failure mode and extent by elevation, adhesion results, joint geometry problems, any hazardous content, and a specification and staging for the programme.

sections.heading: Replacing, bridging or redesigning joints
sections.markdown:
Fire-rated joints that have been replaced with ordinary sealant are corrected first. Otherwise the standard programme is cut out and replace, done properly; bridge seals and joint redesign cover the joints that a straight replacement would not cure.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cut out and replace | Remove the old sealant completely, clean and prime the faces, install a new backing rod and bond breaker, and apply and tool new sealant to the right profile. | The standard programme. |
| Bridge or overband seals | A preformed silicone strip bonded over the joint. | Where the old sealant cannot be fully removed, the joint is too narrow, or the substrate is weak. |
| Joint redesign | Widen joints that are too narrow for their movement, or change to a lower-modulus product. | Where joints fail by over-extension, or pull the substrate apart. |
| Fire-rated joints | A tested system matched to the joint width, movement and required rating. | Wherever fire-rated joints are missing, gapped or replaced with ordinary sealant. |
| Hazardous sealants | Removal under a hazardous materials method, including treatment of contaminated adjacent substrate. | On buildings of the PCB era, where testing confirms it. |

Interactions: sealant programmes share access with façade inspections, glazing work and cleaning, and are most economical when combined; adjacent coatings may need to be renewed at the same time.

Where the façade has no second line of defence, resealing is the whole defence and its cycle must be planned and kept; where it has one, resealing protects a system that also needs its drainage and flashings maintained.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Survey and testing are a lump sum with rates per test. Sealant replacement is measured by linear metre of joint by joint type, with bridge seals and fire-rated joints priced separately. Access is usually the dominant cost on multi-storey façades. PCB removal adds containment, disposal and substrate treatment.

What drives the cost: access (rope access, building maintenance units, mast climbers or scaffold), the total length of joints by type, cut-out difficulty, substrate repair, and hazardous material controls where older sealants contain PCBs. Commonly missed: fire-rated joints, window perimeter seals inside as well as out, and compatibility testing.

The programme recurs: a façade resealed today will need it again within one to two decades on exposed elevations. It is coded as lifecycle; patching is repairs and maintenance; fire-rated joint repairs are code compliance.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a look at the joints cannot: when they were last renewed and with what, whether old sealants contain PCBs, and which joints must be fire-rated. Ask for them before specifying a programme.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Date, extent, product and contractor of the last sealant programme, and its warranty | When the joints were last renewed, with what, and whether a warranty applies. |
| Façade inspection reports noting joint condition by elevation | Which elevations are failing first. |
| Leak log and maintenance log | Where leaks recur, and how often joints have been patched. |
| Façade specification naming sealants, coatings and panel finishes, for compatibility | Which sealants, coatings and finishes must be compatible. |
| Hazardous materials register, including any PCB testing | Whether old sealants contain PCBs. |
| Fire-stopping records for slab edges and fire-separating joints | Whether joints at slab edges and fire walls are fire-rated. |
| Compatibility and adhesion test results from the last programme | Whether the last programme was tested for compatibility and adhesion. |
| Access arrangements and their certification for close inspection | How the joints can be reached for close inspection. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Sealant joints are misread when a failure is patched without asking how it failed, when an intact-looking joint is assumed still to be bonded, and when every leak is blamed on the sealant.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| A failed joint is a failed joint | Where a joint has failed tells you why. Look at which face the sealant has left, and whether the substrate came with it. |
| It looks intact, so it is sound | A joint that looks intact can still have lost adhesion. Pull a tab of sealant by hand at a sample of joints before deciding a façade is sound; adhesion loss is often only visible when tested. |
| Resealing will stop the leak | A leak that persists after the visible joint was resealed points to a missing or blocked second line of defence: cavity drainage, weep holes and flashings. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets standards for selecting sealants and designing joints, rules for fire-rated joints, and its own arrangements for paying for and inspecting them. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Sealants and joints | Façade sealants are specified to the ISO 11600 classification of movement capability. | BS 6213 guides the selection of construction sealants, BS 6093 the design of joints, and BS EN ISO 11600 classifies sealants by movement capability. | ASTM C920 specifies elastomeric joint sealants, ASTM C1193 guides their use and ASTM C1472 the calculation of joint movement; ASTM C1521 sets the adhesion test. |
| Fire-rated joints and hazards | Fire-rated joints follow the National Construction Code, with fire resistance tested to AS 1530.4 and installed to AS 4072.1. | Fire-stopping falls under Approved Document B. | The EPA publishes guidance on PCBs in caulk in buildings built or renovated between 1950 and 1979. |
| Ownership and inspection | On strata buildings, façade joints are common property and a frequent sinking-fund omission. | On leasehold blocks, a sealant programme is a service-charge item subject to section 20 consultation. | Façade ordinances record sealant condition as part of each examination. |

sections.heading: Worked example: leaks that return after every patch
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 1990s precast office has leaks at window heads on its west and south elevations, patched repeatedly over five years. The sealant is in several colours, the original is hard and crazed, and at several joints the newer sealant has peeled cleanly from one face. There is no record of a full sealant programme.

Several colours mean patching rather than a programme, and sealant peeled cleanly from one face is adhesive failure, here from patching over old sealant without full removal. Failure concentrated on the west and south points to exposure, and the original sealant is past its life.

So the register carries a full cut-out-and-replace programme as a condition line, staged by elevation starting with the west and south, adhesion testing at sample joints first, and a check that any joints at slab edges are fire-rated.

pages.title: Service Corridors
pages.question: How do back-of-house service corridors fail, and why are they a fire safety concern?
pages.answer: Service corridors are often required exits, yet they become overflow storage for pallets, stock and bins, and exit doors are locked for security. Trolleys gouge walls and damage low services; overhead pipes leak unnoticed; waste spills bring pests into tenancies. Blocked exits and locked exit doors are fire safety breaches; mark no-storage zones, provide storage elsewhere, and protect walls and services at trolley height.
