pages.searchTitle: Service corridors and back-of-house: blocked exits, propped doors, damage and pests

questions.question: Can tenants store goods in the service corridor?
questions.answer: Not where it is an exit. Storage in exit corridors is a fire safety breach, not a housekeeping issue.

questions.question: Can exit doors be padlocked for security?
questions.answer: No. Security locks on exit doors must release on alarm and on power failure.

questions.question: Why are pests getting into tenancies near the service corridor?
questions.answer: Usually waste spills and gaps in the corridor walls. Seal the gaps, and manage the waste.

questions.question: Should the building fix one tenant's mess?
questions.answer: Usually not. Problems in one section point to a particular tenant or operation, and the fix is lease enforcement.

questions.question: How long does service corridor wall protection last?
questions.answer: 10 to 20 years; floor coatings and paint last 5 to 10.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Service corridor problems show at operational times as stock in exits, propped and locked doors, damage at trolley height, leaks, spills and pests, and in inspection and incident records. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On site | Pallets, stock and bins in corridors; exits partly or fully blocked | Blocked exits, fire doors and security |
| On site | Fire doors propped or damaged; security locks on exit doors | Blocked exits, fire doors and security |
| On site | Gouged walls and broken corner guards at trolley height | Impact damage and leaks |
| On site | Leaks and staining from overhead services | Impact damage and leaks |
| On site | Spills, odour and pest evidence | Odour, hygiene and access to services |
| On site | Dark sections; failed emergency lights and exit signs | Blocked exits, fire doors and security |
| In the records | Fire safety inspection findings and orders | Standards by country |
| In the records | Incident records | Blocked exits, fire doors and security |
| In the records | Pest control reports | Odour, hygiene and access to services |
| In the records | Security incident logs | Blocked exits, fire doors and security |
| In the records | Trolleys, cleaning machines and waste bins parked permanently in the corridor | Blocked exits, fire doors and security |
| In the records | Valves and isolation points obscured by stored goods or racking | Odour, hygiene and access to services |
| In the records | Unauthorised people in back-of-house areas | Blocked exits, fire doors and security |

sections.heading: What the space does and what it contains
sections.markdown:
Service corridors are the back-of-house routes that connect loading docks, kitchens, plant rooms, waste rooms, stores and tenancies out of public view. They carry trolleys, pallets, waste and staff, and overhead they usually carry the building's services. In shopping centres and many commercial buildings, they are also the required fire exits from tenancies, so they must stay clear even though they are used as overflow storage. Functionally a service corridor must allow goods and people to move safely, protect the services above it, keep fire separation and exits intact, and stay secure from the public.

| Element group | Typical provision | What matters for the space |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Floor | Sealed concrete, vinyl or epoxy | Trolley and pallet jack traffic; spills; cleaning |
| Walls and protection | Blockwork or plasterboard with corner guards and rails | Impact damage |
| Doors | Fire doors, tenancy back doors, security doors | Fire separation; security; egress hardware |
| Overhead services | Ducts, pipes, cable trays, sprinkler mains | Leaks; impact; access |
| Lighting and emergency lighting | Utility lighting | Visibility; egress |
| Signage | Exit signs, tenancy identification | Egress and deliveries |

Because they are out of public view, service corridors are a reliable indicator of how well a building is really managed, and inspectors often go there first.

sections.heading: How long it stays fit for purpose
sections.markdown:
Floor coatings and paint in service corridors last five to ten years and wall protection ten to twenty, while fire and security doors last fifteen to twenty-five, with hardware replaced sooner. Operations, not age, wear these spaces out: every delivery and bin run takes something from them.

| Component or quality | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Floor coatings | 5 to 10 years | Traffic; spills; cleaning |
| Wall protection | 10 to 20 years | Impact |
| Fire and security doors | 15 to 25 years; hardware sooner | Abuse; traffic |
| Paint | 5 to 10 years | Damage |
| Lighting | 15 to 20 years for LED | Technology |

What shortens fitness for purpose: overflow storage from tenants and operations; trolley and pallet jack impact on walls, doors and services; spills from waste and kitchens; neglect because the public never sees them.

Back-of-house corridors are refurbished far less often than public spaces, so their condition often lags the rest of the building by a decade or more. Their fitness depends more on management than on materials: a corridor in poor repair but kept clear is safer than a freshly painted one full of pallets.

sections.heading: Blocked exits, fire doors and security
sections.markdown:
Pallets, stock, bins and equipment left in service corridors narrow or block the exits that tenancies and staff rely on in a fire. In shopping centres this is one of the most common fire safety breaches found by inspectors.

Doors along service corridors are propped for deliveries, damaged by trolleys and fitted with security locks that do not release, compromising both fire separation and escape.

Back doors left open, broken locks and unmonitored access let the public and intruders into back-of-house areas.

Service corridors are often exits as well as delivery routes, and few people see them, so they drift: a pallet left for an hour becomes a week's storage, and a door propped for deliveries stays propped. The safety question is whether the corridor is clear and openable at its worst moment, which is why observations are recorded with the time they were made.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Corridors used as stores | Insufficient storage for tenants or operations. Storage provision review. | Provide storage elsewhere, mark no-storage zones, and enforce through the leases. |
| Exit doors locked | Security concerns overriding egress. Security review. | Fit security locks that release on alarm and on power failure. |
| Problems concentrated in one section of corridor | A particular tenant or operation. Mapping who uses that section, and when. | Enforce the lease with that tenant, rather than changing the building. |
| A long route to an exit, or a dead end, after racking or partitions were added | Travel distance extended by the layout. Distance to the nearest exit or point of choice measured against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Remove the obstruction or restore the route, and check against the fire strategy. |

sections.heading: Impact damage and leaks
sections.markdown:
Walls, corners, door frames and low services are struck by trolleys, pallet jacks and bins; sprinkler pipes and ducts damaged at low height leak or fail.

Pipes, drains and ducts overhead leak into the corridor; because few people see the space, leaks run for a long time.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Doors damaged at trolley height | No protection or poor door selection. Inspection. | Fit protection plates and buffer rails at trolley height, or more robust doors. |
| A sprinkler pipe or duct dented at low height | Struck by trolleys or pallet jacks. Damage at trolley height along the route. | Repair or replace the service, and fit guards at low height. |
| Stains on the corridor ceiling or floor | A leak from overhead pipes, drains or ducts. Moisture readings, and the run of the service above. | Repair the leak, and add drip protection where services cross. |
| Dim sections of corridor | Failed fittings or lighting not suited to the use. Lux survey against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Replace failed fittings and add lighting where the survey falls short. |

sections.heading: Odour, hygiene and access to services
sections.markdown:
Three problems in service corridors spread beyond them: odours that drift into tenancies and public areas, spills and gaps that let pests through, and stored goods that cut off access to the valves and dampers overhead.

Waste, kitchen exhaust leakage and poor ventilation make service corridors smell, and odours migrate into tenancies and public areas through doors and gaps.

Waste spills, food residue and damp floors attract pests that then move into tenancies and kitchens.

Overhead valves, dampers and cable trays above service corridors are reached by ladder from the corridor; when stock, racking or tenant equipment occupies the space, maintenance becomes difficult and isolations in an emergency are slow.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pests in tenancies near the corridor | Waste spills and gaps in corridor walls. Pest reports. | Seal the gaps in the corridor walls, and improve waste management and cleaning. |
| Valves and isolation points hidden behind stock or racking | Stored goods blocking access to services. Isolations cannot be reached by ladder from the corridor. | Clear and mark access zones beneath valves, dampers and trays. |
| Goods stacked close to sprinkler heads in the corridor | Spray pattern obstructed. Clearance below the deflectors measured against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Clear the stacking and mark the limit on the wall. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Exits blocked; exit doors locked; fire doors propped | safety · 4 Essential | Clear and rectify now. |
| Leaks or service damage | failure · 3 Important | Repair now. |
| Fire safety inspections due | deadline · 3 Important | At the prescribed interval. |
| Impact damage; hygiene; poor lighting | condition · 2 Planned | Repair in the near term. |
| Finishes and protection at end of life | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Renew. |
| Egress role of corridors not documented | check · 2 Planned | Review. |
| Normal | nil · 1 Routine | Routine. |

Because service corridors are often exits, findings about storage and doors are graded as safety even when the corridor is in poor condition otherwise; condition items can wait, egress cannot.

Repeat breaches by the same tenant are a management finding as well as a safety one.

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A building surveyor with a fire safety consultant and the centre or facilities manager. The checks below walk the corridors at operational times, map who uses each section and when, and identify which corridors are exits.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Corridor walk | At operational times: storage, door positions, damage, leaks, hygiene, lighting and security. |
| Egress review | Which corridors are required exits, their widths, and the hardware on exit doors. |
| Fire door and security interface test | . |
| Services survey | Overhead for leaks, damage and access. |
| Storage demand review | With tenants and operators. |
| Use mapping | Who uses each corridor, for what and when, including delivery and waste schedules. |
| Access to services check | Whether isolation valves, dampers and boards can be reached quickly. |
| Hygiene and pest review | With the pest control contractor. |

The report should list egress breaches, damage and a management and works plan.

Inspections at different times of day show the true condition: corridors are often cleared for audits and refilled afterwards.

sections.heading: Clearing, protecting and managing
sections.markdown:
Blocked exits, locked exit doors and propped fire doors come first. After that, the work gives stored goods somewhere else to go, protects walls, doors and services at trolley height, and enforces corridor use through the leases.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Clear exits | Clear exits and mark no-storage zones on floors and walls, with regular checks and enforcement through leases. | Wherever exit corridors hold stored goods. |
| Storage provision | Provide storage elsewhere, so corridors are not used for it. | Where tenants or operations have nowhere else to store. |
| Impact protection | Corner guards, buffer rails and door protection plates at trolley height, and guards for low services. | Where damage concentrates at trolley height. |
| Door hardware | Fire doors with hold-open devices where deliveries require, and security locks that release on alarm. | Where doors are propped for deliveries or locked for security. |
| Durable finishes | Sealed or epoxy floors and washable walls. | Where floors and walls wear or stain. |
| Leak repair and drip protection | Repair leaks, and protect against drips. | Wherever overhead services leak. |
| Pest proofing and waste management | Seal gaps, and manage waste. | Where pests or spills are found. |
| Lease enforcement | Clauses requiring tenants to keep corridors clear, with notices and recovery of clearance costs. | Wherever particular tenants cause the problems. |
| Ventilation improvements | Improve ventilation to remove odours. | Where odours migrate into tenancies and public areas. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Management measures are low cost. Impact protection and door hardware are itemised. Floor coatings by area. Corridor works are usually done out of hours. Safety items are code compliance; finishes and protection are lifecycle.

Impact protection installed once is cheaper than repeated repairs to walls, doors and services. Clearing and enforcement is an operating cost, partly recoverable from tenants. Finishes are renewed on long cycles because the space is out of public view. Fire safety orders for blocked exits can bring penalties and closures far costlier than providing storage.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what one visit cannot: which corridors are exits, who uses each section, and whether obstructions have been enforced against. Ask for them before deciding between lease enforcement and building works.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Fire safety inspection reports and any orders | Whether inspectors have found breaches, and whether orders are outstanding. |
| Egress drawings identifying exit corridors | Which corridors are exits. |
| Lease clauses on back-of-house use | What tenants may do in back-of-house areas. |
| Incident and security logs | Whether incidents and intrusions point to a pattern. |
| Pest control reports | Whether pests are a recurring problem. |
| Delivery and waste schedules | When corridors are busiest, and with what. |
| Notices issued to tenants for obstructions | Whether obstructions have been enforced against. |
| Records of clearance costs recovered | Whether clearance costs are recovered. |
| Building management plan for back-of-house areas | How back-of-house areas are meant to be run. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Service corridors are misread when storage in them is treated as housekeeping, when one bad section is taken for a building-wide problem, and when a single visit is taken to show their condition.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| It is a housekeeping issue | Service corridors that serve as exits must stay clear and openable. Storage in exit corridors is a fire safety breach, not a housekeeping issue. |
| The whole building needs storage | Recurrent problems in one section usually point to a particular tenant or operation; problems throughout point to a building-wide shortage of storage or poor management. Matching problems to users decides whether the fix is a lease enforcement or a building change. |
| One visit shows the condition | Record the time and conditions of each observation, because the condition of these spaces changes with operations and the worst state is the one that matters for safety. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market requires exits and exit corridors to be kept clear and exit doors to open, and places those duties on whoever controls the building. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Exits, doors and duties | The National Construction Code sets egress requirements, and fire safety inspections by councils and fire services commonly find blocked back-of-house exits in shopping centres; retail leases can make tenants responsible for keeping corridors clear. | The Regulatory Reform (Fire Safety) Order 2005 requires escape routes to be kept clear; the responsible person must manage back-of-house routes. | NFPA 101 and the International Fire Code require exit access to be kept clear and exit doors openable; fire marshals inspect. |

In all three countries, fire services and building authorities can issue orders and fines for obstructed exits, and in serious cases close premises until they are cleared. Insurers may treat repeated egress breaches as poor risk management. Retail and commercial leases commonly give landlords the right to clear obstructions and recover costs from tenants, but only if the clauses are used.

sections.heading: Worked example: a shopping centre's back-of-house
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A shopping centre's service corridor, which is also an exit for twelve tenancies, has pallets and bins along one section behind two food tenancies. An exit door at the end carries a padlock fitted after a break-in, the corner guards are broken, and pests have been reported in the neighbouring tenancies.

Storage in an exit corridor and a padlocked exit door are safety findings. Problems concentrated behind two tenancies point to those tenants, which makes lease enforcement the fix there, while pests near food tenancies point to waste spills and gaps in the corridor walls.

So the register carries the padlocked door and the obstructions as safety lines now, a lock that releases on alarm and power failure, lease notices to the two tenants, pest proofing, and new corner guards.

pages.title: Skylights, Dormers & Glazed Atria
pages.question: How do skylights, roof sheets and atrium roofs fail, and when are they a safety hazard?
pages.answer: Roof lights are first a fall-through hazard and second a weathertightness item. Polycarbonate and fibreglass sheets yellow and become brittle with UV and cannot bear a person at any age; an unprotected roof light on a roof people walk on is a safety finding regardless of condition. Leaks come from kerb flashings and atrium seals at the bottom of slopes. Overhead glass must hold together when broken; older atria with monolithic toughened or wired glass may not.

pages.searchTitle: Skylights, roof lights and atria: fragility, leaks, overhead glass and smoke vents

questions.question: Are skylights safe to walk on?
questions.answer: Treat every roof light and translucent sheet as fragile unless a current non-fragility certificate says otherwise. Age makes them weaker, not stronger.

questions.question: Why are my polycarbonate roof sheets yellow?
questions.answer: UV embrittlement: with age the sheets yellow, haze and turn brittle, letting in less light and growing more fragile. Plan replacement with non-fragile rated products, and protect them meanwhile.

questions.question: Why did an overhead glass pane crack on its own?
questions.answer: Read the fracture. A pair of small fragments at a point of origin in toughened glass points to a nickel sulphide inclusion; a single crack meeting the edge at right angles points to thermal stress.

questions.question: Where do skylights usually leak?
questions.answer: At the kerb and its flashings, above all where the detail relies on sealant alone, and in atria at the gaskets and pressure plates at the bottom of each slope.

questions.question: How long do roof lights last?
questions.answer: Polycarbonate sheeting 10 to 20 years, fibreglass sheeting and acrylic domes 15 to 25, roof windows 25 to 40, and atrium framing 30 to 50.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Roof light problems show inside as drips, heat and glare, from above as yellowed or patched sheets, and under an atrium as staining and cracked panes. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Inside | Drips at the base of an atrium slope or along a glazing bar after rain: seals or gaskets | Leaks at kerbs, seals and dormers |
| Inside | Drips from frames on cold mornings without rain: condensation | Condensation, heat and glare |
| Inside | A stain spreading around a skylight kerb on the ceiling below: the kerb flashing | Leaks at kerbs, seals and dormers |
| Inside | Spaces under roof lights uncomfortably hot in summer and glaring at midday | Condensation, heat and glare |

| Inside | Rotten or stained timber around lanterns and dormer windows | Leaks at kerbs, seals and dormers |
| From aerial imagery | Number and layout of roof lights; discoloured, yellowed or patched sheets | Fragility, embrittlement and hail |
| From aerial imagery | Roof lights without mesh, covers or guardrails on roofs with plant or walkways | Fragility, embrittlement and hail |
| From aerial imagery | Debris and staining on atrium roofs | Leaks at kerbs, seals and dormers |
| From aerial imagery | Dark or patched roof lights in a regular run, showing which have been replaced and which are original | Fragility, embrittlement and hail |
| From aerial imagery | Dormers with sagging roofs, open cheeks or staining below the sill | Leaks at kerbs, seals and dormers |
| On the roof | Yellowing, crazing and brittle surfaces; cracks at fixings | Fragility, embrittlement and hail |

| On the roof | Opening vents: actuators, seals, and whether they have been fixed shut | Smoke vents |

| Under an atrium | Netting or temporary screens installed below the glass, a sign that someone was already worried about falling glass | Overhead glass and atrium structure |

sections.heading: Types of roof light
sections.markdown:
This element covers every opening in a roof that lets in light, and the structures built up from the roof plane to do it: in-plane translucent sheets in profiled roofs, framed and domed skylights on kerbs, roof windows, patent glazing, glazed atrium roofs, lanterns, and dormers.

Roof lights are judged on four things at once: whether they keep the weather out, whether they let in the right amount of light without overheating the space, whether anyone can fall through them, and, where they open, whether they do their job in a fire. Older roof lights were chosen for the first two; current practice puts the last two first.

| Form | Where it is found | Main risk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| In-plane polycarbonate or fibreglass sheets | Industrial and warehouse roofs | Fragile: fall-through; UV embrittlement |
| Domed acrylic or polycarbonate on kerbs | Commercial flat roofs, schools | Embrittlement; kerb flashings |
| Roof windows | Houses and loft conversions | Flashings; seals; condensation |
| Patent glazing | Older industrial, stations, institutions | Bars corroding; wired glass; seals |
| Glazed atrium roofs | Shopping centres, offices, institutions | Overhead glass; seals; structural steel |
| Lanterns | Heritage buildings | Timber decay; leaded joints |
| Dormers | Houses and heritage stock | Cheeks, flashings and support |

Overhead glass must hold together when broken. Codes require laminated glass, or toughened glass with a protective screen, in sloped and overhead glazing. Older atria often have wired glass or monolithic toughened glass that would not meet that requirement now.

Era and use shape what to expect. Warehouses and factories from the 1960s onward carry in-plane fibreglass and later polycarbonate sheets, often in regular runs across the roof, and many of them sit in asbestos cement roofs of the same era. Schools and commercial flat roofs carry domed acrylic or polycarbonate skylights on timber or metal kerbs. Shopping centres of the 1980s and 1990s carry large atrium and mall roofs of patent glazing or curtain wall sections. Victorian and Edwardian buildings carry lanterns and patent glazing with lead or putty seals.

Each roof light is a hole in two systems at once: the weatherproofing, where its kerb and flashings meet the [roof covering](https://moyneross.com/technical/roof-coverings) or [membrane](https://moyneross.com/technical/waterproofing-membranes), and the roof's safety, where it creates a fragile surface on the route people walk ([Roof Safety Systems](https://moyneross.com/technical/roof-safety-systems)). Large atria add a third: they are façades laid on their side, with the glass, seals and framing of a curtain wall but exposed to standing water, debris and the full weight of anyone who steps onto them ([Glazing Systems](https://moyneross.com/technical/glazing-systems)).

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Roof lights are among the shortest-lived parts of a roof. Polycarbonate sheets last ten to twenty years and acrylic domes fifteen to twenty-five, against thirty to fifty for atrium framing, and every year in the sun makes translucent sheets more brittle and more fragile.

| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Polycarbonate sheeting | 10 to 20 years | UV protection grade; exposure |
| Fibreglass sheeting | 15 to 25 years | Resin and gel coat |
| Acrylic domes | 15 to 25 years | UV; impact |
| Atrium framing | 30 to 50 years | Coatings; drainage |
| Atrium seals and gaskets | 15 to 25 years | UV; movement |
| Roof windows | 25 to 40 years | Flashings; hardware |
| Dormers | With the roof; cheeks and flashings 30 to 50 years | Cladding and flashings |
| Patent glazing bars | 50 to 80 years; seals and putty 15 to 25 | Corrosion of steel bars; paint; lead or putty seals |
| Laminated overhead glass | 30 years and more | Interlayer delamination at edges; seal failure |
| Automatic opening vents and smoke vents | Mechanisms 15 to 25 years | Actuators, seals and controls; testing regime |

Roof lights usually reach the end of their life well before the roof around them. On industrial roofs, the translucent sheets are often on their second or third replacement while the metal sheet remains, and their age is the best single measure of how fragile they have become.

Within a run of identical sheets, ages differ: sheets replaced after storms sit beside originals, and the originals are the ones most likely to fail under a person's weight. Recording installation or replacement dates for every roof light is the simplest way to know which are oldest.

What shortens life: uV: polycarbonate and fibreglass yellow, craze and become brittle, faster on products without a UV-protected face or installed upside down; hail and impact, which crack domes and sheets and shatter ageing ones; poor kerb and flashing details, sealant-only junctions and kerbs lower than the water that ponds around them; condensation on cold frames and single glazing over humid spaces, which runs down frames and rots timber kerbs and lanterns; debris on atrium roofs blocking gutters and holding water against seals; foot traffic and objects dropped by trades working nearby.

What lengthens it: uV-protected products, specified with a stated life, and replaced on that cycle rather than at failure; proper kerbs and flashings rather than sealant-only details; atrium gutters and seals cleaned and inspected on a schedule, from safe access; ventilation and heating beneath roof lights over humid spaces, so condensation does not run down frames.

sections.heading: Fragility, embrittlement and hail
sections.markdown:
Translucent roof sheets and skylights cannot take a person's weight, and polycarbonate becomes more brittle as it ages. Falls through fragile roofs and roof lights are a leading cause of deaths in roof work in all three jurisdictions. An unprotected roof light on any roof that people walk on is a hazard regardless of condition.

Ultraviolet light breaks down the plastics used in roof lights. Polycarbonate yellows, hazes and loses its impact strength, especially where its UV-protected face was installed facing down or the protection has weathered off; fibreglass loses its gel coat, exposes its fibres and goes dark; acrylic domes craze. Light transmission falls with every year, and the sheet becomes progressively more brittle, so the oldest sheets on a roof are both the dimmest and the most dangerous.

Hail cracks acrylic domes and shatters ageing polycarbonate and fibreglass, often across a whole roof in one storm; the damage may not leak at once but leaves a roof full of weakened sheets. Atrium glass is usually rated for hail but its seals and cappings can be damaged.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Yellow, hazy roof sheets | UV embrittlement. Age; brittle surface. Treat as fragile: in US workplaces skylights must be guarded, screened or covered, and covers must carry at least twice the load that may be placed on them (OSHA 1910.29). | Protect them now with mesh, covers or guardrails, and plan replacement with non-fragile rated products. |
| Cracked domes and sheets across a roof after a storm | Hail. Storm date; damage on many units; exposed sheets worst. | Cover or protect the damaged units now, then replace them. |

sections.heading: Leaks at kerbs, seals and dormers
sections.markdown:
Kerbs that are too low let ponding water over the top; flashings lapped the wrong way direct water under the covering; sealant-only details last a few years before they leak. On profiled roofs, in-plane translucent sheets leak at their laps with the adjacent metal where the profiles do not match exactly, where fixings have loosened in the softer sheet, or where the sheet has shrunk and cracked around its fixings.

Atrium and patent glazing leak at gaskets, pressure plates, capping joints and the junctions between glazing bars, most often at the bottom of each slope, where water collects and runs over the transom, and at changes of slope and hips. Gaskets shrink and harden with UV, leaving gaps at corners; drainage channels inside the glazing bars, which carry away water that gets past the outer seal, block with dirt and overflow inward.

Dormers have more junctions per square metre than any other part of a roof: cheeks, sills, the dormer roof, its gutter and the window itself, each with its own flashings. Cheek flashings and sills leak, timber cheeks and sills decay, and dormers added in loft conversions can lack adequate support, trimming members or tie-down from the roof structure, showing as sagging or cracking around the opening.

Atrium roofs collect leaves, bird fouling and grit in their gutters and at the bottom of each slope, where they block drainage and hold water against seals. Cleaning access is often poor, so the maintenance that would prevent leaks is the maintenance that is skipped.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Leaks around a skylight kerb | Kerb flashing detail. Water test. | Rebuild the kerb with an upstand to current height and proper flashings. |
| Leaks at the bottom of atrium slopes | Gasket or pressure plate failure. Seals shrunk; water test. | Replace the gaskets and pressure plates, and clear the drainage channels. |
| Leaks at a translucent sheet lap with the adjacent metal | Profile mismatch or lap sealant failure. Sheet profile differs from the metal; sealant missing or perished. | Replace the sheet with one matching the metal profile, and reseal the laps. |
| Leaks at the bottom of a dormer cheek or around its window | Cheek and sill flashings. Water test at the cheek; decay in the dormer framing. | Renew the cheek and sill flashings, and replace decayed timber. |
| Water standing in atrium gutters after rain | Blocked or undersized gutters. Debris; outlet capacity against the atrium area. | Clear the gutters, and check outlet capacity against the atrium area. |
| Dormer roof sagging or cracking around the opening | Inadequate support from the roof structure. Trimming members and support checked from inside. | Add support where the roof structure was not adequately trimmed. |

sections.heading: Overhead glass and atrium structure
sections.markdown:
Overhead glass must stay in place when broken, which is why current codes require laminated glass or a protective screen. Monolithic toughened glass can break spontaneously from nickel sulphide inclusions and fall as a shower of small fragments; wired glass cracks from rusting wire at unsealed edges and from thermal stress where it is partly shaded; heat-strengthened or annealed glass can fall in large pieces. Laminated glass cracks but stays in the frame. Many older atria and canopies still have glass that would not be accepted overhead today.

Atrium roofs are carried on steel or aluminium frames that are themselves exposed to water from failed seals and condensation. Corrosion at gutters and bearings, and movement of the supporting structure, load the glazing and open joints.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cracked overhead pane with no impact | Thermal stress, wire corrosion or nickel sulphide. Glass type and fracture pattern. | Protect the area below now; read the fracture pattern, and reglaze with laminated glass. |

sections.heading: Condensation, heat and glare
sections.markdown:
Single-glazed skylights and uninsulated aluminium frames are the coldest surfaces in the roof. In humid spaces (pools, kitchens, bathrooms, crowded malls) condensation forms on them, runs down and drips, and is often mistaken for a leak. Thermally broken frames and insulated glazing reduce it.

Roof lights admit far more solar heat per square metre than walls or windows do. Large areas of older, clear roof lights overheat spaces below and load the air conditioning; retrofitted films and shading are common responses, and the heat load is often a reason to reduce roof light area at replacement ([Energy Efficiency Upgrades](https://moyneross.com/technical/energy-efficiency-upgrades)).

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Drips from frames in cold weather, no rain | Condensation. Cold frames; humid space. | Ventilate and control humidity in the space below. |
| Space overheating beneath clear roof lights | Solar gain. Temperatures follow the sun; roof light area large for the space. | Films or external shading now; fewer, better-performing units at replacement. |

sections.heading: Smoke vents
sections.markdown:
Many roof lights open, for ventilation or as automatic smoke vents that open in a fire to let smoke out of atria, stairs and large spaces. Actuators seize, seals perish, controls are disconnected during alterations, and vents are painted shut or fixed closed to stop leaks. A smoke vent that will not open is a failed fire safety system, not a weathering defect ([Smoke Management Systems](https://moyneross.com/technical/smoke-management-systems)).

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Smoke vent fails to open on test, or has been fixed shut | Actuator, control or seal failure; vent disabled to stop leaks. Test from the fire panel; actuator condition. | Repair or replace the actuator, seals and controls, reconnect the vent to the fire system, and test it. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unprotected fragile roof lights where people work; overhead glass that is not laminated over occupied areas, with breakage history | safety · 4 Essential | Protect now: mesh, covers, guardrails or restrict access. |
| Monolithic toughened or wired glass in overhead positions above occupied space | safety · 4 Essential | Protect below or replace with laminated glass. |
| Leaks damaging interiors | failure · 3 Important | Repair now. |
| Smoke vents that do not open, or have been disabled | failure · 4 Essential | Restore now; the building's fire strategy relies on them. |
| Smoke vent testing overdue under the fire safety maintenance regime | deadline · 4 Essential | Test by the due date. |
| Embrittled sheets; seals at end of life | condition · 3 Important | Replace in the near term. |
| Condensation dripping onto finishes or stock | condition · 2 Planned | Improve ventilation, heating or glazing in the near term. |
| Roof lights at age | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Replace on cycle, usually with the roof covering. |
| Overhead glass of unknown type in an atrium | check · 2 Planned | Identify glass type. |
| Minor discolouration | nil · 1 Routine | Clean. |

A roof light carries two kinds of finding. Its fragility and its overhead glass are about people and are graded on who is near it; its leaks and condition are about the building and are graded on what they are doing to it. The same roof light can be a safety finding and a lifecycle finding at once.

The grading follows what a finding demands, not the size of the eventual bill.

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A roofing surveyor inspects from safe access; a façade engineer inspects atrium glazing. The checks below start with fragility, then leaks, the dormers, overhead glass and smoke vents.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Inventory | Of every roof light with type, size, condition and protection. |
| Fragility assessment | From product data. |
| Glass identification | In atria and overhead glazing. |
| Water testing | Of kerbs and glazing joints. |
| Structural inspection | Of atrium framing. |
| Smoke vent function test | With the fire services contractor, operating each vent from the fire panel. |
| Drone survey | To count, map and photograph every roof light on large or fragile roofs without walking on them. |
| Dormer inspection from inside | Support members, decay and the junction with the roof structure. |
| Light transmission | And discolouration readings where daylight performance matters. |
| Atrium structure | Inspection of steel, gutters and bearings from access equipment. |
| Incident review | Falls and near misses on the roof. |

The report should give a roof light inventory with type, fragility, protection and condition; atrium glass types and any non-laminated overhead glass; leak paths found by testing; and the protection needed before anyone next works on the roof.

Every roof light is recorded, not a sample, because one unprotected fragile sheet is enough to cause a fall.

sections.heading: Protecting, repairing or replacing
sections.markdown:
Protection comes first and should never wait for replacement: mesh, covers or guardrails cost little per roof light. Repairs and replacement then follow what is failing, from kerbs and seals to embrittled sheets, overhead glass and smoke vents.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Protection first | Safety mesh under sheets, covers or guardrails around skylights and domes, and walkways that keep people away from them. | At once, wherever people work near fragile roof lights; inexpensive per roof light, and it should never wait for replacement. |
| Replacement with non-fragile rated products | Ideally with integral mesh, on a planned cycle so sheets do not reach the brittle stage. | Where sheets are embrittled or at the end of their life. |
| Kerb rebuild | Upstands to current heights and proper flashings, replacing sealant-only details. | Where kerbs leak or rely on sealant alone. |
| Atrium reglazing | Laminated glass, new gaskets and cappings, and cleared drainage channels; or protective screens below where reglazing must wait. | Where overhead glass is the wrong type, or seals and gaskets have failed. |
| Smoke vents | Repair or replace actuators, seals and controls, reconnect them to the fire system, and test on the required cycle. | Wherever vents fail to open, have been disabled, or testing is overdue. |
| Dormer repair | New cheek and sill flashings, decayed timber replaced, and support added where the roof structure was not adequately trimmed. | Where dormers leak, decay or sag. |
| Heat and glare control | Films, external shading, or fewer, better-performing units at replacement. | Where the spaces below overheat or glare. |
| Interim covers and exclusion zones | Covers over roof lights, and areas kept clear. | Where replacement is delayed. |

Choosing between them starts with people. Wherever anyone may work near a roof light, protect it now, whatever its condition. Then decide on condition: replace brittle sheets on a cycle, rebuild failing kerbs, reglaze atria with laminated glass, and restore any vent the fire strategy relies on.

Interactions: roof light replacement on industrial roofs is usually done with the roof covering, and with asbestos cement roofs it is part of the licensed removal; atrium reglazing needs protection and closures below; protection works are often the cheapest and most urgent part of any roof light scope. Replacement is also the time to reconsider the area and type of roof lights: fewer, better-performing units with integral fall protection usually cost less to run and maintain than a like-for-like replacement of every original sheet.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Replacement is priced per unit or by area; protection per unit or by length of guardrail. Access dominates. Atrium reglazing is a lump-sum project with protection to the floor below.

What drives the cost: access and protection over occupied space, the number and spread of roof lights, kerb rebuilding, and for atria the size and weight of the glass and the method of lifting it in. Commonly missed: interim covers or exclusion zones while replacement is awaited, cleaning access, and replacement of adjacent roof sheeting where profiles do not match.

Fall protection is code compliance; replacement is lifecycle; repairs are repairs and maintenance.

Safety mesh, covers and guardrails are inexpensive per roof light and should not wait for replacement. Atrium reglazing needs protection decks or scaffolds over occupied floors and out-of-hours work, which often exceed the cost of the glass. Industrial roof lights are usually replaced in the same contract as the roof covering, with licensed asbestos removal where the surrounding sheeting contains it.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a look from below cannot: which roof lights are certified non-fragile, what the overhead glass is, and which vents the fire strategy relies on. Ask for them before anyone works on the roof.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Roof light inventory with type, installation or replacement dates, and non-fragility certificates | Which roof lights are certified non-fragile, and how old each is. |
| Glass schedules for atria and any overhead glazing | Whether overhead glass is laminated, or a type that can fall. |
| Leak logs, especially for atria and dormers | Where leaks recur, especially in atria and dormers. |
| Fall protection installation and inspection records, and records of any falls or near misses on the roof | Whether fragile roof lights are protected, and whether anyone has fallen or nearly fallen. |
| Hazardous materials register for the surrounding roof sheeting | Whether the sheeting around the roof lights contains asbestos. |
| Atrium maintenance, cleaning and structural inspection records | Whether the atrium is cleaned, maintained and structurally inspected. |
| Smoke vent maintenance and test records, and the fire strategy showing which vents it relies on | Which vents the fire strategy relies on, and whether they work. |
| Any heat-load or daylighting assessment for the spaces below | Whether the spaces below overheat, and why. |
| Storm and hail claims affecting roof lights, and what was replaced | Which roof lights were damaged in storms, and what was replaced. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Roof lights are misread when their fragility is judged by how they look, and when a cracked overhead pane is assumed to have been hit by something.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| It looks strong enough to stand on | Treat every roof light and translucent sheet as fragile unless a certificate shows otherwise. Age makes them weaker, not stronger. |
| A fragility test will settle it | Reading fragility does not need a test. Assume any translucent sheet, dome or roof light is fragile unless a current non-fragility certificate says otherwise, and assume it is more fragile the older, yellower and more brittle it looks. The question is not whether it would hold a person, but whether anyone can walk or fall near it, and what stops them. |
| A cracked pane was hit by something | Fracture patterns in overhead glass follow the same reading as in vertical glazing: a pair of small fragments at a point of origin inside toughened glass points to a nickel sulphide inclusion; a single crack meeting the edge at right angles points to thermal stress; cracks radiating from a point point to impact. In wired glass, cracks starting at the edge with rust staining mean the wire has corroded where the edge was not sealed. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets standards for roof lights and overhead glazing, requires fragile surfaces to be protected, and requires smoke vents to be tested. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each, with energy and heritage rules.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Roof lights and glazing | AS 4285 covers skylights, and AS 1288 overhead glazing. | BS 5516 covers sloped glazing. | International Building Code Section 2405 covers sloped glazing and skylights. |
| Fragile surfaces | The work health and safety regulations and the Safe Work Australia code of practice on falls require fragile surfaces to be protected. | The Work at Height Regulations 2005 require fragile surfaces to be identified and protected; the Advisory Committee for Roofsafety publishes the standard test for non-fragility (ACR[M]001); the Construction (Design and Management) Regulations 2015 require fragile surfaces to be identified to anyone working on the roof. | OSHA 29 CFR 1910.28 and 1926.501 require skylights to be protected by covers, guardrails or screens. |
| Smoke vents | Where roof lights serve as smoke vents, they are essential safety measures maintained and tested to AS 1851. | Smoke vents required by Approved Document B must be maintained and tested under the Regulatory Reform (Fire Safety) Order 2005. | Smoke and heat venting follows NFPA 204 where required, with inspection and testing set by the fire code. |
| Energy and heritage | Energy provisions in Section J limit roof light area and set performance for larger installations. | Listed buildings need consent to alter historic lanterns, patent glazing and dormers. | The energy code limits skylight area and sets their thermal and solar performance. |

In strata and leasehold buildings in all three jurisdictions, roof lights over individual dwellings may belong to the dwelling while the roof is common property, which decides who pays.

sections.heading: Worked example: an atrium pane that cracked on its own
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 1990s office has a glazed atrium over its reception. One overhead pane has cracked with no sign of impact, there are drips at the bottom of two slopes after rain, and the glass schedule cannot be found. Elsewhere on the roof, yellowed and brittle polycarbonate roof lights sit on the route to rooftop plant.

The cracked pane comes first. A pair of small fragments at a point of origin would point to a nickel sulphide inclusion in toughened glass, and toughened glass can fall. Until the glass type is known, the area below is protected and the overhead glass is a check finding; if it proves to be monolithic toughened or wired glass above people, it is a safety finding. The drips at the bottom of the slopes point to the gaskets or pressure plates. The yellowed roof lights on the plant route are fragile and need protection now.

So the register carries the roof lights on the plant route and the area below the cracked pane as safety lines now, identification of the overhead glass as a check line, likely reglazing with laminated glass, and new gaskets and cappings for the leaking slopes.

pages.title: Slab on Ground
pages.question: How do ground slabs and warehouse floors fail, and which defects matter?
pages.answer: Fine shrinkage cracks are normal. What matters is movement and joints: curled panel edges rock and break under forklifts; open joints lose their arrises; fill settles and clay moves, dishing slabs and tilting racking; moisture rising through slabs without vapour barriers destroys new flooring. Never cut a slab before scanning for post-tensioning tendons. Warehouse floors must also be judged against the flatness the current racking and forklifts need.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about slab on ground; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Structural condition, joints, surface integrity

pages.searchTitle: Concrete slabs on ground: cracking, curling, joints, moisture and flatness

questions.question: Are cracks in a concrete slab serious?
questions.answer: Cracks that stay hairline and even are not moving; those that widen, displace or step across their length are. Gauge studs across a few cracks for several months settle it.

questions.question: Can I core or cut my concrete slab?
questions.answer: Not until drawings and scanning have confirmed there are no post-tensioning tendons or embedded services. Cutting a tendon is dangerous and weakens the slab.

questions.question: Why do slab corners rock under forklifts?
questions.answer: Curling: the panel edges lift as the slab dries. Grouting under the lifted panels and grinding the high edges corrects it.

questions.question: Why is new flooring blistering on our slab?
questions.answer: Usually moisture vapour coming through the slab. In-situ relative humidity testing confirms it, and a surface membrane goes down before new flooring.

questions.question: How long do industrial floor joints last?
questions.answer: Joints and arrises 10 to 25 years, joint sealants and fillers 5 to 10, and hardeners and coatings 5 to 15.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Slab problems show in the crack pattern, at the joints, in the floor levels and racking, and in floor finishes that blister or debond. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On site | Crack pattern: fine random, at re-entrant corners, along a line, or widening and displaced | Cracking, curling and settlement |
| On site | Joints: broken arrises, rocking panels, failed sealant, trip edges | Joints, surface wear and post-tensioning |
| On site | Floor levels: dishing, doming, steps; racking out of plumb | Cracking, curling and settlement |
| On site | Damp patches, efflorescence and blistered or debonded floor finishes | Moisture, flooring and termites |
| On site | Gaps between slab and walls; skirtings lifting | Cracking, curling and settlement |
| On site | Termite mud tubes at slab edges and penetrations | Moisture, flooring and termites |
| In the records | Slab design and loading, including racking and forklift loads | Investigation before the scope |
| In the records | Flatness specifications and surveys | Cracking, curling and settlement |
| In the records | Post-tensioning drawings | Joints, surface wear and post-tensioning |
| In the records | Floor finish failure history | Moisture, flooring and termites |
| In the records | Termite inspection records | Moisture, flooring and termites |
| In the records | Forklift operators avoiding certain joints or aisles, and goods damaged in transit across the floor, which are early operational signs of joint failure | Joints, surface wear and post-tensioning |

sections.heading: Types of slab
sections.markdown:
A slab-on-ground is a concrete floor cast directly on prepared ground, usually over a vapour barrier and compacted fill. In houses it is often also the footing, stiffened with edge and internal beams. In warehouses and industrial buildings it is a heavy-duty working surface carrying racking, forklifts and stored goods, with joints to control cracking and surface tolerances set for the equipment that runs on it.

| Type | Where it is found | Main issues |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stiffened raft and waffle pod slabs | Australian houses on reactive clays | Edge movement; cracking; termite entry at penetrations |
| Conventional slab with thickenings | Houses and low-rise | Settlement of fill; shrinkage cracking |
| Post-tensioned slab | Houses on expansive soils in the US; some commercial | Tendons must not be cut; corrosion at anchorages |
| Industrial floor slab, jointed | Warehouses, factories, retail | Joint damage from wheels; curling; flatness |
| Jointless steel-fibre slab | Modern warehouses | Random cracking; flatness |
| Older slabs without vapour barriers | Pre-1970s buildings | Moisture through the slab; rising damp; flooring failure |

Warehouse floors are increasingly specified for flatness because very narrow aisle forklifts and tall racking need level surfaces; a floor that was fine for its original use can be inadequate for a new tenant's equipment.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
A slab lasts the life of the building, but its working surface does not: industrial joints and arrises last ten to twenty-five years, hardeners and coatings five to fifteen, and joint sealants five to ten. In a warehouse, the joints and the flatness decide when work is due.

| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Concrete slab | Life of the building | Ground movement; load; moisture |
| Industrial joints and arrises | 10 to 25 years | Wheel traffic; joint design |
| Joint sealants and fillers | 5 to 10 years | Traffic; movement |
| Vapour barrier | Life of the slab if intact | Damage at construction |
| Floor hardeners and coatings | 5 to 15 years | Traffic; chemicals |

What shortens life: hard-wheeled forklifts crossing open joints, which break the edges; loads beyond design: heavier racking, point loads, storage; soil movement beneath the slab: reactive clay, fill settlement, leaking pipes; moisture rising through slabs without vapour barriers; chemicals: acids, sugars and oils attacking concrete surfaces.

The slab itself outlasts almost everything on it; the joints, surface and the ground beneath decide how long it stays serviceable for its use.

sections.heading: Cracking, curling and settlement
sections.markdown:
Concrete shrinks as it dries. Fine random cracks and cracks at re-entrant corners are normal; they matter only if they widen, displace or let water and termites through.

Slabs dry faster at the top than the bottom, so panel edges lift (curl). Joints then rock under traffic, break down and crack the slab beneath the curled edge.

Poorly compacted fill settles; reactive clay shrinks and swells; leaking under-slab pipes soften the ground. Slabs crack, dish or dome, and pull away from walls.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fine random cracks, no displacement | Drying shrinkage. Pattern; age; stability. | No structural repair; route and seal them where they affect finishes. |
| Panel corners rocking at joints | Curling. Level survey across joints. | Grout under the lifted panels and grind the high edges. |
| Slab dished near the centre or edges dropping | Settlement or clay shrinkage. Level survey and soil investigation, with offsets graded on the asset’s market’s floor scale (Thresholds by market). | Investigate the soil; lift and stabilise by injection, or manage the loads. |
| Racking leaning | Floor out of level or settlement under baseplates. Survey. | Survey the floor; add baseplates, relocate the racking, or stabilise the slab. |
| Cracks in a house slab that have opened over a year | Movement beyond drying shrinkage. Crack width graded on the asset’s market’s slab scale (Thresholds by market). | Monitor widths and levels, and have an engineer assess cracks in the moderate band or above. |

sections.heading: Joints, surface wear and post-tensioning
sections.markdown:
Forklift wheels hammer open joints, breaking the arrises (edges); sealants fail; load transfer dowels are missing or ineffective so panels move independently. Broken joints damage forklifts and goods and become trip hazards.

Dusting, scaling and delamination of weak or poorly finished surfaces; chemical attack in food and industrial plants; abrasion in heavy-traffic aisles.

Tendons in post-tensioned slabs carry very high forces. Drilling or cutting into them during alterations can release them violently and weaken the slab; anchorages corrode where water reaches them.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Broken joint edges in forklift aisles | Wheel impact on open joints. Joint width; forklift wheel type. | Rebuild the arrises; install armoured joints in heavy-traffic aisles. |

sections.heading: Moisture, flooring and termites
sections.markdown:
Moisture vapour rising through slabs without vapour barriers, or with damaged ones, debonds adhesives, swells timber and blisters vinyl and epoxy coatings. It is a common cause of flooring failure when old slabs get new finishes.

In termite regions, cracks, slab edges and service penetrations are hidden entry routes for subterranean termites into wall framing.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Floor finish blistering or debonding | Moisture vapour through the slab. In-situ relative humidity testing. | Test the slab's relative humidity; lay a surface membrane before new flooring. |
| New flooring planned over a recent or damp slab | Slab moisture not yet tested. In-situ relative humidity probes to ASTM F2170, read against the limit the flooring manufacturer sets. | Test before laying; use a moisture-tolerant system or a surface membrane where the reading exceeds the limit. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Trip edges in walkways; settlement under racking causing lean; damaged post-tensioning | safety · 4 Essential | Isolate area and fix now. |
| Slab broken up in operational aisles | failure · 3 Important | Repair now. |
| Joint deterioration; curling; moisture-driven flooring failures | condition · 3 Important | Repair in the near term. |
| Joint sealants and surface treatments at end of life | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Renew on cycle. |
| Slab capacity or flatness unknown for a new use | check · 3 Important | Survey and assess. |
| Fine shrinkage cracks | nil · 1 Routine | Seal where needed. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A structural or pavement engineer, with a flooring specialist for moisture problems. The checks below read the crack pattern and the floor levels, then confirm what is embedded in the slab before anything is cut.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Crack and joint mapping | Across the floor. |
| Level and flatness survey | Against the tolerance the use requires and, for house slabs, the asset’s market’s floor scale (Thresholds by market). |
| Joint condition | Arris damage, load transfer, rocking under load. |
| Moisture testing | By in-situ relative humidity probes to ASTM F2170 before new flooring, against the flooring manufacturer’s limit. |
| Cores | For thickness, strength and reinforcement. |
| Scanning | By ground-penetrating radar for tendons and services before cutting. |
| Under-slab services | CCTV and pressure testing where leaks are suspected. |
| Load assessment | Against racking and equipment loads. |
| Joint movement monitoring | With gauges where panels appear to be moving, to separate curling from settlement. |
| Termite inspection | At slab edges, penetrations and expansion joints in termite regions. |

The report should give the condition, flatness and capacity against the use, causes of distress, and repair options.

sections.heading: Repairing joints, levelling or replacing panels
sections.markdown:
Most slab work is repair to the surface and joints: rebuilding arrises, correcting curl and sealing cracks. Settlement, moisture and loading problems need investigating first, and nothing is cut or cored until tendons and services have been ruled out.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Joint repair | Rebuild broken arrises with polymer or epoxy mortars, install steel armoured joints in heavy-traffic aisles, and fill with semi-rigid fillers. | Where joints are broken or open in forklift aisles. |
| Curl correction | Grout under lifted panels and grind high edges. | Where panel corners rock at joints. |
| Crack repair | Routing and sealing, or epoxy injection. | Where cracks are moving, or affect finishes or traffic. |
| Slab lifting and stabilisation | Grout or polyurethane injection. | Where the slab has settled. |
| Grinding and toppings | Restore flatness. | Where the floor is out of level for its use. |
| Moisture mitigation | Surface membranes before new flooring. | Where moisture vapour through the slab defeats floor finishes. |
| Local replacement | Replace broken panels. | Where panels have broken up. |
| Termite management | At slab edges and penetrations. | In termite-prone areas. |
| Load management | Relocate heavy racking or point loads away from weak areas, add baseplates to spread loads, or restrict loads until strengthening. | Where loads exceed what the slab can carry. |
| Coatings and hardeners | Renew them in chemical and abrasion zones. | To protect the surface where it wears. |
| Under-slab pipe repair | Relining, or rerouting above the slab. | Where pipes beneath fail, avoiding breaking out the floor. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Surveys are lump sums. Joint repairs are priced by linear metre; armoured joints by length; panel replacement by area; grinding and toppings by area; moisture membranes by area. In operating warehouses, out-of-hours work and racking relocation add significantly.

Joint and surface renewal are repairs and maintenance or lifecycle; tenant-driven flatness upgrades sit with the tenancy; safety fixes are immediate.

Repairs timed around tenant shutdowns or between leases are usually far cheaper than work in a fully operating warehouse.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a walk across the floor cannot: what the slab was designed to carry, whether it is post-tensioned, and what the lease promises the tenant. Ask for them before any cutting, coring or change of use.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Slab design, loading and flatness specification | What the slab was designed to carry, and how flat it must be. |
| Post-tensioning drawings | Whether the slab is post-tensioned, and where the tendons run. |
| Flatness and level surveys | Whether the floor is still flat enough for its use. |
| Floor finish failure history | Whether moisture has defeated finishes before. |
| Termite inspection records | Whether termites have entered through the slab. |
| Racking and forklift specifications | What loads and wheels the slab now carries. |
| Previous repair records | What has already been repaired. |
| Lease clauses on floor loading and flatness | What loading and flatness a tenant may rely on. |
| Racking inspection reports noting floor issues | Whether racking safety is already affected. |
| Records of coring, cutting or slab penetrations | Whether the slab has been cut, and where. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Slabs are misread when every crack is taken as a sign of movement, and when a slab is cut before anyone has checked what is inside it.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| Every crack is movement | Cracks that widen, displace or step across their length are moving; cracks that stay hairline and even are not. Gauge studs across a few representative cracks for several months settle the question. |
| It is only concrete, so cut it | Never drill, core or saw a slab until the absence of post-tensioning tendons and embedded services has been confirmed by drawings and scanning. Cutting a tendon is dangerous and weakens the slab. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets design standards for slabs and industrial floors, and standards for finishes, moisture testing and termite management. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Design | AS 2870 governs residential slabs and AS 3600 concrete structures; Concrete Institute and CCAA guides cover industrial floors. | The Concrete Society's TR34 sets industrial floor design and flatness; BS EN 1992 covers concrete design. | ACI 360 covers slabs on ground and ACI 302.1 floor construction; PTI publishes design of post-tensioned slabs on expansive soils. |
| Finishes, moisture and termites | AS 3660.1 covers termite management at slab edges and penetrations. | BS 8204 covers screeds. | ASTM F2170 sets in-situ moisture testing. |

In all three jurisdictions, warehouse leases commonly specify the floor loading and flatness a tenant may rely on, and fit-out works that cut or core the slab need engineering approval. Racking installers and operators also have safety obligations for racking on uneven or damaged floors under workplace safety law, which can force floor repairs at short notice.

sections.heading: Worked example: rocking joints in a warehouse aisle
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 2000s warehouse slab has broken joint edges along its main forklift aisle, and panel corners rock as forklifts cross. Operators avoid two aisles, and a racking inspection has noted one bay leaning. The tenant now wants to core the slab for new services.

Rocking corners point to curling, and broken edges in the aisles to wheel impact on open joints. The leaning bay needs a survey of the floor beneath its baseplates. Before any coring, the absence of post-tensioning tendons and embedded services must be confirmed by drawings and scanning.

So the register carries the leaning racking as a safety line, joint repair with armoured joints and curl correction in the aisles as condition lines, and scanning before coring as a check line, with the lease checked for the flatness the tenant may rely on.

pages.title: Smoke Management Systems
pages.question: How do smoke management systems fail, and how do you know they will keep escape routes clear?
pages.answer: Smoke systems fail as systems, not components. Interfaces to the fire alarm and AHUs break, so fans do not start or AHUs feed the fire floor. Pressurised stairs drift too high (doors cannot be opened) or too low (smoke enters) as doors, seals and relief dampers change. Exhaust systems lose make-up air. Fans and dampers that run only in tests seize. Only an integrated test proves the system.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about smoke management systems; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Stair pressurisation, smoke spill fans, smoke curtains
