pages.searchTitle: Smoke control: stair pressurisation, smoke exhaust, dampers and integrated testing

questions.question: Why can't the stair doors be opened during a fire test?
questions.answer: Usually the stair pressure is too high, often after new seals or with a failed relief damper. Measure the door opening force, and rebalance the pressurisation.

questions.question: If every smoke fan runs, does the system work?
questions.answer: Not necessarily. A system that has not passed an integrated test since the last major change to the building is unproven, even if every fan runs on its own.

questions.question: How often should smoke control be tested?
questions.answer: Routine component tests, plus a full integrated test annually and after any change; in the United States, NFPA 92 sets semi-annual tests for dedicated systems and annual tests for non-dedicated ones.

questions.question: Why does smoke reach the stairs in a drill?
questions.answer: The stair pressure is too low, or the fans do not start on alarm. A pressure measurement and an interface test separate the two.

questions.question: How long does smoke control equipment last?
questions.answer: Smoke exhaust and pressurisation fans 20 to 25 years; dampers, actuators, curtains and control panels 15 to 20.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Smoke control problems show at the fire fan control panel, at stair doors during a test, and at fans, dampers, curtains and make-up air paths. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| In the building | Fire fan control panel showing faults or manual overrides | Interfaces and testing |
| In the building | Stair doors hard to open, whistling or slamming during tests | Stair pressure and make-up air |
| In the building | Smoke curtains obstructed by fittings; smoke dampers inaccessible | Equipment and alterations |
| In the building | Make-up air louvres blocked; car park storage blocking jet fans | Stair pressure and make-up air |
| In the building | Fans with belts missing or corroded casings | Equipment and alterations |
| In the records | Fire engineering report and smoke control design | Investigation before the scope |
| In the records | Integrated test reports, with pressures, airflows and door opening forces | Interfaces and testing |
| In the records | Routine service records for fans, dampers, curtains and vents | Equipment and alterations |
| In the records | Cause-and-effect matrix | Interfaces and testing |
| In the records | Annual certification | Standards by country |
| In the records | Relief dampers in stairs stuck open or closed | Stair pressure and make-up air |
| In the records | Fire fan control panel without current labelling or zone plans | Interfaces and testing |

sections.heading: Types of smoke control
sections.markdown:
Smoke management systems keep escape routes clear of smoke and give fire-fighters usable access. Smoke, not flame, kills most people in building fires, so these systems are central to life safety in tall, large and complex buildings. They include stair and lift shaft pressurisation; smoke exhaust from atria, malls and large spaces; zone smoke control using the air conditioning in fire mode; car park smoke exhaust and jet fan systems; smoke curtains and smoke doors; natural smoke vents (automatic opening vents in residential corridors and stairs); and the fire fan control panel and fire-rated wiring that run them.

| System | Where it is found | How it works |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stair pressurisation | Tall buildings in Australia, Britain and the US | Fans push air into stairs so smoke cannot enter when doors open |
| Zone smoke control | Offices with central air conditioning | Fire floor exhausted, adjacent floors pressurised, using AHUs in fire mode |
| Atrium and mall smoke exhaust | Shopping centres, atria, large halls | Fans or vents remove smoke from high level to keep a clear layer above people |
| Car park smoke and heat exhaust | Enclosed car parks | Ducted exhaust or jet fans move smoke to exhaust points |
| Smoke curtains | Atria, lift lobbies, shopfronts | Fabric barriers that drop on alarm to contain smoke |
| Automatic opening vents (AOVs) | Residential corridors and stairs, especially in Britain | Vents open on alarm to release smoke |
| Fire fan control panel | Buildings with mechanical smoke control | Manual override for fire-fighters, status indication |

Smoke systems are designed together with the building: door positions, leakage paths, air make-up and the fire detection cause-and-effect. Changes to any of these (new doors, new seals, enclosed atria, altered AHUs) can stop a system working as designed even though every fan runs.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Smoke control equipment lasts fifteen to twenty-five years: fans twenty to twenty-five, and dampers, curtains, vent actuators and control panels fifteen to twenty. A system's working life can end sooner, though, when the building around it changes and the design no longer fits.

| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Smoke exhaust and pressurisation fans | 20 to 25 years | Rarely run; motor and bearing condition |
| Smoke dampers and actuators | 15 to 20 years | Rarely operated; seize |
| Fire fan control panels | 15 to 20 years | Vendor support |
| Smoke curtains | 15 to 20 years | Fabric; motors; batteries |
| AOV actuators and controls | 15 to 20 years | Weather; operation |
| Fire-rated cabling | Life of the building | Damage; alterations |

What shortens life: disuse: fans and dampers that run only in tests seize; building changes that alter leakage and air paths; controls replacement that moves fire functions onto non-fire-rated systems; incomplete testing that checks components but not the system.

sections.heading: Interfaces and testing
sections.markdown:
Smoke systems start on a signal from the fire detection system. Changes to the fire panel, BMS or AHU controls break interfaces so fans do not start, start in the wrong mode, or AHUs keep supplying air to the fire floor. Fire functions moved onto a building management system that is not designed for fire duty may not work in a fire.

Testing fans and dampers individually does not show the system works. Only an integrated test, with the fire alarm triggering the full sequence and pressures, airflows and door forces measured, does.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| AHUs supply air to the fire floor in a test | Cause-and-effect fault. Integrated test. | Repair the interface, update the cause-and-effect matrix, and retest. |
| No pressure or airflow readings since commissioning | Performance unproven. US Department of Defense guidance operates dedicated smoke control systems semi-annually and others annually, recording airflows and pressure differences for comparison with acceptance results (UFM 3-601-02). | Commission a measured test, and keep the readings for comparison next time. |

sections.heading: Stair pressure and make-up air
sections.markdown:
Pressurised stairs must hold smoke back without making doors too hard to open: Australian, British and US standards cap door opening forces, at about 110, 100 and 133 newtons respectively. New door seals, closers and lobbies raise pressures until doors cannot be opened by occupants; failed relief dampers, missing doors and new openings drop pressures so smoke enters.

Exhaust systems need replacement air to move smoke. Make-up air paths blocked by new shopfronts, closed doors or failed inlet vents reduce exhaust to a fraction of design.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Stair doors cannot be opened during a test | Pressure too high (new seals, failed relief). Door opening force measurement against the limits for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Measure the opening force; rebalance the pressurisation, and repair or add relief dampers. |
| Smoke in stairs during a drill | Pressure too low or fans not starting. Pressure measurement; interface test. | Measure the pressure and test the interfaces; rebalance, or repair the fans. |
| Atrium smoke fills too low in modelling or tests | Make-up air shortfall or enclosure changes. Airflow measurement; layout review. | Measure the airflow; restore or add make-up air paths, and review the layout with a fire engineer. |

sections.heading: Equipment and alterations
sections.markdown:
Fans, dampers, curtains and vents operated only in tests seize, lose belts, or have motors that fail; smoke dampers corrode; curtains snag on new fittings.

Atria enclosed with new floors, malls subdivided, car parks partitioned for storage, and stair doors held open all change smoke behaviour against the design.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fans run but dampers stay shut | Seized dampers or actuator failure. Damper inspection. | Replace the seized dampers or actuators, and retest. |
| Smoke vent obstructed, or replaced with a smaller unit | Vent area short of the design. Free area measured against the design and the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Measure the free area, and restore it. |
| New plant or screens close to a smoke shaft head | Discharge compromised. Outlet height and clearances against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Survey the shaft head against the design, and move or remove obstructions. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| System does not start on alarm; stair doors cannot be opened; stair pressurisation failed; AOVs not opening | safety · 4 Essential | Rectify now; interim measures. |
| Routine and integrated testing due | deadline · 4 Essential | At the prescribed interval. |
| Fans or dampers failed | failure · 4 Essential | Repair now. |
| Equipment worn; partial interface faults | condition · 3 Important | Repair in the near term. |
| Equipment at end of life | lifecycle · 3 Important | Replace. |
| No integrated test since changes | check · 3 Important | Integrated test. |
| Normal | nil · 1 Routine | Routine. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A fire engineer leads, working from the fire engineering report or smoke control design, with a mechanical services engineer and the fire services contractor. Testing is done out of hours, with the fire brigade and monitoring centre notified. The checks below start with the integrated test record, then measure pressures, airflows and door opening forces.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Design review | The smoke control design basis, performance criteria (pressures, airflows, smoke layer heights), cause-and-effect, and any performance solutions that rely on the system. |
| Change review | Every alteration since design that could change smoke behaviour or air paths, including new doors and seals, enclosed atria, subdivided malls, car park storage, and replaced AHUs or controls. |
| Equipment inspection | Fans (bearings, belts, motors, temperature rating), smoke dampers and actuators, relief dampers, curtains, vents, fire fan control panel, fire-rated cabling and power supplies. |
| Integrated test | Initiated from the fire alarm in each smoke zone: confirm the full sequence starts, AHUs switch correctly, dampers move, curtains drop, vents open, and fire-fighters' overrides work. |
| Measurement | Stair pressure differentials with doors open and closed, door opening forces at every stair door, exhaust and make-up airflows, and car park jet fan coverage, against the limits for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). |
| Secondary power | Confirm the system runs from the emergency supply where required. |

The report should state whether the system meets its design performance today, list every failed function and measurement, identify changes that have compromised it, and set out rectification or redesign.

sections.heading: Repairing, rebalancing or redesigning
sections.markdown:
Everything here turns on the integrated test: a system that has not passed one since the building last changed is unproven. Repairs and rebalancing follow what that test measures, and a redesign follows major alterations.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Repair interfaces | Repair interfaces and update the cause-and-effect matrix; return fire functions from general building management controls to fire-rated controls where they were moved. | Wherever the system does not start, or starts the wrong things, on alarm. |
| Rebalance stair pressurisation | Adjust fan speed, add or repair barometric relief dampers, or add variable speed control. | So pressure holds smoke back and door opening forces stay within limits. |
| Restore make-up air | Reopen or add inlet paths, automate inlet doors and vents, and remove obstructions. | Where make-up air is short. |
| Replace equipment | Fans with temperature-rated units, seized dampers and actuators, curtain motors and batteries, and vent actuators. | Where equipment has seized, failed or reached the end of its life. |
| Car parks | Clear storage and partitions from jet fan paths; reposition or add fans. | Where storage or partitions block the jet fans. |
| Redesign after major alterations | A fire engineer revises the design and performance solution. | After alterations that change the spaces the system serves. |
| Testing regime | Routine component tests, plus a full integrated test annually and after any change. | Always. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Routine servicing and integrated testing are recurring costs; integrated tests need several trades present out of hours. Interface and controls repairs are itemised or lump sums. Equipment replacement is per item, with temperature-rated fans and dampers costing more than standard equipment. Rebalancing is a lump sum. Redesign after alterations is a lump-sum fire engineering and construction project, usually carried by the alteration that caused it.

Testing and safety rectification are code compliance; equipment replacement is lifecycle; repairs are repairs and maintenance.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a look at the fans cannot: whether the system has passed an integrated test since the building last changed, and what that test measured. Ask for them before relying on the annual certificate.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Fire engineering report and smoke control design, including performance solutions | What the system is designed to do, and what the building's approval relies on. |
| Commissioning report and latest integrated test report, with measured pressures, airflows and door forces | Whether the system works as a whole, with measured pressures, airflows and door forces. |
| Routine service records for fans, dampers, curtains, vents and the fire fan control panel | Whether fans, dampers, curtains and vents are serviced. |
| Cause-and-effect matrix | What the alarm should start and stop. |
| Annual certification | Whether the system was certified at its last review. |
| Records of alterations since the system was commissioned | Whether the building has changed since the system was proved. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Smoke control is misread when every fan running is taken to mean the system works, when a stair door that is hard to open is taken as a door fault, and when smoke in a stair is blamed on weak fans.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| Every fan runs, so it works | A smoke system that has not passed an integrated test since the last major change to the building should be treated as unproven, even if every fan runs on its own. |
| The stair door is faulty | A stair door that cannot be opened during a test usually points to pressure that is too high, from new seals or a failed relief damper. Measuring the door opening force settles it. |
| Smoke in the stair means weak fans | It may be pressure that is too low, or fans that do not start on alarm. A pressure measurement and an interface test separate the two. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets where smoke control is required, standards for its design and components, and how it is tested and maintained. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Requirements | The National Construction Code sets smoke hazard management by building class and height (Part E2); performance solutions often rely on smoke control. | Approved Document B, BS 9999 and BS 9991 set requirements. | International Building Code Section 909 governs smoke control. |
| Design and components | AS 1668.1 sets the design of smoke control systems and the door opening force limit for pressurised stairs. | The BS EN 12101 series covers smoke control components, including pressure differential systems in BS EN 12101-6. | NFPA 92 sets design; NFPA 101 limits door opening forces. |
| Testing and maintenance | AS 1851 sets routine service; smoke control systems are essential safety measures with annual certification. | Responsible persons must keep systems maintained, and the Fire Safety (England) Regulations 2022 require higher-risk residential buildings to report defects in key fire safety equipment. | NFPA 92 sets testing, with dedicated systems tested semi-annually and non-dedicated systems annually; NFPA 4 covers integrated testing of fire protection and life safety systems. |

sections.heading: Worked example: stair doors that will not open after a refurbishment
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 1990s office tower had its stair doors refitted with new seals during a refurbishment. In the next fire drill, wardens struggled to open several stair doors against the pressurisation. The last integrated test predates the refurbishment, and the relief dampers have not been checked since.

Doors that cannot be opened point to pressure that is too high: new seals make the stairs tighter, and a relief damper stuck shut cannot release the excess. Stair doors that cannot be opened are a safety finding. And with the building changed since its last integrated test, the whole system is unproven.

So the register carries the stair doors as a safety line now, rebalancing the pressurisation with the relief dampers repaired, and a full integrated test, with measured pressures, airflows and door forces, as a deadline line.

thresholds.rule: Door opening force at the handle no more than 110 N; air flowing through open stair doors at 1 m/s

source.title: Stair pressurisation performance in high-rise buildings (Fire, 2023, 6(4), 132)

thresholds.rule: Corridor or lobby vent on an external wall: free area at least 1.5 m²; smoke shaft: section at least 1.5 m², with vents of at least 1 m²

source.title: Approved Document B, Volume 1: Dwellings (2026 online version)

thresholds.rule: At least 0.5 m above surrounding structures within 2 m, and at least 2.5 m above the ceiling of the highest storey served

pages.title: Solar Photovoltaic (PV) Systems
pages.question: How do rooftop solar systems fail, and what risks do they bring to the roof and building?
pages.answer: Solar arrays fail at their electronics and connections more than their panels. Inverters fail at 10 to 15 years and generation stops silently. Mismatched or wet DC connectors and rooftop DC isolators arc and start roof fires. Panels degrade slowly, faster with hot spots and cracks. Arrays leak at penetrations, hide the roof covering, add load, and must be removed for re-roofing. Burnt connectors or isolators mean isolate now.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about solar photovoltaic (pv) systems; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.

questions.question: Are burnt solar isolators dangerous?
questions.answer: Yes. Burnt or discoloured DC isolators and connectors are a fire hazard; have a qualified person isolate the array, since DC wiring stays live while the sun shines.

questions.question: Why is our solar output low?
questions.answer: Compare the strings: one weak string points to a fault in that string, while uniform decline points to soiling, degradation or the inverter.

questions.question: How long do solar inverters last?
questions.answer: String and central inverters 10 to 15 years, and microinverters and optimisers 15 to 25; modules 25 to 30.

questions.question: What happens to solar panels when the roof is replaced?
questions.answer: The array is removed and reinstated for the re-roofing; the ownership or lease terms decide who pays and arranges it.

questions.question: Do solar arrays need rapid shutdown?
questions.answer: In the United States, NFPA 70 Article 690 requires rapid shutdown at the roof to protect fire-fighters.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Solar problems show on the roof as damaged modules, burnt connectors, loose frames and leaks, at the inverter as fault lights, and in generation data against what the array should produce. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On the roof | Discoloured, cracked or burnt modules; hot spots on thermal imaging | Inverters, modules and soiling |
| On the roof | Cables lying on the roof surface; connectors in water | DC fire risk, batteries and firefighting |
| On the roof | Burnt or discoloured DC isolators and connectors | DC fire risk, batteries and firefighting |
| On the roof | Corroded frames and clamps; loose modules | Roof, frames and compliance |
| On the roof | Debris and bird nesting under arrays | Roof, frames and compliance |
| On the roof | Leaks below mounting penetrations | Roof, frames and compliance |
| At the inverter | Error lights and fault codes | Inverters, modules and soiling |
| At the inverter | Inverter in direct sun or a hot room | Inverters, modules and soiling |
| At the inverter | Monitoring showing zero or reduced generation | Inverters, modules and soiling |
| In the records | Generation data against expected output | Inverters, modules and soiling |
| In the records | Installation certificates and compliance documents | Investigation before the scope |
| In the records | Roof structural assessment for the array | Roof, frames and compliance |
| In the records | Power purchase or lease agreements | Roof, frames and compliance |
| In the records | Battery installation and compliance records | DC fire risk, batteries and firefighting |

sections.heading: Types of solar installation
sections.markdown:
A solar photovoltaic system generates electricity from sunlight. It comprises modules (panels) on mounting frames, DC cabling and connectors, DC isolators, inverters (string inverters, microinverters or optimisers with a central inverter) that convert DC to AC, AC connection to a switchboard, metering, monitoring, and often batteries. Systems on roofs interact with the roof covering, structure, lightning protection and fire-fighting access.

| Form | Where it is found | Character |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Residential rooftop with string inverter | Houses | Small; inverter is the weak point |
| Microinverters or optimisers | Houses and commercial from the 2010s | Module-level electronics on the roof; more parts, better shading performance |
| Commercial rooftop arrays | Warehouses, retail, offices | Large; penetrations or ballast on the roof; roof replacement interaction |
| Ballasted arrays on flat roofs | Commercial flat roofs | No penetrations; weight and wind uplift |
| Battery systems | Houses and commercial | Fire risk; location and separation rules |
| Building-integrated PV | Façades and canopies | Part of the envelope |

Ownership varies. Arrays may be owned outright, leased, or installed under a power purchase agreement with a third party that owns the equipment and holds rights over the roof; these arrangements constrain re-roofing and sale.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Modules last twenty-five to thirty years, losing about half a per cent of output a year, and their frames as long, but string and central inverters last only ten to fifteen. The roof beneath often needs replacing before the array does.

| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Modules | 25 to 30 years, losing about half a per cent of output a year | Quality; heat; defects |
| String and central inverters | 10 to 15 years | Heat; surges |
| Microinverters and optimisers | 15 to 25 years | Heat on the roof |
| Mounting frames | 25 to 30 years | Coastal exposure; fixings |
| DC connectors and isolators | 10 to 25 years | Installation quality; water ingress |
| Batteries | 10 to 15 years | Chemistry; cycling; heat |

What shortens life: poor installation: mismatched connectors, cables on roof surfaces, isolators exposed to sun and water; heat on inverters mounted in sun or in hot rooms; coastal exposure on frames and fixings; shading and soiling that cause hot spots; wind on poorly fixed or ballasted arrays.

sections.heading: DC fire risk, batteries and firefighting
sections.markdown:
DC circuits on roofs carry high voltages that arc when a connection is poor. Mismatched connectors from different manufacturers, poorly crimped connectors, and rooftop DC isolators that take in water have caused roof fires. In Australia, rooftop DC isolators were a known fire source and are no longer mandatory under the current PV array standard.

Arrays generate DC voltage whenever there is light, so fire-fighters cannot simply isolate them. Without rapid shutdown, labelling and clear access pathways, fire services may limit roof operations on buildings with arrays.

Lithium battery systems can enter thermal runaway, producing fire and toxic gases; location, separation and ventilation rules apply.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Burn marks at isolators or connectors | DC arcing. Inspection. | Have a qualified person isolate the array; replace with matched, correctly installed parts. |
| Rooftop DC isolators cracked, discoloured or full of water | Isolator failure and fire risk. Inspection of enclosures and terminals. | Replace the isolators with suitable rated units, protected from weather. |
| Battery installed in a habitable room, escape path or unventilated space | Battery location against the standard. Location, clearances and enclosure against AS/NZS 5139. | Relocate or enclose the battery as the standard requires. |

sections.heading: Inverters, modules and soiling
sections.markdown:
Inverters are the commonest failure: electronics fail from heat, surges and age, typically within 10 to 15 years. A failed inverter stops generation without any visible sign on the roof.

Modules lose output slowly; defects accelerate it: hot spots from cell cracks or shading, potential-induced degradation, delamination, moisture ingress, junction box failures, and microcracks from hail or foot traffic.

Bypass diodes in module junction boxes let current pass shaded or damaged cells; when they fail, sections of a module overheat or stop producing. Junction boxes that lose their seal let in water and can arc.

Dust, bird droppings and leaves reduce output and create hot spots; birds nesting under arrays damage cabling and block drainage on the roof below.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No generation; inverter fault light | Inverter failure. Error codes; monitoring. | Replace the inverter, and add monitoring with alerts. |
| Output below expected | Shading, soiling, degradation or string fault. String measurements; thermal imaging. | Compare the strings; clean, trim shading, or repair the weak string. |
| Hot cells on thermal image | Cell cracks or shading. Thermography; electroluminescence. | Replace the defective modules. |
| Monitoring offline or showing no data | Faults going unnoticed. Monitoring connection and history. | Restore monitoring, and set alerts for zero or low output. |

sections.heading: Roof, frames and compliance
sections.markdown:
Penetrations for mounting leak if poorly flashed; frames trap debris and water; roof coverings under arrays cannot be inspected or maintained; re-roofing requires removal and reinstatement of the array. Arrays add load the roof structure must carry, and ballasted arrays can shift in wind.

Dissimilar metals, poor fixings and coastal air corrode frames and clamps; modules can come loose in wind.

Inverters must meet grid connection standards and network settings; older inverters may not meet current requirements, and export limits may constrain output.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Roof leaks under the array | Mounting penetrations. Water test. | Reseal the penetrations, or remove and reinstate the array at re-roofing. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Burnt connectors or isolators; exposed live DC; loose modules; battery overheating | safety · 4 Essential | Isolate now. |
| Inverter failed; no generation | failure · 3 Important | Repair or replace now. |
| Degradation, corrosion, leaks | condition · 2 Planned | Repair in the near term. |
| Inverters at end of life; array at end of life | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Replace on cycle. |
| Roof structure not assessed; PPA terms unknown | check · 2 Planned | Assess. |
| Normal | nil · 1 Routine | Clean and maintain. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A licensed solar installer or electrical engineer. The checks below compare generation with what the array should produce, string by string, then inspect the DC connectors, isolators and roof penetrations.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Generation analysis | Against expected output for the system size, orientation and weather. |
| Visual and thermographic inspection | Of modules, connectors, isolators, cabling and frames. |
| String testing | Open-circuit voltage, current, insulation resistance. |
| Inverter inspection | And fault history. |
| Roof inspection | Penetrations, covering under the array, structural capacity. |
| Compliance check | Against grid connection and installation standards. |
| Contract review | Ownership, leases, PPAs. |
| Electroluminescence imaging | Where cracks or hail damage are suspected. |
| Earth fault and insulation testing | Of DC circuits. |
| Battery inspection | Location, separation, ventilation, detection and the battery management system's fault history. |
| Fire service access | Rapid shutdown, labelling and roof pathways where required. |

The report should state generation performance against expectation, safety defects, roof and structural effects, compliance, and the remaining life of inverters and modules.

sections.heading: Making safe, repairing or replacing
sections.markdown:
Burnt connectors and isolators come first: the array is isolated by a qualified person, since DC wiring stays live while the sun shines. After that, monitoring finds failed inverters quickly, and the array is planned around the roof beneath it.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Replace connectors and isolators | Matched, correctly installed parts. | Wherever connectors or isolators are burnt or discoloured. |
| Inverter replacement | A new inverter. | Where the inverter has failed or reached the end of its life. |
| Module replacement | Replace defective modules. | Where modules are cracked, burnt or show hot spots. |
| Cable management | Lift cables off roof surfaces. | Where cables lie on the roof or connectors sit in water. |
| Frame repairs | Repair and refix the frames. | Where frames and clamps corrode or modules are loose. |
| Cleaning | Clean the modules. | Where soiling cuts output. |
| Array removal and reinstatement | Remove and reinstate the array. | For re-roofing. |
| Battery relocation | Relocate or separate batteries. | Where their location does not meet the rules. |
| Labelling and shutdown | Labels for fire services and rapid shutdown where codes require it. | Wherever codes require it, and for the safety of fire services. |
| Monitoring | Monitoring with alerts. | So failed inverters are found within days, not months. |
| Bird proofing | Proof the array's edges. | To stop nesting and cable damage. |

Interactions: re-roofing under an array means removal, storage and reinstatement by a licensed installer, recommissioning, and often updating to current standards; batteries may need relocation; lightning protection must bond the array.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Inverter replacement is priced per inverter and recurs at 10 to 15 years, so it belongs in the register as a recurring line. Module replacement is per module, often limited by matching availability. Connector, isolator and cabling remediation is priced per string. Array removal and reinstatement for re-roofing is a lump sum that can be a large share of a re-roofing project and should sit in the roof line. Monitoring and cleaning recur. Batteries are replaced on their own cycle.

Inverter and battery replacement are lifecycle; DC fire-risk rectification is immediate; repairs and cleaning are repairs and maintenance. Under a power purchase agreement, many of these costs sit with the system owner, and the register should say so.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a look at the roof cannot: whether the array generates what it should, who owns it and the roof beneath, and whether the roof was assessed to carry it. Ask for them before any re-roofing.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Installation certificates, single-line diagrams and compliance documents | How the array is wired, and whether it was certified. |
| Generation monitoring data since installation | Whether the array produces what it should. |
| Inverter, module and workmanship warranties | What is still under warranty. |
| Roof structural assessment for the array | Whether the roof was checked to carry the array. |
| Ownership, lease or power purchase agreement terms, including roof access and re-roofing provisions | Who owns the array, and who pays to move it for re-roofing. |
| Network connection approval and export limits | How much the array may export. |
| Battery installation compliance and location records | Whether batteries are installed where the rules allow. |
| Maintenance and cleaning records | Whether the array is cleaned and maintained. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Solar arrays are misread when burnt connectors are treated as a fault to schedule, and when total output is read without comparing the strings that make it up.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| A burnt connector can wait | Burnt or discoloured DC isolators and connectors are a fire hazard. The array should be isolated by a qualified person until repaired; DC wiring stays live while the sun shines. |
| Total output tells the story | Comparing strings tells you more than the total: one weak string points to a fault in that string; uniform decline points to soiling, degradation or the inverter. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets standards for PV installation and safety, inverters and grid connection, and batteries. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Installation and safety | AS/NZS 5033 governs PV array installation, and its current edition no longer requires rooftop DC isolators. | BS 7671 Section 712 covers PV installations; the IET Code of Practice for grid-connected solar PV sets practice. | NFPA 70 Article 690 governs PV systems, including rapid shutdown at the roof to protect fire-fighters; UL 61730 lists modules and UL 1741 inverters. |
| Inverters, batteries and connection | AS/NZS 4777.1 and 4777.2 cover inverter installation and grid performance; AS/NZS 5139 covers battery installation and location; installers must be accredited under the national solar accreditation scheme; network service providers set export limits and connection requirements. | MCS certification is needed for most incentive schemes; connection follows Engineering Recommendations G98 and G99; fire-safety guidance addresses PV on roofs. | IEEE 1547 sets interconnection; the International Fire Code sets rooftop access pathways and setbacks. |

sections.heading: Worked example: an array that went quiet
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A warehouse's rooftop array has produced almost nothing for four months, unnoticed because no one reads the monitoring. The inverter shows a fault light, one DC isolator on the roof is discoloured, and the roof beneath the array is due for replacement within five years.

The discoloured isolator comes first: it is a fire hazard, and the array is isolated by a qualified person until it is repaired. The fault light points to a failed inverter, which went unnoticed for months without alerts. The roof's remaining life means the array will need removing and reinstating.

So the register carries the isolator as a safety line now, inverter replacement with monitoring alerts, and array removal and reinstatement planned with the re-roofing, with the ownership terms checked for who pays.

pages.title: Specialised Occupancy Areas
pages.question: How do laboratories, clinical spaces and teaching rooms fail, and which findings are safety-critical?
pages.answer: Specialised spaces fail when their critical services drift or their use changes. Fume cupboards lose containment as exhaust weakens; emergency showers go untested and deliver stagnant water; medical gas systems are altered without certification; isolation rooms lose pressure; classrooms echo and get stuffy as occupancy rises. Spaces converted to new uses without upgraded services fall short. Fume cupboard, safety shower, medical gas and ligature findings are safety-critical.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about specialised occupancy areas; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Classrooms, lecture theatres, laboratories, wards, purpose-built spaces

pages.searchTitle: Laboratories, clinical and teaching spaces: fume cupboards, medical gases, isolation rooms

questions.question: What should happen when a fume cupboard alarms?
questions.answer: Take it out of use, test the face velocity and the duct, and rebalance or replace the fan before it is used again.

questions.question: Why does the safety shower run brown?
questions.answer: Water stagnating between tests. Activate it weekly, flush until clear, and keep a log.

questions.question: Who can work on medical gas systems?
questions.answer: Specialists, under a permit, with the system tested and recertified after any change.

questions.question: Why are classrooms tiring by the afternoon?
questions.answer: Often low outdoor air as occupancy rises, with noise or echo making speech hard to follow. Measure carbon dioxide and reverberation.

questions.question: How long do fume cupboards last?
questions.answer: Laboratory fit-outs and fume cupboards last 15 to 25 years, and emergency showers 15 to 20.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Problems in specialised spaces show at fume cupboards, showers, gas outlets and nurse call points, in finishes and fittings, in rooms that echo or go stuffy, and in test and accreditation records. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On site | Fume cupboard test labels and face velocity indicators; alarms sounding or silenced | Laboratories: exhaust, showers and chemicals |
| On site | Safety showers and eyewash blocked, untested, or without test tags | Laboratories: exhaust, showers and chemicals |
| On site | Chemicals stored on benches and floors rather than in ventilated cabinets | Laboratories: exhaust, showers and chemicals |
| On site | Medical gas outlets, alarms and zone valves: labelling, damage, test records | Healthcare: medical gases, infection control and ligatures |
| On site | Damaged clinical flooring and walls; open seams | Healthcare: medical gases, infection control and ligatures |
| On site | Classrooms that echo or are stuffy when full | Teaching spaces |
| On site | Nurse call points missing or not working; ligature points in sensitive areas | Healthcare: medical gases, infection control and ligatures |
| In the records | Fume cupboard performance tests | Laboratories: exhaust, showers and chemicals |
| In the records | Safety shower and eyewash test logs | Laboratories: exhaust, showers and chemicals |
| In the records | Medical gas certification and permits | Healthcare: medical gases, infection control and ligatures |
| In the records | Isolation room pressure monitoring | Healthcare: medical gases, infection control and ligatures |
| In the records | Nurse call test records | Healthcare: medical gases, infection control and ligatures |
| In the records | Accreditation reports | Healthcare: medical gases, infection control and ligatures |

sections.heading: What the space does and what it contains
sections.markdown:
Specialised occupancy areas are purpose-built spaces whose function sets demanding requirements: classrooms and lecture theatres in education buildings, laboratories in research, education and industry, and wards, treatment rooms and clinical spaces in healthcare and aged care. Each depends on services and finishes that ordinary space does not need, such as fume extraction, emergency showers, medical gases, nurse call, infection-control finishes, acoustic performance and controlled ventilation. They are judged on whether they still meet the standards of their use, which change faster than the buildings that house them.

| Space | Critical provisions | What commonly fails |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Classrooms | Acoustics, ventilation, daylight, power and AV | Noise and reverberation; stuffiness; worn finishes |
| Lecture theatres | Raked seating, AV, egress, acoustics, ventilation | Ageing AV; seating; air supply for full rooms |
| Teaching and research laboratories | Fume cupboards, exhaust, gases, emergency showers and eyewash, chemical storage, acid-resistant drainage | Exhaust performance; untested safety showers; chemical storage |
| Hospital wards and clinical rooms | Medical gases, nurse call, infection-control finishes, pressure-controlled rooms | Gas system compliance; finishes; isolation room pressures |
| Aged care rooms | Nurse call, accessible bathrooms, tempered water, falls prevention | Nurse call coverage; scalding risk; trip hazards |
| Mental health spaces | Ligature-resistant fittings and safe design | Ligature points; damaged fittings |

sections.heading: How long it stays fit for purpose
sections.markdown:
Laboratory fit-outs, fume cupboards and medical gas outlets last fifteen to twenty-five years and emergency showers fifteen to twenty, while nurse call systems last ten to fifteen and classrooms are refurbished every fifteen to twenty. A change in how the space is used ends its fitness for purpose more often than wear.

| Component or quality | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Laboratory fit-out and fume cupboards | 15 to 25 years | Research needs; exhaust performance |
| Emergency showers and eyewash | 15 to 20 years | Testing; water quality |
| Medical gas outlets and alarms | 15 to 25 years | Compliance; clinical change |
| Nurse call systems | 10 to 15 years | Vendor support |
| Classroom refurbishment | 15 to 20 years | Pedagogy; technology |
| Lecture theatre AV | 7 to 10 years | Technology |
| Clinical finishes (sheet vinyl, wall protection) | 10 to 20 years | Cleaning regimes; damage |

What shortens fitness for purpose: changing use: new research, teaching methods or models of care that the space was not built for; rising standards for safety, infection control and ventilation; intensive cleaning with aggressive chemicals in clinical areas; technology turnover in AV, nurse call and laboratory equipment.

sections.heading: Laboratories: exhaust, showers and chemicals
sections.markdown:
Fume cupboards must draw air in at a set face velocity to contain fumes. Exhaust fans that weaken, dampers that drift, too many cupboards on one system, and changes to room supply air reduce containment, exposing users to chemicals. Discharge stacks too low or near intakes re-entrain exhaust into the building.

Safety showers and eyewash stations that are not run regularly deliver stagnant, contaminated or no water when needed; those with blocked paths or no tempered water are unusable in an emergency.

A fume cupboard protects its user only while air flows into it at the right speed. That flow depends on the fan, the dampers, how many cupboards share the system and the room's supply air, so containment drifts with any of them, and only a face velocity test shows where it stands.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fume cupboards alarming low flow | Exhaust fan, damper or balancing problem. Face velocity and duct tests. | Take the cupboard out of use; test face velocity and the duct, then rebalance or replace the fan. |
| Chemical odours in corridors | Exhaust re-entrainment or containment failure. Smoke tests; stack location. | Smoke test the containment; raise or relocate the stack away from intakes. |
| Brown water from safety shower | Stagnation from infrequent testing. Test log. | Activate it weekly, flush until clear, and keep a test log. |
| Chemicals stored on benches and floors | No ventilated, segregated storage. Containers outside cabinets, and incompatible chemicals together. | Provide ventilated, segregated cabinets and stores. |
| Fume cupboard face velocity never tested, or tested years ago | Containment unverified. Face velocity and containment test against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Test every cupboard, repair or replace failures, and set an annual test. |

sections.heading: Healthcare: medical gases, infection control and ligatures
sections.markdown:
Oxygen, medical air, vacuum and other gases are life-critical. Leaks, failed alarms, incorrectly labelled outlets, and works without permits create clinical and fire risks. Medical gas systems need specialist testing and certification after any change.

Damaged finishes, open joints in flooring, porous surfaces, and isolation rooms that have lost their pressure differentials undermine infection control in healthcare and aged care.

In mental health and some aged care settings, fittings that can be used as ligature points, and damaged or replaced fittings that reintroduce them, are serious patient safety risks.

Healthcare spaces carry services patients depend on: gases that must flow and alarm correctly, rooms that must hold their pressure, and fittings that must not become ligature points. Each is life-critical, which is why work on them runs under permits and specialist testing.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Isolation room pressure alarms | Door seals, supply and exhaust balance. Pressure monitoring. | Restore the door seals and the supply and exhaust balance, and keep monitoring. |
| A medical gas outlet without a clear label, or an alarm panel in fault | A medical gas system out of control. Labels missing or wrong, and alarms untested. | Have a medical gas specialist test and certify it, under permit. |
| Open seams in clinical sheet flooring | Infection-control finishes that have failed. Joints lifting at seams and coving. | Replace with seamless flooring and coved skirtings. |

sections.heading: Teaching spaces
sections.markdown:
Classrooms with long reverberation and noisy ventilation make speech hard to understand; rooms with low outdoor air become stuffy as occupancy rises, with measurable effects on learning.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Classroom complaints of noise and fatigue | Reverberation, ventilation noise or low outdoor air. Acoustic and CO₂ measurement. | Measure reverberation and carbon dioxide; add acoustic treatment, quieter ventilation and more outdoor air. |

sections.heading: Change of use
sections.markdown:
The most common finding in specialised spaces is a space doing a job it was not built for. A laboratory in an old office or a repurposed ward can look right and still lack the exhaust, gases, drainage or safety equipment the new use needs.

Laboratories converted from offices, wards repurposed, and classrooms subdivided without upgrading services often fall short of what the new use requires.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| An office floor now used as a laboratory, or a repurposed ward | A change of use the services never followed. Exhaust, gases, drainage or safety equipment unchanged from the old use. | Review the services against the new use, and upgrade them. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fume cupboards failing containment; untested or blocked safety showers; medical gas faults; ligature points in mental health areas | safety · 4 Essential | Take out of use and rectify now. |
| Critical service failed (exhaust, gases, nurse call) | failure · 3 Important | Restore now. |
| Statutory testing, certification or accreditation due | deadline · 3 Important | At the prescribed interval. |
| Worn finishes; acoustic and ventilation shortfalls | condition · 2 Planned | Improve in the near term. |
| Fit-out and specialist equipment at end of life | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Refurbish. |
| Use changed without a review of services | check · 2 Planned | Assess. |
| Normal | nil · 1 Routine | Routine. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A building services engineer with specialists for laboratories, medical gases, acoustics or healthcare engineering, working with the users' safety officers. The checks below start by comparing what each space is used for with what it was designed for, then test the critical services: exhaust, showers, gases, pressures and nurse call.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Use review | What each space is now used for against what it was designed for. |
| Laboratory safety testing | Fume cupboard face velocity and containment, exhaust system capacity, stack discharge, safety showers and eyewash, chemical storage and gas systems. |
| Healthcare engineering review | Medical gas testing and certification, isolation room pressures and air changes, nurse call coverage, infection-control finishes. |
| Teaching space review | Reverberation time, background noise, CO₂ in use, lighting and AV. |
| Patient safety review | For ligature risk in relevant settings. |
| Records and accreditation review | . |

The report should list safety items for immediate action, compliance and accreditation status, and a refurbishment programme aligned with users' plans.

sections.heading: Testing, restoring and upgrading for the use
sections.markdown:
Fume cupboards failing containment, untested safety showers and medical gas faults come first, with the equipment out of use until it is tested and repaired. After that, critical services are rebalanced and controlled by permits, and spaces whose use has changed are upgraded to suit it.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Laboratory exhaust | Rebalance, replace fans, add variable air volume fume cupboard controls, raise or relocate stacks. | Wherever fume cupboards fail containment or alarm. |
| Safety showers and eyewash | Weekly activation, tempered supply, clear access, replacement where faulty. | In every laboratory and chemical area. |
| Chemical storage | Ventilated, segregated cabinets and stores. | Wherever chemicals sit on benches and floors. |
| Medical gases | Repairs and certification by specialists under permit. | Wherever medical gas faults are found or works are planned. |
| Infection-control finishes | Seamless flooring with coved skirtings, cleanable wall protection. | Where clinical finishes are damaged or porous. |
| Isolation rooms | Restore pressures and monitoring. | Where isolation rooms lose their pressure. |
| Teaching spaces | Acoustic treatment, quieter ventilation, increased outdoor air, updated AV. | Where classrooms echo, or are noisy or stuffy. |
| Ligature-resistant fittings | Ligature-resistant fittings in sensitive areas. | In mental health and some aged care settings. |
| Refurbishment | Refurbishment matched to the current use. | At the end of the cycle. |
| Change-of-use upgrades | When a space is repurposed, bring its exhaust, gases, drainage, finishes and safety equipment up to the new use before occupation, not after. | Whenever a space is repurposed. |
| Permit systems | Permit systems for work on medical gases, laboratory exhaust and isolation rooms, so changes are controlled and recertified. | Wherever these services exist. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Testing and certification recur. Safety rectification is itemised per item. Laboratory and clinical refurbishments are lump sums per room or suite, usually large because of services, and constrained by the need to keep research, teaching or care going. Teaching space upgrades are per room. Specialist equipment is often owned by the user rather than the building, so ownership must be settled.

Safety and certification are code compliance; refurbishment is lifecycle; upgrades for a change of use sit with that change.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a walk-through cannot: whether fume cupboards contain, whether showers run clean, whether gases are certified, and whether a space's use has outrun its services. Ask for them before any change of use.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Fume cupboard and laboratory exhaust test records | Whether fume cupboards contain fumes at the required face velocity. |
| Safety shower and eyewash test logs | Whether showers and eyewash are run and tested. |
| Medical gas certification and permit records | Whether medical gases are certified, and works controlled. |
| Isolation room pressure monitoring records | Whether isolation rooms hold their pressures. |
| Nurse call test and maintenance records | Whether nurse call works everywhere it should. |
| Accreditation and inspection reports | What accreditors and inspectors have found. |
| Acoustic and ventilation assessments of teaching spaces | Whether classrooms suit teaching. |
| Records of changes of use and the engineering reviews that accompanied them | Whether changes of use were engineered. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Specialised spaces are misread when failed critical equipment is left in use, when every problem is treated as wear, and when a space that looks the part is assumed to have the services its use needs.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| Keep using it until it is fixed | Fume cupboards that fail containment tests, untested emergency showers, and medical gas faults are safety findings. Take the equipment out of use until tested and repaired. |
| It is worn out | Most findings in these spaces trace back either to drift in a critical service that was once right, or to a change of use the services never followed; the first needs testing and rebalancing, the second needs a design review. |
| It looks like a laboratory, so it works as one | Laboratories converted from offices and repurposed wards often keep the old use's exhaust, gases, drainage and safety equipment. Check the services against the current use, not the room's appearance. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets standards for laboratory ventilation and fume cupboards, medical gases, healthcare and teaching spaces. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Laboratories, healthcare and teaching spaces | AS/NZS 2243 covers safety in laboratories and AS/NZS 2243.8 fume cupboards; AS 4775 covers emergency eyewash and showers; AS 2896 covers medical gas systems; the National Safety and Quality Health Service Standards and aged care quality standards apply; AS/NZS 2107 sets recommended acoustic levels for interiors including classrooms. | Health Technical Memoranda set healthcare engineering standards, including HTM 02-01 for medical gases and HTM 03-01 for ventilation; BS EN 14175 covers fume cupboards; Building Bulletin 93 sets acoustic design for schools and Building Bulletin 101 ventilation. | NFPA 99 covers healthcare facilities including medical gases; ANSI Z358.1 sets weekly activation of emergency showers and eyewash; ASHRAE 110 tests fume cupboard performance; ANSI S12.60 covers classroom acoustics; accreditation bodies such as The Joint Commission inspect healthcare facilities. |

sections.heading: Worked example: a laboratory in a former office
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A university converted an office floor into teaching laboratories ten years ago. Several fume cupboards alarm on low flow, the corridor smells of solvents on busy days, the safety shower runs brown when tested, and chemicals are stored on benches because the cabinets are full.

Containment alarms and odours in the corridor point to an exhaust system that has drifted, or was never sized for the cupboards now on it, and an untested shower is a safety finding. Behind both sits a change of use whose services may never have been reviewed.

So the register carries the failing cupboards and the shower as safety lines, out of use until tested, face velocity and stack tests, ventilated chemical storage, and a services review of the floor against its laboratory use.

thresholds.rule: Average of 0.5 m/s, with no reading below 0.3 m/s; tested at least every 12 months

pages.title: Specialist & Non-Standard Features
pages.question: How should bespoke features such as indoor pools, saunas and cellars be recorded and assessed?
pages.answer: Specialist features are recorded so they count in a building's capital picture, but they are kept out of cohort comparisons so they do not distort benchmarks. Judge them mostly by their effect on the rest of the building: indoor pools, spas, saunas and cellars push moisture into walls and roofs; pools and aquariums overload floors; water near electrics is a hazard; bespoke systems become unrepairable when suppliers disappear.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about specialist & non-standard features; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Genuinely unique one-off elements with no standard home \u2014 capture for completeness only; excluded from cohort convergence
