pages.searchTitle: Specialist features: indoor pools, saunas, cellars, smart homes and their effect on buildings

questions.question: Can an indoor pool damage the house?
questions.answer: Yes. Without dehumidification and vapour control, its moisture condenses in walls and roofs, causing rot and corrosion out of sight.

questions.question: Can my floor take a spa or aquarium?
questions.answer: Only if an engineer confirms it. Pools, spas and aquariums add loads the floor may not have been designed for.

questions.question: What if the smart home system's supplier has gone?
questions.answer: Plan to replace the platform with an open alternative, since bespoke systems cannot be repaired without their supplier.

questions.question: Should an unused feature be removed?
questions.answer: Often. Decommission it with the services made safe and the fabric repaired.

questions.question: How long does pool and spa plant last?
questions.answer: 8 to 15 years; smart home platforms last only 5 to 10.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Specialist feature problems show as condensation, corrosion and odour around the feature, sagging floors, electrics near water and undocumented controls, and in approvals, manuals and service records. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On site | Condensation, mould or corrosion around pools, spas, saunas and cellars | Moisture, chemicals and the rest of the building |
| On site | Sagging or cracked floors under heavy features | Structure, electrics and occupant safety |
| On site | Electrical equipment near water | Structure, electrics and occupant safety |
| On site | Proprietary control panels without documentation | Obsolescence, records and insurance |
| On site | Unusual features with no records | Obsolescence, records and insurance |
| In the records | Approvals and engineering for features | Structure, electrics and occupant safety |
| In the records | Manuals and supplier details | Obsolescence, records and insurance |
| In the records | Service records | Obsolescence, records and insurance |
| In the records | Corrosion of fixings, light fittings and ventilation around pools | Moisture, chemicals and the rest of the building |
| In the records | Steam or chemical odour in other parts of the house | Moisture, chemicals and the rest of the building |
| In the records | Feature controls that no one in the household knows how to operate | Obsolescence, records and insurance |
| In the records | Removed features with services capped and left behind | Obsolescence, records and insurance |
| In the records | Dehumidifiers running constantly near the feature | Moisture, chemicals and the rest of the building |
| In the records | Rust staining or efflorescence on walls next to pools and saunas | Moisture, chemicals and the rest of the building |

sections.heading: Types of specialist feature
sections.markdown:
Specialist and non-standard features are the bespoke items some homes and buildings contain that do not fit any other element: wine cellars, home cinemas, indoor pools and spas, saunas and steam rooms, home lifts, safe rooms, recording studios, large aquariums, smart home systems, heritage and artistic features, and similar. In the Moyne Ross framework this element is a capture-only holding pen: items are recorded so they are counted in a building's capital picture, but they are kept out of cohort comparisons, because averaging a wine cellar or an aquarium across buildings would distort the benchmarks for everything else.

| Feature | Main risks to the building | What to record |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Indoor pools and spas | Humidity, condensation and corrosion in the building fabric; chemical storage; load | Plant, dehumidification, structure, safety |
| Saunas and steam rooms | Moisture and heat in walls and ceilings; electrical | Vapour control, ventilation, electrical |
| Wine cellars | Cooling equipment; condensation in walls | Climate control, vapour barriers |
| Home cinemas and studios | Electrical and heat load; acoustic construction | Ventilation, power |
| Large aquariums and water features | Floor load; leaks; electrical near water | Structure, leak protection |
| Home lifts | See accessibility lifts | Servicing, safety |
| Smart home and automation systems | Obsolescence; cyber; dependency on one integrator | Platform, support, documentation |
| Heritage and artistic features | Specialist repair; fragility | Significance, conservation needs |

Recording them consistently, even when rare, keeps nothing out of the building's capital story.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Pool and spa plant lasts eight to fifteen years, sauna heaters and steam generators ten to fifteen, cellar cooling eight to twelve, and smart home platforms only five to ten. The supplier often matters more than the age: a bespoke system ends when no one can repair it.

| Feature | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pool and spa plant | 8 to 15 years | Chemicals; use |
| Sauna heaters and steam generators | 10 to 15 years | Water quality; use |
| Cellar cooling units | 8 to 12 years | Run hours |
| Smart home platforms | 5 to 10 years | Vendor support |
| Aquarium systems | 10 to 15 years | Maintenance |

What shortens life: moisture escaping into the building fabric; specialist suppliers leaving the market; lack of documentation, so new owners cannot maintain features.

The life of specialist features is less predictable than ordinary elements because it depends on bespoke products, specialist suppliers and the care of each owner. Many are removed rather than replaced when they reach the end of their life, particularly when new owners do not value them.

Smart systems often age fastest.

sections.heading: Moisture, chemicals and the rest of the building
sections.markdown:
The most serious risk from many specialist features is to the rest of the building: indoor pools, spas, saunas, steam rooms and cellars generate moisture that, without vapour control and ventilation, condenses in walls and roofs, rotting timber, corroding steel and growing mould.

Indoor pool chemicals and their by-products corrode metalwork, fixings and ventilation equipment and affect air quality throughout the house if the pool hall is not separated and ventilated.

An indoor pool evaporates water into the air every day, and a sauna or steam room releases it in every session. Unless that moisture is removed by dehumidification and kept out of the structure by vapour control, it condenses in walls and roofs, where rot and corrosion progress out of sight.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mould and rot around an indoor pool | Inadequate dehumidification and vapour control. Humidity logging; fabric inspection. | Log humidity; add dehumidification, ventilation and vapour control, and repair the damaged fabric. |
| A steam or chemical smell elsewhere in the house | A pool hall or steam room not separated from the rest of the building. Odour and humidity readings in adjoining rooms. | Separate it with sealed doors and its own ventilation. |
| Corroded fixings, light fittings and ventilation around an indoor pool | Pool chemicals and their by-products attacking metalwork. Corrosion concentrated in the pool hall. | Replace corroded items with suitable materials, and improve the ventilation. |

sections.heading: Structure, electrics and occupant safety
sections.markdown:
Specialist features can hurt people directly: by overloading a floor not designed for them, by bringing water and electricity together, and through the burns, slips, drowning and entrapment that saunas, pools and safe rooms carry.

Pools, spas, aquariums and heavy equipment add large loads that the floor may not have been designed for.

Water near electrical equipment, sauna heaters near combustible linings, and high electrical loads in cinemas and studios create shock and fire risks.

Saunas, steam rooms and pools carry burns, slips and drowning risks; safe rooms and lifts can trap occupants without communication.

Each feature also adds maintenance burden that few owners plan for.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Floor deflection under a spa or aquarium | Load beyond design. Engineering check. | Have an engineer check the load; strengthen the floor or reduce the load. |
| Tripping circuits | Electrical faults in wet areas. Electrical test. | Test the circuits; add RCD protection, and separate equipment from water. |
| A sauna heater close to timber linings | A fire hazard. The clearance between heater and linings. | Correct the clearance to the heater's requirements. |
| A pool or spa without a barrier, or with a gate that stays open | Child drowning risk. Barrier height, gaps, climbable zones and gate closing measured against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Repair or install the barrier, and fix the gate to close and latch from any position. |

sections.heading: Obsolescence, records and insurance
sections.markdown:
Some features increase insurance risk or limit insurer appetite, and their effect on value varies widely: features that one buyer values, another sees as a liability.

Bespoke systems depend on specialist suppliers and integrators; when they disappear, features cannot be repaired.

Features installed by previous owners often come without manuals or records, leaving new owners unable to maintain them safely.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Feature cannot be repaired | Supplier gone. Supplier search. | Search for a supplier; replace the platform with an open alternative, or decommission the feature. |
| Services capped and left behind where a feature was removed | A decommissioning never finished. Capped pipes and cables, and damaged fabric, where the feature stood. | Make the services safe, and repair the fabric. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Electrical hazards near water; overloaded floors; pool and spa safety failures | safety · 4 Essential | Isolate now. |
| Feature failed; moisture damaging the building | failure · 4 Essential | Repair now. |
| Statutory inspections of pools or lifts due | deadline · 3 Important | As required. |
| Condensation; ageing plant | condition · 3 Important | Repair in the near term. |
| Feature at end of life | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Replace or remove. |
| Feature undocumented | check · 2 Planned | Record and assess. |
| Normal | nil · 1 Routine | Routine. |

Because these features are excluded from cohort averages, their grading matters for the individual building only; the moisture, load and electrical risks they create for the building are graded the same way as any other finding.

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A building surveyor records and assesses each feature, bringing in specialists for pools, electrical safety, structure and building physics as needed. The checks below inventory every feature with its supplier and records, then look past each one to the fabric around it, where moisture, load and chemicals do their damage.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Inventory | Of every specialist feature with type, age, supplier, approvals and documentation. |
| Building fabric check | Around moisture-producing features: humidity logging, moisture readings, thermal imaging and inspection of roof spaces and walls. |
| Structural check | Of floors carrying heavy features. |
| Electrical safety test | Of wet-area and high-load installations. |
| Supplier and support check | For bespoke systems. |

The report should record each feature for the capital picture, state any risks it poses to the building, and recommend keep, repair, replace or remove.

Capture-only recording does not mean light assessment: the risks to the building still need checking.

Owners' knowledge of operation should be recorded too.

sections.heading: Protecting the building, making safe or removing
sections.markdown:
Electrical hazards near water, overloaded floors and missing pool and spa safety measures come first. After that, the question for each feature is whether it is damaging the rest of the building, and whether it is worth keeping at all.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Moisture control | Dehumidification, ventilation and vapour barriers for pools, saunas, steam rooms and cellars. | Wherever pools, spas, saunas, steam rooms or cellars produce moisture. |
| Structural work | Structural strengthening or load reduction under heavy features. | Where a floor carries more than it was designed for. |
| Electrical rectification | Electrical rectification with RCD protection and separation from water. | Wherever electrical equipment sits near water. |
| Documentation | Compile manuals, supplier details and maintenance requirements. | For every feature without records. |
| Platform replacement | Platform replacement for unsupported smart home systems with open alternatives. | Where a platform's supplier has gone. |
| Removal | Removal of features that cost more to keep than they are worth. | Where the feature has become a liability. |
| Separation | Separation of pool halls and steam rooms from the rest of the building with sealed doors and their own ventilation. | Where moisture or chemicals reach other rooms. |
| Safety measures | Barriers, alarms, emergency stops and communication where people could be trapped or injured. | Wherever people could be trapped or injured. |
| Decommissioning | Decommissioning with services made safe and fabric repaired. | Wherever a feature is removed. |
| Monitoring | Humidity and leak sensors around moisture-producing features so damage is caught early. | Around every moisture-producing feature. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Costs vary widely and are bespoke: specialist servicing recurs, moisture control and strengthening are lump sums, and removal is a lump sum with making good. These items are recorded in the building's capital picture but excluded from cohort averages.

Safety items are immediate; replacement is lifecycle; building damage repairs are condition items.

Removal often costs less than continued repair and may add value.

Specialist servicing often requires the original supplier.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a look at the feature cannot: whether it was approved and engineered, who can repair it, and whether it has already damaged the building. Ask for them before valuing or insuring the feature.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Approvals and engineering for each feature | Whether each feature was approved and engineered. |
| Manuals and supplier contacts | How each feature is maintained, and who can repair it. |
| Service records | Whether the features are serviced. |
| Electrical certificates | Whether electrical work near water was certified. |
| Insurance terms affected by the feature | How the feature affects insurance. |
| Heritage listing where relevant | Whether heritage rules limit changes. |
| Records of moisture or corrosion damage around the feature | Whether the feature has damaged the building. |
| Decommissioning records for removed features | Whether removed features were made safe. |
| Operating instructions held by the owner | Whether the owner can operate the feature safely. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Specialist features are misread when they are judged by their own condition rather than their effect on the building, when their age is taken as the guide to their risk, and when every feature is assumed to add value.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| Judge the feature by its condition | Record specialist features so they are counted, but judge them by their effect on the rest of the building. The fabric damage they cause usually matters more than the feature itself. |
| Old means at risk | A feature's age is less telling than its surroundings. Look at the fabric around it, the supplier behind it and the records that come with it. |
| Every feature adds value | A feature one buyer values, another sees as a liability, and some limit what insurers will cover. Where a feature costs more to keep than it is worth, removing it properly is a legitimate option. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets rules for pool and spa safety, for electrical work near water, and for the structure and ventilation that heavy or wet features need. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Pools, electrics and specialist installations | Building approval is needed for many features; pools and spas follow AS 1926 for barriers and state registration; electrical work follows AS/NZS 3000, including wet area zones. | Building regulations apply to structural, electrical and ventilation aspects; BS 7671 governs electrical installations in pools and saunas. | Local building and electrical codes apply, with NFPA 70 covering pools, spas and saunas; pool barriers follow the International Swimming Pool and Spa Code. |

In all three countries, many specialist features need building approval, and features installed without it can affect insurance, sale and certification. Pools and spas carry barrier and safety rules regardless of how they are classified in the capital picture, and electrical work in wet areas is tightly regulated. Heritage features may be protected by listing.

sections.heading: Worked example: an indoor pool in a house
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 2000s house has an indoor pool off the living area, with a dehumidifier that runs constantly. The pool hall's light fittings and fixings are corroded, a chlorine smell reaches the bedrooms, rust stains mark the wall beside the pool, and no one in the household knows how the pool's control panel works.

Judge the pool by its effect on the house. Constant dehumidification and rust staining point to more moisture than the hall can handle, probably condensing in the walls; corroded metalwork and the smell elsewhere point to a pool hall not separated from the house. The missing records leave the plant unmaintainable.

So the register carries electrical safety around the pool and the corroded fittings as safety lines, opening up the wall to check the fabric, upgraded dehumidification and vapour control, sealed doors to the house, and the manuals and supplier details compiled.

thresholds.rule: At least 1200 mm high; no more than 100 mm under the barrier; a 900 mm non-climbable zone; 300 mm clear inside; boundary fences used as barriers at least 1800 mm

pages.title: Specialist Hydraulics
pages.question: How do pools, recycled water systems and water features fail, and which findings are life-safety issues?
pages.answer: Specialist hydraulics fails on safety before condition. Pool and spa outlets without compliant covers or with single drains can trap and drown; pool gates that do not self-close and latch defeat child barriers; chlorine and acid stored together can release gas; recycled and rainwater pipes connected to drinking taps contaminate the supply; spas and fountains grow Legionella. Shells, finishes and plant then wear on predictable cycles.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about specialist hydraulics; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.

pages.searchTitle: Pools, spas and recycled water: entrapment, pool gates, chemicals and cross-connections

questions.question: When must a pool be closed?
questions.answer: When outlet covers are missing or broken, or gates do not self-close and latch. Close the pool or spa until they are fixed.

questions.question: Why is the pool losing water?
questions.answer: Beyond evaporation, a crack in the shell, a plumbing leak or a failed finish.

questions.question: Why does the pool plant room corrode?
questions.answer: Chlorine fumes from poor storage or ventilation. Separate and bund the chemicals, and ventilate the room.

questions.question: Can recycled water pipes connect to taps?
questions.answer: Not to drinking water outlets. A purple pipe at a basin or kitchen tap is a cross-connection.

questions.question: How long does a pool last?
questions.answer: Concrete shells 30 to 50 years; finishes 10 to 20, and filters 10 to 15.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Specialist hydraulic problems show at pools as outlet covers, gates and surfaces, in plant rooms as chemical smells and corrosion, at recycled water outlets, and in testing and certificates. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On site | Pool outlet covers: present, intact, secured, compliant labels; number of drains | Entrapment, barriers and pool shells |
| On site | Pool fences and gates: self-closing and self-latching, heights, gaps, climbable objects nearby | Entrapment, barriers and pool shells |
| On site | Plant room: chemical storage separation, bunding, ventilation, smell of chlorine, corrosion of equipment | Chemicals, water quality and features |
| On site | Pool surfaces: etching, loose tiles, cracks, water loss | Entrapment, barriers and pool shells |
| On site | Recycled and rainwater pipes and outlets: colour and labelling, signage at taps | Recycled water and cross-connections |
| On site | Water features: cleanliness, slime, foam, treatment equipment | Chemicals, water quality and features |
| On site | Staining or leaks under podium pools | Entrapment, barriers and pool shells |
| In the records | Pool water testing logs | Chemicals, water quality and features |
| In the records | Pool barrier compliance certificates | Entrapment, barriers and pool shells |
| In the records | Chemical safety data and storage register | Chemicals, water quality and features |
| In the records | Recycled water validation and testing | Recycled water and cross-connections |
| In the records | Water feature Legionella management | Chemicals, water quality and features |
| In the records | Leak and repair history | Entrapment, barriers and pool shells |

sections.heading: Types of specialist system
sections.markdown:
Specialist hydraulics covers water systems beyond ordinary supply and drainage: swimming pools and spas with their filtration, heating and chemical dosing plant; rainwater harvesting and recycled or greywater systems that supply toilets, irrigation and cooling; water features and fountains; and irrigation systems. Each brings its own hazards: drowning and suction entrapment, toxic chemicals, cross-connection of non-drinking water into drinking supplies, and Legionella from aerosols.

| System | Where it is found | Main hazards |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Swimming pools and spas | Apartment buildings, hotels, gyms, schools, aged care, leisure centres | Drowning, suction entrapment, chemical exposure, microbial contamination, slips |
| Pool plant rooms | With every pool | Chlorine gas from mixed chemicals, confined spaces, electrical hazards in wet areas |
| Rainwater harvesting | Houses, schools, commercial buildings | Cross-connection with drinking water; mosquitoes; contamination |
| Recycled and greywater systems | Green-rated commercial buildings, precincts with third-pipe networks | Cross-connection; treatment failure; odour |
| Water features and fountains | Lobbies, plazas, landscaping | Legionella from aerosols; slips; electrical |
| Irrigation | Landscaping, green roofs and walls | Backflow into drinking water; leaks onto membranes |

Recycled and harvested water is carried in separately identified pipes (purple or lilac in Australia and the United States, with marked pipes in Britain) and must never be connected to drinking water outlets. Most cross-connections are created years after construction by plumbers who did not recognise the pipe.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Concrete pool shells last thirty to fifty years, but their finishes last ten to twenty, filters ten to fifteen, and pumps and heaters less. Gates, outlet covers and chemical storage decide safety long before the shell decides the budget.

| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Concrete pool shells | 30 to 50 years | Waterproofing; ground movement; chemical balance |
| Pool surface finishes (render, tiles, membranes) | 10 to 20 years | Water chemistry; maintenance |
| Pool filters | 10 to 15 years; media 5 to 10 | Backwashing; water quality |
| Pool pumps and heaters | 8 to 15 years | Chemicals; run hours |
| Chemical dosing equipment | 8 to 12 years | Corrosive environment |
| Rainwater tanks | 20 to 40 years | Material; sediment |
| Recycled water treatment plant | 15 to 20 years; membranes and lamps sooner | Maintenance; feed quality |
| Irrigation systems | 10 to 20 years | UV; damage; controllers |

What shortens life: poor water chemistry in pools, which etches finishes, corrodes metalwork and damages plant; corrosive plant rooms where chlorine fumes attack electrical equipment, steel and controls; neglected treatment of recycled and harvested water, which lets systems foul and smell; ground movement and leaking pool shells that undermine surroundings.

sections.heading: Entrapment, barriers and pool shells
sections.markdown:
Pool and spa outlets with single drains, missing or broken covers, or flow rates too high for the cover can trap hair, limbs or bodies against the outlet, causing drownings and serious injuries, particularly to children. Dual drains, compliant covers and safety vacuum release systems prevent it; older pools often lack them.

Pool fences and gates that do not self-close and self-latch, gaps under or through fences, and climbable objects placed nearby defeat the barriers that prevent child drownings.

Pool shells crack and leak through ground movement and failed waterproofing; finishes etch, delaminate and loosen tiles; leaks undermine surrounding paving and structures, and on podium pools leak into car parks and plant below.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pool losing water beyond evaporation | Shell crack, plumbing leak or failed finish. Bucket test; dye test; pressure testing. | Find the leak, and repair the shell, plumbing or finish. |
| Gate that does not latch | Hinge or latch failure. Inspection. | Close the pool; repair the hinge or latch. |
| Pool fence low, with gaps under it or climbable objects beside it | Barrier not stopping a child. Height, gaps and climbable zones measured against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Raise or repair the barrier, and clear the non-climbable zone. |

sections.heading: Chemicals, water quality and features
sections.markdown:
Chlorine and acid stored or dosed together, or mixed by accident during deliveries, release chlorine gas. Plant rooms without ventilation, bunding, separation of chemicals and signage put staff and the public at risk; dosing failures overdose or underdose pools.

Pools and spas with poor filtration, disinfection or turnover grow bacteria and parasites; spas are the highest risk because of warm water and aerosols, and are a known source of Legionella.

Fountains and water features recirculate warm water and create aerosols; without treatment and cleaning they grow Legionella and have caused outbreaks.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Corroded equipment and electrical panels in the plant room | Chlorine fumes from poor storage or ventilation. Inspection. | Separate and bund the chemicals, and ventilate the plant room. |
| Cloudy water and complaints of irritation | Filtration or chemical dosing problems. Water testing; turnover check. | Repair the filtration and dosing, and test the water. |
| Slime and foam in water features | Inadequate treatment. Water testing. | Set treatment and cleaning regimes, or decommission the feature. |

sections.heading: Recycled water and cross-connections
sections.markdown:
Recycled, greywater and rainwater pipes connected to drinking water outlets, or drinking water top-up connections without backflow protection, contaminate the drinking supply. The risk grows with every later alteration.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Purple pipe connected to a basin or kitchen tap | Cross-connection. Dye or tracer testing. | Remove the cross-connection, and label the system. |
| Rainwater or recycled water tank with no backflow protection to the mains | Cross-connection risk. Backflow device at the mains connection; device test record. | Fit and test a suitable backflow prevention device. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Unsafe pool outlets; pool barriers failed; chemical storage able to release chlorine gas; cross-connection to drinking water; Legionella in a spa or feature | safety · 4 Essential | Close, isolate or rectify now. |
| Pool or treatment plant failed; podium pool leaking into structure | failure · 3 Important | Repair now. |
| Pool barrier inspection or registration due | deadline · 4 Essential | By the regulatory date. |
| Worn finishes, ageing plant, corroded equipment | condition · 3 Important | Repair in the near term. |
| Plant and finishes at end of life | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Replace on cycle. |
| No water management plan; no barrier certificate | check · 2 Planned | Assess. |
| Normal | nil · 1 Routine | Routine maintenance. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A pool and aquatic specialist, hydraulic engineer and, for water quality, a water hygiene specialist. The checks below start at the pool gate and the outlets, then the plant room and water testing logs, and trace recycled water pipes to their outlets.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Pool safety inspection | Outlet covers and their ratings, number and spacing of drains, safety vacuum release systems, signage, depth markings and lifesaving equipment. |
| Barrier inspection | Against the applicable standard: height, gaps, gates, latches, non-climbable zones, and any certificate or registration requirements. |
| Plant room inspection | Chemical storage and segregation, bunding, ventilation, dosing controls, electrical condition, confined space status. |
| Water quality review | Testing logs, turnover rates, filtration performance, disinfection levels; laboratory sampling where needed. |
| Leak investigation | Of pool shells and pipework by bucket, dye and pressure tests. |
| Cross-connection survey | Of recycled, greywater and rainwater systems by tracing and dye testing. |
| Water feature review | Under a Legionella risk assessment. |

The report should state safety defects and immediate actions, regulatory compliance, water quality management, plant condition and remaining life, and a capital plan.

sections.heading: Making safe, refurbishing or treating
sections.markdown:
Unsafe outlets, failed barriers and chemical hazards come first, and the pool or spa closes until they are fixed. After that, the work refurbishes the shell and plant, and keeps recycled water and features treated and separate from drinking water.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Outlet upgrades | Compliant anti-entrapment covers, dual drains or safety vacuum release systems, and flow rates within the cover rating. | Wherever outlet covers are missing, broken or non-compliant. |
| Barrier rectification | Self-closing and self-latching gates, heights and gaps fixed, climbable objects removed, and certification obtained. | Wherever gates or barriers fail. |
| Plant room upgrades | Separated and bunded chemical storage, ventilation, automatic dosing with alarms, signage and emergency procedures. | Where chemicals are stored together or the room is poorly ventilated. |
| Pool refurbishment | Shell repairs, new waterproofing, finishes, tiles and coping. | Where the shell leaks or finishes fail. |
| Filtration and plant replacement | New filtration and plant, sized to the bather load and turnover required. | Where plant is failing or undersized. |
| Cross-connection removal | Remove cross-connections, with backflow protection on drinking water top-ups and clear labelling. | Wherever recycled water reaches drinking water outlets. |
| Treatment upgrades | Upgraded treatment for recycled water systems, with validation and monitoring. | Where recycled water quality is not proven. |
| Water feature treatment | Treatment and cleaning regimes, or decommissioning. | Where features grow slime or foam. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Water testing, plant maintenance and barrier inspections recur. Outlet and barrier rectification are lump sums and usually urgent. Plant room upgrades and pool refurbishment are lump sums, with refurbishment closing the pool for weeks. Pool plant replacement is per item. Recycled water plant overhauls are lump sums with membrane and UV lamp replacement on cycles.

Safety and barrier rectification are code compliance; refurbishment and plant replacement are lifecycle; maintenance is repairs and maintenance. In apartment buildings, pools are often one of the largest sinking fund items.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a look at the pool cannot: whether the barriers are certified, whether the water has been tested, and whether recycled water has been validated. Ask for the barrier certificate first.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Pool barrier compliance certificates and registration | Whether the pool barriers are certified and registered. |
| Pool water testing logs and health department inspection reports | Whether the water is tested and safe. |
| Outlet cover specifications and installation dates | Whether the outlet covers are compliant. |
| Chemical storage register and safety data sheets | Whether chemicals are stored safely. |
| Recycled or rainwater system validation and testing records | Whether recycled or rainwater is validated and tested. |
| Water management plan covering spas and features | How Legionella is managed in spas and features. |
| Pool refurbishment and leak history | Whether the pool has leaked before, and how it was repaired. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Pools and recycled water are misread when a broken outlet cover or a gate that does not latch is treated as a repair to schedule, and when purple pipes are treated as labelling.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| The pool can stay open | Missing or broken pool outlet covers and pool gates that do not self-close and latch are life-safety failures. Close the pool or spa until they are fixed. |
| Purple pipes are just labelling | A purple pipe connected to a basin or kitchen tap is a cross-connection between recycled and drinking water. Remove it, protect drinking water top-ups against backflow, and label the system clearly. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets rules for pool barriers, outlets and water quality, and for non-potable water systems. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Pools, barriers and non-potable water | Pool barriers follow AS 1926.1 with state registration and certification regimes (for example in New South Wales and Queensland); outlets follow AS 1926.3; public pools are regulated by state health departments; recycled and rainwater systems follow AS/NZS 3500.1 and state health guidelines. | HSG179 sets health and safety guidance for swimming pools, and the Pool Water Treatment Advisory Group (PWTAG) sets water treatment practice; rainwater harvesting follows BS EN 16941-1 and BS 8515; the Water Supply (Water Fittings) Regulations govern cross-connections. | The Virginia Graeme Baker Pool and Spa Safety Act requires anti-entrapment drain covers on public pools and spas; the Model Aquatic Health Code and state health codes govern public pools; ASHRAE 188 covers Legionella risk in features and spas; plumbing codes cover non-potable water systems. |

sections.heading: Worked example: a podium pool with a gate that will not latch
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. An apartment building's podium pool has a gate that no longer self-latches, one outlet cover is cracked, and staining has appeared on the car park ceiling below. The plant room smells strongly of chlorine, with acid and chlorine stored side by side.

A cracked outlet cover and a gate that does not latch are life-safety failures: the pool closes until they are fixed. Chemicals stored together in a poorly ventilated room are a hazard too. The staining below points to a leak from the shell, plumbing or finish.

So the register carries the gate, the outlet cover and the chemical storage as safety lines now, with the pool closed, and leak finding and repair of the shell or plumbing as a failure line.

thresholds.rule: At least 1200 mm high; no more than 100 mm under the barrier; a 900 mm non-climbable zone; 300 mm clear inside; boundary fences used as barriers at least 1800 mm

source.title: Pool fences: requirements for pool barriers

pages.title: Specialist Suppression Systems
pages.question: How do gaseous, pre-action and other specialist suppression systems fail, and when do agent rules end their life?
pages.answer: Specialist suppression fails at the room and the rules. Gaseous systems discharge into rooms that no longer hold gas because cables and doors were added, so the fire reignites. Halon, HFC agents and PFAS foams are restricted, ending the life of sound systems. Carbon dioxide systems kill if safeguards fail. Panels left in manual stop discharge. Kitchen systems fail when nozzles are greased up and links not replaced.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about specialist suppression systems; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.

pages.searchTitle: Gas suppression, kitchen and foam systems: room integrity, halon, PFAS and safety

questions.question: Why must room integrity be retested after works?
questions.answer: A gaseous system in a room that no longer holds gas will discharge and fail to put the fire out. Any works that penetrate the room can break its integrity.

questions.question: Do halon systems have to be removed?
questions.answer: Halon is restricted in all three markets: in Australia it is used only under permit, and in the United Kingdom only for listed critical uses. Decommission it through approved channels.

questions.question: Is a carbon dioxide system dangerous to people?
questions.answer: It can be. Rooms protected by carbon dioxide need lock-off valves, alarms, signage and procedures, or a safer agent.

questions.question: What should replace PFAS firefighting foam?
questions.answer: Fluorine-free foam, with the system fully cleaned and the old concentrate and rinse water disposed of under environmental rules.

questions.question: How often are kitchen suppression links replaced?
questions.answer: Fusible links are replaced at least annually, and the nozzles kept matched to the appliances below them.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Suppression problems show at the cylinders and panel, in the protected room itself as new holes and unsealed doors, and in the records of what agent is installed. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On site | Cylinder labels: agent, fill date, test date; pressure gauges | Agents, regulation and occupant safety |
| On site | Panel faults; isolations; manual or lock-off positions | Detection, pre-action and kitchen systems |
| On site | New penetrations and gaps in protected rooms; doors without seals or closers | Room integrity and change of use |
| On site | Warning signs and alarms at protected rooms | Agents, regulation and occupant safety |
| On site | Kitchen nozzles greasy or out of position | Detection, pre-action and kitchen systems |
| On site | Foam concentrate type and labels | Agents, regulation and occupant safety |
| In the records | Design and agent quantity calculations | Investigation before the scope |
| In the records | Room integrity test reports | Room integrity and change of use |
| In the records | Service and cylinder test records | Detection, pre-action and kitchen systems |
| In the records | Halon or foam registers and decommissioning records | Agents, regulation and occupant safety |
| In the records | Room doors fitted without closers or seals after works | Room integrity and change of use |
| In the records | Raised floors and ceilings opened for cabling | Room integrity and change of use |
| In the records | Abort and manual release switches without labels or covers | Agents, regulation and occupant safety |

sections.heading: Types of specialist system
sections.markdown:
Specialist suppression systems protect spaces and hazards where ordinary sprinklers are unsuitable or insufficient: data and communications rooms, switchrooms, archives, museums, heritage buildings, commercial kitchens, flammable liquid stores, aircraft hangars and industrial processes. They use gas, water mist, foam, wet chemical or water released only after detection confirms a fire.

| Type | Where it is used | Character |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Inert gas (IG-541, IG-55, nitrogen, argon) | Data rooms, archives, switchrooms | Lowers oxygen to suppress fire; safe for occupants at design concentrations; large cylinder banks |
| Chemical clean agents (HFC-227ea, FK-5-1-12) | Data rooms, telecoms, control rooms | Compact; HFC-227ea is subject to HFC phase-down; FK-5-1-12 supply changed after a major producer stopped making PFAS |
| Halon | Legacy systems in some aviation, defence and older installations | Ozone-depleting; banned for new use; restricted to critical uses |
| Carbon dioxide | Unoccupied machinery spaces, industrial | Lethal at extinguishing concentrations; strict safeguards |
| Pre-action sprinklers | Data rooms, freezers, heritage | Pipes dry until detection opens a valve, then heads operate |
| Deluge | Transformers, process hazards | Open heads; all discharge together |
| Water mist | Heritage, hotels, machinery spaces | Fine droplets; less water; system-specific design |
| Kitchen wet chemical | Commercial cooking hoods | Suppresses cooking oil fires; linked to gas and power shutdown |
| Foam systems | Hangars, fuel stores, industrial | Older foams contain PFAS and are being phased out |

Gaseous systems only work if the protected room holds the gas for the required time. Every cable, pipe and door added to the room after commissioning can let the gas escape, so room integrity is as important as the cylinders.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Suppression systems last twenty to thirty years in their cylinders and valves, and fifteen to twenty in their panels, but regulation often ends an agent's life first: halon is already restricted, HFC agents fall under fluorinated gas rules, and PFAS foams are being withdrawn.

| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Gas cylinders and valves | 20 to 30 years with periodic hydrostatic testing | Pressure testing intervals; corrosion |
| Detection and control panels | 15 to 20 years | Vendor support |
| Pre-action valves | 20 to 30 years | Maintenance; water quality |
| Kitchen system cylinders and links | Fusible links replaced at least annually | Grease; heat |
| Foam concentrate | 10 to 20 years | Storage; type; regulation |
| Water mist pumps and nozzles | 15 to 25 years | Water quality; nozzle blockage |

What shortens life: room integrity lost by later penetrations and doors; agent regulation: halon, HFC and PFAS controls end the useful life of systems that are mechanically sound; panel obsolescence; grease on kitchen system nozzles and links.

sections.heading: Room integrity and change of use
sections.markdown:
Gaseous systems are designed to hold an extinguishing concentration for a set time. New cable penetrations, raised floor and ceiling changes, gaps under doors, and new ductwork let the gas leak away, so the fire reignites when the concentration falls. A door fan integrity test shows whether the room still holds.

A room fitted out for one use and later used for another (more equipment, storage, people) can outgrow its design.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Room integrity test fails | Penetrations and gaps added. Door fan test. | Seal every penetration with tested products, fit door seals and closers, and retest. |
| Door fan test predicts a short hold time | Room too leaky to hold the agent. Predicted hold time against the design and the limits for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Seal the leaks with tested products and retest. |
| Walls, ceilings or doors damaged after a discharge | Peak pressure beyond what the enclosure can take. A discharge produces a peak of roughly 240 to 1,200 Pa for a fraction of a second, while suspended ceilings take only about 50 Pa (SFPE). | Have pressure relief sized and fitted, and restrain ceiling tiles. |

sections.heading: Agents, regulation and occupant safety
sections.markdown:
Halon production ended in developed countries in 1994; remaining systems must be decommissioned or justified. HFC-227ea is being phased down with other HFCs. A major producer of FK-5-1-12 stopped making PFAS products, changing supply. Older firefighting foams contain PFAS and are being banned or restricted in Australia, Britain, the European Union and many US states, with clean-up obligations.

Carbon dioxide systems kill people who are in the room when they discharge; pre-discharge alarms, time delays, lock-off valves and signage must work. Inert gas systems lower oxygen to levels that are safe only for short exposures at design concentration.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Halon cylinders present | Legacy system. Labels. | Plan decommissioning through approved channels, and replacement with a permitted agent. |
| Foam concentrate of older type | Likely PFAS-containing foam. Product data; testing. | Test the foam; replace PFAS foam with fluorine-free foam, cleaning the system and disposing of the old concentrate. |
| Carbon dioxide cylinders with no recent weight record | Agent quantity unknown. US Department of Defense guidance verifies high-pressure carbon dioxide by weighing every two years, and checks pre-discharge time delays annually (UFM 3-601-02). | Weigh the cylinders and check the time delays; recharge any cylinder found short. |

sections.heading: Detection, pre-action and kitchen systems
sections.markdown:
Systems release only when detection confirms a fire, usually from two detectors. Faulty detectors, disabled panels, and abort or manual release switches left in the wrong position stop discharge or cause accidental discharge.

Pre-action pipework that holds water from tests corrodes; supervisory air leaks; valves fail to trip.

Nozzles blocked with grease, fusible links not replaced, appliances moved from under nozzles, and gas shutoff interlocks bypassed.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Panel in manual or isolated | Left after works or a false discharge. Panel status. | Return the panel to automatic, and find out why it was left isolated. |
| Kitchen system label older than six months | Servicing lapsed. US Department of Defense guidance inspects wet chemical systems semi-annually, checking the hazard has not changed and replacing fusible links (UFM 3-601-02). | Restore six-monthly servicing, and check the nozzles against the current appliances. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Carbon dioxide safeguards failed; system isolated in a protected room; kitchen system disabled | safety · 4 Essential | Rectify now. |
| Room integrity failed | failure · 4 Essential | Seal now. |
| Halon, HFC or PFAS foam requiring decommissioning or replacement under rules | deadline · 4 Essential | By the regulatory date. |
| Servicing and integrity testing due | deadline · 4 Essential | At the prescribed interval. |
| Panel or detection ageing | condition · 3 Important | Repair. |
| System at end of life | lifecycle · 3 Important | Replace. |
| Design basis unknown after change of use | check · 3 Important | Review. |
| Minor faults found and fixed at service | nil · 1 Routine | Routine maintenance. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A fire services engineer leads, with a suppression specialist for the system type and, for kitchens, the hood and suppression contractor. The checks below start with room integrity and the agent, then test detection, controls and safeguards.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Design review | Hazard, agent, design concentration and hold time, room volume, and whether the room’s use, contents and occupancy have changed; pipework changes need the design recalculated against the discharge time for the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). |
| Room integrity test | By door fan for gaseous systems, predicting hold time against the design and the asset’s market (Thresholds by market), with leaks located by smoke pencil or thermal imaging. |
| Cylinder and agent inspection | Weight or pressure against the label, hydrostatic test dates, valves, discharge pipework and nozzles, mounting. |
| Detection and control test | Detectors, two-stage confirmation logic, pre-discharge alarms, time delays, abort and manual release, lock-off valves, interfaces to air handling shutdown and dampers. |
| Occupant safety review | For carbon dioxide and inert gas systems: signage, alarms, lock-off procedures, room access controls. |
| Regulatory review | Of the agent: halon status, HFC phase-down, foam PFAS content and any decommissioning or clean-up obligations. |
| Pre-action checks | Supervisory air, low-point drains, internal condition, trip test. |
| Kitchen system inspection | Nozzle positions against current appliances, grease, fusible links, gas and power shutdown interlocks, manual release. |

The report should state whether the system will suppress a fire in the room as it now is, the safety position, the agent's regulatory status, and works or replacement needed.

sections.heading: Restoring, recharging or replacing
sections.markdown:
A gaseous system is only as good as the room around it, so room integrity comes first, retested after any works. After that, the work follows the agent: some must be decommissioned under regulation, and some, such as carbon dioxide, need safeguards for anyone in the room.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Restore room integrity | Seal every penetration with tested products, fit door seals and closers, seal raised floors and ceilings, then retest. | Wherever the room fails its integrity test. |
| Recalculate and recharge | Recalculate the agent quantity and recharge. | Where room volume or use has changed. |
| Replace regulated agents | Decommission halon through approved channels; plan replacement of HFC-227ea systems; move to inert gas or other permitted agents, which may need more cylinder space and pressure relief venting. | Wherever a regulated agent is installed. |
| Replace PFAS foam | Fluorine-free foam, with full system cleaning and disposal of old concentrate and rinse water under environmental rules. | Wherever foam concentrate contains PFAS. |
| Panel and detection replacement | Supported equipment. | Where panels or detection are ageing or unsupported. |
| Carbon dioxide safety measures | Lock-off valves, alarms, signage and procedures, or replacement with a safer agent. | Wherever carbon dioxide protects a room people enter. |
| Pre-action corrosion control | Nitrogen supervisory gas, drainage and pipe replacement. | Where pre-action pipework corrodes. |
| Kitchen systems | Reposition nozzles to match appliances, replace links, restore interlocks, and clean regularly. | Where nozzles are greasy or out of position, or appliances have changed. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Servicing, room integrity testing and cylinder testing recur. Room sealing is a lump sum per room. Agent replacement is a lump-sum project per protected space, including new cylinders, pipework, nozzles, pressure relief and commissioning. Halon decommissioning and PFAS foam replacement carry disposal and clean-up costs that can be significant. Kitchen system servicing recurs, with replacement per hood.

Servicing, integrity and safety rectification are code compliance; agent replacement driven by regulation is a deadline item; system replacement at end of life is lifecycle.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a look at the cylinders cannot: whether the room still holds its gas, what agent is installed, and whether the room has been opened up since it was tested. Ask for them before any works in a protected room.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Design and agent quantity calculations | What the system was designed to protect, and with how much agent. |
| Room integrity test reports with hold times | Whether the room holds the gas long enough to put a fire out. |
| Service, cylinder weight and hydrostatic test records | Whether cylinders are full and tested. |
| Detection and control test records | Whether the system will release when it should, and only then. |
| Halon register and decommissioning records; foam product data and PFAS status | Whether a regulated agent or PFAS foam is present. |
| Carbon dioxide safety procedures and lock-off records | Whether people are protected from a carbon dioxide discharge. |
| Kitchen system service records and link replacement dates | Whether kitchen systems are serviced and their links current. |
| Records of works in protected rooms | Whether the room has been penetrated since it was last tested. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Specialist suppression is misread when the system is judged without the room around it, and when a failed integrity test is blamed on the wrong cause.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| Full cylinders mean protection | A gaseous system in a room that no longer holds gas will discharge and fail to put the fire out. Room integrity must be retested after any works that penetrate the room. |
| A failed integrity test means ageing seals | A protected room that fails its integrity test after recent works points to the works; one that fails without recent works points to ageing seals, doors and dampers. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets standards for gaseous, kitchen, foam and pre-action systems, and restricts halon, some HFC agents and PFAS foams. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Gaseous systems | AS 4214 and ISO 14520 cover gaseous systems; AS 1851 sets routine service, including room integrity checks. | BS EN 15004 and BS ISO 14520 cover gaseous systems. | NFPA 2001 covers clean agent systems, including annual enclosure integrity checks, and NFPA 12 carbon dioxide, with strict personnel safety requirements. |
| Regulated agents and foam | Halon is controlled under the ozone protection legislation, with use only under permit; several states and the Commonwealth restrict PFAS firefighting foams. | Halon use is restricted to listed critical uses; HFC agents fall under fluorinated gas regulations; PFAS foam restrictions apply under UK and EU chemical rules. | EPA and state rules restrict PFAS foams; NFPA 11 covers foam. |
| Kitchen and pre-action | Kitchen suppression follows the relevant Australian Standard and AS 1851. | Kitchen systems follow LPS 1223. | NFPA 17A covers wet chemical systems, and NFPA 13 and 25 pre-action systems. |

sections.heading: Worked example: a server room opened for new cabling
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A server room is protected by a clean agent system, with cylinders full and serviced on time. Last year the raised floor and ceiling were opened for new cabling, and the door's seal was lost when the door was replaced during the works. The last room integrity test predates the works.

A gaseous system in a room that no longer holds gas will discharge and fail to put the fire out, however full the cylinders. Any works that penetrate the room call for a new integrity test. The opened floor and ceiling and the unsealed door make failure likely, and if it fails, the works are the cause rather than ageing seals.

So the register carries a room integrity test as a check line now, resealing of the floor, ceiling and door with tested products, and a retest with its hold time, with the agent recalculated if the room's volume has changed. If the test fails, the room is a failure line until it is resealed.

thresholds.rule: At least 10 minutes, or long enough for trained personnel to respond; end of hold commonly taken at 80 per cent of the minimum design concentration

pages.title: Storage & Archive Areas
pages.question: How do storerooms and archives fail, and which storage findings are safety issues?
pages.answer: Stores fail through what is put in them. Compactus and archives overload upper floors; goods stacked to the ceiling block sprinklers; plastics and batteries outgrow sprinkler designs; incompatible chemicals stored together without bunding or ventilation risk toxic gas and fire; e-bikes charged in basement cages start fires. Archives under pipes or in damp basements are destroyed by leaks and mould. Most fixes are management, but floor overloads and chemical hazards need action now.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about storage & archive areas; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
