questions.question: Can we put compactus shelving on an upper floor?
questions.answer: Only after an engineer has checked the floor. Compactus full of paper can impose loads far above an ordinary office floor's design.

questions.question: How close can storage be to sprinklers?
questions.answer: Not within the clearance zone below the heads. Mark maximum stacking heights so stored goods do not block the spray.

questions.question: Can cleaning chemicals be stored together?
questions.answer: Not if they react, such as chlorine and acids, or oxidisers and flammables. Separate them into bunded, ventilated storage.

questions.question: Can e-bikes be charged in storage cages?
questions.answer: They should not be. Battery fires are intense and can reignite; provide a charging room with detection instead.

questions.question: Why are archive boxes going mouldy?
questions.answer: A damp basement or poor ventilation. Dehumidify, stabilise the temperature, and check for leaks.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Storage problems show as goods under sprinklers, heavy shelving upstairs, pipes over archives, chemicals together, batteries charging and mould, and in load, dangerous goods and flood records. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On site | Storage within the clearance zone under sprinkler heads; stacked to the ceiling | Fire load, sprinklers and batteries |
| On site | Compactus and heavy shelving on upper floors; cracks or deflection in the floor | Floor loads |
| On site | Pipes running above archives and stores; water staining on boxes | Water and the archive environment |
| On site | Chemicals stored together without bunding or segregation; corroded containers | Dangerous goods |
| On site | E-bikes and batteries in basement cages; charging cables run to outlets | Fire load, sprinklers and batteries |
| On site | Mould on boxes or walls; pest evidence | Water and the archive environment |
| On site | Storage spilling into corridors, stairs and plant rooms | Fire load, sprinklers and batteries |
| In the records | Floor loading design and approvals for compactus | Floor loads |
| In the records | Dangerous goods register and manifest | Dangerous goods |
| In the records | Sprinkler design basis | Fire load, sprinklers and batteries |
| In the records | Leak and flood history | Water and the archive environment |
| In the records | Building rules on storage cages and charging | Fire load, sprinklers and batteries |
| In the records | Fire doors to stores propped open to make access easier, and stores left unlocked | Fire load, sprinklers and batteries |

sections.heading: What the space does and what it contains
sections.markdown:
Storage and archive areas hold goods, records and materials: general storerooms, paper and media archives, compactus and mobile shelving rooms, cleaners' stores, chemical and dangerous goods stores, and resident and tenant storage cages in basements. Functionally a store must carry its load, keep its contents safe from fire, water, pests and theft, keep hazardous materials segregated, and not obstruct escape or fire protection. Stores are easy to overlook because they are rarely visited, yet they concentrate fire load, floor load and hazardous materials in one place.

| Type | Where it is found | What matters for the space |
| --- | --- | --- |
| General storerooms | All building types | Fire load, sprinkler clearance, egress, housekeeping |
| Archives and compactus rooms | Offices, councils, law firms, hospitals | Floor loading; water protection; environmental control |
| Cleaners' and chemical stores | All managed buildings | Segregation, ventilation, spill containment |
| Dangerous goods stores | Industrial, laboratories, pool plant, workshops | Separation distances, bunding, signage, ventilation |
| Resident and tenant storage cages | Apartment and office basements | Fire load; sprinkler coverage; lithium batteries; security |
| Rack storage in warehouses | Logistics and retail | Sprinkler design; racking safety; floor flatness |

In apartment buildings, resident storage cages in basements are common property spaces filled with private belongings, so fire and battery risks there are shared by everyone in the building.

sections.heading: How long it stays fit for purpose
sections.markdown:
Mobile shelving and storage cages last twenty to thirty years, chemical cabinets fifteen to twenty-five, and archive environmental control fifteen to twenty. A store's fitness for purpose changes whenever its contents do, which is why the survey starts with what is actually in it.

| Component or quality | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mobile shelving and compactus | 20 to 30 years | Load; track wear |
| Storage cages | 20 to 30 years | Damage; corrosion in damp basements |
| Chemical storage cabinets | 15 to 25 years | Corrosion; damage |
| Archive environmental control | 15 to 20 years | Equipment life |
| Fitness for the stored contents | Changes whenever contents change | New uses; denser storage |

What shortens fitness for purpose: denser or heavier storage than the room was designed for, such as compactus added to an office floor; changes in what is stored, from paper to plastics, from tools to lithium batteries, without reviewing fire protection; water from pipes running overhead and basement flooding; neglect in rooms nobody visits.

sections.heading: Floor loads
sections.markdown:
Compactus and mobile shelving full of paper impose loads far above ordinary office floor loads. Installed on upper floors without engineering, they cause cracking and deflection and, in extreme cases, threaten the floor.

Paper is heavy. Mobile shelving packed with files concentrates far more load on a floor than the desks it replaced, and the floor shows it slowly, as cracks and deflection, if at all. The check is a calculation against the floor's design, made before the shelving is filled.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Floor cracks under a compactus room | Overload beyond design. Load calculation against design. | Have an engineer check the loads; move the storage over beams or to a lower floor, limit its density, or strengthen the floor. |
| New compactus on an upper floor with no engineering on record | Heavy storage added without a load check. No approval or calculation on file. | Have the floor checked against the load before the shelving is filled. |
| Archive boxes or compactus on a floor designed for offices | Load beyond the floor’s design. The design imposed load compared with the storage load, against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Have an engineer confirm the capacity before loading further. |

sections.heading: Fire load, sprinklers and batteries
sections.markdown:
Stores concentrate combustible material. Storage stacked close to sprinkler heads blocks their spray; high-piled plastics exceed what the sprinkler system was designed for; doors to stores are propped; and stores without detection let fires grow unseen.

E-bikes, scooters and batteries stored and charged in basement cages and stores are a growing fire source; such fires are intense, produce toxic gases and can reignite.

Stores overflowing into corridors and stairs, and blocked access to fire equipment, valves and switchboards, are common in buildings where storage is scarce.

Basement stores also sit where floods arrive first, so stored contents and the services that pass through stores are at combined risk.

A store's danger depends on what is in it, not what it was built for. High-piled plastics where paper was planned, batteries charging in cages, and goods stacked into the spray zone of the sprinklers each push the store beyond its design without any change to the building.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sprinklers blocked by stacked goods | Housekeeping and inadequate storage space. Clearance measurement. | Clear and mark maximum stacking heights; upgrade the sprinklers if the stored hazard has outgrown them. |
| E-bikes charging in basement storage cages | Battery charging in stores. Cables run from outlets into cages, with batteries left on charge. | Ban charging in cages and stores, and provide a charging room with detection. |
| Store doors propped open, or stores with no detection | Fire separation and early warning defeated. Doors wedged for access, and no detectors in the store. | Close the doors or fit hold-open devices linked to the alarm, and add detection. |
| Boxes stacked up close to the sprinkler heads | Spray pattern blocked from above the goods. Clearance below the deflectors measured against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Lower the stacks and mark the limit on the racking. |

sections.heading: Dangerous goods
sections.markdown:
Chemicals stored together that react (such as pool chlorine and acids, oxidisers and flammables), without bunding, ventilation or separation, can release toxic gas, cause fires or contaminate drains.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Corroded fittings near a chemical store | Fumes from incompatible or unventilated storage. Inventory; ventilation check. | Separate incompatible chemicals into bunded, ventilated cabinets or rooms. |
| No register of what is stored where | Dangerous goods not recorded. No manifest, and quantities unknown. | Inventory the store, and keep a register and manifest. |

sections.heading: Water and the archive environment
sections.markdown:
Archives and stores under pipework, plant rooms, wet areas or in flood-prone basements suffer leaks and floods that destroy records and stock. Archives should never sit under water pipes.

Paper, film and media need stable temperature and humidity; damp basements grow mould, and pests (silverfish, rodents) damage records.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mould on archive boxes | Damp basement or poor ventilation. Humidity logging. | Dehumidify, stabilise the temperature, and remove damp-damaged material. |
| Water-stained boxes | Leaks from overhead pipes. Pipe route survey. | Reroute the pipes or add drip trays and leak detection, and raise storage off the floor. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Floor overload; incompatible dangerous goods; storage blocking sprinklers or egress; battery charging in cages | safety · 4 Essential | Remove or rectify now. |
| Flood or leak damaging stored contents | failure · 3 Important | Stop the water now. |
| Dangerous goods notification or manifest due | deadline · 3 Important | As required. |
| Damp, pests, poor housekeeping | condition · 2 Planned | Improve in the near term. |
| Shelving and cages at end of life | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Replace. |
| Storage loads and contents unknown | check · 2 Planned | Survey. |
| Normal | nil · 1 Routine | Routine. |

Storage findings are graded by consequence: a store whose contents could start, feed or spread a fire, overload a floor, or release toxic gas is a safety grade; a damp or untidy store of inert goods is a condition grade.

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A building surveyor leads, with a structural engineer for heavy storage, a fire engineer for storage hazard and sprinkler adequacy, and a dangerous goods specialist where chemicals are stored. The checks below record what is actually stored in each room, with its weight and combustibility, then compare it with the floor, sprinkler and storage design.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Storage survey | Of every store: contents, height, density, clearances to sprinklers, access to fire equipment and egress. |
| Floor load assessment | For compactus, archives and heavy storage against the floor's design. |
| Sprinkler adequacy review | Against the actual stored commodity and height. |
| Dangerous goods review | Inventory, quantities, compatibility, separation, bunding, ventilation, signage, and notification thresholds. |
| Water risk review | Pipes above stores, flood levels, drainage. |
| Environmental monitoring | In archives: temperature, humidity, pests. |
| Battery charging review | In basement stores and cages. |

The report should list safety findings by store, the capacity and suitability of each, and works and management changes.

sections.heading: Making safe, separating and protecting
sections.markdown:
Overloaded floors, incompatible chemicals, storage blocking sprinklers and battery charging come first. After that, the work protects stored contents from water and damp, enforces housekeeping, and reduces what has to be stored at all.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Load control | Relocate heavy storage to ground floors or over beams, strengthen floors, or limit shelving density. | Wherever heavy storage exceeds what the floor was designed for. |
| Sprinkler clearance | Marked maximum stacking heights, and sprinkler upgrades where the stored hazard has outgrown the design. | Wherever goods are stacked into the sprinklers' spray zone. |
| Dangerous goods stores | Segregated, bunded and ventilated cabinets or rooms, with signage, spill kits and a current register. | Wherever chemicals are stored. |
| Water protection | Reroute pipes, add drip trays and leak detection, raise storage off floors in basements. | Wherever stores sit under pipes or in flood-prone basements. |
| Archive environment | Dehumidification, stable temperature, pest control. | Where records suffer from damp, heat or pests. |
| Battery policy | Ban charging in cages and stores, provide designated charging rooms with detection. | Wherever residents or staff store e-bikes and batteries. |
| Housekeeping | Housekeeping rules enforced with regular checks. | In every store. |
| Records digitisation | Digitise records to reduce paper archives and their floor and fire loads. | Where paper archives overload floors or fill stores. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Most storage findings are fixed by management at little cost. Floor strengthening and sprinkler upgrades are lump sums. Dangerous goods cabinets and stores are itemised. Archive environmental control is a lump sum with running costs. Leak protection is itemised. Safety items are code compliance; equipment replacement is lifecycle.

Digitising or offsiting archives can avoid floor strengthening and free valuable space. Dangerous goods non-compliance can bring regulatory penalties and insurance consequences that far exceed the cost of proper stores.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a look into each store cannot: what the floor and sprinklers were designed for, what dangerous goods are kept, and what has been lost to water before. Ask for them before any change of use or contents.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Floor loading design and approvals for heavy storage | Whether heavy storage was engineered and approved. |
| Dangerous goods register and manifest | What dangerous goods are kept, and how much. |
| Sprinkler design basis for storage areas | What the sprinklers were designed to protect. |
| Leak and flood history affecting stores | Whether stores have flooded or leaked before. |
| Building rules on storage cages and battery charging | What the rules say about storage cages and battery charging. |
| Archive environmental monitoring records | Whether the archive's environment is stable. |
| Insurer conditions on storage | What the insurer requires of storage. |
| Inventory of stored contents by room | What is actually stored, room by room. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Stores are misread when overloading and chemicals are treated as housekeeping, when a store is judged by its design rather than its contents, and when one visit is taken to show its condition.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| It is a housekeeping matter | Overloaded floors, blocked sprinklers, incompatible chemicals and battery charging in basement stores are safety findings, not housekeeping. |
| The store was designed for this | Most storage findings come from a mismatch between what the store was designed for and what is now in it, so begin by recording the actual contents and their weight and combustibility. |
| One visit shows the condition | Record the time and conditions of each observation, because the condition of these spaces changes with operations and the worst state is the one that matters for safety. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets rules for storing dangerous goods, for floor loads, and for sprinkler protection of stored goods. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Dangerous goods, loads and sprinklers | Work health and safety regulations govern hazardous chemicals, with AS 1940 for flammable liquids and AS 3780 for corrosives; state laws set dangerous goods notification thresholds; AS/NZS 1170.1 sets floor loads for storage; sprinkler design for storage follows AS 2118.1. | The Dangerous Substances and Explosive Atmospheres Regulations 2002 (DSEAR) and COSHH govern chemicals; BS EN 1991-1-1 sets storage loads; the responsible person must manage fire risk in stores. | OSHA hazard communication and flammable liquid standards and NFPA 30 govern chemical storage; NFPA 13 sets sprinkler design for storage; ASCE 7 sets storage live loads. |

Insurers in all three countries commonly set conditions on storage heights, battery charging and chemical storage.

Records retention laws may also apply.

sections.heading: Worked example: an archive moved upstairs
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A tenant moved its archive into compactus shelving on the fourth floor of a 1980s office, with no engineering on record. Cracks have appeared in the ceiling below, boxes in one corner are water-stained under a chilled water pipe, and cleaning chemicals, including chlorine and acid, share a cupboard in the same store.

Most storage findings come from a mismatch between what a store was designed for and what is now in it. Paper in compactus can overload a floor designed for offices, and the cracks below point to it. Chlorine and acid together can release toxic gas. The stained boxes point to the pipe above.

So the register carries the floor load and the chemicals as safety lines now, an engineer's load check with the shelving relocated or reduced, the chemicals separated into bunded, ventilated storage, and the pipe rerouted or fitted with a drip tray and leak detection.

thresholds.measure: Floor imposed loads (IBC Table 1607.1, as adopted in Massachusetts)
thresholds.rule: Offices 50 psf (2.4 kPa); light storage 125 psf (6.0 kPa)

source.title: 780 CMR Table 1607.1 Minimum uniformly distributed live loads (Massachusetts State Building Code, adopting the IBC table)

thresholds.rule: At least 457 mm (18 in) to the top of storage

source.title: 29 CFR 1910.159 Automatic sprinkler systems
source.publisher: US Occupational Safety and Health Administration

pages.title: Stormwater Drainage
pages.question: How do site stormwater systems fail, and why do buildings flood in large storms?
pages.answer: Stormwater systems fail by blockage and obstruction. Litter, sediment and roots block pits and pipes; detention tanks lose storage and orifices block; treatment devices fill and bypass. Buildings flood in big storms most often because overland flow paths have been blocked by fences, walls and landscaping, sending water into basements and ground floors. Many detention systems carry legal maintenance obligations on title.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about stormwater drainage; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Surface pits, pipes, on-site detention/retention systems

sources.title: Australian Rainfall and Runoff
The SuDS Manual (C753)
Stormwater

pages.searchTitle: Stormwater drainage: blocked pits, detention tanks, flooding and what to fix first

questions.question: Why does the site flood only in big storms?
questions.answer: Usually because an overland flow path is blocked or the system's capacity is exceeded. Check the surface first: fences, walls and landscaping across low points are common causes.

questions.question: Does an on-site detention tank need maintenance?
questions.answer: Yes. Orifices block, sediment fills the storage and covers get buried. In Australia the maintenance is often required by a covenant on title.

questions.question: Why does the same pit keep blocking?
questions.answer: A blocked pit or pipe, or roots where it runs near trees. A CCTV survey shows which.

questions.question: What causes damp behind retaining walls?
questions.answer: Often blocked subsoil drains. Inspection and flushing confirm it; drains that cannot be cleared need renewing.

questions.question: How long do stormwater pipes last?
questions.answer: Concrete and PVC pipes 50 years and more, clay and older pipes 50 to 80; treatment media 1 to 5 years and subsoil drains 15 to 30.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Stormwater problems show after rain: ponding, silt marks, water where it should not be. On a dry day the signs are the pits, the grates and what stands in the water's way. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On site | Ponding on paved areas and around pits after rain; silt and debris marks | Blocked pits, pipes and subsoil drains |
| On site | Grates broken, missing or sitting proud; pits full of sediment | Blocked pits, pipes and subsoil drains |
| On site | Water entering basements, car parks or ground floors in storms | Overland flow and capacity |
| On site | Fences, walls and landscaping across low points | Overland flow and capacity |
| On site | Detention tank access covers missing, buried or sealed | Detention and treatment |
| On site | Treatment devices overflowing or full | Detention and treatment |
| In the records | Stormwater drawings and design | Investigation before the scope |
| In the records | On-site detention design and maintenance obligations | Detention and treatment |
| In the records | Cleaning and maintenance records | Blocked pits, pipes and subsoil drains |
| In the records | Flood history | Overland flow and capacity |
| In the records | CCTV surveys | Blocked pits, pipes and subsoil drains |
| On site | Erosion, scour and sediment fans at outlets and on slopes below the site | Overland flow and capacity |
| On site | Water discharging onto neighbouring land or footpaths from the site | Overland flow and capacity |

sections.heading: What the system covers
sections.markdown:
Stormwater drainage collects rainwater from roofs and paved areas and carries it to the public system or to on-site treatment and storage: surface pits and grates, channel drains, underground pipes, subsoil drains, on-site detention tanks that hold water and release it slowly, retention and harvesting tanks, gross pollutant traps and treatment devices, bioretention basins and swales, and the overland flow paths that carry water safely when pipes are full. Roof gutters and downpipes have their own page.

| Element | Where it is found | Main issues |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Surface pits and grates | Car parks, paved areas, landscaping | Blockage; broken grates; trip and wheel hazards |
| Underground pipes | All sites | Root intrusion; cracking; displacement; sediment |
| Subsoil drains | Behind retaining walls, under pavements, around footings | Silting and root blockage |
| On-site detention (OSD) tanks | Newer urban sites in Australia, Britain and the US | Orifice blockage; sediment; access; legal maintenance obligations |
| Gross pollutant traps and treatment devices | Car parks and commercial sites | Full of litter and sediment; bypassing |
| Bioretention and swales | Newer sites with water-sensitive design | Clogging; planting loss; erosion |
| Overland flow paths | All sites | Blocked by fences, walls and landscaping |

Stormwater is designed for a storm of a given size. When pipes and pits are full, water must flow safely across the surface along overland flow paths, away from buildings. Fences, walls, landscaping and new structures that block those paths send floodwater into buildings, basements and car parks.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Stormwater pipes and pits last fifty years and more; what fails first is the maintenance. Treatment media need replacing every one to five years and subsoil drains within decades, and blockage causes most failures long before the pipes wear out.

| Element | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Concrete and PVC stormwater pipes | 50 years and more | Roots; ground movement; installation |
| Clay and older pipes | 50 to 80 years | Roots; joint failure |
| Pit structures and grates | 30 to 50 years | Traffic loads; corrosion |
| On-site detention tanks | 50 years and more | Maintenance; access |
| Treatment device media and filters | 1 to 5 years | Sediment load |
| Subsoil drains | 15 to 30 years | Silting; roots |

What shortens it: sediment and litter from car parks, construction and landscaping; tree roots entering joints; traffic over pits and grates not rated for it; lack of maintenance of detention and treatment devices.

The pipes usually outlast the building; the maintainable parts (grates, treatment media, detention screens and orifices) set the real maintenance cycle.

sections.heading: Blocked pits, pipes and subsoil drains
sections.markdown:
Roots enter pipe joints and grow into masses that block flow and crack pipes; ground movement displaces joints; pipes crushed by traffic or construction collapse.

Leaves, litter, sediment and debris block grates, pits and pipes; water then ponds on pavements, enters buildings and basements, and overflows into neighbouring land.

Silted or root-blocked subsoil drains let groundwater build up behind retaining walls, under slabs and around footings, causing damp, heave and wall failure.

Stormwater connected to the sewer overloads it in storms; sewer connected to stormwater pollutes waterways. Both are breaches.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ponding at one pit after every storm | Blocked pit or pipe. Inspection; CCTV. | Clear the pit and pipe; survey by CCTV if it recurs. |
| Repeated blockage downstream of trees | Root intrusion. CCTV. | Cut the roots as an interim, then reline or replace the damaged pipe. |
| Damp behind retaining walls and under slabs | Blocked subsoil drains. Inspection; flushing. | Flush the subsoil drains, and renew them if they cannot be cleared. |
| Long, flat stormwater runs silting up | Gradient too shallow. Levels survey against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Relay the run to fall, or add access for regular flushing. |

sections.heading: Detention and treatment
sections.markdown:
Detention tanks release water through small orifices that block with debris; tanks fill with sediment and lose storage; access covers are buried or sealed. Failed detention increases flooding downstream and on the site itself, and in many places the owner has a legal obligation to maintain it.

Gross pollutant traps and filters fill with litter and sediment and then bypass, discharging pollutants; clogged media stops working.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Detention tank never empties or empties instantly | Blocked orifice or missing orifice plate. Inspection. | Clear or replace the orifice plate and screens, remove sediment, and reinstate accessible covers. |
| Treatment devices or pit baskets full of litter and sediment | Maintenance lapsed. Device inspection; maintenance records against the agreement. | Clean the devices and set a maintenance schedule. |

sections.heading: Overland flow and capacity
sections.markdown:
Systems sized for older rainfall data or smaller paved areas are overwhelmed when sites are extended, paved over, or when design rainfall intensities are revised upward.

Fences, retaining walls, landscaping, sheds and raised paving built across overland flow paths force floodwater into buildings and basements during large storms.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Site floods in large storms only | Overland flow blocked or system capacity exceeded. Flow path review; design capacity. | Check the overland flow path first, then the design capacity; restore the path before upsizing pipes. |
| Water entering the building at a low threshold in storms | Overland flow reaching the building. Levels at thresholds against the flow path. | Raise thresholds, regrade, or add grated drains at the entry. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Broken or missing grates in traffic or pedestrian areas; flooding into switchrooms or basements | safety · 4 Essential | Make safe now. |
| Collapsed pipes; blocked system causing flooding | failure · 3 Important | Repair now. |
| On-site detention maintenance required by title or council | deadline · 4 Essential | As required. |
| Sediment build-up; roots; failing devices | condition · 3 Important | Clean and repair in the near term. |
| Treatment media and devices at end of life | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Replace. |
| No drawings; detention obligations unknown | check · 3 Important | Investigate. |
| Normal | nil · 1 Routine | Routine cleaning. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A civil or hydraulic engineer, with a drainage contractor for cleaning and CCTV. The checks below start at the surface, because flooding is often a blocked flow path rather than a pipe problem, then go underground by CCTV.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Drawings and obligations review | Stormwater design, detention and treatment requirements, and any covenants or council conditions. |
| Pit and pipe inspection | Lift grates, measure sediment, CCTV pipes, with pipe falls compared with the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). |
| Detention tank inspection | Access, orifice plates, screens, sediment, storage volume. |
| Treatment device inspection | Litter and sediment levels, media condition. |
| Overland flow path survey | Obstructions and levels against design. |
| Subsoil drain flushing and inspection | . |
| Connection check | For illegal cross-connections. |
| Capacity check | Of the system against current design rainfall and the paved area now draining to it, especially after extensions. |
| Storm observation | Where practicable, observe the site in heavy rain to see where water actually goes. |

The report should state system condition, flood risk, compliance with detention and treatment obligations, and a maintenance plan.

sections.heading: Cleaning, repairing and restoring
sections.markdown:
Most stormwater work is cleaning and restoring what is already there: pits, pipes, detention tanks and flow paths. Capacity upgrades come last, once the surface and the existing system have been checked, because floodwater is often a blocked path rather than an undersized pipe.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cleaning programme | Scheduled cleaning of grates, pits, pipes, detention tanks and treatment devices, with extra visits after storms and leaf fall. | Always; obligations on title often require it. |
| Pipe repairs | Root cutting as an interim, then relining or excavation and replacement of damaged pipes. | Where roots or damage cause repeated blockage. |
| Grate replacement | Load-rated grates suited to the traffic, with heel-safe and bicycle-safe patterns in pedestrian areas. | Wherever grates are broken, missing or sit proud. |
| Detention restoration | Clear or replace orifice plates and screens, remove sediment, and reinstate accessible covers so maintenance can be done. | Where a tank never empties or empties at once, or cannot be reached for maintenance. |
| Overland flow path restoration | Remove, lower or open fences, walls and landscaping that block flow, and regrade where needed so water passes the building safely. | Where fences, walls or landscaping block the path water takes in a storm. |
| Subsoil drain renewal | Renew the subsoil drains behind retaining walls and under pavements. | Where they cannot be flushed clear. |
| Capacity upgrades | Larger pipes and pits, additional inlets, or added detention where flooding recurs. | Where flooding recurs once the flow paths and the existing system are clear. |
| Treatment device servicing | Service the devices and replace their media. | On the device's cycle, typically every one to five years for media. |
| Correct illegal connections | Separate stormwater from sewer where they are connected. | Wherever a survey finds them. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Cleaning and inspection recur, often annually and after major storms, and are best carried as recurring maintenance. Pipe repairs are priced by length; relining by length and diameter; grates and pits per item. Detention restoration is a lump sum, often modest unless access must be rebuilt. Overland flow path works range from minor fence changes to regrading. Capacity upgrades are lump-sum civil projects. Treatment media is replaced on a cycle.

Cleaning is repairs and maintenance; detention and treatment compliance is code compliance; flood protection works are risk-driven; replacement is lifecycle.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a dry-day inspection cannot: what the system was designed for, what the owner is obliged to maintain, and where the site has flooded. Obligations recorded on title bind the owner whether or not anyone remembers them.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Stormwater drawings and design | Where the water is meant to go, and what the system was designed for. |
| On-site detention and treatment obligations, covenants and maintenance plans | What the owner must maintain, and how often, under title or council conditions. |
| Cleaning and maintenance records | Whether pits, pipes and tanks have been cleaned as required. |
| CCTV surveys | The condition of the pipes underground, and where roots have got in. |
| Flood history | Where and how often the site has flooded. |
| Council correspondence on stormwater | Whether the council has raised concerns about the system. |
| Records of flooding events and insurance claims | What flooding has cost, and whether insurers have been involved. |
| Council orders or notices about stormwater | Whether there are outstanding orders to comply with. |
| Records of site extensions or paving since the stormwater design | Whether more water now runs off the site than the system was designed for. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Stormwater problems are easily blamed on the pipes, when the cause is often on the surface, or in maintenance that nobody has done for years.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| Flooding in storms means the pipes are too small | Floodwater entering basements and ground floors in storms is often a blocked overland flow path or detention system rather than a pipe problem. Check the surface first. |
| A detention tank looks after itself | Orifices block, sediment fills the storage and covers get buried; the maintenance is often an obligation on title. |
| One blocked pit is a one-off | Ponding at the same pit after every storm points to a blocked pit or pipe; repeated blockage downstream of trees points to roots. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market regulates stormwater through design standards and through conditions that oblige owners to manage it on site. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out the design standards and the on-site obligations.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Design | AS/NZS 3500.3 covers stormwater drainage; Australian Rainfall and Runoff sets design rainfall and flood guidance. | Approved Document H covers rainwater drainage; the CIRIA SuDS Manual sets sustainable drainage practice. | Plumbing codes cover building storm drainage. |
| On-site obligations | Councils impose on-site detention and water quality conditions, often backed by covenants on title requiring owners to maintain them. | Planning conditions and, in Wales, statutory approval regimes require SuDS and their maintenance. | Local stormwater codes and permits under the Clean Water Act set on-site management; maintenance agreements are often recorded against property. |

In strata and condominium schemes in all three countries, site stormwater, detention and treatment systems are common property, and maintenance obligations recorded on title bind the owners corporation; failure to maintain can lead to council orders and liability for flooding of neighbours.

sections.heading: Worked example: a basement car park that floods in storms
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 2000s office building's basement car park takes water down its ramp in heavy storms, though not in ordinary rain. A garden wall was built across the low side of the site some years ago, and the on-site detention tank's access cover is buried under landscaping.

Flooding only in large storms points to an overland flow path or capacity, not a blocked pipe. The garden wall across the low point is the first suspect: it blocks the path water used to take past the building. The buried cover means the detention tank cannot have been maintained, and a blocked orifice or a tank full of sediment would make things worse.

So the register carries flooding into the basement as a safety line, restoring the flow path and the detention tank as failure lines, and a check of the title for maintenance obligations. A capacity upgrade is considered only if flooding recurs once those are done.

thresholds.rule: 75 mm and 100 mm drains no flatter than 1:100; 150 mm at 1:150; 225 mm at 1:225

pages.title: Structural Core
pages.question: How do cores, shear walls and bracing fail, and how do alterations undermine a building's stability?
pages.answer: Lateral systems rarely wear out; they are cut and removed. Cores and shear walls collect openings for services and doors until capacity is lost; bracing is removed from warehouse bays and fit-outs for new layouts; steel bracing connections corrode. Soft-storey buildings over open parking are especially vulnerable in earthquakes. Missing bracing in a portal frame or significant unengineered core openings need temporary bracing and an engineer now.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about structural core; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.

pages.searchTitle: Cores, shear walls and bracing: openings, removed bracing and seismic retrofit

questions.question: Can bracing be removed for a new door?
questions.answer: Not without an engineer's design. Removed bracing needs temporary bracing at once, then permanent bracing reinstated or relocated to suit the new layout.

questions.question: Can I core through a lift or stair core wall?
questions.answer: Never without a structural engineer's design. Core walls and shear walls matter far more than the loads they carry day to day suggest.

questions.question: What is a soft storey?
questions.answer: An open or weak storey, often a ground floor of parking or shops beneath residential floors, which is vulnerable in earthquakes. Several US cities require such buildings to be retrofitted.

questions.question: Why does our building sway in the wind?
questions.answer: Noticeable sway may reflect reduced stiffness or simply the design limits of a tall building. Monitoring and an assessment tell them apart.

questions.question: How long does structural bracing last?
questions.answer: Steel bracing and connections last the life of the building if protected; their coatings are renewed as they wear.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Lateral system problems show as openings cut through core walls, bays missing their bracing, diagonal cracking in shear walls, and occupants noticing sway. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On site | Openings, cores and chases in lift and stair core walls; new risers and doors through shear walls | Openings and removed bracing |
| On site | Missing bracing in warehouse bays; bracing rods slack, bent or disconnected | Openings and removed bracing |
| On site | Diagonal cracking in core and shear walls | Soft storeys, cracking and movement |
| On site | Occupants noticing sway in wind in taller buildings | Soft storeys, cracking and movement |
| On site | Open ground floors under residential floors in seismic areas | Soft storeys, cracking and movement |
| On site | Corrosion at bracing connections and base plates | Connections and construction defects |
| In the records | Structural drawings showing the lateral system | Investigation before the scope |
| In the records | Records of coring and openings with engineering | Openings and removed bracing |
| In the records | Fit-out drawings showing bracing changes | Openings and removed bracing |
| In the records | Seismic evaluations and retrofit orders | Standards by country |
| In the records | Post-earthquake inspections | Soft storeys, cracking and movement |
| In the records | Penetrations in core walls grouped closely together around new risers, or near wall ends and corners, where they matter most | Openings and removed bracing |

sections.heading: Types of lateral system
sections.markdown:
The structural core and bracing system keep a building upright against sideways forces: wind, earthquake and the small imperfections that would otherwise let a frame sway and buckle. In multi-storey buildings this is usually a concrete core around lifts and stairs, sometimes with additional shear walls; in steel buildings it may be braced bays or rigid moment frames; in low-rise sheds and houses it is bracing in walls and roofs. Because these elements carry little vertical load, their importance is easy to overlook when cutting openings or removing walls.

| System | Where it is found | Main vulnerabilities |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Concrete lift and stair cores | Offices and apartments of most eras | Openings cut for services and doors; construction defects |
| Concrete shear walls | Apartments, car parks, mid-rise | Penetrations; removal in alterations |
| Steel braced frames | Steel buildings, warehouses, portal frames | Bracing removed; corroded connections |
| Moment-resisting frames | Steel and concrete buildings | Connection detailing in older seismic design |
| Timber wall and roof bracing | Houses and low-rise | Bracing panels removed or cut in renovations |
| Transfer structures | Podiums and mixed-use buildings | High loads; alterations; detailing |

Seismic design requirements have tightened over time in all three countries, most heavily on the US west coast. Older buildings in seismic regions, including soft-storey buildings with open ground floors over parking, can have lateral systems far weaker than current standards require.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Cores, shear walls and bracing last the life of the building if they are protected and left intact. What shortens their life is rarely wear: it is the accumulated openings, removed bracing and corroded connections that steadily reduce what the lateral system can resist.

| Element | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Concrete cores and shear walls | Life of the building | Alterations; durability |
| Steel bracing and connections | Life of the building if protected | Corrosion; removal |
| Timber bracing panels | Life of the building if kept | Renovations; decay |
| Seismic retrofit elements | Life of the building | Maintenance; damage in earthquakes |

Lateral systems rarely wear out. What shortens their effective life is change:

What shortens it: openings and penetrations cut through cores and shear walls for doors, ducts and pipes; bracing removed in fit-outs and alterations, often because it obstructs a new layout; corrosion of steel bracing and connections in exposed or damp areas; added height or mass that increases lateral loads; earthquake damage that weakens the system for the next event.

sections.heading: Openings and removed bracing
sections.markdown:
Core and shear walls are cored and cut for new services, risers and doors throughout a building's life. Each opening removes concrete and may cut reinforcement; several near each other, or near wall ends and corners, can significantly reduce capacity and create weak points. Cores are often more penetrated than any other element.

In warehouses, bracing bays are removed or relocated for new doors and racking; in offices, braced partitions are removed in fit-outs; in houses, bracing walls are removed to open up living areas. Without bracing, frames sway and can buckle or collapse in wind or earthquake.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Many cores and openings through a lift core | Accumulated service penetrations. Survey against drawings; engineering review. | Survey against the drawings; get an engineering review, with strengthening around openings where needed. |
| Warehouse bay without the bracing shown on drawings | Bracing removed for doors or racking. Drawing comparison. | Install temporary bracing now; reinstate or relocate it to an engineer's design. |
| Building now taller or more public than its original class | Robustness short of the new consequence class. In England offices and flats over 15 storeys fall in Class 3 and need a systematic risk assessment, while those over 4 storeys sit in Class 2b (Approved Document A, Table 11). | Have the lateral system and robustness assessed before the change. |

sections.heading: Soft storeys, cracking and movement
sections.markdown:
Buildings with open ground floors (for parking or shopfronts) beneath stiffer upper floors concentrate earthquake movement in the ground storey, which can collapse. Many such buildings in California have been required to retrofit.

Diagonal cracking in shear walls and cores indicates shear distress; cracking at the base or at openings can indicate overload or settlement; excessive sway in wind shows reduced stiffness.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Diagonal cracks in a shear wall | Shear distress from overload, settlement or past earthquake. Engineering assessment. | Get an engineering assessment, then repair or strengthen. |
| Noticeable sway in wind | Reduced stiffness or design limits. Monitoring; assessment. | Monitor the sway, and have it assessed. |
| Rust staining or spalling on concrete core walls | Reinforcement corrosion. Carbonation depth and chloride at bar depth: the carbonation front marks a fall in pH from about 12.5 to 8.5, shown by phenolphthalein on a fresh break, and the chloride threshold is generally taken as 0.2 to 0.4 per cent by mass of cement (Institute of Corrosion). | Map the corrosion, repair the concrete, and protect it against further carbonation or chloride. |

sections.heading: Connections and construction defects
sections.markdown:
Steel bracing connections corrode where water collects; older moment frame connections in seismic regions were found after the 1994 Northridge earthquake to fracture in a brittle way and have since been the subject of retrofit guidance.

Cores and walls can have cold joints, honeycombing and poorly compacted concrete, particularly at congested reinforcement, and later reveal these through leaks and cracking.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Slack or bent bracing rods | Movement, impact or corrosion. Inspection. | Inspect, then retension, repair or replace the rods and their connections. |
| Lift doors binding or guide rails out of line | Core movement or settlement. Verticality survey of the core; the lift contractor’s alignment records. | Survey the core and have an engineer review it before the lift is realigned. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bracing removed in a portal frame building; significant openings in cores without engineering; earthquake damage | safety · 4 Essential | Brace temporarily and engineer now. |
| Shear distress cracking | failure · 4 Essential | Repair and strengthen now. |
| Seismic retrofit required by ordinance | deadline · 4 Essential | By the ordinance date. |
| Corroded bracing connections; minor unengineered penetrations | condition · 3 Important | Repair in the near term. |
| Protective coatings on exposed bracing at end of life | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Recoat on cycle. |
| Lateral system unknown; seismic adequacy unassessed in seismic regions | check · 3 Important | Assess. |
| Normal | nil · 1 Routine | Routine. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A structural engineer leads; a seismic specialist joins in seismic regions. The checks below compare the lateral system as built with the drawings, then look for distress in walls, bracing and connections.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Drawing review | To identify the lateral system and compare it with the building as it now is. |
| Penetration survey | Of cores and shear walls, with scanning to locate reinforcement before any new coring. |
| Bracing survey | In steel and timber buildings for missing, altered or damaged members. |
| Condition survey | For cracking, corrosion and concrete defects, with carbonation depth and chloride content tested where reinforcement corrosion is suspected (Institute of Corrosion). |
| Structural analysis | Of lateral capacity with the openings and changes accounted for. |
| Seismic evaluation | To the recognised method for existing buildings in seismic regions. |
| Monitoring | Of sway or crack movement where concerns exist. |

The report should state the lateral system's adequacy, the effect of alterations, any urgent measures, and strengthening options.

Where drawings are missing, the lateral system may have to be inferred from the structure itself, which takes opening up and scanning.

sections.heading: Bracing, strengthening or retrofitting
sections.markdown:
Removed bracing gets temporary bracing at once, until a permanent design is in place. After that, the work restores what has been cut or corroded and, in seismic regions, strengthens the building to current expectations, with controls so the next cut is engineered.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Temporary bracing | Bracing installed wherever bracing has been removed. | At once, until permanent replacement. |
| Reinstated or relocated bracing | Bracing designed by an engineer to suit the new layout. | Wherever bracing has been removed for doors or racking. |
| Strengthening around openings | Steel frames, fibre-reinforced polymer or added concrete. | Where openings have weakened cores or shear walls. |
| Seismic retrofit | New shear walls or braced frames, strengthened connections, soft-storey strengthening, and base isolation for important buildings. | In seismic regions, and wherever an ordinance requires it. |
| Connection repair | Repair and recoat corroded bracing. | Where connections and base plates corrode. |
| Concrete repair | Repair defects and cracks. | Where construction defects or cracking are found. |
| Controls on future penetrations | A permit system and penetration register for cores and shear walls. | Always; it stops the next unengineered opening. |
| Post-earthquake assessment and repair | Rapid safety evaluation, then detailed assessment and repair of damaged elements before reoccupation. | After an earthquake. |
| Documentation | Mark core and shear walls on fit-out drawings and on site. | So trades know not to cut them. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Assessment and analysis are lump sums. Temporary bracing is an immediate cost. Strengthening and seismic retrofit are lump-sum projects, often large, which may require tenants to vacate. Bracing reinstatement in warehouses is per bay. Penetration management is a low-cost procedure that avoids large future costs.

Safety items are immediate; ordinance retrofits carry deadlines; strengthening is a condition or code compliance item; recoating is lifecycle.

Seismic retrofits often attract incentives or are tied to ordinance timetables, which affect funding and programme.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a walk-through cannot: what the lateral system is, what has been cut or removed since, and whether the building's seismic adequacy has been assessed. Ask for them before any fit-out that touches cores, shear walls or bracing.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Structural drawings showing the lateral system | What the lateral system is, and where it runs. |
| Records of coring and openings in cores and shear walls, with engineering | Which openings in cores and shear walls were engineered. |
| Fit-out and alteration drawings affecting bracing | Whether fit-outs have removed or moved bracing. |
| Seismic evaluations, retrofit orders and completion records | Whether a seismic retrofit is required, and whether it was completed. |
| Post-earthquake inspection reports | What was found after past earthquakes. |
| Penetration permits or register | Whether new penetrations are controlled. |
| Earthquake insurance terms and any seismic assessment used for lending | Whether insurance or lending depends on a seismic assessment. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Cores and bracing are misread when their importance is judged by the loads they carry day to day, and when bracing missing from a bay is assumed to have been redundant.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| It carries little load, so it can go | Never cut, core or remove core walls, shear walls or bracing without a structural engineer's design. Their importance is not obvious from the loads they carry day to day. |
| The bracing was not needed | A warehouse bay without the bracing shown on the drawings has usually lost it to doors or racking. It needs temporary bracing now, and a permanent design to suit the new layout. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets wind and earthquake loads and design standards, and rules for assessing and altering existing structures. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Loads and design | AS/NZS 1170.2 sets wind actions and AS 1170.4 earthquake actions; AS 3600 and AS 4100 govern concrete and steel; earthquake design has applied nationally since the 1990s. | Approved Document A, including requirements to avoid disproportionate collapse, and the Eurocodes govern design; seismic design is rarely required. | ASCE 7 sets wind and seismic loads. |
| Existing buildings | The National Construction Code requires structural adequacy for alterations. | The Institution of Structural Engineers publishes guidance on appraisal of existing structures. | ASCE 41 governs the seismic evaluation and retrofit of existing buildings, and the International Existing Building Code alterations; Los Angeles and San Francisco require soft-storey and non-ductile concrete retrofits. |

Insurance and lending in seismic regions increasingly depend on a building's seismic assessment in all three markets where earthquake risk is material.

sections.heading: Worked example: bracing removed for a new roller door
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 1990s portal-framed warehouse had a new roller door installed in an end bay during a tenant fit-out. The structural drawings show cross bracing in that bay; on site there is none, and no engineering for its removal is on record. The rods in the next bay are slack.

Bracing removed from a portal frame bay is a safety finding: its importance is not obvious from the loads it carries day to day, but it is what holds the building against wind. The slack rods next door may now be taking more than they were designed for.

So the register carries the missing bracing as a safety line now, with temporary bracing until an engineer designs a permanent arrangement around the door, the slack rods inspected and retensioned, and the bracing marked on fit-out drawings.

pages.title: Structural Frame
pages.question: How do concrete, steel and timber frames deteriorate, how do you read the cracks, and when is a frame unsafe?
pages.answer: Frames deteriorate where protection fails. Carbonation reaches thin-covered steel and cracks concrete along the bars; chlorides from accelerators, vehicles or sea air pit reinforcement with little warning, worst in car parks. Alkali-silica reaction map-cracks concrete. Steel corrodes where water reaches it, including encased steel behind masonry. Alterations cut openings, cores and tendons. Cracks around columns on top of flat slabs can signal punching shear and need urgent attention.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about structural frame; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
