questions.question: Are cracks around columns on a car park deck serious?
questions.answer: They can be. Cracks radiating around columns on the top of a flat slab can indicate punching shear distress; it needs an engineer urgently and may need propping.

questions.question: Why does concrete spall along the reinforcement?
questions.answer: The steel is corroding, from carbonation across a facade with low cover, or from chlorides in car parks and near the sea. Testing at bar depth shows which.

questions.question: Why isn't a patch repair enough in a car park?
questions.answer: In chloride-contaminated concrete, patches can accelerate corrosion next to them unless combined with protection such as cathodic protection.

questions.question: What is alkali-silica reaction?
questions.answer: A reaction within the concrete that causes map cracking, often with white gel. Petrographic examination of cores confirms it.

questions.question: How long do car park decks last?
questions.answer: Typically 30 to 60 years before major repair, with protective coatings and membranes renewed every 10 to 20.

questions.question: Why is concrete breaking away near the drains in the parking garage?
questions.answer: Chloride-induced corrosion of the reinforcement. Repair with cathodic protection, and fix the deck drainage and membranes.

questions.question: Is a sagging floor with cracked partitions a structural problem?
questions.answer: It can be: deflection beyond what the floor was designed for. Survey the deflection, compare it with the design, and have an engineer advise on loads or strengthening.

questions.question: Why is rust coming through the brickwork in lines up the building?
questions.answer: Steel encased in the masonry is corroding. Open up, treat and recoat the encased steel, or replace badly corroded members.

questions.question: What do diagonal cracks near the ends of a concrete beam mean?
questions.answer: Shear distress. Get an engineering assessment; the remedy is strengthening with plates, wraps or added members.

questions.question: Why is the concrete cracking in a map pattern with white deposits?
questions.answer: That is the pattern of alkali-silica reaction. Confirm it by petrographic examination of cores; have an engineer assess, and strengthen where needed.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Frame problems show as cracks along reinforcement and spalled concrete, map cracking, cracks around columns on slab tops, rust bleeding through finishes, and sagging members. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On site | Cracks running along the line of reinforcement, with rust staining; spalled concrete exposing bars | Carbonation and chlorides |
| On site | Map cracking with gel deposits, suggesting alkali-silica reaction | Alkali-silica reaction and problem concretes |
| On site | Cracks radiating around columns on the top of car park and podium slabs, and deflection near columns | Punching shear and alterations |
| On site | Water ponding on car park decks; failed joints and membranes; staining on soffits | Carbonation and chlorides |
| On site | Corroded steel at bases, connections and perimeter; rust bleeding through encasement | Steel corrosion and fire damage |
| On site | Sagging beams or slabs; cracks in partitions below | Punching shear and alterations |
| On site | Openings, cores and cut elements not shown on drawings | Punching shear and alterations |
| In the records | Structural drawings and calculations | Investigation before the scope |
| In the records | Previous condition surveys, concrete testing and repairs | Investigation before the scope |
| In the records | Records of alterations and their engineering | Punching shear and alterations |
| In the records | Car park inspection reports where required | Standards by country |
| In the records | Fire history | Steel corrosion and fire damage |

sections.heading: Types of frame
sections.markdown:
The structural frame is the skeleton of columns, beams and their connections that carries a building's floors, roof and envelope to the foundations. Frames are reinforced concrete (cast in place or precast), structural steel, composite steel and concrete, timber (sawn, glulam and, increasingly, cross-laminated timber), or combinations. The frame's condition depends on what protects it: concrete cover protecting reinforcement, coatings and fire protection on steel, and dryness for timber.

| Type and era | Where it is found | What it implies |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Steel frame encased in masonry or concrete, 1900s to 1940s | Early offices, warehouses, department stores | Hidden corrosion of encased steel; rust jacking of the encasement |
| Reinforced concrete with calcium chloride accelerators, 1950s to 1970s | Offices, car parks, apartments | Chloride-induced reinforcement corrosion, often aggressive |
| High alumina cement concrete, 1950s to early 1970s (Britain) | Precast beams in schools, offices, industrial roofs | Strength loss with age and moisture |
| Large panel precast systems, 1960s to 1970s | Residential towers, especially in Britain | Robustness of joints; progressive collapse risk |
| Post-tensioned concrete, 1970s onward | Car parks, offices, apartments | Tendon corrosion; damage during alterations |
| Multi-storey car park flat slabs, 1960s to 1990s | Car parks | Chlorides from vehicles; punching shear at columns |
| Modern concrete and steel frames, 1990s onward | Most commercial and residential | Usually sound; issues come from alterations and water |
| Mass timber (glulam, CLT), 2010s onward | New offices, schools, apartments | Moisture during construction and in service; connections |

The era and type of frame tell you where to look. Car parks deserve particular attention: they combine exposed concrete, chlorides carried in on vehicles, water ponding and cycles of wetting and drying, and some older designs are vulnerable to punching shear failure around columns.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
A reinforced concrete or protected steel frame lasts the life of the building, often a hundred years and more, but its protection does not: coatings and membranes on concrete last ten to twenty years, exposed steel twenty-five to fifty between recoats, and car park decks thirty to sixty before major repair.

| Element | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Reinforced concrete frame | Life of the building, often 100 years and more | Cover; carbonation; chlorides; water |
| Car park decks and ramps | 30 to 60 years before major repair | Chlorides; drainage; protection coatings |
| Structural steel frame, protected | Life of the building | Coating and fire protection; water |
| Exposed steel | 25 to 50 years between major recoating | Corrosivity of the environment |
| Timber and mass timber frames | Life of the building if dry | Moisture; connections; fire protection |
| Protective coatings and membranes on concrete | 10 to 20 years | Traffic; UV; product |

What shortens life: low cover to reinforcement, which lets carbonation and chlorides reach the steel early; chlorides: added as accelerators in older concrete, carried in on vehicles from salted roads, or from sea air; water: leaking roofs, failed membranes, ponding car park decks and blocked drainage; alterations: openings cut, columns removed, tendons cut, loads changed; fire, which weakens concrete, steel and timber.

sections.heading: Carbonation and chlorides
sections.markdown:
Concrete protects steel through its alkalinity. Carbon dioxide from the air slowly neutralises it from the surface inward; when this carbonation front reaches the reinforcement and moisture is present, the steel corrodes. The rust expands, cracking and spalling the concrete along the bars. It is slow, widespread and most common where cover is thin.

Chlorides break down the protective layer on steel even in alkaline concrete, producing localised pitting that can remove a large part of a bar's section with little surface sign. It is the main cause of serious deterioration in car parks, marine structures and concrete built with chloride accelerators, and can be structurally significant before spalling appears.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cracking and spalling along bars across a facade or soffit | Carbonation-induced corrosion. Carbonation depth at the steel; low cover. The carbonation front marks a fall in pH from about 12.5 to 8.5, shown by phenolphthalein on a fresh break (Institute of Corrosion). | Patch repair, then anti-carbonation coatings or realkalisation. |
| Localised spalling in a car park, especially near joints and drains | Chloride-induced corrosion. Chloride content at bar depth, against a threshold generally taken as 0.2 to 0.4 per cent by mass of cement (Institute of Corrosion); half-cell potentials. | Repair with cathodic protection, and fix the deck drainage and membranes. |

sections.heading: Alkali-silica reaction and problem concretes
sections.markdown:
Some aggregates react with alkalis in cement to form a gel that swells with moisture, cracking concrete in a map pattern and sometimes causing expansion that distorts elements. It develops over decades and needs moisture.

High alumina cement concrete, used in British precast beams in the 1950s to 1970s, loses strength as it converts with age, heat and moisture, and led to collapses in the 1970s. Reinforced autoclaved aerated concrete planks are covered on the roof structure page.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Map cracking with white gel | Alkali-silica reaction. Petrographic examination of cores. | Confirm by petrographic examination; have an engineer assess, and strengthen where needed. |

sections.heading: Punching shear and alterations
sections.markdown:
In flat slabs without beams, the slab around each column carries very high shear. Reinforcement corrosion, deterioration and added load (soil and landscaping on podium decks, resurfacing) can lead to a slab punching through around a column, and once one column fails the load can cascade. Older car parks and podiums are the main concern.

Openings cut through slabs and walls, cores drilled for services, columns removed, beams notched, post-tensioning tendons cut, and heavier loads from new uses all change how the frame carries load. Many are done without engineering.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cracking around columns on the top of a flat slab | Punching shear distress. Engineering assessment; deflection survey. | Call an engineer urgently; prop if advised, restrict loads, and add punching shear reinforcement. |
| Diagonal cracks near beam supports | Shear distress. Engineering assessment. | Get an engineering assessment; strengthen with plates, wraps or added members. |
| Vertical cracks at mid-span soffits | Flexural cracking from load or loss of capacity. Load review against the design loads and the asset’s market (Thresholds by market); reinforcement check. | Review the loads and check the reinforcement; restrict loads or strengthen. |
| Beams or slabs visibly sagging, with cracked partitions | Deflection beyond serviceability. Level survey against the design limits and the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Survey the deflection, compare it with the design, and have an engineer advise on loads or strengthening. |

sections.heading: Steel corrosion and fire damage
sections.markdown:
Steel frames corrode where water reaches them: perimeter columns and beams behind leaking façades, steel encased in masonry, connections and base plates in damp basements, and exposed steel in car parks and industrial buildings.

Fire spalls concrete and reduces the strength of exposed reinforcement, buckles and weakens steel, and chars timber. The structure may stand after a fire with reduced capacity.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rust bleeding through masonry at column lines | Encased steel corrosion. Opening up. | Open up, treat and recoat the encased steel, or replace badly corroded members. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Punching shear distress; significant section loss at critical members; spalling over occupied areas; post-fire damage | safety · 4 Essential | Prop, exclude and engineer now. |
| Corrosion with loss of section in members; cut tendons | failure · 4 Essential | Repair or strengthen now. |
| Statutory car park or milestone inspection due | deadline · 4 Essential | At the prescribed interval. |
| Corrosion and spalling without significant section loss; ASR; failed car park membranes | condition · 3 Important | Repair programme in the near term. |
| Protective coatings and membranes at end of life | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Renew on cycle. |
| Problem concretes possible; alterations unengineered; no survey of a car park | check · 3 Important | Assess. |
| Isolated minor cracking | nil · 1 Routine | Monitor. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A structural engineer experienced in existing structures leads, with a concrete testing specialist for durability. The checks below read the crack pattern first, then test the concrete and open up the steel to establish the cause and the loss of section.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Desk study | Drawings, calculations, construction era and materials, previous surveys and repairs, alterations and their approvals. |
| Visual and hammer survey | Of exposed surfaces, mapping cracks, spalls, rust staining and delamination. |
| Cover survey | By covermeter or radar, and reinforcement location before any drilling. |
| Carbonation depth | Testing at a sample of locations. |
| Chloride profiles | From dust samples at increasing depths to the reinforcement, against a threshold generally taken as 0.2 to 0.4 per cent by mass of cement (Institute of Corrosion). |
| Half-cell potential and resistivity mapping | To locate active corrosion in chloride-contaminated areas. |
| Cores | For strength and petrographic examination for alkali-silica reaction, high alumina cement and other problems. |
| Opening up | At representative locations to measure section loss of bars and steel members. |
| Structural assessment | Of capacity against current loads, including punching shear for flat slabs. |
| Monitoring | Of deflection and crack movement where needed, against span/250 overall and span/500 after partitions (The Structural Engineer). |

The report should state the deterioration mechanisms, their extent and rate, structural capacity, safety issues and a repair and protection strategy with timing.

sections.heading: Repairing, protecting or strengthening
sections.markdown:
Punching shear distress and serious section loss come first, with propping where an engineer advises. Most of the rest is concrete repair and protection, chosen for whether corrosion is driven by carbonation or chlorides, since the right repair depends on which.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Patch repair | Break out damaged concrete, clean or replace reinforcement, and reinstate with repair mortars to recognised repair principles. | For carbonation damage; in chloride-contaminated concrete, only combined with other protection. |
| Cathodic protection | Impressed current or galvanic anode systems that stop corrosion in chloride-contaminated concrete. | Widely used in car parks and marine structures. |
| Electrochemical treatments | Realkalisation of carbonated concrete, and chloride extraction. | Where corrosion is widespread but the concrete is sound. |
| Protective coatings and membranes | Anti-carbonation coatings on facades, and traffic membranes on car park decks. | To keep water and chlorides out. |
| Drainage | Fix falls, outlets and joints on car park decks. | Wherever water ponds. |
| Strengthening | Fibre-reinforced polymer wraps and plates, steel plates and brackets, additional columns or beams, and punching shear reinforcement. | Where capacity is lost or loads have grown. |
| Steel repair | Blast, repair and recoat; replace badly corroded members; open up and treat encased steel. | Wherever steel corrodes. |
| Fire damage repair | Repair after assessment. | After a fire. |
| Load control | Restrict loads and remove surcharge from podiums. | While capacity is in doubt. |
| Demolition and replacement | A new structure. | Where repair is uneconomic or the structure is unsafe. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Investigation is a lump sum, with testing rates per sample. Patch repair is priced by area or volume of concrete, with access, propping and protection of the area below as major components; repairs in occupied car parks are phased by bay. Cathodic protection is priced by area with monitoring that recurs for its life. Membranes by area, recurring on their cycle. Strengthening is priced per element or as a lump sum.

The usual shape is two-part: investigation first, then a repair programme sized from it, often phased over years. Repairs to stop active deterioration are condition items; membranes and coatings are lifecycle; statutory inspections are deadlines; safety items are immediate.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a visual survey cannot: what the frame was designed for, what earlier testing found, and what has been cut or added since. Ask for them before any repair is specified, since the method depends on the cause.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Structural drawings and calculations | What the frame was designed to carry. |
| Previous structural surveys, concrete testing and repair records | What earlier testing found, and what was repaired. |
| Records of alterations, openings and coring, with engineering | Whether the frame has been cut or altered, and with what engineering. |
| Car park condition surveys and statutory inspection reports | Whether statutory car park inspections are current. |
| Cathodic protection monitoring records where installed | Whether cathodic protection is still working. |
| Fire history and any post-fire assessments | Whether a fire has affected the frame, and how it was assessed. |
| For strata buildings, capital works or reserve study entries for structural repair | Whether strata funds have provided for structural repair. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Frames are misread when cracks around columns on a flat slab are taken for ordinary cracking, and when every spall is repaired the same way regardless of its cause.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| Cracks on a slab top are ordinary | Cracking around columns on the top surface of flat slabs, especially in older car parks and on podiums carrying soil or landscaping, can indicate punching shear distress. It needs an engineer urgently and may require propping. |
| A patch repair fixes corrosion | Patches in chloride-contaminated concrete can accelerate corrosion next to them (the incipient anode effect) unless combined with other protection, such as cathodic protection. The cause decides the repair. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets standards for designing and repairing concrete and steel structures, and some impose periodic inspections of car parks and older buildings. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Design and repair | AS 3600 governs concrete structures, AS 4100 steel and AS 1720 timber; repairs follow recognised concrete repair practice. | The Eurocodes (BS EN 1992 concrete, 1993 steel, 1995 timber) govern design, and BS EN 1504 concrete repair and protection; the Institution of Structural Engineers publishes guidance on appraising existing structures. | ACI 562 governs assessment and repair of existing concrete structures, and the International Existing Building Code alterations. |
| Inspections and duties | Strata buildings carry structural repairs as common property, and New South Wales adds duties for building defects in apartment buildings. | The Building Safety Act 2022 adds structural safety duties for higher-risk buildings; CROSS collects structural safety reports. | New York City requires periodic inspection of parking structures, and Florida requires milestone structural inspections of condominium buildings of three or more storeys and structural integrity reserve studies. |

sections.heading: Worked example: cracks around columns on a car park roof
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 1970s car park has a flat-slab top deck, now used for overflow parking and carrying planters added later. Cracks radiate around several columns on the top surface, water ponds on the deck, and the soffits below show rust staining and spalls near the joints.

Cracks radiating around columns on the top of a flat slab can indicate punching shear distress, made worse by the planters' added load: it needs an engineer urgently and may need propping. The spalls near the joints point to chloride-induced corrosion, fed by the ponding water.

So the register carries the slab around the columns as a safety line now, with loads restricted and the planters removed, testing for chlorides as a check line, and repair with cathodic protection and a traffic membrane, with the drainage fixed, as condition lines.

thresholds.rule: Sag beyond span/250 impairs appearance; after partitions, deflection may be limited to span/500; brittle finishes damaged at L/500 or 20 mm, whichever is less

source.title: Deflection and preliminary vibration effects on structural elements (The Structural Engineer, 89(5), 2011)

thresholds.measure: Floor imposed loads (IBC Table 1607.1, as adopted in Massachusetts)
thresholds.rule: Offices 50 psf (2.4 kPa); corridors above the first floor 80 psf (3.8 kPa); light storage 125 psf (6.0 kPa)

source.title: 780 CMR Table 1607.1 Minimum uniformly distributed live loads (Massachusetts State Building Code, adopting the IBC table)

pages.title: Sub-floor & Crawlspace
pages.question: How do sub-floors and crawlspaces fail, and what causes decay and pest damage beneath floors?
pages.answer: Sub-floors fail when they get damp. Raised ground levels, paving and extensions block vents; leaks and downpipes wet the ground; timber then rots at stumps, bearers and joist ends. Termites enter through stumps and bridged barriers; in damp climates dry rot spreads through masonry. Uneven, springy floors and musty smells are the early signs. Remove the moisture source before replacing timber.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about sub-floor & crawlspace; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Soil condition, ground vapour barriers, sub-floor ventilation

pages.searchTitle: Sub-floors and crawlspaces: rot, termites, stumps, ventilation and damp

questions.question: Why is my floor springy under the bathroom?
questions.answer: Decay under bathrooms, kitchens and laundries usually points to a plumbing leak or failed wet area waterproofing above. Fix the source before replacing the timbers.

questions.question: How do I know if it is dry rot?
questions.answer: White strands spreading across masonry and fungal fruiting bodies point to dry rot. It needs specialist identification and treatment, with the moisture source removed.

questions.question: Is termite damage covered by insurance?
questions.answer: Often not. Many policies exclude termite damage, so prevention and regular inspection carry the risk.

questions.question: Why does the house smell musty?
questions.answer: Often poor sub-floor ventilation or damp ground. Clearing and adding vents, a ground vapour barrier, or mechanical ventilation dries it out.

questions.question: How long do termite barriers last?
questions.answer: Physical barriers and ant caps 20 to 50 years, and chemical barriers 5 to 10.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Sub-floor problems show inside as springy or sloping floors and musty smells, outside as blocked vents and mud tubes, and below as soft timber and damp ground. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| From inside and outside | Floors uneven, springy or sloping; cracks in plaster at floor level | Termites and stumps |
| From inside and outside | Vents and air bricks blocked, buried or painted over; ground levels close to or above floor framing | Services, ventilation and radon |
| From inside and outside | Musty smell inside; mould on skirtings | Services, ventilation and radon |
| From inside and outside | Mud tubes on stumps, piers and walls; damaged timber at the surface | Termites and stumps |
| In the sub-floor | Soft, cracked or stained timber at stumps, bearers and joist ends | Wet rot and dry rot |
| In the sub-floor | Standing water, damp soil, leaking pipes | Services, ventilation and radon |
| In the sub-floor | Ant caps missing or bridged | Termites and stumps |
| In the sub-floor | White strands or fruiting bodies of fungus | Wet rot and dry rot |
| In the sub-floor | Clearance from ground to timber | Services, ventilation and radon |
| In the records | Timber pest inspections and treatment records | Investigation before the scope |
| In the records | Restumping records | Drying, treating and replacing |
| In the records | Damp and timber treatment guarantees | Wet rot and dry rot |
| In the records | Radon tests | Services, ventilation and radon |

sections.heading: Types of sub-floor
sections.markdown:
A sub-floor or crawlspace is the space beneath a suspended ground floor: timber floors on bearers, joists and stumps or piers in older Australian houses; suspended timber ground floors on sleeper walls with air bricks in British terraces and semis; and crawlspaces under timber floors in American houses. The space must stay dry and ventilated, or the timber above decays and pests thrive.

| Form | Where it is found | Main issues |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Timber floor on stumps or piers, open sub-floor | Australian Victorian, Federation and inter-war houses; Queenslanders on high stumps | Stump decay and sinking; termites; ventilation |
| Suspended timber floor on sleeper walls with air bricks | British houses before about 1950 | Blocked air bricks; joist end decay; dry rot |
| Vented crawlspace | Older American houses | Humidity, mould, decay |
| Conditioned or encapsulated crawlspace | Newer and retrofitted US houses | Depends on vapour barrier and dehumidification |
| Concrete suspended ground floor with void | Some modern buildings | Ventilation; services; ground gases |

Ventilation is usually the deciding factor. Ground levels raised by paving and gardens, extensions built over vents, and air bricks blocked with debris or paint turn a dry sub-floor into a damp one.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Bearers and joists last sixty to a hundred years if kept dry, but timber stumps last thirty to sixty, chemical termite barriers five to ten, and vapour barriers twenty to thirty. A sub-floor's life depends almost entirely on keeping it dry, ventilated and inspectable.

| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Timber stumps | 30 to 60 years | Moisture; termites; treatment |
| Bearers and joists | 60 to 100 years if dry | Ventilation; leaks; pests |
| Ant caps and termite barriers | 20 to 50 years; chemical barriers 5 to 10 | Bridging; disturbance |
| Vapour barriers | 20 to 30 years | Damage; coverage |
| Sub-floor vents and air bricks | Life of the building if kept clear | Blockage |
| Crawlspace dehumidifiers | 8 to 12 years | Run hours |

What shortens life: blocked ventilation from raised ground levels, paving and extensions; water from leaking plumbing, overflowing downpipes and poor site drainage reaching the sub-floor; insufficient clearance between ground and timber; bridged termite barriers.

sections.heading: Wet rot and dry rot
sections.markdown:
Timber that stays above about 20 per cent moisture decays. Joist ends bearing on damp walls, bearers over wet ground, and stumps at ground level go first. Decayed timber is soft, cracked across the grain and darkened.

In Britain and other damp climates, dry rot (Serpula lacrymans) spreads from damp timber across masonry and through walls, destroying floors and joinery well away from the original source. It is identified by white strands, orange-brown fruiting bodies and cuboidal cracking.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Soft joist ends at external walls | Wet rot from damp walls or blocked vents. Moisture readings. | Clear the vents and lower the ground levels; replace the decayed timber. |
| White strands across masonry and fruiting bodies | Dry rot. Identification. | Remove the moisture source; cut out affected timber well beyond the visible damage, and treat the masonry. |
| Damp ground or standing water under the floor | Water reaching the sub-floor. Inspection after rain; ground falls; downpipe and plumbing discharge. | Regrade, connect downpipes, fix leaks, and lay a ground membrane where the ground stays damp. |

sections.heading: Termites and stumps
sections.markdown:
Subterranean termites, a major risk across most of Australia and the southern United States, enter through the sub-floor via stumps, piers and bridged barriers, hollowing timbers from inside. Borers attack sapwood in drier conditions.

Timber stumps rot and sink, concrete stumps crack and lean, and floors become uneven, springy and cracked. Restumping is a standard Australian repair.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Uneven floors in a house on timber stumps | Decayed or sunken stumps. Sub-floor inspection. | Restump, and replace decayed bearers and joists. |
| Hollow timbers with mud | Termites. Inspection; termite detection. | Treat with chemical barriers or baiting, fix ant caps and remove bridges; replace damaged timber. |
| Floor framing close to the ground | No room to ventilate or inspect. Ground clearance under the lowest member against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Lower the ground or improve access, and keep the clearance clear of stored material. |

sections.heading: Services, ventilation and radon
sections.markdown:
Three conditions here concern what else is in the sub-floor besides its timber: the pipes, drains, wiring and insulation that run through it, the air that sits in it, and, in radon-affected areas, the gas that rises into it from the ground.

Leaking pipes, disconnected drains and damaged wiring in sub-floors cause decay, contamination and hazards. Older sub-floors may hold asbestos debris.

Insulation added beneath floors without care can also trap moisture against timber or block vents, turning an energy upgrade into a decay problem.

Poorly ventilated crawlspaces grow mould, which affects indoor air above, and allow condensation on cold surfaces and services.

In radon-affected areas, gas collects in crawlspaces and enters the house through the floor. Ventilation and sealing reduce it.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Musty smell and mould | Poor ventilation or damp ground. Humidity and ventilation check, with vent area against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Clear and add vents, lay a ground vapour barrier, or add mechanical ventilation. |
| Damp only below one area | Plumbing leak or downpipe discharge. Inspection. | Fix the plumbing leak or downpipe. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Floor collapse risk from decay or termites; radon above action levels | safety · 4 Essential | Prop and remediate now. |
| Active termites; dry rot; failed stumps | failure · 4 Essential | Treat and repair now. |
| Blocked ventilation; damp; decay starting | condition · 3 Important | Repair in the near term. |
| Stumps and chemical barriers at end of life | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Restump; renew barriers. |
| No timber pest inspection; inaccessible sub-floor | check · 3 Important | Inspect. |
| Normal | nil · 1 Routine | Routine inspection. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A timber pest inspector and building surveyor; a structural engineer for extensive decay. The checks below read where the decay sits, which points to the moisture source, then identify any rot or termites.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Sub-floor inspection | Of stumps, piers, bearers, joists, and ground, with probing and moisture readings. |
| Timber pest inspection | To the relevant standard, with non-invasive detection where needed. |
| Ventilation assessment | Vent area, cross-flow, blockages and clearances, against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). |
| Level survey | Of floors. |
| Plumbing and drainage check | For leaks. |
| Radon test | In affected areas, against the action level that applies (4 pCi/L in the United States, US EPA). |
| Asbestos check | For debris and old materials. |
| Access | Where crawl access is too low or blocked, small access openings or camera inspection may be needed to see critical areas such as joist ends under bathrooms and kitchens. |
| Fungus identification | By a specialist where decay is found, distinguishing wet rot from dry rot, because the treatment and extent of removal differ. |
| Termite monitoring | With in-ground stations or detection equipment where activity is suspected but not seen. |

The report should state timber condition, pest activity, causes of damp, and repairs.

sections.heading: Drying, treating and replacing
sections.markdown:
Every repair here depends on removing the moisture first: ventilation, leaks, downpipes and site drainage. Then decayed and damaged timber is replaced, termites and dry rot are treated by specialists, and access is made so the sub-floor can be inspected again.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ventilation | Clear and add vents, lower ground levels, and add mechanical sub-floor ventilation where cross-flow is poor. | Wherever the sub-floor is damp or musty. |
| Fix water sources | Plumbing leaks, downpipes and site drainage. | First, wherever water reaches the sub-floor. |
| Restumping and timber replacement | Restump, and replace decayed bearers and joists. | Where stumps have failed or timber has decayed. |
| Termite management | Chemical barriers or baiting, ant caps, and removing bridges. | Wherever termites are active or barriers have lapsed. |
| Dry rot treatment | Remove the moisture source, cut out affected timber well beyond visible damage, and treat masonry. | Wherever dry rot is identified. |
| Ground vapour barriers | A barrier laid over the ground. | Where damp ground keeps the sub-floor humid. |
| Crawlspace encapsulation | Encapsulation with dehumidification. | In suitable climates. |
| Radon mitigation | Measures to keep radon out of the living space. | Where radon testing shows a need. |
| Access openings | Openings so the sub-floor can be inspected in future. | Wherever the sub-floor is inaccessible; a requirement for effective termite management in Australia. |
| Under-floor insulation | Insulation installed so it does not block ventilation or trap moisture. | When insulating the floor. |
| Asbestos removal | Removal of debris and old materials by licensed contractors. | Where the sub-floor holds asbestos debris. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Inspections recur annually in termite regions. Restumping is priced per stump or per house. Timber replacement by length. Termite barriers by perimeter length, recurring. Ventilation works itemised. Encapsulation by area.

Restumping and timber replacement are lifecycle or repairs; termite management recurs; active infestations are immediate.

Access is the main cost driver: low, obstructed or partly enclosed sub-floors make every task slower, and extensions over old sub-floors may require floors to be lifted from above. Dry rot remediation can extend into walls, plaster and joinery well beyond the floor. Annual timber pest inspections and periodic barrier renewal should be carried as recurring lines in termite regions.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a torch in the sub-floor cannot: whether termites have been found and treated, what earlier inspections said, and whether the insurance covers what is found. Ask for them before any repair is priced.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Timber pest inspection reports and treatment records | Whether termites or decay have been found, and how they were treated. |
| Restumping and sub-floor repair records | What has been replaced, and when. |
| Damp proofing and timber treatment guarantees | Whether past treatment is still guaranteed. |
| Radon test results | Whether radon is a concern. |
| Plumbing leak history | Whether leaks above are wetting the sub-floor. |
| Pre-purchase or periodic building and pest inspection reports | What earlier inspections found. |
| Records of extensions built over the sub-floor | Whether extensions have blocked ventilation or access. |
| Insurance terms on termite and decay damage | Whether termite and decay damage is covered. |
| Asbestos register for older houses | Whether debris or old materials in the sub-floor contain asbestos. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Sub-floor problems are misread when active termites and dry rot are treated as ordinary repairs, and when decayed timber is replaced without asking where the moisture came from.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| Termites and dry rot are ordinary repairs | Active termites and dry rot are progressive and spread unseen. Both need specialist identification and treatment, and the source of moisture must be removed. |
| Replace the rotten timber and move on | Decay concentrated under bathrooms, kitchens and laundries points to plumbing leaks or failed wet area waterproofing above; decay along external walls points to blocked vents, high ground levels or damp walls; decay spread evenly across the sub-floor points to general ventilation failure. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets rules for termite protection, timber decay and sub-floor ventilation, and guidance on radon. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Termites and decay | AS 3660.1 sets termite management for new buildings and AS 3660.2 for existing ones; AS 4349.3 covers timber pest inspections. | The Property Care Association publishes guidance on timber decay and dry rot. | Termite protection is required in many regions. |
| Ventilation and radon | The National Construction Code sets sub-floor ventilation and clearance. | Approved Document C covers resistance to moisture, including ventilation of suspended floors; the UK Health Security Agency maps radon. | The International Residential Code sets crawlspace ventilation or conditioning; the EPA recommends radon testing and mitigation. |

Pre-purchase timber pest inspections are standard in Australian residential sales, and termite damage and dry rot often affect insurance and lending in all three countries; many insurance policies exclude termite damage, so prevention and inspection carry the risk.

sections.heading: Worked example: a springy floor under a bathroom
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 1920s weatherboard house on timber stumps has a springy floor in its bathroom and a musty smell in the hall. In the sub-floor, the joists and bearers under the bathroom are soft and stained and the soil beneath is damp, while the timbers elsewhere are sound. Two vents on the same side are buried by a garden bed.

Decay concentrated under a bathroom points to a plumbing leak or failed wet area waterproofing above, not to the sub-floor as a whole; the buried vents add to it locally. The timbers are replaced only after the leak is found and fixed, or they will rot again.

So the register carries the bathroom floor as a failure line, finding and fixing the leak and the wet area waterproofing first, replacement of the decayed joists and bearers, and the vents cleared, with a timber pest inspection to rule out termites.

thresholds.rule: At least 150 mm under the lowest member; 400 mm where termite management relies on inspection

source.title: NCC 2025 Housing Provisions, Part 6.2 Subfloor ventilation

thresholds.rule: At least 2,000, 4,000 or 6,000 mm² per metre of wall in climate zones A, B and C; half where the ground is sealed with a membrane; 50 per cent more where excessively damp; spaced evenly, no more than 600 mm from corners

source.title: NCC 2025 Housing Provisions, Part 6.2 Subfloor ventilation

pages.title: Sub-metering
pages.question: How do sub-metering systems fail, and when do metering errors become a billing or compliance problem?
pages.answer: Sub-metering fails quietly. Current transformers are installed with the wrong ratio, on the wrong circuit or reversed; fit-outs move circuits so meters measure the wrong tenancies; communications fail and data stops. Reconciling sub-meters against the main meter exposes most errors quickly. Meters used to bill tenants or residents must meet legal measurement rules, and embedded networks carry regulatory obligations; monitoring-grade meters used for billing invite disputes.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about sub-metering; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Enhanced energy and water sub-metering for monitoring and reporting
