pages.searchTitle: Sub-metering: why meters mislead and how to check them

questions.question: How do I know if our sub-meters are right?
questions.answer: Reconcile them against the main meter. Any significant unexplained difference means something is wrong in the meters, the mapping or the data.

questions.question: Why is a sub-meter reading negative?
questions.answer: The current transformer is usually installed backwards. Inspection confirms it; reversing it and recommissioning the meter fixes it.

questions.question: Can sub-meters be used to bill tenants?
questions.answer: Only with meters that meet the rules for billing: in Australia, national measurement law; in the United Kingdom, the Measuring Instruments Regulations 2016. Billing with unapproved meters is a deadline finding.

questions.question: Why does our metering data have gaps?
questions.answer: Usually a communications or battery failure. Alarms for data gaps catch them early.

questions.question: How long do sub-meters last?
questions.answer: Electronic electricity meters typically 15 to 20 years, but battery-powered communications and data gateways 5 to 10, and mechanical water meters lose accuracy after 10 to 15.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Metering errors show in the data before anywhere else: totals that do not reconcile, flat lines, readings that cannot be right. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On site | Meters without clear labels of what they measure | Wiring, mapping and accuracy |
| On site | Meters showing zero or impossible readings | Wiring, mapping and accuracy |
| On site | Dead displays on battery-powered meters | Missing meters and data gaps |
| On site | Boards altered since metering was installed | Wiring, mapping and accuracy |
| In the data | Sub-meter totals that do not add up to the main meter | Wiring, mapping and accuracy |
| In the data | Flat lines or gaps in data | Missing meters and data gaps |
| In the data | Tenancy consumption that does not match occupancy or hours | Wiring, mapping and accuracy |
| In the data | Negative readings on current transformer meters | Wiring, mapping and accuracy |
| In the records | Metering schedule and single-line diagrams | Wiring, mapping and accuracy |
| In the records | Meter pattern approvals and verification certificates for billing meters | Billing and legal rules |
| In the records | Recharge and billing records, and tenant disputes | Billing and legal rules |
| In the records | Embedded network registrations and exemptions | Billing and legal rules |
| In the records | Tenants or residents questioning their bills, often the first sign of mapping or ratio errors | Billing and legal rules |
| In the data | Ratings that change sharply without a physical change to the building | Missing meters and data gaps |

sections.heading: Types of meter
sections.markdown:
Sub-metering measures electricity, water, gas and thermal energy below the utility meter: by tenancy, apartment, floor, plant item or end use. It serves two different purposes with different requirements. Billing meters charge tenants or residents for what they use and must meet legal metrology rules; monitoring meters show where energy and water go, support ratings and catch faults, and need accuracy and reliable data but not legal approval. Many buildings have meters installed for one purpose being used for the other.

| Type | Where it is found | Main issues |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Electricity sub-meters with current transformers | Tenancies, floors, plant | Wrong ratios, reversed polarity, wrong circuits |
| Whole-current electricity meters | Apartments, small tenancies | Communications; accuracy approval for billing |
| Water sub-meters | Apartments, tenancies, cooling towers, irrigation | Mechanical wear; batteries in pulse units |
| Gas sub-meters | Tenancies, kitchens, plant | Approval; access |
| Thermal (heat and chilled water) meters | Heat networks, shared plant | Sensor accuracy; flow meter fouling |
| Embedded network meters | Apartments and shopping centres where the owner on-sells energy | Regulatory obligations; billing systems |
| Data loggers and gateways | Most networked metering | Communications failure; data gaps |

Metering also underpins compliance: ratings, disclosure and building performance standards rely on accurate whole-building and end-use data, and metering errors can misstate a building's performance to buyers, tenants and regulators.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Meters outlast their usefulness more often than they wear out. Electronic meters last fifteen to twenty years, but communications, batteries and data platforms fail far sooner, and accuracy declines before a meter stops working.

| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Electronic electricity meters | 15 to 20 years | Technology; communications |
| Mechanical water meters | 10 to 15 years before accuracy drops | Volume passed; water quality |
| Battery-powered meter communications | 5 to 10 years | Battery life |
| Thermal meters | 10 to 15 years | Sensor drift; flow meter fouling |
| Data gateways and software | 5 to 10 years | Vendor support; networks |

What shortens it: fit-outs that move circuits without updating which meter measures what; communications that fail silently, leaving data gaps; vendor platforms that close or change; network changes, such as retirement of older mobile networks used by meter modems.

Meter hardware usually outlasts the communications and software around it, which is where most metering systems fail first.

sections.heading: Wiring, mapping and accuracy
sections.markdown:
Electricity sub-meters that use current transformers are commonly installed with the wrong ratio programmed, transformers on the wrong phase or circuit, or polarity reversed. The meter then reads a fraction, a multiple or the wrong load entirely, sometimes for years.

After fit-outs and alterations, circuits are moved between boards and meters no longer measure the areas their labels say. Tenants are billed for each other's use, and plant energy is attributed to the wrong place.

Mechanical water meters under-read as they wear; thermal meters drift as temperature sensors age and flow meters foul.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sub-meters add up to much more or less than the main meter | Ratio, polarity or mapping errors, or missing meters. Reconciliation; spot load checks. | Reconcile against the main meter, then check ratios, polarity and mapping with spot load checks. |
| Negative or reversed readings | Current transformer installed backwards. Inspection. | Reverse the current transformer and recommission the meter. |
| Tenant consumption far from expected | Wrong circuits measured. Load tracing. | Trace the loads and correct the circuit allocation and mapping. |
| Larger building with only one main electricity meter | Metering below the market’s rules. Meters against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Add meters at the next switchboard work. |

sections.heading: Missing meters and data gaps
sections.markdown:
Loads added after the metering design (new plant, EV chargers, tenant equipment on common supply) are often not metered at all, so the main meter and sub-meters never reconcile and costs are absorbed by the owner or spread unfairly.

Meters keep counting but communications fail, batteries die, or gateways lose connection; monitoring dashboards show gaps or flat lines that nobody notices.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Data flat for weeks | Communications or battery failure. Gateway status. | Restore communications or batteries, and set alarms for data gaps. |
| Meters installed but nobody reviews the data | Metering without use. Who receives reports and what action follows. | Set up monthly review with exception alerts. |

sections.heading: Billing and legal rules
sections.markdown:
Meters used to bill tenants or residents generally need approved patterns and verification under national measurement law. Monitoring-grade meters used for billing expose owners to disputes and regulatory action.

Owners who on-sell electricity or gas through embedded networks take on regulatory obligations for metering, billing, hardship and customer protections. These are tightening in several Australian states.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Billing disputes | Mapping errors or unapproved meters. Audit. | Audit the meters and mapping; correct past bills where errors are found. |
| Tenants billed from estimates despite meters being fitted | Meters unread or untrusted. Reading records; meter approvals. | Verify the meters and move billing to actual readings. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Billing with unapproved meters or under embedded network rules not met | deadline · 4 Essential | Rectify to the legal requirement. |
| Metering system failed; no data for billing | failure · 2 Planned | Restore now. |
| Mapping errors; ratio and polarity faults; data gaps | condition · 2 Planned | Correct in the near term. |
| Meters at end of life or on retiring networks | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Replace. |
| No reconciliation or metering schedule | check · 2 Planned | Audit. |
| Accurate and reconciled | nil · 1 Routine | Routine. |

Metering findings are rarely about physical safety; their weight comes from money and compliance, because errors in billing meters affect every tenant's charges and errors in monitoring meters undermine ratings and performance standard reporting.

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
An electrical engineer or metering specialist, with legal advice where billing or embedded networks are involved. The checks below establish what each meter measures, whether it was installed correctly, and whether the totals reconcile.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Metering audit | Inventory of every meter with type, approval, location, what it measures and how it communicates. |
| Reconciliation | Of sub-meters against the main meter over a representative period. |
| Spot checks | Of current transformer ratios, polarity and the circuits measured, by clamp measurement. |
| Mapping verification | Against current single-line diagrams and tenancy layouts. |
| Data review | For gaps and failures. |
| Compliance review | Of billing meters and embedded network obligations, with metering coverage checked against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). |

The report should give a corrected metering schedule, faults found, compliance status and a remediation plan.

Reconciliation over several weeks, comparing sub-meter totals with the main meter by hour, separates constant errors (ratios, missing meters) from intermittent ones (communications, failing meters).

sections.heading: Fixing the metering
sections.markdown:
Most metering faults are cheap to correct once found: a reversed current transformer, a wrong ratio, a circuit moved in a fit-out. The harder work is keeping the metering right after every change, and putting right any bills that relied on wrong data.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Correct installation faults | Correct ratios, polarity and circuit allocation. | Wherever reconciliation or spot checks find errors. |
| Update mapping and labelling | Update mapping and labelling after fit-outs, as part of every fit-out sign-off. | After every fit-out. |
| Replace meters | Replace meters that are not approved for billing, are inaccurate or are on retiring networks. | Where meters bill without approval, have lost accuracy or run on networks being retired. |
| Communications and alarms | Improve communications and set alarms for data gaps. | Where data drops out or runs flat. |
| Add meters | Add meters where ratings or performance standards need end-use data. | Where ratings or performance standards need data the meters do not give. |
| Embedded network compliance or exit | Bring the embedded network into compliance, or exit it. | Depending on the obligations and the economics. |
| Commissioning standard | Commission every new or moved meter with a clamp-meter check of ratio, polarity and circuit, recorded in the metering schedule. | For every new or moved meter. |
| Validation rules | Rules in the data platform that flag gaps, flat lines, negative readings and reconciliation differences automatically. | Wherever metering data is used for billing or ratings. |
| Tenant recharge corrections | Recalculate past bills where errors are found, and agree adjustments. | Wherever errors affected past bills. |
| Open data formats | Formats that let metering data move between platforms when vendors change. | When choosing or changing a data platform. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Audits are lump sums. Meter corrections are itemised. Meter replacement and additions are per meter plus installation and communications. Data platforms are recurring subscriptions. Errors corrected in tenant recharges can produce refunds or recoveries.

Billing compliance is code compliance; metering for ratings is often code compliance or improvement; replacement is lifecycle; corrections are repairs and maintenance.

Correcting long-standing billing errors can involve refunds to tenants for overcharging or unrecovered costs for undercharging, which may exceed the cost of fixing the meters.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what reading a meter cannot: what each meter is meant to measure, whether it was commissioned, and whether the totals reconcile. Ask for them before relying on any sub-meter for billing or ratings.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Metering schedule and single-line diagrams | What each meter measures, and whether that is still true. |
| Meter approvals and verification certificates for billing meters | Whether meters used for billing are approved and verified. |
| Reconciliation reports | Whether the sub-meters add up to the main meter. |
| Tenant recharge methods and disputes | How costs are passed on, and where they have been challenged. |
| Embedded network registrations, exemptions and compliance records | Whether the embedded network meets its obligations. |
| Data platform contracts and access | Who holds the data, and whether it can be moved. |
| Commissioning records for each meter | Whether each meter was checked for ratio, polarity and circuit when installed. |
| Data platform validation reports | Whether gaps and errors in the data are being caught. |
| Records of loads added since metering was designed | Whether new loads are being measured, or missed. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Sub-meter data is easily taken at face value because it comes from an instrument. Most errors lie in what a meter measures or how its data is mapped, not in the meter itself.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| The meters are new, so the readings are right | Current transformers can be installed with the wrong ratio, on the wrong circuit or reversed. Reconciling sub-meters against the main meter is the quickest test of a metering system. |
| A tenant's high bill means high use | It can mean the meter measures the wrong circuits after a fit-out. Trace the loads before disputing the use. |
| A flat line means nothing was used | Data flat for weeks usually means a communications or battery failure. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
The rules on metering turn on what the data is used for: billing, re-billing residents, or ratings. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each in turn.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Meters used for billing | Meters used for trade must meet national measurement law administered by the National Measurement Institute. | The Measuring Instruments Regulations 2016 govern billing meters. | Weights and measures authorities oversee meter accuracy. |
| Re-billing and networks | Embedded networks are regulated by the Australian Energy Regulator with state rules; Victoria is restricting new embedded networks in residential buildings. | The Heat Network (Metering and Billing) Regulations 2014 require meters on heat networks. | State public utility commissions regulate sub-metering and re-billing of utilities to residents. |
| Metering for ratings and new buildings | NABERS requires metering to rate buildings; the National Construction Code requires energy monitoring facilities in larger new buildings. | Approved Document L and CIBSE TM39 guide metering in non-domestic buildings. | Benchmarking and building performance standards in many cities require whole-building data that sub-metering supports. |

sections.heading: Worked example: tenant bills that do not add up
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A multi-tenant office recharges electricity from sub-meters. The sub-meters total well over the main meter, one tenant's meter reads negative, and a tenant that moved floors last year disputes its bills.

Reconciliation is the first test, and it has failed: something is wrong in the meters, the mapping or the data. The negative readings point to a current transformer installed backwards, and the disputed bills to a fit-out that moved circuits without updating which meter measures what.

So the register carries a metering audit as a check line now, correction of the installation faults and mapping as condition lines, and a recharge correction for the bills that relied on the wrong data. Billing with unapproved meters would add a deadline line.

thresholds.rule: Over 500 m²: time-of-use metering of gas and electricity; over 2500 m²: separate meters for air conditioning, lighting, appliance power, central hot water and lifts

source.title: NCC 2025 Volume One, Part J9 Energy monitoring and on-site distributed energy resources

pages.title: Terminal Units
pages.question: How do fan coils, VAV boxes and chilled beams fail, and how do you assess hundreds of them?
pages.answer: Terminal units fail by population. Fan coil condensate drains block and leak into ceilings; VAV dampers stick and airflow sensors drift, so zones get too much or too little air; reheat valves stick and heat and cool together. Chilled beams drip when water is below room dew point. Behind most comfort complaints is a mix of failed actuators, drifted sensors and controls overrides. Assess them by sample and controls data, not one by one.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about terminal units; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: FCUs, VAV boxes, chilled beams

sources.title: Guideline 36: High-Performance Sequences of Operation for HVAC Systems
AS 1668.2:2024 The use of ventilation and air conditioning in buildings, Part 2: Mechanical ventilation in buildings
AS/NZS 3666.1:2011 Air-handling and water systems of buildings: Microbial control, Part 1: Design, installation and commissioning
Approved Document F, Volume 2: Buildings other than dwellings

pages.searchTitle: Fan coils, VAV boxes and chilled beams: leaks, comfort complaints and controls

questions.question: Why is one zone always too hot?
questions.answer: Often its VAV box is at full open: undersized for the load, or starved by the supply upstream. BMS trends show it.

questions.question: Why are there stains below the fan coils?
questions.answer: Blocked or overflowing condensate drains. A drain programme clears them, with overflow switches above sensitive areas.

questions.question: Why do chilled beams drip?
questions.answer: Chilled water below the room's dew point. Dew point control and condensation sensors prevent it.

questions.question: Do all terminal units need inspecting?
questions.answer: No. A sample inspection plus controls data tells you more, and the data usually shows where the problems are.

questions.question: How long do fan coil units last?
questions.answer: Fan coil units 15 to 20 years, with fan motors and VAV controllers and actuators 10 to 15; VAV box casings last 20 to 30.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Terminal unit problems show in the ceiling as stains, in occupied zones as hot and cold complaints and noise, at the units themselves, and above all in the controls data. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| In the building | Stained ceiling tiles below fan coils; water marks on fit-outs | Fan coils and induction units |
| In the building | Hot and cold complaints concentrated in particular zones | VAV boxes and controls |
| In the building | Noise from fan coils; draughts from diffusers | Fan coils and induction units |
| In the building | Musty smells from fan coils | Fan coils and induction units |
| At the units (sample) | Drain pans: standing water, slime, corrosion | Fan coils and induction units |
| At the units (sample) | Filters: overloaded, missing | Fan coils and induction units |
| At the units (sample) | Coils: dust, corrosion, leaks | Fan coils and induction units |
| At the units (sample) | Actuators: position against command | VAV boxes and controls |
| At the units (sample) | Labels and controller types; asbestos in induction units | Fan coils and induction units |
| In the BMS | Zones in manual override | VAV boxes and controls |
| In the BMS | VAV boxes at full open (starved) or minimum (oversupplied) | VAV boxes and controls |
| In the BMS | Reheat valves open while cooling | VAV boxes and controls |
| In the BMS | Controllers offline | VAV boxes and controls |
| In the BMS | Temperature trends showing persistent deviations | VAV boxes and controls |
| In the records | Maintenance logs and reactive call-outs for leaks and comfort | Investigation before the scope |
| In the records | Test and balance reports after fit-outs | VAV boxes and controls |
| In the records | Controller types and support status | VAV boxes and controls |

sections.heading: Types of terminal unit
sections.markdown:
Terminal units deliver heating and cooling to individual zones from the central plant and air handling system. They are numerous: a single office floor can have dozens, and a tower hundreds. Their condition is assessed as a population, by sample and by controls data, rather than one by one.

| Type | Where it is found | How it works |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fan coil unit (FCU), two-pipe or four-pipe | Offices, hotels, apartments, from the 1960s | A fan blows room air over chilled and heating water coils; condensate drains from a pan |
| Variable air volume (VAV) box, with or without reheat | Offices from the 1980s | A damper varies supply air to a zone; a controller reads airflow and room temperature |
| Fan-powered VAV box | Offices, especially in the United States | VAV box with a fan mixing plenum air |
| Active chilled beam | Offices and laboratories from the 2000s | Primary air induces room air over a chilled water coil; no fan, no drain |
| Passive chilled beam or chilled ceiling | Offices | Natural convection over chilled water coils or panels |
| Induction unit | Offices of the 1960s and 1970s | High-pressure primary air induces room air over a coil; perimeter units under windows |
| Perimeter heating: radiators, convectors, trench heaters | All building types | Hot water or electric heating at the façade |
| Constant volume reheat boxes | Older offices, laboratories | Constant airflow with reheat |

Terminal units are where the tenant meets the building's systems, so they are often relocated, added and altered in fit-outs. Lease make-good obligations frequently cover them, and their ownership and maintenance responsibility can be split between owner and tenant.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Fan coil units last fifteen to twenty years and VAV box casings twenty to thirty, but their motors, controllers and actuators last ten to fifteen. In most buildings it is the controls on the units, rather than the boxes themselves, that decide when work is due.

| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fan coil units | 15 to 20 years | Fan motors; coils; drain pans |
| FCU fan motors | 10 to 15 years | Run hours |
| VAV box casing and damper | 20 to 30 years | Rarely limiting |
| VAV controllers and actuators | 10 to 15 years | Electronics obsolescence |
| Airflow sensors | 10 to 20 years, with recalibration | Dust fouling; drift |
| Chilled beams | 25 to 30 years | Coil cleaning; condensation control |
| Induction units | 25 to 35 years | Mostly at end of life now |
| Control valves and actuators | 10 to 15 years | Water quality; use |

What shortens life: blocked condensate drains on fan coils; lack of filter maintenance in fan coils; poor water treatment, which blocks small coils and valves; fit-out changes that relocate units, cut ductwork and lose commissioning; obsolete controllers that cannot be replaced like for like.

sections.heading: Fan coils and induction units
sections.markdown:
Fan coil drain pans block with dust and slime, overflow, and drip into ceilings and onto fit-outs; pans corrode; drain pipework sags and holds water. Water damage to ceilings below fan coils is one of the commonest maintenance calls in office buildings, and the pans are also a microbial growth site.

Fan motors fail and bearings get noisy; filters clog and dust fouls coils; small coils block with sludge from poorly treated water; valves stick.

Induction units at the perimeter suffer blocked nozzles, fouled coils, noisy high-pressure primary air and leaking valves. Many are fifty years old, and some contain asbestos in linings and insulation.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ceiling stains below fan coils | Blocked or overflowing condensate drain. Drain pan inspection. | Clear the drain, fix the falls and traps, and fit overflow switches above sensitive areas. |
| Fan coil filters clogged or missing | Maintenance lapsed. Filter condition and dates on a sample of units. | Restore filter changes on a schedule, and clean coils and pans. |

sections.heading: VAV boxes and controls
sections.markdown:
Damper actuators fail, leaving boxes stuck open or closed; airflow sensors foul and drift so the controller delivers the wrong airflow; reheat valves stick open so the box heats and cools at once, wasting energy; controllers lose communication or become unsupported. Many problems hide behind controls overrides.

Over years of fit-outs and maintenance, setpoints drift, schedules are overridden, zones are put in manual, and units fight each other (one heating while its neighbour cools). The equipment works but the building performs badly.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Zone too hot, VAV box at full open | Box undersized for the load, or upstream supply starved. Airflow measurement; load change. | Check the upstream supply and the box sizing, and rebalance. |
| Zone too cold, VAV box at minimum | Minimum airflow too high or reheat failed. Settings; reheat valve. | Lower the minimum, or repair the reheat. |
| Heating and cooling at the same time | Reheat valve stuck or controls fighting. BMS trends. | Free the reheat valve, and recommission the sequences. |
| Many zones in manual override | Controls problems worked around. BMS point list. | Fix the faults behind the overrides, then recommission. |
| Stuffy meeting rooms with VAV boxes at minimum | Outside air short when the box turns down. Airflow and carbon dioxide in the room against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Reset minimum airflows for ventilation, or add demand-controlled ventilation. |

sections.heading: Chilled beams
sections.markdown:
Chilled beams have no drain. If the chilled water supply is colder than the room dew point, they condense and drip. They depend on dew point control and on dry primary air; failures of either cause dripping.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Dripping from chilled beams | Chilled water below room dew point. Water temperature; humidity; dew point control. | Add dew point control and condensation sensors. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Water leaking onto electrical equipment; asbestos in deteriorating induction units | safety · 4 Essential | Isolate now. |
| Widespread leaks damaging fit-outs | failure · 3 Important | Clear drains and repair now. |
| Many units with failed actuators, drifted sensors or blocked drains | condition · 3 Important | Programme in the near term. |
| Units at end of life; unsupported controllers | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Plan replacement, often floor by floor. |
| No sample inspection; controls data unavailable | check · 2 Planned | Sample inspection and controls audit. |
| Isolated faults | nil · 1 Routine | Routine maintenance. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A mechanical services engineer leads, with the controls contractor operating the BMS during the inspection. The checks below read the controls data first, then inspect a sample of units where the data points.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Sample inspection | Of a representative share of units of each type on each floor, weighted to areas with complaints and leaks: drain pans and drains, filters, coils, fans and motors, valves and actuators, controllers, casing and insulation. |
| Functional testing through the BMS | Command a sample of VAV dampers, valves and fans and confirm the response at the unit; read airflow and temperature against setpoints. |
| Controls audit | Overrides, alarms, offline controllers, trend data for zone temperatures and VAV damper positions, controller models and vendor support. |
| Airflow measurement | At a sample of VAV boxes and diffusers; comparison with test and balance records. |
| Comfort survey and complaint analysis | To locate problem zones. |
| Asbestos check | Of induction units and older fan coils. |
| Fit-out review | Changes to layouts, ceilings and ductwork since commissioning. |

The report should give fault rates by type and floor, controller support status, the controls faults found in the trends, safety items, and a strategy: repair and recommission, retrofit controls, or replace floor by floor.

sections.heading: Recommissioning, retrofitting or replacing
sections.markdown:
Water on electrical equipment and asbestos come first. After that, most of the work is recommissioning and a drain programme, with controls retrofits and floor-by-floor replacement timed to lease expiries and fit-outs.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Drain programme | Clean and treat fan coil drain pans and drains on a schedule; fix falls and traps; condensate overflow switches on units above sensitive areas. | Wherever fan coils leak. |
| Fan motor upgrade | Electronically commutated motors, cutting energy and noise. | Where fan motors are worn or noisy. |
| Coil cleaning | Coil cleaning and a filter regime. | Where coils and filters are dirty. |
| Controls retrofit | Replace unsupported unitary controllers and actuators with open-protocol controllers, often in the same programme as a BMS upgrade. | Where unitary controllers are unsupported. |
| Airflow sensor recalibration | Recalibrate airflow sensors, with test and balance. | Where VAV boxes starve or oversupply zones. |
| Recommissioning | Setpoints, deadbands, schedules, and sequences to stop simultaneous heating and cooling. | Where heating and cooling fight, or zones sit in override. |
| Chilled beam protection | Dew point control and condensation sensors. | Where beams drip. |
| Replacement | Floor by floor, timed with lease expiries and fit-outs, sometimes moving from fan coils to VAV or chilled beams. | At the end of the units' life. |
| Induction unit replacement | Replacement with asbestos removal and new perimeter systems. | Where induction units are at end of life or contain asbestos. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Sample inspection and controls audits are lump sums. Repairs and motor replacements are per unit. Controls retrofits are per unit or per floor. Replacement is per unit or per floor including ceiling works, ductwork and pipework connections, controls and commissioning, and is usually timed with tenancy changes. Lease make-good obligations can carry part of the cost of units altered by tenants.

Replacement is lifecycle; repairs, recommissioning and drain maintenance are repairs and maintenance.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a ceiling inspection cannot: which zones fail and how often, how the units behave over time, and whether their controllers are still supported. Ask for the BMS trends before opening ceilings.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Maintenance logs and reactive call-out records, especially for leaks and comfort | Which zones leak or fail, and how often. |
| Test and balance reports, original and after fit-outs | Whether the system was rebalanced after fit-outs. |
| BMS point lists and trend data for zones and terminal units | How the zones and units actually behave over time. |
| Controller types, firmware and vendor support status | Whether the unit controllers are still supported. |
| Asbestos register for older units | Whether older units contain asbestos. |
| Fit-out records and lease make-good obligations | What tenants must reinstate when they leave. |
| Comfort survey or complaint records | Where occupants are uncomfortable. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Terminal units are misread when every unit is inspected one by one, and when a zone that is too hot or too cold is blamed on the box that serves it.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| Inspect every unit | Terminal units are assessed as a population. A sample inspection plus controls data tells you more than inspecting every unit, and the controls data usually shows where the problems are. |
| The box in the hot zone is faulty | A VAV box at full open in a zone that is too hot may be undersized for the load, or starved by the supply upstream. A box at minimum in a zone that is too cold may have its minimum set too high, or a failed reheat. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets standards for comfort, ventilation, energy and hygiene that terminal units must meet, and rates buildings partly on how they perform. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Standards and ratings | AS 1668.2 sets ventilation and AS/NZS 3666 microbial control for air-handling systems including terminal units; NABERS Energy and Indoor Environment ratings reflect terminal unit and controls performance; lease make-good clauses commonly address tenant alterations to terminal units. | Approved Documents F and L apply; the British Council for Offices guide to specification sets market expectations for office conditions; BESA TR/19 covers hygiene; air-conditioning energy inspections apply to systems over 12 kW. | ASHRAE 55 sets thermal comfort, 62.1 ventilation and 90.1 energy, and Guideline 36 sets VAV and other terminal sequences; state energy codes such as California's Title 24 add requirements. |

Asbestos rules in all three jurisdictions govern work on older induction units and fan coils with asbestos-containing linings or insulation.

sections.heading: Worked example: hot and cold complaints on one floor
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 1990s office floor served by VAV boxes generates constant hot and cold complaints. BMS trends show a third of the zones in manual override, several boxes at full open in hot zones, and reheat valves open while cooling elsewhere. Two ceiling tiles below fan coils in the lift lobby are stained.

Controls data tells you more than inspecting every unit. Zones in override are workarounds for faults; boxes at full open in hot zones point to undersizing or the supply upstream; reheat open while cooling means heating and cooling are fighting. The stained tiles point to blocked fan coil drains.

So the register carries recommissioning as a condition line, with airflow sensors recalibrated and the floor rebalanced, a drain programme for the fan coils, and a controls retrofit where the unitary controllers are unsupported.

thresholds.rule: 10 L/s per person

source.title: Approved Document F, Volume 2: Buildings other than dwellings

thresholds.rule: Below 800 ppm suggests good ventilation; consistently above 1500 ppm calls for action

pages.title: Trade Waste Systems
pages.question: How do grease arrestors and other trade waste devices fail, and when do they put the building in breach?
pages.answer: Trade waste devices fail by being too small, too full or bypassed. An arrestor sized for a café cannot treat a busy restaurant; missed pump-outs leave grease and solids filling the tank and turning septic; hydrogen sulphide corrodes concrete and baffles until grease passes straight through; fit-outs connect dishwashers around it. Utilities then issue notices and fines. Blockages downstream of an arrestor point at the arrestor; upstream, at kitchens or drains.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about trade waste systems; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.

pages.searchTitle: Grease arrestors and trade waste: blockages, pump-outs, utility notices, oil interceptors

questions.question: Why do the drains keep blocking with grease?
questions.answer: Blockages downstream of the arrestor point at the arrestor; blockages upstream point at kitchen practices or the drains.

questions.question: How often should a grease arrestor be pumped out?
questions.answer: As often as the utility requires and the actual loading demands, with dockets kept on site.

questions.question: Who pays for trade waste upgrades in a multi-tenant building?
questions.answer: Leases should require tenants to maintain their devices and fund the upgrades their use requires.

questions.question: Why is there an oil sheen at the car park stormwater outlet?
questions.answer: A full or bypassed oil interceptor. Empty it, replace the media and repair the alarm.

questions.question: How long do grease arrestors last?
questions.answer: Concrete 20 to 40 years, steel 15 to 25, and plastic and fibreglass 25 to 40.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Trade waste problems show at arrestors as odour, broken covers and alarms, in kitchens as fat in the drains, in the street as sewer blockages, and in dockets and utility notices. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On site | Arrestor location, size and covers; odour around lids | Corrosion, odour and covers |
| On site | Fat build-up in kitchen drains and frequent blockages downstream of kitchens | Overload, pump-outs and bypasses |
| On site | Pump-out labels or dockets; date of the last service | Overload, pump-outs and bypasses |
| On site | Oil interceptor alarms and level indicators | Oil interceptors |
| On site | Cracked or rocking covers in trafficked areas | Corrosion, odour and covers |
| On site | Dishwashers and floor wastes connected directly to the sewer | Overload, pump-outs and bypasses |
| In the records | Trade waste agreement or consent with discharge limits | Standards by country |
| In the records | Pump-out dockets and frequency | Overload, pump-outs and bypasses |
| In the records | Utility notices, sampling results and fines | Overload, pump-outs and bypasses |
| In the records | Tenant kitchen specifications | Overload, pump-outs and bypasses |
| In the records | Drain blockage history | Overload, pump-outs and bypasses |
| In the records | Kitchen staff pouring fat, oil and food scraps into sinks rather than collecting them, a management issue that overloads even well-sized arrestors | Overload, pump-outs and bypasses |
| In the records | Sewer overflows or utility crews attending blockages in the street outside the building | Overload, pump-outs and bypasses |

sections.heading: Types of trade waste device
sections.markdown:
Trade waste systems treat liquid waste from commercial and industrial activities before it enters the public sewer, so fats, oils, solids and chemicals do not block sewers or harm treatment plants. They are governed by agreements or consents with the water utility that set what may be discharged, how it must be treated, and how often treatment devices must be emptied and sampled.

| Device | Where it is found | What it removes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Grease arrestors (grease traps, grease interceptors) | Restaurants, food courts, hotels, hospitals, schools, aged care | Fats, oils and grease from kitchens |
| Oil and silt interceptors (light liquid separators) | Car parks, car washes, workshops, fuel areas, loading docks | Oils, fuels and sediment |
| Silt and plaster traps | Workshops, dental and craft rooms | Solids |
| Lint traps | Commercial laundries | Fibres |
| Neutralising or dilution pits | Laboratories, schools, hospitals | Acids and alkalis |
| Dosing and pre-treatment plant | Industrial processes | Process contaminants |

Most arrestors are concrete, steel or plastic tanks in the ground or in basements, with baffles that slow the flow so grease floats and solids settle. They work only if they are sized for the flow and emptied before they fill. When a tenancy changes from a café to a high-volume restaurant, the arrestor that served the café can be overwhelmed.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Concrete grease arrestors last twenty to forty years and steel fifteen to twenty-five, while plastic and fibreglass units and oil interceptors last twenty-five to forty. Most failures come sooner, from loads the arrestor was never sized for and pump-outs that are too infrequent.

| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Concrete grease arrestors | 20 to 40 years | Hydrogen sulphide and acid attack on concrete |
| Steel arrestors | 15 to 25 years | Internal corrosion |
| Plastic and fibreglass arrestors | 25 to 40 years | Ground movement; lid damage |
| Oil interceptors | 25 to 40 years | Alarms; baffles; coalescer media |
| Baffles and internal fittings | 10 to 20 years | Corrosion |
| Access covers | 15 to 30 years | Traffic loads; corrosion |

What shortens life: infrequent pump-outs, which leave acidic, septic waste in contact with concrete and steel for long periods; hot water and chemical cleaners discharged into arrestors, which carry grease straight through and attack the tank; traffic loads on covers not rated for vehicles; undersizing for the current use, so devices are overloaded continuously.

sections.heading: Overload, pump-outs and bypasses
sections.markdown:
An arrestor sized for a small café cannot treat the flow from a commercial kitchen. Grease passes through to the sewer, blocking the building's drains and the public sewer, and the utility issues notices or fines. Food court and multi-tenancy buildings often have shared arrestors whose capacity was set for an earlier tenant mix.

Arrestors must be emptied at a frequency set by the utility or the agreement. When pump-outs lapse, grease and solids fill the tank, overflow to the sewer, and turn septic and odorous.

Dishwashers, floor wastes and sinks connected around the arrestor, or arrestors bypassed after blockages, discharge untreated waste. Connections added in fit-outs are a common source.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Grease blockages in drains downstream of the arrestor | Arrestor undersized, full or with corroded baffles. Size against flow; pump-out dates; internal inspection. | Pump out more often, repair the baffles, or upsize the arrestor. |
| Grease blockages upstream of the arrestor | Kitchen practices or drain defects. CCTV; kitchen practices. | Change kitchen practices, and CCTV the drains. |
| Utility notice for high fats in discharge | Overload or bypass. Sampling; connection survey. | Remove bypasses, and upsize or add arrestors. |
| No pump-out dockets for months, or dockets with no volumes | Arrestor not being emptied as the permit requires. Pump-out records against the trade waste agreement. | Set a pump-out contract at the permitted frequency, and keep the dockets. |

sections.heading: Corrosion, odour and covers
sections.markdown:
Hydrogen sulphide and acids from decomposing waste attack concrete above the liquid line and corrode steel baffles and fittings. Corroded baffles let grease pass straight through; failed walls leak into the ground.

Septic arrestors release odours into kitchens, basements and public areas through failed seals and lids. Hydrogen sulphide makes arrestor pits dangerous confined spaces.

Covers in car parks and service lanes crack and break under vehicles, creating trip and fall hazards and letting stormwater in.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Strong odour at lids | Septic arrestor from infrequent pump-outs, or failed seals. Pump-out records; seal inspection. | Pump out more often, and seal the covers. |
| Broken covers | Covers not rated for traffic. Cover rating. | Fit heavy-duty covers rated for the traffic. |

sections.heading: Oil interceptors
sections.markdown:
Oil interceptors fill with oil and silt, alarms fail, and coalescer media clog. A full interceptor discharges oil to the sewer or stormwater system, which is an environmental offence.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Oil sheen at stormwater outlets from a car park | Full or bypassed oil interceptor. Interceptor levels. | Empty the interceptor, replace the media and repair the alarm. |
| Oil interceptor alarm silenced or never fitted | Full interceptor not detected. Alarm and level probe test; service records. | Repair or fit the alarm and empty the interceptor. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Broken covers in trafficked areas; hydrogen sulphide exposure; oil discharging to stormwater | safety · 4 Essential | Make safe and contain now. |
| Arrestor overflowing; sewer blocked | failure · 3 Important | Pump out and clear now. |
| Utility notice or agreement requiring upgrade or sampling | deadline · 4 Essential | By the utility's date. |
| Corroded baffles and tank; undersized for current use | condition · 3 Important | Repair or upgrade in the near term. |
| Arrestor at end of life | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Replace. |
| No trade waste agreement; capacity not checked after tenancy changes | check · 2 Planned | Assess. |
| Normal | nil · 1 Routine | Routine pump-outs. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A hydraulic engineer or licensed plumber with liquid waste contractor support; confined space procedures for entry. The checks below start with the trade waste agreement and pump-out dockets, then open the arrestors and trace which fixtures drain through them.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Inventory | Of every pre-treatment device, its size, material, age and what it serves. |
| Capacity check | Of each arrestor against the current kitchen fixtures, meals and flow, using the utility's sizing method. |
| Internal inspection | After pump-out: walls, baffles, inlet and outlet fittings, seals and covers. |
| Connection survey | By dye testing to confirm every fixture that should discharge through the arrestor does, and nothing bypasses it. |
| Records review | Trade waste agreements, pump-out frequency against requirements, utility sampling and notices. |
| Oil interceptor checks | Levels, alarms, media and outlet condition. |
| Cover load ratings | Against the traffic over them. |

The report should state compliance with the utility's requirements, capacity against current use, condition, bypasses, and the works and pump-out frequency needed.

sections.heading: Pumping out, repairing or upsizing
sections.markdown:
Broken covers in trafficked areas and gas exposure come first. After that, most of the work is a pump-out regime set to the real loading, connections corrected so everything that should pass through the arrestor does, and upsizing where tenancies have outgrown it.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Pump-out regime | Set to the utility's requirement and the actual loading, with dockets kept on site. | Wherever arrestors fill or turn septic. |
| Upsizing or additional arrestors | Larger or additional arrestors, usually as a condition of the new tenancy. | Where tenancies have outgrown the existing devices. |
| Internal repair | Replace corroded baffles and fittings; reline concrete tanks with acid-resistant linings. | Where baffles or tanks corrode. |
| Replacement | Plastic or fibreglass units. | Where concrete or steel tanks have failed. |
| Connection corrections | Route dishwashers, floor wastes and sinks through the arrestor and remove bypasses. | Wherever fixtures bypass the arrestor. |
| Heavy-duty covers | Covers rated for the traffic, with gas-tight seals. | Where covers crack or rock in trafficked areas. |
| Oil interceptor servicing | Emptying, media replacement and alarm repair. | Where interceptors fill or alarms fail. |
| Tenant obligations | Lease clauses requiring tenants to maintain their devices and fund upgrades their use requires. | In every multi-tenant building with food or vehicle tenancies. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Pump-outs recur at the required frequency and are usually a tenant or service charge cost. Internal repairs and relining are lump sums per device. Replacement or upsizing is a lump sum including excavation in kitchens, basements or car parks, which can disrupt tenants. Utility fees and fines are operating costs that capital works avoid. Cover replacement is per cover.

Utility-required upgrades carry deadlines; replacement is lifecycle; pump-outs and repairs are repairs and maintenance; tenant-driven upsizing should sit with the tenancy.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what lifting a lid cannot: what the utility requires, how often the arrestor is pumped out, and which fixtures actually drain through it. Ask for the agreement and dockets first.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Trade waste agreements, permits or consents, with discharge limits | What the utility allows the building to discharge. |
| Pump-out dockets for the last two years | Whether pump-outs keep up with the loading. |
| Utility notices, sampling results and any fines | Whether the utility has found problems or fined the building. |
| Drawings showing arrestors and the fixtures connected to them | Which fixtures drain through each arrestor. |
| Tenant kitchen fit-out specifications | What each tenant's kitchen discharges. |
| Drain blockage history downstream of kitchens | Where grease blocks the drains, which points to the cause. |
| Oil interceptor service and alarm records | Whether oil interceptors are serviced and alarmed. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Trade waste is misread when every grease blockage is blamed on the arrestor, and when the owner who holds the agreement is assumed to carry the cost alone.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| Blockages mean the arrestor | Grease blockages downstream of an arrestor point at the arrestor; blockages upstream point at kitchen practices or the drains. The location tells you which to fix. |
| The owner holds the agreement, so the owner pays | In multi-tenant buildings the agreement is often in the owner's name while tenants generate the waste. Leases should require tenants to maintain their devices and fund the upgrades their use requires. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market requires consent or an agreement to discharge trade waste, and sets standards for grease and oil separators. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Trade waste and separators | Water utilities set trade waste requirements through agreements or permits, with arrestor sizing, pump-out frequencies and sampling (for example Sydney Water and the Melbourne retailers); AS/NZS 3500.2 governs the plumbing; confined space entry follows AS/NZS 2865. | Discharges of trade effluent need consent from the water company under the Water Industry Act 1991; grease separators follow BS EN 1825 and light liquid separators BS EN 858; local authorities enforce on food premises where fats block sewers. | Local pretreatment programmes under the Clean Water Act and municipal fats, oils and grease ordinances set requirements; plumbing codes set grease interceptor sizing; oil separators follow local and environmental rules. |

Lease terms matter in all three jurisdictions: in multi-tenant buildings, the agreement is often in the owner's name while tenants generate the waste, so leases should allocate pump-out, upgrade and fine costs to the tenant whose use requires them.

sections.heading: Worked example: a food court that outgrew its arrestor
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A shopping centre food court shares one grease arrestor installed when it had four tenancies; it now has nine. Drains downstream block with grease every few weeks, the utility has issued a notice for high fats in the discharge, and pump-out dockets show visits every three months.

Blockages downstream of the arrestor point at the arrestor, here undersized for nine kitchens and pumped out too rarely. The utility notice makes it a deadline.

So the register carries the utility notice as a deadline line, a pump-out regime set to the actual loading now, an additional or larger arrestor as a condition line, and lease clauses so tenants fund the upgrades their use requires.

pages.title: Upper Floor Slabs & Structures
pages.question: How do upper floors fail, and when does a change of use overload them?
pages.answer: Floors fail from overload, alterations and water. Mobile shelving, archives, plant and water features can exceed design loads; concrete floors keep deflecting for years and crack partitions below; coring without scanning cuts post-tensioning tendons; water corrodes composite decking; timber joists are notched by trades and decay at damp bearings. Check design loads against current use before accepting heavy tenants or equipment.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about upper floor slabs & structures; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Concrete, composite, or timber-joisted floor structures

pages.searchTitle: Upper floors: sagging, overload, cut tendons, decking corrosion and timber joists

questions.question: Can I drill or core through my floor slab?
questions.answer: Not until the tendons and reinforcement have been located by drawings and scanning. Cutting a post-tensioning tendon is dangerous and reduces capacity.

questions.question: Why is the floor sagging under our storage?
questions.answer: Usually overload: heavy storage, mobile shelving or plant beyond what the floor was designed for. Move heavy items over beams and columns, and check the loads against the design.

questions.question: Does a change of use need a structural check?
questions.answer: Yes. Changes of use, such as office to residential or office to laboratory, trigger structural review in all three markets, and may need strengthening before approval.

questions.question: Why does our timber floor feel springy?
questions.answer: Undersized joists, lost strutting, or notching for services. Sistering joists, restoring strutting and repairing bearings stiffen it.

questions.question: How long do floor screeds last?
questions.answer: Screeds and toppings 20 to 50 years, and composite decking 40 to 80; concrete floors themselves last the life of the building.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Floor problems show as sagging or sloping floors, cracks in partitions and ceilings below, cracked or stained soffits, and heavy loads or cut holes on the floor itself. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On site | Floors noticeably sloping or sagging; ponding on balconies and podiums | Deflection, overload and vibration |
| On site | Cracks in partitions and ceilings below; doors binding | Deflection, overload and vibration |
| On site | Cracks on slab soffits; rust staining from decking or reinforcement | Post-tensioning, precast and decking |
| On site | Heavy storage, mobile shelving, plant or water features on upper floors | Deflection, overload and vibration |
| On site | Cored holes and cut openings in slabs | Post-tensioning, precast and decking |
| On site | Notched and drilled joists; springy floors; decay at joist ends | Timber floors |
| In the records | Structural drawings with design loads | Investigation before the scope |
| In the records | Post-tensioning drawings | Post-tensioning, precast and decking |
| In the records | Records of coring and openings | Post-tensioning, precast and decking |
| In the records | Change of use approvals | Standards by country |
| In the records | Floor loading notices | Deflection, overload and vibration |
| In the records | Load notices on floors and racking, or their absence where heavy storage is present | Deflection, overload and vibration |
| In the records | Patched or filled holes in slabs whose history is unknown | Post-tensioning, precast and decking |

sections.heading: Types of floor
sections.markdown:
Upper floors carry occupants, furniture, partitions, storage and equipment and transfer them to beams, walls and columns. They are reinforced concrete flat slabs or beam-and-slab floors, post-tensioned slabs, precast hollowcore planks, composite slabs on steel decking, timber joists and boards, and, more recently, cross-laminated timber panels. Each has characteristic weaknesses: deflection and cracking in concrete, tendons in post-tensioned slabs, bearings in precast, corrosion of decking, and notching, decay and bounce in timber.

| Type | Where it is found | Main vulnerabilities |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Reinforced concrete flat and beam-and-slab floors | Offices, apartments, institutions | Deflection; cracking; corrosion in wet areas |
| Post-tensioned slabs | Offices, apartments, car parks from the 1970s | Tendons cut during alterations; anchorage corrosion |
| Precast hollowcore planks | Commercial and residential from the 1970s | Bearing length; cutting; water in cores |
| Composite slabs on steel decking | Steel-framed offices and car parks | Decking corrosion; holes cut through ribs |
| Timber joists and boards | Houses, terraces, older commercial | Notching and drilling; decay at bearings; bounce |
| Cross-laminated timber | New mid-rise buildings | Moisture; vibration; fire protection |

Floors are designed for imposed loads that depend on use: offices, homes, assembly areas, storage, libraries and plant rooms all differ. A change of use or tenant can put loads on a floor that were never designed for it, particularly compactus and mobile shelving, archives, server racks, gym equipment and water tanks.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Concrete, post-tensioned and precast floors last the life of the building if their tendons and reinforcement stay protected, and dry timber joists eighty to a hundred and fifty years. Composite decking lasts forty to eighty years, and screeds and toppings twenty to fifty.

| Element | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Concrete floors | Life of the building | Water; alterations; overload |
| Post-tensioned slabs | Life of the building if tendons protected | Water at anchorages; alterations |
| Hollowcore planks | Life of the building | Bearings; cutting |
| Composite decking | 40 to 80 years | Corrosion where wet |
| Timber joists | 80 to 150 years if dry | Decay; notching; insects |
| Floor screeds and toppings | 20 to 50 years | Cracking; debonding |

What shortens life: overload from changed uses, storage and heavy equipment; alterations: openings cut, cores drilled, joists notched for services; water from leaking wet areas, roofs and plant; long-term creep in concrete, which keeps deflections growing for years.

Floors rarely reach the end of their structural life; their limits come from the loads placed on them and the holes cut through them.

sections.heading: Deflection, overload and vibration
sections.markdown:
Concrete floors continue to deflect for years after construction as concrete creeps. Long spans and thin slabs sag; partitions below crack, doors bind, and on balconies and podiums water ponds. Deflection is usually a serviceability problem, but large or increasing deflection can signal loss of capacity.

Mobile shelving, archives, plant, water features and heavy equipment can exceed design loads by a wide margin. Overloaded floors crack and deflect, and in extreme cases fail.

Light, long-span floors in timber, steel and post-tensioned concrete can be lively under footfall, a comfort problem that matters for sensitive uses such as laboratories and hospitals.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sagging mid-span and cracked partitions below | Creep deflection or overload. Level survey and load review, against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Survey the levels and review the loads; restrict loads or strengthen. |
| Cracks under heavy storage areas | Overload. Loads against design. | Move heavy items over beams and columns, limit storage, and post load notices. |
| Lively floor under footfall | Low stiffness and mass. Vibration measurement. | Measure the vibration; add stiffness or mass. |
| Partitions cracking along their head on an upper floor | Slab deflection after the partitions were built. Deflection since the partitions went in, against span/500, or 20 mm for brittle finishes (The Structural Engineer). | Fit deflection heads to the partitions, and have the slab assessed if movement continues. |
| Heavy plant, compactus or stock on an existing floor | Loads beyond the design imposed load. Load review against the design loads, the floor’s capacity and the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Move heavy items over beams and columns, spread the load, or strengthen the floor, and post load notices. |

sections.heading: Post-tensioning, precast and decking
sections.markdown:
Drilling and coring into post-tensioned slabs without scanning can cut tendons, releasing them violently and removing part of the slab's capacity. Water reaching unbonded tendon anchorages at slab edges corrodes them.

Precast planks need adequate bearing on supports; short bearings and planks cut near their ends for services are vulnerable. Water trapped in hollow cores freezes or corrodes strands.

Steel decking under composite slabs corrodes where water leaks through from wet areas, car park decks or roofs, losing its role as reinforcement.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Broken concrete around a cored hole | Tendon or reinforcement cut. Scanning; drawings. | Scan and check the drawings; get specialist repair if a tendon has been cut. |
| Rust staining on decking soffits | Water through the slab above. Leak source above. | Stop the leak above, then repair the decking. |

sections.heading: Timber floors
sections.markdown:
Joists are notched and drilled by plumbers and electricians, cutting through critical zones; joist ends decay where they bear on damp walls; floors are springy or bouncy where joists are undersized or have lost strutting; insects attack timber.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Springy timber floor | Undersized joists, lost strutting, or notching. Inspection. | Sister or replace joists, restore strutting, and repair bearings. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Floors overloaded beyond design; cut tendons; severe decay at joist bearings | safety · 4 Essential | Remove loads or prop now. |
| Significant deflection or cracking from overload or damage | failure · 4 Essential | Strengthen or repair now. |
| Decking corrosion; notched joists; creep deflection affecting finishes | condition · 3 Important | Repair in the near term. |
| Screeds and toppings at end of life | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Renew. |
| Design loads unknown for current or proposed use | check · 3 Important | Assess capacity. |
| Minor shrinkage cracking | nil · 1 Routine | Monitor. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A structural engineer, with scanning specialists for coring and concrete testing as needed. The checks below compare what the floor now carries with what it was designed for, then locate anything embedded before a hole is cut.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Load review | Current and proposed uses against design loads, including specific heavy items. |
| Level survey | Of deflections, repeated over time where growth is suspected, against span/250 overall and span/500 after partitions (The Structural Engineer). |
| Scanning | Of slabs to locate tendons and reinforcement. |
| Condition survey | Of soffits, decking, bearings and timber. |
| Opening up | Of timber floors to inspect joists and bearings. |
| Vibration measurement | For sensitive uses. |
| Capacity assessment | For the intended use. |
| Load testing | In special cases where calculations cannot confirm capacity, carried out under engineering control. |
| Cores and concrete testing | To confirm strength and reinforcement where drawings are missing. |

The report should state floor capacity against use, condition, any overload or damage, and strengthening options.

Investigations are best timed before a lease commits to a use, so capacity limits are known at negotiation.

sections.heading: Controlling loads, strengthening or repairing
sections.markdown:
Load control comes first and costs least: move heavy items over beams and columns, limit storage, and post load notices. Strengthening and repair follow where loads cannot be reduced or the floor has been damaged.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Load control | Relocate heavy items over beams and columns, limit storage, and post load notices. | First, wherever loads approach or exceed the design. |
| Strengthening | Fibre-reinforced polymer on concrete, added steel beams, or additional supports. | Where loads cannot be reduced or capacity has been lost. |
| Tendon repair | Specialist repair of cut tendons or corroded anchorages. | Wherever a tendon has been cut or an anchorage corroded. |
| Decking repair | Repair the decking, after stopping the leak above. | Where composite decking corrodes. |
| Timber floor repair | Sister or replace joists, restore strutting, repair bearings, and replace decayed timber. | Where joists are notched, undersized, unstrutted or decayed. |
| Vibration control | Added stiffness or mass, or tuned mass dampers for special cases. | Where floors are lively underfoot. |
| Penetration controls | Scanning and engineering for every new hole. | Always. |
| Tenant controls | Lease clauses setting floor load limits and requiring engineering approval for heavy equipment and storage. | In every let building. |
| Screed and topping replacement | New screeds or toppings. | Where cracked or debonded toppings add load without strength. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Assessment is a lump sum. Strengthening is priced per element or as a lump sum. Timber repairs per joist or per area. Load relocation is an operational cost. Scanning per area or per location.

Strengthening for a new use sits with the change of use; repairs are condition items; safety items are immediate.

The cost of a heavy-use tenancy often includes structural strengthening that should be recovered through the lease rather than absorbed by the owner. Scanning before every coring job is inexpensive compared with repairing a cut tendon.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a level survey cannot: what each floor was designed to carry, whether it is post-tensioned, and what tenants have been allowed to put on it. Ask for them before any change of use or new heavy equipment.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Structural drawings with design loads | What each floor was designed to carry. |
| Post-tensioning drawings | Whether the slabs are post-tensioned, and where the tendons run. |
| Coring and opening records | Where the slabs have been cut, and whether it was engineered. |
| Change of use approvals | Whether a change of use was approved with the structure checked. |
| Floor load notices and tenant equipment schedules | What tenants keep on each floor, and whether notices limit it. |
| Lease clauses on floor loads | What loads tenants may place under their leases. |
| Engineering approvals for heavy tenant equipment | Whether heavy equipment was engineered before it went in. |
| Deflection monitoring records where available | Whether deflection is still increasing. |
| Timber pest and decay reports for timber floors | Whether timber floors have decay or pests. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Upper floors are misread when a slab is cored or cut before anyone has checked what runs through it, and when a floor that looks fine is assumed to carry whatever is placed on it.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| It is only a hole | Never core, drill or cut into a floor slab until tendons and reinforcement have been located by drawings and scanning. Cutting a post-tensioning tendon is dangerous and reduces capacity. |
| The floor looks fine, so it can carry more | Heavy storage, mobile shelving, plant and water features can exceed what a floor was designed for long before it shows. Check the design loads before any change of use or heavy equipment. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets imposed floor loads by use, design standards for concrete and timber floors, and rules for when a change of use needs the structure checked. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Loads and design | AS/NZS 1170.1 sets imposed floor loads by use; AS 3600 governs concrete, and AS 1684 and AS 1720 timber. | BS EN 1991-1-1 sets imposed loads; the Concrete Society publishes guidance on post-tensioned floors. | ASCE 7 sets live loads; ACI 318 governs concrete design. |
| Change of use | A change of use needs building approval showing the structure is adequate. | Approved Document A applies to material changes of use. | The International Existing Building Code governs changes of occupancy. |

In all three jurisdictions, leases and building management rules commonly set floor loading limits, and strata or condominium by-laws restrict alterations that cut slabs. Changes of use (for example, office to residential, or office to laboratory) trigger structural review under each country's rules for existing buildings, and may require strengthening before approval. Post-tensioned slabs need specialist contractors for any repair or alteration.

sections.heading: Worked example: a records store on an office floor
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 1980s office tenant has installed mobile shelving packed with paper records across one bay of an upper floor. The floor now sags visibly at mid-span, partitions on the floor below have cracked, and there is no load notice or engineering approval for the shelving.

Sagging at mid-span with cracked partitions below, directly beneath heavy storage, points to overload rather than creep. Mobile shelving full of paper can exceed an office floor's design load long before it shows. Moving the load is the first step; strengthening follows only if the tenant must keep it there.

So the register carries the overloaded bay as a safety line now, with the shelving relocated over beams or reduced and a load notice posted, a load review against the design as a check line, and lease controls on floor loads for the future.

thresholds.rule: Sag beyond span/250 impairs appearance; after partitions, deflection may be limited to span/500; brittle finishes damaged at L/500 or 20 mm, whichever is less

source.title: Deflection and preliminary vibration effects on structural elements (The Structural Engineer, 89(5), 2011)

thresholds.measure: Floor imposed loads (IBC Table 1607.1, as adopted in Massachusetts)
thresholds.rule: Offices 50 psf (2.4 kPa); corridors above the first floor 80 psf (3.8 kPa); light storage 125 psf (6.0 kPa)

pages.title: Ventilation Systems
pages.question: How do car park, kitchen, laboratory and toilet exhaust systems fail, and which failures are safety findings?
pages.answer: Dedicated ventilation fails on hazards, not comfort. Kitchen ducts accumulate grease beyond the hood and catch fire; car park CO sensors drift so fans do not start, or run constantly and mask the fault; fume cupboards lose face velocity and alarms get silenced. Toilet exhaust ducts disconnect and dump moisture into voids. Large exhaust without make-up air pulls flue gases back into buildings. Most of these systems have prescribed testing or cleaning intervals.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about ventilation systems; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
