pages.searchTitle: Exhaust and ventilation: car parks, kitchen grease, fume cupboards and make-up air

questions.question: Is grease in kitchen exhaust ductwork a fire risk?
questions.answer: Yes. Grease beyond the hood is a safety finding; the full system needs cleaning, at a frequency set by the cooking volume.

questions.question: How often should kitchen exhaust be cleaned?
questions.answer: By cooking volume: in the United States, NFPA 96 sets inspection from monthly for solid fuel cooking down to annually for low volume; in the United Kingdom, BESA TR/19 Grease sets the frequencies.

questions.question: Why do the car park fans never run?
questions.answer: Usually failed or disabled carbon monoxide sensors. Replace and calibrate them, and restore automatic control.

questions.question: Why is there mould in the bathrooms?
questions.answer: Often failed exhaust, or exhaust discharging into the roof space. Reconnect the ducts, replace the fans and extend the discharges outside.

questions.question: How long do car park CO sensors last?
questions.answer: 5 to 10 years, with regular calibration.

questions.question: Why do the car park fans run all the time?
questions.answer: The sensors have failed safe, or the controls have been overridden. Replace failed sensors and remove the overrides.

questions.question: Why is there a smell of exhaust fumes in the lift lobby of the car park?
questions.answer: Carbon monoxide is reaching people. Test the sensors and fan staging, and add extract or separation at occupied points.

questions.question: Why can we smell cooking or exhaust inside the building?
questions.answer: Exhaust is re-entering, or the building is at negative pressure. Move the discharge away from intakes, or rebalance the make-up air.

questions.question: Why is there mold in the roof space above the bathrooms?
questions.answer: The exhaust has failed or is discharging into the void. Reconnect the ducts, replace the fans, and extend the discharges outside.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Ventilation problems show in car parks, kitchens and laboratories as sensors, grease and alarms, in the building as mould, odours and slamming doors, and in the test and cleaning records. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On site | Car park: CO sensor locations and calibration labels; jet fans running or dead; storage blocking airflow | Car park ventilation |
| On site | Kitchen: grease on hoods, filters and accessible duct sections; fan casing grease; cleaning labels | Kitchen exhaust |
| On site | Labs: fume cupboard test labels, face velocity alarms, sash condition | Fume cupboards |
| On site | Bathrooms: fans running; condensation and mould; discharge points on façades and roofs | Make-up air, re-entry, toilet exhaust and MVHR |
| On site | Exhaust discharges relative to intakes and windows | Make-up air, re-entry, toilet exhaust and MVHR |
| On site | Doors slamming or hard to open (pressure imbalance) | Make-up air, re-entry, toilet exhaust and MVHR |
| In the records | Essential safety measure records for car park and kitchen exhaust | Standards by country |
| In the records | Kitchen exhaust cleaning certificates and frequencies | Kitchen exhaust |
| In the records | Fume cupboard and LEV test reports | Fume cupboards |
| In the records | CO sensor calibration records | Car park ventilation |
| In the records | Complaints of odour or fumes | Make-up air, re-entry, toilet exhaust and MVHR |

sections.heading: Types of ventilation system
sections.markdown:
Ventilation systems here are the dedicated supply and exhaust systems that serve particular spaces and hazards, separate from the general air conditioning: car park ventilation, toilet and bathroom exhaust, commercial kitchen exhaust, laboratory fume cupboards and fume extraction, garbage room and plant room exhaust, local exhaust ventilation for workshops, and whole-dwelling mechanical ventilation in apartments. Smoke exhaust and stair pressurisation for fire are covered on the fire services pages.

| System | Where it is found | What it protects against |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Car park ventilation (ducted or jet fans), often with CO control | Basement and enclosed car parks | Carbon monoxide and vehicle exhaust |
| Toilet and bathroom exhaust | All buildings | Odour and moisture; mould |
| Commercial kitchen exhaust (hood, grease filters, ductwork, fan) | Restaurants, hotels, hospitals, schools | Grease, heat, smoke; grease fires in ductwork |
| Fume cupboards and lab exhaust | Laboratories, schools, hospitals | Toxic and flammable vapours |
| Local exhaust ventilation (LEV) | Workshops, industrial processes | Dust, fume and vapour at source |
| Garbage and plant room exhaust | Apartments, commercial | Odour; heat; refrigerant |
| Whole-dwelling mechanical ventilation (MVHR, continuous extract) | Newer apartments, especially in Britain | Indoor air quality and condensation in airtight dwellings |
| Make-up air | Kitchens, labs, large exhaust systems | Balances exhaust so the building is not starved of air |

Many of these are life-safety or occupational health systems with statutory testing regimes: car park ventilation and kitchen exhaust are commonly essential safety measures; fume cupboards and LEV have periodic test requirements; kitchen exhaust cleaning frequencies are prescribed by standards and insurers.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Exhaust and car park jet fans last fifteen to twenty years and kitchen exhaust fans ten to fifteen, while carbon monoxide sensors last five to ten with calibration. Welded kitchen exhaust ductwork lasts twenty-five to forty years, if it is kept clean of grease.

| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Exhaust fans (general) | 15 to 20 years | Run hours; corrosion in wet exhaust |
| Car park jet fans | 15 to 20 years | Moisture; exhaust contaminants |
| CO sensors | 5 to 10 years, with calibration | Sensor technology; drift |
| Kitchen exhaust fans | 10 to 15 years | Grease; heat |
| Kitchen exhaust ductwork (welded steel) | 25 to 40 years | Cleaning access; grease fires |
| Fume cupboards | 15 to 25 years | Chemicals; sash mechanisms; controls |
| MVHR units | 15 to 20 years | Filter maintenance; fan motors |

What shortens life: grease build-up in kitchen exhaust; corrosive vapours in laboratory and wet area exhausts; lack of maintenance on systems that run out of sight; changes of use: a car park converted to storage, a kitchen with heavier cooking, a lab with new chemicals; disconnected ductwork in risers and ceilings.

sections.heading: Car park ventilation
sections.markdown:
Carbon monoxide sensors drift or fail, so fans either do not start when they should (CO builds up) or run continuously (wasting energy and masking the fault). Jet fans corrode in damp basements and are disabled when noisy. Supply air paths are blocked by storage or doors kept shut.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Car park fans never run | CO sensors failed or disabled. Calibration records; sensor test. | Replace and calibrate the CO sensors, and restore automatic control. |
| Car park fans always run | Sensors failed safe, or controls overridden. BMS; sensor test. | Replace failed sensors and remove overrides. |
| Exhaust fumes lingering at car park pay stations or lift lobbies | Carbon monoxide reaching people. Readings at occupied points against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Test sensors and fan staging, and add extract or separation at occupied points. |

sections.heading: Kitchen exhaust
sections.markdown:
Grease condenses in hoods, filters, ductwork and fans. Without regular cleaning to the full length of the duct, it accumulates to the point where a flare-up at the cooker ignites the duct. Kitchen duct fires spread through buildings, which is why cleaning frequencies are set by cooking volume and type.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Grease visible in ducts beyond the hood | Cleaning frequency or extent inadequate. Cleaning records; inspection. | Clean the full system, add access panels, and set the frequency to the cooking volume. |

sections.heading: Fume cupboards
sections.markdown:
Face velocity falls as fans wear, ducts leak or the building's pressure regime changes; sashes stick; alarms are silenced; cupboards are used for chemicals they were not designed for. Exhaust discharged too low or near intakes re-enters the building.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Fume cupboard alarms silenced | Low face velocity. Face velocity test against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Restore the alarm; test face velocity, and repair the fans and ductwork. |

sections.heading: Make-up air, re-entry, toilet exhaust and MVHR
sections.markdown:
Large exhaust without matching make-up air puts the building under negative pressure: doors slam or resist opening, flues backdraught (pulling combustion gases into the building), and dust and contaminants are drawn in through the envelope.

Exhausts discharging near air intakes, operable windows or terraces re-enter the building. Kitchen odour, car park fumes and laboratory vapours are the usual complaints.

Fans fail, ducts disconnect in ceilings and risers, and moisture is discharged into roof spaces and voids instead of outside, causing mould and decay.

MVHR filters are never changed, fans are switched off by residents because of noise, and boost controls do not work; condensation and mould follow in airtight apartments.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mould in bathrooms and roof spaces | Exhaust failed or discharging into voids. Fan and duct inspection. | Reconnect the ducts, replace the fans, and extend discharges outside. |
| Odour in occupied areas | Exhaust re-entry or negative pressure. Discharge locations; pressure test. | Move the discharge away from intakes, or rebalance the make-up air. |
| Flue spillage from appliances | Negative pressure from exhaust. Combustion and pressure test. | Stop using the appliance; add or rebalance make-up air. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Grease build-up in kitchen ductwork; car park ventilation not responding to CO; fume cupboard failing test; flue spillage from negative pressure | safety · 4 Essential | Stop use or clean and repair now. |
| Kitchen exhaust cleaning, fume cupboard or LEV testing due | deadline · 4 Essential | At the prescribed interval. |
| Fans failed; exhaust disconnected | failure · 3 Important | Repair now. |
| Sensors drifting; fans worn; poor balance | condition · 3 Important | Repair in the near term. |
| Systems at end of life | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Replace on cycle. |
| No records for safety-related systems | check · 2 Planned | Test and inspect. |
| Normal wear | nil · 1 Routine | Routine maintenance. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A mechanical services engineer, with specialists for kitchen exhaust, fume cupboards and LEV. The checks below start with the safety-related systems, car park, kitchen and laboratory exhaust, and their test and cleaning records, then the general exhaust and make-up air.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Records review | Essential safety measures, cleaning certificates, test reports, calibration records. |
| Car park | CO sensor tests with calibration gas, fan operation, airflow paths. |
| Kitchen exhaust | Inspection of hood, filters, the full length of ductwork through access panels, fan; grease depth measured against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). |
| Fume cupboards | Face velocity and containment testing to the relevant standard, and alarm function, against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). |
| LEV | Thorough examination and test of capture and airflow. |
| Toilet exhaust | Sample airflow checks; riser and duct inspection. |
| Pressure regime | Building pressure relative to outside; make-up air. |
| Discharge review | Distances to intakes and windows. |
| Smoke test | Of exhaust discharges to see where plumes travel. |

The report should give the status of every safety-related system, test results, cleaning adequacy, and recommended works.

sections.heading: Restoring, cleaning or rebalancing
sections.markdown:
Kitchen grease, unresponsive car park ventilation and failing fume cupboards come first, as safety findings. After that, the work restores general exhaust and the balance of make-up air, and moves discharges away from intakes.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Car park | Replace and calibrate CO sensors; repair or replace jet fans; clear airflow paths. | Where CO sensors or jet fans have failed. |
| Kitchen exhaust | Clean the full system; add access panels; set cleaning frequency to cooking volume; replace fans; fire suppression in hoods. | Wherever grease builds up beyond the hood. |
| Fume cupboards | Repair fans and ductwork; rebalance; replace cupboards; raise discharge stacks. | Where cupboards fail face velocity tests. |
| Toilet exhaust | Reconnect ducts; replace fans; extend discharges outside. | Where bathrooms grow mould, or exhaust discharges into voids. |
| Make-up air | Add or rebalance. | Where doors slam, odours spread or appliances spill. |
| Discharge relocation | Move discharges away from intakes. | Where exhaust re-enters the building. |
| MVHR | Maintenance programmes; quieter fans; resident guidance. | In homes with mechanical ventilation with heat recovery. |

Interactions: kitchen exhaust changes often require fire-rated duct enclosures and access panels through finished spaces; fume cupboard and lab exhaust changes need the whole lab pressure regime rebalanced; car park changes interact with smoke exhaust and fire systems.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Kitchen exhaust cleaning, fume cupboard and LEV testing, and CO sensor calibration are recurring contracts at prescribed frequencies. CO sensor replacement and fan replacement are itemised. Kitchen exhaust duct replacement, access panel installation and fire-rated enclosures are lump sums. Fume cupboard replacement is per cupboard, with ductwork and controls. Discharge relocation and make-up air systems are lump sums.

Testing, cleaning and safety rectification are code compliance and recur; replacement is lifecycle; repairs are repairs and maintenance.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a look at the fans cannot: whether kitchen exhaust has been cleaned along its whole length, whether fume cupboards pass their tests, and whether car park sensors are calibrated. Ask for them first, since most of these systems are safety measures.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Essential safety measure records and annual statements for car park and kitchen exhaust | Whether car park and kitchen exhaust were certified at the last review. |
| Kitchen exhaust cleaning certificates showing the extent cleaned, with frequency | How much of the kitchen exhaust was cleaned, and how often. |
| Fume cupboard face velocity and containment test reports | Whether fume cupboards contain fumes at the required face velocity. |
| LEV thorough examination reports | Whether local exhaust ventilation has been examined. |
| CO sensor calibration records and car park ventilation test records | Whether car park ventilation responds to carbon monoxide. |
| Complaint records for odour, fumes or doors | Where odours, fumes and pressure problems occur. |
| Mechanical drawings showing exhaust discharge locations and air intakes | Where exhausts discharge relative to intakes. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Ventilation is misread when its safety-related systems are treated as ordinary maintenance, and when fans that are running are assumed to be doing their job.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| It is a maintenance item | Kitchen exhaust ductwork with grease beyond the hood, car park ventilation that does not respond to carbon monoxide, and fume cupboards that fail face velocity tests are safety findings, not maintenance items. |
| The fans are running, so it works | Car park fans that always run may have sensors that failed safe or controls that were overridden, and fume cupboards whose alarms have been silenced may have low face velocity. Running is not the same as working. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets standards for car park and general ventilation, kitchen exhaust cleaning and fire safety, and laboratory exhaust. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Car parks and general ventilation | AS 1668.2 sets ventilation including car parks with CO control. | Approved Document F. | The International Mechanical Code covers car park ventilation. |
| Kitchen exhaust | AS 1668.1 covers kitchen exhaust fire aspects. | BESA TR/19 Grease sets kitchen extract cleaning frequencies. | NFPA 96 sets kitchen exhaust inspection frequencies (monthly for solid fuel cooking, quarterly for high volume, semi-annually for moderate, annually for low volume). |
| Laboratories and maintenance | AS/NZS 2243.8 governs fume cupboards; car park and kitchen exhaust systems are commonly essential safety measures maintained under AS 1851 and state regulations. | COSHH requires LEV thorough examination at least every 14 months; fume cupboards follow BS EN 14175. | ANSI/ASSP Z9.5 covers laboratory ventilation. |

Planning conditions often govern kitchen exhaust discharge and odour control in all three countries.

sections.heading: Worked example: grease beyond the hood
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A restaurant on the ground floor of an office building has a current kitchen exhaust cleaning certificate, but grease is visible in the duct beyond the hood where an access panel has been opened, and the certificate does not say how much of the system was cleaned. Upstairs, tenants complain of cooking odours near a fresh air intake.

Grease beyond the hood is a safety finding, not a maintenance item, whatever the certificate says: the cleaning has covered the hood, not the full system. The odours upstairs point to exhaust discharging near an intake and re-entering the building.

So the register carries the kitchen exhaust as a safety line now, cleaned along its full length with access panels added and the frequency set to the cooking volume, and the discharge moved away from the intake.

thresholds.rule: Average of 0.5 m/s, with no reading below 0.3 m/s; tested at least every 12 months

thresholds.rule: Deposits of no more than 200 microns

pages.title: Verandahs, Balconies & Balustrades
pages.question: How do balconies, decks and balustrades fail, what are the warning signs, and which findings mean closing them?
pages.answer: Balconies fail where you cannot see: corroding top steel at the root of a concrete cantilever, decayed ledgers on timber decks, rusting post bases inside slab pockets, membranes leaking at thresholds. A cantilever tip lower than its root with cracking along the wall line, a balustrade that moves under hand pressure, or a missing toughened glass panel means closing it now. Older balustrades below current height are a risk even where upgrade is not mandated.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about verandahs, balconies & balustrades; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.

pages.searchTitle: Balconies, decks and balustrades: dropped cantilevers, leaks, loose rails and glass

questions.question: Is a balcony with a dropped edge dangerous?
questions.answer: It can be. A cantilever whose tip has dropped relative to its root, with cracking along the wall line, should be closed to use until an engineer has assessed it.

questions.question: Why does the unit below leak under our balcony?
questions.answer: Often a failed membrane at the threshold, but leaks are also blamed on the balcony when they come from the door sill or window frame above. Water test them separately.

questions.question: Is a wobbly balustrade serious?
questions.answer: Yes. A balustrade that moves under hand pressure is a safety finding; close the balcony until it is refixed or replaced.

questions.question: Can I put a spa or heavy planters on my balcony?
questions.answer: Only with engineering. Heavy planters, spas and enclosures can overload a balcony not designed for them.

questions.question: How high must a balcony balustrade be?
questions.answer: At least 1 m in Australia, 1100 mm for external balconies in most UK buildings, and 42 inches in US buildings other than houses, where 36 inches is allowed.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Balcony problems show underfoot and at the rail, as leaks in the unit below, from the street as drooping edges and rust staining, and close up at thresholds, post bases and ledgers. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Inside | A balcony or deck that bounces, slopes outward or feels different underfoot from when it was new | Cantilevers and overload |
| Inside | A balustrade that moves when you lean on it, or a glass panel that rattles in its fixings | Balustrades and glass |
| Inside | Leaks, stains or swelling floor finishes in the unit below or inside the door, worst after rain on the balcony | Membranes, thresholds and enclosures |
| Inside | Rust stains running down the slab edge or soffit, or around post bases | Cantilevers and overload |
| Inside | Water that stands against the door sill after rain | Membranes, thresholds and enclosures |
| Street or aerial | Balcony slab edges drooping relative to the floor line above or below; tips lower than roots | Cantilevers and overload |
| Street or aerial | Spalling and rust staining on slab soffits and front edges; efflorescence on soffits | Cantilevers and overload |
| Street or aerial | Rust at the base of balustrade posts; posts out of line; missing glass panels; replaced glass in a different tint | Balustrades and glass |
| Street or aerial | Balustrades visibly below the height of their neighbours or with horizontal rails | Balustrades and glass |
| Street or aerial | Timber decks with sagging joists, staining at the house wall line, decayed post bases | Timber decks, ledgers and heritage verandahs |
| Street or aerial | Heritage verandahs with missing lace, leaning posts, sagging beams | Timber decks, ledgers and heritage verandahs |
| Close up on site | Cracking on the top surface along the wall line; drummy tiles; tiles cracked in a line parallel to the wall | Cantilevers and overload |
| Close up on site | Movement of balustrades when pushed by hand; corrosion at post bases and clamps; cracked concrete around post pockets | Balustrades and glass |
| Close up on site | Threshold height: water ponding against the door sill; falls towards the building | Membranes, thresholds and enclosures |
| Close up on site | Ledger fixing type and condition; rust on hangers and fasteners; soft timber when probed | Timber decks, ledgers and heritage verandahs |
| Close up on site | Glass type markings on balustrade panels; edge chips in toughened glass | Balustrades and glass |
| In the records | Strata defect claims and leak logs concentrated at balconies | Membranes, thresholds and enclosures |
| In the records | Balustrade certificates and glass specifications; any engineer's report on balconies | Balustrades and glass |
| In the records | Occupant alteration approvals: tiling, enclosures, spas, planters | Membranes, thresholds and enclosures |

sections.heading: Types of balcony and balustrade
sections.markdown:
Balconies, verandahs and decks are elevated platforms attached to or projecting from a building, and balustrades are the barriers that stop people falling from them. They combine structure, waterproofing and a life-safety barrier in one element, often over occupied space or a footpath, which is why their failures are among the most serious on any building.

| Form | Where it is found | Critical points |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cantilevered concrete slab continuous with the floor | Apartments and offices from the 1950s | Top reinforcement near the upper surface, under the tiles and membrane; the root where the slab passes the wall line |
| Steel or precast balconies bolted or hung on the frame | Apartments from the 1990s | Connection brackets and bolts; thermal break connectors |
| Timber deck on a ledger fixed to the house | Houses and townhouses | Ledger fixing to the wall; joist hangers; post bases; fasteners in treated timber |
| Post-supported balcony or verandah | Houses, heritage terraces, low-rise | Post bases and footings; beam connections; roof drainage on verandahs |
| Heritage verandah with cast iron or timber | Victorian and Edwardian terraces in Australia; heritage stock elsewhere | Cast iron corrosion and fracture; timber decay at post bases and floor edges |
| Juliet balcony | Apartments and houses | Fixings of a balustrade across an opening with no platform |

Balustrades are steel, aluminium, timber, masonry, wire or glass. Glass balustrades are either framed, point-fixed with clamps or spigots, or frameless in a base channel; the glass is toughened, laminated or toughened laminated. Older balustrades were often lower than current codes require and had horizontal rails children can climb; current codes in all three jurisdictions set minimum heights, limit openings, and in Australia restrict climbable elements where the fall is large.

These are among the few building elements that can kill people suddenly. A balcony carries its occupants over a drop, often with the critical steel or timber hidden under tiles, membranes and cladding, and its failure gives little warning. Its condition is read through the [membrane](https://moyneross.com/technical/waterproofing-membranes) that keeps water out of it, the [structure](https://moyneross.com/technical/structural-frame) it hangs from, and the balustrade that stops people falling from it ([Glazing Systems](https://moyneross.com/technical/glazing-systems) for glass balustrades).

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
A concrete balcony lasts fifty to eighty years and more, but its membrane lasts fifteen to twenty-five, steel balustrades twenty-five to forty, and a timber deck structure only fifteen to thirty. Water reaching the reinforcement, the ledger or the post bases is what cuts these lives short.

| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Concrete cantilever slab | 50 to 80 years and more | Cover to top steel; waterproofing over it; chloride exposure |
| Steel balcony frames and brackets | 40 to 60 years | Coating cycle; coastal exposure; water at connections |
| Timber deck structure | 15 to 30 years | Timber species and treatment; ground clearance; fastener corrosion |
| Membrane under tiles | 15 to 25 years | Falls, threshold height, outlets |
| Tiles and bedding | 20 to 30 years | Membrane condition; movement joints |
| Steel balustrades | 25 to 40 years | Paint or galvanising; post-base detail |
| Aluminium balustrades | 30 to 50 years | Finish; fixings; dissimilar metals |
| Glass balustrade fittings and glass | 25 to 40 years | Clamp and spigot corrosion; glass type; edge damage |

Life is set by water. The parts that stay wet longest, the slab root at the wall, post bases, ledgers against the house, board ends and outlets, fail first, usually long before the visible surfaces suggest anything is wrong.

What shortens life: water at the wrong level: flat or reversed falls, blocked outlets, low thresholds that let water run back to the door and the structure; hollow posts cast into or grouted onto slabs, which fill with water and rust from inside; treated timber with copper-based preservatives (ACQ and similar) that corrode plain galvanised nails, screws and hangers; coastal exposure and spray from pools; alterations by occupants: tiles laid over membranes without care, planters, spas, enclosures, fixings drilled through the membrane; overloading: heavy planters, hot tubs and crowding on timber decks.

What lengthens it: falls away from the building and outlets kept clear, so water never stands at the threshold or the slab root; drained post bases and side-fixed balustrades rather than posts set in pockets in the slab; approval for occupant changes: no tiling over membranes, no enclosures, planters or spas without engineering; periodic close inspection of balustrade fixings and glass, and of the underside of decks and cantilevers; stainless or hot-dip galvanised fixings for ledgers and joist hangers, compatible with the timber treatment.

sections.heading: Cantilevers and overload
sections.markdown:
A concrete cantilever carries its load in the top reinforcement, close to the upper surface. Water passing a failed membrane, chlorides from coastal air or old calcium chloride additives, or low cover lets that steel corrode. It loses section unseen at exactly the point of highest stress, the root at the wall line. The slab cracks along the wall line on its top surface, then rotates and sags at its tip; spalling appears on the soffit edge and at the front face.

Balconies are designed for people, not for what occupants later put on them. Heavy planters, spas, water features, barbecues on raised hearths and crowds at a party can exceed what a cantilever or ledger was built for, most dangerously when the structure has already lost capacity to corrosion or decay.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Crack along the wall line on the top surface; tip of the slab lower than its root | Top reinforcement corrosion or overload in a cantilever. Half-cell and cover readings at the root; chloride or carbonation at bar depth; rotation measured by level. | Close the balcony until an engineer has assessed it; strengthen it, or replace it where section loss at the root is severe. |
| Spalling on the soffit and front edge | Corrosion of edge and bottom bars. Rust staining along bar lines; low cover. | Repair the concrete to a recognised repair standard. |

sections.heading: Timber decks, ledgers and heritage verandahs
sections.markdown:
Timber decks most often collapse at the ledger, the beam fixed to the house wall. Nails withdraw, bolts corrode, and water trapped between ledger and wall decays both. Joist hangers corrode in treated timber. Collapse is sudden and typically happens when the deck is crowded.

Post bases in contact with soil or paving, floor board ends, and beams where water lodges decay first. Termites attack timber in contact with the ground in Australia.

Cast iron lace, brackets and columns corrode and are brittle: they crack rather than bend, and a rusted fixing can let a heavy section fall. Verandah gutters and roofs overflow onto posts and floors.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Deck separating from the wall; bounce; stained wall line | Ledger fixing failure and decay. Nails or corroded bolts at the ledger; soft timber behind. | Close the deck; fit a new ledger with through-bolts and lateral load connectors. |
| Deck bouncing or sloping outward | Ledger, joist or post failure, or overload. Ledger fixings corroded or withdrawn; joists decayed at bearings. | Close the deck; replace the failed ledger, joists or posts, or rebuild it. |
| Cracks in cast iron lace or columns | Corrosion and brittle fracture. Rust at fixings; cracked sections that move. | Replace cracked sections with matching castings. |

sections.heading: Balustrades and glass
sections.markdown:
Steel posts set in pockets or core holes in the slab fill with water, rust from inside, and burst the concrete around the base. The post looks sound above the floor and is loose at its root. Bolted base plates corrode under the plate.

Monolithic toughened glass can break spontaneously from nickel sulphide inclusions and falls out of the frame as fragments, leaving no barrier. Laminated glass stays in place when broken. Clamps and spigots loosen and corrode; glass in base channels can rotate when the channel fixings or packers fail.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Rust and burst concrete at a balustrade post base, post loose | Water in hollow post or pocket. Post moves at the root under hand pressure; water inside when drilled. | Rebuild the post base with a drained or solid post on a surface-mounted plate above the membrane. |
| Missing glass panel with fragments below | Spontaneous breakage of monolithic toughened glass. Glass marked toughened, not laminated; no impact. | Close the balcony; replace monolithic toughened glass with laminated glass. |
| Low balustrade, wide gaps, or rails children could climb | A barrier that will not prevent a fall. Height, openings and climbable rails measured against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Raise, infill or replace the barrier to the current requirement. |

sections.heading: Membranes, thresholds and enclosures
sections.markdown:
Balconies over occupied space depend on a membrane under the tiles. It fails at the threshold where the door sill meets the balcony, at upstands, at outlets and at balustrade post fixings drilled through it. Water leaks into the unit below, saturates the screed, and on concrete balconies reaches the reinforcement.

Glass enclosures, retractable screens and new tiling change how water drains and add weight and wind load. Tiles laid over an existing membrane without falls hold water against it; enclosures block the drainage the balcony relied on and hide the structure from inspection.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Leak to the unit below at the door line | Membrane failure at the threshold. Flood test at the threshold; low or reversed upstand. | Flood test the threshold separately from the door sill; raise the upstand and renew the membrane. |
| Drummy and cracked tiles over the whole balcony | Membrane failure with saturated bedding. Flood test; moisture in the screed. | Re-membrane: remove tiles and screed, correct the falls, renew the membrane and outlets, and re-tile. |
| Water standing against the door sill | Falls towards the building or threshold too low. Level survey; threshold height against the balcony surface. | Correct the falls and threshold height when re-membraning. |
| Leaks below that began after tiling or an enclosure | Occupant alteration to the waterproofing. Alteration dates; tiles over membrane; drainage blocked. | Establish the alteration, then restore the membrane and drainage. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Balustrade that moves under hand pressure, missing glass panel, loose post; cantilever rotation or root cracking; decayed or loose deck ledger | safety · 4 Essential | Close or barricade immediately; engineer within days. |
| Cantilever tip dropped with cracking along the wall line; deck ledger separating from the wall | safety · 4 Essential | Close the balcony or deck now and prop. |
| Heavy planters, spas or enclosures on a balcony not designed for them | condition · 4 Essential | Remove or assess the load before further use. |
| Leaks damaging the structure or units below; spalling exposing reinforcement | failure · 4 Essential | Repair now; extent from investigation. |
| Post-base corrosion without looseness; membrane leaks without structural damage; fastener corrosion on decks | condition · 3 Important | Programme repair in the near term. |
| Membranes and coatings at age without leaks | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Renewal on cycle. |
| California exterior elevated element inspection due; strata order | deadline · 4 Essential | Timing set by the statute or order. |
| Balustrades below current height or with climbable rails, compliant when built; monolithic toughened glass balustrades at height | check · 3 Important | Assess risk by use and fall height; upgrade where children use the space or where the risk warrants. |
| Cosmetic coating wear, isolated drummy tile | nil · 1 Routine | Routine care. |

> Codes rarely require existing compliant balustrades to be upgraded, but a balustrade below current height or with climbable rails on an apartment balcony is a foreseeable risk. Upgrade is usually justified where children use the space and the fall is large.

The grading follows what a finding demands, not the size of the eventual bill.

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A structural engineer leads, with a waterproofing consultant for membranes. On apartment buildings, a sample of balconies is inspected, weighted to the most exposed and oldest; every timber deck and every glass balustrade over a public area is inspected. The checks below test every balustrade by hand and read the shape of each balcony, then flood test the membrane and threshold separately from the door above.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Level survey | Of cantilever tips against roots to detect rotation. |
| Hammer survey | Of soffits, edges and tiles; cover and half-cell potential surveys at the root; chloride and carbonation testing at bar depth. |
| Opening up | At thresholds, outlets and post bases; removal of tiles at the root where corrosion is suspected. |
| Flood testing | Of membranes. |
| Load testing | Of balustrades to the design horizontal load where fixings are doubtful, with height and openings measured against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). |
| Ledger inspection | From below, with probing of timber and removal of a sample fastener. |
| Glass identification | Of balustrade panels. |
| Occupant alteration survey | Tiling, enclosures, planters and spas recorded for each balcony inspected. |

The report should state for each balcony inspected the structural condition, rotation measured, membrane condition, balustrade compliance with the code at the time and current code, and urgent actions.

sections.heading: Closing, repairing or rebuilding
sections.markdown:
A balcony or deck showing structural warning signs, or a balustrade that moves, is closed to use first. The repairs then follow the cause: concrete repair or strengthening at the root, a new membrane with correct falls and upstands, rebuilt post bases, or a new ledger.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Concrete repair | Break out, treat or replace reinforcement and reinstate to a recognised repair standard; strengthen with additional steel or external brackets; replace the balcony where section loss at the root is severe. | Where reinforcement corrodes, or the cantilever has rotated. |
| Re-membrane | Remove tiles and screed, correct falls and threshold upstands, lay a new membrane and outlets, and re-tile. | Where the membrane has failed. |
| Post bases | Cut out and rebuild with drained or solid posts on surface-mounted plates above the membrane. | Where post bases corrode or burst the concrete. |
| Balustrades | Refix or replace; raise height with extensions; infill climbable sections; replace monolithic toughened glass with laminated or heat-soaked laminated glass. | Where balustrades move, fall short of current height, or use monolithic toughened glass at height. |
| Timber decks | A new ledger with through-bolts and lateral load connectors, new joists and hangers with compatible fasteners, or a full rebuild. | Where ledgers, joists or posts have decayed or corroded. |
| Heritage verandahs | Repair cast iron with matching castings, replace decayed timber in kind, and restore roof drainage. | On heritage verandahs. |

Interactions: on apartment buildings balconies are repaired as a programme, unit by unit, with residents moved off the balcony during works; re-membraning usually means new tiles, new thresholds and often new balustrades, so balustrade upgrades are best done at the same time.

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Inspection is priced per balcony with a lump sum for testing. Works are priced per balcony unit for concrete repair and re-membrane, per linear metre for balustrades, and per square metre for membranes and tiling. Access by scaffold or swing stage dominates on multi-storey buildings, and work inside occupied units adds time and cost.

What drives the cost: access (scaffold or mast climbers over the full façade, or work from each unit), the number of balconies, tile and finish removal, threshold and door alterations, and resident disruption. Commonly missed: making good finishes in the unit below, door and window sill changes, and statutory inspection reports where required.

Two-part lines are normal. Balustrade upgrades and statutory inspections are code compliance; membranes are lifecycle; concrete and fixing repairs are repairs and maintenance, or lifecycle when replacement is needed; make-safe is immediate.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a walk along the balconies cannot: what each was designed to carry, whether its membrane was flood tested, and what occupants have added. Ask for them before attributing a leak or a defect.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Structural drawings of balconies and decks; balustrade certificates and glass specifications | What each balcony and deck was designed to carry, and what its balustrades are certified for. |
| Membrane specification and warranty; flood test records | What the membrane is, and whether it was flood tested. |
| Any engineer's report on balconies, and statutory inspection reports where required | What engineers have already found. |
| Leak logs and defect claims concentrated at balconies | Whether leaks and defects cluster at the balconies. |
| Records of occupant alterations: tiling, enclosures, planters, spas | What occupants have added or altered. |
| Maintenance records for outlets, coatings and timber decks | Whether outlets, coatings and decks are maintained. |
| Statutory balcony or exterior elevated element inspection reports, where required | Whether statutory inspections are current. |
| Engineering for any enclosures, spas or heavy planters added by occupants | Whether heavy additions were engineered. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Balconies are misread when a dropped cantilever is treated as a finishing defect, and when every leak below a balcony is blamed on its membrane.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| A dropped tip is cosmetic | Rotation of a cantilever is a structural warning. A balcony whose tip has dropped relative to its root, with cracking along the wall line on top, should be closed to use until an engineer has assessed it. |
| The leak below is the balcony membrane | A leak into the unit below is often blamed on the balcony membrane when it comes from the door sill or window frame above it. Water test the frame and sill separately from the balcony surface ([Sealants & Joints](https://moyneross.com/technical/sealants-and-joints)). |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets the height, openings and loads of barriers, standards for balcony design and membranes, and in some places periodic inspection. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Barriers and guards | The National Construction Code requires barriers where a fall is 1 m or more, at least 1 m high (865 mm on stair flights), with openings that do not pass a 125 mm sphere and no climbable elements between 150 mm and 760 mm where the fall is more than 4 m; glass in barriers follows AS 1288. | Approved Document K sets guarding heights (1100 mm for external balconies and edges of floors in most buildings) and limits openings to 100 mm where children may be present; BS 6180 covers barriers. | International Building Code Section 1015 requires guards of 42 inches where the drop exceeds 30 inches, with a 4-inch sphere limit, and Section 1607 sets guard loads; the International Residential Code allows 36-inch guards in houses. |
| Design, inspection and liability | External membranes follow AS 4654.2 and imposed loads AS/NZS 1170.1; balconies are a leading item in strata defect claims, and New South Wales adds duties under the Design and Building Practitioners Act 2020. | BS 8579 covers the design of balconies and terraces; regulation 7(2) restricts combustible materials in balconies of relevant buildings. | California requires periodic inspection of exterior elevated elements: every six years for apartment buildings under SB 721 and every nine years for condominiums under SB 326. |

sections.heading: Worked example: a leak below a retiled balcony
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 2000s apartment has a tiled concrete balcony. The unit below reports a leak at its ceiling near the door line, and the tiles across the whole balcony sound drummy. The owner retiled over the original tiles last year, and one glass balustrade panel rattles in its clamp.

The rattling panel comes first: a balustrade that moves is a safety finding. For the leak, the door sill and frame above are water tested separately from the balcony surface, since leaks are often blamed on the membrane when they come from the frame. Drummy tiles across the whole balcony, and last year's retiling, point to a membrane failure with saturated bedding, possibly caused by the alteration.

So the register carries the balustrade as a safety line now, separate water tests of the door frame and a flood test of the balcony as check lines, and re-membraning with corrected falls and threshold upstand as a failure line if the flood test confirms it.

thresholds.rule: Required where the surface is 1 m or more above the ground beneath; at least 1 m high; openings that will not pass a 125 mm sphere; above 4 m, no climbable horizontal elements between 150 mm and 760 mm

source.title: NCC 2025 Volume One, Part D3 Construction of exits

thresholds.rule: At least 1100 mm high; no openings that pass a 100 mm sphere

source.title: Approved Document K (2013 edition incorporating 2016 and 2020 amendments)

pages.title: Water Conservation
pages.question: Where do buildings waste water, and how do you find and fix it?
pages.answer: Most avoidable water use is leaks, timed urinal flushing and poorly controlled cooling towers, not fixture choice. Night flow on the main meter with the building empty reveals leaks and timed urinals in minutes. Efficient fixtures help, but very low flows on old drains cause blockages and weak showers invite tampering. Rainwater and recycled systems that fail quietly revert to mains water. Metering that someone reads holds the savings.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about water conservation; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Water-efficient fixtures (WELS rated), rainwater harvesting

pages.searchTitle: Water conservation in buildings: leaks, urinals, cooling towers and what to fix

questions.question: Where does most wasted water go?
questions.answer: Leaks, timed urinal flushing and poorly controlled cooling towers, more than fixture choice.

questions.question: How can I tell if a building has a hidden leak?
questions.answer: Read the main meter with the building empty. Flow at night means leaks or timed urinals, and isolating zones finds the source. Wet ground or lush patches on dry days suggest a buried leak.

questions.question: Why does a cooling tower use so much water?
questions.answer: Mostly through bleed. Poor bleed control wastes water; control by conductivity with good water treatment reduces it.

questions.question: Do low-flow toilets cause blockages?
questions.answer: They can in old drains, where low flows cannot carry waste. A CCTV survey of the drains confirms it.

questions.question: Why isn't our rainwater tank saving water?
questions.answer: If the tank overflows while the building draws mains water, the harvesting system is not supplying its end uses. Check the pumps and valves.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Most wasted water is never seen; it shows on the meter, at night, and in the bills. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On site or in data | Night flow on the main meter when the building is empty | Leaks, urinals and fixtures |
| On site or in data | Cisterns running or trickling into pans | Leaks, urinals and fixtures |
| On site or in data | Urinals flushing in empty toilets | Leaks, urinals and fixtures |
| On site or in data | Cooling tower overflow or constant bleed | Cooling towers, kitchens and process water |
| On site or in data | Irrigation running in rain | Irrigation and alternative water |
| In the records | Water bills and meter data | Leaks, urinals and fixtures |
| In the records | NABERS Water or similar ratings | Standards by country |
| In the records | Fixture schedules | Leaks, urinals and fixtures |
| In the records | Cooling tower water treatment reports | Cooling towers, kitchens and process water |
| On site | Wet ground, lush patches or water running in gutters on dry days, which suggest buried leaks | Leaks, urinals and fixtures |
| On site | Equipment discharging cooling water continuously to drain | Cooling towers, kitchens and process water |
| On site | Rainwater tanks overflowing while the building draws mains water, showing the harvesting system is not connected or working | Irrigation and alternative water |
| On site | Showerheads and taps with restrictors removed | Leaks, urinals and fixtures |

sections.heading: Water saving measures
sections.markdown:
Water conservation covers the measures that reduce a building's water use: efficient taps, showers, toilets and urinals; leak detection and repair; cooling tower water management; efficient irrigation; rainwater harvesting and water recycling (whose systems are covered on the specialist hydraulics page); and metering that shows where water goes. In offices and commercial buildings, cooling towers, toilets and leaks dominate use; in apartments, showers, toilets and leaks.

| Measure | Where it is found | Watch points |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Efficient taps and showerheads | All buildings | User satisfaction; tampering |
| Dual flush and efficient toilets | All buildings | Cistern leaks; drainage carry in old pipes |
| Waterless and efficient urinals | Commercial and public buildings | Odour and maintenance; old timed flushing systems |
| Leak detection and metering | Larger buildings | Meters not read; data ignored |
| Cooling tower water management | Buildings with water-cooled chillers | Bleed control; cycles of concentration |
| Efficient irrigation | Landscaped sites | Leaks; running in rain |
| Rainwater harvesting and recycling | Newer buildings | Treatment; cross-connection |

Labelling schemes help choose fixtures: the Water Efficiency Labelling and Standards scheme is mandatory in Australia, the Unified Water Label is used in Britain, and WaterSense is the US Environmental Protection Agency's voluntary label.

Water conservation also reduces energy, because heating, pumping and treating water all use it; in buildings with large hot water loads, efficient showerheads cut gas or electricity use as much as water.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Water saving measures last only as long as they keep working as intended. Fixtures and controls need renewing within ten to twenty years, and the savings depend on leaks being found and controls not being bypassed.

| Measure | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tapware and showerheads | 10 to 20 years | Water quality; use |
| Toilets and cisterns | 20 to 30 years; internals 5 to 10 | Valve and seal wear |
| Urinal controls | 10 to 15 years | Sensors; batteries |
| Water meters | 10 to 20 years | Accuracy; batteries |
| Irrigation controllers | 8 to 12 years | Technology |

What shortens it: silent leaks in cisterns and pipes; timed urinal flushing running day and night; tampering with flow restrictors by dissatisfied users; unread meters, so waste goes unnoticed.

Water savings decay quickly without maintenance: a cistern valve that starts to pass, a urinal sensor that fails into continuous flushing, or a restrictor removed by a tenant can undo years of savings within weeks, and nothing visible signals it except the meter.

sections.heading: Leaks, urinals and fixtures
sections.markdown:
Leaking cisterns, dripping taps and hidden pipe leaks waste large volumes silently. In many buildings leaks are a significant share of total use, and night flow on the main meter is the simplest test.

Older urinals on timed cisterns flush around the clock whether used or not; replacing them with sensor or waterless systems is one of the largest savings in commercial buildings.

Showers with poor spray and taps with weak flow lead users to remove restrictors or complain until fixtures are replaced.

Very low-flush toilets on long, shallow-graded or old drains can leave solids behind, causing blockages; water efficiency must be matched to the drainage.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Night flow with the building empty | Leaks or timed urinals. Night flow test; isolate zones. | Isolate zones to find the source; repair leaks and fit sensor urinal controls. |
| Water use rising with no change in occupancy | New leak. Sub-meters. | Use the sub-meters to find the leak, then repair it and set leak alarms. |
| Blockages after toilet replacement | Low flows in old drains. CCTV; drain grades. | Survey the drain by CCTV; upgrade it where low flows cannot carry waste. |
| Toilets or urinals running constantly | Failed fill valves or flush controls. Dye test in cisterns; urinal controls. | Repair or replace the valves and fit urinal controls. |

sections.heading: Cooling towers, kitchens and process water
sections.markdown:
Cooling towers lose water by evaporation and bleed; poor water treatment forces excessive bleed. Bleed control tied to conductivity and good treatment raises cycles of concentration and cuts water use.

Commercial kitchens, laundries and process equipment such as single-pass cooling of refrigeration and ice machines can use large volumes; single-pass cooling in particular wastes water continuously and is prohibited in some places.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| High cooling tower water use | Poor bleed control. Treatment records. | Control bleed by conductivity, with good water treatment. |
| Constant flow from equipment | Single-pass cooling. Inspection of kitchen and plant. | Replace single-pass cooling with air-cooled or closed-loop equipment. |

sections.heading: Irrigation and alternative water
sections.markdown:
Outside the building, water is lost to irrigation that runs to a timer rather than the weather, and to alternative water systems that no longer supply what they were built for. Both waste water that nobody sees.

Irrigation running on fixed timers in rain, broken sprinklers and leaking drip lines waste water outdoors, often the largest use on landscaped residential sites in summer.

Rainwater and recycled systems that fail revert to mains top-up, so the saving disappears without anyone noticing.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Summer peaks in water use | Irrigation or cooling towers. Sub-meters; seasonal pattern. | Use the sub-meters to separate irrigation from the cooling towers; fit smart controllers and rain sensors. |
| Tanks full but mains use unchanged | Harvesting system not supplying end uses. Pump and valve checks. | Check the pumps and valves, and reconnect the system to its end uses. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cross-connection of recycled water to drinking water | safety · 4 Essential | Isolate now. |
| Major leak | failure · 2 Planned | Repair now. |
| Water restrictions or rating requirements | deadline · 4 Essential | As required. |
| Leaks, timed urinals, poor tower control | condition · 2 Planned | Fix in the near term. |
| Fixtures at end of life | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Replace with efficient fixtures. |
| No water audit | check · 2 Planned | Audit. |
| Normal | nil · 1 Routine | Monitor. |

Water findings are rarely urgent for safety, but a large hidden leak can damage structure and finishes, which raises it to a failure grade.

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A hydraulic engineer or water auditor leads, with the cooling tower water treatment contractor and landscape contractor where relevant. The checks below establish where the water goes, whether it flows when the building is empty, and which systems are wasting it.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Water audit | Consumption broken down by end use (amenities, cooling towers, irrigation, kitchens, process) from bills, sub-meters and fixture counts. |
| Night flow test | Read the main meter over a period when the building is empty to quantify leaks and continuous flows. |
| Fixture survey | Flow rates of taps and showers, flush volumes, urinal controls, and condition of cistern valves and seals. |
| Cooling tower review | Bleed control, cycles of concentration, overflow and drift. |
| Irrigation audit | Leaks, overspray, controllers and rain sensors. |
| Alternative water check | Whether rainwater and recycled systems are actually supplying their end uses. |
| Drainage check | Before installing very low-flush fixtures on old drains. |

The report should identify the largest uses and losses, quick fixes, fixture upgrades, and a metering and monitoring plan.

sections.heading: Saving water
sections.markdown:
Most avoidable water use is leaks, timed urinal flushing and poorly controlled cooling towers, so the first measures are repairs and controls, not new fixtures. Metering with alarms keeps the savings, because leaks return unseen.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Leak repair | Repair cisterns, taps and pipework, then fit leak alarms on sub-meters. | Wherever night flow or rising use shows a leak. |
| Urinal controls | Sensor flushing or waterless urinals in place of timed cisterns. | Wherever urinals flush on a timer in empty toilets. |
| Efficient fixtures | Fixtures chosen for user satisfaction as well as rating, to avoid tampering. | When fixtures reach the end of their life. |
| Cooling tower bleed control | Bleed controlled by conductivity, with good water treatment. | Where tower water use is high or bleed is constant. |
| Irrigation upgrades | Drip irrigation, smart controllers and rain sensors. | Where irrigation runs in rain or drives summer peaks. |
| Alternative water restoration | Repair harvesting and recycling systems so they supply their end uses. | Where tanks overflow while the building draws mains water. |
| Metering with alarms | Alarms on night flow and unusual consumption. | In every building, so leaks are caught early. |
| Drain upgrades | Upgraded drains where low-flow fixtures cause blockages. | Where blockages follow toilet replacement in old drains. |
| Single-pass cooling replacement | Air-cooled or closed-loop equipment in kitchens and plant. | Wherever equipment discharges cooling water continuously to drain. |
| Tenant engagement | Shared consumption data, and water clauses in leases. | In tenanted buildings. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Audits are lump sums. Leak repairs and urinal controls are small itemised costs with quick paybacks. Fixture replacement is per fixture, usually timed with refurbishment. Cooling tower controls and irrigation upgrades are lump sums. Metering is per meter plus a monitoring subscription.

Leak repair is repairs and maintenance; fixture replacement is lifecycle; ratings and restrictions can create deadlines.

Water savings often also cut sewer charges and the energy used to heat and pump water, so paybacks are usually better than the water bill alone suggests.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a walk-through cannot: how much water the building uses, where it goes, and whether it flows when the building is empty. Ask for at least two years of bills and any meter data before judging the building.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Water bills for at least two years | How much water the building uses, and how that has changed. |
| Sub-meter data and night flow readings | Where the water goes, and whether it flows when the building is empty. |
| NABERS Water or similar ratings | How the building compares with others like it. |
| Fixture schedules with ratings | What fixtures are installed, and how efficient they are. |
| Cooling tower water treatment reports | Whether bleed is controlled, and how much water the towers use. |
| Irrigation controller settings and records | Whether irrigation runs to the weather or to a fixed timer. |
| Alternative water system maintenance records | Whether harvesting and recycling systems supply their end uses. |
| Records of leaks found and repaired | Where leaks recur. |
| Any water efficiency plan or audit | What has been recommended, and what has been done. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Water waste is often blamed on fixtures, when most of it comes from leaks and controls nobody sees. Comparing use per occupant or per square metre with benchmarks shows whether a building is unusually wasteful before any detailed investigation.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| Efficient fixtures are the answer | Most avoidable water use is leaks, timed urinal flushing and poorly controlled cooling towers, not fixture choice. |
| No visible leaks means no leaks | Night flow on the main meter with the building empty shows leaks or timed urinals that nobody sees; wet ground or lush patches on dry days suggest buried leaks. |
| A rainwater tank saves water | Only if it is connected and working. A tank overflowing while the building draws mains water shows a harvesting system that is not supplying its end uses. |
| Low-flow toilets always help | In old drains, low flows can cause blockages, and the drains may need upgrading with the fixtures. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market labels efficient fixtures, but the rules beyond that differ. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out the fixture schemes, the rules for new buildings and ratings, and restrictions and support.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Fixtures | The Water Efficiency Labelling and Standards scheme requires labelling of taps, showers, toilets and urinals; plumbing codes set minimum efficiency for new fixtures. | The Unified Water Label grades fixtures. | WaterSense labels efficient fixtures; federal and state standards set maximum flow rates, with stricter limits in states such as California. |
| New buildings and ratings | NABERS Water rates offices. | Approved Document G sets a water efficiency limit for new homes; BREEAM rewards water efficiency in non-domestic buildings. | Some cities require water benchmarking alongside energy. |
| Restrictions and support | Water utilities and states impose restrictions in droughts. | Water companies offer audits. | Water utilities and states impose restrictions in droughts, as California has; many utilities offer rebates for WaterSense-labelled fixtures. |

In all three countries, strata and condominium buildings commonly have a single water meter, so individual waste is shared by all owners; sub-metering apartments changes behaviour and is required or encouraged in some places.

sections.heading: Worked example: an office that uses water at night
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 1980s office with a cooling tower and landscaped grounds has water use well above benchmark for its size. The main meter shows flow overnight with the building empty, and the urinals flush on a timer.

Night flow with the building empty points to leaks or timed urinals, and here both are possible. Isolating zones overnight separates them: if flow stops when the urinal supply is isolated, sensor controls are the fix; if it continues, a leak is in the pipework. The cooling tower is the other suspect, checked against its treatment records for bleed control.

So the register carries a water audit as a check line, leak repair and urinal controls as condition lines, and bleed control on the tower if the records show constant bleed. Sub-meters with night-flow alarms keep the savings from drifting back.

pages.title: Water Supply
pages.question: How do building water supplies fail, and which failures put drinking water quality or the building at risk?
pages.answer: Water supply fails by corrosion, pressure and contamination. Galvanised steel narrows and runs brown; copper pinholes in some waters; brass fittings in plastic systems dezincify; polybutylene fails. The safety findings are about water quality: backflow devices that are untested or missing on hazard connections, cross-connections from alterations, lead service pipes and solder, and Legionella in cold storage tanks. Seized isolation valves turn small leaks into building-wide outages.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about water supply; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.
pages.frameworkDescription: Incoming services, storage tanks, backflow prevention devices
