pages.searchTitle: Water supply pipework: brown water, pinhole leaks, backflow, lead and pressure

questions.question: Why is the water brown after a weekend?
questions.answer: Usually corroding galvanised steel pipework. Plan its replacement, riser by riser.

questions.question: How often must backflow devices be tested?
questions.answer: Typically annually, as the water utility or the local cross-connection control programme requires.

questions.question: Why does our water meter run at night?
questions.answer: A hidden leak or running cisterns. Find and repair it, and add smart metering to catch the next one.

questions.question: Why do the pipes bang when taps close?
questions.answer: Water hammer from high pressure or fast-closing valves. Pressure-limiting valves and water hammer arrestors cure it.

questions.question: How long does water pipework last?
questions.answer: Copper and PEX 50 years and more; galvanised steel 40 to 60, often less; brass fittings in plastic systems 10 to 30.

questions.question: Why is the water pressure weak on the upper floors?
questions.answer: The pressure is below what the fixtures need. Check valves, filters and boosters, and resize the supply if needed.

questions.question: Why do the copper pipes keep getting pinhole leaks in the same places?
questions.answer: Pitting corrosion from the water chemistry. Test the water chemistry, and replace the affected runs.

questions.question: Why is the backflow valve dripping?
questions.answer: A device leaking from its relief port has fouled or failed check valves. Service or replace the device, and test it.

questions.question: Why are the brass fittings leaking on the plastic pipework?
questions.answer: Dezincification of the brass. Replace the fittings with dezincification-resistant brass.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Water supply problems show at taps as brown water and low flow, in pipework as crusted fittings and banging, at backflow devices and tanks, and in consumption and leak records. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| On site | Pipe materials visible in plant rooms, risers and under fixtures | Corrosion, leaks and valves |
| On site | Brown water on opening taps; low flow at upper floors or far outlets | Corrosion, leaks and valves |
| On site | Water hammer noise; loose pipe supports | Lead and pressure |
| On site | Green or white crusting on brass fittings (dezincification) | Corrosion, leaks and valves |
| On site | Backflow devices: test tags, leaks from relief ports, bypasses | Backflow and tanks |
| On site | Tank lids, screens, overflows and condition | Backflow and tanks |
| On site | Damp and staining on walls and ceilings near pipe runs | Corrosion, leaks and valves |
| In the records | Water consumption trends, especially night-time use | Corrosion, leaks and valves |
| In the records | Backflow device register and test certificates | Backflow and tanks |
| In the records | Leak and repair history by location | Corrosion, leaks and valves |
| In the records | Water quality testing, including lead where relevant | Lead and pressure |
| In the records | Tank cleaning and inspection records | Backflow and tanks |

sections.heading: Types of pipework
sections.markdown:
Water supply covers drinking and service water from the utility connection to the outlets: the incoming main and meter, backflow prevention devices that stop building water flowing back into the public supply, pressure-limiting valves, storage and break tanks, distribution pipework, risers and isolation valves, sub-meters, and cold water to fixtures and equipment. Hot water plant and booster pumps have their own pages.

| Material | Typical era and use | What it implies |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lead | Service pipes in older housing: Britain before about 1970, US lead service lines into the 1980s | Lead in drinking water; replacement programmes in Britain and the United States |
| Galvanised steel | Pre-1970s in all three countries; some commercial risers later | Internal corrosion and tuberculation; brown water; falling flow |
| Copper | Most buildings from the 1950s onward | Long-lived; pinhole pitting in some waters; erosion at high velocity |
| Polybutylene | US and some Australian housing, late 1970s to mid 1990s | Fittings and pipe failures; often replaced proactively |
| PEX and other plastics | From the 1990s | Durable; brass fittings can dezincify; UV degradation if exposed |
| Ductile iron and PE | Large incoming mains and site services | Corrosion of iron; joint failures; ground movement |

In apartment and commercial buildings, water often passes through break tanks and booster pumps before reaching upper floors. Tenancies and apartments are sub-metered, and the owner's infrastructure stops at each lot's isolation valve or meter. Where a building has cooling towers, irrigation, fire services or process water, backflow devices separate each hazard from the drinking supply.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Copper and PEX pipework last fifty years and more, but galvanised steel lasts forty to sixty and often less, and brass fittings in plastic systems ten to thirty. Water chemistry decides how long copper actually lasts.

| Component | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Copper pipework | 50 years and more | Water chemistry; velocity; installation |
| Galvanised steel pipework | 40 to 60 years, often less | Water chemistry; internal corrosion |
| PEX pipework | 50 years and more | UV exposure; fittings |
| Brass fittings in plastic systems | 10 to 30 years | Dezincification in aggressive waters |
| Backflow prevention devices | 15 to 25 years with annual testing | Water quality; debris; maintenance |
| Pressure-limiting valves | 10 to 20 years | Debris; diaphragms |
| Cold water storage tanks | 20 to 40 years | Material; lining; access and cleaning |
| Isolation valves | 15 to 30 years | Rarely operated; seize |

What shortens life: aggressive water chemistry that pits copper, dezincifies brass and corrodes steel; high pressure without limiting valves, which stresses joints and fittings and causes water hammer; high velocity in undersized pipes, causing erosion at bends and fittings; stagnation in tanks and dead legs, which affects water quality; ground movement on buried services.

sections.heading: Corrosion, leaks and valves
sections.markdown:
Galvanised steel corrodes from the inside: the zinc is consumed, the steel rusts and builds tubercles that narrow the bore, flow falls, and water runs brown after periods of no use. Copper can pit in certain waters, producing pinhole leaks that recur along the same runs. Brass fittings in plastic systems can lose zinc (dezincification), becoming porous and weak, and leak or fail.

Leaks under slabs, in walls and in ceiling voids waste water, damage finishes and structure, and are found through rising consumption or damp. Polybutylene and failed fittings are common sources.

Valves never exercised seize, so a leak on one floor means shutting down the building. This turns small repairs into major outages.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Brown water after periods of no use | Corroding galvanised steel. Pipe material; internal inspection of a removed section. | Plan replacement of the galvanised pipework, riser by riser. |
| Repeated pinhole leaks in copper on the same runs | Pitting corrosion from water chemistry. Leak history; water analysis; pipe section examination. | Test the water chemistry, and replace the affected runs. |
| Leaks at brass fittings in a plastic system | Dezincification. Fitting examination; product type. | Replace with dezincification-resistant brass. |
| Night-time water use with the building empty | Hidden leak or running cisterns. Meter readings; leak detection. | Find and repair the leak, and add smart metering. |

sections.heading: Backflow and tanks
sections.markdown:
Where building water connects to a hazard (cooling towers, fire systems, irrigation, laboratories, chemical dosing, boilers), a drop in mains pressure can draw contaminated water back into the drinking supply. Backflow devices prevent it only if they work; devices that are not tested can fail open without any sign. Unprotected cross-connections created by alterations are a public health risk.

Cold water storage tanks with poor lids, missing insect screens and sediment build-up allow contamination; warm tanks in roof spaces and plant rooms grow Legionella. Tanks that are oversized for current use hold water too long.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Backflow device leaking from the relief port | Fouled or failed check valves. Device test. | Service or replace the device, and test it. |
| Testable backflow devices with no test record in the last year | Protection unverified. Device register and test reports against the water authority’s requirements. | Test every device, repair failures, and lodge the reports. |

sections.heading: Lead and pressure
sections.markdown:
Lead service pipes and lead solder in older plumbing release lead into water, especially after it has stood. In the United States, federal rules now require lead service lines to be identified and replaced; in Britain, water companies and owners share responsibility for lead pipes on either side of the boundary.

High mains pressure without limiting valves bursts flexible hoses, wears tap washers and valves, and causes water hammer: the banging when valves close fast, which loosens supports and fatigues joints. Low pressure at upper floors points to booster problems, undersized risers or corroded pipes.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Banging when taps close | Water hammer from high pressure or fast-closing valves. Pressure measurement against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Fit pressure-limiting valves and water hammer arrestors. |
| Weak flow at upper floors or remote outlets | Pressure below what fixtures need. Pressure logging at the outlets, against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). | Check valves, filters and boosters, and resize the supply if needed. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator or ordinance sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Failed backflow device on a high-hazard connection; unprotected cross-connection; lead above drinking water limits; Legionella in cold storage | safety · 4 Essential | Isolate or rectify now; notify the utility or health authority where required. |
| Burst main or major leak; no water to the building | failure · 3 Important | Repair now. |
| Backflow testing due; lead service line replacement under a programme | deadline · 4 Essential | At the prescribed interval or date. |
| Galvanised corrosion, recurring copper leaks, dezincification, seized valves, high pressure | condition · 3 Important | Repair in the near term. |
| Pipework at end of life | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Plan replacement, often riser by riser. |
| Pipe materials unknown; no backflow register | check · 3 Important | Survey. |
| Normal | nil · 1 Routine | Routine. |

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A hydraulic engineer or licensed plumber leads, with a water treatment specialist where corrosion or quality is in question. The checks below start with the backflow register and consumption data, then trace pipe materials and leaks through plant rooms and risers.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Materials survey | Of incoming services, risers, branches and fittings. |
| Backflow audit | Every hazard connection identified, with the device type checked against the hazard rating and tested. |
| Pressure and flow measurement | At the incoming main, at the top floors and at remote outlets, against the asset’s market (Thresholds by market). |
| Water quality testing | Lead and copper at outlets after standing; Legionella and bacterial counts in storage. |
| Pipe sampling | Remove sections of corroded or leaking pipe for examination. |
| Leak detection | Meter tests, acoustic and thermal methods for hidden leaks. |
| Tank inspection | Internal condition, lids, screens, temperatures. |
| Valve operation | Exercise isolation valves and record those that fail. |

The report should state pipe materials and condition, backflow compliance, pressure and flow adequacy, water quality, leaks and a replacement strategy.

sections.heading: Testing, repairing or replacing
sections.markdown:
Backflow protection comes first, since devices fail without visible signs and an untested device is unproven. After that, the work follows the pipe materials: replacement riser by riser, better fittings, pressure control, and lead removal where testing warrants it.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Backflow | Install or upgrade devices to suit each hazard, and set up annual testing. | Wherever devices are missing, untested or unsuited to the hazard. |
| Pressure control | Pressure-limiting valves and water hammer arrestors. | Where pressure is high or pipes bang. |
| Replacement | Replace galvanised, polybutylene and pitting copper pipework, riser by riser, with temporary supplies. | Where pipework corrodes, leaks repeatedly or reaches the end of its life. |
| Fitting replacement | Dezincification-resistant brass. | Where brass fittings leak in plastic systems. |
| Lead removal | Replace lead service pipes and remove lead solder where testing warrants. | Where testing warrants. |
| Tank works | Clean, reline, fit sealed lids and screens, or remove redundant tanks. | Where tanks are dirty, unsealed or redundant. |
| Valve replacement | Valves so floors and risers can be isolated individually. | Where the building cannot be isolated in sections. |
| Leak repairs | Repair leaks, and add smart metering to find future leaks quickly. | Wherever water is lost. |
| Water quality management | Flushing programmes for little-used outlets and dead legs, and removal of redundant branches so water does not stagnate. | Where outlets are little used or branches are redundant. |

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Backflow testing recurs annually per device; device replacement is per device. Pipe replacement is priced by length or per riser, with access, finishes and temporary supply as major components in occupied buildings. Valve replacement is per valve. Tank works are lump sums. Lead service line replacement is a lump sum and may be shared with the utility under its programme.

Backflow and water quality compliance are code compliance; pipework replacement is lifecycle; repairs are repairs and maintenance.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a look at the pipes cannot: whether backflow devices have been tested, where leaks recur, and whether lead is present. Ask for the backflow register first.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Backflow device register and test certificates | Whether every backflow device has been tested in the last year. |
| Water consumption data, ideally by sub-meter | Whether water is being lost, and when. |
| Leak and repair history | Where leaks recur, which points to the cause. |
| Water quality test results, including lead where relevant | Whether the water is safe, including for lead. |
| Tank cleaning and Legionella records | Whether tanks are clean and Legionella is managed. |
| Hydraulic drawings showing pipe materials and isolation | What the pipes are made of, and how sections can be isolated. |
| Utility notices about lead pipes or backflow | Whether the utility has required action. |
| Pressure readings at the incoming main and upper floors | Whether pressure is too high at the main or too low upstairs. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Water supply is misread when an untested backflow device is assumed to work, and when repeated leaks on the same run are repaired one at a time.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| The backflow device is fine | Backflow devices fail without visible signs. A device that has not been tested in the last year should be treated as unproven, and in some jurisdictions the water utility can disconnect the supply until it is tested. |
| Fix each leak as it comes | Repeated pinhole leaks in copper on the same runs point to pitting corrosion from the water chemistry; repairing them one by one misses the cause. Test the water, and replace the affected runs. |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market governs water services and backflow protection, and requires backflow devices to be tested and water quality, including lead, to be managed. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out each.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Water services, backflow and quality | AS/NZS 3500.1 governs water services and backflow prevention, with testing of devices under AS/NZS 2845.3 typically required annually by the water utility; plumbing work is licensed and certified in each state; pressure-limiting valves are required where mains pressure is high. | The Water Supply (Water Fittings) Regulations 1999 (and Scottish byelaws) govern fittings and backflow protection, with WRAS approval of products; the HSE Approved Code of Practice L8 covers Legionella control in cold water systems; water companies and owners have lead pipe replacement responsibilities on either side of the boundary. | The International and Uniform Plumbing Codes govern water supply; states and utilities run cross-connection control programmes with annual testing of backflow assemblies; the EPA's Lead and Copper Rule Improvements require water systems to replace lead service lines over the coming decade. |

sections.heading: Worked example: brown water and night-time use
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 1960s office has galvanised steel water pipework. Brown water comes from the taps after weekends, the meter shows steady water use overnight with the building empty, and the backflow device at the main has no test tag from the last two years.

Brown water after periods of no use points to corroding galvanised steel; night-time use with the building empty points to a hidden leak or running cisterns. The untested backflow device is unproven, and the utility may require a test.

So the register carries the backflow device as a deadline line, tested and serviced, leak finding with smart metering as a condition line, and replacement of the galvanised pipework riser by riser as a lifecycle line.

thresholds.rule: Working pressure at least 50 kPa at outlets; static pressure no more than 500 kPa within the building

pages.title: Waterproofing Membranes
pages.question: How do flat roof and deck membranes fail, how do you tell a detail failure from a failed roof, and when must a roof be stripped rather than patched?
pages.answer: Membranes fail at details first: upstands, terminations, outlets and penetrations, then seams. Leaks in a line point to seams; one leak under a penetration is a detail repair; leaks that move around and continue after rain mean wet insulation, which keeps leaking after every patch and rules out recovering. EPDM shrinks and tears at upstands; old PVC turns brittle. Establish whether the insulation is wet before choosing repair, recover or replace.
pages.limitations: General technical guidance about waterproofing membranes; it describes how these elements behave, not the condition of any particular building, and it carries no prices.

pages.searchTitle: Flat roof membranes: leaks, wet insulation, ponding and when to repair or replace

questions.question: Why does my flat roof keep leaking after repairs?
questions.answer: Often because the insulation beneath is wet. A dry membrane over wet insulation will keep leaking after every repair; establish whether the insulation is wet before patching, recovering or coating.

questions.question: Why does the leak appear far from where the water gets in?
questions.answer: Water runs along the deck before it drips, travels in wet insulation, and on ballasted or paved roofs travels on top of the membrane under the overburden.

questions.question: Can a new membrane go over the old one?
questions.answer: Only where the insulation is proven dry by survey, the deck is sound, falls are adequate and the code allows the extra layer. Otherwise it seals in whatever is beneath.

questions.question: Are blisters in a flat roof membrane serious?
questions.answer: Dry blisters over the field are not structural on their own; they come from trapped moisture or poor adhesion. Monitor them, and repair any that split.

questions.question: How long does a flat roof membrane last?
questions.answer: Built-up roofing, TPO and PVC 15 to 25 years, EPDM 20 to 30, protected modified bitumen 20 to 30, and liquid-applied coatings 8 to 20.

questions.question: Why does the flat roof stay wet for days after rain?
questions.answer: Ponding from inadequate falls, blocked outlets or a deflected deck. Clear the outlets, survey the levels, and correct the falls or add outlets.

questions.question: Why does the flat roof feel spongy when you walk on it?
questions.answer: Wet insulation under the membrane. Core and moisture-survey the roof, and remove the wet insulation before any repair.

questions.question: Why did the roof start leaking after new plant or cables were installed?
questions.answer: A later penetration sealed with mastic and no proper flashing. Replace the mastic seal with a proper flashing.

questions.question: Why is the roof leaking in a straight line?
questions.answer: A seam has failed. Probe every seam on the roof, and reweld or re-tape the open laps.

questions.question: Why is the membrane tearing where the roof meets the wall?
questions.answer: The membrane has shrunk and pulled tight at the upstands. Renew the upstand details, allowing for the shrinkage.

sections.heading: What you'll notice
sections.markdown:
Membrane problems show inside as drips and stains, from above as ponding and patches, on the roof as open seams and soft areas underfoot, and below the roof as staining on soffits. Start with what you see or what the records hold, then follow it to the part of the page that explains it.

| Where | What you see | Read next |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Inside | A drip under one penetration, outlet or upstand that appears with each heavy rain: a detail failure | Details, seams and penetrations |
| Inside | Leaks that move from place to place, or keep dripping for days after the rain stops: water travelling in wet insulation | Wet insulation, inverted and green roofs |
| Inside | Stains in a line across a ceiling or soffit: an open seam above | Details, seams and penetrations |
| Inside | Water at the head of the walls below a parapet: the upstand, termination or coping, not the field of the roof | Details, seams and penetrations |
| Inside | Drips from a cold roof on clear mornings without rain: condensation in the roof build-up, not a leak | Wet insulation, inverted and green roofs |
| From aerial imagery | Ponding marks and dark rings where water has stood; vegetation in ballast and at outlets | Ponding and wind |
| From aerial imagery | Patches in different materials; areas of new membrane; coatings over old membranes | Ageing, blisters, coatings and movement |
| From aerial imagery | Plant added since the roof was laid, with its supports through the membrane | Details, seams and penetrations |
| From aerial imagery | Lifted or billowing single-ply at corners and perimeters after wind | Ponding and wind |
| On the roof | Open seams and laps; blisters; splits over deck joints and board edges | Ageing, blisters, coatings and movement |
| On the roof | Upstands lower than the water line; terminations pulled out; sealant at terminations failed | Details, seams and penetrations |
| On the roof | Outlets corroded, blocked, detached or set above the membrane level | Ponding and wind |
| On the roof | Soft or spongy areas underfoot: wet insulation beneath | Wet insulation, inverted and green roofs |
| On the roof | EPDM bridging at upstands; brittle PVC that cracks when folded | Ageing, blisters, coatings and movement |
| On the roof | Wrinkles and ridges in the membrane over moving insulation boards | Ageing, blisters, coatings and movement |
| Below the roof | Staining, blistering paint and efflorescence on soffits; drips at deck joints | Details, seams and penetrations |
| Below the roof | Corrosion of steel deck and fixings visible from below | Wet insulation, inverted and green roofs |
| Below the roof | Leaks that continue for days after rain stops: water held in insulation | Wet insulation, inverted and green roofs |
| Below the roof | In car parks under podiums, staining and corrosion in lines along joints | Details, seams and penetrations |
| In the records | Membrane specification, installer and warranty, with date | Investigation before the scope |
| In the records | Leak register and repair history; repeated repairs in different places | Details, seams and penetrations |
| In the records | Roof surveys, core reports and moisture surveys | Wet insulation, inverted and green roofs |

sections.heading: Types of membrane
sections.markdown:
Waterproofing membranes are the continuous waterproof layers on flat and low-slope roofs, podiums, plant decks, terraces, planters and balconies. They sit on a structural deck, usually with insulation above or below, and are often hidden under ballast, paving on pedestals, soil or tiles. The membrane turns up at parapets and walls, terminates under flashings, and is penetrated by outlets, plant supports and balustrade posts.

| Type | Typical use and era | Character |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Built-up roofing (BUR): bitumen and felt in layers | Commercial flat roofs, 1950s to 1990s | Thick, robust; surface ages and crazes; blisters between plies |
| Modified bitumen sheet (SBS, APP), torch-on or self-adhered | Commercial and residential roofs from the 1980s | Durable; laps are the weak line; heat at installation |
| Mastic asphalt | British flat roofs and decks, long history | Very durable when protected; cracks with movement |
| Single-ply TPO | Commercial roofs from the 2000s | Heat-welded seams; reflective; product generations vary |
| Single-ply PVC | Commercial roofs from the 1980s | Welded seams; plasticiser loss causes shrinkage and embrittlement in older products; incompatible with bitumen and some foams |
| EPDM rubber | Commercial roofs from the 1980s | Taped or glued seams; shrinks with age, pulling at perimeters |
| Liquid-applied (polyurethane, acrylic, PMMA, polyurea) | Balconies, wet areas, roof restoration | Seamless; life set entirely by film thickness and preparation |
| Cementitious and crystalline | Planters, basements, water tanks | Rigid; cracks with movement |

How insulation is arranged decides how failure plays out. In a warm roof the insulation is above the deck and under the membrane; a leak saturates the insulation, which then holds water across a wide area. In an inverted roof the insulation is above the membrane, protecting it, and is held down by ballast. In a cold roof the insulation is below the deck, and condensation in the deck or void becomes the risk.

Falls matter as much as the membrane. A flat roof is never truly flat: each market sets a minimum finished fall so that water reaches the outlets (Thresholds by market). Roofs laid dead flat, or that have deflected since, pond; ponding shortens the life of almost every membrane and loads the structure ([Roof Structure](https://moyneross.com/technical/roof-structure)).

A membrane is also only as good as what it meets: the outlets and overflows that drain it ([Rainwater Systems](https://moyneross.com/technical/rainwater-systems)), the upstands and copings at parapets ([Plant Screens & Parapets](https://moyneross.com/technical/plant-screens-and-parapets)), the insulation above or below it ([Insulation](https://moyneross.com/technical/insulation)), and every pipe, duct and plant support that passes through it.

sections.heading: How long it lasts
sections.markdown:
Membranes last fifteen to thirty years depending on type and protection, and liquid coatings less, but a membrane's life is decided at its details: upstands, outlets and penetrations fail long before the field wears out.

| Membrane | Typical life | What moves it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Built-up roofing | 15 to 25 years | Surfacing and maintenance; ponding |
| Modified bitumen, protected | 20 to 30 years | Ballast or paving above it |
| Modified bitumen, exposed | 15 to 20 years | UV; foot traffic |
| Mastic asphalt, protected | 30 years and more | Movement; solar protection |
| TPO | 15 to 25 years | Product generation; seam quality |
| PVC | 15 to 25 years | Plasticiser loss; compatibility |
| EPDM | 20 to 30 years | Seam method; shrinkage |
| Liquid-applied coatings | 8 to 20 years | Film thickness; preparation; product |
| Inverted roof membranes (insulation and ballast above) | 30 years and more | Protected from UV and thermal shock; life set by details and drainage |
| Green roof and planter membranes | Life of the planting build-up, if root resistant | Root barrier; drainage layer; access for repair |

Where a membrane sits in the build-up matters as much as what it is made of. An exposed membrane takes the full daily swing of temperature and the sun's ultraviolet; one buried under insulation, ballast or paving is protected from both and can last twice as long, but is far harder to inspect and repair. A product's life on a specification sheet assumes it is installed and protected as designed.

Life is uneven across a roof. The areas around plant, along walkway routes, at low points that pond and at the upstands facing the weather age first, and many membranes are replaced because their details have failed while the field is still serviceable.

What shortens life: ponding from flat or reversed falls, deflecting decks and blocked outlets; foot traffic and plant on unprotected membranes; plant installed later through the membrane without proper penetration details; uV exposure on membranes intended to be protected; movement at upstands, deck joints and changes of material; roots in planters and green roofs without a root barrier; incompatible materials: PVC in contact with bitumen or polystyrene; solvents on EPDM.

What lengthens it: clear outlets and working overflows, checked after every major storm and at least twice a year; walkways and raised plant supports, so nothing sits directly on the membrane and no one walks on it unprotected; protection and ballast kept in place on inverted and protected roofs; displaced ballast exposes the membrane to sunlight and wind; a permit system for roof work, so trades who penetrate the membrane are known and the penetration is sealed by the roofer; early repair of details: upstands, terminations and penetration seals renewed before water reaches the insulation.

sections.heading: Details, seams and penetrations
sections.markdown:
Membranes rarely fail first in the open field. They fail at upstands where the membrane turns up a wall and is terminated, at outlets, at penetrations, at thresholds and at changes of level. Terminations pull out of their chases or bars; upstands are too low, so water ponding against them rises over the top; outlets corrode, detach from the membrane or sit above the membrane surface so water never reaches them; and door thresholds onto roofs and podiums are built flush with the membrane, leaving nothing to stop wind-driven water entering.

Single-ply seams that were under-welded, over-welded or contaminated with dirt or moisture open over time, first where the membrane is most stressed by wind and movement. EPDM tape and adhesive seams debond with age and heat. Bitumen laps lift where the torching was cold or the surface dirty. Seam failures run in lines across the roof, following the roll widths, and on mechanically fastened roofs they often coincide with the fastener rows.

Most membranes are breached after they are laid: plant supports bolted through, cables and pipes for new equipment, antenna and solar mounts, each sealed with mastic rather than a proper flashing. Plant vibration and thermal movement then work those seals loose. A roof with a clean original installation and a leak history usually has a story of later trades.

Membranes are walked on by trades servicing plant, cleaning gutters and installing equipment, and are punctured by dropped tools, screws and sharp debris. Damage concentrates on the routes people take and around plant, which is why a membrane can be sound across most of a roof and failing along a path to the air-conditioning units.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Single leak under a penetration or upstand | Detail failure. Water test or electronic leak detection at the detail. | Water test or use electronic leak detection at the detail, then renew it. |
| Leaks in a line across the roof | Seam failure. Probing seams finds open laps along the line. | Probe every seam on the roof, and reweld or re-tape the open laps. |
| Leak under newer plant or a cable penetration | Later penetration sealed with mastic. Penetration post-dates the membrane; no proper flashing. | Replace the mastic seal with a proper flashing. |
| Leak at a wall head below a parapet | Upstand too low, termination failed, or coping and wall above leaking. Water test above the termination first, then the upstand. | Test from the top down: the coping and wall first, then the upstand. |
| Punctures and patches along the route to plant | Foot traffic and dropped tools. Damage concentrated on the access path; no walkway. | Repair the punctures, and lay walkways to the plant. |

sections.heading: Wet insulation, inverted and green roofs
sections.markdown:
In warm roofs, water entering through any defect spreads through the insulation below the membrane. Wet insulation loses its thermal value, adds load, rots timber decks, corrodes steel decks and fixings, and keeps feeding leaks long after the original defect is repaired. It is the most expensive hidden failure on a flat roof, because the roof cannot simply be re-covered.

Where the membrane is buried under insulation, ballast, pavers or planting, its condition cannot be seen, and leaks travel along it before appearing below. Insulation boards can float and shift in heavy rain if not restrained; ballast is scoured by wind at corners and edges; paving on pedestals traps debris that blocks drainage. Any repair means lifting everything above the membrane first.

Roots find their way into any weakness, which is why planted roofs need a root-resistant membrane or barrier. Drainage layers clog with fines over time, leaving the membrane under saturated soil, and the load of wet soil was often underestimated on retrofit installations.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Leaks moving around, continuing after rain | Wet insulation spreading water. Cores show saturated insulation; thermography shows wet areas. | Core and moisture-survey the roof; widespread wet insulation means strip and replace. |
| Spongy areas underfoot | Wet insulation. Cores and moisture survey. | Core and survey; remove the wet insulation before any repair. |
| Leaks on a ballasted or paved roof appearing far from any visible defect | Water travelling beneath the build-up. Electronic leak detection locates the breach. | Use electronic leak detection to locate the breach under the build-up. |
| Drips from the soffit of a cold roof on clear mornings | Condensation within the build-up. Vapour control and ventilation absent; timing follows temperature, not rain. | Add vapour control and ventilation; see Insulation. |
| Wet soil and leaks below a planter | Root ingress or blocked drainage layer. Roots through the membrane; drainage layer clogged. | Clear the drainage layer, and repair the membrane with a root barrier. |

sections.heading: Ageing, blisters, coatings and movement
sections.markdown:
Bitumen surfaces craze (alligatoring), lose their mineral surfacing and harden. PVC loses plasticiser, shrinks and becomes brittle. EPDM shrinks and pulls at its perimeter, bridging across the angle at upstands until it tears.

Moisture or air trapped between layers or under the membrane expands in heat and forms blisters, which crack when walked on. Splits form over deck joints, at insulation board edges and where the membrane is stressed by thermal shock or movement.

Liquid membranes fail where they were applied too thin, over damp or dusty substrates, or across cracks that move. They crack, peel and blister, often over the whole area, and the cause is usually the original application.

Exposed membranes on dark roofs reach high surface temperatures in sun and drop sharply when a storm passes or the sun sets. The repeated expansion and contraction concentrates at joints in the deck, the edges of insulation boards and changes of material, where splits open. Movement joints in the building beneath a roof need matching joints in the membrane; where they are missing, the membrane tears along the line of the structural joint.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Membrane pulled tight at upstands, tearing at the angle | EPDM shrinkage. Membrane bridges the angle; field is slack-free. | Renew the upstand details, allowing for the shrinkage. |
| Membrane cracks when folded; shrinkage at laps | PVC plasticiser loss. Age and product; cracking at stress points. | Plan replacement; the membrane is at the end of its life. |
| Blisters over the field | Trapped moisture or poor adhesion. Blisters cut show moisture; not structural on their own. | Leave dry blisters alone and monitor them; repair any that split. |
| Liquid coating peeling over large areas | Application thickness or substrate. Film thickness readings; substrate condition. | Check film thickness and the substrate; strip and reapply where the coating has failed. |
| Split running in a straight line across the roof | Unaccommodated movement over a deck or structural joint. Split follows a joint below; no movement joint in the membrane. | Form a movement joint in the membrane over the joint below. |

sections.heading: Ponding and wind
sections.markdown:
Water standing for more than a couple of days after rain accelerates ageing, deposits dirt that holds more water, and on light decks adds load that deflects the deck, which holds more water. Ponding is a symptom of inadequate falls, blocked outlets or a deflecting structure, and treating it as a membrane problem misses the cause.

Mechanically fastened single-ply membranes rely on fasteners into the deck. Corroded or under-specified fasteners, and corners and perimeters with too few, let the membrane billow and tear in wind.

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Ponding lasting days, staining in rings | Inadequate falls, blocked outlets or deck deflection. Level survey; outlet condition; deck deflection measured. | Clear the outlets, survey the levels, and correct the falls or add outlets. |

sections.heading: Older membranes and asbestos
sections.markdown:
Bitumen felts, mastics and some coatings applied before the 1990s can contain asbestos, as can older flashings and outlet surrounds. They are safe in place but must be identified before cutting, coring or stripping ([Hazardous Materials](https://moyneross.com/technical/hazardous-materials)).

| What you see | Likely cause, and what confirms it | Next step |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Old bitumen felt, mastic or roof coating on a building of the 1950s to 1980s | Possible asbestos in the membrane, mastic or coating. Asbestos register; sampling by a competent person before cutting or stripping. | Sample first; overlay where suitable, or remove under asbestos controls. |
| Grey fibrous sheet or board beneath an old membrane | Possible asbestos substrate. Inspection and sampling at an opening. | Avoid drilling or cutting until sampled; plan removal or encapsulation with the re-roof. |

sections.heading: How serious it is
sections.markdown:
Findings are graded by what they demand: safety (can hurt someone now), failure (failed and damaging the building), condition (distress present and progressing), lifecycle (renewal due on age and exposure), deadline (a regulator, ordinance or order sets the date), check (investigate before sizing works) and nil (cosmetic or stable).

| Finding | How serious | What it means for timing |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Membrane torn or lifted by wind; ballast displaced at corners and edges over public areas | safety · 4 Essential | Secure now. |
| Ponding on a light deck with visible deflection; outlets blocked with water rising | safety · 4 Essential | Clear and relieve now. |
| Active leaks damaging structure, services or occupied space | failure · 3 Important | Repair now; establish whether the insulation is wet. |
| Wet insulation over a wide area beneath a warm roof | failure · 3 Important | Plan strip and replace; repairs alone will not stop the leaks. |
| Seams opening, details failing, membrane brittle at upstands | condition · 3 Important | Programme detail repairs or recover in the near term. |
| Membrane splits over structural or deck joints | condition · 3 Important | Install movement joints and repair in the near term. |
| Later penetrations sealed with mastic only | condition · 3 Important | Flash properly at the next roof works. |
| Membrane at the end of its expected life, no leaks | lifecycle · 2 Planned | Plan replacement with the insulation, falls and drainage. |
| Planted or paved roof with leaks and no access to the membrane | check · 3 Important | Locate the breach (electronic leak detection) before lifting the build-up. |
| Leak history on a warm roof with no moisture survey | check · 3 Important | Survey before choosing repair, recover or replace. |
| Pre-1990s bitumen felts and mastics of unknown status | check · 3 Important | Sample before cutting, coring or stripping. |
| Minor surface ageing, isolated dry blisters | nil · 1 Routine | Routine maintenance. |

On warm roofs the grading turns on the insulation. A membrane defect over dry insulation is a repair; the same defect over saturated insulation is a failure that only stripping will cure, whatever the membrane surface looks like.

The grading follows what a finding demands, not the size of the eventual bill.

sections.heading: Investigation before the scope
sections.markdown:
A roofing consultant or building surveyor leads, with a specialist leak detection contractor where needed. The checks below locate the leak in relation to the roof above, then establish whether the insulation beneath is wet.

| Check | What it covers |
| --- | --- |
| Visual survey | Of the field, seams, upstands, terminations, outlets and penetrations, with a plan of defects. |
| Core cuts | To identify the build-up, membrane type and layers, and insulation condition; cores sealed after. |
| Moisture survey | By infrared thermography at night, capacitance or impedance meters on a grid, or nuclear moisture gauges. |
| Electronic leak detection | (low-voltage or high-voltage methods) to locate breaches, including under ballast or overburden; ASTM D7877 guides the methods. |
| Flood testing | Of balconies and small decks, checking deck capacity first. |
| Seam probing | On single-ply roofs. |
| Fastener pull-out tests | On mechanically fastened roofs. |
| Hazardous material sampling | Of older bitumen felts, mastics and flashings before cores are cut or the roof is stripped. |
| Deck inspection from below | Where it can be reached: corrosion of steel decks and fixings, decay in timber decks, and deflection under ponding. |
| Drone and level survey | Of falls, ponding and the layout of outlets, overflows, plant and penetrations. |

The report should state the build-up, membrane type and age, defects and their locations, the extent of wet insulation, and whether the roof can be repaired, recovered or must be stripped.

sections.heading: Repairing, recovering or replacing
sections.markdown:
The choice turns on what lies beneath the membrane. Details and seams can be repaired on a roof whose insulation is dry; a sound but ageing membrane can be recovered or coated; and wet insulation over a wide area leaves only strip and replace.

| Option | What it involves | When it is right |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Detail repairs | Renew upstands, terminations, outlets and penetration flashings, raise low upstands where possible, and replace mastic-only seals with proper flashings. | Often the best value on a roof whose field and insulation are sound. |
| Seam repair | Reweld or re-tape seams, or overlay with cover strips. | After probing the whole roof to find every open lap, not only the one that leaked. |
| Recover | A new membrane over the old. | Only where the insulation is proven dry by survey, the deck is sound, falls are adequate and the code allows the extra layer; faster and cheaper than stripping, but it seals in whatever is beneath. |
| Restoration coatings | Coatings over sound, ageing membranes, extending their life by years. | With a dry substrate, compatible chemistry and correct film thickness; they do nothing for wet insulation or failed details. |
| Strip and replace | Remove membrane and wet insulation to the deck, repair the deck, correct falls with tapered insulation, and install new membrane, upstands, outlets and overflows. | The only cure for widespread wet insulation. |
| Drainage | Add outlets and overflows, correct falls, lower outlets set too high, and clear and maintain them. | Wherever water ponds for days or outlets block. |
| Protection | Walkways to plant, raised plant supports on proper bases, protection boards under pavers and ballast, and a permit system for roof work. | Wherever people and plant cross the membrane. |
| Movement joints | Joints in the membrane over structural joints and at changes of deck. | Where splits follow joints below. |

Choosing between them turns on the insulation. A dry build-up can be repaired or recovered; a wet one must come off, whatever the membrane looks like. Recovering over a wet roof seals the water in, and codes limit how many times a roof may be recovered before it must be stripped to the deck.

Interactions: replacing a membrane usually means lifting and reinstating whatever sits on it (ballast, pavers, planting, plant), which can cost more than the membrane itself. Insulation upgrades may be required by the works ([Insulation](https://moyneross.com/technical/insulation)), roof safety systems and plant supports are renewed with it ([Roof Safety Systems](https://moyneross.com/technical/roof-safety-systems)), and the outlets and overflows should be checked against the roof's catchment ([Rainwater Systems](https://moyneross.com/technical/rainwater-systems)).

sections.heading: Cost shape
sections.markdown:
Moisture surveys and cores are lump sums. Detail repairs are itemised per outlet, penetration or linear metre of upstand. Replacement is priced by area with separate lines for strip-out, wet insulation removal, deck repair, new insulation and falls, upstands and outlets, and reinstatement of ballast, pavers, planters and plant. Reinstatement is often the largest component on terraces and podiums.

What drives the cost beyond area: what sits on the membrane (ballast, pavers, planting, plant) and must be lifted and reinstated, the extent of wet insulation, deck repairs, new falls, the number of upstands and penetrations, access and crane lifts, and work over occupied space. Commonly missed: temporary relocation of plant, roof safety systems, outlets and overflows, and hazardous material removal in older roofs.

The usual shape where leaks exist and insulation status is unknown is two-part: moisture survey, then a conditional envelope that is a detail repair if the insulation is dry and a strip-and-replace if it is wet. Replacement is lifecycle; detail repairs and outlet clearing are repairs and maintenance.

sections.heading: What to ask the owner or agent for
sections.markdown:
The records settle what a walk across the roof cannot: what the membrane is and how old, where it has leaked, and whether the insulation beneath has been tested. Ask for them before any patching, recovering or coating.

| Record | What it settles |
| --- | --- |
| Membrane specification, manufacturer, installer and warranty, with installation date and whether the warranty is transferable | What the membrane is, how old, and whether a warranty still applies. |
| Leak register, repair history, and any leak investigation, moisture survey, core results or electronic leak detection reports | Where it has leaked, and whether the insulation has been found wet. |
| Roof drawings showing falls, outlets, overflows, movement joints and the build-up | How the roof is meant to drain and move. |
| Records of plant, cables, solar and other penetrations added since installation, and who sealed them | Which penetrations came later, and who sealed them. |
| Outlet cleaning and roof maintenance schedule, and the roof access permit system | Whether outlets are kept clear and work on the roof is controlled. |
| Defect claims and expert reports, especially inside statutory defect or warranty periods | Whether defects are already in dispute, and within which periods. |
| Hazardous materials register entries for older felts, mastics and flashings | Whether older felts, mastics and flashings contain asbestos. |
| For planted and paved roofs, the build-up design, root barrier details and access arrangements for the membrane | How a buried membrane can be reached and protected. |

sections.heading: Common misreads
sections.markdown:
Membrane leaks are misread when the leak is assumed to sit directly above the drip, or when the membrane is patched without asking what lies beneath it.

| What is assumed | What is closer to right |
| --- | --- |
| The leak is directly above the drip | Begin with where the leak is in relation to the roof above. Directly beneath a detail, the detail is the suspect. Beneath open field, look for a seam or a puncture up-slope, since water runs along the deck before it drips. Far from anything, especially on warm roofs, assume water is travelling in wet insulation, and on ballasted or paved roofs, assume it is travelling on top of the membrane under the overburden. |
| A patch will stop it | A dry membrane over wet insulation will keep leaking after every repair. Before patching, recovering or coating a warm flat roof with a leak history, establish whether the insulation is wet. |
| Water at the wall head is the membrane | Water at the top of a wall below a roof is often blamed on the membrane when it comes from the coping, the wall above or a window head and runs down behind the upstand. Test from the top down ([Sealants & Joints](https://moyneross.com/technical/sealants-and-joints)). |

sections.heading: Standards by country
sections.markdown:
Each market sets standards for membranes and their falls, drainage and fire performance, and has its own rules on defects. For Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, the table sets out the membrane standards, drainage, fire and wind, and upgrades and defects.

|  | Australia | United Kingdom | United States |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Membrane standards | The National Construction Code calls up AS 4654.1 and AS 4654.2 for external above-ground membranes; AS 4654.2 sets design and installation requirements including minimum falls, upstand heights and termination details, and AS 3740 covers internal wet areas. | BS 6229 sets the code of practice for flat roofs with continuously supported coverings, calling for a finished fall of at least 1 in 80, usually achieved by designing to 1 in 40; BS 8217 covers reinforced bitumen membranes and BS 8218 mastic asphalt; industry guidance from the National Federation of Roofing Contractors and the Liquid Roofing and Waterproofing Association supplements the standards. | International Building Code Chapter 15 governs roof assemblies, minimum slopes and re-covering over existing roofs; single-ply membranes follow ASTM D6878 (TPO), D4434 (PVC) and D4637 (EPDM), and ASTM D7877 guides electronic leak detection. |
| Drainage, fire and wind | Roof drainage follows AS/NZS 3500.3. | Roof coverings must meet external fire performance requirements (typically a BROOF(t4) classification), which affects green roofs, solar arrays and some liquid systems; Approved Document B and regulation 7(2) bear on roof build-ups on relevant buildings. | Edge securement must be tested to ANSI/SPRI/FM 4435/ES-1, and insurers commonly require FM-approved assemblies for wind uplift and fire; roof coverings carry a fire classification (Class A, B or C under ASTM E108 or UL 790), required according to construction type and location. |
| Upgrades and defects | On strata buildings, roof, podium and balcony membranes are usually common property and a leading head of defect claims; New South Wales and Victoria have statutory defect and warranty periods for waterproofing. | Approved Document L applies thermal upgrades on renovation. | State law sets the periods for construction defect claims, which vary from state to state. |

sections.heading: Worked example: a flat roof that keeps leaking after repairs
sections.markdown:
An illustrative example of the reasoning, not an inspected building. A 1980s office has a warm flat roof with a modified bitumen membrane. Leaks have been patched three times in two years, each in a different place, and the latest keeps dripping for days after the rain stops. Plant was added on the roof later, with its supports sealed through the membrane in mastic.

Leaks that move around and continue for days after rain point to water travelling in wet insulation, which is why the patches have not held: a dry membrane over wet insulation keeps leaking after every repair. Cores and a moisture survey come before anything else. The mastic seals at the plant supports are a separate condition finding.

So the register carries a moisture survey as a check line now. If the insulation is wet over a wide area, strip and replace is the only cure, as a failure line; if it is dry, the plant penetrations get proper flashings and the seams are probed across the whole roof. A recover or a coating waits until the survey is in.

thresholds.rule: 1 in 100 (10 mm per metre)

source.title: AS 4654.2-2012 Waterproofing membranes for external above-ground use, Part 2: Design and installation

thresholds.rule: 1 in 80 (12.5 mm per metre)

source.title: BS 6229:2025 Flat roofs with continuously supported flexible waterproof coverings

thresholds.rule: About a quarter inch per foot (about 21 mm per metre, roughly 1 in 50)

source.title: 2024 International Building Code

Thesis · 12 min read Read → Part IV · 05 The Cap Rate Doesn’t See the Roof Income-based valuation is built to price rent, not concrete. Capital requirements enter as broad allowances, if at all, which leaves a gap between what a building is worth on paper and what it will cost to own. Thesis · 4 min read Read → Part V · 01 Reading a Building as Capital A building can be read as architecture, as a set of defects, or as income. Reading it as capital means asking what each part will ask of its owner, when, and how sure we are. Each paper answers one question, so start wherever yours is. Read the seven parts → A building. An ambition. A conversation. Send us a building. We’ll read it. docs.title: How we use AI
docs.kind: The practice
docs.blurb: How AI fits inside the Moyne Ross system, and where it stops.
docs.text: AI one part of system model does not do arithmetic maths MR Index final decision professional judgement quality checks AI and the practice | Moyne Ross Moyne Ross Approach Insights About Portal Start your strategy Moyne Ross / AI Judgement, given room How AI changes building and capital advice, where it stops, and who stands behind the result. “The slow part of building advice was never the judgement. It was everything around it.” Moyne Ross The argument Most of a surveyor’s time has gone into producing the report: finding records, reading them, measuring, pricing, assembling. The judgement clients actually rely on was fitted into whatever time was left. AI changes that balance. It can take on the reading, the cross-checking and the first draft, at a scale no person can match, so professional time moves to where it matters: the building, the evidence that is missing, and the decision in front of you. That is why Moyne Ross was built. 01 Reading at scale A building leaves traces everywhere: planning records, permits, imagery, listings, maintenance logs, past reports. Few assessments read them all, and fewer read them against each other. The MR engine searches, reads and compares that evidence together, alongside any documents you share. Where sources agree, confidence rises. Where they conflict, the conflict is recorded rather than smoothed over. Every finding is held as documented, observed or inferred , so you can see what kind of claim it is. More evidence, read more carefully, before anyone forms a view. 02 How the engine works The engine was built around the real work of assessing a building, and it keeps each part of that work in its proper hands. Evidence Research and your documents establish the asset, its history and known works. Gaps stay visible. Assessment One framework across structure, services and space: condition, action, cost basis, timing and confidence. Calculation Costs, horizons and the MR Index are calculated by code from structured inputs, not written by the model. Checks More than forty automated checks look for gaps, contradictions and claims the evidence cannot support. Review A chartered surveyor reviews the assessment before it is issued as advice. The model proposes. The platform calculates. The surveyor decides. Each step leaves its working on the page, so it can be questioned afterwards. See what that looks like inside the Capital Register . 03 Every number shows its working A capital figure is only as good as what sits behind it. In a Moyne Ross strategy, every priced line carries its cost basis: the scope assumed, the quantities, what is included and excluded, the date, and how firm the footing is. Where a figure is a planning allowance rather than a quote, it says so. Where the evidence stops short, the register prices the inspection and goes no further. Confident language is not allowed to outrun the evidence, and the checks are built to catch it when it tries. Honest uncertainty is more useful than false precision. 04 What it changes for you Your building’s strategy, usually within a working day, from its address alone, looked over before release. Because the production is faster, the conversation can start earlier and go further. A different holding period, a refurbishment, a change of use: alternatives can be explored together within the agreed brief, with the register as the shared reference. And the record stays live. New evidence, a quotation or a change of plan can be brought in and the strategy updated, rather than the work going stale in a document. You also work with fewer layers. The person who built the engine is the person who reviews your building and talks it through with you. 05 Where the line is AI does not inspect your building. It does not certify compliance, perform the final arithmetic, calculate the MR Index or take responsibility for the instruction. A Capital Strategy issued as professional advice is reviewed and approved by the responsible chartered surveyor for its agreed purpose. A desktop assessment and an inspection-supported assessment rest on different evidence, and the strategy says which it is. The engine extends judgement. It never replaces it. 06 Accountable, by design RICS’s Responsible use of artificial intelligence in surveying practice standard took effect on 9 March 2026. It informs how Moyne Ross works: appropriate use, data and provider assessment, professional judgement, clear communication with clients, and accountability. Moyne Ross is not currently an RICS-regulated firm, and this page does not claim RICS approval or certification of the engine. For any instruction, you can ask how material AI outputs were assessed, which assumptions affect their reliability, and whether further verification is needed. The extent of professional indemnity cover, including for AI-assisted work, is addressed before an instruction is accepted; this page does not itself confirm cover. The detail Systems, data and your choices The practical arrangements behind the approach above. Open any section. The systems we use We use large language models to assist with research and analysis. They are general-purpose systems; Moyne Ross supplies the building methodology, evidence rules and output structure. The platform supports different providers, including Anthropic (Claude), Google (Gemini) and OpenAI, depending on the feature and selected configuration. The provider used for a confidential instruction forms part of the processing arrangements explained to the client. A new provider is not authorised to receive private material merely because the platform can connect to it. Relevant changes are disclosed before the affected processing, with permission obtained where required. Data retention and model-training terms differ by provider, product and account settings. We do not promise that information is retained only while a response is generated. Our Privacy & Cookie Policy explains this distinction and how to ask about the arrangements for your instruction. Issued strategies and working outputs An issued Capital Strategy records the professional advice for the agreed instruction. Where the portal offers interactive AI tools, such as chat or a generated working report, their status is different: those responses and reports may not have been individually reviewed or adopted as advice. If a working output suggests a material new conclusion, ask us to review it and, where appropriate, incorporate it into the advice or a revised strategy. Generating a report does not by itself make its contents a newly issued professional opinion. The scope, permitted reliance and any further work are governed by your client agreement and instruction. How we manage uncertainty AI can produce convincing but incorrect statements, miss relevant evidence or give undue weight to a weak source. An apparently precise cost is still only as reliable as its scope, quantity, rate and assumptions. Our approach combines: Evidence distinctions: separating documented information, observations and inference, with gaps and uncertainty kept visible. Structured assessment: consistent coverage of building fabric, services and the spaces they support, within the agreed scope. Separate calculations: code-based cost roll-ups and MR Index scoring from the structured assessment. Automated checks: checks for structural, arithmetic and completeness problems, alongside advisory signals that inform review. Professional judgement: consideration of the material findings, their limitations and their suitability for the client’s decision. Further investigation: identifying questions that require better records, site evidence or the appropriate specialist. These measures reduce risk; they do not eliminate uncertainty or guarantee that every issue is identified. The speed of generation does not determine whether an assessment is suitable to rely on. How we handle your data AI services may receive relevant asset documents, images, questions and assessment context, and may process them outside Australia. Private and confidential material requires an appropriate processing basis and express written permission before submission. We seek to minimise unnecessary personal information and address restrictions on third-party material before it is used. The permissions for delivering an instruction are distinct from permission to publish a client case study or use identifiable material for model development. See our Privacy & Cookie Policy for providers, overseas processing, retention, research use and your choices. Your questions and choices You can ask which AI systems are involved, why they are used, what their relevant limitations are and how they affect your work. We will provide an appropriate written explanation, including relevant reliability reasoning and safeguards, while respecting security, confidentiality and third-party rights. You can also contest a proposed use of AI, request correction or raise a complaint through our contact form . We aim to acknowledge concerns within five business days and give a substantive response within twenty business days, or explain when a response will follow. The complaints process in our Terms sets out the next steps. AI is integral to an engine-generated Capital Strategy. A wholly AI-free version of that product is not offered. If you have restrictions on a provider or particular information, raise them before sharing the material so we can consider whether a different evidence basis or scope can meet your needs. Updated 24 October 2026. Moyne Ross / AI Better evidence. More time for judgement. One person accountable. Start with an address. We’ll read the building before anything else is agreed. docs.title: The MR Index
docs.kind: Methodology
docs.blurb: The decision layer: how much attention a building needs, and how soon, from MR 1 to MR 5.
docs.text: MR Index score band MR 1 MR 2 MR 3 MR 4 MR 5 rating condition elements attention how serious how soon no costs capital position The MR Index | Methodology Reference | Moyne Ross Moyne Ross Approach Insights About Portal Start your strategy Methodology / The MR Index The MR Index How much of the building needs attention, how serious it is and how soon. One reading, on a scale from MR 1 to MR 5. Every Capital Strategy carries one. This page explains what the Index is reading, how a building ends up on a band, and what the band is telling you. How it is read ↓ Start your strategy → One reading, five bands Illustrative building · forty elements Element by element Each square is one element of the building Needs nothing Needs a check Needs works: lighter is routine or later, stronger is serious and soon Reads as MR 3 · Mid-cycle refresh 01 Why a single score A Capital Register runs to forty lines or more. The first question anyone asks of it is simpler than that: how bad is it? The MR Index answers that first. It gives back one position for the decade ahead, so an owner, a board or a buyer sees the shape of what is coming at a glance, then turns to the register for the why. Condition, not cost A large building is not marked down for being large, and an expensive repair counts for no more than a cheap one of the same seriousness. The costs stay in the register, for planning. The same way, every time The band is worked out from the register itself, line by line. Nobody decides it, and it does not drift as prices move. It tells you where the building stands. What to do about it is the conversation that follows. 1 Minimal 2 Routine 3 Mid-cycle 4 Elevated 5 Major 02 Three questions, every element By the time the register is complete, every element of the building, from the footings to the fire panel, has been looked at and judged. The Index asks the same three things of each one. Does it need attention? Over the next ten years, will this element need work, need someone to look before anyone can say, or need nothing at all? Works A check Nothing How serious? If it were left, what would it cost the building: its safety, its function, its value? Essential Important Planned Routine How soon? Is this a matter for the coming year, the middle of the decade, or later? Within a year Years two to five Years six to ten 03 The band reads the whole building Picture the building as a field of squares, one for each element. Light up the ones that need attention, more strongly the more serious and the sooner. The band is a reading of that whole picture. A building with a few faint squares late in the decade reads lightly. A building where most of the field is lit, much of it strongly, reads heavily. Three examples, drawn to the same scale: MR 1 Minimal requirements MR 3 Mid-cycle refresh MR 5 Major intervention Needs nothing Needs a check Needs works: lighter is routine or later, stronger is serious and soon Illustrative buildings of forty elements. A real register commonly reads between thirty and fifty. 04 The five bands The reading lands on one of five bands. Each describes a kind of decade, not a verdict on the building. Where the lines between them fall is set against buildings Moyne Ross has assessed, and reviewed as that library grows. MR 1 Minimal requirements Little needs attention, and nothing serious any time soon. MR 2 Routine profile What is needed is routine or already planned, and spread across the decade. MR 3 Mid-cycle refresh A clear set of elements needs attention, some of them important. This decade needs a plan. MR 4 Elevated programme Serious elements need attention, often within a few years, or too many questions are still open. MR 5 Major intervention So much of the building needs serious, early attention that the decision itself changes. 05 What the Index is, and is not The Index says what condition a building is in. It is not a verdict on whether the building is good, beautiful or worth buying. Not a valuation A prime building in a tightly held precinct can read MR 5 and still be the right acquisition. A heritage building often reads heavily simply because so much of it deserves care. Nor is the Index a cost estimate; the register carries the costs. Same band, different decisions Someone holding for ten years reads an MR 4 one way; someone weighing a refurbishment or a change of use reads it another. The Index is the shared starting point. The plan comes from your objectives. Since October 2026 The Index has read condition rather than cost since October 2026. Earlier strategies were banded from cost-weighted measures, still kept for reference, and any of them can be read again under the current method. Five bands. See where yours sits. Send us an address. The first read comes back with the building’s band and the register behind it, before anything is agreed.
