docs.blurb: The line-by-line capital document behind every strategy, with the cost basis on every row.
docs.text: Capital Register cost basis uncertainty range worst case provisional sum horizon horizons three horizons first year years 2 to 5 years 6 to 10 0 1 2 5 6 10 condition action impact confidence arithmetic timing The Capital Register | Methodology Reference | Moyne Ross Moyne Ross Approach Insights About Portal Start your strategy Methodology / The Capital Register The Capital Register Every element of the building, costed across the decade, with the evidence for every cost carried on its own row. It sits at the centre of every Moyne Ross Capital Strategy. This page shows what you receive, how to read it, and why each number can be challenged. What you receive ↓ Start your strategy → One row, from a real strategy 1970s distribution warehouse · Q3 2026 Roof · Item 4.1 Metal deck roofing across the distribution warehouse 01 · Condition Severe oxidation and coating breakdown across the older bays; water ingress risk to stock below. 02 · Action Staged re-sheeting of the corroded sections, with a roofing consultant’s inspection first. 03 · Cost basis Planning range $1.8M–$3.4M for 20,000–25,000 m², ex GST, Q3 2026. Purlins excluded. 04 · Impact 4 · Essential 05 · Confidence Medium 06 · Timing 1 yr $35K 2–5 yr $2.6M 6–10 yr None Item total $2.64M 01 What you receive A Capital Strategy is a reviewed, ten-year view of what your building will ask of your capital, why, and how sure we are. It comes in six connected parts. The register is the engine room; this is what sits around it. Moyne Ross / Capital Strategy Desktop assessment · Q4 2026 Mixed-use building · inner Melbourne A sound frame, a tired envelope. c.1960s · two storeys · retail with offices above 10-year capital requirement $1.42M 1 yr $96K 2–5 yr $718K 6–10 yr $606K MR Index MR 3 Mid-cycle refresh Register 46 elements assessed Executive summary The capital sits in the roof, the façade and plant near the end of its life. The structure shows no evident concern. Most of the decade’s spend falls in years two to five, led by roof renewal and mechanical replacement; the façade allowance depends on an inspection that should come first. Illustrative excerpt with sample figures, in the layout of an issued strategy. The story An executive summary in plain words: where the building stands, what matters most, and what is still uncertain. The capital position The ten-year total, and how it falls across the next year, years two to five, and years six to ten. The MR Index One score for the decade ahead, from MR 1 to MR 5, calculated from the register. How to read it . The register Every element of structure, services and space, row by row: condition, action, cost, timing, impact and confidence. The cost basis Behind every priced line, how the number was built, what it includes and excludes, and how firm it is. A living record Your building’s private place in the portal, by invitation, with report and spreadsheet exports, updated as evidence and plans change. Then, with you: the questions worth investigating, the options the building could support, and the next sensible step. 02 One method, different answers The method is the same on every row. What changes is what the evidence supports. The roof above is a large, well-evidenced exposure. The five rows below each reach a different kind of answer, reproduced from issued strategies and anonymised. 01 Urgency, earned Most of a decade's capital never belongs in the first year. This row does: the failure is active, and water is reaching an occupied room below. Early learning centre, regional Victoria · built 2018 · Q3 2026 External Elements · Item 6.6 Landscaping & Play Areas: Upper Play Deck Waterproofing & Drainage Outlet Failure (Timber-Framed Structure) Impact 4 · Essential Confidence Medium Timing 1 yr $152.5K 2–5 yr None 6–10 yr None Condition, action and cost basis Condition The upper play deck's turf-over-membrane system is failing as one continuous sequence. Inadequate membrane falls and outlet restrictions cause persistent water ponding and biological growth. Saturation is tracking through the plywood substrate into the children's room below and bleeding down the rear elevation, presenting an imminent risk of premature fungal decay and structural loss across concealed joists, blocking, and LVL framing if unaddressed. Action Allow for full turf strip-out and bituminous membrane removal across the confirmed multi-bay extent, reinstated with a flanged clamping-ring outlet, tapered firring to falls, reworked upstand flashing, a sub-turf drainage layer, structural timber framing repair from localized joist/blocking replacement through to full LVL deck relay, and render/soffit make-good, a range of $95,000–$195,000. A specialist waterproofing and structural engineering inspection will confirm the actual figure, and its cost is included. Includes Turf strip-out and disposal, full bituminous membrane removal and replacement with a flanged clamping-ring outlet termination, tapered firring to falls, continuous upstand flashing reworked at the parapet and post-penetration cluster, a drainage layer beneath reinstated turf, spot render and soffit make-good at the confirmed staining path, and structural timber repair ranging from multi-bay joist/blocking replacement to full LVL deck relay. Excludes Remediation beyond the deck footprint and its confirmed drainage path, structural upgrades beyond like-for-like member replacement, internal reinstatement to the room below (costed separately at 5.3). Item total $152.5K 02 Where the evidence stops Impact 4, and no works figure. Nothing yet supports one, so the register prices the inspection and stops there. 1912 heritage building, inner-north Melbourne · Q4 2026 Substructure · Item 1.1 Foundations: Original masonry footings beneath the original building Impact 4 · Essential Confidence Low Timing 1 yr $4.5K 2–5 yr None 6–10 yr None Condition, action and cost basis Condition Original early-twentieth-century foundations are likely shallow masonry footings beneath the two-storey brick shell. No major façade displacement is apparent across the visible street elevations, but concealed footing geometry and movement history remain unknown across the full approximately 564 m² building. Differential movement could crack heritage masonry and disrupt later structural alterations. Action Commission a structural engineer to inspect accessible lower-level fabric, review visible cracking and assess footing performance before major fit-out, rooftop works or façade intervention. The objective is to confirm structural capacity and movement risk at the original-building and later-alteration interfaces. Includes Site inspection, visible crack review, accessible lower-level observations and concise structural advice. Excludes Trial pits, geotechnical testing, monitoring, design documentation and remedial works. Item total $4.5K 03 Heritage fabric Conservation repair rather than replacement: compatible materials, protection of original fabric, and exclusions that keep the range honest. 1912 heritage building, inner-north Melbourne · Q4 2026 Façades · Item 3.1 Masonry/Brickwork: Principal heritage street elevations Impact 3 · Important Confidence Medium Timing 1 yr $8.5K 2–5 yr $137.5K 6–10 yr None Condition, action and cost basis Condition The principal elevations retain extensive red face brickwork, projecting pilasters and decorative white masonry dressings. Local staining, aged pointing and weathered decorative interfaces are visible, particularly around parapet-level details. The façade is a prominent heritage asset; moisture entry through open joints or failed flashings could accelerate brick and internal-finish damage. Action Allow for conservation cleaning, mortar renewal, local brick and dressings repair, and parapet weathering works to the heritage elevations, a range of $85,000–$190,000. A heritage façade specialist inspection will confirm the actual figure, and its cost is included. Includes Access, cleaning, local repointing, brick replacement, decorative repair and minor flashings. Excludes Full façade reconstruction, structural rebuilds, hidden lintel replacement and permit fees. Item total $146K 04 An inference, labelled as one No fault is reported, and the row says so. It names the statutory regime that sets the inspection, and keeps the age-based reasoning visible as reasoning. 1990s broadcasting and office tower, Japan · Q4 2026 Fire Services · Item 9.1 Fire Detection & Alarm Systems Impact 4 · Essential Confidence Medium Timing 1 yr ¥4M 2–5 yr ¥122.5M 6–10 yr None Condition, action and cost basis Condition Fire detection and alarm infrastructure across a 21-storey occupied tower is a life-safety system subject to mandatory periodic inspection under Japan's Fire Service Act. At 30+ years, original-era detection panels and field devices are a plausible candidate for parts obsolescence even absent any reported fault. Action Allow for fire alarm control panel and detector network replacement across all floors, a range of ¥85,000,000–¥160,000,000. A fire engineer inspection will confirm the actual figure, and its cost is included. Includes Fire alarm control panel replacement, detector network renewal, integration with smoke management. Excludes Sprinkler system works (priced separately), structural fire separation works. Item total ¥126.5M 05 Sound work, left alone Coatings refreshed in 2023 are not pulled forward. The recoat sits in years seven to nine, with a review before it. 1990 office building, inner south-east Melbourne · Q3 2026 Façades · Item 3.6 External Coating Systems: Architectural Masonry Paint & Render Impact 2 · Planned Confidence Low Timing 1 yr None 2–5 yr None 6–10 yr $60K Condition, action and cost basis Condition External acrylic elastomeric paint system applied to concrete spandrels, parapets, and side/rear masonry boundary walls. Facade coatings were selectively refreshed during the late 2023 works, presenting uniform adhesion and colour retention with minor road grime accumulation on upper returns. Action Allow for commercial pressure washing, localized crack priming, and dual-coat elastomeric repainting of all external concrete and masonry surfaces, a range of $35,000–$78,000. A painting specialist inspection will confirm the actual figure, and its cost is included. Includes Access plant, surface prep, crack patching, two-coat exterior paint. Excludes Structural render replacement. Item total $60K 03 Every number can be challenged Each finding is graded by where it comes from. Documented findings rest on records or supplied material, observed findings on what the evidence shows, and inferred findings on the building’s era, type and context. The grade travels with the finding, so an assumption never quietly becomes a fact. The cost basis is the audit trail, and it shows how each number was built. Every priced line carries one: what kind of figure it is, the quantity it was applied to, what it includes and excludes, and its date. A planning allowance is presented as a planning allowance, not as a market price, so a quotation or a new survey can be tested against it line by line. The register puts a price on uncertainty instead of hiding it. Where the evidence stops short, the register says so. Partial evidence gets a range and the assumptions that could move it. Where investigation is the right next step, it is priced as its own line rather than hidden behind “to be confirmed”. Inspection tightens the ranges; the discipline is the same either way. That makes the register a shared reference as the plan develops. A quote, a survey or a change of direction can be brought in, and the position updated within the agreed engagement. 04 What the register is not The register isn’t a condition report, a maintenance schedule or a compliance checklist. Those answer technical questions: what the building is, what to do about it routinely, what regulators need to see. The Capital Register is a capital document. It tells the owner what the building will ask of their capital over the next ten years, how sure we are, and when. See the method in use in When the Building is Not the Asset and The Economics of Heritage . The thinking behind it is set out in Timing Is Not Risk , Documented, Observed, Inferred , Pricing What You Don’t Know and The Register, Not the Report ; A Register Read End to End shows how to read one. docs.title: When the Building is Not the Asset
docs.kind: Part II: What buildings become
docs.blurb: When most major systems reach end of life at once and the site carries a development option worth more than the renewed building. A Capital Strategy on a 1970s Melbourne office found a $1.5 million ten-year requirement, about $1,820 per square metre of lettable area. With an approved residential scheme on the site, most of that spend falls away for a developer, and the strategy’s job becomes confirming which pathway the capital should follow.

It also found that, for the most likely buyer, almost none of it mattered.  capital strategy redevelopment versus refurbishment ageing office development consent Melbournecapital strategy redevelopment versus refurbishment ageing office development consent Melbourne when to redevelop instead of refurbish building worth less than land 1970s office capital requirement development consent value dual pathway propertywhen to redevelop instead of refurbish building worth less than land 1970s office capital requirement development consent value dual pathway propertywhen to redevelop instead of refurbish building worth less than land 1970s office capital requirement development consent value dual pathway property A Capital Strategy on a small office in one of Melbourne’s most tightly held inner-city precincts produced something more useful than a condition report. It showed the moment a commercial building stops being valued for what it is and starts being valued for what it could become.

The building needed about $1.5 million over ten years. For one kind of buyer that figure was the whole story. For another it was almost irrelevant. This study sets out why, and what it says about reading ageing stock in supply-constrained locations.  Research note

An asset study first published on 10 February 2026 and rewritten on 4 November 2026. The building is anonymised. The figures are from a desktop Capital Strategy prepared from public evidence without inspection; they are planning allowances at the date of assessment. Deepened 11 November 2026 against the Technical Library: the wall-tie question behind the facade allowance and the concrete tests that gate a retained frame.

## The asset

The property is a four-level office on a corner site of about 300 square metres, built in the mid-1970s, with roughly 820 square metres of lettable area and on-site parking. It sits in a heritage overlay precinct with a non-contributory grading, so the existing building carries no heritage protection of its own. At assessment it was vacant and offered by international expression of interest.

It came with an approved development consent for a six-level residential building of four apartments, designed by one of Australia’s best-known architecture practices.

## What the register found

The building was read as a desktop assessment from public evidence, without physical inspection, using the [Capital Register](/methodology/capital-register) method. The ten-year requirement came to about $1.5 million: roughly $320,000 in the first year, $845,000 in years two to five and $330,000 in years six to ten. About $263,000 of it sat in provisional sums, items that need specialist investigation before they can be priced with confidence. The largest items in the ten-year registerElementAllowanceWhat drives itMechanical services$255,000Central plant beyond its expected service lifeLift$180,000Single passenger lift needing full modernisationElectrical services$177,000Main switchboard, distribution boards and emergency lightingFire services$135,500Detection, sprinklers and passive fire; extent depends on scope of future workFacade$85,000Interim repairs to weathered 1970s brickwork and jointsHazardous materials$30,000Audit and initial management; worst case $120,000 to $250,000 for removal

Moyne Ross Capital Strategy, February 2026. Planning allowances, not quotations.

None of this is unusual. It is what a 1970s office looks like after decades of being held rather than managed. Mechanical systems original or first-generation replacements; electrical infrastructure older than modern loads; fire services designed to the standards of their day; a facade never upgraded for thermal performance, its brickwork of an age that usually means galvanised steel [wall ties](/technical/masonry-brickwork#ties), whose corrosion is the concealed question behind weathered joints. Every major system was approaching end of life at once. [The 1970s Office](/insights/the-1970s-office) explains why that generation of buildings tends to arrive at this point together.

## Where the question changes

The approved scheme reframes almost every line. It involves partial demolition, complete facade replacement and a vertical extension from four levels to six. For a buyer acquiring to build it, the services, lift and envelope that drive the register become part of a new project rather than renewals of the old building. The plant is not replaced like for like; the switchboard is not upgraded on its current basis. What remains relevant is narrower: the condition and capacity of whatever structure is retained to carry the extension. For a frame of the mid-1970s that means [concrete testing](/technical/structural-frame#investigation) before design, not after: cover, carbonation depth and chloride at the depth of the steel, since concrete of the era sometimes carried calcium chloride accelerators, and a retained frame that needs cathodic protection changes the scheme’s cost. Even the [asbestos](/technical/hazardous-materials) question changes character, from a maintenance liability into a demolition management cost.

So the same listing contains two different investments. For a buyer continuing commercial use, the $1.5 million is real: about $1,820 per square metre of lettable area over the decade, much of it early, on a small building in a precinct where office demand is soft. For a developer, the building’s condition matters mainly through the retained structure. What they are pricing is the land, the consent, the architect, the precinct’s scarcity and the cost of the new building.

## What the strategy is for

A conventional pre-purchase report would have listed the defects and compliance gaps and stopped. That answers what the building needs. It does not answer the question an allocator actually faces: given what it would cost to keep this building competitive, and what its alternative use is worth, which pathway should the capital follow?

Here the answer was clear. Simultaneous end of life across the major systems, the hazardous materials exposure and the fire services renewal argued against continued operation with a premium residential consent sitting in the drawer. The Capital Strategy’s role was not to guide retrofit spending but to confirm that redevelopment, not refurbishment, was the rational use of the capital. [Hold, Improve, Reposition or Exit](/insights/hold-improve-reposition-or-exit) sets out that decision in general form.

## The broader pattern

The pattern is increasingly common in inner Melbourne and in other cities with fixed land supply. Buildings from the 1970s and early 1980s are reaching the point where several major systems need replacing together. Where they sit in precincts whose supply is constrained by heritage overlays and planning controls, and where residential demand is strong, the value of the building separates from its income once a development option exists. The building becomes a vessel for the land and the consent.

The clocks behind that arithmetic are set out element by element in the Technical Library: how long [cooling plant](/technical/central-cooling-plant#service-life), [lifts](/technical/passenger-and-goods-lifts#service-life) and [electrical supply](/technical/main-electrical-supply#service-life) last, and what shortens them.  In the register

The register priced the building as it stands, then the strategy read it against the approved scheme: under development intent, the services and envelope lines fall away and the retained structure becomes the question.   Key signal

When every major system reaches end of life at once and the site holds a better consent, the register’s job is to show which pathway the capital should follow.

Accessed 3 November 2026.

## Questions

### When should an ageing office be redeveloped rather than refurbished?

When the ten-year capital requirement to keep it competitive is large relative to its income, several major systems need replacing at once, and the site supports a more valuable use that planning will allow.

### What did the ten-year requirement come to?

About $1.5 million, or roughly $1,820 per square metre of lettable area, with about $263,000 in provisional sums awaiting investigation.

### Why does the same building mean different things to different buyers?

An owner continuing commercial use must fund the renewals. A developer with an approved scheme replaces most of what those renewals would fix, so the land and consent carry the value.

Owners should read their buildings for what they can physically do, not only for what they currently earn.

That era is turning, and the buildings that make, store and power things are being repriced.  real assets financial repression capital cycle industrial real estate replacement costreal assets financial repression capital cycle industrial real estate replacement cost movement to real financial repression real estate Russell Napier buildings capital cycle industrial property return to real assets replacement cost commercial propertymovement to real financial repression real estate Russell Napier buildings capital cycle industrial property return to real assets replacement cost commercial propertymovement to real financial repression real estate Russell Napier buildings capital cycle industrial property return to real assets replacement cost commercial property For forty years the most rewarded skill in property was financial. Interest rates fell almost without interruption, credit was cheap and abundant, and value came from the spread between what a building earned and what its debt cost. The building itself was a container for that arithmetic.

That arrangement is turning. The turn is uneven, contested and slower in some markets than others, but its direction is visible in policy, in prices and in the buildings people now want to own. This paper sets out the macro argument briefly, then translates it into what an owner should look for in a building.  Research note

A Letter first published on 5 February 2026, rewritten and checked on 4 November 2026. Macro views attributed to Russell Napier are his arguments, not Moyne Ross forecasts. Construction price figures are from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics (as tabulated by the Associated General Contractors of America), the Australian Bureau of Statistics and BCIS.

## Forty years of falling money

The United States ten-year Treasury yield peaked above 15 per cent in September 1981 and fell, with interruptions, to about 0.5 per cent in August 2020. Across those four decades almost every asset priced off that rate rose in value, and property rose with it. Much of the gain came from the falling discount rate rather than from anything the buildings did.

The end of that era was abrupt. Between February 2020 and early 2022 the US M2 money supply grew by roughly 40 per cent. Inflation followed, central banks raised rates hard, and the assumption that debt could always be refinanced more cheaply broke. [Forty Years of Cheap Money](/insights/forty-years-of-cheap-money) traces what that did to how buildings were held and maintained.

## The argument for a structural turn

The financial historian Russell Napier argues that the turn is structural rather than cyclical. In his account, governments heavily indebted after the pandemic will prefer to erode that debt through inflation held somewhat above target, while directing savings toward domestic and strategic ends: financial repression, in the old phrase. He expects the regulatory state to keep expanding, industrial policy to be dressed in the language of national security, and capital controls to become thinkable again.

Those are Napier’s forecasts, not settled facts, and reasonable economists dispute them. But the direction of policy since 2022 has broadly run his way: tariffs and onshoring incentives in the United States, strategic investment programmes in Europe and Australia, and governments openly steering pension and insurance capital toward domestic infrastructure. [Industrial Policy Comes Home](/insights/industrial-policy-comes-home) follows that thread into industrial buildings.

Napier’s most useful idea for property investors is the capital cycle. The best returns tend to come from sectors where capital has been scarce for years, so supply is thin when demand turns. For a generation, very little capital went into productive capacity in high-cost economies, because competing with low-cost manufacturing elsewhere made poor sense. If that calculus is reversing, the buildings and land able to house production are undersupplied relative to where demand is heading.

## Replacement cost has moved

The clearest evidence that the physical world is being repriced is the cost of building it. In the United States, the producer price index for new nonresidential building construction rose 42.5 per cent between February 2020 and December 2025, against 25.7 per cent for consumer prices. The index for new office construction rose 50.3 per cent. In Australia, the national building construction output price index rose about 35 per cent in the five years to September 2026. BCIS forecasts United Kingdom tender prices to rise a further 14.1 per cent over the five years to 2031.

When it costs this much more to build, existing buildings that can do what new ones would be built to do become more valuable, because the alternative is expensive and slow. The same arithmetic runs the other way for owners of buildings that need major renewal: every year of deferral is priced in a currency that has been losing value against construction. [The Building That Has to Earn Its Hedge](/insights/the-building-that-has-to-earn-its-hedge) works through what that means for property as an inflation hedge.

## What production asks of a building

If more of the economy makes things, someone has to house the making. Most industrial stock was built for a different job. The logistics sheds that dominate industrial portfolios were designed to store and move goods manufactured elsewhere: large, cheap, quick to build, close to highways and ports, with modest electrical supply and floors designed for racking.

Production asks for different things, and most of them are physical attributes that cannot be added cheaply after construction. What a distribution shed typically provides, and what production tends to needAttributeTypical distribution shedProduction or energy-intensive useWhere it shows in a registerElectrical supplySized for lighting, docks and forklift chargingSeveral times the connected load, often with redundancyIncoming supply, transformer, main switchboardFloor slabDesigned for racking point loadsHeavy plant, vibration control, embedded servicesStructure: slab capacity and conditionStructure and heightLong spans, clear height for rackingCrane rails, mezzanines, roof-hung servicesStructure: frame and roof capacityProcess servicesMinimalProcess water, compressed air, extraction, drainageMechanical and hydraulic servicesFire and hazardous materialsStorage hazard classProcess hazards, dangerous goods, battery storageFire services and complianceOperating patternShift-based logisticsContinuous or multi-shift productionPlant duty, maintenance regime, service lives

Moyne Ross practice, generalised. Requirements vary widely by process; each building needs its own reading.

[Power](/technical/main-electrical-supply#capacity) is usually the binding constraint. A building with spare supply capacity, or land with a grid connection that can be upgraded quickly, holds an attribute the market increasingly prices. Large power transformers have carried lead times of well over two years, and connection queues in Britain and Australia have been long enough that governments have had to reform them. [Energy Becomes a Building Function](/insights/energy-becomes-a-building-function) sets out the evidence.

## Where the financial playbook strains

A great deal of commercial property was bought on a playbook that worked well for fifteen years: borrow cheaply, optimise the spread between income and debt, hold operating costs down, defer capital works to the next owner, and sell before the bills arrived. The playbook assumed that debt would always roll.

Higher and less predictable rates test that assumption directly. Refinancing becomes harder and dearer, and the capital that was deferred is still there, now priced at today’s construction costs. Deferral was never free; it was a loan from the building, and the interest shows up as condition. [Deferred Maintenance Is Debt](/insights/deferred-maintenance-is-debt) makes that case in full.

Napier adds a warning about geography: in past episodes of financial repression, capital that could move freely across borders found it could not easily move back. If he is right even in part, where an asset sits, and under which rules, matters as much as what it is.

## What this means for an owner

The movement to real does not make every physical asset a good one. Prime and secondary buildings are diverging sharply in every market Moyne Ross covers, and a building that cannot do what the next occupier needs is not rescued by the macro tide. The turn rewards specific attributes: supply capacity, structure, adaptability, location relative to labour and infrastructure, and a capital position that is understood rather than deferred.

That changes what due diligence asks. Income still matters. But the questions that decide the next decade are physical: what can this building carry, power and become, what will it need and when, and what would it cost to build its replacement today. That is the reading a [Capital Strategy](/insights/what-a-capital-strategy-is) is designed to give.  In the register

A register in this frame records the building’s physical capacity alongside its renewals: incoming supply and switchboard headroom, slab and frame capacity, and the services that limit change of use.   Key signal

When replacement cost outruns inflation, physical capacity becomes scarce and deferred renewal becomes expensive. Read the building for what it can do.

## Questions

### What is the movement to real?

A shift in capital and policy away from financial engineering and asset-light models toward productive capacity and physical assets, driven by higher inflation, industrial policy and the end of four decades of falling interest rates.

### Does this mean all real estate will rise in value?

No. The evidence points to divergence: buildings with scarce physical attributes such as power capacity, structure and adaptability gain, while buildings that cannot meet new requirements lose ground.

### What should investors check first?

Electrical supply capacity, structural capacity, adaptability for new uses, and the building’s ten-year capital position at current construction costs.

docs.blurb: It turns supply capacity, roof structure and grid connection into primary value drivers. New Australian commercial buildings under NCC 2025 must install rooftop solar, fleet electrification brings megawatt-scale overnight charging loads, and disclosure rules make a building’s energy performance visible. An older warehouse may need roof strengthening, a supply upgrade and switchboard work, and the binding constraint is often whether the local network can take the load or the export at all.

By 2030 its tenants will need it to generate power, charge fleets and report its emissions.  warehouse electrification rooftop solar warehouse EV fleet charging depot industrial property capex NCC 2025warehouse electrification rooftop solar warehouse EV fleet charging depot industrial property capex NCC 2025 warehouse solar structural capacity electrification industrial real estate EV truck charging depot power NCC 2025 solar mandate warehouses industrial building grid connectionwarehouse solar structural capacity electrification industrial real estate EV truck charging depot power NCC 2025 solar mandate warehouses industrial building grid connectionwarehouse solar structural capacity electrification industrial real estate EV truck charging depot power NCC 2025 solar mandate warehouses industrial building grid connection The energy transition is changing what an industrial building is, structurally rather than cosmetically. A warehouse that served for twenty years as a storage box is being asked to become a node in an energy network: to generate power, to carry the charging load of an electric fleet, and to report its emissions to regulators and investors.

Most industrial underwriting has not caught up. It still turns on location, lease expiry and rent reversion, which all still matter. But a new layer of due diligence is emerging that asks what the building can do with electrons, and the gap between what a 2010 warehouse can deliver and what a 2030 occupier will need has a cost attached to it.  Research note

A research note first published on 2 February 2026, rewritten and checked on 4 November 2026. The original described NCC 2025 as requiring full-coverage solar; the requirement is the smaller of the available roof area or a per-square-metre output, so this version says so. Fleet counts in the original have been removed because they dated quickly. NCC adoption dates are as published by the states at review. Deepened 11 November 2026 against the Technical Library: the J9D4 charging readiness rule, roof lives by exposure for the sequencing question, and the battery fire rules.

## Three forces, one building

The first force is regulation. The National Construction Code 2025, released by the Australian Building Codes Board on 1 May 2026, requires new commercial buildings, warehouses included, to install on-site [solar](/technical/solar-photovoltaic-systems) under clause J9D5. The requirement is to cover the available roof area, with exclusions for trafficable areas, plant space and shading, or to meet a minimum output per square metre of conditioned floor area, whichever is smaller; buildings that use gas must add further solar. For a largely unconditioned warehouse the second test can be much the smaller. Adoption is a staircase, state by state, with several states on NCC 2022 until at least May 2027 ([where each state stands](/insights/australia-supply-constraint-and-the-staircase-code#where-each-state-stands)).

The groundwork was laid earlier. NCC 2022 required new commercial buildings to keep at least 20 per cent of the roof clear for future solar and to provide switchboard space for solar and batteries. For warehouses specifically, Part B of NCC 2022 added a requirement to allow for the future [structural load](/technical/roof-structure#loads) of solar panels, because long-span steel roofs are especially sensitive to it. Warehouses designed before that change were not.

The same edition reaches the car park: under clause J9D4, new buildings must be ready for future charging, with dedicated boards on each storey sized for 7 kW chargers in a set share of spaces, 20 per cent for warehouses and factories ([the values, kept by market](/technical/electric-vehicle-charging#thresholds)).

The second force is operational. Fleet electrification has moved from pilots to orders, and an electric fleet charges at the depot, overnight, every night. The third is disclosure. Australia’s mandatory climate reporting under AASB S2 began for the largest entities with financial years starting on 1 January 2025, and NABERS now rates warehouses and cold stores, so the energy performance of industrial buildings is becoming visible and comparable.

## What a 2010 warehouse was built for

Consider a typical 10,000 square metre warehouse built around 2010: a portal frame with a metal deck [roof](/technical/roof-coverings#service-life), designed for lights, a few dock levellers and forklift charging, on an incoming supply of a few hundred amps. Its roof was engineered for the cladding, insulation and code-minimum loads. It was not designed for the permanent weight of solar panels and their racking, or for the extra wind uplift they create.

A structural engineer assessing that roof for a large array will model the portal frame and, in many cases, find that purlins or rafters need strengthening. That work is done from inside, often while the building is operating. It is rarely trivial and always cheaper to design in than to add. [The Roof Nobody Designed for Solar](/insights/the-roof-nobody-designed-for-solar) works through the structural reading.

## The charging load

Fleet charging is where the electrical gap becomes stark. The arithmetic is simple, and the numbers below are illustrative rather than a specification. Illustrative overnight charging load for a depot fleetFleetCharger rating eachConnected loadWhat it implies10 electric trucks80 kW0.8 MWLikely beyond the original supply; switchboard and supply upgrade25 electric trucks80 kW2.0 MWNew or enlarged transformer and network connection25 trucks, staggered by smart charging80 kWAbout 1.0 to 1.2 MW peakLoad management can halve the peak, not remove it

Moyne Ross illustration. Charger ratings, duty cycles and diversity vary; a specialist load assessment sets the real figure.

A building on a few hundred amps cannot carry that. The supply needs enlarging, the transformer may need replacing or supplementing, and the main [switchboard](/technical/main-electrical-supply#capacity) needs reconfiguring. Large transformers have carried lead times of well over two years, and distribution transformers months rather than weeks, so the electrical upgrade sets the programme more often than the building works do.

## The connection is the hidden constraint

Before any of that, someone has to establish whether the local network can accept the solar export or deliver the [charging load](/technical/electric-vehicle-charging#capacity). Distribution networks in outer-suburban industrial precincts, in places like Truganina, Pakenham and Kemps Creek, were designed for historical load profiles. Solar export and megawatt-scale charging change those profiles fundamentally. A site may face export limits that cap the value of its roof, or import limits that cap its ability to charge a fleet. These are commercial risks, not engineering details.

There is also a sequencing problem on the roof itself. Exposure decides how sharp it is: a metal deck of 2010 inland may well outlast an array, since coated steel lasts forty years and more in benign conditions, but the same sheet within about a kilometre of surf may last fifteen to twenty-five, and a [membrane](/technical/waterproofing-membranes#service-life) roof fifteen to twenty-five at best. A roof with ten years of life left, under panels designed for twenty-five, forces either a costly removal and reinstallation of the array when the roof fails, or an early roof replacement that rewrites the capital plan. Getting the order of works right is worth real money, and it depends on knowing the roof’s condition before the solar is specified.

## The cost gap is the investment case

Bringing a 2010 warehouse to a standard an electrifying occupier will accept involves some combination of roof strengthening, roof renewal timed to the array, a supply and transformer upgrade, switchboard reconfiguration, chargers and space for batteries with fire separation, since lithium systems can enter thermal runaway and their location, separation and ventilation are regulated in each market ([batteries and DC fire risk](/technical/solar-photovoltaic-systems#dc)). The cost varies widely by building and by network, which is precisely why it belongs in the capital plan rather than in a footnote.

That gap is both the stranded-asset risk and the opportunity. Owners who know which of their buildings can be brought up to standard, at what cost and how fast the network can respond, can upgrade ahead of lease events and capture the tenants who need it. Owners who find out at lease expiry compete on rent alone. [Energy Becomes a Building Function](/insights/energy-becomes-a-building-function) and [After Rent](/insights/after-rent) follow the same argument into supply capacity and energy income.  In the register

For an industrial building, the register carries roof structure and remaining roof life alongside the incoming supply, transformer, switchboard and the network’s known export and import position.   Key signal

An industrial building’s energy readiness is set by its roof, its supply and its network. Read all three before underwriting an electrifying tenant.

## Questions

### Does NCC 2025 require solar on warehouses?

Yes, for new commercial buildings including warehouses, once a state adopts NCC 2025: solar covering the available roof area, or a minimum output per square metre of conditioned floor area, whichever is smaller.

### Did NCC 2022 already address solar on warehouses?

Yes. It required 20 per cent of the roof to be kept clear and switchboard space for solar and batteries, and for warehouses added a requirement to allow for the future structural load of panels.

### What limits an electric fleet depot?

Usually the electrical supply and the network connection. Charging 25 trucks can need around 2 MW of connected load, which often means a new transformer and network approval.

That logic is acquiring competition, because a building that can generate, store and shift electricity can earn money that does not depend on who is inside. The second line is still small for most buildings. It is growing, and it rewards a different set of physical attributes.  Research note

A Letter first published on 29 January 2026, rewritten and checked on 4 November 2026. The original cited a full-system battery cost of around US$125 per kilowatt-hour falling 93 per cent since 2010; the 93 per cent figure is BloombergNEF’s average pack price, and this version states the pack and stationary figures separately. Deepened 11 November 2026 against the Technical Library: the life of a heat pump against a boiler, and metering as the precondition for a second income line.

## The wrong argument for electrification

Building electrification has mostly been argued on emissions and compliance: mandates, deadlines and the threat of stranded assets. That case has run into hard limits. In November 2025 New York agreed in a court filing to delay its All-Electric Buildings Act, due to start on 1 January 2026, until a federal appeal is decided. Berkeley’s ban on gas connections in new buildings was struck down by a federal appeals court in 2023. Grid constraints and affordability have made forced electrification politically fragile.

The stronger case has little to do with being green. It is about control.

## Control, not compliance

A gas boiler has two states. It burns fuel and makes heat, and it has no useful relationship with the electricity system. It cannot respond to a price signal or sell anything back.

An electric building is different in kind. A heat pump with a variable-speed compressor can modulate continuously. Add a battery and the building can shift when it draws power. Add controls that understand tariffs and forecasts, and it can move load away from expensive hours before anyone notices. Connect it to an aggregator and it becomes part of a virtual power plant, paid for services the grid needs. Electricity lets a building measure, store, shift and respond; combustion does not. Electric plant also runs on a shorter clock. An air-to-water heat pump lasts fifteen to twenty years, against twenty-five to thirty-five for a cast iron or steel boiler, so the capital plan has to carry a faster replacement cycle ([heating plant lives](/technical/central-heating-plant#service-life)).

## The cost curve has moved

The barrier was always cost, and the cost has fallen faster than most capital plans assume. BloombergNEF’s 2025 survey put the average lithium-ion battery pack price at US$108 per kilowatt-hour, 93 per cent below 2010. Packs for stationary storage fell 45 per cent in a single year to US$70 per kilowatt-hour, the cheapest of any use for the first time.

Those are pack prices, not installed systems. Enclosures, power electronics, fire protection, installation and [connection](/technical/main-electrical-supply#capacity) add substantially, and costs in Australia, Britain and the United States sit above the Chinese prices that drive the global average. But the direction is unambiguous, and a battery that was hard to justify on a commercial roof five years ago is now a routine feasibility question.

## A second income line

Each part of the second line has a different counterparty, different physical needs and a different degree of certainty. Treating them as one number is the most common mistake in feasibility work. Energy income lines open to a commercial buildingLineWho paysWhat the building needsHow firmSolar used on siteNo one: it avoids purchased energyRoof capacity and structure, inverter, switchboard spaceFirm while tariffs holdExported solarRetailer or network, at feed-in or wholesale ratesExport approval from the network; often limitedVariable; export caps commonShifting with a batteryAvoided peak tariffs and demand chargesBattery space, fire separation, switchboard capacityModerate; depends on tariff designFlexibility and demand responseAggregator or system operatorControllable plant and meteringContracted, but programmes changeElectric vehicle chargingFleet operators, tenants, the publicSupply capacity, often a transformer upgradeStrong where fleets are committedEnergy services to tenantsTenants, under the lease or an embedded networkMetering, billing and regulatory complianceRegulated; varies by jurisdiction

Moyne Ross practice, generalised. Rules for export, embedded networks and flexibility markets differ by state and country.

Most of these lines need metering before they need anything else, and in some markets the meters are already required. In Australia, new buildings over 2,500 square metres must meter air conditioning, lighting, appliance power, central hot water and lifts separately, and those over 500 square metres need time-of-use metering of gas and electricity ([the values, kept by market](/technical/sub-metering#thresholds)).

At system scale the value is large. The US Department of Energy’s 2021 roadmap for grid-interactive efficient buildings estimated that they could save the US power system between US$100 billion and US$200 billion over two decades. For an individual building the sums are modest beside rent, but they are not nothing, and they compound with avoided cost.

## What changes in tenant selection

If the second line becomes material, the financial test is no longer the only test. An owner starts asking questions that never appeared in a leasing brief. Does this tenant’s demand fall in daylight hours, when the roof generates? Does it run equipment that can be shifted without hurting operations? Does it bring a fleet that charges overnight under a long commitment? A tenant whose load complements the building can be worth more than one paying slightly higher rent with a profile that fights it.

This should not be overstated. Rent will remain the dominant income for almost every commercial building, and covenant strength still matters most. But at the margin, energy fit becomes a leasing criterion, and leases that share the value of the building’s energy systems between owner and tenant become a product worth designing.

## The constraint is the connection

The hardest limit is usually the connection rather than the technology. Networks cap exports, connection upgrades take time, and the equipment needed to enlarge a supply has had long lead times. A building that wants to export from its roof or charge a fleet overnight may find the network cannot take it for years.

That is why the infrastructure decisions made at renewal matter so much. Switchboard capacity, spare ways, the incoming supply, roof structure and space for a battery with proper [fire separation](/technical/solar-photovoltaic-systems#dc) are cheap to provide when the building is being renewed and expensive to add afterwards. A building renewed without them competes on rent alone. A building renewed with them keeps the second line open.  In the register

The register carries the attributes that keep a second income line open: supply capacity, switchboard headroom, roof structure for solar, battery space and fire separation, and controllable plant.   Key signal

The value of a building’s energy systems depends on its connection to the grid. Check the supply and the export position before modelling the income.

## Sources

Named sources consulted for this paper. Consequential claims link to their source in the text. Reviewed 3 November 2026; next review by 3 November 2027.
- [Lithium-ion battery pack prices fall to $108 per kilowatt-hour](https://about.bnef.com/insights/clean-transport/new-record-lows-for-battery-prices/), BloombergNEF. Accessed 3 November 2026.
- [Li-ion battery pack prices fell 8% since last year](https://www.energy-storage.news/?p=91801), Energy-Storage.news. Accessed 3 November 2026.
- [New York agrees to delay implementation of the All-Electric Buildings Act](https://www.harrisbeachmurtha.com/insights/new-york-agrees-to-delay-implementation-of-the-all-electric-buildings-act/), Harris Beach Murtha. Accessed 3 November 2026.

## Questions

### Can a commercial building earn money from energy?

Yes. Through solar used on site, exports, battery shifting, flexibility payments and vehicle charging. For most buildings the sums are modest beside rent but growing.

### Have battery costs really fallen?

BloombergNEF’s 2025 survey found stationary storage battery packs fell 45 per cent in a year to US$70 per kilowatt-hour. Installed system costs are higher and vary by country.

### What limits a building’s energy income?

Usually the grid connection: export limits, supply capacity and the time it takes to upgrade a connection.

docs.title: The Economics of Heritage
docs.kind: Part III: The stock we already have
docs.blurb: Expect two costs. Heritage controls raise the cost of ordinary renewal through specified materials, methods and approvals. And a century of undocumented change leaves structural, roof and compliance questions that only investigation can answer. A ten-year Capital Strategy on a 1912 Melbourne fire station came to $1.69 million, about 54 per cent of the asking price, with first-year spend led by investigation rather than repair.

Heritage controls raise the cost of ordinary renewal through specified materials, methods and approvals. And a century of undocumented change leaves structural, roof and compliance questions that only investigation can answer. A ten-year Capital Strategy on a 1912 Melbourne fire station came to $1.69 million, about 54 per cent of the asking price, with first-year spend led by investigation rather than repair. A Capital Strategy on a 1912 Preston fire station found a ten-year requirement of $1.69 million against a $3.1 million asking price. The heritage premium was only part of it. The unknowns were the rest. A Capital Strategy on a 1912 Preston fire station found a ten-year requirement of $1.69 million against a $3.1 million asking price. The heritage premium was only part of it. The unknowns were the rest.  heritage building capital expenditure adaptive reuse heritage premium investigation Victoriaheritage building capital expenditure adaptive reuse heritage premium investigation Victoria heritage building capex heritage premium renewal cost adaptive reuse capital plan heritage listed building due diligence Victorian Heritage Register permitheritage building capex heritage premium renewal cost adaptive reuse capital plan heritage listed building due diligence Victorian Heritage Register permitheritage building capex heritage premium renewal cost adaptive reuse capital plan heritage listed building due diligence Victorian Heritage Register permit A Capital Strategy on a heritage-listed former fire station in Preston, in Melbourne’s north, set out what owning an adaptively reused civic building actually asks of capital. Designed in 1912 and now home to a cafe and offices, it was listed at $3.1 million across two titles.

The numbers tell a story that reaches well beyond this one asset. Heritage raises the cost of ordinary work, but the larger exposure in a building of this age is what nobody knows.  Research note

An asset study first published on 28 January 2026 and rewritten on 4 November 2026. Figures are from a desktop Capital Strategy at the date of assessment; they are planning allowances, not quotations. The description of Victorian heritage approvals is general and is not legal advice. Deepened 11 November 2026 against the Technical Library: why lime pointing matters, what a roof of 1912 conceals beneath its covering, and the record that resolves fire certification.

## The ten-year picture

The ten-year requirement came to $1.69 million: about 54 per cent of the asking price, simply to maintain and operate the building at its current use. How it falls across the decade matters as much as the total. The ten-year requirement by horizonHorizonAllowanceWhat leads itYear one$142,300Compliance verification and investigation: foundations, roof, structural timber, fire certificationYears two to five$711,000Facade conservation, heritage painting, timber window restorationYears six to ten$832,000Lifecycle replacement of services and finishesTotal$1.69 millionAbout 54% of the $3.1 million asking price

Moyne Ross Capital Strategy, January 2026. Planning allowances, not quotations.

Much of the first year is spent finding out rather than fixing. The items graded low confidence, genuine unknowns awaiting investigation, came to $46,500 on their own. Before capital can be deployed with confidence, the owner needs to know what it is dealing with.

## Why heritage costs more

Heritage controls raise the cost of ordinary renewal in predictable ways. Repointing has to use lime mortar compatible with the original brick, not modern cement: a solid wall of this age relies on soft lime joints to absorb and release moisture, and hard cement pointing drives salts and frost into the brick itself, shortening a life that is otherwise a century and more ([how such walls work and fail](/technical/masonry-brickwork#what-it-is)). [Windows](/technical/glazing-systems#frames) are restored rather than replaced. Paint schemes follow documented colours. Access is restricted by what can be fixed to historic fabric. And work needs approval. In Victoria, a place on the Victorian Heritage Register needs a permit from Heritage Victoria under the Heritage Act 2017, while a place protected only by a local Heritage Overlay needs a planning permit from the council under Clause 43.01 of the planning scheme. The two routes have different tests, timeframes and conditions.

Here the envelope alone, repointing, heritage painting and window restoration, accounts for $633,000 over the decade. That is the cost structure of authenticity rather than a fault in the controls, and what matters to an allocator is whether it is priced into the acquisition or discovered afterwards.

## The information gap

What stands out is how much remains unknown in a prominent, listed building. The foundation type and capacity were unverified. The condition of the roof’s structural timber was concealed, and in a roof of 1912 that matters: slate and terracotta coverings can last eighty years and more, but the nails, battens and timber at wall plates, valleys and gutter lines beneath them do not, and a roof re-covered in heavier tiles at some point can have spread at the eaves ([what timber roofs of this kind do](/technical/roof-structure#timber)). The status of fire compliance certification was unclear. In Victoria, the annual essential safety measures report is the first document that shows whether fire systems are being maintained, and its absence is itself a finding ([The Living Record](/insights/the-living-record)). More than a century of progressive change, with little documentation, creates uncertainty that is systematic rather than incidental.

That is typical of heritage assets, not exceptional. The register handles it by pricing what it can and carrying what it cannot as provisional allowances with explicit worst-case budgets: $180,000 to $280,000 for foundation risk, $185,000 to $245,000 for roof replacement risk. A false single figure would look more confident and be less true. [Pricing What You Don’t Know](/insights/pricing-what-you-do-not-know) explains the method.

## What the income can carry

The office tenancy generates $43,264 a year. Against a ten-year requirement of $1.69 million, the income cannot carry the building on its own. The investment case rests on something else: development upside, which the listing pointed to as airspace for rooftop activation, or capital growth in Preston’s civic precinct.

The strategy endorsed the asset conditionally. The fundamentals are real: a prominent corner, a successful adaptive reuse, two titles that give flexibility, and genuine heritage significance. But it set prerequisites before capital is committed: complete the investigation programme, establish the heritage approval pathway for the main works, and verify the leases.

## For heritage allocators

Heritage assets trade on significance and on the appeal of adaptive reuse. Underneath, they commonly carry deferred maintenance, gaps in compliance verification and higher lifecycle costs that marketing material does not show. The discipline that protects capital is simple to state: investigate before deploying, carry unknowns as provisional allowances with worst cases, and budget explicitly for the heritage premium.

What matters is whether that investigation programme happens in due diligence before exchange, or after settlement when the capital is already committed. The fabric that programme reads, from [old masonry](/technical/masonry-brickwork) to [slate, lead and tile roofs](/technical/roof-coverings#service-life) and [decorative features](/technical/architectural-and-decorative-features), is set out element by element in the Technical Library.  In the register

The register separated the heritage premium from the unknowns: envelope work priced to conservation standards, and foundation, roof and fire compliance carried as provisional allowances with worst-case budgets.   Key signal

In a heritage building the first year buys knowledge. Price the investigation before committing to the works.

## Sources

Named sources consulted for this paper. Consequential claims link to their source in the text. Reviewed 3 November 2026; next review by 3 November 2027.
- [The Capital Register: methodology reference](https://moyneross.com/methodology/capital-register), Moyne Ross. Accessed 3 November 2026.
- [Do I need a permit?](https://www.heritage.vic.gov.au/permits-and-approvals/do-i-need-a-permit), Heritage Victoria. Accessed 3 November 2026.
- [Local heritage protection](https://www.planning.vic.gov.au/guides-and-resources/guides/all-guides/local-heritage-protection), Victorian Government, Planning. Accessed 3 November 2026.

## Questions

### Why does heritage work cost more?

Controls specify compatible materials and methods, favour repair over replacement, restrict access to historic fabric and require approval, all of which raise the cost of ordinary renewal.

### What approvals does heritage work need in Victoria?

Places on the Victorian Heritage Register need a permit from Heritage Victoria under the Heritage Act 2017. Places protected by a local Heritage Overlay need a planning permit from the council under Clause 43.01.

### How should unknowns be priced?

As provisional allowances with explicit worst-case ranges, resolved by investigation, rather than as a single figure that implies more certainty than exists.

docs.kind: Part II: What buildings become
docs.blurb: AI compresses routine cognitive work such as drafting, formatting and first-pass analysis, which can be done anywhere. What remains is judgement, synthesis and the conversations where trust is built, which benefit from presence. The evidence so far is demand concentrating in the best space while secondary space carries the vacancy. Buildings that provide genuinely good shared infrastructure for that remaining work hold their value; buildings that only offer floor plates compete on price.

What it leaves behind is the work that needs people together, and that work wants better space, not more of it.  office demand AI and office space flight to quality office vacancy amenityoffice demand AI and office space flight to quality office vacancy amenity AI office demand will AI reduce office space 10 percent office flight to quality office vacancy office amenity shared space prime versus secondary officeAI office demand will AI reduce office space 10 percent office flight to quality office vacancy office amenity shared space prime versus secondary officeAI office demand will AI reduce office space 10 percent office flight to quality office vacancy office amenity shared space prime versus secondary office The common account of AI and offices runs in a straight line. AI makes workers more productive; more productive workers mean fewer workers; fewer workers need less space. Sell office, buy industrial.

The straight line misses what is actually happening. Moyne Ross rebuilt its own practice around AI tools, and the compression is real: reporting that took most of a week now takes a fraction of it. But the need for a place to work together did not disappear. What changed was what that place is for.  Research note

A Letter first published on 28 January 2026, rewritten and checked on 4 November 2026. The vacancy figures are the latest available at review from the Property Council of Australia, Savills, CBRE and Colliers; they use different definitions and should be read as direction rather than a like-for-like comparison. Deepened 11 November 2026 against the Technical Library: what fewer, busier days ask of ventilation, partitions and lifts, with the English ventilation values.

## What compresses, and what does not

AI compresses the routine: drafting, formatting, gathering information, first-pass analysis, the tasks that filled calendars and could be done anywhere. Much of that work is now done faster by people with tools, or by the tools alone.

What does not compress is judgement: synthesis, and the moment of deciding what the information means. The conversation in which trust is built or lost. The room where the decision is made. Call it the ten per cent that remains. It has different spatial needs from the ninety per cent that is shrinking, and those needs are about quality rather than quantity.

## The evidence so far

If AI were simply shrinking [office](/technical/commercial-office-areas) demand, vacancy would be rising across the board, and it is not. What the data shows in every market Moyne Ross covers is concentration: occupiers are taking less space overall and better space within it. Office vacancy, latest readings by market and gradeMarketOverall vacancyBest spaceReadingSydney CBD13.3% (July 2026)Prime 13.2% against secondary 14.9% (January 2026)Premium-grade demand leading the recoveryMelbourne CBD18.9% (July 2026)Highest vacancy of the Australian capitalsOversupply still working throughBrisbane CBD10.2% (July 2026)Not reported separatelyTightest of the threeCentral London7.2% (Q2 2026)Grade A was 94% of first-half take-upDemand almost entirely for the best spaceUnited States18.2% (Q3 2026)Prime 11.9%; Midtown Manhattan prime 1.9%Ten straight quarters of positive absorption

Property Council of Australia Office Market Reports; Savills; CBRE. Definitions differ by source and are not directly comparable.

Even AI itself is a source of demand. Colliers reported that AI-related firms took 11 per cent of London office take-up in the first quarter of 2026. The firms building the tools want to be together, in good space, near each other.

## The fit-out fallacy

The instinctive response is to make the office nicer: breakout zones, a coffee bar, bright colours, collaboration spaces. A beautiful [fit-out](/technical/partitioning-systems#fitout) inside a culture where people retreat to their desks with headphones on is theatre. The space signals collaboration; the behaviour signals isolation.

Culture creates the ten per cent; space cannot. But space can support it or obstruct it, and that is where an owner has leverage, because the owner controls the base building and the common areas, and nothing else.

## The building as shared infrastructure

Every tenant in a conventional building solves the same problem alone. Each builds its own meeting rooms, too small and booked solid. Each builds a breakout area that looks good in photographs and sits empty most of the week. Each pays for space it underuses while lacking the space it actually needs.

A building can solve that collectively. Properly soundproofed rooms at several scales, bookable by any tenant. Event space for a quarterly all-hands without hiring a venue. Quiet space for focused work. Somewhere good to host a client. Provided as base-building infrastructure, these let tenants take less demised space and still have what the ten per cent needs.

This has physical consequences that show up in a capital plan. Shared rooms need ventilation that responds to variable occupancy, acoustic separation, controls that work, and lifts and [amenities](/technical/public-amenities#capacity) sized for people arriving at the same time. A building whose services were designed for a steady, evenly spread workforce may need renewal to support a pattern of fewer, busier days. The failures are recognisable: a meeting room on a [VAV box](/technical/terminal-units#vav) that turns down to its minimum and goes stuffy within the hour; [partitions](/technical/partitioning-systems#rating) that stop at the ceiling, so conversations carry between rooms; lifts that cope with a steady day and queue at nine. In England, offices are ventilated to 10 litres per second of outside air per person, and the guidance treats carbon dioxide consistently above 1,500 ppm as calling for action, a level a full meeting room on a turned-down box can reach ([the values, kept by market](/technical/air-handling-units#thresholds)).

## For owners and investors

If you hold office, ask whether the building offers something tenants cannot easily provide for themselves; whether demand comes back matters less. A building with the floor plates, services and common areas to host the ten per cent well has a proposition that survives compression. A building that offers only floor plates and a lobby is selling the shrinking use case to tenants who need less of it every year.

There is real uncertainty here. Organisations are conservative, leases are sticky, and running shared space well is a different skill from conventional property management. The shift may take longer than the logic suggests. But the direction in the data is consistent: the best space is scarce and the rest is not, and AI is so far reinforcing that divide rather than closing it.  In the register

For an office, the register reads the services that decide whether shared space can work: ventilation and controls for variable occupancy, acoustic separation, lift capacity and amenities.   Key signal

AI is concentrating demand in the best space. The question for an owner is whether the building can host the work that still needs people together.

## Sources

Named sources consulted for this paper. Consequential claims link to their source in the text. Reviewed 3 November 2026; next review by 3 November 2027.

- [Sydney CBD office market steadies as tenants keep chasing quality](https://www.propertycouncil.com.au/media-releases/sydney-cbd-office-market-steadies-as-tenants-keep-chasing-quality), Property Council of Australia. Accessed 3 November 2026.
- [Melbourne office market stabilising, but nation’s highest vacancy underscores work ahead](https://www.propertycouncil.com.au/media-releases/melbourne-office-market-shows-signs-of-recovery-but-nations-highest-vacancy-underscores-work-ahead), Property Council of Australia. Accessed 3 November 2026.
- [Central London office market research](https://www.savills.com/research_articles/255800/393427-0), Savills. Accessed 3 November 2026.
- [U.S. office figures, Q3 2026](https://www.cbre.com/insights/figures/q3-2026-us-office-market-report), CBRE. Accessed 3 November 2026.
- [London offices snapshot, April 2026](https://www.colliers.com/-/media/files/emea/uk/publications/other-publications/regional-snapshots/london/london-offices-snapshot--apr-2026.ashx?sc_lang=en-gb), Colliers. Accessed 3 November 2026.

## Questions

### Will AI reduce demand for office space?

AI reduces the routine work that can be done anywhere. The evidence so far shows demand concentrating in the best buildings while secondary space carries the vacancy, rather than a uniform decline.

### What is the 10% office?

The share of office work that still benefits from presence: judgement, synthesis and relationship-building. It asks for better shared space rather than more desks.

### What can an office owner control?

The base building and common areas. Providing good shared rooms, event space and quiet space as infrastructure is where an owner has leverage.

docs.kind: Part V: Reading a building
docs.blurb: Mostly not. Large property datasets are being consolidated, but data alone rarely becomes a decision. The advantage lies in synthesising whatever evidence exists, public and private, into a reading of the building that states what is documented, what is observed and what is inferred. A method that is honest about its own confidence is harder to copy than a database.

The real advantage is the method that turns fragments of evidence into a capital decision, and says how sure it is.  property technology property data evidence synthesis G-NAF due diligenceproperty technology property data evidence synthesis G-NAF due diligence proptech data moat is proprietary data the moat property data synthesis G-NAF address data Australia UPRN property identifierproptech data moat is proprietary data the moat property data synthesis G-NAF address data Australia UPRN property identifierproptech data moat is proprietary data the moat property data synthesis G-NAF address data Australia UPRN property identifier Property technology spent fifteen years building consumer apps while the more consequential opportunity sat underneath: the layer that connects the physical reality of a building to the decisions made about it. The question of who owns that layer is being settled now, and much of the industry is looking at the wrong thing.

The prevailing view is that proprietary data is the moat. Own the data, own the market. This note argues that the advantage lies elsewhere, in the method that turns imperfect evidence into a decision and is honest about how sure it is.  Research note

A note first published on 28 January 2026, rewritten and checked on 4 November 2026. The original was written after a PropTech Australia panel and included figures and claims that could not be verified at review; these have been removed. It also described Britain as lacking a national address reference, which overlooked the UPRN.

## The consolidation is real

The large platforms are buying data layers. CoStar completed its acquisition of the 3D capture company Matterport in 2025 and then of the Australian portal Domain. Virtual inspection, once a pandemic stopgap, is becoming a standing record of a property’s interior. Each acquisition adds a layer of information about buildings that did not previously exist at scale.

Compliance is building trust infrastructure too. From 1 July 2026, Australian real estate professionals became subject to anti-money laundering and counter-terrorism financing obligations, enforced by AUSTRAC. The first year is friction. What usually follows in regulated industries is better-structured data: identity established once, verified and reused, rather than photocopied at every step of a transaction.

## Why owning data is not the advantage

Anyone who has worked with the large proprietary property datasets knows how little of their value is realised. The data exists; the insight often does not. Records sit in systems built for listing and transaction, not for asking what a building will need over the next decade, and little of it describes condition, services or capital at all.

Meanwhile, a credible reading of a commercial building can be built from fragments: listing photographs, an information memorandum, planning and permit records, energy ratings, aerial imagery and public registers. Moyne Ross produces Capital Strategies this way. The output is partly synthetic, and that is the point: the analytical layer that should exist, but does not, is constructed from whatever evidence is available. The competitive advantage lies with whoever can turn the data that exists into a decision, not with whoever owns the most of it.

## Synthesis has to be honest

Synthesis is only valuable if it is honest about what it rests on. A reading built from fragments must say which conclusions come from documents, which from observation, and which are inferences from a building’s age, type and context. Without that, synthetic intelligence is just confident guessing. [Documented, Observed, Inferred](/insights/documented-observed-inferred) sets out how Moyne Ross grades its evidence, and [What Public Evidence Can Tell You](/insights/what-public-evidence-can-tell-you) what a desktop reading can and cannot establish.

This is also where AI changes the economics. It makes synthesis fast enough to be routine, but it makes the grading discipline more important, not less, because a model will produce a fluent answer whether or not the evidence supports it. The method has to keep the model honest.

## The address spine

Synthesis depends on joining records about the same place. Australia has an unusual advantage here in the Geocoded National Address File, G-NAF, an authoritative national address index released as open data, which lets planning, permit, transaction and environmental records be attached to a stable reference.

Britain has an equivalent in the Unique Property Reference Number, the UPRN, which identifies every addressable location and is now open for reuse. The United States has no single national identifier with the same reach, so joining records across jurisdictions remains harder there. Where a stable address spine exists, the synthesis problem becomes tractable at national scale. National property reference identifiersMarketIdentifierWhat it enablesAustraliaG-NAF (Geocoded National Address File)Joining planning, permit, transaction and overlay records to one addressUnited KingdomUPRN (Unique Property Reference Number)Joining records about each addressable location across government and industryUnited StatesNo single national identifierJoins rely on parcel numbers and address matching, which vary by county and state

Moyne Ross summary at review. Coverage and licensing vary; check the current terms of each dataset before relying on it.

## Where the value goes

Strata and owners-corporation records are a clear example of value lost to fragmentation. Buildings worth many millions are governed by volunteer committees making capital decisions with little data, while insurance adequacy, fund balances and maintenance history sit in silos invisible to buyers until it is too late. What those records should show, and how shared areas wear while funds fall short, is set out in the Technical Library’s page on [common internal areas](/technical/common-internal-areas#collective); [Why Shared Buildings Defer](/insights/why-shared-buildings-defer) shows what the pattern means for capital.

The broader lesson for allocators is to value capability over inventory. A business that owns a large dataset but cannot turn it into a decision is holding a cost. A method that can read a building from incomplete evidence, say how confident it is, and improve as better evidence arrives is the asset.  In the register

The register records the evidence behind every finding and grades it, so a reading built from public fragments says plainly which conclusions are documented, observed or inferred.   Key signal

Data becomes valuable when a method turns it into a decision and says how sure it is. Ask what a finding rests on, not how big the database is.

## Sources

Named sources consulted for this paper. Consequential claims link to their source in the text. Reviewed 3 November 2026; next review by 3 November 2027.

- [Unique Property Reference Numbers (UPRNs)](https://www.geoplace.co.uk/addresses-streets/location-data/the-uprn), GeoPlace. Accessed 3 November 2026.
- [Summary of AML/CTF obligations for tranche 2 entities](https://austrac.gov.au/node/1158), AUSTRAC. Accessed 3 November 2026.

## Questions

### Is proprietary data the moat in property technology?

Rarely on its own. Much proprietary property data is underused. The durable advantage is a method that turns available evidence into decisions and grades its own confidence.

### Can a building be assessed from public evidence?

Partly. Listing material, planning and permit records, energy ratings and imagery support a desktop reading, provided it states which conclusions are documented, observed or inferred.

### What is G-NAF?

The Geocoded National Address File, Australia’s authoritative national address index, released as open data. Britain’s equivalent is the Unique Property Reference Number.

docs.title: Forty Years of Cheap Money
docs.kind: Part I: The turn
docs.blurb: From the early 1980s to 2020, falling rates compressed property yields so steadily that much of the value created in commercial real estate came from the cost of money rather than from the buildings themselves. With rates normalised, returns have to come from income and physical performance again, so capital needs that were easy to ignore become central to value.
