How did four decades of falling interest rates change the way commercial buildings were valued and maintained?  From the early 1980s to 2020, falling rates compressed property yields so steadily that much of the value created in commercial real estate came from the cost of money rather than from the buildings themselves. With rates normalised, returns have to come from income and physical performance again, so capital needs that were easy to ignore become central to value. From the early 1980s to 2020, falling rates compressed property yields so steadily that much of the value created in commercial real estate came from the cost of money rather than from the buildings themselves. With rates normalised, returns have to come from income and physical performance again, so capital needs that were easy to ignore become central to value. From the early 1980s to 2020, falling rates compressed property yields so steadily that much of the value created in commercial real estate came from the cost of money rather than from the buildings themselves. With rates normalised, returns have to come from income and physical performance again, so capital needs that were easy to ignore become central to value.  Falling interest rates priced buildings like bonds and let their physical condition fade from the valuation. That era is over, and the building is coming back into the price. Falling interest rates priced buildings like bonds and let their physical condition fade from the valuation. That era is over, and the building is coming back into the price.  interest rates cap rate compression commercial real estate valuation deferred capital expenditure real assetsinterest rates cap rate compression commercial real estate valuation deferred capital expenditure real assets falling interest rates and property values yield compression why capex was ignored higher for longer real estate bond-like propertyfalling interest rates and property values yield compression why capex was ignored higher for longer real estate bond-like propertyfalling interest rates and property values yield compression why capex was ignored higher for longer real estate bond-like property For most of the working lives of the people who now run property portfolios, the price of money only went one way. Long bond yields in the United States sat in the teens in the early 1980s and fell, with interruptions, to below one percent in 2020. Australia and Britain followed the same arc. Every asset priced against a discount rate rode that slope, and commercial buildings rode it harder than most.

This paper is about what that long slope did to the way buildings were understood. It argues that cheap money made the physical building the least important part of a property investment, and that the end of cheap money is putting it back at the centre.  Research note

Checked 3 November 2026. The US ten-year Treasury yield peaked at about 15.8 per cent in September 1981 and fell to about 0.5 per cent in August 2020. Policy rates reached record lows in 2020: 0.1 per cent at both the Reserve Bank of Australia and the Bank of England. Tightening in 2022 and 2023 took the RBA cash rate to 4.35 per cent and Bank Rate to 5.25 per cent. Easing followed in 2024 and 2025, then reversed: the RBA raised its cash rate four times in 2026 to 4.60 per cent by September, the Federal Reserve raised its target range to 3.75 to 4.00 per cent in September 2026, and Bank Rate, cut to 3.75 per cent in December 2025, has been held since. The argument about yield compression and deferral is a thesis, not a measured finding. Deepened 4 November 2026 with policy rate history and current settings from the three central banks.

## The bond with a roof

A commercial building with a long lease to a strong tenant looks, to a financial model, very much like a bond. A stream of contracted income, a capitalisation rate, an exit value. As rates fell, the rate at which that income was capitalised fell with them, and values rose without anything happening to the building at all.

Over four decades, a large share of the value created in commercial property came from yield compression. The same building, with the same roof and the same plant, was worth more each cycle because money was cheaper. Owners who did nothing to the asset could still post strong returns.

When value comes from the discount rate, the building becomes a wrapper around the income. Its fabric is a detail, and details get deferred.

## What compression hid

Compression did not just inflate values. It changed behaviour. If a building’s value rises five percent a year from falling yields, a roof replacement that dents the next two years of income looks like a poor use of money. Deferral is rewarded. The building can be sold to the next owner at a lower yield before the roof becomes anyone’s emergency.

Over time this produced a recognisable pattern across ageing stock in all three markets we watch: plant run past its expected life, envelopes patched rather than renewed, compliance upgrades postponed until a trigger forces them. None of it shows in a valuation built on income and a market yield. It shows in the plant room. We have written elsewhere about [deferred maintenance as debt without a statement](/insights/deferred-maintenance-is-debt); cheap money is how that debt was able to accumulate for so long.

## A simple illustration

Take a building earning one million dollars of net income a year. Capitalised at eight per cent it is worth twelve and a half million. Capitalised at five per cent it is worth twenty million. Nothing about the roof, the plant or the tenants has changed; the market’s required yield has. Over four decades, a large share of the value change in commercial property worked this way, and it rewarded owners for holding rather than for improving.

Now run the same arithmetic the other way. If yields move out from five to six per cent, the same income is worth about sixteen and two-thirds million, a fall of one sixth, again with nothing changed in the building. An owner who also discovers a deferred capital programme of two million dollars takes both hits at once. That is the position many holders of older stock found themselves in after 2022.

## Three markets, one slope

The pattern was shared. Australian, British and American policy rates followed the same long descent and the same sharp reversal, and commercial property yields in all three tracked them with a lag. The differences lie in lease structures and in who carries capital: net leases in the United States pass more operating cost to tenants, while British repairing leases and Australian outgoings regimes allocate it differently. But the core effect, value created by the price of money rather than by the building, was common to all three.

## The slope in three numbers

The shape of the forty years is clearest in the policy rates themselves: a high starting point, a long descent to almost nothing, and a sharp climb back. Policy rates: the long descent and the reversalAround the early peakThe floorAt review (November 2026)Australia: RBA cash rateAbout 17.5% (1990)0.10% (November 2020)4.60%, after four increases in 2026United States: federal funds rateAbout 19 to 20% (1981)0 to 0.25% (March 2020)3.75 to 4.00%, after a September 2026 increaseUnited Kingdom: Bank Rate17% (November 1979)0.10% (March 2020)3.75%, unchanged since December 2025US 10-year Treasury yieldAbove 15% (September 1981)About 0.5% (August 2020)

Reserve Bank of Australia; Federal Reserve; Bank of England; Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis (DGS10). Early peaks are approximate.

The table explains the paper’s argument in one reading. For four decades, almost any asset priced off these rates rose in value because the rates fell. From 2022 the direction reversed in all three markets at once. Rates are now well below their 1980s peaks but far above their floor, and nothing in the 2026 increases suggests a quick return to the conditions that made deferral cheap.

## When the tide goes out

The rate shock of 2022 and 2023 reversed the slope. Yields moved out, values fell, and the source of return that had carried the sector for forty years stopped working. The easing that followed proved brief: in 2026, with inflation pushed up again by energy prices, the Reserve Bank of Australia raised its cash rate four times and the Federal Reserve raised its target range. Few serious allocators now expect a return to the near-zero world of the last decade.

In a world without compression, return has to come from two places: income growth and the physical capacity of the building to keep earning it. Both run through the building. A tenant will pay for a space that works and leave one that does not. A lender will look harder at what the next ten years of capital will take. A buyer will ask what the previous owner left undone.

That is the building coming back into the price. The capital requirement, which was a footnote when values rose on their own, becomes one of the main variables in the return.

## Back to the building

The questions a good building surveyor has always asked are now capital-markets questions. How long will the chillers last? What does the roof need, and when? Which compliance upgrades will a refurbishment trigger? These were once due-diligence detail. They now decide whether the asset earns its place in a portfolio.

It also changes what an owner should want to know before acting. A ten-year view of capital, built line by line with its evidence visible, turns the physical building back into something that can be reasoned about alongside income and yield. That is the work of a [Capital Strategy](/insights/what-a-capital-strategy-is), and it is the thread that runs through every part of this publication. This is a reading of the rate cycle, and a sustained return to very low real rates would weaken it; we hold it as a working view.  In the register

Cheap money shows up in a register as clusters of plant and envelope items sitting in the 1 yr and 2–5 yr horizons on ageing stock, often with condition well past typical service life.   Key signal

When yield compression stops carrying returns, the capital requirement of the physical building becomes one of the main drivers of value rather than a footnote.

## Sources

## Questions

### Why did falling interest rates encourage deferred maintenance?

When values rise from falling yields, spending capital that reduces near-term income looks unattractive and the asset can be sold before deferred work becomes urgent. The incentive was to defer, and many ageing buildings carry the result.

### Does the end of cheap money make buildings worse investments?

Not necessarily. It makes them different investments. Return depends more on income and physical performance, which rewards owners who understand their buildings and plan capital deliberately.

docs.title: The Building That Has to Earn Its Hedge
docs.kind: Part I: The turn
docs.blurb: A building hedges inflation only if its income can rise with prices and its capital needs do not inflate faster than that income. Because construction and building-services costs can rise faster than general inflation, deferred works become more expensive each year, and a building with a heavy capital programme can lose much of its hedge.

Whether a building actually behaves like one depends on its leases and on how fast its own capital needs inflate.  inflation hedge construction cost inflation commercial property lease indexation capital expenditureinflation hedge construction cost inflation commercial property lease indexation capital expenditure is property an inflation hedge construction costs rising faster than inflation capex inflation rent indexation and capex cost of deferring worksis property an inflation hedge construction costs rising faster than inflation capex inflation rent indexation and capex cost of deferring worksis property an inflation hedge construction costs rising faster than inflation capex inflation rent indexation and capex cost of deferring works Real assets are meant to protect capital when money loses value. Land is finite, replacement cost rises with prices, rents follow. If the macro view in [The Movement to Real](/insights/the-movement-to-real) is right and inflation runs warmer than central bank targets for a long time, that protection matters more than it has for a generation.

But a building is a machine sitting on land, and machines wear out on a schedule that inflation does not care about. Whether a particular building hedges inflation is a question about that building, not about property as a class.  Research note

Checked 3 November 2026. In Australia, construction cost indices ran well ahead of the Consumer Price Index from 2021: the Cordell Construction Cost Index, a private index, recorded 11.9 per cent growth in residential construction costs over 2022, its largest annual rise on record outside the introduction of the GST, before slowing to 2.6 per cent in the year to June 2024 with costs still around 30 per cent above pre-pandemic levels. Construction costs outpacing consumer prices is episodic rather than a constant. Producer price indexes in Britain and the United States showed similar pressure in the same period. Lease indexation practice varies by market and lease. Deepened 4 November 2026 with construction and consumer price series from the BLS (via AGC), the ABS and BCIS.

## The hedge is a claim, not a property

The case for property as an inflation hedge rests on income. If rents rise with prices, the real value of the income holds. That depends on the lease. Fixed annual reviews below inflation, long terms without market reviews and incentives that eat into effective rent can all leave income trailing prices for years.

Even where the lease works, income is only half the picture. The other half is what the building will ask of its owner over the same period, and that half is rarely modelled with the same care.

## Capex is a short position on construction costs

Every planned replacement in a building is, in effect, a commitment to buy construction at some future price. Roofing, lifts, chillers, switchboards, fire systems: all of these are priced in the construction and services markets, and those markets have their own inflation. In the years after 2020, building costs in Australia, Britain and the United States rose faster than consumer prices, driven by materials, labour shortages and long equipment lead times. The pressure eased from 2024, but the episode showed how quickly the gap can open, and the energy-price shock of 2026 has brought input costs back into view.

An owner with a large deferred programme is therefore short construction inflation. Each year of deferral is a year in which the eventual cost can rise faster than the income meant to pay for it. The hedge leaks through the plant room.

A building with a light capital programme and well-indexed leases is a strong hedge. A building with a heavy programme and soft leases can be a weak one, whatever the asset class says.

## What the numbers show

The gap between construction prices and general inflation is no longer a theoretical risk. It has been measured in all three markets, and in the United States it is large. Construction prices against consumer pricesMeasureConstruction pricesConsumer pricesGapUnited States, Feb 2020 to Dec 2025+42.5% (new nonresidential building, BLS PPI)+25.7% (CPI-U)16.8 pointsUnited States, new office only+50.3%+25.7%24.6 pointsUnited States, peak year (2022)+19.9%+8.0%11.9 points in one yearAustralia, Sep 2021 to Sep 2026About +35% (ABS building construction output index)Not compared over the same periodAnnual non-residential building inflation 4.8% to September 2026United Kingdom, forecast to Q3 2031+14.1% (BCIS all-in tender price index)Not forecast hereTender prices +3.2% in the year to Q3 2026

US: BLS producer price indexes as tabulated by the Associated General Contractors of America. Australia: ABS producer price indexes. UK: BCIS five-year forecast.

Put simply: works priced at $1 million in February 2020 would have cost about $1.43 million by the end of 2025, while rent indexed to consumer prices rose about 26 per cent. A building whose income tracked inflation and whose capital plan tracked construction lost about a sixth of its real capacity to fund its own renewal in under six years.

The gap did not open evenly. Most of it arrived between 2021 and 2023, when US construction prices rose 5.2, 19.9 and 7.9 per cent in successive years. In 2024 and 2025 they rose only 0.1 and 1.6 per cent. Construction inflation does not always run hot; it moves in surges that income rarely matches, and a capital plan that assumes general inflation will be caught out by the next surge.

## Testing the hedge on one building

A practical test needs three inputs. First, the income path: how the leases index, when they review to market and when they expire. Second, the capital path: the register’s ten-year programme, by horizon. Third, an assumption about construction cost escalation relative to general inflation, which can be varied. With those, an owner can see whether net income after capital holds its real value under a warmer inflation regime, or leaks.

Two buildings with identical leases can give opposite answers. One has a light programme spread across the decade and keeps most of its hedge. The other has a heavy mid-decade programme in roofing, plant and facade, priced in a construction market that has run ahead of CPI, and gives a large part of its hedge back. A valuation does not show the difference; a register does.

## Lease structure decides who holds the risk

Who actually bears that capital inflation depends on the lease. Under fully net structures common in the United States, many outgoings and some capital items pass to tenants, though structural and major replacement items often stay with the owner. In Australian and British leases, the line between recoverable outgoings, tenant repair obligations and landlord capital varies widely by lease and by asset. We explore the mechanics in [Who Pays](/insights/who-pays-make-good-dilapidations-and-net-leases); the point here is that the same building can be a good hedge for one owner and a poor one for another, depending on what the leases say.

## Earning the hedge

Earning the hedge is mostly a matter of knowing the capital position early. If the major replacements over the next decade are visible, with a sensible range and timing for each, an owner can decide which to bring forward before costs rise, which to defer with confidence, and which to stage. That is a different posture from discovering the chiller is failing in a hot summer and buying a replacement at whatever price the market sets that month.

It also changes how an acquisition should be read. A building bought as an inflation hedge should be tested against its own capital programme, priced in the same inflationary world the hedge is meant to protect against. If the programme is heavy and early, part of the hedge has already been spent.  In the register

Inflation exposure sits in the timing columns: large items in the 2–5 yr horizon are the ones most sensitive to construction cost movements before they are bought.   Key signal

An owner with a heavy deferred capital programme is effectively short construction inflation, which can erode the inflation protection the asset is meant to provide.

## Questions

### Why can construction costs rise faster than general inflation?

Construction and building-services prices respond to materials, specialist labour supply and equipment lead times, which can move independently of consumer prices. When those markets are tight, the cost of planned building works can rise faster than rents.

### Does bringing capital works forward always beat inflation?

No. Replacing a system early gives up remaining service life and ties up capital. The useful question is item by item: what the remaining life is, what failure would cost, and how sensitive the price is to waiting.

docs.title: Industrial Policy Comes Home
docs.kind: Part I: The turn
docs.blurb: As governments in Australia, Britain and the United States steer capital toward domestic manufacturing, energy and defence supply chains, demand grows for buildings that can host production rather than storage. Production asks for power, floor capacity, services, compliance and resilience that many existing sheds were never built to provide, so the gap between specification and requirement becomes a capital question.

Production asks more of a building than storage ever did.  industrial policy onshoring manufacturing buildings industrial real estate building specificationindustrial policy onshoring manufacturing buildings industrial real estate building specification onshoring and industrial property manufacturing versus warehouse building industrial policy real estate power supply for manufacturing shed specification gaponshoring and industrial property manufacturing versus warehouse building industrial policy real estate power supply for manufacturing shed specification gaponshoring and industrial property manufacturing versus warehouse building industrial policy real estate power supply for manufacturing shed specification gap For thirty years the rich world exported its production and imported finished goods. The buildings followed. Factories closed or became warehouses, and the industrial real estate that boomed was the distribution box: big, simple, low in services, built to hold goods rather than make them.

That arrangement is being reversed by policy. The details differ and will keep changing, but the direction is shared. Australia, Britain and the United States now all speak openly about industrial strategy, supply-chain security and domestic capability in energy, defence, critical minerals and advanced manufacturing. Capital is being steered toward making things at home.  Research note

Checked 3 November 2026. Australia’s Future Made in Australia Act 2024 received royal assent on 10 December 2024, establishing a National Interest Framework for public investment; the UK published its Modern Industrial Strategy on 23 June 2025; the United States enacted the CHIPS and Science Act in 2022. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act of July 2025 then curtailed US clean-energy incentives: wind and solar projects lose the main credits unless construction began by 4 July 2026 or they are in service by the end of 2027, and the commercial building energy-efficiency deduction ends for construction beginning after 30 June 2026. Individual programmes change with governments; the direction of policy, toward domestic capability in energy, critical minerals, advanced manufacturing and defence, is shared. Deepened 4 November 2026 with US Census manufacturing construction spending, 2022 to August 2026. Deepened 11 November 2026 against the Technical Library: process drainage and dangerous goods, and what a production use asks of slab joints and post-tensioned floors.

## Policy with a postcode

Industrial policy has a physical address. A subsidy for battery assembly, a defence contract, a critical-minerals processing plant: each of these lands in a building somewhere, usually in an existing industrial precinct because that is where zoning, labour and transport already are. The demand shows up first as enquiries for sites and existing sheds, long before any new plant is built.

This is the practical expression of the macro argument in [The Movement to Real](/insights/the-movement-to-real). Capital cycles reward the sectors that went unfunded for years. Domestic production capacity is one of them, and it needs buildings.

## The money is real, and it moves

Industrial policy is visible in concrete. In the United States, construction spending on manufacturing facilities rose from about $125 billion in 2022 to about $236 billion in 2024, as the CHIPS and Science Act and clean-energy incentives drew in semiconductor, battery and solar plants. It then eased: $220 billion in 2025, and an annual rate of about $171 billion by August 2026, as some projects completed and some incentives were cut back. Policy instruments and the evidence of buildingMarketInstrumentBuilding signalUnited StatesCHIPS and Science Act (2022); clean-energy manufacturing credits, narrowed in 2025Manufacturing construction $125bn (2022), $202bn (2023), $236bn (2024), $220bn (2025); about $171bn annual rate (August 2026)AustraliaFuture Made in Australia Act 2024 (assent 10 December 2024)A national interest framework for public investment in strategic industriesUnited KingdomModern Industrial Strategy (23 June 2025)Eight priority sectors, with an emphasis on energy costs and grid connection for industry

US Census Bureau construction spending (TLMFGCONS, via FRED). Australian and UK instruments as enacted or published; their effect on construction is not yet separately measured.

The American series carries a warning as well as a signal. Policy can move capital quickly, and it can move it back. An owner positioning industrial stock for production should underwrite the physical capability, which lasts, rather than a particular incentive, which may not.

## What production asks of a building

A warehouse needs a dry roof, a flat [slab](/technical/slab-on-ground#cracking), clear height, docks and enough power for lighting, racking and a few chargers. A production building asks much more. Electrical capacity sized for process equipment. Floor slabs that can take point loads and vibration. Compressed air, process water, extraction and drainage, with [trade waste](/technical/trade-waste-systems#arrestors) pretreatment where the process discharges anything but domestic sewage. Fire and hazardous-materials compliance for what is stored and made, from [dangerous goods stores](/technical/storage-and-archive-areas#chemicals) to the separation of battery and charging areas. Often round-the-clock operation, which changes how plant and envelope wear.

Each of those requirements is a line in a capital programme. Each can also be a reason a building cannot be used at all without major works.

The difference between a storage shed and a production building is mostly invisible from the street. It sits in the [switchboard](/technical/main-electrical-supply#capacity), the slab and the services.

## A production readiness reading

A production readiness reading asks six questions of each building in an industrial portfolio. What is the incoming electrical supply, and what would increasing it involve? What is the slab designed for, and what condition is it in? Can the [roof structure](/technical/roof-structure#loads) take extraction plant, solar or both? What does the fire strategy permit in terms of process, storage and hazardous materials? Are there process services, compressed air, water, drainage, gas, to build on? And what does the site allow for vehicles, hardstand and expansion?

The answers sort a portfolio into three groups: buildings that can host production with modest works, buildings that can with significant works, and buildings that are distribution boxes and will stay that way. Each group has a different capital strategy and a different place in the market that industrial policy is creating.

## The specification gap

Much of the existing industrial stock in all three markets was built for distribution or light industry. Some of it can adapt; some cannot without works that approach the cost of building new. The gap between what a shed was designed for and what a production occupier now needs is where value is being made and lost.

Power is usually the binding constraint. Increasing a site’s electrical supply can involve network studies, new substations and long lead times on transformers and switchgear, as we discuss in [Energy Becomes a Building Function](/insights/energy-becomes-a-building-function). Floor capacity is the next: a slab designed for racking loads may not take heavy machinery without strengthening, and the joints matter as much as the thickness, since open joints without working dowels let panels move independently and break up under wheeled traffic ([joints and wear](/technical/slab-on-ground#joints)). Post-tensioned slabs add a further caution: cutting into one to set down machinery can release a tendon. Roof structures may not take the extraction plant or solar arrays that come with the new use.

## Reading the shed for production

The question for an owner of industrial stock is which of these buildings could host the occupiers that policy is creating, what it would take, and in what order. That is a building question before it is a leasing one: supply capacity, slab, structure, services, fire strategy, hazardous materials.

Portfolios of sheds are worth reading in two layers, the familiar income and location layer and a physical-capacity layer that asks what each building can become. The second layer is where the next decade of value is likely to be decided. Industrial policy is political and reversible, so this view will be revised with the programmes that drive it.  In the register

Production readiness surfaces in a register through electrical supply, slab and structure, fire services and roof structure items, frequently carrying wide ranges until supply capacity and loads are confirmed.   Key signal

Industrial policy creates demand for buildings that can host production, and the binding constraints are usually power supply, floor capacity and services rather than location.

## Questions

### Can an existing warehouse be converted to manufacturing use?

Sometimes. It depends on electrical supply, floor slab capacity, roof and structural capacity, services and fire compliance for the intended process. Each needs checking against the specific occupier’s requirements before value is assumed.

### Why is electrical supply often the main constraint?

Increasing a site’s supply can require network approvals, new substations and equipment with long lead times. Unlike most building works, it is partly outside the owner’s control.

docs.title: Energy Becomes a Building Function
docs.kind: Part I: The turn
docs.blurb: As heating, transport and equipment electrify while grids struggle to add connections, the electrical capacity a building already holds becomes scarce and valuable. Switchboards, substations, supply agreements and gas services move from background utilities into core capital lines that shape what a building can be used for and what it will cost to keep competitive.
docs.text:
Energy Becomes a Building Function Energy Becomes a Building Function Energy Becomes a Building Function Energy Becomes a Building Function  Why is a building’s electrical capacity becoming a key factor in commercial property value? Why is a building’s electrical capacity becoming a key factor in commercial property value? Why is a building’s electrical capacity becoming a key factor in commercial property value? Why is a building’s electrical capacity becoming a key factor in commercial property value?  As heating, transport and equipment electrify while grids struggle to add connections, the electrical capacity a building already holds becomes scarce and valuable. Switchboards, substations, supply agreements and gas services move from background utilities into core capital lines that shape what a building can be used for and what it will cost to keep competitive. As heating, transport and equipment electrify while grids struggle to add connections, the electrical capacity a building already holds becomes scarce and valuable. Switchboards, substations, supply agreements and gas services move from background utilities into core capital lines that shape what a building can be used for and what it will cost to keep competitive. As heating, transport and equipment electrify while grids struggle to add connections, the electrical capacity a building already holds becomes scarce and valuable. Switchboards, substations, supply agreements and gas services move from background utilities into core capital lines that shape what a building can be used for and what it will cost to keep competitive.  Electrification and grid constraint are turning a building’s energy capacity into one of its most valuable and least understood attributes. Electrification and grid constraint are turning a building’s energy capacity into one of its most valuable and least understood attributes.  building electrification grid capacity switchboard replacement gas phase-out commercial real estate energybuilding electrification grid capacity switchboard replacement gas phase-out commercial real estate energy electrical capacity commercial property value grid connection constraint buildings gas to electric conversion building main switchboard upgrade electrification capexelectrical capacity commercial property value grid connection constraint buildings gas to electric conversion building main switchboard upgrade electrification capexelectrical capacity commercial property value grid connection constraint buildings gas to electric conversion building main switchboard upgrade electrification capex For most of the last century, energy was something a building consumed. It arrived through a gas main and an electrical supply sized when the building was designed, and nobody thought about either until a bill or a fault forced them to. Energy was an operating cost, not a building attribute.

That is changing quickly. Heating is moving from gas to electric heat pumps and vehicles from fuel to charging, occupiers are adding equipment that draws more power, and rooftops are generating. In all three of our markets, electricity networks are struggling to connect new demand as fast as it arrives.  Research note

Checked 3 November 2026. A 2024 National Renewable Energy Laboratory report found distribution transformer lead times of up to two years, roughly four times pre-2022 norms. Since then the picture has split: distribution transformers have eased to around 30 weeks, while large power transformers average more than two years and generator step-up units passed 160 weeks in early 2026, according to Wood Mackenzie data cited by the Congressional Research Service. In Britain, connections reform cut the queue for new generation and storage from over 700 gigawatts to 283 in December 2025, with revised offers issued through 2026. In Victoria, new homes and most new commercial buildings must be all-electric from 1 January 2027; elsewhere gas restrictions vary and some have been reversed. Deepened 4 November 2026 with electrical plant lead times (Wood Mackenzie data, secondary reporting) and the December 2025 results of Britain’s connections reform. Deepened 11 November 2026 against the Technical Library: switchboard, breaker and transformer lives, and the Australian rules for charging readiness and metering.

## Capacity is the new location

Grid connection has become one of the slowest parts of any project. Network operators in Australia, Britain and the United States have all faced long queues for new connections and upgrades, and the equipment that sits between the grid and a building, transformers and high-voltage switchgear, has had long lead times. A building that already holds a generous supply has something a newer competitor may wait years for.

This is why we think of electrical capacity the way the market has always thought of location. It is partly fixed, hard to add, and it determines what a site can be used for. The argument runs through [When the Shed Becomes a Power Station](/insights/when-the-shed-becomes-a-power-station) for industrial stock, but it applies to offices, retail and mixed-use buildings too.

## The switchboard as a capital line

Inside the building, the main [switchboard](/technical/main-electrical-supply#capacity) is where this becomes physical. An older board may be at the end of its life, short of spare capacity, or built to standards that make modification difficult. The clocks run at different speeds: a main switchboard lasts thirty to forty years, but its breakers lose manufacturer support after twenty to twenty-five, and an oil-filled transformer can run thirty to fifty years while a dry-type one manages twenty-five to thirty-five ([supply lives](/technical/main-electrical-supply#service-life)). Replacing it can mean a shutdown, temporary supply and coordination with the network. It is rarely a large line in isolation, but it often gates everything else: electrified heating, chargers, solar and batteries all need somewhere to connect.

In many ageing buildings the switchboard is the quiet bottleneck. Nothing on the [electrification](/technical/energy-efficiency-upgrades) wish-list can happen until it does.

## Why the supply is hard to add

Increasing a building’s electrical supply is rarely a matter of asking. It usually involves an application to the network operator, a study of local network capacity, and sometimes a new or upgraded substation, either on site or in the street. The equipment involved, transformers and high-voltage switchgear, has had long lead times since 2022. In the United States, federal laboratory research documented waits of up to two years for distribution transformers at the 2024 peak; those have since eased, but large power transformers still commonly take more than two years. Australian and British owners report similar delays for substation equipment and network works.

The consequence is that supply capacity behaves like a scarce asset. An owner who already holds it can offer electrified heating, fleet [charging](/technical/electric-vehicle-charging#capacity) or process loads quickly. One who does not may wait years, at a cost that is partly outside their control. That asymmetry is now showing in leasing conversations for industrial and logistics space, and it is starting to appear in office and mixed-use buildings planning to electrify.

## The equipment queue

Adding supply is limited by the equipment needed to connect to the network as well as by the network’s capacity. Lead times for electrical plant lengthened sharply from 2021 and have only partly eased. Lead times for electrical plant, United StatesEquipmentLead timeReadingDistribution transformersAbout 30 weeks (mid-2025)Eased from earlier peaksLarge power transformersAbout 128 weeks on average (mid-2025)More than two yearsGenerator step-up transformers143 weeks, and over 160 weeks by early 2026The longest queue in the chainMedium-voltage switchgearAbout 44 weeks (mid-2025)Often sets the programme for a building upgradeHigh-voltage circuit breakersAbout 125 weeks (second half of 2025), against 77 in 2023Lengthening, not easing

Wood Mackenzie data as reported by POWER magazine and other trade sources; secondary reporting. Australian and UK lead times follow the same global supply chain but are not separately published.

Prices moved with the queues: power transformer prices were reported to have risen about 77 per cent since 2019. For a building, the practical point is that a supply upgrade needing a new transformer is a multi-year programme item, and it should enter the capital plan years before the load it serves.

## Britain reorders the queue

Britain’s transmission connection queue had grown beyond 700 gigawatts, far more than the system could ever connect. Reform approved by Ofgem in 2025 reordered it around readiness and strategic need. The results published in December 2025 left 283 gigawatts of generation and storage and 99 gigawatts of demand in the new pipeline. Only about 13 gigawatts of new transmission demand can connect before 2030, with a further 86 gigawatts from 2030 to 2035.

At distribution level, UK Power Networks reported that 59 per cent of its customers secured a place in the reformed queue and that the queue more than halved. Reform reallocates capacity rather than creating it. For a building or a site that needs a larger connection, the queue position is now a property attribute in its own right.

## Reading the energy chain

In a register, the energy chain reads in order: incoming supply and its agreement; main switchboard, age, capacity and spare ways; sub-mains and distribution; heating and hot water plant and its fuel; roof capacity for generation; space and fire strategy for storage; and metering and controls. Some links are already regulated for new buildings: in Australia, the 2025 code requires car parks ready for future charging and separate metering of major services in buildings over 2,500 square metres ([charging values](/technical/electric-vehicle-charging#thresholds), [metering values](/technical/sub-metering#thresholds)). Each link has its own condition and timing. The useful judgement is about the weakest link, because that is the one that sets the pace for the rest.

## Gas: from utility to liability

The other side of the shift is gas. Gas [boilers](/technical/central-heating-plant#boilers) and gas services were once the cheap, reliable default. In many jurisdictions they now face carbon limits, disclosure, rising network charges and, for new buildings, outright restriction. A building that relies on gas for heating has a conversion in its future even if the date is uncertain.

That conversion is not a like-for-like swap. Heat pumps run at lower temperatures, may need different distribution, take roof or plant space and add electrical load. The [After Rent](/insights/after-rent) paper makes the case that electrification is ultimately about control, not compliance. Whatever the motive, the capital consequence is the same: gas-dependent plant has a shortened useful life in the minds of tenants, lenders and buyers, whatever its physical condition.

## What this asks of the register

In a Capital Strategy, energy capacity should be read as a system rather than a set of separate items. The supply, the main board, distribution, heating plant, roof capacity for generation and the space for storage or charging belong to one story. Reading them together tells an owner what the building can become and in what order the works need to happen.

It also changes how to read timing. A switchboard with five years of physical life may still need to move earlier if it blocks a heating conversion that a tenant or a regulation requires. That is a decision, not a condition rating, and it belongs in the conversation with the owner. If connection queues clear and equipment lead times normalise, capacity becomes easier to add and this argument loses some of its force; we will say so when it does.  In the register

Energy capacity appears across several rows: supply and main switchboard, distribution, heating plant, roof structure and generation, each with its own timing but one shared dependency.   Key signal

Electrical capacity is becoming as decisive for commercial property as location, and the switchboard often gates every other electrification decision.

## Questions

### Why does gas heating shorten a plant’s useful life?

Carbon limits, disclosure, network charges and occupier expectations can make gas-dependent plant obsolete before it is physically worn out. The physical condition may be fine while the economic life is shrinking.

### What should an owner check first about a building’s energy capacity?

The size and age of the incoming supply and main switchboard, the spare capacity available, and whether a supply increase would need network works. Those answers frame every later electrification decision.

docs.title: What AI Takes Out of the Building
docs.kind: Part I: The turn
docs.blurb: AI subtracts routine desk work from offices and routine control from building operations, while adding demand for power, connectivity and monitoring. The result is buildings that hold fewer people doing more consequential work, run by software that exposes the age of their controls, and draw more on electrical and digital infrastructure.

AI removes routine work from offices and routine decisions from building operations. Both subtractions change what a building needs to be.  artificial intelligence office demand building management systems smart buildings workplaceartificial intelligence office demand building management systems smart buildings workplace AI impact on office buildings building management system upgrade AI and office space demand smart building controls obsolescence office occupancy densityAI impact on office buildings building management system upgrade AI and office space demand smart building controls obsolescence office occupancy densityAI impact on office buildings building management system upgrade AI and office space demand smart building controls obsolescence office occupancy density The common story about AI and property is short: AI makes office workers more productive, firms need fewer of them, offices empty out. In [The 10% Office](/insights/the-10-office) we argued that this misses what is actually happening inside firms. The work that remains is the work that needs people together.

This paper takes the next step. AI is a subtraction, but it subtracts in two places at once: from the work done in buildings and from the work of running them. Both have physical consequences.  Research note

Checked 3 November 2026. The International Energy Agency reported in April 2026 that data centre electricity use grew 17 per cent in 2025 to about 485 terawatt-hours and projects around 950 terawatt-hours by 2030, about 3 per cent of global electricity demand. The description of building management system obsolescence reflects common practice experience; controller support and integration capability should be confirmed with the system vendor for any particular building. Deepened 4 November 2026 with early market evidence on AI and office demand. Deepened 11 November 2026 against the Technical Library: controls lives and the support clock, the commonest cyber exposure, and the VAV turn-down failure behind uneven occupancy.

## Subtraction first

The first subtraction is desk volume. Drafting, formatting, reconciling and first-pass analysis are moving to software. The floor space that housed that work, rows of workstations and the storage and back-office functions around them, has less reason to exist.

What remains is denser in meaning but not necessarily in people. Rooms for decisions, client work, teaching and the conversations where trust is built. These ask for different things from a building: better acoustic separation, flexible meeting space, good air and light, reliable connectivity, and services that cope with uneven occupancy, empty on Friday and full on Tuesday.

For the base building, uneven occupancy is a services problem. Plant sized for steady full occupancy runs inefficiently at partial load. Older systems without good zoning heat and cool whole floors for a handful of people, while [VAV boxes](/technical/terminal-units#vav) that turn down to a fixed minimum leave the one busy meeting room short of outside air.

## The building learns to run itself

The second subtraction is in operations. Building management has been largely a matter of schedules, set points and someone responding to complaints. Analytics and AI-driven controls can now predict loads, detect faults and tune plant continuously. That only works if the building can be read and controlled: [sensors](/technical/integrated-building-systems#interfaces), metering, networked controllers and plant that responds to commands.

Software-defined operation exposes the age of the controls. A building with a closed, obsolete management system cannot benefit, however good the software above it.

Many buildings from the 1990s and 2000s carry management systems whose controllers are no longer supported, built on proprietary protocols that are hard to integrate. Their replacement used to be discretionary. It is becoming the condition of participating in how buildings will be run.

## A controls reading

Reading a building’s readiness for software-defined operation comes down to a few questions. What is the [building management system](/technical/building-management-and-control-system), which version, and is it supported? Are the controllers on an open protocol, such as BACnet, or a closed proprietary one? How much of the plant is metered and sub-metered, and how much reports its state? Do the major items, chillers, boilers or heat pumps, air-handling units, accept commands at variable output, or only on and off? And is there a secure network path from the building’s systems to the software that would analyse them, separated from tenants and the internet in the way current cyber guidance expects? In practice the commonest exposure is basic, a controller reachable from the internet on its default password or a device on the building network that no one can name ([cyber exposure](/technical/integrated-building-systems#cyber)).

The answers also date the system. Head-end hardware lasts five to eight years and its software five to ten before a major upgrade; plant controllers fifteen to twenty; and it is the end of vendor support, not wear, that usually ends them ([controls lives](/technical/building-management-and-control-system#service-life)). A system installed in 2005 has had its head end replaced twice if it has been kept current, and its controllers are at the end of support either way.

Many buildings of the 1990s and 2000s answer poorly on most of these. That is a capital line rather than a crisis, and often one of the cheapest ways to improve both performance and energy ratings in an older building.

## What arrives

AI also adds. It adds compute, which needs power and cooling, whether in a data hall or a server room on a floor. It adds connectivity requirements, from fibre into the building to coverage across it. It adds monitoring, which turns parts of the building into data sources. The building-as-host argument in [The Building as Host to Machines](/insights/the-building-as-host-to-machines) develops this further.

## What the market shows so far

If AI were simply emptying offices, the evidence would show it in vacancy. What it shows instead is concentration, and in places AI is adding demand rather than removing it. AI and office demand: early evidenceSignalReadingSourceAI-related firms’ share of London office take-up, Q1 202611%ColliersMidtown Manhattan prime office vacancy, Q3 20261.9%CBREUS national office vacancy, Q3 202618.2%, with ten straight quarters of positive net absorptionCBRE

Early and partial evidence. AI’s effect on headcount is a slower variable than leasing cycles.

The subtraction this paper describes is real at the level of tasks and desks. At the level of buildings, the first effect has been to sharpen the divide between space that people want to be in and space they do not. The capital question is the one this paper ends on: whether the base building’s services and controls can support fewer, more purposeful occupants.

## Capital follows the subtraction

The capital consequence is a shift in where money goes: less into floor-plate fit-out at scale, more into the base-building systems that make a smaller, better-used building work. Zoned and responsive mechanical plant, modern controls, electrical capacity, connectivity, and the quality of the shared spaces that bring people in.

The dividing line in office stock may not run between prime and secondary at all. It may run between buildings whose services and controls can adapt to fewer, more purposeful occupants, and buildings that cannot without a deep refurbishment. Much of this depends on how far and how fast firms actually change the way they work, and occupancy evidence over the next few years will test it.  In the register

These shifts appear as building management system, controls, metering and mechanical zoning items, often rated for functional rather than physical obsolescence.   Key signal

AI subtracts desk work and routine operations at the same time, moving capital toward base-building controls, responsive plant and connectivity rather than floor-plate fit-out.

## Questions

### Does AI mean office buildings need less capital spending?

It changes where capital goes more than how much. Fit-out at scale may shrink, while controls, responsive mechanical plant, electrical capacity and shared spaces become more important.

### Why are older building management systems a problem?

Many use unsupported controllers and closed protocols that cannot integrate with modern analytics. Without replacement, the building cannot benefit from data-driven operation.

Australia’s mandatory climate reporting began phasing in from 2025, Britain finalised its own sustainability reporting standards in 2026, and in the United States federal rules have stalled while California presses ahead. Portfolio reports have grown thick with scenarios.

Physical risk is different. It does not live in a report. It lives in the box gutter that overflows in a cloudburst, the switchroom in the basement, the chiller that cannot keep up on the fourth day of a heatwave.  Research note

Checked 3 November 2026. Flood Re supports flood cover for eligible households in the UK and does not extend to commercial property. Australian mandatory climate-related financial reporting under AASB S2 began for the largest entities from financial years starting 1 January 2025, with further groups from July 2026 and July 2027. Britain published final UK Sustainability Reporting Standards on 25 February 2026. In the United States, the SEC proposed rescinding its climate disclosure rule on 29 May 2026, California’s climate-risk reporting law has been enjoined since November 2025, and its emissions reporting law is proceeding. ## From disclosure to drainage

Disclosure asks an owner to describe exposure. Buildings ask an owner to deal with it. The two meet only when the reported risk is translated into elements, actions and timing. A flood exposure becomes a question about where the main switchboard, lift motors and pumps sit relative to likely water levels. A heat exposure becomes a question about cooling capacity, plant ratings and envelope performance. A storm exposure becomes a question about roof fixings, [gutters](/technical/rainwater-systems#capacity), downpipes and facade anchors.

Many existing buildings were designed for a climate envelope that is shifting. Drainage sized for historic rainfall intensities, plant selected for historic peak temperatures, roofs fixed for historic wind loads. None of that makes a building unsafe by default. It does mean the margins are thinner than they were.

## Insurance prices the building

Insurers have been pricing physical risk ahead of most owners, though not in a straight line. Headline commercial property rates have been falling since 2024 as reinsurance capacity returned: Marsh reported global property rates down 10 per cent in the third quarter of 2026. That is the insurance cycle, not the hazard. Exposure still reaches a building through deductibles, sub-limits, exclusions and rebuild-cost inflation, and in the most exposed locations through cover that is hard to place at all. Australian home premiums rose an average of 7.2 per cent a year between 2010 and 2025, against 3.1 per cent wage growth, according to APRA. In Britain, the Flood Re scheme supports household flood cover but does not extend to commercial property, which is priced on its own exposure.

When insurance becomes the first place a physical risk is priced, the building’s condition and configuration start to show up in its operating cost, its financeability and its sale.

An owner who can show what has been done, flood barriers, raised plant, upgraded drainage, can argue for better terms. One who cannot is priced on the assumption that nothing has.

## Where the risk reaches the asset

Because headline commercial rates are falling, it is tempting to read physical risk as easing. The signals in the market say otherwise, once they are separated. Insurance signals at reviewSignalReadingSourceGlobal commercial property rates, Q3 2026Down 10%, after falls of 12% and 9% in the two previous quartersMarsh Global Insurance Market IndexUS commercial property rates, Q3 2026Down 10%MarshPacific (Australia and New Zealand) commercial property rates, Q3 2026Down 14%MarshAustralian home premiums, 2010 to 2025Up 7.2% a year on average, against 3.1% wage growthAPRADriver of Australian premiumsBuilding cost inflation identified as a key factorACCC insurance monitoring

Commercial rates reflect the reinsurance cycle as well as hazard; household premiums in exposed regions have continued to rise.

Physical risk reaches a commercial building through more than the premium. Deductibles and sub-limits for flood, storm and [hail](/technical/roof-coverings#storms) determine how much of a loss the owner carries. Rebuild-cost inflation raises the sum insured, and with it the premium, even where the rate falls. Lenders increasingly ask for evidence of resilience before they will finance an exposed asset. And in the most exposed locations, the question is not price but whether cover can be placed at all.

For the register, this means the resilience items in this paper, plant location, drainage capacity, roof drainage and cooling margins, protect against damage and keep the building insurable on terms a buyer and a lender will accept.

## The elements climate reads first

Physical climate risk concentrates in a familiar set of elements. Roof drainage and box gutters. Basements, ground-floor plant and electrical rooms. Cooling plant and its capacity margin. Facade sealants, fixings and glazing. External ground levels and site [stormwater](/technical/stormwater-drainage#flooding). Bushfire-exposed vents, gutters and combustible elements on urban fringes.

Each has a design basis the climate is moving. In Australia, eaves gutters are typically designed for a storm with a 5 per cent chance in any year and box gutters for a 1 per cent chance, because a box gutter that overflows brings water inside ([the values, kept by market](/technical/rainwater-systems#thresholds)); published design intensities have been revised upward in many places since older buildings were designed, so a box gutter that met its original design can be undersized today. A basement switchroom is the classic single point of failure, where water on a board is both an immediate hazard and a long outage ([switchroom risks](/technical/main-electrical-supply#capacity)). Cooling margins thin twice over: air-cooled chillers last fifteen to twenty years, less near the coast, and the hottest days are the ones they were never sized for.

These are ordinary register items. What changes is how they are read. A gutter at mid-life might be a 6–10 year item on condition alone, and a 2–5 year item once its capacity against current rainfall intensity is considered. That is the kind of judgement we discuss in [Timing Is Not Risk](/insights/timing-is-not-risk): risk changes the case for acting, while timing still follows the evidence.

## A resilience reading

A resilience reading starts with exposure and ends with elements. Exposure comes from hazard mapping and history: flood levels, overland flow paths, bushfire overlays, wind regions, heat. Elements come from the building: where the main switchboard, lift motors, pumps and generators sit relative to plausible water levels; how roof drainage, box gutters and overflows are sized against current rainfall intensities; how much margin cooling plant has on hot days; how facades and roof fixings are designed for wind; what vents, gutters and combustible elements face fire.

Joining the two produces a short list of targeted works: raising or protecting critical plant, adding overflow capacity, upgrading fixings, ember-proofing vents, adding cooling margin. Most are modest. Their value lies as much in what they show an insurer or lender as in what they prevent.

## Holding the line

The step itself is modest. Identify the elements that carry the building’s climate exposure, check them against current conditions rather than design-era assumptions, and decide which deserve earlier attention. Most will be targeted works rather than wholesale change.

Portfolio heat maps hide this. Two buildings on the same flood map can carry very different exposure depending on where their plant sits and what has already been done, which is a reason to look below the map at the building. Insurance markets move, and the pressure on particular elements will follow claims evidence rather than this paper.  In the register

Physical climate exposure appears through roof drainage, basement and ground-level plant, cooling capacity, facade and site stormwater items, with impact ratings that reflect consequence rather than condition alone.   Key signal

Physical climate risk acts on specific elements, and insurers are pricing it now, which makes plant location, drainage and cooling margins capital questions rather than disclosure items.

## Questions

### What building elements are most exposed to physical climate risk?

Typically roof drainage and gutters, basement and ground-floor electrical and mechanical plant, cooling capacity, facade sealants and fixings, and site stormwater, plus bushfire-exposed elements in fringe locations.

### Is climate disclosure the same as climate resilience?

No. Disclosure describes exposure. Resilience comes from physical changes to specific elements, which need to be identified, prioritised and timed in a capital plan.

docs.title: The Building as Host to Machines
docs.kind: Part II: What buildings become
docs.blurb: Machines need power, cooling, floor capacity, connectivity and fire protection in quantities that people never did. As occupiers add compute, automated handling, batteries and charging, the building’s electrical, structural, mechanical and fire systems become the limit on what it can host.

As occupiers add compute, automated handling, batteries and charging, the building’s electrical, structural, mechanical and fire systems become the limit on what it can host.  Occupiers increasingly bring machines rather than people: compute, robots, batteries and chargers. Machines are demanding tenants, and they ask the building for things it may not have. Occupiers increasingly bring machines rather than people: compute, robots, batteries and chargers. Machines are demanding tenants, and they ask the building for things it may not have.  automation lithium-ion battery fire safety data rooms automated warehouses building services capacityautomation lithium-ion battery fire safety data rooms automated warehouses building services capacity buildings for robots and automation battery storage fire risk building server room cooling office automated warehouse slab flatness EV charging building capacitybuildings for robots and automation battery storage fire risk building server room cooling office automated warehouse slab flatness EV charging building capacitybuildings for robots and automation battery storage fire risk building server room cooling office automated warehouse slab flatness EV charging building capacity Buildings were designed around people: floor loads for desks and filing, ventilation for breathing, power for lights and a computer per person, and fire strategies for paper, furniture and fit-out.

A growing share of what occupiers bring through the door is machinery: servers and network equipment, robotic picking systems, battery storage, charging banks for vehicles and forklifts, sensors and the infrastructure that connects them. Machines are a new kind of tenant, and they are demanding ones.  Research note

Checked 3 November 2026. NFPA 855 sets requirements for the installation of stationary energy storage systems in the United States and is widely referenced elsewhere; fire services in Australia and Britain, including the London Fire Brigade, have issued guidance on lithium-ion battery risks from e-bikes, scooters and storage. The IEA projects data centre electricity demand of around 950 terawatt-hours by 2030, roughly double 2025. Specific requirements depend on the jurisdiction, the system and the insurer. Deepened 4 November 2026 with Uptime Institute rack density data and a summary of battery installation standards in each market. Deepened 11 November 2026 against the Technical Library: office and storage floor loads in the United States, and e-bike charging as the everyday battery case.

## Machines want power and cooling

Machines convert electricity into work and heat. A rack of modern computing equipment can draw as much [power](/technical/main-electrical-supply#capacity) as a whole floor of office workers once did, and all of it ends up as heat that must be removed. An automated warehouse runs conveyors, shuttles and chargers continuously. A fleet depot may need more power at night than the building uses all day.

The building’s supply, switchboards, distribution and [cooling](/technical/central-cooling-plant) plant were sized for a different load profile. Adding machines often means adding capacity, and as [Energy Becomes a Building Function](/insights/energy-becomes-a-building-function) sets out, capacity is now one of the hardest things to add.

## How dense the machines have become

The pace of change is easiest to see in computing racks, the clearest case of a machine asking more of a building than people ever did. Rack power density: typical against AIMeasureReadingSourceAverage rack density, excluding purpose-built high-density sitesAbout 7.5 kW (2025)Uptime Institute Global Data Center SurveyMost common rack densityAbout 11 kW (2026), up from 9 kWUptime Institute, 2026 surveyOperators whose densest rack is below 30 kW82% (2025)Uptime InstituteOperators with a rack of 50 kW or more9% (2025)Uptime InstitutePoint at which liquid cooling is typically usedAbove about 50 kW per rackUptime InstituteLeading AI racks100 kW and more, with designs moving towards several hundredUptime Institute

Uptime Institute survey data as reported by Data Center Knowledge and others.

For a building that was never designed as a data hall, the lesson is that a single AI rack can draw what an entire [floor](/technical/upper-floor-slabs-and-structures#deflection) of offices once did, and reject the same heat into one small room. Hosting that is a question of supply capacity, cooling plant, structure and, increasingly, water for liquid cooling, not of floor area.

## Battery rules by market

The [fire question](/technical/automatic-sprinkler-systems) has its own standards, and they differ. In the United States, NFPA 855 governs the installation of stationary energy storage systems. In Australia, AS/NZS 5139 covers battery systems connected through inverters, mainly at smaller scale, with larger installations relying on fire engineering and insurer requirements. In Britain, PAS 63100 sets out fire protection for domestic battery storage, and commercial installations rely on fire engineering and insurer guidance. For an owner, the consistent points are separation, ventilation, detection and access for firefighters, and an insurer who has been told before the system is installed, not after.

## Machines want the floor to behave

Automated handling systems ask for slab flatness and load capacity that older industrial floors may not meet. Very narrow aisle and high-bay racking concentrates loads at the feet of tall structures. Robots tolerate far less unevenness than forklifts and people. Heavy [batteries](/technical/solar-photovoltaic-systems#dc) and equipment cabinets put point loads on suspended floors in offices and mixed-use buildings. In the United States, for example, an office floor is designed for 50 psf (2.4 kPa), less than half the 125 psf (6.0 kPa) required for light storage ([the values, kept by market](/technical/upper-floor-slabs-and-structures#thresholds)), so a battery room or a server row on an office floor is an engineering question before it is a fit-out.

A slab that has served for twenty years can become the reason a building cannot host the next occupier. Floor capacity is rarely on a marketing sheet, and it is expensive to change.

## Machines change the fire question

Lithium-ion batteries are the clearest example. Battery storage, e-bike and scooter charging, forklift fleets and vehicle chargers bring a fire hazard that behaves differently from the fires most building fire strategies were designed around. Fire authorities and insurers in all three of our markets have been issuing guidance and tightening expectations on where batteries sit, how they are separated and how fires would be fought.

The commonest case is e-bikes and scooters charging in corridors, stairs and basement storage cages, each a fire the building’s strategy never imagined ([how it shows up](/technical/storage-and-archive-areas#fire)). For an existing building, this can mean new compartmentation, detection, suppression, ventilation or simply a different location for the equipment. It can also mean that an insurer prices the building differently once the machines arrive.

## A hosting capacity statement

Owners who expect machine-heavy occupiers benefit from preparing a short hosting capacity statement for each building, drawn from the register. Spare electrical capacity at the main switchboard and the supply, and what increasing it would involve. Cooling headroom in the base-building plant and space for supplementary cooling. Floor loading and, for industrial space, slab flatness and joint condition. Riser and cable path capacity. And the fire strategy’s position on batteries, charging and high-value equipment.

A statement like this answers a prospective occupier’s first questions quickly and honestly. It also tells the owner which buildings to market to which kind of occupier, and which upgrades would widen the field.

## What hosting asks of the owner

An owner does not control what occupiers bring, but does control what the base building can support. The useful work is to know the limits before the enquiry arrives: spare electrical capacity, cooling headroom, slab capacity and flatness where relevant, riser space for cabling, and what the fire strategy would need to accept batteries or charging.

Those limits belong in the Capital Strategy as facts and as decisions. Some buildings will host machines easily, some only with targeted works and some not at all, and knowing that early is as valuable as knowing the opposite. How much of this reaches ordinary commercial stock, rather than purpose-built facilities, is the open question we are watching.  In the register

Hosting capacity shows up across supply and switchboard, mechanical cooling, slab and structure, risers and fire services rows, often as conditional allowances tied to a specific future use.   Key signal

As occupiers bring machines rather than people, electrical capacity, cooling headroom, floor performance and battery fire strategy decide what a building can host.

## Sources

## Questions

### Why do lithium-ion batteries change a building’s fire strategy?

Battery fires can develop and spread differently from ordinary fit-out fires and can be hard to extinguish. Where batteries are stored or charged, separation, detection, ventilation and suppression may need to change, and insurers may reassess the risk.

### Can any warehouse floor take automated handling equipment?

Not necessarily. Automated systems can require tighter floor flatness and higher load capacity than older slabs provide. The slab should be checked against the specific system before committing.

docs.title: Retail as Service Infrastructure
docs.kind: Part II: What buildings become
docs.blurb: Retail space is shifting from places that display goods to places that deliver services: health and medical uses, food, fitness, collection and returns, and local fulfilment. These uses ask more of loading, services, hydraulics, power, accessibility and opening hours, so the capital needs of retail buildings move from shopfront refresh toward services and infrastructure.
