In the United States, building rules are made city by city and state by state. A growing number of cities now cap what existing buildings may emit, and that turns plant replacement into compliance.  Local Law 97 building performance standards property condition assessment reserve study United States commercial real estateLocal Law 97 building performance standards property condition assessment reserve study United States commercial real estate Local Law 97 2030 limits building performance standards US cities property condition assessment ASTM E2018 Florida structural integrity reserve study US commercial building capex complianceLocal Law 97 2030 limits building performance standards US cities property condition assessment ASTM E2018 Florida structural integrity reserve study US commercial building capex complianceLocal Law 97 2030 limits building performance standards US cities property condition assessment ASTM E2018 Florida structural integrity reserve study US commercial building capex compliance In Australia and Britain, the building rules that matter most are set nationally or by large states. In the United States they are set by thousands of jurisdictions. Model codes are adopted and amended locally. Energy policy for existing buildings is driven largely by cities and a handful of states. The result is a patchwork, and capital planning has to start with the address.

This note reads the American setting for its capital consequences. It is not legal advice.  Research note

Checked 3 November 2026. Local Law 97 applies to most New York City buildings over 25,000 square feet, with emissions limits from 2024 and materially stricter limits from 2030; Urban Green Council’s analysis of 2024 benchmarking data found that 43 per cent of covered buildings already meet the 2030 limits; the penalty is 268 dollars per tonne above the limit. Washington DC’s mayor proposed pausing that city’s standard in 2025. Florida’s milestone inspection and structural integrity reserve study requirements apply to condominium and cooperative buildings of three or more habitable storeys. Other city and state standards cited are current as understood at the review date and vary in metric and timetable. Deepened 4 November 2026 with Local Law 97 first-year compliance data and a summary of other performance standards. Deepened 11 November 2026 against the Technical Library: the federal refrigerant, lead, PCB, fire door and electrical clearance rules that move cost wherever a building is.

## Cities cap existing buildings

Building performance standards limit the energy use or emissions of existing buildings, not just new ones. New York City’s [Local Law 97](https://www.nyc.gov/site/buildings/codes/ll97-greenhouse-gas-emissions-reductions.page) is the best known. It applies to most buildings over 25,000 square feet, set its first limits from 2024 and tightens them significantly from 2030, with a penalty of 268 dollars per tonne of emissions above the limit. Urban Green Council’s analysis of 2024 [benchmarking](/technical/sub-metering) data found that only 43 per cent of covered buildings already meet the 2030 limits.

Other cities and several states have adopted their own standards, including Boston, Washington DC, Denver, Colorado, Maryland and Washington State, each with its own metrics and timetables. Several have faced delays, and in 2025 Washington DC’s mayor proposed pausing implementation there. Many more cities require annual energy benchmarking and publish the results.

Where a performance standard applies, the replacement of a gas boiler is no longer just a maintenance decision. It is a compliance strategy with a penalty attached to getting it wrong.

## What the first year showed

New York’s Local Law 97 reached its first compliance deadline in 2025, and the results are the first real evidence of how owners respond to a performance standard with penalties attached. Of 29,031 buildings required to report, about 7 per cent did not file. Of those that did, about 95 per cent met their emissions limits. Penalties collected so far are modest, around $270,000 from roughly fifteen buildings, against a statutory rate of $268 per tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent over the limit.

The first period was always going to be the easy one; the limits tighten sharply from 2030. What the first year shows is that most owners can meet a lenient limit with operational changes and modest works, and that the capital question arrives at the second step, when plant replacement and electrification become hard to avoid. Selected building performance standards in force or adoptedJurisdictionCoversKey point at reviewNew York City (LL97)Buildings over 25,000 sq ftFirst period 2024 to 2029; tighter limits from 2030; $268 per tCO2e over the limitWashington State (CBPS)Tier 1 commercial over 220,000 sq ftFirst compliance deadline 1 June 2026Evanston and West HollywoodLocal building stockAdopted standards in 2025Benchmarking onlyMore than 35 jurisdictionsAnnual energy reporting; no performance cap

NYC Department of Buildings via Facilities Dive; Institute for Market Transformation. About fifteen state and local governments had adopted performance standards by 2025.

## Reading a building against a performance standard

A performance standard converts a building’s energy use into an emissions figure using factors for electricity, gas and steam, and compares it with a limit set by occupancy type and floor area. The reading an owner needs is therefore in four steps. Benchmark the current position from the energy data most cities already require. Model the limits for each compliance period against that position. Identify which measures close the gap, in order of cost and disruption: controls and operations, lighting, [heating](/technical/central-heating-plant) plant and electrification, envelope. And time those measures against plant life and lease events so that compliance is achieved by replacement at the right moment rather than by premature spend or penalty.

In the register, the same works appear as ordinary plant, controls and fabric rows. What changes is their timing field, which is set by the compliance period as well as by condition, and their cost basis, which records the penalty exposure that makes the timing matter.

## The condition assessment culture

American commercial real estate has a well-established due diligence product in the property condition assessment, commonly performed to the ASTM E2018 standard and often required by lenders. It typically identifies immediate costs and projects replacement reserves over a term, frequently around ten to twelve years, alongside a separate Phase I environmental site assessment. [Due Diligence Across Three Markets](/insights/due-diligence-across-three-markets) compares it with Australian and British practice.

Lender-driven assessments are efficient and consistent, but they are often designed around a loan rather than an owner’s strategy. A capital plan built for decisions asks different questions of the same building.

Some of the questions have federal answers that move cost wherever the building is. A comfort cooling system holding 50 lb or more of an ozone-depleting refrigerant must be repaired once it leaks more than 10 per cent of its charge a year ([refrigerant](/technical/central-cooling-plant#thresholds)). Paint is lead-based at 1.0 mg/cm² by XRF or 0.5 per cent by weight, which decides how a renovation proceeds ([lead](/technical/hazardous-materials#thresholds)). Caulk installed between 1950 and 1979 can carry up to 40 per cent PCBs ([sealants](/technical/sealants-and-joints#thresholds)). Fire door assemblies are inspected every year under NFPA 80, and the clear working space in front of electrical equipment is fixed by OSHA ([fire doors](/technical/passive-fire-protection#thresholds), [switchrooms](/technical/main-electrical-supply#thresholds)). The Technical Library keeps these as United States values, apart from the Australian and British ones.

## Net leases and reserves

Net leases are common, especially triple-net structures in single-tenant retail, industrial and some office assets, where tenants carry taxes, insurance and many operating costs. Even so, structural and major replacement items often remain with owners, and the line between repair and capital varies by lease.

In shared residential and mixed-use buildings, reserve studies estimate future capital needs. After the 2021 collapse at Surfside, Florida introduced mandatory milestone structural inspections and structural integrity reserve studies for condominium buildings of three or more habitable storeys, a reminder that underfunded shared buildings can become a safety issue, as discussed in [Why Shared Buildings Defer](/insights/why-shared-buildings-defer).

## Insurance and physical risk

The United States is where insurance retreat from physical risk is most visible, with insurers withdrawing from or repricing exposed regions. For owners, building-level resilience, plant location, roof systems, flood protection, increasingly shows up in insurance terms. [Climate as Physical Risk](/insights/climate-as-physical-risk) develops this. Local standards change with local politics and litigation, and this note is reviewed every six months.  In the register

American registers in performance-standard cities carry plant and controls rows timed against compliance periods, with penalty exposure recorded in the cost basis rather than merged into the works cost.   Key signal

In US cities with building performance standards, emissions limits that tighten over time turn plant replacement and controls upgrades into compliance timing decisions.

## Questions

### Which buildings does New York City’s Local Law 97 cover?

Most buildings over 25,000 square feet, with emissions limits that began in 2024 and become significantly stricter from 2030. Exemptions and alternative pathways apply to some building types.

### What is a property condition assessment?

A due diligence report on a commercial property’s physical condition, commonly prepared to the ASTM E2018 standard, typically identifying immediate repair costs and projecting replacement reserves over a term, often for a lender.

Knowing the equivalents avoids comparing different things as if they were the same.

Owners and investors who work across Australia, Britain and the United States often find that the same idea has three names, and that similar names can mean slightly different things.

This field guide sets out the equivalents that matter most for building capital. They are close equivalents, not identical: scope and legal effect differ.  Research note

Terms are given as commonly used in professional practice in each market at the review date. Legal definitions, measurement standards and professional titles vary within countries as well as between them; where a term has legal effect, the governing instrument and local advice decide. Deepened 4 November 2026 with a table of measurement and cost terms across the three markets. Deepened 11 November 2026 against the Technical Library: values kept by market, the same discipline applied to physical rules.

## Due diligence and surveys
- Technical due diligence (Australia, also used in Britain) · building survey or building condition survey (Britain) · property condition assessment, often to ASTM E2018 (United States). Each assesses physical condition and likely capital needs before a transaction.
- Building consultant or building surveyor in the consultancy sense (Australia) · chartered building surveyor (Britain) · property condition assessor or consultant (United States). In Australia, a registered building surveyor is also the statutory role that issues building permits, which is a different job.
- Environmental site assessment, contamination report (Australia) · environmental report (Britain) · Phase I environmental site assessment, often to ASTM E1527 (United States).

[Due Diligence Across Three Markets](/insights/due-diligence-across-three-markets) compares how these are scoped.

## Leases and recoveries
- Make good (Australia) · dilapidations, reinstatement and yielding up (Britain) · surrender condition or restoration obligations (United States). What a tenant must do to the premises at lease end.
- Outgoings (Australia) · service charge (Britain, multi-let) · common area maintenance, operating expenses and pass-throughs (United States).
- Gross and net leases (Australia) · full repairing and insuring lease (Britain) · gross, modified gross and triple-net leases (United States).

[Who Pays](/insights/who-pays-make-good-dilapidations-and-net-leases) reads what these structures mean for capital.

## Areas, costs and the standards behind them

Some of the most expensive mistranslations are about area and cost, because a figure can be correct and still not mean what the reader assumes. Measurement and cost terms across the three marketsConceptAustraliaUnited KingdomUnited StatesLettable office areaNet lettable area (PCA method of measurement)Net internal area, or IPMS under RICS standardsRentable area under BOMA standardsRecoverable running costsOutgoingsService chargeOperating expenses, common area maintenanceRestoring premises at lease endMake goodDilapidations, reinstatement, yielding upRestoration, surrender conditionShared-building reserveSinking fund or capital works fundReserve or sinking fund (often voluntary)Reserve fund, set by a reserve studyPre-purchase building reportTechnical due diligenceBuilding survey or technical due diligenceProperty condition assessment

Moyne Ross summary. Standards change; confirm which edition a figure was measured or prepared under.

The habit that prevents most errors is the first one this paper names: ask what the number includes, and under which standard it was produced.

## Shared buildings and funds
- [Strata](/technical/common-internal-areas#collective) title, owners corporation or body corporate (Australia) · leasehold flats with a freeholder or residents’ management company, or commonhold (Britain) · condominium and homeowners association (United States).
- Sinking fund, capital works fund or maintenance fund (Australia) · reserve or sinking fund within the service charge (Britain) · reserve fund, with a reserve study to set it (United States).

## Three habits that prevent mistranslation

First, ask what the number includes. A capital figure may or may not include design fees, contingency, preliminaries, tax and access costs, and the conventions differ by market. Second, ask what the area is. Net lettable area, net internal area and rentable square feet are measured differently and can differ by ten per cent or more for the same floor. Third, ask what the horizon is. A ten-year forecast, a twelve-year reserve table and a schedule of immediate works are not the same instrument, and only one of them is comparable with another building’s ten-year forecast.

Moyne Ross keeps these on the cost basis of every line: currency, measurement basis, inclusions and exclusions, base date. It is unglamorous, and it is what makes cross-border comparison honest. The Technical Library applies the same discipline to physical rules: every measured value is kept by market, so an Australian fire door gap, an English one and an American one sit in separate tables and are never read as each other ([an example](/technical/passive-fire-protection#thresholds)).

## Performance and measurement
- NABERS ratings and Commercial Building Disclosure (Australia) · Energy Performance Certificates and Display Energy Certificates (Britain) · ENERGY STAR scores and city benchmarking (United States).
- Net lettable area (Australia) · net internal area (Britain) · rentable and usable square feet, often to BOMA standards (United States). Floor area definitions differ, so capital per square metre or square foot is only comparable once the basis is aligned.
- Essential safety measures and annual fire safety statements (Australian states) · fire risk assessment under fire safety legislation (Britain) · fire inspections and code compliance under local adoption of model codes (United States).   In the register

Moyne Ross registers use one structure across markets, structure, services and space with the same six fields, while the cost basis records currency, measurement basis and local terminology so lines are not blended across jurisdictions.   Key signal

Equivalent terms across Australia, Britain and the United States are close but not identical, so capital figures should only be compared once scope, measurement and currency are aligned.

## Sources

- [E2018 revision](https://newsroom.astm.org/e2018-revision), ASTM International. Accessed 3 November 2026.

## Questions

### Is make good the same as dilapidations?

They address the same idea, a tenant’s obligations about the premises’ condition at lease end, but the legal framework, process and typical outcomes differ between Australia and Britain. Lease terms and local advice govern the detail.

### Can capital costs per square metre be compared across countries?

Only with care. Floor area definitions, currency, tax treatment and what is included in each cost can all differ, so the basis needs aligning before comparison.

This note describes typical practice. Scope is always set by the engagement, and individual reports vary widely.  Research note

Descriptions of practice in each market are general and reflect common scope at the review date. The ASTM E2018 standard for property condition assessments and ASTM E1527 for Phase I environmental site assessments are American voluntary consensus standards; RICS publishes professional standards and guidance for building surveys and technical due diligence used in Britain and internationally; Australian practice follows professional and client-driven scope rather than a single national standard. Deepened 4 November 2026 with the governing due diligence documents in each market. Deepened 11 November 2026 against the Technical Library: standards by country and values kept by market, at element level.

## Australia

Australian technical due diligence is commonly carried out by building consultants, with engineers for services and structure as required. A typical report covers the condition of structure, envelope and services, statutory compliance including the building’s fire safety and essential safety measures records, and a capital expenditure forecast, often over ten years. Environmental, make-good and specialist issues may be separate.

Reports tend to be written for the purchaser and its financiers, and the capital forecast often feeds directly into the price negotiation and the investment model.

## Britain

In Britain, chartered building surveyors lead most commercial building surveys and technical due diligence, again with engineers for mechanical and electrical systems. Reports commonly cover condition, deleterious and [hazardous](/technical/hazardous-materials#jurisdiction-notes) materials, statutory compliance, energy performance in light of minimum standards, and a capital schedule. Because so much British commercial property is leased, the interplay between condition and lease obligations, service charges and dilapidations often receives particular attention.

[The energy rating as a letting rule](/insights/britain-when-the-energy-rating-becomes-a-letting-rule) has made EPC pathways a growing part of British due diligence.

## United States

In the United States, the property condition assessment is a well-defined product, commonly prepared to the ASTM E2018 standard and frequently commissioned for a lender. It typically identifies immediate costs, items needing prompt attention, and projects replacement reserves over a term, often around ten to twelve years, usually through a walk-through survey and document review rather than intrusive investigation. A Phase I environmental site assessment is normally a separate report, and seismic risk reports are common in some regions.

The standardisation makes reports consistent and quick to compare. Their framing around a loan can mean they say less about strategy, functional obsolescence or the owner’s options.

The three products answer the same first question, what will this building cost to own, but they are shaped by who usually commissions them.

## The governing documents

Each market’s due diligence rests on a different kind of document, and their status matters when a report is relied on. What governs technical due diligence in each marketMarketGoverning documentStatusNoteAustraliaNo single national standard for commercial due diligencePractice set by consultants and clients’ briefsResidential inspections have AS 4349; commercial scopes are negotiatedUnited KingdomTechnical due diligence of commercial property, first edition (RICS)Published January 2020; reissued April 2023 as a professional standardMandatory for RICS members carrying out this workUnited StatesASTM E2018-24, Standard guide for property condition assessmentsApproved 1 January 2024, replacing the 2015 edition, with more than 140 revisionsThe most cited standard for transactional scopes; ASTM says it is less suited to capital planning

RICS; ASTM International.

For an investor, the practical consequence is that the same words, a due diligence report, describe documents with different scopes, horizons and obligations. Reading the governing document, or asking which one a report was prepared under, is part of reading the report.

## What a good report says about its own limits

The best due diligence reports in any market are explicit about four things. Access: what was and was not inspected, and why. Evidence: which conclusions rest on documents, which on observation and which on inference from age and type. Scope: what was excluded, such as environmental, geotechnical, services testing or compliance audit. And confidence: how firm each capital figure is. A report that is silent on these is harder to use than one that is modest about them, because the reader cannot tell where the risk sits.

When Moyne Ross takes findings from a third-party report into a register, these four things decide the confidence rating on each line and whether an investigation item is needed.

## Reading across them

For an investor working across markets, three differences matter most. Horizons and categories: immediate, short term, replacement reserve and ten-year forecasts are not cut the same way. Evidence: some reports rely on a walk-through, others on deeper investigation, and few say clearly which conclusions rest on which. And purpose: a lender’s report and an owner’s strategy weigh different risks.

A structured register helps bridge them. Expressing every report’s findings as lines with condition, action, cost basis, timing, impact and confidence, in one set of horizons, makes reports from different markets comparable. It is also how Moyne Ross approaches every building, wherever it is. The Technical Library carries the same separation down to the element: each page has its standards by country and its measured values kept by market, so a finding read against one market’s rule is never graded against another’s ([an example](/technical/roof-coverings#jurisdiction-notes)). See [Same Thing, Different Name](/insights/same-thing-different-name) for the terminology.  In the register

Findings from Australian, British or American reports can be expressed in one register structure, with source, measurement basis and currency carried in each cost basis so they are not blended.   Key signal

Due diligence products differ by market mainly because of who commissions them, so comparing them requires aligning horizons, evidence depth and purpose.

## Questions

### What is the difference between a PCA and technical due diligence?

Both assess condition and likely capital needs. A US property condition assessment is often standardised to ASTM E2018 and lender-driven, presenting immediate costs and replacement reserves; Australian and British technical due diligence is often broader in compliance and lease matters and framed for the purchaser.

### Over what period do due diligence reports usually forecast capital costs?

Commonly around ten years in Australian and British practice, and often ten to twelve years for replacement reserves in US property condition assessments, though scope varies by engagement.

The building’s capital needs are the same either way, but who bears each line, and when, depends on the lease and the law that governs it.

It does not, on its own, say who will pay. That depends on the leases, and lease structures vary widely across Australia, Britain and the United States, and between assets in the same market.

This note reads lease structures from a building and capital perspective. The legal effect of any lease is a question for lawyers, and the law in each jurisdiction can limit what a lease achieves.  Research note

Lease structures are described in general terms as commonly encountered in each market. Retail leasing legislation in several Australian states limits what landlords can recover from retail tenants; British dilapidations claims are subject to statutory and common-law limits on damages; American net lease terms vary widely by document. None of this is legal advice, and the lease and local counsel govern. Deepened 4 November 2026 with the section 18(1) cap, the RICS dilapidations standard and a comparison of lease-end mechanisms. Deepened 11 November 2026 against the Technical Library: the fire separation a fit-out can leave compromised, which matters more at lease end than the finishes.

## Australia: outgoings and make good

Australian commercial leases range from gross to net, with tenants contributing to outgoings such as rates, insurance and operating costs depending on the lease. The line between recoverable outgoings and capital is drawn by the lease and, for retail premises, by state retail leasing legislation, which in several states restricts what can be recovered from retail tenants.

At lease end, make-good clauses require tenants to return premises to a specified condition, often removing fit-out and repairing damage. [Make good](/technical/retail-tenancies#tenure) can fund some reinstatement, but it rarely funds base-building renewal, and negotiated settlements often replace physical works.

## Britain: repair, service charge and dilapidations

British single-let commercial buildings are often held on full repairing and insuring leases, placing repair obligations broadly on the tenant. In multi-let buildings, landlords typically carry out common works and recover costs through a service charge, guided by professional codes. The distinction between repair, which may be recoverable, and improvement, which often is not, can decide who pays for major replacements.

At lease end, dilapidations claims address breaches of repairing and [reinstatement](/technical/partitioning-systems#fitout) obligations. The law limits damages in various ways, which is one reason dilapidations rarely deliver a building in the condition the schedule describes.

What a fit-out leaves behind is often more than the schedule sees. Partitions taken to the ceiling rather than the slab, penetrations left open through fire-rated walls, and corridor or riser walls altered without approval all compromise the base building’s [fire separation](/technical/passive-fire-protection#compartments), and the reinstatement that matters is the separation rather than the finishes ([what fit-outs do to walls](/technical/partitioning-systems#fitout)).

Lease structure can move a capital line between parties. It cannot make the building need less.

## The rules that cap the claim

In England and Wales the landlord’s claim at lease end is capped by statute. Section 18(1) of the Landlord and Tenant Act 1927 limits damages for breach of a repairing covenant to the reduction in the value of the landlord’s interest caused by the breach. If the landlord intends to redevelop or substantially alter the building, the cap can reduce the claim to nothing, because the repairs would be superseded.

Practice is set by the Pre-Action Protocol for dilapidations claims and by the RICS professional standard on dilapidations, now in its seventh edition. Claims are expected to be quantified, supported and reasonable, and the courts take account of parties who ignore the Protocol. Landlord and Tenant Act 1927; RICS; state retail leases legislation; lease practice varies widely.

The consequence for a register is that lease end is a capital event whose value depends on the owner’s own plans. A landlord intending to refurbish gets less from a dilapidations claim than one intending to relet as is, and a register that knows the plan can show which.

## United States: gross to triple net

American leases run from full-service gross, where the landlord carries operating costs, through modified gross, to triple net, where tenants pay taxes, insurance and maintenance. Common area maintenance charges recover shared costs in multi-tenant assets. Even in net leases, roof, structure and major system replacements often remain with the landlord, sometimes recovered over time through amortisation where leases allow.

## Reading lease events against the horizons

The practical exercise is to lay the lease calendar over the register’s three horizons. Where do expiries, breaks, reviews and make-good or dilapidations events fall against the one-year, two-to-five-year and six-to-ten-year columns? A plant replacement due in year four in a single-let building with a lease expiry in year three is a different decision from the same replacement under a lease that runs to year nine. A facade programme may be timed to coincide with vacancy. An energy upgrade that benefits re-letting may be hard to recover from a sitting tenant and easy to fund at expiry.

The register does not decide these questions. It makes them visible, line by line, so that the conversation with lease advisers starts from the building’s actual position rather than from a general allowance.

## What it means for the register

Reading the register through the leases is the practical exercise. Which lines fall on the owner, which on tenants, which are shared, and which are uncertain? When do lease expiries, reviews and make-good or dilapidations events fall against the register’s horizons? A large replacement just before a major lease expiry is a different decision from the same replacement just after a new long lease.

This is one of the clearest places where [the owner’s intentions](/insights/bringing-the-owners-intentions-to-bear) reshape a strategy. The building stays the same; who carries it, and when, does not. Recoverability is best settled with lease advisers; the register’s job is to make the physical position clear enough for that conversation to be precise.  In the register

Registers can note where recoverability under the leases is a question to settle with lease advisers, and lease events such as expiries and make good can be read against the 1 yr, 2–5 yr and 6–10 yr horizons.   Key signal

Lease structure decides who carries each capital line and when, but not what the building needs, so the register should be read through the leases with legal advice on recoverability.

## Questions

### Does a triple net lease mean the tenant pays for a new roof?

Not necessarily. Many net leases still leave roof, structure and major replacements with the landlord, sometimes with recovery over time. The lease wording and local law decide.

### Will make good or dilapidations pay for base-building renewal?

Usually not in full. These obligations focus on the tenant’s premises and lease breaches, and settlements are often negotiated rather than delivered as physical works.

docs.kind: Part VI: Three markets, one building
docs.blurb: Disclosure regimes across Australia, Britain and the United States, including energy ratings at sale or lease, city benchmarking, fire safety records, climate-related reporting and reserve requirements for shared buildings, are making more of a building’s physical performance visible to buyers, tenants and lenders. As information asymmetry shrinks, physical facts become price signals, and owners who understand their buildings first gain an advantage.

Disclosure shrinks the gap between what owners know and what markets price. Energy ratings, benchmarking, fire safety statements, climate reports, reserve studies: more of a building’s physical reality is becoming public. Disclosure shrinks the gap between what owners know and what markets price.  building disclosure energy benchmarking NABERS EPC information asymmetrybuilding disclosure energy benchmarking NABERS EPC information asymmetry commercial building energy disclosure benchmarking ordinance building performance transparency information asymmetry property mandatory disclosure buildingscommercial building energy disclosure benchmarking ordinance building performance transparency information asymmetry property mandatory disclosure buildingscommercial building energy disclosure benchmarking ordinance building performance transparency information asymmetry property mandatory disclosure buildings For most of the history of commercial property, sellers knew more about their buildings than buyers did. Condition, performance, past problems: these were private until due diligence dug them up, and even then only partly. Information asymmetry was a source of profit for those on the right side of it.

That gap is narrowing. Across our three markets, rules increasingly require building information to be published, disclosed at transaction or reported to investors.  Research note

Disclosure regimes cited: the Commercial Building Disclosure programme in Australia for office space of 1,000 square metres or more; Energy Performance Certificates on sale or letting in Britain, with Display Energy Certificates for larger public buildings; benchmarking ordinances and performance standards in a number of American cities, led by New York; and Florida’s requirement that condominium buyers receive milestone inspection reports and structural integrity reserve studies. Climate-related financial reporting is phasing in in Australia and Britain; in the United States the federal rule is proposed for rescission while California’s emissions reporting proceeds. Deepened 4 November 2026 with a comparison of building and climate disclosure by market. Deepened 11 November 2026 against the Technical Library: the measurable tests behind a fire safety record.

## What is now visible

In Australia, most larger offices must disclose a [NABERS](/technical/energy-efficiency-upgrades) Energy rating when sold or leased, and fire safety maintenance records are routinely requested. In Britain, Energy Performance Certificates are required on sale or letting and sit on a public register, and the minimum standards described in [our British note](/insights/britain-when-the-energy-rating-becomes-a-letting-rule) turn them into a letting condition. In the United States, many cities require large buildings to benchmark energy use annually, and several publish the results; cities with performance standards publish compliance data.

Climate-related financial reporting in all three markets is bringing physical and transition risk into investor documents. And for shared buildings, reserve and inspection requirements, such as those introduced in Florida after Surfside, put capital planning on the record.

## Disclosure at review

The direction is toward more disclosure, but not in a straight line, and the United States has moved backwards at federal level. Building and climate disclosure by marketMarketBuilding-level disclosureCorporate climate disclosureAustraliaCommercial Building Disclosure: offices of 1,000 m² and over disclose a NABERS Energy rating when sold or leasedMandatory climate reporting under AASB S2, phased in from financial years starting 1 January 2025United KingdomEnergy Performance Certificates on sale and letting; Display Energy Certificates for public buildingsUK Sustainability Reporting Standards published in February 2026; mandatory scope still being setUnited StatesLocal benchmarking in more than 35 jurisdictions; performance standards in about fifteenSEC proposed in May 2026 to rescind its climate disclosure rule; California’s SB 261 enjoined since November 2025

Australian Government; UK Government; Institute for Market Transformation; status at review.

For building owners the federal retreat in the United States changes less than it seems. The building-level rules that drive capital, benchmarking and performance standards, are local, and they continue to spread.

## From a number to a programme

Take a disclosed metric and ask what moves it. For an energy rating, the answer is usually a known list: controls and operation, lighting, heating and cooling plant, fabric, on-site generation. For a fire safety statement or essential safety measures record, it is the maintained condition of specific systems, each with measurable tests: fire doors that close and seal within set gaps, detectors inside their life, alarms audible at the level the market sets ([fire door values by market](/technical/passive-fire-protection#thresholds), [alarm values by market](/technical/fire-detection-and-alarm-systems#thresholds)). For a reserve study, it is the remaining life of named components. In every case, the disclosed number is the output of physical elements that sit on a register.

An owner who holds that register can read the disclosure as a diagnosis and plan the works that change it. An owner who holds only the number can react to it. Over the next decade, as more of these numbers become public and more of them carry consequences for letting, finance and sale, the difference between those two positions will be worth a great deal.

## Physical facts become price signals

When information is public, it gets priced. Tenants compare energy ratings. Lenders build them into credit terms. Buyers screen out buildings below thresholds. Insurers use condition and resilience data. What was once a technical detail discovered late becomes a visible attribute that shapes demand from the start.

Disclosure does not change a building. It changes how quickly the market notices it.

## Disclosure is not a plan

Disclosure regimes publish outcomes: a rating, a benchmark, a compliance record. They do not say what to do about them, what it will cost, or in what order. A building with a poor rating has a problem everyone can see and a solution nobody has published.

That is where the advantage now lies. Owners who understand the capital path from a disclosed position to a better one, which systems, which sequence, what cost, what timing, can act before the market prices the gap against them. [It’s Not About Owning Data](/insights/its-not-about-owning-data) makes the broader point: as raw information becomes more available, value moves to the ability to turn it into decisions.

## Knowing first

The response that follows is to know your buildings at least as well as the market soon will: read disclosed metrics against the physical register, identify what drives each, and plan the works that would move them.

Disclosure also offers a screening layer across portfolios. It is a starting point, and the building behind each number still has to be read. Disclosure can contract as well as expand, and this note is reviewed every six months.  In the register

Disclosed metrics such as energy ratings and benchmarking results are read against the mechanical, electrical, controls and fabric rows that drive them, turning a published number into a sequence of works.   Key signal

As disclosure makes building performance public, advantage shifts to owners who understand the capital path behind each disclosed metric before the market prices it.

## Questions

### Does disclosure of energy ratings affect commercial property values?

It makes performance visible to tenants, lenders and buyers, which allows it to be priced. The effect depends on the market, the asset and how far the rating sits from thresholds that matter.

### Is a disclosed energy rating enough to plan upgrades?

No. A rating shows an outcome. Planning requires understanding which systems and fabric drive it, what works would improve it, and in what order and at what cost.

This paper describes the Moyne Ross Capital Strategy as published in its methodology references. Scope, fees and timing for any engagement are agreed before work begins. Deepened 4 November 2026 with an account of the work from address to issued strategy, and a comparison with other building documents.

## Six connected parts

A Moyne Ross Capital Strategy has six connected parts. An executive summary in plain words: where the building stands, what matters most and what is still uncertain. The capital position: the ten-year total and how it falls across the next year, years two to five and years six to ten. The [MR Index](/methodology/mr-index): one band for the decade ahead, calculated from the register. The [Capital Register](/methodology/capital-register): every element of structure, services and space, row by row. The cost basis: how each number was built and how firm it is. And a living record: the building’s private place, updated as evidence and plans change.

Each part answers a different question. Together they let an owner see the shape of the decade, the reasons behind it and the decisions it contains.

## What Moyne Ross does, start to finish

The work starts with an address. Moyne Ross gathers the public evidence about the building: listing and marketing material, planning and permit history, energy ratings, imagery, heritage and overlay controls, and whatever the owner can share. From that evidence it builds the Capital Register, element by element, with every finding graded as documented, observed or inferred, and every cost carried with its basis. A surveyor reviews the register before anything is issued; the platform does the arithmetic, and the surveyor takes responsibility for the judgement.

The first read hears the building on its own terms, before the owner’s plans are brought to bear, so that the brief does not shape what the building is found to need. Then the strategy is set against the owner’s intentions: hold, improve, reposition or exit. What arrives is a Capital Strategy in six parts, and a private record of the building that is updated as evidence and plans change.

## How it differs from the documents a buyer already knows

Most owners have seen a condition report, a technical due diligence report or a valuation. A Capital Strategy borrows from each and replaces none of them. A Capital Strategy beside other building documentsDocumentThe question it answersHorizonWhat it producesCondition report or building surveyWhat state is the building in?NowDefects and condition, usually without a decade of costsTechnical due diligenceWhat should a buyer know before purchase?Typically 5 to 10 yearsFindings, risks and cost estimates for a transactionValuationWhat is the building worth?At the valuation dateA value, with capital treated as an allowanceDilapidations scheduleWhat must be put right at lease end?The lease termA schedule tied to lease obligationsCapital StrategyWhat will the building ask of its owner’s capital, when, why and how sure are we?Ten years, in three horizonsA reviewed register, an MR Index band and a living record

Moyne Ross summary. Terms and scope differ by market; see Same Thing, Different Name.

The difference that matters most is the horizon and the record. A report answers a question at a date. A Capital Strategy is built to keep answering as the building, the market and the owner’s plans change.

## What it is not

A Capital Strategy is not a valuation, a quantity surveyor’s estimate, a dilapidations schedule, a compliance certificate or a structural engineer’s report. It draws on the kinds of evidence those disciplines produce and points to where they are needed. Its job is narrower and, for an owner, more directly useful: to set out what the building will ask of its capital and how the owner might respond.

A Capital Strategy is the building expressed as decisions about money and time.

## What an owner does with one

Owners use a Capital Strategy in a few recurring ways. To budget: the horizons give a defensible near-term figure and a planning view of the decade. To prioritise: impact, timing and confidence show what matters most and what to investigate first. To decide: the register supports hold, improve, reposition and exit comparisons, as described in [Hold, Improve, Reposition or Exit](/insights/hold-improve-reposition-or-exit). To communicate: with lenders, insurers, co-owners and buyers. And to remember: kept current, the strategy becomes the building’s living record.

## How the thesis lands

Every force in this publication shows up somewhere in a register. [Electrification](/insights/energy-becomes-a-building-function) in the switchboard and heating plant. [Physical climate risk](/insights/climate-as-physical-risk) in drainage and plant location. [Obsolescence](/insights/three-kinds-of-obsolescence) in the timing of sound systems that a changing world has overtaken. [Concealed conditions](/insights/what-age-conceals) in investigation allowances. A Capital Strategy is where these general arguments become specific lines, with specific evidence, for one asset.

Not every force bears on every building. Part of the work is deciding which do, and how much.

## Two movements

A Capital Strategy is built in two movements. The first hears the building as it is, from its address and the evidence available, without the owner’s plans shaping the read; [Hearing the Building as It Is](/insights/hearing-the-building-as-it-is) explains why. The second brings the owner’s intentions, records and knowledge to bear on the decisions the first read raises, which is the subject of [Bringing the Owner’s Intentions to Bear](/insights/bringing-the-owners-intentions-to-bear).

Then the strategy keeps going. Buildings change, and so should the record of them.  In the register

The Capital Strategy is the register plus its readings: the summary, the capital position by horizon, the MR Index band and the cost basis behind each line.   Key signal

A Capital Strategy is where the general forces reshaping commercial property become specific, evidenced lines and decisions for one building.

## Sources

Named sources consulted for this paper. Consequential claims link to their source in the text. Reviewed 3 November 2026; next review by 3 November 2027.
- [The Capital Register: methodology reference](https://moyneross.com/methodology/capital-register), Moyne Ross. Accessed 3 November 2026.
- [The MR Index: methodology reference](https://moyneross.com/methodology/mr-index), Moyne Ross. Accessed 3 November 2026.

## Questions

### How is a Capital Strategy different from a building condition report?

A condition report describes the state of the building. A Capital Strategy turns that and other evidence into a ten-year view of actions, costs, timing, impact and confidence, with an overall position and decisions for the owner.

### What horizons does a Moyne Ross Capital Strategy use?

Within one year, years two to five, and years six to ten, across a ten-year view.

The owner explains the plan: a refurbishment, a sale, a new tenant, a five-year hold. The adviser then reads the building in light of it.

That sounds efficient, and for some questions it is. But for the first read of a building’s capital position, we think it is the wrong order.  Research note

This paper states a Moyne Ross method principle: the first read is made on the building’s current, business-as-usual terms, and the owner’s intentions are applied afterwards. The observations about attention and briefing are general and drawn from practice. Deepened 4 November 2026 with a table of what the first read records and what it holds back.

## Briefs bend evidence

A brief tells the reader what matters before the reader has looked. An owner planning a sale may unconsciously steer attention away from issues a buyer will find. An owner planning a refurbishment may lead the adviser to discount systems the refurbishment would replace, even if the refurbishment never happens. A tenant’s fit-out plan may focus attention on one floor while the roof above it is the real story.

This happens without any bad faith, because that is how attention works. Knowing the answer someone wants changes which questions get asked.

The first read should be the building speaking for itself. Everything else can be layered on once that voice has been heard.

## Business as usual

The Moyne Ross first read assumes the building continues in its current use, on its current terms. What is its condition? What will it need over ten years if nothing about its use changes? What is uncertain? This business-as-usual baseline is the reference against which every later plan can be measured.

It is built from the address and the evidence available, often [public evidence](/insights/what-public-evidence-can-tell-you) at first, read with the discipline described in [Documented, Observed, Inferred](/insights/documented-observed-inferred). Its uncertainties are visible, and its conclusions are a starting point rather than a verdict.

## What the first read contains

A first read sets out the building’s profile as established from evidence: use, age and how it was dated, construction, size and the main systems. It sets out a ten-year register on business-as-usual terms, with condition, action, cost basis, timing, impact and confidence on every line. It carries an overall capital position and MR Index band. And it states plainly what is uncertain and what would resolve it.

It does not assume a refurbishment, a sale or a new tenant. Those come next, and they are easier to reason about because the baseline is already there.

## What the first read holds back

The discipline of the first read is as much about what it leaves out as what it contains. The first read and what follows itThe first read recordsHeld back until the owner is heardThe building’s profile, dated from evidenceThe owner’s plans for use, tenancy and timingEvery element, graded documented, observed or inferredBudgets and preferred spending patternsA business-as-usual register: what the building needs in its current useOptions for refurbishment, repositioning or saleThe uncertainties and what would resolve themWhich uncertainties the owner wants resolved first

Moyne Ross practice.

Holding the second column back is what makes the first column trustworthy: a baseline written before anyone said what they hoped it would show.

## The read changes the brief

One of the most useful things a first read does is change the questions. An owner who expected to discuss tenancy refresh learns that the facade and fire services are the dominant issue. An owner planning to sell learns that a cheap investigation now could remove the largest uncertainty a buyer would price. An owner thinking about electrification learns that the switchboard gates everything.

If the brief had come first, those findings might have been framed as peripheral. Coming first, the read sets the agenda for the conversation.

## Then the owner

Hearing the building as it is does not mean ignoring the owner. It means sequencing. Once the baseline exists, the owner’s plans, records, knowledge and constraints are brought to bear, line by line, on the decisions it contains. That second movement is described in [Bringing the Owner’s Intentions to Bear](/insights/bringing-the-owners-intentions-to-bear).

The baseline stays on the record. It is what lets an owner see exactly what their plans change, and what they do not.  In the register

The first read produces a business-as-usual register: condition, action, timing and confidence on the building’s current terms, which later strategies are measured against.   Key signal

A first read made on the building’s own terms, before the owner’s plans are applied, avoids bending evidence and often changes what the brief should be.

## Questions

### Does a first read ignore what the owner knows?

No. It sets a baseline from the evidence before plans are applied. The owner’s records and knowledge can still improve that evidence, and their intentions are applied in the next stage.

### Why is a business-as-usual baseline useful?

It shows what the building needs if its use does not change, so the effect of any plan, refurbishment, sale or new tenant, can be measured against it clearly.

It does not tell them what to do. That depends on what they want from the building, and two owners of the same building can rightly reach very different answers.

This is the second movement of a Capital Strategy: bringing the owner’s intentions, records and knowledge to bear on the decisions the first read raises.  Research note

This paper describes the second movement of a Moyne Ross Capital Strategy. How intentions are applied in any engagement depends on the owner, the building and the agreed scope. Deepened 4 November 2026 with a grid of one register read under three intentions.

## Intentions change actions, not condition

An owner planning a deep refurbishment in three years should not replace a lobby finish now. An owner selling next year may resolve a large uncertainty before marketing. An owner holding for twenty years may bring a roof forward to install solar. A tenant committing to a long lease may change which systems matter and who pays for them. In each case the building’s condition is unchanged. The right action and timing are not.

This is why the [MR Index](/methodology/mr-index) reference says the same score can lead to different decisions. The capital position is a fact about the building. The strategy is a fact about the building and its owner together.

## Records sharpen the read

Owners also bring evidence. Maintenance logs, compliance records, drawings, recent works, warranties, surveys and tenant information can confirm, narrow or overturn lines from the first read. An inferred plant age becomes documented. A wide range for a facade becomes a narrow one after an inspection report is supplied. A suspected issue is closed.

The first read listens to the building. The second listens to the owner. A good strategy needs both voices, in that order.

## Three intentions, one building

Take a 1990s office with a mid-decade chiller replacement, a lobby in need of refresh and an energy rating below where the market is heading. An owner selling in eighteen months resolves the largest uncertainty, documents the plant, and leaves the replacement to the buyer with clear information. An owner holding for ten years replaces the chiller with electrified plant at the right moment, sequences the switchboard first and times the lobby with a lease event. An owner repositioning for a different tenant market brings plant, lobby and energy works together into one refurbishment.

The building is identical in all three. The register lines are the same. The actions and timing differ, and each strategy can be read against the same baseline.

## The same building under three intentions

The worked example in this paper is clearest as a grid: the same register lines, read under three different plans. One 1990s office, three intentionsRegister lineHold for ten yearsRefurbish in three yearsSell within eighteen monthsChiller replacement, mid-decadePlan and fund on its own clockFold into the refurbishment scopeDisclose with its evidence; consider early works only if they protect the priceLobby refreshDo it when the leasing case supports itDefer: the refurbishment replaces itA modest refresh may help presentationEnergy rating below the marketImprove controls and plant over the holdDesign the refurbishment to the target ratingExplain the pathway and its cost to buyersLow-confidence facade allowanceInvestigate early and refineInvestigate as part of designInvestigate before marketing so the buyer does not

Moyne Ross illustration. The condition of each line is the same in every column; only the action and timing change.

## Working through the decisions

Bringing intentions to bear means working through the register with the owner: which lines matter most to their plans, which decisions are urgent, which can wait, which depend on each other, and which need investigation before anyone can decide. [A Building Is Forty Decisions](/insights/a-building-is-forty-decisions) describes the shape of that work.

The outcome is a direction the owner can act on, with the reasoning visible: what will be done, when, why, and what remains open.

## Keeping the baseline

The baseline from the first read stays on the record beside the tailored strategy. That matters for two reasons. It shows the owner exactly what their plans change. And if the plans change, as they often do, the strategy can be re-tailored from the same baseline rather than rebuilt.

It also guards against a subtle risk: that a strategy shaped around an intention drops issues the intention made inconvenient. With the baseline visible, nothing disappears without a reason.  In the register

Tailoring changes the action and timing fields on affected rows and records the owner’s reason in the cost basis, while the business-as-usual baseline remains available for comparison.   Key signal

Owner intentions change the right action and timing on many lines without changing the building, so a strategy applies them to a stable baseline rather than replacing it.

## Questions

### Can two owners of the same building have different capital strategies?

Yes. Hold period, refurbishment plans, tenancy, sale timing and risk appetite all change the best action and timing for many items, even though the building’s condition is the same.

### What owner records improve a capital strategy most?

Maintenance and works history, compliance records, drawings, recent surveys, warranties and lease and tenant information typically narrow uncertainty and confirm or correct the first read.

It holds reports from different years, by different advisers, in different formats, with invoices for works, certificates and some drawings. A great deal of knowledge sits in the heads of a facility manager or a former owner, and leaves with them.

The building loses its memory, and every few years someone has to rediscover it.  Research note

This paper describes how Moyne Ross keeps each building’s strategy as a versioned register in a private, invitation-only place for the owner. Retention and access arrangements are set out in the Moyne Ross terms and privacy policy. Deepened 4 November 2026 with a table of recurring regulatory evidence that refreshes a building record. Deepened 11 November 2026 against the Technical Library: the records each element should have.

## Memory as an asset

A living record is a capital register that is kept current. When a survey arrives, the affected lines change. When works are done, they are recorded and the next cycle is set. When a plan changes, the strategy is re-tailored and the reason noted. Each version is kept, so the record shows how understanding of the building developed over time.

A building with a living record carries its knowledge with it. A building without one loses most of what anyone learned about it at every handover.

## Why it is worth keeping

The benefits compound. Decisions are made on current evidence rather than old reports. Uncertainty narrows over time instead of being re-estimated from scratch. Managers and advisers can change without the building losing its history. Lenders and insurers can be shown a credible picture. And at sale, as [What the Next Buyer Will Read](/insights/what-the-next-buyer-will-read) argues, the buyer verifies rather than discovers.

There is also a simpler benefit. Rediscovering a building every few years is expensive and slow. Updating a record is not.

## What keeps a record current

A record stays alive because the building keeps producing evidence. Much of it arrives on a regulatory calendar. Recurring evidence that refreshes a building’s recordEvidenceWhereHow oftenAnnual fire safety statementNew South WalesEvery yearEssential safety measures reportVictoriaEvery yearBuilding Energy Efficiency Certificate for offices of 1,000 m² and overAustraliaValid for up to 12 months, needed when space is sold or leasedFire risk assessmentEngland and WalesKept under regular review, and after significant changeEnergy benchmarking disclosureNew York City and other US jurisdictionsEvery yearFacade inspection for buildings over six storeysNew York CityEvery five years

State and city regulations as summarised at review; obligations depend on building type and size.

Each of these is a small update to the register if the record is kept, and a box of paper if it is not. The difference compounds: after a few cycles, a kept record knows the building better than any single report could.

## What a good record holds

A living record holds the current register with its reasoning; every previous version with what changed and why; completed works with their scope, date and evidence; investigations and their results; the decisions agreed with the owner; and the documents that support them, drawings, certificates, warranties, surveys. What those documents should be is set out for each element in the Technical Library, as the records that prove or disprove a finding, which makes it the checklist a living record fills over time ([fire detection, for example](/technical/fire-detection-and-alarm-systems#what-to-ask-for)). It is organised so that any line can be traced from today’s figure back to the evidence that produced it.

Kept this way, the record is useful to everyone who will ever have to make a decision about the building, which over its life is a long list.

## Versions and agreement

A living record needs discipline. Versions should be clear: what was known at each point and what changed. Anything shown together, a strategy, a report, a summary, should agree, which is why reports are best drawn from the register as views rather than written separately, as [The Register, Not the Report](/insights/the-register-not-the-report) explains. And updates should follow evidence, not convenience.

Moyne Ross keeps each building’s strategy in a private place for the owner, by invitation, where the current version, its history, the notes and what has been agreed sit together.

## Beyond the single owner

Over a long enough period, a building’s living record matters more than any single owner’s tenure. It is the baton described in [Patient Capital and the Long Building](/insights/patient-capital-and-the-long-building): the most useful thing one owner can pass to the next. It is also, in aggregate, how a practice learns. Every record that improves over time teaches something about how buildings of that kind actually behave.  In the register

A living register keeps every version, records completed works and resolved uncertainties on their rows, and carries the reasons for each change.   Key signal

A capital record kept current becomes the building’s memory, preserving knowledge across managers and owners and turning sale and finance into verification rather than discovery.

## Sources

Named sources consulted for this paper. Consequential claims link to their source in the text. Reviewed 3 November 2026; next review by 3 November 2027.
- [Commercial Building Disclosure: is your building disclosure affected?](https://www.cbd.gov.au/node/27), Australian Government. Accessed 3 November 2026.

## Questions

### How often should a building capital plan be updated?

Whenever material evidence arrives, works are completed or plans change, with a periodic review even when nothing obvious has changed. The aim is that the record always reflects current knowledge.

### What should a living building record contain?

The current capital register with its reasoning, a version history, completed works, resolved and open uncertainties, supporting documents and the decisions agreed with the owner.

## Start with the shape

Begin with the capital position: the ten-year total and its split across the first year, years two to five and years six to ten. The split says more than the total. A front-loaded programme means decisions now. A mid-decade bulge means planning time. A back-loaded programme means a building in a quiet phase that will not stay quiet.

Then read the [MR Index](/methodology/mr-index) band. It summarises how much of the building needs attention, how serious and how soon, in one position from MR 1 to MR 5. It is not a verdict on the building. It tells you what kind of decade to expect.

## Find the concentration and the gates

Next, see where the capital concentrates. Is it spread across many systems, or dominated by one, a [roof](/technical/roof-coverings), a facade, central plant? Concentration tells you where attention and investigation will pay off most.

Then look for gating items: single findings that could reshape the programme if confirmed. A structural question, a concealed facade issue, a hazardous material in the way of planned works. These usually sit as investigation items with conditional allowances, as described in [Pricing What You Don’t Know](/insights/pricing-what-you-do-not-know).

Read the shape before the rows. Most of what matters is visible in the split, the band, the concentration and the gates.

## One row, read field by field

The methodology reference shows a single row from an issued strategy: metal deck roofing across the older bays of a 1970s distribution warehouse. Behind it sit the Technical Library’s roof page, which gives coated steel forty years and more inland and fifteen to twenty-five near the coast, with the bottom metre above the gutter going first, and the scale every finding is graded on ([roof coverings](/technical/roof-coverings#service-life)). Reading it field by field shows what each part is for. Reading a register rowFieldWhat the row saysThe question it answersConditionSevere oxidation and coating breakdown across the older bays; water ingress risk to stock belowWhat state is it in, and what is the consequence if nothing is done?ActionStaged re-sheeting of the corroded sections, with a roofing consultant’s inspection firstWhat should be done, and in what order?Cost basisPlanning range $1.8 million to $3.4 million for 20,000 to 25,000 m², excluding GST, Q3 2026; purlins excludedHow was the figure built, and what does it leave out?Impact4, EssentialHow much does this matter to the building?ConfidenceMediumHow firm is the evidence?Timing$35,000 in year one; $2.6 million in years two to five; nothing in years six to tenWhen does the money fall?Item total$2.64 millionWhat does it add to the decade?

Moyne Ross Capital Register methodology reference.

Read together, the fields say something no single one does. The roof matters a great deal, but the money is not urgent: the first year buys an inspection, and the works follow once their scope is known. The exclusion of purlins is the line a buyer’s adviser would circle first.

## Read confidence and the near term

Filter for low-confidence lines. They show where the evidence is thin and where the capital position could move. Then read every first-year line and ask the question from [Timing Is Not Risk](/insights/timing-is-not-risk): why must this happen within twelve months? A good register answers it on each row.

On the warehouse example in the reference, the roof row shows the pattern clearly: strong evidence from aerial imagery, a large exposure, a modest first-year amount for a roofing consultant’s inspection, and the main re-sheeting in years two to five.

## Five questions to ask any register
- Why must each first-year item happen within twelve months?
- Which single findings could reshape the programme, and what would it cost to resolve them?
- Where does the capital concentrate, and is that concentration supported by strong evidence?
- Which lines rest on inference, and does their confidence say so?
- Which lines depend on each other, and is the sequence right?

A register that answers these well is one an owner can act on. One that cannot is one to question.

## Finish with the cost basis

Finally, read the cost basis on the largest lines. How was each figure built? What scope, quantity and assumptions does it rest on? What is included and excluded? How firm is it? This is where you can challenge a number intelligently, and where an owner’s own knowledge, a recent quote, a known constraint, can sharpen it.

Read this way, a register of forty lines becomes a short list of questions worth asking. That list is usually the start of the conversation described in [Bringing the Owner’s Intentions to Bear](/insights/bringing-the-owners-intentions-to-bear).  In the register

The reading order follows the register’s own structure: capital position by horizon, MR Index band, concentration by system, gating and low-confidence rows, first-year rows, then the cost basis on the largest lines.   Key signal

Reading a register from its shape to its evidence, split, band, concentration, gates, confidence, near term, cost basis, turns a dense schedule into a short list of decisions.

## Sources

Named sources consulted for this paper. Consequential claims link to their source in the text. Reviewed 3 November 2026; next review by 3 November 2027.
- [The Capital Register: methodology reference](https://moyneross.com/methodology/capital-register), Moyne Ross. Accessed 3 November 2026.

## Questions

### What is the most important number in a capital register?

Usually not the total, but how it splits across the near term, middle years and later years, together with where it concentrates. Those show what kind of decisions the building will demand and when.

### How can an owner challenge a figure in a capital register?

By reading its cost basis: the scope, quantity, assumptions, inclusions, exclusions and confidence behind it, and testing them against the owner’s own knowledge, quotes or records.

A Capital Strategy makes each option legible by showing what the building needs regardless, what each path adds or avoids, and what remains uncertain, so the owner can compare them on evidence. A Capital Strategy makes each option legible by showing what the building needs regardless, what each path adds or avoids, and what remains uncertain, so the owner can compare them on evidence.  Every capital strategy ends in a choice about the building’s future. The register does not make the choice. It makes each option legible. Every capital strategy ends in a choice about the building’s future. The register does not make the choice. It makes each option legible.  asset strategy hold or sell repositioning refurbishment capital allocationasset strategy hold or sell repositioning refurbishment capital allocation hold or sell commercial building decision reposition versus refurbish asset strategy options building capital strategy exit decision improve or exit propertyhold or sell commercial building decision reposition versus refurbish asset strategy options building capital strategy exit decision improve or exit propertyhold or sell commercial building decision reposition versus refurbish asset strategy options building capital strategy exit decision improve or exit property However detailed the analysis, a capital strategy ends in a choice about the building’s future. Broadly there are four paths. Hold it largely as it is and maintain it well. Improve it within its current use. Reposition it, for a different tenant market or a different use. Or exit.

The register does not choose between them. What it can do is make each option legible, so the choice rests on evidence rather than instinct.  Research note

The four-path framing is a general asset strategy convention. The redevelopment example draws on the published CMP 007 asset study. Deepened 4 November 2026 with the Marks & Spencer Marble Arch case as a public test of refurbishment against redevelopment.

## What the building needs regardless

Every option starts from the same base: what the building needs whatever path is chosen. Safety, current compliance obligations, items failing or causing damage. These are the floor. Even an owner who intends to sell must usually deal with some of them, or price them into the sale.

Above the floor, the paths diverge.

## Four paths, four programmes

Holding as is means following the business-as-usual register: renew systems as they come due, defer consciously where sensible, keep the building competitive within its current market. Improving means adding works that raise performance within the current use: better controls, an energy upgrade, a lobby, end-of-trip facilities. Repositioning means accepting a larger programme to reach a different market or use, a deeper refurbishment, a conversion, a change of tenant type. Exiting means deciding what to do before sale, which uncertainties to resolve and which works to leave to the buyer.

The same register supports all four paths. What changes is which lines are taken up, when, and what is added.

Each path also carries different risk. Holding exposes the owner to obsolescence. Improving exposes them to whether the market rewards the improvement. Repositioning exposes them to construction, approvals and leasing risk. Exiting exposes them to what [the next buyer will read](/insights/what-the-next-buyer-will-read).

## A simple comparison table

For each path, set out four figures from the register: the base programme every path must fund; the additional works the path implies; the conditional allowances still open; and the timing against leases. Add a short note on the main risk each path carries. On one page, an owner can see the capital implication of each option on the same evidence, which is usually enough to narrow the choice to one or two before any detailed feasibility work begins.

## When the building is not the answer

Sometimes the evidence points beyond all four. When the capital needed to keep a building competitive approaches what it can earn, and the land supports something else, redevelopment becomes the rational path, as [When the Building is Not the Asset](/insights/when-the-building-is-not-the-asset) describes. A good capital strategy says so plainly when it is true.

## A public test of refurbish against rebuild

The most visible recent test of this decision is Marks & Spencer’s store at Marble Arch on London’s Oxford Street. The retailer applied in 2021 to demolish the 1930s building and replace it with a new nine-storey building of shops and offices, arguing that the existing store could not be adapted. Westminster approved the scheme, but the government called it in, and in July 2023 the then Secretary of State refused it, citing among other things whether refurbishment had been properly explored and the embodied carbon of demolition.

In March 2024 the High Court quashed that refusal, finding that national planning policy had been misapplied. In December 2024 the decision was remade and permission granted. The case did not settle the general question of retrofit against rebuild, but it made one thing plain: the case for redevelopment now has to be argued from evidence about the existing building, including what refurbishment could achieve and at what carbon and capital cost. The Marble Arch timelineDateEvent2021Application to demolish and rebuild; approved by Westminster City CouncilJune 2022Called in by the Secretary of StateJuly 2023Permission refused1 March 2024High Court quashes the refusal5 December 2024Permission granted on redetermination

Mishcon de Reya; Dezeen; CIBSE Journal.

For an owner weighing the four paths, the lesson is that exit by redevelopment is no longer a quiet choice in many cities. The register that shows what the existing building needs, and what it could become, is the evidence such a decision will be asked for.

## Choosing on evidence

Owners compare paths through the register: the base they must fund anyway, the additional programme each path implies, the uncertainty that remains, and the timing against leases and plans. The comparison does not need to be elaborate to be useful. What matters is that each option is costed and timed on the same evidence.

This is also where the ideas in Capital Made Physical become practical. Whether a building should be held, improved, repositioned or sold depends in part on the forces in [Part I](/insights/the-movement-to-real) and the futures in Part II. The register brings those general arguments down to one building’s options.  In the register

Options are compared on one register: the base rows every path must fund, the additional rows each path adds, and the conditional allowances that remain open under each.   Key signal

Hold, improve, reposition and exit each imply a different capital programme and risk, and a register makes them comparable on the same evidence.

## Sources

Named sources consulted for this paper. Consequential claims link to their source in the text. Reviewed 3 November 2026; next review by 3 November 2027.
- [RICS Valuation, Global Standards (Red Book)](https://www.rics.org/profession-standards/rics-standards-and-guidance/sector-standards/valuation-standards/red-book), RICS. Accessed 3 November 2026.
- [Government grants planning permission for the redevelopment of Marks & Spencer’s flagship store on Oxford Street](https://www.mishcon.com/news/government-grants-planning-permission-for-the-redevelopment-of-marks-and-spencers-flagship-store-on-oxford-street?publication=7403), Mishcon de Reya. Accessed 3 November 2026.
- [Marks & Spencer gets go-ahead for Oxford Street flagship store demolition](https://www.dezeen.com/2024/12/05/marks-spencer-approval-flagship-store-demolition/), Dezeen. Accessed 3 November 2026.
- [High Court overturns Gove’s M&S decision](https://www.cibsejournal.com/news/high-court-overturns-goves-ms-decision/), CIBSE Journal. Accessed 3 November 2026.

## Questions

### What capital works must be done even if a building is being sold?

Typically safety issues, current compliance obligations and failing elements causing damage, or else they are priced into the sale. Discretionary improvements can usually be left to the buyer.

### When does redevelopment make more sense than refurbishment?

Often when the capital needed to keep the existing building competitive approaches what it can earn, and the site supports a more valuable use or form. The decision depends on the building, the land and approvals.

docs.title: Physical Assets Under Management
docs.kind: Part VII: From thesis to building
docs.blurb: Instead of episodic reports at purchase, refinancing or sale, a building’s capital position would be held as a living register and its decisions worked through continuously as evidence, markets and plans change, much as financial assets are managed. The idea treats a portfolio of live registers as physical assets under management, with advice valued by the quality of decisions over time rather than by documents produced.
