What would continuous, ongoing management of a building’s capital position look like?  Instead of episodic reports at purchase, refinancing or sale, a building’s capital position would be held as a living register and its decisions worked through continuously as evidence, markets and plans change, much as financial assets are managed. The idea treats a portfolio of live registers as physical assets under management, with advice valued by the quality of decisions over time rather than by documents produced. Instead of episodic reports at purchase, refinancing or sale, a building’s capital position would be held as a living register and its decisions worked through continuously as evidence, markets and plans change, much as financial assets are managed. The idea treats a portfolio of live registers as physical assets under management, with advice valued by the quality of decisions over time rather than by documents produced. Instead of episodic reports at purchase, refinancing or sale, a building’s capital position would be held as a living register and its decisions worked through continuously as evidence, markets and plans change, much as financial assets are managed. The idea treats a portfolio of live registers as physical assets under management, with advice valued by the quality of decisions over time rather than by documents produced.  The investment world manages financial assets continuously. Buildings are mostly advised on in episodes. The argument of this publication ends with the case for treating physical assets the way capital treats money. The investment world manages financial assets continuously. Buildings are mostly advised on in episodes. The argument of this publication ends with the case for treating physical assets the way capital treats money.  asset management ongoing building advice living record capital decisions real assetsasset management ongoing building advice living record capital decisions real assets ongoing building capital advice continuous asset management buildings physical assets under management building advisory retained future of building consultancyongoing building capital advice continuous asset management buildings physical assets under management building advisory retained future of building consultancyongoing building capital advice continuous asset management buildings physical assets under management building advisory retained future of building consultancy A financial portfolio is never left alone for five years. It is monitored, rebalanced and reported on continuously. Decisions are made as information arrives. The manager is judged by outcomes over time.

Buildings, which are often a large part of those same portfolios, are usually treated differently. Advice arrives in episodes: a due diligence report at purchase, a condition survey at refinancing, a vendor report at sale. Between episodes, the building’s capital position drifts, and nobody is watching it as a whole.  Research note

This closing thesis describes a direction for building advice rather than a service offering. The comparison with continuing service arrangements for lifts and major plant refers to common industry practice. Deepened 4 November 2026 with the ISO 55000 asset management series and a comparison of episodic and continuous advice.

## Episodes and drift

Episodic advice made sense when assessing a building was slow and expensive, and when reports were the only practical output. Each engagement started from scratch, produced a document and ended. The knowledge it created aged on a shelf.

The cost of that model is drift. Systems age past their planned replacement, uncertainties stay unresolved, and regulations and plans change. By the next episode, much of the previous advice is out of date and the building has to be rediscovered, which is the problem [The Living Record](/insights/the-living-record) addresses.

## A different shape of advice

The tools now exist to change that shape. A building can be read quickly from evidence, held as a structured register, and kept current as things change. The expensive part of the old model, rediscovering the building, shrinks. What remains, and grows in importance, is judgement: deciding which of the building’s [forty decisions](/insights/a-building-is-forty-decisions) to make now, which to defer, which to reopen.

When reading a building becomes fast, the value moves to staying with it.

Other industries already work this way with physical equipment. Lifts, escalators and major plant are commonly maintained under continuing service arrangements by people who know the installed base intimately. The idea here is similar, applied to a building’s whole capital position rather than to one system.

## What would make it work

Continuous advice on a building’s capital position needs three things. A structured, versioned register that can be updated cheaply as evidence arrives. A method that keeps judgement visible and challengeable, so that changes are explained rather than asserted. And people who know the building well enough to notice what matters and to talk to its owner about it. The first two are now practical. The third is the part that cannot be automated, and the part owners value most.

## An established discipline, applied to buildings

Continuous management of physical assets is not new. Infrastructure owners, utilities and public estates have run it for decades, and it has an international standard: the ISO 55000 series on asset management, first published in 2014 and revised in 2024. Its premise is the one this paper argues for buildings: decisions about physical assets should be made over their whole life, from current evidence, and recorded so they can be reviewed. Episodic advice and continuous managementEpisodicContinuousTriggerA transaction, a lease event or a failureA calendar, and any new evidenceOutputA report at a dateA register kept current, with its historyUncertaintyFixed at the date of the reportNarrowed as evidence arrivesAcross a portfolioReports in different formats and datesComparable registers on one basisWho carries the knowledgeWhoever read the last reportThe record itself

Moyne Ross summary; asset management principles follow the ISO 55000 series.

Commercial property has been slow to adopt this way of working because its assets change hands and its advice is bought transaction by transaction. That is exactly why the record matters: it is the part of the discipline that survives a change of owner.

## Physical assets under management

Seen at portfolio scale, a set of live registers begins to look like assets under management: physical rather than financial, but held, monitored and decided on continuously. Each register improves as evidence accumulates. Across many buildings, patterns emerge about how real systems age, what works cost and which decisions paid off. That is the argument of [It’s Not About Owning Data](/insights/its-not-about-owning-data) carried to its conclusion: the advantage lies in turning evidence into decisions, repeatedly.

## Where the thesis ends

Capital Made Physical began with a claim that capital is turning back toward the physical, that buildings are becoming operating infrastructure rather than financial wrappers. If that is right, buildings deserve the continuous attention that capital gives to everything else it cares about.

That is the world this publication describes and the one Moyne Ross is built for: buildings read as capital, held as living records, and decided on with care over time, by people who know them. This is the most speculative paper in Capital Made Physical. Within a few years the evidence will show whether owners want continuous attention to their buildings and whether it can be delivered economically, and the paper will be rewritten either way.  In the register

In this model the register never closes: every row is a standing decision, revisited as evidence, markets and the owner’s plans change.   Key signal

As reading a building becomes fast, the value of building advice moves from producing documents to staying with the building and its decisions over time.

## Questions

### How is continuous building advice different from periodic condition surveys?

Periodic surveys produce a snapshot that ages until the next one. Continuous advice keeps a living register current and works through decisions as evidence and plans change, so knowledge accumulates instead of being rediscovered.

### Why compare buildings with financial assets under management?

Both are significant capital that changes value with time and circumstances. Financial assets are managed continuously; the argument is that physical assets increasingly warrant similar ongoing attention to their capital position.

How to read this register How To Read The Register One row, one element Each row is an element of the building: its condition, the action it needs, when that falls, what it is expected to cost, how much it matters and how firm the evidence is. Cost basis Every priced row carries the reasoning behind its number: the scope assumed, the quantities, what is included and excluded, the cost date and how firm the footing is. A planning allowance is presented as a planning allowance, not as a market price. Timing Every allowance carries an intervention window in years. The next-year column is reserved for work whose whole window sits inside the next twelve months. Any other window is shown, as a single placement, in the horizon that holds its midpoint; the window itself is stated in the cost basis. Evidence Desktop or inspection Unless this strategy records a site inspection, the assessment is desktop-based: public records, imagery and material supplied by the client. A desktop assessment cannot establish concealed conditions or replace an inspection where one is needed. Documented, observed, inferred Documented findings are supported by records or supplied material. Observed findings are visible in the evidence available. Inferred findings are reasoned from the building’s era, type and context, and are labelled as such. Where the evidence stops Where nothing yet supports a works figure, the register prices the investigation that would, and stops there. Where an inspection is included, its fee is a separate line added to the works midpoint rather than absorbed into the range. Impact Essential Critical to operation, life safety or compliance. Failure would risk shutdown, a safety incident or regulatory action. Important Significant effect on operation or commercial value. Failure would cause material disruption. Planned Standard lifecycle work within expected replacement cycles. Routine Minor work that can be deferred without material consequence. Confidence High Strong, asset-specific evidence for the scope. Any benchmark, quote or tender relied on is identified at item level. Medium Building-specific evidence combined with standard assumptions for buildings of this type and scale. Low Limited evidence, concealed elements or atypical systems. The range is wider, and the investigation that would narrow it is included. Work Codes CAP Capital expenditure: lifecycle replacement, restoration or end-of-life renewal. R&M Repair and maintenance beyond routine thresholds. BCC Building code compliance: statutory, certification or code-upgrade work. ENV Environmental: efficiency, carbon and environmental compliance. Costs Planning allowances Costs are planning allowances in the strategy currency at Q4 2026. Each row states its own inclusions, exclusions and treatment of preliminaries and tax; these are not assumed to be uniform across the register. Separate interventions Works are planned as discrete interventions unless a row says otherwise. Coordinated procurement may reduce duplicated access and preliminaries; no saving is assumed without project-specific evidence.
